units.la: Mnibus læta, iucundamque veterum rerum & antiquitatis memoriâ, quam Historiam appellamus, fuisse hinc clarè perspicueq; cernimus. Quod cum cæteræ artes & disciplinæ quarum cognitione siue ad vitæ, siue ingenii, siue morum siue religionis cultum ducuntur homines abstrusam aliquam & reconditam scientiam continentes, à paucioribus iisque doctis ac industriis perceptæ & exploratæ sunt, hæc vna popularis & peruulgata, omnibusq; indoctis patet, vt quibus nec otium, nec ingenii facultas ad illa cæterarum artium intima indagandaconcedatur, in hac rerum à maioribus gestarum recordatione atque lucecconquiescant, eaq; imperiti, perinde ac intelligentiores valde multoque etiam sæpe magis delectentur, multum tamen semper interest, quantum commoditatis atque fructus docti ex historiis magis quàm indocti percipiant. Nam dum hi Heroum & magnatum casus varios domi militiæque ad mirantur, dum ob clades & calamitates exercituum, Rerumpublicar. euersiones, ciuitatum vastationes, rerum mutationem, bella, incendia, naufragia, atque horum omnium varietatem, inconstantiam, & arrogantiam magna delectatione affecti & attoniti stupent, neq; aliam vtilitatem optant, aut inesse putant historiæ: quo quidque consilio gestum, quo authore & suasore inceptum, in quem exitum ac euentum ptogressum, quibus modis ad finem deductum quidquid sit, nunquam animaduertunt. Quæ sane viris doctis atque prudentibus, quibus in rebus inutilibus, aut ad necessarium vitæ vsum non spectantibus operam suam nunquam posuere, maxima semper fuit historias scribendi, atque legendi causa. Vt ex antecedentium & præteritarum rerum scientia, quid præsentibus atque secuturis vsu futurum sit, cernere ac prospicere possint. Verum non minor saepe est historias scribendrum quàm legentium culpa. Vt enim legentes non alium plerumque fructum quàm inanem voluptatem vel cognoscendi, vel eadem rursus commemorandi atque oftenrandi imperitè atque inutiliter capiunt: sic scriptores cum non ad veritatem fidemq; rerum gestarum exquisitè, sed ad commendricias vulgoque sparsas fabulas sine delectu liberè perfuseque loquuntur, laboris inutilis, studiúmque stulti populârem laudem vt iniquam mercedem fortasse consequuntur, sed de humana vita pessimè meriti, posteritatem avita cognitione ranquam legitimahæreditate fraudant. Deinde si gravitas aut simultatis alicuius suspicio in scribente appareat, vt aut sallsum dicere audeat, aut verum non audeat, tota rolitur & lex & fides ab historia. Ex his vitiosis historiarum scriptoribus proximi atque pessimi sunt hi, qui partium quæ semper tam bello quàm pace sunt odio ducti, ea quæ vitio verti aut nullo aut pertenui possunt, omnioratione exaggerant, quæ vero maxima laude digna sunt, in his quos factiosi improbabant, aut summo silentio, aut tacita detractione praeterierunt. Hos singularum ætatum scriptores tam varios posteritas tandem mendaces olfecit & exististimavit. Itaque hi perennem laudem retinuerunt, optimeque in ea re de genere humano mereri putantur, qui omnibus illis nugis atque fabulis, quibus pueriles atque anules animi possunt incendi, veritati soli explicandæ & illustrandæ studuerunt. Nam vt in aliis artibus magnus est industriæ laboriœque locus, sic in historia sincerè & accuratè describenda. Si quis enim Thucididem Græcum, autè Latinis Cæsarem & Saluftium, qui res à se aut suis temporibus gestas, quarum certissimam cognitionem habere poterant, diligenter legerit, reperiet quanta sedulitate veritatem exquisierint, deinde quàm plano, fideliqueque sermone eandem expresserint. Qui verò in remotissimam antiquitatem respexerunt, & ex ea eruere ac ad suos transferre conabantur ea, quæ fide digna & suis temporibus oportuna, & posteris tanquam hæredibus relinquenda ac patefacienda sunt, eorum sanè vt virtus arq; opera maior, sic laus debet esse celebrior. Nam Herodotus Græcus, ne quid antiquitatis omisisse videretur, omnia sine delectu congessit, quorumque pletaq; non ab antiquis scriptis, sed à vulgi fabulis accepit. Qui quanquam oratione concinnus sit atque elegans, eorum tamen qui sanè & incorruptè iudicant, auertit ab illa tam coacerunata & referta narrationum multitudine fidem. Et quanquam à quibusdam, quod videturaffectasse historiæ pater dicatur, ab aliis tamen fabularum pater meritò dictus est. Quæ delectationis habeant tantum quantum scriptor volet, verbisque, sententiis, omniáque orationis apparatu adiuuentur, authoritatem tamen nullam debemus, neque fidem commentitiis rebus adiungere. At Liuius Latinus veteribus rerum Romanarum scriptis ab origine repetitis, rectoque & accurato iudicio perpensis atque comparatis, edidit historiam Dominio ac Imperio Romano dignam. In qua nihil est fabulosum, quod authoritate ac testimonio careat, aut quod æquabili & verisimili narratione non videatur ex se legenti fidem gignere. Quæ tam diserta & luculenta rerum anteactarum expressa veritas, si Rebuspublicis ad belli, pacisque administrationem, & ad mundani Imperii diuturnitatem atque conseruationem multum valere existimetur, quo tandem non animo, studioque incitati esse debemus, ad earum rerum veritatem atque falsitatem indagandam, quae in Ecclesia Dei tanquam diuino Regno & Imperio, summi eius Imperatoris nutu, aut ab Antichristo eiusdem praedone ac inuasore gesta esse perhibentur. Namque vt reliquarum artium scientia sine diuina inutilis ac nulla putanda est, sic humanos tantum euentus atque casus, rerum vero diuinarum statum a quo illi dependent, non expendere, supina quaedam est negligentia, & indigna Christianis. Vt cum omnia a maioribus nostris domi, militiaeve gesta digna sint cognitu, tum ea maxima quibus aut firma fuerit, aut vacillans fluctuabatur Ecclesia. Ex quibus intelligemus quando D. Ihesus veritate ac luce fulgens sua eam illustrauerit, quando rursus tanquam nebulis obducto Sole ab oculis Ecclesiae tectus, serpes ille antiquus sele insinuauerit, quibusque artibus atque dolis potentiam suis acquisierit, tum patefacta iterum veritate, quae luctae & concertationes in vtriusque membris de principatu instituta fuerint, quae in carne, quae vero in Dei spiritu succubuerunt atque praualuerint. Quo quidem in genere Eusebium, Socratem & Sozomenum, qui Apostolorum vestigia sequuti, exactati nostrae literis conseruarunt, quae proximis Apostolorum saeculis acta gestaque fuerunt. Item Gregoram, Zonaram, ac Nicephorum, qui orientalium Patriarcharum praefecturas, deinde Palatinam, atque Siluium, qui Romanorum pontificum vitas descripserunt, eiusque generis permultos qui externa nobis scriptis referunt, non modo laudamus, sed admiramur atque suspicimus. Sed plerumque (quod dolendum est) cum in externis, minusque saepe necessariis, nostros totos conteramus, literisque atque ocio fastidiose abutamur, quae in nostra Republica atque Ecclesia domi a primordio gesta sunt, magnopere scire non auemus. In quo vno nos ne dignos quidem hac perbeata omnique diuina largitione affluenti Insula iudicamus, quod dum in alienis regnis sumus curiosi, quae domi geruntur, semper ignoramus, perinde ac patresfamilias, seruique indiligentiores, qui quae a vicinis fiunt sedulo explorant, remque suam domi negligunt. Nam si quis nostram gentem cum externis conferat, reperiet eam et si minutam & exiguam, vicina regna ditione multo latiora omni virtute antecessisse. Res enim bellicas & multitudine praeliorum, & acri dimicatione cum hostibus, crebrisque victoriis partis fortius foeliciusque gessimus, remque publicam melioribus administrauimus & institutis & legibus. Iam vero si, quod est praesentis instituti, de Ecclesiae institutione atque disciplina agere quisquam volet, eam sentiet (vt illa sane tenebrosa errorumque plena tulerunt, tempora) nec accuratius descriptam, nec seueriusc cultam in quacunque prouincia quam in Anglia fuisse, vt causa nulla sit, cur in alienis magis quam in nostris cognoscendis laboremus. Atque hoc in loco veterum huius regni monumentorum siue negligentia, siue iniuidia interierint, & extincta penè sint, interitum atque vastitatem deplorare iure possumus. Namque si quod multi probabiliter fatis existimant, dum inclytus Rex Henricus Octauus quibusdam ad id designatis eruditis viris Anglicanae antiquitatis indagationem, & lustrationem commisisset, & antiquissimorum codicum manuscriptorum in Coenobiis demolitis conditorum acervos atque cumulos permisisset, vt ex ea copia delectum haberent, & ad huius Insulae historiam sincere describendam ea quae oportuna maxime viderentur sumerent, illisque quae cum summo iudicio ǀ( 3 expendere debuissent, leuitate atq; perfunctorie multitudine ipsa librorum confusi & perturbati tranligerunt, aut malitia & rerum nostrarum inuidia (quod de peregrino quodam atque Italo, qui eas satis prolixè ac latinè artigit, à suis in eo munere Collegis dictum atq; scriptum fuit) eadé aut corruperunt, aut penitus deleuerunt, quibus dinis execrandum est, vt ram illustris atque splendidæ getis vetustas in rantam socordiā prauitatemq;, incideret. Et tamen diuino quodam beneficio nuper euenit, vt quemadmodum illa quondam multitudo atque copia quorundam delidia, quorundam vero malitia atque detractatione cōsumpta pene ac dissipara fit, sic quæ iam extat veterū nostrorū Scriptorū paucitas magna sedulitate, multisq; sumptibus cōquisita, & nō modo ex obscuris Bibliothecis atq; latebris, sed ex Pharmacopolarum officinis, cæterisq; vilioribus penetq; culinaris locis (ita enim incuria & inuidia priorum temporum vt Aesopica gemma abignaro & vetri prono gallo spernebatur, abiecta penèq; deleta fuerunt) erata & corrieruata, homines industrios & amantes patriæ ita ad nauandam in Reip. suæ historia operam excitarunt, vt sine peregrinis & alienigenis ipsi ἀπ' ἐαυτῶν rerum hic antiquitus gestarum genuinam atque propriam, nec aliunde sumptam aut muruatam edant historiam. Quibus de causis magnam sane gratiam debemus his qui in tanta antiquitatis nostræ iactura, ipsoq; naufragio, eas tamen in fluctibus nantes reliquias collegerunt, quibus ad rerum nostrarum memoriam tanquam ad portum integri saluiq; perduci possumus. Ac nobis quidem propositum est Britannicæ Ecclesiæ, eiusq; antiquissimæ à primis eius (vt ita dicam) incunabulis originem explicare, tū eam hostilibus incursionibus multis seculis depressam & occultam, & à Gregorio Papa in nouam formam Augustini aduentu commutatam; ad hæc nostra tempora deducere. Quam quidem historiam etsi tot celebres in Anglia Episcopales sedes permultis præclaris monumentis possunt illustrare, duæ tamen existunt præ cæteris magnis nobilitatæ, Cantuariensis nempe & Eboracensis Metropoles. Quarum vtraq; rerum suarum atq; Archiepiscoporum scriptores in uenit: illa Stobæum quendam, hæc Geruasium, ac Stephanum Byrchingtonum Monachos Cantuariensis; atque Richardū de Diceto Paulinæ Ecclesiæ Londinensis Decanum. Qui tamen neq; Archiepiscopos, neq; eorum temporibus in Ecclesiis gesta tam plene tractarunt, atq; persecuti sunt, vt lectori rerum copiam; aut temporum ordinem desiderantí possint satisfacere. Tum Geruasius & Richardus vltra Hubertum Archiepiscopum, qui Iohanne régnate mortuus est non progrediuntur. Stephanus autē in Willielmo Couttey desinit, vt eadem copiosius & accuratius, ad nostra tempora aptius retexenda atque trahenda esse videantur. Et quoniam Cantuariensis Ecclesia ditione maior, dignitate clarior, omniq; amplitudine excellentior cæteris in Anglia sit Ecclesiis (Nā & Eboracensis in prouincia Ecclesiæ, administratione pleniq;, hanc sequitur & imitata est, necvlla alia Ecclesia quid in Ecclesiasticis totius Angliæ rebus singulis æratibus atq; seculis decretum, mutatū, sūcitum, abrogatumq; sit, sicut hæc, cōmemorare potuit) eam potissimum explicandam duximus, vt perspiciatur quibus Satanæ dolis atque technis, Antichristi filius, nempe horrendæ vsurpatæ Romanæ potentiæ seruitus ingenuitate Christianam inuasit in Anglia, quomodo rursus in primæuam suam libertatem, tum, vetereq; natalium splendorem orta atque apprehensa luce Euangelii sese iterum recepit atque vindicauit. Res est itaque his nostris temporibus, quibus profligatis Satanae tenebris illuxit dominus cognitu scita atque oportuna, Cantuariensium Archiepiscoporum ordine à primordio hucusque ducta successio. Quam ex variis antiquis sumptam apte atque concinne hic compositam & cohaerentem videres; ut vnius potius scriptoris series, quam ex multis decerptae authoritates & sententiae videri possint. Antiquitatis tamen tanta à nobis ratio habita est, vt singula pene loca pro certiore testimonii fide authores suos in margine designent.
units.tr: Everyone must see clearly and plainly that the memory of past affairs and antiquity, which we call history, is pleasant and delightful. Although the other arts and disciplines, by whose knowledge men are led to the cultivation of life, of talent, of morals or of religion, contain some abstruse and recondite learning grasped and tested by only a few, and those learned and diligent, this one discipline is popular and widely known and lies open to all the unlearned. Those who are granted neither leisure nor the capacity of mind to probe the inner secrets of the other arts rest content with this recollection and light of things done by their forebears. The unlearned are delighted by it just as much as the more intelligent, and often even more. Yet it always matters greatly how much profit and benefit the learned draw from histories, compared with the unlearned. For while the latter marvel at the various fortunes of heroes and great men at home and in war, and are struck dumb and stupefied with great delight at the defeats and calamities of armies, the overthrow of commonwealths, the devastation of cities, changes of affairs, wars, fires, shipwrecks, and the variety, inconstancy and arrogance of all these, they desire no other usefulness and think history has none. They never notice with what counsel each thing was done, by what author and instigator it was begun, toward what end and outcome it advanced, and by what means it was brought to its conclusion. Learned and prudent men, who have never devoted their effort to useless things or to matters not bearing on the necessary use of life, have always regarded this as the chief reason for writing and reading histories: that from knowledge of earlier and past events they may discern and foresee what will be of use for the present and for what is to come. Yet the fault of historians is often no smaller than that of their readers. Just as readers commonly derive from them no fruit but empty pleasure, either of learning or of recalling and displaying the same things again, carelessly and uselessly, so writers, when they speak freely and copiously, without discrimination, not about the truth and credibility of what was done, but about trifling and commonly circulated fables, perhaps gain popular praise as an unjust reward for their useless labour and zeal. But having deserved very badly of human life, they cheat posterity of its ancestral knowledge, as of a lawful inheritance. Moreover, if any suspicion of partiality or private enmity appears in the writer, so that he either dares to say what is false or does not dare to say what is true, then the whole credit of history, both law and faith, is overthrown. Among these faulty writers of history, the nearest and worst are those who, led by hatred of a party which is always present in war as in peace, exaggerate with every kind of speech those things which can be blamed either not at all or only very slightly, while those things which deserve the greatest praise, in men whom the factious disapprove, they pass over in complete silence or with covert disparagement. Posterity has at last smelled out and judged such writers of every age to be liars, however varied they may be. Therefore those have kept everlasting praise, and are thought to have deserved best of the human race in this matter, who, leaving aside all those trifles and fables by which childish and foolish minds can be inflamed, have striven to explain and illustrate the truth alone. For just as in other arts there is great room for diligence and labour, so there is in describing history sincerely and accurately. If someone reads diligently Thucydides among the Greeks, or among the Latins Caesar and Sallust, who recorded affairs done by themselves or in their own times, of which they could have the most certain knowledge, he will find with what care they sought out the truth, and then how plainly, faithfully and clearly they expressed it. But those who looked back to the most distant antiquity, and tried to draw out from it and carry over to their own people things worthy of belief and fitting for their own times, and which are to be handed down and laid open to posterity as to heirs, the virtue and labour of such men must surely be greater, and their praise ought to be more celebrated. For Herodotus the Greek, lest he should seem to have omitted anything of antiquity, gathered everything without discrimination, and much of what he received came not from ancient writings but from the fables of the common people. Although he is elegant and polished in style, yet to those who judge soundly and without corruption, his heaped-up and crammed multitude of narratives takes away credit. And although by some he is called the father of history, which he seems to have aimed at, yet by others he has been rightly called the father of fables. Such things as have as much delight as the writer wishes, and are helped by words, sentences and every adornment of style, we ought nevertheless to give no authority to, nor add belief to made-up matters. But Livy the Latin, having traced the ancient writings on Roman affairs from their origin, and weighed and compared them with a right and accurate judgment, produced a history worthy of the Roman dominion and empire. In it there is nothing fabulous that lacks authority and testimony, or that by its even and plausible narrative does not seem of itself to beget belief in the reader. If such an eloquent and luminous expression of the truth of past things is judged to be of great value for the administration of war and peace in commonwealths, and for the lasting preservation of the worldly empire, with what zeal and study ought we to be stirred to investigate the truth or falsity of those things which are said to have been done in the Church of God, as in the divine kingdom and empire under the nod of its highest Emperor, or by Antichrist, the plunderer and invader of the same? For just as knowledge of the other arts is to be thought useless and nothing without the divine, so to weigh only human events and chances, and not to weigh the state of divine things on which those depend, is a kind of slothful negligence, and unworthy of Christians. So since all the deeds done by our forebears at home and in war are worth knowing, the greatest are those by which the Church was either made firm or wavered unsteadily. From these we shall learn when our Lord Jesus, shining with truth and light, illuminated it; when again, as if the sun were covered with clouds and hidden from the eyes of the Church, that ancient serpent insinuated himself; by what arts and tricks he acquired his power; then, when the truth was again laid open, what struggles and contests about primacy were undertaken among the members of each side, and which parties succumbed and which prevailed, in the flesh or in the Spirit of God. In this kind of writing, Eusebius, Socrates and Sozomen, who following the footsteps of the Apostles preserved in our writings what was done in the ages nearest the Apostles, deserve not only our praise but our wonder and esteem. Likewise Gregoras, Zonaras and Nicephorus, who described the offices of the Eastern patriarchs, and Platina and Silvius, who wrote the lives of the Roman pontiffs, and very many of that kind who relate foreign matters to us in writing, we not only praise but admire and look up to. But for the most part (which is to be lamented), while we waste ourselves on foreign matters, often less necessary, and abuse our letters and leisure in a fastidious way, we do not greatly wish to know what has been done at home from the beginning in our own commonwealth and Church. In this one thing we judge ourselves not even worthy of this most blessed island, abounding in every divine bounty; for while we are curious about the kingdoms of others, we always remain ignorant of what is done at home, just like heads of households and servants who are too careless, who diligently spy out what is done by their neighbours and neglect their own affairs at home. For if anyone compares our nation with foreign ones, he will find that, though small and slight, it has surpassed neighbouring kingdoms, far wider in dominion, in every virtue. For we have waged the affairs of war, with many battles, sharp fighting with enemies and frequent victories, more bravely and more happily, and we have administered our commonwealth with better institutions and laws. Now indeed, if anyone wishes to treat, as is the present purpose, of the institution and discipline of the Church, he will find (as those dark times full of errors have borne) that in no province was it described more accurately or cultivated more strictly than in England, so that there is no cause why we should labour more in learning about foreign matters than our own. And here, whether through the negligence or the envy of men the ancient monuments of this kingdom have perished and have nearly been extinguished, we may justly lament their destruction and waste. For if, as many reasonably think, when the renowned King Henry the Eighth had committed the investigation and survey of English antiquity to certain learned men designated for this, and had allowed heaps and piles of very ancient manuscript codices, stored in the demolished monasteries, to be at their disposal, so that from that abundance they might make a selection and take those things which seemed most suitable for describing the history of this island sincerely; and these men, confused and disturbed by the very multitude of books, which they ought to have weighed with the greatest judgment, passed over them with levity and carelessly; or, through malice and envy of our affairs (as was said and written of a certain foreigner and Italian who had handled them rather fully and in Latin, by his fellow Collectors in that office), either corrupted them or utterly destroyed them, then it is to be execrated that such an illustrious and splendid antiquity fell into such sloth and perversity. And yet by some divine benefit it has lately happened that, just as that former multitude and abundance, consumed and nearly scattered partly through the sloth of some and partly through the malice and disparagement of others, so the small number of our ancient writers which now survives, sought out with great diligence and at great expense, and recovered and restored not only from obscure libraries and hiding places but from the workshops of druggists and other meaner and almost kitchen places (for through the carelessness and envy of earlier times they were despised like the Aesopic gem among the dung, and cast aside and nearly destroyed), has so stirred up industrious men who love their country to labour in the writing of their commonwealth's history, that they themselves, without foreigners and aliens, publish a genuine and proper history of things done here in antiquity, not borrowed or exchanged from elsewhere. For these reasons we owe great thanks to those who, amid such a loss of our antiquity and its very shipwreck, gathered up those remnants swimming in the waves, by which we may be brought safe and sound, as to a harbour, to the memory of our affairs. And our purpose is to explain the origin of the British Church and its most ancient beginnings, as it were from its first cradle, and to bring it down to our own times: how it was depressed and hidden for many centuries by hostile incursions, and was changed into a new form by the coming of Augustine, sent by Pope Gregory. Although the many famous episcopal sees in England can illustrate this history with very many distinguished monuments, two stand out above the rest as greatly ennobled, namely the metropolitan sees of Canterbury and York. Each of these has found writers of its own affairs and of its archbishops: Canterbury has Stubbs (Stobaeus), a certain monk, and York has Gervase, and Stephen Birchington, monks of Canterbury, and Richard of Diceto, Dean of St Paul's in London. Yet they have not treated and pursued the archbishops, nor the things done in the churches in their times, so fully that they could satisfy a reader who desires an abundance of matters or the order of times. Gervase and Richard do not proceed beyond Archbishop Hubert, who died in the reign of John. Stephen, however, ends with William Courtenay, so that the same matters seem to be more fully and accurately, and more fittingly, to be unfolded and carried down to our own times. And since the Church of Canterbury is greater in jurisdiction, more distinguished in dignity and more excellent in every largeness than the other churches in England (for the church of York in its province, full of administration, follows and imitates it, and no other church could recall so many things decreed, changed, endured, or abrogated in the ecclesiastical affairs of all England in each age and century), we have chiefly judged it to be explained, so that it may be seen by what tricks and devices of Satan the son of Antichrist, namely the horrible servitude of the usurped Roman power, invaded the Christian liberty in England; and how, the light of the Gospel having arisen and been grasped, it again recovered and vindicated for itself its first liberty and its ancient splendour of birth. Therefore, in these our times, when the darkness of Satan has been put to flight and the Lord has shone forth, there is a matter fit and useful to know: the succession of the Archbishops of Canterbury, drawn in order from the beginning down to the present. You would see it gathered from various ancient sources, aptly and neatly arranged and coherent here, so that it may appear as the series of one writer rather than authorities and sayings plucked from many. Nevertheless we have paid such great attention to antiquity that almost every single passage has its authors designated in the margin, for a more certain confidence in the testimony.

units.la: Ac verbis praeterea illis plerumque vsi sumus, quibus Veteres illi scriptores suorum temporum mores actionesque expresserunt. Quae à nobis consulto quidem ideo facta sunt, ne cum Pontificiorum flagitia tam insigniter saepè ab ipsis Monachis & antiquis scriptoribus notata & deprehensa sunt, eadem à nobis ficta seu depravata quisquam comminiscatur, tum ne quacunque in re ab illorum mente & sententia videri possimus recessisse. Cuius quidem rei rationem potius quam cuiuscunque ornatus aut elegantiae habuisse nobis conuenit, qui non ornandae sed purè simpliciterque explicandae veritati studemus. Is si assequamur, harum rerum tot seculis abditarum historiam ad nostrorum hominum notitiam traducamus, eum labórem fructu quem expetimus & speramus, videbimur accepisse. Tantum n. abest vt gloriolam, aurámve popularem sectemur, vt inuidorum etiam, obtrectatorumque voculas, quae optima queque lacerare solent, aequo animo perfetamus.
units.tr: Moreover, we have for the most part used those very words in which the ancient writers of their own times expressed the customs and deeds of their day. We have done this deliberately, so that no one may invent that these things were fabricated or corrupted by us, since the crimes of the Papists have so often been noted and detected by the Monks themselves and by the ancient writers. We have also done so that we may not seem to have departed in any matter from their mind and opinion. For us, who strive to set forth the truth purely and simply rather than to adorn it, it has been fitting to consider this reason rather than any kind of ornament or elegance. If we attain this aim, and bring the history of these matters, hidden for so many centuries, to the knowledge of our fellow men, we shall seem to have received from this labour the fruit we seek and hope for. For we are so far from pursuing a little empty glory or popular applause that we bear with equanimity even the small murmurings of envious and detractors, which are wont to tear to pieces whatever is best.

units.la: Nam si quis ita affectus sunt, vt eos rerum nouitas, aut vetustatis tractatio laedat, aut laboribus alieni videantur eis ingrati, parianteque fastidium, his opus nostrum ex omni Anglicana antiquitate collectum, ac nonullo studio lucubratum, scriptum non esse censemus. Sunt enim duo hominum genera, quorum iniqua temeraria iudicia non formidamus, sed contemnimus. Vnum eorum, qui vni soli studio addicti atque contenti, cetera non modo negligunt, sed carpunt, reprehendunt, ac penitus etiam saepe damnant: alterum eorum qui omni quidè literarum genere versari atque permisceri gaudent, sed dum caeteris intelligentiores, peritioresque haberi & existimari velint, alienaque industriae laudem tollere aut detrahere studeant. Illi canibus comparandi sunt, qui ignotis semper latrant; hi porcis, qui ea prius conculcant, ac luto, caenoque inuoluunt, quae mox auide deuorat. Vtrumque sane perniciosum genus hominum, & à literarum coetu, consuetudineque abigendum. Nam si omnis humanitas, vitaeque cultus elegantior expoliri magis literis, studiisque existimetur, quam parum in literis profecisse videantur aliis (quicquid de se existimentl) hi, qui non modo tam inhumani quam etiam agrestes sunt atque barbari, vt alienam sedulitatem exprobrent, inuentaque reprehendant. Dequibusdam enim qui rebus nouis ita studeant, vt omnia perturbari atque permisceri cupiant, nec alia quam quae ipsi pariunt dogmata, à quoquam probari velint, ne dicamus quicquam grauius, quam censoria castigatione magis quam verborum corruptione opus esse. Qui tumore ac fastidio si velint tabescant, nos in hoc suscepto labore pietati veritatique, non hominum rumoribus obsequuti, nullius siue blando atque ficto allecti, siue iniquo & criminoso sermone deterriti, quicquid diuturna vetustissimorum huius regni monumentorum lucubratione consequi atque indagare potuimus, ad omnium iudicium tanquam publicum discrimen subeundum, in apertam tandem lucem emisimus. In quo benignos candidosque lectores, de duobus, haud secus atq; conuenit exiliter petimus. Primum quod Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ dignitatem, eam quam & temporis diuturnitas, & principum concessiones, & ipsa iura tribuunt, tueamur atq; defendamus. Alterum quod ipsorum Archiepiscoporum etsi non minus vitia, quam recte facta exponamus, non idcirco tamen magis lectores ab illius dignitate abhorreat. Nam, vt Caius Suetonius Tranquillus, qui duodecim primorum Cæsarum vitas, eadem libertate describere dicitur, qua ipsi vixerunt, in quibus multa nefanda facinora commemorauit, pius lectoribus inducere animum non potest, vt imperia atq; Monarchias, quæ ad humani generis utilitatem & salutem (etsi a malis saepe administrantur) a Deo constitutæ sunt, tuentur aut contemnant: sic ea quæ de Archiepiscopis Cantuariensibus scripsimus, in quibus male perperam, fecerunt, cum iure reprehendant, abalienare tamen vllius boni animum a tam vtili atq; necessaria Archiepiscopatus in Ecclesia regenda dignitate, nullo modo debent. Ea tamen vt cunctis, ipsisque adeo inuidis ac maleuolis (quæcunq; euenire possunt) vno dicto respondeamus. Si Papalis illa dominatio ac potentia, quam cæcitate magis & superstitione quam contumacia tuebantur & colebant, abfuisset, nullos aut in rebus diiudicandis prudentiores, aut ab omni luxu continentiores, aut in tota vita modestatiores, magisq; frugi & in pauperes benef icos, & quotiescunque Rempub. capescebat, Regibus atq; regno vtiliores quam Cant. Archiepiscopos plerumq; fuisse sentient. Illa autem Papalis vsurpatio, quæ tum infitar diuini numinis ab omnibus obseruabatur, eos communi magis temporum vitio (quis enim tum fere vixit, quem illa cæcitas non infatuauit) quâ sua propria aut peculiari culpa, aduersos esse sç pè fecit Regibus, aliaq; multa perpetrare, quæ tum putabantur pia, iam profligara caligine manifestatur impia. Id itaq; vni hominum generi precipue vertí vitio non debet, quod perinde omnes occupauit, nec priuatim singulis, sed communiter accidit vniuersis. Tu vero pie candideque lector eum quem sine liuore & detractatione oportet ex hac lucubratione fructum percipe. Cuius tota laus ei tribuenda est, qui eadem vigilantia & sedulitate, qua singula quæ ad Christianam gerendam Ecclesiam sunt necessaria, rimatur atq; colligit, etiâ in istius sedis antiquitatem penitus retrospexit, nosq; peregrinantes ac errantes ad certissimam rerum nostrarum fidem atq; ventatem amanter iterum reduxit domum. Cui vt tam sanctas & salubres dominico gregi vigilias & excubias agendas longæva vita superesse possit, ipsaq; demum æternitas concedatur, bonorum omnium assiduus votis interpellandus est ille magnus gregis pastor D. Iesus: cuius est cum patre atq; paracleto vna, & immensa atq; infinita maiestas.
units.tr: For if there are those so disposed that the novelty of things offends them, or the handling of antiquity wounds them, or the labours of others seem to them unwelcome and breed disgust, we judge that this work, gathered from all English antiquity and written with some diligence, was not written for them. For there are two kinds of men whose unfair and rash judgements we do not fear but despise. One kind consists of those who are devoted and content with a single field of study, and not only neglect everything else but carp at it, find fault with it, and often condemn it outright. The other kind consists of those who delight to be involved in and mixed up with every sort of literature, but, wishing to be thought and regarded as more intelligent and more skilled than others, strive to take away or diminish the praise of others' industry. The former are to be compared with dogs, which always bark at what they do not know; the latter with pigs, which trample underfoot and wallow in mire and filth those things which they then greedily devour. Both are indeed a pernicious kind of men, and to be driven away from the company and fellowship of letters. For if all civility and a more refined way of life are thought to be polished rather by letters and studies, then those who, whatever they may think of themselves, have made little progress in letters, and who are not only as unkind as they are rustic and barbarous, so as to upbraid the diligence of others and find fault with what has been discovered, are far from such refinement. For there are some who pursue new things in such a way that they desire everything to be thrown into confusion and disorder, and who wish no doctrines to be approved by anyone except those they themselves produce; we need not say anything more severe than that such men need correction by censure rather than by the corruption of words. Let them waste away with their pride and disdain if they wish. As for us, in this labour we have undertaken, we have yielded to piety and truth, not to the rumours of men; we have been swayed by no flattering or feigned persuasion, nor deterred by unjust and slanderous talk. Whatever we have been able to obtain and investigate through the long study of the most ancient monuments of this realm, we have at last brought out into the open light, to be submitted to the judgement of all as if to a public trial. In this matter we humbly ask kind and candid readers for two things, and we ask it no less than is fitting. The first is that they should protect and defend the dignity of the Canterbury Church, which both the length of time, the grants of princes, and the laws themselves bestow. The second is that, although we set out the vices of the archbishops themselves no less than their right deeds, readers should not on that account be turned away from the dignity of that office. For just as Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, who is said to have described the lives of the first twelve Caesars with the same freedom with which they lived, and in whom he recorded many wicked crimes, nevertheless cannot bring a pious reader to despise or hold in contempt the empires and monarchies which God has established for the usefulness and salvation of the human race, even though they are often administered by bad men; so likewise, what we have written about the archbishops of Canterbury, in which they have rightly been reproached for wrong and perverse deeds, ought in no way to alienate the mind of any good person from the dignity of the archbishopric, so useful and necessary for governing the Church. Yet, that we may answer all, and even the envious and malicious, in one word (whatever may happen): if that Papal domination and power, which men defended and honoured more through blindness and superstition than through obstinacy, had been absent, they will perceive that the archbishops of Canterbury were for the most part no wiser in judging matters, no more continent from all luxury, no more moderate in their whole life, no more thrifty and beneficent to the poor, and, whenever they took up the government of the commonwealth, no more useful to kings and kingdom. But that Papal usurpation, which at that time was observed by all as if it were the authority of the divine majesty, has often made them opposed to kings, and to do many other things, through the common vice of the times rather than through their own particular or peculiar fault (for who then lived who was not made foolish by that blindness?), and things which were then thought pious are now, with the darkness dispelled, made manifestly impious. Therefore this fault ought not to be charged especially against one class of men, since it occupied all alike, and happened not privately to individuals but commonly to all. And you, pious and candid reader, take from this work the fruit which ought to be gathered without envy and detraction. Its whole praise is to be given to him who, with the same vigilance and diligence with which he searches out and gathers each thing necessary for conducting the Christian Church, has looked back thoroughly even into the antiquity of that see, and has lovingly led us, wandering and erring, back home to the most certain faith and truth of our affairs. That such holy and wholesome watches and vigils may be kept for the Lord's flock by him, and that long life may be granted to him, and at last eternity itself, the great shepherd of the flock, Lord Jesus, is to be entreated by the constant prayers of all good men; to him, with the Father and the Paraclete, belongs one and immense and infinite majesty.

units.la: DE VETVSTATE BRITANNICÆ ECCLESIÆ TESTIMONIA.
units.tr: ON THE ANTIQUITY OF THE BRITISH CHURCH: THE TESTIMONIES.

units.la: RACTATURI de Cantuariensibus Archiepiscopis, qui Dorobernenses antiquitus dicti sunt: quia totius Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ Primates & Metropolitani fuerūt, commodißimum faciemus, si primam Christianæ Ecclesiæ originem, & iostitutionem in Insula Britannica, ex antiquissimis Patrum scriptorumq; testimoniis, tāquam altiùs ducto huius vtilißimæ narrationis principio, declaraverimus. Quadiligentius perpensa & explorata, repperiemus non modò peruetustam eam fuisse, sed etiam ab ipso primùm per Apostolos propagato per orbem Euangelio, non à Romano sede, vt Pontificii coötendunt, & plæriq; imperitè autumant, & initia duxisse, & accepisse incrementa. Gyldas enim antiquissimus inter eos, qui fide digni sunt, Britannicarum rērum scriptor, tradit Britannos iam inde ab ortu Euangelii Christianam suscepisse fidem. Tum Origenes, qui proximis fuit post Apostolos seculis, testatur Britanniam in Christianam consentire religionem. Et cum hoc Tertullianus antiquissimus Ecclesiæ patēt, in Iudæos scribens de gentibus Christianam fidem amplexis, meminit Britanorum. Cuius hæc sunt diserta verba. In quem alium vtiquèrsæ gentes crediderunt, nisi in Christum, qui iam venit? Cui enim & aliæ gentes, Parthi, Medi, &c. vt iam Gerulorum varietates, Mauorum multi sines, Hispaniarum omnes termini, Galliarum diuersæ oationes, & Britannorū inaccessa Romanis loca, &c. Huic ætati finitimus Athanasius, mentionem de his faciens nationibus, quæ ad Sardicum concilium coouenissent. In magno(ioquit) Sardico concilio, hoc stram innocentiam plures quàm trecenti Episcopi suis calculis comprobarunt: qui ex multis prouinciis, Ægypti, Lybiæ, Pentapoleos, &c. Hispaniarum, Galliarum, Britanniatum, eò se ad concilium contulerant. Huc accedit Arelatensis secundi concilij authoritas, in quo disertè exprimitur, Restitutum quendam Londinensem Episcopum ei concilio è Britannia vocatum interfuisse, eiusdemq́ue decretis subscripsisse. Ad extremum in Ecclesiastica Nicephori historia extat eiusdem Athanasij ad Iouinianum Imperatorem Epistola, in quâ scribit. Illud scito, Christianissime Auguste, à seculo hanc esse prædicatam fidem, & hanc ipsam professos esse, qui Nicææ conuenerē patres, ac etiamnum suffragiis suis eam comprobare omnes, quæ passim sunt Ecclesiæ, in Hispania, & Britannia, & Gallia, & Germania. Omnium enim earum quas recensuimus, comperta nobis est sententia, quòd ab eis Epistolas habeamus. Ex quibus manifestò constat authoritatibus, non modò Christianam fidem primis illis temporibus à Britannis receptam, sed Ecclesiam institutam, & Episcopis, singulísq; missitrorum otdinibus distinctam, longè ante Augustini à Gregorio missi huc aduentū fuisse. Quòd si quis tanquam moturus nobis controuersiam, citata testimonia ad eam Britanniam referat, quæ iam Galliæ prouiocia, inter Normannïam & Guasconiam ioterieˉa est: perpendat Tertullianum de Britanniā Romanis inaccessa loquì, sicut hoc versu Virgilium: Et penitus toto diusos orbe Britannos. Itemq́; Senecam Latinum Tragicum: Cuique Britannia terra dedere; Ducibus nostris ante ignoti.
units.tr: Since we are about to treat of the Archbishops of Canterbury, who were anciently called Dorobernenses because they were Primates and Metropolitans of the whole English Church, we shall do best to begin this most useful account from further back, and to set out the first origin and establishment of the Christian Church in the British Island from the most ancient testimonies of the Fathers and writers. When we have weighed and examined these carefully, we shall find that this Church was not only very ancient, but that it had its beginnings and received its growth not from the Roman see, as the Papists contend and as most people unskilfully suppose, but from the gospel itself, first spread throughout the world by the Apostles. For Gildas, the most ancient of those writers of British affairs who are worthy of belief, relates that the Britons had embraced the Christian faith from the very beginning of the gospel. Then Origen, who lived in the age closest after the Apostles, testifies that Britain agrees with the Christian religion. Tertullian, the most ancient father of the Church, agrees with him, for in writing against the Jews about the nations that had embraced the Christian faith, he mentions the Britons. His words are these: "In whom else have all the nations believed, except in Christ, who has already come? For to whom else have other nations believed: Parthians, Medes, etc.; the varieties of the Gaetulians, the many tribes of the Moors, all the borders of Spain, the diverse regions of Gaul, and the places of the Britons which are inaccessible to the Romans, etc." Athanasius, living close to this age, also makes mention of the nations that came together at the council of Sardica. "In the great council of Sardica," he says, "more than three hundred bishops confirmed our innocence with their votes. They had come to the council from many provinces: of Egypt, Libya, Pentapolis, etc.; of Spain, of Gaul, of Britain." To this is added the authority of the second council of Arles, in which it is plainly stated that a certain Restitutus, bishop of London, called to that council from Britain, was present and subscribed to its decrees. Finally, in the ecclesiastical history of Nicephorus there is extant a letter of the same Athanasius to the emperor Jovian, in which he writes: "Know this, most Christian Augustus, that this faith has been preached from the beginning, and that the fathers who met at Nicaea professed it, and that all the churches scattered through Spain, Britain, Gaul and Germany still confirm it by their votes." For we have the opinion of all those we have listed, since we have their letters. From these authorities it is clearly established that the Christian faith was received by the Britons in those first times, and that the Church was not only founded but also distinguished by bishops and by the distinct orders of ministers, long before Augustine was sent here by Gregory. But if anyone, as though about to raise a dispute with us, refers the cited testimonies to that Britain which is now a province of Gaul, lying between Normandy and Gascony, let him consider that Tertullian speaks of Britain as inaccessible to the Romans, as Virgil does in this line: "and the Britons, cut off entirely from the whole world." Likewise Seneca the Latin tragedian: "To whom Britain gave its land, unknown before to our leaders."

units.la: Illa enim Galliæ regio, inter Normanniam & Guasconiam in altum Oceanum porrēcta, à Iulio Cæsare Armorica nuncupata, aduentu Fabii tunc quibusdam Romanis legionibus à Cæsare præfećti, post multos Gallorum motus, in Romanam dedicioöem, scripsicut reliqua Gallia penitus ceßit & conquiecuit. Nec ante Britannia dicta est, quàm à Britannis veteribus huius regni incolis patriam deserentibus, Armoricitêq; inde eiectis & deturbatis occupata, eorum nouo incolatu sic nominata fuit, An Dom. 596. trecentis amplius post prædictos patres annis. Cuius rei certissimum habemus hodiernum argumentum, quòd illi Gallobritanni, vetcris Britannici sermonis Wallis seu Cambris Britannorum in hac Insula residuis vitati, verba atque idioma adhuc adeo retinent, vt ab his facile intelligantur. Præterea nec Restitutus Londinensis Episcopus in Arelatensi concilio nuper commemoratus ex illa Britannia esse potuit. Vt nemini dubium sit, illam de Gallicana Britannia dubitationem a Ponuficiis ineulcaram, esse manifestam, fraudisque plenam calumniam. Sed singulatum in illa priori Britannica Ecclesia rerum gestarum memoria prodita nobis atq; conseruata non est. hæc autem, quæ de vetustate eius diximus, & domesticis atque nostris, & externis testimoniis ac monumentis satis comprobantur.
units.tr: For that region of Gaul, lying between Normandy and Gascony and stretching out into the deep ocean, was called Armorica by Julius Caesar. After many movements of the Gauls, it surrendered to Roman rule, and was quieted, as the rest of Gaul entirely was, when Fabius, then a prefect of certain Roman legions appointed by Caesar, arrived. Nor was it called Britain until the ancient Britons, the inhabitants of this kingdom, abandoned their homeland and, being driven out and expelled from Armorica, occupied it; and it was named Britain from their new settlement, in the year of the Lord 596, more than three hundred years after the aforesaid fathers. Of this we have a most certain argument still present: those Gallo-Britons retain the words and idiom of the old British speech so fully that they are easily understood by the Welsh, or Cambrians, the remnant of the Britons in this island. Moreover, Restitutus, bishop of London, mentioned just now in the council of Arles, could not have come from that Britain. So no one can doubt that the doubt raised by the Papists about Gallican Britain is a manifest and fraudulent calumny. But no individual record of events in that earlier British Church has been handed down and preserved for us. What we have said about its antiquity, however, is sufficiently confirmed both by our own domestic testimonies and monuments and by foreign ones.

units.la: Qvis primo Christi doctrinam tradidit in hac Insula.
units.tr: Who first delivered the doctrine of Christ in this island.

units.la: OSTQVAM ab ipsis Ecclesiæ incunabulis hanc Insulam in fide Christiana fuisse instructam luculenter breuiterq; exposuimus, videamus a quo Doctore primùm institiuta sit: tum quomodo vnà semper creuit, nec aulula penitus defecit vnquàm, etsi multis erroribus ab hostilibus incursionibus, Romanaq; sede huc traductis, tardius sæpe corrupta, sed diuina veritate iterum recepta ocyus recreata semper fuit. Ac primum Paulum ipsum gentium doctorem, cum aliis gentibus, tum nominatim Britannis Euangelium nunciasse post priorem suam Romaz incarcerationem, & Theodoretus, & Sophronius Patriarcha Hictosolymitanus affirmant. Hoc autem quod Pontificii incredibile atq; adeo impossibile statuunt, cum vero cohaereat maximè. Quanquâ n. ipse ad hanc Insulâ profectus nô sit, tamen Claudiæ Rufinæ nobilissimæ Britannæ, & Græcis Latinisq; literis instructæ Christianam religionem suasisse hinc perspicuum est. Multos enim nobiles Britannos Romam Neronis tempore ductos captiuos iussu Neronis tyranni testatur Cornelius Tacitus. Hæc autem Claudia nomen à Claudio Cæsare accepit, post cuius hucadüentum, nobiles Britanni amici & conferderati Populo Romano, hæredibus liberisque suis Romana nomina imponebat. Deinde eadem Claudia Rufo ex Hetrusca nobilitate insigni equiti Romano, tum Tribuno militum, deinde Senatorio nupta, à marito Claudia Rufina dicta est. Rufus sectæ Stoicæ Philosophus ob clementiam morum; mansuetudinem, atq; ingenuitatem & verecundiam tanquam naturâ inditam Pudens dictus est. Qui gravitate & modestia suaadigebat Martialem illum lasciuum & amatorium Poetam, veteri sibi neccsitudine familiarem, calamo plura reformare. Itaq; Martialis tam hunc Pudentem, Rufum ab humanitate, pietate, eruditione, & eloquentia, quâ Claudiâ Britanniaeius coniugem a forma, fœcunditate, fide coniugali, doctrina, linguis & literis laudat. De qua hæc conscripsit carmina. Claudia cæruleis cum sit Ruffina Britannis. Ædita, cur lata pectora plebis habet? Quale decus formæ Romanam credere matres Italides possunt, Atthides esse suam Dii bene, quod sanctos peperit fæcunda marito Quæ sperat generos, quotque puella parum. Sic placeat superis, vt coniuge gaudeat vno Et semper matrî gaudeat illa tribus.
units.tr: Having set out clearly and briefly that this island was instructed in the Christian faith from the very cradle of the Church, let us see by whom it was first taught. Then let us see how it always grew together with the faith and never wholly failed at any time, although it was often corrupted more slowly by many errors, by hostile incursions, and by teachers brought here from the Roman see, and yet, when restored by divine truth, it was always revived more quickly. And first, Theodoret and Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, affirm that Paul himself, the teacher of the Gentiles, announced the gospel to other nations and especially to the Britons after his first imprisonment at Rome. The Papists consider this incredible and even impossible, but it coheres most closely with the truth. For although he himself did not go to this island, it is nevertheless clear from the following that he persuaded Claudia Rufina, a most noble British woman instructed in Greek and Latin letters, to the Christian religion. For Cornelius Tacitus testifies that in Nero's time many noble Britons were led captive to Rome by the tyrant's order. Now this Claudia took her name from Claudius Caesar, after whose coming the noble Britons, friends and allies of the Roman people, used to give Roman names to their heirs and children. Then the same Claudia was married to Rufus, a distinguished Roman knight of Etruscan nobility, then a military tribune, and afterwards a senator; from her husband she was called Claudia Rufina. Rufus, a philosopher of the Stoic sect, was called Pudens, on account of the gentleness of his character, his mildness, his nobility and modesty, as if these were innate in his nature. By his gravity and moderation he persuaded Martial, that wanton and amatory poet, an old friend of his, to revise many of his poems. Thus Martial praises this Pudens, Rufus, for his humanity, piety, learning and eloquence, and praises his wife, Claudia of Britain, for her beauty, fruitfulness, marital faithfulness, learning, languages and letters. About her he wrote these verses: "Claudia, though she is Rufina, born of the sky-blue Britons, why does she have a broad-hearted breeding? What grace of form Italian mothers could believe to be Roman, the Athenian women could claim as their own! May the gods bless her, that being fruitful she has borne holy children to her husband, and hopes for as many sons-in-law as a girl has. So may it please the gods that she rejoice in one husband, and always rejoice in her three children."

units.la: Eadem, Martialis ad virum suum Rufum scripsius accedentis carmina ad Britannos Latinæ linguæ cupidos, cum ipsa Romæ esset, tanquàm Xenia mittere consuevit. De quo idem Martialis.
units.tr: The same Martial, when Claudia was at Rome, used to send to the Britons who were eager for the Latin tongue, as gifts, the verses he had written to her husband Rufus. Of this the same Martial says: "Britain too is said to sing our verses."

units.la: Dicitur & nostros cantare Britannia versus.
units.tr: Dicitur & nostros cantare Britannia versus.

units.la: Sed postea accepta prædicatione diuina, tam Pudentem Rufum Senatorem Romanum, quam Claudiam suam coniugem totamq; suam familiam, Christi fidem amplexos testatur Volaterranus. Pauli autem non Petri fuisse discipulos, non modò tempus & locus concordant, sed ipsius Gentium Apostoli posteriora Timotheum Epistola, cuinis nitâ pertinaci manifestissimè declarat. Quia Timotheum condiscipulû suum salutari à Paulo voluerunt. Vnde Paulus. Salutans Salutant te Eubulus, & Pudens, & Linus, & Claudia, & fratres omnes.
units.tr: But afterwards, when the divine preaching had been received, Volaterranus testifies that Pudens Rufus, a Roman senator, embraced the faith of Christ, as did Claudia his wife and his whole household. That they were disciples of Paul and not of Peter is shown not only by the agreement of time and place, but also by the Apostle of the Gentiles' own later Epistle to Timothy, which declares it most clearly and with persistent insistence, because they wished to send greetings to Timothy, their fellow-disciple, through Paul. Whence Paul: "Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia and all the brothers greet you."

units.la: Hanc itaque iam ad Christum conuersam, non minus est verisimile Christiana dogmata ad Britannos misisse suos, quàm ante acceptam fidem Epigrammata Martialis. Nec verisimile solum sed verum iudicandum est, in tam nobili familia fuisse cum Claudia gentiles suos Britannos qui vna baptizati fuerunt, à quibus Euangelii igniculi per totam gentem Britannam disperso, viritim ad multos peruenerunt. Hæc res siue veritas sit, siue in re tanta veritatis indagatio atque coniectura, videmus tamen quibus nitatur adminiculis, vt multò certiorexistimari debeat, quàm illa fictio Pontificia, suis legationibus fuisse primò inchoatam in Britannia Christianam fidem. Philippus enim Apostolus, qui in Galliam venit, & Euangelii prædicatione plures ad fidem vertit, abluitq; baptismate, cum de Britannia modico freto separata Insula accepisset, a qua Druidum superstitio manabat in Galliam, delegit ex suorum sociorum numero duodecim: quibus Iosephum Arimathiensem, qui Dominum Christum sepulchro condidit, præfecit. Qui cum in Britanniam appulissent, fidem Christi forti pectore prædicabant. An. Dom. 63. Quorum prædicatione etsi Rex Arviragus cum proceribus suis ab inueterata Druidum religione abduei noluit: tamen & tam longinquæ peregrinationis, & modestiæ, morumque manuetudinis eorum opinione permotus, petentibus illis quandam Insulam, in regionis suæ finibus positam, horridam illam tunc quidem & incultam, fluuiisque, rubis, ac paludibus circumseptam, ab incolis Insuuitrim nuncupatam, habitandam & concedit. Ac deinde alii duo reges, huius exemplo, & Iosephi sociorumque piete, vitæque integritate adducti, singulis illis duodecim, singulas terra hidas ex gentis mere sic dictas, dederunt & confirmarunt. Unde & duodecim hidarum nomen adhuc retinent. In hac autem Insula diuino admonitu templum à Ioiepho, & sociis extructum referunt. De qua Augustinus à Papa Gregorio huc missus, primusque (vt mox patebit) Dorouernenfis, seu Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus, sic scribit. Est (inquit) in confinio Occidentalis Britanniæ, quædam regalis insula, antiquo vocabulo Glasicon nuncupata, latis locorum dimensa finibus, piscosis aquis, stagnis circumdata fluminibus, & plurimis humanæ indigentiæ vsibus apta, factique (quod maximum est) dedicata muneribus. In ea siquidem primi Catholicæ legis neophitæ, Ecclesiam nulla hominum arte constructam, vt ferunt, imo humanæ saluti à Deo paratam repererunt: Hæc Augustinus. Sed locus ipse postquàm Iosephus & sociì excesserunt è vita, aliquot interieétis annis, ab incolis deiertus, in solitudinem, sed templo remanente, mutatus, Lucii Regis temporibus, hoc casu iterum repertus, & à Christianis denuò occupatus est. Phaganus & Deruuianus Eleutherii Papæ, ad Lucium Britanniæ Regem legati (de quibus in sequenti narratione dicetur) de hac Iosephi sociorumque in Britannia olim habitatione, aliquid Romæ perciperent, locum ipsum sedulò perquirebant, singulisque Britanniæ regionibus lustratis, tandem dictam Avalonium Insulam, tanquàm solitudinem & desertum penetrantes, penitusque rimantes, Ecclesiam illam quam vicini incolæ à Christi discipulis quondam extructam, & in humanam salutem conditam asserebant, inuenerunt. Quibus, aliisque manifestis signis ac indiciis facilè intellexerunt, eam ipsam fuisse Iosephi, sociorumque in Britannia habitationem, de qua Romæ acceperunt.
units.tr: Now that she had been converted to Christ, it is no less probable that she sent Christian teaching to her own Britons than that Martial's epigrams were sent to them before she received the faith. And it should be judged not only probable but true that in so noble a family there were with Claudia her gentile Britons, who were baptised together with her, and from whom the sparks of the gospel, scattered through the whole British nation, reached many individuals one by one. Whether this is the truth, or in so great a matter only an investigation and conjecture of the truth, we nonetheless see what supports it, so that it ought to be considered far more certain than that Papist fiction, that the Christian faith in Britain was first begun by their legations. For the Apostle Philip, who came into Gaul and by the preaching of the gospel turned many to the faith and washed them in baptism, when he had learned of Britain, an island separated by a narrow sea, from which the superstition of the Druids flowed into Gaul, chose twelve from among his companions, and set over them Joseph of Arimathea, who had laid the Lord Christ in the tomb. When they had landed in Britain, they preached the faith of Christ with brave hearts. In the year of the Lord 63. Although King Arviragus, with his nobles, would not be drawn away from the long-rooted religion of the Druids by their preaching, yet he was moved by the reputation of so distant a journey and by their modesty and gentleness of manners. When they asked him for a certain island, lying within the bounds of his realm, then indeed rough and uncultivated, surrounded by rivers, brambles and marshes, and called Insuuitrim by the inhabitants, he allowed them to live there and granted it to them. Then two other kings, led by his example, and by the piety and integrity of life of Joseph and his companions, gave and confirmed to each of those twelve a single hide of land taken from the people's own land, so called. Whence they still keep the name of the twelve hides. In this island they report that a church was built by Joseph and his companions at divine prompting. Augustine, sent here by Pope Gregory, and the first (as will soon become clear) Archbishop of Dorobernia, or Canterbury, writes of it thus: "There is, he says, on the border of western Britain a certain royal island, anciently called Glasicon, measured out with broad territories, surrounded by fishy waters, marshes and rivers, and suited to many human uses, and dedicated, what is greatest, by the gifts of God. For in it the first neophytes of the Catholic law found a church built by no human art, but, as they say, prepared by God for human salvation." So Augustine. But after Joseph and his companions had departed this life, and some years had passed, the place was deserted by its inhabitants and became a wilderness, though the church remained. In the time of King Lucius it was found again by chance and was once more occupied by Christians. Phaganus and Deruvianus, legates of Pope Eleutherius to King Lucius of Britain (of whom more will be said in the following narrative), when they learned at Rome something of the former dwelling of Joseph and his companions in Britain, searched carefully for the place itself. Having explored every region of Britain, they at last came to the island called Avalonia, as a solitude and desert; penetrating and searching it thoroughly, they found that church which the neighbouring inhabitants asserted had once been built by the disciples of Christ and founded for human salvation. From this and other clear signs and indications they readily understood that this was the very dwelling of Joseph and his companions in Britain of which they had heard at Rome.

units.la: Neque enim à veritate alienum esse poterit, Iosephum petindè, ac alios Apostolos ac discipulos, per totum orbem sparsos, quid singulis in regionibus pro Christo effecisset, quidue siue aduersi, siue commodi sensissent, per nuncios ac literas certiores fecisse coliegas suos, tam Romæ, quàm Hierosolymis, aliisque in locis: aut Eleutherii legatos indagare voluisse ea loca, quæ à Christianis priùs culta Romæ ex antiquis scriptis acceperunt. In hoc itaque loco præfati legati, nouem annorum moram fecerunt, vbi tam res a Iosepho pro fide Christiana gestas, quàm memoratam historiam de Iosephi sociorumque appulsu, regia concessione, templi ædificatione, aliisque nonnullis ex antiquis scriptis acceperunt, quorum memoria ad ipsum Augustinum Romanum, sicuti diximus, deducta, ab eoque prodita est, ne quis suspicetur hoc fabulosum, aut à recenti authore traditum, tenere iam emissum, sed ab ipsa origine petitum, & ab antiquissimis scriptoribus se inuicem succedentibus, ad nostram ætatem & notitiam peruenisse.
units.tr: Nor can it be out of keeping with the truth that Joseph and the other Apostles and disciples, scattered throughout the whole world, informed their colleagues by messengers and letters, both at Rome and at Jerusalem and elsewhere, what each had accomplished for Christ in his region, and what he had experienced, whether adverse or favourable. Nor is it unlikely that Eleutherius's envoys wished to search out those places which, according to ancient writings, Christians had earlier cultivated and had known at Rome. In this place, then, the aforementioned envoys spent a stay of nine years, where they received from ancient writings both the deeds Joseph had done for the Christian faith and the aforesaid history of Joseph's and his companions' arrival, the royal grant, the building of the church, and some other matters. The memory of these, as we have said, was brought down to Augustine of Rome and handed on by him, so that no one may suspect that this is a fable or a tradition from a recent author. Rather, it has been held as already published, and has come down to our age and knowledge from its very origin, passing from the most ancient writers, each succeeding the other.

units.la: Alii Simonem Zelotem in Britanniam venisse, & Euangelium primum nuncIasse, referunt. Quorum vtrumq; verum esse potest. Nam Iosephi socii non nominantur, inter quos fuisse Simonem est verisimile. Iosephus itaque de quo certior est fides, sua & sociorum prædicatione, dilatauit per hanc insulam Euangelium, vt permultos conuersos & baptismate mundatos permeans, & traductum tandem ad Regem ipsum peruenit. Qui Iosepho & socijs modicam tellurem, mille circiter passus ab Wellio oppido seiunctam, in quo olim nobile cœnobium Monasticæ familiæ Benedictini ordinis extructum fuit, adhuc extat templum magnificum, colendam & habitandam concessit. Huic loconomen Glasconiain Avalonia solitudine, Britannicè dicta pupsi. Pomorum Insula: nam Aual Pomum, pupsi Insulam Britanno sermone significat. Hic Iosephus toto reliquę vitæ spacio confecit & Ecclesiæ fundamenta in hac Insula primus iecit: ibique moriens, anno Christo 75. sepultus est. Ex hac prima Euangelii satione, reliquiæ quædam ad Lucii regis tempora perin manserunt. Quæ Euangelium latens atque conditum rursus ipso Rege authore, vt mox patebit, diuulgarunt. Sub Claudio autem Cæsare Euangelii lucernam primùm in Britannia voce Iosephi accensam testatur Georgius Maior.
units.tr: Others report that Simon the Zealot came into Britain and first preached the Gospel. Both of these accounts may be true. For the companions of Joseph are not named, and it is likely that Simon was among them. Joseph, therefore, of whom the trustworthy report is more certain, through his own preaching and that of his companions spread the Gospel through this island, so that, passing through very many who were converted and cleansed by baptism, it at last reached the king himself. To Joseph and his companions he granted a small plot of land, about a thousand paces from the town of Wells, in which a noble monastery of the Benedictine order was once built, and where the magnificent church still stands, to be cultivated and inhabited. They called this place Glastonia, in the solitude of Avalon, which in the British tongue is called "Pupsi" (the Isle of Apples); for "Aual" in the British language means an apple, and "pupsi" an island. Here Joseph spent the whole remainder of his life, and he was the first to lay the foundations of the Church in this island. He died here and was buried in the year of Christ 75. From this first sowing of the Gospel, certain remnants persisted until the time of King Lucius, and these, the Gospel lying hidden and concealed, they again made known, with the king himself as author, as will soon be clear. Under Caesar Claudius, however, George Major testifies that the lamp of the Gospel was first kindled in Britain by the voice of Joseph.

units.la: QVANNO, ET QVOMODO REX BRITANNIÆ LVCIVS Euangelio credens baptizatus fit.
units.tr: IN WHAT YEAR, AND IN WHAT MANNER, KING LUCIUS OF BRITAIN, BELIEVING THE GOSPEL, WAS BAPTIZED.

units.la: VCIVS itaque Coilli Britanniæ Regis pietate omniq; virtute insignis princeps, vnicus filius ad pateroam laudem sua præstantia accedens, Pius, & alter Coillus merito dictus, sceptrum regium anno post Christi aduentum 179. cœpit, idque 12. annis tenuit. Huius temporibus cum edicto Romano de abolenda Druidum superstitione e proscinctis cauebatur, cœpit de religione, & vero Dei cultu, cuius personam studiosus fuit, in primis deliberare. Erat hæc Druidum disciplina, antiquitùs in Britannia reperia, atque inde translata in Galliam. Qui non modo sacrificiis præfuerunt, sed de omnibus publicis priuatisque controuersiis constituebant. Et si quis eorum decretis non obtemperauisset, statim sacrificiis interdicebant, quæ pœna fuit apud eos grauissima. Namque huiusmodi interdicti, impiorum ac sceleratorum numero habebantur, a quibus omnes discedebant, eorumque congressum coosortiumque vitabant. Druides autem neque bello interfuerunt, nec tributa pendebant, sed multis priuilegiis & immunitatibus, magnum iuuentutis numerum ad disciplinam perdiscendam monebant. Docebant animas non interire, sed à corpore in corpus, vt Pythagoras affirmabat, migrare, tum de cœli ac syderum motu, de mundi magnitudine, rerum natura, deque viae potestate suorum Deorum disputabant. Inter quos Mercurium tanquam omnium artium inuentorem, viarum ac itinerum ducem, & ad quæstum, mercaturamq; vim maximam habentem, potissimum colebant. De Ioue, Apolline, & Marte, reliquisque eandem cum cæteris gentibus opinionem habebant: eorum verò doctrina non literis mandata, sed memoriæ fuit, ne aut in vulgus proferretur, aut literarum fiducia iuuentus quæ eam perdiscebat, diligentiam, memoriamuè remitteret.
units.tr: Lucius, therefore, the son of King Coel of Britain, a prince distinguished by piety and every virtue, the only son, adding to his paternal praise by his own excellence, and rightly called "Pius" and another Coel, began to reign in the year 179 after the coming of Christ, and held the sceptre for twelve years. In his time, when by Roman edict the superstition of the Druids was being restrained and abolished, he began to deliberate earnestly about religion and the true worship of God, of which he was zealous. This was the discipline of the Druids, which had been found in Britain in ancient times and from there transferred into Gaul. They not only presided over the sacrifices, but also settled all public and private disputes. If anyone did not obey their decrees, they at once forbade him the sacrifices, which among them was the gravest penalty. For those thus placed under interdict were counted among the impious and the wicked; all withdrew from them, and they avoided their company and fellowship. The Druids, however, took no part in war and paid no tribute, but by many privileges and immunities they encouraged a great number of young men to learn their discipline. They taught that souls do not perish, but pass from body to body, as Pythagoras asserted; they also discoursed on the motion of heaven and the stars, the greatness of the world, the nature of things, and the power and majesty of the immortal gods. Among these they worshipped above all Mercury, as the inventor of all arts and the guide of roads and journeys, who had the greatest power for gain and trade. Concerning Jupiter, Apollo and Mars they held the same opinion as the other nations. Their teaching, however, was not committed to writing but to memory, lest it be made known to the common people, or lest the young men who learned it, trusting in writing, should relax their diligence and their memory.

units.la: Erat eodem tempore Lucius & Romanorum fautor, & Marco Antonio Vero Cæsari summa beneuolentia, ac familiaritate coniunctus. Cuius authoritate & decreto, cum profligandæ esset tantæ authoritatis religio, quæ omnium memoriam superabat: Luciusque de Christiana religione accepisset, quæ nondum authoritate regia publicata, sed viritim per multos priuatos serpsit ac progressa est: diuque incertus & dubius animi, etsi Christum ouncianti-ustacita, vt videtur, fide tandem assensus est, non tamen à suis domesticis & popularibus, ac iosimæ & abiectæ conditionis hominibus more ludrorum, quorum infirmos animos simplicitas Christiana offendebat: sed solennioribus & Regiæ cellistrudini, vt ipse putabat, dignioribus sacris initiari in fide voluit. Cumq; cognouisset, non solum Adrianum, Antoninumque Piū æ quissimos Cæsares edicto suo cauisse, ne amplius in Christianos religionis ergo tantis supplicijs animaduerteretur, verum etiam complures nobiles Romanos eandem fidem à Pontifice Romano accepisse, eorumque exemplo Christianum nomen in singulas prouincias sparsum & disseminatum fuisse, statuit in eadem fide sub Eleutherio tunc Romano Pontifice inaugurari. Ad quem illustres & facundos viros Eluanum Avalonium, & Meduinum Belgam, per quos à Druidum, ad Christi fidem traductus est, cum literis & mandatis legauit. In quibus petiit, vt ad se iam doctrina Christiana imbutum nuncios ac legatos, à quibus baptismate lauaretur, mitteret: quique vnà deferrent Romanas leges, quibus religionis, & Reipub. statum in tegno suo describeret, atque stabiliret. Sed Eleutherius Pius Episcopus, diuino potiùs verbo propagando, quàm suæ famæ illustrandæ studens, summoaffectus gaudio, obtantum Regem Christo lucrifactum, suam operam inanem & superuacaneam, in eo quod postulabatur, iudicauit. Sed neque Britannicæ conuersionis laudem sibi ascripsit aut vendicauit, sed Regi rescripsit, maximam cepisse se ex eius in Christi fide voluptatem. Leges autem Romanas ab eo desiderat as, non esse Christianæ Reipublicæ necessarias, in quibus petmulta sancirentur a Christianis non seruanda. Neque egere eum in legibus condendis authoritate aut opera sua, qui vtramq; haberet paginam Veteris & Noui Testamenti, ex quibus adhibito proceerum concilio, sanctas & omni vitio carentes leges sumere posset: tum authoritate non aliena sed sua fulciretur, qui in suo regno Dei Vicarius esset, eiusque potentiam populo suo repræsentaret. Cuius Epistola quia tam rara & augusta est, totam seriem inseramus.
units.tr: At the same time Lucius was both a friend of the Romans and joined in the greatest goodwill and intimacy with the Caesar Marcus Antoninus Verus. By his authority and decree, since that religion of such great authority, which surpassed the memory of all, was to be overthrown, and since Lucius had learned of the Christian religion, which was not yet published by royal authority but had crept on and advanced privately, man by man, and while he was long uncertain and doubtful in mind, he at length assented to Christ with a silent faith, as it seems. Yet he did not wish to be initiated into the faith by his own household and fellow-countrymen, nor by men of the lowest and most abject condition, who, like jugglers, were offended by the simplicity of the Christians, whose weak minds were repelled by it; he wished instead to be initiated with more solemn rites, which he thought more worthy of royal dignity. When he had learned that not only Hadrian and the most just Caesar Antoninus Pius had by their edict provided that Christians should no longer be punished with such great torments on account of their religion, but also that many noble Romans had received the same faith from the Roman Pontiff, and that by their example the Christian name had been spread and disseminated through each province, he resolved to be consecrated in the same faith under Eleutherius, then Roman Pontiff. To him he sent, with letters and instructions, the illustrious and eloquent men Elvanus of Avalon and Medwinus of Belgium, through whom he was brought from the Druids to the faith of Christ. In these letters he asked that Eleutherius send to him envoys and messengers, already imbued with Christian teaching, by whom he might be washed in baptism, and who would bring with them the Roman laws, by which he might describe and establish the state of religion and of the commonwealth in his kingdom. But Eleutherius the bishop, intent rather on spreading the divine word than on enhancing his own fame, rejoiced greatly, and judged that his own labour was vain and superfluous in what was asked, since the king had been gained for Christ. Yet he did not claim or arrogate to himself the praise of the British conversion, but wrote back to the king that he had received the greatest pleasure from his faith in Christ. He did, however, deny that the Roman laws which he requested were necessary for a Christian commonwealth, since many things were enacted in them which Christians ought not to observe. Nor, he said, did the king need his authority or help in enacting laws, since he held both pages of the Old and New Testament, from which, with the advice of the nobles, he could take holy laws free of every fault; and he would be supported by an authority not foreign but his own, since he was God's Vicar in his kingdom and represented God's power to his people. Since this letter is so rare and august, we shall insert it in full.

units.la: Petistis à nobis leges Romanas & Cæsaris vobis transmitti, quibus in regno Britanniæ vti voluistis. Leges Romanas & Cæsaris semper reprobare possumus: Legem Dei nequaquam. Suscepistis enim nuper miseratione diuina, in regno Britanniæ legem & fidem Christi. Habetis penes vos in regno vtramque paginam, ex illis Dei gratia per concilium regni vestri fume legem & per illam Dei patientia, vestrum reges Britanniæ regnum. Vicarum vero Dei esse in regno iuxta Prophetam Regem. Domini est terra, & plenitudo eius orbis terrarum, & vniuersi qui habitant in eo: & rursum iuxta Prophetam Regem. Dilexisti iusticiam, & odisti iniquitatem: propterea vnxit te Deus tuus oleo lætitiæ, præ consortibus tuis: & rursum iuxta prophetam regem: Deus iudicium tuum. Non enim iudicium neque iustitiam Cæsaris: Filii enim regis gentes Christiana, & populi regni sunt, qui sub vestra protectione & pace & regno degant, & consistant, iuxta Euangelium: Quemadmodum gallina congregat pullos suos sub alis. Gentes vero regni Britanniæ, & populi, vestri sunt, & quos diuisos debetis in vnum ad concordiam & pacem, & ad fidem, & ad legem Christi, & ad sanctam Ecclesiam congregare, reuocare, fouere, manutenere, protegere, regere, vt positis cum eo regnare in æternum, cuius vicarius estis in regno prædicto, qui cum Patre, & Filio.&c.
units.tr: You asked us to send you the Roman laws and the Caesar's laws, which you wished to use in the kingdom of Britain. We can always reject the Roman and Caesar's laws, but never the law of God. For you have recently received, by divine mercy, in the kingdom of Britain the law and faith of Christ. You have in your kingdom both pages, from which, by the grace of God, take law through the council of your kingdom, and by that law, through the patience of God, hold the kingdom of Britain. For you are God's Vicar in the kingdom, according to the Prophet the King: "The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof, the world and all that dwell therein." And again, according to the Prophet the King: "You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows." And again, according to the prophet the king: "O God, give your judgment" (not the judgment or justice of Caesar). For the nations of the Christian kingdom and the peoples are the sons of the king, who live and remain under your protection, peace and kingdom, according to the Gospel: "As a hen gathers her chicks under her wings." The nations, moreover, and the peoples of the kingdom of Britain are yours, whom you ought to gather, recall, cherish, maintain, protect and rule, divided as they are, into one, to concord and peace, to the faith and law of Christ, and to the holy Church; so that, having been set with him, you may reign for ever in the aforesaid kingdom, whose vicar you are, who with the Father and the Son, etc.

units.la: Cum his respondis reuersi Eluanus & Meduinus, tamen à quibus Lucius baptizatus fit, in dubio est. Sunt enim qui ab Eluano & Meduino, propriis ad Eleutherium oratoribus iam cum superiori responso reuersis, baptizatum Lucium esse scribunt. Ex quibus Eluanus ex illo paludoso Iosephi discipulorum & successorum in Avalonia collegio profectus, quique prima illa Euangelii semina à Iosepho conita, per latiores Britanniæ agros disseminauerat, ab Eleutherio Episcopus creatus est. Alter illæ Meduinus Belgius, qui sacræ scientiæ eloquentiam, & Britannici sermonis copiam & facultatem adiunxerat, Britannicæ gentis doctor, qui non in certo aliquo & designato loco, sed vbique per totam Insulam, fidem in Christo prædicaret, ab eodem Eleuthetio institutus est. Alii referunt Phaganum & Deruuianum Romanos, Eluano & Meduino, ab eodem Eleutherio, viris & in sacris literis, & in administranda Ecclesia peritos, tanquam ... seu cooperarios adhibitos, quorum industria & scientia tanto operi perficiundo, quod in extirpando Druidū vetustoillo, & penitus Britannis infito aeinnato errore, tum in sanciendā Christianæ religionis disciplinā ponerentur, esset necessaria. A quibus Lucius, apud quem tum ..., iuxta gentis in re tanta parum valebat authoritas, more acritur Romano baptizatus est.
