Nec est dissimile, quin Eluanus & Meduinus, qui omni cura atque studio propensi, vt ad Euangelium Regem suum allicerent, ei morem gererent ac indulgerent, vt à Romanis, quibus tantum & gratiæ & authoritatis concessit, quòd illorum opæ ad imperium Britannicum euectus sit, potius quam à suis baptizaretur, ne cuni ab instituto alienarent. Itaque vt concedamus à Romanis baptizatum Lucium, quorum tunc fama non principatu & dominatu, sed erebro Martyrio & constantia, ac sincera fidei disciplina, per totam Christianum orbem celeberrima fuit. In hoc tamen omnia quorumcunq; scriptorum testimonia consentiunt & conspirant, Lucium Christianam fidem prius à suis intellexisse, antequam Romani Pontificis operam implorauerat. Quæ qué (ipso Eleutherio teste) Regi Christi Vicario, diuinas paginas, & doctorum ac sanctorum virorum copiam domi habenti non fuit necessaria, et is iucunda sibi, vt potè quibus Romanitam gratiosi essent, ac vt ilisad perfieiendum id, quod in religione instituit, videri possit. Hoe igitur modo baptizatus, fideq; Christiana firmatus & corroboratus Lucius, tam suos Eluanum atque Meduinum, quàm Romanos Phaganum & Deruuianum in concilium adhibuit. Et primùm explosa Druidum omni disciplina, Christianos doctores ad illustrandum Euangelium per totam Insulam Druidum loco præfecit: tum synagogas & templa falsorum deorum quos Druides colebant, & ipsa delubra in Christianas Ecclesias conuertebat, quas doctis & piis verbi ministris replebat: ad extremum, loco Flaminum Episcopatus viginti octo ordinauit, eosdemque in tres provincias, quarum Me{a}tropolis in tribus ecclesiarum regni civitatibus collocauit, distinxit. Prima fuit Londinensis provincia, quae Loegriæ & Cornubiæ finibus continebatur. Secunda Eboracensis, quæ Northumbriæ, Deiræ, Albaniæque fuit præfecta. Tertia prouincia in Cambria fuit, cuius præsectura in urbe Legionum confedebat. Lucius autem non suæ tantum, sed externis, fiuitimisque gentibus in Christi fide instituendis magnam operam dabat. Diuinis enim rebus sic in Britannia compositis, exercitum in Galliam eduxit, vt eam gentem nō sibi sed Christo subiugaret. Vbi eum Duces sui bellica tractarent officia, ipse in Euangelio prædicando assiduus fuit. Eiusque soror Emerita tanto Euangelii flagrauit ardore, vt pro Christiana fide ipsa Martyrium passa fit. Hoc itaque modo Christiana religio, in Britanniam ab Iosepho primum inducta, sub Lucio regali potentia publicè recepta, sinegulis ministrorum ordinibus distincta, ab Episcopis gubernata & fulta fuit, cuiusque sic instituendæ ipsius tantum Lucii Regis, non aliena, aut Romani Pontificis authoritas, sed modicum inde auxilium, peritum magis & desideratum, quàm necessarium accessit. Quod tam diuinum ac immensum beneficium, tanquàm diuina quædam prærogatiua huic Insulæ cœlitus concessa existimari debet. Quòd ex omnibus gentibus hæc Euangelium, deleris superstitiosis ritibus, primùm publicè ac integrè professa est. A qua prosessione (vt proximo loco declarabimus) deinceps nunquàm deflexit.
units.tr: Eluanus and Meduinus returned with this answer, but it is doubtful by whom Lucius was baptized. Some write that Lucius was baptized by Eluanus and Meduinus, who had already returned to Eleutherius with the earlier reply as envoys of their own. Of these, Eluanus, who came from that marshy college of Joseph's disciples and successors at Avalon, and who had spread through the wider fields of Britain those first seeds of the Gospel sown by Joseph, was made bishop by Eleutherius. The other, Meduinus the Belgian, who had joined to his knowledge of sacred learning a fluency and facility in the British tongue, was instituted by the same Eleutherius as teacher of the British people. He preached faith in Christ not in some fixed and designated place, but everywhere throughout the whole island. Others report that the Romans Phaganus and Deruuianus were brought in by Eleutherius as assistants to Eluanus and Meduinus, men skilled both in sacred letters and in administering the Church. Their diligence and knowledge were needed to complete so great a work, namely to root out the ancient error of the Druids, which was innate and deeply implanted in the Britons, and to establish the discipline of the Christian religion. Lucius, with whom then ... and in so great a matter the authority of his people counted for little, was baptized in the Roman manner by these men. It is not unlikely that Eluanus and Meduinus, who were most eager, with all care and zeal, to win their king to the Gospel, were willing to humour and indulge him, so that he would rather be baptized by the Romans, to whom he had granted so much favour and authority (since it was by their help that he was raised to the throne of Britain), than by his own people, lest he alienate them from his purpose. So let us grant that Lucius was baptized by the Romans, whose reputation at that time was famous throughout the whole Christian world not for rule and domination, but for frequent martyrdom, constancy and the pure discipline of faith. Yet in this all the testimonies of whatever writers agree and concur: Lucius had understood the Christian faith from his own people before he sought the help of the Roman Bishop. Indeed, as Eleutherius himself bears witness, he had no need of this for a king who had at home the divine writings and a supply of learned and holy men, unless it was pleasing to him, since the Romans were agreeable to him, and so that he might appear to be bringing to completion what he had set up in religion. Lucius, therefore, baptized in this way and confirmed and strengthened in the Christian faith, took counsel with his own people, Eluanus and Meduinus, as well as with the Romans Phaganus and Deruuianus. And first, once all the discipline of the Druids had been driven out, he set Christian teachers over the Druids' former posts to illustrate the Gospel throughout the whole island. Then he converted the synagogues and temples of the false gods whom the Druids worshipped, and their very shrines, into Christian churches, which he filled with learned and godly ministers of the Word. Finally, in place of the flamens, he ordained twenty-eight bishoprics, and distributed them into three provinces, whose metropolises he placed in three cities of the kingdom's churches. The first was the province of London, which was contained within the borders of Loegria and Cornwall. The second was York, which was set over Northumbria, Deira and Albania. The third province was in Wales, whose seat of government was in the City of Legions. Lucius, moreover, gave great effort not only to his own people but also to the instruction of foreign and neighbouring nations in the faith of Christ. For when divine matters had been so ordered in Britain, he led an army into Gaul, so that he might subject that nation not to himself but to Christ. While his generals carried on the business of war, he himself was busy preaching the Gospel. His sister Emerita burned with such zeal for the Gospel that she suffered martyrdom for the Christian faith. In this way, therefore, the Christian religion, first introduced into Britain by Joseph, was publicly received under King Lucius's royal power, distinguished into its several orders of ministers, and governed and supported by bishops. In establishing it, the authority of King Lucius himself was alone involved, not that of anyone foreign or of the Roman Bishop; there came from outside only a small help, more welcome and wished-for than necessary. This so divine and immense benefit ought to be regarded as a certain divine prerogative granted from heaven to this island, that of all the nations it was the first to profess the Gospel publicly and wholly, the superstitious rites having been destroyed. From this profession (as we shall declare in the next place) it never afterwards turned aside.

units.la: BRITANNOS CHRISTI FIDEM AMPLEXOS NVN-quam postea desciuisse ad veteres gentium errores. Necum Augustinus Iunior in Insulam venuret. Quosdam etiam ex Anglis ante Augustinum aduentum religionem Christi percepisse.
units.tr: THAT THE BRITONS, HAVING EMBRACED THE FAITH OF CHRIST, NEVER AFTERWARDS FELL AWAY TO THE ANCIENT ERRORS OF THE NATIONS. ALSO, THAT THIS WAS SO BEFORE AUGUSTINE THE YOUNGER CAME TO THE ISLAND. AND THAT SOME OF THE ENGLISH HAD RECEIVED THE RELIGION OF CHRIST BEFORE THE COMING OF AUGUSTINE.

units.la: LLA itaque Pontificiorum inanis laudis de Britannica gente per se conuersa arrogatio, & fide propria earet, & permultis antiquissimis argumentis, ipsisque adeo suis refellitur. Quod enim Innocentius in Epistola quadam condemnans omnes Aphricanas & Occidentales Ecclesias, vel à Petro, vel ab eius & successorum suorum discipulis in Christo fuisse generatas, præterquam quod hoc ineptum & falsum arguunt Maidelburgensis authores historiæ, & ostentationis aeglorioiæ, mundanæque aequirendæ potentiæ ipse potius quàm à veritate profectum: ex ipsis indubitatæ fidei scripturis certum est, Paulum illum gentium doctorem, negasse se a Petro vocatum aut missum, qui etiam Occidentales Ecclesias, & Hispaniam ipsam ab oriente remotissimam peragrauit. Ipseque testatur Euangelium per eum ad omnes gentes peruenisse.
units.tr: That empty boast of the Papists, by which they arrogate the British nation to themselves, is therefore both without foundation in its own right and refuted by very many of the most ancient arguments, and even by their own. For Innocent, in a certain epistle condemning all the African and Western Churches, claimed that they had been begotten in Christ either by Peter or by the disciples of Peter and his successors. Apart from the fact that the authors of the Magdeburg history argue that this is both foolish and false, and that it proceeded from ostentation, empty glory and the desire to acquire worldly power rather than from the truth, it is certain from the indubitable writings of Scripture that Paul, that teacher of the Gentiles, denied that he had been called or sent by Peter. He also travelled through the Western Churches and Spain itself, the most remote of lands from the East. And he himself testifies that the Gospel reached all nations through him.

units.la: Præterea nec Philippus, Iosephus, aut Simon Zelotes à Petro fidem acceperunt, sed ab ipso Domino. A quibus Euangelica luce primùm illustratam Britanniam supra commemorauimus.
units.tr: Moreover, neither Philip, nor Joseph, nor Simon the Zealot received the faith from Peter, but from the Lord himself. We have already mentioned that Britain was first illumined by the light of the Gospel through these men.

units.la: Huic sanctæ semperque obseruandæ scripturarum auctoritati accedant & historiarum Ecclesiasticarum authores. Sulpicius Seuerus, quinon modò hunc nostrum Romanum, sed illum integerrimum patrem Augustinum Afrumantecessit, cum de occidentalibus Episcopis ad Ariminense concilium ipsius Imperatoris atque etiam de statu Ecclesiastico non modico, sed de Arianismo, qui totum suum imperium perturbauit, qui se ab illa re esi disiunxerant, conuocatis, meminit Britannos etiam Episcopos interfuisse. Equibus tres, (nihil enim reticendum est) venijudicio habebantur cæteris occidentalibus Episcopis, quòd cum illi ex promissa Imperatoris largitione se alere in illo concilio suis opibus fieri recusabant, isti inopes à fisco necessaria haurirebant.
units.tr: To this authority of the Scriptures, which is holy and must always be observed, let the writers of ecclesiastical histories be added. Sulpicius Severus, who surpassed not only our Roman but also that most upright father Augustine of Africa, when he records that the Western bishops were summoned by the Emperor himself to the council of Ariminum, and that a great controversy about the ecclesiastical state arose, not only over Arianism, which had thrown the whole empire into disorder, but also over those who had separated themselves from that matter, says that British bishops too were present. Of these, three (for nothing must be concealed) were judged inferior to the other Western bishops, because, when the others refused to be maintained at that council at their own expense from the Emperor's promised largesse, these three, being poor, drew their necessities from the treasury.

units.la: Hoc, author in Britannis Episcopus contra occidentalium Episcoporum censuram, laudi humanæ vertit, quòd vt quondam Socrates ex Atheniensi Prytanæo ali se dignum putabat, sic illi ex publico promissio fisco, potius quam ex singulorum indulgentia, quæ vitis authoritatem habere debentibus semper fuit contemptui, noceßitatem suam subleuabant.
units.tr: The author turns this, against the judgment of the Western bishops, into human praise. Just as Socrates once thought himself worthy to be maintained at the Athenian Prytaneum, so these men relieved their need from the public treasury, which had been promised, rather than from the generosity of individuals. Such generosity has always been despised by those who ought to have authority in their way of life.

units.la: Huie adiiciamus Gennadii Catalogum illustrium virorum, qui refert Xysti vrbis Romæ Episcopi, qui ante Augustinum fuit, tempore quendam Fastidium Britanniarum (sic enim eius verba sunt) Episcopum, scripsisse ad Fatalem quendam de vita Christiana librum unum, & alium de viduitate seruanda sana, & Deo digna doctrina. Ad hanc autem Pontificiorum opinionem minuendam non externis solum, sed lùm,sed domesticis exemplis ac testimoniis abundamus. Quorsum enim spectat illius integerrimi,doctissimiq; Gildæ Britanni tam acris & vehemens in sui temporis cleros inuectio, quem paulò ante Augustini illius Romani aduentum claruisse constat. Quid illa de Theono, & Thadioco Londoniensi ac Eboracensi Archiepiscopis, post patriam à Saxonibus occupatam,& Christianitatem turbatam, sedes suas deserentibus, & in Cambriam atque Cornubiam profugientibus, crebra in historiis mentio? Quid quod eodem testimonio confirmatur:Cum barbara gens Saxonum pagana superstitione cæcata totam Christianitatē delere contenderat:tamen Christiana fidem sub Lucio accepptam,tam in aquilonari quàm in illa Insulæ parte, quam Britanni suis sedibus pulsi tenebant,integram viguisse. Quæ etiam(Beda teste)in tranquillitate & pace, vsque ad Diocletiani tempora permansit per totam Insulam integra. In quibus crudeli insectatione vexata, Albanus, Amphibalus, Aaron & Iulius,sanctiac Euangelii prædicatione confpicui viri (eodem Beda referente) Martyrio candidati fuêre. Deinde Constantinus ille Magnus,quiomnium Cæsarum primus per orbem Romani Imperii Christianam fidem Imperiali authoritate propagauit, ex Helena matre Chiuilliana & Britanna natus est, & Maximus qui interfecto Imperatore Gratiano in Imperium crudelirer & tyrannicè inuasit, posteaq; à Theodosio primo victus fuit , Christianum exercitum è Bri- rannia duxit in Galliam. Præterea ( eodem Beda authore ) Arrianæ sectæ furor in Britannica Ecclesia fœuir, quæ paulò post hincejecta & explosa fuit, catholica fide ao reseruata. Quid item , quod de Canono Armoricæ rege pagano, Christianas puellas vi abducente, suisq;ad suscipiendam prolem concedente,traditum? Quæ tamen restiterunt,nec Paganis Christ non fidentibus,corporis sui eopiam facere voluerunt. Quid de constante Monachoe Monasterio Amphibali,quod Ventanæ in Britannia fuit, Constantino Regi succeßuro extracto ? Quid de Germani in Britanniam aduentu, ad Pelagianismum primo delendum,deinde eodem renouato prorsus extirpandum,à quo etiam, & à Lupo, Britanni à Scotis atq; Pictis armis petiti, adiuti atq; vindicati sunt. Cuius rei rectius intelligatur,paulò altius ducenda ratio est. Restitutam quendam Londinensem Episcopum ante diximus Gallicano cuidam Concilio interfuisse, & afsensum eius decretis adhibuisse. Quòd Christiana religio(vt videtur)firmioribus tunc in Britannia fietit, quàm in Gallia viribus, quò magis expetebant Galli, vt suis quoquè in religione decretis, Britanni alicuius Episcopi consensus & authoritas accederet. Cùm iraqne Pelagiana hæresis, per Agricolam quendam Pelagii discipulum, in Britanniam illata esset, latiusq; serpsisset, Britanni Guitelino iamdudum mortuo etsi doctore caterent, qui tam auersam ab acceptis in Christi fide institutis disciplinam refelleret, tamen fidem nullis suasionibus aut argumentis victi deserebant: sed moti illa sui Archiepiscopi Restituti ad Gallicana Concilia firmandaaccersitit:recenti memoria,huius etiam spiritualis belli exunguendi auxilium mutuum à Gallicanis Episcopis vicissim implorabant. Itaque cleri Synodus à Britannis implorata decreuitin Gallia, Germanum Antisiodărenem, & Lupum Trecafinum Episcopos, viros fide ac virtute diuina pollenies, rum sermone facundos,&in differendo acres,ad Britannos mittendos, vt hinc Pelagiæ hę- resium nascenti,diuino verbo resisterent. Qui Synodo parentes,nauigatione huc perducti, Verolamii populi,clericiq; consensum statuunt. Quò immensa populi multitudo cum coniugibus& liberis vndique concurrit:tanta tum Britannis inerat Christianæ fi- dei firmiter retinendæ cupiditas, vtq; ipsius Historiographi verbis vtar. Astabant (inquit) partes disparicondicione dissimiles: Inde diuina fides: hinc humana præsumptio: hinc pietas,inde superbia:hinc Christus,inde Pelagius author omnis prauitatis. Primo inlocobeatissimi sacerdotes copiam disputandi aduersariis præbuerunt, qui solanuditate verborum diù inaniter & aures occuparunt & tempora. Deinde Antistites venerandi,torrentes eloquii sui,cum Apostolicis & Euangelicis imbribus perfudetunt. Miscebatur sermo proprius cum diuino,& assertiones molestissimas lectionum testimonia sequebantur. Conuincitur vanitas, & perfidia confutatur:ita vt tad singulas verborum obiectiones,erraßefe,dum nequit respondere,fateatur. Populus arbiter vix manus continet,iudicium cum clamore testatur. Post hunc diem ita ex animis omnium suasio iniqua deleta est, vt Sacerdotum doctrinam sitientibus desiderijs sedtarentur. Quibus peractis Episcopi ad Gallicanas suas sedes, Britannis eorum opera à Pelagianismo vendicatis, & in Euangelio firmatis teuersi sunt. Magnum est etiam Britannorum perfectæ in Christum fidei argumentum,illa
units.tr: To this we may add Gennadius's Catalogue of Illustrious Men, which reports that in the time of Xystus, Bishop of the city of Rome, who came before Augustine, a certain Fastidius, Bishop of the Britons (for these are his words), wrote one book to Fatalis on the Christian life, and another on maintaining widowhood in a sound and God-worthy teaching. Yet we abound in domestic examples and testimonies, not only foreign ones, to diminish this opinion of the Papists. For what does the very upright and most learned Gildas the Briton's so sharp and vehement invective against the clergy of his own time pertain to? He is known to have flourished shortly before the arrival of that Roman Augustine. What of the frequent mention in the histories of Theonus and Thadiocus, Archbishops of London and York, who abandoned their sees after the country was occupied by the Saxons and Christianity disturbed, and fled into Wales and Cornwall? Moreover, by the same testimony it is confirmed that, although the barbarous Saxon nation, blinded by pagan superstition, strove to destroy all Christianity, nevertheless the Christian faith received under Lucius flourished unimpaired both in the northern part of the island and in that part which the Britons, driven from their seats, still held. This too (as Bede bears witness) remained unbroken throughout the whole island in tranquillity and peace until the time of Diocletian. In that persecution, which raged with cruel harassment, Alban, Amphibalus, Aaron and Julius, men conspicuous for their holy preaching of the Gospel (as Bede again reports), were made candidates for martyrdom. Then that Constantine the Great, who was the first of all the Caesars to propagate the Christian faith by imperial authority throughout the world of the Roman Empire, was born of Helena his mother, who was of British and Chiuillian origin. And Maximus, who after killing the Emperor Gratian seized the empire cruelly and tyrannically, and was afterwards defeated by Theodosius the First, led a Christian army out of Britain into Gaul. Furthermore (on the same authority of Bede), the fury of the Arian sect raged in the British Church, but shortly afterwards it was driven out and expelled, the Catholic faith being preserved. Likewise there is what is related of Canon, a pagan king of Armorica, who by force carried off Christian maidens and, for the sake of begetting offspring, handed them over to his people; yet they resisted and, since the pagans were not believers in Christ, were unwilling to yield their bodies to them. What of the constant monk of the monastery of Amphibalus, which was at Wentana in Britain, who was dragged out when Constantine was about to succeed as king? What of the coming of Germanus into Britain to destroy Pelagianism first, and then, when it was revived, to root it out completely? By him also, and by Lupus, the Britons, having been attacked by the Scots and Picts with arms, were aided and defended. To understand this matter more correctly, the account must be taken a little further back. We mentioned earlier that Restitutus, Bishop of London, took part in a certain Gallican council and gave his assent to its decrees. Since the Christian religion (as it seems) was then stronger in Britain than in Gaul, the Gauls the more earnestly desired that the consent and authority of some British bishop should also be added to their decrees on religion. When therefore the Pelagian heresy had been brought into Britain through a certain Agricola, a disciple of Pelagius, and had spread more widely, the Britons, although they had a teacher, Guitelinus, long since dead, who might have refuted so perverse a departure from the institutions received in the faith of Christ, nevertheless were giving up the faith, won over by no persuasions or arguments; but moved by this, they summoned their Archbishop Restitutus to strengthen the Gallican councils, and, the memory being still fresh, they in turn implored the aid of the Gallican bishops to extinguish this spiritual war as well. Accordingly the synod of the clergy, implored by the Britons, decided in Gaul to send Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre, and Lupus, Bishop of Troyes, men powerful in the faith and divine virtue, eloquent in speech and keen in disputation, to Britain, so that they might resist the budding Pelagian heresy with the divine word. Obeying the synod, they were brought here by sea and settled the consent of the people and clergy of Verulamium. Thereupon a huge multitude of people, with their wives and children, gathered from everywhere: so great at that time was the eagerness of the Britons to hold firmly to the Christian faith. To use the very words of the historian: "There stood by" (he says) "parties unlike in condition: on one side divine faith, on the other human presumption; here piety, there pride; here Christ, there Pelagius, the author of all depravity. At first the most blessed priests gave their adversaries the opportunity of disputing, who for a long time vainly occupied both ears and time with the mere volubility of words. Then the venerable prelates, pouring forth the streams of their eloquence, drenched them with the showers of the Apostles and the Gospel. Their own discourse was mingled with the divine, and the most troublesome assertions were followed by testimonies from the readings. Vanity is convicted, and treachery refuted, so that at each objection to their words, the opponent, unable to answer, confesses his error. The people, as judges, can scarcely restrain their hands; they bear witness to their judgment with a shout. After this day the unjust persuasion was so thoroughly erased from the minds of all that they were refreshed with the desires of thirsting for the teaching of the priests." When these things were done, the bishops returned to their Gallican sees, the Britons having been, by their labour, rescued from Pelagianism and confirmed in the Gospel. There is also a great proof of the Britons' perfect faith in Christ in that complaint and grievance which they lodged vehemently against their king Vortigern: "that the unbelieving Hengist had joined his daughter to himself in marriage." Wherefore the nobles, incensed, deposed Vortigern from the royal power and set up his son Vortimer as king. He, having gained the kingdom, restored the Christian churches which had fallen and been demolished through his father's wrong, and he held the ministers of the Word in the highest esteem. Next to him in rank and age, Aurelius, to repair the churches, held a meeting of the whole clergy. And when battle for the faith was joined between him and Hengist, and Hengist was taken, Aurelius received from Heldanus Claudius, Bishop of Chester, counsel to put him to death. Then Octa, besieged by the same Aurelius, surrendered himself into his power and authority with these words: "They are yours, my gods; I believe I revere your God." Then, the war being waged so successfully and peace secured, turning his mind to the Church, he appointed Sampson as Bishop of York and Dubritius as Bishop of the City of Legions. Then Arthur, a Christian king, when Sampson had been driven out by the Saxons, appointed his chaplain Pyramus in place of Dubritius, who had died, and Tremorus in their place. What more? Aurelius, killed by poison through a physician, was buried not in royal and splendid fashion but in the Christian manner, by bishops and abbots, in the year of the Lord 417. To these are added what is told of Uther Pendragon, created by the assembly of the people and clergy together, and celebrating the feast of Easter with due honour, in the year of the Lord 498; then of the fury of the Saxons laying waste the Christian churches, 511; of Uther Pendragon buried in the Christian rite, and of Arthur his son, after his father's death, made king in the same way, consecrated by Dubritius, the bishops and the magnates, in the year

units.la: expostulatio & quærela, qua in Vortigernum suum regem vehementèr egerunt: quod Hengistus infidelis filium matrimonio sibi iunxisset. Quare infensi proceres, Vortigerno Regia potestate abdicato, Vortimeram eius filium regem creabant. Hic potitus regno, Christianas Ecclesias paterno vitio lapsas ac demolitas restaurauit: verbiq; ministros in summo precio habuit. Huic tam ordine quàm ætate proximus Aurelius, ad reparandas Ecclesias totius Cleri habuit conuentum. Et cum inter hunc, & Hengistum iniretur pro fide prælium & Hengistus captus esset, Aurelius ab Heldano Claudio Ceftrensi Episcopo concilium de eo trucidando accepit. Tum Octa ab eodem Aurelio obsessus, in suam deditionem & potentiam his verbis se tradidit: Vestri sunt ꝺᵢ meᵢ, Deumq, tuum reuerere credo. Tum tam fœliciter gesto bello pace parta, ad Ecclesiam animum vertens, t o Sampsonem Eboracensem, & Dubritium in vrbe Legionum Episcoposcreauit. Deinde Arthurus Rex Christianus, Sampsone a Saxonibus eiecto, capellanum suum Pyramum, Dubritioq; mortuo, Tremoricum eorum loco constituit. Quid quòd Aurelius ex veneno pet Medicum interfectus, ab Episcopis & Abbatibus, non tam regali & splendido, quam Christiano more sepultus est Anno Domini. 417. His accedunt quod ferturde Vterpendragone, Populi simul ac Cleri conuentu creato, & Pascatis festum honore debito celebrante, anno Dom. 498. Tum de Saxonum furore Christianas Ecclesias vastantium. 511. De Vterpendragone Christiano ritu sepulto, deque Arthuro eius filio, post patris obitum, Rege à Dubritio, Episcopis, & magnatibus pari modo sacrato, anno.
units.tr: This complaint and grievance, which they lodged against their king Vortigern, was that Hengist, an unbeliever, had joined his son to himself in marriage. Because of this, the enraged nobles deposed Vortigern from royal power and made his son Vortimer king. Once he had taken the kingdom, he restored the Christian churches that had fallen and been torn down through his father's wickedness, and he held the ministers of the Word in the highest honour. Next after him in rank and in time came Aurelius, who called a gathering of the whole clergy to repair the churches. When battle was joined for the faith between him and Hengist, and Hengist was taken, Aurelius received from Heldanus Claudius, Bishop of Chester, counsel to put him to death. Then Octa, besieged by the same Aurelius, surrendered himself into his power and authority with these words: They are yours and mine; I believe you reverence your God. Then, with the war so happily waged and peace won, Aurelius turned his mind to the Church and appointed Sampson as Bishop of York and Dubricius as Bishop in the City of Legions. Afterwards King Arthur, a Christian, when Sampson had been driven out by the Saxons, set up his chaplain Pyram in his place after Dubricius died, and Tremorinus in theirs. Moreover, Aurelius was poisoned by a physician, and was buried by the bishops and abbots not with royal and splendid pomp, but in the Christian manner, in the year of the Lord 417. To these are added what is reported of Uther Pendragon, who was created king by the assembly of people and clergy alike, and who celebrated the feast of Easter with due honour, in the year of the Lord 498; then of the fury of the Saxons laying waste the Christian churches, 511; of Uther Pendragon, buried in the Christian rite, and of his son Arthur, who after his father's death was likewise consecrated king by Dubricius, the bishops and the nobles, in the year 516.

units.la: 516. Qui Scorum & Pictorum Episcopis, in Insula Stagni, & lacus Lomnudi obsessis, 2 o illis cum lachrimis petentibus, delictorum poenam remisit, & in gratiam ac misericordiam accepit. 522. Tum de Gwenhwyuare regina, quæ Arthurum metuens ad Monasterium Iulii Martyris, in vrbem Legionum confugit, in eoque religionis habitum suscepit. 541. Et ante hæc Constantinus duos Medredi filios interemit, vnum Wentanæ, in Ecclesia sancti Amphiboli iuxta altare, alterumcæsobio quodam Londinensi vi ereptum. Anno. 543. Nec præterea fuit de Columbano illo claro Scoro in Britanniam veniente. An. 566. Deqj septem Britannis Episcopisi qui ad concilium ab Augustino vocatum conuenerunt: nec de 2100. Christianis Philosophis in Banchorensi cœnobio victum & vestitum propria industria,ex diui Pauli institute quærentibus. Quæ tot tantaq; Presbyterorum, Monacho 3 o rum, præsulum, Episcoporum, Ecclesiarum, cœnobiorum, sediumq; vetusta nomina, quæquouis seculo extiterunt, etsi prætermittantur, tamen futuri temporis, ipsius Augustini ætate, eorumq; qui eum sequuti sunt recordatio, satis probat Euangelium, quod primis illis Apostolorum temporibus in Britannia nunciatum, non modò semper retentum firmiter, sed singulis seculis auctum & dilatatum creuisse. Quodquè ne ab ipsis Saxonibus supra modum ꝺꝰ ꝺꝯ ꝺꝰ fuit, tandem diuino instinctu, & suasione fideꝺ sui cœpit. Ethelbertus enim Cantii Rex, cum ad eum ab eodem Augustino venissent legati nunciatum, venisse iam Augustinū, vnà cum aliis è Roma, eiusque suo populo, de Christo optimū ferre nuncium. Fama (inquit) ad me huius Christianæ religionis peruenit: ex gente 4 o enim Francorum vxorem duxi Bertam, ex Christianis parentibus ipsam Christianam, quæ mihi à parentibus his conditionibus data est, vt ritum fidei ac religionis Christianæ,cum Episcopo Lybdhardo eius adiutore inuiolatam retinere liceret. Præterea permultos reges Anglosaxonesin Christiana fide institutos,non ab Augustino aut eius successoribus,sed ante aduentum illorum exist imandum est, nisi non nostris solùm, sed externis & Germanorum historiis fidem pariter detrahamus. Namq; refert Mumsterus, Anno Dom. 601. venisse ex Anglia virum quendam insignem,regiostemmate natum, dictum Osfonem, qui traie sto Rheno in vo is habuit stabilire fidem Christi, quamque ad rem primus iecit Monasterii Sc hutternensis fundamenta. Multos autem Saxones reges Osfas dictos, ex nostris liquet monumentis. Sed ex ipso Beda verisimilimum est 5 o hunc OffamArhelfridi Regis Berniciorum filium fuisse, qui ex Acia Ellæ Regis Deirorum filia septem filios genuerat: Eanfridum, Ofwaldum, Ofwinum, O kacum, Ofwidum, Osam, & nostrum de quo tractamus Offam. Nam & tempore non discrepant, & regio in qua natus est, pene è regione ostii fluminis Rheni, quod illum traiecisse Mumsterus scribit, positaest. Christianam autem doctrinam à Columbano vel eius discipulis accepit: quod etiam ex aliis Bedæ verbis colligi potest. Toto (inquit) tempore, quo regnaut Edwinus filii præfati regis Edelfridi, qui ante eum regnauerat, cum magna nobilium iuuenum ute apud Scotus siue Pictos exulabant. Itaque ad doctrinam Scotorum catccatechisati, & baptizatis gratia sunt recreati. Hæc Beda.Sed Augustinū Romanas potius consuetudines ac ceremonias, ne dicam superstitiones induxisse, & ad Papalem illum dominatum in Anglia obtinendum, se callide insinuasse, & Anglicanas Ecclesias ex Romanis ritibus instituisse, potius quàm Euangelium prædicasse satis constat.
units.tr: Arthur, who, when the bishops of the Scots and Picts were besieged on the island of Stagnum and on Loch Lomond, pardoned them the penalty of their offences when they begged him with tears, and received them into favour and mercy. In 522 there is the account of Queen Gwenhwyfar, who, fearing Arthur, fled to the monastery of St Julius the Martyr in the City of Legions, and there took the habit of religion. In 541, and before this, Constantine slew two sons of Meredydd, one in the church of St Amphibalus beside the altar at Wentana, and the other, who had been snatched by force, at a certain cloister in London. In 543 there is also the account of that famous Scot, Columban, coming into Britain. In 566 there is the account of the seven British bishops who assembled at the council summoned by Augustine, and of the 2,100 Christian philosophers in the monastery at Bangor who sought food and clothing by their own labour, following the institution of St Paul. The many and great ancient names of elders, monks, prelates, bishops, churches, monasteries and sees, which arose in every age, even if they are passed over, nevertheless prove sufficiently, by the memory of them in Augustine's own time and among those who followed him, that the gospel which was proclaimed in Britain in those first times of the Apostles was not only firmly retained, but grew and spread in every age. And this, which was not altogether... (at last, by divine impulse and the persuasion of his own faith, it began to be so). For Ethelbert, King of Kent, when envoys came to him from the same Augustine announcing that Augustine had come, together with others, from Rome, and that they bore the best tidings of Christ to his people, said: "Report of this Christian religion has reached me. For I have taken as wife Bertha of the Franks' race, a Christian herself from Christian parents, who was given to me by her parents on these terms: that she be allowed to keep the rite of the Christian faith and religion inviolate, together with Bishop Liudhard, her helper." Moreover, we must consider that very many Anglo-Saxon kings were instructed in the Christian faith not by Augustine or his successors, but before their arrival, unless we take away faith equally from our own histories and from foreign and German ones. For Munster reports that in the year of the Lord 601 there came from England a certain distinguished man of royal lineage, called Osfo, who, having crossed the Rhine, undertook to establish the faith of Christ in those parts, and was the first to lay the foundations of the monastery at Schuttern for this purpose. Now, that many Saxon kings were called Offa is clear from our records. But from Bede himself it is most likely that this Offa was the son of Ærfrith, king of the Bernicians, who had begotten seven sons by Acha, daughter of Ælle, king of the Deirans: Eanfrith, Oswald, Oswiu, Oslac, Oswudu, Osa, and our Offa, of whom we are speaking. For both the times do not disagree, and the region in which he was born lies almost opposite the mouth of the Rhine, which Munster writes that he crossed. But he received Christian teaching from Columban or his disciples, which can also be gathered from other words of Bede. "For the whole time," he says, "during which Edwin, son of the aforesaid King Ethelfrith, who had reigned before him, reigned, many young nobles of great number lived in exile among the Scots or Picts. So they were catechised in the teaching of the Scots, and having been baptised, they were restored by grace." Thus Bede. But that Augustine introduced Roman customs and ceremonies, not to say superstitions, and cunningly insinuated himself to win that papal domination in England, and that he established the English churches on Roman rites rather than preached the gospel, is quite clear.

units.la: Sub Lucio enim Rege (vt antea diximus) in tribus Britanniæ provinciis, Loegria, Albania, atque Cambria, tres Metropoleis institutæ sunt. Quarum Albanensis septem Episcopis præfuitin Cambria Legionensis, ad Menevium translata postea totidem: in Loegria autem Londinensis, quoniam ea provincia maior & nobilior Insulæ pars fuit, quatuordecim diocæses regebat. Christianaitaque religioë Loegrensi, atque feré ex Albanensi provincia: per Anglosaxones pulsa & deturbata, in Cambria retenta, & primis illis Christianis ritibus ab Asianis seu orientalibus Ecclesiis per Lucium regem acceptis, adhuc publicè culta fuit. Diocæses autem Cambriæ hæ fuerunt, Henetorensis, Tauensis, Paternensis, Banchorensis, Elluiensis, Wiccensis, ac Morganensis. Cum quibusin primo ad se connocato cleri concilio, quod Wigorniæ habebatur, de Romanæ sedis vetustate & authoritate, de Petri successione, de Pontificis in reliquas Christianas Ecclesias principatu, & vt Romano more baptizarent, prædicarent, ac pascha celebrarent, pluribus egit Augustinus. In quo Concilio Dionotus quidam Britannus Banchorensis coenobiarcha, vir doctrina & eloquio celebris, grauiter, & docte de non approbanda apud eos Romanorū authoritate disputabat, fortiterq; tuebatur Meneuësis Episcopi in illa provincia aratam iurisdictionem, libros; perdoctos scripsit, vnum de conseruandis eorum ritibus, alterum defensorum sedis Meneuensis, afferens, non esse tutum aut commodum Britannis ab vsitatis in religione ceremoniis recedere, vel Romanorum saltum sustinere, coque magis, quòd nondum Cambri Anglosaxonibus parebant. In quoomne Augustini institutum, & concilium versabatur, vt Anglis Britannos, & Romanæ Ecclesiæ Anglicanam, suæq; iurisdictioni Meneuensem provinciam subiceret. Quod & Lælandus antiquitatis indagator satis sedulus testatur. Debuerat (inquit) Gregorius admonuisse Saxones gentem perfidam, vt si sincerè Christianisimum admittere vellent, Britanniæ imperium quod contra sacramentum militiæ per tyrannidem occupaverant, iustis dominis ac posse ssoribus restituerent. Augustinus enim, quod Dionotus persentir, præextu fidei, gentem aduenam in alieno confirmauit imperio, vt suam & Romanam iurisdictionem dilataret. Longe dissimilis Palladio, tune Scotorum Apostolo, qui Constantinum eorum regem (teste Polidoro) multis precibus hortatus est, ne gentem Saxonum impiam contra Britannos Christianos, armis iuuaret. Itaque quæ in cantu, processione, suffragiis, adorationibus, Missis, templis, sanctorum nominibus appellandis, & huiusmodi Romanis superstitiosis ceremoniis, in ea Synodo decernere voluit Augustinus, à Britannis qui in Meneuensi provincia, à Saxonibus, & se, & religionem tuebantur, reiecta fuerunt. Inter quos vigebat Christianitas, quæ sub Eleutherio publicè instituta nunquam postea defecit: vt in Augustini vita fusius deinc ep: decla rabimus.
units.tr: Under King Lucius (as we said earlier), three metropolitan sees were founded in the three provinces of Britain: Loegria, Albania and Cambria. The Albanian metropolis had seven bishops under it. In Cambria, Legionensis, later transferred to Menevia, had the same number. In Loegria, London governed fourteen dioceses, since that province was the greater and more noble part of the island. The Christian religion in Loegria and nearly all of the province of Albania was driven out and overthrown by the Anglo-Saxons, but it was kept in Cambria, and there, with those primitive Christian rites which Lucius had received from the Asian or Eastern churches, it was still practised openly. The dioceses of Cambria were these: Henetorensis, Tauensis, Paternensis, Banchorensis, Elluiensis, Wiccensis and Morganensis. At the first council of clergy which Augustine called together at Worcester, he argued at length about the antiquity and authority of the Roman see, about the succession of Peter, about the supremacy of the Pope over the other Christian churches, and about the British churches baptizing, preaching and keeping Easter in the Roman manner. In that council a certain Briton, Dionothus, abbot of Bangor, a man famed for learning and eloquence, argued gravely and learnedly against accepting Roman authority among them. He also firmly defended the long-established jurisdiction of the bishop of Menevia in that province. He wrote two learned books, one on preserving their rites and one defending the see of Menevia, asserting that it was neither safe nor advantageous for the Britons to depart from their customary religious ceremonies or to submit to the leadership of the Romans, all the more because the Welsh were not yet subject to the Anglo-Saxons. The whole purpose of Augustine's programme and of that council was to subject the Britons to the English, the English church to the Roman church, and the province of Menevia to his own jurisdiction. The diligent investigator of antiquity, Leland, also bears witness to this. Gregory, he says, ought to have admonished the Saxons, a faithless people, that if they sincerely wished to embrace Christianity, they should restore to its rightful lords and possessors the kingdom of Britain, which they had seized by tyranny in violation of the sacred oath of military service. For Augustine, as Dionothus perceived, under the pretext of faith, strengthened a foreign people in another's kingdom, in order to extend his own and the Roman jurisdiction. Palladius, then apostle of the Scots, was very unlike him: he urged Constantine, their king (according to Polydore), with many prayers not to help the impious Saxon race with arms against the Christian Britons. Therefore the things Augustine wished to decree in that synod, concerning chanting, processions, suffrages, adorations, Masses, temples, the naming of saints and similar Roman superstitious ceremonies, were rejected by the Britons in the province of Menevia and by the Saxons who defended themselves and their religion. Among these people Christianity flourished, having been publicly established under Eleutherius, and it never afterwards failed; as we shall declare more fully in the life of Augustine.

units.la: QVORVNDAM LONDINENSIVM ARCHIEPISCOPORVM nomina, & res gestæ.
units.tr: The names and deeds of certain Archbishops of London.

units.la: Ondinenses Episcopos Britannorum temporibus & multos fuisse, & doctrina, pietate, prudentia insignes, ex his paucis quos adhuc ex monumentis nostris habemus, intelligere licet. Nam & Restitutum Londinensem Episcopum adiisse Arelatensem in Galliis Synodum, in coq; subscripsisse antea diximus. Quì vt ex aliorum scriptis discimus, cum Hilario Pictauiensi Episcopo coniugato familiaris, & ipse coiugatus fuit. Hunc sequutus quidam Guitelinus Londinensis Metropolitanus, cuius præter cæteros singularis in fide constantia, in patriam pietas, & in regerenda solertia, literis prodenda atque illustranda est. Cum enim ob crebras hostiles & barbaras incursiones Romani tributum Britannis remittere, quam assiduam operam ferre maluisset, hi omni veneratione dignus pater, patriam quam à Romanis desertam & hostibus expositam vidit, & Christiana consolatione roborauit atque animauit, & re ipsa iuuit, nec à fide Christiana, nec à patriæ charitate, periculis procellisque vnquam separatus: & ad implorandum auxilium ad minoris Britanniæ seu Armoricæ Regem profecturus. Durate, inquit Guis, ac in fide Christianâ peffiftite Ipsum innocentem, ne in his periculis deficiatis, sed animo forti, constanti, & alaacri, fidem, libertatem, & patriam ab hostibus, Pictis & Scotis, infulam assiduè & incontinenter infestantibus vindicetis. Postea in Armoricam profectus, egit cum Episcopis illius regionis suis confratribus de vicino Britannorum suorum periculo, ad eos celeriter quoque peruenturo, fi opem maturam non attulerint. Regnabant tunc in Armorica Aldroenus, rex a Canano quartus, qui perspecta viri grauitate & prudentia, illum in honore maximo habuit. A quo Rege Episcopus auxilii interiturae patriae cum ludu & gemitibus supplex petiit, & vt barbaris, Deoq; inuitis expulsus, ipse populum regnumq; Britannicum ad suum imperium poteftatemq; reduceret. Cui rex ex peititiffe sequendam illud Britanniæ regnum respondit: nunc autem tantis calamitatibus afflictum, sibi fuifq; proceribus esse spretum & contemptum. Verumtamen quoniam maiores fui eam Insulam quondam tenuissent, fratrem suum Constantinum illuc cum duobus militum millibus classe iranfmiffurum, vt fi diuina ope hostes repelleret, diademate regio insigniretur & gloriose patrum honorifica pace polliderat. Cui episcopus & summas gratias egit: & vocato Constantino Viro militiæ scientissimo: Vincit (inquit) Christus, Christus regnat, Christus imperat: adsit ergo Christus Regi Britanniæ. Ecce defensionem nostram, ecce ipes & gaudium nostrum perpetuum. Classe itaque parata traiecit in Britanniam cum Constantino & militibus Episcopus, ad Totonefii portum appulsus. Quorum aduentu cogaito, Britanni in latibulis & speluncis hostium formidine, multis & referus agminibus conclusi erumpunt ad Constantinum & Episcopum suum concurrunt, iunctisq; copiis in hostes barbaros & impios sæuo impetu feruntur. Quibus ex Infula tota eiectis, & profligatis, tam beati viri opera in fide Christiana, & patriis sedibus vna permanserunt. Hoc etiam tempore tributum Romanis antea pensitatum solui amplius desiit. Parta victoria Constantinus Cicefiriæ, quæ Britannico sermone Caer Caer appellatur, apud populum pro concione laudatur, & Rex Britanniæ decernitur; coniunxq; ei ex nobili Romanorum prosapia procreata, & sub Guitelino sanctissimo Episcopo educata, ac in fide Christiana instituta datur. Ex qua tres inclytos filios, Constantem, Aurelium Ambrofianum, & Vterpendragonem, tam in fide Christiana, quam humana virtute ftrenuos generauit. Constantem primogenitum in ordine Monachali educandum in Ecclesia Amphibali Wintoniæ poluit. Aurelium & Vterpendragonem, sancto Episcopo Guitelino educandos commisit. Ac postquam decennio fœliciter Britannis imperaffet Conftantinus, à quodam Pictô seruulo suo, eodemq; proditore, quem in colloquium quoddam pritaturum in uiam virgulro adhibuit, est interemptus. Eodemq; tempore, & integerrimus præsül Guitelinus optimè de patria meritus, obiit Britannia pastore simul & Rege destituta.
units.tr: That there were many bishops of London in the time of the Britons, distinguished for learning, piety and prudence, may be gathered from the few of them whom we still have from our records. For we said earlier that Restitutus, bishop of London, attended the synod at Arles in Gaul and subscribed to its decrees there. As we learn from the writings of others, he was a friend of Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, who was himself married, and Restitutus was married too. He was followed by a certain Guitelin, metropolitan of London, whose singular steadfastness in the faith, devotion to his country and diligence in governing deserve to be recorded and celebrated in writing. For when the Romans, because of frequent hostile and savage raids, had preferred to remit the tribute to the Britons rather than keep up their constant efforts on their behalf, this father, worthy of all veneration, strengthened and encouraged his country, which he saw deserted by the Romans and exposed to enemies, with Christian consolation, and helped it in fact. Never separated from the Christian faith or from love of his country, nor from its dangers and storms, he was about to set out to seek aid from the king of Lesser Britain, or Armorica. "Endure," he said, "and persist in the Christian faith. Do not fail in these dangers, but with a brave, steadfast and eager spirit defend your faith, your liberty and your country from the enemies, the Picts and the Scots, who constantly and without restraint harass the island." Afterwards he went to Armorica and discussed with the bishops of that region, his fellow bishops, the nearby danger to his Britons, which would soon reach them too if they did not bring timely help. At that time Aldroenus, the fourth king from Conan, reigned in Armorica. Having recognised the bishop's seriousness and prudence, the king held him in the highest honour. The bishop begged this king as a suppliant, with mourning and groans, for help for his perishing country, so that the Britons, expelled by barbarians against God's will, might be restored under his rule to the people and kingdom of Britain. The king replied that the kingdom of Britain was indeed worth pursuing, but that now, afflicted by such calamities, it was despised and scorned by him and his nobles. Nevertheless, since his ancestors had once held that island, he promised that he would send his brother Constantine there by fleet with two thousand soldiers, so that if by divine help he drove back the enemies, he would be invested with the royal diadem and would gloriously win honourable peace. The bishop gave him the warmest thanks, and summoned Constantine, a man most skilled in warfare. "Christ conquers," he said, "Christ reigns, Christ rules. May Christ therefore be with the King of Britain. Behold our defence, behold our constant joy." So, with the fleet readied, the bishop crossed over to Britain with Constantine and the soldiers, and landed at the harbour of Totonefium. When their arrival became known, the Britons, who had been shut up in hiding places and caves through fear of the enemy, in many crowded bands, burst out and ran to Constantine and their bishop. Joining their forces, they charged the savage and impious enemy with fierce assault. When the enemy had been driven out and routed from the whole island, through the work of so blessed a man they remained together in the Christian faith and in their ancestral homes. At this time too, the tribute formerly paid to the Romans ceased to be paid. After the victory, Constantine was praised before the people in an assembly at Cicestria, which in the British tongue is called Caer Caer, and was declared king of Britain. He was given in marriage a woman of noble Roman lineage, who had been brought up by the most holy bishop Guitelin and instructed in the Christian faith. By her he begot three famous sons, Constans, Aurelius Ambrosius and Uther Pendragon, vigorous both in the Christian faith and in human virtue. He placed the firstborn, Constans, to be educated in the monastic order in the church of Amphibalus at Winchester. He entrusted Aurelius and Uther to be educated by the holy bishop Guitelin. After Constantine had ruled the Britons happily for ten years, he was killed by a certain Pict, a servant of his and also a traitor, whom he had taken with him on the road for a private conversation into a thicket. At the same time the most upright prelate Guitelin, who had deserved so well of his country, died, and Britain was left bereft of shepherd and king at once.

units.la: Hinc post belli motus sedatos, inter regni proceres de imperio orta est contentio. Nam Regis Constantini filii post Guitelini mortem, in Armoricam missi sunt, quiq; ob teneram ætatem regnare, aut partes suas tueri non poterant. In illa itaque ciuili discordia Vortigernus quidam Geuiseorum Consul, postiundi postea regni ipse, Constantem Regis primogenitum, iam Monachum, è cœnobio extractum, Londinum adductum, & populo osstensum, vix suffragante populo, magna cum feditionatione Regem creat. Et pari temeritate mortuo Guitelino, nec praesente aliquo Episcopo, ipse propriis manibus Episcopi vice, Constantis capiti coronam imponebat. Deinde adolescenti incauto insidias struens, regni thesaurum in suam custodiam dari procurabat, eiq; suasit, vt Pictis potiùs quàm Britannis sedes vocitesq; tueretur ac defenderet. Itaque centum Pictí ad perpetrandam illam fraudem, quam Vortigernus in regem meditabatur, parati, ad corporis tuitionem constituti sunt. Horum omnium gratiam cum muneribus & blanditiis collegisset Vortigernus, quadam die, cum largius in aula regis potauisset, simulauit se è Britannia discessurum, quod annuus ei rediutus, quo quinquaginta militibus stipendia prouideret, non superesset. Quo audito, Pictî Regis custodes iam poti: Monachum (inquiunt) istû trucidemus, vt Vortigernus regno potiatur: & impetu in regem subito fa&to, eo; interfecto, Vortigerno diadema detulerunt. At Vortigernus, vt lachrimis proditionem simularet, prorupit in fletum, & Londinensibns, vbi hoc feelus commissum est conuocatis, Pictos proditores capite punit. Et callide paulatim defleto suo scelere, tandem coronam sibi imposuit, sed quorumcunque principum malitiam actyrannidem superauit, & quicquid flagitiosum fuit, & pietati virtutiq; maxime aduersum perpetrauit. Quorum omnium poenas in senectute subiit, cum ob Hengisti Pagani filiam nuptam regno à proceribus eiectus est.
units.tr: After the disturbances of war had subsided, a dispute over the rule arose among the nobles of the kingdom. For the sons of King Constantine had been sent into Armorica after Guitelin's death, and because of their tender age they could neither reign nor defend their own rights. In that civil discord, a certain Vortigern, consul of the Gewisse, who afterwards himself gained the kingdom, dragged Constans, the king's firstborn, who was already a monk, out of his monastery, led him to London, and showed him to the people. Scarcely with the people's consent, and amid great sedition, he made him king. And with the same rashness, Guitelin being dead and no bishop present, he himself placed the crown on Constans' head in the bishop's place. Then, plotting against the unwary young man, he arranged for the treasury of the kingdom to be handed into his own keeping, and persuaded him to favour the Picts rather than the Britons in guarding and defending his dominions. So a hundred Picts were made ready to carry out the treachery Vortigern was plotting against the king, and were appointed to guard his person. Having won the favour of all of them with gifts and flattery, Vortigern one day, after drinking rather freely in the king's hall, pretended that he would leave Britain, since his annual income, from which he could provide pay for fifty soldiers, no longer sufficed. When the Pictish guards of the king heard this, now drunk, they said, "Let us slaughter this monk, so that Vortigern may gain the kingdom." They made a sudden attack on the king, killed him, and brought the diadem to Vortigern. But Vortigern, to feign grief over the treachery, burst into tears. Summoning the Londoners, in whose city this crime had been committed, he punished the Pictish traitors with death. Then, gradually and cunningly lamenting his own crime, he at last placed the crown on his own head. But he surpassed in wickedness and tyranny any princes whatever, and committed every shameful deed most opposed to piety and virtue. He paid the penalty for all of these in old age, when, because he had married the daughter of the heathen Hengist, he was expelled from the kingdom by the nobles.

units.la: Atque hæc de Guitelino Londinensi Archiepiscopo, ob summa in patriam merita celebrando viro dicta sint. Post Guitelinum sedit Voadinus Londinensis Archiepiscopus, idq; vt est credibile, nullo interiecto, quiAn. Dom. 436. occisus est. Tum Glocestrensis quidam Episcopus, nomine Theonus, a sede Glocestrensi in Episcopum Londinensem translatus est, Anno gratiae. 553. An vero hic alius fuit ab eo Theono Episcopo Londinensi, de quo hanc mentionem facit Ibri Roffensis author, qui cum Thadiocoo Ehoraeensi, & reliquis clericis atq; Britannis patriam a Saxonibus occupatam deserens, in Walliam atq; Cornubiam secessit, anno Christi. 586. non definimus.
units.tr: So much for Guitelinus, Archbishop of London, a man to be celebrated for his great services to his country. After Guitelinus, Voadinus sat as Archbishop of London, and, as is credible, without anyone being interposed, he was killed in the year of the Lord 436. Then a certain bishop of Gloucester, named Theonus, was translated from the see of Gloucester to the bishopric of London in the year of grace 553. Whether this was a different man from that Theonus, Bishop of London, whom the author of the Book of Rochester mentions, who, along with Thadiocus of York and the other clergy and Britons, abandoned their country occupied by the Saxons and retreated into Wales and Cornwall in the year of Christ 586, we do not decide.

units.la: DE EPISCOPALIVM SEDIVM ORIGINE, MVTATIONE, & maioritate in Anglia.
units.tr: Concerning the origin, transfer and primacy of the episcopal sees in England.

units.la: ELETA Druidum disciplina, Flaminibusq; explosis: viginti octo Episcopatus tribus Metropoliticis prouinciis distinctos in Britannia sub Lucio rege constitutos antea diximus. Metropoleis autem in tribus celeberrimis regni vrbibus, Londini, Eboraci, & in vrbe Legionum collocabantur. Relegato vero Episcopi celebriores locos quasi consultò vitabant, & in humilioribus magisq; solitariis, orationi, contemplationiq; diuinae congruis, sedes staruas statuerunt. Quod eò est verisimilius, etsi nec res ipsa, nec historia id probarer, quòd Druides ipsi, quorum loca Episcopi occupabant, sub robustioribus arboribus & quercubus, ad eruenda daemonum oracula latitabant: vnde & quercum significat, Druides appellabantur. Tum Saxonum aduentu, & religio, & Episcoporum sedes deturbatae, elistinna & imperio, ex casibus euentisq; varie sequutis, singulas pene sensisse eorum limina est historia. Ae primò de Metropolitanis sedibus varietate nonnulla mutatis dicamus, ab vrbe Legionum, (quae etsi minima, tamen in Christiana religione constantissime diurisimeq; permansit) ordinetes A Lucio enim ad Arthuri regis tempora duravit: tum & sub Episcopo Dauide Mcheuiam migrauit: vbi postquam plures sedissent Archiepiscopi, tandem flaua peste, quae Ictericia dicebatur, in Cambria feruente, Sampson Archiepiscopus, sumpto secum pallio, Armoriam adiit, & Dolensi sedi praesedit. Post hunc 24. Episcopi, pallio ob inseitiam, pauperatem vel contemptum Romanorum rituum carentes, Meneuiq; sedebant, qui ab illius gentis Episcopis sacrabantur, eosq; etiam vt suos suffraganeos consecrare soliti sunt, nulla Catuarienfi, aut cuiuncque alteri Ecclesiae professa iuratauae subiectione, vsque ad Riebardi primi vel vt alii volunt Henrici primi imperium, qui primus Cambrienses episcopos vrgebat, ad parendum Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo, tanquam Primati: quod tunc inceptum, postea Henrico 5. regnante Bonifacius Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus, legatione per singulas cathedrales Ecclesias Cambriae fungens, siue cum gratia impetrauit, siue legatina vi impetrauit atq; perfecit. Hinc constat Cambrienses ecclesias in Cantuariensi Metropolis ditionem per Augustini conuentionem nondum venisse, de longe post finitas inter Cantuar: & Eboracensem Archiepiscopum, de prouinciarum & iurisdictionis magnitudine controuersias.
units.tr: We have said earlier that, once the discipline of the Druids and their flamens had been driven out, twenty-eight bishoprics were established in Britain under King Lucius, distinguished into three metropolitan provinces. The metropolitan churches were placed in the three most famous cities of the kingdom: London, York, and the City of Legions. Afterwards the bishops deliberately avoided the more famous places and set up their fixed seats in humbler and more secluded spots, suited to prayer and divine contemplation. This is the more likely, even if neither the thing itself nor history proves it, because the Druids themselves, whose places the bishops occupied, used to hide beneath sturdy trees and oaks in order to draw out the oracles of demons. That is why they were called Druids, a name that signifies an oak. Then, with the coming of the Saxons, both religion and the sees of the bishops were overthrown, and history shows that, through the various chances and events that followed, nearly every one of their thresholds was felt by the enemy. First, let us speak of the metropolitan sees, which underwent some changes. The City of Legions, though very small, remained most constant and long-lasting in the Christian religion, from the time of Lucius down to the times of King Arthur. Then, under Bishop David, it moved to Menevia. There, after several archbishops had held the see, at last, when a yellow plague called the jaundice was raging in Wales, Archbishop Sampson took his pallium with him, went to Armorica, and presided over the see of Dol. After him, twenty-four bishops, lacking the pallium through ignorance, poverty, or contempt for Roman rites, held the sees of Menevia. They were consecrated by bishops of that nation, and they customarily consecrated their own suffragans too, without any acknowledged subjection to Canterbury or to any other church. This lasted until the reign of Richard I, or, as others prefer, of Henry I, who first pressed the Welsh bishops to obey the Archbishop of Canterbury as their primate. This was begun then, but later, under Henry V, Boniface, Archbishop of Canterbury, acting as legate through the cathedral churches of Wales, obtained and carried through the matter, either by favour or by the force of his legatine authority. From this it is clear that the Welsh churches did not come under the rule of the metropolis of Canterbury through Augustine's agreement, and that the disputes between the Archbishops of Canterbury and York over the extent of their provinces and jurisdiction arose long afterwards.

units.la: Proximo loco de Londinensi disseramus. Haec vsque ad Anguftini primi Cant. Archiepiscopi tempora ab ipsa Lucii institutione Metropolitanam dignitatem, ob Saxonum metum & potentiam exirà conspectum, lueemq; vulgi, elam semper retinuit annis amplius trecentis. Ecclesia autem eiusdem Cathedralis vsque ad aedificationem templi Paulini, quod Ethelbertus Saxonum Rex extruxit, fuit ea quae iam est in monte frumentario, qui Cornhill, seu Cornmell vulgariter appellatur, Ecclesia S. Petri Paroechialis, vt ex historiola in eadem conseruata liquet. Sed Augustinus siue Ethelbertus Cathedralis tiorum Regis & hospitis sui gratia, siue quia Londonia tunc regis Ethelberti non erat, sed Seberti nepotis sui, siue ea charitate & benevolentia, qua ipsos Cantios se ad eos apulsum tam benigne exciperi est prosecutus: siue quòd Cantium fuit tunc prima & praecipua Britanniae provincia, cuius Regis ditioni caeteri reges parebant. Nam Cantianis ex antiqua probitatis praerogatiua prima in exercitu obtinere aciem, vt innata gibi fecrocitate, militiq; eopia primo hostium conatus elidant, eaq; forma exteris Angli praelati, Cantuariensi Ecclesiae patent. Etsi Longini Pallium acceperit Augustinus, & ei primatus ab Ethelberto fege assignatus, nec Gregorio ipso contradicente, & snecedentibus eoepiscopis ista praerogativa palam stabilita fuit.
units.tr: Next we shall discuss London. From the time of Lucius's establishment of the see, down to the times of Augustine, the first Archbishop of Canterbury, London kept its metropolitan dignity for more than three hundred years, held in reverence by the common people, though it was overshadowed by fear and the power of the Saxons. The cathedral church of London, until the building of St Paul's, which King Ethelbert of the Saxons erected, was the church that now stands on the hill called Cornhill, or in common speech Cornmarket, the parish church of St Peter, as is clear from a little history preserved in that same church. But whether Augustine or Ethelbert chose Canterbury rather than London for the cathedral, whether out of favour to the king and to his own host, or because London was then not under King Ethelbert but under his nephew Sebert, or out of the love and goodwill with which the Kentish people had so kindly received him when he landed among them, or because Kent was then the first and chief province of Britain, to whose king the other kings paid obedience, the reason is uncertain. For the men of Kent, by the ancient privilege of their valour, held the first place in the army, so that by their innate fierceness and multitude of soldiers they might break the first assaults of the enemy. By this manner the English are said to have been led by foreigners, and this is the basis of the Canterbury church's claim. Even though Augustine received the pallium from Gregory, and primacy was assigned to him by King Ethelbert, and Gregory himself did not object, and this privilege was openly confirmed by his successors.

units.la: Ad quam rem certius perpendendam tam ipsius Gregorii, quàm aliquot istorū Romanorū pontificum testimonia proferenda sunt. Quæ valeant quæ possunt authoritate, antiq; tamen pari valent, qua sunt pmulta hodierno vsu salubriter retenta. Neq; enim vrait lure conuictulus omnium rerum quæ à maioribus gesta sunt, ratione possumus redere, itaque enim plerāq; ex his quæ salubriter constituta sunt, subuertercntur facilime. Sed contra calumniantes ostendamus optimis ac commodissimis rationibus, ac sine cuiusque episcopalis sedis iniuria, Metropolitanam dignitatem Cantuariæ primò locatam fuisse.
units.tr: To weigh this matter more certainly, the testimonies of Gregory himself and of several Roman pontiffs must be brought forward. Such testimonies have as much authority as they can have, and yet they are of equal weight with antiquity, since many things are kept today to good effect by long usage. For we cannot give a rational account of every custom handed down by our ancestors, and so most of the things that have been wisely established would be very easily overturned. But against those who slander, let us show, by the best and most convenient reasons, and without injury to any episcopal see, that the metropolitan dignity was first established at Canterbury.

units.la: REVERENDISSIMO ET SANCTISSIMO FRATRI AVGVSTINO Cantuariensi Episcopo: Gregorius servus servorum Dei.
units.tr: To the most reverend and most holy brother Augustine, Bishop of Canterbury: Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

units.la: VM certum sit pro omnipotenti Deo laborantibus, ineffabilia æterni regni præmia seruari: nobis tamen necesse est, eis honorum beneficia tribuere. vt in spiritualis operis studio ex remuneratione valeant multiplicius insudare. Et quia noua Anglorum Ecclesia, adomnipotentis Dei gratiam, eodem Domino largiente, & te laborante, perducta est, visum tibi palliu in ea, ad sola missarum solemnia agenda concedimus, ita vt pet loca lingula 12. Episcopos ordines, qui tuæ subiaceant ditioni, quatenus Londinensis ciuitatis episcopus, semper in posterum a Synodo propria debeat conseruari, atq; honoris pallium ab hac sancta & Apostolica (cui 12 Deo authore deseruio) sede percipiat. Ad Eboracū vero ciuitatem volumus te Episcopum mittere, quem ipse iudicaueris ordinatetta dumtaxat, vt si eadem ciuitas cum finitimis locis verbum Dei receperit, ipse quoque duodecim Episcopos ordinet, & Metropolitani honore perfruatur: Quia ei quoq; (si vita comes fuerit) pallium tribuere Domino fauente proponimus: quem tamen tuæ fraternitati volumus dispositioni subiacere. Sit vero inter Londinensis & Eboracensis ciuitatis Episcopos posterum honoris distinctio, vt ipse prior habeatur, qui prius fuerit ordinatus. Communi autem concilio, concordi actione, quæ sunt pro Christi zelo agenda, disponant vnanimiter, recte sentiant, & ea quæ senserint, non solum eos Episcopos quos ordinauerit, sed etiam omnes Britanniæ sacerdotes, habeat (Domino Deo nostro Iesu Christo authore) subiectos: quatenus ex lingua & vitæ sanctitatis, recte credendi, & bene viuendi normam percipiant: atq; officium suum fide ac moribus exequentes, ad cœlestia, cum Domino volueris, regna pertingât. Deus te incolumem custodiat Reuerendissime frater. Data 10. die Kal. Iunij, imperante domino nostro Mauricio Tiberio piissimo Augusto anno 19. post consulatum eiusdem Domini anno 18. indictione 4. Missæ sunt hæ literæ per Mellitum.
units.tr: Since it is certain that rewards of the eternal kingdom, beyond all telling, are kept for those who labour for almighty God, it is nonetheless necessary for us to bestow on them benefits of honour, so that in the pursuit of spiritual work they may be able to toil more abundantly by reason of their reward. And since the new Church of the English has been brought into being by the grace of almighty God, the Lord granting it and you labouring, we grant you the use of the pallium in it, for celebrating the solemnities of the Mass alone, so that you may ordain twelve bishops in its various places, who shall be subject to your rule. Thus the bishop of the city of London shall always hereafter be consecrated by his own synod, and shall receive the honour of the pallium from this holy and apostolic see, which, by God's authority, I serve. We wish you to send a bishop to the city of York, whomever you yourself shall judge fit to ordain. If that city, together with the neighbouring places, receives the word of God, he too shall ordain twelve bishops and enjoy the honour of a metropolitan. To him also, if he survives you, we propose, with the Lord's favour, to give the pallium; yet we wish him to be subject to the arrangement of your brotherhood. Let there be a distinction of honour between the bishops of London and York for the future, so that he who was ordained first shall be regarded as the senior. Let them decide together, by common counsel and harmonious action, what must be done for the zeal of Christ, and let them agree unanimously and think rightly. And what they decide shall be binding, not only on the bishops whom you ordain, but also on all the priests of Britain, under the authority of our Lord God Jesus Christ, so that from the teaching and holiness of life they may receive the rule of right belief and good living, and, fulfilling their office in faith and conduct, may come, when the Lord wills, to the heavenly kingdom. May God keep you safe, most reverend brother. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, in the nineteenth year of his rule, the eighteenth year after the consulship of the same lord, indiction four. These letters were sent by Mellitus.

units.la: Sed licet pallium Londinum ad eum à Gregorio missum sit, videriq; posset Gregorium, de Metropoli Londini tenenda cogitasse, Augustinus, tamen consilio ad hoc quod facere senserat, meditato, ab Etherio Arelatensi Episcopo à quo sacratus fuit, neque Londinensis, neq; Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus, sed vniuersali nomine Anglorum Episcopus creabatur, vt liberum sibi sit, in quacunque veleret regni regione seclusum suam collocare. Itaque ptædictis rationibus motus, & siue Ethelberto, siue Cantiis obsequutus, Archiepiscopatus obsoleta insignia Londino traduxit Cantuariam. Id quod à Merlino vaticinio prædictum quidam asserunt his verbis: Dignitas Dorobernia adornabit Dorobernum. Quam vt firmaret, viuus (vt in vita eius dicetur) Laurentium successorem constituit, nec Metropolitæ sedis mutatio euenit. Sed nec duodenario Episcoporum numero à Gregorio præscripto, nec maioritate in Eboracensem altetam metropolim, durante Augustini vita, Cantuariensis sedes coritenta fuit. Quin Augustinus solum indultam authoritatem ad posteros, succesisuto; propagare, ditionemq; Cantuariensem, vlra fines à Gregorio constitutos dilatare studens, suam prouinciam & Cambriæ diocesis, & locupletiori cultioriq; Insulæ parte ornauit, ac Eboracensem Botealibus magisq; in cultis finibus conclusit, ac à sua separauit. Qua quidem in re etsi tam celebettlmæ Londinensi ciuitati, quam Eboracensi prouinciæ, contra mentem fortassis Gregorii, (vt quibusdam placet) iniuria primo facta videri possit, tamen illa authoritas quæ tunc arrogata & vsurpata videbatur, postea tam regiis in Anglia dectetis, quam Papalibus rescriptis, cum penes illos fuisset Ecclesiasticarum rerum potestas, ita corroborata & firmata fuit, vt iam diu sine omni controuersia, in certum iudicatumque transierit.
units.tr: But although the pallium was sent to him at London by Gregory, and it might seem that Gregory had thought of holding the metropolis at London, Augustine, with a plan deliberately made for what he had resolved to do, was consecrated by Etherius, Bishop of Arles, and was created neither Bishop of London nor Archbishop of Canterbury, but Bishop of the English as a whole, so that he would be free to fix his seat in whatever region of the kingdom he wished. Accordingly, moved by the reasons mentioned above, and yielding either to Ethelbert or to the Kentish people, he transferred the old insignia of the archbishopric from London to Canterbury. Some assert that this was foretold by a prophecy of Merlin in these words: "The dignity of Dorobernia shall adorn Dorobernum." To confirm this, while still alive (as will be told in his life), he appointed Laurence as his successor, and no change of the metropolitan see took place. But the Canterbury see did not remain content with the number of twelve bishops prescribed by Gregory, nor with the primacy over the Metropolis of York, while Augustine was alive. Indeed, Augustine, intent on extending to posterity the authority granted to him, and on enlarging the rule of Canterbury beyond the limits set by Gregory, adorned his province with the diocese of Wales and with the richer and better cultivated part of the island, and he confined the Bernician territory of York to the rougher and less cultivated lands and separated it from his own. In this matter, though it may seem, as some think, that a wrong was first done to the very famous city of London and to the province of York, perhaps against Gregory's intention, nevertheless that authority, which then seemed to have been claimed and usurped, was afterwards so strengthened and confirmed, both by the royal decrees in England and by papal rescripts, since the power over ecclesiastical affairs lay with those authorities, that for a long time it has passed without any dispute into a settled and recognised judgment.

units.la: Sed ne iniquis coniecturis à veritate ad suspiciones torqueatur historia, æquius est existimare Augustinum ne præter Gregorii voluntatem atque mentem Cantuariæ potius quam Londini sedem suam instituisse. Etsi enim Gregorius primis illis ad Augustinum literis quibus pallium miserit, loci atque gentis ignarus, duarum tantum ciuitatum Londini scilicet & Eboraci, quæ celeberrimæ putabatur, meminerit. Fuit tamen eodem tempore Ethelbertus Cantii rex omnium Angliæ regum potentissimus, utpote qui imperii sui fines ad Humbrum fluuium propagare curauerat, tum ipsa Cantuaria iurisdictione amplissima, ad quam reliquæ Angliæ gentes Iuris habendi causa maxime confluebant. Ipseq; Ethelbertus ad fidem conuersus non modo Augustiniense cœnobium Cantuariæ, & ecclesiam Roffensem, sed Londini Paulinam ecclesiam primus condidit. Quibus rebus motus Gregorius cum auctum Euangelium inter Anglos ab Ethelberto & Cantuaricnibus intellexerat, non præscriptam prius rationem Augustino seruandam, sed rem suo arbitrio tam in hac quàm in omnibus causis ecclesiasticis moderandam relinquit. Id quod ex Gregorianis responsis ad vndecim Augustini quæstiones intelligi potest.
units.tr: But lest history be twisted by unfair guesses into suspicion, it is fairer to think that Augustine did not establish his see at Canterbury rather than London against Gregory's wish and intention. For although in his first letters to Augustine, with which he sent the pallium, Gregory, being ignorant of the place and the people, mentions only two cities, London and York, which were thought most celebrated. Yet at that same time Ethelbert, king of Kent, was the most powerful of all the kings of England, since he had taken care to extend his realm as far as the river Humber, and Canterbury itself had very extensive jurisdiction, to which the other English peoples flocked especially to obtain justice. Ethelbert himself, once converted to the faith, was the first to found not only the monastery of St Augustine at Canterbury and the church of Rochester, but also the church of St Paul at London. Moved by these things, when Gregory learned that the gospel had been spread among the English by Ethelbert and the Canterbury people, he did not impose on Augustine a method to be kept as prescribed beforehand, but left the matter to be governed at his own discretion, in this as in all ecclesiastical causes. This can be understood from Gregory's replies to Augustine's eleven questions.

units.la: RESPONSIO GREGORII PAPÆ AD TER- tiam interrogationem Augustini.
units.tr: THE REPLY OF POPE GREGORY TO AUGUSTINE'S THIRD QUESTION.

units.la: Ovit fraternitas tua Romanæ Ecclesiæ consuetudinem: in quase meminit enutritam. Sed mihi placet vt siue in Romana, siue in Gallicanorum, seu in qualibet Ecclesia aliquid inuenisti quod plus omnipotenti Deo possit placere, solicitè eligas: & in Anglorum ecclesia, quæ adhuc ad fidem noua est, institutione præcipua quæ de multis ecclesiis colligere potuisti, infundas exempla. Non enim pro locis res, sed pro bonis rebus loca amanda sunt. Ex singulis ergo quibusque ecclesiis, quæ pia, quæ religiosa, quæ recta sunt elige: & hæc quasi in fasciculo collecta apud Anglorum mentes in consuetudinem depone.
units.tr: Your brotherhood knows the custom of the Roman Church, in which you remember you were brought up. But it is my pleasure that, if you have found anything in the Roman Church, or in the Gallican or any other church, that may please almighty God more, you carefully choose it, and that you introduce into the church of the English, which is still new to the faith, the best practices you have been able to gather from many churches. For things are not to be loved for the sake of places, but places for the sake of good things. Therefore from each church choose whatever is pious, religious and right, and, having gathered these together as in a bundle, lay them down as custom in the minds of the English.

units.la: Hunc Pontificem Romani qui proximè sequuti sunt, sedem Metropolitanam, ita Cantuariæ confirmarunt, vt ab ea diuelli nephas esse decreuerunt. Namq; ad Ethelbertum primo, deinde ad Iustum Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum, qui tertius fuit ab Augustino, Bonifacius Papa scribens non modò affirmat, Metropolim ab ipso Gregorio sub Augustino Cantuariæ fuisse institutam, sed sub Anathematis & gehennalis mortis pœna præcepit, ne à quoquam illhac alio transferatur, vt ex ipsis literis hic insertis apparet.
units.tr: The Roman pontiffs who immediately followed this pontiff so confirmed the metropolitan see at Canterbury that they decreed it a sin to tear it away from there. For Pope Boniface, writing to Ethelbert first and then to Justus, Archbishop of Canterbury, who was the third after Augustine, not only affirms that the metropolis at Canterbury was founded by Gregory himself under Augustine, but also commands under the penalty of anathema and of hellish death that it be transferred from there by no one, as appears from the letter itself inserted here.

units.la: LITERA BONIFACII QVINTI PAPÆ, AD ETHELBERTVM Regem, & Iustum Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum, &c.
units.tr: LETTER OF POPE BONIFACE V, TO KING ETHELBERT AND JUSTUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, etc.

units.la: Omino excellentissimo atq; præcellentissimo filio regi Ethelberto Bonifacius Episcopus seruus seruorum dei.
