Dum Christianitatis vestræ integritas ita circa conditoris sui cultum excreuerit, vt longè lateq; resplendeat, & in omni mundo annunciata vestra Deo dignæ operationis augmenta referat, innumeras largitori omnium bonorum gratis Deo exoluimus: qui nos de excelso prospexit & in tato virtutum culmine erexit. Quapropter gloriolè fili quod ab apostolica sede per Coepiscopum nostrum Mellitum pustulasti, libenti animo coriecdimus, id est, vt vestrabenignitas in Monasterio in Dorobernensi ciuitate constituto (quod sanctus doctor vester Augustinus beatæ memoriæ Gregorii discipulus; sancti Saluatoris nomini consecrauit: cui ad præceris præsse dignosctur dilectissimus frater noster Laurentius,) licenter per omnia monachorum regulariter viuentium habitationem statuat, apostolica auctoritate decernentes, vt ipsi vestræ salutis prædicatores monachi monachorum gregem tibi associent, & eorum vitam sanctitatum moribus exornent. Quæ nostra decreta si quis successorum nostrorum, siue Regum, siue Episcoporum, Clericorum, seu laicorum irrita facere tentauerit, a principe apostolorum Petro, & a cunctis successoribus suis ana hematis vinculo subiaceat quoadusque quod temerario ausu peregit, Deo placita facti factione pœniteat, & huius in quietudinis veram emendationem faciat. In Christo valeas Domine fili. Missa per manu Melliti Episcopi Londinensis. Anno Dominicæ incarnationis. DCXV.
units.tr: To the most excellent and most eminent son, King Ethelbert, Boniface, Bishop, servant of the servants of God. Since your Christianity has so grown in the worship of its Maker that it shines far and wide, and the reports of its works, worthy of God, are proclaimed throughout the whole world, we give countless thanks to God, the giver of all good things, who looked down on us from on high and raised us to such a height of virtue. Therefore, glorious son, we gladly grant what you requested from the Apostolic See through our fellow bishop Mellitus: namely, that your kindness may freely establish, in the monastery built in the city of Canterbury (which your holy teacher Augustine, a disciple of the blessed Gregory of happy memory, dedicated to the name of the holy Saviour, and over which our most beloved brother Laurence is known to have presided before him), a dwelling for monks living under a rule. By apostolic authority we decree that these preachers of your salvation, the monks, shall join the flock of monks with you, and adorn their life with the morals of holiness. If any of our successors, whether kings, bishops, clergy or laymen, should attempt to make these our decrees void, let him be bound by the chain of anathema from the prince of the apostles, Peter, and from all his successors, until he repents before God of the rash deed he has done, and makes a true amendment of this disturbance. Farewell in Christ, lord son. Sent by the hand of Mellitus, Bishop of London. In the year of the Lord's incarnation, 615.

units.la: DIlectissimo fratri suo Bonifacius Episcopus seruus seruorum Dei Suscepto vestræ dilectionis apicibus, in quibus reperimus inter alia plurimos ex gentilibus idem degentibus, Deo omnipotente & Domino nostro Iesu Christo auxiliante commissos, maximè autem in partibus Cantii ad veri Dei nostri fidem vestris laboribus esse perductos, valde gratulari fumus. Edbaldi quoque regis animum ad vestræ agnitionis viam esse correctum Dominum omnipotentem laudauimus, qui suf nominis sui crementum, vestrique laborum fructum non deseruit, sicut ipse prædicatoribus Euangelii veraciter repromisit. Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus vitæ vsque ad consummationem seculi. Multa est clementia apud Dominum, multa est in vobis demonstrata, cum aperiantur corda barbarorum gentium ad suscipiendum prædicationis verbum singulare mysterium. Verùm proficerent, vestris meritis est eorum Saluatio procurata, Domino dicente. Qui perseuerauerit in finem, hic saluus erit. Cognoui siquidem in vestris syllabis vt sanctæ recordationis prædecessor noster Gregorius constituit Augustinum & omnibus successoribus suis in posterum Metropolitanam & primitiuam sedem in ciuitate Dorobernia, vbi caput totius genitis Anglorum à diebus paganorum habetur. At verò nunc per reuelationem Iesu Christi qui est origo & caput Christianitatis, eadem ciuitas exaltatur, & orthodoxa fides quæ est radix nobilissima ibidem collocatur, vt ex illa seges eius vberrimum fructum boni operis ad pabulum cœlestis patriæ omnes inde sulani metere queant. O quam fœlix illa ciuitas, quæ meruit in se Christum habitatorem habere. Fœlix illa ejuitas & totagens cum illas superna misericordia visitare non dedignata sit, quos ante mundi creationem prædestinauerat sibi sociare. Quare absit ab omni Christiano vt ex illa ciuitate Dorobernia aliquid minuatur, aut in aliud mutetur nunc vel futuris temporibus, quæ à prædecessore Domino Papa Gregorio statura sunt quomodo res humanæ quasi uentur. Sed magis ex auctoritate beati Petri Apostolorum principis id ipsum præcipientes firmamus, vt in Dorobernia ciuitate semper in posterum Metropolitanus totius Britanniæ locus habeatur, omnesque prouinciæ regni Anglorum prædicti loci Metropolitanæ Ecclesiæ subiiciantur, immutilata & perpetua stabilitate decreuimus. Hanc autem Ecclesiam vt pote specialiter consistentem sub potestate & tuitione sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ si quis conatus fuerit imminuere, eique de concessa potestatis iure quicquam abstulerit, auferat eum omnipotens Dominus de libro vitæ suæ, sciatque se sub anathematis vinculis esse innodatum. Deus te incolumem custodiat Reuerende frater.
units.tr: To his most beloved brother, Boniface, Bishop, servant of the servants of God. Having received the letters of your affection, in which we found, among other things, that very many of the Gentiles dwelling there have been committed to Almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and, above all, that in the parts of Kent they have been brought by your labours to the faith of our true God, we rejoice greatly. We have also praised the Lord Almighty that the mind of King Eadbald has been turned toward the way of your knowledge; he has not forsaken the increase of his name and the fruit of your labours, just as he himself truly promised to the preachers of the Gospel: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the world. Great is the mercy of the Lord, and great is the grace shown in you, since the hearts of barbarous nations are opened to receive the word of preaching, a singular mystery. Indeed, that they might advance, their salvation has been secured by your merits, the Lord saying: He who shall persevere to the end, he shall be saved. For I have learned from your letters that our predecessor of holy memory, Gregory, appointed Augustine, and all his successors in future, to the metropolitan and primatial see in the city of Canterbury, where the head of the whole English nation has been held since the days of the pagans. But now, through the revelation of Jesus Christ, who is the origin and head of Christianity, that same city is exalted, and the orthodox faith, which is the noblest root, is planted there, so that from it all may gather a most abundant harvest of good works for the food of the heavenly homeland. O how happy that city, which has deserved to have Christ dwelling in it! Happy that city, and the whole nation, since the heavenly mercy has not disdained to visit those whom it had predestined before the creation of the world to be joined to itself. Wherefore, far be it from any Christian that anything be diminished from that city of Canterbury, or changed into something else, now or in future times, since these things have been established by our predecessor, the lord Pope Gregory, as human affairs roll on. But rather, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we command and confirm the same, and decree with an unchanged and perpetual firmness that in the city of Canterbury there shall always in future be held the metropolitan place of all Britain, and that all the provinces of the aforesaid kingdom of the English shall be subject to the metropolitan church of that place. If anyone should attempt to diminish this church, which especially stands under the power and protection of the holy Roman Church, and should take away anything from the right of power granted to it, may Almighty God blot him out of the book of his life, and may he know that he is bound in the chains of anathema. May God keep you safe, reverend brother.

units.la: Posthunc Honorius Papa Honorio Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo scripsit, vt in ciuitate Dorobernia, Metropolitanus locus & honor Archiepiscopatus, & caput omnium Ecclesiarum Anglorum semper in posterum habeatur, & à nulla persona pet aliquam malam suationem ab alium locum mutetur. Iustus autem cum Paulinum Eboracensem Archiepiscopum ordinauit, eius sedem Eboracensem Cantuariensi Metropoli subiecit. Sicut(inquit) Cantium subiiciatur Romæ, quod ex ea fide accepit: ita Eboracum subiiciatur Cantuariæ, quæ eò prædicatores misit. Sieut igitur Cantuariæ sedes prima fuit in fide, ita prima sicut honore. Quam dignitatem atque prærogativam Cantuariensis Metropolis septem deinceps Romani Pontifices, cum Cantuariensis Archiepiscopos confirmarent, tanquam ab ipso Gregorio acceptam, primoque institutam renouarunt. Vt si quis hanc rem altius consideraverit, ne necesse fuisse quidem Augustinum à Gregorii præscripto iudicabit, sed ipsum Gregorium mutato postea consilio, quid è re maximè sit Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ Augustini iudicio permisisse. Itaque Augustinus libera sibi facta à Gregorio potestate Angliam suo arbitrio iudicio que in religione instituere, huius loci commodicatem sequutus, quæ & cultu vrbanior, & suis suationibus propensior, & rebus egregiis clarior, & exteris vicinisque nationibus notior fuit, tum ab ipso Ethelberto rege tanta munificentia magnificentia alle&tus, Catuariensis Archiepiscopus potius quam Lodinensis dici voluit. Nec minus amicitiæ atque necessitudinis quàm ipsi antiquitati & originitanto honorem videtur detulisse, vt in gente atque ciuitate quam primo instituit atque constituit totius prouinciæ Metropolitanum tanquam oraculum statuatur.
units.tr: After this, Pope Honorius wrote to Honorius, Archbishop of Canterbury, that in the city of Canterbury the metropolitan place and honour of the archbishopric, and the head of all the churches of the English, should always be held in future, and that no person, by any evil persuasion, should move it to another place. Justus, moreover, when he ordained Paulinus, Archbishop of York, made his see of York subject to the metropolis of Canterbury. "As Kent," he says, "is subject to Rome, from which it received the faith, so York is to be subject to Canterbury, which sent preachers to it. Therefore, as the see of Canterbury was first in the faith, so let it be first in honour." This dignity and pre-eminence the metropolis of Canterbury, as having been received from Gregory himself and first instituted by him, afterwards renewed, when seven Roman Pontiffs in succession confirmed the archbishops of Canterbury. So that if anyone considers this matter more deeply, he will judge that it was not even necessary for Augustine to follow Gregory's prescription; rather, Gregory himself, having later changed his plan, left to the judgement of Augustine what would be most advantageous to the English Church. Therefore Augustine, his power being freed by Gregory, chose to establish England in religion according to his own will and judgement, following the convenience of this place, which was both more civilised in its worship, more inclined to his persuasions, more distinguished in its notable affairs, and better known to foreign and neighbouring nations; and, being so attracted by the great munificence and magnificence of King Ethelbert himself, he wished to be called Archbishop of Canterbury rather than of London. And he seems to have conferred this honour no less out of friendship and close connection than out of regard for the antiquity and origin of that place, so that in the nation and city which he first founded and established, the metropolitan of the whole province should be set up as an oracle.

units.la: NIhis autem quæ prædicta sunt tria mihi videntur esse notanda: videlicet qua de causa Sanctus Gregorius voluerit vt Archiepiscopus Arelatensis Augustinum Anglorum sacrasacraret Episcopum, cum tot inprasentiarum sint Archiepiscopi Angliae viciniores, forte tunc temporis tot Episcopi non fuerunt, vel crescente paulatim Ecclesia creuit & gloria, vt Episcopos in Archiepiscopos temporis intervallo Romana commutaret Ecclesia. Cur autem in Anglia tres Archiepiscopos instituerit, scilicet Cantuariensem, Londoniensem & Eboracensem, vt singuli suos numero. 12. haberent suffraganeos, resin propatulo est. Aut enim error erat scriptoris velociter scribentis, vt nomina transponeret civitatum, aut existimauit Gregorius, licet sancti spiritus esset sacrarium, vt civitates in Anglia nobilissimae ab inuicem aequali distarent proportione, & Cantuariensis esset in capite, Eboracum in fine, Londonia vero in mediterraneo terrae. Statum itaque sciens Augustini, situm vero terrae nescientes, de tribus Archiepiscopis instituendis scripsit, vt supra dictum est. Attamen omnia ipsius Augustini suppositi dispositioni. Cum Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus. 12. haberet suffraganeos, vbi nam Londinensis suos. 12. reperire poterit, certe nusquam competenter apparet. Idcirco dispositioni diuinae cuncta suppositae debent esse Praetereanotandum est, quaratione nitantur qui dicunt & scribunt beatum Gregorium Pallia misisse tribus Archiepiscopis, Cantuariensi scilicet Augustino qui sedit annis. 16. & Laurentio qui post Augustinum sedit annis. 5. qui conuniuncti faciunt annos. 16. cum ipse Gregorius non sederit nisi annis. 13. menslibus. 6. & diebus decem: quae cum ulterius omnia cohaerent non possunt, nam & solam perpendo rationem, quam etiam in scriptis vidi, licet non authenticis, & a senioribus audiui, videlicet quod Papa Ac Augustinum omnia suo modo in Anglia statuendi a Gregorio potestatem adeptum, haec etiam impulit causa, cur Cantuariae Metropolitanam sedem collocarit. Quod Cantii quos primo lucrifecisser, humanitate vrbanitateque caeteras Anglorum gentes superate, & in vitae cultu atque moribus non multum a vicinis Gallis (qui politia eleganciaque Anglos anteibant) differte, ipsius Iulii Caesaris testimonio per hiberum. Quodque ab his Augustinus tam humaniter tractatus locum impositio suscepto que suo religionis in Anglia negocio tibi & successuris, qui peregrini & Itali diu fuerunt, tutum atque commodum delegisset. Londinenses autem & Insulae penè mediterraneos, & in alterius regni finibus, hempè Essexiae tum positos, tardiusque ad fidem conuersos, necessitate magis quam voluntate reliquisse: eoque concilio Cantuariae concilio, quod vnà cum suis, Ethelberti Regis & Cantiorum coniunctae ciuitatis, ire ac redire tutius facilius atque potuisset, magis quam vt in maritimo, ac vicinioti Insulae loco, Papae seu cuiquam in tumultibus inte stitiis adesset, opemue ferret, an expectaret. Verum eo fuit Cantuariensis sedis authoritas magis consolidata, quod cum Offa Merciorum Rex, Lamberto Archiepiscopo & Cantuariensibus infestus, annuente Adriano tum Pontifice Romano, fortasse muneribus ad id corrupto, Metropolim Cantuariae adeptam, in vrbe suis tegni mediterranea, quae Lichfieldia nuncupatur, sub Aldulpho Archiepiscopo & Primate constitutes: postea sub Kenulpho tege in Metciorum regno Offa succedente, iterum Cantuariae restituta est, omniaque quae fecisset Offa ad nihilum redacta, vtriusque iutis carentia, a Leone tunc Pontifice pronunciata sunt: vtex vtriusque iam Kenulphi, quam Leonis scriptis & refectis literis, in Athelardi Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi vita inseritis recitatis; liquidò constare potest. Tum authoritati Cantuariensi tuendae atque stabilendae accesserunt crebrae inter Metropolitanos luctae & controuersiae, in quibus Cantuariensis vel provocantes vel relucantes semper vicit atque superauit. Metropolis autem Eboraci constituta, cui Albania subiecta fuit, etsi abilla sede nunquam dimota & aulla fit, tamen haec Insula in duo tantum regna, Angliam scilicet & Scotiam diuisa, deficiente Albania, quae fuit prouincia & alterius regni pars maxima fuit, minuta valde & perexigua, fiad Cantuariam referatur, existiman potest. Quare permoti illius sedis Archiepiscopi, repetebant crebrò aliquas diocaeses, vt Wigorniensem atque Lincolniensem, quibus obtentis in magnitudine prouinciae Cantuariensibus Archiepiscopis penè pares esse poterant: & aequipollentem a Gregorio constitutam Eboracensem cum Cantuariensi iurisdictionem obtinerent: vtć à sua Synodo, suaque prouincia, perinde ac Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi sacrarentur : nec subiectionem quocunque modo Archiepiscopis Cant. vlla lege promitterent, aut iurarent. In quibus omnibus litibus atque controversiis (vt suis locis opportunius demonstrabitur) Eboracenses Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis potentia (cuius plerumque fuit & Angliæ Regibus, & Romanis Pontificibus ipsa vicinitate, & origine sedis suæ quasi coniuncta, maior authoritas) causa sua victi ceciderunt : vt non tam ex prima institutione, quam ex sequuta contentione, in qua principes atque pontifices semper Cantuariæ primas defenderunt, Cantuariensis provincia magnitudinem & potentiam suam æquissimam esse iudicatur. Sub Lanfranco enim (vt in eius vita patebit) & Gulielmi concilio (qui armis & victoria regnum obtinuit) & pontificum variis rescriptis, hæc inter Cantuar. & Eborac. Archiepiscopos totiès redintegrata contentio, sic pacata, & ad concordiam redacta est : vt prouinciarum fines Humbto flumine statuerentur, & vt in omnibus diuinum cultum tangentibus decretis ac negociis, Eboracensis provincia subdatur Cantuariensi: & vt Eboracensis Archiepiscopus cum suo Clero, concilio à Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo indićo, atque congregato interfit. Deinde vt Eboracensis Archiepiscopus cum suis suffraganeis, sacratum Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum, Cantuariam, vel ad alium eius prouinciæ designatum locum accedant, & vt Eboracenses Archiepiscopi consecrandi per Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem Cantuariæ, vel in Cantuariensi provincia consecrenrur. Ad extremum, vt utrique Metropolitano suus honos, distinctus tamen tribuatur: Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus totius Angliæ primas: Eboracensis vero Angliæ primas edicto nuncupatus. Hæc lis, etsi ita composita fuerit, postea tamen querundam Archiepiscoporum Eborac. renovata fuit importunitate, qui victi causa ceciderent. Nec desunt, qui Archiepiscopum Eboracensem quendam Thomam, suffraganei vice, in consecratione Sampson Wigorniensis Episcopi, sub Anshelmo functum fuisse scribant. Ira & maioritatem, & provinciæ magnitudinem, Cantuariensis sedem omnino firmatam rot annis occupavit, & Eboracensem ad Boreales fines relegavit, & ad subiectionem redegit. Eboracensis autem sedes quanquam à constituto primum loco non migravit, eius tamen authoritas quasi sopita 30. annis cessavit. Edwinus enim rex (qui Edelbertam filiam Adelberti Regis Cantuariæ vxorem duxit) postquam cum Paulinus (qui post appulsum Augustini cum 40. sociis in Angliam missus erat à Pontifice etiam, cum 12. alis Clericis, in auxilium Augustino) cum Eboracensi civitate, & adiacente provincia, ad Christi fidem converterat, hostili manu à Ceadwalla Britonum, & Pœanda Merciorum regibus infestatus, bello periit. Cuius morte rebus turbatis, Paulinus tunc Eboracensis Archiepiscopus ab Augustino institutus & consecratus recessit, nauigioque Cantuariam cum Edelberta Regina, sumpto secum pallio profugit: vbi perhumaniter ab Honorio tunc Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo acceptus, Roffensi diocesi præficitur: non victus inopia (vt perperam ex vanissima coniectura collegit Polydorus) sed ipsa vi, & temporum magis quam serum necessitate Archiepiscopalem sedem deserens. Perinde enim dicere poterat Reginam Adelbertam, non necessitate sed paupertate fugisse. Eo ita absente vacavit sedes, donec Egbertus Episcopus frater Regis, Pontificali authoritate pallium recuperauisset. Annoque post Paulini discessum 30. Vlfridus in Eboracensi sede instituitus est. Nunc Metropoliticis mutationibus & dignitatibus expositis, inferiores Episcopatus in vtraque provincia secundum earum varietates & mutationes percurramus. Ante Augustini aduentum, vastatas à Saxonibus in Eboracensi & Londinensi provinciis, Episcopales sedes vnà cum religione eiectæ, exiitimare conuenit. Ideoque de Cambriæ sedibus Episcopalibus, quæ fidem retinuerunt, & notior, & certior est historia, cuius provinciæ Episcopatus supra commemorauimus. Ad cæterarum notitiam & intelligentiam hoc ordine peruenietis. Sefendum est Britannis in Walliam, Cornubiam, & Galliam ætis, Anglos atque Saxones potitam à se Insulæ partem, in septem regna diuisisse Quotum primum, occiduam Insulæ regionem, hos comitatus. Southamtonam, Betkeriam, Wilcetiam, Dorcestrensem, Somersetensem, Surrensem. Deuonensem, & Cornubiam continens, Westfaxonia vocabatur, Secundi ab australibus Saxonibus, Southsaxonia, seu Sodthsexia dicta, illi comitatum, partemq; Surræ tenebat. Tertii regnū Cætii finibus continebatur. Quartū ab orientalibus, Eftfaxonia nuncupata, Londinum, Midlesexiam, Essexiam, ac Hertfordensis parto comcomprehendebat. Quintum ab Orientalibus etiam Estanglia nominata, per Norfolciam, Suffolciam, Cantabrigiensem, Elamqué Insulam extensum est. Sextum in mediterraneis situm, Mercia sic dicta, ab Anglico nomine Merce / quod limen, regionisq; alicuius fines significat, quia à cæterorum finibus hoc tangentibus, circumseptum & inclusum fuit, aut (vt aliî volunt) à Latino nomine Mercés, quia totius Insulæ mediterrulum locuples fuit, & Mercibus eò vndiq; portaris abundabat, quia à cæterorum finibus hoc tangentibus circumseptum & inclusum fuit. Hoc autem regnum per comitatus, Lincolniensem, Northamptonensem, Rutlandiam, Huntingdonensem, Bedfordiensem, Buckingamiensem, Oxfordiensem, Cheftrensem, Derbensem, Nottingamensem, Staffordensem, Warwicensem, Glocestrensem, Wigorniensem, & partem Herefordensis late patebat. Septimum fuit Northumbrorum regnū, quod Eboracensem, Dunelmensem, Northumbriam, Cumbriam, Westhumbriam, & Lancastriam comitatum ambitu suo cinxit. In his septem regnis, Episcopatus septem primò ab Anglia & Saxonibus post receptū Euangelium institui fuerunt, sed variis & incertis sedibus; postea ordinibus locisq; distincti, & numero dilatati sunt.
units.tr: Of the matters just mentioned, three seem to me worth noting. The first is why Saint Gregory wished the Archbishop of Arles to consecrate Augustine as bishop of the English, since there are now more archbishops of England nearer at hand. Perhaps there were not so many bishops at that time, or perhaps, as the Church grew little by little, its size and glory increased, so that the Roman Church changed bishops into archbishops over time. The second is why he set up three archbishops in England, of Canterbury, London and York, so that each should have twelve suffragans. The reason for this is plain enough. Either a hurried scribe transposed the names of the cities, or Gregory, although he was a treasury of the Holy Spirit, thought that the noblest cities of England should lie at equal distances from one another, with Canterbury at the head, York at the far end, and London in the middle of the land. So, knowing the position of Augustine's see but not the lie of the land, he wrote about appointing three archbishops, as stated above. Yet all these arrangements must be subject to the disposition of divine providence. Since Canterbury had twelve suffragans, it nowhere clearly appears where London could find its twelve. Everything placed under that arrangement must therefore be left to the divine disposition. The third matter to note is on what grounds those argue and write that the blessed Gregory sent palliums to three archbishops, namely to Augustine of Canterbury, who held the see for sixteen years, and to Laurence, who succeeded Augustine and held it for five; together these make sixteen years, whereas Gregory himself held his office for only thirteen years, six months and ten days. These figures cannot all be reconciled. I weigh only the reasoning, which I have also seen in writings, though not authentic ones, and heard from my elders. It is that the Pope had given Augustine the power to order everything in England in his own way, and this same consideration led him to place the metropolitan see at Canterbury. The men of Kent, whom he first won over, surpassed the other English peoples in courtesy and refinement; their way of life and customs differed little from those of the neighbouring Gauls, who excelled the English in civil polity and elegance, as Julius Caesar himself testifies. Augustine was treated so kindly by them that he chose a safe and convenient place for himself and his successors, who were long foreigners and Italians, to establish the seat of his religious business in England. He left the Londoners, and the islanders who lived almost inland, on the borders of another kingdom (Essex, as it then was), and slower to be converted to the faith, more from necessity than from choice. By that decision he placed the seat at Canterbury, where he and his people, together with King Ethelbert and the city allied to the men of Kent, could come and go more safely and easily, rather than in a maritime island near the coast, where he might be present for the Pope or anyone else in the disturbances and intervals, bring help, or wait for it. The authority of the see of Canterbury was further strengthened by the following events. King Offa of the Mercians, hostile to Archbishop Lambert and the men of Canterbury, with the approval of Adrian, the Roman Pontiff then in office, and perhaps with the Pope bribed for that purpose, obtained the metropolitan dignity from Canterbury and established it at Lichfield, an inland city of his kingdom, under Aldulph as archbishop and primate. Afterwards, under King Kenulph, who succeeded Offa in the kingdom of the Mercians, it was restored to Canterbury, and all that Offa had done was annulled and declared void by Pope Leo, as can be clearly established from the writings of both Kenulph and Leo, and from the letters, restored and inserted, that are recited in the life of Athelard, Archbishop of Canterbury. To the defence and consolidation of Canterbury's authority there were added frequent struggles and disputes among the metropolitans, in which Canterbury, whether challenging or resisting, always won and prevailed. The metropolis of York was established, to which Albania (Scotland) was subject. Although that see was never removed and never ceased to exist, this island came to be divided into only two kingdoms, England and Scotland, since Albania, which had been a province and by far the greater part of the other kingdom, had declined and become very small and slight, so that it may be thought to have been brought under Canterbury. Moved by this, the archbishops of that see repeatedly sought certain dioceses, such as Worcester and Lincoln. If they obtained these, they could have been nearly equal to the archbishops of Canterbury in the size of their province, and they would have held a jurisdiction equal to the one Gregory had assigned to York. They would then be consecrated by their own synod and within their own province, just as the archbishops of Canterbury were, and they would promise or swear no subjection to the archbishops of Canterbury by any law. In all these disputes and controversies (as will be shown more fittingly in their places), the archbishops of York were defeated and fell in their cause, overcome by the power of the archbishop of Canterbury. That power was generally the greater, both for the kings of England and for the Roman pontiffs, because of its proximity and because its see was in a sense joined to theirs by origin. Thus the province of Canterbury is judged to have the most just magnitude and power, not so much from its first institution as from the contention that followed, in which princes and pontiffs always defended the primacy of Canterbury. Under Lanfranc (as will appear in his life), and by the council of William, who gained the kingdom by arms and victory, and by various papal rescripts, this contention between the archbishops of Canterbury and York, so often renewed, was pacified and brought to concord. The boundaries of the provinces were fixed at the river Humber. In all decrees and matters touching divine worship, the province of York was made subject to Canterbury. The archbishop of York, with his clergy, was to attend a council summoned and convened by the archbishop of Canterbury. Then the archbishop of York with his suffragans was to go to Canterbury, or to another place in the province designated by the consecrated archbishop of Canterbury, and the archbishops of York were to be consecrated by the archbishop of Canterbury, at Canterbury or within the province of Canterbury. Finally, each metropolitan was to be given his own honour, yet a distinct one: the archbishop of Canterbury as primate of all England, and the archbishop of York as primate of England by edict. Although this dispute was settled in this way, it was afterwards revived by the persistent importunity of certain archbishops of York, who fell in their cause when defeated. Nor are there lacking those who write that a certain archbishop of York, Thomas, acted in the place of a suffragan at the consecration of Samson, bishop of Worcester, under Anselm. Thus the see of Canterbury, having firmly secured both greater authority and the magnitude of its province, held that position for many years, relegated York to the northern borders, and reduced it to subjection. The see of York did not, indeed, migrate from its originally appointed place, but its authority, as if asleep, ceased for thirty years. King Edwin, who married Ethelburga, daughter of King Ethelbert of Kent, had, after Paulinus was converted to the faith (Paulinus had been sent by the Pontiff, together with twelve other clerics, to assist Augustine, who had come to England with forty companions), converted the city of York and the neighbouring province to faith in Christ. But he was attacked by hostile hands, those of Ceadwalla, king of the Britons, and Penda, king of the Mercians, and perished in battle. With affairs thrown into confusion by his death, Paulinus, then archbishop of York (instituted and consecrated by Augustine), withdrew and fled by ship to Canterbury with Queen Ethelburga, taking the pallium with him. There he was most courteously received by Honorius, then archbishop of Canterbury, and was set over the diocese of Rochester. He did not, as Polydore Vergil foolishly conjectured, flee because he was overcome by poverty; he left the archiepiscopal see because of the force of events and the necessity of the times rather than of the men. For one could just as well say that Queen Ethelburga fled not from necessity but from poverty. With him absent, the see stood vacant until Egbert, bishop and brother of the king, recovered the pallium by pontifical authority. Thirty years after Paulinus's departure, Wulfrid was installed in the see of York. Having now set out the changes and dignities of the metropolitans, let us run through the lesser bishoprics in each province, according to their variations and changes. Before Augustine's arrival, it is reasonable to suppose that the episcopal sees in the provinces of York and London, laid waste by the Saxons, were cast out along with the religion. The history of the episcopal sees of Wales, which kept the faith, is therefore both better known and more certain, and of their provinces' bishoprics we have spoken above. You will come to know the rest in the following order. It must be said that the Britons, driven into Wales, Cornwall and Gaul, divided into seven kingdoms the part of the island that the Angles and Saxons had seized. The first, which contained the western region of the island, was called West Saxony, and comprised these counties: Southampton, Berkshire, Wiltshire, Dorset, Somerset, Surrey, Devon and Cornwall. The second, belonging to the southern Saxons, was called South Saxony or Sussex; it held the county of Sussex and part of Surrey. The third kingdom was contained within the borders of Kent. The fourth, from the eastern Saxons, was called East Saxony, and comprised London, Middlesex, Essex and part of Hertfordshire. The fifth, also called East Anglia from the east, extended through Norfolk, Suffolk, Cambridgeshire and the Isle of Ely. The sixth, situated inland, was called Mercia, from the English word for boundary or border of a region [Merce], because it was surrounded and enclosed by the borders of the others that touched it; or (as others prefer) from the Latin word for merchandise [Mercés], because the inland of the whole island was rich and abounded with goods brought in from every side. This kingdom extended widely through the counties of Lincoln, Northampton, Rutland, Huntingdon, Bedford, Buckingham, Oxford, Cheshire, Derby, Nottingham, Stafford, Warwick, Gloucester, Worcester, and part of Hereford. The seventh was the kingdom of the Northumbrians, which enclosed within its circuit the counties of York, Durham, Northumberland, Cumberland, Westmorland and Lancashire. In these seven kingdoms, seven bishoprics were first instituted in England by the Saxons after the reception of the Gospel, but in various and uncertain sees. Afterwards they were distinguished by orders and places, and their number was enlarged.

units.la: ORIGO ET MVTATIO SINGVLARVM EPISCOPALIVM SE- DIVM in Anglia, iuxta Heptarchiam.
units.tr: THE ORIGIN AND CHANGES OF THE SEVERAL EPISCOPAL SEES in England, according to the Heptarchy.

units.la: TAQVE in Cantii regno sub Ethelbertô rege, Augustinus Anglorum Episcopus ab Atclatensi Episcopo in Gallia ordinatus est, qui primam sedem reliquarum Metropoliticam Cantuaria locauit. In hac ipse Anglorum Apostolatum seu Episcopatum gessit annis 16. Posteaque iustum præsbyterum suum Roffensi sedi, quam instituit, præfecit. Eodemque anno in Eastsaxoniæ regno, Londinensi Episcopus Mellitus, qui Sebertō Regi orientalium Saxonum Euangelium nunciauit, ab eodē Augustino primus constituitur. Australium aūt Saxonū primus Episcopus fuit Wilfridus, qui Deiris & Bernicēfibus antea Eboraci præsidebat, sed inde ab Egfrido Rege pulsus, Romam profectus est, redieuntque in Angliam, cum à prouincialibus suis propter Regis offensam, recipi non poterat, venit ad Ethelwaldum Australiun Saxonum Regem in Mercia, quondam sub Wolfero Rege ab Egfrido victo & cieco baptizatum, australiesque Saxones fide primus imbuit Christiana. Huic Ethelwaldus Rex insulam quandam Seleheli.i. vitulorum Insulam nuncupatam donauit, in qua Mercios ab Egfrido, qui id regnum Marte superauerat, in exilium actos recipere: ibi Wilfridus Monasterium condidit, Merciōque ad se profugos, permultosque alios Monastica disciplina continuit, & illius regni Episcopatum gessit. Deinde Egfrido mortuo ad suos reuertus est. Itaque hic Australium Saxonum Episcopatus, ab Insulæ nomine, Selehensis primò dictus fuit: in quo cum viginti ordine sedissent Episcopi, à quodam Stigando 11. Episcopo ad Cicestrium, vbi nunc residet, traductus est. Westsaxoniam latam (vtante dixi mus) prouinciam primus ad fidem conuertit, & Pontificali authoritate rexit Birinus ab Honorio Pontifice ad Kinogilsum illius prouinciæ Regem missus. Hic Episcopalem sedem Dorcestriæ posuit. Sed vtroque tam Kinogifo Rege, quàm Birino antiliteritmortuo, Agilbertus quidam Gallus accitus ex Hybernia à Kinewalo Rege Kinogilsi filio, illius gentis Episcopus creabatur, quem quia Rex Gallicè loquentem vix intellexerat, suæ nationis atque linguæ virum facundum nomine Wina, in Gallia procurauit ordinari, posteá queprouinciam suam in duas distribuit parochias, alteramque Wentan.1. Wintonia statuit, cui in consulio Agilberto Wina præfecit, quod isiniquo animo ferentis in Gallias discesserit, ibique senio confectus moritur. Post hunc Wina solus totam Westsaxoniam prouinciam administrauit, quo casu Dorcestriæ sedes Episcopalis haberi desiit, & ab Wintonia aliquandiu abfuit. Sed Hedda secundus à Wina illius gentis Episcopus, inter quem & Winam Elentherius medius intercessit, Episcopalem sedem iterum Wintoniam reduxit, ibique sitmauit atque fixit. Itaque illa modica scriptorum dissensio, vtrum à Wina, an ab Hedda, Wintoniensis Episcoparus initium accepit, facilè dissoluitur, si existimauerimus id, quod à Wina inceptum & inchoatum fuit, ab Hedda perfectum & absolutum fuisse. Successione enim vicini, solo Eleutherio interiecto, fuerunt. Sed Hedda mortuo dissectus iterum in duas sedes Episcopatus fuit, vna Wintoniæ restabat, altera ad Shirbomiam, quæ Shirborn Monachorum in Southampronensi comitatu etiamnum dicitur, institiuta est. In hac Aldelmus primus sedit, post eum 25. quorum ultimus Osmundus eam sedem suam sub Edwardo Rege maiore Sa-
units.tr: And so, in the kingdom of Kent under King Ethelbert, Augustine, bishop of the English, was ordained by the bishop of Arles in Gaul, and he made Canterbury the metropolitan see, the first of the rest. In it he himself held the apostolate or bishopric of the English for sixteen years. Afterwards he set over the see of Rochester, which he founded, his own priest, Justus. In the same year, in the kingdom of East Saxony, Mellitus, who announced the gospel to Sebert, king of the East Saxons, was made the first bishop of London by the same Augustine. The first bishop of the South Saxons was Wilfrid, who had previously presided at York over the Deirans and Bernicians. Driven out from there by King Egfrid, he went to Rome, and when he came back to England he could not be received by his own people, because of the king's displeasure. He came to Ethelwald, king of the South Saxons in Mercia, who had once been baptized under King Wulfhere, after being defeated and blinded by Egfrid, and he was the first to imbue the South Saxons with the Christian faith. King Ethelwald gave him a certain island called Selsey, that is, the Island of Calves, where he was to receive the Mercians who had been driven into exile by Egfrid, who had overcome that kingdom in war. There Wilfrid founded a monastery, and he kept under his care the Mercians who had fled to him, and many others, in monastic discipline, and he held the bishopric of that kingdom. Then, when Egfrid had died, he returned to his own people. Thus this bishopric of the South Saxons was first called the Selsey see, from the name of the island. After twenty bishops had sat in it, it was transferred by a certain Stigand, the eleventh bishop, to Chichester, where it now resides. Birinus, sent by Pope Honorius to Kinegils, king of that province, was the first to convert West Saxony, a wide province, as I have said above, and to rule it with pontifical authority. He set the episcopal see at Dorchester. But when both King Kinegils and Birinus had died, a certain Gaul, Agilbert, was summoned from Ireland by King Kenwalh, son of Kinegils, and was made bishop of that people. Because the king had scarcely understood him speaking French, he arranged for a fluent man of his own nation and language, named Wine, to be ordained in Gaul. Afterwards Agilbert divided his province into two parishes, and set up the other at Wentan, that is, Winchester, and he placed Wine over it in Agilbert's place, because Agilbert, bearing this with an unhappy mind, went off to Gaul and there died worn out with age. After him Wine alone administered the whole province of West Saxony. By this chance the episcopal see at Dorchester ceased to be held, and it was for some time absent from Winchester. But Hedda, the second bishop of that people after Wine, with Eleutherius intervening between him and Wine, brought the episcopal see back again to Winchester, and there established and fixed it. Thus that slight disagreement among the writers, whether the bishopric of Winchester began with Wine or with Hedda, is easily resolved if we think that what was begun and initiated by Wine was completed and finished by Hedda. For they were successive, with only Eleutherius interposed. But when Hedda had died, the bishopric was again divided into two sees. One remained at Winchester, and the other was established at Sherborne, which is still called Sherborne Abbey in Hampshire. Aldhelm sat first in this see, and after him twenty-five, the last of whom, Osmund, moved his see under King Edward the Elder to Salisbury.

units.la: risburiam remouit. Tum ob huius prouinciæ magnitudinem tempore Edwardi Regis & Plegmundi Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi, tres aliæ sedes erectæ fuerunt: prima Wiltoniensis, siue Sunnangiensis, in qua Athelstanus primus, post quem 7. in ea sede fuerunt, sedebat. Hæc etiam dicti Regis tempore in Sarisburiam translata desiit. Secunda Cridinensis seu Vnnanicnsis, in qua Eadulphus primus fuit Episcopus, eique succedebant decem, quorum vltimus Owrus Cornubiensem prætulatum fuit copulauit. Quem sequutus Leofricus coniunctis illius sedes sub Edwardo rege, Exeniæ collocauit, vbi nunc sitæ sub vna permanent. Tertia fuit Wellensis, siue Fontanensis Ecclesia, in qua Althelmus, & Wulfhelmus, qui postea Cantuarienses Archiepiscopi fuerunt, ordine primi sedebant. Tum paulò post Iohannes de Villula, veterem illam Fontanensem Ecclesiam Bathoniam transtulit. Quæ duæ sedes in vnam iam diu coalescentes, ab vno Præsule regantur, prætinaque vtriusque sedis nomina tenent. In orientali Anglia quæ Northfolciam, Suffolciamque continet, primus Episcopatum gessit Fœlix natione Burgundus, qui Sigeberticum orientalium Anglorum Regem, Erthenwaldi Apostatæ filium in Christiana fide instituit, ad quod ab Honorio Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo missus est, An. Dom. 630. Hic Donwicki sedebat, cumque in illa sede sequuti tres, quorum Bisus vltimus, cum tanta corporis infirmitate laboraret, vt administrationi prouinciæ impar esset, diuisa in duas sedes Diocæsis fuit, quarum vna Donwicki, in comitatu Suffolciæ, altera Northelmæ in Norfolcia habebatur. Illius primus Episcopus Bradwinus, cui 12. huius Heatra, cui 10. successerunt. Et postquam in illis locis desierant Episcopales sedes in nouam sedem, quæ Thetfordia nuncupatur, per Herfastum Episcopum iterum coniunctus & mutatus illius regni Episcopatus fuit. Sed paucis deinde labentibus annis, Wilhelmo Rufo Angliæ regnum tenente, Herebertus Lofinga Eftangliæ Episcopus, Episcopatum illum Nordouici moderna in sede stabiliuit. Sequitur Merciorum regnum omnium maximum, & per plurimos comitatus diffusum. In quo Rex Penda (seu Pæda (cuius filius Weadda Eanfledam Ofwini Northumbrorum Regis Christiani filiam coniugali amore expetiuit, nuptiaque non alia conditione, quam si Weadda Christianus fieret, concilari potuissent) Euangelium prædicari permisit. Post has nuptias capitales intercesserunt Ofwino cum Penda inimicitiæ, bellumque atrox gestum, in quo Penda victus & interfectus est, & Ofwinus Merciorum regnum suo coniunxit, in eoque Diuinas quidam à Finano Dei-30 rx Bernicix que (de quibus proximo loco dicturi sumus) Secundo Episcopo, primus Merciorum Episcopus eius mandato ordinatus est. Hunc sine certa sede sequuti sex Merciorum Episcopi, quorum vltimus Sexulfus, latè patentem prouinciam Episcopalibus Ecclesiis 5. distinxit, tempore Regis Etheldredi, qui quartus post Pendam fuit. Quarum Ecclesiarum nominalia cum sint, Herefordensis, in qua Peuca: Wigornensis, in qua Bosetus: Lichfeldensis, quæ illius gentis primaria habita est, in qua Headda: Leogernensis siue Leycestrensis, in qua Wilfridus, & Lindesensis, in qua Geadethus primus sedebat: sed postea Celdredus Leycestrensis Episcopus oFauus & vltimus, hæc deserta ad Couentrensem Ecclesiam secessit, quam Petrus eius successor Lichfeldensis adunauit. Eodemque modo Ofwinus oFauus, & postremus Lindisensis Episcopus, suam parochiam 40 cum Leogernensi à Celdredo derelicta coniungens, vtramque Dorcestriam migrans secum transportauit: cuius sedis Eadulphus decimus & vltimus eam sedem ad veterem regionem reduxit, & Lincolnia fixit. Quæ diocæsis magnitudine laborans sua, detracta in Elienfi diocæsi (cuius primus Episcopus Herueus fuit) ab Henrico primo, nec non Petriburgensi, atque Oxoniensi ab Henrico octauo, etsi aliquantulum diminuia, Comitatuum tamen numero adhuc est maxima. Tres etiam alij Episcopatus ab eodem Rege Henrico 8. erectis: Brystolensis, Gloucestrensis, & Cestrensis, quæ Henrici 8. tempore Eboracensi prouinciæ additæ est. His itaque diocæsibus præter Cestrensem Cantuariensis prouincia tandem suis numeris perfecta & absoluta constat. Iamad Northumbrorum prouinciam & Eboracensem alteram Metropolitum vltimo loco accedimus, cuius Rex Edwinus, coniugata sibi Ethelberti Regis filia à Paulino primo Eboracensi Episcopo(quem Iustus Cant. Archiepiscopus ordinauit & Honorius Papa pallio donauit)ad fidem conuersus, coniugata cum regina pallioque in Cantium reuertfus est. Interea silebar in ea regione religio. Sed paulò post Ofwaldus Edwini frater, quituribaro, & alio occupato suo regno in Scotia exulauerat, Christianamque fidem acceperat, fratris regno restitutus, propagandæ per totam suam prouinciam Christianæ religionis cupiditate ductus, duabus regionibus Deiræ scilicet & Berniciæ, quæ totum Northumbrorum regnum cōtinet,
units.tr: Then, because of the size of this province, in the time of King Edward and of Plegmund, archbishop of Canterbury, three other sees were erected. The first was Wilton, or Sunningy, where Athelstan sat first, and after him seven in that see. This too, in the time of the said king, was transferred to Salisbury and ceased to exist. The second was Crediton, or Wunnanceaster, where Eadulf was the first bishop, and ten succeeded him, the last of whom, Oure, joined the Cornish prelacy. Following him, Leofric, having united their sees under King Edward, placed them at Exeter, where they now remain joined under one. The third was the church of Wells, or Fontanensis, in which Athelm and Wulfhelm, who afterwards became archbishops of Canterbury, sat first in order. Then, a little later, John de Villula transferred that old church of Wells to Bath. These two sees, long since coalesced into one, are now ruled by one prelate and keep the names of both. In East Anglia, which contains Norfolk and Suffolk, the first to hold the bishopric was Felix, a Burgundian by birth, who instructed Sigebert, king of the East Angles, son of the apostate Erkenwald, in the Christian faith. He was sent to do this by Honorius, archbishop of Canterbury, in the year of the Lord 630. He sat at Dunwich, and after him three sat in that see, the last of whom, Bisi, laboured under such bodily weakness that he was unequal to the administration of the province. The diocese was then divided into two sees, one at Dunwich in Suffolk, the other at North Elmham in Norfolk. Its first bishop was Bradwin, who was succeeded by twelve, and in this place Heathored by ten. And after the episcopal sees had ceased in those places, the bishopric of that kingdom was again joined and transferred, through Bishop Herfast, to a new see called Thetford. But a few years later, while William Rufus held the kingdom of England, Herbert Losinga, bishop of East Anglia, established that bishopric in its present see at Norwich. Next comes the kingdom of Mercia, the largest of all, spread over many counties. In it King Penda (or Peada), whose son Wedda sought in marriage Ealhflaed, daughter of Oswiu, the Christian king of the Northumbrians, and the marriage could be arranged only on condition that Wedda became a Christian, permitted the gospel to be preached. After this marriage, deadly enmity arose between Oswiu and Penda, and a fierce war was waged in which Penda was defeated and killed, and Oswiu joined the kingdom of Mercia to his own. In it, a certain Diuma, sent by Finan, second bishop of the Deirans and Bernicians (of whom we shall speak in the next place), was ordained by his command as the first bishop of the Mercians. After him six bishops of the Mercians followed without a fixed see, the last of whom, Sexwulf, divided the widely extended province into five episcopal churches in the time of King Ethelred, who was the fourth after Penda. The names of these churches are Hereford, in which Putta sat; Worcester, in which Bosel; Lichfield, which was regarded as the chief of that people, in which Headda; Leicester, or Leicester, in which Wilfrid; and Lindsey, in which Geadda was the first to sit. But afterwards Ceolred, bishop of Leicester, the last of that line, deserted it and withdrew to the church of Coventry, which his successor Peter, bishop of Lichfield, united to his own see. In the same way Oswin, the last bishop of Lindsey, uniting his parish with Leicester, which had been abandoned by Ceolred, moved both to Dorchester and carried them with him there. Eadwulf, the tenth and last bishop of that see, brought it back to its old region and fixed it at Lincoln. This see, labouring under the burden of its own great size, had parts taken away from it: the diocese of Ely, whose first bishop was Hervey, was detached from it by Henry I; and likewise Peterborough and Oxford by Henry VIII. Though these were somewhat reduced, the see still has the largest number of counties. Three other bishoprics were also erected by the same King Henry VIII: Bristol, Gloucester, and Chester, and Chester was added to the province of York in the time of Henry VIII. Thus, except for Chester, the province of Canterbury, with these dioceses, stands complete and finished in its proper numbers. Now we come, in the last place, to the province of the Northumbrians and the second metropolitan see, York. Its king, Edwin, after marrying the daughter of King Ethelbert, was converted to the faith by Paulinus, the first bishop of York (whom Justus, archbishop of Canterbury, ordained, and Pope Honorius gave the pallium). Having married the queen, he returned to Kent with the pallium. Meanwhile religion lay silent in that region. But a little later Oswald, brother of Edwin, who had gone into exile in Scotland when another man had seized his kingdom, and had received the Christian faith there, was restored to his brother's kingdom. Moved by a desire to spread the Christian religion throughout his whole province, he set over the two regions of Deira and Bernicia, which make up the whole kingdom of the Northumbrians, Aidan, who had been ordained in Scotland.

units.la: Ioan. 3. tinet, Aidanum in Scotia ordinatum praefecit. Harum regionum Episcopatus, Meirnolefis primo dicebatur, postea Lindisfarnensis ob Insulae nomen, in qua Aidanus Christi Ecclesiam aedificauit, & Episcopatus sedem posuit. Post Aidanum rres Episcopi ibi sederunt. Virinus Tudda: quo defuncto Alefredus Northumbriae Rex misit Wilfridum (postea australium Saxonum Episcopum, cuius ante meminimus) ad Agilberrum Parisiorum in Gallia Episcopum, sui regni Episcopum consecrandum. Cum q; moram diuturniorem in Gallia Wilfridus fecisset, Rex Osvini filii sui suasu misit Ceddam a Cant. Archiepiscopo, ad Eboracensem iterum praesulatum ordinandum, qui in peregrinatione erans peruenit ad Winam primum Wintoniensem Episcopum, ab eoq; sacratus, Eboracum Archiepiscopali authoritate reuertus rexit. Postea rediit Wilfridus, cuius aduentu Cedda secessit in Monasterium Lestingha, & Wilfridus Archiepiscopatum suscepit, solusq; totam prouinciam gessit. Orta deinde inter eū & Egfridum Regem, vt ante diximus, dissensione, australes Saxones petiit, cuiusq; loco Bosa Eboraci successit. Inde huc vsque Archiepiscopalis dignitas Eboraci continuo retentata est. Quae Metropolis habet 12. parochias quondam continebat. Ecclesiam beatae Mariae prope ciuitatem, vlita amnem Vse: Ecclesias Riponensem, Beuerlacensem, Dunelmensem, Lindefurnensem, Haggelstal. defem. Candidae case vel Galoudiae, Deiterem, Bernicienem, Cumbrensem iuxte Carleolensem, Ceftrensem & Ecclesiam Pictorum, praeter Ecclesias Scoticas, in quibus ante separata regna crebris se bellis infestantia, Eboracensis Archiepiscopus Metropolitani & Primatisiure fungebatur. Et longe postquam diuisa essent regna, ob eamq; diuisionem defecisset ab Eboracensi Metropoli Scotia, quidam Foderochus Ecclesiae S. Andreae (quae postea Scotiae Metropolis fuit) Episcopus, venit ad Thomam tunc Eboracensem Archiepiscopum, deliberatumq; fassus est, quod ab Anglicana Ecclesia defecisset, ad quod Malcholini Regis, & Reginae Margaretae concilio & imperio adductus fuit, ne contra patrum decreta quicquam Eboracensis sedi detraheret. Huic Thomae Vrbanus Papa exprobrat, quod tam facile professionem subiectionis Cantuariensis Archiepiscopo profecisset, in praeiudicium Romanae Ecclesiae, quae pacatas controuersias soler reftitucere, vt appellatione sua ad Papam facta lucri aliquid accrescerent. Hunc Thomam sequitus est, post Girardum, qui t6. Archiepiscopus fuit, alter Thomas dictus iunior, qui hos Episcopos in Scotia consecrauit, Michaelem Episcopum Glasquensem, Wimundum de Syder, & Radulphum ab Orcadensibus electū, qui tum presbyter fuit in Ecclesia S. Petri Eboraci. Eboracensis etiam sedes habet sibi subditum Sodorensem Episcopatum in insula Manna, quę Monaida, seu Monauia, quam Anglii Mannam vocant, appellatur. Hane falso credit Polydorus esse Monam veterem Druidum Insulam, quae iam Anglesea vocatur. Itaque causa non est, cur a Cantuariensi illatam in parochiarum paucitate Eboracensi sedi minuriam, quis quaeratur aut existimet. Modernae enim, & praesentis paucitatis non tam Cantuariensis quam ipsos Eboracenses Archiepiscopus authores fuisse ecerum est. Quas quinque dioeceses, primam vltra amnem Vse in Ecclesia Christi prope ciuitatem: secundam ad Ripon: terriam ad Beuerlay positam: quartam in Haugustaldensi Ecclesia: & quintam in casa candida locatam ipsa Metropolis devoraui, & in suum corpus traiecit, vt auioris verbis vtar: multo alter quam Cantuariensis Metropolis, quae Archiepiscopatu tantum Cambriam priuauit, & sedem Meneuensem in Episcopalem mutauit, illamq; prouinciam suae Cantuariensi subiicit: nec vt Eboracensis, vastaur penitus & abforsit. A quo tantum abfuit, vt a proximis finitimisq; sibi sedibus destruendis abhorruit, vt quia vicinum Episcopum sibi originis necessitudine coniunctum habere voluit, non in aliena, sed in propria Cantii parochia nouam Episcopalem sedem Roffae constituerat. Itaque adiunctis & unitis Eboracensi Metropoli, seu potius in eum modum exhaustis praedictis quinque dioecesibus, vt indigenis nō modo memoriam, sed nc suspicione sui vllam reliquerint tum Albania Pictorum, dioecesi detracta duae tantum superfuerunt subiectae: Cumbrensis olim, iam Carlilensis diocesis parochia, & Dunelmensis, quae sua freta potentia etiam eum Metropoli contendebat, & ab eius subiectione se ex ius proprie vendicare nisa est. Quibus ad dilatandū illius Metropolis territorium in Ceftrenfi coenobio erectus ab Henrico octauo, Episcopatus restitutus & adiectus est. Pictorum autem Episcopalem sedem (cuius Bedam meminit) ignorat praedictus Nicholaus.
units.tr: Ioan. 3. continet, appointed Aidan as bishop of these regions while he was ordained in Scotland. The see of these regions was first called Meirnolefis, and afterwards Lindisfarne, from the name of the island in which Aidan built the Church of Christ and established the seat of the bishopric. After Aidan, three bishops sat there: Virinus, Tuda and Tudda. When Tudda died, Alfred, king of Northumbria, sent Wilfrid (afterwards bishop of the South Saxons, whom we mentioned earlier) to Agilbert, bishop of Paris in Gaul, to be consecrated as bishop of his kingdom. When Wilfrid had stayed a long time in Gaul, King Oswy, at the urging of his son, sent Chad from Archbishop Deusdedit to be ordained again to the see of York. On his journey he came to Wine, the first bishop of Winchester, who consecrated him; returning to York with archiepiscopal authority, he governed the see. Afterwards Wilfrid came back, and on his arrival Chad withdrew to the monastery at Lastingham, and Wilfrid took up the archbishopric and alone administered the whole province. Then, as we said before, a quarrel arose between him and King Ecgfrith, and he went to the South Saxons; in his place Bosa succeeded at York. From then until now the dignity of the archbishopric of York has been continuously maintained. This metropolis has twelve parishes, which once comprised: the Church of St Mary near the city, beyond the river Ouse; the churches of Ripon, Beverley, Durham, Lindisfarne, Hexham, Whitby (or Galloway), Dehere, Bernicia, Cumbria near Carlisle, Chester, and the Church of the Picts; besides the Scottish churches, in which, while the kingdoms were separate and often at war with one another, the archbishop of York exercised metropolitan and primatial jurisdiction. And long after the kingdoms had been divided, and Scotland on account of that division had withdrawn from the metropolis of York, a certain Fothad, bishop of the Church of St Andrews (which afterwards became the metropolis of Scotland), came to Thomas, then archbishop of York, and confessed that he had deliberately withdrawn from the English Church; he had been led to do so by the counsel and command of King Malcolm and Queen Margaret, so that he would not take anything away from the see of York contrary to the decrees of the Fathers. Pope Urban rebukes this Thomas, because he had so readily made a profession of subjection to the archbishop of Canterbury, to the prejudice of the Roman Church, which is accustomed to restore settled controversies, so that some gain might accrue to it from an appeal made to the Pope. After this Thomas came another Thomas, called the Younger, who succeeded Girard, the sixth archbishop; he consecrated these bishops in Scotland: Michael, bishop of Glasgow; Wimund of Sodor; and Radulph, elected by the people of Orkney, who was then a priest in the Church of St Peter at York. The see of York also has the bishopric of Sodor subject to it, in the Isle of Man, which is called Monaida or Monavia, and which the English call Man. Polydore falsely believes this to be Mona, the ancient island of the Druids, now called Anglesey. Therefore there is no reason why anyone should seek or suppose that the smallness of the York see in the number of parishes was caused by Canterbury. For it is well known that the present and recent small number was brought about not so much by the archbishop of Canterbury as by the archbishops of York themselves as its authors. For the metropolis itself, as I may use the words of an author, devoured the five dioceses mentioned above, namely: the first beyond the Ouse, in the Church of Christ near the city; the second at Ripon; the third placed at Beverley; the fourth in the church of Hexham; and the fifth located at Whitby, and drew them into its own body, far differently from the metropolis of Canterbury, which deprived Wales only of its archbishopric and changed the see of Menevia into a bishopric, subjecting that province to its own Canterbury; nor did it lay waste and wholly swallow up these sees as York did. Canterbury was so far from shrinking from the destruction of neighbouring and adjoining sees that, because it wished to have a neighbouring bishop joined to itself by ties of origin, it set up a new episcopal see at Rochester, not in foreign territory but in its own parish of Kent. Therefore, when the aforesaid five dioceses had been added and united to the metropolis of York, or rather drained in that manner, so that they left to the natives not only no memory but no suspicion of themselves, then, with the diocese of Scotland (Albania of the Picts) taken away, only two subject dioceses remained: the one formerly of Cumbria, now a parish of the diocese of Carlisle, and that of Durham, which, relying on its own power, even contended with the metropolis and tried to claim its own right, independent of its subjection to it. To extend the territory of that metropolis, a bishopric erected by Henry VIII in the monastery of Chester was restored and added to them. As for the episcopal see of the Picts (of which Bede makes mention), the aforesaid Nicholas is ignorant of it.

units.la: Nunc vtriusque prouinciae dioeceses cum comitatibus quos nunc obtinent, repetamus. Ceftriam itaq; Ceftriam, Comitatum & Rychmondia & Lancastriam, partemq; Flynt & Dynbigh in Wallia comitatuum continet. Dunelmensis autem ipsum Dunelmensem atq; Northubriā: Carlisle, Cubria, Westmoriam Westbumbriamq; comitatus cingit.
units.tr: Now let us repeat the dioceses of each province together with the counties which they now hold. The diocese of Chester therefore contains the county of Chester, Richmond and Lancaster, and part of the counties of Flint and Denbigh in Wales. The diocese of Durham contains Durham itself and Northumberland. Carlisle encloses the counties of Cumberland, Westmorland and Westbumbria.

units.la: Istis sex comitatibus adiecti duo, qui Eboracensem diocæsem statuunt: ipsum nempe Eboracum & Nottinghamia prouinciam ipsam absoluunt: altehius autem prouinciæ, quæ tam ditione quam iurisdictione maior est, sunt in Anglia 18. dioeceses. Cantuarien sis cum Roffeoli, ipsum Cantium comitatum continet. Loodiocnsis quoq; Essexiam, Midelsexiam, partemq; Hertfordensis comitatus, Ciceftrensis Southsexiam, Wiotonien sis Southamtonensem, Surram & Vedem Insulam: Sarisburiensis Wilcheriam, & Bercheriam: Exoniensis & Deuoniam & Cornubiam. Bathoniensis & Welilensis simul iunctæ Somersetum. Glocestrensis Glocestrensem : Wigorniensis Wigorniensem, & partem Waruicensis: Herefordensis Herefordeolem, & partem Salopiensis: Couentrensis & Lichfeldensis vna copulatæ, Staffordensem, Derbiensem, &c; reliquam partem Warwicensis, nec non Salopiensis, & partem eam, quæ ad Repillum fluuiom spectat. Tum Lincolniesem omnium maximam sex terminant comitatus, Lincolniensis, Leycestrensis, Huntingtona, Bedfordiensis, Buckinganiesis, & reliqua pars Hertefordensis: Elienensem, Cantabrigia, ipsaque Elis Insula: Nordouiceniensis, Norfolcia atq; Suffolcia. Oxfordiensem Oxfordiensis: Petersburgensem Northamptona, & Rutlandia: Bristoliensem; Dorcestria. Quibus 18. in Anglio dioecesibus, addendæ sunt Walliæue Cambriæ diocæses, quæ & Archiepiscopatu proprio priuatæ, & oumero extenuatæ sunt, septe videlicet in quatuor abeuntibus, quæ sunt: Mencuensis, quæ ad sanú S. Dahidis sedet, Landauensis, Banchorensis, & Asiaensis siue Elwensis. In exteris antiquioribus mutationes ex causis suo ordine in hac historia recensendis contigere. Gulielmi etiam Regis tempore, sub Lanfranco Cant. Archiepiscopo in concilio Londinii habito, constitu-tum & decretum fuit, ut Episcoporum sedes, quæ vt diximus, in frequentatis a populo iocis non erant, sed in abditis atq; solitariis, iam ad ciuitates & celebriora regni loca migrarent. Vnde Dorcestrensis sedes primo Lincolniâ, ac Lichfeldensis Cestriâ, Ramesburiensis & Schirburoensis Sarisburiâ, Wellensis Bathoniâ, Cornubiensis & Cridiensis Exoestria deducta sunt. Tum Oriecotales ac Mediterranei Saxones, qui vuigatos Eslexiae & Midde-lesexiae comitatus incolent, Londinensi dioecesi subiiciuntur. Adhæc septentrionales & australes Anglos, populù latè patenté, qui Norfolciae Suffolci dicûtur, duabus dioecesibus primò distinctos, vna tandem dioecesis Thetfordiæ primo instituta, indeq; Norvicum translata, continebat. Elienfis verò sedes, quæ primò Monasterium fuerat, à Lincolniensicui subiectus, separata, sua dioeceß, sub Henrico 1. Rege instituta, Cantabrigiâ sem comitatum & insulam Elienensem complexa est: Quod Lincolniensi iurisdictioni detractâ territorium ab Henrico Rege datâ io ciusdé Episcopi dildonem Spalding, vrbe Regia compensatum est.
units.tr: To these six counties are added two which make up the diocese of York: namely York itself, and Nottingham, which completes the province itself; but the other province, which is greater both in wealth and in jurisdiction, has eighteen dioceses in England. Canterbury, together with Rochester, contains the county of Kent itself. London also contains Essex, Middlesex, and part of the county of Hertford. Chichester contains Sussex; Winchester, Southampton, Surrey and the Isle of Wight; Salisbury, Wiltshire and Berkshire; Exeter, Devon and Cornwall. Bath and Wells, joined together, hold Somerset. Gloucester holds Gloucestershire; Worcester holds Worcestershire and part of Warwickshire; Hereford holds Herefordshire and part of Shropshire; Coventry and Lichfield, united as one, hold Staffordshire, Derbyshire, etc., the rest of Warwickshire, as well as Shropshire, and that part which faces the river Trent. Then Lincoln, the largest of all, is bounded by six counties: Lincolnshire, Leicestershire, Huntingdonshire, Bedfordshire, Buckinghamshire, and the rest of Hertfordshire. Ely contains Cambridge and the Isle of Ely itself. Norwich contains Norfolk and Suffolk. Oxford is coextensive with Oxfordshire. Peterborough contains Northamptonshire and Rutland. Bristol, Dorset. To these eighteen English dioceses must be added the dioceses of Wales, which have been deprived of their own archbishopric and reduced in number, namely seven have passed into four, which are: Menevia, which sits at the shrine of St David; Llandaff; Bangor; and Asaph or Elfael. In the other, older sees changes occurred for causes which will be recounted in their proper order in this history. In the time of King William, too, under Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, it was established and decreed in a council held at London that the seats of the bishops, which, as we have said, were not in places frequented by the people but in hidden and solitary spots, should now migrate to cities and more famous places of the kingdom. Hence the see of Dorchester was first moved to Lincoln, and that of Lichfield to Chester; the sees of Ramsbury and Sherborne to Salisbury; Wells to Bath; and those of Cornwall and Crediton to Exeter. Then the Eastern and Middle Saxons, who inhabit the counties of Essex and Middlesex, were made subject to the diocese of London. Moreover, the northern and southern English, a widely spread people called Norfolk and Suffolk, were first divided into two dioceses, and afterwards one diocese, first established at Thetford and then transferred from there to Norwich, contained them. The see of Ely, which had first been a monastery, was separated from its subjection to Lincoln and, established as its own diocese under King Henry I, embraced Cambridgeshire and the Isle of Ely; because territory had been taken away from the jurisdiction of Lincoln, it was compensated by King Henry with the town of Spalding, a royal town, given to the same bishop.

units.la: Nunc Episcoporum vtriusq; prouinc. æ numero descripto, eorum etiam munera, quæ vt suffraganei Archiepiscopo suo præstabant, communę munerum dignitates, quibus alterum antecellit, explicemus. Magnopere enim semper laborabant in loco aliquo & dignitate pares Primatem & Metropolitanum suum haberi. Idq; & suum proprium, & sedis suæ honorem maximum esse putabant. Primus itaque sub primate honos, Londinensi Episcopo delatus est. Is in Synodo & Collegio Episcoporum, Cant: prouincie Decanus dictus est. Qui quicquid à Metropolitano decretum per prouinciam fiiam mandabatur, literis suis ad inferiores præsules exequutus, debitæ iuxe exequutioois eundem per literas mandato remissio fecit certiorem. Itaq; per huoc, & totius prouinciæ Cleros ad Synodos celebrandas conuocari, & legitima primatis fui monita peragere confuerunt. Tum in profligatis illis papisticis ritibus pompolis atq; solennibus, io synodis & conuentibus sleri, coram Archiepiscopo fuit Millidicus. Ob quæ vomima munera, io synodis & sessionibus Episcoporum, proximus illi Archiepiscopo locus à dexteris concessus est, nisi Eboracensis adesset, quo intercuniente & a dextris sedente, Londinensis sinistras obtinuit. Post Londonensem Wintoniensis in summo honore apud primatem fuit, quia Cancellarius eius nomioabatur. Huius proprium munus fuit in missis, in synodo per Londinensem celebratis, auream pacem accipere, eandemq; ad Archiepiscopum osculandam deferre, & alcari reterte. Sed & Londioensi sede vacante, Episcopatui in remotis agente, Wintoniensis eius vices suscepit, & Subdecanus Cant. prouincia dicebatur. Huius honoris causa, vt Londinensis dextras, sic Wintoniensis sinistras Archiepiscopo proximus occupauit. Sed Eboracesi præsente, à sinistris propter Londinensem sedebat. Quàm grata autem fuissent Suffraganeis hæc honoris officia, sub primate suo gesta, ex Iohannis Pountois Winton. Episcopi literis, Richardi Grauefend, tunc Episcopi Londinen. mortui vices ageotis, ad Iohannem Peckam Cant. Archiepiscopum scriptis apparet.
units.tr: Now that the number of the bishops of both provinces has been described, let us also explain their duties, which they performed as suffragans to their archbishop, and the common dignities of office by which one excels another. For they always laboured greatly to be considered, in some place and dignity, peers of their primate and metropolitan. And they thought this was both their own proper honour and the greatest honour of their see. The first honour below the primate was therefore conferred on the bishop of London. He was called dean in the synod and college of the bishops of the province of Canterbury. Whatever was decreed by the metropolitan and sent through the province, he carried out by his letters to the inferior prelates, and he informed the primate by letter that the due execution had been carried out. Thus, through him, the clergy of the whole province were accustomed to be summoned to hold synods and to carry out the lawful admonitions of their primate. Then, in those abolished papistical rites, the pompous and solemn ones, when something was done in the synods and assemblies before the archbishop, he was the one who read out the ... (?) Because of these first duties, in the synods and sessions of the bishops, the place next to the archbishop was granted on his right; but if the archbishop of York was present, the bishop of London, who sat on his right when the other intervened, took the left. After London, the bishop of Winchester held the highest honour with the primate, because he was called his chancellor. It was his particular duty, in masses celebrated by the bishop of London in the synod, to receive the golden peace and carry it to the archbishop to be kissed, and to bring it back to the altar. But also when the see of London was vacant, the bishop being absent on business, the bishop of Winchester took over his duties and was called sub-dean of the province of Canterbury. For this honour he occupied the place on the right of the archbishop, just as the bishop of London did, and the place on the left, but when the archbishop of York was present he sat on the left next to the bishop of London. How welcome these honorary duties performed under their primate were to the suffragans appears from the letters of John Pontoise, bishop of Winchester, written to John Peckham, archbishop of Canterbury, on behalf of Richard Gravesend, then acting for the deceased bishop of London.

units.la: Ex Archivo
units.tr: From the archive.

units.la: Epistola Iohannis Winton. ad Iohannem Peckam Cant. Archiepiscopum.
units.tr: The letter of John of Winchester to John Peckham, Archbishop of Canterbury.

units.la: Eucre dissimo in Christo Patri & Domino charissimo, suus devotus Capellanus, quicquid potest obedientiæ, reuerentiæ & honoris. Præeminentiæ vestræ literas per harum baiulum nobis missas recepimus 11. die Decembris, quæ mixturam quandam doloris & gaudii continebant: Inücit nimirum animo nostro mæstitiâ, quòd hominê gratum Deo, iustû, mâsuetum & pium, & his diebus malis regno Angliæ tam necessarium, bonæ memoriæ Dominum, Richardum Londini Episcopum ab hac luce mors amara subtraxit, sed materiam quandam gaudi & cõsolationis submi nistrat, quòd excellentiam vestram, ad nostra, & Ecclesiæ nostræ Winton. iura conseruanda & augenda literarum earundem relatu cognouimus quandam spiritualis dilectionis prærogatiua folicitam & internam, pro quo vestræ dignationi gratæ licet exiles & tantis meritis impares, quantas pro tempore possumus exhibemus. Ex hoc nempe laudis & honoris titulum vestra præcellens dignitas promeretur, quæ ramen fe reputat honoratam, cùm, qui singulis quibusq; debetur fratribus, honor debitus non negatur. Ait enim beatus Gregorius: meus honor est fratrum meorum solidus vigor. Verùm quia alibi scribitur, tempore indigemus, vt aliquid maturius agamus, ne præcipitemus consilia & operanostra, neque eorum ordinem corrumpamus, deliberanone nostram super hoc fecimus. Quod eiùs vices eo mortuo vel absente, gerere & exequi ad nos tanquam ad vestrorum Suffraganeorum Subdecanum iure coniugudinario dictas pertinere, consultis nostris dilectis filiis, Priore & Capitulo nostro Wintoni: cum omni celeritate accommoda absque morâ dispendio rescribemus: firmum semper habentes propositum & promptum gerere animum ad vestra præcepta & beneplacita exequenda. Incolumitatem vestram in longa tempora protendat altissimus ad regimen Ecclesiæ sponsæ suæ. Scriptum apud Farnham die prædicto.
units.tr: To the most reverend father in Christ and most dear lord, his devoted chaplain offers whatever obedience, reverence and honour he can. We received on the 11th day of December your letter, sent to us by the bearer of these presents, which contained a mixture of grief and joy. Grief, indeed, has crept into our minds because the bitter hand of death has taken from this light the good lord Richard, Bishop of London, a man of blessed memory, pleasing to God, just, gentle and pious, and very necessary to the realm of England in these evil days. But it also supplies a matter for joy and consolation: from the account of that letter we have learned that your excellency, zealous and diligent in keeping and enlarging the rights of our Church of Winchester and of ourselves, has a certain prerogative of spiritual affection towards us. For this we offer your dignity, though we are humble and unequal to such great merits, as much service as we can for the time being. Your preeminent dignity earns from this the title of praise and honour, yet it considers itself honoured, since the honour due to each of the brethren is not withheld. For blessed Gregory says: "My honour is the firm vigour of my brethren." But because it is written elsewhere that we need time in order to act with more maturity, so that we do not rush our counsels and deeds or upset their order, we have made our deliberation on this matter. As to the fact that, with him dead or absent, it belongs to us, as subdean of your suffragans, by customary right to exercise and carry out his duties, we will reply, after consulting our beloved sons, our Prior and Chapter of Winchester, with all speed, without delay or expense, always holding the firm purpose and a ready mind to carry out your commands and pleasure. May the Most High extend your safety for a long time for the governance of his spouse, the Church. Written at Farnham on the aforesaid day.

units.la: Capellanus vester Wintoniensis.
units.tr: Your chaplain of Winchester.

units.la: Nam præter dictas eminentias & prærogatiuas, etiam Reges Londinensib. & Winron. Episcopis, Archiepiscopis Cant. mortuis vel absentibus, tanquam eorum Vicarii in Coronatione vngi & sacrari solebant. Quaratione Edwardus Rex eius nominis II. ab Hentico Woodlock Wintoniensi Episcopo consecratus fuit, absentis Archiepiscopi mandato, quòd Robertus Winchelsheytum Archiepiscopus ab exilio, in quod ab Edwardo 1. actus erat nondum reuersus fuerat, vt in vita ciusdem Roberti deinceps declarabitur. Post Wintoniensem Lincolniensis Vicecancellarius fuit: Tum Salisburiensis Præcentor: deinde Wigorniensis Capellanus & Roffensis Cruciger Metropolitani fuit fuerunt.
units.tr: For besides the said eminences and prerogatives, the kings were also accustomed to be anointed and consecrated at their coronation by the Bishops of London and Winchester, as vicars of the Archbishop of Canterbury when he was dead or absent. In this way Edward II was consecrated by Henry Woodlock, Bishop of Winchester, by the command of the absent Archbishop, because Robert Winchelsey, the Archbishop, had not yet returned from the exile into which he had been driven by Edward I, as will be declared hereafter in the life of the same Robert. After Winchester, he was Vice-Chancellor of Lincoln; then Precentor of Salisbury; then Chaplain of Worcester, and Cross-bearer of the Metropolitan of Rochester.

units.la: Quibus honoribus & Primati suo ar&tius denuncabantur, & præ ceteris illustriotes habebantur. Atque hoc in loco commodum est, eas quoque profecturas, quasin sefionibus supremi Concilii, quod Parlamentum dicitur, vtriusque prouinciæ tenent Episcopi recensere. Primo itaque loco seder Cant. 2. Euorac. Archiepiscopus; 3. Londinensis Episcopus; 4. Dunelbensis; 5. Wintonienfis, qui & nobilitati illius ordinis in Angliaga Ter ii Præsatus procerum illius ordinis interiori semper adest cohilio. Reliqui post hos 5. Episcopos sine sedium suarum discrimine, vt consecratione priores, ita locis potiores & digniores censentur. Quod si quis Episcoporum Regi fuerit à secretis, is post 5. Episcopos prædictus primus locum capit.
units.tr: These honours and dignities were also more closely announced to their Primate, and were regarded as more illustrious than the rest. And here it is fitting to list also the seats which the bishops of each province hold in the sessions of the supreme council which is called Parliament, since they will be useful. In the first place sits the Archbishop of Canterbury; second, the Archbishop of York; third, the Bishop of London; fourth, the Bishop of Durham; fifth, the Bishop of Winchester, who also, as the aforesaid, is always present in the inner council of the nobles of that order in England. The rest after these five bishops are regarded as more worthy and more important in place, without regard to the arrangement of their seats, as they were earlier in consecration. But if any bishop has been a secretary to the King, he takes the first place after the aforesaid five bishops.

units.la: Atque hi quidem prouinciales Episcopi Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi Suffraganei censentur & appellantur. Habent & ipsi sub se suffraganeos, qui ea, absentibus Episcopis, vel aliis grauioribus occupationibus detentis, gerunt, quæ ordinis tantum, non Iurisdictionis Episcopalis sunt. Sed & hi consecrationem ab Archiepiscopo Cant. percipiunt, professionemq; Archiepiscopo iurant. Loca autem in quibus licet Episcopis suos suffraganeos constituere sunt hæc.
units.tr: These provincial bishops are reckoned and called suffragans of the Archbishop of Canterbury. They also have suffragans under them, who carry out, when the bishops are absent or occupied with other weightier business, those things which pertain only to order and not to episcopal jurisdiction. But these also receive consecration from the Archbishop of Canterbury and swear the oath of profession to the Archbishop. The places in which bishops may appoint their suffragans are these.

units.la: Ac postquam Cantuariensem sedem dignitate sua Eboracensem ita vicisse dociuimus, videamus quomodo Oceanum ipsum transiens tandem Hiberniam, ipsamq; Galliam intrisdictione superauit. Hybernenses Episcopos à suis postulatos, vel electos à Cantuariensibus Archiepiscopis, confirmari atque sacrari solitos esse, ex his constare potest. Quod defuncto Donato Dublinie ciuitatis Episcopo, populi cleriq; cum consensu, quidam Coenobii S. Albani Monachus Hybernensis vocatus Samuel, electus fuit à Rege Hiberniæ qui Mutierdach tum dicebatur, communiq; decreto, vt secundum gentis illius antiquum morem à Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo sacrandus ad Anshelmum missus est.
units.tr: And after we have shown that the see of Canterbury surpassed the see of York in its dignity, let us see how, crossing the ocean itself, it finally extended its jurisdiction over Ireland and even over Gaul.
