From this it can be established that the Irish bishops, when nominated by their people or elected, were accustomed to be confirmed and consecrated by the Archbishops of Canterbury. When Donatus, bishop of the city of Dublin, had died, with the consent of the people and clergy, a certain monk of the monastery of St Alban, an Irishman called Samuel, was chosen by the King of Ireland, who was then called Muirchertach, and by common decree he was sent to Anselm to be consecrated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, according to the ancient custom of that people.

units.la: Qui hominem aliquandiu secū honorifice detinuit, & de Ecclesia Dei secundū eius verbum regēdum diligenter instructum, & canonicā subiectionem ex visitato veteriq; more professum in Episcopatus Dublinensis officium promouit. Hæc autem consecratio octauo die post Pasche festum ab Anselmo mirisfrantibus sibi in hoc officio, quatuor prouinciæ Cantuariensis Episcopis suffraganeis suis Wintoniæ celebrabatur. Qui nouus Dublinie Episc. tanti patris benedictione literarum de sua consecratione, Regi populoque Hyberniæ scriptarum testimonio gaudens, a popularibus suis reditum eius gratulanubus, in suam sedem honorifice susceptur. Hæc autem Cantuariensis sedis auctoritas ab Eugenio Pontifice aliquantulum labefactata posse videri. Quin Iohannem quendā Romanæ Ecclesiæ Cardinalem præsbyterū cognomento Paparo destinauit legatum in Hyberniam cum quatuor pallijs, quorum vnum Episcopo Dublinie impartiuit, & reliqua tria tribus aliis Hybernie Episcopis, subiectiq; eorum vnicuiq; 5. aliis Episcopos.
units.tr: Anselm kept the man with him for some time with honour, and, having diligently instructed him in governing the Church of God according to his word, and having him profess canonical obedience according to the accustomed and ancient custom, he promoted him to the office of the see of Dublin. This consecration was celebrated by Anselm on the eighth day after the feast of Easter at Winchester, with four bishops of the province of Canterbury, his suffragans, assisting him in this office. The new bishop of Dublin, rejoicing in the blessing of so great a father and in the testimony of the letters written about his consecration to the King and people of Ireland, was received honourably into his see by his countrymen, who congratulated him on his return. Moreover, the authority of the see of Canterbury may seem to have been somewhat weakened by Pope Eugenius. Indeed, he sent as legate to Ireland a certain John, a priest and cardinal of the Roman Church, surnamed Paparo, with four pallia, one of which he gave to the bishop of Dublin, and the other three to three other Irish bishops, and each of these had five other bishops subject to him.

units.la: Tamen & hoc contra consuetudinē antiquorum, & dignitatē Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ, à qua solebant Hyberniæ Episcopi consecrationis accipere benedictionē & non tam ad Cantuariensis sedis minuedā authoritatē, quā ad certū Episcoporū numerū statuendū, q pro Metropolitani olim indistinctè arbitrio multiplicabantur, vt singulì Episcopi plures Episcopatus quasi parochiatim & ecclesiatim possiderent, factum fuisse decernitur. Ab Anshelmo enim iterum petitum ab Hybernensibus alterius Episcopi consecrationis auxilium certum est ex Regis prædicti, Episcoporum atque procerum ad cundem literis. Quod totum negotium atq; decretum inseruimus, ne rei gestæ veritatem v el verbo tenus immutasse videamur.
units.tr: Yet it is decided that this too was done contrary to the ancient custom and to the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, from which the Irish bishops were accustomed to receive the blessing of consecration. This was done not so much to diminish the authority of the see of Canterbury as to fix a certain number of bishops, which formerly had been multiplied at the indiscriminate discretion of the metropolitans, so that individual bishops possessed several bishoprics, as it were parish by parish and church by church. It is certain that the Irish asked Anselm again for the help of another bishop's consecration, as is clear from the letters of the aforesaid King, bishops and nobles to the same Anselm. We have inserted this whole business and decree so that we may not seem to have altered the truth of the event even in words.

units.la: Rex Hybernia Murchertachus nomine, & Dofnaldus Episcopus cum czteris Episcopis: & quique nobiles cum clero & populo ipsius Insulæ miserunt nuncios ad literas ad Anhselmum, innotefcêtes ei quandam ciuitatem Watesferdiam nomine, in vna suarum prouinciarum esse, cui ob numerosam ciuium multitudinem expediret Episcopum institui, simulque petentes, quatenus ipse primatus quem super eos gerebat potestate, & qua sungebatur apostolica fretus auctoritate, sanctæ Christianitati ac necessariæ pleiun vilitati instituendo eis Pontificem subueniret. Iam enim secula multa transiegant, in quibus eadem ciuitas absque prudentia & cura pontificali consistens per diuersa tentationum pericula iactabatur. Elegerant autem idemipsi in hoc officium quendam suæ gentis virum vocatum Malchum, cumque sacrandum cum communi decreto ad Anshelmum transmiserunt. Decretum autem hoc:
units.tr: Muirchertach, King of Ireland, and Donald, bishop, together with the other bishops, and the nobles together with the clergy and people of the same island, sent messengers with letters to Anselm, informing him that a certain city called Waterford lay within one of their provinces, and that because of its large population of citizens it was expedient that a bishop be set over it; and at the same time they asked that he, relying on the power of the primacy which he held over them and on the apostolic authority which he exercised, would provide them with a pontiff to establish holy Christianity and necessary unity. For many ages had already passed in which that same city, lacking wisdom and pontifical care, had been tossed about by various dangers of temptation. They had chosen for this office a certain man of their own nation called Malchus, and they sent him with a common decree to Anselm to be consecrated. The decree, however, was this:

units.la: Anshelmo Dei gratia Anglorum Archiepiscopo, clerus & populus oppidi Watesfordiæ cum Rege Mucherdacho & Episcopo Dofnaldo, salutem in Domino. Pater sancte, et secitas ignorantiæ nos diu detrimenta salutis nostræ sustinere coegit, quia magis elegimus seruiliter Dominico iugo colla subtrahere, quàm liberaliter pastoralí obedientiæ subesse. Nunc autem quantum proficiat pastoralis cura cognoscimus, cum aliarum rerum similitudines ad mentem reuocamus, quia sine regimine nec exercitus bellum, nec nauis marinum audet acceptare periculum. Naucula ergo nostra inundans dedita fluctibus, sine pastore contra callidum hostem qua ratione pugnabit? Proinde nos, et Rex noster Mucherthachus, & Episcopus Dofnaldus, & Dermec Dux noster frater regis, elegimus hunc præsbyterum Malchum, Walchelini Wintoniensis Episcopi Monachum nobis sufficientissimè cognitum, natalibus & moribus nobilé, Apostolica & Ecclesiastica disciplina imbutum, fide catholicum, prudentem, morbus temperatum, vita castum, sobrium, humilem, affabilem, misericordem, literatum, hospitalem; suæ domui bene præpositum, non neophitum, habentem testimonium bonum in gradibus singulis. Hunc nobis petimus à vestra paternitate ordinari Pontificem, quatenus regulariter nobis præesse valeat, & prodesse, & nos sub eius regimine salubriter Domino militare possimus. Vt autem omnium nºstrum votain huius electionem conuenire noscatis, huic decreto canonico promprissima voluntate singuli manibus propriis roborantes subscripsimus. Ego Muchertachus Rex Hyberniæ subscripsi. Ego Dermaeth Dux, frater Regis subscripsi. Ego Dofnaldus Episcopus subscripsi. Ego Ferdomuachus Lugdunensis Episcopus subscripsi. Subscripserunt his multi plures, quos nos breuitatis sludentes notare, non necessarium duximus.
units.tr: To Anselm, by the grace of God Archbishop of the English, the clergy and people of the town of Waterford, together with King Muirchertach, and Bishop Donald, greetings in the Lord. Holy father, the blindness of ignorance has long forced us to suffer the losses of our salvation, because we preferred to withdraw our necks slavishly from the Lord's yoke rather than to submit freely to pastoral obedience. Now, however, we recognise how much pastoral care profits, when we call to mind the likeness of other things: for without a commander neither an army dares to undertake battle, nor a ship dares to undertake the perils of the sea. Therefore our little boat, flooded and given over to the waves, without a shepherd, by what means will it fight against the crafty enemy? Accordingly we, and our King Muirchertach, and Bishop Donald, and Dermot our leader, brother of the king, have chosen this presbyter Malchus, a monk of Walchelin, Bishop of Winchester, well known to us, noble by birth and character, imbued with apostolic and ecclesiastical discipline, catholic in faith, prudent, temperate in disposition, chaste in life, sober, humble, affable, merciful, learned, hospitable, well set over his household, not a novice, having a good testimony in each of his grades. We ask of your fatherhood that he be ordained as our pontiff, so that he may be able to preside over us regularly and to be of benefit, and that under his governance we may serve the Lord healthfully. And so that you may know that the wishes of all of us agree in this election, we have each subscribed with our own hands, most readily, strengthening this canonical decree. I, Muirchertach, King of Ireland, have subscribed. I, Dermot, duke, brother of the King, have subscribed. I, Donald, bishop, have subscribed. I, Ferdomnach, bishop of Lugdunum, have subscribed. Many more subscribed besides, whom we, aiming at brevity, judged it unnecessary to note.

units.la: Cum igitur animadueritisset Anshelmus eos iusta & vtilia petere, petitionem eorum libens annuit. Eiusdem ergo Pontificem, diligenter in iis quæ sacra, iubet authoritas examinatum, ac multorum eum vitæ suæ testimonio dignum Episcopatu comprobatum, sumptâ ab eo ex more de subiectionis suæ obedientia prosessione, sacrauit eum Cantuariæ (Kal. Ianuarii, assistentibus, & cooperantibus sibi in hac ministerio duobus Episcopis suis, Radulpho Scilicet Cicestrensi, & Gundulpho Roffensi. Itaque Cantuariensis sedis authoritati illa Adriani per suum legatum Archiepiscoporum in Hybernia constitutione adtum magis & adiuntu, s derogatum fuit: vt pote qui nihilominus Cantuariensem primatem in omnibus agnoscunt suum. Et quia Angliæ Episcopatus recensuimus, commodissimum in hoc loco videtur, etiam Hibernlæ Episcopatus, Archiepiscopatibus & prouinciis suis distinctos enumerare. Itaq; Archiepiscopatus quatuor sub Eugenio constituti sunt hi. Primus Armachensis primas, sub quo sunt 8. Lugdunensis, Rharensis, Thuenensis, Chonderensis, Rathpotensis, Ceneuercensis, Ardachacdensis, Cluenerardensis: Secundus est Cassilensis Archiepiscopus, sub quo hi vndecim contineantur, Ligmorensis legatus, Tumelethensis, Eluanumensis, Arcinorensis, Lumpniacenis, Kildareuensis, Waterfordensis, Arthfortensis, Rosensis, Finiabrensis, Korcenfis. Tertius est Dublinensis Archiepiscopus, cui subiacent quinq;, Binstagniehsis, Læthelensis, Eariplonensis, Ferdinensis, Kildarensis.
units.tr: When Anselm perceived that they were asking for just and useful things, he gladly granted their petition. He therefore had the man examined carefully in those matters that sacred authority requires, and, since many attested to his worth for the episcopate by the testimony of his life, he approved him. After taking from him, as is customary, a profession of obedience to his subjection, he consecrated him at Canterbury on the Kalends of January, with his two bishops assisting and cooperating with him in this ministry, namely Ralph of Chichester and Gundulf of Rochester. Thus the authority of the see of Canterbury was somewhat diminished by that constitution of Hadrian, made through his legate, which set up archbishops in Ireland, yet those archbishops nonetheless acknowledge the Canterbury primate as their own in all things. Since we have reviewed the bishoprics of England, it seems most convenient here to list also the bishoprics of Ireland, distinguished by their archbishoprics and provinces. Four archbishoprics were accordingly established under Eugenius. The first is the primacy of Armagh, under which are eight: Louth, Rahan, Tuam(?) [as printed: Lugdunensis, Rharensis, Thuenensis, Chonderensis, Rathpotensis, Ceneuercensis, Ardachacdensis, Cluenerardensis]. The second is the archbishop of Cashel, under whom these eleven are contained: the legate of Limerick, Tumelethensis, Eluanumensis, Arcinorensis, Lumpniacenis, Kildareuensis, Waterfordensis, Arthfortensis, Rosensis, Finiabrensis, Korcenfis. The third is the archbishop of Dublin, to whom five are subject: Binstagniehsis, Laethelensis, Eariplonensis, Ferdinensis, Kildarensis.

units.la: Quartus est Tuamensis Archiepiscopus, sub quo & alii quinq; sunt, Chieufernensis, Magioniensis, Achatorneñsis, Killathensis, Alimensis. Atque hi omnes 53. Episcopatus vsitato & antiquissimo Hibernici regni iure ac instituto, Cantuariensi sedi, vt Metropoli patent.
units.tr: The fourth is the archbishop of Tuam, under whom are five others: Chieufernensis, Magioniensis, Achatorneñsis, Killathensis, Alimensis. All these together make fifty-three bishoprics, which by the customary and most ancient law and institution of the kingdom of Ireland are subject to the see of Canterbury as their metropolitan.

units.la: Scotia etiam quanquàm ab Eboracensi Prouincia ob regnorum diuisionē penè coactase sciunxit, tamen Cantuariensem Ecclesiam, vndè gubernandi, suamq; prouinciæ regendi iura sumeret, vt matrem agnouit: Nam cùm Scotiæ reges in suo regno Metropoliticam Ecclesiam qnæ cæteris præsideret, à Romanis Pontificibus postularent, primò Sixtus quartus Pontifex, S. Andreæ Episcopum, totius Scotiæ Primatem & Metropolitanum, Romanæ sui sedis legatum constituit. Identq; ne Episcopi Scotiæ in suo regno capite carerent, quanquàm reclamante Eboracensi Archiepiscopo, hàc 12. sedes Metropoliticæ S. Andreæ subiecit, Rossensem, Brechinensem, Glasguensem, Dunkelddensem, Aberdonensem, Catlanensem, Danublacensem Candidæ casæ, seu Galouidiæ, Moranensem, Orcadensem, Lismorensem, & Pictorum: non Sodorensem vt quidam scribit. Huius enim sedes in Manna Insula est, quæ Eboracensi paret Metropoli. Deinde Innocentius octauus Wilhelmo Shenes Regis Scotiæ ad se Oratorem, in eadem Metropolitica Ecclesia cum Primatis & Legatinæ authoritatis iure collocauit, eumq; & suos successores ad obseruantiam, imitationemq; huius nostræ Metropolis his verbis adstrinxit.
units.tr: Scotland too, although it was almost compelled by the division of the kingdoms to separate from the province of York, nonetheless acknowledged the Church of Canterbury as its mother, from which it would take the rights of governing and ruling its province. For when the kings of Scotland asked the Roman pontiffs for a metropolitan church in their kingdom to preside over the others, Pope Sixtus IV first appointed the bishop of St Andrews, primate and metropolitan of all Scotland, as legate of his Roman see. And so that the bishops of Scotland should not lack a head in their kingdom, he subjected to the metropolitan see of St Andrews twelve sees, although the archbishop of York protested: Ross, Brechin, Glasgow, Dunkeld, Aberdeen, Caithness, Dunblane, Candida Casa or Galloway, Moray, Orkney, Lismore, and the Picts. (Not Sodor, as some write; for its see is in the Isle of Man, which belongs to the metropolis of York.) Then Pope Innocent VIII, to William Sheves, ambassador of the King of Scotland to himself, granted a place in the same metropolitan church with the rights of primate and legate, and he bound him and his successors, in these words, to observe and imitate this our metropolis:

units.la: In concernentibus Archiepiscopalia, Primarix, & huiusmodi Legationis officia, iura, & eorum liberum exercitium, honores, onera, & emolumenta obiicerent, teneant firmiter, ac inuiolabiliter studeant perimplere laudabiles consuetudines inclitæ Metropolitanæ Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis, cuius præsul legatus natus existit. Illas hîcac si de verbo ad verbum exprimerentur, pto expressis haberi volentes, qualescunque sint, ad præsatam prouinciam, Archiepiscopatum, Primatiam, & Legationem S. Andreæ, & illius Ecclesiæ, Monasteria, beneficia Ecclesiastica, Episcopos, Abbates, Canonicos, Vicarios, generales conuentus, & personas, clerum & populum eiusdem dictæ auctoritate extendimus, iudicimus, & institutimus, ac volumus pari modo consuetudines huiusmodi, sicut in dicta Cantuariensi prouincia & legatione obseruantur, in regno & prouincia Scotiæ prætactis, in posterum perpetuis futuris temporibus inuiolabiliter obseruari.
units.tr: In matters concerning the archiepiscopal, primatial and similar offices, rights and duties of legation, and their free exercise, honours, burdens and emoluments, they shall firmly hold, and shall be careful to fulfil inviolably, the praiseworthy customs of the renowned metropolitan Church of Canterbury, whose prelate is by birth legate. Wishing those customs, whatever they are, to be regarded as expressed as if they were set down word for word here, we extend, judge and institute them for the aforesaid province, archdiocese, primacy and legation of St Andrews, and for that church's monasteries, ecclesiastical benefices, bishops, abbots, canons, vicars general, convents and persons, clergy and people, by the authority of the same; and we will that such customs, as they are observed in the said Canterbury province and legation, be inviolably observed in the aforesaid kingdom and province of Scotland for all future time.

units.la: Præterea cum Reges Angliæ Normandiam, Guasconiam, Acquitaniam prouincias Gallicas sua ditione tenuissent, Episcopatibus vacantibus, spiritualatis seu Ecclesiasticæ iurisdictionis custodia penes Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum remansit, qui Vicarios suos in illis dioecesibus & prouinciis delegauit. Tum si quis ad Romanam sedem appellausset, etiam ad Cantuariensem, ne in iuris sui possessione turbaretur, simul appellauit. Quæ appellatio, quia possessionis tuedæ causa, ne lite pendente immutaretur, fuit interposita, tuitoria dicta est. Huius autem appellationis recipiendæ vim, non alteri cuiquam Archiepiscopo concessam legimus: vt si in Eboracensi, vel vicinis prouinciis, appellare quis ad Principem velleri, si possessionem interim tueri ac defendere cupit, Cant. Archiepiscopum inuocabit. Hisce breuiter expositis, ad Cantuar. sedis priuilegia accedemus, si prius aliam ex Anacleto huius insulæ diuisionem inseruiremus. Heptarchia ante commemorata longè post Christum fuit, ideoque notior est historia, huius autem veritatem quia latet plures, iuxta veterum testimonia proferemus. Britannia habuit prouincias quinque, videlicet. Britannium primam, Britanniam secundam, Flauiani, Maximiam, & Valentiam. Prima occidentalis Insulæ pars est, in qua Britones Bruto & Coryneo ducibus primò appuli sedes statuerunt. 2. Cantium est in quo deinde Brutus & sui incolæ fuerunt. 3. Flauia (quæ & Mercia dicitur) quia mercibus diues, cuius caput Londinum. 4. Maximia i. Eboraca ab Imp. Maximo vocata. 5. verò Valentia, à Valente Imperatore sic dictæ est. Albania quæ nunc scz. abusiuè Scotia dicitur, sic quoriduatum à viris sanctis prædictis duobus fuerat, vtin occidentali Insulæ parte, quæ & nunc adulterino vocabulo Wallia dicitur, propriè vero Cambria, à Kambro Bruti filio dicta, vrbs legionum Metropolis fuerat 12. Suffraganeos habens Dorobernia quæ nuno Cantuaria dicitur, à Dun Britannico quod est aqua, quoniam aquis abundat, sic nuncupata, Metropolis ab australi Thamiæ fluuij parte. 12. Suffraganeos habens. Eboraca (quæ nunc dicitur Eboracum) Metropolis 12. Suffraganeos habens. Et vrbs quæ nunc S. Andreæ forsan dicitur, totidem Suffraganeos habens, olim Albadicta est, vnde & Albania Prouincia, vel potius ab Albanacto Bruti filio nuncupata. Cumq; hoc ordine distincta ducentis annis & pluribus Britannica Ecclesia floruisset, superuenit gens Saxonica, quæ nunc Anglica dicitur, à Britonibus inuitata, vt contra Pictos & Scotos, qui boreales Insulæ partes occupauerant, Britonum stipendiis militarent. Tandem verò cum valde creuisset, iunctò cum bostibus fœdere, & ipsi quoq; peiores hostes effecti, miris proditionibus incolas ad occiduas partes Insulæ propulerunt, totamq; terram residuam, quam & Angliam vocarunt à natali suo Saxonix solo, quod lingua eorum Engelond vocabatur, id est, Angularis terra, Britanniam occupatam sic nominantes, nec non & Scotiæ partem non modicam, destructis Ecclesiis ritu gentilitatis, quoniam gentiles erant, fœdauerunt, Britonibus nihilominus Christi fidem in occiduis Insulæ finibus iuconcusse seruantibus. His sic se habentibus missus est à Gregorio Augustinus Monachus in Angliam, qui duas tantum in Anglia
units.tr: Moreover, when the kings of England held the Gallic provinces of Normandy, Gascony and Aquitaine under their dominion, the custody of the spiritual or ecclesiastical jurisdiction, while the bishoprics were vacant, remained with the archbishop of Canterbury, who delegated his vicars in those dioceses and provinces. Then, if anyone appealed to the Roman see, he also appealed at the same time to Canterbury, so that he would not be disturbed in the possession of his right. This appeal, because it was lodged in order to protect possession, so that nothing might be altered while the suit was pending, was called protective (tuitoria). We read that the power of receiving this appeal was granted to no other archbishop: so that if anyone in the province of York, or in neighbouring provinces, wished to appeal to the Prince, and desired meanwhile to protect and defend his possession, he would invoke the archbishop of Canterbury. Having briefly set out these matters, we shall come to the privileges of the see of Canterbury, if first we insert another division of this island from Anacletus. The heptarchy mentioned above was long after Christ, and so its history is better known; but since the truth of the earlier division is hidden from many, we shall set it forth according to the testimony of the ancients. Britain had five provinces, namely: first Britain, second Britain, Flavia, Maxima and Valentia. The first is the western part of the island, where the Britons, under their leaders Brutus and Corineus, first landed and established their seats. The second is Kent, where afterwards Brutus and his people lived. The third is Flavia, also called Mercia, rich in merchandise, whose capital is London. The fourth is Maxima, that is York, named after the Emperor Maximus. The fifth, Valentia, is so called from the Emperor Valens. Albania, which is now improperly called Scotland, was thus divided by the two holy men mentioned above, so that in the western part of the island, which is now also called Wales by a corrupted name, but properly Cambria, named after Kambrus, son of Brutus, there was the city of Legions, the metropolis, having twelve suffragans. Dorobernia, which is now called Canterbury, named from the British word dun, which means water, because it abounds in waters, is the metropolis on the southern side of the river Thames, having twelve suffragans. York (now called Eboracum) is a metropolis having twelve suffragans. And the city which is now perhaps called St Andrews, having as many suffragans, was formerly called Alba, whence the province of Albania, or rather named after Albanactus, son of Brutus. Since the British Church flourished, distinguished in this order, for two hundred years and more, the Saxon people arrived, who are now called English, invited by the Britons to serve as mercenaries against the Picts and Scots, who had occupied the northern parts of the island. At last, when they had greatly increased, and having also made a league with their enemies, they themselves became worse enemies, and by monstrous treacheries drove the inhabitants to the western parts of the island, and occupied the rest of the land, which they called England, and Britain they named after their native Saxon soil, which in their language was called Engelond, that is, the angular land. They also defiled no small part of Scotland, destroying the churches in the manner of the heathen, since they were heathens. Meanwhile the Britons kept the faith of Christ unshaken in the western borders of the island. With matters thus standing, Augustine, a monk, was sent into England by Gregory, who established only two metropolises in England, namely Canterbury and York.

units.la: 10 Metropoles constituit, Doroberniam scilicet & Eboracum. Doroberniæ, quam sibi sedem elegerat, totam Angliam fere, quia 12. vel 13. Episcopatus amplos continebat, subiecit. Hæc Girald. Sed istius non immorabimur, ad propositum reuertamur.
units.tr: 10 He subjected almost all England to Canterbury, which he had chosen as his seat, since it contained twelve or thirteen large bishoprics. Thus Giraldus. But we shall not linger on this; let us return to our purpose.

units.la: CANTVARIENSIS SEDIS PRIVILEGTA & Prærogatiua.
units.tr: The Privileges and Prerogative of the See of Canterbury

units.la: 20 VNE singularum sedium origine ac mutatione, nec non Cantuariensis sedis eminentia & dignitate expositis, operæ precium erit, huius quoque sedis Prærogatiuam atque Priuilegia, tam ea quæ ipsa origine vetustatéque, quam quæ Principum indulgentia atque concessione tenet, seorsim, parce tamen narrare. Nam vt diximus, Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis authoritas, non certis atque definitis Archiepiscopalis aut Metropoliticæ iurisdictionis cancellis concluditur, sed ordinaria, libera, peneque arbitraria per suam prouinciam excurrit & diffunditur. Cuius quidem potestatis & authoritatis vt ab ipsa origine ducatur, vtque facilis ac in promptu esse possit, rationem ostendamus. Augustino primum, vt in eius vita patebit, potestatem indulsit Gregorius Regum ad Christianam fidem conuertorum authoritate, per totam Angliæ Episcopos ordinandi, Ecclesiastica & iura describendi, ritus ceremoniasque instituendi. Hic in sua prima ordinatione quam ab Etherio Arelatensi Episcopo in Gallijs acceptit, siuli cœrtæ sedi astrictus, sed Anglorum Episcopus, seu Apostolus dictus est. Ac postquam eo nomine ordinatus esset, tantæ dignitatis sedem Cantuariæ locauit. Deinde Theodorus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus sextus ab Augustino: summus Angliæ Pontifex ordinatus & appellatus fuit. Ab hoc itaque initio Ecclesiasticarum rerum summa potestas penes Cantuarienses Archiepiscopos, tamquam ipsis Regulis, inter quos septem regionibus diuisum tum regnum fuit ad fidem conuersis, quam à posterioribus Regibus qui vna ditione totum regnum gubernabant, approbata semper remansit. Adeo vt in concilio quod apud Barrum sub Vrbano Papa 2. contra Græcos Spiritus sancti processionem à Deo Filio dependentes celebrabatur, in quo docte Anshelmus cum Cant. Archiepiscopus eorum errorem refellit. Vrbanus Papa adiuentu eius
units.tr: 20 Since the origin and changes of each see have been set out, and the eminence and dignity of the see of Canterbury have been explained, it will be worth the effort to describe briefly the prerogative and privileges of this see as well, both those it holds by its very origin and antiquity and those it holds by the indulgence and grant of princes, and to treat them separately. For, as we have said, the authority of the archbishop of Canterbury is not confined within fixed and defined limits of archiepiscopal or metropolitan jurisdiction, but runs and spreads through his province in an ordinary, free and almost arbitrary way. Let us show the reason for this power and authority, from its origin, so that it may be easy to grasp and ready to hand. As will appear in his life, Gregory first granted to Augustine the power, by the authority he held over the kings converted to the Christian faith, of ordaining bishops throughout England, of drawing up ecclesiastical laws, and of instituting rites and ceremonies. In his first ordination, which he received in Gaul from Etherius, bishop of Arles, he was bound to no fixed see, but was called bishop or apostle of the English. And after he had been ordained under that title, he placed the see of such dignity at Canterbury. Then Theodore, the sixth archbishop after Augustine, was ordained and called the supreme pontiff of England. From this beginning, therefore, the highest power in ecclesiastical affairs lay with the archbishops of Canterbury, just as it lay with the kings, among whom the kingdom was then divided into seven regions converted to the faith; and this power, approved by the later kings who ruled the whole kingdom under one dominion, always remained. So much so that at the council held at Bari under Pope Urban II against the Greeks, who make the procession of the Holy Spirit depend on God the Son, where learned Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, refuted their error, Pope Urban, on his arrival,

units.la: 40 lætus: Hunc, inquit, pro Magistro teneamus, & quasi comparem, veluti alterius orbis Apostolicum & Patriarcham iure venerandum censeamus. Sed Pontifices Romani hac authoritate præditos Cant. Archiepiscopos vt suos legatos nominabant, vt authoritatem quam iure suo obtinebant, à sede Romana sumere viderentur. Non aliter atque Henrico octauo Regi inignem illum & verum fidei defensoris titulum Papa diplomate suo dedit, verius ne quod eiusdem posset annos suas vires deferet atque frangeret. Hæc sunt plurimæque Papalis callidnitas & astutia, vt quorum authoritatem in administratione Ecclesiastica maximam esse cognosceret, iso omnium Regnorum Dominium affectans, eos suos legatos voluit dici, vt quæcunque in administratione sua gesserit, id tanquam vniuersali authoritate fieri viderentur. Hac ratione non modo in
units.tr: 40 joyfully said: "Let us hold him as our master, and esteem him as our equal, and rightly regard him as the apostolic patriarch of another world, to be venerated." But the Roman pontiffs, who called the archbishops of Canterbury, endowed with this authority, their legates, did so in order that the authority they held by their own right might seem to be derived from the Roman see. In the same way, the Pope gave King Henry VIII that famous and true title of Defender of the Faith by his own diploma, lest perhaps it should weaken and break the king's own power. These are the great craft and cunning of the Papacy: since it knew that their authority in ecclesiastical administration was very great, and aiming at dominion over all kingdoms, it wanted them to be called its legates, so that whatever they did in their administration might seem done by universal authority. In this way not only in

units.la: 50 Anglia Cantuariensem & Eboracensem, sed in reliquis Regnis Christianis celebriores legatos, suos nominauit in Scotia Archiepiscopum S. Andreæ; in Germania Archiepiscopum Salisburgensem, in Gallia Remensem, in Italia Pisanum, & in Hungaria Strigoniensem Archiepiscopum; quorum omnium authoritas tanta fuit, vt cum inferioribus suis prouinciis quibusque præsatis in omni ordinaria iurisdictione concurrerent.
units.tr: 50 England did it name the archbishops of Canterbury and York its legates, but in the other Christian kingdoms it named the more famous ones as well: in Scotland the archbishop of St Andrews; in Germany the archbishop of Salzburg; in France the archbishop of Reims; in Italy the archbishop of Pisa; and in Hungary the archbishop of Esztergom. The authority of all of them was so great that, together with the lesser provinces of each, they shared in every ordinary jurisdiction.

units.la: Itaque Ecclesia Metropolitica Cantuariensis quædam habet iura cum cæteris communia, legibusque descripta, quædam absoluta, ubique singularia quæ legibus ex-
units.tr: So the metropolitan church of Canterbury has some rights in common with the others, described in the laws, and some absolute rights, everywhere peculiar to it, which are not expressly stated in the laws.

units.la: presse non sunt. Præscripta legibusque definita iura, sunt huiusmodi Prouinciaiurum Episcoporum post suam electionem & Regiam approbationem confirmatio & consecratio, in qua tamen est aliquid singulare. Nam in Ecclesia Christi Cant. celebranda est, nec in quocunque alio loco quantumuis celeberrimo, legitimè id fieri potest, quamuis vt alibi fiat Decani & capituli Cant. consensus de consuetudine accedere debeat. Ad hanc rem Episcopi sacrati grandia olim tributa praestabant. Veluti consecrationis die qui Dominicus esse debet, noctisque ante gressa, omnes familiæ Archiepiscopi sumptus sacratus lautissimo instructo conuiuio sustinebat, & in sacratione cappam professionalem Archiepiscopo donabat. Postridie discedens Archiepiscopo remunerationis præmium loco Centum librarum vel Marcas pro Episcopatus sciliect exiguitate aut magnitudine locique distantia dabat. Tapeta sua atque vestes soluta pecunia ab Archiepiscopi Capellanis redimebat. Pecuniam etiam largam inter Archiepiscopi famulos distribuebat. Crucifero Archiepiscopi quadraginta solidos, totidemque Marischaleho donabat. Quæ tam copiosa quondam largitas in ulto consecrationis die, ad modicam decem librarum summam Archiepiscopo iam contracta eit, aliqua præterea, sed pertinuit in famulatum libertalitate diffusa. Pro cappis autem professionalibus xx. sup. in vnufcuiusque Episcopi consecratione Cantuariensi Ecclesiæ præstantur. Quilibet etiam consecratus in sua inauguratione Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi iuramento pollicetur obedientiam Canonicam, & defensionem omnium Cantuar. Ecclesiæ Priuilegiorum atque libertatum.
units.tr: The rights prescribed and defined by law are these: the confirmation and consecration of the bishops of the province after their election and royal approval. In this there is, however, something singular. For it must be celebrated in the church of Christ at Canterbury, and it cannot lawfully be done in any other place, however famous, although for it to be done elsewhere the consent of the dean and chapter of Canterbury ought by custom to be given. In connection with this, bishops, when consecrated, formerly paid large dues. On the day of consecration, which had to be a Sunday, and on the night before, the whole of the archbishop's household was provided for at the consecrated bishop's expense, with a most lavish banquet; and at the consecration the bishop gave the archbishop a professional cope. The next day, on departing, he gave the archbishop, as a reward, a hundred pounds or marks, according to the smallness or largeness of the bishopric and its distance from the place. He redeemed his carpets and garments from the archbishop's chaplains for money. He also distributed a generous sum among the archbishop's servants, giving forty shillings to the archbishop's cross-bearer and as much to the marshal. This once copious generosity on the day of consecration has since shrunk to a modest sum of ten pounds for the archbishop, with some other payments spread out in largesse to the servants. For the professional copes, twenty shillings are paid to the church of Canterbury at each bishop's consecration. Every consecrated bishop also promises at his inauguration canonical obedience to the archbishop of Canterbury, and the defence of all the privileges and liberties of the church of Canterbury.

units.la: Adhæc visitandi, Synodos & concilia cogendi, inferiorum negligentias defectusque supplendi, appellationes recipiendi, ad easque referendi, debilibus & infirmis Episcopis Coadiutores assignandi, Vicarios generales atque commissarios non habentibus aut idoneos non habentibus constituendi, præterea indulgendi, tollerandi atque dispensandi & similia, nota satis sunt scriptisque legibus prodita iura. Quæ vero sua sunt peculiaria atque propria, aut in ciuilibus honoribus priuilegiisque consistunt, aut in Ecclesiasticis. Ciuilibus enim multis honoribus tam ante, quam post conquestum multi Angliæ Reges Cant. Archiepiscopos affecerunt: vt cum Nobilium & magnatum haeredes, qui in minore sunt ætate, antequam legitimam ætatem attingunt, in fide atque clientela regia quam Guardiam seu custodiam nuncupant, iure Regni retinentur, Henricus. 3, Rex Angliæ Comitis Gloceftriæ hæredes, quoties in minore ætate ad eam haereditatem peruenirent, in authoritate & tutela Cantuariensium Archiepiscoporum esse voluit, eiusdemque Comitis maneria de Tunbridge, Horfmondem, Bradlyd, Veileston, Meliton & Petrys, quamdiu in minori esset ætate, in eorundem custodia esse statuit, vtque ab Archiepiscopis Cantuariensibus tanquam a primis illius Sol Dominis, quatuor militum præstitis Feodis ac seruitiis Glocestriæ Comites eadem maneria accepta agnoscerent, in vniuscuiusque Archiepiscopi introniizatione eis inserviebant, & Senefchalli sui atque Principalis Pincernæ officia gerebant.
units.tr: Besides these, the rights to visit, to call synods and councils, to make good the negligences and defects of inferiors, to receive appeals and refer them, to assign coadjutors to weak and infirm bishops, to appoint vicars general and commissaries to those who lack them or have none suitable, and further to grant indulgences, toleration and dispensations, and similar things, are well known and set out in written laws. Those rights, however, which are his own and peculiar, consist either in civil honours and privileges or in ecclesiastical ones. For many English kings, both before and after the Conquest, have honoured the archbishops of Canterbury with many civil honours. Thus, when the heirs of nobles and magnates who are under age are held, before they reach legal age, in the king's faith and clientage, which they call wardship or custody, by the law of the realm, King Henry III of England wished the heirs of the earl of Gloucester, whenever they came to that inheritance while still minors, to be under the authority and guardianship of the archbishops of Canterbury. He also decreed that, while the earl was a minor, the manors of Tonbridge, Horsmonden, Bradley, Wiveliscombe, Milton and Petham should be in the custody of the same archbishops. And so that the earls of Gloucester should acknowledge that they received these manors from the archbishops of Canterbury, as the first lords of that lordship, for the fees and services of four knights, they served each archbishop at his enthronement and performed the offices of his steward and chief butler.

units.la: Qui cum hæc eo tempore impendunt seruitia, certis quibusdam Feodis atque præmiis vicissim remunerari solebant. Eodem etiam seruitij genere D. Coniers Baro, & D. Strangwayes maneria de Whiuelton, Semer, Efton, Alderwicke, Pothon, & Dominion in Eboracensi comitatu tenent. Oxonii item Comes, Baronesque D. Rosse, & D. Darcie ad obsequia & seruitia militaria Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo præstanda pro quibusdam suis præditis maneriisque astringuntur. In quorum seruitiorum iuribus fruendis, Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi Prærogatiua aliorum subditorum iura antecellit. Hæc est enim regni iure prærogatiua regia. Vt cum plurium diuersi status & conditionis prædiorum & maneriorum pluribus primariis soli Dominis, plura tribuunt militaria seruitia. Si princeps fit variis prædit aut manerii principalis Dominus, is reliquorum Dominorum tota iuraad se prærogatiua Regia deducit atque trahit. Ita quotiescunque huiusmodi hæres in minori sit ætate, Princeps remotis cæteris Dominis totam illius tutelam & curationem nanciscitur, quo iure totius etiam hæreditatis, quanquam pluriorum fundis diuisæ emolumenta percipit. At Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi prærogatiua præ cæteris hoc habet præcipuum, vt quicunque a Principe terras tenent, siue in ipso præstipuo ac principali seruitio, quod Capitale vocant, siue in militari fi alias a Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo militaribus seruitubus alligatas habeat, eatrum emolumenta atque iura quamdiu minor sit, Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi deferuntur. Hoc autem tam eximium ius, vetustissimum, semperque obseruatum fuit. Nuper vero cum pro Manerio de Flete in Cantio, quod Edwardus Oxoniensis Comes tunc minor in militari seruitio Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi debito tenet, res in contoueriam veniret, perspecta penitus lege quæ de Regis prærogatiua lata est, perpensisque instrumentis atque monumentis quæ Archiepiscopus proferebat, rerumque anie ante pro terris Baronum Rosse, Coniers, & Darcy temporibus Henrici 6. & Henrici 8. similiter iudicatarum authoritate, à celeberrimo prudentissimoq; viro D. W. Cecilio equite aurato, iam Barone Burleighe, Regiæ Maiestatis consiliario, & præcipuo secretario, curiæq; Guardiarum & liberationum Regiarum, in quia de huiusmodi minorum atque seruiturum iure disceptatur, Magistro atque præside, cum Regii procuratoris aliorumque à Regiis consiliis in eacuria Præsentium consensu, decretum est commoda & emolumenta Manerii de Flete, ratione minoris ætatis, Oxoniensis Comitis, ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum pertinere, omniaque quæ antea quam Archiepiscopus pro iure suo propositum esset, atq; docuisset, ad Regios vius perceptafuntur, eodem decreto ei restituta fuerunt.
units.tr: Those who performed these services at that time were customarily rewarded in turn with certain fees and rewards. By the same kind of service, Lord Conyers, baron, and Lord Strangways hold the manors of Whiveton, Semer, Easton, Alderwick, Pothon and Dominion in the county of York. Likewise at Oxford the earl, and the barons Lord Ross and Lord Darcy are bound to render military duties and services to the archbishop of Canterbury for certain of their own estates and manors. In enjoying the rights of these services, the prerogative of the archbishop of Canterbury surpasses the rights of other subjects, for this is the royal prerogative under the law of the realm. When several estates and manors of different status and condition, belonging to several chief lords, owe several military services, and the prince is the principal lord of one of them or of the manor, he draws to himself, by royal prerogative, all the rights of the other lords. Thus whenever such an heir is under age, the prince, the other lords being set aside, obtains the whole guardianship and care of him, and by that right receives the profits of the whole inheritance, although it is divided among several estates. But the prerogative of the archbishop of Canterbury has this chief point above the others: whoever hold lands from the prince, whether in the chief and principal service which they call capital, or in military service, or otherwise bound to the archbishop of Canterbury by military services, their profits and rights, for as long as they are minors, are conveyed to the archbishop of Canterbury. This most remarkable right is very ancient and has always been observed. Recently, however, when the matter of the manor of Flete in Kent, which Edward, earl of Oxford, then a minor, holds in military service owed to the archbishop of Canterbury, came into dispute, the law concerning the royal prerogative was thoroughly examined and the instruments and records which the archbishop produced were weighed, together with the earlier judgments made in the time of Henry VI and Henry VIII concerning the lands of Lords Ross, Conyers and Darcy. By the authority of the most famous and prudent man, Sir William Cecil, knight, now Lord Burghley, councillor and chief secretary of His Royal Majesty, and master and president of the court of Wards and Liberates, in which such disputes about the rights of minors and of those owing service are heard, with the consent of the royal attorney and of others from the royal councils present in that court, it was decided that the profits and emoluments of the manor of Flete, by reason of the minority of the earl of Oxford, belong to the archbishop of Canterbury; and whatever had been received for the king's use before the archbishop set out and demonstrated his right was restored to him by the same decree.

units.la: Idem munificentissimus pariter ac religiosus rex Henr. 3. summa libertate & immunitate tam familiam quam prædia atque maneria Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi muniuit. Multas omnes atque poenas, quas famuli, servi, ministri, vasalli, coloni, aut tenentes Archiepiscopi incurrerent, siue à lege, siue à Iudice irrogarentur, Cantuariensibus Archiepiscopis concessit: easque a Regiis Iudicibus ac ministris exigi aut petiprohibuit.
units.tr: That most munificent and at the same time religious king, Henry III, protected both the household and the estates and manors of the Archbishop of Canterbury with the greatest liberty and immunity. He granted to the Archbishops of Canterbury all fines and penalties that their servants, slaves, ministers, vassals, tenants or holders incurred, whether imposed by law or by a judge, and he forbade royal judges and officers to demand or exact them.

units.la: Iohanneś Pius Rex Huberto rum Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo authoritatem concessit, vt vetera Feoda in antiquissimo illo seruitio quod Gauelkind appellatur vlitata, ad militaria seruitia, & designatos ac præscriptos pro illis seruitiis reditus tam ferrer, vtque illius generis tenentes ac coloni pari cum reliquis Archiepiscopalium prædiorum possessoribus immunitate gauderent.
units.tr: King John granted to Hubert, Archbishop of Canterbury, authority that the old fees, in that most ancient service called gavelkind, should be changed into military services, and that the rents designated and prescribed for those services should be paid, and that tenants and farmers of that kind should enjoy the same immunity as the other holders of archiepiscopal estates.

units.la: Deinde Henricus 6. Iohanni Stafford Archiepiscopo concessit, vt Cantuariensiū Archiepiscoporum tenentes, residentes ac firmarii, a prouisoribus & victualium captoribus, pro hospitio regio deinceps semper liberentur.
units.tr: Henry VI granted to John Stafford, Archbishop, that the tenants, residents and farmers of the Archbishops of Canterbury should from then on always be freed from purveyors and takers of provisions for the royal household.

units.la: Hoc Priuilegium inclitus Rex Henricus octauus W. Waramo suisc; succesfotibus iidem confirmauit, ac insuper commemorauit, vt ab omni Panagio, Pesagio, Laftagio, Stallagio, Cariagio, Pescagio, Picagio, Terragio, Tronagio, Pontagio, Chunnagio, Ankeragio, Wharfagio, omniq; secta ad shiras & hundred, & lasta hundredorum, a quibus ante immunes erant, quietiessent ac soluti.
units.tr: The renowned King Henry VIII confirmed this privilege to William Warham and his successors, and further declared that they should be quit and free from every pannage, pesage, lastage, stallage, cariage, pescage, piccage, terrage, tronage, pontage, chimnage, anchorage, wharfage, and all suit at shires and hundreds and lasts of hundreds, from all of which they had previously been immune.

units.la: Eodem etiam famulos, ministros ac colonos a tributi pensatione, quæ pto his oneribūs quæ prisei iuris vocabulis Tollagium & Mutagium vocant, ac Thelonio omniq; alia præstatione quacunq;, oneribusq; tam impositis, quam imponendis per totam Angliam perpetuis futuris temporibus penitus soluit ac liberauit.
units.tr: Likewise he entirely released and freed the servants, ministers and tenants from the payment of tribute, which, with these burdens, are called by the old legal names tallage and motage, and from toll and every other payment whatever, and from burdens both already imposed and yet to be imposed, throughout all England, for all future time.

units.la: In Cantuariensi etiam Ecclesia illius ciuitatis Præsides ac Recatores, quos Maiores ac Balliuos nuncupant, clauesque quas Masas vocant Magistratus insignia sibi à lictoribus suis præferri non permittebatur. Quia in ea Ecclesia illorum cessabat authoritas.
units.tr: In the Church of Canterbury, in that city, the presidents and recorders, whom they call mayors and bailiffs, were not permitted to have their maces, which they call keys, carried before them by their lictors as the insignia of magistracy, because there their authority ceased.

units.la: Necnon in Episcopatu Roffensi Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus plenum ius patronatus obtinebat, cumq; sicut alia sui iuris patronatus Ecclesiastica beneficia liberè conferebat. Eoque vacante non modo spiritualium, sed & temporalium administrationem, custodiamque retinebat: eaque Feodalia seruitia, quæ pro terris præsiisque Episcopalibus Regibus iam deferuntur, ab Episcopis Roff. Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo tantum illius sedis patronoq; atque conditori tribuebantur. Aliaque permulta sunt Cantuariensis sedis in legibus regni municipalibus commemorata priuilegia, quorum nonulla desuetudine contrariisque legibus sublata sunt, reliqua vi pristina & authoritate constat. Quæ quidem vt qualia olim fuerint, ac iam (quatenus saluis Regni legibus fieri possit) adhuc in vsu esse possunt, non contendendi vt ea mordicus retineamus studio, a nobis repeturis: Sed ab his ad maiora Ecclesiasticæ suæ authoritatis potestatisque spacia, quæ huius loci acinstituti magis propria sunt, accedamus. In his primum ac præcipuum munus est, quod Angliæ Reges imperium suscipientes à Cantuariensibus Archiepiscopis sacrari & coronari volebant, iuramentiq; vinculo astringi Reipublicæ, vt sceptrum gladiumq; Regium ad regni tutelam atque salurem gerant. Hæc enim Regalis sacratio atque coronatio Cant. Archiepiscoporum semper fuit propria, vt in sequenti historia sæpius declarabitur. Regias etiam nuptias Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi coniungunt; & benedicunt. Cum enim in Windesoriæ castro quod in Salisburiensi diocæsi sirum est, Salisburiensis Episcopus Episcopali iure tanquam in propria diocæsi in Henrici Regis primi cum Atheleida Godefridi Lotharingiæ Ducis filia nupsit anno sui regni. 11. Eorum celebrationi se audacter ingessisset, ab omnibus proceribus acclamatum est, hocius Cantuariensium Archiepiscoporum esse proprium: Regesque ac Reginas vbicúnque in Anglia degerent, eius esse speciales atque domesticos (vt Gervasius diserte loquitur) Parochianos, totumque regnum etsi diuersis dioecesibus distinctum sit, ratione primatus eius esse Parochiam. Atqne haec adeo verasunt vt Regiae procerumque oblationes, siue in Regio sacello, siue in quacunque Ecclesia Cathedrali, Conventuali, vel Parochiali, praesente Archiepiscopo inter sacra factae, nec illius dioecesis Episcopo, neo Conventuali aut Capitulo, hecipsi Sacelli Regii Decano, nec Parocho, aut alteri cuicunque, sed Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi soli debeantur. Nam in his quae ad diuinum cultum in primis pertinent, praecipua semper fuit cura atque solicitudo Archiepiscopi. Huic proximum quoque Eboracensis Archiepiscopus non modo ab Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi se electum confirmari, aut sacrari in Cantuariensi Ecclesia petit, sed & ipse ad Archiepiscopum Cant. confirmandum aut consecrandum in eadem Ecclesiam accedit, & in sua sacratione obedientiam profitetur. Archiepiscopi quoque & Metropolitani Hyberniae, & Archiepiscopo nostro sua confirmationis & consecrationis iura capiunt, & ad huius fedis obseruantiam atque cultum se astringunt. Tum ipsi Prouinciales fui Suffraganei & Episcopi tenentur singuli aliquem ab Archiepiscopo Cant. nominatum in bonarum literarum studiis alere & exhibere, donec eidem de competenti beneficio Ecclesiastico sit prouisum. Sed nec in vita solum, & consecrationis suae tempore huiusmodi officia Archiepiscopo suo tribuunt, sed mortui annulos, & sigilla cuncta, praeter eum quotoptimus sit relinquunt. Quidam etiam vt Asaphensis & Banchorensis in Wallia Episcopi, praeter ea quae diximus munera, equum suum generosum quem Paleafrendum appellant, fraeno ornato atque sella instructum Archiepiscopo debent. Roffensis vero Episcopos, qui Capellanus Archiepiscopi habetur, praeterea donat cuppam seu cyphum argenteum, canesque venaticos. His accedant Archidiaconatus Cantuariensis vacantis iura. Archidiaconi enim Cantuarienses Suffraganeos a Primate sacratos in sedes suas Episcopales ex more inducunt, quibus id muneris obeunt tibus, equus cella & fraeno ornatus, cyphus argenteus & decem Marcae tributum. Vacante vero Archidiaconatu Archiepiscopus ea dona percipit. Antiquius enim Episcopus quidam S. Martini dictus. Archidiaconi Cantuariensis munere fungebatur, quo tandem deleto Lanfrancus Archidiaconatum erexit atque stabiliuit, & Archidiaconum Cantuariae primus posuit.
units.tr: Likewise in the diocese of Rochester the Archbishop of Canterbury held full right of patronage, and, as with his other ecclesiastical benefices in his gift, he conferred them freely. When that see was vacant he retained the administration and custody not only of spiritual but also of temporal affairs. The feudal services which are now rendered to kings for the lands and possessions of bishops were attributed by the bishops of Rochester to the Archbishop of Canterbury alone, as patron and founder of that see. There are very many other privileges of the see of Canterbury recorded in the municipal laws of the realm; some of them have been abolished by disuse and by contrary laws, while the rest remain in their former force and authority. We shall not, in order to know what they once were and how far, with the laws of the realm preserved, they may still be in use, set them out with the zeal of contending that we must hold them tooth and nail. Rather let us pass from these to the greater spheres of his ecclesiastical authority and power, which are more proper to the purpose and undertaking of this place. Among these, the first and chief office is that the kings of England, when taking up the rule, wished to be consecrated and crowned by the Archbishops of Canterbury, and bound by the tie of an oath to the commonwealth, that they would bear the sceptre and royal sword for the protection and safety of the realm. For this royal consecration and coronation has always been proper to the Archbishops of Canterbury, as will be declared more often in the following history. They also join in and bless royal marriages. When the Bishop of Salisbury, in the castle of Windsor, which lies in the diocese of Salisbury, presumed boldly to thrust himself, by episcopal right as in his own diocese, into the celebration of the marriage of King Henry I with Adeliza, daughter of Godfrey, Duke of Lorraine, in the eleventh year of his reign, it was declared by all the nobles that this was the proper right of the Archbishops of Canterbury. Kings and queens, wherever they lived in England, were their special and domestic parishioners (as Gervase plainly says), and the whole realm, though divided into different dioceses, is by reason of his primacy one parish. And these things are so true that royal and noble offerings, whether made during sacred rites in the royal chapel or in any cathedral, conventual or parish church, in the presence of the Archbishop, are owed not to the bishop of that diocese, nor to the convent or chapter, nor to the dean of the royal chapel himself, nor to the parson or anyone else, but to the Archbishop of Canterbury alone. For in those matters which pertain chiefly to divine worship, the care and solicitude of the Archbishop has always been the greatest. Next to him, the Archbishop of York not only asks to be confirmed or consecrated by the Archbishop of Canterbury in the Church of Canterbury, but he himself also comes to that Church to confirm or consecrate the Archbishop of Canterbury, and in his own consecration he professes obedience. The Archbishops and Metropolitans of Ireland also take their rights of confirmation and consecration from our Archbishop and bind themselves to the observance and reverence of this see. Then, each of his own suffragans and bishops of the province is bound to maintain and support, in the study of good letters, someone nominated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, until that person is provided with a suitable ecclesiastical benefice. And they render these duties to their Archbishop not only in his life and at the time of their consecration, but on their death they leave their rings and all their seals, except the best, to him. Some also, such as the bishops of St Asaph and Bangor in Wales, besides the duties we have mentioned, owe their Archbishop a noble horse, which they call a palfrey, furnished with bridle and saddle. The bishop of Rochester, who is regarded as the Archbishop's chaplain, also gives a silver cup or bowl and hunting dogs. To these are added the rights of the Archdeaconry of Canterbury when it is vacant. For the archdeacons of Canterbury customarily induct into their episcopal sees the suffragans consecrated by the Primate, and for performing this service they receive a horse with bridle and saddle, a silver cup, and a tribute of ten marks. But when the archdeaconry is vacant, the Archbishop receives those gifts. For earlier a certain bishop, called St Martin, performed the office of archdeacon of Canterbury; when this office was later abolished, Lanfranc erected and established the archdeaconry and was the first to appoint an archdeacon of Canterbury.

units.la: His expositis iam ad ea quae Iurisdictionis sunt, quaeque iure quodam peculiari Archiepiscopo Cant. competunt, veniamus. Huius Iurisdictionis magna vis & authoritas semper fuit. Nam cum Archiepiscopus & Metropolitanus non aliam in sua Prouincia iurisdictionem vendicare sibi possit, quam quae iure expresso & definita fit, nec ad suum tribunal euocare ex Episcoporum dioecesibus quemplam; nisi prouocando, aut aliis moedis in iure expressis ab Episcopo proprio recesserit, & Archiepiscopum adierit: Cantuariensis tamen Archiepiscopus, in quacunque suae Prouinciae dioecesi ac Parochia, etiam appellatione nulla interposita singulas ac vnusquisque suas causas querelasque diiudicandas potest suscipere. Quae iurisdictio, tam tacito omnium consensu, vsuque longaevo, quam Regni institutis latisque legibus in iuris vigorem necessitatemque iamdiu tran-fit.
units.tr: Having set these things out, let us now come to those matters which belong to jurisdiction and which by a certain peculiar right pertain to the Archbishop of Canterbury. The great force and authority of this jurisdiction has always been considerable. For although an Archbishop and Metropolitan can claim in his province no jurisdiction other than that which is expressed and defined by law, nor summon anyone from the dioceses of bishops to his tribunal, unless that person has departed from his own bishop by appeal or by other means expressed in law and has approached the Archbishop, yet the Archbishop of Canterbury may take up and adjudicate the individual causes and complaints of each and every person in any diocese and parish of his province, even with no appeal having been lodged. This jurisdiction, by the tacit consent of all, by long usage, and by the institutions and broad laws of the realm, has for a long time passed into the force and necessity of law.

units.la: Adhaec ipsarum appellationum iura, quae omnibus Metropolitanis competunt, in hac tamen sede fuit prope singularia. Nam ab inferioribus iudiciis ad hunc Metropolitanum omissis mediis appellatur, & non gradatim vt iura praescribunt. Statimque appellatione recepta, vetat eos a quibus appellatum est, mandatis vt dicitur prohibitoriis, ne causam ad suum tribunal per appellationem delatam vlterius tractent, neue quisquam in appellantis praeiudicium attentent aut faciant; quod iura sine causae cognitione fieri haud permittunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the rights of appeal itself, which belong to all Metropolitans, were in this see nearly peculiar. For appeal is made from the lower courts to this Metropolitan with the intermediate stages omitted, and not step by step as the laws prescribe. And immediately upon receiving the appeal he forbids, by what are called prohibitory mandates, those from whom the appeal was made to proceed further with the case brought before his tribunal by appeal, and forbids anyone to attempt or do anything to the prejudice of the appellant. The laws do not permit this to be done without examination of the cause.

units.la: Praeterea cum in his causis, in quibus iam ad Regiam Maiestatem appellatur, Archiepiscopus de causa controuersa summarie cognouit, reliqui controuersiae possessionem intuam appellationis reseruato. Et haec appellatio, quia possessionis tuenda causa interposita erat, tutoria dicta est. Culus praesidio vt possessionem firmaret, non modo litigantibus, sed ipsis Romani Pontificis Iudicibus delegatis inhibuit, neue pendente quacunq; innouatione possessionem a sede eiectam turbarent, aut appellantis praeiudicium inferrent. Ad hoc possessionis tuendae auxilium implorandum, non modo ex sua Prouincia, sed ex Eboracensi, atque Hyberniae, aliisque Prouinciis Gallicanis, quae quondam in Anglia Regis ditione fuerunt, omnesque Papam prouocantes olim confugerunt. Cum autem in illa, vt diximus, potestate sit inferiorum praelatorum defectus & negligentias supplere, hoc ille nulla prius negligentiæ coniunctione, probationeq; praehabita facit, eorumq; gesta arbitrio, libitoq; suo reuocat, ac reformat.
units.tr: Moreover, in those causes in which appeal has already been made to the royal Majesty, when the Archbishop has summarily examined the disputed cause, he reserves possession of the remaining controversy until the outcome of the appeal. And this appeal, since it was lodged for the sake of protecting possession, was called tutorial. By its protection, in order to make possession secure, he forbade not only the litigants but even the judges delegated by the Roman Pontiff to disturb, while any innovation was pending, the possession ejected from the see, or to cause prejudice to the appellant. To obtain this aid for protecting possession, not only from his own province but from the province of York, from Ireland, and from other Gallican provinces which were once under the king's rule in England, all who appealed to the Pope formerly took refuge. Since, as we have said, it is within his power to supply the defects and negligences of inferior prelates, he does this without any prior proof or previous finding of negligence, and recalls and reforms their acts at his own pleasure and discretion.

units.la: Sedis etiam Episcopalis in sua Prouincia cuiuscunq; vacantis authoritas, quæ iure communi in Ecclesiæ Capitulo vel Conuentu tanquam in reliquo corpore manet, in Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo consistit. Sed hanc authoritatem alteri plerumq; mandare solet, qui vtoto satis nomine, illius diocæsis quæ Episcopo carer, Custos spiritualitatis nuncupatur. Hac praerogatiua omnia illius vacantis Dioecesis Episcopalia iura ad Archiepisc. deuenerunt, veluti visitandi, instituendi & reliqua, fructus etiam quorum cunque beneficiorum vacantium ad suos vsus percipiendi. Quod quia primus annuus valor vniuscuiusque Ecclesiastici beneficii vacantis Principi persoluitur, æquiore vtic iure incubentibus conceditur. Beneficia item, quæ iuris patronatus illius vacantis Episcopatus fuerit, si se custodie vacarent, liberè conferebat, quod iam Regale censeretur ius, non Archiepiscopale. Quanquam in Assaphensi Episcopatu huius iuris possessionem vsq; ad regnum Henr. 8. reuniuit.
units.tr: The authority of an episcopal see that is vacant in any province, which under common law remains in the chapter or convent of the church as in the rest of the body, rests with the Archbishop of Canterbury. He usually commits this authority to another, who, under the general name, is called Custos spiritualitatis of the diocese that lacks a bishop. By this prerogative all the episcopal rights of that vacant diocese pass to the archbishop, such as visiting, instituting and the rest, and he takes for his own use the fruits of any vacant benefices. Because the first year's value of every ecclesiastical benefice when vacant is paid to the prince, it is granted to incumbents by a fairer right. Likewise, benefices in the patronage of that vacant bishopric, if they fell vacant during the custody, he conferred freely; this is now regarded as a royal right, not an archiepiscopal one. Yet in the bishopric of St Asaph he retained possession of this right until the reign of Henry 8.

units.la: Episcopatus & Dioecesis suæ Prouinciæ quandocunq; & quocunq; ordine sibi videbitur expedire, visitat. Indicta vero & pendente visitatione Archiepiscopali, tam Suffraganei quam inferiores praelati ordinaria sua Iurisdictione abstinent, omniaq; per Archiepiscopum, eiusque commissarios expediuntur. Causaq; ad se in visitatione delatas, iudiciaq; tum capta, finita vel relaxata visitatione retinet ac definit. Ac praeter hanc Archiepiscopalem visitationem, diocæses quotiescunque vacauerint, iure ordinario visitat.
units.tr: He visits the bishoprics and dioceses of his province whenever and in whatever order seems expedient to him. When an archiepiscopal visitation has been announced and is in progress, both suffragans and lesser prelates refrain from their ordinary jurisdiction, and everything is dispatched by the archbishop and his commissaries. He keeps and decides the causes brought before him in the visitation, and the judgments given there, whether they are concluded or relaxed once the visitation is over. Besides this archiepiscopal visitation, he also visits dioceses in the ordinary way whenever they fall vacant.

units.la: Tamq; late patent huius Archiepiscopatus Prinilegia, vt in loca firmissima septa ac munita priuilegiis se insinuent. Multa enim loca quæ a Metropolitica & ordinaria Iurisdictione seiuncta procurarunt, ab huius tamen authoritate immunia ac tuta esse non poterant. Iuter quæ illæ celebres Cantabrigiensis & Oxoniensis in Anglia Academiæ, quamquam priuilegia iura & exemptionis priuilegia sibi quondam a Papa concedi procurarunt, illis tamen authoritate postea Regia irritis ac rescissis, in Cantuariensi Archiepiscopi authoritatem se reddiderunt, & tam visitationes suas subire coguntur, quam ad Synodalia sua concilia per Cancellarios accedunt.
units.tr: The privileges of this archbishopric extend so widely that they insinuate themselves into the most secure and fortified places, protected by privileges. For many places that had secured their separation from metropolitan and ordinary jurisdiction could not be safe and free from this authority. Among them are the famous English universities of Cambridge and Oxford. Although they had procured for themselves, from the Pope, privileges, rights and exemptions, these were later annulled and rescinded by royal authority, and they have submitted themselves to the authority of the Archbishop of Canterbury. They are compelled to undergo his visitations, and their chancellors attend his synodal councils.

units.la: In Cantabrigiæ Collegio S. Petri, cuius Elienfis Episcopus est patronus, ea sede vacante, tam præfectum quam socios admittit, & vni Scholarium cui gratificari voluerit, vacantem societatem confert. Oxonii Collegiorum omnium animarum & Mertonensis est patronus, ac in vtrisque ordinariam & omnimodam Iurisdictionem exercet.
units.tr: In St Peter's College, Cambridge, of which the Bishop of Ely is patron, when that see is vacant the archbishop admits both the master and the fellows, and confers the vacant fellowship on whichever scholar he wishes to favour. At Oxford he is patron of All Souls College and of Merton College, and in both he exercises ordinary and full jurisdiction.

units.la: His iuribus atque priuilegiis firmata Cantuariensi potentia, cum iam in eius esset potestate, vt diximus, Prouincialia cuncta negocia arbitrio suo moderari atque temperare, euenit vt eum Testamentorum probationes & Insinuationes, bonaque intestatorum administrandi commissiones ad Ecclesiasticum forum spectarent, & restatorum ac intestatorum plerumque bona in variis parochiis dispersa essent & dissipata, nec legitimus aut scriptus hæres ea recuperare poterat, nisi Testamenti insinuationem, aut administrandi authoritatem sibi a loci ordinario commissam sub authentico sigillo in foro Regio indicaret: ne diuersis hæredibus a diuersis ordinariis eandem authoritatem postulatibus, defunctorum bona vendi & iuris daretur, quod ob locorum & poscentium multitudinem atque varietatem sæpe contigit, Prouinciales subditi pro huiusmodi Testamentorum insinuatione, & bonorum administratione petendad Metropolitani tributum plerumque confluebant, Id Prouinciales Præsules ægrè ferebant, hoc sibi iusadimi, & a loco pulcherrimo quoque sua tribunalia deserebant.
units.tr: With the power of Canterbury thus strengthened by these rights and privileges, and since it was now in his power, as we have said, to regulate and moderate all provincial business at his own discretion, it came about that the proving of wills and their insinuation, and the commissions to administer the goods of intestates, belonged to the ecclesiastical court. The goods of the dead, often scattered and dissipated across various parishes, could not be recovered by a lawful or named heir unless he showed the insinuation of the will, or the authority to administer committed to him by the local ordinary, under the authentic seal in the royal court. This was to prevent the goods of the dead from being sold and distributed when different heirs sought the same authority from different ordinaries, which often happened because of the number and variety of places and claimants. Provincial subjects therefore often flocked to the metropolitan and paid him a fee for the insinuation of such wills and the administration of goods. The provincial bishops bore this badly, claiming that this right was taken from them, and they deserted their tribunals in that most beautiful place as well.

units.la: Itaque cum Metropolitano suo in hac controuersia sæpe luctabantur & contendebant, & instabant eius authoritatem certis Metropolitani finibus septam ac contentam esse debere. Hæc autem Testamentorum, bonaque defunctorum administrandi iura non a Cantuariensi, sed ab ordinaria Episcoporum authoritate esse petenda. Sed in hac controuersia enituit max. Caut. Archiepiscopi potestas atque vis. Planè enim docuit strictis illis Archiepiscopi seu Metropolitani finibus suam potestatem non arctari, sed quia totius Angliæ nou modo primas, sed ordinarius & Episcopus primò iustitutus fuit, & præsse se illis, vt suis Suffraganeis, & æquiore conditione in suæ Prouinciæ Dioecesibus eum illis Iurisdictionem & authoritatem gerere. Præterea ius istud antequam vendicaret, à Prouincialibus sæpissimè promeque delatum fuisse, ideoque accepisse ab illis potius quam se exegisse omnibus iuste videri posse. Ipsi enim inhquum putabant defunctorum bonis multis territoriis diuisis cogendos hæredes ad tam varia tribunalia,certius atque iustius consultum esse tam hæredibus quam legatarijs atque creditoribus in vno foro quàm in pluribus litigare. Illos deinde ne Suffraganeos certis teneri legibus, in sua autem Prouincia suæ foliis post Principum esse potestatis æquum & bonum legibus permisceré,illorum defectus non in facto solùm sed in iurez se supplendos & adiuuandos. Illorum iurisdictione liuum multitudinem in propositis causis crescere,& in infinitum deduci,sua vero minui & amputari, Non sanè iuriam illis facere,qui suo tantum iure,quod summa æquitate niitur,vtatur. Hæc crebro repetita multisq; annis agitata controuersia contra Episcopos, secundum Metropolitanum tandem definita desiit.
units.tr: So they often struggled and contended with their metropolitan over this dispute, insisting that his authority ought to be enclosed and confined within fixed metropolitan limits, and that the rights to probate wills and to administer the goods of the dead should be sought from the ordinary authority of the bishops, not from Canterbury. But in this controversy the power and might of the most reverend Archbishop of Canterbury showed itself. For he clearly demonstrated that his power was not restricted by those narrow limits of archbishop or metropolitan, since he was instituted not only as primate of all England but also as ordinary and bishop from the first, and that he presides over the bishops as his suffragans and exercises jurisdiction and authority within the dioceses of his province alongside them, on a fairer footing. Moreover, that right had very often been offered to him by the provincial clergy before he claimed it, so it could fairly be held that he had received it from them rather than seized it himself. For they judged it unjust that heirs, with the goods of the dead divided among many territories, should be compelled to appear before so many tribunals. It was more certain and more just to serve heirs, legatees and creditors alike by litigating in one forum rather than in several. Further, while the suffragans were bound by fixed laws, it was right and good that in his own province he should, after the power of the princes, be permitted by lawful means to temper the laws. Their defects were to be made good and supplied by him not only in fact but in law. Under their jurisdiction the multitude of cases in question grew and was drawn out endlessly, whereas under his it was reduced and cut short. Certainly he does no wrong to others by using only his own right, which rests on the highest equity. This controversy, repeated often and debated for many years against the bishops, was at last decided in favour of the metropolitan and came to an end.

units.la: Vniuscuiusq; autem Episcopi defuncti bona vel secundùm eius tabulas administrandacommittit,si testatus decesserit,vel sine tabulis,si intestatus,etsi illius singula bona vniusiurisdictionis ambitu connocantur.
units.tr: He also commits the goods of any deceased bishop to be administered according to his will if he died testate, or, if intestate, without a will, even though all the individual goods of the bishop lie within the bounds of one jurisdiction.

units.la: Hæc & alia permulta Cantuariensi sedi indulta priuilegia iuraq; consuetudine quæsita,etsi quàdam contraria legibus sublata sint,plerasq; tamen pristinam vim ac firmitatem retinent.
units.tr: These and many other privileges granted to the see of Canterbury, and rights acquired by custom, although some contrary ones have been abolished by law, nonetheless for the most part retain their former force and firmness.

units.la: Nam inclytissimus Henricus.8.Rex An.Dom.1534. exclusa & exacta suo Regno tot annis vsu capta authoritate Papali,& fucato illo Monachismo eiecto(qui vt in sequenti parebit historia, perpetuum fuit omnium Principibus cum Clero interiectarum turbarum seminarium) muliq; Papalibus ceremoniis delectis,Cantuariensis sedis Priærogatiam,lege tam suo quàm totius populi consensu lata stabiliuit,totumq; illud legum rigorem mitigandi ius quod dispensare dicitur, quod vsucapione sibi Romanus Pontifex vendicauit & vsurpauit,in Archiepiscopum Cant.similislege lata transtulit. In qua lege cautum est ne præter diuina,Regiqúe atq; Regni auita iura Cantuariensis quicquâ decerneret.
units.tr: For the most renowned King Henry 8, in the year of the Lord 1534, having excluded and expelled the papal authority, which had been usurped in his kingdom for so many years, and having cast out that feigned monasticism (which, as will appear in the history that follows, was a perpetual seedbed of the disturbances stirred up by princes together with the clergy), and having rejected many papal ceremonies, established by a law passed with the consent of himself and of the whole people the prerogative of the see of Canterbury. By a similar law he transferred to the Archbishop of Canterbury the whole right of mitigating the rigour of the laws, which is called dispensing, and which the Roman Pontiff had claimed and usurped by prescription. In this law it is provided that the Archbishop of Canterbury shall decree nothing beyond the divine law, the royal law and the ancient rights of the realm.

units.la: Hanc igitur tam latè patentem Iurisdictionem vt absoluerer,fora varia,& tribunalia ordinauit,quæ Doctis peritisq; iudicibus, aduocatis, procuratoribus, scribis, notariis,& actuariis ad causas agendas & iudicia reddenda parata ac instruxit.
units.tr: So that I might set out this jurisdiction, which extends so widely, he ordained various courts and tribunals, and equipped them, ready for conducting cases and giving judgments, with learned and skilled judges, advocates, proctors, scribes, notaries and clerks.

units.la: Primum & antiquissimum Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi consistorium, Alma curia de Arcubus London vulgariter appellatur.Nomen a Templo Beatæ Mariæ Londini dedicato,cuius culmen ad similitudinem intenti arcus in summo euruatum & quasi ad uncum est,dicitur sumpsisse. Iudex qui huic consistorio præest, Decanus de'Arcubus, vel officialis almæ curiæ Cantuariensis de Arcubus nuncupatur. Decanus autem à quarundam in Londinensi ciuitate Parochiarum,quæ a iurisdictione Londinensis Episcopi exemptæ, & Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo subiectæ sunt numero 13.qui decanatum constituit,dictus est. Ex earum Parochiarum numero est illa Arcuati templi Parochia, in quo templo hic Decanus, qui eas Parochias regit, pro tribunali sedet. Huius est authoritas ordinaria atque libera,ad omnium in Cant. prouincia appellationes referibit nulla antegreßacausæ cognitione,& in illis tuitoriis appellationibus,de quibus ante diximus,is solus appellantes tuetur ac defendit.In hac curia duo sunt scribæ ac librarii, qui Registrarii dicuntur. Quorum vnus acta iudicii,iudicisque decreta ac sententias in iure scribit,hic actuarius appellatur. Alter testes in iure priusiuratos scrutim ac diligenter examinat &excquirit,eorumque depositiones,partiumque ad libellos & allegationes responsiones describit,tum omnia iudicii acta,veteraque dictæ curiæ monumenta in ordinem redacta custodit,ideoque Registri seu tabularii custos nuncupatur. Aduocatorum in ea curia numerus sexdecem antiquitus constitutus est, sed pro Archiepiscopi iure atque voluntate est arbitrarus.Hic Doctores legum in celebri aliqua studiorum vniuersitate ordinantur,antequam ad hoc tam infigne tribunal accedunt. Et vt certius atque diligentius Clientibus de iure respondeant,antiquitus constituit fuit, vt tam ordine sacerdotali, quàm beneficiis Ecclesiasticis animarum curam habentibus,quamdiu in illa aduocatione exercentur,abstineant. Postea verò Regni statuto,in ordinis illius gratiam indulkum fuit,vt ab his beneficiis quæ residentiam requirunt, aduocationis suæ causa,inoffensa statuti sanctione abesse possent. Cum ex eo numero quispiam vel moritutis fuerit,vel ordinem deseruerit, Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus literis commissionalibus ad Decanum missis alium deligna.Is die aliquo iuridico in Aduocatorum coetu,à duobus aduocatis ad Decanû pro tribunali sedente deducitur. Illi Decano porrigit Archiepiscopales literas,quibus publicè perlectis,inaugurandum Doctorem laudant,moribus adeo commodis,iurisque tanta peritia affirmant, vt in suum numerum ascifcendum putent, Id à Decano fieri petunt:qui iuramentum ei defert de authoritate Regia agnoscenda,
units.tr: The first and most ancient consistory of the Archbishop of Canterbury is commonly called the Arches Court of London (Alma curia de Arcubus). It is said to take its name from the church of St Mary in London dedicated to her, whose roof is vaulted at the top like a bent arch, almost in the shape of a hook. The judge who presides over this consistory is called the Dean of the Arches, or the official of the Arches Court of Canterbury. The dean takes his title from the thirteen parishes in the city of London that are exempt from the jurisdiction of the Bishop of London and subject to the Archbishop of Canterbury, and which he constitutes as a deanery. Among these parishes is that of the arched church, in which church this dean, who governs those parishes, sits on his tribunal. His authority is ordinary and free. He hears all appeals from throughout the province of Canterbury without any prior examination of the cause, and in those protective appeals of which we spoke earlier, he alone protects and defends the appellants.
