In this court there are two scribes and keepers of books, who are called registrars. One of them writes down the acts of the court, and the judge's decrees and sentences in law; he is called the actuary. The other diligently examines and questions the witnesses sworn in court, writes down their depositions and the parties' responses to libels and allegations, and keeps all the proceedings and the ancient records of the court arranged in order. He is therefore called the keeper of the registry or archives. The number of advocates in this court was fixed in ancient times at sixteen, but it is left to the archbishop's right and will. These men are made doctors of law in some famous university of studies before they come to this distinguished tribunal. So that they may give clients more sure and diligent advice on the law, it was established long ago that, as long as they are engaged in that advocacy, they should abstain both from clerical orders and from ecclesiastical benefices with the cure of souls. Afterwards, however, by a statute of the realm, it was granted in favour of that order that for the sake of their advocacy they might be absent, without offence to the statute's sanction, from those benefices which require residence. When any member of that number has died or left the order, the Archbishop of Canterbury, by letters of commission sent to the Dean, designates another. On some court day, in the assembly of advocates, he is led by two advocates to the Dean sitting on his tribunal. They hand the Dean the archiepiscopal letters, which are read publicly, and they commend the doctor to be inaugurated, affirming him to be of such agreeable morals and of such great skill in law that they think he should be admitted to their number. They ask the Dean to do this. He administers to him an oath concerning acknowledgment of the royal authority

units.la: { } ... agnoscenda, de fideli aduocatione & patrocinio, de grata defensione panperum, & de licita lustration Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi & Ecclesiæ iurium, libertatum, priuilegiorumque propugnatione atque tuitione. Quo iuramento publice præstito, Decanus hunc nouidum dictæ curiæ Aduocatum pronunciat, eiqueque in aduocatorum subselliis locum a dextris vel sinistris suis assignat. Ad hunc locum duobus illis aduocatis deducitur. Statimque Decanus nodosam aliquam & controuersam in iure quæstionem, de qua in vtramque partem dici posset, proponit. Decanus ipse in vtramque partem disputat, cumque perorauerit, expectat noui Aduocati sententiam. Huic dicere incipienti imponitur à Decano silentium. Hoc silentium anno durat, in quo nouus aduocatus tacituRnus peneque mutus reliquorum aduocatorum auditor, in Archiepiscopali foro sedet. Doctores seu aduocati huius fori prioritatis suæ ordine, amictu doctorali in superioribus sedent subselliis, Decano iudici in exponendis clientium suorum desideriis reuerenter assurgunt, Decanumque diebus iuridicis bini prioritatis suæ ordine subsequentes, à suo Collegio ad Consistorium ducunt atque reducunt. In eadem curia Procuratores decem litigantium causas tractant, Hi de rei controuersiæ facto intigant, iudicoque, ac scribam similibus quibus legum bacchalaurii amicti vestibus pene circumstant, nam Aduocatorum subselliæ paulo sunt a sede iudicis remotiora. Illi libellos, responsiones, materias, allegationes aut iam conceptas iudici tradunt, aut scribæ dictant, quoties que de luse ambigitur, procurator clientis sui aduocatum inuocat. Is assurgens de iure rei disseruit, si ab alterius partis aduocato contradictum sit, & sit in ambiguitate difficultas, quæ statim a iudice explicari nequit: iudex eam litem in alium diem refert, monetque aduocatos, vt ad proferenda & enucleanda de ea quæstione infra diem constitutos sibi adsint. Eo facto in lite progrediuntur. Procuratores idem iuramentum præstant, cum in eum ordinem ascribuntur, quod Aduocati, eosque cum iudice ad forum accedentes ab eoque decedentes sequuntur. His non licet sine aduocatorum consilio causas assumere, aut de iure, quod imperite & temere sæpe faciunt clientibus respondere, illique perinde ac aduocati sermone vtuntur latino, si quis secus fecerit, indicta illico à Decano poena plectitur. Prima huius fori institutio ac origo, aut monumentis tabularum & detectis ac amissis, aut librariorum negligentia incerta est. Sed constat esse periucundum: Nam Alexander 3. qui Romanus Pontifex fuit, Henrico secundo regnante ad Decanum de Arcubus rescripsit. Et Robertus Kilwarbeius Cantuar. Archiepiscopus, qui obiit Anno Domini 1172. abrogatis veteribus & obsoletis illius curiæ legibus nouas condidit. Proxima huic & quasi uterina adeoque gemella curia, Cantuariensis Audientia nuncupatur. Hæc omnes etiam Prouincialium querelas, causas & appellationes recipit. Sed illa antiquior atque nobilior celebratur. Nam huius origo hæc fuit, quod plurimas causas Archiepiscopus ipse extra forum domi definiuit, de quibus antequam pronunciaret, peritis in iure doctisque viris, quos Auditores suos nominauit, discutiendas commisit. Ideoque hæc Domestica penè fuit & familiaris Archiepiscopi curia, & causarum auditores eum vbique sequuti sunt. Finitimus & coniunctus his quondam fuit Archiepiscopi Cancellarius, qui ea quæ contentiose iurisdictionis non erant, sed officii mei, gerebat. His duo scribæ seu tabellliones inseruiebant. Cancellario Principalis Archiepiscopi Registrarius, qui acta mei officii scripsit ac monumentis mandabat: Alter causarum curiæ audientiæ actuarius dictus est. Quæ duo munera à duobus adhuc diuisa & dispertita administrantur. Sed Cancellarii & Auditorum officia in vnum diu collata sunt, quiin Ecclesia Paulina & Londinensi Consistorio iudicia dat. Huius tribunal ab eisdem Aduocatis & Procuratoribus, quibus Arcuata curia frequentatur, aliis enim permissum non est in propositis ibi causis versari. Eademque iura atque consuetudines vtriusque curiæ sunt. In eodem etiam loco de hereditatibus ab intestato, eu testamento desatis, deque testamentorum atque legatorum iure ab alio iudice qui Custos, Magister siue Commissarius Cantuariensis Prærogatiuæ appellatur, iura reddunturs. Qui etiam peculiarem habet atque suum scribam, qui Prærogatiuæ Cant. curiæ Registrarius vocatur. Ab hoc iudice testamentorum quæ ad ius Præerogatiuam Cant. (de quo ante diximus) spectant insinuationes, bonaque intestatorum administrandi commissiones decernuntur. Quæ omnia negocia in eadem Archiepiscopi a domestico iudice olim administrabantur, sed litium multitudine crescente, stata pro his causis Londinicuriaest, quæ etsi dignitate inferior sit, tamen copia & vbertate fructuum ceteras vincit atque superat. Iidemque etiam Aduocati & Procuratores causas in hac curia curant, qui in prioribus.
units.tr: ... acknowledging royal authority, of faithful advocacy and patronage, of gracious defence of the poor, and of the lawful upholding and protection of the rights, liberties and privileges of the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Church. Once this oath has been publicly taken, the Dean declares this new advocate of the said court and assigns him a place on the advocates' benches, to his right or left. He is led to this place by the two advocates. Straightaway the Dean puts forward some knotty and disputed point of law, on which something could be said on either side. The Dean himself argues both sides, and when he has finished speaking he waits for the opinion of the new advocate. As he begins to speak, the Dean imposes silence on him. This silence lasts a year, during which the new advocate, quiet and almost mute, sits in the Archbishop's court as a listener to the other advocates. The doctors or advocates of this court sit on the higher benches in doctoral dress, each in the order of his seniority, and rise respectfully when the Dean as judge explains the wishes of their clients. On court days, two of them at a time, following in order of seniority, escort the Dean from their College to the Consistory and back again. In the same court, ten proctors handle the causes of litigants. They take up the facts of the matter in dispute and stand about the judge and the scribe in gowns much like those of bachelors of law, for the proctors' benches are a little further from the judge's seat than the advocates' are. They hand to the judge the libels, answers, papers and pleas, either already drafted or dictated to the scribe; and whenever there is doubt about the law, the client's proctor calls on an advocate. The advocate rises and argues the point of law. If the advocate of the other side has contradicted him, and there is a difficulty in the ambiguity which the judge cannot at once resolve, the judge adjourns the suit to another day and warns the advocates to be present within that day to put forward and clear up the question. When this is done, the suit proceeds. The proctors take the same oath when they are enrolled in their order as the advocates do, and they follow the advocates and the judge as they come to the court and leave it. They may not take up causes without the advice of the advocates, nor answer clients about the law, which they often do unskilfully and rashly; and they use the Latin language just as the advocates do. If anyone acts otherwise, he is at once punished with a fine imposed by the Dean. The first establishment and origin of this court is uncertain, either because the records have been lost or destroyed, or through the carelessness of the copyists. But it is certain that it is very ancient: for Alexander III, who was Roman Pontiff, wrote to the Dean of the Arches in the reign of Henry II. And Robert of Kilwardby, Archbishop of Canterbury, who died in the year of our Lord 1172, abolished the old and obsolete laws of that court and framed new ones. Next to this court, and as it were its twin and sister, is the Canterbury Audience, which also receives all the complaints, causes and appeals of the provincials. But that court is reckoned the older and more distinguished. Its origin was this: the Archbishop himself decided very many causes at home outside the court, and before he pronounced on them he committed them to be examined by men skilled in law and learned, whom he named his auditors. So this was almost a domestic and familiar court of the Archbishop, and its auditors followed him wherever he went. Closely connected with these in former times was the Archbishop's Chancellor, who handled matters that were not of contentious jurisdiction but of my office. Two scribes or notaries served these. Under the Chancellor was the principal registrar of the Archbishop, who wrote down the acts of my office and committed them to the records; the other is called the actuary of the audience court. These two offices are still administered separately, though they were long combined in one. He who gives judgments at the Consistory of St Paul's and London has the same advocates and proctors who frequent the Arches court, for others are not permitted to be engaged in the causes heard there; and the rights and customs of both courts are the same. In the same place, rights are also administered concerning inheritances without a will, and concerning the law of wills and legacies, by another judge who is called the Keeper, Master or Commissary of the Canterbury Prerogative. He also has his own scribe, who is called the Registrar of the Prerogative Court of Canterbury. From this judge are issued the probates of wills that pertain to the Canterbury Prerogative (of which we spoke before), and the commissions for administering the goods of those who died intestate. All these matters were formerly administered in the Archbishop's domestic court, but as the number of lawsuits grew, a fixed court for these causes was established in London, which, although lower in dignity, surpasses and outdoes the others in the abundance and richness of its fees. The same advocates and proctors manage the causes in this court as in the former ones.

units.la: Tandem eiecta prorsus authoritate papali, cum Henricus octauus, vt diximus, iuris Ecclesiastici moderationem & æquitatem lege lata in Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo potuisset, constituta noua curia est, eiusque iudex præfectus, qui desideria cognoscit eorum, qui iuris quandoq; rigidi atq; stricti relaxationem petunt, & Registrarius qui concessas dispensationes in scriptaretert. Ille Magister seu custos facultatum, hic earum Registrarius appellatur. Hæc curia quia litigiola non est, in ædibus Archiepiscopi sine foro & tribunali plerumq; excercetur.
units.tr: At last, when the papal authority had been utterly thrown out, Henry VIII, as we have said, was able by statute to moderate and temper the ecclesiastical law in the Archbishop of Canterbury; and a new court was set up, with a judge placed over it, who hears the requests of those who sometimes seek relief from the rigour and strictness of the law, and a registrar who writes down the dispensations granted. The one is called the Master or Keeper of faculties, the other their Registrar. Because this court is not litigious, it is usually held in the Archbishop's house, without a bar or tribunal.

units.la: Habet etiam Archiepiscopus Cant. in nonnullis Prouinciæ suæ Dioecesibus Parochias quasdam à iurisdictione Episcopali & Archidiaconali quacunq; separatas, sibiq; peculiares. Quibus peculiares præsunt iudices, qui peculiarium Decani appellantur, quibus etiam peculiares atq; proprij Registrarii adiunguntur. Hæ autem Parochiæ ordine secundùm diocæses scripiæ sequuntur: Decanatus de Archubus. Ecclesia sancti Vedasti. Ecclesia sancti Dunstani in Oriente. Ecclesia sancti Leonardi in Castlesope. Ecclesia S. Dionysij Backchurch. Ecclesia sanctorum sanctorum Lombardstreet. Ecclesia sancti Michaelis in Corneill Lane. Eccl. beatæ Mariæ Bothaw. Ecclesia sancti Michaelis in Riola, alias Pater noster. Ecclesia beatæ Mariæ Aldermaria. Ecclesia sancti Pancratii. Ecclesia beatæ Mariæ de Archubus. Ecclesia omnium sanctorum in Bredstreet. Eccl. S. Iohan. Euangelistæ in Maslonstreet. Decanatus de Shorham. Ecclesia de Shorhá cū Capella de Offord. Ecclesia de Eynesford. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Derueth. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Ferningham. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Beale. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Eaxde. Ecclesia de Northfleete. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Mepham. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Clyne. Ecclesia de Greau. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Parleigh. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Huntington. Ecclesia de Peckham. Vicaria eiusdem. Eccl. de Wrotham cum capella. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Eightham. Ecclesia de Seaueache. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Penhurst. Ecclesia de Chiddingstone. Ecclesia de Hanet. Ecclesia de Gillingham. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Brasted. Ecclesia de Sundrehe. Ecclesia de Chenening. Ecclesia de Orpington cum Capella. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Hese. Ecclesia de Keston. Ecclesia de Halsted. Ecclesia de Woodland. Ecclesia de Eastmalling. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Iflel. Decanatus de Croydon. Ecclesia de Hazeow. Vicaria eiusdem. Ecclesia de Hese. Vicaria eiusdem. Hi omnes Decanatus & Parochiæ ab Episcoporum & Archidiaconorum iurisdictione liberati, Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo soli subiiciuntur. Præterea mos & consuetudo Archiepiscoporum Cantuariensium ab antiquo fuit & est, vt in terris suis vbicunque per Angliam sint, nullus Episcoporum præter se ius aliquod habeat, sed humana simul & diuina omnia, velut in propria diocæsi in sua dispositione consistant.
units.tr: The Archbishop of Canterbury also has, in some of the dioceses of his province, certain parishes separated from episcopal and archidiaconal jurisdiction of every kind and peculiar to himself. Peculiar judges preside over these, who are called Deans of the peculiars, and peculiar and proper registrars are attached to them as well. These parishes follow in order, according to the dioceses in which they are written: Deanery of the Arches. Church of St Vedast. Church of St Dunstan in the East. Church of St Leonard in Eastcheap. Church of St Dionysius Backchurch. Church of All Saints, Lombard Street. Church of St Michael in Cornhill. Church of St Mary Bothaw. Church of St Michael in Riola, otherwise Paternoster. Church of St Mary Aldermary. Church of St Pancras. Church of St Mary of the Arches. Church of All Saints in Bread Street. Church of St John the Evangelist in Watling Street. Deanery of Shoreham. Church of Shoreham with the chapel of Offord. Church of Eynesford. Its vicarage. Church of Darenth. Its vicarage. Church of Farningham. Its vicarage. Church of Beal. Its vicarage. Church of Eccles. Church of Northfleet. Its vicarage. Church of Meopham. Its vicarage. Church of Cliffe. Church of Cobham. Its vicarage. Church of Parley. Its vicarage. Church of Hollington. Church of Peckham. Its vicarage. Church of Wrotham with the chapel. Its vicarage. Church of Eight Hatch. Church of Seal. Its vicarage. Church of Penshurst. Church of Chiddingstone. Church of Hanet. Church of Gillingham. Its vicarage. Church of Brasted. Church of Sundridge. Church of Chevening. Church of Orpington with the chapel. Its vicarage. Church of Hayes. Church of Keston. Church of Halstead. Church of Woodlands. Church of East Malling. Its vicarage. Church of Ifield. Deanery of Croydon. Church of Hayes. Its vicarage. Church of Hayes. Its vicarage. All these deaneries and parishes, freed from the jurisdiction of bishops and archdeacons, are subject to the Archbishop of Canterbury alone. Moreover, it has been and is the custom and usage of the Archbishops of Canterbury from of old that, in their lands wherever they are throughout England, no bishop has any right except themselves, but all matters, both human and divine, stand at their disposal, just as in their own diocese.

units.la: In Cantio autem, quod sua propria est Dioecesis atq; iurisdictio, Consistorium Cantoriæ statuit. Eius præses Commissarius Consistorii Episcopalis Cantr. appellatur, qui hius actæ excipit, & scriptis mandat, Consistorii Episcopalis Cantr. Registrarius etiam vocatur. Huic commissario non omnia generaliter mandantur, sed quædam in specie de legantur, multioribus & grauioribus causis Cancellarii audientiæ reiseruatis.
units.tr: In Kent, which is its own diocese and jurisdiction, the consistory of Canterbury has been established. Its president is called the commissary of the episcopal consistory of Canterbury, who receives the acts and has them written down. He is also called the registrar of the episcopal consistory of Canterbury. Not all matters are entrusted to this commissary in general terms; certain ones are assigned to him specifically, the greater and more serious causes being reserved to the chancellor of the audience.

units.la: His itaque Priuilegiis, Prærogatiuis, eminentiis, immunitatibus, tribunalibus, aris, curiis Cantr. Archiepiscopi dignitas, tanquam suis numeris perfecta & absoluta constat. Quarum rerum fides ne dubia & incerta sit, sciendum est ea partim ex Archiuis turris Londinensis, partim ex domesticis Archiuis in publica Cantuariensis sedis custodia reposita fuisse desumpta. Quæ eam vim habent, vt ea sine aliis probationum adminiculis plenam non legentibus solum, sed & iudicantibus fidem faciunt. Ipsiis namq; ærebris Suffraganeorum cum Metropolitano, de iurisdictione, iudicis & controuersiis, in quibus Suffraganei semper fuceumbebant, cum Metropolitanus iurisdictionem suam, & iure primæuo fundatam, & diuturnuo via firmatam, ex his monumentis docere, negabant Suffraganei suorum actorum & registri authoritatem ad id probandum sufficere, quia in proprio registro custodita scripta, priuata non publica, esse nodiciam, da.
units.tr: By these privileges, prerogatives, eminences, immunities, tribunals, altars and courts, the dignity of the archbishop of Canterbury stands complete and perfect in all its parts. So that the proof of these things may not be doubtful or uncertain, it should be known that they were drawn partly from the archives of the Tower of London and partly from the domestic archives kept in public custody at the see of Canterbury. These records have such force that, without other supports of proof, they win full credence not only from readers but also from judges. For in the very disputes of the suffragans with the metropolitan, concerning jurisdiction, judgments and controversies, in which the suffragans always used to lose, when the metropolitan sought to show from these records that his jurisdiction was founded on primitive right and confirmed by long usage, the suffragans denied that the authority of his acts and register was sufficient for proving this, since writings kept in one's own register are private, not public.

units.la: At verò cum & temporis diuturnitas, & actorum frequentia, & à multo iudicio ne pe Metropolitano mandare, & à suis officialibus & notariis personis publicis diu seruata custodia, simul iuncta vnius generis, & similia instrumenta proferebantur ab annorum gestorum multitudinem, mandatis authoritatem, ad ministrationem dignitatem obtinuit Archiepiscopus, vt ex suis Archiuis prolata & editæ instrumenta, sine authentica, & in formam publicam redacta, siue priuata in solito & consueto registri loco custodiæ causa posita, sine alterius probationis ope idem ex se fieri, atque suffraganei dum eneruare Metropolitani sui vires studuerunt, ipsi non modo debilitati, sed & tractati ceciderunt. Prædictæ etiam consuetudines, prærogatiuæ, & priuilegia Metropolitanæ sedi tam firmiter infixæ hæreant, vt (nisi aperta lege) tolli & auelli haud possint, atque Suffraganei, eâ Metropolitanus tolerantia & conniuentia (quod æquisbilitate sua sæpe solet) iuri suo aliquandiu cedat, multaq; temitat, & a Suffraganeis vsurpari, vellongit, simi temporis tractu sinat, Archiepiscopalia tamen iura acquirere sibi, aut Metropolitanum excludere vel prohibere, propter iurisdictionis causas quod fiebat præsumptus nulla præscriptione possunt iurisdictionis enim suæ habenas, & relaxatum vult, & cadu ducit ad se cum necesse est.
units.tr: But since the length of time, the number of acts, and the long-kept custody by his officials and notaries, who are public persons, together with the similar kind of instruments produced over the many years of recorded business, gave the archbishop authority and standing, it was accepted that instruments produced and issued from his archives, whether unauthenticated, or put into public form, or private and placed for safekeeping in the usual and customary place of the register, could by their own force, without any other proof, be treated in the same way. While the suffragans strove to weaken the powers of their metropolitan, they themselves fell, not only weakened but also roughly handled. The aforesaid customs, prerogatives and privileges cling so firmly to the metropolitan see that they cannot be removed or torn away except by an express law. The suffragans, through the metropolitan's tolerance and connivance (which by his equity he is often accustomed to show), yield some of their right for a time and allow many things to be usurped by them over a long lapse of time. Yet they cannot by prescription acquire archiepiscopal rights for themselves, or exclude or prohibit the metropolitan, in matters of jurisdiction, on the ground that such things were presumptuously done. For he wishes to hold the reins of his jurisdiction, and when they have been relaxed, he draws them back to himself whenever necessary.

units.la: Nunc Cantuariensis sedis Prærogatiua & Priuilegiis satis breuiter expositis, patiendo ipsa Cantuariæ titulate dicamus: deinde ad Gregorium, & Augustinum, cum sequutos Cantuarienses Archiepiscopos ordine accedamus. In quorum vitis gestisq; declarandis, authorum qui illorum remporum scriptoriam, potius quam elegantioris stylitationem habere contendit, ne quacunq; etiamsi minutiss imam re, ab historiæ veritate deflexisse videamur.
units.tr: Now that the prerogative and privileges of the see of Canterbury have been set out briefly enough, let us, by the favour of God, speak of the title itself of Canterbury; then we shall come in order to Gregory and Augustine, and the archbishops of Canterbury who followed them. In setting out their lives and deeds, I have aimed to write as a chronicler of those times rather than to seek a more elegant style, so that, even in the smallest matter, we may not seem to have departed from the truth of history.

units.la: DOROVERNIÆ, SEV CANTVARIÆ scriptio.
units.tr: DOROVERNIÆ, SEV CANTVARIÆ scriptio.

units.la: Antium, quod atroc hissima & humanissima Britanniæ habita seruer per fuit prouincia, ad austrum Solemq; Orientem Oceano Germanico, ad aquilonem vberrimo Thamesi fluuio, ad Occidentem Sueuram, ac Sussexia prouincias, quas Angli Comitatus appellant, cingitur. Hæc & agrorum feracitate fœcunda, populoq; generoso, ac potenti fefa rita, plures vrbes, villasq; in locis, ob aquas & sylvas vicinas humanæ habitationi commodioribus condidit, & ob marium timos portus, quos multos habet peregrinorum consuetudine, Galliæq; vicinitate magis quam reliquæ huius Insulæ regiones à scriptoribus perhibetur. Quibus leni tionibus, & moribus cultior, & opibus diuior iure existimatur. Huius regionis antiquissima ciuitas nunc appellatur Cantuaria. Nam Ptolomaeus Durnouernum nominat: deinde sequentibus seculis immutato populi idiomate, nunc Dorovernum, nunc Durouernum, nunc Dorobernia, nunc Dorobrinia, nunc Doroucernia, dicta fuit: quae consimilia nomina, ab antiquo Britannico vocabulo <bl>Dwr</bl> / quod aquam significat, deducta fuisse hinc quidam coniiciunt, quod fluuius qui eam praeterlabitur, antiquus <bl>Dwr</bl>, nunc Stower appellatur: indeque vicus per eum extensus, <bl>Stowerstreat</bl>, etiamnum dicitur. Cantuariae autem nomen a Saxonibus, qui fugatis Britannis Cantium tenebant, impositum hac origine fuit. A Rudibrasio prudentissimo Britannorum Rege haec Cantiorum celeberrima Ciuitas, ante Christi incarnationem, 890. condita, ab eo quae Caer Kent id est, Cantiorum eiusdem dicta est, quia iura hic Cantiis dari iudiciaq; exerceri solebant. Itaque aduenru suo Saxones eandem Cantwarabirige, id est, Cantiorum virorum curiam, appellabat: Ware enim Saxonice, pluralis est numerus Wer, quod virum significat: Byrig autem eadem lingua iudicii locus, tribunal, seu curia est abilla prima nominis nota paulatim Anglica voce ac Canterburie: Latina omissis duabus syllabis Cantwara, deinde Cantuaria deuenit: quae omnibus eam ciuitatem seruate denotantibus, iam in usu est.
units.tr: Kent, which was regarded as the most fierce and yet the most humane province of Britain, is bounded to the south and the east by the German Ocean, to the north by the very fertile river Thames, and to the west by Surrey and Sussex, which the English call counties. Rich in fertile fields and in a noble and powerful people, it has founded many towns and villages in places more suited to human habitation because of the nearby waters and woods. Because of its safe harbours, which many foreigners use, and its proximity to Gaul, it is said by writers to be more civilised than the other regions of this island. By its mild climate and its customs it is rightly judged more cultivated, and by its resources more wealthy. The most ancient city of this region is now called Canterbury. Ptolemy calls it Durnouernum; then in the following centuries, as the speech of the people changed, it was called now Dorovernum, now Durouernum, now Dorobernia, now Dorobrinia, now Doroucernia. Some conjecture that these similar names were derived from the ancient British word Dwr, which means water, because the river that flows past it, formerly called Dwr, is now called the Stower; and the street extended along it is still called Stowerstreet. The name Canterbury, however, was given by the Saxons, who, after driving out the Britons, held Kent, and it arose from this origin. This most famous city of the men of Kent was founded by Rudibras, the most prudent king of the Britons, 890 years before the incarnation of Christ, and was called by him Caer Kent, that is, the city of the men of Kent, because it was customary there to give laws and to hold courts for the men of Kent. Therefore on their arrival the Saxons called it Cantwarabirig, that is, the court of the men of Kent: for Ware in Saxon is the plural of Wer, which means man, and Byrig in the same language means a place of judgement, a tribunal or court. From the first part of this name, gradually, in English it became Canterburie, and in Latin, with two syllables dropped, Cantwara, and then Cantuaria. This form, which all who speak of that city now use, is in use.

units.la: Quidam hanc ciuitatem eam esse putant, quae in extremo Cantii promontorio excelsa arce portuq; celebri dicitur Douerum, a quo ad Caletum maritimum ex alteta parte in Gallia oppidum secundis ventis spirantibus, quatuor horis breuissimus fit traiectus. Quos similitudine nominis deceptos ac perturbatos errare perspicuum est. Ptolomaeus enim Dnraruennum mediterraneam esse scribit Cantii ciuitatem, non maritimam. Deinde Beda Iustum ab Augustino in ea Cantii ciuitate Episcopum ordinatum scribit, quae a Dorouernia 14 fere passuum milibus ad occidentem distat, Quaeq; a primo eius conditore Roff Rofecestria dicta fuit. Quilocorum situs & distantia illorum errorem arguit. Abest enim a Douero Roffa triginta duobus passuum millibus, abeoque ita facet, vt in septentrionem magis quam in occidentem spectet, Cantuaria autem duodecim miliaribus mari abest, teste Ptolomaeo sub longitudine gradus 21. Huc Hengistus & Horsa Saxonum duces a Vortigerno Britannorum Rege opem sibi contra Pictos laturi, aeciti appulerunt, qui eiectis postea Britannis ciuitatem pariter totamq; Pronunciam tenuerunt. Deinde cum Cantium ab vno Rege regeretur, fuit haec ciuitas illius Regni Metropolis. Cumq; Augustinus in Angliam ad Ethelbertum Cantii Regem accedeceret, caput Imperii Regis Ethelberti dicebatur. Hanc muro cinctam Augustino Ethelberus eum Regalibus turribus priuilegiisq; donauit, ipse vero Xaculut recessit, ibique palarium sibi statuit: sed Augustinus in ea sedem Archiepiscopalem primo statuit, cuius celebritate atque fama trans regni ac Imperii Anglicani Metropolis deinceps semper floruit. Templum autem ante Saxonum Imperium a Romanis quondam extructum fuit Cantuariae, Saluatoris nomini dedicatum, quod ad Augustini tempora parietibus atq; tecto integrum extabat.
units.tr: Some think that this city is the one that is said to lie on the far tip of Kent, with a high fortress and a famous harbour, Dover, from which the shortest crossing, in four hours with favourable winds, is made to Calais, a town on the other side in Gaul. But it is clear that those who are misled and confused by the similarity of the names are in error. For Ptolemy writes that Durnovernum is an inland city of Kent, not a maritime one. Next, Bede writes that Justus was ordained bishop by Augustine in that city of Kent which lies about fourteen miles west of Canterbury and which was called Rochester from its first founder. The positions and distances of these places prove their error. Rochester is thirty-two miles from Dover, and lies so that it faces north rather than west. Canterbury, however, is twelve miles from the sea, according to Ptolemy, at a longitude of 21 degrees. Hither Hengist and Horsa, leaders of the Saxons, were summoned and landed, having been invited by Vortigern, king of the Britons, to bring him help against the Picts. Afterwards, when the Britons had been driven out, they held the city and the whole province alike. Then, when Kent was ruled by one king, this city was the metropolis of that kingdom. And when Augustine came into England to King Ethelbert of Kent, it was called the seat of King Ethelbert's power. Ethelbert, having enclosed this city with a wall, gave it to Augustine together with royal towers and privileges; but he himself withdrew to Reculver, and set up a palace for himself there. Augustine, however, first established an archiepiscopal see in this city, and by its renown and fame it has ever since flourished as the metropolis of the whole kingdom and English empire. Moreover, before the rule of the Saxons, a temple dedicated to the name of the Saviour was once built at Canterbury by the Romans, and it still stood whole, with walls and roof, until the time of Augustine.

units.la: QVA OCCASIONE AVGVSTINVS A GREGORIO IN ANGLIAM MISSVS EST.
units.tr: QVA OCCASIONE AVGVSTINVS A GREGORIO IN ANGLIAM MISSVS EST.

units.la: Ontificii qui primam in Anglia Euangelii sationem sibi acceptam ferri cupiunt, tradunt de Augustini huc a Gregorio mittendi occasione suis annalibus non indignam fabulam: In viu tum Romanis fuisse formosissima mancipia abducta ex Anglia in foro publice vendere. Quae Gregorius tum Presbyter Romanus cum eo forte transisset conspicatus, & venustatem tantam admiratus, eorum vicem ferrent doluisse, quod tam pulcherrimi hominum genus verum Deum ignorarent. Moxq; de Gentis nomine quaesiuit, cui responsum est quod Angli vocarentur: & recte inquit, nam & angelicas habent facies, & tales Angelorum coelestium decet esse coheredes. Deinde de qua illius gentis provincia exiisset: cui quod ex Deiborealiter ius regionis provincia exisset, responsum est.
units.tr: The Papists, who wish the first sowing of the Gospel in England to be credited to them, relate, in their annals, a not unworthy story about the occasion for sending Augustine here from Gregory. At that time, they say, there were very beautiful slaves brought from England and sold publicly in the marketplace at Rome. Gregory, then a Roman presbyter, happened to pass by them, and seeing them and admiring their great beauty, grieved for their condition, that so handsome a race of men should be ignorant of the true God. He at once asked what the name of the people was, and was told that they were called Angles; and rightly, he said, for they have angelic faces, and such people ought to be co-heirs of the heavenly angels. Then he asked from what province of that people they had come; and he was told that they came from Deira, which is a region of Britain.

units.la: At ille provinciae nomini alludens, perinde atque gentis fecisset, bene inquit Deiri, id est de ira Dei eruti, & ad misericordiam Christi vocati. Ultimo de illius Provinciae Regis nomine interrogarit, cumque accepisset quod Elle diceretur. Alleluia (inquit) landem Dei creatoris illi in partibus oporteat cantari. Itaq; suscepto papatu nihil sibi prius faciendum duxit, quam tam pulcherram & eandidam gentem in Christiana vocare societatem, eaq; de causa Augustinum eum sua potentia in Angliam destinauit. Sed Pontificiorum historia tantis mendaciis referta & assueta semper fuit, vt nec verum quidem aliquid enunciare nisi permista vanitate potuit. Vt enim concedamus Augustinum huc missum à Gregorio, tamen nec hanc fuisse legationis suæ causam, eamque non gratuitam à Gregorio & Augustino, sed ab ipsis Anglis Euangelii desiderio expetitam, occupationem quàm ipsum Gregorium testem proferre debemus neminem. Cum enim Augustinus & Romani vulgari sermone neque ad verbum declarandum, neque ad vllam vitæ consuetudinem cum Anglis loqui potuissent, scripsit Gregorius duas literas, vnas ad Theodoricum, & Theodebertum Francorum Reges; alteras ad Brunichildam reginam, in quibus rogauit, vt Augustinum in eo munere peragendo iuvarent. Quarum litteratum verba, quæ de hac re mentionem faciunt, duximus inserbenda.
units.tr: Playing on the name of the province, as if he had made a pun on the people, he said, "Well, Deiri," that is, rescued from the wrath of God, and called to the mercy of Christ. Finally he asked the name of the king of that province, and when he learned that he was called Ælle, he said, "Alleluia! The praise of God the Creator must be sung in those parts." Therefore, on assuming the papacy, he thought nothing should be done by him before he called so beautiful and fair a people into Christian fellowship, and for this reason he sent Augustine into England with his authority. But the history of the Papists has always been so full of great lies and so accustomed to them that it has never been able to state even a true thing without mixing in some falsehood. For even if we grant that Augustine was sent here by Gregory, yet this was not the cause of his mission, nor was it undertaken without request, freely, by Gregory and Augustine, but was sought by the English themselves from their desire for the Gospel. And for this we ought to call no witness other than Gregory himself. For since Augustine and the Romans could speak neither in the vernacular language to explain the word of God, nor to hold any ordinary conversation of life with the English, Gregory wrote two letters: one to Theodoric and Theodebert, kings of the Franks, the other to Queen Brunhild, in which he asked them to help Augustine in carrying out that task. We have thought fit to insert the words of these letters that speak about this matter.

units.la: Peruenit ad nos Anglorum gentem ad fidem Christianam Deo miserante desiderantes velle conuerti, sed Sacerdotes tui è vicino negligere: & desideria eorum cessare sua adhortatione succendere. Ob hoc igitur Augustinum seruum Dei præsentium portatorem, cuius zelus & studium nobis est cognitum, cum aliis feruis Dei prævidimus illoc dirigendum. Quibus etiam iniunximus, vt aliquos secum è vicino debeant presbyteros ducere, cum quibus eorum possumus mentes agnoscere, & voluntatem admonitione sua (quam Deus donauerit) adiuuare, &c.
units.tr: It has come to us that the English people, by the mercy of God, desire to be converted to the Christian faith, but that your priests nearby neglect them, and do not stir up their desires by their exhortation. For this reason, therefore, we have decided to send Augustine, the servant of God, the bearer of these present letters, whose zeal and diligence are known to us, together with other servants of God, to that place. We have also instructed them that they should bring with them some presbyters from nearby, with whom they may be able to recognise their minds and assist their will by their admonition (which God has granted), and so on.

units.la: IN ALTERA AD BRVNIGILDAM EPISTOLA.
units.tr: IN THE SECOND LETTER TO BRUNHILDA.

units.la: Ndicamus ad nos peruenisse Anglorum gentem Deo annuentem velle fieri Christianam: sed Sacerdotes qui in vicino sunt pastorale ergo illas solicitudinem non habere. Quorum ne animæ in æterna damnatione valeant deperire, curæ nobis fuit præsentium portatorem Augustinum, &c.
units.tr: We say that word has reached us that the English nation, with God's assent, wishes to become Christian; but the priests who are nearby do not have the pastoral care for this. Lest their souls perish in eternal damnation, we have taken care to send Augustine, the bearer of these letters, etc.

units.la: Iam vero si quod Gregorius ipse retulit, Christianam religionem Angli desideraverunt; vtrum ex Augustini & Romanorum prædicatione, quorum eis vox adhuc ne audita fuit, postea intelligi non potuit: an ex veteribus Britannorum scintillis & monumentis ne adhuc quidem penitus deletis & extinctis; credibilius est hoc eis desiderium incessisse. Nam a vicinis sacerdotibus aduluari eos non potuisse narrat ipse Gregorius. Fortasse non minus ob Britannos tam perfide & crudeliter exactos, quàm ob tam immanta & funesta inter se bella, quibus nullis seruatis pactionibus se inuicem infestabant, & quod adduci ad fœdera conseruanda, & Britannorum itiuris resarciendas Christiana suasione non potuerunt; ideoque vt indignos Christiana communione fuisse in tanto peccato & iniuria desertos. Quod si Augustinus aduentu suo aggressus esset, eique ablata restituere suasisset, vtrum dignissime & in perpetuum Lælandus notauit, non Ethelberti Regis accessisset Regiam, sed ad Monachismum reiectus in Anglia nihil profecisset. Illa vero eos in Britannos crudelius sæuire docuit, sed videamus quam Christianam fidem in Anglorum animos aduentu suo ingenerauit, secum ne allatam Roma, ab a Britannis acceptam tradita-tamq; domi priùs. Etenim si Paulo gentium Doctori credimus fidem ex auditu, & anditum ex nunciatione verbi Dei ad nos peruenire ; quomodo ab hoc non intellecto accipere fidem potuerunt. Deinde Beda qui nihil homini detraxit, enumeratis quæ fecit ac institutiones cæteris, de prædicatione sua ne verbum quidem facit. At baptizauit vno die multa hominum millia, qui baptismus aut inuersus ac reciprocus fuit, aut hi quos baptizauit, non à se erant sed ab aliis ante ad fidem conuersi. Iohannes qui Iudæis primus baptizauit, venit prædicans, sicut baptismo sed à prædicatione, & nuciatione Euangelii exortus est. Hoc Augustinum in Anglia fecisse quis scriptor vnquam prodidit, facere non potuisse docent Epistolæ Gregorianæ. Ceremoniarum profecto fuit hic, Romanorum; rituum non Christianæ fidei, aut diuini verbi Apostolus Anglis, eosque Romanos ac Pontificios, potius quam Christianos aut Euangelicos agere docuit. Id quod ex veteribus ipsorum Saxonum legibus & prædicationibus ante Augustini huc aduentum emissis ac diuulgatis, diutinaq; ptouidentia etiam idiomate iam diu obliuione desueto, & in aliud translato conseruatis, nuperq; ad refellendum huc primum pontificiorum de Augustino errorem repertis atq; editis probabitur luculenter. Primum enim pontificiam in Encharistia transubstantiationem, inanemque corporis præsentiam negant, ac Eucharistiam ter ad minus toti populo distribuendam in utroque Panis ac Vini genere, tam ad sanguinis quam ad corporis Dominici commemorationem statuunt, tum sanctas scripturas etiam à laicis sedulò ae exquisitè ad animarum suarum salutem scrutandas, à quibus etiam orationem Dominicam, Symbolum Apostolorum, & Decalogum firmiter materna lingua teneri memoria oportere, eademq; à sacerdotibus etiam prompte ac memoriter dicenda, Euangeliaq; populo perlegenda vulgari sermone. Hic mos vsque ad Normannorum victoriam in Anglia duravit, & quia paulatim idioma tum coepit immutari, Euangelia paulò post Normannorum aduentum ante Wiclifi tempora in vulgarem sermonem iterum traducta sunt. Praeterea simulac hra non esse colenda docebant, neque clericis interdicta iure diuino coniugia, qui etiam nuptiis non obstantibus administrabant sacra, nec ad coelibatum se voto vllo aut professione astringere volebant. Ad extremum legum de Ecclesiasticis causis negotiis q; ferendarum potestatem esse penes Principes cum Parlamenti authoritate & consensu, cosque Dei Vicarios esse iure, maximáq; Christianae Ecclesiae curam habere debere affirmabant. Quae quidem antiqua veteris Ecclesiae Britannicae dogmata, diuq; post illas Romanas praeferuras ab ipsis Saxonibus retenta quàm sint verbo Dei, ac hodiernis huius regni institutis consentanea, & à Romanis discrepantia, omnimoq; contraria & abhorrentia, videre si velint clarissime possunt omnes, praesertim hi qui antiquitatem, ia sacris rebus tanquàm ducem sequuntur, quique non aeternitatis, sed temporis momentis, & prioribus ac posterioribus seculis atque eiusdem sita definiri volunt. Augustinum autem ex his de quibus tam acriter hostiliterq; cum Britannis contendebat, in quibus pauca de doctrina Christiana, sed de Romano dominatu & potentia, ac pontificis ritibus decertabat, ceremoniosum (ut ita dicā) magis quàm religiosum fuisse ex eius vita infelicius descripta patebit, in qua copiosè suoq; magis loco explicatur ea, quae ad huc videntur pertinere, lā vt ad illam fabulā, a qua digressi sumus redeamus. Si Gregorius Augustinū ad Deeros Elfleda, illorum Regem mittere statuisset, cur Catuariam potius quàm illuc appulsus cum Ethelbertho cōsedit, nec ad illos profectus est. Homo mollis atq; Monachus, humanitate Regis Ethelberti in Cantio gente fructuosa & perbenigna, tantis affectus honoribus, ab aquilonaribus Deirorum regionibus pruinosis atq; suis eadem ductus humanitate retentus est. Ita Christianitatem & institutum Gregorii, vicit humanitas Augustini.
units.tr: Now, if it is true, as Gregory himself reports, that the English desired the Christian religion, it is more credible that this desire arose from the ancient sparks and monuments of the Britons, which were not yet wholly erased and extinguished, than from the preaching of Augustine and the Romans, whose voice had not yet been heard by them and so could not afterwards be understood. Gregory himself says that they could not be won over by the priests nearby. Perhaps this was owing no less to the Britons, who had been treated so treacherously and cruelly, than to the immense and deadly wars among themselves, in which they harassed one another without keeping any agreements; and because they could not be brought, by Christian persuasion, to keep covenants and make restitution to the Britons, they were therefore left as unworthy of Christian fellowship, in such great sin and injustice. But if Augustine had confronted them on his arrival and persuaded them to restore what they had taken, then (as Lælandus most justly and perpetually noted) he would not have come to the court of King Ethelbert, but, cast back into monkery, would have achieved nothing in England. Yet Augustine taught them to rage more cruelly against the Britons. Let us see, however, what Christian faith he instilled into the minds of the English by his coming, since he did not bring it with him from Rome, but received it from the Britons, and had handed it down at home before. For if we believe Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, that faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the proclamation of the word of God, how could they receive faith from one whom they did not understand? Next, Bede, who detracted nothing from anyone, when he lists what Augustine did and the institutions he made for others, says not a word about his preaching. But he baptized many thousands of men on one day; and that baptism was either overturned and reversed, or those whom he baptized had not been converted to the faith by him but earlier by others. John, who first baptized the Jews, came preaching; baptism arose from preaching and the proclamation of the gospel, not the reverse. That Augustine did this in England no writer has ever reported, and the letters of Gregory show that he could not have done it. He was certainly a teacher of Roman ceremonies, not of the rites of the Christian faith or of the divine word; he taught the English to act as Romans and Papists rather than as Christians or Evangelicals. This will be clearly shown from the ancient laws and sermons of the Saxons themselves, which were issued and published before Augustine's arrival here, and were preserved through long providence, even in a language long since fallen into disuse and translated into another; these have lately been found and published here, for the first time, to refute the Papists' error about Augustine. For they deny the papist transubstantiation in the Eucharist and the empty presence of the body; they establish that the Eucharist is to be distributed at least three times to the whole people, in both kinds of bread and wine, as a memorial of the Lord's blood as well as of his body; and they hold that the holy Scriptures are to be searched diligently and exactly by the laity for the salvation of their souls; that the Lord's Prayer, the Apostles' Creed and the Decalogue must be firmly held in memory in the mother tongue, and that these must be recited promptly and from memory by the priests too, and that the Gospels are to be read to the people in the vernacular. This custom lasted in England until the Norman conquest; and because the language gradually began to change, the Gospels were translated again into the vulgar tongue a little after the Norman arrival, before the time of Wycliffe. Moreover, they taught that images are not to be worshipped, and that marriage is not forbidden to the clergy by divine law; they even administered the sacred rites while married, and were unwilling to bind themselves to celibacy by any vow or profession. Finally, they affirmed that the power of making laws concerning ecclesiastical causes and business belongs to the princes, with the authority and consent of Parliament, and that the princes are by right God's vicars and ought to have the greatest care of the Christian Church. How consistent these ancient doctrines of the old British Church, retained by the Saxons themselves long after those Roman arrogances, are with the word of God and with the present institutions of this realm, and how contrary and abhorrent they are to the Romans, all men can see most clearly if they wish, especially those who follow antiquity as their guide in sacred matters, and who want things defined not by the moments of eternity but by time, and by earlier and later centuries and their circumstances. Yet that Augustine was more ceremonious (so to speak) than religious, in those matters over which he contended so bitterly and hostilely with the Britons, in which he disputed little about Christian doctrine but much about Roman domination, power and the rites of the pontiff, will appear from his unhappily written life, in which what pertains to this matter is set out fully and in its proper place. But to return to that story from which we have digressed: if Gregory had decided to send Augustine to Deira, to Elfleda, their king, why did he settle in Kent with Ethelbert instead of going there after landing? A soft man and a monk, he was held back in Kent, a people fruitful and most kindly disposed to Ethelbert's humanity, honoured with such great dignities, and drawn by the same humanity from the frosty northern regions of the Deirans. Thus the humanity of Augustine overcame the Christianity and the institution of Gregory.

units.la: AVGVSTINVS.
units.tr: Augustine.

units.la: NNo Mauritii Imperatoris 14.qui fuit annus Domini 596. & post appulsum Anglorum in hanc Britanniæ Insulam. 150. mittitur in Angliam Augustinus à Gregorio Pontifice Romano, vt collapsam iam & penitus delerani, in ea Insulæ parte, quam Angli occupauerant, Christi religionem instauraret. Acceptis igitur Comitibus circiter quadraginta Augustinus, iter in Angliam aggreditur. Cum vero aliquantum itineris confecissent, & ad ipsam Regionem propius accederent, quò commodius susceptum opus peragerent, de ipsius populi moribus, natura, & indole á finitimis perquisiuerunt: responsum est, gentem esse immanem, bellicosam, & iniractabilem.
units.tr: In the fourteenth year of the Emperor Maurice, which was the year of the Lord 596, and 150 years after the landing of the English in this island of Britain, Augustine was sent into England by Gregory, Bishop of Rome, to restore the Christian religion in that part of the island which the English had occupied, where it had fallen and was almost wholly destroyed. Augustine therefore took on about forty companions and set out on the journey to England. When they had travelled some distance and were drawing nearer to the region itself, they inquired of their neighbours about the character, nature and disposition of the people, so that they might carry out the work they had undertaken more conveniently. They were told that the nation was savage, warlike and intractable.

units.la: Quo audito, reçi inuicem deliberata, in propositio pergere pertimuerunt. Augustinum ergo domum remittunt, qui supplicater à Pontifice peteret, vt ipsis ab itinere tam periculoso, bona cum venia liceret desistere.
units.tr: On hearing this, they deliberated among themselves and were afraid to go on with the undertaking. So they sent Augustine back home, to beg the Pope that they might be allowed, with good grace, to give up so dangerous a journey.

units.la: Recognita, Gregorius obnixè cum Augustino agit, vt ad socios redeat, exponit ei, quam foret opus illud Deo gratum, ipsis honorificum, Anglis salutare, simulque literas setus argumenti ipsi Augustino ad socios dat. Acceperat etiam literas Augustinus ad Etherium Arelatensem Archiepiscopum, in quibus cum rogat Gregorius, vt Augustinum humaniter exeipiat, vt in hoc Britannico negocio ipsum consilio auxilioq; iuuet. Harum & superiorum literarum forma extat in Ecclesiastica historia Bedæ Lib.1.ca.23. Iam vero idioma Anglicanum Romanis erat incognitum, & propterea per interpretes agi oportuit: & quia Anglis cum Francis propter vicinitatem iamdiu erat commercium, adsciscit sibi aliquot Francos Augustinus, qui interpretum munere fungerentur. Paratis omnibus nauem conf. endunt, ventis vela dant, Angliam recta contendunt, & ad Insulam Cantii, quæ Thanatos dicitur, nauem appellunt.
units.tr: Gregory, when this was reported to him, urged Augustine earnestly to return to his companions. He explained how pleasing that work would be to God, how honourable to them, and how salutary for the English, and at the same time he gave Augustine letters of the same purport for his companions. Augustine had also received letters to Etherius, Archbishop of Arles, in which Gregory asks that he receive Augustine kindly and help him with counsel and support in this British business. The text of these and of the earlier letters is extant in Bede's Ecclesiastical History, Book 1, chapter 23. Now the English language was unknown to the Romans, so the business had to be conducted through interpreters. And since the English had long had dealings with the Franks because of their proximity, Augustine took some Franks to himself to serve as interpreters. When everything was ready, they fitted out a ship, gave sail to the winds, made straight for England, and put in at the island of Kent called Thanet.

units.la: Egressi in litus, Augustinus, (qui cæteris in hoc negocio à Pontifice præficiebatur) aliquot ex Comitibus suis, cum interpretibus Gallis, ad Ethelbertum Anglorum Regem mittit. Hi postquam ad Regem admissi sunt, quæ illis mandauerat Augustinus, Regi exponunt: venisse aliquot Romæ viros, qui ad illum & vniuersum populum Anglicanum lætum habeant & salutare nuncium, cuius vt velint obtemperare, æterna in cœlis vita cum Deo viuo & vero potirentur.
units.tr: Having landed, Augustine (who had been placed by the Pope in charge of the others in this business) sent some of his companions, with the Gallic interpreters, to Ethelbert, King of the English. When they were admitted to the King, they set out to him what Augustine had instructed them to say: men had come from Rome who brought him and the whole English people a joyful and saving message, and if they were willing to obey it, they would win eternal life in heaven with the living and true God.

units.la: Legationem hanc Rex benignè excipit, suis imperat, vt necessaria omnia nouis hospitibus suppeditentur: ipse breui de hoc tam salutari nuncio plura audituros. Post paucos dies Rex Thanatum venit, Augustinum cum suis ad se euocat, colloquiū ineunt, Regi & vniuerso Comitatu prædicant. Rex quamvis ad primam prædicationem assensum non dederit, tamen nec a nomine Christiano prorsus abhorruit, neq; religionem ipsam penitus ignorauit, quippe qui vxoris Bertæ Christianæ, & Lybhardi Episcopi operam, in ea aliquantulum erat instructus. Atqui cum secum reputaret viros istos ad se, sua de causa è longinquis venisse, omnia illis (vt par est) officia humanitatis exhiber. Hospitio igitur excipiuntur, in regni Ethelberti Ciuitate Dorouernensi (quatum totius quidem Angliæ ditionis erat Metropolis) Regiis aluntur sumptibus, sedem sane commodam ad Euangelium promulgandum nacti sunt, nec id facere, à Rege sunt prohibiti. Quid multis opus est? Multi Christo nomen dederunt, crediderunt, & baptizati sunt.
units.tr: The King received this embassy kindly, and ordered that everything necessary be supplied to the new guests; he said that they would soon hear more about this so salutary message. After a few days the King came to Thanet and summoned Augustine with his companions to him. They held a conference and preached to the King and his whole retinue. Although the King did not assent at the first preaching, yet he did not altogether shrink from the Christian name, nor was he wholly ignorant of the religion, since he had been somewhat instructed in it through the efforts of his Christian wife Bertha and Bishop Liudhard. Moreover, reflecting that these men had come from far away on his account, he showed them all the courtesies of hospitality, as was fitting. They were therefore received as guests in the city of Canterbury in Ethelbert's kingdom (which was indeed the metropolis of the whole of England's dominion), were supported at royal expense, and found a convenient seat for proclaiming the Gospel; nor did the King forbid them to do so. Why say more? Many gave their names to Christ, believed, and were baptized.

units.la: Erat autem prope ipsam ciuitatem versus orientem fanum, in honorem Sancti Martini antiquitus constructum, dum adhuc Romani Britanniam incolerent, ibi Regina cum Lybhardo Episcopo orare consueverat: ibi igitur primò Christiani confluere, sacra peragere, psallere, missasque celebrare (non eas quidem priuatas, sed in quibus Euchari stiam populo distribuere soliti sunt) prædicare etiam & baptizare publicè ceperunt donec Rex ipse tandem conuersus, & vniuersus populus Christo lucrifactus est. Tum vero ecclesias collapsas restituunt, novas ædificant, prophanaras & pollutas consecrant. Christianam religionem per omnem regionem vndiq; stabiliunt. Quin etiam Rex Augustino & comitibus suis, domum honestam apud Stablegate in Dorouernensi urbe concessit, Possessionibus etiam satis amplis eandem locupletauit, ita vt res tota opti-
units.tr: Now near the city, towards the east, there was a temple built long ago in honour of St Martin, while the Romans still inhabited Britain; there the Queen used to pray with Bishop Liudhard. There, therefore, the Christians first began to gather, to perform sacred rites, sing psalms, and celebrate masses (not private ones, but those in which they were accustomed to distribute the Eucharist to the people also). They began to preach and baptize publicly, until at last the King himself was converted and the whole people was won for Christ. Then they restored the churches that had fallen into ruin, built new ones, and consecrated those that had been profaned and polluted. They established the Christian religion throughout the whole region. Indeed, the King granted Augustine and his companions a respectable house at Stablegate in the city of Canterbury, and enriched it with fairly ample possessions, so that the whole business seemed to have gone very well.

units.la: Bedæ Lib. 1, Cap. 5. mè successisse videri posse. Iam vero Anglorum Episcopus Augustinus dici & esse volebat: quapropter Arelatem ad Archiepiscopum Etherium sele contulit, & ab eo in Archiepiscopum genti Anglorum ordinatus est. Statim vt domum reuertius est, misit Romam Laurentium Presbyterum & Petrum Monachum, qui Pontifici Gregorio Anglos fidem Christi amplexos, & se eorum Archiepiscopum factum esse nunciarent. Insuper & de quibusdam ad precentis Ecclesiae statum spectantibus Gregorium consuluit, quae quidem, vna cum responsis Gregorii comperies in Ecclesiastica historia Bedae, Lib. i. Laurentius & Petrus paulo post in Angliam reuertentes, literas quidem plures a Pontifice attulerunt, ac primas ad Ethelbertum Regem, vna cum muneribus, in quibus Pontifex & Regi & sibi gratulatur: Regi, quod ad veri Dei & Christi fui notitiam peruenerat: sibi, quod id sua opera & industria factum esset. Ad Augustinum etiam binas adferunt, quarum in vnis significat, se illi pallium misisse, vasa etiam sacra & vestimenta altarium, ornamenta quoque Ecclesiarum, saccerdotalia, ceruicalia indumenta, reliquias sanctorum, ac codices complures, denique vniuersa quae ad cultum Dei ac ministerium Ecclesiae somniabat necessaria, simul etiam insinuat, quemadmodum ipse Episcopos per Britanniam debeat constituere.
units.tr: Bede, Book 1, chapter 5. Augustine now wished to be called, and to be, bishop of the English. So he betook himself to Archbishop Etherius at Arles, and was ordained by him as archbishop for the English people. As soon as he returned home, he sent Laurence the presbyter and Peter the monk to Rome, to tell Pope Gregory that the English had embraced the faith of Christ, and that he himself had been made their archbishop. He also consulted Gregory about certain matters concerning the present state of the Church. You will find these, together with Gregory's replies, in Bede's Ecclesiastical History, Book 1. Laurence and Peter, returning to England a little later, brought several letters from the Pope. The first, to King Ethelbert, came together with gifts, in which the Pope congratulates the King (because he had come to the knowledge of the true God and Christ) and himself (because this had been brought about by his own labour and diligence). They also brought two letters to Augustine. In one of these the Pope says that he had sent him the pallium, as well as sacred vessels, altar vestments, church ornaments, priestly and clerical garments, relics of saints, and several codices; in short, everything he judged necessary for the worship of God and the ministry of the Church. At the same time he hints at how Augustine ought to appoint bishops throughout Britain.

units.la: In alteris vero monet, ne de virtutibus suis gloriatur, neue miracula quae facta sunt, sibi deputet, sed Britannis in illutem a Deo doraia existimet. Tradiderant etiam literas Vigilio, qui Etherio in Archiepiscopatu Arelatensi successerat, in quibus sibi pergratum fuisse demonstrat, adiutum fuisse in negocio Britannico ab Arelatensibus Augustinum. Haec literae datae sunt. 10. Cal. Iulii, impetante adhuc Mauritio An. Dom. 601. Exempla ipsarum prostant apud Bedam in Lib. superius commemorato. Postquam Augustinus sedem Episcopalem Doruerniae in Regia ciuitate sortitus esset, fanum aliud, quod ibi ab antiquis Romanis positum erat, nomine Sancti Saluatoris & Domini nostri Iesu Christi (Regę concedente) insigniuit. Palatium etiam Regni sui cum adiacentibus Augustino Rex donauit, ipse vero Xaculuer/quod secus mare situm est, ecclesiae, vbi palatium sibi & successoribus suis statuit, quo etiam in loco coenobium construxit, cuius vltimus Abbas Wenredus fuit. Coemiterium etiam locum sepulturis idoneum extra Cantuariae ciuitatis muros ad orientem, instigante Augustino fecit: nondum enim consuetudo erat intra ciuitatem quemquam sepelire, vsque ad Cuihbertum Archiepiscopum Cant. qui intra ciuitates passim fieri coemeteria procurauit, Pontifice Rom. id ex illius intercessione concedente.
units.tr: In the other letter he warns Augustine not to boast of his virtues, nor to ascribe to himself the miracles that have been performed, but to consider them as given by God for the salvation of the Britons. They had also delivered letters to Vigilius, who had succeeded Etherius in the archbishopric of Arles, in which Gregory shows how very pleasing it was to him that the people of Arles had helped Augustine in the British business. These letters were dated ten days before the Kalends of July, while Maurice was still emperor, in the year of the Lord 601. Copies of them survive in Bede, in the book mentioned above. After Augustine had obtained the episcopal see of Canterbury in the royal city, he dedicated to the Holy Saviour and our Lord Jesus Christ another church which the ancient Romans had built there (with the King's consent). The King also gave Augustine his palace with its surroundings. He himself built a church at Reculver, which lies beside the sea, where he established a palace for himself and his successors; in this place he also built a monastery, whose last abbot was Wenredus. At Augustine's urging, he also made a cemetery outside the walls of the city of Canterbury, to the east, a place suitable for burials. For it was not yet the custom to bury anyone within the city, until Archbishop Cuthbert of Canterbury arranged for cemeteries to be made inside cities everywhere, with the consent of the Roman Pontiff, obtained through his intercession.

units.la: Rex etiam Monasterium ad orientem non longe ab ipsa ciuitate erexit, in quo rogatu Augustini ædem etiam diuis Apostolis Petro & Paulo a fundamentis extruxit, idque Monasterium donis ornauit amplissimis, vbi ipsius Augustini & Doruernensium Archiepiscoporum, Regumq; Cantiorum corpora inhumari solebant. Hoc postea non Augustinus, sed qui illi viuenti electus successit, Laurentius consecrauit. Quibus praeclare positis fundamentis initiis, Regium Doruernense, quod Augustinus ab Ethelberto donoaccepera, succedentium deinceps semper fuit, Archiepiscoporum Palatium. Atque hoc modo conuersos ad Christianam religionem Anglos, posita mq; primam ab Augustino in Doruernensi ciuitate atq; Prouincia Ecclesiam esse putant. Sed valde dolendum est Anglorum coluerit ionem in illa tempora incidisse, in quibus collapsa Ecclesiae doctrina atq; disciplina, multum ab antiqua veritate puritate ad superstitionum errores degenerauit. Quinquam n. venerandus Presbyter Beda scribat, Augustinum suosque sociis primitiua Ecclesiae vitam ac doctrinam in instituenda Anglorum Ecclesia imitatos, tamen res ipsa declarat non minus Romanae superstitionis, quam Christianae religionis Augustinum Anglis Magistrum atq; praeceptorem fuisse. Nam & Romana Ecclesia etiam Gregorio praesidente & authore, harum omnium superstitionem caput & origo fuit, indeque non modo in Anglia ab Augustino inductae, sed in varias orbis Christiani regiones disseminatae late diuanarunt. Gregorius enim Melito in Angliam ad Augustinum profiscenti utiliter praecipiens, de non diruendis fanis quae a gentilibus Anglis Doemonibus consecrabantur, ita scribit, vt deletis Idolis Fanaipsa conseruarentur, & ad Christianae Ecclesiae ritus cultumque diuinum a gentilitis prophanationib. per aquae benedictae asperionem, altarium constructione, & reliquiarum collocatione, veneratione mq; expiarentur: & ipsi Augustino ad missarum solemnia celebranda Pallii, item vasa sacra, altariu vestimenta, Ecclesiarum ornamenta, saccerdotalia atq; Clericalia indumenta, sanctorum Apostolorum ac Martyrum reliquias se misisse dicit. Ex quibus videmus quantae tum in Romanam Ecclesiam coecitates & errores irrepserant. Nec huiusmodi solum malis sanctiora Ecclesiae instituta deptauata sunt, sed ex illa de vnius in Ecclesia pastoris imperio atque
units.tr: The King also built a monastery to the east, not far from the city itself. At Augustine's request, he built from the foundations a church dedicated to the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and he adorned that monastery with very generous gifts. There the bodies of Augustine himself, of the archbishops of Canterbury, and of the kings of Kent used to be buried. This church was afterwards consecrated not by Augustine but by Laurence, who had been chosen to succeed him while he was still alive. With these beginnings so splendidly laid, the royal palace at Canterbury, which Augustine had received from Ethelbert, has ever since been the palace of the succeeding archbishops. In this way, they think, the English were converted to the Christian religion, and the first church was established by Augustine in the city and province of Canterbury. But it must be greatly lamented that the conversion of the English fell in those times when the doctrine and discipline of the Church had collapsed, and it degenerated far from ancient truth and purity into the errors of superstition. For although the venerable presbyter Bede writes that Augustine and his companions imitated the life and teaching of the primitive Church in founding the English Church, the matter itself shows that Augustine was a teacher and instructor of the English in Roman superstition no less than in the Christian religion. For the Roman Church, with Gregory presiding over it and as its author, was the head and origin of all these superstitions, and from it they were introduced not only into England by Augustine, but were spread far and wide into various regions of the Christian world. For Gregory, advising Mellitus usefully as he set out for England to join Augustine, writes that the temples which the heathen English had consecrated to demons should not be destroyed, but that, the idols being removed, the temples themselves should be preserved, and cleansed of their pagan pollution for the rites and divine worship of the Christian Church, by sprinkling with holy water, building altars, and placing relics there. He also says that he had sent to Augustine himself the pallium for celebrating the solemnities of the mass, likewise sacred vessels, altar vestments, church ornaments, priestly and clerical garments, and relics of the holy Apostles and Martyrs. From these things we see how great blindness and error had then crept into the Roman Church. Nor were the holier institutions of the Church corrupted by such evils alone; but from the rule and power of one pastor in the Church, and

units.la: Lib. Ecd. Cant. Lib. Ref. atque potestate contentione, quàm Iohannis Constantinopolitani Patriarchæ ambitio viuente adhuc & acerrimè reclamante Gregorio excitauit, non modò ad superstitionē & sacrorum omnium prophanationem, sed etiam ad impietatem atque Antichristi Regnum patefacta fuit ianua. Antea enim inaudita erant & incognita illa superborum titulorum omina, summus pontifex, & vnicum Ecclesiæ in terris caput, Christi vicarius, & similia, quibus iofolescere postea cœpit Romanorum pontificum audacia, quibusq; parere sub æternæ mortis pœnis omnes iubentur. Et Gregorius illam Iohannis ambitionem, cum se vniuersalem orbis Episcopum dici voluit, multis diris execratus, nullam sibi aut Romanæ Ecclesiæ admi prærogatiuam cooqueftus est, sed appellationem ipsam ad Man. ... hactius (inquit) superbia, quid aliud nisi propinquia iam esse Antichristi tempora designatur. Quia illum videlicet imitatur, qui spreta Anglorum societate ascendere conatus est culmen singularitatis & alibi. Ego autem fidenter dico, quisquis se vniuersalem Episcopum vocat, vel vocari desiderat, in elatione sua Antichristum præcurrit, qua superbiendo se exteris præponit. Atq; hoc modo Iohannis cupiditati & libidini omnibus Ecclesiis imperandi Gregorius pie fortiterq; restitit. Verùm eo mortuo, & Mauritio Imperatore interfecto (de quo eum in somnis ante admonitum quidam tradunt) Phocas Romanis quà Constantinopolitanis ciuibus amicior, quia in Mauritii locù suffectus sine contentione aut contradictione cuiusquam Romæ coronatus est, Bonifacio Tertio, qui seciundus à Gregorio fuit, eum quem Iohannes Constantinopolitanus vendicabat, & Gregorius recusabat primatus titulum concessit, vt is summus pontifex, Romaque omnium Ecclesiarum caput diceretur. Neque tamen hoc Phocæ beneficium Romanis pontificibus multum profuit centum quadraginta deinceps annis. Nam Aphrica atq; Asia pontifici nunquam paruerunt. Gallia verò & Germania etiam se adiunxerunt, non tamen obtemperabant, nisi in his quibus libitum esset, donec Zacharias Pontifex Pipino Gallię Regnum affectanti adiutor fuit, vt Hilderico legitimo Rege, quem stupidum & insensatum vocabant, amoto & in Monasterium detrusto, Gallisque pontificis authoritate a subiectionis iuramento absolutis Regnum occuparet. Pro quo beneficio hoc à Pipino præmium ac mercedem tulit, vt in Gallicanas Ecclesias Romanus semper pontifex iurisdictionem haberet. Deinde Stephanus Tertius pootifex elatus suæ sedis amplitudine, quasi in Imperatoras atque Reges ius haberet, Constantinum Copronimum, Cooftantinopolitanum Imperatorem, quia contra imaginum veneratio nem Synodum instituisset, priuauit imperio, & insignia, dignitates, titulosq; imperii in Papinum ac Francorum Reges transstulit. Quibus adminiculis & accessionibus iam erecta pontificum Romanorum pontificiorum potestas tandem firmata fuit, cum Adriani pontificis ope Carolus Magnus imperio potius, occidentales omnes Ecclesias Episcopis Romanis subiecit. Atq; hic etiam(quod dici solet) manus manum fricare cepit. Namq; Adrianus pontifex Lateranensi indicto concilio, siue vim ac potentiam Constantinopolitanum Cæsarum, quorum maiestatem lædeat, imperiumq; minueret, formidans, siue præda, cum Carolus in imperium allenum, ille in Ecclesias alienas rueret, diuisa & communicata, se atq; omnes Occidentales Episcopos tutelæ committ Caroli, sanxitque Anathematè proscriptioque bonorū; ne tam Romanus pontifex quàm cæteri Episcopi electionum confirmationes & Ecclesiarum inueniturasa Carolo magno Imp. fuisq; successoribus caperent: tum vt suam etiam in Ecclesias dominationem perinde stabiliret, primus instituit vt illa Romanaditiplomata quæ literas Apostolicas atq; bullas appellant, quo cæteris sigillis firmiora & diuturniora viderentur, obsignaretur plumbo, cum antea tantum cera vterentur. Ita pontificia dominatio quàm Gregorius tantopere detestatus est, eo mortuo sub Phoca Imp. & Bonifacio Papa inchoata, centum septuaginta deinceps annis indies creuit, tàdemq; Carolo magno Imp. & Adriano primo pontifice conspirantibus ad summum culmen magnitudinemq; uenit. Quà potestatis amplitudinè pontifices simulatquè nactiesent, Ecclesiæ gubernatione occupauit ambitio, vitæq; cõtinentia luxus, & religione vndiq; iniuafit fupftitio. Omnis diuinus cultus in cæremoniarū multitudine atq; magnificentia existimabatur cõsistere, & loco verbi plusquam aniles, atq; pueriles fabulæ annũciabatur populo. Quarũ si quædam proferamus, etsi scribentium authoritate atq; dignitate hon carebant, tamen quàm similia delirorum aut mente captorum somniis fuerunt, facile erit existimare. Iohannes Turpinus Archiepisc. Remensis, Caroli magni (vt ipse scribit) in eastris contra Saraceoos socius, foluq; ex Episcopis inter primarios Galliæ principes seu 11. pares ascriptus de eius morte ita scribit. Secum Viennæ quodam die altari in Ecclesia
units.tr: Lib. Ecd. Cant. Lib. Ref. The contest over power and authority, which the ambition of John, Patriarch of Constantinople, stirred up while he was still alive and loudly protesting against it, opened the door not only to superstition and the profanation of all sacred things, but also to impiety and the kingdom of Antichrist. Before this, those proud titles were unheard of and unknown: "supreme pontiff," "the one head of the Church on earth," "Vicar of Christ," and similar names, by which the audacity of the Roman pontiffs later began to swell, and to which all are commanded to submit on pain of eternal death. Gregory cursed John's ambition with many dreadful curses, when John wished to be called "universal bishop of the world." Gregory claimed no such prerogative for himself or for the Roman Church, but referred that very title to Man. ... "So far, he says, is pride; what else does it signify than that the times of Antichrist are now at hand? For he imitates the one who, having spurned the fellowship of the English, tried to climb to the summit of singularity..." And elsewhere: "I say with confidence that whoever calls himself, or desires to be called, universal bishop, goes before Antichrist in his own pride, since in his arrogance he sets himself above others." In this way Gregory piously and bravely resisted John's greed and lust to rule over all the Churches. But after Gregory died, and the Emperor Maurice was killed (some report that Gregory had warned him of this beforehand in a dream), Phocas, who was more friendly to the Romans than to the citizens of Constantinople, was crowned at Rome without any dispute or objection from anyone, since he had been raised to the place of Maurice. He granted to Boniface III, who was the second after Gregory, the title of primacy which John of Constantinople had claimed and Gregory had refused, so that this man should be called supreme pontiff and Rome the head of all Churches. Yet this favour of Phocas did little good to the Roman pontiffs for the next hundred and forty years. For Africa and Asia never obeyed the pontiff. Gaul and Germany did join themselves to him, but they obeyed only when it suited them, until Pope Zacharias helped Pepin, who was aiming at the kingdom of Gaul. Childeric, the lawful king, whom they called stupid and senseless, was removed and shut up in a monastery, and the Gauls, released from their oath of allegiance by the authority of the pontiff, lost their kingdom to Pepin. For this service Pepin paid him a reward: the Roman pontiff was to have jurisdiction over the Gallican Churches for ever. Then Pope Stephen III, puffed up by the greatness of his see, as if he had a right over emperors and kings, deprived Constantine Copronymus, Emperor of Constantinople, of his empire, because he had called a council against the veneration of images, and transferred the insignia, dignities and titles of empire to Pepin and the kings of the Franks. With these aids and additions the power of the Roman pontiffs, the papal power, was at last made firm, when, with the help of Pope Hadrian, Charles the Great, rather than governing an empire, subjected all the Western Churches to the Roman bishops. And here too, as the saying goes, hand began to rub hand. For Pope Hadrian, having summoned a council at the Lateran, fearing either the power and might of the Constantinopolitan emperors, which would injure their majesty and diminish their empire, or else booty, since Charles was rushing on another's empire and he on other Churches, divided and shared the spoils: he committed himself and all the Western bishops to the protection of Charles. He also decreed by anathema and proscription of goods that neither the Roman pontiff nor the other bishops should take confirmations of elections or the investitures of Churches from Charles the Great, the emperor, or his successors. Then, so that he might establish his own domination over the Churches in the same way, he was the first to order that those Roman documents which they call apostolic letters and bulls should be sealed with lead, so that they would seem firmer and more lasting than other seals, whereas before they had used only wax. Thus the papal domination, which Gregory had so greatly detested, begun under the Emperor Phocas and Pope Boniface after Gregory's death, grew daily for the next hundred and seventy years, until at last, with Charles the Great as emperor and Hadrian I as pontiff working together, it came to the highest peak of greatness. As soon as the pontiffs had obtained this extent of power, ambition seized the government of the Church, luxury took the place of a continent life, and superstition invaded religion on every side. All divine worship was thought to consist in a multitude and magnificence of ceremonies, and instead of the Word, more than old-wives' and childish fables were announced to the people. If we bring forward some of them, it will be easy to judge how like they are to the dreams of madmen or lunatics, even though they did not lack the authority and dignity of their writers. John Turpin, Archbishop of Reims, who (as he himself writes) was a companion of Charles the Great in the camp against the Saracens, and who is counted among the twelve peers, the chief princes of Gaul, writes thus about Charles's death. "One day at Vienne, while he was saying Mass at the altar in the church..."

units.la: afflictisset, in itinere raptum, Psalmumq; (Deus in adiuorium) cantu extorsum, conspex sse innumera terrorum militum agmina transire, acin Lolharingiam tendere, atque aquodam illius gregis Aethiopi simile, qui czeteros lentius insequeretur, quasfuisse quo illa pergerent agmina, illumq; respondisse, ad Caroli magni mortem, vt eius animam in Gehennam raparent. Tum Archiepiscopus, adiurote, inquit, per nomen Domini nostri Iesu Christi, vt peracto itinere tuo ad me reuerti non renuas. Deinde psalmo vix absoluto celeriter cum czteris redeunte rogat quid egisset. Cui ille, tot inquit ac tantos lapides ac ligna Basilicarū fuarū in platera supendit, magis appedetur bona, q malaeius opera, & idcirco eius animam à nobis abstulit, qbus dictus Dæmon euanuit. Ita; infert Turpinus; intellexi eadem die Carolum ex hac luce migrasse, & subsidiis beati Iacobi cui Ecclesias multas ædificauerat, ad superna merito Regna subuectum.
