Hac operum & sanctorum fiducia ita extenuatam, peneq; abiectam in Christo poneodam fidem videmus, vt salutis & redemptionis nostræ laus hominibus nostrisque gestis aferipta sit. Atque huius simile commentum eadem ætate de cultu beatæ Mariæ excogitatum est. Fuisse hominem religionem Christianam ore profitentem, sed adeo dissolutum & flagitiis deditum, vt nulla cuiquam bono de eius salute spes esse poterat. Consueuit tamen omni alio diuino cultu neglecto, indies beatam Mariam cenries Inuocare, & anglicam salutationem dicere. Itaque cum ægritudine summa laboraret in extremo raptus, & quasi mortuus à Dæmonibus ad Dei tribunal ductus, ae propter infinita scelera ad inferni supplicia postulatus est, Deus eum tot inquinatum vitiis ac peccatis adiudicauit Dæmonibus, verum laua iama ab Deo æternæ mortis sententia interuenit Maria, exhibuit ; Christo filio suo schedulas, in quibus scriptum fuit quoties eam cum angelica salutatione inuocasset Dæmones turfus peccatorum multitudine vrgebat, & in scriptis proferebant. Ita virtusq; tam beatæ Mariæ quam Dæmonum scriptis in lance positis peccatorum scripta orationum schedulas deprimebant. Cumq; Maria se nihil pro quo interces sit, proficere vidisset, eiusmodi ad Christum filium suum supplicatione vsæst. Recordare dilecte quod de mea sub-stantia receperis sub tantiam, vilibilem, palpabile, & passibilem, & da mihi vnā gutam sanguinis tui fusam pro peccatoribus in passione tua. Et ille, inipossibile (inquit) est tibi aliquid denegari. Verumtamen scias quod vnica gutta sanguinis mei præponderat omnibus peccatis totius mundi. Accipe itaq; quod petisti, quam accipiens posuit ad stateram, & omnia prædicta peccata quasi fauillam præponderabat. Tum dæmones discedentes confusi, clamabant dicentes. Nimis miseri cors est Domina Christianis. Vnde deficimus quotiens se de conflictu intromisset. Reducta est ergo anima ad corpus, & ipse postea conualescens omnia narrauit, & factus est Monachus. Numnam Poëtarum fabulæ, aut eorum qui confulio (sicur Lucianus) mendacia scribunt, figmenta, his narrationibus sunt ineptiora? Quæ tamen authores habent magnæ authoritatis atque famæ, & pro concionibus narrabantur, vt Populum super stitione excæcarent. Nec vt mortuis solis sed etiam mutis picturis & Imaginibus diuinus honos haberetur, attributa sunt ligneis lapideisq; statuis stupenda miracula. In Siria confossam lancea fuisse à quodam Iudæo in Christianorū contemptum & ludibrium Imaginem Christi, ex qua sanguis v berrime mox effluxit, Iudæumque prodigii metu perculsum, ne sanguis diffusus periret vas vulneri supposuisse, quo qui vt sunt ægroti valetudine recuperabant. Tum sanguis longe lateque mullus perue-nit Mantuam, vbi propter crebra miracula magno in pretio habitus est. Quibus auditis Carolus Imperator ad Leonem Papam scripsit, vt de hoc eum certiorem redderet. Leo vero Mantuam proficiscens approbato Christi sanguine ob frequentiam miraculorum, quod & alii pontifices post eum fecerunt, ad Carolum pergit, certúq; de præmissis fecit. Hanc superiorum temporum super stitionum atque vanitatem posterioris scriptores imitati sunt, vt Vincentius in historiarum speculo scribit. Quandam fuisse Albantam extra Rodulphi castrum quæ Dolis vocabatur positum, in qua super Ecclesiæ columna Imago beatæ Mariæ Christum Iesum puerum amplexibus suis tenentis sculpota fuit. Ad quam cum mulier quædam paupercula orandi gratia accessisset, exprobrabant ei duo in atrio stantes viri fatuitatem, quorum vnus in imaginem iecit lapides, eoque ictu brachium pueri confregit, à quo humi prolapso guttæ sanguinis distillabant, perinde ac si viui hominis brachium fuisset, moxque ille qui lapides proiecit exspirauit, cui cum altera fuccurrere cadenti vellet, à Dæmonibus arreptus est, & postridie mortuus est. Turba deinde frequens conuenit, vt Imaginem, & profluentem sanguinem videret, qua inspectante imago descidit ornamentum, quo præcinda lapideum, detraxitque collo monile, pectusque ad mammillas denudauit, ob iniuriam atque igniominiam sibi; filiogi illata.
units.tr: ...had afflicted himself, and on the journey he was snatched away, and while he was chanting the psalm (Deus in adiutorium), he saw innumerable troops of terrible soldiers passing by and heading into Lorraine; and to one of that crowd, who resembled an Ethiopian and was following the others more slowly, he asked where those troops were going. He answered that they were carrying the soul of Charles the Great to Gehenna at his death. Then the Archbishop said, "I adjure you by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ that, when your journey is finished, you do not refuse to return to me." Then, when the psalm was barely finished, he returned quickly with the others and asked what he had done. The other replied, "I hung so many and such great stones and timbers of your basilicas in the balance that the good works outweighed his evil ones, and for this reason we have taken his soul from us," and with these words the demon vanished. "So," Turpin adds, "I understood that on that same day Charles had departed from this light, and by the help of blessed James, to whom he had built many churches, had been rightly carried to the heavenly kingdoms." We see that faith in Christ has been so weakened and almost cast down by this confidence in works and saints that the praise of our salvation and redemption is ascribed to men and their deeds. A similar fiction about the worship of the blessed Mary was devised in the same age. A man who professed the Christian religion with his mouth, but was so dissolute and given to crimes that no one could hope for his salvation, nevertheless, neglecting all other divine worship, used to invoke the blessed Mary every day a hundred times and say the English Hail Mary. So when, at the end, he was lying in very great sickness, and as if dead was led by the demons to God's judgement seat and was condemned to the punishments of hell for his infinite crimes and sins, God judged him to the demons, as one so stained with vices and sins. But then Mary, the blessed one, intervened and showed to Christ her Son some slips of paper on which was written how often he had invoked her with the angelic salutation. The demons again pressed him with the multitude of his sins and brought forth their written records. Thus the slips of prayers, written by the blessed Mary and the demons, were placed in the scales, and the written record of sins was weighed down by the prayers. When Mary saw that she was achieving nothing for the man on whose behalf she was interceding, she made this supplication to Christ her Son: "Remember, beloved, that you received from my substance a substance visible, palpable and passible, and give me one drop of your blood, shed for sinners in your passion." And he answered, "It is impossible for anything to be denied you. Yet know that one drop of my blood outweighs all the sins of the whole world. Take then what you asked," and placing it in the scales, it outweighed all the said sins like a spark. Then the demons, departing in confusion, cried out, "The heart of the Lady is too merciful toward Christians. We are defeated whenever she enters the conflict." So the soul was returned to the body, and the man, afterwards recovering, told everything, and became a monk. Are not the fables of the poets, or the lies of those who write fictions (like Lucian), more absurd than these stories? Yet these tales have authors of great authority and fame, and they were told in sermons to blind the people with superstition. And not only to dead things, but also to dumb pictures and images, divine honour was given, and stupendous miracles were attributed to wooden and stone statues. In Syria, it is said, an image of Christ was pierced with a lance by a Jew, to the contempt and mockery of the Christians, and blood immediately gushed forth copiously; and the Jew, struck with fear at the portent, placed a vessel under the wound so that the blood spilled should not be lost, and with it the sick recovered their health. Then the blood spread far and wide, and reached Mantua, where, because of frequent miracles, it was held in great esteem. When this was heard, the Emperor Charles wrote to Pope Leo to inform him of it. Leo, setting out for Mantua, approved the blood of Christ because of the frequency of the miracles, as other pontiffs after him also did, and went on to Charles and gave him certain information about these matters. Later writers have imitated this superstition and vanity of earlier times, as Vincent writes in his Mirror of History. There was, they say, a certain Albanta outside the castle of Rudolph called Dolis, in which, on a column of the church, an image of the blessed Mary was carved, holding the child Jesus in her embrace. When a poor woman came to this image to pray, two men standing in the courtyard reproached her for her foolishness; one of them threw stones at the image, and with that blow broke the arm of the boy, from which drops of blood dripped as if from the arm of a living man. Soon the man who had thrown the stones died, and when another man tried to help him as he fell, he was seized by demons and died the next day. Then a large crowd gathered to see the image and the flowing blood, and while they watched, the image, which had been cut from stone, let fall its ornament; the man took a necklace from its neck and laid bare its breast down to the nipples, because of the injury and disgrace done to it and to its Son.

units.la: Quam stupendam fabulam non modò feriò narrat author, sed & sanguinem illum ac imaginem reuulsa veste nudatam, oculis suis conspexisse scribit. Et in Hibernia fingunt anre Anglorum adnentum crucem in templo trinitatis Dublinæ crucifixo simulimam, quæ & loquuta est, & inter duos cives de contractu diffidentes testimonium veritati perhibuit. Eadem; & fures alienà rapientes ad ablatorum confessionem restitutionēq; coegit. Infinitum esse cætera fabularum portenta enumeraque, quibus infinitis librire-plentur narrare, hæc tantum recensuimus vt quanta caligine illa tempora laborarunt lectores perspicerent, & Deo gratias assiduas funderent nos tandem veritate Euangelii illustratos, & tantis tenebris ereptos esse. Itaque vt ab his ad ea quæ de Angustino, ipsoq; Gregorio dicenda sunt redeamus. Certum est Gregorium, ersi illum vniuersalis ac suffimi Pontificis ritulum abominatus sit seruorum Dei primus appellauerit, suisque successoribus humilitatis speciem, quàm verbo magis quàm re secuti sunt, præscripserit, tamen superstitioni vsq; adeo deditum fuisse, vt sua aliorumque somnia inter vetas divinationes retulerit. Namq; per Romanæ ciuitatis forum transiens, quod Traianus optimus princeps ædificiis decorarat, cum illius bonitatis ac iustitiæ erga viduam quandam reminisceretur, ad diui Petri Apostoli Basilicam slens celeriter accurrit, vbi innegertimi clementissimiq; Imperatoris infidelitatem ac errores lachrymis deplorans, Deum pro eo abinfernalibus pœnis redimendo dicitur exoralle, noctequè proxima accepisse in somnis à Deo responsum, se de Traiano pro quo tantis lachrymis deprecatus esset, ealege exauditum, nec deinceps pro pagano quocunque preces efunderet. Illud autem pietatis opus, quod Gregorium adtam ardentes pro Traiano preces impulit commemorarur suius in Florilego. Quip ro manuetudine & exhibitione Iustitiæ à pœnis infernalibus per lachrymas beati Gregorii, quinquennis amplius post mortem suam annis Traianum meruisse liberari scribit. Hæc igitur & eiusmodi innita delira atque somnia pro veris tunc miraculis celebrari ceperunt, populumque a recto & sincero Dei cultu deprauarunt. Vt non satis fælix Anglorum statu videri posset, qui his temporibus ab Augustino, & magistro suo Gregorio ad Christianam fidem conuersi sunt, in quibus cum ambitio timulerunt, plus, errorum ipsis in secta. Sed etsi (vt diximus) Romani Pontificis in Ecclesias principatus in hac Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ origine atque fundatione incæperit & centum quadraginta deinceps annis sensim creuerit, ac sub Carolo magno confirmatus atque stabilitus fuerit, fuit adhuc tamen Imperatorum maior quàm Pontificum in quibusCUNQUE siue diuinis siue ciuilibus rebus agendis authoritas. Namq; Præsalorum in Ecclesiis inuestituræ, & electionum confirmationes ad Imperatores pertinebant, & conciliorum indicendorum atque appellationem sinigendarum supremæ lexæ potestas penes eos fuit. Namque ipsius Caroli iussu quinque conciliæ de statu Ecclesiæ reformando celebrata sunt, vnum Moguntiæ, alterum Rhemis, tertium Cabillone, quartum Arelati, quintum vero in Turonibus. Ipse etiam Gregorius (cui eam viuendi scribendique sincentatem quàm Pontificii ascribunt non tribuimus) non tam cupidè ad se causas Ecclesias rapuit, quin Principibus ius suum relinqueret, in tantum vt muliebri Ecclesiasticam iurisdictionem permiserit. Nam cum Mennam Episcopum canonica purgatione absolutum dimisisset, eum nihilominus Brunichildæ Francorum Reginæ rursus porgandum misit, quæ causa in gloffographis & commentariis fusius explicatur. Sed de his pro nostro instituto satis, in quibus longius ideo proueclsumus, ne iactare tam strenuæ Pontificii debeant accepram ab illis Christianam religionem, quos tantatum, eum Gregorius præfuit, doctrinæ corruptela infecisset, morumque disciplina in ritus quosdam & obseruationes superstitiosas recidisset, Qui religionis fucus, cultusque simulatus, vsque ad Henrici 8. Regis nostri triumphum imperium, quòd post Augustini huc aduentum nongentis amplius fuit annis, singulis ætatibus crescente Pontificum potestate simul cum libidine auctus duraurt, ab eoq; vna cum Pontificis potestate sic abiectus & profligatus est, vt Euangelii Luci veritatis locus esse ceperit.
units.tr: Nor does the author merely relate this marvellous tale; he also writes that he saw with his own eyes the blood and the image, stripped of its garment when the clothing was torn away. And in Ireland they invent that a cross in the Trinity church at Dublin, made like the crucified, was set up by the English and both spoke and bore witness to the truth between two citizens who disagreed about a contract. The same cross also compelled thieves who had seized other men's goods to confess and make restitution. It would be endless to list the other monstrous fables, with which countless books are filled. We have recounted only these, so that readers may see how great the darkness in which those times laboured, and may pour out continual thanks to God that we have at last been illumined by the truth of the Gospel and rescued from such great shadows. And so, to return from these matters to what must be said about Augustine and Gregory himself: it is certain that Gregory, although he abominated the title of universal and supreme Pontiff, and was the first to call himself servant of the servants of God, and prescribed to his successors a show of humility which they have followed more in words than in deeds, nevertheless was so given over to superstition that he reckoned his own dreams and those of others among true divinations. For passing through the forum of the Roman city, which the excellent Emperor Trajan had adorned with buildings, he recalled that prince's goodness and justice toward a certain widow. Hurrying quickly to the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, he lamented with tears the unbelief and errors of that most merciful and noble emperor, and is said to have prayed to God to redeem him from the punishments of hell. That night, he received in dreams an answer from God that Trajan, for whom he had besought with such tears, had been heard on that account, and that he should no longer pour out prayers for any pagan whatever. The work of piety which moved Gregory to such ardent prayers for Trajan is recorded in his Florilegium. For through the tears of the blessed Gregory, Trajan, on account of his gentleness and the practice of justice, merited to be freed from infernal punishments, as he writes, more than five years after Gregory's death. These and such like unheard-of follies and dreams then began to be celebrated as true miracles, and they corrupted the people from the right and sincere worship of God. So the state of the English could not seem very fortunate, since in these times they were converted to the Christian faith by Augustine and his master Gregory, and along with the ambition they took on more errors in their sect. But although (as we have said) the principate of the Roman Pontiff over the Churches began in this origin and foundation of the English Church, and grew gradually over the following one hundred and forty years, and was confirmed and established under Charles the Great, the authority of the Emperors was still greater than that of the Popes in whatever matters were handled, whether sacred or civil. For the investiture of prelates in the churches and the confirmation of elections belonged to the Emperors, and the supreme power of calling councils and hearing appeals lay with them. Indeed, by Charles's own command five councils were held to reform the state of the Church: one at Mainz, another at Rheims, a third at Chalon, a fourth at Arles, and a fifth at Tours. Gregory himself (to whom we do not ascribe that sanctity of life and writing which the Papists ascribe to him) did not so eagerly snatch the causes of the Churches to himself as to leave their right to princes; indeed he so far conceded ecclesiastical jurisdiction to a woman that, when he had dismissed Bishop Minnas, absolved by canonical purgation, he nevertheless sent him back to be examined by Brunhild, Queen of the Franks. This matter is explained at greater length by the glossators and commentators. But enough of these things for our purpose. We have gone on at such length so that the Papists may not boast so loudly of the Christian religion received from men whom, while Gregory presided, the corruption of doctrine had infected, and whose discipline of morals had relapsed into certain rites and superstitious observances. This mask of religion and feigned worship lasted, until the triumph of our King Henry VIII, for more than nine hundred years after Augustine's arrival here. It grew with the power of the Popes in every age, and increased together with lust, and it was cast down and overthrown together with the Pontiff's power, so that the Gospel, the light of truth, began to have its place.

units.la: Quod in hac historia declarabimus. Britannos à Lucii Regis, & Eleutherii Papæ tempore Christianam retinuisse fidem, vt nunquam inter eos deficeret certum est, sed quia à Romanæ Ecclesiæ ritibus discrepabant, conuocari ex his Episcopos atque eruditiores auxilio Ethelberthi Regis fecit Augustinus, vt de rebus controversis disceptarent, ac in vna sententia conuenirent. Namq; eius Regis ditio maxima erat, ita vt tèporibus pacatis cæterarum provinciarum Reges Cantiorum Regi parebant. Cùmq; ad locu quondam in vicinorum atque occidentali Saxonum confinio, qui lingua Anglosaxonica Antiquarii Ang. Ant. vocatur, convenissent, petiit Augustinus, ut Britannicam Ecclesiam in caeremoniis atque religionis summa suae in Anglia nuper instituta conformare, Romanaeque subiicerent. Quod precibus, suasionibus, atque minis perficere tentavit Augustinus. At illi neque Augustino se subiicere, neque ab antiquis ecclesiarum ritibus quos ab Apostolis acceperant, nec Romanae solum, sed quarumcunque Ecclesiarum ritibus praeferrent, discedere velle dicebant. Ita cum in hac nihil profecisset, ab Ilam indixit Synodum Augustinus, ad quam Britanni frequentiores quam antea convenerunt. Septem enim Episcopi Britannorum Herefordensis, Tauensis, Paternensis, Bancorensis, Gluiensis, Vniacensis, ac Morganensis convenerunt. Aderat etiam clericorum ingens numerus, maximè verò Monachorum professorum ex nobilissimo Coenobio, quod Saxones Bancornaburg appellabant, quod circa 1200. Monachos, ex quibus maximè idoneos et indocti eliquis ministrabant, victum ipsum et vestium opetis suppeditabant, continebant. Horum Abbatum Dunecus dicebatur. Antequam autem hiac Britannorum multitudo ad Augustinum accessit, pium quendam et sapientem Anachoritam consuluerunt, verum Augustini sua usu violatas traditiones desererent. Quibus ille, si homo, inquit, Dei est, illi morem gerite. Quomodo verò, inquiunt illi, hoc constabit nobis? Ex hac, inquit Augustinus, humilis ac mitis sit, verisimile est eum Christi onus portare, vobisque portandum offerre velle: sin verò elatus sit ac superbus, a Deo non est, nec a vobis audiendus. Adhuc inquiunt, qui cognoscemus. Ingrediatur, inquit ille, in Synodo prior, tum si vobis adunctantibus allurrexerit, Christi famulus est, illique in omnibus obtemperate: sin secus fecerit, voique ipse pracuerit, negligatur vicissim et aspernetur a vobis. Intrauit itaque prior in Synodum Augustinus cum fastu et pompa, eum Apostolatus sui vexillo, crucesque argentea, letania, processione, iconibus, reliquiis, canticis, aliisque triumphis nugis tanquam sanguinarius et superbus Monachus. Et Britannis ingredientibus non modò non assurrexit, sed nec charitatis aut benevolentiae signum vsui vllouo gestu declarauit, propositi, si in tribus saltem secum convenirent, ut pascha, et baptismus Romano ritu celebrarentur, et Anglis verbum Dei secum vna praedicarent, etiam in aliis dissiderent, aequo animo toleraturum. Atillicum hominis fastum arrogantiamque notarent, nullaei in re obsequi volebant, nec solum vetustaracie repugnabatur, verum etiam suos visus et obseruationes omnibus praeminentiores Eleutherii Papae authoritate pronunciabant. Affirmabant etiam caeremonias non solùm a Sancto Eleutherio pontifice primo institutore suo, ab ipsa pene infantia Ecclesiae dicatas, verùm a sanctis patribus suis, Dei amicis ac Apostolorum sequacibus hactenus observatas, quas non deberent mutare propter nouos dogmaticas. Adhaecneque illum suum Archiepiscopum habituros, cum Archiepiscopum iam Legancestriae commoratum haberent, eui deberent et vellent parere, externo verò Episcopo se minimè subiectos fore. Quo respondo Augustinus ira percitus, illis futura bellapromisit, ac mortis vitionem, quae mox sequebatur, ferociter minabatur. Quam Augustini atrocitatem eò magis mirati conuenit, quòd Gregorius ad illum scripserit, non esse necessarium in omnibus Ecclesiis caeremoniarum similitudinem obseruare, sed vnamquamque sibi optimas eligere debere. Sed Augustinus ad Papalem principatum, suamque iurisdictionem tespexit, Gregorii praeceptaque non sequutus, qui dulcissimis conuinis illum dominatum proscindit. De Britannis autem Augustino resistentibus, sic scribit Mantuanus in Fastis. Adde quòd & patres ausi taxare latinos: Causabantur eos fulte, imprudenter, & aquo Durius ad ritum Roma voluisse Britannos Cogere, & antiquum tam precipitanter amorem Tam stolide temerasse ausu. Concedere Roma Debuit, aebant, potius quam rumpere pacem Humana quia iuris erant, modo salua manerent Lex divina fides, Christi doctrina senatus Quam primus tulit ore suo: quia tradita ab ipso Christi erat, humana docere & lumine vitae. &c.
units.tr: What we shall make clear in this history is that the Britons had retained the Christian faith from the time of King Lucius and Pope Eleutherius, and it is certain that it never failed among them. But because they differed from the rites of the Roman Church, Augustine, with the help of King Ethelbert, arranged that bishops and the more learned men among them should be summoned, so that they might debate the controverted matters and come together in one judgement. For the dominion of that king was very great, so that in peaceful times the kings of the other provinces obeyed the king of Kent. When they had assembled at a certain place on the border of the neighbouring West Saxons, which in the Anglo-Saxon tongue is called [...], Augustine asked that the British Church should conform to him in the ceremonies and the chief points of religion, which he had recently established in England, and submit to Rome. He tried to bring this about by entreaties, persuasions and threats. But they said that they would neither submit to Augustine, nor depart from the ancient rites of the churches which they had received from the Apostles, and that they would prefer those rites not only to the Roman but to those of any churches whatever. Since he had achieved nothing in this, Augustine then called a synod, to which the Britons came in greater numbers than before. For seven bishops of the Britons came together: those of Hereford, Tavistock (Tauensis), Paternensis, Bangor, Gloucester, Wroxeter (Vniacensis), and Morgannwg. There was also a great number of clergy, and above all of professed monks from the most noble monastery, which the Saxons called Bancornaburg (Bangor), which contained about twelve hundred monks, of whom the most suitable and learned ministered to them, supplying them with food and clothing. Their abbot was called Dunecus. Before this multitude of Britons came to Augustine, they consulted a certain pious and wise anchorite, whether they should abandon the traditions handed down to them, which Augustine's practice had violated. He answered them: "If he is a man of God, follow his custom." "But how," they said, "will this be established for us?" "By this," said Augustine, "if he is humble and gentle, it is likely that he bears the yoke of Christ and wishes to offer it for you to bear; but if he is proud and arrogant, he is not from God, and you should not listen to him." "Still," they said, "how shall we know?" "Let him enter the synod first," said the anchorite, "and if he rises to you when you approach, he is a servant of Christ, and you should obey him in all things; but if he does otherwise, and wishes to be preferred to you, let him be neglected and despised by you in turn." So Augustine entered the synod first, with pomp and display, carrying the banner of his apostolate and a silver cross, with a litany, procession, images, relics, chants and other such trifles, like a bloody and proud monk. And when the Britons entered, he not only did not rise, but did not show by any gesture a sign of charity or goodwill. He proposed that if they would agree with him in at least three matters, namely that Easter and baptism were celebrated by the Roman rite, and that they preached the Word of God together with him to the English, he would tolerate with an equal mind their disagreement in other matters. But they, noting the man's pride and arrogance, would not yield to him in any point; and not only did they refuse to abandon their ancient custom, but they declared that their own customs and observances were to be preferred to all others by the authority of Pope Eleutherius. They also affirmed that their ceremonies had been established not only by Saint Eleutherius, the first Pope who had been their founder, and dedicated almost from the infancy of the Church, but had been observed until then by their holy fathers, friends of God and followers of the Apostles, and that they ought not to change them on account of new dogmas. Moreover, they said they had their own archbishop, for at Legecester (Chester) an archbishop had been living, whom they ought and were willing to obey, but they would not be subject to a foreign bishop at all. To this Augustine, roused to anger, promised them future wars, and ferociously threatened the death that soon followed. All the more is this cruelty of Augustine to be wondered at, since Gregory wrote to him that it was not necessary to observe a uniformity of ceremonies in all churches, but that each should choose the best for itself. But Augustine looked to papal primacy and his own jurisdiction, and did not follow Gregory's precepts, who, with the sweetest persuasions, had cut down that dominion. Concerning the Britons who resisted Augustine, Mantuan writes thus in the Fasti: "Add that they dared to censure the Latins, Charging them with folly and imprudence, and with too harsh a wish To compel the Britons to the Roman rite, And to have so rashly violated the ancient love. Rome, they said, ought to have yielded rather than break the peace, Since these were human laws, provided that the divine law, The faith, the doctrine of Christ, remained safe, Which the first senate bore from his own mouth, Because it was handed down by Christ himself, To teach human things with the light of life, etc."

units.la: Et sanè illa prima de Romanis ritibus inducendis per Augustinum tunc excitata contentio, quae non nisi clade & sanguine innocentium Britannorum poterat sedari, ad nostra recentiora tempora, cum simili pernicie, cædeq; Christianorū peruenit. Cū enim illis gloriosis ceremoniis a pura primitiuæ Ecclesiæ simplicitate recesserunt, non de vitæ sanctitate, de Euangelii prædicatione, de Spiritus Sancti vi & consolatione multum laborabant, sed novas indies altercationes, de novis ritibus per Papas singulos additis, qui nemnem tam excelso gradu dignum iudicabant, qui aliquod ceremoniosi, non dicam, monstrosi, inauditi & inusitati, non adiecisset, instituebant, suggestaq; & scholas, fabulisrixisq; suis implebant. Nā prima Ecclesiæ species simpliciot, & integro, ac interno Dei cultu ab ipso verbo præscripto candida, nec vestibus splendida, nec magnificis structuris decorata, nec auro, argento, gemmisque fulgens fuit. Etsi liceat his exterioribus vt, modoanimum abillaiocorioni & integro Dei cultu non abducunt, quod quidem in summo, ah ipso Domino recordandæ salutis ostræ symbolo Ecclesiæ traditio, nempe Eucharistiæ mysterio cernitur. Eius primo ceremonia in calicibus ligneis, & communibus vestibus, a sanctioribus, quàm qui deinceps sequuti sunt, præsbyteris administrabatur: & quòd in Myssarum tanta precum, collectarum, canonum lectionumq; varietate ac multitudine refertarum solenniis id sacramentum administrari voluit Pontificii, scimus ex eodem Martino Pænitentiario, ipsam missam sic dictam, & sacramenti illius traditionem, non alia quàm sola oratione dominica, à Petro io orientalibus reglionibus, vel, vt alii volunt, à Iacobo Hierosoliymis fuisse celebratum: & sic à Christi primo instituto ducentis amplius annis in prima Ecclesia duravit: donec eam Zepherinus 16. Romanus Pontifex, quorundam suasionibus ad pulchriorem materiam formamq; mutare voluit. Vrbanus vero 18. Pootifex lepidè alludens: nunc, ioquit, verendum est, ne aureis calicibus plumbei vel ligneis ministrent sacerdotes. Quod dicto arguit suum illud seculum, quod multò propius, quàm Augustini à Christo & Apostolis abfuit, curiosis ac morosis ritibus, ab illa primæva, & rectàsimplicitate Euangelica degenerasse. Illa autem in Romana Ecclesia rituum multitudo, ad immensum, illius magni Augustini Hipponensis in Africa Episcopi temporibus, ita creuerat, vt quæ stus st. Christianorum in ceremoniis ac ritibus ob multitudinem duriorem tunc fuisse conditionem, quàm Iudæorum, qui etiam tempus libertatis non agnoouerint, legabitus tamen sarcinis, non humanis præsumptionibus subiiciebantur: nam pauciorib{us} in diuino cultu, quàm Christiani, ceremoniis vtebatur. Quisi se sensisset, quantus deinde per singulos Papas coaceruatus cumulus accessit, modumChristianum,credo, ipse statuisset, qui hoc malum tunc in Ecclesia viderat. Videmus enim ab illa ceremoniarum cõhtentione nedom Ecclesiam esse vacuam: quinhomines alioquin dosti atq; pii de vestibus & huiusmodi nugis adhuc rixoso magis & militari, quàm aut Philosophico, aut Christiano more inter se digladiantur & contendunt. Hanc autem calicum in aurea vasa mutationem ex Triburiensi Coocilio, sub Arnolfo Imperatore inito, describamus.
units.tr: And indeed that first dispute over introducing Roman rites, stirred up by Augustine, which could be settled only by the slaughter and blood of innocent Britons, came down to our more recent times with similar ruin and slaughter of Christians. For when they had departed from the pure simplicity of the primitive Church by those glorious ceremonies, they laboured not so much over the holiness of life, the preaching of the Gospel, and the power and comfort of the Holy Spirit. Instead they stirred up new disputes every day over new rites added by individual Popes. They thought no one worthy of so exalted a rank who had not added some ceremonial, I will not say monstrous, unheard-of and unusual, rite, and they filled their sermons and schools with these things, and with their fables and wranglings. For the earlier form of the Church was simpler. Its inward and whole worship of God was prescribed by the Word itself; it was not splendid in vestments, nor adorned with magnificent buildings, nor glittering with gold, silver and jewels. Although it is permitted to use these outward things, provided they do not draw the mind away from the pure and whole worship of God, the Church's tradition from the Lord himself, the symbol of remembering our salvation, is seen most of all in the mystery of the Eucharist. At first its celebration was administered with wooden chalices and common vestments, by elders more holy than those who followed afterwards. And we know from the same Martin the Penitentiary that the Papists wished this sacrament to be administered with the solemnities of the Mass, crammed with such a variety and multitude of prayers, collects, canons and lessons. The so-called Mass itself, and the handing down of that sacrament, was celebrated with nothing but the Lord's Prayer, from Peter in the eastern regions, or, as others hold, from James at Jerusalem. And so it continued in the primitive Church for more than two hundred years from Christ's first institution, until Zephyrinus, the sixteenth Roman Pontiff, at the persuasion of some, wished to change it to a more beautiful matter and form. Urban, the eighteenth Pontiff, alluding wittily, said: "Now we must fear lest priests minister with leaden or wooden chalices instead of golden ones." By this saying he shows that his own age, which was much nearer to Christ and the Apostles than Augustine's, had degenerated from that primitive and right evangelical simplicity by curious and fussy rites. Now in the Roman Church the multitude of rites had grown so immensely in the time of that great Augustine, bishop of Hippo in Africa, that the condition of Christians in ceremonies and rites was then harsher, because of their number, than that of the Jews. The Jews, who did not even know the time of liberty, were nevertheless burdened with burdens, though not with human presumptions; for they used fewer ceremonies in divine worship than the Christians. Had he seen how great a heap was afterwards piled up by each successive Pope, I believe he would himself have set a Christian limit, he who had already seen this evil in the Church. For we see that the contention over ceremonies has not only left the Church far from free; men otherwise learned and pious still fight and contend with one another over vestments and such trifles in a more quarrelsome and military manner than in a philosophical or Christian one. Let us now describe this change of chalices into golden vessels, as recorded by the Council of Trebur, held under Emperor Arnulf.

units.la: De Vasculis Cap. XVIII.
units.tr: On Vessels, Chapter XVIII.

units.la: Asa quibus sacra consiciuntur mysteria, calices sunt & paterae. De quibus Bonifacius Martyr & Episc. interrogatus, si liceret in vascu-lis ligneis sacramenta conficere respondit. Quondam sacerdotes aurei ligneis calicibus vtebatur, nunc è contra lignei sacerdotes, aureis vtuntur calicibus. Zepherinus 16. Romanus Episcopus, patenis vitreis missas celebrari constituit.
units.tr: Among the things with which the sacred mysteries are performed are chalices and patens. Concerning these, Boniface, martyr and bishop, being asked whether it was lawful to celebrate the sacraments in wooden vessels, replied: "Formerly priests of gold used wooden chalices; now, on the contrary, wooden priests use golden chalices." Zephyrinus, the sixteenth Roman bishop, decreed that masses be celebrated with glass patens.

units.la: Tum deinde Vrbanus 5. Pontifex omnia ministeria sacrata, fecit argentea. In hoc enim sicut & in religiuis cultibus, magis & magis increuerunt temporum, decus succreuit Ecclesiarum. Nostris enim diebus (vt decreto sanctissimo) qui serui patrisfamilias sumus, ne decus matris Ecclesiæ imminuatur, sed magis cultus mulerur & amplificetur, statuimus vt deinceps, nullus sacerdos sacrum mysterium eorporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi Domini nostri in ligneis vasculis vllo modo conficere præsumat, neundepacari debet, inde irascatur Deus. Nos vero ad Synodum Angustiniauam reuertemur. Inter alia quæ Britannis Augustinus suasisse dicitur, hoc ab historicis ideo commemoratur, quia insignis postea cladis erat occasio. Rogauit Britannos vt se Archiepiscopum reciperent, & vt communem secum Anglis euangelizandi laborem susceiperent: At Britanni, quia abillis patriis sedibus erant pulsi, id facere recusauerunt, addentes, se merito Anglos & eorum religionem odisse: quia illis erant tanquam canes habiti, ideoque immerito contempti. Hoc responsum Britanhorum non illibenter captauit Augustinus. Inde enim se occasioòem nactum ratus est, vnde neglectum & contemptum sui in illis vlciscererur. Cupide igitur hanc consuetudinem ad Ethelbertum Regem defert, eandemq; Rex non inuitus arripuit. Is instigat Edelfridū Regem Northumbrorum cognatum suum, etsi paganum, aduersus Britannos, qui quidem cum numeroso & prope stupendo exercitu, Legeceftriam ab Anglis sic dicta, Britonibus vero Caer legion appellatam, venit: ibi enim Brochmal Britannorum dux aduentum hostium expectarat: quò etiam confugerat Abbas Dinoth cum ingenti sacerdotū, Eremitarum & Monachorum numero, maximè verò de Monasterio Bangor. Hi peracto triduano ieiunio Deum orabāt, vt à barbarorum gladiis populum suum protegeret. In hos primùm arma verti Rex iubet, quos etiam Dux Brochmal à primo hostiū aduentu pertetrefactus, turpiter terga dans, inermes ac nudos hostium gladiis exposuit: 50. solum viri fuga sibi consuluerunt: reliqui ad 1200. gladio Edelfredi trucidati sunt. Narrat Beda Augustinum diuino edoctum oraculo, bellum hoc Britonum Episcopis & Clericis in consilio Augustiniano prædixisse: cùm tamen verisimilius sit, ipsum communicato cum Ethelberto Rege consilio, eius belli infferendi non conscium modo, sed etiam causam fuisse. Visus est enim illo Rege familiarissimè, cuius soafu & impulsu diximus Edelfridum hanc calamitatem Britannis inflixisse. Atqui sane dicitur Augustinus in primo de istis ritibus colloquio, cùm illis precibus persuaderi nō poterat, comminatum esse: quare non est abimile eius instigatione hoc bellum Britannis esse paratum, si se illi in a. congressu non conformaren: quidam etiam Legiocestriæ Augustinum obuium fuisse regibus adid præsium præcinctis tradunt. Quin etiam huic coniecturæ suffragari videtur Amandus Xicrixiensis, vir ex ordine fratrum minorum, cuius ipsius verba subiiciam. Cū enim, inquit, Britones fuerunt catholici, Saxones gentiles erant, ad quos conuertendos misit beatus Gregorius, Augustinum & Mellitum, qui Saxones conuerterunt. Sed cum Augustinus vellet Episcopos & Abbates Britonum adducere authoritate Apostolica, vt cum Legatum receiperent, & cum eo Anglis prædicarent, mota est dissensio propter eorum inobedientiam ad sanctum Augustinum, & sic motum fuit bellum inter Britonum Regulos & Saxonum Regulos: quia nam conuersi volebant Britones Augustino subdere. Quidam ascribunt Bedæ testimonio hanc stragem Britannis illatam Augustino iam antemortuo, quod sane suppositium est, nec in libris Bedæ Saxonicis habetur. Alijeam ad annum 605. referunt, ipso adhuc superstite, quibus propterea assentior, quia apud omnes constat Edelfridum Northumbrorum Regem hoc ipso anno Britones subiugasse, & tributarios Anglis fecisse. Nam si quod faciunt pontifices, ex quibus unq; sine authoritate & delectu authoribus, nobis sumere quæ velimus, liceret, vt illi ex suis historiis Christianam religionem in Anglia institutam aut restitutam Augustino suo totam tribuunt: si cnos ex nostris eadem authoritate atque fide, probare possimus, religionem abillo vel euertam & deletam, vel depravatam & corruptam fuisse. Idque a Merlino prædictum fuisse dicitur his verbis. Delebitur iterum religio, & transmutatio primarū fidei. Dignitas Londoniæ ad Dorobernium Q iod per Gormundum fuisse factū aut Augustinum, qui 1100. Banchorenses in Wallia Monachos fecit occidi, còquod non obedierunt sibi in concilio, planè docet Alexander Ecclesiensis. Mirum enim est, quòd de religione delenda, & primarum sedium mutatione & Londinensi dignitate Cantuariam transferenda vno vaticinio, verbisq; cohærentibus prædixit Merlinus. Postquam Augustinus Anglo saxones ad Christianam religionem inxta Romanos ritus perduxerat, imprimum obiit, sedem dicitur, Ethelberto primo ex Anglorum Regibus Christiano adhucregnante, an. 611. 7. Kal. Iunii. postquam 16. annos sedisset, vt plures tradunt: quamuis multum laborat Thomas Sportus in Chronico suo, aliique Monachi, Augustinū non tam longuum fuisse, sed multo ante tempore obiisse, vt suprādictæ Wallensis cladis suspicioné ac infamiam ab illo auerterent. Positum est corpus eius foris iuxta Ecclesiam beatorum Apostolorum Petri & Pauli (cuius superiùs meminimus) extra muros ciuitatis ad orientem. Eaenim adhuc nec perfecta fuit, nec de more dedicata. Mox vero ac dedicata est, translatum est corpus eius in porticum illius templi aquilonarem, ibiq; honore, quod deberat, sepulcum: in qua etiam porticu succedentiū Archiepiscoporum corpora inhumari solitafunt, vtiq; ad Theodorum, qui cum sui fuisset sequentibus Episcopis ahibi in eadem Ecclesia ac conditus est, eò quod prædicta porticus non erat capax plurium. Extructum est etiam in eius porticus medio altare in honorem beati Gregorii, in quo singulis quibusque sabbatiis nuñæ solenniores celebrabantur Tumulo Augustini hoc epitaphium inscriptum est. Hic requiescit diuus Augustinus, Dorobernensis Archiepiscopus primus, qui olim huc à beato Gregorio Romanæ urbis pontifice directus, & a deo operatione miraculorum suffultus, & Ethelbertum Regem, & gentem illius ab idolorum cultu ad fidem Christi perduxit. Erat hic Augustinus statura procera & arrecta, ita vt à scapulis populo superemineret: faciem amabilis, & Reuerenda frons, mediate suis coloribus resultabat fcneftrata, fcpius discalceatus ibat, nudis pedibus pertuftrando, callos plantis attrauiffe. Non multò ante Augustini obitum Bonifacius 3. in Sabiniani Pontificis mortui locum surrogatur, qui post suscepeam admiristrandi prouinciam confestim eum Phoca egit, vt Romana Ecclesia esset omnium aliarum caput; quod ægrè nec sine multa contentione concessum fuit. Tunc etiam dira humani generis pestis, impia Mahumeti religio originem accepit. Inter Abbatiarum multitudinem, quæ huius temporis in Britannia fuerunt, Abbatia Petri & Pauli Cantuariæ dignitate cæteras omnes longè antecelluit.
units.tr: Then afterwards Urban the fifth Pontiff made all the sacred ministries of silver. For in this, as in religious rites, the more the times increased, the more the splendour of the Churches grew. For in our own days, by a most holy decree, since we are servants of the Father of the family, lest the dignity of Mother Church be diminished, but rather her worship be increased and enlarged, we decree that from now on no priest shall presume in any way to celebrate the holy mystery of the body and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord in wooden vessels, lest God be provoked from the very quarter whence he ought to be appeased. But let us return to the Synod of Augustine. Among the other things which Augustine is said to have urged on the Britons, historians record this one because it was afterwards the occasion of a notable disaster. He asked the Britons to receive him as their archbishop, and to take up with him the common labour of preaching to the English. But the Britons, because they had been driven from their ancestral seats, refused to do so, adding that they rightly hated the English and their religion, since they had been treated by them as dogs and therefore unjustly despised. Augustine eagerly seized upon this answer of the Britons. For he thought he had found an occasion by which to avenge the neglect and contempt shown to himself among them. Eagerly, therefore, he reported this to King Ethelbert, and the King not unwillingly seized upon it. He incited Edelfrid, King of the Northumbrians, his kinsman though a pagan, against the Britons. Edelfrid came with a numerous and almost astonishing army to Legeceaster, as the English call it, or Caerlegion, as the Britons call it. For there Brochmael, leader of the Britons, had awaited the coming of the enemy; thither also had fled Abbot Dinoth with a great number of priests, hermits and monks, especially from the monastery of Bangor. These men, having kept a three-day fast, prayed to God that he would protect his people from the swords of the barbarians. The King ordered arms to be turned first against them. Brochmael, terrified at the first approach of the enemy, shamefully turned his back and exposed the unarmed and naked men to the enemy's swords. Only fifty men saved themselves by flight; the rest, about 1200, were slaughtered by the sword of Edelfrid. Bede relates that Augustine, taught by a divine oracle, foretold this war to the bishops and clergy of the Britons in the council held by Augustine. Yet it is more probable that he, having taken counsel with King Ethelbert, was not only aware of the waging of this war but was even its cause. For he was seen to be very intimate with that King, at whose persuasion and impulse we have said Edelfrid inflicted this calamity on the Britons. Indeed it is said that Augustine, in the first conference about these rites, when he could not persuade them by prayers, threatened them. So it is not unlike that this war was prepared against the Britons at his instigation, if they did not conform to him at the meeting. Some also relate that Augustine met the kings at Legecester, girded for battle. Indeed Amandus Xicrixiensis, a man of the order of the Friars Minor, seems to support this conjecture, and I shall add his own words. "For when," he says, "the Britons were Catholics and the Saxons were gentiles, blessed Gregory sent Augustine and Mellitus to convert them, and they converted the Saxons. But when Augustine wished to bring the bishops and abbots of the Britons under apostolic authority, so that they would receive him as legate and preach with him to the English, a dissension arose on account of their disobedience to St Augustine, and so war was stirred up between the kinglets of the Britons and the kinglets of the Saxons, because the Britons, having been converted, wished to submit to Augustine." Some ascribe this slaughter inflicted on the Britons to Augustine when he was already dead, citing the testimony of Bede. This is certainly spurious, and it is not found in Bede's Saxon books. Others refer it to the year 605, while Augustine was still alive, and I agree with them, because it is agreed by all that Edelfrid, King of the Northumbrians, subdued the Britons that same year and made them tributary to the English. For if it were permitted to us to take from our own histories, with the same authority and without choice of authors, whatever we wish, as the pontiffs do, from whose histories they attribute wholly to their Augustine the establishment or restoration of the Christian religion in England, then we could prove from our own histories, with the same authority and faith, that religion was either overthrown and destroyed by him or depraved and corrupted. And this is said to have been foretold by Merlin in these words: "Religion will be destroyed again, and the change of the first faith." That the dignity of London was transferred to Canterbury by Gormund or by Augustine, who had 1100 monks of Bangor in Wales killed because they did not obey him in council, Alexander of Ecclesia plainly teaches. For it is remarkable that Merlin foretold in one prophecy, and in coherent words, the destruction of religion, the change of the primary sees, and the transfer of the dignity of London to Canterbury. After Augustine had brought the Anglo-Saxons to the Christian religion according to Roman rites, he died first, as is said, in his see, while Ethelbert, the first of the English kings, was still reigning as a Christian, in the year 611, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, after having sat sixteen years, as most report. Although Thomas Sprott in his Chronicle, and other monks, labour much to show that Augustine did not live so long but died much earlier, so that they might turn away from him the suspicion and infamy of the aforesaid Welsh slaughter. His body was placed outside, beside the church of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul (which we mentioned above), outside the city walls to the east, for that church was neither yet finished nor dedicated in the customary way. But as soon as it was dedicated, his body was transferred into the northern porch of that temple and there given the honour it deserved, in a tomb. In this porch also the bodies of succeeding archbishops were customarily buried, up to Theodore, who, with his successors, was buried in the same church, because the said porch was not large enough to hold more. An altar was also built in the middle of that porch in honour of blessed Gregory, at which more solemn masses were celebrated on every Saturday. On Augustine's tomb this epitaph is inscribed: "Here rests holy Augustine, first archbishop of Canterbury, who was once sent here by blessed Gregory, pontiff of the city of Rome, and, supported by God's working of miracles, led King Ethelbert and his people from the worship of idols to the faith of Christ." This Augustine was tall and upright in stature, so that he overtopped the people by the shoulders; his face was lovely and his brow reverend, and it was mottled with its own colours. He often went barefoot, having by walking drawn calluses on the soles of his bare feet. Not long before Augustine's death, Boniface III was substituted in the place of the deceased Pontiff Sabinian, who, after taking up the administration of his province, at once brought it about with Phocas that the Roman Church should be the head of all the others; this was granted with difficulty and not without much contention. Then too the dire pest of the human race, the impious religion of Mahomet, took its origin. Among the multitude of abbeys which existed in Britain at this time, the Abbey of Peter and Paul at Canterbury far surpassed all the rest in dignity.

units.la: II. Laurentivs.
units.tr: II. Laurentius.

units.la: Vc̄cessit Augustino Dorobernia Laurentius, natione Romanus, vir doctrina & moribus clarus, quem sibi adhuc superstes successorem delegit Augustinus, nè se mortuo Ecclesia recens posita; pastore vel modico tempore destituta, ad gentilismum denuo relaberetur: vel etiam veritus, ne fede tantillum vacante, dignitas Me- tropolitica alio transferretur: vt vt fuit, Augustinum non fefellit Laurentius. Statim enim atque Archiepiscopatus gradu positus est, quam ille religionem, quoscunque fructus instituerat, hic promouere atque stabilire omni diligentia, studio, solicitudine, exhortationibus, & contributis bonorum operum exemplis adnitebatur: neque solum rectoris Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ curam gessit, sed etiam Britannios veteres, qui metu Anglorum in desertis Walliæ sese abdiderant, Scotos etiam, & Hybernos adhuc in Christianæ fidei dogmate rudiores plenius erudire; & ad cosdem ritus studuit perducere. Nam cum Scoti, quemadmodum de Britannis in Augustino dictum est, Pascha diuerso à Romanis modo celebrarent, ipsoque Ecclesiastica distribuerunt consuetudine & more Romanæ Ecclesiæ in pluribus differret, ex Episcopis suis cum literis ad eos legasse dicitur Laurentius, maiorem in modum contendens & obse- crans, vt se Romanæ Ecclesiæ velit cohinngere, receptosque vbiuis ritus, & Catholicas traditiones admittere. Scripsitque etiam dicitur ad sacerdotes Britonum, significans se ve- hementer cupere, ipsos iam disperses & palantes, ad unile Christi & Ecclesiæ vnitatem congregare. Superiorioris Epistolæ principium extat in Ecclesiastica historia Bedæ Lib: 2. cap. 4. hæc autem nusquam reperitur. Et quanquam his literis nonnihil profecisse Laurentium refert Beda, iamque ad concordiam superius distensentes propendere videretur, atque adeo pet omnem regionem constitutæ religio & firmata putaretur, non multo tamen post totius religionis perturbatio, enerfioque sequuta est. Moritur enim Christianissimus princeps Ethelbertus, vnaque cum eo moritur religio Christiana. Illi successit Edbaldus, Rex Anglorum ab Hengesto sextus, admodum puer, filius patris per omnia dissimilis. Is postquam adolecuerat, susque iuris factus est, genio paulatim indulsit, tandemque se vitarique suam omni vitiorum genere contaminauit. Inter cætera, quæ ille scelerate itique peccatum, uxorem patris concupisse, nupsisseque dicitur: quæ etiam nuptiæ fuerunt subsecuntia omnium malorum origo & causa. Hisce enim copulis infaustis infandisque, cum religio Christiana adueratur, eius primo eum cepit tædere, postea displicere infestari, abominari. Ingenium Regis, populus (vt assolet) sequutus est, Laurentio nihilominus iisdem scribit, hortans, monens, vt in cœpta professione permaneret. Cum vero nihil se, neque ad Regem, neque apud populum cerneret profi- cere, quinetiam odium & crudelitatem tyrannidem adusus Christianos (qui pauci erant) iisdem asper, statuit tandem è Britannia discedere, & sequi in Galliam Mellitum & Iustum, quos alibi demonstrabimus, à filiis Liberri, Regis orientalium Saxonum excepit. Pridie ergo quam proficisceretur, lectum sibi in Ecclesia Apostolorum Petri & Pauli sternì iuberi, in quo postquam recubuisset, multis precibus, suspiriis & lachrymis, Ecclesiæ salutem & incolumitatem Deo commendauit. Finitis precibus se quieti dat: quam prius in vero obdormisset, illico ei visus est in somnis adesse Petrus, ipsum corripere, castigare; loris & flagellis cædere, quòd immemor mandati Augustini & officii sui, metu suppliciti gregem Christi sibi commissum Lupis rapacibus laniandum relinquere. Hoc spectaculo perterrefactus, consilio repente mutatoque incœpto destitit. Edbaldus etiam rex, vbi, quæ Laurentio accidissent, ei nuntiatum est, reinouitate percul- sus est. sus, 'defuncti veniam à Laurentio petiit, repudiatoque protinus turpi conlugio ad sanitatem rediit, Mellitum etiam & iustum domum reuocauit: anteacta denique vita emendata, Christi religionem promouere coepit. Templum etiam beatæ Mariæ in Coenobio S. Petri ædificauit, quod tamen non Laurentius, sed suæ cessor eius Mellitus consecrauit.
units.tr: Laurentius, a Roman by birth, a man distinguished for learning and character, succeeded Augustine at Canterbury. While he was still alive, Augustine chose him as his successor, lest after his death the newly planted Church, left for even a short time without a minister, should slip back into heathenism. Or perhaps Augustine feared that, with the see left even briefly vacant, the metropolitan dignity would be transferred elsewhere. However that was, Laurentius did not disappoint Augustine. As soon as he was raised to the archiepiscopal office, he strove with all diligence, zeal and care, by exhortation and by the example of good works, to advance and establish the religion that Augustine had begun. He did not only take charge of the Church of the English. He also set himself to instruct more fully the ancient Britons, who had hidden themselves in the wilds of Wales for fear of the English, and likewise the Scots and the Irish, who were still rather ignorant of the doctrine of the Christian faith, and to bring them to the same rites. For although the Scots, as was said of the Britons in the account of Augustine, celebrated Easter in a manner different from the Romans, and although they differed in many points of ecclesiastical usage and custom from the Church of Rome, Laurentius is said to have sent letters to their bishops, urging and beseeching them very earnestly to join themselves to the Church of Rome, and to accept the rites and Catholic traditions observed everywhere. He is also said to have written to the priests of the Britons, declaring how greatly he desired to gather them, now scattered and wandering, into the unity of Christ and of the Church. The beginning of the former letter is extant in Bede's Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 4; this latter one is found nowhere. And although Bede reports that Laurentius made some progress by these letters, and although those who had dissented seemed now inclined to concord, and the religion was thought to be established and firmly settled throughout the whole land, nevertheless not long afterwards there followed a disturbance and weakening of the whole religion. For the most Christian king Ethelbert died, and with him the Christian religion died too. He was succeeded by Eadbald, the sixth king of the English from Hengest, a mere boy, a son wholly unlike his father. When he grew up and came into his own authority, he gradually indulged his inclinations, and at last defiled himself with every kind of vice. Among other wicked and abominable sins, he is said to have lusted after his father's wife and to have married her; and this marriage became the source and cause of all evils that followed. For with these unhappy and unspeakable unions, while the Christian religion was still growing, he first began to be weary of it, then to dislike it, to be hostile to it, and to abhor it. The people followed the king's disposition, as is customary. Nevertheless Laurentius wrote to him, exhorting and warning him to persevere in the profession he had begun. But when he saw that he was accomplishing nothing, neither with the king nor with the people, and that the king, taking up hatred and cruelty as a tyrant, treated the Christians (who were few) harshly, he at last resolved to leave Britain and to follow Mellitus and Justus into Gaul, whom we shall show elsewhere were received by the sons of Liberrus, king of the East Saxons. On the day before he set out, he ordered a bed to be laid for him in the church of the Apostles Peter and Paul. When he had lain down there, with many prayers, sighs and tears, he commended the safety and welfare of the Church to God. When the prayers were finished he gave himself to rest; and as soon as he had fallen asleep, Peter seemed to stand beside him in a dream, to rebuke him and to chastise him, beating him with thongs and whips, because, forgetful of Augustine's charge and of his own duty, he was abandoning through fear of punishment the flock of Christ committed to him, to be torn by ravening wolves. Terrified by this vision, he at once gave up his plan and changed his purpose. When King Eadbald was told what had happened to Laurentius, he too was struck with remorse. He asked the dead man's pardon, and at once, rejecting his shameful marriage, he returned to soundness of mind. He also recalled Mellitus and Justus home. At length, his former life amended, he began to advance the religion of Christ. He also built a church of blessed Mary in the monastery of St Peter, which, however, was consecrated not by Laurentius but by his successor Mellitus.

units.la: Moriturque enim Laurentius eo ipso anno, quo Edbaldus Rex fidem Christi amplexus erat, atque in porticu Ecclesiæ Petri iuxta Augustinum sepultus est. Est opinio à Monachis profecta, eaque à posteris libenti magis ac grato assensu, quàm vero receptā, omnes Cantuarienses Archiepiscopos Monachos fuisse, à primo Augustino ad Stigandum. Arentis hic Laurentius, de quo hactenus egimus, Monachus planè non fuit, sed Præsbyter, idipsum affirmante Beda Lib 1. cap. 27. Interea (inquit) vir Domini Augustinus venit Arelatens, & ab Archiepiscopo eiusdem eiustatis Ethelo, iuxta quod iussu sancti patris Gregorii acceperat, Archiepiscopus genti Anglorum ordinatus est: reuersusq; Britanniam misit Romam Laurentium Præsbyterum, & Petrum Monachum, &c.
units.tr: Laurentius died in the same year in which King Eadbald embraced the faith of Christ, and he was buried in the porch of the church of Peter, next to Augustine. There is an opinion, started by the monks and accepted by later writers more with pleasure and approval than on sound grounds, that all the Archbishops of Canterbury, from the first Augustine down to Stigand, were monks. But this Laurentius, of whom we have so far spoken, was plainly not a monk but a presbyter, as Bede affirms in book 1, chapter 27: "Meanwhile (he says) the man of God Augustine came to Arles, and was ordained archbishop of the English nation by the archbishop of that province, Aetherius, as he had received instruction from the holy father Gregory. Returning to Britain, he sent to Rome Laurentius the presbyter and Peter the monk, etc."

units.la: III. MELLITVS.
units.tr: III. MELLITUS.

units.la: NGlis ad fidem Christi conuersis, cùm quadraginta illi Comites, quos secum attulerat Augustinus, prædicando Evangelio non sufficerent, Britanni verò operam iuam plane destituerunt, significat Gregorio per literas Augustinus, macssem quidem multam esse, operarios verò paucos. Mittuntur ergo a Gregorio in supplesmentum, Mellitus Romanus Abbas, Iustus, Paulinus, Rufinianus, aliíque complures verbi Dei ministri, quorum primum fuisse Mellitum vel hinc coniicere facilis est ratio. Ad illum enim iam longius in itinere prosectum, scripsit Gregorius, vesuo nomine cum Augustino agerent, de dolis in Anglia destruendis, sanis Ethnicis in Christiana templa mutandis, altaribus constituendis, de sacrificiis vel conuiuiis in Dei laudem & honorem instituendis. Discedit ergo Roma Mellitus An. Dom. 601. Annoque post. 3. illum Episcopi titulo & honore insigniuit Augustinus, eiusque otientales Saxones Thamefi fluuio à Cantio diuisos, & orientali maricontiguos comemisit concedentes. Horum Metropolis Londinum est, ciuitas ad ripam fluminis posita, suis ipsius incolis frequens, alienigenarum etiam, eò (commercii gratia) confluentium multitudine illustris atque celebris. Quibus etsi heo tempore Seberus imperaret, sub Ethelbertō tamen (cuius etiam nepos eratex sorore Pauli) prouinciam administrauit. Suos enim fines Ethelbertus ad confinia Humbri fluminis extendebat.
units.tr: When the English had been converted to the faith of Christ, and the forty companions whom Augustine had brought with him were not enough for preaching the Gospel, and the Britons had entirely withdrawn their help, Augustine wrote to Gregory that the harvest was indeed great but the labourers few. Therefore Gregory sent, to supply the need, Mellitus the Roman Abbot, Justus, Paulinus, Rufinianus, and several other ministers of the Word of God. That Mellitus was the first of them one may easily gather from this reasoning: Gregory wrote to him when he had already set out on his journey further, asking him to act in his name with Augustine concerning the destruction of idols in England, the changing of heathen shrines into Christian churches, the setting up of altars, and the establishing of sacrifices or feasts to the praise and honour of God. So Mellitus left Rome in the year of the Lord 601, and in the following year Augustine honoured him with the title and dignity of bishop, and committed to him the East Saxons, who are separated from Kent by the River Thames and border on the eastern sea, and who agreed to this. Their metropolis is London, a city lying on the bank of the river, crowded with its own inhabitants and made famous by the multitude of foreigners who flock there for trade. Although Sebert then ruled over them, he governed the province under Ethelbert (whose nephew he was, through his sister, the sister of Paulinus). For Ethelbert extended his borders as far as the confines of the River Humber.

units.la: Eius igitur nomine, & authoritate (vt verisimilè est) vsus Mellitus, Sebertum Regem ac reliquum populum ad Christianæ religionis professionem perduxit, & salutari baptismatis unda perfudit. Hisita prospere succedentibus, Rex Ethelbertus Londini Ecclesiam Paulo fundamentis extruxit, & in ea Episcopalem sedem statuit, cui Mellitum eleCtum & Episcopum consecratum præsecit. Ab eadem etiam altera Dnus Petro ad Westmonasterium pari operis fastigio erecta est. Mellitus Episcoparus sui An. 4. Romam profectus est, cum Bonifacio Pontifice tractaturus de rebus ad Anglicanam Ecclesiam necessariis.
units.tr: By Ethelbert's name and authority, as is very likely, Mellitus brought King Saberht and the rest of the people to profess the Christian religion, and bathed them in the saving water of baptism. With these things succeeding well, King Ethelbert built a church at London in honour of Saint Paul, with foundations laid, and established in it an episcopal see, over which he set Mellitus, elected and consecrated as bishop. Another church, dedicated to Saint Peter at Westminster, was erected by the same king with equal splendour of workmanship. In the fourth year of his episcopate, Mellitus went to Rome to treat with Pope Boniface about matters necessary for the English Church.

units.la: Quo etiam tempore Bonifacius Synodum coegerat Episcoporum Italiæ in qua de moribus Monachorum & pace decerneret. Huic Synodo Mellitus interfuit, omniaque ibi sancita & decreta, sua authoritate & subscriptione confirmauit, ac in Britanniam rediens, eadem Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ obseruanda dedit. Literas etiam à Bonifacio, vtas ad Ethelbertum Regem, alteras ad Archiepiscopum Laurentium, tertias ad vniuersum populum Anglicanum attulit. His peractis Mellitus Londinum reuertitur, ibiq;, quamdiuliuit, commoratus Episcopali munere fungitur. An. 6. postquam is reuersisset ad Romã, moritur Ethelbertus Rex Cantiorum eodemque anno Sebertus nepos, qui post se tres reliquit filios, Serredum, Sisuardum, & Sigebertum, In quibus nihil sancti, nullus Dei metus, nulla religio erat. Abhostrebant inprimis à nomine Christiano, & veræ religionis præcipua mysteria irridere soliti sunt. Celebrante enim aliquando Pontifice missarū solemnia, illi de industria adesse volucrunt, cumque eò peruenitisset, vt Eucharistiā populo de more Pōnifex porrigeret, sibi etiā inter cæteros dari postularūt. Cur nō, inquiunt, panē illū nigidū nobis etiā porrigis quē patri nostro Sabæ (sic. n. eū appellabat) dare solebat, & adhuc populo darenō desstis? Respòdit Mellit, si vultis ablui soteillo salutari quēadmodū pater vester, porestis etiā panis sacti pricipes esse: alioqnec sibi dare, nec illis accipere fas esse. Qua Episcopi responsione, grauiter ad iram commoti sunt, parumque abfuit, quin illi sibidem manus nefarie iniicerent; regni vero finibus illico exire manda runt. Expulsus ad hunc modum Londino Mellitus Cantuariam ad Laurentium Archiepiscopum se se contulit, qui conditione fuit omnino non meliore. Ex morte enim Ethel berti, cui successerat Edbaldus; Cantii etiam res Christianæ eo ipso tempore cuerse & profligatæ sunt. Aliquandiu igitur boni Antistites, quemadmodu labenti Ecclesiæ subleuarent deliberantes, cum eidem nulla ratione opitulari se posse cernerent, cedere tandem impietati tyrannorum potius statuerunt, quam sese certo & imminenti periculo, nullo cum commodo religionis obiicere. Profugit ergo confestim Mellitus cum iusto Roffensi Episcopo in Galliam: nec ita multo post ingruescente Edbaldi crudelitate, i dem Laurentio faciendum etat. Quemadmodum autem Laurentius consilium prose ctionis mutarit, Edbaldumque Regem ad fidem conuerterit, superius in ipsius vita vide reest. Conuerso Edbaldo domum Mellitus a Laurentio reuocatus est. Cum autem a Londinensibus Christi religionem plane repellentibus non reciperetur, in Cantio per manere eogitur. Eodem ipso anno, quo reuersus est ab exilio Mellitus, mortuur Laren tiusque iusque loco Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis surrogatus est, Quo Archiepiscopaleni dignitatem administrante, iustus Roffensem regebat. Ille duo pariter & solicitudine Episcopali munere fungeretur, exhortatorias & congratulatorias literas a Bonifacio ac ceperunt, qui post Deusdedit Ecclesiæ Rom. præsul An. Dom. 614. Erat Mellitus no bilium ortus familia, mentis vero celsitudine quam natiuitate illustrior, terrena omnia de spexisse dicitur, spirasse cœlestia: Et quanquam corpore infirmus & valetudinarius iam diu fuerat, animo tamen fortitudine strenuo. Podagra vitam finiuit & in portion Petri cum Augusti. & Laurentio sepultus est. Circiter hoc tempus Mahometes pseudopropheta Epilepsia seu comitiali morbo laborans, quoties vi morbi in terram cadere cogebatur, Gabrielem Angelum sibi comparuisse & collocutum esse simulauit; eiusque splendorem cum ferre non posset, consternatus concidisse. Tandem vero, cum eo to lum omnibus absentibus morbus opprimeret, volutatus vt lutulentius sus, & ex ore ipsi tuam turpiter euomeris a poris merito dilatiarus est.
units.tr: At that time Boniface had also convened a synod of the bishops of Italy, in which he was to decree concerning the morals of monks and concerning peace. Mellitus was present at this synod, and with his authority and signature confirmed everything that was there sanctioned and decreed. Returning to Britain, he handed these same decrees to the English Church to be observed. He also brought letters from Boniface: one to King Ethelbert, another to Archbishop Laurence, and a third to the whole English people. This done, Mellitus returned to London, and remaining there for as long as he lived, he discharged the episcopal office. In the sixth year after Mellitus had returned to Rome, King Ethelbert of Kent died, and in the same year Saberht his nephew died too, leaving three sons, Saered, Sigheard and Sigebert. In these there was nothing holy, no fear of God, no religion. They shrank above all from the Christian name, and were accustomed to mock the chief mysteries of the true religion. Once, when the bishop was celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass, they came there on purpose. When the bishop, as was his custom, was offering the Eucharist to the people, they demanded that it be given to them too among the rest. "Why," they said, "do you not also give us that black bread which you used to give our father Saba (for so he called him), and still give to the people?" Mellitus replied: "If you wish to be washed in the saving font as your father was, you may also be partakers of the holy bread; otherwise it is not lawful for me to give it to you, nor for you to receive it." At this answer of the bishop they were gravely angered, and it wanted little that they would impiously lay hands on him. Instead they ordered him to leave the borders of the kingdom at once. Thus driven out of London, Mellitus betook himself to Canterbury, to Archbishop Laurence, who was in no better condition. For after the death of Ethelbert, whom Eadbald succeeded, the Christian cause in Kent too was then overturned and ruined. For a while the good bishops deliberated how they might relieve the falling Church; but when they saw that they could in no way help it, they decided at last to yield to the impiety of tyrants rather than expose themselves to certain and imminent danger with no advantage to religion. Mellitus therefore fled at once to Gaul with Justus, bishop of Rochester. Not long after, as the cruelty of Eadbald grew, the same was to be done by Laurence. But how Laurence changed his plan of departure and converted King Eadbald to the faith is seen above in his life. With Eadbald converted, Mellitus was recalled home by Laurence. But since he was not received by the Londoners, who utterly rejected the Christian religion, he was forced to remain in Kent. In the same year in which Mellitus returned from exile, Laurence died, and Mellitus was made Archbishop of Canterbury in his place. While he administered the archiepiscopal dignity, Justus governed Rochester. When both of them performed the episcopal office with care, they received letters of exhortation and congratulation from Boniface, who, after Deusdedit, was bishop of Rome in the year of the Lord 614. Mellitus was born of a noble family, and was more illustrious in greatness of mind than in birth. He is said to have looked down on all earthly things and to have breathed after heavenly ones. Although he had long been weak in body and ailing, he was vigorous in strength of spirit. He ended his life by gout, and was buried in the portico of Saint Peter's with Augustine and Laurence. About this time the false prophet Mahomet, suffering from epilepsy or the falling sickness, whenever the force of the disease compelled him to fall to the ground, pretended that the angel Gabriel had appeared to him and talked with him; and since he could not bear the brightness of the angel, he fell down dismayed. At last, when the disease overcame him while all were absent, he rolled about like a filthy pig, and foaming shamefully from his mouth, he was deservedly struck down.

units.la: IIII. Iustus.
units.tr: IIII. Justus.

units.la: VSTVS Mellito & Paulino Romæ proficiscentibus socius a Grego rio Pontifice datus, Roffensi Episcopatui, quo tepore Mellitus Lon dinensi, ab Augustino adhuc viuente, præpositus est. Is parem cum Mellito fortunæ sleam subiuit (exulauit enim cum eo An. Dom. 618. vt superiu annorarum est) excepto quod cum Mellitus a Londi nensibus pulsus reditum non admitteretur, iustus sedi suæ coniunctu restitutus est, cuitamdiu præfuit, quam Mellitus vixit. Eo mortuo ad Dorobernensem Archiepiscopatum translatus est. Primo Pontificatus sui anno, a Bo nifacio 5. Rom. Pontifice, pallium cum literis de more accepit. In illis Bonifacius, quilam pridem a Phocæ obtinuerat, vt Romana Ecclesia esset omnium Ecclesiarum caput, subiectionem & obedientiam Ecclesiæ Rom. a Mellito postulauit. Adhortatur etiam, vt Ep̄iscoporū in commodioribus Angliæ parrebus ordinaret: Is igitur Paulinum consocium suum, virum sanctum & prudentem, Archiepiscopum Eboracensem hac occasione crea uit, An. Dom. 625. Erat Edbaldo Cantiorum Regi innupta soror Ethelberga. Huius consortium Ed winus Northumbriæ Rex vt adhuc a fide alienus expetiit, ac per legatos illam sibi da ri postulauit. Respondit est, nisi esse fas Christianam virginem homini Ethnico & Pagano locari, nec fore fides & sacramentorum cœlesti Regi prius præstitum, terreni Regis suadente iusto & Paulino, quibus spes erat; hæc occasione Christi religionem a Nor thumbris ahiplexaram iri. Commodum enim rati sunt Edbaldus & iustus, vt Paulinus virginis comitatu adhiberetur, tum ad fouendam religionem in suis; si forte Pagani ad gentilismum se adderent, tum etiam ad ipsos Paganos ad Christi religionem conuertendos, sicd commode fieri posse videret. In quo utroque ita se gessit, & profecit Paulinus, ut & suos à Paganismo prudenter converteret, & Paganos ad Christianismum hortando conuerteret. Edwino & Northumbris hoc modo conuersis, Paulinus ante à iustito in Cantio ereatus Eboracensis Archiepiscopus primus admissus est. Iustus postquam religionem Christianam diu multumque promouisset, defunctus in humanis esse 4. Idus Nouembris. An. Dom. 634. Sepultus est in Ecclesia Sanctorum Apostolorum Cantuariæ. Quo tempore diem etiam obiisse Edbaldus dicitur.
units.tr: Justus, given by Pope Gregory as a companion to Mellitus and Paulinus when they set out from Rome, was placed over the bishopric of Rochester, at the time when Mellitus was set over London while Augustine was still alive. He shared Mellitus's fortune (for he was exiled with him in the year of the Lord 618, as noted above), except that when Mellitus was driven out by the Londoners and not allowed to return, Justus was restored to his own see, which he governed for as long as Mellitus lived. On Mellitus's death he was translated to the archbishopric of Canterbury. In the first year of his pontificate he received the pallium with letters, as was customary, from Boniface V, Pope of Rome. In those letters Boniface, who had long before obtained from Phocas that the Roman Church should be the head of all churches, demanded submission and obedience to the Roman Church from Justus. He also urged him to ordain bishops in the more convenient parts of England. Accordingly, on this occasion Justus made his companion Paulinus, a holy and prudent man, archbishop of York, in the year of the Lord 625. Edbald, king of Kent, had an unmarried sister, Ethelberga. Edwin, king of Northumbria, still a stranger to the faith, sought her in marriage and asked through envoys that she be given to him. It was answered that it was not lawful to join a Christian virgin to a heathen and pagan man, and that this could not happen unless the faith and sacraments were first rendered to the heavenly King, the earthly king being persuaded by Justus and Paulinus, in whom hope lay; and that by this occasion the Northumbrians would embrace the religion of Christ. For Edbald and Justus thought it advantageous that Paulinus should attend the virgin, both to foster religion among her people, should the pagans perhaps relapse into heathenism, and also to convert the pagans themselves to the religion of Christ, as he saw could conveniently be done. In both respects Paulinus conducted himself and made progress, so that he prudently turned his own people away from paganism and, by exhortation, converted the pagans to Christianity. Edwin and the Northumbrians having been converted in this way, Paulinus, who had earlier been created archbishop of York by Justus in Kent, was the first to be admitted. Justus, after promoting the Christian religion long and greatly, departed this life on the fourth day before the Ides of November in the year of the Lord 634. He was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles at Canterbury. At about the same time Edbald is said to have died as well.

units.la: V. HONORIVS.
units.tr: V. HONORIVS.

units.la: VSTO defuncto Honorius patria Romanus, venerandus pater, & in sacris literis non vulgariter eruditus, quippe qui Gregorii magni fuerat discipulus, Romæ in Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem electus est, & a Paulino Eboracensi Archiepiscopo Lindocolniæ consecratus. Hic quintus erat ab Augustino Dorobernensis Ecclesiæ antistes, ab Honorio Romano Pontifice eius nominis primo, pallium cum literis accepit, in quibus concessit Rom. Pontifex, vt moriente alterutro Cantuariensi seu Eboracensi Archiepiscopo, is qui superuiueret, potestatem haberet alterius sedis Archiepiscopum ordinandi, vt deinceps non sit necesse petere graviora itinera Romam contendendo fatigari. Honorius accepto pallio ecreauit Episcopum Fœlicem Burgundum virum Apostolicum, eumque ad orientales Anglos misit, qui sedem habuit Episcopalem in ciuitate Dunmock, alias Dunwich. primus fundauit An. Dom. 636. quanquam alii Regem Sigisbertum Fœlicis Burgundi consilio eam instituisse scribunt. Fœlice mortuo Thomam Diaconum eius in iltius locum opportune substituit: strenuus ac peruigil diuinæ militiæ dux & Imperator, aliis in acie diuina cadentibus alios surrogare sedulo adnittitur, ne deficiente forte milite, hostis locus in castra Dominica pateret irruendi. Neque solum Episcopos tanquam superiores turrium custodes Ecclesiæ superimposituit, sed etiam prouidiam suam primus in parochias diuidens, inferiores ministros ordinauit, quos etiam sacerdotes instruit & adhortatur, vt plebem Dei comiter & paenitenter non doctrina solum, sed etiam vitæ probitate erudirent: his enim intedeulos & à fide alienos citius capi, quam seueris obiurgationibus & austeritate morum. Huius etiam tempore turbatæ erant res Northumbrorum: interficitur enim Edwinus Rex quem Paulinus baptizarat, ipsèque Paulinus fugere coactus, in Cantium regreditur, vbi ab Honorio Episcopatu Rofensi donatus est. Ethelbergam Edwini defuncti Regis Northumbrorum uxorem, & Edwaldi Regis Cantiorum sororem virginem velauit: quæ ad villam Limming sibi a fratre data, Monasterium condidit. Honorius postquam vitæ suæ cursum implerat, ex hac vita migrauit, & in porticu cum superioribus sepelitur.
