units.tr: Uzo, when Honorius was dead, a Roman by birth, a venerable father, and not commonly learned in the sacred letters, having been a pupil of Gregory the Great, was elected Archbishop of Canterbury at Rome, and was consecrated at Lincoln by Paulinus, Archbishop of York. He was the fifth from Augustine to hold the chair of the Canterbury Church. From Honorius, the first of that name, Roman Pontiff, he received the pallium with a letter, in which the Roman Pontiff granted that, when either the Archbishop of Canterbury or the Archbishop of York died, the survivor should have the power of ordaining the archbishop of the other see, so that from then on it would not be necessary to travel the long journey to Rome and be worn out by the toil. Having received the pallium, Honorius consecrated Felix the Burgundian, an apostolic man, and sent him to the East Angles, who founded a episcopal see in the town of Dunmock, otherwise Dunwich, in the year of the Lord 636, although others write that King Sigebert instituted it on the counsel of Felix the Burgundian. When Felix died, Honorius opportunely substituted Thomas, his deacon, in his place: a vigorous and watchful leader and commander of the divine army, who, when others fell in the divine battle line, zealously strove to put others in their place, lest, if a soldier should perhaps be lacking, a place should be open for the enemy to rush into the Lord's camp. Nor did he only set bishops over the Church as superior watchmen of the towers, but also, being the first to divide his care into parishes, he ordained lesser ministers, whom he also instructed and exhorted, as priests, to teach the people of God courteously and patiently, not only by doctrine but also by integrity of life; for by these means those who were wandering and alien to the faith were more quickly taken than by severe rebukes and austerity of manners. In his time also the affairs of the Northumbrians were troubled: for King Edwin, whom Paulinus had baptized, was killed, and Paulinus himself, forced to flee, returned to Kent, where he was given the bishopric of Rochester by Honorius. Honorius veiled Ethelburga, the wife of the dead King Edwin of the Northumbrians and sister of Eadbald, King of the Kentish men, while still a virgin; she, having been given to her by her brother at the estate of Lyminge, founded a monastery there. Honorius, having completed the course of his life, departed from this life and was buried in the porch with his predecessors.

units.la: VI. DEVSDEDIT, SIVE, ADEODATVS.
units.tr: VI. DEUSDEDIT, OR ADEODATUS.

units.la: OST Honorium electus est (fede prius vacante per annum & 6. menses) Archiepiscopus Dorobernensis, de gente occidentalium Saxonum oriundus, Deusdedit, qui vita & eruditione insignis, primus ex Anglis Archiepiscopus à Deo datus est. Patria enim lingua Frith'ona vocabatur. Sed ob merita eius in Remp. præclara, nomé Saxonicum abeleetus Dei ministris, in Angelicum fuit commutatum, & Deusdedit dictus est: gratia namq; Dei, illum ad opus Sancti ministerii elegit, sumpto sacerdotali officio in timore Dei perseuerauit permansit. Hic ab Ithamaro antistite Roffensi consecratus est: quia post Paulinum nullus adhuc erat Archiepiscopus Eboracensis, ad quem id muneris ex reiscripto Pontificali pertinebat. Obiit Deusdedit Ecclesiæ Dorobernensis Archiepiscopus pridie Idus Iulii An. Dom. 664. vltimusque in aquilonari portico Ecclesiæ Apostolorum Petri & Pauli secundus est. Hoc tempore tradiitur Benalt Episcopus, Abbate Sancti Augustini, coeruum & instructore Bedæ, artem consiciendi vitrii in Anglia adinuenisse, & occultiorum artium libros induxisse. Monasterium suum Adriano, q ex Roma est Theodoro (qui proximus Deusdedit subsecutus est) in Angliam aduenit, religiouit. Tã graui morbo hoc tempore laborasse Anglos comemorat lib. Roff. vt se populus ad præcepta maris frequenter conferret, vt inde se in mare præcipites darent celeri enim morte à cruciatu liberari potius eligebant, quam diutius intabescendo miserè perire. De hac pestilentia sic scribit Bedæ: An. Dominicæ incarnationis 664. facta estccest eclipsis Solis die tertio mensis Maii, horam circiter decimam diei, quod etiam anno mox subita pestilentia lues subsequuta est, quæ depopulatis prius australibus Britanniæ plagis, Northumbrorum quoque provinciam corripiens, & acerba clade diutius longe lateque desæviens, magnam hominum multitudinem stravit. Hac peste sacerdos Iuba Episcopus Northumbrorum interiit. Hyberniam quoque eadem clade peruasit. » Nam cum tempore Synodi & Colmanni Episcoporum ex Anglis multi tum nobiles, tum plebeii ... (text partly illegible in scan)
units.tr: After Honorius, Deusdedit was elected Archbishop of Canterbury (the see having been vacant for a year and six months). He was of the West Saxon people, and was distinguished for his life and learning. He was the first Archbishop of Canterbury given by God from among the English. His native name was Frithona, but on account of his outstanding services to the commonwealth, his Saxon name was changed by the ministers of God into an English one, and he was called Deusdedit (given by God), for the grace of God chose him for the work of the holy ministry. Having taken up the priestly office, he persevered and continued in the fear of God. He was consecrated by Ithamar, bishop of Rochester, because after Paulinus there was as yet no Archbishop of York, to whom this office belonged according to the Pontifical. Deusdedit, Archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, died on the day before the Ides of July, in the year of the Lord 664, and was the last buried in the north porch of the Church of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the second to be so buried. At this time it is handed down that Bennet, bishop, abbot of St Augustine's, the companion and teacher of Bede, introduced the art of making glass into England, and brought in books of the more secret arts. He founded his monastery in the time of Adrian, who came from Rome into England, and of Theodore, who succeeded Deusdedit. The Book of Rochester records that the English were at this time afflicted by so grievous a disease that the people frequently went to the sea's edge, and threw themselves headlong into the sea, for they preferred to be freed from their torment by a swift death rather than to perish wretchedly by wasting away over a long time. Bede writes thus about this pestilence: In the year of the Lord's incarnation 664, there was an eclipse of the sun on the third day of May, at about the tenth hour of the day. In the same year a sudden plague followed, which first laid waste the southern parts of Britain, then seized the province of Northumbria, and raging widely and for long with bitter slaughter, cut down a great multitude of people. By this plague Jaruman (Iuba), bishop of the Northumbrians, perished. The same calamity also overran Ireland. For at the time of the Synod and of Colman, bishops, many of the English, both noble and common, ...(text partly illegible in scan)

units.la: VII. THEODORUS.
units.tr: VII. THEODORUS.

units.la: Post quam Deusdedit mortuus est, vacante non modico tempore Ecclesia Dorobernensi, missus est Romam a Regibus Egberto Cantiorum & Oswio Northumbrorum, Wigardus presbyter, vir doctissimus natione Anglus, qui in Archiepiscopum Cant. ordinaretur. Cuncta Oswius Northumbrorum Rex, munera ad Romanum Pontificem, valaurea atque argentea tradidit. Wigardo Romam adveniente, pestilentia ibi grauiter sævienti, quo quidem ipse, pitiusque ... (text partly illegible in scan)
units.tr: After Deusdedit died, and the Church of Canterbury had been vacant for no small time, Wigard, a presbyter, a most learned man and an Englishman by birth, was sent to Rome by the kings Egbert of Kent and Oswy of Northumbria, to be ordained Archbishop of Canterbury. Oswy, king of Northumbria, gave gifts of gold and silver to the Roman Pontiff. When Wigard arrived in Rome, where a plague was raging severely, he himself ... (text partly illegible in scan)

units.la: Hinc ab Adriano Pontifice, quem tamen non alium lege adhuc Vitalianus, quam ... Theodorus, cum Græcus esset, moribus & ritibus Romanis conformatum ut Ecclesiam Anglicanam introduceret.
units.tr: Hence, from Pope Adrian, whom Vitalian had not yet ... (other persons were not to be chosen), Theodore, although he was a Greek, was conformed to Roman customs and rites, so that he might introduce the English Church.

units.la: Bed. Lib. 4. cap. 1. Anno 668. Cap. 2.
units.tr: Bede, Book 4, chapter 1. In the year 668, chapter 2.

units.la: Episcopos enim aliquos, diuerso a Romanis more confecrarros ea sola de causa pro arbitrio suo, vel dignitate plane moutt, vel Canonice coegit ordinari, lusetiam & superioritatem sedis propriæ ita exercuisse dicitur, vt non tam iudicio & consilio regeret, quam impetu animi & perturbatione rupi videretur. Reliquis igitur huius viri virtutes, quæ sane vulgares non fuerunt, hæc minima suæ dignitatis asserenda pertinacitas non medioctitas obcurauit. Quanquam enim post Britanniam ab Angis occupatam feli- ciora tempora & ecclesiastica non fuerunt, quam cum ille Cantuariæ præsidebat: multum tamen detraxit eius gloriæ, inimicia Episcoporum delectio, ac præcipuæ quidem Wil- fridi Eboracensis Archiepiscopi, quem ille indignè sua sede pepulit, virum sibi & vitæ sanctitate & erudizione & industria, si non superiorem, at certè omnium iudicio parem. Cuius etiam illius temporis eruditi, qui multi erant, quantum Theodoro & debebant & deferebant. Nam eum non minorem scripturarum scientia, quam Theodorus prædicus esset, quam in literis humanioribus multum excelluit, Poetica, Arithmetica, Astronomia, Musica, Latina quoq; & Græca lingua, quas sane discipinas auditoribus suis, quos moli- tos habuit, vnà cum ecclesiasticarum lectione copiose contradixit. Hunc igitur tantum vi- rum, quem ita immodere & præter meritum persecuendo, & multum nocuit Ecclesiæ pa- rentali, ecclesiastico non fuerint. Hac de re ita scribit Will. Malmesburiensis Lib. de Pontificibus Theodorum enim sedem Apostolicam misisse Beda narrat, omnium antiquitum Cantuariæ, vigorem Pontificalem in tota Britannia exercuisse. Denique & vitra & citra Humbrum Episcopos hos pro placito abegisse, hos potuisse. In ipsa Eboraco, aliarum vibium Præsules consecratos, & (vt in vita beati Wilfridi legitur) eiusdem ciuitatis Pontifices Ceddam & ipsum Wilfridum, sed ratione, sed vi repulisse, vbi videri & doleri potest humanam miseriam, quod videlicet, quantalibet quis sanctitate polleat, non ad ple- nam perfectionem morte cum ad suum tuo oculi Britanniæ conroversias inter se ege- rint. Siquidem Theodorus Wilfridum iniusté, quantum nostra habet coniectura, eloquent. Wilfridus Romano Papæ Agathoni (multis ante periculis tactatus) querelam deduxit: modestè fame, vt quinque Apostolicæ sedem directis accusationibus vrge- ret, nec innocentiam suam ducere permitteret. Eius enim verba hæc sunt in fugge- ttione quam obrutit Papæ. Quid autem accideritt, vt Theodorus sincere iudicis Ar- chiepiscopus (me superstitiosus in sede, quam fuerit indignus) disposuit ab aliquo consensu Episcopi, tres sua authoritate (mea humilitate non atque sensu) ordinaret Epi- scopos: vt omittere quam vigere pro illo viri reverendi conducerunt, quem quidem, eo quod ab hac Apostolica sedis summa est directus, accusate non audeo. Iraquo quamlibet nec iudicio cohibiri Rom. vidimus, quod Wilfridus iudicatus & ad sedem suam remissus fuerit, non tamen sem obtinuit, Regis Egfridi violentia, cum præsertim Theodorus vel obsisterret ex sententia, vel permitteret ex conuenientia. Idem est am ab hoc Theodoro Hibernia Wilfridum iniuriam, vt dignus est acerbe verbis exagitat. Necesari(inquit) potuit manifestissima Theodori iniuria. Cum enim Wilfridus protribunali Regem adhibere, iniuriarum causam exponendas: Nihil(dixit Theodorus) rearasi bi opponimus. Sed quod constituimus, rarum esse volumus. Quo dicto quid ab sint, quasi dicerem. Sic volo, sic iubeo, stat pro ratione, voluntas.
units.tr: For he is said to have compelled some bishops, consecrated in a manner different from the Romans, for that reason alone, to be ordained again, at his own discretion, plainly by dignity or canonically; and he is also said to have exercised the authority of his see in such a way that he seemed to govern not so much by judgement and counsel as by the violence and disturbance of his temper. Therefore the rest of this man's virtues, which were certainly not ordinary, were obscured by this least creditable stubbornness in asserting his dignity. For although after the occupation of Britain by the Angles there were no happier times, either for the Church, than when he presided at Canterbury, yet the hatred of bishops, and above all of Wilfrid, Archbishop of York, whom he unworthily drove from his see, greatly detracted from his glory. Wilfrid was a man equal, if not superior, to him in holiness of life, learning and diligence, and at least, by the judgement of all, his equal. How much the learned men of that time, who were many, owed to Theodore and deferred to him, ... Wilfrid, excelling in humane letters, poetry, arithmetic, astronomy, music, and both Latin and Greek, taught these disciplines copiously to his many pupils, together with the reading of the Church. Therefore it was not to the Church's advantage that so great a man should be persecuted so immoderately and beyond his deserts. William of Malmesbury writes thus about this matter in his book On the Pontiffs: Bede relates that Theodore, sent by the Apostolic See, exercised pontifical authority throughout the whole of Britain, in the most ancient church of Canterbury. He also expelled bishops at his pleasure, on both sides of the Humber, and appointed others. In York itself, he consecrated the presidents of other cities, and (as is read in the life of blessed Wilfrid) drove out of the same city Cedd and Wilfrid himself, not by reason but by force. Here one may see and lament human wretchedness: however much a man may excel in holiness, he does not attain full perfection, since the Britons and the English waged controversies among themselves. For Theodore, as far as our conjecture goes, unjustly accused Wilfrid. Wilfrid brought his complaint (having been harassed by many dangers before) to Agatho, the Roman Pope, and, in a modest manner, so that he might urge the Apostolic See with five direct accusations, and not allow his innocence to be dishonoured. For his words are these, in the letter which he gave to the Pope: "But as to what happened, that Theodore, the sincere judge and archbishop (I, though unworthy of the see, am superstitious), by the consent of some bishop, ordained three bishops by his own authority, (not by my humility and not with my agreement), so that it might be better to omit than to speak of that reverend man, whom, because he was sent by this summit of the Apostolic See, I do not dare to accuse." Thus, although we have seen that Wilfrid was judged and sent back to his see, he nevertheless did not keep it, by the violence of King Ecgfrith, since Theodore either opposed him by his judgement or allowed it by agreement. Likewise Hibernia (Ireland) harshly censures the manifest injury done by this Theodore to Wilfrid, as he deserves. "A most manifest injury of Theodore's," it says, "could not have been avoided. For when Wilfrid, at the tribunal, called upon the king to explain the cause of the injuries, Theodore said: 'We oppose nothing to your reasons, but what we have decided, we wish to be rightly decided.'" By this saying, what more did he say than if he had said: "Thus I wish, thus I command; for reason, let the will stand."

units.la: Anno Domini 678. hæc inter Theodorum & Wilfridum orta dissensio est: quo etiam tempore Cometam per tres integros menses apparuisse Beda narrat: Matutinis horis oriebatur, excelsam radiantis flammæ quasi columnam præ- se ferens. Ac hæc quidem ita se habent. Quo enim anno Wilfridus Romam Britanniam rediit, & provincia sua per Theodori inimicitias prohiberetur, (quanquam fidele Euangelium promulgarit) ingens mortalitas multas Britanniæ provincias corripuit. In provincia etiam occidentali Saxonum per 3 integros annos non pluit. Vnde populus præterquam quod morbo, etiam fame præter modum afflictus est. Idem etiam Beda narrat: sæpe 40. homines, sæpe plures fa- mis acerbitate non ferentes, ad matris ripas se contulisse, seseque inde iunctis manibus fluctibus absorbendos miseré præcipitasse. Duas suo tempore Synodos Theodorus conuocasse dicitur. Primam Hæresiorum in qua decreta decem sancta sunt. Capita huius Synodi habebis apud Bedam. Cum hæc Synodus celebraretur, moritur Egbertus Rex Cantuariorum, mense Iulio, cui successit Lotharius frater eius. Secundam Synodi conuocauit apud Clyff.inxta Roffam.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 678 this dispute arose between Theodore and Wilfrid. At this time, too, Bede relates, a comet appeared for three whole months; it rose in the early morning, bearing a lofty column, as it were, of shining flame. These things stand thus. In the year that Wilfrid returned from Rome to Britain, and his province was hindered by the enmities of Theodore (although he had preached the faithful Gospel), a great mortality struck many provinces of Britain. In the western province of the Saxons it did not rain for three whole years. Hence the people were afflicted beyond measure not only by disease but also by famine. The same Bede relates: often forty people, often more, unable to bear the bitterness of hunger, betook themselves to the banks of the river, and, joining hands, miserably threw themselves to be swallowed by the waves. Theodore is said to have summoned two synods in his time. The first was a synod against heresies, in which ten holy decrees were issued. You will find the chapters of this synod in Bede. While this synod was being held, Egbert, king of the Kentish men, died in July, and was succeeded by his brother Lothair. The second synod he called at Clofesho, near Rochester.

units.la: Atqui cum audiret fide Ecclesiæ Constantinopolitanæ hæresi Eutychiana plurimum esse tor- batam, est eclipsis Solis die tertio mensis Maii ; horam circiter decimam diei, quo etiam anno mox subita pestilentiæ lues subsequuta est, quæ depopulatis prius australibus Britanniæ plagis, Northumbrorum quoque prouinciam corripiens & acerba clade diutius longè lateque desæuiens, magnam hominum multitudinem strauit. Hac peste sacerdos Iuba Episcopus Northumbrorum interiit. Hyberthiam Insulam quoq; eadem clades peruasit. Nam cum tempore Sinani & Colmanni Episcoporum ex Anglis multi tum nobiles, tum plebii nõ diuinæ lectionis & conuenientioris vitæ gratia recesserant, Monasticam vitam professi, ibi & posteris suis Monasterium, quod Rathmelsigi dicitur, comparauerant: hos omnes aut peste absumptos esse, aut per ignota loca dispersos Beda ibidem refert.
units.tr: But when he heard that the faith of the Church of Constantinople was greatly troubled by the Eutychian heresy, there was an eclipse of the sun on the third day of May, about the tenth hour of the day. In the same year a sudden outbreak of plague followed. It first laid waste the southern parts of Britain, then seized the province of the Northumbrians and raged for a long time, far and wide, with bitter slaughter, and it struck down a great multitude of people. Iuba, a priest and bishop of the Northumbrians, died in this plague. The same calamity also struck the island of Ireland. For in the time of the bishops Sinanus and Colmanus, many English, both nobles and commoners, had left their homes for the sake of divine reading and a more fitting way of life. They had professed the monastic life, and there they had established for themselves and their descendants a monastery called Rathmelsigi. Bede reports in the same place that all of these either were carried off by the plague or were scattered into unknown regions.

units.la: VII. THEODORVS.
units.tr: VII. THEODORE.

units.la: Postquam Deusdedit mortuus est, vacante non modico tempore Ecclesia Doroberneñ, missus est Romam à Regibus Egberto Cantiorum, & Oswio Northumbrorum, Wigardus presbyter, vir doctissimus, natione Anglus, qui in Archiepiscopum Cant. ordinaretur. Cui etiam Oswius Northumbrorum Rex, munerad Romanum Pontificem, vasa aurea atque argentea tradidit. Wigardo Romam aduenienti, pestilis illic grauiter sæuiebat, qua quidem ipse, priusquam Episcopus crearetur, cum omnibus prope comitatu interiit. De Wigardi morte Vitalianus Papa Oswium Regem Northumbrorum certiorem facit: ipse interim eum suis Romæ deliberans, quem in Angliam loco defuncti idoneum Archiepiscopum mitteret. Erat hoc tempore in Monasterio Viridano, quod est non longe à Neapoli Campaniæ, Abbas Adrianus, natione Afer, vir in sacris literis & omni disciplinarum genere peritissimus. Hunc ad se vocatum Papa Vitalianus Archiepiscopum Cant. creasse voluit. Is W. Malmesb. sese tanto oneri sustinendo imparem professus, honorem humiliter recusauit. Cum verò excusationem Pontifex non admitteret, inuenturum se esse pollicitus est hominem magis idoneum, qui ipsum & ætate & eruditione præcellerent: hac conditione dimissus est. Familiaris fuit Adriano Theodorus Monachus, natus Tharsi, ibidem disciplinis instructus, quibus antea diximus Adrianum, vir ætate etiam venerandus, annum enim egit 66.
units.tr: After Deusdedit died, the Church of Canterbury stood vacant for no small time. Then Wigard, a presbyter, a most learned man and an Englishman by birth, was sent to Rome by the kings Egbert of Kent and Oswy of Northumbria, to be ordained Archbishop of Canterbury. King Oswy of Northumbria also gave him gold and silver vessels as a gift for the Roman Pontiff. When Wigard arrived in Rome, a plague was raging there severely, and before he could be made bishop, he died there, almost all his retinue with him. Pope Vitalian informed King Oswy of Northumbria of Wigard's death, and meanwhile he himself considered at Rome whom to send to England as a suitable archbishop in the dead man's place. At this time there was at the monastery of Viridanum, not far from Naples in Campania, an abbot named Hadrian, an African by birth, a man most skilled in Holy Letters and in every kind of learning. Pope Vitalian summoned him and wished to make him Archbishop of Canterbury. Hadrian, (marginal: William of Malmesbury) professing himself unequal to so great a burden, humbly refused the honour. But when the Pontiff would not accept his excuse, Vitalian promised that he would find a man better suited, who would surpass him both in age and in learning; on this condition Hadrian was dismissed. Theodore, a monk born at Tarsus, who had been instructed in the same disciplines we have mentioned earlier in Hadrian's case, was a close friend of Hadrian; he was also a man venerable for his age, for he was sixty-six years old.

units.la: hic ab Adriano sistitur Pontifici, quem tamen non alia lege admisit Vitalianus, quàm si Ex Archiuo. ipse Adrianus cum eo vna in Angliam proficisceretur, ac diligenter prospiceret, ne quid Theodorus, cum Græcus esset, moribus & ritibus Romanis contrarium in Ecclesiam Anglicanam introduceret. Cum in hoc Pontifici consensisset Adrianus, Theodorus Cogita. Subdiaconus factus est, ac quia tonsuram Apostoli Pauli more orientalium habuerat; quapropter ... Romæ commoratus est, donec illi coma crescerat, quò in coronam Romano more tadi posset. Deinde Archiepiscopus ordinatus, & à Vitaliano Papa Rothæ consecratus est, anno salutis humanæ 668. primo Aprilis; qui fuit dies Dominicus. Eodem W. Malmesb. ritio, 6. Kal. Iunii, vnà cum Adriano in Angliam iter occupat, cum magna authoritate Ex Archiuo. ligandi & soluendi. Hi expeditum iter in Angliam non habuerunt, imminens enim hyemis eos aliquandiu Massiliæ detinuit. Postea cum in Galliam peruenissent, eos Ebronius, vir in maxima authoritate & gratia cum Rege Galliæ remotatus est. Tandem vero Theodorus dimittitur, & ad portum Conuentuunis perductus est, Vnde etiam afflictus impeditus valetudine non ita pridem fuit.
units.tr: This man was presented to the Pontiff by Hadrian, yet Vitalian admitted him only on the condition that Hadrian himself should go with him into England and carefully see to it that Theodore, since he was a Greek, should not introduce into the English Church anything contrary to Roman customs and rites. Hadrian agreed to this at the Pontiff's request. (Marginal: Consider this.) Theodore was made subdeacon, and because he had worn the tonsure in the manner of the Eastern churches, in the style of the Apostle Paul, he stayed at Rome until his hair had grown back, so that he could receive the crown in the Roman manner. Then he was ordained archbishop and consecrated at Rome by Pope Vitalian, in the year of human salvation 668, on the first of April, which was a Sunday. (Marginal: William of Malmesbury.) On the sixth day before the Kalends of June, Theodore set out on the journey to England together with Hadrian, with the great authority of binding and loosing. (Marginal: From the archive.) They did not have a smooth journey to England, for an approaching winter detained them for some time at Marseilles. Afterwards, when they had reached Gaul, Ebronius, a man of the greatest authority and favour with the King of the Franks, kept them there. At last Theodore was let go and brought to the port of Conuentuunis, from which he was afterwards troubled and hindered by ill health for some time.

units.la: Adrianus autem ab Ebronio retinetur: suspectus enim illi erat, de mandatis ab Imperatore ad Reges Angliæ perferendis contra regnum Gallicanum: Illetamen non multò post, cum se Ebronio purgauisset, Theodorum in Britanniam subsequitur, qui eum Cænobio B. Petri Apostoli Cantuariæ, vbi Archiepiscopi sepeliri solent, donauit. Venit Theodorus Cantuariam, An. 1. postquam consecratus est, 6. Kal. Ianuarii. Hic bibliothecam copiosam tam è Græcis quàm Latinis libris secum in Angliam adauexit, quorum nonnulli Græco idiomate conscripti apud nos manent: videlicet, Opera Homeri Græco chataderæ ita eximiè & exquisitè descripta, vt librorum impressorum veritarem superent: volumen grande est, charta etiam antiquior. Homeliæ Chrysostomi folio pargemenæ: Psalmi Dauidici: Ιώσηφ Iosephi eadem lingua conscripta: opera sane ob eximiam literarum scripturam nostro seculo rara, & quæ perpetuæ memoriæ famâ obtinere mereantur. Huic Theodoro omnis Anglicana Ecclesia (quod reliquis Episcopis non fecit) libenter sese subiecit: isque peragrata tota Insula, Paschæ celebrationem, reliquosque Romanos ritus vbique stabiliuit: tantumque abfuit, vt aliquid à Romana Ecclesia alienum faceret, vt eius authoritatem contentiose nimis putetur propugnasse.
units.tr: Hadrian, however, was detained by Ebronius, for Ebronius suspected him of carrying orders from the Emperor to the kings of England against the kingdom of the Franks. Yet not long afterwards, when he had cleared himself to Ebronius, Hadrian followed Theodore into Britain. Theodore gave him the monastery of St Peter the Apostle at Canterbury, where the archbishops are usually buried. Theodore came to Canterbury in the first year after his consecration, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January. Here he brought into England a rich library, drawn from both Greek and Latin books, some of which remain among us, written in Greek: namely, the works of Homer in Greek characters, so exquisitely and finely written that they surpass the accuracy of printed books; it is a large volume, and the paper is older still. The homilies of Chrysostom on parchment leaves; the Psalms of David; the Joseph [Ἰώσηφ] written in the same language. These works, because of the remarkable beauty of their script, are rare in our century, and deserve to hold the fame of perpetual memory. To this Theodore the whole English Church (which it did not do for the other bishops) willingly submitted itself. He travelled through the whole island and everywhere established the celebration of Easter and the other Roman rites. And he was so far from doing anything alien to the Roman Church that he is thought to have defended its authority too contentiously.

units.la: Episcopos enim aliquot, diuerso a Romanis more consecratos ea sola de causa pro arbitrio suo, vel dignitate plane movit, vel Canonice coegit ordinari. Iusticiam & superioritatem sedis propriae ita exercuisse dicitur, vt non tam iudicio & consilio regere, quam impetu animi & perturbatione rapi videretur. Reliquas igitur hulus viri virtutes, quae sane vulgares non fuerunt, haec minima fuit dignitatis asserendae pertinacitas non mediocriter obscuratur. Quanquam enim post Britanniam ab Anglis occupatam fugitioratempora & eruditiora non fuerunt, quam cum Ille Cantuariae praesidebat: multum tamen detraxit eius gloriae, immerita Episcoporum deiectio, ac praecipue quidem Wilfridi Eboracensis Archiepiscopi, quem ille indigne sua sede depulit, virum sibi & vitae sanctitate & eruditione & industria, si non superiorem, at certe omnium iudicio parem: cui etiam illius temporis eruditi, qui multi erant, quantum Theodoro & debebant & deferebant. Nam cum non minore scripturarum scientia, quam Theodorus praditus esset, tum in literis humanioribus multum excelluit, Poetica, Arithmetica, Astronomia, Musica, Latina quoque & Graeca lingua, quas sane disciplinas auditoribus suis, quos multos habuit, vna cum scripturarum lectione copiose contradidit. Hunc igitur tantum virum tam immoderate & praeter meritum persequendo, & multum nocuit Ecclesiae packi, & male consuluit famae suae. Hac de re sic scribit Will. Malmsburiensis Lib. de Pontificibus Theodorum enim a sede Apostolica missum Beda narrat, omnium antiquitum Cantuariae, vigorem Pontificalem in tota Britannia exercuisse. Denique & vltra & citra Humbrum Episcopos hos pro placito abegisse, hos posuisse. In ipsa Eboraco, aliarum vrbium Praesules consecrasse, & (vt in vita beati Wilfridi legitur) eiusdem ciuitatis Pontifices Ceddam & ipsum Wilfridum, seu ratione, seu vitio repulisse, vbi videri & doleri potest humana miseria, quod videlicet, quantalibet quis sanctitate polleat, non ad pesnum peruicaces mores exuat: quod illi duo oculi Britanniae controuersias inter se egerint. Siquidem Theodorus Wilfridum iniuste, quantum nostra habet coniectura, ejecerit: Wilfridus Romano Papae Agathoni (multis ante periculis iactatus) querelam detulit: modeste sane, vt qui neque Apostolicum sedem directis accusationibus vrgeret, nec innocentiam suam fluctuare permitteret. Eius enim verba haec sunt in suggestione quam obtulit Papae. Quid autem acciderit, vt Theodorus sanctissimus Archiepiscopus (me superstite) in sede, quam (licet indignus) dispensabam absque consensu cuiusuis Episcopi, tres suae authoritate (mea humilitate non acquiescente) ordinaret Episcopos: omittere magis quam vrgere pro eiusdem viri reuerentia conducere, quem quidem, eo quod ab hac Apostolicae sedis summitate sit directus, accusare non audeo. Itaque quamuis hinc iudicio consilii Rom. videmus, quod Wilfridus iudicatus & ad sedem suam remissus fuerit, non tamen rem obtinuit, Regis Egfridi violentia, cum praesertim Theodorus vel obsisteret ex sententia, vel permitteret ex conniuentia. Idem etiam alibi Theodorum hanc in Wilfridum iniuriam, vt dignus est acerbe verbis exagitat. Nec eclari (inquit) potuit manifestissima Theodori iniuria. Cum enim Wilfridus pro tribunali Regem adiisset, iniuriarum causam expostulans: Nihil (dixit Theodorus) reatus tibi opponimus. Sed quod constituimus, ratum esse volumus. Quo dicto quid absurdius quasi diceret. Sic volo, sic iubeo, stat pro ratione, voluntas.
units.tr: For he moved several bishops, who had been consecrated in a manner different from the Romans, purely on that ground, either deposing them at his own discretion or compelling them to be ordained canonically. He is said to have exercised the justice and superiority of his own see in such a way that he seemed to rule less by judgement and counsel than to be carried away by impulse and passion. Thus the other virtues of this man, which were certainly not ordinary, are not a little obscured by this one fault, his obstinacy in asserting his dignity, the least of his faults. For although the times after the English had occupied Britain were not more fortunate or more learned than the time when he presided at Canterbury, yet the undeserved deposition of bishops greatly diminished his glory, especially that of Wilfrid, Archbishop of York, whom he unworthily drove from his see. Wilfrid was, in holiness of life, learning and diligence, if not superior to him, at least in the judgement of all equal to him. The learned men of that time, who were many, owed and paid to Theodore as much as they could. For although Theodore was endowed with no less knowledge of the Scriptures, he also excelled greatly in the humane letters: poetry, arithmetic, astronomy, music, and the Latin and Greek tongues, which disciplines he taught copiously to his many pupils together with the reading of Scripture. By persecuting so great a man so immoderately and beyond his deserts, he greatly harmed the Church and ill served his own reputation. William of Malmesbury writes thus on this matter in his book On the Pontiffs: "For Bede relates that Theodore, sent from the Apostolic See, exercised the pontifical power of the oldest see of Canterbury throughout the whole of Britain. Finally, both beyond and on this side of the Humber, he drove these bishops out at his pleasure and set others in their place. In York itself he consecrated the prelates of other cities, and (as is read in the life of the blessed Wilfrid) he cast out of that same city's bishopric Chad and Wilfrid himself, whether for reason or from vice. Here one can see and lament human misery: that, however holy a man may be, he does not strip off obstinate manners to the end; and that those two eyes of Britain contended with each other. For Theodore, as far as our conjecture goes, unjustly expelled Wilfrid. Wilfrid brought his complaint to the Roman Pope Agatho (having been tossed about by many dangers before), and he did so with moderation, since he neither pressed the Apostolic See with direct accusations nor allowed his innocence to waver. For these are his words in the petition he presented to the Pope: 'But why it happened that Theodore, the most holy Archbishop, in my lifetime, in the see which (though unworthy) I administered, without the consent of any bishop, ordained three bishops by his own authority, my humility not agreeing, it is better to pass over than to press, out of reverence for that man, whom I dare not accuse, since he was sent from this summit of the Apostolic See.' Therefore, although by the judgement of the Roman council we see that Wilfrid was adjudged and sent back to his see, he did not obtain the matter, owing to the violence of King Egfrid, since Theodore either resisted by his own judgement or permitted it by his connivance." The same writer elsewhere censures this injury done by Theodore to Wilfrid harshly, as it deserves: "Theodore's manifest wrong could not be concealed. For when Wilfrid went before the tribunal of the King to complain of the injury, Theodore said, 'We oppose no charge to you. But what we have decided, we wish to stand.' What could be more absurd than this saying, as if he meant, 'Thus I will, thus I command; my will stands in place of reason.'"

units.la: Anno Dominicae incarnationis 678. haec inter Theodorum & Wilfridum orta dissensio est: quo etiam tempore Cometam per tres integros menses apparuisse Beda narrat: Matutinis horis oriebatur, excelsam radiantis flammae quasi columnam praeferens. Ac haec quidem stella (vt solet) ingentem Britanniae calamitatem portendebat. Quo enim anno Wilfridus Romam in Britanniam rediit, & provincia sua per Theodori inimicitias prohibeatur, (quanquam ut fidelis Euangelium promulgarit) ingens mortalitas multas Britanniae provincias corripuit, in provincia etiam occidentali Saxonum per 3. integros annos non pluit. Unde populus praeterquam quod morbo, etiam fame praeter modum afflictus est. Idem etiam Beda narrat. Saepe 40. homines, saepe plures fagis aceribitatem non ferentes, ad maris ripas se contulisse, seseque inde iunctis manibus fluctibus absorbendos miserae praecipitasse. Duas suo tempore Synodos Theodorus conuocasse dicitur. Primam Herefordiae, in qua decreta decem sancita sunt. Capita huius Synodi habebis apud Bedam. Cum haec Synodus celebraretur, moritur Egbertus Rex Cantiorum, mense Iulio, cui succedit Lotharius frater eius. Secundam Synodum conuocauit apud Chff.iuxta Roffam.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord's incarnation 678, this dissension arose between Theodore and Wilfrid. At the same time, Bede relates, a comet appeared for three whole months. It rose in the morning hours, carrying before it what looked like a tall column of blazing flame. This star, as usual, portended a great calamity for Britain. For in the year when Wilfrid returned to Britain from Rome, and his province was kept from him by Theodore's hostility (although as a faithful man he had proclaimed the Gospel), a great pestilence seized many provinces of Britain; in the western province of the Saxons it did not rain for three whole years. Hence the people were afflicted beyond measure not only by disease but also by famine. Bede also relates this: often forty men, often more, unable to bear the want, betook themselves to the shores of the sea and, joining hands, threw themselves wretchedly into the waves to be swallowed up. Theodore is said to have summoned two synods in his time. The first was at Hereford, in which ten decrees were enacted. You will find the chapters of this synod in Bede. While this synod was being held, Egbert, King of Kent, died in the month of July, and his brother Lothair succeeded him. The second synod he called at Chff., near Rochester.

units.la: Atqui cum audiret fide Ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae haeresi Eutychinia plurimum esse turbatam, omnes huius Synodi Episcopos, Sacerdotes & Doctores, cuius essent fidei, scrutatus est: quos cùm sanos & Orthodoxos reperisset, eos in eadem confirmauit. Atq; ve hic religionis status esset solidior, quinq; illa Sacrata & vniuersalia concilia apud Græcos olim habita Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ proposuit, quæ eadem libenter amplexata. Prima fuit Synodus Nicæna contra Arium, vbi congregati fuerunt 318. patres. 2. Ephesina ex 200. patribus contra Nestorium: 3. Chalcedonensis, vbi aderant 230. Episcopi contra Eutychē & Nestorium: 4. Constantinopolitana 150. patrū contra Macedonium & Eudoxū: 5. etiam ibidē temporibus Iustiniani, contra Theodorū, Theodoricū, & Cyrillum. An. 679. cōfertograui prælio Inter Edilredū Regem Merciorū & Egfridū Regem Northanhumbrorū, occisus est iuxta flumen Trenta Elbumi frater Regis Egfredi iuuenis annos natus 14. Huius interitus cum fratrem grauiter irritaret, odiūq; Regum hac occasione inexpiabile videretur: Theodori tamen monitis vterq; acquieuit, paxq; inter eos, eorumq; regna (intercedente ptx sule) conciliata, multo deinde tempore perduruit. Magno etiam in precio & authoritate fuit tum Romanis omnibus, tum etiam Agathon: Romano Pontifici, quæ ex eius ad illum literis perquam familiaribus colligimus, quæ scriptæ sunt tempore primi concilii habiti Constantinopoli: ex illa Epistola hæc verbadepromptimus. Spectabamus deinde de Britannia Theodorum confamulum ac Coepiscopum nostrum, magnæ Insulæ Britanniæ Archiepiscopum & Philosophum, cum aliis qui ibidem hactenus demorantur, exinde ad humilitatem nostram coniungere, & hac causa Concilium liucusque distulimus. Videtur lector, quanti eum Agatho fecerit, quem tam honorifice compellauit, cuiusq; causa concilium vaiuerfale distulerit. Hos libros scripsit. Summam pœnitentialem, patrum Canones; otdinationes Cleri, de fide contra Eutychem, & alia. Non multo ante obitum Erkenwaldum Londinensem Episcopum consecrauit. Alios Eboraci ordinauit, Eadhedum, Bosam & Eatam, primusq; fuit qui Pontificalem in Anglia vigorem exercuit. Cum senex esset ac plenus dierum, defunctus est, 19. die Septembris. anno. 690. cum annum iam ageret. 88. quem le numerum annorum, & non vlirà victurum somnio admonitus prædicere solebat. Sedit annos. 21. Sepultus est in Ecclesia beati Petri, sed non in prædicta porticu, vtitimus enim ibidem positus fuit Deusdedit. Paulò antequam moreretur accertsuisse Londinum dicitur ad se Wilfridum & Erkenwaldum, quibus cum deliĉta confiteretur, nullo conscientiam suam ita perturbari & terreri professus est, quam quod Wilfridum contra ius & fas, vel ipse sede iniuste exuerit, vel exui permiserit. Wilfridum igitur supplicit er rogat, vt iniuriam remitteret, vtrosque, vt apud Deum pro ipso intercederent. Præclare hoc sane quod refuperit. At vero Theodorus, vir apud omnem posteritatem venerandus, & multum celebrandus fuisset, si huius infamiæ labem omnino non contraxisset.
units.tr: But when he heard that the Church of Constantinople was greatly disturbed by the Eutychian heresy, he examined all the bishops, priests and teachers of this synod as to what their faith was. When he found them sound and orthodox, he confirmed them in it. So that the state of religion might be more secure, he set before the English Church the five sacred and universal councils that had long been held among the Greeks, and the English Church gladly embraced them. The first was the Nicene Synod against Arius, where 318 fathers met. The second was the Ephesine, of 200 fathers, against Nestorius. The third was the Chalcedonian, where 230 bishops were present, against Eutyches and Nestorius. The fourth was the Constantinopolitan, of 150 fathers, against Macedonius and Eudoxius. The fifth was also held at Constantinople, in the time of Justinian, against Theodore, Theodoret and Cyril. In the year 679 a hard-fought battle took place between Ethelred, king of the Mercians, and Ecgfrith, king of the Northumbrians. There fell beside the river Trent Elbum, a brother of King Ecgfrith, a young man of fourteen years. Since this death grievously provoked the king his brother, and the hatred between the kings seemed on this occasion irreconcilable, both yielded to the admonitions of Theodore. Peace was made between them and their kingdoms, through the mediation of the archbishop, and it lasted for a long time afterwards. Theodore was also held in great esteem and authority, both by all the Romans and by Agatho the Roman Pontiff. We gather this from his very friendly letters to him, which were written at the time of the first council held at Constantinople. From that letter we take the following words: "We were then looking to bring Theodore, our fellow-servant and fellow-bishop, archbishop of the great island of Britain and a scholar, together with others who have so far remained there, from there to our lowliness; and for this reason we have so far put off the council." Consider, reader, how highly Agatho esteemed him, whom he addressed so honourably, and for whose sake he postponed the universal council. Theodore wrote these books: a penitential summary, the canons of the Fathers, ordinations of the clergy, a book on the faith against Eutyches, and others. Not long before his death he consecrated Erkenwald, bishop of London. He ordained others at York, Eadhed, Bosa and Eata, and he was the first who exercised the pontifical authority in England. When he was old and full of days, he died on 19 September, in the year 690, in his eighty-eighth year. He used to foretell this number of years, admonished by a dream, saying that he would not live beyond it. He sat for twenty-one years. He was buried in the church of St Peter, but not in the aforesaid porch, for Deusdedit was the last to be laid there. Shortly before he died, he is said to have sent for Wilfrid and Erkenwald to London. When he confessed his sins to them, he declared that his conscience was troubled and terrified by nothing so much as the fact that he had either himself unjustly and against right and law deprived Wilfrid of his see, or had allowed him to be deprived. He therefore earnestly begged Wilfrid to remit the wrong, and asked both of them to intercede with God on his behalf. Truly this was an admirable thing to have done. But Theodore, a man to be venerated and greatly celebrated by all posterity, would have been so indeed, had he not wholly incurred the stain of this infamy.

units.la: Nam præter reliquas eius virtutes eximiè doctus fuit, ac post mortem in disciputis, qui multi erant & præclari, quasi viuens. In his fuit S. Beda, Iohannes Beuerlacensis, Albinus venerabilis cœnobii Augustinensis Cantuariæ Abbas, Tobias Rofensis Episcopus, qui latinam ita & Græcam linguam, vt nariuam calluisse dicitur. Albinum Beda ingenuè agnoscit adiutorem fuisse luctoriæ suæ colligendæ, in linguis etiam Thobiæ patem facit.
units.tr: For, besides his other virtues, he was exceedingly learned, and after his death he lived on, as it were, in his disciples, who were many and distinguished. Among them were St Bede, John of Beverley, Albinus, abbot of the venerable monastery of St Augustine at Canterbury, and Tobias, bishop of Rochester, who is said to have known both Latin and Greek as if they were his native tongue. Bede frankly acknowledges that Albinus helped him to collect his history, and he also calls Tobias his father in languages.

units.la: VIII. BIRTHVALDVS.
units.tr: VIII. BIRTHWALD.

units.la: VCCESSIT Theodoro Cant. Birthualdus, natione Anglus, hunc primum fuisse ex Anglis Archiepiscopum falsò prodidit Polidorus Virgilius, superiores omnes Italos aut Romanos faciens, in quo quitè dupliciter erravit. Deusdedit enim secūdus ab hoc, degente occidentalium Saxonum fuit, & Theodorus ante istum proximus, de Tharso Ciliciæ oriundus erat. Fuit Birthualdus Abbas cœnobii Raculf. positi iuxta ostium aquilonare fluminis Gentad, prope Insulam Thanet, hodie Raculuer appellatur. Electus est in Archiepiscopum Birthualdus Anno Dom. 692. primo die mensis Iulii, à Godwino Metropolitano Walliæ, vel (vt refert Beda) Galliæ ordinatus est. Proximo post electionem anno. 3. Kalend. Iulii, pridie Kal. Septembr. plenam sedis suæ possessionem accepit. Scripturarum scientia non mediocri imbutus fuit, & in Ecclesiastica disciplina satis instructus, Theodoro tamen pdecessori æqualis non fuit. Birthualdo Sergius Pont. eius nominis primus, omnis Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ primatu per literas cōcessit. Quo tempore videlicet: An. gratiæ. 693. In a Rex Westsaxonum, vendicare disposuit combustionem Mollitiis cognati fui, Sed Rex Cantii Withredus cum Cantuarienfibus suis humiliter obtulam veniens. 3750. libras pro nece adolescentis dedit. Et sic: Lis finita fuit, pax confirmata reuixit. Canfam necis tradunt quidam, quia Cantuarienses praedictum Mollonem praefractiorem in defendendis imaginibus (vt tum solennis quaestio erat) quam par fuit, viderent. Sedente Birthualdo Episcopimulti in Anglia per illum ordinati sunt: in quibus praecipui fuerunt: Daniel Episcopus Winton. & Thobias Winton. & Thobias Episcopus Roff. quorum hic Latinae Graecae, & Saxonicae lingnae cognitione, eruditione etiam multiplici exteros omnes sui temporis longe anteceelluit. Huic Birthualdo vitio vertitur, quod adiutor, aut potius Author fuerit Alfrico Regi Northumbrorum, denuo expellendi e sede sua Wilfridum, qui annos quinque à restitutione sua Prouinciam Eboracensem prudenter, & quiete administrauerat. Nam quo tempore Wilfridus Episcopatu pulsus est, prouinciae suae Eboracensi praepositi sunt duo à Theodoro ordinati Episcopi, Bosa & Eatra: quorum hic Bernicorum, ille Deirorum Prouinciam accepit: hic in Eboracensi, ille in Hagustaldensi Ecclesia sedem statuit. Eatra defunctus in sua prouincia successit. Ioannes Beuetlacensis. His locis suis cedere coacti sunt post Wilfridi restitutionem. Eiecti igitur Episcopi, qui ante infesti Wilfrido fuerunt, iam maiori odio in eum concitati, vnà cum Hida Abbatissa, quae simultates cum Wilfrido pariter gessit, nouas quoque ad Regi Alfrido deferunt eumque denuo in Wilfridum incendunt. Birthualdum etiam figmentis variis in Wilfridum concitatis, ad iram prouocant. Ille Regem instigat: Rex caeca cupiditate ductus, Wilfridum omnibus praediis exuit, bonisque spoliat, & Episcopatu pellit. Vtq; res non inordinate procedere videretur, decretum Theodori Archiepiscopi praetexunt, latum quidem, cum Theodorus & Wilfridus graues inimicitias inter se exercerent, cum tamen non ignorauerant (Wilfrido id etiam affirmante) Theodorum ante mortem (vt in eius vita dictum est,) animo compunctum iniuriarum contra Wilfridum poenituisse. Sed cum nulla ratione Regi persuadere poterat, tamen voluntati eius non cessit. Sponte iure & Episcopatu suo cedere noluit, etsi ad id faciendum & Alfricus Rex, & Birthualdus Archiepiscopus, minis, & blandimentis eum alliecre non desisterent. Violenter igitur à Rege finibus Northumbrorum expellitur. Ad Regem Mereiorum, quem familiarem habuit, confugit, à quo sane & beneuole, & honorifice exceptus est: mortuoq; Sexulfo Lichefeldensi Episcopo, eius Episcopatus totius Ecclesiae Merciorum curam illi commisit. Rex postquam eum vi Episcopatu eiecerat, tamen vt iure etiam expulsus videretur, Birthualdi consilio Synodum Episcoporum conuocari facit, in quo Wilfridus, vt resignaret, adducereturiaut si id non faceret, perstentium Episcoporum suffragiis potius quam iniuria Regis mutere suo pulsus videretur. Wilfridus cum ad hoc Concilium vocatus esset, vim metuens primò quidem abnuit, postea vero ne causae suae cognitionem subterfugere videretur, fide data interesse placuit: sperauitque tam fratres suos & coepiscoposque aequiores habituram se, quam expertus est. Nam quam primum in Concilium ingreditur, omnes tanquam ad id iam diu compositi illum verbis conuiciis & calumniis iritemperanter exagitant: tandem vero, tum Theodori Archiepiscopi decretis parere vellet, captiose interrogant. Ille fraudem persentiens respondebat, se illis Theodori decretis obtemperaturum, quae à sacris canonibus non dissentirent. Acerbe etiā in eos inuectus est, quòd ea Theodori decreta, quae iam annos xii. sopita quieuerant, malitiose in eontumeliam fratris refricarent: praesertim cum eadem decreta authoritate 3. Pontificum Rom. Agathonis, Benedicti, Sergii, ad nihilum redacta planteq; reficiassadiu ante fuerunt. Huic concilio Rex Alfricus interfuit, ac eum se propositò frustratum videt, suosq; abs se subornatos Episcopos in contentione à Wilfrido superatos videret, animo offensa Birthualdum intuitus in haec verba prorupit. Si haec ita sint (pater) opprimam eum per violentiam. Quae Regis verba, quanquam graue quondam Wilfrido minitari viderentur, tamen inimicis merito displicuerunt. Quanquàm eum Episcopatu suo pelli libenter voluerunt: tamen authoritatem Pontificis Romani, (qua omnis ipsorum gratia, & existimatio nitebatur) à Rege directe violari noluerunt. Wilfridum ergo alia via adoriuntur. Exponüt ei quàm noxiae, & periculosae essent discordiae in Ecclesia Dei, nouellam vero & iam pridem positam Ecclesiam aliis multis controuersiis agitari, quas quidem cum ad Episcopos spectaret componere, eos id commode facere non posse, si ipsi inter se digladiarentur: eum igitur orant & obtestantur, vt sponte vellet de iure suo & Episcopatu decedere. Praeterquam enim quod ea ratione Regis animum vehementer iam in ipsum exacerbatam, omnes huius Synodi Episcopos, Sacerdotes & Doctores, cuius essent ædei, scrutaratus est: quos cum sanôr& Orthodoxos reperisset, eosin eadem confirmauit. Atq; vt hic religionis status esset sollidior, quinq; illa Sacrata & valuersalia concilia apud Græcos olim habita Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ proposuit, quæ eadem libenter amplexata. Prima fuit Synodus Niczna contra Arium, vbi congregati fuerunt 318. patres. 2. Ephesina ex 200. patribus contra Nestorium: 3. Chalcedonensis, vbi aderant 230. Episcopi contra Eutyche & Nestorij: 4. Constantinopolitana 150. patrû contra Macedonium & Eudoxiu: 5. etiam ibidé temporibus Iustiniani, contra Theodorici, & Cyrillum. An. 679. cóserto graui prælio inter Edilredû Regem Merciorû & Egfridû Regem Northanhumbrorû, occisus est inxta flumen Trenta Elbumi frater Regis Egfredi iuuenis annos natus 14. Huius interitus cum fratrem grauiter irritaret, odiúq; Regum hac occasione inexpiabile videretur: Theodori tamen monitis vtercq; acquieuit, paxq; inter eos, cõrumq; regna (interea dente præsule) conciliata, multo deinde tempore perduravit.
units.tr: Birthwald, an Englishman by birth, succeeded Theodore at Canterbury. Polydore Virgil falsely reports that he was the first Englishman to become archbishop, making all his predecessors Italians or Romans, and in this he erred in two ways. For Deusdedit, the second after Birthwald, was a West Saxon, and Theodore, the one immediately before him, was born at Tarsus in Cilicia. Birthwald had been abbot of the monastery of Reculver, situated near the northern mouth of the river Genta, close to the Isle of Thanet, now called Reculver. Birthwald was elected archbishop in the year of our Lord 692, on the first day of July, and was ordained by Godwin, metropolitan of Wales, or (as Bede reports) of Gaul. In the year after his election, on the third day before the Kalends of July, that is the day before the Kalends of September, he took full possession of his see. He was imbued with no small knowledge of the Scriptures and was sufficiently instructed in church discipline, yet he was not equal to Theodore his predecessor. Sergius, the first Pope of that name, granted by letter to Birthwald the primacy of the whole English Church. At that time, namely in the year of grace 693, Ine, king of the West Saxons, resolved to avenge the burning of Mollo, his kinsman. But Wihtred, king of Kent, came humbly with his men of Canterbury and gave 3750 pounds for the killing of the young man. And so the dispute was ended, and peace, once confirmed, was restored. Some report the cause of the killing: the men of Canterbury saw that the aforesaid Mollo was more obstinate than was fitting in defending images (as was then a common question). While Birthwald presided, many bishops were ordained in England by him; the most notable among them were Daniel, bishop of Winchester, and Tobias, bishop of Rochester, who in knowledge of Latin, Greek and Saxon, and in manifold learning, far surpassed all the foreigners of his time. Birthwald is faulted for having been the assistant, or rather the instigator, of Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians, in expelling Wilfrid from his see a second time; Wilfrid had administered the province of York wisely and quietly for five years since his restoration. For at the time Wilfrid was driven from his bishopric, two bishops ordained by Theodore, Bosa and Eata, were set over his province of York: of these, the one received the province of the Bernicians and the other that of the Deirans; the one fixed his seat in the church of York, the other in that of Hexham. Eata, on his death, was succeeded in his province by John of Beverley. These men were compelled to give up their places after Wilfrid's restoration. The bishops thus ejected, who had previously been hostile to Wilfrid, now stirred up with still greater hatred against him, together with Abbess Hild, who had likewise carried on quarrels with Wilfrid, brought fresh accusations to King Aldfrith and inflamed him again against Wilfrid. They also provoked Birthwald to anger by various fabrications against Wilfrid. He in turn stirred up the king; the king, led by blind desire, stripped Wilfrid of all his estates, robbed him of his goods, and drove him from his bishopric. And so that the matter might not seem to proceed irregularly, they put forward a decree of Archbishop Theodore. This decree had indeed been passed when Theodore and Wilfrid were carrying on grave enmity between them; yet they were not unaware (Wilfrid himself affirming it too) that Theodore, before his death, as was said in his life, his mind pricked with remorse, had repented of the wrongs done to Wilfrid. But although Wilfrid could by no means persuade the king, he nevertheless did not yield to his will. He refused to give up his right and his bishopric of his own accord, although King Aldfrith and Archbishop Birthwald did not cease to entice him to do so with threats and flatteries. Therefore he was violently expelled from the borders of Northumbria by the king. He fled to Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, whom he had counted as a friend, and was received by him kindly and honourably; and when Sexwulf, bishop of Lichfield, had died, the king committed to Wilfrid the care of the whole church of the Mercians. After the king had driven him from his bishopric by force, yet so that he might seem to have been expelled also by right, at Birthwald's counsel he caused a synod of bishops to be convened, in which Wilfrid was to be brought to resign; or, if he did not do so, he would appear to have been removed from his see by the votes of the persisting bishops rather than by the king's injustice. When Wilfrid was summoned to this council, fearing violence, he at first refused; afterwards, lest he seem to shun the hearing of his cause, he resolved to attend under a pledge of safe conduct, and hoped that his brethren and fellow bishops would be fairer to him than he found them to be. For as soon as he entered the council, they all, as if long prepared for this very purpose, harassed him immoderately with words, insults and slanders; at last they craftily asked whether he would obey the decrees of Archbishop Theodore. He, sensing the trap, replied that he would obey those decrees of Theodore which did not dissent from the sacred canons. He also attacked them bitterly, because they maliciously revived, to his brother's insult, those decrees of Theodore which had lain dormant for twelve years; especially since the same decrees had been wholly annulled long before by the authority of three Roman pontiffs, Agatho, Benedict and Sergius. King Aldfrith was present at this council, and seeing himself frustrated in his purpose, and his bishops, whom he had suborned, overcome by Wilfrid in the dispute, he was offended in mind; looking at Birthwald, he burst out in these words: "If these things are so, father, I will crush him by violence." These words of the king, though they seemed to threaten grave danger to Wilfrid, nevertheless deservedly displeased his enemies. Although they were glad to have him driven from his bishopric, they were unwilling that the authority of the Roman Pontiff, on which all their credit and reputation rested, should be openly violated by the king. They therefore assailed Wilfrid by another way. They set before him how harmful and dangerous discords were in the Church of God, and how the young church, planted long since, was troubled by many other controversies, which it belonged to bishops to settle; and that they could not do this conveniently if they themselves were fighting among themselves. They therefore begged and entreated him to be willing of his own accord to give up his right and his bishopric. Besides, by this means the king's mind, already greatly embittered against him, was ... ; and he examined all the bishops, priests and teachers of this synod, whose churches they were; and whom he found sound and orthodox, he confirmed in the same. And so that the state of religion here might be more solid, he set before the English Church the five sacred and universal councils once held among the Greeks, which it gladly embraced. The first was the Synod of Nicaea against Arius, where 318 fathers were gathered; the second was Ephesus, of 200 fathers, against Nestorius; the third was Chalcedon, where 230 bishops were present against Eutyches and Nestorius; the fourth was Constantinople, of 150 fathers, against Macedonius and Eudoxius; the fifth was also held there in the times of Justinian, against Theodore and Cyril. In the year 679, when a grievous battle had been joined between Ethelred, king of the Mercians, and Ecgfrith, king of the Northumbrians, near the river Trent, Elfwine, brother of King Ecgfrith, a youth of fourteen years, was killed. Since this death greatly provoked his brother, and the hatred of the kings seemed on this occasion irreconcilable, yet both acquiesced in Theodore's admonitions; peace was brought about between them and their kingdoms, while Theodore was presiding, and afterwards lasted a long time.

units.la: Magno etiam in precio & anthoritate fuit tum Romanis omnibus, tûm etiam Agathoni Romano Pontifici, quæ ex eius ad illum litteris petquam familiaribus colligimus, quæ scriptæ sunt tempore primi concilii habiti Constantinopoli: ex illa Epistola hæc verba deprompsimus. Sperabamus deinde de Britannia Theodorum confamulum ac Coepiscopum nostrum, magnæ insulæ Britanniæ Archiepiscopum & Philosophum, cum allis qui ibidem hactenus demorantur, exinde ad humilitatem nostramconiungere, & hac caussa Concilium hucusque distulimus. Viderit lector, quanti cum Agatho fecerit quem tam honorifice compellauit, cuiusq; causa concilium vniuersale distulerit. Hos libros scripsit. Summam pœnitentialem, patrum Canones, ordinationes Cleri, de fide contra Eutychem, & alia. Non multo ante obitum Erkenwaldum Londinensem Episcopum consecrauit Alios Eboracio ordinauit, Eadhedum, Bosam & Eatam, primusq; fuit qui Pontificalem in Anglia vigorem exercuit. Cum senex esset ac plenus dierum, defunctus est. 19. die Septembris. anno. 690. cum annum iam ageret. 88. quem sc numerum annorum, & non vltrà victurum somnio admonitus prædicere solebat. Sedit annos 21. Sepultus est in Ecclesia beati Petri, sed non in prædicta porticu, vbi multa enim ibidem positus fuit Deusdedit.
units.tr: He was also held in great esteem and authority, both by all the Romans and by Agatho, the Roman Pontiff himself, as we gather from the letters Agatho wrote to him, rather familiar in tone, at the time of the first council held at Constantinople; from that letter we have taken these words. "We had hoped then to join to our humility from Britain Theodore, our fellow-servant and fellow-bishop, archbishop and philosopher of the great island of Britain, together with the others who have hitherto remained there; and for this cause we have hitherto deferred the council." Let the reader see how highly Agatho esteemed the man whom he addressed so honourably, and for whose sake he deferred the universal council. He wrote these books: a penitential summa, the canons of the fathers, the ordinations of the clergy, on the faith against Eutyches, and others. Not long before his death he consecrated Erkenwald, bishop of London; he ordained others at York, Eadhed, Bosa and Eata; and he was the first who exercised pontifical vigour in England. When he was an old man and full of days, he died on 19 September, in the year 690, in his 88th year, a number of years which, warned by a dream that he would live no longer, he used to predict. He held the see for 21 years. He was buried in the church of St Peter, but not in the aforesaid porch, where many had already been buried, including Deusdedit.

units.la: Paulò antequam moreretur accerfuisse Londinum dicitur ad se Wilfridum & Erkenwaldum, quibus eum delicta confiteretur, nullo conscientiam suam ita perturbari & terreri professus est, quàm quod Wilfridum contra ius & fas, vel ipse sede iniuste exuerit, vel exui permiserit. Wilfridum igitur supplicit rogat, vt iniuriam remitteret, vtroque, vt apud Deum pro ipso intercederent. Præclare hoc sane quod resipuerit. Arverò Theodorus, vir apud omnem posteritatem venerandus, & multum celebrandus fuisset, si huius infamiæ labem omnino non contraxisset.
units.tr: Shortly before he died, he is said to have summoned Wilfrid and Erkenwald to London, and to them he confessed his sins. He declared that nothing troubled and terrified his conscience so much as the fact that he had either himself unjustly and contrary to right and law deprived Wilfrid of his see, or had allowed him to be deprived. He therefore humbly asked Wilfrid to forgive the wrong, and asked both of them to intercede for him with God. Truly, this was a laudable repentance. But Theodore, a man to be revered and greatly celebrated by all posterity, would have been even more so had he not contracted the stain of this infamy at all.

units.la: Nam præter reliquas eius virtutes eximiè doctus fuit, ae post mortem in discipulis, qui multi erant & præclati, quasi viuens. In his fuit S. Beda, Iohannes Beuerlacensis, Albinus venerabilis cœnobii Augustinensis Cantuariæ Abbas, Thobias Roffensis Episcopus, qui latinam ita & Græcam linguam, vt natinam callui se dicitur. Albinum Beda ingenuè agnoscit adiutorem fuisse historiæ suæ colligendæ, in linguis etiam Thobiæ parem facit.
units.tr: For, besides his other virtues, he was exceedingly learned, and after his death he lived on, as it were, in his disciples, who were many and distinguished. Among them were St Bede, John of Beverley, Albinus, abbot of the venerable monastery of St Augustine at Canterbury, and Tobias, bishop of Rochester, who is said to have known Latin and Greek as well as his native tongue. Bede openly acknowledges that Albinus helped him in gathering his history, and he makes him equal to Tobias in languages.

units.la: VIII. Birthvaldvs.
units.tr: VIII. Birthwald.

units.la: Vccessit Theodoro Cant. Birthualdus, natione Anglus, huic primum fuisse ex Anglis Archiepiscopum falsò prodidit Polidorus Virgilius, superiori tempore Romanos faciens, in quo quidem dupliciter errauit. Deusdedit enim secundus ab hoc, de gente occidentalium Saxonum fuit, & Theodorus ante istum proximus, de Thatso Ciliciæ oriundus erat. Fuit Birthualdus Abbas cœnobii Racul: posita iuxta ostium aquilonare fluminis Gentad, ptopeInsulam Thanet, hodie Xacustur appellatur. Electus est in Archiepiscopum Birthualdus Anno Dom. 692. primo die mensis Iulii, & à Godwino Metropolitano Wallia, vel (vt tefert Beda) Galliæ ordinatus est. Proximo post electionem anno. 3. Kalend Iulii, priedie Kal. Septembr. plebam sedis suæ possessionem accepit. Scripturarum scientia non mediocri instructus fuit, & in Ecclesiastica disciplina satis instructus, Theodoro tamen pdecessori æqualis non fuit. Birthualdo Sergius Pont. eius nominis primus, omnis Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ primatû per literas cõcessit. Quo tepore videlicet: An. gratiæ. 693. Ina Rex West Saxonum, vendicare dispositi combustionem Mollinis cognati sui, Sed Rex Cantii Withredus cum Cantuariensibus suis humiliter obtiam veniens, 3750. libras pro nece adolescentis dedit. Et sic: Lufinita fuit, pax confirmata est. Causam necis tradunt quidam, quia Cantuarienses praedictum Mollonem praefactionem in defendendis imaginibus (ut tunc solennis quae fuit) quam parfuit, viderent. Sedente Birthualdo Episcopi multi in Anglia per illum ordinati fuerunt: Daniel Episcopus Winton. & Thobias Winton, & Thobias Episcopus Rosi. quorum hic Latinae Graecae, & Saxonicae linguae cognitione, eruditione etiam multiplici caeteros omnes sui temporis longe antecelluit. Huic Birthualdo vitio vertitur, quod adiutor, aut potius Author fuerit Alfrico Regi Northumbrorum, denuo expellendi e sede sua Wilfridum, qui annos quinque a restitutione sua Provinciam Eboracensem prudenter, & quiete administrarat. Nam quo tempore Wilfridus Episcopatu pulsus est, provinciae suae Eboracensi praepositi sunt duo a Theodoro ordinati Episcopi, Bosa & Eatra: quorum hic Pernicierum, ille Dagoram Provinciam accepit: hic in Eboracensi, ille in Hagustaldensi Ecclesia sedem fixit. Eatra defunctus, in provincia suae cessit. Ioannes Beuerlacensis. Hi locis suis cedere coacti sunt post Wilfridi restitutionem. Eiecti igitur Episcopi, qui ante infesti Wilfrido fuerunt, iam maiori odio eum concitati, unam Hida Abbatissa, quae simultates cum Wilfrido pariter gesserunt, nouas querelas Regi Alfrido deferunt eumque denuo in Wilfridum incendunt. Birthualdum etiam stigmatis variis in Wilfridum concitatis, ad iram provocant. Ille Regem instigat: Rex caeca cupiditate ducitur, Wilfridum omnibus praediis exuit, bonis spoliat, & Episcopatu pellit. Vtque res non inordinate proceedere viderentur, decretum Theodori Archiepiscopi praetexunt, iuxta quod, cum Theodorus & Wilfridus graues inimicitias inter se exercerent, tamen non ignorauerunt (Wilfrido id etiam affirmante) Theodorum ante mortem (vt in eius vita dictum est,) animo compunctum iniuriarum contra Wilfridum poenituisse. Sed cum nulla ratione Regi persuadere poterat, tamen voluntati eius non cessit. Sponte n. iure & Episcopatu suo cedere noluit, etsi ad id faciendum & Alfricus Rex, & Birthualdus Archiepiscopus, minis, & blandimentis eum allicere non desisterent. Victoriosus igitur à Rege finibus Northumbrorum expellitur. Ad Regem Merciorum, quem familiarem habuit, confugit, à quo sane & benevole, & honorifice exceptus est: mortuoq; Sexulfo Lichesfeldensi Episcopo, eius Episcopatus totius Ecclesiae Merciorum curam illi commisit. Rex postquam eum vi Episcopatu eiecerat, tamen vt iure etiam expulisse videretur, Birthualdi consilio Synodum Episcoporum convocari facit, in quo Wilfridus, vt resignaret, adduceretur: aut si id non faceret, praesentium Episcoporum sufragiis potius quam iniuria Regis munere suo pulsus videretur. Wilfridus cum ad hoc Concilium vocatus esset, vim metuens primo quidem abnuit, postea vero ne causae iuxta cognitionem subterfugere videretur, fide data interesse placuit: sperauit etiam fratres suos & coepiscopos aequiores habituros se, quam expertus est. Nam quam primum in Concilium ingrederetur, omnes tanquam ad id iam diu compositi illum verbis provocando, conuitiis & calumniis intemperanter exagitant: tandem vero, num Theodori Archiepiscopi decretis parere vellet, captiose interrogant. Ille fraudem perspiciens respondebat, se illis Theodori decretis obtemperaturum, quae a sacris canonibus non dissentirent. Acerbe etiam in eos inuectus est, quod ea Theodori decreta, quae iam annos 21. sopita quiescerent, malitiose in contumeliam fratris refricarent: praesertim cum eadem decreta authoritate 3. Pontificum Rom. Agathonis, Benedicti, Sergii, ad nihilum redacta planeque reiecta diu ante fuerunt. Huic concilio Rex Alfricus interfuit, ac eum se proposito frustratum videt, suosque abs se subornatos Episcopos in contentione a Wilfrido superatos videret, animo offensa Birthualdum intuitus in haec verba prorupit. Sihaec ita sint (pater) opprimam eum per violentiam. Quae Regis verba, quanquam graue quondam Wilfrido minitari viderentur, tamen inimicis merito displicuerunt. Quanquam n. eum Episcopatu suo pelli libenter voluerunt: tamen authoritatem Pontificis Romani, (qua omnis ipsorum gratia, & exiitimatio nitebatur) a Rege directe violari nolnerunt. Wilfridum ergo alia via adoriuntur. Exponunt ei quam noxiae, & periculosae esset discordia in Ecclesia Dei, nouellam vero & iam pridem positam Ecclesiam aliis multis controuersiis agitari, quas quidem cum ad Episcopos spectaret componere, eos id commode facere non posse, ipsi inter se digladiarentur: eum igitur orant & obtestantur, vt sponte veller de iure suo Episcopatu decedere. Praeterquam enim quod ea ratione Regis animum vehementer iam in ipsum exaceracerbatum lenirent, Ecclesiam etiam Dei hac contentione turbatam pacaret: quasi re fi illorum votis annueret, ipsis quidem gratum faceret, Ecclesiæ Dei perutile, & ad proprii nommis laudé gloriosum. Wilfridus hac oratione, quanrumcunq; artificiosa, non movetur: quin etiam obiicit, iptos de se non ita esse meritos, vt ad eorum nutum iure suo cederet reneatur. Ac quod ad Ecclesiæ utilitatem spectat, si illis afensum præberet, maioracidem mala illaturum se inde verebatur: nam cum ille Paschæ Romanorum pernomen Northumbriam propagasset, cum Antiphonarum institutisset, ordinem Benedicti promovisset, multaq; alia in Ecclesiam induxisset, ea omnia tanquam abolita recisa forent, si fe ipse damnaret, cum plerumq; res ipsæ a personis authoritatem & accipiant & amittant.
units.tr: Birthwald, an Englishman by birth, succeeded Theodore at Canterbury. Polydore Virgil falsely reported that he was the first Englishman to become archbishop, thereby favouring the Romans in earlier times, and in this he erred in two ways. For Deusdedit, the second after Theodore, was of the race of the West Saxons, and Theodore, the one immediately before Birthwald, was born at Tarsus in Cilicia. Birthwald was abbot of the monastery of Reculver, situated near the northern mouth of the river Gentad, close to the Isle of Thanet, now called Reculver. Birthwald was elected archbishop in the year of our Lord 692, on the first day of July, and was consecrated by Godwin, metropolitan of Wales, or (as Bede reports) of Gaul. In the year after his election, on the third day before the kalends of July, or the day before the kalends of September, he took possession of his see before the people. He was furnished with no small knowledge of the Scriptures and was sufficiently trained in church discipline, yet he was not equal to his predecessor Theodore. Sergius, pope, the first of that name, granted by letter to Birthwald the primacy of the whole English Church. At that time, namely in the year of grace 693, Ine, king of the West Saxons, intended to avenge the burning of his kinsman Mollo. But Withred, king of Kent, came humbly to meet him with his Canterbury men and gave three thousand seven hundred and fifty pounds for the killing of the youth. And so the dispute was ended, and peace was confirmed. Some give as the cause of the killing that the men of Canterbury had seen the said Mollo, as was then the custom, zealously engaged in defending images. While Birthwald presided, many bishops in England were ordained by him: Daniel, bishop of Winchester, Tobias of Winchester, and Tobias, bishop of Rochester. Of these, this Tobias far surpassed all the others of his time in his knowledge of Latin, Greek and Saxon, and in his manifold learning. Birthwald is faulted for being the helper, or rather the author, of King Aldfrith of the Northumbrians in expelling Wilfrid once again from his see. Wilfrid had administered the province of York prudently and quietly for five years since his restoration. For at the time when Wilfrid was driven from his bishopric, two bishops ordained by Theodore, Bosa and Eata, had been set over his province of York. Of these, the one received Bernicia and the other Deira; the one fixed his seat in the church of York, the other in the church of Hexham. Eata, after his death, gave way in his province. John of Beverley. These were forced to yield their places after Wilfrid's restoration. The bishops thus ejected, who had been hostile to Wilfrid before, were now roused against him with even greater hatred. Together with Hild the abbess, who had likewise quarrelled with Wilfrid, they brought new complaints to King Aldfrith and inflamed him again against Wilfrid. They also provoked Birthwald to anger by stirring up various slanders against Wilfrid. He urged on the king, and the king, led by blind desire, stripped Wilfrid of all his estates, plundered his goods, and drove him from his bishopric. So that the matter might not seem to proceed irregularly, they put forward a decree of Archbishop Theodore, according to which, although Theodore and Wilfrid had waged grave enmity against each other, nevertheless they did know (as Wilfrid himself also affirmed) that Theodore, before his death, as was said in his life, had been stung in conscience and repented of his wrongs against Wilfrid. But although he could by no means persuade the king, Wilfrid did not yield to his will. For he was unwilling to give up his right and his bishopric of his own accord, although King Aldfrith and Archbishop Birthwald did not cease to lure him to do so with threats and flatteries. Overcome, therefore, he was driven by the king from the bounds of Northumbria. He fled to Ceolwulf, king of the Mercians, whom he counted as a friend, and was received by him kindly and honourably. When Sexwulf, bishop of Lichfield, died, the king entrusted to Wilfrid the care of his whole bishopric, that is, of the whole church of the Mercians. After the king had driven him from his bishopric by force, yet so that he might seem to have expelled him also by right, he caused, on Birthwald's advice, a synod of bishops to be convened, at which Wilfrid was to be brought to resign. Or, if he did not do so, he might seem to have been deprived of his office by the votes of the bishops present rather than by the king's injustice. When Wilfrid was summoned to this council, fearing violence, he at first refused. Afterwards, however, lest he seem to shirk the case by avoiding a hearing, he resolved, having given his pledge, to attend. He also hoped that his brothers and fellow bishops would deal more fairly with him than they proved to. For as soon as he entered the council, they all, as if long prepared for this, provoked him with words and harassed him immoderately with reproaches and calumnies. At length they asked him craftily whether he would obey the decrees of Archbishop Theodore. He, seeing the trap, replied that he would obey those decrees of Theodore which did not conflict with the sacred canons. He also attacked them bitterly for maliciously reviving, to his insult as a brother, those decrees of Theodore which had lain dormant for twenty-one years, especially since the same decrees had long before been annulled and utterly rejected by the authority of three Roman pontiffs, Agatho, Benedict and Sergius. King Aldfrith was present at this council. Seeing that his purpose was thwarted, and that the bishops he had suborned were being worsted by Wilfrid in the dispute, he was offended in mind, and looking at Birthwald, he burst out in these words: "If these things are so, father, I will crush him by violence." These words of the king, though they seemed to threaten grave danger to Wilfrid, nevertheless deservedly displeased his enemies. For although they were glad to see him driven from his bishopric, they were unwilling that the authority of the Roman pontiff, on which all their own favour and reputation rested, should be openly violated by the king. So they attacked Wilfrid by another route. They set before him how harmful and dangerous discord in the Church of God was. They said that the young and long-established Church was troubled by many other controversies, which it was the business of the bishops to settle, yet they could not settle them conveniently while they themselves were tearing each other apart. They therefore begged and entreated him to be willing, of his own accord, to give up his right and withdraw from his bishopric. For besides softening the king's mind, already violently embittered against him, and calming the Church of God, troubled by this strife, it would, as though he had in fact granted their wishes, please them, be most useful to the Church of God, and gloriously redound to his own praise. Wilfrid was not moved by this speech, however artful it was. He even objected that they had not deserved so well of him that he should be bound to give up his right at their nod. As for the Church's advantage, he feared that if he gave them his assent he would bring greater evils upon it. For since he had spread the Roman Easter throughout Northumbria, introduced the Antiphonal, promoted the Rule of Benedict, and brought many other things into the Church, all these would be cut off as if abolished, should he condemn himself, since things very often receive and lose their authority from the persons who hold them.

units.la: Quod autem ad se fuamq; laudem attinet, vituperio potius & dedecori id sibi suturum at, si ietam senem & 40. annorum Episcopum deiici paterentur. Popnlo enim (ut suspiciosus est) non facile persuaderi posse, ipsum innocente sponte potius cessisse, quam crimimosum merito esse iecium. Hoc colloquio nihil aliud effectum est, nisi quod Wilfridus, qui antea non gravaret Episcopatu suo carvere, nunc ad eundé recuperandú cupiens ... ita male commentō hoc adnerfaris cessit.
