Dimisso concilio Wilfridus Romam proficisci tur, rogat pontificem, vt causam suam cognoscere dignetur. Quid multa? Adversarii accusantur, Romam veniunt, artificiose contra Wilfridum a Brithualdo instructi, illum graviter coram Pontifice, multisq; aliis Episcopis accusant. Atque illud inprimis, vt capitale scelus Wilfrido obiicinnt, quòd in superiore concilio dixisset, nolle se Theodori Archiepiscopi decretis morem gerere. Ille sic ita generaliter loquutum negat, tantum iis, quæ canonum decretis non repugnarent, iubens obsequium præstare: Quantum vero canonum authoritat detrahat, in tontem hne accusatore iudicis sententiam subire, neminem latere putat. Qua in re eum Wilfridus singulari modestia causam suam ageret, omnium iudicio probatus criminis illati inuidiam pepulit: aduersarii pudore suffusi, & ipse frustrati discedunt. Pontifex Anglorum Regibus Ethelredo Mercioum, & Alfrico Northumbrorum referibit. Audisse quidem se inter Wilfridum & reliquos Episcopos, &, quantum ipse coniectura assequi poterat, Wilfridum esse innocentem. Verùm quia principales partes accusationum & iniuriarum non aderant, consulo ret, vt Brithualdus Synodum Episcoporum denuo Britanniæ conuocet, cui Bosam & Ioannem interesse cogeret, & sic vtraque parte audita litem componerent. Sin autem Bosa & Ioannes adesse nollent, aut iudicio non acquiescerent, omnes coram ipso Romæ sub anathematis pœna comparerent. Wilfridus domum redieni has Rom. Pontificis literas Ethelredo Regi Merciorum (quiiam monachatum susceperat) tradidit: ille qui seipsum potestate regia prius exuerat, a Kenredo tamen Vlfarli fratris filio, quem suo loco Regem constituerat, obtinuit, vt pro tenore literarum Wilfridi causa agereiur. Brithualdus etiam Archiepiscopus Cant. Wilfrido anterius infestissimus, comminationibus Rom. Pontificis perterrefactus, in causa succubuit. Alfricus vero Northumbrorum Rex constanter in proposito persistit, iniquum esse exclamans, virum bis ab omnibus Angliæ Episcopis reiectum, ad mandatum Rom. Pontificis restituri. Accidit, vt paucis post diebus Rex morturetur, cui Osredus filius successit. Abillo Berthfridus (quo Rex familiarissime vsus est) auctor & gratia obtinuit, vt Synodus in Northumbria congregaretur vbi (pertinacier renitentibus aduersariis) Wilfridus fauente Rege superior euasit. Qui post aliquot annorum quietam in fede possessionem, lecto decumbens testamentum condidit, & bona omnia in quatuor partes diuisit. Vnam eamque optimam Romanæ Ecclesiæ, cuius authoritate omnibus semper iniuriis exemptus, & honoribus restitutus fuit: alteram pauperibus tertiam cornobiorum præpositisque quartam laboris sui comitibus indiuidiuis: qui nondum terras quibus se sustentarent, acceperant, legauit. An. 4. post Wilfridum restitutum Birthualdus concilium Wigorniæ conuocat: Eius commentu hanc fuisse causam referunt historiæ. Egwinus qui fuit Abbas Eueshamensis, & Wigorniensis Episcopus, sæpius factam sibi esse apparitionem virginis Mariæ suspicatus est, & propterea diuæ virgini honorem aliquem exhibere in animo habuit. Romam igitur iter capit, & Constantino Pontifici exponit, quemadmodum illi sæpe Maria in formam visa & collocuta sit, eius rei gratia mitum in mundum abillo contendit, vt Wigorniæ, vbi sibi Dei gentrix apparuerat, cœnobium & templum construere liceret. Pontifex Egwino de visione fidem habens, ipsius petitioni facile annuit; ipsumq; datum cum literis dimittens, Birthualdum admonet, vt quamprimum conuiliam non feligiosorum modo, sed etiam regni procerum, eo loci conuocet, vbi Egwino diua virgo apparuerat.
units.tr: As for himself and his own reputation, it would bring him rather disgrace and dishonour if they allowed the aged man, a bishop of forty years, to be deposed. For the people, being suspicious by nature, could not easily be persuaded that he had resigned of his own accord and innocently, rather than being removed as one deserving blame for a crime. Nothing else was achieved by this conference, except that Wilfrid, who had previously had no objection to giving up his bishopric, now, eager to recover it, gave way to this opposition, which was so badly devised. After the council was dismissed, Wilfrid set out for Rome and asked the pontiff to deign to hear his case. What more is there to say? His opponents were accused, came to Rome, and, cleverly instructed against Wilfrid by Berhtwald, brought grave charges against him before the Pontiff and many other bishops. Above all, they put forward as Wilfrid's capital crime that at the earlier council he had said he was unwilling to obey the decrees of Archbishop Theodore. He denies that he spoke in such general terms, saying he had ordered obedience only to those things which did not conflict with the decrees of the canons. How much this detracts from the authority of the canons, and that anyone who brings such an accusation submits himself to the judge's sentence, he thinks no one fails to see. In this matter Wilfrid pleaded his cause with singular modesty, and, approved by the judgement of all, he dispelled the odium of the charge brought against him. His opponents, overcome with shame, and they themselves, departed frustrated. The Pontiff wrote to the English kings, Ethelred of the Mercians and Alfrith of the Northumbrians. He had indeed heard the dispute between Wilfrid and the other bishops and, as far as he could conjecture, judged Wilfrid innocent. But because the principal parts of the accusations and injuries were not present, he advised that Berhtwald convene again a synod of the bishops of Britain, compelling Bosa and John to attend, so that, both parties having been heard, they might settle the dispute. But if Bosa and John were unwilling to attend, or did not abide by the judgement, all were to appear before him at Rome under penalty of anathema. Wilfrid, returning home, handed the letters of the Roman Pontiff to Ethelred, king of the Mercians, who had himself taken monastic vows. Ethelred, who had earlier stripped himself of royal power, nevertheless obtained from Ceonred, son of his brother Wulfhere, whom he had set up as king in his place, that Wilfrid's case be pleaded in accordance with the tenor of the letters. Berhtwald, archbishop of Canterbury, who had formerly been most hostile to Wilfrid, terrified by the threats of the Roman Pontiff, gave way in the cause. But Alfrith, king of the Northumbrians, persisted steadfastly in his purpose, exclaiming that it was unjust for a man rejected twice by all the bishops of England to be restored at the command of the Roman Pontiff. It happened that a few days later the king died, and his son Osred succeeded him. Through Berhtfrith, whom the king had used most intimately, as adviser and favourite, it was obtained that a synod be gathered in Northumbria, where, the adversaries resisting stubbornly, Wilfrid prevailed with the king's favour. After some years of quiet possession of his see, Wilfrid, lying in bed, made a will and divided all his goods into four parts. The first and best he gave to the Roman Church, by whose authority he had been freed from all injuries and restored to honours; the second to the poor; the third to the monasteries and their superiors; and the fourth, undivided, to his companions in labour who had not yet received lands on which to support themselves. In the fourth year after Wilfrid's restoration, Berhtwald convened a council at Worcester. Histories report that the cause of it was this. Ecgwine, who was abbot of Evesham and bishop of Worcester, often suspected that the apparition of the Virgin Mary had been made to him, and therefore intended to show some honour to the divine Virgin. He therefore set out for Rome and explained to Pope Constantine how Mary had often appeared to him in bodily form and spoken with him. For this reason he earnestly asked, in a remarkable way, that he might be allowed to build a monastery and church at Worcester, where the Mother of God had appeared to him. Pope Constantine, believing Ecgwine's account of the vision, readily granted his petition; sending him away with letters, he admonished Berhtwald to convene as soon as possible a council not only of the clergy but also of the nobles of the realm, in the place where the divine Virgin had appeared to Ecgwine.

units.la: Quid in hac Synodo decretum sit memoriæ non prodiitur, illud autem, cuiusmodi Sic adorationem imaginum permissam esse nõnulli scribunt, quàm verè, non statuamus, sanè sic esse credibile est, tum quòd Constantinus Pontifex, (quin iubente hæc Synodus conuncata est) hoc tempore in Italia, concilium ibi habito decreuerat, vt imagines sanctorum in Ecclesiatum parietibus depingerentur, tum etiam quòd huic concilio Winfridus natione Anglus incerfuit, qui postea cum Moguntinensis esset Episcopus, & Bonifacius dictus, non solum clericorum connubia prohibuit, sed etiam coniugatos, vxores repudiare, coegit. Huius tempore Anno Domini 729. apparuerunt duæ Cometæ, altera Solem præcedebat orientem, altera sequebatur occidentem, illa diem, hæc noctem comitabatur, mortalibus & noctium, & diernum periculu & calamitatem portendentes. Mense Ianuario duobus fere Septimanis vitæ sunt. Hoc anno montur Egbertus Sacerdos, ipso Paschatis die, cuius festi celebritatem Romano more Huenses Monachi ex illius institutio obseruabant. Columbanus etiam, qui Pictos septentrionales ad fidem Christi conuerterat, de quo scribit Beda. Qualiscunque fuerit ipse, nos (inquit) de illo certò tenemus, quod reliquit successores magna continentia regularis institutione insignes. In tempore quidem summæ festiuitatis dubios circulos sequentes (vt pote qui bus longe vltra vrbem positis, nemo Synodalia Paschalis obseruantiæ decreta porrexerat) tantum ea in Prophetiis, Euangelicis & Apostolicis literis discere poterant, pietatis & Castitatis opera diligenter obseruantes. Permansit autem huiusmodi obseruantia Paschalis apud eos tempore non pauco, vsque ad annum Dominicæ incarnationis 716. per annos 150. hæc Beda. Apud Britones etiam post Bedæ mortem permansit. Quo tempore præsulatum adiit Birthualdus, regnabant in Cantio Wilredus & Swinfardus fratres, qui Ecclesiam S. Martinii in Villa Douernensi ædificarunt, Monachosque, ibi viuentes amplis possessionibus ditarunt. Anno 695. Helwaldus & Hebaldus presbyteri, à Britannia in regionem Frisonum præcedi gratia venientes, Martyrio ibidem coronabantur.
units.tr: What was decreed in this synod is not recorded, but that the adoration of images was permitted in it, as some write, we do not determine how truly. It is certainly credible that it was so, both because Pope Constantine, who indeed had this synod convened by command, had at this time decreed, in a council held in Italy, that images of the saints be painted on the walls of churches, and also because Winfrid, an Englishman by birth, who was afterwards bishop of Mainz and called Boniface, took part in this council. He not only prohibited the marriages of clerics but also compelled married men to repudiate their wives. In his time, in the year of the Lord 729, two comets appeared: one went before the sun as it rose, the other followed it as it set; the one accompanied the day, the other the night, portending danger and calamity to mortals both by night and by day. In January they were visible for almost two weeks. In this year Egbert the priest died on the very day of Easter, whose festival the monks of Iona had observed in the Roman manner under his instruction. Columban also, who had converted the northern Picts to the faith of Christ, of whom Bede writes: "Whatever he was, this we hold for certain about him, that he left successors distinguished by great regular continence." At the time of the highest festivity, they followed uncertain cycles, since they lived far beyond the city, and no one had brought them the synodal decrees on the observance of Easter. They could learn only from the Prophets, the Gospels and the apostolic letters, diligently observing works of piety and chastity. This observance of Easter remained among them for no short time, until the year of the Lord's incarnation 716, that is, for 150 years, thus Bede. It also remained among the Britons after Bede's death. At this time Berhtwald came to the episcopate. In Kent reigned the brothers Wilred and Swaefheard, who built the church of St Martin in the township of Dover and enriched the monks living there with ample possessions. In the year 695 the priests Helewald and Hewald, who had come from Britain into the region of the Frisians to preach, were crowned with martyrdom there.

units.la: Sub hoc Birchtualdo Wintoniæ & Schirborniæ fuerunt duo Episcoparus, regnantes apud occiduos Saxones Ina Rege, qui primus concessit illud tributum, vulgò dictum Peter Pence soluendum Ecclesiæ Rom. Moritur Birthualdus. An. Dom. 731. Idibus Ianuarii, sepultusque est in Ecclesia Cant. Sedit annos 38. menses 3. dies 14.
units.tr: Under this Berhtwald there were two bishops, of Winchester and of Sherborne, while Ine reigned among the West Saxons. Ine was the first to grant that tribute, commonly called Peter's Pence, to be paid to the Roman Church. Berhtwald died on the Ides of January in the year of the Lord 731 and was buried in the church at Canterbury. He sat for 38 years, 3 months and 14 days.

units.la: IX. TAXWINVS.
units.tr: IX. TAXWINUS.

units.la: NVNC eodem quo Birthualdus moriebatur, factus est Archiepiscopus Cant. Taxwinus Mercius, alias Cadwinus vel Scadwinus Monachus ordinis S. Benedicti in Abbatia Bretton, quanquam aliter non fuisse Monachum scribunt. Beda sacerdotem illum fuisse Monasterii Brenton in prouincia Mercitorum constanter affirmati Confessarius, et anno 1. Gregorii. 3. Pontificis Romani in ciuitate sua à Daniele Wentano, Ingwaldo Londinensi, Aldwino, Lichfeldensi, & Aldulfo Rosi, Episcopis. Vt sua relligiose cuiusque, & in sacris literis egregie instructus. Anno post consecrationem 2. exorta est inter sedem Cant. & Eboracensem de primatu controversia, qua de causa ipse Romam profectus est, vbi à Gregorio Pontifice Pallio donatus, primatus etiam conformationem accepit, deinde in Anglia celebri cunctem contendit. Non multò post duos Episcopos ordinauit. De huius gestis pauca tamen aut tibi memoria dignum reperimus. Ad huius tempora historiam suam Beda perduxit, vir moderatus sermone suo gentis res gestas conscribens. Cui sanè ob id pluris quam debet posteritas, quòd plurima scripta dignissima literarum monumentis tradidit, quorum memoria (si non retinuisset) obliuionis nube tegeretur. Taxwinus, vbi tres integros annos fecisset, dierum claudit extremum, an. 794. & Cantuariæ honorifice tumulo conditus.
units.tr: Now, on the same day on which Birthwald died, Taxwin the Mercian, also called Cadwin or Scadwin, a monk of the order of St Benedict in the abbey of Bretton, was made Archbishop of Canterbury, though writers say he was otherwise not a monk. Bede states that he was a priest of the monastery of Brenton in the province of the Mercians, a man of steady and proven confessor's character, and that in the first year of Gregory III, Roman Pontiff, he was consecrated in his own city by Daniel of Winchester, Ingwald of London, Aldwin of Lichfield and Aldulf of Rochester, bishops. He was religious in his own way and excellently instructed in sacred letters. In the second year after his consecration a controversy over primacy arose between the see of Canterbury and that of York. For this reason he himself went to Rome, where he was presented with the pallium by Pope Gregory, and received also confirmation of his primacy; afterwards he returned to England and contended in a celebrated manner throughout the land. Not long after, he ordained two bishops. Yet we have found few deeds of his worth recording. Bede brought his history down to this time; he was a man of moderate style who wrote the deeds of his nation. Posterity owes him, for this reason, more than it ought to, because he handed down many writings most worthy of literary monuments, whose memory (had he not preserved it) would be covered by the cloud of oblivion. Taxwin, after he had completed three full years, closed his last day in the year 794, and was honourably buried at Canterbury.

units.la: X. NOTHELMVS.
units.tr: X. NOTHELM.

units.la: Oubelmus Londinatarpus, & ibidem Episcopus, inde ad Archiepiscopatum Cantuariensem translatus est, anno 1. præfati Gregorii 3. & ab eodem Romæ consecratus, à quo etiam Pallium anno sequente accepit. Hunc, cum adhuc in vrbe Londinensi presbyter esset, sibi multum adgesta Anglorum colligendæ proiisse, Bedaio Ecclesiasticæ historiæ prologos sictatur. Plurima enim ex Romani Pontificis scrutinio in Anglia aduexerat, quæ historiæ illius inferre cõmodissimum fuerat. Hic, si quid dignum memoria gessit, id omne silentio inuoluitur. Accidit, vt post pancorum annorum quietam in sede possessionem, graui morbo correptus interiret, sepultus in Ecclesia Cant. iacet. Hic tertius erat ex Cant. Archiepiscopis presbyter restante Beda: præter Wigardum, qui presbyter etiam in Archiepiscopum ante Theodorum ordinatus fuisset, si non prius Romæ ex peste ingrauescente perijsset, quàm consecrari poterat.
units.tr: Nothelm, bishop of London, and bishop there, was then transferred to the archbishopric of Canterbury in the first year of the aforesaid Gregory, the third (of his reign?), and was consecrated at Rome by him, from whom he also received the pallium in the following year. While he was still a priest in the city of London, he is said to have devoted himself greatly to gathering up materials of the English past, and to have assisted Bede in his Ecclesiastical History. For he had brought from the Roman archives many documents that it would have been most useful to insert into that history. He himself, if he did anything worthy of memory, has all of it wrapped in silence. It happened that, after a quiet possession of the see for some years, he was seized by a grave illness and died; he was buried in the church of Canterbury, where he lies. He was the third archbishop of Canterbury who was a priest while Bede survived, apart from Wigard, who had been ordained priest and would have been made archbishop before Theodore, had he not died at Rome of a raging plague before he could be consecrated.

units.la: XI. CVTHBERTVS.
units.tr: XI. CUTHBERT.

units.la: CVthbertus ex illustri Anglorum prosapia ortus, erat primò Herefordensis in Merciâ Episcopus, inde Nothelmo mortuo ad Cant. Archiepiscopatus translatus est, anno Pontificatus Gregorii 3. nono, dominicæ verò incarnationis. 740. Hortatu Bonifacii Moguntinensis Episcopi, cui Cuthbertus erat contemporaneus, & Ethelbaldi Regis Merciorum auxilio Synodum in Anglia conuocauit, apud Clyst iuxta Roffam. Huius Synodi hæc causa fuit. Præter modum æras hæc genio indulgebat, omnium turpitudinis generi dedita fuit, nec ij solum per seculares homines impuritas grassata, sed etiam clericalis ordo fredissimè corruptus est. Reges legitimas nuptias deserentes, virginibus, iisque monialibus sese turpiter immisçuerunt, Regumq; exemplis sequuti optimates, spretis propriis uxoribus, adulteras sibi, easq; sanctimoniales asciuerunt. Sanctimoniales ipsæ, quò se vendibiliores facerent, vtq; facilius ad amorem illi, reges, proceres, & alios quosq; homines allicerent, sub cultu vario, laticiuo, sumptuoso, & (vt authoris verbis vtar) sub vestitus pompa pudicitiam suam prostituebant. Quin etiam Monachi, animo quidem & intrinsecus obscuri, exterpo tamen corporis apparatu, nitescere fulgerêq; voluerunt: hinc facilis conic dura est, ipsos iisdem vitiis, quibus Sanctimoniales miserè coinspurcatos fuisse. Externus enim corporis cultus affectum animi, internum prodit & indicat. Episcopi etiam atque Presbyteri, quorum erat, hæc tam in laicis quam clericis reprehendere & pœnam irrogare, ad omnium sceleta conniuerunt: ipsi suam vitam perdite degebant, rixas & armaminter segregabant, lectioni scripturarum non attendebant, conciohandi munus ratissimè obibant, unde fiebat, vt vulgus hominum in tam crassa vetsaretur ignorantia, vt vix, aut articulos fidei, aut orationem dominicam idiomate suo dicere potuerint. Hæc sceleraa & impium Dei contemptum, non multò post Cuthberti obitum irruptio Danorum in Anglis puniuit & vindicauit. Quibus vitiis, vt facilius occurreretur, hæc Synodus apud Clyst congregata est. Anno Domini. 747. Cui consilio interfuerunt Ethelbaldus Merciorum Rex, cum omnibus regni sui prouincibus: Cuthbertus Cant. Archiepiscopus, Roffensis Episcopus, Totta, Hunita, ac Podda Merciorum Episcopi, Humfredus & Hereualdus occidentalium Saxonum præsules, Atwius Lindisiæ Prouinciæ, & Siega austrialium Saxonum Episcopi, aliiq; complures doctrina & moribus probatissimi. Huius Concilii capita quaedam breuibus perstringere commodissimum putamus.
units.tr: Cuthbert, sprung from the noble stock of the English, was first Bishop of Hereford in Mercia, and afterwards, on the death of Nothelm, was transferred to the archbishopric of Canterbury, in the ninth year of Pope Gregory III, and in the year of the Lord's incarnation 740. At the urging of Boniface, Bishop of Mainz, who was a contemporary of Cuthbert, and with the help of Ethelbald, King of the Mercians, he summoned a synod in England, at Clyst near Rochester. The cause of this synod was as follows. The age was given over to self-indulgence beyond measure, and was abandoned to every kind of wickedness; and this impurity raged not only among laymen but the clerical order too was most shamefully corrupted. Kings, deserting their lawful marriages, shamefully mixed themselves with virgins, and with nuns too; and the nobles, following the kings' example, cast off their own wives and took to themselves adulteresses and nuns. The nuns themselves, to make themselves more marketable and to lure kings, nobles and all other men more easily into love, prostituted their chastity under a varied, luxurious and sumptuous dress—to use the author's own words, "under the pomp of their clothing." Moreover the monks, though dark in mind and within, wished to shine and gleam in an outward display of the body; hence it is easy to conclude that they too were foully defiled by the same vices as the nuns. For outward bodily adornment betrays and indicates the inward disposition of the mind. The bishops and presbyters too, whose duty it was to rebuke these things in laity and clergy alike and to inflict punishment, winked at the crimes of all: they themselves lived dissolute lives, scattered quarrels and armed conflicts among themselves, did not attend to the reading of the Scriptures, and very rarely performed the office of preaching. As a result the common people were kept in such gross ignorance that they could scarcely say, in their own language, either the articles of faith or the Lord's Prayer. These crimes and this impious contempt of God were punished and avenged not long after Cuthbert's death by the invasion of the Danes into England. To make these vices easier to meet, this synod was gathered at Clyst, in the year of the Lord 747. Taking part in this council were Ethelbald, King of the Mercians, with all the provinces of his realm; Cuthbert, Archbishop of Canterbury; Bishops Totta of Rochester, Hunita, and Podda of the Mercians; Humfrith and Hereward, prelates of the West Saxons; Atwi of the province of Lindsey; and Siega, Bishop of the South Saxons; and several others most approved for learning and morals. We think it most convenient to set out briefly some of the chapters of this council.

units.la: Primum decreto sancitum fuit ne quis in sacros ordines admitteretur, qui non integritate morum bene apud omnes audiret. Vt sacræ scripturæ lectioni per Monasteria assiduè operam navarent. Vt Dominicam orationem & Symbolum Apostolicum Anglicò idiomate discant & do-cerent. Vt modesta voce sacra in Ecclesiis canant. Vt dies Dominicus summo cum honore teneatur. Vt Regum & Principum salutem publicis precibus Deo commendarent, &c.
units.tr: First, it was decreed that no one should be admitted to holy orders who was not well spoken of by all for integrity of life. That they should be diligent in reading Holy Scripture throughout the monasteries. That they should learn and teach the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed in the English language. That they should sing sacred songs in the churches with a modest voice. That the Lord's Day should be kept with the highest honour. That they should commend the welfare of kings and princes to God in public prayers, etc.

units.la: Alia sunt huius Synodi acta permulta, quæ nos sicco pede præterire vtilissimum duximus: Hæc autem omnia Cuthbertus Archiepiscopus Cant. post Synodum dissolutum; per Rinebartum Diaconum suum Bonifacio Moguntino Archipræsuli mira celeritate transmisit: quæ ille grato accipiens animo, sine mora ad Ethelbaldum Anglorum Regem literas dedit, quorum exemplar hic subscribemus.
units.tr: There are very many other acts of this synod, which we thought it most useful to pass over lightly; but all these things Cuthbert, Archbishop of Canterbury, after the synod was dissolved, sent with remarkable speed through his deacon Rinebert to Boniface, the chief bishop of Mainz; and he, receiving them with a grateful mind, without delay wrote a letter to Ethelbald, King of the English, a copy of which we subjoin here.

units.la: Epistola Bonifacii ad Ethelbaldum Anglorum Regem.
units.tr: Letter of Boniface to Ethelbald, King of the English.

units.la: OMINO charissimo, & in Christi amore, cæteris regibus Anglorum præferendo, Ethelbaldo, Bonifacius Archiepiscopus, legatus Germanicus Romanæ Ecclesiæ, perpetuam in Christo, charitatis salutem. Confitemur coram Deo, quia, quando prosperitatem vestram & fidem, & bona opera audimus, lætamur. Quando autem adversum, vel in cuentu bellorum, vel periculo animarum de vobis cognoscimus, tristamur. Audimus enim quod de cælestinis interpellatus, furta, & rapinas prohibes, pacem diligis, viduas & pauperes tueris: ob quæ gratias Deo agimus. Quòd vero legitimum matrimonium fugis, si præter exteras castitatis sacerdos esset laudabile: sed quia in luxuria, & adulterio etiam cum Sanctimonialibus voluptas est vituperabile, & damnabile. Nam & famam gloriæ vestræ coram Deo & hominibus cŏfundis: & inter idololatras constituit, & tèplu Dei violasti. Quapropter (fili charissime) pœnitentiam agas & memorare, quam turpe sit, ut tu, qui multis gentibus, domo Dei, dominaris, ad iniuriam eius, sis libidinis servus. Audimus præterea quòd optimates pene omnes gentis Merciorum, exemplo tuo legitimas uxores deserat, & adulteras frequentes, sanctimoniales constuprent. Quod quàm alienum sit ab honestate, doceat vos a- liarum gentium institutio. Nam in antiqua Saxonia, ubi quàm est Christi cognitio, si virgo in paterna domo maritata, subconiuge fuerit adulterata, manu propria sti angularis ctemant, & supra fossam sepultæ, corruptorem suspendunt aut cingulo tenus vestibus abscissis flagellant eam calce matronæ, & cultellis pungunt, & de villa in villam inter se deducunt noxæ flagellatrices, donec interimant. Insuper & Winzedi (quod est fœtidissimus genus horrinum, hunc habens morem, ut mulier (viro mortuo) se in rogo mittent vivere ... ut præcipitet. Si ergo gentiles Deum ignorantes tantum zelo castitatis habeant, quid ... bi conuenit (fili charissime) qui Christianus & Rex es? Parce ergo animæ tuæ, parce multitudini populi tui, tuo pereutis exemplo, de quorum animabus reddituros es ratio- nem. Attende & illud: quòd ut gens Anglorum, sicut in Gallia & in Italia, & ab ipsis Pa- ra extra commixtione sit gens ignaua, & Dei contemptrix, quæ perditis moribus patriam pessundet. Sicut Burgundialibus & Prouincialibus & Hispanis contigit: quos Sarraceni multis annis propter peccata præterita infestarunt. Præterea nunciatum est nobis, quòd multa priuilegia Ecclesiarum, & Monasteriorum auferens, etiá ad hoc ingens faci-nus, duces tuos prouoces: sed animo reuoluas quàm quàm graues vindicta Dcus in priores Reges exercuit huius culpæ cöscios, quam in tear gumus. Nam Celredum prædecessorem, fluprat orem Sanctimonialium, & Ecclesiasticarum immunitatum violatorem, splendide cum suis comitibus epulantem, spiritus malignus arripuit, & sine confessione & viatico, cum Diabolo sermocinanti, & legem Dei detestanti, animam extorsit. Ofteduum quoq; Regem Deirorum & Berniciorum ciusdem scelerisreum, ita efficit ... numegit, ut regnum, in iuuenili ætate, consimili morte amitteret. Carolus quoq; princeps Francorum, Monasteriorum multorum euersor, & Ecclesiasticorum bonorum in usus proprios commutator, post assiduos corporis dolores horrenda morte consumptus est. Quapropter (fili charissime) paterne, & obnixe deprecamur, ut non despicias consilium patrum tuorum, qui Dei amore moti, Celsitudinem tuam mente instituere studeat. Nihil enim bono regi salubrius, quàm, si Italia commissa cum arguantur, libenter emendet. Salomon enim dicit, qui diligit disciplinam, diligit sapientiam. Idem (fili charissime) ostendentes consilium iustum, ob testamur & obsecramus per patrem omnipotentem Deum, & Filium eius Iesum Christum, & Spiritum sanctum, ut recorderis, quàm fugitiua sit vita præsens, & quàm breuis, & quàm momentanea delectatio spurcæ carnis, & quàm ignominiosum sit, ut breuis vitæ homo, mala exempla in perpetuum, posteris relinquat. Incipe ergo meliorib⁹ moribus vitam componere, & præceritos errores iuuentutis corrigere, ut hic coram hominibus laudem habeas, & in futura vita, æterna gloria gaudeas. Valeat celsitudinem, tuam & bonis operibus proficere optamus.
units.tr: To the most beloved lord Ethelbald, to be preferred above the other kings of the English in the love of Christ, Boniface, Archbishop, legate of Germany to the Roman Church, sends perpetual greeting in Christ and in charity. We confess before God that when we hear of your prosperity, your faith and your good works, we rejoice; but when we learn of adversity concerning you, whether in the outcome of wars or in peril to souls, we grieve. For we hear that, having been admonished by the heavenly ones, you forbid thefts and robberies, you love peace, and you protect widows and the poor; for these things we give thanks to God. But as for your fleeing lawful marriage, it might be praiseworthy in a priest apart from outward chastity; yet since pleasure in lust and adultery, even with nuns, is blameworthy and damnable, you are also bringing shame upon the reputation of your glory before God and men, and you have placed yourself among idolaters and have violated the temple of God. Therefore, dearest son, repent, and consider how shameful it is that you, who rule over many nations and over the house of God, should be the slave of lust to the injury of him. We hear moreover that almost all the nobles of the people of the Mercians, following your example, desert their lawful wives and frequently defile nuns. How far this is from honesty the custom of other nations may teach you. For in ancient Saxony, where the knowledge of Christ is not yet, if a virgin married in her father's house was defiled by an adulterer, the matrons, with their own hands, cut off the hair of her head and, burying her in a pit, hang the seducer above the trench or, stripping her garments down to the waist, flog her with the heel; they pierce her with knives, and the avenging women lead her from village to village until they kill her. Besides, the Wends (which is a most foul and savage people, having this custom, that a woman, when her husband has died, is cast alive into his funeral pyre...) so that she may perish headlong. If therefore Gentiles who are ignorant of God have such zeal for chastity, how fitting is it, dearest son, that you, who are a Christian and a king, should do otherwise? Spare therefore your soul, spare the multitude of your people, whom you strike down by your example, and for whose souls you must render an account. Attend also to this: that the English people, if it is not kept apart from intermingling with the Pagans, as has happened in Gaul and in Italy, will become an idle people and a despiser of God, and by its corrupt manners will ruin its country, as happened to the Burgundians, the Provincials and the Spaniards, whom the Saracens harassed for many years on account of their past sins. Moreover, we have been told that you incite your leaders even to this huge crime, that you take away many privileges of churches and monasteries. But consider in your mind how grievously God avenged this crime on earlier kings who were conscious of it, which we ourselves are afraid of. For the evil spirit seized Ceolred, your predecessor, a debaucher of nuns and a violator of ecclesiastical immunities, while he was feasting splendidly with his companions, and he wrung out his soul without confession and viaticum, while he talked with the Devil and cursed the law of God. Likewise Oswald, king of the Deirans and Bernicians, guilty of the same wickedness, was so struck down that in his youthful age he lost his kingdom by a similar death. Charles also, prince of the Franks, the overthrower of many monasteries and the diverter of ecclesiastical goods to his own uses, was consumed by a horrible death after continual bodily pains. Therefore, dearest son, we earnestly and fatherly beseech you not to despise the counsel of your fathers, who, moved by love of God, strive to instruct your Highness in mind. For nothing is more wholesome for a good king than, when Italy is committed and he is rebuked, to amend willingly. For Solomon says, "he who loves discipline loves wisdom." Likewise, dearest son, we show you this just counsel, and we testify and beseech you through God the Father almighty, and his Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, that you remember how fleeting the present life is, how brief, and how momentary the delight of the filthy flesh, and how shameful it is that a man of brief life should leave bad examples to posterity forever. Begin therefore to order your life by better manners, and to correct the errors of your youth that you have committed, so that you may have praise here before men, and in the future life may rejoice in eternal glory. We pray that your Highness may also advance in good works. Farewell.

units.la: Eius etiam argumenti literas, Bonifacius Cuthberto Archiepiscopo misit, in quibus præcipuè hortatur, ut Clericos & Sanctimoniales de splendore & pompa vestium acriter increpet, quippe cum tanta libidinum ingluvie, tam fœda vitiorum labe conspurcaChristum profitentes minimo decerent, essi Romana sœde Christianæ religionis vnica potestas (quæ sed nis morum Magistram, vtcunque idem solam præceptricem fallacissime vendicat, ipsos Paganos crudelitate, sagittis, & perditis facinoribus permultis gradibus superet. Idem etiam Zachariam Papam grauiter adhortatur, vt quosdam Paganicos abusus Romæ grassantes eradicet, præcipue vero barbaram illam in plateis dimicandi ferè tanquam in choros contueudinem, & sacrilega quadam, & obscœna canendi morem quotidianum. Addit peraterea, nunciarum illi esse à quibusdam, Romanas mulieres Paganorum esse famas, quod philacteria, & ligaturas in brachiis & cruribus gestas habeant; & publicè vanum sic prostituant. Quæ omnia propagandæ veritatis, non in incrementò sed impedimento nimium sunt. Nam eum hominis alioqui rudes & barbari hæc ibi vitia grassari videant, peccandi licentiam liberè datam sibi existimant. Aliæ sunt, quæ Romano Pontifici Bonifacius incuiciat; verùm quia nihil ad nos, illius non immorabimur. Ad Cuthbertum nostrum, unde defleximur, reuertamur oratio. Ille Ecclesiam suam cathedralem Christi, honore aliquo insignire cupiens, cùm nullâ honorabili sepultura adornatam videret, indignum rattus est, defunctorum Archiepiscoporum corporibus suam Ecclesiam spoliare & ad Monasterium Petri & Pauli, Sanctiquè Augustini ea semper transferri. Iauit ergo secum rationem, quonam modo hanc consuetudinem irritam faceret. Itaque ad Regem Eadberrum in Cantio tum regnantem accedit, ab eo precibus contendit, vt prædictum sepulturæ morem mutaret, & mutatum suo Regio edicto confirmaret, quod partim pre-
units.tr: Boniface also sent letters on the same subject to Archbishop Cuthbert, in which he chiefly urges him to rebuke sharply the clergy and nuns for the splendour and pomp of their clothing, since those who profess Christ ought, with such a gluttony of lusts and such a foul stain of vices, to be least of all adorned; although the Roman see, which falsely claims for itself alone the power of teacher of morals in whatever way, surpasses even the Pagans in cruelty, arrows and many kinds of wicked crimes. He also earnestly exhorts Pope Zachary to root out certain Pagan abuses raging at Rome, above all that barbarous custom of fighting in the public squares almost as in dances, and that sacrilegious and obscene custom of singing daily. He adds moreover that he has been told by some people that Roman women imitate the practices of the Pagans, in that they wear amulets and charms on their arms and legs, and so publicly make a vain display of themselves. All these things are not an increase but a very great hindrance to the spreading of the truth. For when rude and barbarous men see these vices flourishing there, they think that a license to sin has been freely given to them. There are other matters which Boniface lays upon the Roman Pontiff; but since they have nothing to do with us, we shall not dwell on them. Let our discourse return to our Cuthbert, from whom we have digressed. He, desiring to adorn his cathedral church of Christ with some honour, when he saw it lacking any honourable burial, judged it unworthy that the bodies of deceased archbishops should be stripped from his church and always transferred to the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul, and of Augustine. He therefore turned over in his mind how he might make this custom void. And so he went to King Eadberht, then reigning in Kent, and begged him with entreaties to change the aforesaid custom of burial, and to confirm the change by his royal edict, which he at last obtained partly by pre-

units.la: cario, partim etiam precio interueniente tandem obtinuit. An. Dom. 758. Cuthbertus morbo correptus grauì, mortem animadvertit sibi impendere: Itaque in Ecclesia sua seorsim docetes, totam familiam suam & connectitum Monachorum Christi (qui suum de Sepultura mandatum facile exequi erant paratissimi) ad se vocatum, iureiurando astringit, ne qua infirmitatis aut mortis suæ fama volitaret, unde aliquod suctus indicium publicum fieret: neue exequiæ celebrarentur, donec corpus per aliquot dies humo conditum fuisset. Tertio post sepulturam, che campanis pulsatur, certus rumor mortis diuulgatur. Quo audito, Aldhumus Sancti Augustini Abbas cum sociis accessit, caduer Archiepiscopi uixta nitudo pristinus, secum ablaturus. At vbi iam sepultum repertus & antiquum etiam sepulturæ consuetudinem Regia autoritate sublatam didicit, frustrarus voto, domum tum suis reuertitur. Quàm iniquo animo, hocillis iam cognitum, Monachi Augustiniensis tulerint, ex historia quorundam ibi Monachorum planè compertum habemus: Cuthbertum enim ob causam prædictam, hominem doli plenum, vulpina callidutate furtum denique serpentinum interficientem marrem quidam appellant. Alij referunt Cuthbertum nonuiti ipsa maiore Ecclesia fuisse numulo conditum, sed in Ecclesia ei pene contiguo, in honorem Iohannis Baptistæ ab ipso fabricata, quod idcirco extruxit, vt & baptisteria, & examinationes iudiciorum pro diuersis causis, ad correctionem scelerum, illic celebrarentur, & Archiepiscoporum corpora in ea sepelirentur. Hanc vero Iohannis Ecclesiam, multis annorum transactis seculis, cum Ecclesia Christi, & officinis, flamma deuoratur: Ecclesiam Christi postea Lanfrancus Archiepiscopus repatauit. Ari. Dom. 741. Monasterium in Eboraco ciuitate succensum est. Anno 745. Visi sunt in aere igneî ictus ea ætate rarisne ante intellectis, qui pene per totam Angliam visi sunt Kal. Ianuarii. An. Dom. 747. stellarum de cœlo casus ita omnes terrore affecit, vt consummationem seculi instare putarent.
units.tr: treaties, partly also by an intervening payment. In the year of the Lord 758, Cuthbert, seized by a grievous sickness, perceived that death was hanging over him. Therefore, in his church, having summoned apart his whole household and the associated monks of Christ (who were most ready to carry out his command concerning his burial), he bound them by oath that no report of his illness or death should fly abroad, whereby some public sign of it might be made, and that no funeral rites should be celebrated until the body had been laid in the earth for some days. On the third day after the burial, when the bells were rung, a certain rumour of his death was spread abroad. On hearing this, Aldhun, abbot of Saint Augustine's, came with his companions, intending to carry off the body of the Archbishop, as was the old custom. But when he found that it had already been buried, and learned that the ancient custom of burial had been abolished by royal authority, he was frustrated in his wish and returned home with his men. How unhappily the monks of Augustine's took this news, we have plainly learned from the history of certain monks there: for they call Cuthbert, on account of the aforesaid matter, a man full of guile, who with fox-like cunning and at last with serpentine theft had caught the body. Others report that Cuthbert was buried not in the greater church itself but in a church almost adjoining it, built by himself in honour of John the Baptist, which he erected for this reason: that baptisteries and the hearings of judgements in various causes, for the correction of crimes, might be held there, and that the bodies of archbishops might be buried in it. But this church of John, many centuries having passed, was devoured by flame together with the church of Christ and its workshops; the church of Christ was afterwards repaired by Archbishop Lanfranc. In the year of the Lord 741, the monastery at the city of York was burned. In the year 745, fiery strokes were seen in the air, of a kind rarely understood before that age, which were seen almost throughout all England on the Kalends of January. In the year of the Lord 747, a fall of stars from heaven so affected everyone with terror that they thought the end of the age was at hand.

units.la: XII. BREGWINVS.
units.tr: XII. BREGWINUS.

units.la: Bregwinus ex antiqua Saxonia claris parentibus oriundus, postea pueritia excellerat, factis literis operam dedit, cuius amore raptus, in Angliam natiuo relicto solo, se contulit, vbi propter modestiam & morum integritatem, tantam apud omnes gratiam iniuit, vt in numerum reliquorum incolarum & ciuium asciscerentur. In sacris vero literis tantos progressus fecit, vt mortuo tunc Cuthberto Cant. Archiepiscopo solus dignus haberetur, qui in Archiepiscopatu etiam inuitus succederet. Bonis operibus ita claruit, vt omnes sui temporis multis gradibus anteceelleret. Is de præfata mutatione sepulturæ Archiepiscoporum Cant. gesta prædecessoris sui pro raro habens, iisdem quoque vestigiis insistit, ad cuius confirmationem, tam regiæ, quàm Apostolica authoritas ex sua instigatione intercessit. Cumque tres annos Ecclesiam suam probe administrasset, spiritum exhalauit non tamen illius obitus publicè cogaticus erat, quàm in Ecclesia Ioannis ioxta præcursores suum sepultus fue-rat. Tum demum mortis eius fit diuulgatio, Lanterimus, executæ de more petitionis. Quod vbi conuenerunt S. Augustini innouit, confestim Lambertus ibidem Abbas, Ecclesiam S. Trinitatis, sine Christi, armato militi ingrediatur, vt corpus defuncti violenter abduceret, si quam ei illius voto morem gerere denegarent. Aut vbi iam cum sepultum, sque dolo, vt prius circumuentum vidisset, spe conatuque frustratus, dolore & pœnitentia percussus, domum cum sociis reuertitur, appellationes pro sancto & libertate sui Monasterii, & iniurijs illatis, ad summum Pontificem variis interposuit. Circa idem tempus sancta de cœlo nix decidit, quæ gelu & frigore tantam moxglaciem contraxerat, vt ab illo fluminis arboreibus, oleraque manu ex parte arauerunt, & admodum malor parafame interiit. Tunc etiam vrbes multæ, Monasteria, villæque per diuersa locaconstituta, repentino ignis incendio pericrutit videlicet, Strechburg, Wenta cantas, Lodinium, Eboracum, Donacestria, aliaque permulta loca: fulmen etiam horribile tunc cohibetur ferunt, quod plurimis terrorem incussit. Quantum verò timoris, fulminis horror incusseret, quod tunc vndecunque peruasit, aliis discutiendum relinquo.
units.tr: Bregwin, born of an ancient Saxon family of distinguished parents, excelled from boyhood and devoted himself to letters. Seized by his love of learning, he left his native soil and went to England. There, on account of his modesty and the integrity of his character, he won such favour with everyone that he was admitted among the remaining inhabitants and citizens. In sacred letters he made such progress that, when Cuthbert, Archbishop of Canterbury, died, he alone was thought worthy to succeed him in the archbishopric, even though he was unwilling. He shone in good works so that he surpassed all his contemporaries by many degrees. Regarding the aforesaid change in the burial of the Archbishops of Canterbury, he thought his predecessor's acts worthy of note and followed the same footsteps; to confirm it, both royal and apostolic authority were interposed at his instigation. When he had administered his Church well for three years, he breathed his last. Yet his death was not made public so much as he was buried in the church of John, beside his predecessors. Then at last news of his death was spread, and the customary petition was made. When the monks of St Augustine's learned of this, Lambert, the abbot there, at once entered the church of the Holy Trinity with an armed soldier, so that he might violently carry off the dead man's body if they refused to comply with his wish. But when he saw that the body had already been buried and that he had been outwitted by trickery, he was frustrated in hope and effort, struck with grief and penitence. He returned home with his companions and lodged various appeals with the supreme Pontiff, on behalf of the sanctity and liberty of his monastery and for the injuries done to it. About the same time, holy snow fell from heaven, which by frost and cold formed such thick ice that the trees and herbs by that river were in part torn up by hand, and many people perished of famine. Then too many cities, monasteries and villages, situated in various places, were suddenly endangered by fire, namely Strechburg, Wenta, Lodinium (London), York, Doncaster, and very many other places. They also say that a dreadful thunderbolt then struck, which terrified many. How great the fear caused by the horror of the lightning, which then struck from every quarter, I leave for others to discuss.

units.la: XIII. Lambertus, vel Lambertus.
units.tr: XIII. Lambertus, vel Lambertus.

units.la: ONACHI Ecclesiæ Christi pastoris solatio priuati, ancipiti cura diu attractu fluctuabant, quem loco defuncti præficerent. Læberti prædicti Abbatis S. Augustini, summam in repetendo, ac profecto ius suum iure atque iudicio constantiam, & eam in tebus Ecclesiasticis, quam secularibus, singularem prudentiam animaduertunt, tumentque tamen nes, appellationes ad Papam factas prosequendo, sepulturam Archiepiscopi oportum precio, vel precepto solitum locum teducerer. Quòigitur huicmalo venientiocyus occurreretent, Lambertum Abbatem in Archiepiscopum eligunt, futurum spectantes, vt fratres Augustinianis auxilio tanti patris ortbati, etsinon bi nectiam, amote tamen, & teuerentia, qua Lambertum prosequebatur, ducti, ab inceptis appellationibus desisterent. Quæ spes, vt exitus ret declarauit, ipsos non fefellit. Lambertus itaque, ab Abbate Monasterii D. Augustini, Archiepiscopus Cant. factus, à Paulino Papæ nominis primo, pallio donatus est. Hunc Offa Rex Mercio-rum (quòd graues cum Cantuariensibus inimicitias gereret) primatu, omnibusque prædi-is, quæ in sua ditione habuit, spoliate cogitans, regnum quæ suum Mercciorum, Archiepiscopatus honore insignire cupiens, ab Adriano Papa legatis mittit petiit, vt Eadulfum Lichefeldensem Episcopum pallio donaret, omnibusque Regni sui Episcopis præficeret: quam rem facile obtinuit, Papa verisimilibus Apostolicis argumentis (id est, pecuniis) persuasus. Romanienim Pontifices, varia supraque vires negocia suscipientes, facilime vel in multis illicitis, ad assensum trahuntur. Eadulfo igitur Lichefeldensi Episcopo, Merciorum, Episcopalem celsitudinem administranti subiiciebantur hi Merciorum Episcopi: Denebertus Wigorniensis, Werebertus Legecestrensis, Eadulphus Sinacestrensis, Wlmardus Herefordensis, necnon & ocientalium Anglorum Episcopi, scilicet: Harardus Helinhamensis & Tidferth Domuensis. Sed vero Cantuariensi, Londinensis, Wintoniensis, Roffensis, Sireburnensis, ansitites dumLambertus sedit, tantum supeturi fuerunt, etsi neque sumptui, neque labori pepercerit, vt sedem suæ priritiæ dignitati restitueret. Quidam verò referunt, cum legati ab Adriano Papa in Angliam missi, concilium apud Calchuth in Prouincia Northumbrorum tenuissent Anno 787, ibi Lambertum, Archiepiscopatus præfatam partem, Episcopo Lichefeldensi remissile. Sed Lambertus postquam annos plutimos Præsulatus dignitatem magna cum constantia, nec minore labore, tenuisset, vitæ eximum iam sibi instare prægiens, cupiensque antecessorum suorum statuta de sepeliendis Archiepiscopis lata in nihilum redigere, & sepulturam ad antiquum reducere locum, iussit, vt de mortuo corpus ad Ecclesiam Apostolorum Petri & Pauli, Sanctique Augustini sepeliendum deferretur. Cuius præcepto & voluntati facile paruerunt. Defunctus enim in capitulo S. Augustini, honorificè traditur sepulturæ. Circa hoc rempus Badnlf, siue Beadulf, Episcopus Candidæ Casæ, olim vocatæ Viternæ, vlximus Episcoporum eius loci constitutus est. Citò enim defecit Episcopatus, quod in extremis Anglorum finibus situs Scotorum & Piētorum depopulationis nimium obnoxius fuerit. Illic Niniantus terræ mandabatur, uatione Britannus, qui primus in illis partibus Christum euangelizauit. Sedente Lamberto Cathedrae ciuitas iniuria Eorumredi Merciorum tyranni, cremata & solo æquata fuit, quo etiam anno ipse iusta Dei vindicta incendio miserè periit. Tunc etiam stellas de cœlo cadentes mirum in modum quiuis conspicabantur.
units.tr: The Church of Christ, deprived of the comfort of its pastor, long wavered in uncertain anxiety over whom to set in the place of the dead man. Noticing the great steadfastness of the aforesaid Abbot Lambert of St Augustine's in pursuing his claim, and his rightful resolve in matters of law and judgement, and his singular prudence in Church affairs as much as in secular ones, and fearing that appeals to the Pope would continue, and that the archbishop's burial would be returned to its usual place by payment or by command, they therefore elected Abbot Lambert as archbishop, to meet this evil more quickly. They hoped that the brothers of St Augustine's, bereft of the help of so great a father, would, though not moved by this, yet led by love and the reverence they showed to Lambert, give up the appeals they had begun. This hope, as the outcome showed, did not deceive them. So Lambert, made archbishop of Canterbury from the abbot of the monastery of St Augustine, was given the pallium by Pope Paul the First. Offa, King of the Mercians, because he bore grave enmity against the men of Canterbury, thought of stripping them of the primacy and of all the estates they held in his dominion. Wishing to adorn his kingdom of Mercia with the honour of an archbishopric, he sent envoys to Pope Adrian asking that he would give the pallium to Eadulf, bishop of Lichfield, and set him over all the bishops of his kingdom. This he easily obtained, the Pope being persuaded by plausible apostolic arguments, that is, by money. For Roman pontiffs, undertaking affairs of many kinds beyond their strength, are very easily drawn to assent, even in many unlawful matters. So the Mercian bishops were made subject to Eadulf, bishop of Lichfield, who administered the episcopal dignity of the Mercians: Denebert of Worcester, Werebert of Leicester, Eadulf of Sidnacester, Wlmard of Hereford, and also the bishops of the East Angles, namely Harard of Elmham and Tidferth of Dunwich. But the sees of Canterbury, London, Winchester, Rochester and Sherborne survived only so long as Lambert sat, although he spared neither expense nor labour to restore his see to its former dignity. Some, however, report that when legates sent by Pope Adrian into England held a council at Calchuth in the province of Northumbria in the year 787, Lambert there surrendered the aforesaid part of the archbishopric to the bishop of Lichfield. But Lambert, after he had held the dignity of the prelacy for many years with great steadfastness and no less labour, foreseeing that the end of his life was at hand, and wishing to annul the decrees of his predecessors concerning the burial of archbishops and to restore burial to its ancient place, ordered that after his death his body should be carried to be buried in the church of the Apostles Peter and Paul and of St Augustine. His command and wish were readily obeyed, for when he was dead he was honourably laid in the chapter house of St Augustine's. About this time Badulf, or Beadulf, bishop of Candida Casa, formerly called Whithorn, was appointed the last of the bishops of that place. For the bishopric soon failed, because it lay on the farthest borders of the English and was too exposed to the ravaging of the Scots and Picts. There Ninian, a Briton by birth, who first preached Christ in those parts, was committed to the earth. While Lambert sat in the see, the city of the see was burned and levelled to the ground by the injustice of Eorred, tyrant of the Mercians, and in that same year Eorred himself perished miserably in a fire, by the just vengeance of God. Then too, anyone could see stars falling from heaven in a wonderful manner.

units.la: Non multò post in cœlo rubea signa & visu horrida post occasum Solis apparuerunt: Serpentes visi sunt in Suthsexia, ac si è terra scaturirent. Sanguinem etiam pluebat. Hæc prodigia, signa erant & prognostica itæ Dei, malorumque in Britannia futurorum. Breui enim post per Danorum latrocinia, urbium depopulatio, & hominum magna strages subsequuta permultos annos duravit. Nec mirum, nam & merum, & verum Dei cultum abiecerant, pieratem omnem exuerant, & viciorum sordibus taa occalluerant, ut sanum consilium nihil apud eos valeret.
units.tr: Not long afterwards, red signs appeared in the sky after sunset, dreadful to behold. Serpents were seen in Sussex, as though springing out of the earth. It even rained blood. These portents were signs and omens of the wrath of God and of the evils that were to come upon Britain. For soon afterwards, through the robberies of the Danes, the plundering of cities and a great slaughter of men followed, and lasted for very many years. Nor is this surprising, for they had cast off both the pure and the true worship of God, had put off all piety, and had become so hardened by the filth of vices that sound counsel had no weight with them.

units.la: XIV. ATHE- LARDVS.
units.tr: XIV. ATHELARDUS.

units.la: THELARDVS siue Edhelardus primò Abbas Malduni, deinde Wintoniensis Episcopus, postremò ob virtutem sapientiam, & favorem procerum Archiepiscopus Cant. fuit, anno Imperii Offæ Regis Merciorum 35. Adriant Papæ 21. Ac tertio ante Præsulatum Leonis 4. qui Papa in Epistola quadam sua ad Kenulfum Regem Merciorum testimonium Athelardo tribuit sanctissimi, clarissimi, & perinsignis Præsulis, & bonis moribus ornati. Ostendit autem Merciorum Rege mortuo, nec non filio eius Edgfrido egregio luuene (qui cum patre regnaret, vnà cum patre animam effluit) Kenulfus Cuthberti filius diadematæ Regio coronatur. Ad hunc Athelardus cum Eaubaldo Eboracensi Archiepiscopo accessit, vt cum eo de amissa Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ dignitate ageret. Kenulfus igitur Rex ab Archiep. f oris certior factus, quantum nefas diminuendo Cantuariensem Prouinciam ante cessit eius Offa commisisset, pristinam illi dignitatem restituit. Missis igitur ad Leonem Papam, Adriant successorem suis, & omnium Anglorum Pontificum litteris (ipso Archiepiscopo Athelardo legationem bene & fideliter fungente) quod petiit, impetrauit: vnde Alcuinus Caroli Magni præceptor, his verbis Athelardo gratulatur. Audita prosperitate itineris vestri, & reuersionis in patriam: & quomodo ab Apostolico suscepti fuistis, toto cordis affectu gratias egi Domino Deo, qui magno clementiæ dono, prospero itinere, viam vestram dirigens, dedit vobis gratiam in conspectu Apostolici, votiq; compotem redire in patriam concessit, & primi Doctoris nostri sacratissimam sedem adprehensitem dignitatem per re iterum reducere dignatus est.
units.tr: Thelardus, or Edhelardus, was first abbot of Malmesbury, then bishop of Winchester, and last, on account of his virtue, wisdom and the favour of the nobles, archbishop of Canterbury. This was in the 35th year of Offa, king of the Mercians, the 21st year of Pope Adrian, and the third year before the pontificate of Leo IV. In a certain letter of his to Kenulf, king of the Mercians, Pope Leo bore witness that Athelard was a most holy, most distinguished and singularly eminent prelate, adorned with good morals. When the Mercian king died, and his son Edgfrid, an excellent young man (who had reigned together with his father and died with him), Kenulf, son of Cuthbert, was crowned king. Athelard came to him together with Eadbald, archbishop of York, to discuss with him the loss of the dignity of the church of Canterbury. King Kenulf, therefore, having been informed by the archbishop how great a wrong Offa had committed in diminishing the province of Canterbury, restored to it its former dignity. Letters were then sent to Pope Leo, successor of Adrian, and to all the English prelates, and Archbishop Athelard himself carried out the embassy well and faithfully, and obtained what he sought. Hence Alcuin, the tutor of Charlemagne, congratulated Athelard in these words: "On hearing of the success of your journey and of your return to your country, and of how you were received by the Apostolic See, I gave thanks with my whole heart to the Lord God, who, in His great gift of mercy, directing your way with a prosperous journey, gave you favour in the sight of the Apostolic See, granted that you should return home with your wish fulfilled, and deigned to restore again the dignity of the most sacred see of our first teacher, which you had recovered."

units.la: Quod etiam Eaubaldus Eboracensis Archiepiscopus mutuis probitatis officiis adiutor Athelardo Cant. Archiepiscopo fuit, quò hæc inuasio quàm Offa, Rex Merciorum in Cant. Ecclesiam fecerat, ad nihilum redigeretur. Idem etiam Alcuinus in alia epistola ad eundem Athelardum scriberet. Audiens salutem & prosperitatem vestram, & conuentum cum Eboracensi Archiepiscopo filio meo Eaubaldo, satis mihi placuit, speranti ex vestræ colloquio sanctitatis, vnitatem Sanctæ Ecclesiæ iterum renouari, quæ partim discussa est nulla ratione habita, sed quadam potestatis cupiditate. &c. Athelardus, postquam sedis suæ pristinam dignitatem recuperauisset, literas etiam à Papa decretum Kenulfum Regem Merciorum. Quas vero ad Papam prius literas dederit, non erit alienum à nostro instituto hic inserre.
units.tr: Eadbald, archbishop of York, also helped Athelard, archbishop of Canterbury, by the mutual good offices of uprightness, so that the wrong which King Offa of the Mercians had done to the church of Canterbury might be brought to nothing. Alcuin wrote the same thing in another letter to the same Athelard: "Hearing of your health and prosperity, and of your meeting with the archbishop of York, my son Eadbald, I was very glad, hoping that from your conference with such holiness the unity of the holy Church would be renewed again, a unity which was partly broken, not from any reasonable cause, but from a certain greed for power, etc." After Athelard had recovered the former dignity of his see, he also obtained from the Pope a decree in favour of King Kenulf of the Mercians. It will not be out of place for my purpose here to insert the letter which he sent to the Pope beforehand.

units.la: EPISTOLA KENULFI MERCIORUM REGIS ad Leonem Papam.
units.tr: LETTER OF KENULF, KING OF THE MERCIANS, TO POPE LEO.

units.la: DOMINO beatissimo, & veræ amantissimo Leoni, Sanctæ & Apostolicæ sedis Romanæ Pontifici, Kenulfus gratia Dei Rex Merciorum, cum Episcopis ducibus, & omnibus sub nostra ditione, dignitatis gradu sincerissimæ dilectionis in Christo salutem. Gratias omnipotenti Deo semper agimus, qui Ecclesiam suo præcioso sanguine acquisitam inter diuersas mundi huius procellas nouis semper duis ethus, prioribus ad vitam sumptis assuefecit ad portum salutis attractum, eumque nouali luce infundere quatenus nullo sit tenebrarum errore fuscata, sed veritatis inoffensio pede gradiatur; undemerito omnis per orbem exultat Ecclesia. Quia cum omnium verus remunerator bonorum, gloriosissimum gregis sui pastorem Adrianum perpetuò remanentandum, super æthera duxisset: quia tamen oibus, pia erexit prouidentia pastorem, qui scit ouile Dominicum ad caulas vitæ, non infersus agitare. Nos quoque merito, quos exiremitas orbis tenet, eodem modo præ czeteris gloriamur, quia illius salus & illius prosperitas est nobis perennis exultatio: quia vnde tibi Apostolica dignitas, inde nobis veritas fidei innotuit. Quapropter opportunū arbitror tuis sanctissimis iussis aurem obedientiæ nostræ humiliter inclinare, & quæ tuæ pietati ritè nobis sequenda videantur, omni conatu implenda. Quæ verò rationi contraria deprehensa fuerint, citius declinanda, ac interim à nobis omnibus modis reseçenda. Sed modò ego Kenulfus Dei gratia Rex, excellentiam tuam humilis exoro, vt te sine offensione animi nostri, de protectu nostro vt optamus liceat alloqui, quatenus me inclinem gremium pietatis tuæ tranquilla pace percipias, & quem meritorum facultas nulla eripuit, git, large benedictionis tuæ vbertate, ad plebem suam Regendam locupletet: vt vna mecum gentem quam vestra Apostolica authoritas fidei rudimentis imbuere studuit, per intercessionem tuam, contra impetus exterorum omnipotens erigat, & perte, regnum quod ipse Deus dedit nobis, dilatare dignetur. Hanc benedictionem, omnes qui ante ipsum receptro præfuerunt Merciorum, meruerunt abantecessoribus tuis adipisci: hanc ipse humilis peto, & à vobis (ô sanctissime) cupio impetrare, quatenus inprimis adoptionis forte me tibi filium suscipias, sicuti te in patris persona diligo, & totis obedientiæ viribus semper amplector. Decet enim inter tãtas personas fides sancta seruari, & muliolata caritas custodiri. Quia paterna pietas, filiorum fœlicitas in Deo esse credenda est, secundum illud Ezechiæ: Pater filius notam faciet veritatem tuam Domine. In quibus verbis te (amande genitor) imploro, vt filio tuo tametsi indigno, veritatem Domini tuis verbis Sacrosanctis notam facere non deneges: vt per tuam sanam erudinonem (Deo adiuuante) ad melioris vitæ propositum merear peruenire. Quinetiam (dulcissime) cum omnibus Ep. scopis nostris, & cuiusque dignitatis apud nos persona, deprecor, vti nobis de multimodis inquisitionibus, super quibus maximam subtilitatem vestram, d gnum diximus perquirere, benigne respondeas: ne sanctorum traditio patrum, & abillis tradita nobis Regula quali incognita, quouis modo vicietur in nobis. Sed fer mo tuus directus in nobis in charitate & manuetudine veniat, vt per Dei misericordiam profuturum in nobis percipiat fructum. Primum namque est, quod Pontifices nostri, ac peritissimi quique in nobis dicunt, quòd contra Canones & Apostolica statuta, quæ nobis à patre beatissimo Gregorio dirigente, statuta sunt, (sicut vos scitis) authoritas Dotobernensis Metropolitani in duas scinditur parochias: cuius, (eodem patre mandante) ditioni debent subiacere Episcopi. Sicut per Ecclesias nostras legitur in epistola, quam fratri, & Coepiscopo Augustino direxit, de duobus Metropolitanis Episcopis, Londoniæ videlicet & Eboraei, quam etiam apud vos haberi non dubitamus. Sed ipse primum Pontificalis aspex, qui tunc Londoniæ sub ornamento, & honore Pallii fuerat consecratus, pro eo Roberniæ oblatus est atque concessus. Nam quia beatæ memoriæ Augustinus, qui verbum Dei (imperante Gregorio) Anglorum genti ministrabat, & gloriosissimæ Ecclesiis præfuit Saxoniæ, in eadem ciuitate diem obiit, & corpus illius in Basilica beati Petri Apostolorum Principis (quam successor eius Laurentius sacrauit) conditum fuisset: visum est eundem gentis nostræ sapientibus, quatenus illi ciuitati Metropolitanus honor habeatur, vbi corpus eius tumulo conditum est, qui his partibus fidei veritatem inseruit. Cuius itaque (sicut vos scitis) dignitatis honorem, primum Rex Offa propter inimiciam cum venerabili Lamberto, & gente Cantuariorum acceptam auertere, & in duas parochias diuidere nixus: & pius Coepiscopus & anteccessor vester Adrianus, rogata prædicti Regis facere coepit, quod prius nemo præsumpsit, & Merciorum Præsulem pallio exuit. Neutrum tamen ex his coarguimus, in quibus Christus (vt credimus) æterna victoria triumphat. Sed tamen excellentiam vestram humiles exoramus (cui a Deo merito sapientiæ clauis collata est) vt super hac causa, cum sapientibus vestris quæ gratis: & quicquid vobis videatur, nobis posteà feruandum referre dignemini: ne tunica Christi inconsutilis, aliquid inter nos dissensionis Schisma patiatur. Sed per vestram sanam doctrinam, (vt defideratamus) ad veræ pacis vnitatem dirigatur. Magna enim humilitate simul & dilectione hæc tibi scripsimus (Papa beatissime) clementiam tuam profusius precates, quatenus ad ea quæ necessaria vobis à nobis explicata sunt, benigne & iuste respondeas. Sed & illa Epistola, quam Athelardus Archiepiscop coræ cuctis prouinciali b. Episcopis nostris missa: tiplicius de suis & totius Britanniæ causis & necessitatib. tibi scripsit, pio amore pfeverati digneris: & qcqd de reb. q in ea scripta sunt, fidei normula poscat, pagina nobis veritatis patefacere. paterer accere memineris. Praeterito anno legationem meam etiam, & Episcopum per Wadam Abbatem misimus. At ille accipiens illam legationem negligenter, imo insipienter dedu-xit. Sed modo ubi modicam amoris gratiam per Brine presbyterum & Fuldas, & Cenolbri hit ministros meos (pater amande) misi to, quod est tuo maculas cum literis precans, ut benigne suscipias, & benedictionem tuam nobis dare digneris, Omnipotens Deus te longaevo tempore, ad laudem suae Ecclesiae custodiat incolumem.
units.tr: To the most blessed lord, and most loving of the truth, Leo, Pontiff of the holy Apostolic See of Rome: Kenulf, by the grace of God king of the Mercians, with the bishops, leaders and all who are under our rule, sends greeting in Christ of the most sincere affection and of due honour. We always give thanks to almighty God, who, amid the various storms of this world, has ever guided the Church, purchased by His precious blood, with new tides, and has brought it to the harbour of salvation by means of former ones, and who has caused the light of day to shine upon it, so that it may not be darkened by any error of shadows, but may walk without stumbling in the way of truth; wherefore the whole Church throughout the world rightly rejoices. For when the true rewarder of all good men had taken up his glorious shepherd of the flock, Adrian, to heaven, to remain there for ever, yet by his devoted providence he raised up for all a pastor who knows how to lead the Lord's sheep to the folds of life without any harm. We too, whom the farthest end of the world holds, rightly glory above others in the same way, because his salvation and prosperity are to us a lasting joy; for from you, the Apostolic dignity, the truth of the faith has become known to us. Wherefore I think it fitting to bow humbly the ear of our obedience to your most holy commands, and with every effort to carry out whatever seems rightly to be followed by us in your piety. But whatever is found to be contrary to reason is to be rejected quickly, and meanwhile by us all in every way cut off. But now I, Kenulf, king by the grace of God, humbly beg your excellence that, without offence to your mind, I may be permitted to speak with you about our protection, as we desire, so that you may receive me into the bosom of your piety in calm peace, and that He who has not taken away the power of my merits may enrich, with the abundant largesse of your blessing, the people He has committed to my rule; that, together with me, He may through your intercession raise up against the assaults of foreigners the nation which your Apostolic authority has taken pains to imbue with the first principles of the faith, and may deign to enlarge the kingdom which God Himself has given us. All who before me have held the sceptre of the Mercians have deserved to obtain this blessing from your predecessors; this I, though humble, ask for, and, O most holy one, desire to obtain from you: that first you would receive me as a son by adoption, as I love you in the person of a father and always embrace you with all the strength of my obedience. For among such great persons holy faith ought to be kept, and a sincere love maintained; for paternal piety and filial happiness are to be believed to exist in God, according to that saying of Hezekiah: "The father shall make known thy truth, O Lord." In these words I beseech you, beloved father, that you will not refuse to make known the truth of the Lord by your holy words to your son, however unworthy he is, so that through your sound teaching (God helping) I may deserve to attain to the purpose of a better life. Moreover, most sweet father, I pray, together with all our bishops and every person of whatever dignity among us, that you would kindly answer us concerning the many kinds of questions, on which we have said that your very great subtlety ought to be sought out; lest the tradition of the holy fathers, and the rule handed down to us from them, be in some way violated among us as if unknown. But let your teaching come to us directed in charity and gentleness, so that by the mercy of God it may bear profitable fruit in us. For first, our prelates and the most learned among us say that, contrary to the canons and apostolic statutes which were laid down for us by the most blessed father Gregory (as you know), the authority of the Metropolitan of Canterbury is split into two parishes, under whose jurisdiction, by the same father's command, the bishops ought to be subject. As we read in our churches in the letter which he sent to his brother and fellow bishop Augustine, concerning the two metropolitan bishops, namely of London and of York, which we do not doubt is also held by you. But the first pontifical rank was then offered and granted to Rochester, which had been consecrated at London with the ornament and honour of the pallium. For when Augustine of blessed memory, who, under Gregory's command, ministered the word of God to the English people and presided over the most glorious church of the Saxons, died in that city, and his body was buried in the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles (which his successor Laurence consecrated), it seemed good to the wise men of our nation that the honour of metropolitan should be held by that city where his body, which had brought the truth of the faith to these parts, lies in the tomb. This dignity, as you know, King Offa first strove to take away, on account of his enmity with the venerable Lambert and the people of Canterbury, and to divide it into two parishes; and your pious fellow bishop and predecessor Adrian began to grant what the aforesaid king asked, which no one had previously presumed to do, and he stripped the bishop of the Mercians of the pallium. Yet we do not condemn either of these things, in which Christ, as we believe, triumphs with eternal victory. Nevertheless we humbly beg your excellence (to whom by God's gift the key of wisdom has been committed) that, concerning this matter, you would deign to refer it to your wise men, and afterwards to let us know what you think should be kept by us, lest the seamless tunic of Christ suffer any schism of dissension among us, but rather, through your sound teaching, as we desire, be directed to the unity of true peace. For with great humility and at the same time with affection we have written these things to you, most blessed Pope, earnestly begging your clemency that you would kindly and justly answer the things which we have set forth to you as necessary. And that letter also, which Archbishop Athelard sent to all our provincial bishops, in which he wrote to you more fully about his own and all Britain's causes and needs, may you be pleased to receive with loving piety; and whatever is written in it on matters which the rule of faith requires, may you be pleased to reveal to us in a page of truth. Remember not to hold us in contempt. Last year we also sent our embassy and a bishop through Abbot Wada. But he, receiving that embassy carelessly, or rather foolishly, carried it through. Now, however, through Priest Brine and my ministers Fulda and Cenolbriht, I have sent a small gift of love, dear father, together with letters, praying that you would graciously receive it and deign to give us your blessing. May almighty God keep you safe for a long time, to the praise of His Church.

units.la: RESPONSTO LEONIS PAPAE AD LITERAS Kenulfi Regis.
units.tr: The reply of Pope Leo to the letter of King Kenulf.

units.la: DOMINO excellentissimo filio Kenulfo Regi Merciorum Provinciae Saxoniae Leo Papa. Veniens ad sacratissima limina Apostolorum Petri & Pauli, tam orationis vota fideliter soluens, quam nostrae Apostolicae sedi causam sui Sacerdotii suggerens, Reverendissimus & Sanctissimus frater Athelardus, Archiepiscopus Dorobernensis Ecclesiae obtulit nobis vestrae Regalis excellentiae syllabas, quibus in duabus epistolis a vobis directis plenis fidei rectae, magnam humilitatem reperientes, Omnipotenti Deo gratias retulimus, qui vestram prudentissimam excellentiam in nobis ordinavit atque decoravit erga beatum Petrum Apostolorum principem, & nobilem habere dilectionem, & in omnibus Apostolicis humiliter consentire censuris. Porro in una ex illis epistolis reperimus, qualiter gratiam nostrae Apostolicae functionis (si iuxta suisteris) animā vestram pro nobis benigne posuisseris Imo & nostra prosperitati multum in Domino congaudeatis, & quando nostra dulcitudine admonitionis literae ad vestras vhanimitatis aures pervenerunt, cum omni suavitate cordis & gaudio spirituali, quasi filii paternum munus suscipere fraternit. Fatebantur vero & hoc, quod aliquantulum ex vestra facultate benedictionem nobis offerri demandari idest. 120. manculas, quas cum magno amore pro animae vestrae salute suscepimus. Et praedictus Archiepiscopus cum sociis honorifice ac benigne susceptus est, & adiuvari eum in necessitatibus suis libenter fecimus. Interea credentes vestrae prudentiae, & excellentiae, ubi fetebatur in ipsis tuis Regalibus apicibus, quod nostris Apostolicis sanctionibus nullus Christianus contraire praesumit: ideo totis nixibus nostris, ea quae tuo regno expediunt committere atque praedicare coniamur, ut ea quae vobis praefatus frater noster Athelardus Archiepiscopus, seu tota Synodus Evangelicae atque Apostolicae doctrinae, sanctorumque patrum, necnon praedecessorum nostrorum sanctorum Pontificum canonica censura praedicante, vestrae Regali excellentiae, seu cunctis principibus gentis vestrae, & universo populo Dei dilecti, nequaquam in Orthodoxa eorum doctrina quippiam resistere debeatis, Domino & redemptore nostro in evangelio dicente: Qui vos recipit, me recipit. Et, qui recipit prophetam in nomine prophetae, mercedem prophetae accipiet. Quanto magis pro ipsa spe de dicto Archiepiscopo, quem nobis valde, honorificatis, laudastis (sicut & est) videlicet, clarissimus & peritissimus. Et quia illum scitis prudentem, bonis ornatum moribus, Deoqi & hominibus dignum, ecce filii dulcissime, & amantissime, atque praestantissime, Rex bone, in his tuis affectionibus collaudamus Deum omnipotentem, qui talem vobis demonstravit Anglia. Qui sicut verus pastor ad studia & doctrinam sanctarum Scripturarum, & dignam poenitentiam valet inducere eos, qui sub ditione sacerdotali eius existunt: & eruere animas eorum ex inferno inferiori, & ab igne inextinguibili, deducens eos in portum salutis, & offerre pro illis hostiam dignam & immaculatam, in conspectu divinae Maiestatis omnipotenti Deo. Et quia multum nobis praenominatus Archiepiscopus, in omni sanctitate sua, & vitae conversatione vitro ritu placuit valde, authoritate beati Petri Apostolorum principis, cuius (vel immeriti) vices gerimus, ut ille talem praebuimus Praesulatum: ut si quis piam ex subiectis suis, tam Regibus, & Principibus, quam viliorum populo transgressus fuerit Dominica mandata, excommunicet eum, vita poenitente: & si impoenitens fuerit, sit vobis sicut Ethnicus & Publicanus. De Athelardo vero iam facto Archiepiscopo Dorobernensis Ecclesiae, sicut a nobis popposcit vestrorum Praesulum excellentia, ut ei ius suum facere tum, de ipsis diocesibus suis, tam Episcoporum, quam Monasteriorum, quibus illicitè (ut vos cognoscitis) & spoliatus est, & a venerabili sede eius possessiones, quas dudum retinuit, ablatae sunt: nos per omnia enucleatius tractantes in iucto scrinio nostro reperimus, S. Gregorii praedecessoris nostri, in integro ipsam parochiam num. 12. dato Angustino Archiepiscopo tradidit, & confirmatis Episcopos consecrandi: unde & suos veritate ipsi reperta ordinatione, sive confirmationem nostra Apostolica authoritate illi in integro (sicut antiquitus fuerunt) confituentes,reddidimus,& priuilegium confirmationis iecundum sacrorum Canonū censuram, Ecclesiæ suæ obseruandum tradidimus.
units.tr: To the most excellent lord and son, Kenulf, King of the Mercians, in the province of Saxony, Leo, Pope. The most reverend and most holy brother Athelard, Archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, came to the most sacred thresholds of the Apostles Peter and Paul, faithfully fulfilling his vows of prayer, and also laying before our Apostolic See the matter of his priesthood. He presented to us the letters of your royal excellency. In the two letters you sent, full of sound faith and great humility, we found cause to give thanks to Almighty God, who has ordained and adorned your most prudent excellency toward us, toward the blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, so that you hold a noble affection for him and humbly agree with all Apostolic judgments. Moreover, in one of those letters we found that you had kindly taken to heart the office of our Apostolic function, and that you rejoice greatly with us in the Lord over our prosperity. When the letters of our sweet admonition reached your ears, you received them as sons receive a father's gift, with all gentleness of heart and spiritual joy. They also confessed that they had sent us, from some part of your means, a blessing, namely one hundred and twenty mancus, which we received with great love for the salvation of your soul. The aforesaid Archbishop, with his companions, was received honourably and kindly, and we gladly helped him in his needs. Meanwhile, trusting your prudence and excellence, since it was stated in your royal letters themselves that no Christian presumes to oppose our Apostolic decrees, we therefore strive with all our effort to commit and proclaim those things which are useful for your kingdom.
