You ought in no way to resist in their orthodox teaching those things which our aforesaid brother Athelard, the Archbishop, or the whole Synod, declares to your royal excellency, or to all the princes of your nation and to the whole beloved people of God, from the teaching of the Gospel and the Apostles, the sayings of the holy Fathers, and the canonical judgments of our predecessors, the holy Popes. Our Lord and Redeemer says in the Gospel: "He who receives you receives me; and he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet's reward." How much more, then, on account of the hope we have in the said Archbishop, whom you greatly honoured and praised before us (as indeed he is), namely most famous and most skilled. And since you know him to be prudent and adorned with good morals, worthy of God and of men, behold, most sweet, most loving, and most excellent son, good King, in these your dispositions we praise Almighty God, who has shown such a man to you in England. As a true minister, he is able to lead to the study and teaching of the holy Scriptures and to worthy repentance those who are under his priestly authority, to rescue their souls from the lower hell and from unquenchable fire, leading them into the harbour of salvation, and to offer for them a worthy and spotless sacrifice in the sight of the divine Majesty, to Almighty God. And since the aforesaid Archbishop, in all his holiness and manner of life, has pleased us greatly, by the authority of the blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, whose place we hold, though unworthily, we have granted him such a primacy that if any of his subjects, whether kings and princes or the common people, transgresses the commandments of the Lord, he may excommunicate him, while he remains unrepentant; and if he remains impenitent, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican. Concerning Athelard, now made Archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, as your excellency of bishops asked us, that his right be restored to him in his dioceses, both of bishops and of monasteries, from which he was unlawfully despoiled (as you know), and whose possessions, which he formerly held, were taken from his venerable see: we, examining the matter in every detail, found in our sealed chest that our predecessor, Saint Gregory, gave the whole parish, number 12, to Archbishop Augustine, and granted him the power of consecrating bishops. Therefore, having found the truth of that ordinance, by our Apostolic authority we have restored to him in full (as they were in ancient times) his bishops, and, confirming them, we have delivered to his Church the privilege of confirmation, to be observed according to the judgment of the sacred canons.

units.la: Hæc tam solerti diligentia Athelardi, qua dignitates & prædia sedis suæ Metropoliticæ amissa recuperauit, nomen suum excelso,sublimiq; in loco, atque in illustri quadam specula constitutum est,quod nulla obliuionis nube deleri, nedum regi potuit. Nam præterquam quod Caniuum ob summa in hanc sedem merita, arrestatio huiusmodi des deferre necessariò cogitur: tota etiam Anglia, sedis illegitimæ iugo oppressa, & ab
units.tr: By the same skilful diligence with which Athelard recovered the dignities and estates of his metropolitan see that had been lost, his name was set on high, in a lofty place and upon a certain illustrious watchtower, so that it could not be blotted out, much less dimmed, by any cloud of oblivion. For, besides that the Canterbury see, on account of its great merits, is necessarily compelled to bring forward such evidence, all England, oppressed by the yoke of an illegitimate see, and ...

units.la: Anno 792. Carolus Francorum Rex librum Synodalem Constantinopoli sibi delarum in Britanniam misit: in quo multa verae fidei contraria reperta sunt: atque illud inprimis (quod omnium pene orientalium Doctorum, nec non & trecentorum, aut eoam- plius Episcoporum assensu confirmatum est) imagines adorari debere, id quod Ecclesia Dei maxime detestatur. Aduersus hanc haeresim Alcuinus Diaconus Cantuariensis coenobu Abbas, post Caroli Magni praeceptor epistolam eleganrem, variis scripturarum testimoniis fulcitam dictauit, quam vna cum eodem libello Francorum Regi attulit. Huius consilio & instigatione Carolus Rex postea Parisiense gymnasium extruxit.
units.tr: In the year 792, Charles, King of the Franks, sent to Britain the Synodal book which had been brought to him from Constantinople. In it many things contrary to the true faith were found, and especially this (which was confirmed by the assent of almost all the eastern teachers, and also of three hundred or more bishops): that images ought to be adored, which the Church of God utterly detests. Against this heresy Alcuin, deacon of Canterbury and abbot of a monastery, afterwards teacher of Charles the Great, dictated a learned letter, supported by various testimonies of Scripture, and brought it to the King of the Franks together with the same little book. By his counsel and urging, King Charles afterwards built the university at Paris.

units.la: Anno Christi 793 Et Britrici Regis Occidentalium Saxonum, 11 dia prodigiamisferam Anglorum genrem perterruerunt: Siquidem fulminatterribilia, flammeque Dracones per aera volitare subinde conspiciebatur, quae signa miseriae pestes sunt subsequutae. Dani enim cum Norwegensibus irruptione facta in Northumbriam & Lindisfarnensem Insulam, omnia ferro & face profrarunt, Ecclesias Christi diruerunt, incolas neci dederunt. Hanc cladem Simeon Dunelm.his verbis grauius inculcat.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 793, in the days of Brihtric, King of the West Saxons, portents terrified the fierce nation of the English. For terrible thunderbolts were seen, and fiery dragons were often seen flying through the air, and these signs were followed by plagues of misery. The Danes, together with the Norwegians, made an invasion into Northumbria and the island of Lindisfarne, and laid everything waste with sword and fire, overthrew the churches of Christ, and put the inhabitants to death. Simeon of Durham presses this disaster more heavily with these words:

units.la: An. Dom. 793. Idus Ianuarii: Pagani ab aquilonari climate, nauali exercitu, vt aculeati crabrones Britanniam veniendo, hac illacque, vt rapacissimi lupi discurrerunt, praedati sunt, momorderunt, interfecerunt non solum iumenta, onera, ceteraque animalia, verumetiam sacerdotes, Leuitas, chorosque Monachorum atque Sanctimonialium. Veniunt ad Lindisfarnensem Ecclesiam, miserabili praedatione vastant cuncta, calcant sancta pollutis vestigiis, altaria suffodiunt, & omnia thesauraria sanctae Ecclesiae rapiunt. Quosdam e fratribus interfecerunt, nonnullos etiam vinctos secum assumunt, perplurimusque opprobriis vexatos, nudos proiciunt: aliquos in mari demergunt.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 793, on the Ides of January, heathens came from the northern region with a naval army, running hither and thither over Britain like stinging hornets, like most ravenous wolves; they plundered, they tore, and they killed not only beasts of burden, loads, and other animals, but also priests, Levites, and the choirs of monks and nuns. They came to the church of Lindisfarne, laid waste everything with miserable plunder, trampled holy things with polluted feet, dug up the altars, and seized all the treasures of the holy Church. Some of the brothers they killed, some they took with them in chains, and very many they cast out naked, vexed with insults; some they drowned in the sea.

units.la: Hi sariis insulam praedati, & sibi inuicem de prelio prospere gesto congratulantes discedunt. Nec minus miseram conditionem secum annus sequens attulit. Idem enim Pagani portu Egfridi Regis vastato, Monasterium Doni amnis praedarunt. Causae vero tantae calamitatis irruptione hostium iam inceptae, & per trecentos annos continuatae (nam ad Wilhelmi Normanni tempora, bas miserias Britannia sustulit) grauissima hominum scelera & impietas erant, quae partim recensui, cum de Cuthberto Cant. Archiepiscopo agerem parum ea sunt, quorum causa Gildas suam gentem tam acerba inuectiua proseritur. Ad scelera namque proclives, omnem pudorem exuerant, metum diunum abiecerant, vitam, vt pecora, in flagitiorum sordibus traducebant. Praefatus ergo Alcuinus, graui cura, & solicitudine labefactatus atque conuulsus, Anglorum plures literis vrget: in quibus eorum calamitates acerbo ludu, & scelera graui quaerela proscindit. Litteras quas ad Higebaldum Lindisfarnensem Episcopum dedit, placuit hic aferibere. Beatissimi patris Cuthberti Episcopi in Christo filiis, Higbaldo Episcopo, & omni congregationi Lindisfarnensis Ecclesiae, Alcuinus Diaconus salutem. Vestrae charitatis familiaritas me multum laetificare solebat: sed verba vicem tribulationis calamitas (licet absentem) me contristauit: quod Pagani contaminauerunt sanctuaria Dei: & fudeuit satguinem sanctorum in circuitu altaris: calcauerunt corpora sanctorum in templo, quasi sterquilinium in platea. Quae est fiducia Ecclesiis Britanniae, si sanctus Cuthbertus cum tanto Sanctorum numero suam non defendit Ecclesiam. &c. Quos item hortatur, ne a moribus antecessorum ita turpiter degenerent, neque luxui, gulae & inspeccantiae indulgentes profestionis suae dignitatem tanta labe conspurcarent: ob scelerum. grauitate haec ut- sia sustulerant, grauiora passuri, nisi trahitos turpiter annos melioris vita copenhagen. In fine literarum addit: Cum Dominus noster Rex Carolus hostibus per misericordiam Dei subditis, domum reuertetur, nos (Deo iuuante) ad eum venire disponemus. & si quid tunc vel de pueris, qui in captiuitate ducti sunt a Paganis, vel de aliis necessitatib. vestris proficere porrigimus, diligenter ad effectum perducere curabimus. Quas vero debet literas ad Offam Regem Mercitorum, non erit ab instituto nostro alienum hic referre. Ego (inquit) parotus erant. nis eram cum muneribus Caroli Regis ad vos venire, & ad patriam reuerti: sed melius mihi visum est, propter pacem gentis mee in peregrinatione remanere, nescienes quid apud eos fecissem, inter quos nullus securus esse vel in salubri concilio proficere poterit. Ecce loca sancta a Paganis vastata, altaria periuria fœdata, Monasteria adulterijs violata, terra sanguine dominorum & principum maculata. Ad Eboracenses sic scribit. Non anni auaritia (restis est mihi cogitor cordis) Franciam veni, nec remansi, sed causa Ecclesiasticæ necessitatis.
units.tr: Having plundered the island in this way, and congratulating one another on the successful battle, they departed. The following year brought no less wretched a state with it. The same heathens, having laid waste the harbour of King Ecgfrith, plundered the monastery at the mouth of the river Don. The causes of so great a calamity, begun by the invasion of enemies and continued for three hundred years (for Britain endured these miseries until the times of William the Norman), were the gravest crimes and impieties of men. Some of these I have recounted, when I was dealing with Cuthbert, Archbishop of Canterbury; they are the reason why Gildas denounced his own nation in such bitter invective. Being prone to wickedness, they had cast off all shame, had put aside the fear of God, and spent their lives, like beasts, in the filth of vices. Therefore Alcuin, shaken and torn by heavy care and anxiety, urged many of the English by letters, in which he rebuked their calamities with bitter sorrow and their crimes with heavy complaint. The letter which he wrote to Higbald, Bishop of Lindisfarne, I have thought fit to set down here: "Alcuin the deacon, to the sons in Christ of the most blessed father, Cuthbert the bishop, to Bishop Higbald and to the whole congregation of the Church of Lindisfarne: greeting. The familiarity of your charity used greatly to gladden me, but the calamity of your tribulation, though I am absent, has saddened me with words: the heathens have defiled the sanctuaries of God, and poured out the blood of the saints around the altar; they have trampled the bodies of the saints in the temple like dung in the street. What confidence is there for the Churches of Britain, if Saint Cuthbert with so great a number of saints does not defend his own Church?" And so on. He likewise exhorts them not to degenerate so shamefully from the morals of their ancestors, nor, indulging in luxury, gluttony, and greed, to defile the dignity of their profession with such a stain: because of the gravity of their sins, they were suffering these things, and would suffer greater things, unless they amended their shamefully wasted years with a better way of life. At the end of the letter he adds: "When our Lord King Charles, by the mercy of God, shall return home with the enemies subdued, we shall (with God's help) arrange to come to him; and if we then put forward anything useful about the boys who were led into captivity by the heathens, or about your other needs, we shall take care to bring it diligently to effect." But the letter which he wrote to Offa, King of the Mercians, it will not be out of place for my purpose to report here: "I," he says, "was prepared to come to you with the gifts of King Charles, and to return to my country; but it seemed better to me to remain in exile for the peace of my people, not knowing what I might have done among those people, among whom no one can be safe, or be able to make progress even in a wholesome council. Behold, holy places are laid waste by the heathens, altars are defiled by perjuries, monasteries are violated by adulteries, the land is stained with the blood of lords and princes." He writes thus to the people of York: "It was not for the sake of avarice (God is my witness in my heart) that I came to France, nor did I remain there, but for the sake of the Church's necessity."

units.la: Ad Ethelredum Regem, qui tertius post Egbertum regnauit, hæc verba habet. Ecce Ecclesia sancti Cuthberti sacerdotum, Dei sanguine aspersa, omnibus spoliata ornamentis, & locus omnis in Britannia Paganis gentibus datur ad depraedandum. Et vbi primum post discessum S. Paulini ab Eboraco Christiana Religio a nostra gente sumpsit exordium, ibi miseriæ & calamitatis sumpsit initium. Quid significat pluuia sanguinis quadragesimali tempore in Eboracensi ciuitate (quæ caput beatitotius regni est)? quam in Ecclesia beati Petri Apostoli vidimus, de borealibus domus, sereno aere, de summo tecti minaciter cadere? Nonne potest iudicati de borealibus partibus venire sanguinem super terram? Nostrum regnum Northanhumbrorum pene periit, intestinis dissensionibus, & fallacibus iuramentis. Scribit etiam ad Wiorenses, apud quos Beda vixerat, & obierat, ex obliquo fecisse arguens, quod ne faciant, rogat. Affuescant pueri astare laudibus superni Regis, non vulpium fodere cauernas, non leporum fugaces sequi cursus: discant nunc sacras Scripturas, vt aetate perfecti, alios docere possint. Recogitate nobilissimum nostræ aetatis Magistrum, Bedam Presbyterum, quale habuit in iuuentute discendi studium, talem nunc habet inter homines laudem, & multo maiorem apud Deum remunerationis gratiam. Ad Athelardum Cantuar. Archiepiscopum de quo nunc agimus, hæc scribit. Hoc dico propter flagellum, quod nuper accidit paribus insulæ, quæ prope trecentis & quadraginta annis, inhabitata est a paten- tibus nostris.
units.tr: To King Ethelred, who reigned third after Egbert, he addresses these words: "Behold, the church of St Cuthbert, sprinkled with the blood of God's priests, stripped of all its ornaments, and every place in Britain is given up to the heathen nations to plunder. And where first, after the departure of St Paulinus from York, the Christian religion took its beginning among our people, there the beginning of misery and calamity has arisen. What does the rain of blood mean, which we saw in Lent in the city of York (which is the head of the blessed kingdom), falling threateningly from the roof of the church of the blessed Apostle Peter, from the north side of the house, in clear air? Can it not be judged that blood has come upon the earth from the northern parts? Our kingdom of Northumbria has nearly perished through internal dissensions and deceitful oaths." He also writes to the men of Wearmouth, among whom Bede had lived and died, and, rebuking them somewhat obliquely, asks them not to do so: "Let boys grow accustomed to stand at the praises of the heavenly King, not to dig the dens of foxes or chase the fleeting courses of hares. Let them now learn the sacred Scriptures, so that when grown they may be able to teach others. Call to mind our most noble teacher of this age, Bede the Presbyter: as great as was his zeal for learning in youth, so great is the praise he now has among men, and a far greater reward of grace with God." To Athelard, archbishop of Canterbury, of whom we are now speaking, he writes thus: "I say this on account of the scourge which lately fell upon the inhabitants of this island, which for nearly three hundred and forty years has been inhabited by our fathers."

units.la: Sed vt ad Gildæ restimonium reuertatur, ille tamen solitudinis in Anglia refert, iniuriosam principum auaritiam, & rapinam inexplebilem, iudicium insignem corruptelam & atrocem iniustitiam, praesulum praedicantium linguorum & inertiam, plebis profusam luxuriem, & intemperantiam: quos omnes, pudor retinere, modestia regere, verecundia temperare nullo modo poruit. Adhæc Bonifacius Moguntinensis Archiepiscopus, cuius restimonium (cum sermo erat de Cuthberto Cantuar. Archiepiscopo) aliquoties produximus, ipsum Athelardum Cantuar. Archiepiscopum quod Clericis in vestium splendore nimium indulgeat, gratius increpat. Monet etiam, vt cum Roma iter habeat, & Carolum Magnum vitiles, Clericos vel Monachos verticoloribus & splendidis vestibus indutos comitatui suo non adhibeat, quod Gallorum clerus modestiam in apparatu retinere solet.
units.tr: But to return to the testimony of Gildas: he indeed speaks of the desolation in England, the injurious avarice of the princes and their insatiable rapine, the notorious corruption of judgment and the savage injustice, the idleness and the tongues of the preaching prelates, the boundless luxury and intemperance of the common people. Shame could in no way restrain all these, nor modesty govern them, nor decency temper them. Besides, Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, whose testimony (when we were speaking of Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury) we have cited several times, more pointedly rebukes Athelard himself, archbishop of Canterbury, because he indulges the clergy too much in the splendour of their garments. He also advises that, when he has occasion to travel to Rome, he should not take with him, as companions, clergy or monks clothed in variegated and showy garments before Charlemagne, since the clergy of the Gauls are accustomed to keep moderation in their apparel.

units.la: Atqui vtre pauci complectamur, Henricus Huntendunensis hæc refert: Proculsu tempo- ris inter Anglos virtus omnis adeo defecerat, vt gentes qualcunque proditione superarent, cuius sceleris, etsi infamia notati, nihil tamen eos puduit. Hinc facile constare potest, cur tanto furore iustitia Dei in Anglos exarserit, quippe quos tam graui malo, tam longo tempore afflígi passus sit. In historiis postius ac Britonum quinque plagis insulam hanc percussam legimus: verum quarta per Danorum irruptionem illata, exteris longe crudelior & immanior fuit. Romani siquidem Britanniam in dignorem suam breui redegerant, subactam legibus dominorum splendide regebant. Picti vero & Scoti crebras infructiones ex boreali parte Britanniæ faciebant: quam tamen omni ex parte non aggrediebantur, sepius etiam accepto graui malo ad sua recurrentes, plures annos ab hostibus impetu sibi temperabant. Saxones autem pro virium suarum magnitudine continuo terram hanc praelio infestantes, subiugebant, subactam fortiter retinebant, retentam ipsam dide edificabant, ad sicut bonis legibus administrabant.
units.tr: But, lest we dwell on too few, Henry of Huntingdon relates these things: "Within a short time, all virtue among the English had so failed that any peoples whatever overcame them by treachery, and though marked with the infamy of this crime, they were not at all ashamed of it. Hence it can easily be seen why the justice of God blazed out against the English with such fury, since he allowed them to be afflicted with so grievous an evil, over so long a time. In histories we read that this island was struck by five plagues, both of the Britons and of the Romans; but the fourth, brought in by the invasion of the Danes, was far more cruel and savage than the others. For the Romans had soon reduced Britain to their own dignity, and, once subdued by their laws, ruled it splendidly. The Picts and Scots indeed made frequent raids from the northern part of Britain, yet they did not attack it on every side; often, having received a heavy blow, they returned to their own lands and for many years refrained from attacks on it. The Saxons, however, according to the greatness of their strength, continually assaulting this land in war, subdued it, held it bravely once subdued, built it up when held, and governed it by good laws.

units.la: Normanni postea hanc terram hostiliter inundantes, castris pacis, præcipua régni propugnacula obsidione cingebant, quibus facile superatis, & tributariis factis, vitam, libertates, leges, & antiqui regni benigne concesserunt. Dani vero certam omnem magna militum manu sæpius inuadebant, non regnandi studio, sed prædandi, non victoriæ sed victus cupiditate, non gloriolæ, sed praedioli spe, ut statim quia in fugam verterentur, lucri auctus nihil accreuit: cum classis hostium instructior fuisset appulsa aliis regni loca occupaverunt. Nam cum Regem Anglorum in barbaros bonos... ritualem partem prædantes, copias, instructorem in professione accurrit ouncius, referens. ingentem Paganorum classem & austrafia Britanniæ litrora appulisse, vrbes & villas late depopulari, stannia cœde & incendio replere. Quo die et doenit, aher, occidentales Anglię partes multis armatorum millibus repleras ferens, quibus nisi celeriter occurrunt actum esse de eorum vita: tam enim vos in fugam versos ferro & face a tergo perisequebantur. Eodem aut postero die tertius vix spiritum trahens accelerat ille Danorum appulsum in plagas boreales, utcpidè refert domorum conflagrationem, honorum direptionem, infantium miseram cædem, cuiusque singularem cladem proponit. His tot simisis rumoribus acceptis, & maioribus periculis immeritus Rex & populus tamen ore percussi, mærore & sordibus obruti, variis curarum fluctibus iactabantur, quo se verterent. Ita ut victoria elatos, nedum lætos effecit, quod vix vlla salutis reliquia spes esset.
units.tr: Afterwards the Normans, invading this land like enemies, surrounded with siege the fortresses of peace and the chief bulwarks of the kingdom; when these were easily overcome and they had made the land tributary, they graciously granted life, liberties, laws and the ancient kingdom. But the Danes, with a great band of soldiers, attacked again and again, not with the zeal to reign but to plunder, not out of desire for victory but for booty, not for glory but in hope of a little gain; so that, as soon as they were turned to flight, nothing of profit accrued to them. When a fleet of the enemy, better equipped, had landed, they occupied other places of the kingdom. For when ... the rumour came that a great pagan fleet had landed on the southern shores of Britain, laying waste towns and villages far and wide, filling the lands with slaughter and fire. On that day... another reported that the western parts of England were filled with many thousands of armed men, unless they quickly came to the rescue of which their lives would be undone; for they pursued the fleeing with sword and torch from behind. On the same or the following day the third, scarcely drawing breath, hurried in with the news of the Danes' landing in the northern regions, and related with horror the burning of houses, the plundering of goods, the wretched slaughter of infants, and set forth the singular disaster of each individual. Having received so many terrible reports, and though not yet exposed to greater dangers, the king and the people, stricken in heart, overwhelmed with grief and filth, were tossed by the various waves of their cares as to where they should turn. So that, though raised by victory, they were not even made glad, since there was scarcely any remnant of hope of safety."

units.la: Anno Domi.797. Circa Solem, tres circuli visi sunt.
units.tr: In the year of our Lord 797. Around the sun three circles were seen.

units.la: Anno sequenti Londinò subito casu inflammatis plurimis ædes & hominum multitudo perierunt.
units.tr: In the following year, at London, by a sudden accident, many houses were set on fire and a multitude of people perished.

units.la: Anno 799. Naves plurimæ in Britannico mari vitæ pestilentis partim fractæ & collisæ, partim submersæ sunt.
units.tr: In the year 799. Many ships in the British sea were partly broken and dashed together, partly sunk, by a pestilential tempest.

units.la: Anno 800. Kal. Jan. ventus tam vehemens & violentus ab Africa flauit, ut urbes prostraverit, arbores radicitus evulserit, more supra cancellos & ripas irruptos cuiusque generis animalia perdidit.
units.tr: In the year 800, on the first day of January, a wind so vehement and violent blew from Africa that it overthrew cities, tore up trees by the roots, and destroyed animals of every kind that had broken in over the walls and banks.

units.la: Hoc tempore Carolo per Leonem Papam corona Imperatoris insignito, Imperium à Græcis ad Gallos & Germanos translatum est, quia occasione, & alis plurimis de religione controversiis ducti Græci, ab Ecclesiæ Romanæ obedientia se imperpetuum subtraxerunt, eumque per Romanos Pontifices ad obtegendum & Ecclesiæ suæ vastatem reuerti sepius interpellaretur, referebere solebant: vosmet à motus subiturus, non subtraximus nos à vobis.
units.tr: At this time, when Charlemagne had been decorated with the crown of emperor by Pope Leo, the empire was transferred from the Greeks to the Gauls and Germans; for the Greeks, led by that occasion and by many other controversies about religion, withdrew themselves for ever from obedience to the Roman Church. And when they were often urged, through the Roman pontiffs, to return to the defence and protection of their Church, they were accustomed to reply: "We have not withdrawn ourselves from you, but you yourselves have withdrawn from us."

units.la: Non multo post Athelardus morbo oppressus decubuit, & post paucos dies animam efflauit. Anno patræ salutis 806. & in Ecclesia Christi, nō sancti Augustini sepulchro iacet, Athelardus ex Lamberti prædecessoris sui flaruit & decretum hilaridum faciens (quæ de sepelendis Archiepiscopis lata esset, tum etiam Cuthberti & Bregwini antecessorum suorum vetigiis insistens, iubet ex mortuo corpus, non in ipsa Augustini, sed in Christi Ecclesia reponi. Hinc adeo factum est, ut illius loca Monachis ne religiosis, partim metu, ne Reges qui Archiepiscopos iis illa hæc & oneroris fraudulenti gravius offenderent, eorum demum in sepulchro insigni dignitatis consueret, nullam deinceps apud summum Pontificem ea de re querelam aut actionem instituerint. Nam ita sepultura Cant. Archiepiscoporum ad Ecclesiam Christi posita semper pertinuit.
units.tr: Not long after, Athelard, overcome by sickness, took to his bed, and within a few days breathed out his soul, in the year of our salvation 806. He lies buried not in the sepulchre of St Augustine but in the church of Christ. Athelard, following the footsteps of his predecessors Cuthbert and Bregwin, and having changed the decree of his predecessor Lambert concerning the burial of archbishops, ordered that his body after death be placed not in St Augustine's but in Christ Church. Hence it came about that the monks of that place, partly fearing that the kings would more heavily offend the archbishops by such fraudulent burdens, and partly because they had been accustomed to gain distinction from those burials, did not thereafter bring any complaint or lawsuit about this matter before the supreme Pontiff. For thus the burial of the archbishops of Canterbury has always belonged to Christ Church.

units.la: XV. FREDVS.
units.tr: XV. FREDVS.

units.la: Fredus Cantuariensis antea Monachus, ad Archiepiscopalem dignitatem Romæ, à Leone 4. Pontifice Romano electus. Pallium etiam confirmationis accepit, Kenulfi Regis Merciorum tertio, & Christi incarnati 806. Nono Archiepiscopatus anno Romam prosectus est, de negociis quibusdam Ecclesiæ actus, quorum veritas historiis non prodidit, comitem itineris Wibertum Sirebertensem Episcopum habuit. Hic, vel hinc hil dignum memoria gessit, aut quam minimum quod ullum i confecit præterea. Quidam referunt Leonem Papam Iunioris misisse cum Anglis Sedibus Legatos Cardinales, datis literis & potestate Apostolica, ad hunc Wlfredum Archiepiscopum, Doroberniæ, exterioris Anglorum Episcopos, qui de Kenelmo Rege Merciorum puerò septennî, clam inter sectò ab Athelberto in valle profunda vocata Clente, proximiæ Cornubiæ diligenter perquirentes. Quod facilius consilio Quendrediæ Reginæ perpetratum finisse compertum est, vt post Rempublicam solam administrasset. Interea putat Carolus Rex Galliæ Alcuino pio episcopo suo, Monasterium sancti Martini Turonensis, Abbatis iuris regendum committi, eò quod Monachi ad salutem ad ubi regati, fortis veritas indicabant gentie in adelgebant.
units.tr: Fredus, formerly a monk of Canterbury, was elected to the archiepiscopal dignity at Rome by Pope Leo IV. He received the pallium of confirmation in the third year of Kenulf, king of the Mercians, and in the year of the incarnate Christ 806. In the ninth year of his archiepiscopate he set out for Rome on certain business of the Church, the truth of which the histories have not recorded. Wibert, bishop of Sherborne, was his companion on the journey. Here he did nothing worth remembering, or at least nothing of note, and he accomplished nothing else of consequence. Some report that Pope Leo, the younger, sent cardinal legates to the English Sees, with letters and apostolic authority, to Wulfred, archbishop of Canterbury, and to the bishops of the southern English, to search diligently for Kenelm, the seven-year-old king of the Mercians, who had been secretly slain by Ethelbert in a deep valley called Clent, near Cornwall. It was found that this had been carried out more easily by the counsel of Queen Quendred, so that she might govern the state alone. Meanwhile, King Charles of the Franks committed the monastery of St Martin of Tours to Alcuin, his pious bishop, to be governed by him as abbot, because the monks, who had been driven out, were said to have been... (the text here is too corrupt to render with certainty).

units.la: Quorum iniunctionem quod quidem Monachi a ipsi iesse, duo Angelis ingurdo gentiam ingressi, omnes Monachos loci illius expetebant, vt videant ut ... Anno Domini 808. ... ; annus Mogunt ... ;
units.tr: Of the injunction which the monks themselves... two angels entering the land... all the monks of that place sought... in the year of the Lord 808... the year at Mainz...

units.la: Anno Mor. Poinanensis Fuisse, quæ Mogun Imperator, Anno lxiii... Carolus Rex non est... ut vna quidem hilarus supra aquam apparet. Anno. 817. Schola Anglorum (Thomæ scilicet hospitale) Romæ quondam ædificata, igne combusta est. Hanc Ine Westsaxonum Rex paucis annis ante Bedæ obitum construxit, Anno Dom. 727. vt Reges Angliæ, eorumq; affines, vtq; Episcopi, Presbyteri & clerici in doctrina & fide Catholica (qua appellatione Romani religionē suam soli dignantur) ecclē instituerentur: qui primo aduersum ab illis sententies, tandem, in Romana fide satis instructi & confirmati ad sedes suas rediebant. Huic Anglorum Scholæ Romani Pontifices à temporibus Augustini primi Archiepiscopi Dorobernensis exerciuia litterarum publica propter assiduas hæreses interdicebant, quæ sub aduentu Anglorum in Britanniam pullulabant, permixtis inter se Christianis cum Paganis, qui vera fidei dogmata fœdè corruperant. Iuxta hanc Scholam, idemRex Ine Ecclesiam beatæ virginis posuit, in qua Anglis Romam adnenientibus diuina mysteria peragere, & mortuos suos ibidem peregrinantes sepelire licuit. Atq; vt hæc ein omnem posteritatem rata haberentur, publico edicto decretum est, per Saxonum occidentalium regnum, quòd Ine Rex administrabat, vt de singulis familiis denarius vnus (qui anglicè Romscot dicitur) beato Petro & arz Romanæ annuatim mitteretur, ad Anglorum ibidem commorantium inopiam subleuandam.
units.tr: In the year... of Poitiers, which the emperor... in the sixty-third year... King Charles is not... so that indeed one appears cheerful above the water. In the year 817 the English School (namely the hospice of St Thomas), once built at Rome, was destroyed by fire. This school Ine, king of the West Saxons, had founded a few years before the death of Bede, in the year of the Lord 727, so that the kings of England, their kinsmen, and the bishops, priests and clerics might be instructed in doctrine and the Catholic faith (a name which the Romans alone deign to give to their own religion). At first they were ... but finally, sufficiently instructed and confirmed in the Roman faith, they returned to their sees. For this English School the Roman Pontiffs, from the time of Augustine, the first archbishop of Canterbury, publicly forbade the teaching of letters because of the constant heresies which sprang up on the arrival of the English in Britain, when Christians were mixed with pagans, who had foully corrupted the true dogmas of the faith. Next to this school the same King Ine built the church of the Blessed Virgin, in which the English arriving at Rome were permitted to celebrate the divine mysteries and to bury their dead who died there while on pilgrimage. And so that these arrangements might be held valid for all posterity, it was decreed by public edict throughout the kingdom of the West Saxons, which King Ine governed, that from each household one penny (called in English Romescot) should be sent every year to blessed Peter and to the city of Rome, to relieve the poverty of the English who dwelt there.

units.la: Anno 819. tanta peste Ecclesia Cant. laborauit, vt omnes Monachi præter quinq; morte perierint. Per id temporis Amalarius quidam floruit, qui in epistola ad Lodowicum asserit, Papam rectorem non esse totius Christianæ religionis, quantum ad homines pertinet.
units.tr: In 819 the Church of Canterbury suffered such a plague that all the monks, except five, perished. About this time a certain Amalarius flourished, who in a letter to Lewis asserts that the Pope is not the ruler of the whole Christian religion, so far as men are concerned.

units.la: Non multò ante Kenulphus Mercioram Rex Abbatiam Winchombe à fundamentis extruxerat, quam dedicari vehementer instabat, cuius celebritati & ipse Rex interfuit. Breui post Wlfredus Cant. Archiepisc. multis precibus apud Kenulphum condescendebat, vt Cantii Regem, quę in vinculis tenebat, libertate donaret: quod tandem impetrato, oportunitate victus Rex concedebat. Post hæc Wlfredus graui morbo correptus, ante mam exhalauit: sepultus est in Ecclesia Christi Cantuariæ.
units.tr: Not long before this, Kenulf, king of the Mercians, had built the abbey of Winchcombe from its foundations, and he urgently pressed for its dedication, at whose celebration the king himself was present. Shortly afterwards Wulfred, archbishop of Canterbury, with many prayers persuaded Kenulf to grant freedom to the king of Kent, who was held in chains; and at length, the request having been granted, the king, won over by the occasion, consented. After this Wulfred, seized by a severe illness, breathed his last within a short time. He was buried in the Church of Christ at Canterbury.

units.la: XVI. THEOLOGILDVS.
units.tr: XVI. THEOLOGILDVS.

units.la: HEOLOGILDVS siue Fleogildus prius Abbas Cant. post ad Archiepiscoparus culmen peruasit, Syredum successorem habuit. Hic repentina morte correptus in Archiepiscoporum Cathalogo non recensentur: Sepultus in Ecclesia Christi Cantuariæ iacet.
units.tr: Theologildus, or Fleogildus, was first abbot of Canterbury and afterwards seized the height of the archbishopric; he had Syred as his successor. He, seized by a sudden death, is not counted in the catalogue of archbishops; he lies buried in the Church of Christ at Canterbury.

units.la: XVII. CELNOTHVS.
units.tr: XVII. CELNOTHUS.

units.la: HEOLOGILDO defuncto Celnothus, alias Ciathredus Decanus Cantuar. Ecclesiæ successit in Archiepiscopatu: hic à Gregorio Papa pallium accepit: sepultus est in Ecclesia Christi Cantuar. postquam iedifset in sede sua. 38. annis. De quo tot annis sedente, nihil momoriæ prodiruum esse miramur, cum grauissimis periculis & maximis molestiis circumseptus fuerit. Siquidem bis per Danos sub eo Cantuati sedes grauiter afflicta fuit, & tam variis procellarum fluctibus agitara, ita vt horrenda rerum omnium transmutatio videretur. Anno enim Archiepiscopatus sui secundo, & Egbrithi Regis occidentalium Saxonum. 33. & Christi. 833. exercitus Danorum in Angliam rediit, 38. anno, postquam apud Donemouth, iine Doni annis superati, fuga saluti suæ consulabant. Primum igitur Shepeiam insulam prædati discedunt: deinde cum 35. nauibus omni armorum genere instructis proximo post anno apud Carram appulsis, Egbrithus Rex bellum intulit, illi vero multis & grauibus damnis illatis superiores euadunt, prostratis & cæsis quoibus Episcopis Heresfrido Wint. & Migfrido Syreburgensi vnà cum duobus ducibus Dudda & Osliota. An. 5. Archiepiscopi, & Adulfi Regis Westsaxonum primo, pyratæ Danorum per totam insulam vagantes omnia ferro & face prosternebant. Quibus auditis Adulfus Rex exercitu compa-rat, ipse partem copiarum ad regni propugnaculum secum retinet, alteram Wlfardo Consuli ducendam tradit, vt contra Danos Haintonæ cum 33. nauibus appulsos pugnam iniret, de quibus post multam hostium cædem commissam victoriæ laudem deportauit. Sed & in Danos alia regni loca infestantes, Athelmus Consul, acceptis à Rege militibus pugnauit, quibus ancipiti prælio diu dimicantibus tandem prostrato Consulo, exercitu fugato, Dani victoria potiti triumphantur.
units.tr: After Theologild died, Celnoth, also called Ciathred, Dean of the church of Canterbury, succeeded him in the archbishopric. He received the pallium from Pope Gregory and was buried in the church of Christ at Canterbury, after he had sat in his see for 38 years. We are surprised that nothing has been handed down about someone who sat for so many years, since he was surrounded by the gravest dangers and the greatest troubles. Twice under him the see of Canterbury was severely afflicted by the Danes, and it was tossed by such various waves of storms that every thing seemed to be turned upside down. In the second year of his archbishopric, and the 33rd year of Egbert, king of the West Saxons, in the year of Christ 833, the army of the Danes returned to England. In the 38th year, after they had been defeated at Donemouth, at the mouth of the river Done, they sought safety in flight. First they plundered the Isle of Sheppey and then departed. The next year they landed at Carhampton with thirty-five ships fitted out with every kind of weapon, and King Egbert made war on them. They, however, came off victorious after inflicting many grievous losses: the bishops Heresfrid of Winchester and Migfrid of Sherborne were struck down and slain, together with the two leaders Dudda and Osliota. In the fifth year of the archbishop, and the first year of Ethelwulf, king of the West Saxons, the Danish pirates roamed through the whole island and laid everything waste with sword and fire. Hearing this, King Ethelwulf assembled an army. He kept part of his forces with himself to defend the kingdom and handed the other part to the consul Wulfhard to lead against the Danes, who had landed at Hamptonshire (Haintona) with thirty-three ships, so that he might join battle with them. After a great slaughter of the enemy, he carried off the praise of victory. But also against the Danes who were harassing other parts of the kingdom, the consul Athelm fought with soldiers received from the king. The battle was long and doubtful, but at last the consul was struck down, his army was put to flight, and the Danes, gaining the victory, celebrated their triumph.

units.la: Anno sequenti Herebertus Consul comparato exercitu, bellum cum Danis apud Merfware sedentibus redintegrauit, sed aduersa visus fortuna & ipse dux periit, & milites profligati sunt. Eodem anno Paganorum exercitus orientales Angliae partes inuasit, & populi numerum inanitum ferro & face trucidauit.
units.tr: The following year the consul Herebert raised an army and renewed the war against the Danes, who were settled at Merfware. But he was checked by adverse fortune: he himself, the leader, perished, and his soldiers were routed. The same year a host of pagans invaded the eastern parts of England and slaughtered a great number of people with sword and fire.

units.la: Anno proximo interiora terrae loca subito impetu circa Cantuariam & Roffecestriam multitudinem magnam prostrauerunt.
units.tr: The next year they suddenly attacked the inland regions around Canterbury and Rochester and laid many people low.

units.la: Anno post quinto Albanus Episcopus Syreburnensis, cum duce Ernulfo & suis Summerfetenibus, & duce Osredo atq; suis Dorsetensibus, contra Danorum exercitum apud Pedredesmuthe pugnaminare parabant, & Deo opem ferente multos eorum prosternebant, reliquos in fuga verterunt. Alfanus hic Episcopus magnae authoritatis & potentiae fuit, in consiliis prudens, eiusdem cū Swithuno Episc. Wintoniensis, sedes vicinae fuerunt, sed moribus & vita dissimiles. Swithunus enim in terrenis nauseans Monachi otium omnino amplexus est: Alfanus vero forensium quoq; cura in se susceperat. Nā cum temporibus Egbrithi Regis Westsaxonum, & Adelulf filii eius quinquaginta annos cum summa rerum copia & quiete in Episcopatu transegisset, Egbrithò Regi Cantuaritas & & orientales Anglos bellicis laboribus ipse Episcopus subegit. Conspicatus etiam Adelulfi indolem ad mansuetudinem nimis propensam, sedulis admonitionibus ad prudentem regni administrationem inetta bat, & contra Danos, inulam infestantes, (ipso pecunias e fisco suo ministrante, & exercitum comparante) languentem regis animum accendebat. Multaq; per eum in huiusmodi rebus & fortiter inchoata, & perfecta feliciter, quisquis annales legerit, inuenict.
units.tr: Five years later Alfan (Albanus), bishop of Sherborne, together with Duke Ernulf and his men of Somerset, and Duke Osred with his men of Dorset, prepared to fight the Danish army at Pedredesmouth. With God's help they struck down many of the enemy and put the rest to flight. This Alfan was a bishop of great authority and power, prudent in counsel. His see and that of Swithun, bishop of Winchester, were close together, but they differed in character and way of life. For Swithun, disgusted with worldly things, wholly embraced the leisure of a monk, whereas Alfan took upon himself the cares of public affairs as well. For in the times of Egbert, king of the West Saxons, and of his son Ethelwulf, he had spent fifty years in the bishopric with great wealth and quiet. Then, in warlike labours, the bishop himself subdued Kent and the East Angles for King Egbert. Seeing that Ethelwulf's nature was too inclined to mildness, he urged him with earnest admonitions to govern the kingdom prudently, and he roused the king's sluggish spirit against the Danes who were harassing the island, supplying the money from his own treasury and equipping the army. Whoever reads the annals will find that many things of this kind were bravely begun and happily completed through him.

units.la: Anno vigesimo Celnothi Archiepiscopi, Regis Athuulfi. 16. Christi. 851. magnus exercitus Paganorum cum trecentis quinquaginta nauibus in ostium Thamesis fluminis adueniens urbes praeclaras & pluribus annis inclytas, Doroberniam scilicet urbem Cantuariorum, & Londinum miserè depopulati sunt: Regemq; Merciorum Berwlsum, qui eorum vim & furorem repellere conabatur in fugam verterunt. Quo praelio feliciter gesto, Dani animo elati, omnes copias suas ano proximo Santhreiam admouent, quibus occurrebat Athelwlfus Westsaxonum Rex, cum magna strenuorum militum manu, inter quos ita anci ... pugna dimicarum est, vtincernam esset, vter victoriae laudem deportaret. Et quanuis in eo nondum feliciter a Rege pugnatum sit, quidem per maximam dier partem superior fuerat & victoriam pene obtinuerat, Sole tamen iam in occasu: palmas amisit: verum beneficio noctis, & tenebrarum adiutus, victi dedecus non subiit Sequentu praelio ingentem hostium multitudinem parua manu profligauit.
units.tr: In the twentieth year of Archbishop Celnoth, the sixteenth of King Ethelwulf, in the year of Christ 851, a great army of pagans came with three hundred and fifty ships to the mouth of the river Thames. They miserably laid waste the famous cities, renowned for many years, namely Canterbury, the city of the men of Kent, and London, and they put to flight King Burgred of the Mercians, who tried to repel their violence and fury. After this battle was successfully fought, the Danes, elated in spirit, brought all their forces the next year to Sandwich, where King Ethelwulf of the West Saxons met them with a large band of brave soldiers. The battle between them was fought so evenly that it was hard to tell which side would carry off the praise of victory. And although the king did not fight successfully in that engagement, for for most of the day he had been the stronger and had nearly won the victory, yet with the sun now setting he lost the palm. But aided by the cover of night and darkness, he did not suffer the shame of defeat. In the following battle he routed a huge multitude of the enemy with a small band.

units.la: Eodem etiam anno Paganorum exercitus in hac regione, apud Insulam Thanet hyemabat: cumq; anno sequenti, dux Ealtherus cum Canuiis, & Hudacum Suihresensibus manus coeruissent, multis millibus vtrinq; cesis, & naufragio submersis, vtrq; ducum praedictorum bello occubuerunt.
units.tr: In the same year the pagan army wintered in this region, at the Isle of Thanet. In the following year, when Duke Ealhere with the men of Kent and Hudda with the men of Surrey joined battle, many thousands were slain on both sides and some were drowned in shipwreck. Both of the aforementioned leaders fell in the war.

units.la: Anno Celnothi Archiepiscopi 14. Christi. 855. magnus Danorum exercitus in Insula Sheppeya hyemem transigebat.
units.tr: In the fourteenth year of Archbishop Celnoth, in the year of Christ 855, a great Danish army spent the winter on the Isle of Sheppey.

units.la: Quinto post anno maior hostium numerus ex indiciis Wintoniam aggrediutur, capit, & lolo aequauit. Non ita multo post Swithunus eiusdem loci Episcopus senio consectus animam exhalauit.
units.tr: Five years later a greater number of the enemy, acting on inside information, attacked Winchester, took it, and levelled it with the ground. Not long afterwards Swithun, bishop of that place, worn down by old age, breathed out his soul.

units.la: Anno sequenti Danorum piratae rursus in Insula Thannet hyemarunt, firmumq; foedus cum Cantuariis pepigerunt, quibus pecuniam pro foedere conferuando Cantuarii polliciti sunt. Sed Dani vulpium more ex indiciis noctu castris erumpentes, foedere ruperunt, maioris lucri, totam orientalem Cantii plagam depopulari sunt.
units.tr: The following year the Danish pirates again wintered on the Isle of Thanet and made a firm treaty with the men of Kent, for which the Kentish men promised money to keep the treaty. But the Danes, like foxes, sallied out of their camp by night, broke the treaty, and for greater gain laid waste the whole eastern part of Kent.

units.la: Anno Christi. 866. maxima Paganorum classis de Danubia Britanniam aduecta, in Eastanglia hyemauit, tantumq; praedati sunt, vt maior pars militum ex pedestribus fuerunt.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 866 a very great fleet of pagans, brought to Britain from the Danube, wintered in East Anglia. They plundered so much that most of their soldiers were left on foot.

units.la: Anno proximo ob orientalibus Anglis ad ciuitatem Eboracum castra mouebant, ferro & flamma vsq; ad Tinemuth omnia depopulantes. Quo tempore Northumbri ciuilibus bellis inter se affecti Regem legitimum Osbrichum regno expulerunt: & tyrannum quendam, Eltanomine, nulla regali progenie ortum, adimperii regimen suscipiendum elegerunt. Sed Danorum iniuria infestari, saluti reipublicae consulunt, & elite compolita Osbrichus & Elta in Danos viriuin suarum neruos intendunt, & Eboracum adeunt. Quorum aduentu Paganis timore perculsi in vrbem confugiunt, & intra moenia se continentes vim propulsare conantur. Christiani fugam timorem illorum animadvertentes, etiam intra urbis moenia a tergo insecutantur, murum demoliuntur, facto in urbem impetu, Pagani metu & necessitate victi eorum irrumpunt, caedunt, fugant, & strenue prosternunt. Northumbrenses praeter spem miseræ cæsi, vtrosq; Reges amittunt, qui superfuerant fodere into pacem cum Danis fecerunt. Quibus subiugati, & vectigalibus factis Dani Egbertum praefecerunt, regnantq; super Northanhumbros vltra Tyne. 6. annos. Haec sunt Eboraci 18. Kal. Apr. Eodem anno Alfanus Episcopus Byrebumensis, cuius fama minus laudabus apud omnes euchitur, defunctus est, & Byrebumæ sepultus.
units.tr: The next year they moved their camp from the East Anglians to the city of York, laying waste everything with sword and flame as far as Tynemouth. At that time the Northumbrians, divided by civil wars, expelled their lawful king Osbricht from the kingdom and chose a certain tyrant, Ella by name, who was not of royal descent, to take up the rule of the realm. But being harassed by the injuries of the Danes, they took thought for the safety of the commonwealth. Laying aside their quarrel, Osbricht and Ella turned their strength against the Danes and came to York. At their arrival the pagans, struck with fear, fled into the city and, holding themselves within the walls, tried to beat off the attack. The Christians, seeing the fear of those men, pursued them even within the city walls from behind, broke down the wall, and made a sudden assault into the city. The pagans, overcome by fear and necessity, rushed out, slaughtered and put to flight, and vigorously overthrew them. The Northumbrians were cut down beyond all hope, and both kings were lost. Those who survived made peace with the Danes. Subdued and made tributary, they were placed under Egbert, whom the Danes set over them, and he ruled over the Northumbrians beyond the Tyne for six years. These events took place at York on the 18th day before the Kalends of April. The same year Alfan, bishop of Sherborne, whose reputation is spoken of with less praise by all, died and was buried at Sherborne.

units.la: Anno Christi 868. Cometa terribilis conspicue visa est. Breui post dictus Paganorum exercitus Northumbris relictis Snolingamum adiit, cum quibus Burredus Merciorum Rex pacem iniit. Pagani vero celeriter ad Northumbros redeuntes, ibi annum integrum consederunt, nulla ratione habita in omnes ferro & face furorem exercentes. Toto itaq; hoc tempore, quo sedit Celnothus Archiepiscopus Cant. tam variis procellis agitato, tamq; turbulentis tempestatibus referto, nullusita a calamitate immunis fuit atque ille.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 868 a terrible comet was seen. Soon afterwards the pagan army left Northumbria and went to Nottingham (Snolingamum), where Burgred, king of the Mercians, made peace with them. But the pagans quickly returned to Northumbria and stayed there a whole year, raging against everyone with sword and fire. So throughout this whole time, while Celnoth sat as archbishop of Canterbury, tossed by such various storms and filled with such turbulent tempests, no one was free from calamity, and he himself least of all.

units.la: Anno Christi 87c. Eadmundus Orientalium Anglorum Rex commisso cum Danis proelio occubuit, cumq; eo Humbrictus Episcopus Helmhamensis, qui Regem eundem in regni fastigium euexerat.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 870 Edmund, king of the East Angles, fell in battle with the Danes, and with him Humbert, bishop of Helmham, who had raised that king to the summit of the kingdom.

units.la: Eodem anno Danorum iniuria Monasterium de Colbingham in australibus finibus Scotiae situm, sex mille passibus a Berwico versus borcam distans, spoliatum: hoc tempore ac locis Abbatissa Danorum praecepto incendio traditi sunt. Deinde Monasterium ad mare situm Lindisfarne Monachorum, in quo sedes tum erat Cathedralis, cum Lindisfarnensi bibliotheca, concremarunt: Tinemuthense Monalium, Girwicense, & Wiremuthense sexcentos Monachos sub Benedicto Nursino institutos, (inter quos Beda Presbyter legitur educatus) depopulati sunt: nec non & Sreneshalense Monachorum, quod Hilda Abbatissa fundaut. Hinc Dani a fluminibus Humbri gressi, haec etiam funditus evertebant coenobia: In Orientalium Anglorum regno Croulandiam, Thomeiam, Ramesciam, Haustede, (quod nunc Burgum Sancti Petri dicitur) cum insula Elicosi & coenobio foeminarum, in quo Ethelreda regina olim Abbatissa officio perfuncta est. Quo rempore Warkingh Mooasterium ad millibus passuum Londino ad orientem distans concrematum fuit. Huius cladis participes fuit Certesia (vulgo Churchesey) Monachorum coenobium 15. millibus passuum distans Londino ad occidentem, de quo haec habet Wilhelmus Malmesburiensis. Dertesium Monasterium non caruit rerum necessariarum copia, vsque ad Danos, (vt cæteræ) locum illum petierant, Ecclesia succensa cum Monachis & Abbate. Tradunt etiam Episcopalem sedem orientalium Saxonum apud Seham tunc incendio periisse. Scham villa est stagno vicina, nauigaturis ad Heli quondam vix tutorat nunc facta via per paludes iter daturus transitur pedibus. Sunt illic indicia diruta, & a Danis in cenis Ecclesiae, quae incolas simul exuitos ruina sua operuit. Ad haec Sanctimoniales Christi ... immunes ab his malis non fuerunt, iniquidem Anno Dom. 871. praed. & ... Paganorum exercitus, occidentales Saxones repetens Readingum venit, quod est in meridiana Thamesis fluminis ripa, in illa plaga, quae dicitur Barfleur, vbi coenobium spoliatum & direptum solo exquarunt. Friderwidze etiam coenobium per Danos emersum fuit ... Mon. Hamburgense, de quo Roffensis. Hamburgense (inquit) Monasterium ... Dani ... nefanda Danorum prouinicias cæde crudeli vastauerat iusto Dei iudicio, propter peccata Anglicæ gentis id ex genere. De Wenlochensis Monasterii subuersione per Danos, sic habet Wilhelmus Malmesbur. Apud Wenloch fuit antiquissima Sanctimoniali domus, in qua sanctissima M. Ibur ga, soror sanctæ Mildredæ, neptis Pendæ regis Merciorum ex filio, transegit vitam & sepulta est. Sed locus omnino inculrus & deserius, omnibus antiquitatis monumetis violentia hostili & temporu vetustate spoliatus. Regnante Edgaro Rege Winchilcombense Monasterium solo fere nomine stabat: & Dei hurst coenobiu antiquitatis inane simulachru fuit. Verisimile igitur est, vtraq; hoc tempore reliquorii cladi communicasse. Monasterium etiam Sancti Petri Gloucestriæ violento hostium impetu prostratum fuit. Reanduoz etiam fuit Monasterium celebre, ad quod Dani relicta Lindisfa, celeri cursu aduolabant, & ex eius spolio hyemem ibi totam transigebant. Iam quoniam in mensem Danorum crudelitatis incidimus, non incommodum erit hic referre calamitates, quas ex illorum ad insulam Thanet appulsu suffinuerit Mildredæ coenobiu, cum suis septuaginta ... virginibus vestalibus, quas ibi primum Theodorus, Dorobernensis Archiepiscopus su-pstitiose velasset: quàm hoc tempore mancipias Capgraujus ita vita Mildredæ silentio nō pre-terit. Pirate (inquit) Danorum in Insulam irrumpentes, hos cædunt, illos laniant, sic-gula vastantes virgines sanctas cum suo Monasterio voraci flamma combiurunt. Quid di-cam de Monasterio Sancti Augustini Dorobernię omnium primo & antiquissimo, Ro-manorum Pontificum, & Regum Cantiorum priuilegiis adeo superbo, quibus fretus ab omnibus subiectione & obedientia sui Archiepiscopalis, immune se putabat, ipso hoc officium, obseruantiam, & honorem ab Archiepiscopo sibi debitum reddere, vt semper electus loci Abbas, cum benedicteretur, non ad illum accederet, sed Archiepiscopus ad Ab-batem, [Gr-edibile] ... Danorum furor & rabies grassata sit, ita vt illorum vim, ne Wallgrum quidem Monarchi effugere, & iniuriam propulsare potuerint. Nam Anno Domini 876. Iugar & Halfdene cum 23. nauibus de Dacia regione (in qua hyemaueranɨ) egressi sunt, vt lupi feroces, & multorum ibi Christianorum sanguinem fuderunt, plurimosque cœnobiis faces admouendo, (solo zquarunt. Quid multis: ausim pro certo affirmare, Deum nulli genti (ne Iudæis quidem) maiorem latitudinem calamitatem, quam hac tempestate Angliæ Monachis, & Sanctimonialibus: ita vt ad annum vsq; sextum Athelredi Archiepiscopi Dorobernensis, (qui fuit Celnothi successor) sive ad annum sextum Alfredi Regis, (qui ei moru Danorum in sylvis locisq; abditis se occultaverat) totus eorum ordo penitus conciderit, & per nonaginta aut eo amplius annorum spacium sirmi obductus fuerit: nonnullum ih omnibus austrasiis Angliæ provinciis, sed in borealibus etiam plus quam debeat, centis annis, scilicet ad annum Dom. 1074. qui fuit Wilhelmi Normanni eogitiomen te conquestoris septimus, & Lanfranci Archiepiscopi Cant. tertius, teste Simeone Dunel-mensi: cuius testimonium operæ precium duximus hoc in loco commemorare. An-no (inquit) Dom. 1074. tres de provincia Merciorum Monachi, pauperes scilicet spiritu, diuinitus missi, in prouinciam Northumbrorum, venerunt Eboracum, petentes ab Hugone filio Baldrici, (qui tunc vicecomitis munus obibat) vt eis ducem itineris constitueret, vsque ad locum qui Munekaccestre, (id est) Monachorum ciuitas appellatur, quæ nunc noui castelli nomen obtinet. Quò conducti ad tempus ibidem morari nectebant: verum nullo antiquorum Christi seruorum ibi repertis, ad Gyrnum iter arripiunt, vbi præ graui ruina, Monachorum vila sedes vix comparuit: Ecclesias ditiutas, domos radicitus euersas conspicere licuit. Horum adueniam Episcopus Walcherus maximè gratulatus, hospitio liberaliter suscepit. Nomina eorum hæc fuere: Aldwinus ætate & moribus prior. Secundus Alfwius: Tertius Renisfridus: quorum la-bore & industria tria in regione Northanhombrorum Instaurata sunt Monasteria, vinum Dunelmi apud sacrum Cuthberti cadauer, in honorem sanctæ Mariæ virginis: al-terū Eboraci, in honorem ciusdē Dei genitricis Mariæ vbi nobile cœnobium constructū primum habuit Abbatem Stephanum: post hunc Richardum: deinde Gaulfridnum nunc vero Seuerinum. Tertium autem, in loco, qui quondam Streoneshath (id est) Si-nus fari, nunc vero Whitby appellarut, hodie Abbatem habet Benedictum. Deniq; postquam sæuissima Paganorum deuastatio, gladio ac flamma, Ecclesias & Monasteria in cineres redegerat, deficiente pene Christianitate vix aliquæ superstiturunt Ecclesiæ, hæ vero virgulis, ac sano contextæ: nullum tamen vspiam Monasterium per ducentos annos restauratum fuit, sidemomnino sublata, & eultu vero religionis penitus obsoleto; Monachorum nomen erat prouincialibus inauditum: religiosorum ordo incognitus; Monachalis habitus omnes in admirationem traxit. Ast vbi prædicti res viri familiarius aliquandiu inter eos vitam degissent, populus conspicatus eorum dexteritatem, & ecclebrem religionis morem, cœpit & ipsè a barbarie ad melius vitæ genus deflectere; ita restaurandis Ecclesiis operam impendere, collapsas renouare, nouas erigere. Plurestreliĉta seculari vita Monachalem assumpserunt: atq; hi de provincialibus pauci: deremotis verò Angliæ partibus, plures celebritate locorum, & virtutis illorum fama incitati, hilari fronte, & animo lubeti sead eorum amicitiam & ordinem adiungebant. Hæc libuit in medium proferre, vt occultum Dei indicium in obrudis Monachorū cultibus superstitiosis & diabolicis, ac in delendo eorum nomine & memoria, per multa annorum curricula probè animaduertamus, & altius animo perpendamus. Horum tunc loco succedebant presbyteri, qui in coniugio legitimo pie viuebant (quos Wilhelmus Malmesbur. vocat ignotas cœnobiorum incolas). Tunc vero Deus optimus maximus, præbuit se magis mitem atque placatum erga Anglicanam gentem, siquidem cum hostibus dimicaturi, victoriæ laudem semper reportabant, liberati à Danorum crudelitate, & tuti ab omni externo hostium impetu viuque ad tempora Edgari permanserunt: sub quo Monachorum fœda superstitio de integro non solum instaurata est, verumetiam ita subiro in immensum creuit, ut nulla superiore memoria tot Monachorum & Monacharum diuerticula nostra tragens scaruerit, quod hoc vno Rege Regnante in australibus solum Angliæ provinciis. Quo mortuo multo magis quam ante ira Dei commota est, maxime in Sodomiticam Monachorum turbam, cuius rei fides postea ipsorum Monachorum verbis & testimonio planius comparebit.
units.tr: In the same year, by the injury of the Danes, the monastery of Colbingham, situated in the southern borders of Scotland, six thousand paces north of Berwick, was despoiled. At that time and in those places, by the Danes' order, the abbess was handed over to the fire. Then they burned the monastery of the monks at Lindisfarne, situated by the sea, where the cathedral see then was, together with the Lindisfarne library. They laid waste the nunneries of Tynemouth, Gyrwe and Wearmouth, which had six hundred monks instituted under Benedict of Nursia (among whom Bede the presbyter is recorded as having been educated), and likewise the monastery of monks at Streoneshalh, which Abbess Hild founded. From there the Danes, advancing from the rivers of the Humber, overthrew these monasteries down to their foundations too: in the kingdom of the East Angles, Crowland, Thorney, Ramsey, Haustede (now called Peterborough), together with the island of Ely and the nunnery where Queen Etheldreda once served as abbess. At the same time Warkworth monastery, about twenty miles east of London, was burnt. Sharing in this disaster was Chertsey (commonly Churchesey), a monastery of monks fifteen miles west of London, concerning which William of Malmesbury writes as follows. The monastery of Dertesium had not lacked a supply of necessary things, until the Danes, as they had done elsewhere, made for that place; the church was set on fire together with the monks and the abbot. They also report that the episcopal see of the East Saxons at Seham then perished by fire. Seham is a village near a pool; ships once sailed there towards Ely, but now a road has been made through the marshes, and the journey is made on foot. There are traces there of ruined buildings, and of the church burnt by the Danes, whose ruin buried the inhabitants along with it. Beyond these, the nuns of Christ were not spared from these evils, for in the year of the Lord 871 aforesaid, a host of pagans, making for the West Saxons, came to Reading, which lies on the southern bank of the Thames, in that district called Barfleur, where they stripped the monastery, plundered it and levelled it to the ground. The monastery of Frideswide was also overthrown by the Danes. Concerning the monastery of Hamburgh, Rochester writes: "The monastery of Hamburgh (he says) ... the Danes ... had laid waste the provinces of the wicked with cruel slaughter, by the just judgment of God, on account of the sins of the English nation of that kind." Concerning the destruction of the monastery of Wenlock by the Danes, William of Malmesbury writes thus: "At Wenlock there was a very ancient house of nuns, in which the most holy Milburga, sister of St Mildred and granddaughter through a son of King Penda of the Mercians, spent her life and was buried. But the place is wholly uncultivated and deserted, stripped by hostile violence and the passing of time of all the monuments of antiquity." In the reign of King Edgar, Winchcombe monastery stood almost in name only, and the monastery of Deerhurst was an empty image of antiquity. It is likely, therefore, that both shared at this time the ruin of the rest. The monastery of St Peter at Gloucester was also overthrown by the violent onslaught of the enemy. Repton too was a famous monastery, to which the Danes, leaving Lindisfarne, hastened with swift course, and from its plunder they spent the whole winter there. Since we have now come to speak of the cruelty of the Danes, it will not be out of place to relate here the calamities which the monastery of Mildred, with its seventy vestal virgins, whom Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury, had first veiled there, suffered from their landing on the Isle of Thanet; which Capgrave, in his life of Mildred, does not pass over in silence. "The pirates of the Danes (he says) bursting into the island, butcher some, tear others apart, laying waste everything, and with voracious flame burn the holy virgins together with their monastery." What shall I say of the monastery of St Augustine at Canterbury, the first and most ancient of all, so proud in the privileges of the Roman pontiffs and the kings of Kent, relying on which it thought itself exempt from all subjection and obedience to its archbishop, so that it did not owe its archbishop this duty, observance and honour; so that the abbot elected for that place, when he was blessed, did not go to the archbishop, but the archbishop came to the abbot ... the fury and rage of the Danes raged, so that not even the monarchs of Wales could escape their force or repel the injury. For in the year of the Lord 876, Ivar and Halfdan, with twenty-three ships, set out from the region of Denmark (where they had wintered), like fierce wolves, and shed the blood of many Christians there, and by applying torches to very many monasteries, levelled them to the ground. To be brief: I would dare to affirm for certain that God has visited no nation (not even the Jews) with a greater calamity than the monks and nuns of England suffered in this period, so that until the sixth year of Athelred, Archbishop of Canterbury (who was Celnoth's successor), or the sixth year of King Alfred (who had hidden himself from the Danes in woods and secret places), their whole order utterly collapsed and for ninety or more years remained buried under thick cover. Some remained in all the southern provinces of England, but even in the northern ones more than ought to have, for a hundred years, namely until the year of the Lord 1074, which was the seventh year of William the Norman, called the Conqueror, and the third of Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, as witnessed by Simeon of Durham, whose testimony we have thought worth recording in this place. "In the year of the Lord 1074 (he says), three monks from the province of Mercia, poor in spirit indeed, sent by God, came into the province of the Northumbrians to York, asking Hugh, son of Baldric (who then held the office of sheriff), to appoint them a guide for their journey as far as the place called Munecaceastre, that is, the city of monks, which now bears the name of Newcastle. Hired for this, they stayed there for a time; but finding none of the ancient servants of Christ there, they set out for Jarrow, where, because of the great ruin, scarcely any trace of a monastic seat appeared; churches could be seen stripped bare, houses utterly overthrown. Bishop Walcher, greatly rejoicing at their arrival, received them generously as his guests. Their names were these: Aldwin, first by age and character; second Alfwy; third Reinfrid. By their labour and industry three monasteries were restored in the region of Northumbria: one at Durham, beside the holy body of Cuthbert, in honour of the Virgin Mary; another at York, in honour of the same Mary, Mother of God, where a noble monastery, first built, had as its first abbot Stephen; after him Richard; then Geoffrey, and now Severinus. The third, in the place which was formerly called Streoneshalh (that is, the bay of the lighthouse), but now is called Whitby, today has Benedict as its abbot. Finally, after the most savage devastation of the pagans had reduced churches and monasteries to ashes with sword and fire, Christianity almost failing, scarcely any churches survived, and those were built of wattles and straw; yet no monastery was restored anywhere for two hundred years, the faith entirely extinguished and the worship of true religion quite obsolete. The name of monk was unknown to the provincials, the order of religious was unfamiliar, and the monastic habit drew everyone to wonder. But when the aforesaid men had lived among them for some time, more familiarly, the people, seeing their skill and the famous manner of their religion, began themselves also to turn from barbarism to a better way of life: they devoted effort to restoring churches, repairing the collapsed and raising new ones. Several, leaving secular life, took up the monastic life; of these, few were provincials, but from the remote parts of England more came, stirred by the fame of the places and the virtue of those men, and with cheerful countenance and willing mind joined their fellowship and order." These things it has pleased us to bring forward, so that we may carefully observe, and weigh more deeply, the hidden judgment of God in the superstitious and diabolical worship of the monks, and in the blotting out of their name and memory over the many course of the years. In their place succeeded presbyters, who lived piously in lawful marriage (whom William of Malmesbury calls the unknown inhabitants of the monasteries). Then indeed God, the best and greatest, showed himself milder and more placated towards the English nation: whenever they were about to fight their enemies, they always carried off the praise of victory, freed from the cruelty of the Danes and safe from every external assault of enemies, and so they remained down to the times of Edgar. Under him the foul superstition of the monks was not only restored anew, but also grew to an immense size, so that in no earlier memory had so many houses of monks and nuns filled our land, and this under one king reigning in the southern provinces of England alone. When he died, the anger of God was stirred far more than before, especially against the sodomitical crowd of monks, of which fact the evidence will appear more plainly afterwards from the monks' own words and testimony.

units.la: Anno Dom. 853. qui fuit annus unde vigesimus Celnothi Archiepiscopi Cant. Ethelwlfus filium suum Elfredum (quem præ cæteris unicè complexus est) cum annum ætatis quintum ageret, Romam cum multo nobilium comitatu transmisit. Quem Leo Papa, sui patris rogatu v nxit in Regem, & in filium sibi adoptatum confirmauit: & benedictum ad patrem remisit. Duobus post annis pater Ethelwlfus (a nonnullis Adulphus vocatus) decimam Regni sui partem omnis Regii vectigalis immunitate donauit, quod ad sempiternam sui memoriam, Ecclesiis dedit, amore diuino raptus (ut refert Simeon Dunelmensis) & animam suam redemptuturus. Non ita multo post Romam profectus, assumpto secu suo filio, quæ iam antehac eo miserat, ibique tributu vocatu Romefeot, quod multis annis ante & post Anglia penitabat, Sancto Petro obtulit, coram Leone
units.tr: In the year of our Lord 853, which was the twentieth year of Archbishop Celnoth of Canterbury, Ethelwulf sent his son Alfred, whom he loved above all the others, to Rome with a large retinue of nobles when the boy was five years old. At his father's request Pope Leo anointed him king and confirmed him as his adopted son, and he sent him back to his father blessed. Two years later his father Ethelwulf (called Adulphus by some) gave a tenth part of his whole kingdom free of all royal tax. He gave it to the churches as a perpetual memorial of himself, moved by divine love (as Simeon of Durham reports) and about to redeem his soul. Not long afterwards he set out for Rome, taking with him his son, whom he had already sent there earlier, and in the presence of Pope Leo he offered to St Peter the tribute called Romescot, which England had paid for many years before and after.

units.la: Papa, Romæque annum integrum moratus, Anglorum Scholam (cuius antehac meminimus) Thomæ hospitale vocaram, & paulo ante eius aduentum incendio consumptam restaurauit. Quo peracto Roma in patriam rediens, iudicham Caroli Calui Francorum Regis filiam cum in Anglia aduectam in vxorem duxit, cum qua duobus annis viuens, post morbo correptus obiit, sepultus Wintoniæ cuius ciuitatis fuit (priusquam vxores vllas duxerat) & Monachus & Episcopus. Sed Egberto patre defuncto, factus est Rex: acceptaque nobili vxore filia Burredi Regis Merciorum, quatuor ex ea filiosque genuit. Tradunt nonnulli Leonem Papam præfatum, licentiam dedisse Adelulfo, vt vxorem duceret, liberosque procrearet, quod pareret eius sine hæredepræter illum interierat. Inter cetera quæ gesfuit Adelulfus Rex, singulis vitæ posterioribus annis, religionis amo-
units.tr: While in Rome he stayed a whole year. He restored the English School (which we have mentioned before), called the hospice of St Thomas, which had been destroyed by fire shortly before his arrival. When this was done he returned home from Rome and married Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, whom he had brought into England. He lived with her two years, then fell ill and died. He was buried at Winchester, of which city he had been both monk and bishop before he took any wife. After his father Egbert died he became king. He took as his wife a noble woman, the daughter of Burgred, king of the Mercians, and had four sons by her. Some relate that Pope Leo granted Ethelwulf the king licence to marry and beget children, since his earlier wife had died leaving no heir except him. Among the other things King Ethelwulf did in the later years of his life, he was driven out of his mind by a love of Papal religion beyond all measure.

units.la: re Papalis supra modum dementatus, trecentas maneussas denariorum (valet mancussa duobus solidis & sex denariis) Romam deferri curauit. Centum in honorem S. Pauli Apostoli eadem de causa: centum vero in vsum ipsius Papæ. Quam munificentiam adimpleuit eodem anno quo Roma rediit. Quibus operibus suis ut deuotis, non liberaniure & sibi Papæ purgatorio, multo minus pauperum Regnum cœlorum, vt Pomerorum turba miseram plebem supra modum in fraudem illexit, & hisce præstigiis dæmoniacis fascinauit: non ergo mirum si gravius in populum furor & ira Dei tumxuit, & in immensum accreuit, ob summum religionis contemptum, qui tunc passim grassatus est. Huc etiam tendit, quod Luitpertus Moguntinensis Archiepiscopus (qui post Leonem quartum Pontificatum Romæ obtinebat) Epistolam ad Ludouicum Cæsarem misit,
units.tr: He had three hundred mancuses of silver (a mancus is worth two shillings and sixpence) sent to Rome. A hundred were for the honour of St Paul the Apostle, for the same reason, and a hundred for the use of the Pope himself. He fulfilled this generosity in the same year he returned from Rome. Believing that by these works, as if they were devout, he would be freed from the Pope's purgatory, and much less would win the kingdom of heaven, the throng of pontiffs led the wretched common people far beyond measure into error and bewitched them with these diabolical tricks. It is therefore no wonder that the fury and wrath of God swelled more heavily against the people and grew beyond measure, because of the very great contempt for religion that then raged everywhere. To this also belongs the fact that Luitpert, Archbishop of Mainz (who held the papacy at Rome after Leo IV), sent a letter to the Emperor Louis,

units.la: qua Papam non solum grauiter peccare, verum etiam plurimis modis errare indicat: eundemq; Imperatorem, vt eum mature castiget, & ad meliorem frugem cogat, hortatur. Anno quo obiit Celnothus Archiepiscopus, sedes Episcopalis Orientalium Anglorum (quæ antea fuit Dompne, vulgo Dunwich) translata fuit ad Elmbam. Huius causam reddit Wilhelmus Malmesb. Tempore (inquit) Bedicani Regis Merciorum, & Egbrithi Regis Westsaxonum, Humbrichus & Wilredus fuerunt Episcopi Orientalium Anglorum. Sed eodem Ludekano & antecessore eius Burredo inuadentibus prouinciam, etiş Episcopis necessariorum copia sublata fuit. Et quidem vtraque Reges intra Regionem, prouinciali ineurfu extincti sunt. Cessarunt tamè Episcopatus, & ex duobus vnus factus, sedem apud Elmham villam non adeo magnam accepit. Hæc ille. Vnum adhuc restat,
units.tr: in which he showed that the Pope not only sinned grievously but also erred in many ways. He urged the Emperor to rebuke him promptly and force him to better conduct. In the year Archbishop Celnoth died, the episcopal see of the East Angles (formerly at Dommoc, commonly called Dunwich) was transferred to Elmham. William of Malmesbury gives the reason: "In the time," he says, "of Beorred, king of the Mercians, and Egbert, king of the West Saxons, Humbert and Wilred were bishops of the East Angles. But when Ludeca and his predecessor Beorred invaded the province, the supply of necessities for the bishops was cut off. Indeed both kings were killed within the region by a raid on the province. The bishoprics nevertheless ceased, and of the two, one was made, and it took its see at the village of Elmham, which was not very large." So far he. One thing remains,

units.la: quod silentio præterire nullo modo possumus, tempore horum 17. Archiepiscoporum Cant. sedisse in vrbe Romana 40. Papas Hoc quo fato contigerit, lectoris iudicio liberū relinquimus. Celnothus vero inter tot turbines & procellas immunis ab hisce malis fuit, atq; vbi plurimos annos sedisset, tandem morbo correptus expiravit, sepultus est in Ecclesia Christi Cantuariæ.
units.tr: which we can by no means pass over in silence: in the time of these seventeen archbishops of Canterbury, forty Popes sat in the city of Rome. By what fate this happened we leave to the judgement of the reader. Celnoth, however, amid so many whirlwinds and storms, was free from these evils. After sitting for many years, he was at last seized by illness and died. He was buried in the Church of Christ at Canterbury.

units.la: XVIII. ATHELREDVS.
units.tr: XVIII. Athelred.

units.la: ATHELREDVS vir venerandus, & in rebus diuinis insigniter eruditus, Monachus primò Ecclesiæ Christi Cant. deinde Episcopus Wintonn. post Ethelredi Regis munificentia, ad sedem Dorobernensem est assumptus. De cuius gestis hoc solum literis traditum reperimus, quod Anno Dom. 872. septimo Idus Iunii, die Pentecostes Werſfridum Wicciorum antistitem(defunc\to Alcuino) consecrauit. Huius eruditio tanta laude celebrabatur, ut cum foeliciffimus Princeps Alfredus excellentis doctrinæ viros in sua Regia curia foueret & alteret, inter hos, in aulam vocarus Wertridus, ráquam antesignanus præluceba. Hic Dialogorum libros Gregorii primi Romani Pontificis in linguam, Saxonicam transtulit. Ea ætate Iohannes Engena, natione Ealdefaxo (dictus Scotus, quòd in Hybernia versaretur) in Monasterio S. Dauidis Meneuiæ claruit. Is bellorum meru in Galliam ad Ludovicum Regem profugit, cui Dionysium transtulit, aliosque scripsit libros, qui quòd aliquàex parte diffonabant à fide Catholica, hæreticus est à Ni-colao Pontifice 1. habitus, cuius infamiæ meru ad Alfredum Angliæ Regem declinauit, cuius liberis præceptor est adhibitus. Postea Melduni resedit, vbi postaliquot annos à pueris quos docebat (vt feruntur) graphiis pforarus, animâ exhalauit. Iacuit aliquandiu in obscura sepultura, in beati Lanrentii Ecclesia quæ fuerat infandæ cædis conscia. Sed vbi diuinus fauor multis noctibus super eum lucem indulsit igneam, admoniti Monachi, eû in maiorem transtulerunt Ecclesiam, & ad finitram altaris ponentes, his Martyrium eius verbis prædicauerunt.
