Claudituř hoc tumulo sanctus Sophista Iohannes, Qui ditatus erat iam viuens dogmate mire: Martyrio tandem Christi conscendere regnum, Quo meritis sancti regnant per secula cuncti.
units.tr: Athelred, a venerable man and remarkably learned in divine matters, was first a monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, then bishop of Winchester. Through the generosity of King Ethelred, he was afterwards raised to the see of Canterbury. The only record of his deeds that we have found in writing is that in the year of our Lord 872, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, the day of Pentecost, he consecrated Werfrith, bishop of the Wiccians, on the death of Alcuin. His learning was celebrated with such high praise that when the most fortunate prince Alfred cherished and promoted men of outstanding learning at his royal court, Werfrith, summoned to the court, shone among them like a standard-bearer. He translated the Dialogues of Gregory the First, Roman Pontiff, into the Saxon tongue. At about this time John Erigena, by nation a Saxon (called Scot because he lived in Ireland), flourished in the monastery of St David's at Menevia. Because of the wars he fled to France, to King Louis, to whom he dedicated a translation of Dionysius, and he wrote other books. Because some of these in part disagreed with the Catholic faith, Pope Nicholas the First held him a heretic. Fearing this infamy, he turned aside to Alfred, King of England, to whose children he was appointed tutor. Afterwards he settled at Meaux, where, after some years, pierced with styluses by the boys he was teaching (as they say), he breathed out his soul. He lay for a while in an obscure grave in the church of blessed Lawrence, which had been party to the unspeakable murder. But when divine favour for many nights shed a fiery light over him, the monks, being warned, transferred him to the greater church and, placing him on the left of the altar, proclaimed his martyrdom in these words: "Here in this tomb is shut up holy sophist John, who, while living, was already wondrously enriched by doctrine; at last, by martyrdom, he ascended to the kingdom of Christ, where all the saints reign for ever by their merits."

units.la: Anno Dom. 860. Methodius Illyricus, vir Doctus, inter Slauos & Vandalos degès vitam, sacras literas in sermonem vulgarem connertit. Ille perutilis Ecclesiæ Christianæ, suscepit laboris imitandum sibi proposuit exemplum, sanctissimum & veruftissimum patrem, Wilfilum Gothorum Episcopum, qui Anno 370. Gothicas reperiens literas vtrûque Testamentum in linguam suam vernaculam traduxit. Perfualit etiam Methodius Illyricus Dalmaticis & Bauaris, vtabolita lingua Latina, vulgari in sacris peragendis verentur: vnde Cleri Principes, Episcopos, & alios ad iram ita concitabat, vt fugain Moravia saluti suæ consulere coactus sit, vbi mortuus atque Olmutiæ sepultus est. Eodem tempore Bulgarorum Episcopi contentionem habuere satis vehementem, cum præfato Nicholao Rom Pontifice, per Guntherum & Theologutum Episcopos, de matrimonii negocio, in quo Pontificem ipsum tyrannum vocabant: cuius etiam tonitrua & fulmina se pro nihilo ducere affirmabant.
units.tr: In the year of our Lord 860, Methodius of Illyria, a learned man who lived among the Slavs and the Vandals, translated the sacred letters into the common tongue. That most useful man of the Christian Church took as a model to imitate in his labour the most holy and most ancient father, Ulfilas, bishop of the Goths, who in the year 370, finding Gothic letters, translated both Testaments into his own native tongue. Methodius of Illyria also persuaded the Dalmatians and the Bavarians to abandon the Latin language and use the vernacular in performing the sacred rites. By this he so stirred up the princes of the clergy, the bishops and others, to anger that he was forced to flee into Moravia to save his life; there he died and was buried at Olomouc. At the same time the bishops of the Bulgarians had a quite violent dispute with the aforementioned Nicholas, Roman Pontiff, through the bishops Gunther and Theologutus, about a matter of marriage, in which they called the Pontiff himself a tyrant, and affirmed that they made nothing of his thunders and lightnings.

units.la: Anno Dom. 881. plurima Gallorum Monasteria à Danis diruta & solo æquata sunt. Athelredus Archiepiscopus post 18. annos in hac sede completos, morbo & senio consectus obiit: Sepultus in Ecclesia Christi Cant. iacet.
units.tr: In the year of our Lord 881, very many monasteries of Gaul were destroyed by the Danes and levelled with the ground. Archbishop Athelred, after eighteen completed years in this see, worn out by sickness and old age, died. He lies buried in Christ Church, Canterbury.

units.la: XIX. Plegmvndvs.
units.tr: XIX. Plegmundus.

units.la: Legmvndvs genere Mercius, literarum sacrarum scientia reli-quos fui temporis præstàs, (Athelredo mortuo) Archiprefulelectus, Romæ à Formoso Papa sacratus est, pallium-que accepit, vnà cum potestatis Metropoliticæ plenitudine summa. Primò in Insula Cestria, quæ ab incolis Plegmundusham dicitur, annos complures Heremiticam vitam ducebat, deinde Alfredo Regi præceptor adhibitus est, quem præcæteris singulari fauore Rex prosequebatur. Habuerat enim alios sibi familiares Asserium Menevensem, Grimbaldum, & Iohannem Scotum presbyteros, quorum labore & industria Psalterium Dauidicum in sermonem Anglicanum transtulit, cuius priore parte vix absoluta expirauit, cuius filium Edwardum Plegmundus Arch. more maiorum coronaRegia apud Singstone insignivit. Postea 7. vno die Episcopos in Ecclesia Cant. consecrauit, quorum suo loco mentionem faciemus.
units.tr: Plegmund, a Mercian by birth and the most learned in Holy Scripture of all the men of his time, was elected archbishop after Ethelred's death. He was consecrated at Rome by Pope Formosus and received the pallium, together with the full power of a metropolitan. At first he lived the life of a hermit for several years on the island of Chester, which the inhabitants call Plegmundsham. Afterwards he was taken on as tutor to King Alfred, who favoured him above all others with singular affection. The king also had other intimate companions, the priests Asser of Menevia, Grimbald and John the Scot. With their labour and diligence Alfred translated the Psalter of David into the English tongue. He died after finishing only the first part of it. Archbishop Plegmund, following the custom of his ancestors, crowned Alfred's son Edward at Kingston. Afterwards, on a single day, he consecrated seven bishops in the church of Canterbury, of whom we shall make mention in their proper place.

units.la: Anno Christi. 889. Plegmundus, omnesque Angliæ Episcopi, atque viri religiosi ex præcepto Regis Alfredi, fidelium elecmosynas collegerunt: colle&asque Romam, atque Hierosolymam cum magna Thesauri sui parte ipsemet Rex per Athelmum Episcopum Winton. transmisit. Officium enim officio iuuatur, & manus manu fricat, Epicharmi Comici testimonio. Prius enim ad instantiam & deprecationem Regis Alfredi, Marianus Papa Scholam commorantium Saxonum Romæ, omnis Tributi immunitate donauetat, & plurima dona præsentato Regi transmiserat: Inter quæ mirandæ antiquitatis monumenmonumentum sanctissimum, magnam scilicet partem illius erucis, in qua filius Dei pro salute hominum pependit.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 889, Plegmund and all the bishops of England, together with religious men, collected alms from the faithful at the command of King Alfred. The alms were gathered and sent to Rome and Jerusalem, with a large part of the king's own treasure, by the king himself through Ethelm, bishop of Winchester. For "one service is helped by another, and one hand rubs the other," as the comic poet Epicharmus testifies. Earlier, at the request and entreaty of King Alfred, Pope Marinus had granted the school of the Saxons living at Rome exemption from every tax, and had sent many gifts to the king. Among these was a most sacred monument of wonderful antiquity, namely a large part of that cross on which the Son of God hung for the salvation of men.

units.la: Anno Dom. 905. Plegmundus Cant. Archiepiscopus, vna cum Rege magnifico, cognomento Edwardo seniore concilium magnum Episcoporum, Abbatum, fidelium, procerum, & populorum in provincia Gewisiorum i. (in illa parte Angliæ, quæ in plaga australi sita est fluminis Thamesis) conuocauit. Fuerat autem Regio illa iam septem annos præhostium vi & impetu furioso, Episcoporum solicitudine & cura pastorali destituta: vnde salubriter constitutum est in hac Synodo, vt pro duobus Episcopis, quorum vnus Wintoniæ, alter Sireburniæ sedem habuit, quinque crearentur antistites, necgrex Domini pastorum cura orbatus luporum lanienæ & voracitati subduceretur. Quorum antistitum sedes hoc nomine appellantur, Wintonia, Sireburnia. Wellia, Cridium & Petrocium, quod est iuxta Wallenses aquilonares, ad flumen Heremuthe posita villula. Celebrato itaque concilio, & Canonica electione facta, constituit Plegmundus Archiepiscopus in sede Wintoniensi Brithestanum in Wellensi Athelmum (qui post Plegmundum factus est Archiepiscopus Dorobernensis:) in Cridiensi Eadulfum in Sireburnensi Wolstanum: & in Petrociensi Athelstanum. Sed & in aliis provinciis ordinauit duos Episcopos: Australibus Saxonibus (quorum antistites sedem habuerunt Cicestriæ) virum idoneum, Burnegum præfecit: Merciis vero Kenulfum ad civitatem Dorcestriæ. Hi omnes vno die Dorobernie ab Archiepiscopo Plegmundo consecrati sunt. Non multo post, sacerdotes parochiarum distributione, superfuerunt Episcopo Wintoniensi provinciæ Hamptoniensis, Sutherensis, & Wilcensis, cum Insula Vecta. Præterea Edwardo Rege adhuc viuente Wilcensis pagus suum habuit Episcopum, cuius sedes Ramisberiæ fuit: Syreburnensis vero Episcopus habebat Summersetam: Wellensis Dorcestriam & Barkeriam: Cridiensis, provinciam Deuonien sem: Petrociensis, Cornubiensem patriam. Quidam referunt septem annos destitutam fuisse omnem Regionem Gewisiorum (id est) Westsaxonum Episcopis, quam ob rem Anno Dom. 904. Formosus Papa in Angliam Episcopos misit, quibus potestatem excommunicandi, & maledicendi Regem Edwardum, & subditos eius dabat, eum antehac benedictionem à sede Sancti Petri, quam dederat Gregorius genti Anglorum, receperant. Quare causa Edwardus Rex Synodum prædictam nobilium Anglorum congregauit, cui præsidebat Plegmundus Archiepiscopus, inter pretans distincte verba Apostolicæ legationis, solutoque consilio idem Archiepiscopus Romam cum honorificis muneribus adiit, & offensum Papæ animum magna humilitate placauit, decretis Regis recitatis, quæ Apostolico ita placuerunt, vt & sua authoritate confirmauerit, & hæc edicta ad nihilantem perpetuo anathemate damnarit. Circa hoc tempus tradunt quidam grauem litem & contentionem de Eucharistia per Fredenardum quendam equitem auratum concitatum fuisse, cui respondebat Paschasius Monachus. Tempus efficeminatum hoc fuisse Warnerus in fasciculo temporum pronunciat: fides (inquit) tum valde deficere cœpit, & Clerici maleficiis erant dediti, consurgentibus sectis.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 905, Plegmund, archbishop of Canterbury, together with the illustrious king Edward the Elder, summoned a great council of bishops, abbots, faithful men, nobles and people in the province of the Gewisae, that is, in that part of England which lies on the southern shore of the Thames. That region had for seven years been left without bishops, deprived of the care and pastoral solicitude of its shepherds, through the violence and furious assault of enemies. Therefore it was wholesomely decided in this synod that, in place of the two bishops, one of whom had his seat at Winchester and the other at Sherborne, five prelates should be appointed, so that the flock of the Lord, bereft of its pastors, might not be handed over to the slaughter and greed of wolves. The seats of these prelates are named as follows: Winchester, Sherborne, Wells, Crediton, and Pedrocium (Padstow), which is a small village near the northern Welsh, on the river Heremuth. The council having been held and a canonical election made, Archbishop Plegmund appointed Brihtstan to the see of Winchester, Athelm to Wells (who after Plegmund became archbishop of Canterbury), Eadwulf to Crediton, Wulfstan to Sherborne, and Athelstan to Padstow. In other provinces too he appointed two bishops: for the southern Saxons, whose prelates had their seat at Chichester, he set over them a suitable man, Burhhelm; and for the Mercians he appointed Cenwulf to the city of Dorchester. All these were consecrated together on one day at Canterbury by Archbishop Plegmund. Not long afterwards, when the parishes had been distributed among the priests, the bishop of Winchester retained the provinces of Hampshire, Surrey and Sussex, together with the Isle of Wight. Moreover, while King Edward was still living, the district of Wilton had its own bishop, whose seat was at Ramsbury. The bishop of Sherborne had Somerset, the bishop of Wells had Dorset and Berkshire, the bishop of Crediton had the province of Devon, and the bishop of Padstow had the country of Cornwall. Some report that the whole region of the Gewisae, that is, the West Saxons, had been without bishops for seven years. For this reason, in the year of the Lord 904, Pope Formosus sent bishops into England, to whom he gave power to excommunicate and curse King Edward and his subjects; they had previously received the blessing from the see of St Peter, which Gregory had given to the English nation. Therefore King Edward gathered the aforesaid synod of English nobles, over which Archbishop Plegmund presided. Interpreting the exact words of the apostolic legation, and the council having been dissolved, the same archbishop went to Rome with honourable gifts and, with great humility, appeased the offended mind of the Pope. The decrees of the king were read out, and they so pleased the apostolic see that the Pope confirmed them by his own authority, and condemned to perpetual anathema anyone who should annul these edicts. Around this time some report that a grave quarrel and dispute about the Eucharist was stirred up by a certain Fredenard, a gilded knight, and that the monk Paschasius answered him. Warner, in his Fasciculus temporum, declares that this was an effeminate age: "Faith (he says) then began to fail greatly, and the clergy were given over to wickedness, and sects arose."

units.la: Anno Dom. 906. Cometa apparuit fere per dimidium annum, præsagientibus nonnullis inde multam sanguinis effusionem, magnam hominum cædem, & stragem, quæ paulo post in prælio inter Danos & Anglos commisso subsequuta est. In quo vtriusque gentis, ingens nobilium numerus corruit. Mirabitur fortasse quispiam, quod causæ sit, quod toties Danorum irruptionis in Angliam meminerimus, cum à nostro instituto cuilia immisceri negocia alienissimum esse debeat. Hic breuiter perpendat iustum Dei iudicium, in puniendis Anglorum flagitiis, nunc Monasteriorum conflagratione, nunc vrbium depopulatione, nunc terræ hiatu, nunc aliis supplicii generibus, eo quod omne religionem penitus contempserant, metum Dei exuerant, ad scelera & libidines nimiū proclives essent. Nam præterquam quod in populo omne vitiorum genus late serpebat, etiam bonarum artium obliuio ita vndique peruaserat, vt ne in Pontificibus quidem ceterisque Principibus, quicquam eluceseceret, quod ad vitam bene instituendam promoueret: recta exoleuerant institutia, templorum vastatio neminem affecit, pietatis exemplä sordebant, liberalium artium amor concideratur, stupor, & amentia quædam, obliuioque morum hominum animos penitus peruaserat: Papalis dignitas (impiorum Pontificum culpa) eo dementiae processerat, vt iam ludibrio esset for didissimo cuique: nec mirum, eum tam dira pietatis obliuio eorum mentes irrepserit, tam fœda scelerum libido impunè omnia loca occupavit, capite ipso ægro, & turpissimæ infamiæ nota conspurcaro, vt nec que personæ quam sustinebant, nec loci quem occupabant, rationem vllam habe-rent. Si ergo lumen O Ecclesia quod in te est, tenebra fuerint, ipsa tenebra quanta? vere igitur affirmare licet, si quid in illis moderati, aut decori fuit, id non tam sua sponte, quam Regum, Imperatorum, & in quorum tutela essent, metu & Reuerētia praestitisse. In hac tam misera rerum omnium facie Plegmundus moritur, & in Ecclesia Christi Cant. cum caeteris sepulturam obtinuit.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 906 a comet appeared for about half a year. Some foretold from it great effusion of blood, a great slaughter of men and carnage, which indeed followed shortly after in the battle fought between the Danes and the English, in which a huge number of nobles of both nations fell. Someone may perhaps wonder why we have so often mentioned the Danish invasion of England, since matters of war ought to be entirely foreign to our purpose. Let him briefly weigh here the just judgment of God in punishing the crimes of the English, now by the burning of monasteries, now by the plundering of cities, now by the opening of the earth, now by other kinds of punishment, because they had utterly despised all religion, cast off the fear of God, and were far too prone to wickedness and lust. For besides the fact that every kind of vice crept widely among the people, the forgetfulness of good arts had so pervaded everywhere that nothing shone forth even among the bishops and the other princes that might promote the right ordering of life. Sound institutions had fallen into disuse; the devastation of churches affected no one; the examples of piety were despised; love of the liberal arts was extinguished; a kind of stupor and madness, and forgetfulness of morals, had thoroughly possessed men's minds. Through the fault of wicked popes the papal dignity had sunk to such a degree of folly that it had become a laughingstock to the most foul of men. Nor is it surprising that, when such dire forgetfulness of piety had crept into their minds, such foul lust for crimes occupied every place unpunished, with the head itself sick and befouled by the mark of the most shameful infamy, so that they had no regard either for the persons they bore or for the place they held. If therefore, O Church, the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness itself? It may truly be affirmed that if there was anything moderate or seemly in those men, it was shown not so much of their own accord as through fear and reverence for the kings and emperors under whose protection they were. In this most wretched state of all things Plegmund died, and obtained burial in the church of Christ at Canterbury with the others.

units.la: XX. Athelmus.
units.tr: XX. Athelmus.

units.la: LEGMVNDO succeßit Athelmus, qui primò fuit Abbas Glastonburienßis, deinde ad Episcopatum Wellenßem translatus, post Cant. Archiepiscopus factus. De huius gestis nihil tradunt historiae, ideo neque nos commiserunt quicquam audemus. Ille post aliquot annorum quietam in sede possessionem in morbum incidit, & post varios corporis cruciatus animam exhalauit, & in Ecclesia Christi Cant. sepultus est. Petit id tempus in Occidentalium Saxonum finibus natus est Dunstanus, cuius auunculus Athelmus noster fuit. Roffensis historia portentū quoddam refert, (non dicam, beluae multorum capitum figmentum) aduersum scilicet in lignea vel lapidea statua Christi, cum se eundem in imagine sua â ludaeis pateretur. Ex hac iusceomodi infinitis anilibus fabulis omnis Pontificiorum doctrina constat, quae plane Antichristianum id esse Regnum, & praefigiis Satanae fulciri arguunt: sublato hoc illorum fundamento caetera sponte ruunt. Hisce etiam delirijs plurimorum Archiepiscoporum vitas sequentium refertas, fabulosi Monachi reliquerunt. Hic Athelmus primus iecit fundamenta Monasterii Malmsbur. Rex etiam Ethelstanus Regio diademate peremum insignitus, tres aedes monetis excudendis destinatas, Cantuariae aedificauit, quarum vnam Regi, Archiepiscopo alteram, tertiam vero Abbati Sancti Augustini, in visus exhibuit. Tres similiter Rodecestra, duas Regi, Episcopo vnam, praeter has etiam, Londini octo, Wintoniae sex, Lewis duas, Haftingae duas, Cicestriae vnam, Hamptoniae duas, Warhamae duas, Exceftriae duas, Schafsbury duas, & in quolibet praeterea oppido vnam.
units.tr: Plegmund was succeeded by Athelm, who was first abbot of Glastonbury, then transferred to the see of Wells, and afterwards made Archbishop of Canterbury. The histories hand down nothing of his deeds, so we too dare not commit anything to writing about him. After enjoying a quiet possession of his see for some years, he fell into illness, and after various bodily torments he breathed out his soul, and was buried in the Church of Christ at Canterbury. At that time, on the borders of the West Saxons, Dunstan was born, whose uncle was our Athelm. The History of Rochester relates a certain portent (I will not call it the fable of a many-headed beast): namely, that a statue of Christ, whether of wood or stone, spoke against him when he was suffering insults from the Jews in his image. The whole doctrine of the Papists rests on this kind of endless old wives' tales, which plainly argue that this is the Antichristian kingdom and is upheld by the portents of Satan; once this foundation of theirs is removed, the rest collapses of its own accord. Fabulous monks have also left behind these same follies, which fill the lives of very many archbishops who followed. Athelm was the first to lay the foundations of the monastery of Malmesbury. King Athelstan, the first to be invested with the royal diadem, also built at Canterbury three mints for striking coin, one for the King, another for the Archbishop, and a third, which he showed to view, for the Abbot of St Augustine's. Likewise at Rodecestra three, two for the King and one for the Bishop; besides these, eight at London, six at Winchester, two at Lewes, two at Hastings, one at Chichester, two at Hampton, two at Wareham, two at Exeter, two at Shaftesbury, and one in every other town.

units.la: XXI. Wlfelmus.
units.tr: XXI. Wulfhelm.

units.la: LFELMVS Wellensis etiam primò Episcopus, post Athelmum Archiepiscopus Cant. consecratur. De eo parum aut nihil historici memorant. Reliquiarum vero mentio fit, hoc tempore delatarū per Adulsum filium Baldwini comitis Flandriae, qui legatione huc in Angliam fungebatur, vt quartam Regis Athelstani filiam Hugonii Gallorum Regi in vxorem postula�ret. Peracta legatione varia caepa grandia munera proferebat, Constantini Magni ensem, cui literis aureis antiqui possessoris nomen insculptum fuit. In capulo ferreus infigebatur clauis, quem alterum ex quatuor, quo Christi corpus cruci affixum fuit, constanter affirmabat. Adhaec lanceā Caroli Magni obtulit, qnē si quādo Inuictissimus Imperator cōtra Sarracenos exercitū ducens, in hostem vibraret, victoriae laudem semper deportabat: Atque hanc eam esse, quàm Dominico lateri Centurio impungebat, à pluribus inculcatum fuisse retulit. Nec nō & Mauritii Beatiss. Martyris vexillum, cuius virtus variorum in bello prosperè gestorum acta fuit. Insuper & sanctae crucis partē chrysfallo inclusam, adbęc & spinae Coronae portionem: quae omnia pluribus verbis collaudara, Regi Athelstano tradebat. Quibus verò laudibus foetida Monachorum rabies haec deliria prosequatur, omnē fidei narrationem plane superat. Vnum autem illud silentio praeterire non possumus, quod Malmesbur. ad posteritatis memoriam, tanquam vnicam Coenobii sui tutelam, graiiter inculcar. Nam cum Athelstanus Rex praedictas crucis & coronae partes Coenobio Malmesburiensi dono dedisset, his solis sese ab omni hostium furore & impetu, immunes & maxime tutos somniabat. Proh Deum atq; hominum fidem, quid est Christum blasphemo & virulento ore proscindere, si hoc non sit? Videat ergo lector, quàm caeca nox mentibus mortalium incubuit, cùm hoc e fucos, posthabita veritate tam gnauiter amplectentur.
units.tr: Wulfhelm, first bishop of Wells, was afterwards consecrated archbishop of Canterbury in succession to Athelm. Historians record little or nothing about him. There is, however, mention of relics brought over at this time by Adulf, son of Baldwin, count of Flanders, who was then in England on an embassy to seek the hand of King Athelstan's fourth daughter for Hugh, king of the French. When his embassy was finished, Adulf presented various great gifts: the sword of Constantine the Great, on which the name of its former owner was engraved in gold letters; on its hilt was fixed an iron nail, which he firmly asserted was one of the four with which Christ's body was fastened to the cross. He also offered the lance of Charlemagne, which, he said, whenever that most invincible emperor, leading his army against the Saracens, brandished it at the enemy, always brought him the glory of victory; and he reported that this was the very lance with which the centurion pierced the Lord's side, as many had insisted. Also the banner of the most blessed martyr Maurice, by whose power the victories of many wars were won; and a part of the holy cross enclosed in crystal, and likewise a portion of the crown of thorns. All these he praised at length and handed over to King Athelstan. With what praises the stinking rage of the monks pursues these delusions, it is altogether beyond any credible account to tell. One thing, however, we cannot pass over in silence, which William of Malmesbury, for the memory of posterity, insists upon as the one protection of his monastery. For when King Athelstan had given the aforesaid parts of the cross and the crown to the monastery of Malmesbury as a gift, the monks dreamed that by these alone they were immune from every fury and assault of enemies and most secure. Good God, and faith of men! What is it to tear Christ with a blasphemous and venomous mouth, if this is not? Let the reader see, then, how blind a night has settled on the minds of mortals, when they so eagerly embrace these frauds and set truth aside.

units.la: XXII. Odo Seuerus.
units.tr: XXII. Odo Severus.

units.la: ODO, cognomento Seuerus, in Orientali Angiorum Regione, ex nobili Dacorum prosapia, Ethnicorum tamen, natus est. Hi male affecti erga illum, quòd iuuenilem agerat agens ætatem Christianorum conuentus frequentaret, grauissimis malis afflictum, iore etiam hæreditario indigne spoliabant. Ille relicta patria ad ducem quendam Christianum, Eihelelmum nomine, in aula Regis Edwardi senioris commorantem, se contulit. Dux perspectaiuoenis Indole, præceptoribus Græcæ & Latinæ linguæ periuissimis instituendum tradidit. Quorum cura & labore ad tam eximiam linguarum cognitionē breui peruasit, vt animi sen sumoratione soluta, aut quouis carminum genere sine mora profferre, & confestim quidquid dicere posset. Nō multo post suscepto baptismo, subdiaconatum etiam consilio Domini fui acceptit, in quo strenuè ac diligenter aliquot annos Euangelium prædicans, tandem sacerdotii munus obuiit. Tradunt quidam Odonem sub Edwardo Rege militari munere prius perfunctum, quàm sacris ordinibus initiaretur, atque id sane verum esse, coniectura facile assequi possumus. Nam post suscepem Episcopatus gradum, tribus vicibus illum militare auxilium Regibus præstitisse legimus. Sacratus enim Scirburnensis, vel Sarisburiensis Episcopus Athelstani Regis munificentia, qui cum singulari fauore complexus est, accidit Regem contra Aulafum instructo exercitu expeditionem suscepisse, cuius lateri adhibitus est. Iunctis verinq; copiis Athelstanus Rex Odonis auxilio, hostes facilimè prostrauit, Regales septem duces, quos aduersarii, in subsidium sui conduxerant, interfecit, & Aulafum fugamad naues capessere coegit. Rex potita victoria lætus in patriam reuertitur: & breui post moritur, cui Edmundus frater in Regno successit ... fratris fortitudinem æmulans, Odonem pari amore sibi conciliauit. Inter hæc moritur Wlfelmus Cant. Rex verò Odonis memor illum ad Archiepiscopatum Cant. eligit, & detrectantem impellit. Odo ægrè prabens assensum, aut, Nouerit Britannia tota, me hullo vnquam modo consensurum, vt in Clericali habitu constitutus Ecclesiæ Cantuariensi præsideam, quum nullus antea qui Monachus non fuerat, (quantum ipse coniicere potest) reuixè cognoscitur, quod tamen à veritate longè alienum est. Nam quosdam presbyteros fuisse supra retulimus, ideoque hic repetere non erit institutio nostro commodissimum. Quid verò est, quod insana Monachorum rabies comminisci non audeat, unde aliquod Monachatus sui patrocinium in coniogatos sacerdotes attripiant. Quem ordinem ob illorum coniugium sanctum omnibus spretum & ludibrio habitum Odo conspiciens, prauo Monachorum consilio inductus, ad Elonacense coenobium (quod est prope Aureliam Gallia ciuitatem) se contulit; in quo Monachalem habitum suscepit. Traduntalii Odonem mare noui transfisse, sed missus a Rege legatis ad Floriacense Monasterium, Abbatem loci, cum nonnullis fratribus laeto cursu in Angliam transfuectos, Odoni Religionis habitum tradidisse: vt cunque fuerit, non multum laboramus. Odone Archiepiscopaleu dignitatem administrante, pallium illi ab Agapeto secundo Romano Pontifice defertur. Fult illi cum Athelstano Rege firma familiaritas, quo malitiosè in domo sua interfecto, Eadredus frater eius ab Odone corona Regia est in signitus, cum quo non minor amicitia intercessit.
units.tr: Odo, surnamed Severus, was born in the eastern region of the English, of a noble Danish stock, though a heathen one. His own people, ill-disposed towards him because in his youth he frequented assemblies of Christians, afflicted him with the gravest injuries and unjustly stripped him even of his hereditary property. He left his homeland and went to a certain Christian nobleman named Æthelhelm, who was staying at the court of King Edward the Elder. The nobleman, perceiving the young man's talent, handed him over to tutors most skilled in Greek and Latin to be taught. Through their care and labour he soon attained such remarkable command of the languages that, with his thoughts flowing freely, he could at once put whatever he wished into verse of any kind, without delay. Not long afterwards, having received baptism, and at the advice of his lord, he also accepted the subdiaconate; then, for some years preaching the gospel vigorously and diligently, he at last assumed the office of priest. Some relate that Odo had served in the army under King Edward before he was admitted to holy orders; that this is true we can easily infer by conjecture. For after he took up the episcopal rank, we read that he gave military aid to kings on three occasions. When he had been consecrated bishop of Sherborne, or Salisbury, through the generosity of King Athelstan, who held him in singular favour, it happened that the king undertook an expedition against Anlaf with his army drawn up, and Odo was called to his side. With their forces joined, King Athelstan, with Odo's help, easily routed the enemy, slew seven royal leaders whom the adversaries had brought in as reinforcements, and compelled Anlaf to flee to his ships. The king, having won the victory, returned joyfully to his homeland, and soon after died; his brother Edmund succeeded him in the kingdom ... and, emulating his brother's courage, won Odo's equal affection. Meanwhile Wulfhelm, archbishop of Canterbury, died. The king, mindful of Odo, chose him as archbishop of Canterbury and pressed him, though he was unwilling. Odo, scarcely giving his assent, said: "Let all Britain know that I will never consent to preside over the church of Canterbury while I remain in clerical dress, since, so far as he himself can conjecture, no one who had not been a monk has been known in recent times to hold that office" — which, however, is far from the truth. For we have said above that there were some presbyters, and so it will not serve our purpose to repeat it here. But what is it that the mad rage of the monks does not dare to invent, so as to snatch from it some defence of their monkhood against married priests? Odo, seeing that order, holy in the eyes of all, despised and made a laughingstock because of the marriage of those priests, and induced by the perverse counsel of the monks, betook himself to the monastery of Elnone, near the city of Orléans in Gaul, where he took the monastic habit. Some relate that Odo crossed the sea to the new land, but that envoys sent by the king to the monastery of Fleury brought Odo the habit of religion, the abbot of that place having travelled happily into England with some brethren; however that was, we do not greatly concern ourselves. While Odo was administering the archiepiscopal dignity, the pallium was conferred on him by Agapetus II, the Roman pontiff. He had a firm friendship with King Athelstan ... who was treacherously killed in his own house; his brother Eadred was crowned king by Odo, and with Eadred he had no less friendship.

units.la: An.Dom.940. Aulafus genere Noruegensis; qui Regnante Athelstano Northanhumbrorum finibus expulsus fuerat, maxima classe ad littora expulsus, Eboracum se contulit: deinde australes Angliæ partes inuadens, facto tumultu subito Regnum Angliæ subiugare summis viribus contendebat. Quorum fama cum ad Regem Eadmundum peruenisset, expedito cursu Legecestriam properat, instructo milite armatus Odonem etiam Cant. & Wiltanum Eborac. comitatu sro adhibuit, vbi coniunctis copiis anciptii prælio diu ab vtriusque dimicatum est. His ita cedentibus. Archiepiscopi grauc vtriusque patris disterimen animadvertentes, præcipuè vero Regni subuersionem metuentes, hac conditione inter eos pacem composuerunt, vt Aulasustotam Angliæ Insulam ad bot ealem plagam viæ Regiæ (quæ Watlingstrete dicitur) suæ dicioni subiectam teneret: Eadmundus verò australis ciuitem callis parte contentus pacifice fuerit: quiqm superuiueret. Regni totius regimen obtineret. Mirabitur forsitan quispiam, quid causæ fuit, quod Odo Archiepiscopus tanti fecerit præfatos Reges Eduardum, Ethelstanum, Eadmundum, Eadredum, & sese cum illis tam intima familiaritate & consanguinitate coniunxerit. Res quidem satis aperta est. Munificentissimi enim in Monasteriis erant, quidam etiam summi Monachorum patroni, atq; ideo illorum gesta, etsi indignissima, summis laudib. ad sidera vsque tollebant.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 940: Olaf, of Norwegian stock, who had been driven from the borders of Northumbria in the reign of Athelstan, landed on the coasts with a great fleet and made his way to York. Then, invading the southern parts of England and causing a sudden tumult, he strove with all his strength to subdue the kingdom of England. When the report of these things reached King Edmund, he hastened by a swift march to Leicester, armed with a ready army, and took with him Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, and Wulfstan of York as his companions. There, with their forces joined, they fought a long and doubtful battle against the enemy. As the fight went back and forth, the archbishops, seeing the peril on both sides and especially fearing the overthrow of the kingdom, made peace between them on this condition: that Olaf should hold the whole island of England on the northern side of the royal road called Watling Street, subject to his rule, and that Edmund, content with the part of the south, should hold peacefully the government of the whole kingdom for as long as he lived. Perhaps someone will wonder what the reason was that Archbishop Odo made so much of the aforesaid kings, Edward, Athelstan, Edmund and Eadred, and joined himself to them in such intimate familiarity and kinship. The matter is quite plain. These kings were most generous to monasteries, some even being the chief patrons of the monks, and for that reason the monks raised their deeds, however unworthy, to the stars with the highest praises.

units.la: Eduardus enim Rex in Nouum Monasterium Wintoniæ (quod pater eius Alfredus construxerat) munificentissimus fuit, quippe portionem terræ satis amplam ab Episcopo & Canonicis mercatus est, in qua officinas erigeret, aturi Marci pro vmoquod pedeiolata. Suspenda (inquit Wilhelmus Monachus) profectò Regis abstinentia fuit, vt iuntsafe paterentur emungi pecunia, nolens scilicet de rapina patrem, offerre Deo sacrificium. Nec minor fuit Regis Athelstani liberalitas. Ille enim duo cænobia Middletonense & Micheleiense à fundamentis extruxit, quibus prædia & possessiones satis amplas donauit. Quot præterea noua Monasteria Rex Athelstanus erexerit Wilhelmus Malmesb. se dissimulaturum ait: illud autem silentio non transtuliturum, quòd vix aliquid intota Anglia vetustum fuerit, quod non vel ædificiis, vel ornamentis, vel libris, vel prædiis ditauerit: atq; ita dedita opera, antiqua recentibus inigniora reddidit, Mamesberiaq; cænobio multa largitus est prædia, chartisq; confirmauit. Post hunc Edmundus frater regnum administrabat, qui liberalitate cæteris inferior nullo modo fuit. Glasconienseme enim Ecclesiam magnis prædiis & honoribus cumulauit, & singulare priuilegiū concessit. Edmundo defuncto Eadredus corona regia ab Odidone redimitur, & recupublicam administrans, Dunstanum (vt in vita eius plenius patebit) tam singulari amore prosequutus est, vt omnes regni Thesauros illius custodiæ commendarit: cuius gratia nomen æternis laudibus affecerunt: atq; ita Regum munificentiam pari officio Monachi cōpensabant illorum gesta (plane supra merita) perlxpius celebrando. Post Edmundū regnauit Edwinus adolescens, ille modico amore Monachos & eorum præcipuos alumnos complexus est. Huic Odo Archiepiscopus par pari referre cupiens eodem anno, quo mortem obiit, regis & reginæ diuortium procurauit. vel quòd (vt ambigue quidam referunt) consanguinitate ei coniuncta fuisset, vel quia illam præter vxorem suam vtaduleram adamauit. Traduntaliì Odonem Archiepiscopum tanto furore percitū fuisse in Regis concubinas (quarum plures habebat) vt Ecclesiæ limitibus illis interdixerit. Nec multò post alteram earum, quam Rex præ cæteris vnicè dilexit, armato milite, a curia regis violenter abduxerit, eamq; in facie cadenti ferro notatam, in Hyberniam perpetuo exilio damnauit. Illa vero cicatrice obducta in Angliam rediens, ab Odone iterum capta & subneruata est. Rex id ægrè ferens diu dissimulatum odium, tandem in omnes Britanniæ Monachos exercebat: quippe satellitibus missis, quotquot Monasticam vitam profitebantur, omnibus facultatibus spoliauit, & maioribus postea calamitatibus affecit, ipsumq; Dunstanum Monachorum principem, in Flandria exulare coegit. Hae tempestate acerbalis, & contentio grauis Odoni fuit cum Clero Cant. de pane Eucharistico: Alii post consecrationem, priorem in eo manere substantiam: & panem tantum figuram esse corporis Christi, ac vinum sanguinis affirmabant. Quos Odo non solidis scripturarum argumentis, sed quibusdam præstigiis atque hoc mendaci Satanæ miraculo dilucere contendebat. Celebrante quodam die ante populum missarum solennia, cum gemitu & lachrymis diuinum auxilium implorabat, vt insitum pluribus errorem cœlestì quodam miraculo depelleret. Vbi ad confractionem ventū esset, confestim inter manus ponnificis fragmenta corporis Christi tenentis, sanguis guttatim defluere cœpit cōpunctisad id fortasse digitis. Stans itaq; pontifex, & prægando lachrymas obtrementes fundes, astantes ministros propius accedere iubet. Illi miraculi nouitate perterrefacti alta voce clamant. O te inter homines homines fœlicissimum, cui hodie filius Dei semetipsum in carne dignatus est reuelare. Exora p̄sul sanctissimū, vt in pristinam formā sanguis pīcns commutetur, ne nos propter infidelitatis errorem diutiù vlio sequatur. Orauit ergo, & ad aram respiciens, vbi sanguinem dimiserat, consuetam vinifpeciem reperiebat. Huius rei veritatem lectoris iudicio liberam relinquimus. Atque hoc fuit transubstantiationis papisticæ initium, quam Monachorum fœda turba, pro vero miserę plebi obtrusit. Simile quiddam de Marco cœmmentum legimus, cuiinipso communionis articulo corpus Christi ab Angelo ministratum est. Nec illud est prætereundum, quod de Pyamone presbytero refertur, cui aliquando sacrum Christi corpus offerenti, ante altare Angelus apparuit, absentium fratrum nomina delens, & præsentium literis mandans. Hisce deliriis & somniis tanquam Apollinis oraculà vulgo recepis, miseram plebem in miram fraudē heu nimiū diu illexerunt. Odone sedente synodum vnam, tempore regis Edmundi congregauit, qua dissoluta Epistolam ad Suffraganeos suos misit. Cuius exemplar, quòd erudicionis suæ indicia aliquod esse posset, hic subiiciemus ex Wilhelmo Malmsburie.
units.tr: King Edward was most generous to the New Minster at Winchester, which his father Alfred had built; indeed he bought from the bishop and canons a sufficiently large plot of land on which to erect workshops, paying a mark of gold for each foot of its breadth. "Astonishing indeed," says William the monk, "was the king's forbearance, that they allowed themselves to be drained of money, unwilling, to be sure, to offer God a sacrifice from his father's robbery." Nor was the liberality of King Athelstan any less. For he built from the foundations the two monasteries of Middleton and Michelney, and endowed them with ample lands and possessions. William of Malmesbury says he will pass over how many other new monasteries King Athelstan erected; but this he will not leave unmentioned, that scarcely anything in all England was so old that he did not enrich it with buildings, ornaments, books or lands. Thus by design he made old things more distinguished by new ones, and he bestowed many estates on the monastery of Malmesbury and confirmed them by charters. After him his brother Edmund administered the kingdom, and in liberality he was in no way inferior to the others. For he heaped great estates and honours on the church of Glastonbury and granted it a singular privilege. When Edmund died, Eadred was crowned king by Odo, and governing the commonwealth, he so favoured Dunstan (as will appear more fully in his life) that he entrusted all the treasures of the kingdom to his keeping; for this favour they honoured his name with eternal praises. And so the monks repaid the kings' generosity with an equal service, celebrating their deeds far beyond their merits. After Edmund reigned the young Edwy, who showed little affection for the monks and their chief pupils. Archbishop Odo, wishing to repay him in kind, in the same year in which he died, procured the divorce of king and queen, either because (as some report ambiguously) she was related to him by blood, or because he loved her as an adulteress, besides his own wife. They relate that Odo was so inflamed with fury against the king's concubines, of whom he had several, that he forbade them the boundaries of the Church. Not long afterwards, he forcibly took away from the royal court with armed soldiers the one whom the king loved above all the others, branded her face with a red-hot iron, and condemned her to perpetual exile in Ireland. But when she returned to England after the scar had healed, Odo seized her again and had her hamstrung. The king, bearing this with grief, at last vented on all the monks of Britain the hatred he had long concealed: for he sent out soldiers, stripped of all their goods everyone who professed the monastic life, and afterwards afflicted them with still greater calamities, and forced Dunstan himself, the prince of the monks, to go into exile in Flanders. At this time there was a bitter and grievous dispute between Odo and the clergy of Canterbury about the eucharistic bread. Some affirmed that after consecration the substance remained in it, and that the bread was only a figure of Christ's body and the wine of his blood. Odo contended that they were to be refuted not by solid arguments from Scripture, but by certain tricks and this lying miracle of Satan. Once, as he was celebrating the solemn rites of the mass before the people, he implored divine help with groans and tears, that by some heavenly miracle he might drive away the error planted in many. When he came to the breaking of the bread, at once, between the hands of the pontiff holding the fragments of Christ's body, blood began to flow drop by drop, perhaps from fingers pricked for the purpose. The pontiff stood still, pouring out tears as he prayed, and bade the ministers standing by come nearer. Terrified by the novelty of the miracle, they cried out in a loud voice: "O you most fortunate of men, to whom today the Son of God has deigned to reveal himself in the flesh! Pray, most holy prelate, that the flowing blood may be changed back into its former form, lest it pursue us longer on account of our error of unbelief." So he prayed, and looking at the altar where he had let the blood fall, he found the usual appearance of wine. We leave the truth of this to the judgement of the reader. And this was the beginning of the Papists' transubstantiation, which the foul crowd of monks foisted on the wretched common people as true. We read something similar about Mark, at whose very communion the body of Christ was administered by an angel. Nor is it to be passed over what is told of Pyamon the presbyter: once, as he was offering the holy body of Christ, an angel appeared before the altar, erasing the names of absent brethren and writing down those of the present. These follies and dreams, received by the common people as if they were the oracles of Apollo, have for far too long, alas, enticed the wretched people into a marvellous fraud. While Odo presided, in the time of King Edmund he gathered one synod, and after it was dissolved he sent a letter to his suffragans. A copy of it, which may serve as some evidence of his learning, we shall append here from William of Malmesbury.

units.la: EPISTOLA ODONIS ARCHIEPISCOPI AD SUFFRAGANEOS SUOS.
units.tr: EPISTLE OF ARCHBISHOP ODO TO HIS SUFFRAGANS.

units.la: IRABILI cunctì potentis præsulis polorum elementia opitulante, Ego Odo Ecclesiæ Domini nostri Iesu Christi Archiepiscopus, Doroberniensis ciuitatis Metropolitanus, Episcopis fidei catholicæ compagatoribus spiritualibus charitatis comitatus vigore, meis cōfratribus piscentiū, pisperitate, ethewithereiq decoris beatitudinem. Si aliquo modo fieri posset, vt totius mundi opes, ante nostros ponerentur obtutus, ita vt imperiali munere nobis vnluerfaliter deseruirent, libenter illa omnia distribuerem: meq; ipsum insuper pro vestrarum animarum salute impenderem. Quippe cum meipsum, a vestræ sanctitatis studio eupio & spero corroborari, super eo in quo Dominus Deus nos operarios constituit. Et post multa (quibus onus Pontificatus exponit) subdidi: Ideo humiliter quasi indignus, sed indignus precor & hortor sanctitatem vestram, ne tepide & negligenter in regimine animarum conuersemini: vt non in tempore tremendæ vindictæ conquaratur de vobis Dominus dicens. Pastores non pascebant gregem meum, sed semetipsos. Et iterum: Principes extiterunt & ego ignorau. Sed potius curemus familiam Domini (super quam nos constituit Rectores) vt cibum demus in tempore suo, mensuram tritici, probatam scilicet doctrinam. Et quamvis meritorum qualitate non præsumam consolari & bortari quenquam, quippe qui solus indignus, & innumerabilium culparum teus, gaudeo & indigeo fraternis admonitionibus fideliter corroborari: tamen propter antiquam authoritatem prædecessorum meorum, beatæ scilicet memoriæ Augustini, & aliorum sanctorum, quorum studiis regula Christianitatis ab hac Archiepiscopali sede cunctis finibus Anglorum innotuit: idcirco istos diuinos apices ad vilitatem omnium vestrum citare decrevi, quatenus Rex augustissimus (egregio nomine Eadmudus) eum omni populo suo inimitari gaudeat, quod in nobis, & ex vobis audiat; omneq; gentes quæ vndiq; regali imperio ipsius subleæ sunt, titulos liquidæ nostræ conuersationis, quanter sequi amant, & delectent. Ceterum epistolæ desunt. Creauit hic Oswaldum nepotem suum Episcopum Wigorn. quem postea ad Eboraensem transtulit.
units.tr: By the merciful help of the almighty Lord of the heavens, I, Odo, Archbishop of the Church of our Lord Jesus Christ and Metropolitan of the city of Canterbury, to the bishops, my fellow brothers, companions in the Catholic faith and bound to me by the strength of spiritual charity, wish peace, prosperity and the blessedness of a good life. If it could somehow be done that all the riches of the world were laid before our eyes, so that they might serve us universally by imperial gift, I would gladly distribute all of them, and I would spend myself too for the salvation of your souls. Indeed, I desire and hope to be strengthened by the zeal of your holiness, in the office to which the Lord God has appointed us as workers. And after many things (in which he sets out the burden of the pontificate), I added: therefore I beg and urge your holiness humbly, as one unworthy, indeed unworthy, not to conduct yourselves lukewarmly and carelessly in the governance of souls, lest in the time of dreadful vengeance the Lord complain against you, saying: "The shepherds did not feed my flock, but themselves." And again: "They were princes, and I did not know it." But rather let us take care of the household of the Lord (over which he has set us as rulers), that we give them food in due season, a measure of wheat, that is, sound doctrine. And although by the quality of my merits I do not presume to console or exhort anyone, since I alone am unworthy and full of countless faults, I rejoice in and need to be faithfully strengthened by fraternal admonitions; nevertheless, on account of the ancient authority of my predecessors, of blessed memory, namely Augustine and the other saints, by whose efforts the rule of Christianity became known from this archiepiscopal see to all the borders of the English, I have therefore decided to summon these divine letters for the benefit of all of you, so that the most august king (of excellent name, Eadmund) may rejoice to imitate, with all his people, what he hears of us and from you, and that all the nations which are subject on every side to his royal rule may love and delight to follow the marks of our clear conduct as far as they can. For the rest, the letters are wanting. Here he created Oswald, his nephew, bishop of Worcester, whom he afterwards transferred to York.

units.la: Anno Dom. 952. Eadredus Rex, Eboracensem Archiepiscopum Wlstanum in Withanbiriche in custodiam tradidit, quia frequentes ad eum accusationes deferrebantur, quod ciues Theodfordenses plurimos interfici iussit, vt mortem Abbatis Adelini iniuria illatam vindicaret. Alii in vineula coniectum tradunt, quòd Danis rebellantibus faueret & adiutor esset: breui tamen post reuerentia Clericalis respectu libertate donatur: qui furore & ira obsitum contumeliam percinus protinus expiravit. Odo vero; vbi Cantuarienfem dignitatem plurimis annis rectè administrasset, tandem senio confectus, ani30 mam exhalauit, sepultus in Ecclesia Christi Cantuariensi sub Edwino Anglorum Rege sacet. Quo mortuo Elfinus Winton. Episcopus precio apud Regem Eadgarum obtinebat Cant. Ecclesiæ dignitatem. Ingressus Cæsium ad Odonis tumulum accedebat, quem pedibus conculcatum, grauibus etiam conuitiis proscindebat. Sequenti noctè Odonis effigies illi in somnis visa est, exitium & perniciem minitans. Ille hæc pro nihilo ducens, Romam ad pallium recipiendum eeleri cursu contendebat. In itinere per Alpes tanto algore oppressus fuit, vt nihil aliud remedii ad frigoris iniuriam propulsandam comminisei potuit, quàm vt exenteratorum equorum adhuc spirantium exiis pedes immergerer, quibus Sanctisepulchrum conculcasset: atq; ita miserè vitam finiuit. Post hanc Brithelmus Wellensis Episcopus, ad Archiepiscopatum Cant. electus est, is, quia rebelles correxionis verbere omnino non cohiberet, à Rege Eadgaro ad relictam dignitatem redire iussus est. Cuius loco B. Dunstanus omnium iudicio comprobatus succedebat. 40
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 952. King Eadred handed over Wulstan, Archbishop of York, into custody at Withanbirig, because frequent accusations were brought against him: that he had ordered very many citizens of Thetford to be killed, in order to avenge the unjust death of Abbot Adelin. Others say he was put in chains because he favoured and aided the rebellious Danes; yet shortly afterwards, out of respect for his clerical dignity, he was granted his liberty. He, consumed with fury and anger at the insult, straightway breathed his last. Odo, indeed, when he had administered the dignity of Canterbury well for very many years, at last worn out with age, breathed out his soul, and was buried in Christ Church, Canterbury, under King Edwin of the English. After his death, Elfinus, Bishop of Winchester, obtained the dignity of the Canterbury church through the favour of King Eadgar. On entering, he went to Odo's tomb, which he trampled underfoot and tore apart with heavy abuse. The following night Odo's image appeared to him in a dream, threatening ruin and destruction. He, regarding this as nothing, hastened with all speed to Rome to receive the pallium. On the journey over the Alps he was so overcome by cold that he could devise no other remedy to ward off the harm of the frost than to plunge his feet into the still-breathing entrails of horses, with which he had trampled the holy sepulchre; and so he ended his wretched life. After him, Brithelm, Bishop of Wells, was chosen as Archbishop of Canterbury. Because he did not at all restrain the rebels with the rod of correction, he was ordered by King Eadgar to return to the dignity he had left. In his place, Blessed Dunstan, approved by the judgement of all, succeeded.

units.la: XXIII. Dunstanvs
units.tr: XXIII. Dunstan

units.la: Amqve Ecclesiæ Christianæ aciesiac cæcabatur erroribus, vt veribi diuini lux à pauculissimus cerneretur. In hac erasa & concreta caligine, quæ densior multis annis ante cretiffet indies, Dunstantus natus est: Huius in illo atro seculo ætas artes gesta prodigiosa, portentisq; (quæ illa ceptas miracula vera putabat) plena fuerunt. Itaque quis ac qualis fuerit, ab ipsis incunabulis, vberibusque ac vtero matertis, retexatur. Cuius historia, quoniam à Monasticis illius seculi scriptoribus, W. Malmesb. haurienda nobis est, dabit nobis prudens lector veniam, si adumbratis fictisq; à se Dunstani laudibus præsermisis, eorum tamen verba & narrationes, quæ vitæ suæ veritate ostendunt, sequamur. Natus est anno primo Regis Athelstani in ea Angliæ plaga, quæ ad occidentem posita, tunc Westsaxonia dicta fuit. Parentibus ortus utriusq; nobilibus, Herstario Parte, matreq; Kinedcida, à cuius vtero ne fine portento foetus exiit. Sed ab infantia penè literis institutus, cum ætate esset proueetior, lingua ad eloquendum composita & formata, à parentibus ad Glasconiensem Ecclesiam deductus est. Ibi ingenuas & liberales artes didicit. Nondum enim etas Monasticus illam Ecclesiam occupauit, Abbatisq; nomen penitus erat incognitum, sed artium profeffores regiis alcbantur stipendiis. Si quis autem ab hominum consuetudine ad solitariam vitam fe vellet abducere, modo solus, modo paucioribus conloquiatur, patria relicta, capta in alienaregione opportunitate viuendi vixit peregrinus. Quaocasione Hibernenses quidam nobiles habitandi locum a ciuili turba multitudinequ; seiunctum Glasconiae delegerunt. Ibi adolescentes nobiles ingenuis artibus mercede instruxerunt. Inter quos Dunftanus in illa iuuenili institutione cateris instructior, ad eas artes, musicam, & pingendi atque sculpendi scientiam adiecit. Quibus facultatibus non minus quam nobilitate decoratus, a parentibus ad Athelinum Cantuariensem Archiepiscoporum auunculum suum oblatus est, a quo benigne suscep tus & aliquandiu retentus, ob indolem, nobilitatem, & doctrinam Athelstano Regi (cui consanguinitatis etiam iure deuinctus fuit) commendatur. Rex adolescentem summa fouit gratia, eoque magis, quod lyram tam dulciter iucunde q; pulsaret. Quo etiam nomine matronis aulicis foeminisq; (quibus fibi perinde ac cum Daemonibus frequens commertium fuit) gratissimus habebatur. Illae laficiuum iuuenem pellexerunt, vt sacerdotalis stolae exemplum artificiosa pictura sibi proponeret, quam illae artificioso & acuato opere, setuis auteisq; filijs gemmisq; illustrarent. Earum rogatu hoc opus assumpta cythara Dunstanus aggreditur. In quo perficiundo, fingunt Monachi, Dunstani cytharam a pariete pendentem, & a nullo tactam, cantabat quod sit nora & dulci modulatione melodiam Antiphonae, Gaudentes in celu anima sanctorum, &c. personuisse. Quo prodigioso euentu perterrita familia exclamauit Dunstanum nimis sapere, caq; quae non expedient scire, & ad Regem deferunt cum Daemoniacis technis praestigiisq; imbutum, pleraq; operari. Rex eum illico aulla iussit cedere, eumq; discedentem quidam insidiose sequuti supplicijs affligunt, vinculisq; constrictum in lutosum paludem coniiciunt. Hac contumelia & ignominia affectus venit ad Elphegum aeunculum item suum Wintoniensem Episcopum. Qui illum tu libidinosum & lascium iuuenem, vt a mulierositate auerteret, multis argumentis hortatus est, vt Monachismum ingrederetur. Sed Dunstanus iuuenem mulierem potius ducere, cuius quotidie blanditiis fouerctur, quam Monachali ritu bidentinis indui panniculis maluit. Itaque spreto auunculi sui consilio, ex intestinorum tumore grauissime co?pit aegrotare. Hunc ille morbum sibi coelitus inflictum autumauit, quod Auunculi spreuisset consilium. Itaq; accito Elphego Monachalis superstitionis habitum poposcit, & fe non castitati sed coelibatui vouit. Monachatu fuiscepto in Glasconiensi beatae Mariae Ecclesia, cuius gestit titulum, contiguum & adhaerentem Ecclesiae parietibus cellam suis manibus ad laboribus struxit, quae spelunca magis atque sepulchri quam humanae habitationis formam praeferebat. Huius longitudo quinq; pedum erat, latitudo duorum & semis, altitudo staturam hominis expressit, si quis in defossa terra constitetur. Aliter enim neque satis ad pedes porrigebatur. Ostiolum autem idem fuit quod Paries. Haec erat iuuenl simulanti sanctitatem ex ingenio domus, huc lectus, hoc de mundo spectaculum. Sed de hoc Monacho hi versus facti esse videntur.
units.tr: And while the battle line of the Christian Church was blinded by errors, so that the light of divine truth was discerned by very few, Dunstan was born into this thickened and condensed darkness, which had been growing denser by the day for many years before. The age of that dark century was full of his arts, deeds and prodigies, and of portents (which it then believed to be true miracles). So who and what sort of man he was is revealed from his very cradle, and from his mother's breasts and womb. Since his history must be drawn for us from William of Malmesbury, a monastic writer of that century, the prudent reader will forgive us if, having set aside the praises of Dunstan that were shaped and embellished by that writer, we nevertheless follow the words and narratives which show the truth of his life. He was born in the first year of King Athelstan, in that part of England which lies to the west and was then called Wessex. He was born of noble parents, Heorstan, the father, and Cynethryth, the mother, from whose womb his offspring came forth without any portent. But being educated in letters almost from infancy, and when he was further advanced in age, with his tongue shaped and formed for speaking, his parents led him to the church of Glastonbury. There he learned the liberal and free arts. For as yet no monastic order occupied that church, and the title of abbot was entirely unknown; instead, teachers of the arts were paid from the royal treasury. If anyone wished to withdraw from the company of men into a solitary life, sometimes speaking alone, sometimes with a few, having left his homeland, he lived as a stranger in a foreign region, seizing the opportunity of living there. For this reason certain noble Irishmen chose Glastonbury as a place to dwell, set apart from the civil crowd and multitude. There they taught young noblemen the free arts for a fee. Among these Dunstan, being better instructed than the rest in that youthful training, added to those arts music and the knowledge of painting and sculpture. Adorned with these accomplishments no less than with his nobility, he was offered by his parents to his uncle Athelm, Archbishop of Canterbury, by whom he was kindly received and kept for some time. Because of his natural gifts, his nobility and his learning, he was commended to King Athelstan, to whom he was also bound by the ties of kinship. The king held the youth in the highest favour, all the more because he played the lyre so sweetly and pleasantly. For this reason too he was most welcome to the court ladies and women (with whom he had frequent dealings, as if with demons). These women enticed the lascivious youth to set before himself as a model a picture of a priestly stole, which they would adorn with skilfully and ingeniously worked silks, golden threads and gems. At their request Dunstan took up his lyre and set about this work. While he was finishing it, the monks tell that Dunstan's lyre, hanging from the wall and touched by no one, sang and sounded forth, with a sweet and pleasant melody, the antiphon The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven, and so on. At this prodigious event the household was terrified and cried out that Dunstan knew too much, and was attempting things he should not know; and they reported to the king that he was steeped in demonic arts and tricks and was working many things by them. The king at once ordered him to leave the court; and as he departed, some men followed him secretly and tormented him with punishments, bound him with chains and threw him into a muddy marsh. Affected by this insult and disgrace, he came to his uncle Elphege, likewise Bishop of Winchester. Wishing to turn him away from his lustfulness and lasciviousness, Elphege urged him with many arguments to enter the monastic life. But Dunstan preferred to take as his wife the young woman by whose caresses he was daily cherished, rather than to be clothed in the coarse rags of the monastic rite. Therefore, scorning his uncle's advice, he fell gravely ill from a swelling of the bowels. He judged that this sickness had been sent to him from heaven because he had despised his uncle's counsel. So, summoning Elphege, he asked for the habit of monastic superstition, and he vowed himself not to chastity but to celibacy. Having taken up the monastic life in the church of Blessed Mary at Glastonbury, whose title he bore, he built with his own hands, close to and adjoining the walls of the church, a cell for his labours, which bore more the form of a cave or tomb than of a human dwelling. Its length was five feet, its breadth two and a half, and its height matched the stature of a man if he stood in dug-out earth; for otherwise it would not stretch out far enough for the feet. The doorway was the same as the wall. This was, for a young man pretending to holiness, the house built to his nature, here his bed, here his spectacle of the world. But these verses seem to have been made about this monk.

units.la: Damon languebat, tunc Monachus esse volebat.
units.tr: Damon was sick, and then he wanted to be a monk.

units.la: Damon conualuit, Damon vt ante fuit.
units.tr: Damon recovered, and Damon became what he had been before.

units.la: Qui enim Aunuculi sui consilio concupiscentia nutrimenta oculis amouere debuisset, in hac fabricata spelunca sub sanctitatis specie quotidiano foeminae congressu fruebatur. Haec Alfgina dicta fuit, regali orta sanguine, atque locuples. Quae Christum a nullo distare voluit; praeterquam ad hoc nomen. Cuius ex ore (vt ipsa parabat) melle dulcior fluebat oratio. Itaque tam sancti sermonis suauitate capta, nec domum redire, nec loco illi discedere, sed cum Dunstano piissimo ruinem mentis, viuere, moriqueque statuit. Habitaculum sibi prope eandem Ecclesiam constituit, cuius Dunstano ad conferendum de Christo sermonem assidua fuit, continuata profecto est, pauperibus benigna & larga fuit, plures illius ordinis vitos in eo loco statuit, qui pauperibus distribuit. Res vero atq; pdia Ecclesiastici sunt, eligens Monachorum hic Pater, patronus, & fautor, ex hac tam opima hereditate, quinq; cōdidit Monasteria, & ecclesiae iuncta. Haec segnitatem adhuc
units.tr: He, who ought to have removed the nourishment of desire from his eyes on his uncle's advice, enjoyed daily the company of a woman in this artificial cave under the appearance of holiness. She was called Alfgina, of royal blood and wealthy. She wished to be like Christ in everything except the name. From her mouth, as she herself arranged it, there flowed speech sweeter than honey. So, captivated by the charm of such holy talk, she resolved neither to go home nor to leave that place, but to live and die with the most pious Dunstan, in the ruin of her mind. She built a dwelling for herself near that same church, and she was constant in conversing with Dunstan about Christ. She was indeed persistent, kind and generous to the poor, and she established several monks of that order in that place, who distributed to the poor. But the goods and property belong to the Church. This Father of the monks, their patron and promoter, chose from this rich inheritance and founded five monasteries joined to churches. These things [were] still [...]

units.la: Athel-
units.tr: Athel-

units.la: A helstano, antequam ætatis suæ annum vicesimum attigisset, gessit Dunstanus. Sed mortuo Athelstano Edmundus eius frater imperium gessit, qui hunc tam insignem ficta pietate Monachum speluncæ suæ eduxit & cum proceribus statuit. Proceres vero nunciata Regi de libidinibus eius & præstigiis dispersa fama, cum aula rursus fuoq; consorvo mouent. Monachi hunc fingunt, triduo postquam discesserit, in Regis iterum gratiam prodigiose redisse. Postridie enim Rex in venatione, famulatu casu derelicto, ceruum per deuia fugientem solus insectabatur, cumq; in montis excelsi cacumen canibus egit, ex quo tam ceruus quam canes præcipites cecidere, grandiq; lapsu fracti periere. Rex ipse hucab equo effreni, quem cohibere non poterat vectus, simile præcipitium expectans de salute desperauit. Hoc metu & periculo perplexus inuocauit Deum, meminitq; Dunstani ex aula pridie eiecti, spondit se & Deo religiosius serviturum, & Dunstanum in summo honore habiturum, si id discrimen euaserit. Quo facto & emisso voto, habenæ, quas in cohibendo equo fregerat, redintegrantur, equus quiete restitit, Ceruus & canes reuiuiscunt, Rexq; saluus ad suos redit. Illico ad reducendum Dunstanum missi, nuncii, cui redeunti occurrit Rex, apprehensamq; eius dextram osculatus: Agnosco (inquit) vitorum sanctissime, quid in te committerim malì, ab improbissimis hominibus stimulatus. Gratias ago clementiæ Dei, qui non solum debitum mihi supplicium noluit inferre, sed etiam a præcipitio montis eripiens, longioris vitæ spacium in tuo nomine concesserit. Sit ergo inter nos deinceps perfecta familiaritas: sit in disponendis in Palario & Regno rebus libera semper tibi facultas. Deinde loca in quibus Dunstanus genitus, natus, enutritus, educatus aut versatus fit, Dunstanus ad cœnobia extruenda dedit. Dunstanus itaque sui ordinis Monachorum copiosa collecta muleitndine, cœnobium quòd tunc solum in Anglia fuit, repleuit, ipseq; eorum dux ac Magister Abbatis nomine primus in Anglia appellatus est. Erat tunc temporis quidam Pulfricius Dunstani frater, qui omnia sacularia Monasterii negocia, quibus ex instituto non liceret se Monachis permiscere, foris tractabat. Hic moritur. Monachi autem omnes ad eius funus celebrandum Monasterio exeunt, solus Dunstanus cum adolescente quodam suo discipulo domi remansit. Cumq; in exequiis Monachi morem fecissent, exiuit cum adolescente, Dunstanus inspectum, an Monachi cum fratris cadauere approprinquarent. Illi tunc bres ex more cantus psallentes prope adfuerunt. Interea taxum quoddam volatile ac rotundum per aetem missum, per caput Dunstani ita transiit, ut eius pileum triginta, passibus a capite decussum proiecerat. Qui intercipidus adolescentem discipulum tuum, iussit illud saxum in tertiam iam actum ad ie deferre. Quod ita pondere depressum errat suo, vt ab adolescente ita attolli potuit. Deinde peractis exequiis Dunstanus iussit id saxum Monasterio illatum, tanquam ad sempiternam miraculi memoriam reseruari. Perempto autem a latrunculo quodam nomine Leof, Edmundo Rege, Eadredus frater imperium suscepit. Hunc omnibus iusticiæ pietatisq; laudibus Monachi sicut pius ac monumentis suis celebrant, quòd Dunstanum Proceribus suis omniq; humano genere, præcluifer. Quem Dunstanus etiam charissimum suum solita acclamatione semper appellauit. Hic iuppellectilem suam præcipuam, regalis hæreditatis atque iuris instrumenta, Regni thesauros, & a se acquisitas gazas in Dunstani Monasterio locauit & condidit: regnum denique, corpus, animamq; adeo suam Dunstano commisit. Omnia iam in Dunstani potestatem venerunt, neque quicquam, non modo in publicis regni negociis, sed in suis pene priuatis rebus gerere inconsulto Dunstano ausus est. Proinde regiam is solus vbique potestatem exercuit. In qua totus laboraut, vt Ecclesias, quasi aut ipse, fundauerat, aut ab aliis conditas Danorum incursio destruxerat, renouaret, præduisq; amplis dotaret. Ad hoccotatu Eadredi Regis mortem Dunstanus tepulius & prohibitus est. Qui cum imm sibi mortem perspexisset, thesauros in Dunstani custodia positos, vt de his adhuc viuus disponeret, repetit. Itaque Dunstanus ad Monasterium vbi reponebatur thesaurus profectus, eum iam regiis opibus onustus & sarcinatus reuertetur, vocem è summo ethere demissam sibi nuncuantem audiuit, Eadredum obdormiuisse in Domino. Huic Eadwinus Edmundi filius successit. Qui pleraq; quæ Dunstanus Patris ac auunculi sui temporibus totam Remp. administrans. Ecclesiis adiecerat, iterum detraxit. Quod Dunstanus grauiter ferens, egit Regem liberius increpare. Rex verò eius increpationes leuiter lusit, & minis eū abaula deterruit. Itaq; iam tertio aulareglia Dunstanus abiens, ad Monasterium suum Glastoniæ secessit. Monachi hunc Regem quia Dunstano suo aduersus fuit, inconsiderata libertate seu temeritate scribentes, parum veracunda narratione infami notant turpitudine.
units.tr: Dunstan conducted affairs under Athelstan before he had reached his twentieth year. But when Athelstan died, his brother Edmund held the kingship. He brought this monk, so notable for his feigned piety, out of his cave and set him among the nobles. The nobles, however, when word of his lusts and tricks was reported to the King and the rumour had spread, moved him again, with the court and his fellowship, out of favour. The monks invent that three days after he had left, he returned again to the King's favour by a miracle. For the next day the King, hunting, had by chance left his attendants behind and was pursuing a stag alone as it fled through pathless places. When he drove it with the dogs to the top of a high mountain, both the stag and the dogs fell headlong, and, broken by the great fall, they perished. The King himself, carried off by an unbridled horse which he could not control, expected a similar precipice and despaired of his safety. Perplexed by this fear and danger, he called upon God and remembered Dunstan, who had been cast out of the court the day before. He promised that he would serve God more devoutly and would hold Dunstan in the highest honour, if he came through this peril. With this done and the vow uttered, the reins, which he had broken in restraining the horse, were restored; the horse stopped quietly; the stag and the dogs came back to life; and the King returned safe to his people. Messengers were straightway sent to bring Dunstan back. The King met him as he returned, and kissing his right hand said: "I acknowledge, most holy of men, what evil I did against you, goaded on by the most wicked men. I give thanks to the mercy of God, who not only did not wish to inflict on me the punishment I deserved, but also, snatching me from the precipice of the mountain, granted me a longer span of life for the sake of your name. Let there therefore be from now on perfect friendship between us, and let it always be open to you to arrange affairs in the Palace and the Kingdom as you wish." Then Dunstan gave to the building of monasteries the places in which Dunstan had been born, begotten, nurtured, educated or lived. Dunstan, gathering a large crowd of monks of his order, filled the monastery which alone then existed in England, and he himself, as their leader and master, was the first in England to be called by the title of Abbot. At that time there was a certain Pulfric, Dunstan's brother, who handled outside all the secular business of the monastery, in which by rule monks were not allowed to mix. He died. All the monks went out to the monastery to celebrate his funeral, and Dunstan remained alone at home with a young disciple of his. When the monks had performed the customary rites at the funeral, Dunstan went out with the young man to see whether the monks were approaching with the brother's corpse. Meanwhile some round missile, flying through the air, passed over Dunstan's head in such a way that it threw his cap thirty paces from his head. Astonished, he ordered his young disciple to bring to him that stone, which had come to rest at a distance. It was so weighed down by its own weight that the young man could lift it only with difficulty. Then, when the funeral was over, Dunstan ordered the stone to be carried into the monastery and kept there as a lasting memorial of the miracle. King Edmund having been killed by a certain robber named Leof, his brother Eadred took up the kingship. The monks celebrate him with every praise of justice and piety in their writings, because he [held] Dunstan [in high regard] before his nobles and all mankind. Dunstan too always called him his dearest, with his customary acclamation. He placed and stored in Dunstan's monastery his chief household goods, the instruments of his royal inheritance and right, the treasures of the kingdom and the wealth acquired by himself. In short, he entrusted his kingdom, body and soul to Dunstan. Now all things came into Dunstan's power, and he did not dare to do anything, not only in public affairs of the kingdom but almost even in his own private affairs, without Dunstan's advice. Accordingly, he alone exercised royal power everywhere. In this he laboured wholly to restore the churches which he himself had founded, or which the incursion of the Danes had destroyed after they had been built by others, and to endow them with ample estates. At this point, when the death of King Eadred drew near, Dunstan was checked and forbidden. When Eadred saw that death was already upon him, he asked back the treasures placed in Dunstan's keeping, so that he might dispose of them while still alive. So Dunstan went to the monastery where the treasure was kept, and as he was returning laden and burdened with the royal wealth, he heard a voice sent down from the highest heaven announcing to him that Eadred had fallen asleep in the Lord. Eadwin, son of Edmund, succeeded him. He took away again many of the things which Dunstan, administering the whole commonwealth in the times of his father and uncle, had added to the churches. Dunstan, taking this badly, began to rebuke the King more freely. But the King lightly mocked his rebukes and by threats drove him from the court. So Dunstan, leaving the court for the third time, withdrew to his monastery at Glastonbury. The monks, writing this of the King because he was opposed to their Dunstan, with reckless freedom or rashness, mark him with infamous disgrace by a narrative that has little regard for the truth.

units.la: {y} Ecclesiam quedam sanctus Dunstanus ædificauit. Regem eo ipso die, quo sacratus fuit, cum in frequentissimo conuentu Procerum de regni admonitione ageretur, se abillis cum lusu & saltu leuiter subduxisse, & in venustæ cuiusdam fceminæ, cuius forma deperibat, complexum inuasisse, eamq; in thalamum ductam viiaisse. Omnes Regis immodestia permoti tacitè murmurare coeperunt. Dunstanus autem cum Cynesio Episcopo coosanguineo suo thalamum ingreditur，Regemq; impudicè lascivieotem tamè lecto quàm è thalamo vi trahit, authoritate q; Odonis Cant. Archiepiscopi eiusdem fceminæ consuetudini renunciare fecit. Hoc regis factum dum Monachi cupidius aueot prodere, ipsi se suapte meodacia produnt. Quidam mulierem à Rege concupitam Alfginam, quidam Athelgifam nuncupant. Quidam Regieo sanguinis gradu cognatam, quo iure Pontificio coniugari non poterant; aliùeius concubinam, alii alterius coniugem, quem Rex occidi iusserat, fuisse scribunt. Quibus inter fe dissentientibus & contrariis Monachis, vetustissimus, integerrimus & doctissimus inter eos antiquitatis scriptor, etsi Monachus non fuerat, Henr. Huntingdonensis, nihil scribit de de Edwino graiius: quàm quòd prospete & laudabiliter Rempubl. administraret, bonaque felicitèr gesti imperii initia posuisset, sed anno sui regni quinto immatura morte a patria sublatus fuerit. Ex his Monachorum etsi discrepantibus fabulis, constat Dunstanum impudentissimè in Regis ingressum thalamum, eaque gessisse, quæ sacerdotalis aut Christianæ non sunt verecundiæ. Nam cæteras huius narrationis varietates consultò omittimus. Rex Dunstanum proscripsit, nec aula solum sed regno eiecit, Monasterii Glaseonienfis bona possessionesq; ditipuit, & in Monachos qui tum in Anglia pauci fuerunt, ea gessit, quæ in Odonis vita supra commemorata sunt. Dunstanus in Galliam profugit, & in Glandauensi, vel Blandiuensi cœnobio vno anno exulat. Post eius discessum scribunt Monachi auditam de crypis Monasterioram vocem plaudentis Diaboli gracilem & canoram, quasi mulierculam immoderatè ridentis & cacchinnantis. Cui Dunstanum fiogunt respondeotem, vt de exilio suo non lætetur, quòd eo reuerso triftior erit, quàm nunc exulante gaudere possit. Interea Mercii & Norrenses, ac inter Humbrum & Thamesim mediterranei in Regem arma capiunt. A quibus autem hic tumultus motus fuerat, Monachi cautè omittunt. In hoc tumultu Edgarus Regis frater regni partem obtinet. Hi multis vtrinque illaris præliis regni vires labefactarunt, sed Edgarus tandem potior, conuocato ad Brandanfordiam Regni concilio, fratris Edwini acta & decreta rescindit, ablatas Ecclesiis & Monasteriis opes restituit, Dunstanum q; ab exilio ad pristinum honorem reuocat, deinde ad Episcopatum Wigornensem using nolentem promouit, postea ad Londinensem, tandem biennio vix translato ad Cantuariensem Archiprælatum. Hos omnes Episcopatus inuitum & importunissimo Regis rogatu victum Dunstanum fuscepisse Monachi scribunt, sed Dunstanum laudandi potius quàm veritatis declarandi studio proueđi vanitatem sæpe adhibent orationis. Alibi enim scribunt, cum Eadredus Cridiensem ei Episcoparum obtulisset, isque, quanquàm acerrimè potente & instante tam Rege quàm Regina eius matre repudiatlet, proxima node adfuisse sibi in somnis Petrum, Paulum, sanctumq; Andream strictos gladios manibus tenentes. In Petri gladio hæc sententia literis aureis inscultptafuit. In principio erat verbum. In Pauli & Andreæ gladiis nomina tantum sua. Hos illi gladios offerebant. Andreas qui Patronus & & vitæ suæ Deus assiduè ab eo cultus fuit, hilari cum vultu intuens. Tollite inquit iugum meum super vos, &c. Petrus autem iussit eum lxuam extendere, quàm his verbis molliter ferit. Sit hæc plaga poena tibi abiecti, & signum vlterius non abiiciendi pontificatus. Dunstanus Regi postridie hoc visum narrat. Rex eo nie & dor somnii, Increpauit te (inquit) Petrus quod iugum Domini contempseris. Tres Apostolorum gladii prænuociant tein Ecclesiis illorum nominibus dicatis Pontificiale ius habituram, in Wigornienfi scilicet atque Londinensi. Sed quod in Petri gladio scriptum fuit. In principio erat verbum. Verbum autem est vnigenitus Dei filius, indicat te Cantuariensi Ecclesiæ, quòe Christi nomini dicatur, quondam præfiendum.
