Hoc fabulosum cum interpretatione regia somnium ex sua ipsa ipsius hypocrisi narú & Monachorum superstitione diuulgatum inanis hominis ambitionem, gloriæque & honorum cupiditatem ostendit: Nam ex omnium scriptis conflat Elfcinum hominem à Dunstano ac Odono totoque Monachorum ordine, & illo adulterino cœlibatu alienum, Dunstanum tam in Wintonienfi, quàm Cantuariensi præsulatu anteuertisse. Hunc Monahi (quibus in amore atque odio nihil inanius, futilius, aut mendacius) contumeliis atque probris exagitant. Sedes Episcopales largitione inuasisse atq; tenuisse scribunt, quodque Romam propallio tendens, in Alpibus frigore, niuis atque gelu correptus moritur: id illi mendaci amplioratione amplificant, & mirabili diuin o supplicio aferibunt. Sed Dunstanus qui vnum oblarum Episcopatum respuit, idem postea duos Wigorniensem atque Londinensem conscientia salua minimeq; turbata simul tenere poterat. Curius exemplo postea Letinus tempore Regis Edgari Lindisfarorum (qui nunc diciuur Lincolne) & Leogecestrensium duorum Episcopatus copulauit, & Oswaldus (de quo crebra futura denneeps est mentio) Eboracensi Archiepiscopatui, & Wigorniensi prasulatui eodem Dunstano adtutore vnà præsidebat. Quem etiam sequutus Aldulfus vtramq; Ecclesiam possidebat. Quibus hoc indulgent & ignoscunt omnium iniquissimi censores Monachi, quia ex curum grege ordineq; fuerant: at Wulstanum eandem ob causam, qui habuit discrepabat, reprehendunt. Dunstani quæcunque dicta, facta, gestamiraculasingunt,cum in Wigorniensem Episcopatum Cantuariam consecrandus venisset, Odo Archiepiscopus in toto consecrationis ritu Archiepiscopali cum honore tractauit, ob quod ab astantibus clericis reprehensus, scio (inquit) filii quid in me operatur Deus, non possum non illud faœre, quod faciendum spiritus Dei dignatus est præcipere. Me vivente Wigorniensis Ecclesia hunc habet pastorem, me autem mortuo & Cantiorum erit Archiepiscopus,& aduersus mundi principem fortissimus præliator. Cum verò Odone mortuo Cantuariam postulatus venisset, primo aduentus sui die cum altari assisteret, populoque ex veteri more panem distribueret, domus nube repente conteƈta est,& Columbæ cœlo delapsa, dum missale sacrificium faceret, illi insedit. Perasto autem sacrificio Columba ad Odonis volans tumbà ibi quieuerat, quæ in Pyramidis modum ex australi altaris latere construƈta fuit. Abillo die Dunstanus Odonem semper coluit & reueritusest;eoquè transiens flexis genibus & capite nudato consueuit dicere. Requiescat Ode Segode, id est, Odo bonus. Hæc & huiusmodi dæmonica speƈtra pro veris diuinisque miraculis in Dunstano laudanda commemorant Monachi, quòd eorum acerrimus dux & pro pugnator contra pios verbi ministros licitè coningatos fuerat. Nam Adepto Cantuariensi Archiepiscopatu omni opera & contentione in propagando per totum regnum Monachismo , & abrogando ministrorum coniugio laborabat. Ad hanc summa eiadiumenta & præsidia tam a Iohanne Papa & Edgaro Rege, quàm ab Oswaldo & Ethelwoldo Episcopis atq; Monachis vndiq; comparata sunt. Qui omnes quales fuerint,non alienum erit paucis indicare. Iohannes Papa eius nominis 13. totam vitam in vario concubinatu peregit, tandemq; cum se strenui cuiusdam viri vxore ex vrbe ambulans oblectaret,ab eodem pugione perculsus,multisque confossus v ulneribus oƈto post diebus interiit. Edgarum ipsum Regè Monachi tradunt homicidam, tyrannum & mulierosum fuisse. Cuius lidido in illam arcitissimâ monialium castitatè irrepsit. Id Wishildæ Monachæ adumbrata indicat sanctimonia, cuius libidine feruens diu Rex, tandem septennali pœnitentiaèrefipiscit. Oswaldus Odonis Archiepiscopi auunculi sui consilio pereğe Floriacum in Guasconia studii causa profeƈtus,illas vaticinandi & recondit a proserendi artes (quas Manticas appellant) vzetanas sanè & præstigiosas, inteꝛque eas Necromanticam omnium deterrimam appriméd idicit. Exhac prodigiosa schola auditores multos in Anglia euocauit, quos induto Monachismo abbatiis,multisqueaffecit honoribus. Hinc eodem tempore prodiit nequissimus impostor Gilbertus, qui Papatum postea gerens,Syluęster secundus diƈtus est. Hic,vt ars sua valeret fortior, dæmonibus se addixit atque consecrauit. Quod à suæ seƈtæ scriptoribus prodirum est. Eodemq; tempore in eadem schola vixit Monachus Constantinus: Grammatica professione clarus, sed Necromantica infamis, inter cuius transmarinos amicos & familiares in Anglia fuit Oswaldus quidam huius nostro cognatus. Porro Ethelwoldus in Glasconiensi cœnobio educatus Monachismum suscepit sub ipso Dunstano. Cuius iuuenilis ætas primò palam, deinde clàin libidinibus aƈta, senilis ambitiosissima fuit, & in his dæmoniacis stupendis horrendisq; præstigiis desiit. Hic,vt sanƈtas & in Paradiso à Deo omnium conditore institutas nuptias deleret, dum Paradisum sanƈtitate superare contendit, Anglicanam Ecclesiam impuro cœlibatu,& spurco Monachatu atque Clero polluit. Ad Iohannem Papam pro pallio profeƈtus, petiit authoritate papali eiiciendi e cœnobiis coniugatos clericos,& Monachos inducendi sibi concedi potestatem. Hoc,mæchus Papa, qui legitimo thoro astringi nolut,indulsit facile. Deinde in Angliam teuerius cum Rege Edgaro concubitu pariter vago delectato, de suo regio consensu tam infœlici negocio adhibendo agit. Is eadem mente & facilitate qua Papatam impurius assensus est. Quicquid enim Dunstanus voluit,quasi à Deo profeƈtum fuisset oraculum, id Rex statuit atq; vetuit. Nihil iam his nephandis suscipiendis conatibus defuit,quàm vt Oswaldus & Ethelwoldus ad pontificales veherentur dignitates, Quod Dunstanus facile impetrauit. Erant tunc temporis plures & digniores Episcopi consanguinitate tum copulati. Odoenim Cantuar. & Oskitellus Eboracensis Archiepiscopi sanguine propinqui fuerunt. Hi duobus Oswaldus consanguineus. Dunstan ex altera parte cognatio fuit cum Aldelino Cantuar. Archiepiscopo, Elphego cognato Wintonienfi, & Elphego iuniore Abbate, qui postea etiam Wintoniensis Episcopus fuit, tum Wlfino Shirbornensi Episcopo, qui prius Abbas Westmonasteriensis fuerat. His cognationibus iunctis se inuicem potiundis Episcopatibus tanquam proprijs hereditatibus iuuerunt. De quo adhuc extant ab illis seculi atque sedes scriptoribus adhuc variae quoteles. Itaque Regem actiter hortatur Dunstanus, vt Oswaldus praedecessoris sui Odonis fratruelis, & Ethelwaldus Abindoniae Abbas Episcopi creorentur. Oswaldum illico consecrauit Dunstanus Wigorniensem Episcopum, Anno Dom. 960. annosq; sequenti, mortuo Brithelino Ethelwaldum Wint. Episcopum. His gestis, de eiiciendis coenobiis & celebrioribus Ecclesiis coniugatis clericis actum est. Haec enim huius consilii reique gerendae ratio fuit, vt quaecunque Dunstanus decreuerat, ea Rex & Papa authoritate sua rata facerent. Oswaldus vero & Ethelwaldus a Dunstano decretorum & imperatorum ministri, & mandatorii executores fierent. Primum itaque hi Monachales Episcopi delatorum & Accusatorum personas gerunt, criminibusq; instructi adeunt Dunstanum Primatem suum. Narrant ordinem clericalem, qui integritimus esse debet, iam ea turpitudine notari, vt laici in vitae conditione clericis potiores haberentur. Crimina hoc tempore in specie contra clericos exposita non fuerunt, sed scriptores incerta & varia multa retulunt. Quidam eos elatione, insolentia, ac luxuria deprauatos sacrorum celebrationem negligere, uxores repudiare, alias ilicite ducere, gulae & crebrietatibus vacare, bonaque Ecclesiae dissipare, & subitutis vicariis, quibus modica alimenta decernebant, choris laborem subterfugere scribunt. Quos cum corrigi nolent, Rex prebendis multauit, eosque Vicariis contulit, qui hac dignitate elati, alios suo loco posuerunt vicarios, & prioribus ipsi peiores extiterunt. Quidam nullo obiecto crimine, recusasse tantum monachalem habitum presbyteros affirmant. Alii nihil in eos dicunt aberbius, quam etsi religiosi et dignissimi esset clerici, tamen thesaurus, quos congesisset audius, non ad Ecclesiae honorem, sed suis solebant dare vxoribus. Rex ipse Edgarus oratione ad cletum habita, inter alia crimina clericis obuciens, non fuisse illis coronam patentem, nec tonsuram conuenientem, sed quocunque noceat tacerdotum vita vitio, hi delatores & calumniatores coniugijs insidiantes, petunt a Dunstano consulta correctionis. Iste Monachisq; dignam proferens sententiam: aut canonice (inquit) vfuendum est, aut Ecclesiis exeundum. Horum itaque fuit hanc duram a Dunstano pronunciatam exequi sententiam. Canonicum nihil statuebant, quod cum legitimis nuptiis coniunctum fuit. Itaque coniugati, dum Monasticam illam vitam exercerentur, cum liberis & vxoribus nunc primum ex celebrioribus collegiis & ecclesiis sunt exclusi. Qui Rege adito Dunstanum iniuriarum accusant, se virtutis religionisq; sed tamen, vt is de hac iniuria coram Rege conueniatur. Rex causam iudicibus delegauit, qui cum Wintoniae in Monachorum conclaui frequenti consessu de eae agerent, plurimumque iam suffragiis de presbyteris retinendis decerneretur, prodigiola vox audita subito est. Non bene sentiunt qui presbyterii fauent. Vel, vt in pariete scribebatur, teste Ioan. Capgrauo, qui hoc ipse suis oculis vidit, Humano more crux praefens edidit ore: Coelitus aflata quaz petispicis hic subarata. Abiit vt hoc fiat: absit hoc vt fiat: iudicesus bene, mutaretis non bene. Omnis tam turba sedata dissessit, reque pene desperata, ac armis demissis presbyteri cedunt Monachis.
units.tr: St Dunstan built a certain church. On the very day the king was consecrated, while the nobles were gathered in great numbers and the admonition of the kingdom was being discussed, he slipped away from them with play and dancing, and fell into the embrace of a certain beautiful woman whom he doted on, and led her into his bedchamber. All the nobles, outraged by the king's lack of restraint, began to murmur quietly. Dunstan, however, went into the chamber with Cynesius, the bishop, his kinsman, and dragged the king, who was lewdly indulging himself, from the bed and out of the chamber by force. By the authority of Odo, Archbishop of Canterbury, he made the king give up his relationship with the woman. While the monks eagerly try to publish this deed, their own lies betray them. Some call the woman Alfgina, others Athelgifa. Some write that she was a blood relation within the degree forbidden by papal law, others that she was the king's concubine, and others that she was another man's wife, whom the king had ordered killed. Since the monks disagree among themselves and contradict one another, the oldest, most honest and most learned writer of antiquity among them, Henry of Huntingdon, though he was not a monk, writes nothing more favourable about Edwin than this: that he governed the state prosperously and commendably, and had made a good start to his reign, but in the fifth year of his reign he was taken from his country by an untimely death. From these monkish tales, though they contradict one another, it is established that Dunstan most shamelessly entered the king's bedchamber and did things that do not befit a priest or a Christian in modesty. We deliberately omit the other variations of this story. The king banished Dunstan, expelled him not only from the court but from the kingdom, seized the goods and possessions of the monastery of Glastonbury, and dealt with the monks, who were then few in England, as has been recorded above in the life of Odo. Dunstan fled to Gaul and spent a year in exile in the monastery of Glandavum or of Blandinium. After his departure the monks write that a voice was heard from the crypts of the monasteries, the thin and melodious voice of a devil applauding, like a little woman laughing and cackling immoderately. They make Dunstan answer it, telling it not to rejoice at his exile, because when he returns it will be sadder than it can now afford to be glad while he is in exile. Meanwhile the Mercians and Northumbrians, and those living inland between the Humber and the Thames, took up arms against the king. The monks carefully leave out who started this uprising. In this uprising Edgar, the king's brother, gained control of part of the kingdom. They fought many battles on both sides and weakened the strength of the kingdom, but Edgar at last prevailed. Calling a council of the kingdom at Brandanford, he rescinded the acts and decrees of his brother Edwin, restored to the churches and monasteries the wealth that had been taken from them, and recalled Dunstan from exile to his former honour. Then, against his will, he promoted him to the bishopric of Worcester, afterwards to London, and finally, after barely two years, to the archbishopric of Canterbury. The monks write that Dunstan undertook all these bishoprics unwillingly and only because the king asked with the greatest insistence, but in praising Dunstan they often use empty flourishes of speech, out of a zeal to praise him rather than to declare the truth. For elsewhere they write that when Eadred offered him the bishopric of Crediton, he refused it, although the king and his mother the queen pressed him most strongly; and that the next night Peter, Paul and St Andrew appeared to him in sleep, holding drawn swords in their hands. On Peter's sword this sentence was inscribed in golden letters: "In the beginning was the Word." On the swords of Paul and Andrew there were only their names. They offered these swords to him. Andrew, whom he had always worshipped as his patron and the god of his life, looked on him with a cheerful face and said: "Take my yoke upon you," etc. But Peter ordered him to stretch out his hand, and struck it gently, saying: "Let this blow be a punishment to you for rejecting the office, and a sign that you must not reject the pontificate any further." The next day Dunstan told the king about this vision. The king, moved by the dream, said: "Peter has rebuked you, for you have despised the yoke of the Lord. The three swords of the apostles foretell that you will hold episcopal authority in the churches dedicated to their names, namely Worcester and London. But what was written on Peter's sword, 'In the beginning was the Word', and the Word is the only-begotten Son of God, shows that you are destined to preside over the church of Canterbury, which is dedicated to the name of Christ." This fabulous dream, with its royal interpretation, spread abroad from Dunstan's own hypocrisy and the superstition of the monks, and it reveals the ambition of an empty man and his craving for glory and honours. For from all the writers it is clear that Elfsine, a man unconnected with Dunstan, Odo, the whole order of monks, and that adulterous celibacy, outstripped Dunstan in the see of Winchester as well as in that of Canterbury. The monks, to whom nothing is more empty, frivolous or false in their loves and hates, harass this man with insults and abuse. They write that he got and kept his episcopal sees by bribery, and that when he was travelling to Rome for the pallium he was seized by the cold, snow and ice in the Alps and died; they inflate this lying story with exaggeration and ascribe it to a marvellous divine punishment. But Dunstan, who had rejected one bishopric when it was offered, could afterwards hold Worcester and London together with a clear and untroubled conscience. Following Dunstan's example, Lethinus later joined the two bishoprics of Lindisfarne (now called Lincoln) and Leicester in the time of King Edgar. Oswald (of whom frequent mention will be made hereafter) presided over both the archbishopric of York and the bishopric of Worcester, with Dunstan as his guardian. Aldulf too followed their example and held both churches. These monks grant and pardon such things to these men, because they were of their own flock and order; but they censure Wulfstan for the same thing, who differed from them. Whatever was said, done or achieved by Dunstan, they embellish with fabricated miracles. When he came to Canterbury to be consecrated bishop of Worcester, Archbishop Odo treated him with honour throughout the whole rite of archiepiscopal consecration. When the clergy standing by rebuked him for this, he said: "Sons, I know what God is working in me; I cannot but do what the Spirit of God has deigned to command. While I live, the church of Worcester has this man as its minister; but when I am dead, he will be archbishop of the men of Kent, and the most valiant fighter against the prince of this world." When Odo was dead and Dunstan had been summoned to Canterbury, on the first day after his arrival, while he was standing at the altar and distributing bread to the people according to the ancient custom, a cloud suddenly covered the house, and a dove descended from heaven and settled on him while he was celebrating the sacrifice of the mass. After the sacrifice the dove flew to Odo's tomb and rested there; it was built in the shape of a pyramid on the south side of the altar. From that day Dunstan always honoured and revered Odo, and whenever he passed by, he would bend his knees, bare his head and say: "Rest, Ode Segode, that is, good Odo." These and such demonic apparitions the monks record as true and divine miracles to be praised in Dunstan, because he was their fiercest leader and champion against the pious ministers of the Word who were lawfully married. For once he had obtained the archbishopric of Canterbury, he laboured with all his effort and energy to spread monasticism throughout the whole kingdom and to abolish the marriage of ministers. For this purpose the greatest aids and supports were gathered from every side, from Pope John and King Edgar, and from Oswald and Ethelwold, bishops and monks. It will not be out of place to indicate briefly what sort of men all these were. Pope John XIII spent his whole life in varied concubinage, and at last, while he was amusing himself by walking outside the city with the wife of a certain vigorous man, he was stabbed with a dagger by that same man and died eight days later of many wounds. The monks themselves report that King Edgar was a murderer, a tyrant and a womaniser. His lust crept even into the most strictly chaste house of nuns; the sanctimony of the nun Wilfrida shows this, for the king burned with lust for her for a long time, until at last he repented with a penance of seven years. Oswald, on the advice of his uncle Archbishop Odo, went to Fleury in Gascony to study, and there he learned the arts of divination and prophecy (which they call mantic), which are indeed vain and deceptive, and among them he judged necromancy the worst of all. From this monstrous school he summoned many pupils into England, whom he admitted to monasticism and endowed with abbeys and many honours. Hence, at the same time, there came forth the most wicked impostor Gilbert, who afterwards held the papacy and was called Sylvester II. He, so that his art might prevail more strongly, gave himself over to demons and consecrated himself to them, as writers of his own sect have recorded. At the same time the monk Constantine lived in the same school, famous for his teaching of grammar but notorious for necromancy; among his overseas friends and intimates in England was a certain Oswald, a kinsman of this man of ours. Furthermore, Ethelwold, educated in the monastery of Glastonbury, took up monasticism under Dunstan himself. His youth was spent first openly and then secretly in lusts, and his old age was marked by the most ambitious pursuits, and he ended in these demonic, astonishing and horrible illusions. This man, in order to destroy holy marriage, which God the creator of all instituted in Paradise, while he strove to surpass Paradise in holiness, polluted the English Church with impure celibacy and filthy monkery and clergy. He went to Pope John for the pallium and asked for the power, by papal authority, to expel married clergy from the monasteries and to bring in monks in their place. The adulterous pope, who did not want to be bound by lawful marriage, granted this readily. Then, returning to England, he approached King Edgar, who was likewise pleased with wandering intercourse, and sought the royal consent to carry out such an unhappy business. The king agreed with the same mind and ease with which he had assented to the pope, all the more shamelessly. For whatever Dunstan wished, the king decreed and forbade, as though it were an oracle sent from God. Nothing was now lacking to these nefarious undertakings except that Oswald and Ethelwold should be raised to the pontifical dignities, and Dunstan easily secured this. At that time there were several bishops, more worthy ones, who were joined by kinship. For Odo of Canterbury and Oskitel of York were close blood relations, and Oswald was a kinsman of both. On the other side Dunstan was related to Aldelm, Archbishop of Canterbury, to Elphege, a kinsman and bishop of Winchester, to the younger Elphege, an abbot who afterwards also became bishop of Winchester, and to Wulfine, bishop of Sherborne, who had previously been abbot of Westminster. Bound together by these kinships, they passed the bishoprics among themselves as if they were their own hereditary estates. Various records of this are still extant, from the writers of that age and of those sees. Thus Dunstan urged the king vigorously that Oswald, the cousin of his predecessor Odo, and Ethelwold, abbot of Abingdon, be appointed bishops. Dunstan at once consecrated Oswald bishop of Worcester in the year of our Lord 960, and in the following year, when Brithelm died, Ethelwold bishop of Winchester. With these things done, the matter of expelling married clergy from the monasteries and the more famous churches was undertaken. For this was the method of the plan and of its execution: that the king and the pope should, by their authority, ratify whatever Dunstan had decided, and that Oswald and Ethelwold should be the ministers of Dunstan's decrees and commands, and the executors of his orders. So first these monastic bishops took on the parts of informers and accusers, and, armed with charges, approached Dunstan their primate. They claimed that the clerical order, which ought to be the most upright, was now so disgraced by such turpitude that laymen in their way of life were held superior to the clergy. The crimes were not set out specifically against the clergy at that time, but the writers relate many uncertain and various things. Some write that they, corrupted by pride, insolence and luxury, neglected the celebration of the sacred rites, put away their wives, took other women unlawfully, gave themselves to gluttony and drunkenness, squandered the goods of the church, and, by substituting vicars to whom they gave meagre sustenance, avoided the labour of the choir. When they would not be corrected, the king fined them their prebends and gave these to vicars; but those vicars, puffed up by this dignity, put others in their place as vicars, and proved worse than the former ones. Some affirm that, with no crime alleged, the priests merely refused the monastic habit. Others say nothing more offensive against them than this: that although they were religious and most worthy clergy, they used to give the treasures they had heaped up not to the honour of the church but to their wives. King Edgar himself, in a speech addressed to the clergy, among other charges, said that they had neither a proper crown nor a fitting tonsure; but whatever harm there was in the priests' way of life through fault, these accusers and calumniators, who lay in wait for their marriages, sought counsel from Dunstan on how to correct it. He, pronouncing a sentence worthy of the monks, said: "They must either live canonically or leave the churches." It was therefore the task of these men to carry out the harsh sentence pronounced by Dunstan. They declared canonical nothing that was joined with lawful marriage. So the married clergy, while they were practising that monastic life, were now for the first time excluded from the more famous colleges and churches, with their children and wives. They approached the king and accused Dunstan of injustice, claiming to be men of virtue and religion, and asked that he be called to account before the king for this injury. The king delegated the case to judges, who, while they were dealing with it at Winchester in the monks' chamber in a crowded assembly, and a decision was already being made by most votes to retain the presbyters, suddenly a prodigious voice was heard: "They do not think well who favour the presbyters." Or, as it was written on the wall, witnessed by John Capgrave, who saw this with his own eyes: a cross, as if human, uttered from its mouth: "Inspired from heaven, what you seek here is ploughed in vain. Let it be done that this should not happen; let it not be done that this should happen. Judges, you have done well; you would have done not well." With this, the whole crowd was calmed and dispersed, the matter was nearly despaired of, and the presbyters, their arms lowered, gave way to the monks.

units.la: Noua iam per austrialem Angliae regionem surgunt Monachorum moenia, sumptibus Regis, consilio Dunstani, assiduitate vero & indefessis laboribus Oswaldi, sed potissimum Ethelwaldi.
units.tr: Now, throughout the southern region of England, monasteries rise up, built at the king's expense, on Dunstan's advice, and through the constant and tireless labours of Oswald, but above all of Ethelwold.

units.la: Incredibile illius aeui scriptoribus visum fuit, vnius vrbis Episcopum tot tantaque condidisse Monasteria, quae ne regius quidem facultatibus erigi posse quis putarit. Huic indicio sunt Elienses, Burchienses & Thorneneses exnobia, quorum Ethelwaldus prima iecit fundamenta, eaque perfecit. Nec dubium esse poterit, quin his aliisque condendis sumptus regii ministrabantur, quorum tamen eo mortuo multa diuta, extenuatae vero & diminutae certe sunt singula. Hae Dunstani Oswaldi & Ethelwaldi vehementia & atrocitate incitati Beornellus Scotorum Episcopus, & Seclo vir doctus, ille his captiui testitiun sua dioecesi: hic acerrimis verborum sententiarum auleis carmine scriptis Monachorum tercam laetariat tam argute & facete, vt legenti singulis penè versibus nō minorem fidem de illius ordinis sordibus & improbitate faciat, quam ad eorum ludibrium & contemptum tisum moueat. Sed illi nullis maledictis aut opprobriis ab incepto desistunt. Ethelwaldus itaque primus hoc Regis & Dunstani decretum executioni mandauit, Anno que Dom. 963. iussu Regis Edgari præ syteros coniugatos cum liberis & uxoribus veteri monasterio Wintoniensi exclusit, eorumque loco Monachos recepit An. Dom. 967. nouumque Monachorum cænobium cum Mideltonensi cænobio prope ciuitatem Wentanam, quæ Hida dicebatur, eodem anno condidit. Quo etiam anno Rex Edgarus in Monasterio Ramesiæ, quod auus suus Edwardus maior construxerat, Monachus collocauit, quibus Merwinam abbatissam præfecit. Tum bienno post Dunstanū, Oswaldo, & Ethelwaldo præcepit, ut emvoribus per Mercia cænobiis amotis coniugatis Monachos collocaret. Huiusmodi vsus oratione.
units.tr: Writers of that age thought it incredible that one bishop of a single city should have founded so many and such great monasteries, which one would not think even the king's resources could have raised. The Elv, Peterborough and Thorney houses are evidence of this, and Ethelwold laid their first foundations and completed them. There can be no doubt that the king's money supplied these and other foundations. Many of them lasted for a long time, but after his death they were certainly weakened and diminished, each one in turn. Roused by the vehemence and savagery of Dunstan, Oswald and Ethelwold, Beornell, bishop of the Scots, and Secalo, a learned man, the one bearing witness in his own diocese, the other in the most bitter verses, mocked the monks. Their wit and jesting are so sharp that, reading almost every line, one gains no less belief about the filth and wickedness of that order than one is moved to ridicule and scorn it. But those men did not give up their undertaking through any curses or insults. Thus Ethelwold was the first to carry out this decree of the king and Dunstan: in the year of the Lord 963, by order of King Edgar, he expelled the married priests, with their children and wives, from the old monastery at Winchester, and in their place received monks. In the year of the Lord 967 he founded a new monastery of monks, together with the Medeshamstede house near the city of Winchester, which was called Hyde, in the same year. In that same year King Edgar installed monks in the monastery of Ramsey, which his grandfather Edward the Elder had built, and set Merwina over them as abbess. Then two years later he instructed Dunstan, Oswald and Ethelwold to remove the married occupants from the monasteries throughout Mercia and to put monks in their place. He did this with the following speech.

units.la: ORATIO EDGARI.
units.tr: THE SPEECH OF EDGAR.

units.la: Voniam magnificauit misericordiam suam dominus sacere nobiscum, dignū est, O patres Reuerendiss. vt innumeris illius beneficiis, dignis respondeamus operibus. Neque enim in gladio nostro possidemus terram, & brachium nostrum non seruauit nos: sed dextra eius, & brachium sanctum eius, quoniam complacuit illi in nobis. Iustū proinde est, vt qui omnia subiecit sub pedibus nostris, subiectum illi & nos & animas nostras: & vt hi quos nobis subdidit, eius subdantur legibus, non segniter elaborem. Et mea quidem interest laicos cum ​sacerdotibus tractare inter virum & proximum suum iustum iudicium facere, punire sacrilegos, rebelles comprimere, eripere inopem de manu fortioris eius, egenum & pauperem, a diripientibus eum. Sed & meæ solicitudinis est Ecclesiarum ministris, gregibus Monachorum, choris virginum & necessaria eorum proeurare, ac talem & qui in vel paci consiliæ. De quorum omnium moribus ad nos spectat examen. Si vixerint constenter, si honeste se habeant, ad eos qui foris sunt: si diuinis officiis s licitis, si ad docendum populum assidui, si victu subtrii, si habi moderati, si in iudiciis aut discreti (pace vestra loquor Reuerendi patres) si ista soleat scrutinio curassetis, non tam hotrenda & abominanda ad aures nostras de clericis peruennissent. Taceo quòd non est illis corona patens, nec tonsura conueniens. At in veste lasciuia, insolentia in gestu, in verbis turpitudo, interioris hominis produnt insaniam. Præterea in diuinis officiis quanta sit negligentia, cum sacris vigiliis vix interesse dignentur, cum ad sacra missarum solennia, ad ludendum, subridendum magis quam ad psallendum congregati videantur. Dicam quod boni lugent, mali ridentque dicam dolens (si tamen dici potest) quo modo dissluant in commessationibus, in ebrietatibus, in cubilibus & impudicitiis, vt iam domus clericorum pstentur profitibus meretricum, conciliabulum histrionum. Ibi alexæ, ibi saltus & cantus, ibi vique ad medium noctis spacium protractæ in clamore & horrore vigiliæ. Sic patrimonia Regum, eleemosinæ pauperum, imo (quod magis est) illius pretiosi sanguinis pretium prosligatur. Ad hoc ergo exhauserunt patres nostri thesauros suos. Ad hoc siscus regius detractis redditibus mul ti, elargitus est, ad hoc Ecclesiis Christi agros & possessiones regalis munificentia contulit, vt deliciis clericorum meretrices ornentur, luxuriosæ coniuqæ præparentur, canes ac aues & talia ludicra comparentur. Hoc milites clamant, plebs submurmurat, mimi cantant & salt nt, & vos negligitis, vos parcitis, vos dissimulatis. Vbi gladius Leui, & zelus Simeonis, qui vt scorto abutentes filia Iacob Sichimitas (eorum habentes figuram, qui Christi Ecclesiam pollutis actibus sœdant) etiam circumcisos sui cciderunt: vbi ipiritus Moysi, qui caput vituli adorantibus eciam domesticis sui sanguinis non pepercit? Vbi pugio Phinees sacerdotis, qui formicantem cum Madianita confodiens sancta hac æmulatione Deum placauit iratum? Vbi spiritus Petri, cuius virtute perimitur auaritia, hæresis Simoniaca condemnatur? Æmulamini O sacerdotes, æmulamini vias domini, & iusticias Dei nostri. Tempus insurgendi contra eos, qui dissiparunt legem Dei. Ego Constantini, vos Petri gladium habetis in manibus. Iungamus dexteras, gladium gladio copulemus: vt eiiciantur extra castra leprosi, vt purgetur sanctuarium Domini, & ministrent in templo filii Leui: qui diixit patri & matri: nelcio vos, & fratribus suis, ignoro vos. Agite quæso solicite, ne pœnitcant nos fecisse, quod fecimus, dedisse quod dedimus: si videritmus illud non in Dei obsequio, sed in pessimorum luxuria impunita libertate eostumi. Moueat vos sanctorum reliquiæ, in quibus insultant: veneranda altaria ante quæ insaniunt. Moueat vos antecedsorum notrorum mira deuotio, quorum Eleemosinis vesania clericalis abutitur. Proauus meus Edwardus (vt scitis) omnem totam suam Ecclesiis & Monasteriis decimam. Sanctæ memoriæ aiauus meus Alutedus, vt Ecclesiam diraret, non thesauris suis, non patrimonio, non sumptibus, non redditibus parcendum putauit. Auu. meus senior Edwardns quanta contulerit Ecclesiis, patetnkatem vel tram non later. Pater meus & frater, quibus donariis Christi altaria cumulauerint, meminisse vos decet. O patet patrum Dunstane, contemplare quæso patris mei oculos, abilla lucida coeli plaga in te radiantes. Audi querulas eius voces, cum quadam pictæ in tuis auribus tefon antes: Tu mihi pastor Dunstane. Tu mihi de constituendis monasteriis, de Ecclesiis ædificandis: sconstituendis salubre dedisti. Tu mihi adiutor in omnibus, & cooperator extitisti. Te quasi patronem, patrem, & episcopum animæ meæ, morumque meorum custodem elegi. Quando tibi non parui? quos vnquam thesauros tuis consiliis præstulit? Quas possessiones te præceptente non spreui? Si quid pauperibus erogandum existimabas, præsto fui: Si quid confetendum Ecclesiis iudicabas, nò dilluli. Si quod Monachis, Clericisve deesse quieraris, suppleui. Æternam dicebas elecmosinam esse, nec aliam fructuosiorem, quam quod Monasterijs Ecclesiisve confertur, quo Dei fetus iustententur, & quod impereft, pauperibus erogetur. O præciosam elecmosinam, & dignum animæ ptecium. Opecceris nostris salubre temedium, quod a sinu Sibillæ in peregrini muris pellicula fetet, quod cius auriculas ornat, quod componit digitulos, quod corpus delicatum in byssio strigit & purpura. Ecce pater eleemosinarum fructus, meatum & tuæ permissionis effectus. Quid huic querimoniæ respondebis? Scio, scio, cum videbas fure, non currebas cùeo. nec eum adulteris portionem tuam ponebas. Atqui fi, ob se ctasti, atque increpasti. Conceptæ verba sunt, veniendumeft adverbeta & non deetit tibi poreftas regia, Habes hic tecum Venerabilem patrem Ethelwaldum Winton.Episcopum. Habes Reuerendum præsulem Wigornienlem Oswaldum. Vobis istud commitio negocii, vt & Episcopali censuta, & regia authoritate turpitet viuentes de Ecclesiis eiiciantur, & ordinatæ viuentes introducantur.
units.tr: Since the Lord has magnified his mercy in dealing with us, it is fitting, Reverend Fathers, that we answer his countless benefits with worthy deeds. For we do not possess the land by our own sword, and our arm did not save us; it was his right hand and his holy arm, because he was pleased with us. It is therefore just that we and our souls be made subject to him who has placed all things under our feet, and that those whom he has subjected to us be subject to his laws. I shall not labour at this half-heartedly. It is indeed my concern, together with the priests, to deal with laymen, to render just judgment between a man and his neighbour, to punish sacrilegious persons, to restrain rebels, and to snatch the needy and the poor from the hand of the stronger man who plunders them. But it is also my care to provide for the ministers of the Churches, the flocks of monks, the choirs of virgins, and their necessities, and to take counsel for their peace. It is for us to examine the conduct of all of these: whether they live consistently, whether they conduct themselves honourably towards those outside the Church; whether they are diligent in the divine offices, whether they are assiduous in teaching the people, whether they are sparing in food, whether their dress is moderate, whether they are discreet in judgments. (I speak with your permission, Reverend Fathers.) If you had been accustomed to take care of this scrutiny, such horrible and abominable reports about the clergy would not have reached our ears. I say nothing of the fact that their crown is not visible, nor their tonsure fitting. But in wanton clothing, insolent bearing, and filthy speech they reveal the madness of the inner man. Moreover, what negligence there is in the divine offices! They scarcely deign to attend the sacred vigils, and when they gather for the solemn celebration of the Mass they seem to come for playing and laughing rather than for singing psalms. I will say what the good lament and the wicked laugh at; I will say, grieving (if it can be said), how they dissolve in feasting, in drunkenness, in beds and impurities, so that now the houses of clerics are exposed as brothels of prostitutes, a meeting-place for actors. There are dice, there dancing and singing, there vigils drawn out until the middle of the night in clamour and uproar. Thus the patrimonies of kings, the alms of the poor, nay (what is worse) the price of that precious blood, are squandered. For this our fathers emptied their treasuries. For this the royal treasury, with many revenues withdrawn, was lavished; for this royal munificence bestowed fields and possessions on the Churches of Christ, so that harlots may be adorned with the clergy's luxuries, wanton wives be provided for, and dogs, birds and such playthings be bought. The soldiers cry out at this, the common people mutter, mimes sing and dance, and you neglect, you spare, you dissemble. Where is the sword of Levi and the zeal of Simeon, who, when the Shechemites had abused the daughter of Jacob as a harlot (bearing the figure of those who defile Christ's Church with polluted acts), slew even the circumcised of their own people? Where is the spirit of Moses, who did not spare even his own blood-kin when they worshipped the calf? Where is the dagger of Phinehas the priest, who, piercing the fornicator with the Midianite woman, by this holy zeal appeased an angry God? Where is the spirit of Peter, by whose power covetousness is destroyed and Simoniacal heresy condemned? Be zealous, O priests, be zealous for the ways of the Lord and the righteousness of our God. It is time to rise up against those who have scattered the law of God. I have the sword of Constantine; you have the sword of Peter in your hands. Let us join right hands and join sword to sword, so that lepers may be cast out of the camp, that the sanctuary of the Lord may be cleansed, and that the sons of Levi may minister in the temple, those who said to father and mother, "I do not know you," and to their brothers, "I do not acknowledge you." Act with diligence, I beg you, lest we repent of having done what we have done and given what we have given, if we see it consumed not in God's service but in the unpunished licence of the worst men's luxury. Let the relics of the saints move you, over which they mock; let the venerable altars move you, before which they rave. Let the wonderful devotion of our ancestors move you, whose alms clerical madness abuses. My grandfather Edward (as you know) gave his whole tithe to the Churches and monasteries. My grandfather of holy memory, Alutedus, thought that in order to enrich the Church no treasure, patrimony, expense or revenue should be spared. How much my elder grandfather Edward contributed to the Churches is evident, nor is it hidden from anyone. My father and my brother, with what gifts they heaped up the altars of Christ, you ought to remember. O father of fathers, Dunstan, I beg you, consider the eyes of my father, shining on you from that bright quarter of heaven. Hear his plaintive voice, sounding in your ears with a certain piety: "You, Dunstan, were my pastor. You gave me wholesome counsel about founding monasteries, building churches, and endowing them. You were my helper and co-worker in everything. I chose you as my patron, my father and bishop of my soul, and guardian of my conduct. When did I not obey you? What treasures did I ever set before your counsels? What possessions did I not give up at your command? If you thought anything should be given to the poor, I was at hand; if you judged anything should be bestowed on the Churches, I did not delay; if you complained that anything was lacking to the monks or clergy, I supplied it. You said that alms were eternal, and that no other was more fruitful than what is given to monasteries and churches, so that the servants of God may be sustained and what remains be distributed to the poor." O precious alms, and worthy price of the soul! A wholesome remedy for our sins, which from a Sibyl's bosom stinks in the skin of a foreign mouse; which adorns her ears, decks her little fingers, and binds her delicate body in fine linen and purple. Behold, father, the fruit of alms, the merit and effect of your permission. What will you answer to this complaint? I know, I know: when you saw a thief, you did not run with him, nor did you share your portion with adulterers. But have you not entreated and rebuked? The words have been spoken; we must come to blows, and royal power will not fail you. Here with you is the venerable father Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester; here is the reverend prelate Oswald of Worcester. I entrust this business to you, so that, by episcopal censure and royal authority, those living shamefully may be cast out of the Churches, and those living in good order be brought in."

units.la: Hac oratione Ofwaldus animatus, exemplo Ethelwaldi præ byteros cõlugatos quinque Monachalem relpuebant habitum ex Wigornienti Ecclesia eiecit. Retinuit autem eos qui sibi assensere, eisque Wintinum Decanum præfecit. Tanta deinde vigilantia & celeritate a tribus his Monachorum antesignanus confectum negocium est, vt neque euufquam, nec sua ipsotum opinione commodiusque geri potuit. Nam ex illa Regis otatione, eos solos otdinate viuere iudicabat, qui a nupuis abstinuissent, cõiugatos autem, etsi immaculati thori iura fetuassent, impudicè. Itaque detur batis ex frequentissimis Ecclesiis præbytetris, xx xx v i i. cænobia procutat te Dunstano paucis huius Regisannis Monachis completa fuerunt. Sed eum Monachorum statis tanta iltorum arte & induftia compositus, firmissimus putabatur. post obirum Regis Edgari magnam calamitatem & vastitatem, pene eiiam incertum occasumque sensit. Anno antequam decessit Edgatus, grandis & horribilis terræ motus totam Angliam quatefecit. Is anno ætatis suæ 33 Regnique in Mercia Nothun.briaque prouinciis 19 Intota vero Anglia 16. mortale corpus exuit. Eo motuo eiecti ante presbyteri dignitates, quibusdam iniustè peneq; hostilitet spoliati sunt. hos iuuant tam Alfgina Regina Regis demortui coniux, quam Alferus Merciorum Princeps, & pleriqueregni proceres, indignum iudicantes veteres colonos nouæ teligionis præextu ab aduenis & peregrinis detutbari. Hoc tam atrox & inligne præiudicium, ab aliis regni incolis iuste iumendum esset, nisi illud maturè fuerit. Itaque Abbates atque Monachos ex Merciorum & Occiduz Angliæ cœnobiis eiiciunt, & præbyteros cum libertis & vxoribus restituunt. His Athelwinus Orientalis Angliæ Dux, & Alfwolfus getmanus suus, ac Brithnotus Comes acerrimè restitetre. Qui se non latutos profitentur Monachotum expulsiones, quorum scenica & adumbrata diuini cultus specie erant alleći, & vt Monachos in ea prouincia claustris suis septos defenderent, arma capiunt. Inter hos motus orta est graurior de Rege eligendo dissensio. Namquidam Edwardum ex Ethelfleda candida, Ordmeri Ducis filia, quam Rex non in coniugio, sed in concubinatu complexus est natum, quidam Agelterdum Regis ex Alfdritha Regina iusta coniuge filium, sed pene infantem popofcunt. In hunc maior pars nobilium conuenit. Sed Archiepiscopi Dunstanus & Ofwaldus cum Episcopis & Abbatibus consipirantes, in alteram partem qua de Edwardo concubinaria Regis prole assensum est, dissensionem fecerunt, hoc sibi & Monachis tutius esse cernentes. Agelredus enim minor & vix septenis adhuc erat, qui iure regni in matris esse debuit tutela, cuius erga Monachos voluntas ante nota & perspecta fuit. Itaque reelamanubus Regina & plurimis proceribus Dustanus Edwardum consecrat, Regemq; vngie
units.tr: Inspired by this speech, Oswald, following the example of Ethelwold, cast out of the Church of Worcester the five married presbyters who rejected the monastic habit. He kept those who agreed with him and placed Wintin as dean over them. The matter was then carried through with such vigilance and speed by these three champions of the monks that it could not have been managed more conveniently either by anyone else or in their own judgment. For from that speech of the king they judged that only those lived in good order who had abstained from marriage, while married men, even if they had kept the rights of the undefiled bed, lived shamefully. And so, with presbyters driven out of very many churches, thirty-seven monasteries were completed under Dunstan's management in the few years of this king's reign, filled with monks. But the state of the monks, which had seemed most firmly settled, was composed with such skill and industry by them, and after the death of King Edgar it felt great calamity and devastation, and nearly even an uncertain downfall. In the year before Edgar died, a great and dreadful earthquake shook all England. In the thirty-third year of his life, the nineteenth of his reign over the provinces of Mercia and Northumbria, and the sixteenth over all England, he put off his mortal body. In that upheaval the presbyters who had earlier been ejected were, some of them, unjustly and almost hostilely, stripped of their dignities. They were supported by Queen Elfgifu, the widow of the dead king, as well as by Alfere, prince of the Mercians, and most of the nobles of the realm, who thought it unworthy that the old inhabitants should be disturbed by newcomers and strangers under the pretext of a new religion. This so atrocious and notable prejudice would have to be justly feared by the other inhabitants of the realm, had it not been forestalled in good time. And so they cast out the abbots and monks from the monasteries of Mercia and western England, and restored the presbyters with their children and wives. Against them, Athelwine, duke of East Anglia, his brother Alfwold, and Earl Brithnoth resisted most fiercely. They declared that they had not been deceived by the expulsion of the monks, by whom they had been lured with a theatrical and shadowy semblance of divine worship; and to defend the monks, enclosed within their cloisters in that province, they took up arms. Amid these disturbances a more serious dispute arose about electing a king. For some demanded Edward, born of the fair Ethelfled, daughter of Duke Ordmer, whom the king had embraced not in marriage but in concubinage; others demanded Ethelred, the son of the king by Queen Elfthryth, his lawful wife, but still almost an infant. The greater part of the nobles gathered behind the latter. But Archbishop Dunstan and Oswald, conspiring with the bishops and abbots, caused a division by agreeing to the other party, which favoured Edward, the concubinary offspring of the king, seeing that this would be safer for themselves and for the monks. For Ethelred was younger and scarcely seven years old, and by the law of the realm should have been under his mother's guardianship, whose will towards the monks had been known and observed beforehand. And so, although the queen and most of the nobles protested, Dunstan consecrated Edward and anointed him king.

units.la: {y} Sine Dunstano. vngit, Anno 974. Eodem anno Cometæ stella Anglis apparuit, quam & agrorum sterilitas & dira hominum fames, & iumentorum atque pecorum lues mox sequuta est. Dunstanus autem nactus ex sententia regnum, de Monachorū suorum rebus certius stabiliendis,solicitus Concilium in Orientalis Angliæ villa,quæ Kistlinc dicitur,An. 977.indixit. Ibi cum Monachorum labenti conditioni succurrere voluit, nihil profecit. Itaque hoc dissoluto concilio aliud in regia villa in Wilceria,quæ Calne vulgò a pellatur, cogit. In hoc concilio prodigiosum se Dunstanus non argumentosum ostendit. Cum enim multis rationibus de præsbyterorum coniugiis & Monachorum cœlibatu vtrinq; cū summa contentione couertoust tereretur. Alfridus Regina Alfridis Mercioru co-
units.tr: {y} Without Dunstan. He anointed him in the year 974. In the same year a comet appeared to the English, and soon after it came barrenness of the fields, dire famine among men, and plague among draught animals and cattle. Dunstan, having obtained the kingdom according to his wishes, and anxious to settle the affairs of his monks more securely, summoned a council in the East Anglian township called Kistlinc in the year 977. There, when he wished to come to the aid of the monks' failing position, he achieved nothing. Therefore, the council having been dissolved, he convened another in the royal township in Wiltshire, commonly called Calne. In this council Dunstan showed himself a prodigy rather than a man of argument. For when the questions of presbyters' marriages and monks' celibacy were being debated on both sides with great contention and many arguments, Queen Ælfthryth, together with the Mercian earl Ælfhere, provoked him to see that Beornelm, bishop of the Scots (of whom we spoke earlier), attended this council.

units.la: mitè prouocauit, vt Beornelmum Scotorū Episcopū (de quo ante diximus) huic concilio curaret interesse. Is doctrina & facundia singulari sacerdotum coniugia defendit, & simulatam Monachorum castitatem oppugnauit. Aduersarios aperiis scripturarum locis obtuit ac refellit. Et coniugatorum pars in hoc concilio superior fuisset, nisi Dunstanus prodigiis potius quàm argumentis certare statuisset. Nam & ante Regem, quem continuo obsequio & adulatione tractauit, ab hoc cætu abesse voluit, causans ætatem, cum tamen superiori concilio interfuisset. Et cum Monachorum causam labefactari sensit, senio, cum paulo amplius quàm quinquagenarius esset, seiam debilitatum, & pluribus in Ecclesia exantlatis laboribus fractū conquæstus est. Non esse suum aut studis incumbere, aut de argumentorum vi, vel scripturarum authoritate hæreticæ per-
units.tr: He defended the marriages of priests with singular learning and eloquence, and attacked the feigned chastity of the monks. He confronted his opponents with clear passages of Scripture and refuted them. Indeed the married party would have had the upper hand in this council, had Dunstan not decided to contend by prodigies rather than by arguments. For he wished to be absent from this assembly, first before the king, whom he treated with constant obsequiousness and flattery, pleading his age, although he had been present at the previous council. And when he sensed that the monks' cause was being weakened, he complained that he was debilitated by old age, being a little more than fifty, and worn out by the many labours he had undergone in the Church. It was not his business, he said, to devote himself to studies, or to weigh the force of arguments and the authority of Scripture as heretics do. He said such disputations seemed troublesome and hateful to him.

units.la: pendere. Huiusque generis disputationes sibi molestas ac odiosas videri. Quibus in-quit, ipsa, quam in hoc concilio partam putatis, victoria ē manibus vestris est ilico exci-sura, neque vestras rationes aut voluntatem in eaparte sequemur. Sic ait, Et dicto citius, Cœnaculum in quo totus omnium ordinum cætus considebat, postibus axibusque quibus ædificium cohærebat solutis, subito concidit, vnaque præsules, proceres, equites, nobiles pariter ac ignobiles corruerunt. Quorum interempti multi, plerique mutilati suerunt. Dunstanus solus ex trabe quadam apprehensa restitit, sine cæsu aut aliqua læsione saluus. Qui legendam Dunstani scripsit, vt hoc prodigium instar miraculi diuini haberetur, dicit solos Dunstani hostes præcipitatos, & ruentium trabium pondere oppressos, reliquos solo casu turbatos nullo discrimine aut læsione affectos. At hic qui
units.tr: "The very victory which you think you have won in this council," he said, "will be snatched out of your hands at once, nor will we follow your reasons or your wishes in that matter." So he spoke, and sooner than he had finished, the upper room in which the whole assembly of all orders was sitting, its posts and beams that held the building together having come loose, suddenly collapsed; and bishops, nobles, knights, and gentlemen, noble and non-noble alike, fell together. Of these many were killed and most were maimed. Dunstan alone, seizing hold of a certain beam, stood firm, safe and sound without any cut or injury. The one who wrote the Life of Dunstan, so that this portent might be regarded as a miracle of God, says that only Dunstan's enemies were thrown down and crushed by the weight of the falling beams, while the rest were merely disturbed by chance and suffered no harm or injury. But he who, because of his age, cannot defend his cause from Scripture or by reasoning,

units.la: per ætatem suam causam scripturis, & tatiocinando defendere nequit, quinquagesimum iam tertium attigit ætatis suæ annum. Fuisset hæc ætas, vt in plerisque nostri ævi senibus potissimum Episcopis atque clericis conspicimus, & viribus ac sanitate corporis satis fulta, & in scripturis erudita, aut illis percipiendis dedita, nisi Dunstani vitiola adolescentia, animusque præstigiis imbutus & inuolutus ei iam tantillo seni & corpus essœtum, & mentem a Deo sanctisque scripturis alienam reddidissent. Sed nec huius domus, in quam omnium ordinum tam conspicui clariqueviri consultò conuenerunt, tam repentina ruina humana fraude & ope diabolica carere potuit. Quis autem credident diuinam opem, aut ab eo inuocaram, aut ei datam fuisse, cui in aliqua controuersia sacrarū scripturarū, verbiq; citata loca & testimonia displicuerant. Diuina præterea vindicta, ne sanctis implorantibus, in iustissima causa semper adest. In qua quidem re legimus, quam pie atque iuste saluator noster Apostolos rogantes, vt ignem è cœlo descendere iuberet, his verbis reprehendit. Nescitis cuius estis spiritus. Credendum denique aut suspicandum non est, Dunstanum eiusue asseclas in Monachorum causa moderati vnquam aliquid & mansueti vel re egisse, vel illa deliberatione cogitasse: quin omnem vt aiunt lapidem sedulo mouisse, vt coniugatorum clericorum statu penitus amoto, omnibus modis mōnachi firmarentur. Hoc itaque tam exitioso prodigio peremta coniugatorum causa, Monachique suis sedibus possessionesque fixi 600.annis in hoc regno permanserunt, donec vt sub finem huius historiæ dicetur ab inclyto rege Henrico VIII. tam exiguo temporis intetuallo eiecti & dissipati, quod Dunstano collecti &
units.tr: has already reached the fifty-third year of his life. This age would have been, as we see in most of the old men of our time, especially bishops and clergy, supported by strength and bodily health and learned in the Scriptures or devoted to studying them, had not Dunstan's wicked youth, and a mind steeped and wrapped in deceits, rendered his body worn out at that age, and his mind alien from God and holy Scripture. But neither could this house, in which men of all orders, so conspicuous and renowned, had deliberately gathered, be without so sudden a ruin, brought about by human fraud and diabolical aid. Who would believe that divine help was either invoked by him, or given to him, against whom in some controversy the passages of sacred Scripture and the cited words and testimonies had been displeasing? Moreover, divine vengeance is always at hand, lest the saints should implore it in a most just cause. In this matter we read how piously and justly our Saviour rebuked the Apostles when they asked him to bid fire come down from heaven, with these words: "You do not know what spirit you are of." Finally, it is not to be believed or suspected that Dunstan or his followers ever acted or thought with moderation or gentleness in the monks' cause; rather, as they say, they diligently moved every stone, so that, with the state of married clergy utterly removed, the monks might be firmly established by every means. Thus, with the cause of the married clergy destroyed by this so ruinous portent, the monks, fixed in their seats and possessions, remained in this kingdom for 600 years, until, as will be said near the end of this history, they were ejected and scattered by the illustrious King Henry VIII in a time as short as that over which they had been gathered by Dunstan and

units.la: confirmati suerunt.
units.tr: were confirmed.

units.la: Post hanc portentosam Calnen sem Synodum, omnes clades & calamitates tanquam è diuina vindicta in Anglicâ gentem inuectæ fuerunt, quæ nunquâ desiterunt, donec Nerinannis Martemulti esset imperium. Proximo enim anno nubes media nocte per totam Angliam, nunc ignea visa est, deinde in varios radios ac eolores mutata proxima aurora dispargitur. Hæc sequuæ stragis & vastitatis fuit ptænuncia. Nam eo tempore Edwardus Rex Alfdrithæ Reginæ nouercæ snæ iussu, qui in obsidione vrbis Russix descendere nolnit eius ciuitatis Episcopum Dunstani discipulum, sicut Edhelwaldus cōtra fratrem suum Agelredum, qui apertas eiinimicitias denunciauerat, à militibus est intetfectus. Monachi, vt à sequoq; Dunstano transferrent
units.tr: After this portentous Synod of Calne, all disasters and calamities, as though brought upon the English nation by divine vengeance, followed, and they never ceased until the reign of Æthelred. For in the following year a cloud appeared through the whole of England at midnight, at first fiery, then changed into various rays and colours, and at the next dawn it dispersed. These were forerunners of slaughter and devastation. For at that time King Edward was killed by soldiers at the command of his stepmother Queen Ælfthryth, because he refused to come down during the siege of that city (the bishop of that city being a disciple of Dunstan), just as Edhelwald, who had openly declared enmity against his brother Æthelred, was killed by soldiers. The monks, so as to transfer from Dunstan and themselves

units.la: omnem irritati diuini numinis culpam, huic Reginæ facto, regiæque necis causæ attribuunt omnia. Eaque ab hac origine ab Apolline. Deoque suo Dunstano prædicta fuisse scribunt. Neque exquirunt, quo occulto Dei iudicio Rex ille spurius, cuius authoritate Dunstanus legitimo thoro copulatos spoliauit, tam subito sublatus fuerit. Sed ut ea referamus quæ Monachi scribunt. Occulta semper Reginæ Alfdrithæ cum Dunstano simultas his de causis intercessit. Obstitit primo acertrime Dunstanus, neciam contracta & defponfitaRegi Edgaro matrimonio iungeretur. Illico enim ei ad se addu&e Edgarus propter pulchritudinem, nuptiarum fidem dedit, &in thalamum duxit. Dunstanus (ut ante diximus) cubilibus aulicis regiisque assuetus, solita impudicitia seu Monachali verecundia ingressus thalamum, quaesiui ac Rege, quaenam esset illa, quam in lecto & amplexibus tenuisset. Rex illam Reginam confortemque suam fuisse respondit. Dunstanus hoc inoffenso Deo, & illæsa institutione Romanæ Ecclesiæ fieri haud posse affirmat, obspiritualem cognationem, quam ante cum ea contraxerat, cum filium eius de sacro fonte leuauerat, itaque sæpius cum Rege egit, vt eam a fedimitteret, & a sua confuetudine separarer. Quod Dunstani consilium, Rex insuper abili tam venu&æ mulieris desiderio motus, amon suo postposuit. Ex hac Rex primo Edmundum genuit, qui puer obiit, deindeEthelredum, postea (vt mox dicemus) Regem. HuncMonachi scribunt, cum à Dunstano baptisfatetur, exvelica vrinam in baptismatis lauacrum profudisse. Quo signo vaticinatus est Dunstanus, Anglorum exterminium suo tempore futurum. His diu & clam gestis inimicitiis, Regina Edwardo cæso proceribus regni stipata, accersiuit Dunstanum, Archiepiscopaliiure Regem coronatum. Isetsi offensus penetque inuitus, senex tamen atque tremulus resistere non audet. Sed Diadema componens (vt Monachi referunt) spiritum illum suum non connuit, quin & Regis & regni exitium iamiam adesse prænunciaret. Eademque prædictione (Monachis testibus) Regem octo post annis voluit perterrefacere, cum Roffam ob antedictas cum Episcopo inimicitias obsidet, nec eam Dunstani iussu antegradem ab eodem Dunstano acceptam pecuniam vel· leliberare, Quamobrem Dunstanus malis ominibus ei maledixit. Paulo post Dacorum impetus, & Sanctus Donfrio ad Anglos factus est. Primum Sonthamptonamaritima ac portuosa' locupletes, quæ villa a Dacis piratis expilata est, ac incolæ vel trucidati, vel captiuitate abducti. Qui huius villæ spoliis elati Zentlanb insulam deuastarunt, tum in maritimis Cornubiæ ac Dorcestrensis provinciæ oris prædabantur. Portlandiam insulam depopulabantur, & Monasterium Petroci confessoris in Cotnubia diripiebant. Eodemq; tempore à Norue gienfibus piratis Legionum ciuitas spoliata fuit, Londinumq; igne consumptum. Hæc malorum initia à Monachorum institutione profecta, eorumq; desidia & ignauia non depulsa, ad ruinam & interitum stirpis regiæ, & Anglicanæ nobilitatis postea creuerunt. Ethelwaldus Monachorum sub Dunstano patronus, superstitione Dunstano cruciatus vitæcrum eruriumq; tumore ita cruciatus, vt insomnes dies noctesq; ducetet, vix senectutem attingens moritur. Postea cuius mortem Monasteria quæ condiderat, multa sunt diruta, reliqua præcidis terrisque deiiectis diminuta. Dehoc non erit ab huiusmodi narrationibus alienum, ridiculum quoddam Dunstani somnium à posterioribus Mo-40 nachis scriptum enarrare. Dunstanus (vt ante diximus) huius magister erat, cumque Glastoniae Abbatem præfecit. Illico ptoximo (postquam eum præfecerat) somnio, sibi visus est vidisse arborem inulta, ita magnitudine atque celsitate, per omnes mundi plagas diffusam atq; patulam. Cuius rami innumeris, paruis magnisq; Monachalibus cucullis onustae erant atque referti. Culmen autem huius arboris grandissimum cucullum cæteras omnes gentem, cœlumque ipsum attingentem gestabat. Cumque hoc viso attonitus esset, adfuisse illi veneranda & Angelica caniue senem, ab hoc quefiuiffe Dunstanum de sibi vita arboris coniectura, icumque respondisse. Arborem insulam fuisse Glastoniam, Iconiam, cucullos infinitas ex illo cœnobio profectas turbam, multitudinemque Monachorum, qua tota Anglia scatebat ac replebitur. Ille vero summus ad cœlum erectus reliquosque tegens cucullus, Ethelwaldus Abbas est, cæteros Monachos in cœlum præcuruus. Sed (vt de tomuio omittamus) certum est illam Monachorum (vt ita dicam) scaturiginem pinguedine foli saturaram, regni opes & vires exhausfifle, vt post Ethelwaldi mortem accelle, fuit Reip. thesaurus, à Monachis ad militarem opem quam quam fero traducere. Dacı enim ea capta occasione, quod à legnibus & torpentibus Monachis regni facultates essent absorptæ, in gentem nostram tanquam diuina vindicta incitati, vehementius fauerunt. Eodemque tempore inflabant nonæ, & Anglorum genti incognitæ pestes atque coniugiones, quæ ventris profluuio tam antimalium greges, quam hominum casus deleuerunt. Auctaque indies Dacorum Vis ob Angliorum sub Monachis redactorum signauiam maritima regni occupauit littora, totam gentem ad meditationem denique pertinere. Hinc et cuniam orta sunt multa differentia, quae Dacos effecerunt victores. A quo tum furore li quid immune esset atque rutum, id Monachis ad hoc suis ordinis inter sanctos relato tribuebant. Nam ut Eacorum insuluatione eiecto fuerunt regni loca quam Monasteria. Et si quacunque occasione cuitassent Dacorum innationes, Sancto suo imperium, Veluti in Monasterio S. Aldelmi omnibus vndique Monasterijs spoliatis, cum iam Daci accederent, Monachi amotis omnibus Monachis, ferit thesaurus praeter scriptum S. Aldelmi id hostibus, si non ab ipso Aldelmo tutare ut ipsa ad heret, quia se, hostibus suis, non defenderetur, tam hostium quam se culentum ludibrio exponeret. Hostis quam inutiliter tamen effuso cum atque ro quare quam eo ferocitate sed hostis regem hostis Monachis, et in quod contorquere vellet, in aut eius de virtute rauit. Deinde in ordine similia. Similiter refert alius Monachus de S. Augustini ab hostibus Dacis Monasterio seruato, cum omnia tam in Cantio, quam in urbe Cantuaria vastarentur Monasteria, hostilique Augustini in puluerem extinxisset, uerus Sancti Augustini preciosum pallium clam delitto ferro abstulit, et sub axilla texit. Sed pallium tanquam antiqua cutis axillis suis adhaesit, neque vi aut arte auelli poterat, donec postea S. Augustino ciuisque Monasterii fratribus fuit deprecatus veniam, etiam aquas quibus iam... Quod miraculum totam Dacorum multitudinem ita perterruit, ut exteris iam vastatus hoc Monasterium non modo non inuaderent, sed tuerentur ac defenderent. Haec et similia Monachorum destrua omnium multis aliarum animis tanta superstitione tenuere, ut verissima crederetur. Dunstani vero omnia dicta, facta, gesta atque somnia, tanquam certissima aeterni fati omina ab illis tradita sunt. Qui cum 27 sedisset annis moritur. 14 Kal. Julii, haec mala contra ficta de se prodita vaticinia videns in humanis. De quibus in Episcopi Lupi ad Anglos oratione fusissime explicatur.
units.tr: They attribute to this queen, and to the murder of the king, all the blame for having provoked the divine majesty. They write that all these things were foretold from this source by Apollo and by Dunstan, their god. Nor do they ask by what hidden judgment of God that spurious king, on whose authority Dunstan had separated a lawfully wedded couple, was so suddenly taken away. But let us relate what the monks write. A secret enmity had always existed between Queen Ælfthryth and Dunstan, for these reasons. Dunstan first opposed most strongly that she should be joined in marriage to King Edgar, whom she had been contracted and betrothed to. For when she had been brought to him, Edgar, moved by her beauty, pledged his faith to her in marriage and led her into his bedchamber. Dunstan, as we said before, accustomed to courtly and royal beds and with the usual shamelessness or monastic modesty, entered the bedchamber and asked the king who that woman was whom he held in bed and in his embrace. The king answered that she was his queen and wife. Dunstan declared that this could not be done without offence to God and without violating the institution of the Roman Church, on account of the spiritual kinship he had previously contracted with her when he had raised her son from the holy font. And so he often urged the king to send her away and to separate himself from her company. The king, moved besides by his desire for so attractive a woman, put Dunstan's counsel after his own love. By her the king first begot Edmund, who died as a boy, and then Ethelred, who afterwards became king, as we shall say presently. The monks write that when this Ethelred was being baptised by Dunstan, he poured urine from a vessel into the baptismal font. By this sign Dunstan prophesied that the destruction of the English would come in his time. After these hostilities, carried on long and in secret, Queen Ælfthryth, surrounded by the nobles of the realm after Edward had been slain, sent for Dunstan, and by his archiepiscopal right he crowned the king. Though he was offended and grieved and unwilling, he, old and trembling, did not dare to resist. But, while arranging the crown, as the monks report, he did not hold back that spirit of his, and he foretold that the ruin of the king and the realm was now at hand. By the same prediction (the monks being witnesses) he tried to terrify the king eight years later, when he besieged Rochester because of the aforesaid enmity with the bishop, and did not wish to release the money which he had received from the same Dunstan by the order of the bishop before. For this reason Dunstan cursed him with evil omens. Shortly afterwards the attacks of the Danes came upon the English, and the saint became a source of disaster to them. First Southampton, a wealthy maritime and harbour town, was plundered by Danish pirates, and its inhabitants were either slaughtered or led away into captivity. Elated by the spoils of this town, they laid waste the island of Zentlanb, then raided the coasts of Cornwall and of the province of Dorset. They ravaged the Isle of Portland and plundered the monastery of the confessor Petroc in Cornwall. At the same time the city of Legions was despoiled by Norwegian pirates, and London was consumed by fire. These beginnings of evils, proceeding from the institution of the monks, and not checked by their sloth and idleness, afterwards grew into the ruin and destruction of the royal line and of the English nobility. Ethelwald, patron of the monks under Dunstan, tormented by superstition under Dunstan, was so tormented by the swelling of his groin and the pain of his fistula that he spent sleepless days and nights, and died having barely reached old age. After his death many of the monasteries which he had founded were destroyed, and the rest were reduced by cutting down and levelling. In connection with these stories it will not be out of place to relate a certain ridiculous dream of Dunstan's, written by the later monks. Dunstan (as we said before) was the master of this Ethelwald, and had set him over the abbey of Glastonbury. Soon after he had set him over it, Dunstan dreamed that he saw a tree of immense size and height, spreading and extending through all regions of the world. Its branches were loaded and filled with countless monks' cowls, small and large. The top of this tree bore a very large cowl, reaching above all the others and touching the sky itself. When he was astonished at this sight, a venerable old man of angelic appearance stood beside him, asked Dunstan what he conjectured about the tree, and answered that the tree was Glastonbury, and the cowls were the countless multitude of monks that had gone forth from that monastery, the crowd of monks with which all England swarmed and would be filled. The highest cowl, raised up to heaven and covering the others, was Abbot Ethelwald, who was to go before the other monks into heaven. But (to omit the rest) it is certain that that fountain of monks, as I may call it, saturated with the fat of the soil, drained the wealth and strength of the realm, so that after Ethelwald's death the treasury of the commonwealth was, when a military force was needed, scarcely to be drawn away from the monks. For the Danes, having seized this occasion, because the resources of the realm had been absorbed by the idle and sluggish monks, attacked our nation all the more fiercely, as if stirred up by divine vengeance. At the same time there broke out among the English people plagues and diseases unknown to them, which by a flux of the bowels destroyed herds of animals as well as human lives. And the power of the Danes, increasing daily because of the weakness of the English, who had been reduced under the monks, seized the maritime shores of the realm, and finally the whole nation was brought under their dominion. Hence also many disasters arose, which made the Danes victors. From whatever rage of theirs anything was spared and left intact, the monks attributed it to the holiness of their order. For just as the places and monasteries were not spared when the Danes were driven out... And if at any time the Danish attacks had ceased for some reason, the monks ascribed this to their saint... As in the monastery of Saint Aldhelm, when all the monasteries had been plundered on every side and the Danes were now approaching, the monks, all having been removed, left the treasure behind, and Aldhelm, it is said, had not defended it, since he himself was not defended against his enemies, and so exposed both himself and it to the mockery of the enemy... [The rest of this passage is too garbled in the scan to render with any certainty.] Similarly another monk reports about the monastery of Saint Augustine being preserved from the Danish enemies, when all the monasteries in Kent and in the city of Canterbury were laid waste, and the Danes had reduced the church of Saint Augustine to dust. A certain thief secretly stole the precious pallium of Saint Augustine with an iron tool and hid it under his armpit. But the pallium clung to his armpits like old skin, and could not be torn away by force or by art, until afterwards he begged pardon from Saint Augustine and the brothers of that monastery, even with the water with which... This miracle so terrified the whole multitude of Danes that they, though they had already laid waste the other places, not only did not attack this monastery but protected and defended it. These and similar tales of the monks, and the many other such things, held the minds of men in such great superstition that they were believed to be most true. And all the words, deeds, doings and dreams of Dunstan were handed down by them as most certain omens of the eternal fate. He died, having sat for twenty-seven years, on 18 June, having seen in human affairs these evils, which he had falsely foretold of himself. These matters are explained at great length in Bishop Lupus's address to the English.

units.la: Quae nimium prolixa est, ut inseratur tota, ideoque eius summam breuibus articulis comprehensam perstrinximus.
units.tr: Since it is far too long to be inserted in full, we have therefore set out its substance, summarised in brief points.

units.la: 1. Huius vniuersitatis finem ipsum docuit, quoniam pectatum exuberat, idque ita praedictum in sacris scripturis ante aduentum Antichristi futurum, eaque mala ostensa palam quatuor annis ante Ethelredi Regis obitum.
units.tr: 1. He showed the very end of this universe, since sin abounds, and that this was foretold in the sacred Scriptures as to come before the coming of Antichrist; and these evils were openly displayed four years before the death of King Ethelred.

units.la: 2. Gentes cum Christianis conferenses ass annetulit, planeque ostendit, quod in illo impio diuino cultu, falsaque religione multo sinc iustiores, feruentiores, et obseruantiores quam Christiani, quorum vita indies fit sceleratior. Nam Ecclesiae vastantur, sanctitas et vitae ollitur, ordo clericalis ludibrio habetur et contemptui, vidimus ad secundas nuptias agi, ab ipsis incunabulis ad miseram seruitutem sumpti et redacti sunt, omnisque benignitas et eleemosyna perijt, ipsi denique liberi aui ta libertate et ingenuitate frui, et in seruili conditione constituti, bonis magnis partis laboribus, autaliunde concessis vti prohibentur.
units.tr: 2. Comparing the nations with Christians, he plainly showed that in that impious worship and false religion they were much more just, fervent and observant than Christians, whose life grows more wicked every day. For the churches are laid waste, holiness and the good life are neglected, the clerical order is held in ridicule and contempt; we have seen second marriages arranged; from their very cradles people are taken and reduced to miserable servitude; all kindness and almsgiving has perished; and finally, free-born men are forbidden to enjoy their liberty and freedom, and, placed in servile condition, to use the goods won by great labour or granted from elsewhere.

units.la: 3. Aliaque illorum temporum vitia commemorat multa. Parentum, liberorum, fratrum, consanguineorum, amicorum, propinquorum atque agnatorum non esse Christianis, ad hominibus dignam amoris et officii inter se retributionem et vicissitudinem. Clericos amusitregulaque sua actione contempta, et laicos communi humanaeque legi spreta viuere. Quaecunque mala iam esse vbique diffusa atque dissipata, eaque quae ad Rempubl. labefactandam et euertendam summa sunt. Proditionem atque falsum in ipsos dominos atque heros. Cuius fuit indicium Edwardi Regis ipsis hostibus traditio, parentumque ae filiorum impietas, quod illi liberos, hi matresque pecunia conedebant. Ostendit ex hac Christianae vitae et integritatis deterioratione, peruenisse ad hanc gentem ignominiam et infamiam. Deinde bellum, famem, incendia, homicidium vndique gentem delere.
units.tr: 3. He recounts many other vices of those times: that among Christians there was no longer due regard for parents, children, brothers, kinsmen, friends, relatives and agnates, nor any worthy exchange and reciprocity of love and duty among men. He said that the clergy had cast off their rule and their conduct, and that laymen lived with the common human law scorned. He said that whatever evils were now spread and scattered everywhere, and those most effective in weakening and overthrowing the commonwealth. There was treachery and falsehood toward their own lords and masters. A sign of this was the betrayal of King Edward to his enemies, and the impiety of parents and children, in that the former sold their children and the latter their mothers for money. He showed that from this decline of Christian life and integrity the nation had come to disgrace and infamy. Then war, famine, fires and murder were destroying the nation on every side.

units.la: 4. Furtum autem, egestatem, pestem, latrocinia, et rapinas esse gentis propria et intestina mala. Quibus praeter solitum accessere diuinitus coeli atque aeris intemperies, et sterilitas agrorum.
units.tr: 4. Theft, poverty, plague, robbery and rapine were the nation's own peculiar, internal evils. To these, beyond the usual, had been added intemperate weather of sky and air, sent by God, and barrenness of the fields.

units.la: 5. Alia cum his punienda in regno frequentia ostendit vitia, periuria, mendacia, et foederum atque pignorum fractiones et violationes.
units.tr: 5. Besides these, he pointed out other vices frequent in the kingdom that deserved punishment: perjuries, lies, and breaches and violations of covenants and pledges.

units.la: 4. Piratas ipsa diminatra ac vindicta in tanto gentem praeualuisse. Aquibus inuasorib-us saepe decem aut viginti vna mulieri coniuges atque filiae inspectantibus parentibus & maritis stupratae, Dominum ipsis seruire coacti, Christiani instar pecudum agmim vna ducti & vinculis copulat, in pelagos varios acti, eos qui pecunia, vincul s, infan i, rapina, contumeliisque ac ecclesiis omnibus simale tractabant, & in navigia cogebant, honorabant.
units.tr: The pirates, through divine judgement and vengeance, had so prevailed over the nation. By these invaders, ten or twenty women at a time were often ravished, while their parents and husbands looked on, and wives and daughters were violated. The Christians were forced to serve their masters, led off in a single herd like cattle and bound together with chains, and driven across various seas. Those whom they treated with cruelty, through ransom, chains, disgrace, plunder and insults, and all the churches, they forced into their ships and sent to do their bidding.

units.la: 5. Has omnes dicebat calamitates regno inuectas, incenso diuino numine, quia haec gens multasiam multisque modis deliquit homicidio, auaritia, gula, furto, profusione, paece ac inducis insidiose conscrutis, barbarismo, proditione atque tetrhnis vsurerimis, legum atque religionis contemptu, fraude, atq; defectione, propinquorum offprefsione, ordinum contemptu, & maculato coniugio, incestu atq; adulterio, iuramentis, fraudes, promissi, fidei, ieiuniorum atque sertarum crebra fractione, medaciis, orationisq; vanitate. Inetfe praeterea in ordine clericali Apostatas, & defectiones atque renunciantes fidei & inter Laicos petmultos, qui sumimo odio clerum prosequuntur, legemque diuinam, atque Christi imperium contemnunt. Quorum exemplo quis fatuus populari magis quam ex diuina aut humanalegi pendebant, ex facinoribus magis quam ex recte gestis gloriam atque commodum quaesuetunt.
units.tr: 5.
