He said all these calamities had been brought upon the kingdom, the divine majesty being kindled, because this nation had sinned in many ways: by homicide, avarice, gluttony, theft, extravagance, treacherously contrived peace and truces, barbarism, treason and tyrannical usury, contempt of law and religion, fraud and apostasy, oppression of kinsfolk, contempt of orders, defiled marriage, incest and adultery, oaths, frauds, frequent breaking of promises, faith, fasts and sermons, lies and the vanity of prayer. Moreover, there were apostasies and renunciations of the faith among the clergy, and among the laity many who pursue the clergy with the greatest hatred and despise the divine law and Christ's rule. Following their example, fools who depended more on popular opinion than on divine or human law sought glory and advantage from wrongdoing rather than from what was rightly done.

units.la: 6. Ad extremum vitae prioris emendationem, poenitendam atque nouitarem, omnisque mali vitationem suadens peroravit. Habuit & aliam ad populum Anglicanum conclonem, quae huius temporis historiae nonest propria, quia ad vitam, ad virtutem fingeret dam, nosque ad diuinam volumtatem redeundos, quod vulgare est Theologorum thema, non ad illius aetatis corrigenda vitia peruenit.
units.tr: 6. At the end he urged amendment of the former life, repentance and renewal, and the avoidance of all evil. He also delivered another sermon to the English people, which does not belong to the history of this time, since it aimed at life and virtue and at our return to the divine will, which is a common theme of the theologians, and did not reach the correction of the vices of that age.

units.la: XXIIII. ÆTHELGARVS.
units.tr: XXIV. Æthelgar.

units.la: Efunctu Dunstano successit Æthelgarus, Abbas primo nouiMonasterii Wintoniensis ab Ethelwaldo Winton. Episcopo reatus dea de Selefiensis Episcopus fuit, postea Dacis hanc iniuria intelitanibus, ad Archiepiscopaeam Celiutidinem euectus est. De huius gelitis propter temporum iniuriam, passim omnia loca occupantur, nihil mem sit proditur. Ast vbi annum vnum & menses duos sedit, vita excessit, sepultus in Ecclesia Christi Cant. iauct.
units.tr: After Dunstan, Æthelgar succeeded, first abbot of the new monastery of Winchester, appointed by Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester. He was bishop of Selsey, and afterwards, when the Danes were troubling the land, he was raised to the archiepiscopal seat. Nothing is recorded of his deeds, because of the troubles of the times, when everything was being seized everywhere. But after he had sat for one year and two months, he departed this life and was buried in the church of Christ at Canterbury.

units.la: XXV. SIRICIVS.
units.tr: XXV. Siricius.

units.la: Veecesit Æthelgaro Siricius, qui ex Monacho Glasconiensi Augustinensis, comobii Abbas Dunstani Archiepiscopi beneficio erectus est. Postea vero sub eodem Dunstano ad Episcopatum Wintoniensem euectus fuit. Deinde Æthelgaro defuncto Archiepiscopalem sedem Anno Dom. 989. obtinuit. Quapotius, etsi ante voluete rota fortunae variabili (vt verbis vtar Wilhelmi Thorna) Monachi propter eorum insolentiam scidibus pulsi, & clericis introducti, silenti Hic tamen eqcanefcio quia cupiditate dictus, clericos seculares ciiccte cepit, constitutis rutsum Monachis, cuius vestigiis insistens Aluricus fueeffor, illius conarum ad effectum perduxit. Et plane Wilhelmus Nubergensis ipse Monachus, tamen refert, clericos suo ordini aduersos in Cant. & Wintoniensi Ecclesiis ante inductum Monachismum omnino ministrasse. Post hoc Siricius pacem Christianis ab infidelibus Dacis x. librorum mitibus redemit ad ignominiam sane pencq perniciem totius Regni. Plura huius acta hon commemorantur. Itaque postquam obierat, in Ecclesia Christi Cant. sepultus est. Dedit libros suos valde bonos Ecclesiae Christi Cant.
units.tr: Æthelgar was succeeded by Siricius, who, from a monk of Glastonbury and Augustinian canon, was raised to the headship of a monastery through the favour of Archbishop Dunstan. Afterwards, under the same Dunstan, he was raised to the see of Winchester. Then, on Æthelgar's death, he obtained the archiepiscopal see in the year of the Lord 989. Wherefore, although before (to use the words of William of Malmesbury) the wheel of fortune had turned changeably, and monks had been driven out for their insolence and clerks introduced, here he, led by desire, began to expel the secular clergy again and reinstate the monks. His successor Ælfric, following in his footsteps, brought his undertaking to completion. William of Newburgh, himself a monk, nevertheless reports that before monasticism was introduced, clergy who were hostile to his order had altogether ministered in the churches of Canterbury and Winchester. After this, Siricius bought peace for Christians from the heathen Danes for ten thousand pounds, to the certain disgrace and nearly the ruin of the whole kingdom. Few other of his deeds are recorded. When he died, he was buried in the church of Christ at Canterbury. He gave his very good books to the church of Christ at Canterbury.

units.la: XXVI. Alvrscivs.
units.tr: XXVI. Ælfric.

units.la: Luricius qui & Alfricus dictus est, ex Glasconiensi coenobio similiter prodiit. Primoque Abbas Abindoniae, deinde Wiltunien sium Episcopus, randemque vero Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus defignatus, & a Papa Iohanne pallium accepit. Vbi Cantuariam venit, a Clericorum ordine, a quo minus vellet, suscepeus est. Hic Siricii praedecessoris sui de clericis eiiciendis propositum adimpleuit, omnisque clericos locis suis cedere coegit, & Monachos introduxit. Hoc etiam tempore sedes Episcopalis Lindisfarnensis Dunelmum translata est. Aluricius vbi plures annos Cantuariensem Ecclesiam ab incursu crudeli Danorum pie fortiterque defendisset, obiit Anno domini MC.vi. & Abindoniæ primo sepultus, postea ad Ptiam Cantuariensem Ecclesiam deductus, ibique humatus iacet.
units.tr: Ælfric, who was also called Alfricus, similarly came forth from the monastery of Glastonbury. He was first abbot of Abingdon, then bishop of Wiltshire, and finally was designated archbishop of Canterbury and received the pallium from Pope John. When he came to Canterbury he was received by the order of clerks, though he would have preferred otherwise. He carried out his predecessor Siricius's proposal to eject the clergy: he compelled all the clergy to yield their places and introduced monks. At this time, too, the episcopal see of Lindisfarne was transferred to Durham. Ælfric, having for several years piously and bravely defended the church of Canterbury from the cruel onslaught of the Danes, died in the year of the Lord 1006, and was buried first at Abingdon; afterwards he was carried to the church of Canterbury and lies buried there.

units.la: XXVII. ELPHEGVS.
units.tr: XXVII. Elphegus.

units.la: Lphegus etiam ex prioratu Glasconiæ profectus est, primum Abbas Bathoniæ constitutus est, a splendidissimis parentibus originem ducens, adolescentiæ annos transegit in Monasterio de Pyrtl, vbi religionis habitum suscepit: postea Monasterio egressus Bathoniam se contulit, vbi constructo habitaculo se inclusit, vt corpus nimio vigore redundans ieiuniis & continentia coerceret: vndecad eum magna Monachorum turba, & maiorum suorum origine, & tam exacto genere vitæ insturuto ducta, confluxit. Quibus ille continentiæ legem imdirens, se angusta habitatione conclusit. Mox Monachi ab eo initiati, plurisque fidei & prosessionis immemores, præceptis ab eo continentiæ Regulis non parebant: sed media nocte quæ potationique operam dabant, tam ad lasciuam & omnem intemperantiam prochues, ea quæ dictu turpia sunt perpetrabant. Morruo deinde Wmroniensi Episcopo Ethelwaldo, eiusdem Ecclesiæ Monachi cum Clericis de novo pontifice eligendo, summopere contendebant. Siquidè clerici eiusdem Ecclesiæ scelaratissimam vitam citra Canonum statuta degentes, cum à prefato antistite sepius, vt prauos mores corrigerent, neue quæ praue gesserant, pertinaci spiritu defenderent vellent, rogati, nec eius monitis obsequuti sanctione ac decreto excluti sunt, eorumque loco accitj alij, qui vita digniores habebantur. Itaque Clericis exterminatis Monachi admittuntur, vtiue in Episcopi electione Clerici Clericum, Monachi Monachum, vtrique suę voluntatis fautores, dicitur. Quod cum animadvertisset Dunstanus, ad oratoris anchoram confugit, Dei dumque futurorum scientissimum supplicauit, quatenus dignaretur ostendere, quis regedæ Ecclesiæ dignus foret. Cùm crebro à Leo precibus instaret, sibi visus est videre AthelApostolum talia dicentem. Quid inquit, Charissime contritaris? quid tam lugubris querelas lac hrymando effundis? Surge & Elphego Abbati manuimpone, & Episcopum de solatæ Ecclesiæ constitue, nec te aliquorum potentia prohibeat, cum non ab homine, sed à Deo hæc de illo sententia processit. Nec vero de me te solicitum reddam. Ego sum Andreas filij Dei Apostolus, ruxqe salutis diligentissimum custodem me esse noueris. Sicque exhilaratus Dunstanus, Elphegum, vt russus fuerat, Episcopum Wintoni consecrauit, & ad sedem suam eum honore remisit.
units.tr: Elphegus also came out of the priory of Glastonbury, and was first made abbot of Bath. He was born of very distinguished parents. He spent his youth in the monastery of Pyrton, where he took the monastic habit. Later he left that monastery and went to Bath, where he built a dwelling and shut himself up in it, so that by fasting and abstinence he might restrain a body that was overflowing with excessive vigour. A great crowd of monks, drawn by his noble birth and by so strict a way of life, gathered around him. He imposed on them the rule of continence and enclosed himself in a narrow dwelling. Soon, however, the monks whom he had trained, forgetting much of their faith and profession, would not obey the rules of continence that he had laid down. Instead, during the night, they gave themselves to drinking and to lascivious and every kind of intemperance, and committed things that are shameful to speak of. Then, when Ethelwald, bishop of Winchester, died, the monks and the clergy of that church contended strongly over electing a new bishop. The clergy of that church were living the most wicked lives, contrary to the decrees of the canons. Often asked by the said prelate to correct their depraved ways, and not to defend with obstinate spirit what they had done wrongly, they did not obey his admonitions, and so by sanction and decree they were expelled, and others were brought in to take their place, who were considered more worthy of their life. Thus, with the clergy driven out, the monks were admitted. It is said that in the election of a bishop, the clergy favour a cleric, and the monks a monk, each side favouring its own wish. When Dunstan noticed this, he took refuge in prayer, and he entreated God, who knows all future things, to deign to show who was worthy to rule the Church. As he pressed his prayers repeatedly, he seemed to see the Apostle Andrew saying such things to him: "Why, dearest one, are you worn out? Why do you pour out such mournful complaints with tears? Rise, lay your hand on Abbot Elphegus, and appoint him bishop of the desolate Church. Let not the power of any men hinder you, since this judgment about him has come not from man but from God. Nor shall I make you anxious about myself. I am Andrew, the Apostle of the Son of God, and you may know that I am a most diligent guardian of your welfare." Dunstan, so cheered, consecrated Elphegus as bishop of Winchester, just as he had been before, and sent him back with honour to his see.

units.la: Omnis tunc & Papæ & Dunstani in promouendis Monachis, Clericisque deprimendis cura & solicitudo versabatur, Sicut enim in Wallia quatuor Episcopatus, & in Anglia septendecem fuerunt, ita octo eorum Episcopos Monachos esse debere, quod in aliis ptounciis aut nusquam, aut rarò inuenies, statuerunt. Quia primi Romani in Anglia prædicatores, Augustinus, Mellitus, Iustus & Laurentius Monachi ante fuerunt: in aliis aut octo Episcopalibus sedibus Canonicos seculares, & in vnoCannicos regulares instituendos Episcopos decretum. Cuius rei testimonii ex Iohannis Papæ ad Edgarum Epistola de Wintun Episcopatu lucidum habemus, nec procul à vero esse potest, silei Papæ Epistolas pro reliquis Episcopatibus, vbi Monachi præfuerunt emanasse.
units.tr: At that time all the care and concern of both the Pope and Dunstan lay in advancing monks and in pressing down the clergy. For just as there were four bishoprics in Wales and seventeen in England, they decided that eight of the English bishops should be monks, a thing you will find in other provinces either nowhere or rarely. This was because the first Roman preachers in England, Augustine, Mellitus, Justus and Laurence, had been monks. In the other bishoprics it was decreed that secular canons should be appointed bishops, and in one of them regular canons. We have a clear witness to this in John the Pope's letter to Edgar concerning the bishopric of Winchester, and it cannot be far from the truth that similar letters of the Popes were issued for the other bishoprics where monks presided.

units.la: Iohannes Episcopus, seruus seruorum Dei Eadgaro Regi excellentissimo, atque omnibus Episcopis, Ducibus, Comitibus, Abbatibus, & cunctisfideli populo Anglicæ gentis Christianam salutem & Apostolicam benedictionem. Quoniam semper sunt concedenda quæ rationalibus quærùtur desideriis, oportet vt vestræ piæ petitionis studium in priuilegiis minime offendatur præstandis. Scimus enim gloriose Fili imperii vestri dignitatem zelo diuinæ legis ita vndique munitam, vt indesinenter pro vetabilium locorum percogiret stabiliæ, quatenus prouenient pro labore scholaDominici multiplicetur seruitij, & largitori omnium Deo abunde fructus referantur. Quare Rex inclyte ac fili charissime, quid vestra excellentia per fratrem & Conepiscopum nostrum Dunstanum abhac Apostolica sede, cui hæc immeriti præsidemus, exposcit, omnibus modis concedimus, authoritate Apostolica sancientes, vt de Monasterio in Wintoniæ ciuitate, in honorem S.Trin.& beatiß. Apostolorum Petri & Pauli cõstructo; quod vetus differentia novi illius quod iuxta est cœnobi cognominatur Canonici "Domino & Episcopo, omnib. catholicae fidei circumstantiis ex patefactis culpabilis quam turpitu- "dinibus odibilis, & in eisdem secundum imperatoris coercentur, innocentes ut deferant pro durantes, cui suo "propósito, utpote valde diaboli eliciantur, & sicut vestra sublimitas de deferat, dilecti filii tua "fratres & Concipiscopus nostri Ethelwaldus regularib. discipulis apprime imbutus, Mo"nachorum secundum praeceptae regulae vivuntum gregem enutriat, cuius inibi perpetu"am mansionem statuat. Illeque eorum vitam ita sanctitatis moribus exornet, ut pastore "ad laboris sui praemium vocato, non aliunde quam ex illa congregatione alteri in lo"cum regiminis succedat. Quod si impedientibus (quod absit) peccatis ad hoc pontificale "officium in eadem congregatione idoneus invenire minime posse contigerit, auctoritate "Apostolorum principis Petri cui Dominus ac daturus nostrer ligandi, solvendique, "potestatem contradixit, praecipimus ut nemo ex Clericorum ordine ad huius regiminis "Ecclesiae promoveatur. Sed potius ex alia qualiter congregatione, qui dignus inveniri "fuerit Monachus, assumatur, & huic Ecclesiae praeficiatur. Si quis enim interea, quod "non credimus, haec Apostolicae sedis privilegii decreta irrita facere, & ex quae nobis pie "indulta sunt, intaminatae praesumperit, authoritate eiusdem ecclesiae anathematis vinculo innodatum, & in illo mu"ni iudicii die perpetualiter damnandum. In Christo valeas Domine filii." Sed postea quam hoc decreto elatiores facti Monachi, intolerabilis illorum arrogantia tam Regibus quam Episcopis ipsis ac procenbus vitae est, ab Henrico Rege post conquestum eius nominis primo, intercedentibus & postulantibus id Episcopis instituta fuit, ut Monachi amplius in Episcopatibus non praeficerentur. Cuius decreti causam & historiam in vita Rhodulphi Cant. post Anselmum Archiepiscopi inseritur recitatimus. Elphegus autem, ut Monachi scribunt, ita se omnium moribus conformavit, ut & omnibus charus esset, & nemo, quod ratum est inter homines, eius gloriae inuidet, cum summe in omnes exstitit misericordiae. In se tamen nimium seuerus, & quasi carnifex apparebat. Nam brumae media nocte surgere, niueum & glaciem nudis pedibus transfire, & ad auroram orationi vacare consuevit. Et pransus tam vacuus cibo ferea mensa surrexit, quam accesserit, unde corpus illius ad tantam maciem redactum est ut cum manus inaltum porrigeret, per medias palmarum iunctiuras, claritas aeris perspicua posset. Tam aperta praeterea & ingenuae fuit naturae, ut quiuis ex eius sermone animi sui sensum facile colligere potuisset. Sed confuecuerunt semper Pontificii de suis sanctis stupenda quaedam & monstri similia commemorare, veluti quod Peronius ambulabat eodem, ne carni suae placeret. Pambus noluit plus vno versu. Idixi custodiam. Quiinterrogantia sed de eodem versu respondit, vixxxx annis ipsum implere potui. Qui rogante Episcopo Athanasio, ut ab eremo ad Alexandriam, fleuit de ornatu mulieris. Ammonius dum cum Athanasio venisset Romam, nullum ibi vidit nisi Basilicam Apostolorum Petri & Pauli, qui ad Episcoporum tractus, ne Episcopus esset, suam abiciditaurem. Iohannes pater trium millium Monachorum. Scrapion pater decem millium Monachorum. Discorus pater C. Monachorum, qui ante communionem conscientias singulorum fratrum pandebat. Theonas xx annis tacuit. Helenus igne in sinu portabat. Helias Cx Monachorum pater in eremo solus annis Lxx. Apelles faber ferrum cx fornace crudum trahens manu, nocte faciem daemonis fingentis se informa mulieris pulchrae percussit. Idoros suum elausit Monasterium, intus habens necessaria. Apollo annis x L. vixit in exteriori solitudine. Dorotheus cuius cibus erat panis sex vnciarum, & fasciculus vnus oleris & aqua. Piamon Presbyter cui offerenti corpus Christi in sacramento angelus circa altare apparuit, nomina absentium fratrumque praesentium scribens. Marcus cui hora communionis angelus corpus Christi praebuit. Moses vasa fratrum nocte aqua impleuit, per x stadia, xx vel xx x. eam afferens: quique quatuor latrones suum hospitium infestantes leguitis, crastino eos in commune fratrum humeris portans. Iulianus septuaginta annis in cella reclusus nec visus, nec locutus tam diu est. Haec & his similia infinita non deliria, sed portenta, quaecum Christianus aequae iudicio tolerare potest. Sed ad Elphegum reuertamur, qui Wintoniensis Episcopus Alfrico mortuo, Romae tandem Cant. Ecclesiae pallium accepit. Vir omnibus rebus ornatus, & propagandae pietatis studio, etiam barbaros, qui inter hostes erant, ad veram religionis cultum praedicatione & exemplo adduxit. At seuicentibus ob non solutum tributum Dacis, Ecclesia Christi spoliatur, ipsa Cantua-
units.tr: John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Edgar, most excellent king, and to all bishops, dukes, counts, abbots, and all the faithful people of the English nation, Christian greeting and apostolic blessing. Since those things that are sought by reasonable desires must always be granted, your devout petition ought not to be refused when it comes to bestowing privileges. For we know that your kingdom, glorious son, is so fortified on every side with zeal for the divine law that you unceasingly care for the stability of places set apart for God, so that the fruits of the labour of the Lord's service may be multiplied, and abundant fruit may be returned to God, the giver of all. Therefore, renowned king and dearest son, we grant in every way, sanctioning by apostolic authority, what your excellence requests through our brother and fellow bishop Dunstan from this apostolic see, over which we, though unworthy, preside. Concerning the monastery in the city of Winchester, built in honour of the Holy Trinity and of the most blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, which is called by the old name of Canons, and which is near that new monastery, we decree that it shall be occupied by monks, living according to the rule. Let your brother and fellow bishop Ethelwald, thoroughly trained in the regular discipline, nourish there a flock of monks living according to the rule, and establish a perpetual dwelling for them there. And let him so adorn their life with the morals of holiness that, when the shepherd is called to the reward of his labour, his successor in the place of rule shall be chosen from no other source than that same congregation. But if, through sins that stand in the way (which God forbid), it should happen that no one fit for the episcopal office can be found in that congregation, then by the authority of Peter, prince of the Apostles, to whom the Lord gave the power of binding and loosing, we command that no one from the order of clergy be promoted to rule this church. Rather, whoever is found worthy from another congregation, let him be taken from among the monks and set over this church. If anyone, which we do not believe, should presume to make void these decrees of the privilege of the apostolic see, and to violate what has been piously granted to us, let him be bound by the chain of anathema of this church and be condemned forever on that terrible day of judgment. Farewell in Christ, lord and son." But afterwards, when the monks had been made more arrogant by this decree, their intolerable pride toward kings, bishops themselves and the common people became so great that, at the request and petition of the bishops, Henry the First, after the Conquest, ordered that monks should no longer be set over bishoprics. The cause and history of this decree are recounted in the life of Ralph, Archbishop of Canterbury after Anselm. Elphegus, as the monks write, so conformed himself to the morals of all that he was dear to everyone, and no one envied his glory, which is rare among men, since he was exceedingly merciful to all. Yet toward himself he was excessively severe and appeared almost like an executioner. For in the middle of the night in winter he used to rise, cross snow and ice with bare feet, and devote himself to prayer at dawn. And when he dined, he rose from the iron table as empty of food as when he had sat down, so that his body was reduced to such leanness that, when he stretched his hands high, the clear air could be seen through the middle of his palms joined together. Moreover, he was of such open and frank nature that anyone could easily gather the feeling of his mind from his speech. But the Papists have always been accustomed to recount certain wonderful things about their saints, things like monsters: for example, that Peronius walked about in the same way, so as not to please his flesh. Pambo wished to know no more than one verse. He said, "I have kept it." When asked about the same verse, he answered, "I have been able to fulfil it for sixty years." When Bishop Athanasius asked him to come from the desert to Alexandria, he wept over the adornment of a woman. Ammonius, when he had come to Rome with Athanasius, saw nothing there except the basilica of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and when they wanted to make him bishop, to avoid being made bishop he cut off his ear. John, father of three thousand monks. Serapion, father of ten thousand monks. Dioscorus, father of five hundred monks, who before communion used to lay open the consciences of each of the brothers. Theonas was silent for twenty years. Helenus carried fire in his bosom. Elias, father of a hundred monks, lived alone in the desert for seventy years. Apelles, a smith, drew red-hot iron from the furnace with his hand, and at night struck the face of a demon that was feigning the form of a beautiful woman. Hidoros shut himself in a monastery, having the necessities within. Apollo lived for fifty years in outer solitude. Dorotheus, whose food was bread of six ounces, a bundle of one herb and water. Pinamon, a presbyter, to whom, while he was offering the body of Christ in the sacrament, an angel appeared beside the altar, writing down the names of the absent brothers and of those present. Marcus, to whom an angel gave the body of Christ at the hour of communion. Moses filled the brothers' vessels with water at night, bringing it from ten stadia, or twenty or thirty. He also bound four robbers who were attacking his hospitality, and on the next day carried them on the shoulders of the brothers to the common house. Julian, shut up in his cell for seventy years, was neither seen nor spoke for so long. These things and countless similar ones are not delusions but portents, which a Christian can tolerate no more than with equal judgment. But let us return to Elphegus, who, after Alfric died as bishop of Winchester, at last received the pallium from Rome for the Church of Canterbury. He was a man adorned with every virtue, and by his zeal for spreading piety he brought even the barbarians who were among the enemies to the true worship of religion, by preaching and by example. But while the Danes were raging because the tribute had not been paid, the Church of Christ was despoiled, and Canterbury itself

units.la: Sed confuecuerunt semper Pontificii de suis sanctis stupenda quaedam & monstri similia commemorare Cantuaria capitur, utraque demum comburuntur. Grex Monachorum, turba vitorum & mulierum decimantur, ut decimo quoque per sortes liberato atque salvo, cæteri omnes trucidentur. Ita pro octingentis quatuor vita condonatis septem millia, ducenti triginta quatuor sunt interfecti. Ipse porro Elphegus vii. mensibus, carceribus detentus, postea Grenovicum adductus, ab infidelibus securi percussus obiit, Swano Dano in Anglia regnante. Sed Daeos hoc furore sævientes ira Dei consumpsit.
units.tr: But the Papists have always been accustomed to recount certain marvels and monstrosities about their saints. Canterbury is taken, and at last both are burned. The flock of monks and the crowd of men and women are decimated: every tenth person is chosen by lot and spared, and all the rest are slaughtered. Thus for 804 people spared, 7,234 were killed. Elphegus himself was held in prison for seven months, then brought to Greenwich, and was struck down with an axe by the unbelievers and died, while Swein the Dane reigned in England. But the Danes, raging with this fury, were consumed by the wrath of God.

units.la: Sepultus erat Elphegus in Ecclesia Paulina Londini, indeque mandato Canuti regis, ad Ecclesiam Christi Cantuariæ transferendus in sepulchro conditur. Tanta tamen in delinquentes sevëritate fuit, ut quendam furem pro multiplici reatu flagellis cæsum, mitti iussit in cippum acrioribus suppliciis cruciandum, qui diu in pœnis iacuit. Ethelwaldum proximè ante se Winton. Episcopum summo semper honore coluit & æstimauit.
units.tr: Elphegus was buried in St Paul's Church in London, and then, by the command of King Canute, was transferred to Christ Church in Canterbury and laid in a tomb. Yet he was so severe towards offenders that, when a certain thief, guilty of many crimes, had been beaten with whips, he ordered him to be put in the stocks, where he was to be tortured with harsher punishments, and he lay there a long time in pain. He always held Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester immediately before him, in the highest honour and esteem.

units.la: XXVIII. LIVINGVS.
units.tr: XXVIII. LIVINGUS.

units.la: Iuingus cognomento Electanus, ab Episcopatu Wellensi, quem ante gesserat, post Elphegi mortem ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum pertulatus venit. Huius tempora, quoniam ob Dacorum crebras incursiones turbulentissima, plenaque vastitatis fuerunt, sine alicuius reitanquam ab Archiepiscopo gestæ commemoratione scriptores somnes pertransfenerunt. Sed certum est Monachorum ocium totam Anglorum gentem in tantam ignauiam atque socordiam exemplo suo deduxisse, ut ad repellendos vndique influentes hostes, nec erigere animos, nec vires ai quis copias colligere valeret. Ita nobilis & perbeata patria indigenis inspectantibus, nec resistere audentibus, vicinis barbaris expolita prædæ est. Huius rei vitium Monachi parum æqui iudices vt a se transferrent, Ethelredo Regi totum tributum quem eriam insolenter & immodeste, præterque suum officium, regiamque maiestatem, quia illos nimium exultauerit, coercuit, onerant maledictis. Miserum inertem, vecordem atque supinum vocant.
units.tr: Living, surnamed Electanus, was moved from the bishopric of Wells, which he had held before, to the archbishopric of Canterbury after the death of Elphegus. Since his times were most turbulent and full of devastation because of the frequent incursions of the Danes, the writers passed over them almost in silence, with no record of any deed of the archbishop. But it is certain that the idleness of the monks, by their example, had brought the whole English nation to such cowardice and sloth that they could neither raise their spirits nor gather forces or troops to repel the enemies pouring in from every side. Thus the noble and most blessed country, while its own people looked on and dared not resist, was plundered as prey by the neighbouring barbarians. To shift the blame for this onto themselves, the monks, who were poor impartial judges, heap abuse on King Ethelred, who had restrained them, insolently and immodestly and beyond his office and royal dignity, because (they said) they had exulted too much. They call him a wretched, sluggish, frenzied and lazy man.

units.la: Sed quid ageret cum omnes pene regni facultates à re militari traductæ essent ad ocia Monachorum. Quos etiam certissimum est allexisse, suarumque diuitiarum cupiditate incendisse Danos, quos tam grandi data pecunia arcere, & abigere suis finibus putabant. Namque Dani quo maiori largitione affecti fuerunt, eo sepius factuti prædam accesserre. Quæ quidem insania, hostes atque prædones muneribus non armis profligare, ab ipsis Monachis primo profluxit. Siricius enim primus decreuit, vt grandi soluia pecunia Danai discederent, qua accepta discesserunt. Sed paulo post lucri suauitate deliniti cum maxima copia & multitudine rediere, & in ipsa Monasteria, quæ opulentissima ex accepiis prius donis expetiti sunt, maiori impetu quam in alia quæcunque regni loca irruerunt. Rex ipse sæpe eos insecutus est, & vt patriam liberaret, interfici iussit. Quo quidem facto esti reiecta aliquandiu eorum iugo ab Anglis fuerunt, parata tamen classe coepiosa, crudeliores reuersi sunt. Quos hoc aduentu, dum Elphegus auertere pecunia vellet eos quidem locupletauit, sed sibi atque patriæ incaute & imprudenter (vt diximus) prospexit. Edgari insignis classis, & bellicæ copiæ, quæ solæ resistere debuerūt, cœnubiis ditandis à Dunstano ante dissipatæ & distributæ fuerunt. Nec dubium est quin bellica regni vis neruata, & ociosorum hominum affluentia hostibus satis nota, huius inuasionis atque bellicausa fuit. Sed huc Liuingus (de quo agimus) cum patriam, ita captam & direptam ab hostibus animadverteret, postquam ipse à carceribus, quibus eum Danisepiem menisbus inclusisset, euasisset, profugit in exilium. Ibi de afflicta patria lugens, cum Swani morte pacatæ res essent, & Rex AEthelredus rediisset, ipse quoque reuersus est. Cui reuerso contigit, vt Ethelredo mortuo primo Edmundum AEthelredi filium, qui ob fortitudinem exgnomento ferreum latus dictus est, regis sacris Londini initiaret. Cumque post indictum singulare illud certamen inter eum & Canutum Swani Dani filium, regnum ea conditione, vt virique ab armis discederent, inter eos diuideretur, ac Edmundo ex Corriei cuiusdam insidiis ferreo veru postea intercepto, totum regnum in Canuti potestatem iam venisset, ei etiam Londini regium Diadema imposuit. Ita duobus ab eo Regibus sacratis optabilem pacem post tantas turbas in fine vitæ vidit. Et postquam septem sedisset annis, Ecclesiamque Cantuariensem plurimis ornasset donis, cum gaudio moritur, & in Ecclesia Christi Cantuariæ sepultus in puluereiacet. Anno Domini 1020.
units.tr: But what could he do, when almost all the resources of the kingdom had been diverted from military affairs to the idleness of the monks? It is quite certain that these monks also enticed the Danes and inflamed them with the desire for their wealth, since they thought they could drive them off and expel them from their borders by paying a large sum of money. For the more lavishly the Danes were rewarded, the more often they came back as plunderers. This folly of routing enemies and robbers with gifts rather than arms first flowed from the monks themselves. Siricius was the first to decree that the Danes should depart on payment of a large sum of money, and when they had received it they departed. But a little later, enticed by the sweetness of gain, they returned with the greatest force and numbers, and they attacked the monasteries themselves, which had become the richest from the gifts previously received, with greater violence than any other places in the kingdom. The king himself often pursued them, and to free his country he ordered them to be killed. Although by this deed the English for some time shook off their yoke, the Danes, having prepared a copious fleet, returned more cruel than before. When Elphegus wished to avert them by money, he enriched them by this arrival, but he provided unwisely and imprudently for himself and for his country, as we have said. The distinguished fleet and military forces of Edgar, which alone ought to have resisted, were dispersed and distributed by Dunstan before, in order to enrich the monasteries. And there is no doubt that the weakening of the kingdom's military strength, and the abundance of idle men, well known to the enemy, was the cause of this invasion and war. But Living (of whom we are speaking), when he saw his country thus captured and plundered by the enemy, escaped from the prison in which the Danes had shut him up for some months, and fled into exile. There, mourning his afflicted country, when affairs were pacified by the death of Swein and King Ethelred had returned, he too came back. It fell to him, on his return, that after the death of Ethelred he anointed Edmund, son of Ethelred, surnamed Ironside on account of his courage, as king at London. And when, after that single combat was proclaimed between him and Canute, son of the Dane Swein, the kingdom was divided between them on the condition that both should lay down their arms, and then Edmund was pierced with an iron spear by the treachery of a certain Corriei, and the whole kingdom had come into the power of Canute, he also placed the royal diadem on him at London. Thus, having anointed two kings, after so great troubles he saw a desired peace at the end of his life. And after he had sat for seven years, and adorned the Church of Canterbury with many gifts, he died with joy and lies buried in dust in Christ Church at Canterbury. Anno Domini 1020.

units.la: AGELNOTHVS.
units.tr: AGELNOTH.

units.la: {A}Gelnothus qui idem Egelnotus, Athelnothus, atque Æthelnothus a scriptoribus varie dictus est, propter eximiam & insitam virtutem onomasiaticè bonus appellabatur. Hic nobilis viri Comitis Agelmari filius fuit. Hoc tempore in Ecclesia Christi Cantuariensi permisti cum Monachis, Canonici Cathedrales habitum quidem Monachalem gerebant, sed regulâ atque professione discrepabant. Itaque cùm in illa sacra Cantuariensium per Dacos decimatione 1020. Ibi à Papa Benedicto & palliû, & primatus honorem accepit, ab eoque bracchium D. Augustini Hipponensis Episcopi, a Papa too. talentis argenti comparatum in Angliam reportauit, ac Couentrensi Ecclesiæ dono dedit. Hanc autem Papalem in concedendis palliis auri argentiq; voraginem, tanquâ Charybdin reprehendit, emendauitq; postea Canutus rex, qui ex illorum temporum cæco more, cùm Edmundo mortuo tumulum Imperium solus in Anglia gessit, ad iceleratua expiunda patchali quodam tempore profectus Romam, dona quidem in Papam conjulit ingenio, atque regia, vt illum inexplebilem satiaret gutgitem, sed ab eodem obtinuit, vt Schola Anglorum instituta Romæ, a censu pendendo liberaretur: deinde vt Angli atque Daci sui subditi, dû Romam siue peregrinationis, siue cuiuscunque negociationis causa profiti sfecentur, a Thelonneo, quod viaticum est vectigal, esse ntimmunes. Ad extremum expositæ immodico papali in pallijs tribuendis lucro, etiam impetrauit, vt id deinceps concederetur gratis. De qua impetratione atque concessione lætus, setipsit ad Agelnotum Cantuariensem, & Alfricum Eboracensem Archiepiscopos, aliosq; regni primates atque proceres. Cuius verba, quæ ad hanc rem necessaria sunt, inseruimus.
units.tr: Agelnoth, who is also called Egelnoth, Athelnoth and Æthelnoth by various writers, was called "good" (bonus) by a play on his name, on account of his outstanding and innate virtue. He was the son of a noble man, Count Agelmar. At this time in the Church of Christ at Canterbury, canons were mixed with monks: the cathedral canons wore the monastic habit but differed from the monks in rule and profession. So, when in that sacred Canterbury, after the Danish devastation of 1020, he received there from Pope Benedict both the pallium and the honour of the primacy, he also brought back to England, from the same pope, an arm of St Augustine, bishop of Hippo, purchased for a hundred talents of silver, and gave it as a gift to the Church of Coventry. But the Papal gulf in granting pallia for gold and silver, this Charybdis, was censured and afterwards corrected by King Canute. In the blind manner of those times, after Edmund's death, when he alone held the rule in England, Canute set out for Rome at a certain time to expiate his wicked deeds. He indeed offered gifts to the Pope, with cunning and royal generosity, so as to satisfy that insatiable gullet; but he obtained from him that the English School founded at Rome be freed from paying the tax, and then that the English and his Danish subjects, when they went to Rome either on pilgrimage or for any business, be exempt from the thelonium, which is a road toll. Finally, with the immoderate papal profit from granting pallia exposed, he also obtained that it be granted free of charge from then on. Glad of this concession and grant, he wrote to Agelnoth, archbishop of Canterbury, and Alfric, archbishop of York, and the other chief men and nobles of the realm. We have inserted his words, those that are necessary to this matter.

units.la: Canutus Rex totius Angliæ, & Danemarchiæ, & Norregiæ & partis Swanorum, Agelnotho Mettopolitano, & Alfrico Eboracensi Archiepiscopo, omnibusque Episcopis & Primatibus, & totigenti Anglorum tam nobilibus quàm plebeiis salutem, &c. infra. Conquestus sum iterum coram Domino Papa, & mihi valde displicere dixi, quod mei Archiepiscopi interim angariabantur iminensi atque per uniarum quæ ab eis expetebantur, dum pro palle accipiendo secundum morem Apostolicam sedem exeterent, decretumq; est, ne id deinceps fiat. Cuncta enim quæ a Domino Papa, & imperatore, & a Rege Radulpho ceterisq; Principibus, per quorum terras nobis transitus est ad Romam, pro mex gentis vtilitate postulabam, libenter annuerunt. Et concessa etiam sacramento confirmarunt, sub testimunio quatuor Archiepiscoporum, &xx. 40 Episcopotum, & innumeræ multitudinis ducum & nobilium quæ aderat, &c.
units.tr: Canute, king of all England, Denmark, Norway and part of the Swedes, to Agelnoth, metropolitan, and Alfric, archbishop of York, and to all the bishops and chief men, and to the whole people of the English, both noble and common, greeting, etc. Further on: I have complained again before the Lord Pope, and I said that it displeased me greatly that my archbishops were meanwhile harassed and burdened by immense sums demanded from them, while they were journeying to the Apostolic See to receive the pallium in the customary way; and it has been decreed that this shall not happen again. For the Lord Pope, and the emperor, and King Rudolph, and the other princes through whose lands we have passage to Rome, have most willingly agreed to all that I asked for the advantage of my people. And they confirmed these concessions also with an oath, in the presence of four archbishops, and twenty-forty bishops, and a countless crowd of dukes and nobles who were present, etc.

units.la: Ita pallium ex hac eó concessione atq; iuramento papali non emptum, sed gratuitu deinceps semper fuit, etsi infinitis aliis artibus atque dolis immensos thesauros illa pontificia fraus expreßit atque hausit. Agelnotus autem iam cum pallio reuertius Cantuariam Ecclesiam Christi nondum post Danicum vastationem integre reparatam, totam restaurauit, Canutoque Regi charus in intimis semper ad fuit consiliis. Qui cum Edmundo Regi interfecto condere magnificum atque regium voluit Monasterium, adhibuit sibi tum Agelnorum, cuius solertia praetuyteros eo loco admouit, Monachosque statuit. Etsi in præbyteris extrudendis tam Rex quam Archiepiscopus humanitate summa vsi sunt, namque eos aut ad Monasticam professionem habitumque 50 perduxerunt, aut si profiteri habitumque illum genere noluerunt, collatis sibi aliis tecus, ex quibus solito abundantius victum habercat ac vestitum, in alia loca migrare seceterunt. Hæc regalis sane & Archiepiscopalis, etiam in re superstitiosa, scripta nobisque ab ipsis Monachis prodita benignitas, exemplo debuit esse posteris pontificiis, qui tanta impietate & sauiitia coniugatos clericos & fœdere coniugii, & ab omnium posseßione iure nulla facta compensatione separabant. Monachatus autem in singula celebri ora regni loca fit irrepsit, tamen plerumque cum sacerdotalis ordinis viris permistus fuit. Id quod usum ex permulis constat historiis, tum ex ipsorum Monachorum scriptis maxime. Vt enim ea non repetamus quæ ante commemorata sunt, Aluricius qui suscepto Stirici conatus in Clericis e Monachorū grege penitus extirpandis perfecit, cum pro Archiepiscopatus capiēda pollicebatur venisset Cantuariam, à Clericorum ordine, à quo minime vellet receptus est, de quibus ab Ecclesia sua amouendis, quod tum in animo consilium habuit, postea eum Rege communicauit. In quo narrauit, suam Ecclesiam Cantuariensem ex primi eius per Gregorium & Augustinum ministrumone non ab alio ordine præterquā à Monachorum posidieri oportere, Clericos autem quorum iam multitudo non modo suam sed pleraque alias Monachales Ecclesias in Regno impleuisse, necessitate nō lege inducos. Nā tēpore Celnothi Archiepiscopi Mona- liorum turbam pesteadeo consumpta, & ad tantam paucitatem redactam, ut in Ecclesia Christi Cantuarienti ne quinque Monachi superesse ent. Hac necessitate coactum Celnothum capellanos suos, & parochiales presbyteros, vt numerus orantium assiduus compleretur, ad Monasterium ducere, & cum Monachis comu gere. Iam autem adaucto irerum Monachorum numero non esse fas, quod tunc necessitatis, quæ nunc cessat, tantum fuit, in iuris aut consuetudinis potestatem transferte. Rex assensu Aluricio ualit, vt pro pallio profectus quam celerrime Romam, cum Papa de hac reageret. Clerici accepto hoc Regis cum Aluricio communicato consilio, auro & argento, cuius interuentu de Papæ iudicio ac sententia certi statuebant, onusti, Romam properant. Sed Archiepiscopi Aluricii nuncii, celerius antegressi, Papam prius in suam sententiam traxerunt. Ita clericorum inanis labor pecuniam saltem tantum sibi saluam fecit. Aluricio postea accedenti Papa cum magno honore ad Pœtcialtare pallium ipse impoluit, eui etiam decedenti, quod Aluticius uptauit, Papa imperauit, vt in Ecclesia sua non alium virorum ordinem tolcrateet, quam Monachorum a Gregorio præceptum (vt ipli tradunt) Augustino. Id quod reuersus sine mora perfecit. De qua tam atroci clericis facta iniuria, in Elphegi proximo sequuti Archiepiscopi vita supplicium diuinitus sumptum est. Vt enim ante præsidente Celnotho Monachi fame perempti ad quinquenarium, sic iterum luh Elphego Dacorum iusta crudelitate delci, & ad pauciorem nempe quaternarium numerum diminuti fuerunt. Quæ renouata (vt in oudetuina) paucitas Clericos iterum introduxit. Et quamuis Wil. Malmes ixit met, hoc verisimile non uideri, perturbatos ab Aluricio Clericos, & Monachos introductos fuisse, tamen vtcunque res gesta sit, W. Thorne ipse Monachus hanc Monachorum atq; Clericorum in posteridis Ecclesiis vicissitudinem neque belli, neque peltis, neq; paucitatis ratione (quod alii sibi adulates fiogunt Monachi) sed ipsorum Monachorum insolentia contigisse scribit. Sed Agelnoti Archiepiscopatus in hoc fœlix fuit, quod Regem Cantum bonis attribus instruxit. aut (vt authoris verbis vtat) permulsit. Quo quidem verbo non aliud iudicari voluit, qtaro Reges præliis atque cæde crebra incensos, pacari non posse commodius quam humanitatis attibus. Vt Horatius ait: Nemo adeo ferus est qui non mitesce re possit Si modo culturæ patientem commodet aurem.
units.tr: Thus from this concession and papal oath the pallium has from then on always been given free, not bought, although that papal fraud had by countless other arts and tricks squeezed out and drained immense treasures. Agelnoth, now returned to Canterbury with the pallium, restored entirely the Church of Christ, which had not yet been fully repaired since the Danish devastation, and he was always dear to King Canute and close to his counsels. When King Canute wished to found a magnificent and royal monastery in memory of the slain King Edmund, he took Agelnoth into his counsel; by his skill he brought in canons to that place and established monks. Yet in expelling the canons both the king and the archbishop used the greatest kindness: for they either brought them to the monastic profession and habit, or, if they were unwilling to profess and take that habit, they gave them other benefices, from which they might have a livelihood and clothing somewhat more abundant than usual, and allowed them to move to other places. This kindness, royal and archiepiscopal indeed, even in a superstitious matter, recorded and handed down to us by the monks themselves, ought to have been an example to the later Papists, who with such impiety and savagery separated married clergy from the bond of marriage and from all their possessions, by right and without any compensation. Monasticism, moreover, crept into almost every famous place in the realm, yet it was for the most part mixed with men of the priestly order. This is clear from many histories, and most of all from the writings of the monks themselves. For, not to repeat what has been mentioned before: Aluric, who, having taken up the attempt of Stigand to root out the clergy completely from the monks' flock, came to Canterbury when he promised to seek the archbishopric, was received by the order of clergy, whom he would by no means wish to be received by; of removing them from his church, which he then had in mind to do, he afterwards informed the king. In this he argued that his Church of Canterbury ought, from its first founding by Gregory and Augustine's ministry, to be occupied by no other order than that of monks, while the clergy, whose number had now filled not only his church but also most other monastic churches in the realm, had been brought in by necessity, not by law. For in the time of Archbishop Celnoth the crowd of monks was so consumed by plague, and reduced to such a small number, that in Christ Church at Canterbury barely five monks were left. Compelled by this necessity, Celnoth led his chaplains and parish priests to the monastery, so that the number of those constantly praying might be complete, and had them live together with the monks. But now that the number of monks has increased again, it is not right to transfer into a matter of law or custom what was then a necessity, which now has ceased. The king agreed with Aluric, so that he should set out for Rome as quickly as possible to obtain the pallium, and treat this matter with the Pope. The clergy, having learned of this decision of the king communicated with Aluric, hurried to Rome, loaded with gold and silver, by whose intervention they were confident of securing the Pope's judgment and sentence. But the messengers of Archbishop Aluric, having gone ahead more swiftly, first drew the Pope to their own opinion. Thus the clergy's vain labour at least preserved their money for them. When Aluric afterwards came to the Pope, the Pope himself put the pallium on him with great honour at the altar of Peter; and to him, as he was departing, the Pope enjoined, which Aluric had asked for, that in his church he should tolerate no other order of men than that of monks, as Gregory had prescribed (as they themselves relate) to Augustine. This Aluric carried out without delay on his return. For this so savage injury done to the clergy, divine punishment was exacted in the life of Elphege, the archbishop who followed next. For just as under Celnoth's presidency the monks had been destroyed by famine down to five, so again under Elphege, through the just cruelty of the Danes, they were diminished to an even smaller number, namely four. This paucity, renewed (as in the old story), again introduced the clergy. And although William of Malmesbury thinks it not likely that the clergy were disturbed by Aluric and monks introduced, nevertheless, however the matter was done, W. Thorne, himself a monk, writes that this alternation of monks and clergy in the later churches came about not through war, nor plague, nor fewness of numbers (as some monks, flattering themselves, feign), but through the insolence of the monks themselves. But Agelnoth's archbishopric was fortunate in this, that he furnished King Canute with good qualities, or (to use the author's words) softened him. By which word he meant nothing else than that kings, inflamed by frequent battles and slaughter, cannot be pacified more fittingly than by the qualities of humanity. As Horace says: No one is so savage that he cannot be softened, if only he lends a patient ear to cultivation.

units.la: Deinde quod duos eiusdem Canuti liberos. 1. Haroldum, deinde Hardecanutum consecratū Canuti memor, qui huius boni Archiepiscopi dictis semper acquieuit. Elphegi corpus decennio Londini sepultum Cantuariam deductum in Christi Ecclesia inhumatur. Ipse Agelnothus cum x v i t i annis sedisset, quarto Kalend. Nouembris diem clausit extremum, & in Ecclesia Christi Cant. sepultus iacet. Quo etiam anno crebræ fuerunt in Anglia mortes Episcoporum.
units.tr: Then, mindful of Canute's consecration of his two sons, first Harold and then Harthacnut, who always acquiesced in the words of this good archbishop. The body of Elphege, which had been buried at London for ten years, was brought to Canterbury and laid to rest in the Church of Christ. Agelnoth himself, after sitting sixteen years, closed his last day on the fourth before the Kalends of November, and lies buried in Christ Church at Canterbury. In that same year the deaths of bishops in England were frequent.

units.la: XXX. EDSINVS.
units.tr: XXX. EDSINUS.

units.la: Dfinus, sæpe Elefinus, Ealfius atque Eadfinus dictus sacerdos secularis, & Haroldi Regis primo fuit Capellanus, à quo ad Wintoniensem Episcopatum promotus est. Deinde tam Haroldo Rege, quam Agelnoto Archiepiscopo mortuo, ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscoparum postulatus & expeditus, ab Alexandro Papa pallium accepit regnante Hardecanuto Haroldi fratre. Hunc Archiepiscopalem honorem Edfinus administrare per infirmam atque aduersam valetu. ine non potuit. Itaque Archiepiscopalia omnia iura & emolumenta, cū ipse tanto oneri impar esset, Siwardo cuidam demisit & delegauit. Ex eo Siwardus, Vicarius, Conepiscopus, & Archiepiscopi vices moderans dictus est. Scribunt quidem Hardecanuto mortuo, Edwardum minorem Æthelredi Regis filium qui in Normannia
units.tr: Edfinus, often called Elefinus, Ealfius and Eadfinus, was a secular priest and was first chaplain to King Harold, by whom he was promoted to the bishopric of Winchester. Then, after the deaths both of King Harold and of Archbishop Agelnoth, he was nominated and elected to the archbishopric of Canterbury, and during the reign of Hardecanute, Harold's brother, he received the pallium from Pope Alexander. Because of ill and adverse health, Edfinus was unable to administer this archiepiscopal office. And so, since he was unequal to so great a burden, he handed over and delegated all the archiepiscopal rights and revenues to a certain Siward. From then on Siward was called Vicar, Co-bishop, and one who governed the archbishop's functions. Writers do indeed record that, after Hardecanute's death, Edward the Younger, son of King Æthelred, who had lived in exile in Normandy in great poverty and had found his mother Emma hostile to him, [obtained the kingdom] with the support of Earl Godwin, while the Witan resisted; and at that time, when the forces of the kingdom had come into their power, [...] should not think it foreign to the truth that [this archbishopric was obtained] because of the king's great favour towards him.

units.la: Ex Canuto. pauperrime exulauerat, atque Emmam matrem aduersam sibi senserat, Godwino Comite cum Vnanis renitentibus, in quorum tum poteritatem regni copiæ peruenissent, ad obtinendum in hoc regnum huius Archiepiscopatus ... ob magnam Regis in eum gratiam a vero alienum existimare non debet. Edwardus enim tam regno potitus ab eodem Edlino die Pascha, Elfrico Eboracensi Archiepiscopo, omnibus quæ regni Episcopis & magnatibus altantibus, Wintoniæ consecratus, & cotonatus est, eumque vt Patrem ct lus a cobcuauit. Sed Edlinus diuturna inualitudine ... ... Edlinus Archiepiscopus Christi Ecclesiæ subscripsit.
units.tr: From Canute. For once Edward had taken possession of the kingdom, on Easter Day he was consecrated and crowned at Winchester by this same Edlin, with Ælfric, Archbishop of York, and with the assent of all the bishops and magnates of the realm, and he began to honour him as a father. But Edlin, through long ill health [...] Edlin, Archbishop of Christ's Church, subscribed.

units.la: Ego Edlinus Archiepiscopus Christi Ecclesiæ subscripsi. Huius tempore sedes Episcopalis Cridiensis ad Exoniam deducta fuit, quæ iam vnadiocæsi Devoniam, atque Cornubiam complexa est. Siwardus autem ægritudine ex proprii facinoris indignitate, acturpitudine confectus, defertur Abindoniâ, ibique duobus mensibus in morbo decumbens, moritur ac sepultus est. Edlinus ex voluntate Edwardi Regis inter sanctos relatus est. In his Archiepiscopis quorum turbulenta tempora nihil memorabile peperunt, etsi simus breuiores, ea tamen recensuimus quæ commemorantur a scriptoribus. In his quæ sequuntur Archiepiscopis ob regni atque imperii ad Normannos mutationem, prolixiora ...
units.tr: I, Edlin, Archbishop of Christ's Church, have subscribed. In his time the episcopal see of Crediton was moved to Exeter, which now embraces one diocese comprising Devon and Cornwall. Siward, however, worn down by sickness, by the disgrace of his own crime and by shame, was carried to Abingdon, and there, taking to his bed with illness for two months, he died and was buried. Edlin was, by the will of King Edward, numbered among the saints. Concerning these archbishops, whose turbulent times produced nothing memorable, although we have been briefer, we have nevertheless recorded those things which are mentioned by the writers. In the archbishops who follow, because of the change of the kingdom and empire to the Normans, [the accounts are] longer [...]

units.la: XXXI. ROBERTVS.
units.tr: XXXI. ROBERT.

units.la: O bertus gente Normannus, ex cœnobio Gemeticensi venit in Anglian, accersitus ab Edwardo Rege, cui(ob sua in eum antea in Normannia exulantem merita, amicitiamque quæ Regi cum Wilhelmo Normanniæ Duce tunc intercesserat) charus fuit. Primum Londinensis Episcopus, deinde Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus, eiusdem Regis gratia institutus est. Huius ... cum Heraldo tunc C. mitte in Normanniam missus est, ut Regis benevolentiam, regniquepotiundi ipsum Duci declararet. ... ... ... Godwinus in exilium cum filiis suis actus, eiusdem Archiepiscopi procuratione, opera & consilio quod Reginæ fauebat. Aidwinus Episcopus Emmæ dictus Amasius, Wintoniensis ciuitatis mœnüs se continere, nec inde sub pœna capitis efferre pedem iussus. Reginain his constituta angustiis, literis ad Episcopos, quos sibi fidos intellexerat (quæ Regi traderentur) missis, & excusauit se, & eos solicitauit, vt pro se intercederent, Regemq; rogarent, vt de se legitimam sine mora inquisitiohem haberet, Vel vt lege ageret, & de iectu quam primum cognosceret atq; statueret. Literarum summa erat hæc: torqueri se magis aliena quàm sua infamia, probare se iudicio paratam, & se & Wintoniensem Episcopum iniuste diffamari, filiiq; sui cædis insontem, nec vnquàm contra Regem aliquid esse molitam, placereque sibi ad criminum vitationem, etiam candentis & igniti ferri periculo; hoc tantum petere, vt abiecta cunctatione in Ecclesia S. Swithuni, hæc sua probatio purgatioq; fieret. S. curam enim esse se cogitationis & cōscientiæ proprio testimonio.
units.tr: Robert, a Norman by birth, came into England from the monastery of Jumièges, summoned by King Edward, to whom he was dear, on account of his services to him when he was in exile in Normandy and of the friendship that then existed between the King and William, Duke of Normandy. He was first made Bishop of London and then Archbishop of Canterbury, both by the King's favour. Of this man ... with Harold, who was then ... was sent into Normandy, to declare the King's goodwill and his intention that the Duke should gain the kingdom. ... ... ... Godwin was driven into exile with his sons, through the management, work and counsel of this same Archbishop, because he favoured the Queen. Ealdwine, Bishop, called the lover of Emma, was ordered to keep within the walls of the city of Winchester and not to set foot outside it on pain of death. The Queen, placed in these straits, sent letters to the bishops whom she understood to be loyal to her, to be delivered to the King. In them she excused herself and urged them to intercede for her and to ask the King to hold a lawful inquiry into her without delay, or else to proceed by law and learn and decide the charge as soon as possible. The gist of the letters was this: she was tormented more by others' infamy than by her own; she was ready to submit to judgment; she and the Bishop of Winchester were unjustly defamed; she was innocent of her son's murder and had never plotted anything against the King; and she was willing, to clear herself of the accusation, even to face the peril of red-hot iron. She asked only that, with no further delay, her proof and purgation be made in the church of St Swithun, for she said that her concern was with her own thoughts and conscience, of which she herself was the witness.

units.la: Quòd si in hoc inquisitionis negocio Rex tarderet, & proctastinatione veteretur, scilicet moriturum. In tanta enim pauperate, quæ se ridiculam effecisset, & vulgi opprobrio molestam, inuisam vitam producere non posse, Regemq; filium suum maiori infamia, vulgiq; odio flagraturum, si se Reginam ac matrem, nec testibus, aut legitimis probationibus, nec sua cofessione iudicatam, criminisque experi-entem, tam famosa & arcta custodia puniret. Omnibus enim perinde esse odiosum, si aut mater filium, aut filius matrem tam atroci odio prosequeretur. Eoque magis, quòd in excelso loco dignitatis ambo positi; vt virtutes, sic & vitia vtriusque in omnium oculos conspicua & nota magis incurrunt. Ac Episcopi acceptis Reginæ literis Edwardum Regem consulunt, querelam & preces Reginæ exponunt. Rex facilitate & innocentia sua, (qui nihil vnquam sua sponte, nisi prouocatus ab aliis commisisset perperam,) eorum precibus facilimè superatus esset, nisi restitutisset Archiepiscopus, qui ea tunc apud Regem existimatione fuit, vt sicornicem dixisset esse candidam, assensum ei fuisset. Qui cum Episcopos pro Regina acriter instaré senserat, fraudem secum meditatus, quæ & illos ludere, & Regis animum ad matris gratiam propensum & inclinantem, auertere posse, sic exorsus est. Conuenistis (inquit) fratres Dominum nostrum Regem de matre sua, fera; non fœmina: qua intercessione retorquetis crimen matris in filium. Illa enim (omnium petulantissima) in Regem & minas & conuitia euomuit, & vnà cum Episcopo Wintoni. adultero suo & stupRorum ac libidinū (frequentatore) societate coniunctissimo suo, (etsi callide simulat sanctitatem,) Regem ipsum sacrilegii reū audet arguere, quod illi indigno Episcopo, (quem illa Christum Domini nominabat,) authoritate Regia iuste bona abstulerit. Sed rem ipsam tangamus. Illa adultera Episcopum adulterum purgare vellet crimine. Quis autem purgabit eam; quæ præterquam quòd est adultera, & filii sui Eluredi interfectionem consensu ratam habuit, & Edwardo venenum procurauit. Et quamquam Regia dignitate sit cæteris feminis eminentior, tamen tot tantorumque crimunum suspecta, genere examinationis strictissimo siue disquisitionis grauissimo & ciusmodi personis inuistato, & seculis omnibus inaudito, quò & se, & amalium pariter suum culpa vacare probet. Quod si perferre illæsa poterit, ego, (quia me huic accusationi inscripsi,) honoribus meis (vestro iudicio condemnatus) priuabor, purgatiq; que restituentur, sin purgationis iudicio rea deprehensa fuerit, Monastica vita perpetua includatur. Cuius rei inuidiam atque culpam ne penes Regem esse putetur, in me recipiam. Ac nec vos degenere probationis siue purgationis diutius suspensos teneam, sic statuo. Hæc infamis fœmina, noue ignitos & candentes vomeres nudis pedibus supergrediatur & transeat, quorum quatuor pro suo, quinq; pro Episcopi Wintonien-sis, (quem innocentem asserit,) iudicio sint: Si titubauerit, si singulos vomeres pleno pede non præsterit, si qualitercunq; læsa fuerit, feratur in eam tanquam fornicariam sententia. Quæ etsi aliis durior censura videatur, mihi tamen mitius & indulgentius secum actum videtur, quòd quæ capite plecti debuit, pedibus tantùm probatur. Itaque feuerillimum hoc Archiepiscopi decretum, à Rege & Episcopis (etsi inuitis,) probatur. Adeo tunc Archiepiscopalis authoritas etiam in potentissimos valuit, vt ipsa Regina, nec suis, nec Regis filii sui, nec procerum aut Episcoporum viribus, nec alia ratione quàm innocentia sua prohibere à se tam insignem contumeliam & iniuriam potuit. Dies ad hoc & locus Wintoniæ statuitur. Quò & Rex & Magnates & Episcopi ad vnum omnes conuenere præter Archiepiscopum. Qui Doueri ægritudinem simulabat, vt si præter opinionem suam negocii euentus sequeretur, citò & sine impedimento posset àfugere. Regina huius decreti certior facta, illius atrocitate non minus turbata fuit, quâ si optatissimum nuncium accepisset, Regiq; iussu è Monasterio Wintoniam reducta est, Iamque expiationis dies aderat. Nocte præcedente Reginaad S. Swithunitumulum vigilans orauit, illum inuocauit, votasuz, abillo ti periculo defungeretur redemptionis permutatafecit: tandem post multas vigilias,(obrepente bteui somno,)vidisse in somnis dicitur Sanctum Swithunum assistentem, dicentemque. Constans esto filia, Ego sum Swithunus quem inuocas,ego tecum sum,ne paueas. Confundentur qui te persequuntur, quia cum transferis per ignem,flammanon nocebit te. Tu autem remittes hanc noxam filio tuo. In hoc autem Monasterio, vt diximus,omni contentione & intercessione,Regina petiit tam periculosam purgationem subire, quia in summo fui omnibus in Wentana ciuitate pretio, quòd multis & suis,& matritotum suorum, Edwardi, Canutiq, & Hardecanuti filii sui,Regum prædiis diuiditisque illud ante locupletauerat: tu vniuersi Angliæ Clero charafruit, quòd eos semper in tanta authoritate atque gratia apud Reges tenuisset, vt mirum esse non posset,eorum omnium votis,suffragiis,viribusque eam in tanto discrimine fuisse seruatam. Postridie Rex(assistentibus tibi Episcopis & proceribus) protribunali sedet, quòcum frequens populi Cleticque conuenisset,eductain publicum Reginainterrogatorum id genus examinationis vellet subire. Atillamodico v sa sentio, his verbis Regem affata est. Domine ac fili charissime: Ego Emma mater tua, quæ re vtero sustuli, de proditione in te & Eluredum filios meos, nec non de turpitudine, violataque pudicitia cum huius sedis Episcopo impetita, Deum inuoco, & in corpus meum testor,me nihil eorum,quæ mihi sunt impolita,nec re, nec proposito,aut cogitatione commissi esse: illaque (et maxime rigida) ignis probatione sum contenta, nec dubito, quin Dominus Deus, eadem potentia qua Sufannam ab iniquissimis vaferrimisque iudicibus liberauit, ignisque vim a tribus pueris in ardentem fornacem coniectis prohibuit, me etiam in hoc discrimine,tum a tam iniusti iudicii fraude & seueritate, tum ab ignis sensu tuebitur. His dictis,in templi pauimentis (ex ritu & more benedicti) nouem vomeres, incendiro pene flagrantes collocantur: Reginaque insons,calceis caligisq; exuta, impositi peplo,accreditaque chlamide suecinctaque inter duos tandem Episcopos mediaad tormentum ducta est. Caterum templo in exteriora atrium deductum. Totius autem populi Cleriqueque quali vna voce vlulantis, S. Swithunum inuocantis & exclamantis, S. Swithune libera eam: maximus fletus pene ad coelos sublatus est, tantusque clamoris sonitus vocibus, viribusque omnium factus est, vt sanctus Swithunus vel illico sine mora, vel nunquam occurreret, vt tonitrua reboantia superaret. Credebant enim illa sua vociferatione (vt author refert) Deum ipsum vim pati, coactumque seruum suum Swithunum quasi violenter extractum e cœlo, ad liberandam Reginam dimisurum. Episcopi ductores, etsi a lachrymis cohibere se non poterant, Reginam tamen consolabantur. Et qui illam hortabantur, vt fortiter hoc perferret, nec timeret, magis ipsi quam illa timebant. Illa cuius tota cogitatio sine formidine in precibus defixa fuit, ad locum accedens, (Episcopis pedes illius vtrinque dirigentibus,) nouem vomeres nouem passibus, singulos totius corporis pleno pondere premens, circa supergressa, nec ferrum vidit, nec sensit incendium. Et vberius ab Episcopis ducta. Num me(inquit) extra ecclesiam in qua probanda sum, estis ductur it cur ad vometes non ponor? At illi a lachrymis gaudio subito retuocari, singultientes resposuerunt. Domina Regina respice, hoc artox & arduum negocium mirando diuino auxilio illæ facile transegisti. Quæ sublato peplo respexit, vidit que ferrum, diuinumque agnouit miraculum. Redemmu igitur inquit ad Regem filium meum, vt perspectis meis pedibus, sciat me non aliud mali, quam iniuriam & intolerabilem infamiam esse perpessam. Itaque ad Regem reuertit rem omnem narrant: cui vberrime cadebant lachrymæ, & ad innocentis matris pedes humi iacens. Peccaui, inquit, mater in Deum & in te, quod quil omnem a te propellere iniuriam, infamiamque delere & abstergere debuitfem, tam ancipiti periculo a viro inimicissimo te exponi permisserim. Itaq; indignus sum filius tuus dici. Necipsum Deum, quem semper summa pietate colui, propitium ac secundum mihi futurum suspicor, nisi hoc meum facinus poena aliqua de me sumpta exp. piatur, tuaq; materna indulgentia remittatur. Atilla prohum ad terram erigens filium. Meus ergo te mi fili amor, quacunque, inquit, sive tua, sive alterius iniuria perimi nulla modo potest: mihi itaque plene hanc tua supplicatione satisfactum est sed de Aldwino Episcopo cogitare te oportet, cui perinde ac mihi iniuria fuit illata. Ab eo vehia spectas, & ablata est tuteris, dignum & te Rege, & me matre tua faciès. Itaque accersitus Episcopus a Rege merente & veniam petete, ordinis ac loco (extra quem positus esset,) restitutus, intet Episcopos sedebat. Posteaque, vt admissum in matrem facinus expiaret, Rex ab Episcopis virgis cæsus, tribusque matemis ictibus percussus, in matris gratiam populique venetationem rediit: omnia prædia eum fructibus medio sue interiectio tempore perceptis, Reginæ & Episcopo Winionien si restituuntur. Qui diuinæ liberationis non immemores, utrique tam Regina quàm Episcopus, nomen muneria ad perpetuam nouem vomerum reique gestæ memoriam Monasterio S. Swithuni singuli concesserunt. Quas donationes Rex & ratas confirmauit, & alia duo muneria, scilicet Mconto & Portesland Monasterio prædicto largitus est. Post hæc Rex matris assiduis precibus Comitem Godwinû cum filiis suis, (redditis eis pristinis honoribus) ab exilio reuocauit, & in summo honore habuit. Quorum ac Regis totiusque populi odio, tantaque facti invidia Archiepiscopus laborans profugit, ac in exilium se dedit voluntarium, vbi mortuus tandem in Gemiticenii Monasterio (unde prodierat) sepultus iacet.
units.tr: "If the King were to delay this inquiry and let it drag on, she would die. In such poverty she would make herself a laughing-stock, and, troubled by the scorn of the common people, could not go on living a hated and despised life. And the King her son would be consumed by greater infamy and by the people's hatred if he punished the Queen and his own mother with such a notorious and severe confinement, when she had been convicted neither by witnesses nor by lawful proofs, nor by her own confession, and was being tried on a charge of crime. For it would be equally hateful to everyone if a mother pursued her son, or a son his mother, with such savage hatred. This would be all the more so since both were set in the high place of dignity, so that their virtues and their vices alike are more readily seen and known in the eyes of all. The bishops, having received letters from the Queen, consulted King Edward and set out the Queen's complaint and prayers. The King, through his easy and guileless nature (for he had never done wrong of his own accord, but only when provoked by others), would very easily have been overcome by their entreaties, had not the Archbishop, who then held such esteem with the King that if he had said a raven was white, his word would have been accepted, stopped him. Having perceived that the bishops were pressing hard on behalf of the Queen, he devised a stratagem by which he could both mock them and turn the King's mind, inclined and leaning towards his mother's favour, away from it. He began thus: 'You have approached our lord the King, brothers, about his mother, not as a woman but as a wild beast; by this intercession you turn the mother's crime back upon the son. For she, the most wanton of all women, has poured forth both threats and abuse against the King, and, joined most closely with the bishop of Winchester, her adulterer and companion in debauchery and lust (though she cunningly feigns holiness), she dares to accuse the King himself of sacrilege, because he justly took goods by royal authority from that unworthy bishop, whom she called the Lord's Anointed. But let us come to the matter itself. That adulteress wishes to clear her adulterous bishop of the charge. But who will clear her, who, besides being an adulteress, both consented to the killing of her son Alfred and procured poison for Edward? And although she is more eminent than other women by royal dignity, yet, suspected of so many and so great crimes, she should be put to a most strict kind of examination, a most grievous inquiry, one unheard of and unknown to such persons in all ages, by which she may prove herself free of guilt both for herself and for her lover. But if she can endure it unharmed, I, who have brought this accusation, shall be deprived of my honours (condemned by your judgement), and she shall be restored and cleared. But if, on the judgement of the trial, she is found guilty, let her be confined in perpetual monastic life. Lest the odium and blame of this matter be thought to rest with the King, I will take it upon myself. And that I may not keep you longer in suspense over the proof or purgation, I decide thus: let this infamous woman walk barefoot across nine red-hot plough-shares, of which four are to be for her own judgement and five for the judgement of the bishop of Winchester, whom she claims is innocent. If she stumbles, if she does not step over each share with her whole foot, or if in any way she is injured, let sentence be passed upon her as upon a fornicator. Though to others this censure may seem harsher, to me she seems to be dealt with more mildly and indulgently, since she who ought to have been put to death is tested only in her feet.' And so this most savage decree of the Archbishop was approved by the King and the bishops, though unwillingly. Such was then the power of archiepiscopal authority, even over the most powerful, that the Queen herself, with neither her own strength, nor that of her son the King, nor that of the nobles or bishops, nor by any means except her innocence, could avert from herself so great an insult and injury. A day and place at Winchester were set for this. There the King, the magnates and the bishops all gathered together, except the Archbishop, who pretended to be sick at Dover, so that if the outcome of the affair were other than he expected, he could quickly and unhindered take flight. When the Queen was informed of this decree, she was no less disturbed by its cruelty than if she had received the most welcome news. By the King's command she was led from the monastery back to Winchester, and now the day of purgation was at hand. On the preceding night the Queen kept vigil at the tomb of St Swithun, invoked him, and made a vow that she might come through such danger, offering in exchange a ransom. At last, after many hours of watching, as a light sleep crept over her, she is said to have seen St Swithun standing by her in a dream, saying: 'Be steadfast, daughter. I am Swithun whom you invoke; I am with you; do not fear. Those who persecute you shall be confounded, for when you pass through the fire the flame shall not harm you. You shall remit this injury to your son.' In this monastery, as we have said, with all effort and entreaty, the Queen had sought to undergo so perilous a purgation, because in the city of Winchester she stood in the highest esteem with all men, since she had enriched that church beforehand with estates and gifts, to many and to all her kin, and to the Kings Edward, Canute and Hardecanute her sons. She was also dear to the whole clergy of England, because she had always kept them in such authority and favour with the Kings that it is no wonder that by the vows, support and strength of them all she was preserved in so great a peril. The next day the King, with the bishops and nobles attending him, sat upon the tribunal, while a crowd of people and clergy had gathered; and the Queen, led out into public view, was asked whether she wished to undergo that kind of examination. Then, with a modest voice, she addressed the King in these words: 'Lord and dearest son, I, Emma your mother, who bore you in my womb, call God to witness and testify on my body that I have committed none of the things charged against me, neither in deed, nor in purpose, nor in thought, concerning the betrayal of you and my son Alfred, nor concerning the foul and violated chastity imputed to me with the bishop of this see. I am content with this ordeal, though it is most severe, and I do not doubt that the Lord God, by the same power by which he freed Susanna from the most unjust and crafty judges, and by which he restrained the power of fire from the three youths cast into the burning furnace, will also protect me in this peril, both from the fraud and severity of so unjust a judgement and from the sensation of the fire.' Having said this, nine ploughshares, glowing almost red-hot with fire, were laid upon the pavement of the church, after the blessing and custom of the rite. The Queen, innocent, with her shoes and stockings removed, a cloth thrown over her, and a mantle fastened about her, was at last led to the ordeal between two bishops. Then she was brought out into the outer court of the church. Meanwhile the whole people and clergy, crying out as with one voice, invoking St Swithun and exclaiming, 'St Swithun, free her!', raised such a great weeping almost to heaven, and such a sound of clamour rose from the voices and strength of all, that St Swithun would either come at once without delay or never, to overcome the roaring of thunder. For they believed, by their outcry (as the author reports), that God himself was being forced, and that he would send his servant Swithun, as if violently drawn from heaven, to deliver the Queen. The bishops who led her, though they could not restrain their tears, nevertheless comforted the Queen; and those who urged her to bear this bravely and not to fear were more afraid themselves than she was. She, whose whole thought was fixed in prayer without fear, approached the place, the bishops guiding her feet on either side, and stepped over the nine ploughshares, pressing each one with the full weight of her body, in nine paces. She neither saw the iron nor felt the fire. And she was led further by the bishops. 'Why,' she said, 'since you have led me outside the church in which I am to be tested, am I not placed at the ploughshares?' But they, suddenly called back from their tears by joy, answered her, sobbing: 'Lady Queen, look back: you have accomplished this hard and difficult business with a marvellous divine help.' She, lifting the cloth, looked back, saw the iron, and recognised a divine miracle. 'Let us go back, then,' she said, 'to my son the King, so that, having examined my feet, he may know that I have suffered no other harm than injury and intolerable infamy.' So she returned to the King and related the whole matter; and he, weeping abundantly and lying on the ground at the feet of his innocent mother, said: 'I have sinned, mother, against God and against you, in that I, who ought to have warded off every injury from you and wiped away and erased your infamy, have allowed you to be exposed to so dangerous a peril at the hands of a most hostile man. Therefore I am unworthy to be called your son. Nor do I suppose that God himself, whom I have always worshipped with the greatest piety, will be gracious and favourable to me, unless this my wrongdoing is expiated by some punishment taken from me, and forgiven by your motherly indulgence.' Then she, raising her son from the ground, said: 'My son, your love for me, whatever injury has been done to me by you or by another, can by no means be destroyed; by your entreaty I am therefore fully satisfied. But you must think of Bishop Aldwin, to whom an injury has been done just as to me. You shall take care to restore to him what has been taken away from him, a thing worthy both of you as King and of me as your mother.' Accordingly the bishop was summoned, and the King, deserving pardon, asked for forgiveness; and he was restored to his order and place (from which he had been removed), and sat among the bishops. Afterwards, that he might atone for the crime committed against his mother, the King was beaten with rods by the bishops and struck with three blows of a birch, and returned to his mother's favour and the veneration of the people. All estates, with the fruits gathered in the meantime, were restored to the Queen and to the bishop of Winchester. And they, not forgetful of the divine deliverance, each of them, both the Queen and the bishop, granted gifts to the monastery of St Swithun, as a perpetual memorial of the nine ploughshares and of the deed done. The King also ratified these donations and of his own accord granted two further gifts to the aforesaid monastery, namely Meonstoke and Portland. After this, at his mother's constant prayers, the King recalled Earl Godwin with his sons from exile, restoring to them their former honours, and held them in the highest honour. The Archbishop, troubled by the hatred of these men and of the King and of the whole people, and by the great odium of the deed, fled, and gave himself up to voluntary exile; there, having died at last, he lies buried in the monastery of Jumièges, from which he had come forth."
