units.la: Erat hæc Emma ob pulchritudinem venustatemque corporis ab Ethelredo Regead coniugalem consuetudinem experita, dictaque filia Normanniæ, Richardo Normanniæ Ducetertio, viro incredibili magnanimitate, pectorisque fortitudine prædito, procreata. Qui quia nullum vnquam periculum formidauerat, Richardus impauidus, seu tine metu, cognominatus est. Huius consuetudo fuit, vt vbicunq; prope Ecclesiâ vel cæmiterii transiret, equo in Ecclesiâ orâtô deiceret: Et si Ecclesiâ clausâ non pollet intrare, pto forib. tepli oraret. Itaq; in nocturno quoda itinere Ecclesiâ procul cospicatus, ad eam diuerit, q aperta ingressus, vidit in terreo humanû cadauer iacens sine custodibus, sepultura destinatum. Quo viso non tardatus, ad cancellam oratum festinauit. Et chirothecis detractis ac iuxta se positis aitollens manus, tacitè deuoteque orauit. Finita oratione audiuit a tergo ingentem sonitum quasi commoti & concussi feretri, hominique aperto ore contra se brachia extendentem. At ille nullo modo stupefactus, impositoque sibi crucis signo imperauit cadaueri, vt Dei nomine acquiesceret. Quod cum non secisset, indignatus dux, pertransiit, & educto gladio corpus illud medio diuiecavit, vt hinc inde ex vtraq; feretri parte diuisum caderet: egressufq; templo ad suos venit. Hæc de causâ per Normanniam edixit, ne deinceps cadauera sine custodibus & vigilia relinquerentur, donec sepultura conderentur: vnde postea inoleuit consuetudo, vt mortui sub vigilum custodia seruarentur, donec humarentur in sepultura, qui mos in Angliam è Normannia foriasse traductus est.
units.tr: Emma was the daughter of Normandy, born to Richard, third Duke of Normandy, a man of incredible magnanimity and strength of heart. She had been taken into marriage by King Ethelred for her beauty and bodily grace. Richard was called "the Fearless," or "the Impavid," because he had never dreaded any danger. His custom was that whenever he passed near a church or cemetery, he would dismount from his horse and pray in the church. If the church was locked so that he could not enter, he prayed at the doors. On a night journey he once saw a church from afar and turned aside to it. Finding it open, he went in and saw a human corpse lying on the floor without guards, set aside for burial. Seeing this, he did not hesitate but hurried to the altar rail. He took off his gloves, laid them beside him, raised his hands, and prayed silently and devoutly. When the prayer was finished, he heard behind him a great noise, as of a bier being moved and shaken, and saw the dead man opening his mouth and stretching out his arms against him. But he was in no way startled. He made the sign of the cross over himself and ordered the corpse to be still in God's name. When it did not obey, the duke was indignant. He strode forward, drew his sword, and cut the body in two at the middle, so that it fell apart on either side of the bier. Then he left the temple and returned to his men. For this reason he decreed throughout Normandy that from then on corpses should not be left without guards and a vigil until they were buried. From this, a custom later took hold that the dead were kept under the watch of guards until they were laid in the grave, and this custom is said to have been brought from Normandy into England.

units.la: Ac paulò post Godwinus Comes, cum in splendido & solenni conuiuio ad mensam propter Regem sedisset, & in eorum conspectu pincerna cum potu potperans, vno pedetentibus atque penè lapsus, altero casum vitans, se recepisset, Comes aliudens euestui, quòd tam eltò pes vnus alreri subuenisset, Regi dixit: Hoc modo frater fratri topem ferre oportet. Cui Rex illico respondit. Ita & frater mihi opitulari potuisset, si sibi licuisset per te. Comes ex hoc responso mæstus, frusto panis in manus sumpto, dira sibi imprecans dixit. Faxit Dominus Deus, vt hæc ossi, quam in os mirto, sit mihi exitialis, si fraternæ tuæ cædis author antreus fuerim. Acceptaque offam deglutire non potuerat, sed quasi stranguiatus ilico exspirauit. Quo viso Rex, nec mente nec corpore motus: Extrahite inquit ministratoribus, delapsum sub mensa canem. Quod peregerunt, & Wintoniam ductum sepeliuerunt. Sub hæc tempora Aldwinus Episcopus decessit, cui Stigandus, de quo proxime tractaturi sumus, successit. Et quia ille purgationis modus Reginæ impositus, tum tanti periculi vitatio, morsque Godwini execrationibus optata, incredibile legentibus admirationem poterit afferre, commodissimum erit hoc in loco, ad illud temporum notam ea referre, quæ in huiusmodi purgationis & execrationis genere à veteribus obseruata fuerunt.
units.tr: Shortly after this, Earl Godwin was sitting at a splendid and solemn banquet at the table beside the King. Before their eyes a cupbearer was hurrying with a drink and stumbled on one foot, nearly falling, but recovered himself by bracing with the other. The Earl, remarking on this, said with a jest to the King that it was right for one foot to help the other so quickly, and that in this way a brother ought to bring help to a brother. The King replied at once: "So might my brother also have helped me, if you had allowed it." The Earl, saddened by this answer, took a piece of bread in his hands and called down a dreadful curse on himself: "May the Lord God grant that this morsel, which I put in my mouth, be deadly to me, if I was the author of your brother's murder." But when he took the morsel he could not swallow it. As if strangled, he died on the spot. Seeing this, the King, moved neither in mind nor in body, said: "Drag out the dog that has slipped under the table," and told the servers. They did so, and the body was carried to Winchester and buried. About this time Bishop Aldwin died, and Stigand, of whom we shall speak next, succeeded him. Since that method of purgation imposed on the Queen, the escape from such great danger, and Godwin's death, which was wished for by curses, may well cause incredible wonder to readers, it will be most fitting here to set down, for the notice of those times, what was observed by the ancients in this kind of purgation and cursing.

units.la: Si quis itaque furti, adulterii, homicidii, proditionis, falsi periurii aut cuiusquàm grauioris criminis iusperctus esset, si nec sim testimonio, nec testibus, nec claris perspicuis, probationibus conuinci poterat, accusatore vel iudice id postulante antiquitus constitutum fuit, vt aqua gelida vel feruenti, aut candenti & ignito ferro, manu vel aliqua parte corporis tactus de criminatione probaretur, vt si frigoris vel caloris vim admoto corpore lensisset, reus iudicatetur: sin expers sensus fuisset, à suspicione absolueretur. In tam incredibilem superstitionem penes fetitatem illis seculis cæcitate peruentum est, vt humanis sensibus vim adferrent, vel elementis detraherent.
units.tr: If anyone was accused of theft, adultery, homicide, treason, false oath, or any more serious crime, and could not be convicted by testimony, witnesses, or clear and evident proofs, it was established in antiquity, at the demand of the accuser or judge, that he should be tested concerning the charge by touching cold or hot water, or red-hot iron, with his hand or some other part of the body. If, when the body was applied, he felt the force of cold or heat, he was judged guilty; but if he was without sensation, he was acquitted of suspicion. In those centuries, through the folly of the age, men came to such an incredible superstition and blindness that they tried to force the human senses, or else took away the power of the elements.

units.la: Quoniam quæ quandoque mitacula ad nominis sui gloriam illustrandam, gentibusque notam facicndam potentet & raro effecisset Dominus, ea leuissimis de causis, singulisque priuatis noxis, crebro præscriptis orationculis & exorcismis suis inanibus, & decantatis ex ore potius, quàm corde emissis fieri repetebant. Neque animaduertebat Dominû, cum in carne fuisset, ea præter naturam signa poscentibus, sæpe denegasse. Et Apostolos eadem nisi raro vt gentes ad fidem allicerent, edidisse. Haec autem curiosa nimis criminum exploratio a veteribus Anglis & Saxonibus, prisco nomine Dryhtelum appellabatur. Cuius nominis haec fuit origo & interpretatio. Dryhtin veteri Saxonum lingua (vt quibusdam placet) privandi particula fuit, cum praeponeretur dictionibus: licut Grece. Vt enim, απο, parte, ... sine parte intelligitur Grece: sic Dryh Saxonice aliquid sine parte, Dryh, non pars, sine parte, expers vel nec quicquam significavit. Et adhuc eiusdem nominis visa aliqua moderna lingua retinetur. Paucum enim parua partem a small Dryh/multum, magnam partem a great Dryh: nullam partem, nō Dryh partitur to Dryh dicimus. Dryhtelum igitur, sive Dryhtelium appellabant veteres Saxones, id genus inuestigationis criminum, quo vendicati cruciatibus adhibiti, Ii doloris omnis, & culpae expertes iudicarentur: quasi qui poenam nequicquam sentissent, neque quicquam perpessi ram, vt suspicabatur, conmisissent. Haec autem credulitas, quae tam multos decepit, a duorum Consiliorum Turiensis & Moguntinensis decretis, (quae Zelotypiae legem a Mose descriptam imitabantur,) in populum deducta fuit. Turiensis Concilii haec est constitutio. Si nobilis homo ingenuus in Synodo accusatur, & negaverit, si fidelem eum esse sciverit, cum duodecim ingenuis se purget. Si autem deprehensus fuerit in furto, perjurio aut falso testimonio ad iutamentum non admittatur: sed fit qui in ingenuus non est, cum feruente aqua vel ferro calido se purget. Moguntinini autem Concilii haec constitutio est. Qui presbyterum occidit XII. annos excommunicationi secundum Canones imponatur: aut si negaverit, si liber est cum LXXII. iuret. Si autem servus, super 12. voces meres feruentes se purget: conuictus noxae usque ad ultimum vitae tempus militiae cingulo careat, & absque coniugii spe maneat. Sed etsi praeter haec aquae & ignis in experimentis reis facta pericula, aliae etiam probationes tam in sacra coena ad Eucharistia, quam in seculentis & poculentis institutae sunt, prius tamen de illa elementari, deinde de his posterioribus, inferendi vel auferendi criminis modis dicamus. Omnes autem huius modi expiationes praescriptis quibusdam exorcizandi & creaturas adiurandi formulis celebrabantur. Illa vero elementaris duplex, vt diximus, fuit. Aquosa scilicet & ignea. Aquo vel calefactamulum & ferucns fuit, vel gelida. In hanc accusatus totus iniectus est, & tunc sic crimine vacavit, ad fundum terebatur, Conscientia vero paucentem aqua non recepit, sed tanquam pondere catentem supra leuauit ac sustulit. Hoc vltimum genus purgationis ad purgatorii demonstrationem & confirmationem infert Bernhardus pater, & Doctus & pius, qui vt plurima sanctè & cautè extitit scripsit, tamen vt in pronerbio est, Bernhardus non vidit omnia. Bertulardi verba haec sunt. Quaeliti(inquit)idem (ncmpe hi qui purgatorium non credebant) cum de quibus suspecti videbantur, omnia prorsus suo more negarent, examinati iudicio aquae mendacii inuenti sunt. Cumque iam negarenon possent, quippe deprehensi, aqua eos non recipiente, arrepto, vt dicitur, freno dentibus tam miserè quam liberè impicatem non confessi, sed professi sunt. Haec Bernhardus. Alterum genus aquosae probationis fuit aquae bullientis & feruidae, in quam postulati bracchium cubito tenus immersum, si sine dolore & laesione proferri posset, liberabatur: sin dolorem aut cicatricem quam minimo iudicio significarent, damnabatur. Hoc aquoso probationis genere, Rustici, servi, libertini, asp ricii, & infimae conditionis homines expiari solebant. Sed interdum & nobiliores criminis suspecti, aqua probabantur. Cum Londiniab ipsis civibus nocturna latrocinia perpetrabantur, cuiusdam latronis manus, dum diuitis mercatoris aedes invaderet, in conflictatione abscissa est, unde is captus & carceribus manciparus, cum de vita spem pollicitatione iudicis acciperet si socios proderet, indicauit plures, inter quos quidam Iohannes (cognomento Senex) nobilissimus & ditissimus indicatus est. Qui cū iudicio aquae se absoluere nō potuit, obtulit Regi quingentas Marcas, vt vitam redimeret. Sed quia aquae iudicio periit, Rex nummos repudiauit. Itaq; Iohannes iudicio publico condemnatus ac funeisuspensus est. De Nobilioribus autem & ingenuis suspectis per ferrum candens quaestio habebatur. Quod multiplex fuit: Aut enim vniuscuiusque criminis agebatur, cuius ferrum vnius erat libre: aut fide pluribus, duplex triplexque secundum criminum multitudinem Ordalcum adhibitum fuit, quod pro criminum numero multiplicata pondera continebat. Hoc autem modo solitum est hoc Ordalcum perfici. Reus autem ferrum nuda manu candens ferebat, aut nudis pedibus super ignibus vomeres, singulis à se distantes passibus, totidem passibus incedebat 1 & si adustionem sensisset, aut manibus pedibusue læsus esset, carceribus, morte, exilio, vel eiusmodi legirima pœna plectebatur, vel sine dolore & noxumento soluturus discessit. Nunc expositis huius Ordalij generibus, ostendamus quibus antiquorum Regum Angliæ legibus sancita fuerint, ab Ethelstano ordinetes: quitotum hoc de Ordaleo instituit in magna Synodo apudGeateleiam, ex prudenti Whelmi Archiepiscopi Archiepiscopialiorum, Episcoporum consilio, & rursus in Grateanleano concilio, cui Wistanus Archiepiscopus interfuit, idem confirmauit. Cuius hæ sunt Leges.
units.tr: For the Lord had powerfully and rarely done those miracles which at times he worked to make his name glorious and known to the nations. Men repeatedly claimed that these could be brought about for the slightest reasons and for each private offence, by frequently prescribed little prayers and empty exorcisms, and by incantations uttered more from the mouth than from the heart. They did not notice that the Lord, when he was in the flesh, often refused such unnatural signs to those who demanded them, and that the Apostles had performed the same only rarely, to draw the nations to the faith. This overly curious investigation of crimes was called by the ancient English and Saxons, in their old tongue, "Dryhtelum." The origin and meaning of this name was as follows. "Dryhtin," in the old Saxon language (as some think), was a particle of privation placed before words, as the prefix [ἀ-] works in Greek. Just as "without part" is understood in Greek, so in Saxon "dryh" signified something without a part, that is, "not a part," "without a part," "free of," or "nothing at all." Even now a trace of this word survives in some modern English usage: we say "a small dry" for a small part, "a great dry" for a large part, and "no dry" for no part at all. The ancient Saxons therefore called this kind of investigation of crimes "Dryhtelum" or "Dryhtelium," because those who were subjected to torments and were judged free of all pain and guilt were regarded as having felt no punishment and suffered nothing, and so, as was suspected, to have committed no crime. This credulity, which deceived so many, was introduced among the people by the decrees of two councils, that of Tours and that of Mainz, which imitated the law of jealousy described by Moses. The constitution of the Council of Tours is this: if a free-born nobleman is accused in a synod and denies it, and if he is known to be a faithful man, he is to purge himself with twelve free-born men. But if he is caught in theft, perjury, or false testimony, he is not admitted to the oath; instead, one who is not free-born purges himself with boiling water or hot iron. The constitution of the Council of Mainz is this: whoever kills a priest is to be excommunicated for twelve years according to the canons; or, if he denies it and is free, he is to swear with seventy-two men; if he is a slave, he is to purge himself by walking over twelve red-hot ploughshares. If he is convicted of the harm, he is to be deprived of the belt of military service until the end of his life and to remain without hope of marriage. But besides these trials by fire and water made on accused persons, other proofs were also instituted, both in the holy Supper of the Eucharist and in foods and drinks. We shall speak first of the elemental proof, and then of these later modes of establishing or removing guilt. All such purgations were carried out with certain prescribed formulas of exorcising and adjuring the creatures. That elemental proof, as we have said, was twofold, of water and of fire. The water was either boiling and hot, or cold. In the cold water the accused was wholly immersed, and if he was free of the crime he sank to the bottom; but if his conscience was guilty, the water did not receive him and lifted him up, as if he were resisting its weight. The father Bernard, learned and pious, who wrote for the most part holily and cautiously, brings forward this last kind of purgation to demonstrate and confirm purgatory. Yet, as the proverb says, Bernard did not see everything. Bertulard's words are these: "They (namely, those who did not believe in purgatory), when they were suspected of certain things, denied everything in their usual way. Examined by the judgment of water, they were found to be liars. And when they could no longer deny it, having been caught, the water not receiving them, they took, as they say, the bridle in their teeth. Not so wretchedly nor so freely did they confess their wickedness, but they professed it." So far Bernard. The second kind of watery proof was by boiling and seething water. The accused's arm was immersed up to the elbow, and if it could be drawn out without pain or injury, he was freed; but if they showed pain or a scar, however slight, he was condemned. Rustics, slaves, freedmen, plebeians, and men of the lowest condition were usually cleared by this watery kind of proof. Sometimes, however, even nobler men suspected of crime were tested by water. When nocturnal robberies were committed in London by the citizens themselves, the hand of a certain robber was cut off in a struggle while he was breaking into a rich merchant's house. He was captured and thrown into prison, and when he was promised his life by the judge if he would betray his accomplices, he named several. Among them a certain John, surnamed the Old, very noble and very rich, was pointed out. When John could not clear himself by the judgment of water, he offered the King five hundred marks to redeem his life. But because he perished in the water-ordeal, the King refused the money. So John was condemned by public judgment and hanged. Concerning nobler and free-born suspects, the inquiry was by red-hot iron. This took several forms. Either it was undertaken for a single crime, for which the iron weighed one pound, or, for several crimes, a double or triple ordeal was applied according to the number of crimes, the weights being multiplied in proportion to their number. This ordeal was usually carried out in the following way. The accused carried red-hot iron in his bare hand, or walked barefoot over red-hot ploughshares, set at a distance of paces from one another, going as many paces as there were ploughshares. If he felt the burning, or was injured in hands or feet, he was punished with imprisonment, death, exile, or some such lawful penalty. If he went away unhurt and without injury, he was released. Now that the kinds of this ordeal have been set out, let us show by what laws of the ancient Kings of England they were sanctioned, as ordained by Athelstan. He established all this concerning the ordeal in a great synod at Geateleia, by the wise counsel of Archbishop Wulfhelm and the other archbishops and bishops. Again, at the council of Grateanleano, in which Archbishop Wistan took part, he confirmed the same. These are his laws.

units.la: 1 De Ordalio præcipimus in nomine Dei, & præcepto Archiepiscopi, & omnium Episcoporum, ne aliquis intret Ecclesiam, postquam ignis infertur, vnde iudicium calefieri debet, præter presbyterum, & cum qui ad iudicium iturus est. Et sint mensurati IX. pedes à staca vsque ad Marcam, ad mensuram pedum eius qui ad iudicium ire debet. Et si aquæ iudicium sit, calefiet donec excitetur ad bullitum, & sit alfeatum ferreum vel ær-eum, vel plumbeum vel de argilla: & si vel examen vsque ad Wriste: & si triplex accusatio sit, vsque ad cubitum. Et cum iudiciū paratum erit, ingrediantur ex vtraque parte duo homines, & certi sint, vt ita calidum fit, sicut prædiximus. Introeant totidem ex vtraque parte Iudicij ex longo Ecclesiæ, & sint omnes iciuni, & ab vxoribus suis se abstineant ipsa nocte, & asperget super eos aquam benedictam, & det eis scularicum textum sanctiEuangelij, & signum sanctæ crucis, & nemo faciat ignem diutius, quam benedictio incipiat, sed iaceat ferrum super carbones, vsque ad vltimam collectam: postea mittatur super scaphas, & non sit illic alia loquuno, quam vt precentur sedulò Deum patrem, vt veritatem suam in eo manifestare dignetur. Et bibat accusarus aquam benedictam, & inde conspergatur manus eius qua iudicium purtare debet. Et sic adeat, nouem pedes mensurati distinguantur inter ternos, In primo signo iuxta stacam teneat pedem suum dextrum; in secundo sinistrum, ibidetransferat dextrum pedem in tertium signum quando ferrum proiiciet, & ad sanctum altare festiner, & post insigilletur manus eius; & inquiratur die tertia, si ihmunda sit vel munda in ipsa sig. llatione. Et qui leges istas fregerit, siue ordalium, sit iudicium vel examen fractum in eo, & reddat Regi, Cxx.s.witæ.
units.tr: 1 In the name of God, and by the command of the Archbishop and of all the bishops, we order concerning the ordeal that no one enter the church once the fire has been brought in from which the judgment is to be heated, except the priest and the person about to go to judgment. Let nine feet be measured from the stake to the mark, by the measure of the feet of the person who is to undergo the judgment. If it is the ordeal of water, let the water be heated until it boils, in a kettle of iron, bronze, lead or clay; if it is the examination, the arm is to be plunged up to the wrist, and if the accusation is threefold, up to the elbow. When the judgment is ready, two men shall go in from each side, and let them make certain that it is as hot as we have said. As many shall go in from each side of the judgment along the length of the church, and all shall be fasting, and shall abstain from their wives that very night. The priest shall sprinkle holy water on them and give them the consecrated text of the holy Gospel and the sign of the holy cross. No one shall keep the fire burning longer than the blessing lasts, but the iron shall lie upon the coals until the final collect. Afterwards it is to be put upon the scales, and there shall be no other speech there than that they earnestly pray God the Father to deign to manifest his truth in the matter. Let the accused drink holy water, and let the hand with which he must bear the judgment be sprinkled with it. Then let him approach: nine measured feet are to be marked off among three signs. At the first sign, let him keep his right foot beside the stake; at the second, his left; there he shall move his right foot to the third sign when he casts down the iron, and hasten to the holy altar. Afterwards his hand shall be sealed, and on the third day it shall be examined, whether it is unclean or clean under the seal. Whoever breaks these laws, whether in the ordeal, the judgment or the examination, shall pay 120 shillings to the King.

units.la: 2 Si quis ipsa triplicis Ordalii sententia in fanum irrupisse conuincatur, is prout in libru habetur iudiciali, compensato.
units.tr: 2 If anyone is convicted of having broken into a church by the sentence of the threefold ordeal, he is to be compensated as is laid down in the judicial book.

units.la: 3 De Ordalio simplici statuimus, vt si quis furti suspicus fuetir accusatus, at-que ipsa tandem Ordalii sententia in reos referendus videatur, nec porro habeat, qui side eum sustentet sua, in custodiam mittitor, vnde cum cognati, prout antea est ad sumus, liberanto.
units.tr: 3 Concerning the simple ordeal we decree that if anyone is accused and suspected of theft, and is at last judged guilty by the sentence of the ordeal, and has no one to stand surety for him with his own pledge, he shall be sent into custody. From there, when his kinsmen are present, as was said before, he shall be set free.

units.la: 4 Præterea statuimus vt vnus per omnem ditionem nostram, atque idem sirntim mus, eumq; nemo extra oppidum cudito. Atqui si monetariorum quisquam numinos corruperit, ei manus scelere violata præciditor, atque nummariæ conspicienda fabricæ affigitor. Sinnummi adulterati postulatus aliquis, criminis suspicionem diluete voluerit, candentis ferri quæstione, manum scelens puram atq; immunem ostendito. Quin si ipsa Ordalii sententia reus extiterit, ita vt antea à nobis dictum est, fiat.
units.tr: 4 Furthermore, we decree that there shall be one coinage throughout all our realm, and likewise we command that no one shall mint outside the town. But if any of the moneyers has debased the coin, his hand, which he has violated by the crime, shall be cut off and fixed to the mint in a conspicuous place. If anyone accused of adulterated coin wishes to clear himself of the suspicion of the crime, let him show his hand clean and free of guilt by the test of red-hot iron. Indeed, if the accused is found guilty by the sentence of the ordeal, let it be done as we have said before.

units.la: 7 Qui se Ordalii quæstione examinandum obtulerit, triduo quàm id sit aggressurus, sacerdotem, vt is sacra de more peragat, adito, atque interim pane, sale, aqua & olcribus tantummodo vescitor, missæ præterea illis ipsis diebus interuesto, muntusque suum offerto: Sub ipso autem quo est Ordalium ingressurus die, panem Eucharisticum sumito, ac iureiurando se illius de quo appellatur, sceleris purum, minimeque consciuum iurato: Tum siaqua gelida faciunda est quæstio, ad sesqui vlnam funis in aquam mergitor. Sin ferro fiat candeni, per continuum triduum obsignanda non resignetur manus
units.tr: 7 Whoever offers himself to be examined by the ordeal shall, three days before he undertakes it, go to the priest so that he may perform the sacred rites in the customary manner. Meanwhile he shall eat only bread, salt, water and herbs, shall attend mass on those days, and shall offer his alms. On the very day on which he is to enter the ordeal, he shall take the Eucharistic bread and swear an oath that he is pure of the crime of which he is accused and not complicit in it. Then, if the test is to be made with cold water, a rope of a yard and a half is lowered into the water. But if it is to be made with red-hot iron, the hand shall be sealed for three continuous days and not unsealed.

units.la: CANUTI LEGES DE ORDALEO.
units.tr: THE LAWS OF CNUT CONCERNING THE ORDEAL.

units.la: ESTIS diebus omnibus, quatuor temporum ieiuniis, quadragesimâ, cæterisq; omnibus, quibus rite fuerit indictum ieiunium diebus, omnis Ordalii ac iurisiurandi iurisdictio intermittitor.
units.tr: On all days, on the Ember fasts, in Lent, and on all other days on which a fast has been duly appointed, all jurisdiction of the ordeal and of oath-taking is suspended.

units.la: 2 Si cuius apud centuriatos labefactata fir fides, adeoq; is crebrę fuerit accusationis infamia notatus, vt eum tres simul viri criminentur, alia quàm ex triplici Ordalio excusatio nulla est accipienda. Verù enimuero si herus eius affirmarit, nec iusiurandum violasse seruum, nec iudicio Ordalei (post coactum Wintoniæ Concilium) ceciderit, ex eadem illa centuria fidelem vnum & alterum herus euocato, qui vnà secum iureiurando confirmeut,
units.tr: 2 If a man's credit has been shaken among the hundred men, and he has acquired such a reputation for frequent accusation that three men at once bring charges against him, no excuse is to be accepted other than the threefold ordeal. But if his lord affirms that the slave has neither violated an oath nor fallen under the judgment of the ordeal (after the Council of Winchester was held), then the lord shall summon from that same hundred one or two trustworthy men who together with him confirm on oath

units.la: 1 3 nec hidem iureiurando obstrictam fefellisse seruum, nec Ordalii sententia in reos relatum, nec furti nomine periculosa quicquam, nisi quidem praesto fuerit praepositus aliquis, cuius in hac re citius habeat ponderis, dicti authoritas. Tum si iusiurandum dederint, accusato fiat eligendi potestas, virum simplicis Ordalii sententiam sub bire, an iosiurandum, quod vnius libræ et 30. denarii aequali proportione respondeat, in tribus centuriis praestare voluerit. Sin id illi iureiurando confirmare verebuntur, triplicis Ordalii quaestione reus examinatur: id autem ad quem nam modum fieri oportebit in lege sua plurib[us] referri Canutus. Aut or viros qui praeluerint quinque adhibero, ipse exutus est.
units.tr: 1 3 that the slave has not deceived by breaking an oath which bound him in faith, nor been brought under the sentence of the ordeal for an accusation, nor is in any danger on account of a charge of theft, unless some reeve is present whose word carries more weight in this matter. Then, if they have given their oath, the accused shall have the choice of undergoing the simple ordeal by the sentence of the ordeal, or of clearing himself by oath, which corresponds in equal proportion to one pound and thirty pence, in three hundreds. But if they hesitate to confirm this on oath, the accused shall be examined by the threefold ordeal. How this is to be done, Cnut refers at more length to his own law. Or he shall bring five men who have given the oath, and he himself shall be cleared.

units.la: 1 Seruus si ipsa Ordalii sententia in reos referatur, primo inustus compungitor, 10 atque si secundo Ordalii quaestione examinatus culpae reus fiat, alia quam capitis poena non esto.
units.tr: 1 If a slave is found guilty by the sentence of the ordeal, he shall first be branded, and if after a second examination by the ordeal he is found guilty of the fault, there shall be no punishment other than death.

units.la: 4 Si quis saluri Regis aut Domini sui insidias retenderit, vita et rebus suis omnib. pleoctitor, nisi quidem triplicis Ordalii quaestione crimen diluerit.
units.tr: 4 If anyone lays snares against the life of the King or of his lord, he shall be punished with the loss of life and of all his goods, unless he clears the charge by the threefold ordeal.

units.la: Leges bont Regis Edwardi.
units.tr: The laws of good King Edward.

units.la: 1 e illo quo iudicium fieri debet, veniatilloc ministeri Episcopi cum Clericis suis, et similis iustitia Regis cum legalibus hominibus pronunciaz illius, qui videant et audiant, ut ea quae omnia fiant, et quos Dominus per misericordiam suam, non per merita saluare voluerit, si quieti sint et liberè recedant, et quos iniquitas culpae non Dominus damnauerit, iustitia Regis de ipsis iustitiam faciat.
units.tr: 1. From the time when judgment ought to be given, let the minister of the bishop come with his clerks, and the king's justice with the lawful men, to pronounce on him, so that they may see and hear. Let all these things be done: those whom the Lord has willed to save through his mercy, not through merits, if they are quiet and withdraw freely, and those whom the guilt of iniquity, not the Lord, has condemned, the king's justice shall do justice upon.

units.la: 2 Si quis captiuus exilio destinatus, habuerit vxorem suam in patria subsistentem, et dixerit aliquis parentum murdrati eam nequitiæ fuisse participem, expurget se iudicio Dei, i. Ordalio, quam si elementia Dei et innocentia sua saluauerit, remaneat legalis cum dote sua et maritagio.
units.tr: 2. If a captive destined for exile has his wife remaining in his country, and some kinsman of a murdered man says that she was a participant in the wickedness, let him clear himself by the judgment of God, that is, by ordeal. If he saves himself by God's mercy and his own innocence, he shall remain lawful, with his dowry and marriage portion.

units.la: Has et alias leges boni Regis Edouardi confirmauit Gulielmus Rex, et alii eum sequentes.
units.tr: These and other laws of good King Edward were confirmed by King William and by the others who followed him.

units.la: Lex Gvlielmi Regis.
units.tr: The law of King William.

units.la: ECRETVM est, vt si Francigena appellauerit Anglum de periurio, 30 aut murdro, furto aut homicidio, aut Rau, quod dicitur apertæ rapina, negari non poterit, Anglus se defendat, per quod melius voluerit, aut iudicio ferri candentis aut duello.
units.tr: It is decreed that if a Frenchman accuses an Englishman of perjury, murder, theft or homicide, or of what is called open robbery (rau), which cannot be denied, the Englishman may defend himself by whichever means he prefers, either by the judgment of red-hot iron or by duel.

units.la: Quod Withelmi Regis decretum ante a prioribus Anglis Regibus obseruatum etiam a posterioribus Regibus vsq; ad Iohan. s Regis tempora retentum fuit.
units.tr: This decree of King William, observed beforehand by the earlier English kings, was also retained by the later kings down to the times of King John.

units.la: Atque haec de Ordalio aqua ferroque probando: Nunc alia purgandi genera explicemus. Proxima est igitur Eucharistica, de qua in Cöcilio Wormacensi his verbis statuntum est. Sic saepe contingit, vt in Monasteriis Monachorum furta perpetrentur, idcirco statuimus, vt quoniam ipsi fratres de talibus expurgare se debent, missaeb Abbatae celebretur, vel ab aliquo ex praesentibus fratribus, et sic expleta missa omnes commonicentur in haec verba. Corpus Domini sit tibi hodie ad probationem. Item: Si Episcopo aut Presbytero aliquod maleficium imputatum fuerit, pro singulis missam celebrare debet et communicare, et de singulis sibi imputatis innocentem se ostendat. Quod si non fecerit, quinquennio a liminibus Ecclesiae extraneus habeatur. Eadem quoque purgatio in Anglia Canuti legibus recepta est, vt in L.sua S. Si quis.
units.tr: So much for proving by the ordeals of water and iron. Now let us set out the other kinds of purgation. The next is the Eucharistic one, about which the Council of Worms decreed in these words: "It often happens that thefts are committed in monasteries of monks; therefore we decree that, since the brothers themselves ought to clear themselves of such things, a Mass shall be celebrated by the abbot, or by some one of the brothers present, and, the Mass being finished, all shall communicate with these words: 'May the body of the Lord be to you today for proof.'" Likewise: "If any wrongdoing is imputed to a bishop or a priest, he ought to celebrate a Mass and communicate for each single charge, and show himself innocent of each thing imputed to him. But if he does not do so, let him be regarded as a stranger from the thresholds of the Church for five years." This same purgation was also received in England under the laws of Cnut, in his law, section "If anyone".

units.la: Si quis itaque (inquit) faceredorem ad certam aliquam religionis normam viuentem in erimen vocarit, atque is nullius sibi scelleris conscius fuerit, Missam (si modo id facere non vereatur) celebrato, et Eucharistiae perceptione vniuus calumniā omnè solus contidito: sin triu fuerit accusatio, perceptā (si modo ausus fuerit) Euebaristia, atq; adiudicatis sibi aliis eiusdem ordinis duob. omnè cogitati scelleris suspicione diluito. Si vero eorū, q arq deseruierint aliq, amicis orbatus adeoq; qui secū vnā pariter iurēt nō habes, criminis fuerit postulatus, panè execratione deuotū comesto, atq; de eo fiat, prout diuina feret voluntas, nisi quidem licitum fuerit Eucharistiae perceptione se culpa liberare.
units.tr: "If anyone (he says) calls to account a priest living under some fixed rule of religion, and that man is conscious of no crime, let him celebrate Mass (if he does not shrink from doing so) and, by receiving the Eucharist alone, refute the whole accusation. But if the accusation comes from several, let him, having received the Eucharist (if he dares), and having had two others of the same order adjudged to him, clear away all suspicion of the imagined crime. But if he is accused of a crime and has no friends who will swear together with him, since those who ought to have stood by him have deserted him, let him eat bread consecrated with a curse, and let it be done with him as divine will shall bring, unless it is permitted to free himself from the fault by receiving the Eucharist."

units.la: Hūe spectat quod Lotharius Imperator, de adulterio petitus sub Adriano Papa secundus se, adhibitis proceribus Euchatistiae perceptione purgare voluit: qui omnes eodem anno perierunt, vt Christianus Massæus An. 855. refert lib. 14. diuina ne ordinata virtute, an occulto veneno, quo in eiusmodi mysteriis etiam Papæ perempti sunt, incertum nobis est. Massei autem diserta verba repetamus. Lotharius Imperator deadulterio petitus, se per literas ad Adrianum Papam missas excusare conatus est. Cui respondit Pontifex, si non es adulterû reus, veni Romam. Ereorpus Christi nobisçum sume, venit Imp. negauit adulterium, sumpsit Eucharistiam vna cum principibus suis qui omnes eodem anno perierunt. Lotharius autem vix Placeantiam veniens mortuus est. 8. Augusti.
units.tr: To this belongs what the Emperor Lothair did. Accused of adultery under Pope Adrian II, he wished to clear himself by receiving the Eucharist, with his nobles present; but all of them died in the same year. Whether this came by divine appointed power or by a hidden poison, with which even popes have been destroyed in such mysteries, is uncertain to us. Let us repeat the plain words of Massaeus (Christianus Massaeus, in the year 855, book 14). "Lothair the Emperor, accused of adultery, tried to excuse himself by letter sent to Pope Adrian. The pontiff replied: 'If you are not guilty of adultery, come to Rome. Behold, take the body of Christ with us.' The Emperor came, denied the adultery, and received the Eucharist together with his princes, all of whom died in the same year. Lothair himself, coming to Placentia, died there on the 8th of August."

units.la: Alteru propellédi criminis genus Monomachiâ seu duello expertum fuit. In quo tam accusatorien actor, quàm reus de veritare accusationis & iure actionis in iudicio prius proposuit, atmis decertabant, vt secundum eum qui vicisset aut adueríarium ad deditionem coegisset, iudicaretur. In hoc genere constitutum fuit, vt partes per se vel procuratores, liberos tamen homines, duello experiri poterant.
units.tr: Another kind of clearing oneself from a charge was tried by monomachy, or duel. In this, both the accuser, as plaintiff, and the accused, first laid before the court the truth of the accusation and the right of the action, and then they fought with arms; whoever conquered, or forced his opponent to surrender, was adjudged right. In this kind it was provided that the parties could fight either in person or through proxies, provided they were free men.

units.la: Vtrimum quod scimus periculi genus, in panis hordeacii & Cásei comestione fuit. Qui manducatus insontibus alimento, reis autem iudicio fuit, vtpote à quibus deglutirinon poterat: sed è gula proiectus omnes corporis artus tremore ac pallore affecit. Atq; haec omnia creaturis per certos exorcizandi modos adhibitis fiebant. Quos etsi varios penas innumerabiles recensere non possumus, certos tamen ad singula expiationum genera accommodatos demonstrabimus. Ac primum de ferro & aqua exorcisatis dicamus.
units.tr: Another kind of danger we know of consisted in the eating of barley bread and cheese. Eaten, this food was harmless to the innocent, but for the accused it became a judgment, since they could not swallow it; it was thrown up from the throat, and it affected all the limbs of the body with trembling and pallor. All these things were done with the creatures (bread and cheese) employed through certain modes of exorcism. Although we cannot recount the various and countless penalties, we will nonetheless point out the particular kinds of purgation, each suited to its purpose. And first let us speak of iron and water, when they have been exorcised.

units.la: PVRGATIO PER FERRVM.
units.tr: PURGATION BY IRON.

units.la: OST accusationem legitimè factum & triduum in ieiuniis, & orationE consummatum, sacerdos, vestibus sacris praeter caesulam indutus: ferrum ante altare positum forcipe accipiat, & hymnum irium puerorum decantans, ad ignem deferat. Quo cum peruenerit, dicat sacerdos hanc orationem super locum vbi fiet ignis ad faciendum iudicium.
units.tr: After a lawful accusation, three days of fasting and prayer having been completed, the priest, vested in sacred vestments except for the chasuble, takes the iron placed before the altar with tongs and carries it to the fire, chanting the hymn of the three children. When he has reached the fire, the priest says this prayer over the place where the fire is to be lit for the trial.

units.la: Benedic Domine Deus omnipotens locum istum, vt sit nobis in eo sanitas, sanctitas, castitas, virtus, & victoria, & sanctimonia, humilitas, bonitas, lenitas & plenitudo legis, & obedientia Deo patri & filio & spiritui sancto, hæc benedictio sit semper super hunc locum, & super omnes habitantes in eo, per, &c.
units.tr: "Bless, Lord God almighty, this place, that in it there may be for us health, holiness, chastity, virtue and victory, and sanctity, humility, goodness, gentleness and the fullness of the law, and obedience to God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. May this blessing rest always upon this place and upon all who dwell in it, through, etc."

units.la: Inde sequuntur similes super ignem benedictiones, quibus finitis ad Missam peruentum est, quæ plurimis eius generis exorcismis consarcinata, in celebratione Eucharistiæ his verbis ad reũ participantem vsa est. Corpus hoc & sanguis Domini nostri Iesu Christi firtibi hodie ad probationem. Qua peracta rursus pergit sacerdos ad ferrum purgatorium, multis oratiunculis sanctos sanctasq; omnes inuocans: quo perueniens legit Euangelium. In principio erat verbum, &c. quo perfecto aquam benedictam super ferrum spargit, & signum crucis faciens dicit, in nomine patris. &c. Mox accusatus accipiens ad nouem pedum mensuram ferrum perferat. Huius deniq; manus sub sigillo triduum inclusa tegatur, & si sanies crudescens in vestigio ferri reperiatur, culpabiles & immundus dicatur: sin autem mundus extiterit, laus & gloria deo referatur.
units.tr: Similar blessings over the fire follow, and when these are finished they come to the Mass. This service, patched together from many exorcisms of this kind, uses these words to the accused, who takes part in the celebration of the Eucharist: "May this body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ be to you today for proof." When this is done the priest goes back to the purgatorial iron, invoking all the saints with many short prayers. Arriving there, he reads the Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word," etc. When this is finished he sprinkles holy water upon the iron and, making the sign of the cross, says "In the name of the Father," etc. Then the accused takes up the iron and carries it nine feet. Finally his hand is bound and sealed up for three days. If festering matter is found in the track of the iron, he is pronounced guilty and unclean; but if he is found clean, praise and glory are rendered to God.

units.la: Purgatio per aquam feruentem, eodem ritu, quo per candens ferrum peracta fuit paucis verbis immutatis: loco enim horum verborum. Si hoc candens ferrum tetigerit, haec dicta sunt: si in hanc aquam feruentemmisericorde manum suam. Hac purgatione Sanctus Paternus probatus fuit, huius manus ter immersa lesionem non sensit quamuis Regis ministrillud ipsum attentantes combusti sunt.
units.tr: Purgation by boiling water was carried out by the same rite as purgation by red-hot iron, with a few words changed: in place of "If he has touched this red-hot iron," these words were said: "if he has put his hand into this boiling water." By this purgation Saint Paternus was proved. His hand, dipped in three times, suffered no injury, although the king's servants who tried the same thing were burned.

units.la: Quo etiam tempore Mulgunnus Borealium Britonum Rex edixit per omnem Britanniam vt omnis mendax aqua feruentissima deprehenderetur. Et Cuthbertus Cant. Archicpiscopus, quia has examinationes in Ecclesia Christi Metropolitica Cant. fieri noluit, aliam Ecclesiam in orientali parte maioris Ecclesiæ eidem pene contiguam; in honorem S Iohannis Baptistæ erexit, vt examinationes iudiciorum pro variis causis constitutorum, quæ ad correctionem scelerator um in Ecclesia Dei fieri solent, ibi celebrarentur, & Archiepiscoporum corpora sepelirentur. Et hic error tantis tenebris eam ætatem obduxerat, vt Wilhelmus Malmesburiensis scribat. Omnes qui in Ecclesia Glaseoniensi, ferrp vel aqua examinandi fuerant, & oratione m in ea Ecclesia deponerent, omnes quos illa praesens memoria confitebatur, vno excepto de salute sua tripudiarent.
units.tr: At about the same time Mulgunnus, king of the Northern Britons, decreed throughout all Britain that every liar should be tested by boiling water. And Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury, because he would not have these examinations held in the metropolitan church of Christ at Canterbury, built another church on the eastern side of the greater church, almost adjoining it, in honour of Saint John the Baptist. There the trials of judgments, held for various causes, which are customarily carried out in the Church of God for the correction of wrongdoers, were to be conducted, and the bodies of archbishops were to be buried. This error had so darkened that age with such shadows that William of Malmesbury writes: all who had been examined by iron or water in the church of Glastonbury, and had made their prayers in that church, all whom that memory of the present day records, except one, rejoiced concerning their salvation.

units.la: PVRGATIO PER AQVAM GELIDAM.
units.tr: PURGATION BY COLD WATER.

units.la: ERACTIS (vtante) triû dierû ieiuniis, & factis de more, vt supra descriptimus, datur accusato aqua benedicta, vt bibat, cû hac execratione. Hæc aqua sit tibi in pbationè hodie, deinde aquæ gelidæ, in q̃ mittedus esset teterus,
units.tr: When three days of fasting (as usual) have been completed, and the rites have been performed as we described above, the accused is given holy water to drink, with this curse: "May this water be to you today for proof." Then the accused is cast into cold water.

units.la: 1 4. huiusmodi coniuratio adhibita est. Adiuro te creatura aquæ in nomine Dei patris omnipotentis, quite in principio creauit, & iussit ministrare humanis necessitatibus, qui & iussit te segregare ab aquis superioribus. Adiuro te etiam per ineffabile nomen Dei Iesu Christi Filii Dei viui, sub pedibus cuius mare & elementum diuisum se calcabile præbuit, qui etiam baptizarise in aquarum elemento voluit. Adiuro te etiam per Spiritum Sanctum, qui super dominum baptizatum descendit. Adiuro te per nomen sanctum indiuiduæ trinitatis, cuius voluntate aquarum elementum diuisum est, & populus Israel siccis pedibus statim transiuerit. Ad cuius etiam inuocationem Hebræus ferrum quod de manubrio creatura ferit, super aquam natare fecerat, aut nullo modo suscipias hunc hominem. N. si aliquo est culpabilis de hoc quod ei obicitur, si licet autem per opera aut per consensum, vel per conscientiam, seu per vllum ingenium, sed fac eum natare super te, & nulla possie esse contra te, causa factā, aut vllum præstigium inimici, quod illud possitoccultare. Per nomen autem Christi præcipimus tibi, vt nobis pro nomine eius obedias, cuiomnis creatura seruit, quem Cherubin & Seraphin collaudant, dicentes, sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Dominus Deus exercituum, qui etiam regnat & dominatur per omnia seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: 1 4. The following adjuration was used: "I adjure you, creature of water, in the name of God the Father almighty, who created you in the beginning and commanded you to minister to human needs, and who commanded you to separate from the upper waters. I adjure you also by the ineffable name of God Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, under whose feet the sea and the element showed itself divided and walkable, and who willed to be baptized in the element of water. I adjure you also by the Holy Spirit, who descended upon the baptized Lord. I adjure you by the holy name of the undivided Trinity, by whose will the element of water was divided, and the people of Israel at once passed through with dry feet. At whose invocation also the Hebrew made the iron that had fallen from the handle float upon the water. Do not receive this man N. by any means, if he is guilty in any way of what is charged against him, whether by deed, or by consent, or by conscience, or by any device; but make him float upon you, so that there is no cause against him, and no trick of the enemy that could hide it. We command you by the name of Christ to obey us for the sake of his name, whom every creature serves, whom the Cherubim and Seraphim praise, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts, who also reigns and rules throughout all ages. Amen."

units.la: Postea recitatis aliis exorcismis, rens exuris vectibus aquas Introiit: Quibus si immergeretur, liberabatur, sin vero sustentaretur, nec inundari poterat, damnabatur.
units.tr: After other exorcisms had been recited, the accused, stripped of his clothes, was led into the water. If he sank, he was set free; but if he was held up and could not be submerged, he was condemned.

units.la: EXORCISMVS PANIS HORDEACII ET CASEI.
units.tr: EXORCISM OF BARLEY BREAD AND CHEESE.

units.la: VORVM appensio vnius erat vnciæ, omnibusq; præsentibus ieiunis sacerdos primitus Letanias fecit, deinde huiusmodi precatio ne vsus est.
units.tr: Each of the loaves of bread and the cheeses weighed one ounce. With everyone present fasting, the priest first recited the litanies, and then used a prayer of this kind.

units.la: Domine Iesu Christe qui regnas in cœlis & in terris, & immobiles es in omnibus openbus tuis, dominator dominantium, Deus Angelorum & Patriarchatum, Prophetarum, Apostolorum, Martyrum, Confessorum, Virginum, & omnium electorum, præstaquę; sumus per sanctum & mirabile nomen tuum, vt qui reus est huius furti vel homicidii, aut adulterii seu maleficii, de quo hic nunc requiritur, vel in factō, vel in conscientia, ad appositam ei pro ostensione veritatis, creatura panis sanctificati vel calci, faux eius claudatur, guttur eius stranguletur, & in nomine tuo ante illud reiiciatur quam devoretur, sed & spiritus diabolicus, cui nulla communio cum tua super veritate in hoc negocio ad subuertendum iudicium prauis præstigiorū suorum molitionibus nil prævaleat, sed qui reus & cōfcius est rei præstrat, ad hoc parabolum sanctificati panis, vel calci, & præsertim per Dominici corporis & sanguinis communionem, quę accepit, tremat, & tremendo palleat, & mutabūdus in omnibus mēbris appareat: innoxius vero & inscius sobrie ad salubritatem sui cum omni facilitate, hanc partem panis vel calci in nomine signatam manducando deglutiant, vt cognoscat omnes, quia tu es iudex iustus, qui saluos facis sperantes in te, & non est alius præter te, qui viuis & regnas per omnia secula seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: Lord Jesus Christ, who reignest in heaven and on earth, and art unchanging in all thy works, Lord of lords, God of the Angels and Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs, Confessors, Virgins and all the elect, we beseech thee through thy holy and wonderful name that, if the accused is guilty of this theft, murder, adultery or sorcery, about which he is now being questioned, whether in the deed or in conscience, then, when the creature of consecrated bread or cheese is set before him as a proof of the truth, his throat be closed, his gullet be strangled, and in thy name it be cast out before he can swallow it. And let the diabolical spirit, which has no fellowship with thy truth in this matter, prevail nothing against the judgement by the wicked contrivances of its illusions. But let him who is guilty and conscious of the deed, when he takes the consecrated bread or cheese prepared for this purpose, and especially when he receives the communion of the Lord's body and blood, tremble, grow pale with trembling, and appear unsteady in all his limbs. But let the innocent and unaware eat and swallow this portion of bread or cheese marked in thy name, soberly, for their own well-being and with all ease, so that all may know that thou art the just judge, who savest those who hope in thee, and there is no other besides thee, who livest and reignest for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: Hæ omnes adiurationes ex veteribus missalibus & Pontificalibus Saxonum Libris verbatim excerptæ sunt. In quibus multa, quæ adhuc in vsu a Ponuficiis habentur de vestibus, Templis, altaribus, locis oratoriis, campanis, paneq; & aqua sanctificandis, eisdem adiurationibus ritibusq; describuntur. At illæ tam contrariis legibus quam desnetudine paulatim sublatæ sunt. Hæc verò eadem canonica cœcitate reuinētur. Sed mirū non est hanc varietatē & inconstantiā Papalibus inesse legibus, quæ (vt in proverbio est) omnia precio singunt atq; refingūt. Nā illas omnes, aquæ, ferri, duelli, ac Eucharistiæ purgationes tanq; authore Diabolo fabricatas, Deūq; tentantes tandē post multa secula Pont. Romani prohibebant. Et de reis iudicia sumi nō alia ratione quā spontanea confessione, vel luculentis testimoniis atque probationibus statuebant. Eāq; purgationem, (quod à vulgo receptā est.) vulgarem, hanc suis institutis sanctam canonicam adpellabant. De qua Gregorius primus ad Brunigildam Reginam Francorum, de Menna Episcopo purgando meminit & improbat.
units.tr: All these adjurations have been copied word for word from the old Missals and Pontificals of the Saxons. In them are described many things, still in use among the Papists, concerning the consecration of vestments, churches, altars, oratories, bells, bread and water, with the same adjurations and rites. But those were gradually abolished, partly by contrary laws and partly by disuse. These same things, however, are now bound up again by canonical blindness. But it is no wonder that such variation and inconstancy belong to the Papal laws, which, as the proverb says, fashion and refashion everything for a price. For the Roman pontiffs at length, after many centuries, forbade all those purgations by water, by iron, by duel, and by the Eucharist, as devised by the devil and tempting God. And they decreed that judgements against the accused were to be made in no other way than by voluntary confession or by clear testimonies and proofs. That purgation which the common people had received they called vulgar, while in their own institutions they called this one holy and canonical. Gregory the First, writing to Brunhilda, Queen of the Franks, about Bishop Mennas who was to be purged, mentions it and disapproves of it.

units.la: Postea; Stephanus Papa quintus de parentibus partus opprimentibus, coram Huberto Episcopo Maguntino purgandis non admittit, ferri candentis, vel aquæ feruentis, examinationem. Spontanea. n. confessione inquit, vel testium approbatione publica delicta, habito præ oculis Dei timore, commissa sunt regimini nostro iudicare. Occulta vero & incognita illi sunt relinquenda, qui solus nouit corda filiorum hominum. Monomachiam verò prohibuit Nicolaus, quæ ciuilibus ac lustinianilegibus ante interdicta fuit, cum hæc & huiusmodi sectantes Deum solummodo tentare videntur. Sed utrum illa Eucharistica panis atq; cafei purgatio similiter tollantur, dubitat cum suis glossographis Gratianus, & discepta paululum controuersia, randem eas quoq; abrogari concludit. Quòd quanquâ Sixtus Papa coram Valentiniano Imperatore, ac Leo postea ea purgatione obiecta sibi crimina diluebât, tamé ipsi refcripserût. Suũ exéplu aliis hoc nô eligentib. formâ nô dare, neq; quenquâ nolentem cogere. Id quod euidétius appatet ex sequentium Paparum Epistolis Decretalib. in quibus nô aliâ purgationê quâ canonicam à se descriptam permittebant. Vnde Honorius. 9. qui vixit tempore Iohannis Regis Angliæ, filii Regis Henrici secundi eam purgationem prohibuit. Nouû ne hoc an vsitatum a Pontificiis possit censeri, vt ea quæ priorum patrum ac consiliorum decretis statuta fuerunt, a posteris superstitiosa, Deum tentantia, & contra canones sucta fuisse dicantur. In quo errorem proprium & mutabilitate ostendunt. Etli enim assentior, rectè ac secundum Deum egisse Pontifices, quod huiusmodi nugis ac præstigiis, quæ multis ante eos seculis in summo vsu & existimatione à veteribus culta & obseruata fuerunt, fidem omnem ac authoritatem detraxerint: in hoc tamen desidero illorum siue pietatem siue prudentiam, quòd quæ in eo genere corrigere volebant, in alio detenora effecerút, vt immutata magis & ad nouas superstitiones traducta, quàm penitus deleta & extincta eernantur. Legat enim qui volet recentiores, & nostro præsertim ævo editos Pontificales ac Missales libros, reperiet eos & ceremoniarum multitudine, & peragendi difficultate atq; ædio, & exorcisationis amentia pfiores illos longe superare. Quibus enim non dicam verbis, sed portentis hæc & eiusmodi a Pontificiis adhuc adiurantur. Primarius lapis & cæmentum pro Ecclesia ædificanda, Sal & aqua, Panis benedictus, Dedicatio recentis Ecclesiæ, Altaria, vasa, indumenta, linteamina & ornamenta Ecclesiastica: Altare portatile, calix cum patena, crux nœua, sanctorum imagines, Campanæ atqi signa, cineres, incensus, cum in militum (vt vocant) regularium erectione, armis, enses & vexilla bellica. Hæcomnia, quàm solenni ritu sanctarum scripturarum sententiis ad sua decantationes perperam adhibitis, pontificii peragunt, paucis vidêamus. Lapis cum Cæmento Episcopi manibus primùm aqua benedicta sparsus insculpto crucis signo, his sententiis in fundamento positus est. Lapidem quem reprobauerunt ædificantes, hic factus est in caput anguli. Deinde tu es Petrus, & super hanc Petram. &c: Postea precabantur, vt qui ad petiendam Ecclesiam auxilium dederint, corpotis & animæ salutem consequantur. In dedicatione autem Ecclesiæ iam extrudæ Episcopus Ecclesiam tet circumiens, ostium baculo pastorali ferit hoc psalmi carmine. Attollite Portas: &c: Cui Diaconus intus existens respondet fere examinatus: Quis est iste rex gloriæ: &c. Deinde ingrediens Episcopus in fundamento Ecclesiæ cineribus sparso, Alphabetum Græcum & Latinum baculo describit: tum variis multisq; Episcopi Clericiq; incisibus, rectis, obliquis, retrogradis & transuersis parietes ac pauimenta aqua sparguntur. Cruces in parietibus chrismate cum dextro Episcopi pollice depinguntur: & infinitis penè completis ceremoniis ad extremum precatur, vt populus in ea conueniens per sacerdotum libamina cœlesti sanctificatione seluatus, animæ salutem perpetuam consequatur. Et discedens Portam his verbis Episcopus vngit chrismate. Porta sis benedicta, sanctificata, consecrata, consignata & Deo commendata. Porta sis introitus salutis & pacis: Porta sis ostium pacificum, per eum, qui se ostium & ostiarium appellauit. Non his autem guriis conditum Solomonis templum fuit, quod plura condentis voluntate oblatum Deo, ab ipso consecratum fuit. Altaria autem innumeris huius generis precibus consecrantur, vt quicunq; in hoc altari sacranda libamina deuotus obruleriit, vel sacrata susceperit, subsidia præsentis vitæ accipiat, & remissionem pariter omnium peccatorum consequatur, & gratiam sempiternam redemptionis percipiat. Et, mane surgens Iacob erigebat lapidem in titulum, fundens oleum desuper, votum vouir domino: verè locus iste sanctus est, & ego nescieba: m: acerit Nomen meum ibi, dicit dominus: &, stetit Angelus iuxta aram templi. Si autem reliquias in ara reconderat Episcopus, addidit: Nationes ex longinquo ad te venient, & munera deferent: &c. Euangelium autem eo die legebatur ex s. Matthæi. Si ergo offers munus tuum ad altare. &c. Ad deuouendum autem altare portatile, decantatis plurimis psalmis & orationculis, precabatur Episcopus: Deus qui quondam legem in tabulis condidisti lapideis, & lapideum metallum ad obsequium tui sacrificii condidisti, annuè dignanter, vt quicunque huic altari oblatum, sacratum uè fuerit, nominituo assurgat, religioni proficiat, & fidei sit honori. Calix cum patena
units.tr: Afterwards, Pope Stephen V, concerning parents who had smothered their offspring, would not admit them to be cleared by the trial of red-hot iron or boiling water before Hubert, Bishop of Mainz. "For," he says, "offences committed by spontaneous confession or by the public approval of witnesses, with the fear of God before our eyes, are committed to our government to judge. But hidden and unknown matters are to be left to Him alone who knows the hearts of the sons of men." Nicholas forbade the judicial duel, which had earlier been prohibited by civil and Justinian laws, since those who pursue such things and similar ones seem to tempt God alone. But whether that Eucharistic purgation by bread and cheese is likewise abolished, Gratian doubts together with his glossators, and after a little debate he concludes that these too have been repealed. Although Pope Sixtus, before the Emperor Valentinian, and Leo afterwards cleared the crimes objected to them by that purgation, yet they wrote back that by their example they did not give a form to others who did not choose it, nor compel anyone unwilling. This appears more clearly from the Epistles of the following popes, the Decretals, in which they permitted no purgation other than the canonical one prescribed by themselves. Hence Honorius III, who lived in the time of John, King of England, son of King Henry II, prohibited that purgation. Is it new, or can it be thought customary among the Papists, that those things which were established by the decrees of the earlier fathers and councils should be said by posterity to have been superstitious, tempting God, and contrary to the canons, though they were held in highest esteem and observed by the ancients for many centuries before? In this they show their own error and changeableness. For although I agree that the Pontiffs acted rightly and according to God in stripping such trifles and illusions of all faith and authority, which for many ages before them had been in great use and esteem among the ancients, yet in this I regret their piety or prudence: what they wished to correct in one kind they have made worse in another, so that they are seen to have changed these practices and transferred them to new superstitions rather than wholly destroyed and extinguished them. For let whoever wishes read the more recent Pontificals and Missals, especially those published in our own age, and he will find that in the multitude of ceremonies, the difficulty and tedium of performing them, and the madness of exorcism, they far surpass the older ones. For with what words, I will not say, but with what portents, these and similar things are still exorcised by the Papists! The cornerstone and mortar for building a church; salt and water; blessed bread; the dedication of a new church; altars, vessels, vestments, linen and ecclesiastical ornaments; a portable altar; a chalice with a paten; a new cross; images of saints; bells and signals; ashes; incense; and, in the enrolling of what they call soldiers of the regular orders, arms, swords and battle standards. Let us briefly see how the Papists perform all these things with such solemn ritual, wrongly applying sentences of Holy Scripture to their chants. The stone with mortar is first sprinkled with holy water by the bishop's hands, a sign of the cross is cut into it, and it is set in the foundation with these sentences: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner." Then: "Thou art Peter, and upon this rock," etc. Afterwards they pray that those who have given help toward the building of the church may obtain the salvation of body and soul. At the dedication of a church already built, the bishop, going around the church, strikes the door with his pastoral staff with this verse of the psalm: "Lift up your gates," etc. To this a deacon, standing inside and questioned as if in an examination, responds: "Who is this King of glory?" etc. Then the bishop, entering, writes the Greek and Latin alphabets with his staff on the foundation sprinkled with ashes; then, with various and numerous incisions made by the bishop and clergy, straight, oblique, retrograde and crosswise, the walls and pavements are sprinkled with water. Crosses are painted on the walls with chrism by the bishop's right thumb, and after almost endless ceremonies he finally prays that the people gathering in it, being saved through the offerings of the priests by heavenly sanctification, may obtain the eternal salvation of their souls. And on leaving, the bishop anoints the door with chrism, saying these words: "Be thou blessed, sanctified, consecrated, signed and commended to God. Be thou the gate of salvation and peace; be thou a peaceful door, through him who called himself the door and the doorkeeper." Solomon's temple was not built with such charms, but was offered to God by the will of its builder and consecrated by him. Altars are consecrated with countless prayers of this kind, so that whoever devoutly offers or receives the sacred oblations at this altar may receive help for the present life, likewise obtain remission of all sins, and receive the everlasting grace of redemption. And, "Jacob rising early in the morning set up the stone for a pillar, pouring oil upon it, and vowed a vow to the Lord: surely this place is holy, and I knew it not," and "my name shall be there, saith the Lord," and "the angel stood by the altar of the temple." If the bishop had placed relics in the altar, he added: "The nations shall come to thee from afar and bring gifts," etc. The Gospel read on that day was from Matthew: "If therefore thou offer thy gift at the altar," etc. For dedicating a portable altar, after many psalms and short prayers had been sung, the bishop prayed: "O God, who once didst write the law on tablets of stone and didst appoint stone for the service of thy sacrifice, graciously grant that whatever is offered or consecrated to this altar may rise up to thy name, advance religion, and be to the honour of the faith." The chalice with the paten

units.la: hoc modo benedicuntur: vt quemadmodum Melchisedech sacratus fuit calix: sic hoc vasculū & patena per sacerdotis benedictionē sanctificetur, & corporis ac sanguinis domini nouum sepulchrum fiat. Tum sacris ritibus (tanquam Motis iussu à Maria contextis,) tributa exorcismis vis est arcendi malignos spiritus, & corporalia, noua redemptoris nostri studia dicta sunt. Crux verò nouæ vitæ lignum, per quod veteris ligni ab Adamo sumptio, expiata appellatur. Qui um Episcopus benedictam flexis genibus adorans & osculans precatur, vt orantes, sequeq; inclinantes ad illam, inuentant eorum potis & animæ sanitatem. Et vt lignum crucis sit remedium salutare generi humano, solidita fidei, prosectus operum, redemptio animarum, protectio, solamen ac tutela contra facula iacula infimicorum. Et imaginibus similis optata potestas est, vt quicunq; coram illis sanctum aliquem honorauerit, illius precibus gratiamin præsenti, & æternam gloriā obtineat in futuro. Ac vasis ornamentis sacratis, vt omnis immundus spiritus contusus longè discedat, ab Episcopo petitum est. Pro Campanis adhuc aratis Episcopi intercessionibus postulatum fuit quemadmodum Motis tuba, populus & ad diuinum cultum conuenit, & in hostes inecensus est, & clangore tubarum Hiericontis mœnia corruerunt, & aduentu domini mare fugit, montes exultauerunt, & tota terra tubata est: sic per Campanæ tactum atq; sonitum ædes inuitentur ad sacram matrem Ecclesiam, & cum melodia illius ausribus insonuerit populorum, crescat in eis deuotio fidei, amor spiritualis, procul pellantur omnes insidiæ inimici, fragur grandinum, procella turbinum, impetus tempestatum, temperetur infesta tonitrua, ventorumq; flatus fiant salubriter ac moderate superi, prosternat aerias tempestates, dexterataræ virtutis, vt hoc audientes tintinnabulū tremescant ae fugiant, ante crucis in eo depictum vexillum.
units.tr: They are blessed in this way: just as the chalice was consecrated by Melchizedek, so this little vessel and the paten are to be sanctified through the priest's blessing and made a new sepulchre for the body and blood of the Lord. Then, by sacred rites (as if they had been woven at the command of Moses by Mary), the power of driving away evil spirits is ascribed to exorcisms, and they are called the bodily and new labours of our Redeemer. The cross, however, is called the wood of new life, through which the taking of the old wood by Adam is expiated. When the bishop, kneeling, adores and kisses the blessed cross and prays that those who pray before it and bow down to it may find health of body and soul. And that the wood of the cross may be a saving remedy for the human race: the firmness of faith, the progress of good works, the redemption of souls, protection, comfort, and defence against the fiery darts of enemies. A similar desired power is ascribed to images, so that whoever honours any saint before them may obtain, through that saint's prayers, grace in the present life and eternal glory in the future. The bishop also asked that, by the consecrated ornaments of the vessels, every unclean spirit be crushed and driven far away. For the bells, too, the bishops' intercessions were requested, that just as the trumpet of Moses gathered the people to divine worship and inflamed them against their enemies, and by the clangour of the trumpets the walls of Jericho fell, and at the coming of the Lord the sea fled, the mountains leapt, and the whole earth was shaken, so by the touch and sound of the bell the buildings might be summoned to our holy mother the Church; and when its melody has sounded in the ears of the peoples, devotion of faith and spiritual love may grow in them, all the snares of the enemy may be driven far away, the crash of hailstones, the storm of whirlwinds, the force of tempests may be tempered, the dangerous thunders restrained, the blasts of the winds made wholesome and moderate, the aerial storms laid low, and the right hand of power so that those who hear this bell may tremble and flee before the banner of the cross depicted on it.

units.la: In gladiis, armis, vexillisq; sacrandis precantur Episcopi, vt sint inimicis signa terribilia, atq; sanctis intercedentibus solidamenta, & victoriæ certa fiducia. Panis ad similitudinem quinq; panum, Christi benedictione multiplicatum gustantibus imprecatus fuit, vt receperent salutem tam animæ quam corporis. Iam vero salis aquæq; benedictio, eorundemq; commixtio an non dicitur verbis est exorcismus? Nam post plenum exorcismum adiurat sacerdos, vt sint creaturæ exorcizatae, præcaturq; vt omnibus fumentibus sint salus animæ atque corporis, vt quicunq; eo sale tactum aut respersum fuerit, careat omni immunditia, ab eoque fugiat & disiseedat omnis phantasia & nequitia, ac versutia diabolicæ fraudis, omnisq; spiritus immundus adiutatus exemplo eius salis, qui ab Elisæo prophetæ in aquam projectus sterilitatem deleuit, cum vt aqua excitata sumat effectum, ad abiicicndos dæmones, morbosq; pelledos, vt quicunque eas parsum sit, careat omni immunditia, liberetur a noxa: Non illic reliquit spiritus pestilens, nō ut ea corruptens, discedant omnes insidiæ latentis inimici: & si quid est, quod aut incolumitatē habitantiū inuidet, aut quieti, aspiqione huius aquæ effugiat. Ad extremū, vt cōmixtio salis & aquæ effeiatur salutare sacramentū. In cœnsum etiam benedictum creditur receipete hanc potestatem, vt omnes languores, omnesq; infirmitates, cundaq; insidiæ inimiei, odorem eius sentientes effugiant.
units.tr: Over swords, arms and banners to be consecrated, the bishops pray that they may be terrible signs to the enemies, and firm supports through the intercession of the saints, and a sure confidence of victory. Over bread, in likeness of the five loaves which were multiplied by the blessing of Christ, a prayer was offered that those who eat it may receive salvation of both soul and body. Now, what of the blessing of salt and water, and their mixing together: is this not an exorcism in words? For after the full exorcism the priest adjures the creatures, now exorcised, and prays that they may be a salvation of soul and body to all who use them, so that whoever is touched or sprinkled with that salt may be free from all uncleanness, and that every fantasy, wickedness and cunning of diabolical deceit, and every unclean spirit, may flee and depart from him, following the example of that salt which the prophet Elisha cast into the water and thereby removed its barrenness. Likewise the water, once stirred up by this, takes effect for driving out demons and banishing diseases, so that whoever is sprinkled with it may be free from all uncleanness and delivered from harm. The pestilent spirit is not to leave anything there to corrupt it; let all the snares of the hidden enemy depart; and if there is anything that envies the health of the inhabitants or their rest, let it flee at the sprinkling of this water. Finally, the mixing of salt and water is made a saving sacrament. It is also believed that the blessed food has this power, that when eaten all sicknesses, all infirmities, and every snare of the enemy flee at the smell of it.

units.la: Sed quid huius generis infinita exempla persequar? Cui enim dubium est huiusmodi exorcismis papales ritus & ceremonias abundare, qui ab his, quos in ordinatione Ordalii, vulgarisq; purgationis antiquitus secuta est, quam serò damnabant, aut nihil differunt, aut pluribus magisq; stupendis præstigiis referti sunt. Ac Sanctus Augustinus, qui suo tempore de cetremoniarum multitudine quæstus est, si iam vireret, quid de hoc immensō numero & prolixo earum celebrandarum modo existimare potuerat? Scribit enim Ianuario de ceremoniis loquens. Ipsam tamen religionem quam paucissimis & maxime-ffimis celebrationum sacramentis misericordia Dei esse liberam voluit, seruilibus oneribus pressit, vt tolerabilior sit cōditio Iudæorum, qui etiamsi tempus libertatis non agnouerint, legalibus tamen tarcinis non humanis pta-ssum ptionibus subiiciuntur. Hæc Augustinus. Et sanè valde deflenda est huius temporis conditio, quòd Ecclesiæ Patres eadem mentis acie ab Ecclesia resecare has & eiusmodi ceremonias seu potius nugas, aut nolunt aut non possunt, qua prioraillā Otdaliiviria cernebant atq; corrigebant. Sed illis vt superstitiosis damnatis & deletis, hæc quæ mordieus retinent, quamuis puerilia & deliria sint, ex illis tamen fabricantur atque struunt. Quantò modernis Pontificibus æquior fuit Gregorius qui scribit. Quomodo regulæ sanctorum patrum pro tempore, loco, & persona & negotio instante necessitate tradita sunt. Hi autem nulla neq; temporis, neque loci, neq; negotii, neq; personæ, neq; euiusquam rei quam suæ voluntatis atq; gloriolæ rationem habentes, nc pusillus in rebus veritati cedere voluot. Perpendat secum diligenter lector ex circumstantiis, quas secundum rerum gestarum varietatem atque fidem ex probatissimis singularum ætatum scriptoribus descripsimus, illa quæ miracula affirmabant, fuisse Dæmonis tantum ad decipiendum vulgus per Papalem clerum exercitata ludibria, nec magis dicenda miracula quam fuerunt illa a Pharaonis præstigiatoribus demonstrata.
units.tr: But why should I pursue endless examples of this kind? For who doubts that the Papal rites and ceremonies abound in exorcisms of this sort, which either differ in no way from those that followed the ordeal, the common purgation, in ancient times (which they condemned only late), or are filled with even more amazing trickery? And St Augustine, who in his own time complained of the multitude of ceremonies, if he were alive now, what could he have thought of this immense number and the lengthy manner of celebrating them? For he writes to Januarius, speaking of ceremonies: "Yet the religion itself, which the mercy of God wished to be free with the fewest and most simple sacraments of celebration, has been burdened with slavish burdens, so that the condition of the Jews is more tolerable, who, although they have not recognised the time of freedom, are nevertheless subject to legal burdens, not to human presumptions." So Augustine. And truly the condition of this age is greatly to be lamented, that the Fathers of the Church either will not or cannot cut away from the Church, with the same sharpness of mind, these and similar ceremonies, or rather trifles, which earlier men saw and corrected in the ordeals. But while they condemn and destroy those as superstitious, they fabricate and build these, which they hold on to tooth and nail, although they are childish and absurd. How much fairer to the modern Pontiffs was Gregory, who writes: "How the rules of the holy fathers were handed down according to time, place, person and the pressing need of the business." But these men, having no regard for time, place, business, person, or anything other than their own will and little glory, do not wish to yield to the truth even a jot in any matter. Let the reader carefully weigh for himself, from the circumstances which we have described according to the variety and credibility of the events, drawn from the most approved writers of each age, that those things which they affirmed as miracles were only mockeries of the demon, carried out through the Papal clergy to deceive the common people, and are no more to be called miracles than those demonstrated by the magicians of Pharaoh.

units.la: XXXII. Stigandus.
units.tr: XXXII. Stigand.

units.la: STIGANDVS, unde, aut à quibus originem traxit, nescitur. Certum est autem, (quoconque laborauit vitio,) & magno animo & profundo ingenio, & de patria bene meritum fuisse. Is in Remp. & Episcopatus gerendos, per gratiam Edwardi Confessoris, Regis lenissimi, & sanctissimi Principis (cuius fuerat capellanus,) virtute nec an calliditate irrepserit, pariter incertum est. Nam indoctum & illiteratum plane fuisse constat. Quæ tamen non sibi peculiaris, sed toti Anglicano clero fuit tunc communis insciitia, ut temporis potius quam hominis defectus ceuseatur. Ad Archiepiscopalem celsitudinem his gradibus ascendit. Primum orientalium Anglorum fuit Episcopus apud Helmham. Quem locum deseruit, non tam liberè & sponte, quàm ut Wintoniensi Episcopatu longe uberiori frueretur post obitum Alwini Episcopi. In quo occultarū diu auaritiæ & ambitionis scelus primò, pdidit atq; patefecit. Quare auarus, ambitiosus, & Simoniacus passim nūcupatur. Quæ vita indicauit apertius, quòd Wintoniensi Episcopatu non contentus, cum Regis animum, in Robertum tunc Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum, commotum animadvertisset, eodem siue in exilium eiecto, & sede pulso, siue sponte fugiente, viuente tamen, & superstite, nec abdicato, Archiepiscopatum occupauit. Hic Robertus antea Regi charus, postquam Emmæ Reginæ matri suæ indixisset, ut violatæ pudicitiæ suspicionem, ignitis & incensis vomeribus, nudis suis pedibus supergressus, deleret & abstergeret, eidè postea inuisus fuit. Hunc igitur supplantauit Stigandus, & vitiatis ritibus, ac ceremoniis omissis, iusto tamen regio concessus est, anno eiusdem Regis 10. & Leonis Romani P. 3. Roberti tamen pallio vsus, & primus in habitu clericali, (vt quidam fertur, sed inconsulte) Archiepiscopatu functus est. Hinc prædo dictus, & alienæ possessionis inuasor, qui non per ostium in Christi gregem & ouile intrauit. Nec tamen Archiepiscopatu adepto Episcopatum Wintoniensem dimisit, sed inexplicabili ductus cupiditate, contra morem & institutā Ecclesiæ utrumq; retinuit.
