Et quamuis sæpe a sede Romana accossetetur, tamen vafris dilationibus & muneribus euasit, eiusq; authoritatem contempsit, atque derisit, donec, ut mox dicetur, Wilhelmo Regi pœnas dedisset, quæ nullius superauit callidi-tas & astutia. Hoc igitur Archiepiscopatu, siue astu, siue gratuita Regis largitione potitus, ne summa contentione, oblatisque muneribus, à sede Romana pallium obtinere potuit: etsi tunc omnia Romæ perinde essent væhalia, ac prioribus & recentioribus temporibus. Tandem interuenientibus muneribus, à quodam Benedicto, sui simili, & eiusdem criminis reo impetrauit. Qui excommunicatus & à sacris prohibitus, pari nequitia Romanam sedem inuasit, qua ille Cantuariensem tenuit. Hæc cum gesisset Stigandus, ratus ea tranquilla & diuturna fore, subito sequuta sunt tempora, in Anglia aliquandiu turbulenta, & plena præcellis, calamitosa vero & plane exitiosa Stigando. Nam mortuo Edwardo Rege, (qui ob vitæ integritatem, in regnando iustitiam & continentiam, legumq;, siue a se latatum; siue ex veteribus sumptarum æquitatem, inter sanctos relatus est) succedit Haraldus: Cui Gulielmus Normanniæ Dux, qui, tam ex promisso Edwardi, (cuius hospes in exilio fuerat) quam iuramento Haraldi, (cuius fratres obsides tenuit) Regnum Angliæ vindicare, ob eiusdem iurisiurandi violatam fidem & religionem, bellum indixit, & armato tum Normanorum militem copiosi classe transuexit in Angliam, vbi cum Haraldo praelio perto Marte & instructa acie de imperio dimicando. Haraldus cerebro ex teli ictu transfixo cum Anglo succubuit: Gulielmus & victoria regno potitus est. Has regionum mutationes, ne casu, aut fortuito, nec humanis tantum viribus euenire, non modò a Philosophis, (qui naturales aiunt esse Rerumpub. contuerfiones,) sed à Theologis, (qui quod verissimum est diuinitus fieri asseruerunt,) admonemur. Hoc autem Normannorum Imperium multis ante Edwardum annis, tacitè & quasi diuino oraculo praenuntiatum legimus.
units.tr: It is not known where Stigand came from or from whom he drew his origin. It is certain, however, that whatever his faults, he had a great spirit and a deep intellect and deserved well of his country. How he crept into the state and into the bishoprics, whether by ability or by cunning, through the favour of King Edward the Confessor, a most gentle king and most holy prince (whose chaplain he had been), is equally uncertain. For it is plain that he was unlearned and illiterate. Yet this ignorance was not peculiar to him but common to the whole English clergy at that time, so that it should be counted a failing of the age rather than of the man. He rose to the archiepiscopal dignity by these steps. He was first bishop of the East Angles, at Elmham. He left that see, not so much freely and willingly as so that he might enjoy the far richer bishopric of Winchester after the death of Bishop Alwin. There his long-hidden crime of greed and ambition first came to light and was exposed. For this reason he is everywhere called greedy, ambitious and a Simoniac. His later conduct showed more plainly that, not content with Winchester, when he perceived that the king's mind was turned against Robert, then archbishop of Canterbury, he seized the archbishopric, either after Robert had been expelled into exile and driven from his see, or while Robert, still living and not deposed, was fleeing of his own accord. Robert had been dear to the king before, but afterwards became hateful to him, after he had ordered Queen Emma, the king's mother, to wipe away the suspicion of her violated chastity by walking barefoot over red-hot, glowing ploughshares. So Stigand supplanted him. Although he set aside the rites and ceremonies, he was nevertheless granted the archbishopric by royal grant in the tenth year of the same king and the third year of Pope Leo of Rome. Yet he used Robert's pallium and was the first to hold the archbishopric while wearing clerical dress (as some report, though without good reason). For this he was called a robber and an invader of another's property, one who did not enter the flock and sheepfold of Christ by the door. Nor, having obtained the archbishopric, did he give up the bishopric of Winchester, but, driven by an inexplicable greed, he kept both, against custom and the institution of the Church. And although he was often summoned by the Roman see, he escaped by crafty delays and bribes, and he despised and mocked its authority, until, as will soon be said, he paid the penalty to King William, a penalty that no one's cunning and craft could evade. Having thus got the archbishopric, whether by trickery or by the king's free gift, he was able, though with great effort and with gifts offered, to obtain the pallium from the Roman see, even though at that time everything at Rome was as much for sale as in earlier and more recent times. At last, by the intervention of gifts, he obtained it from one Benedict, who was like him and guilty of the same crime. Benedict, excommunicated and forbidden to perform sacred offices, invaded the Roman see with the same wickedness by which he himself held Canterbury. When Stigand had done these things, thinking they would be calm and lasting, times suddenly followed that were for a while turbulent in England and full of disasters, and calamitous and utterly ruinous for Stigand. For after King Edward died (who, because of his integrity of life, his justice and self-restraint in ruling, and the fairness of the laws, whether he made them himself or took them from the old ones, was counted among the saints), Harold succeeded him. William, Duke of Normandy, against him, claiming the kingdom of England both by the promise of Edward (whose host he had been in exile) and by the oath of Harold (whose brothers he held as hostages), declared war because the faith and religion of that same oath had been broken. He carried a large army of armed Norman soldiers across to England in a fleet, and there, with Harold, he fought a battle over the realm, with the fortune of war even and the battle line drawn up. Harold was struck through the brain by an arrow and fell with the English. William gained the victory and took possession of the kingdom. We are warned that these changes of realms do not happen by chance or accident, nor by human strength alone, not only by philosophers (who say that such upheavals in commonwealths are natural), but by theologians (who have asserted that what is most true, that they happen by divine providence). We read, moreover, that this rule of the Normans was foretold many years before Edward, quietly and as if by a divine oracle.

units.la: Canuto enim Regi, qui aliquot fuit ante Edwardum annis, Brithwoldum quendam (tunc Wentanum Episcopum,) cum in nocturnis excubiis & lucubrationibus subiisset sibi
units.tr: For King Cnut, who lived some years before Edward, a certain Brithwold (then bishop of Wilton), while he was keeping night watches and vigils and was turning over in his mind the royal stock, which had been nearly extinguished and destroyed, fell into a deep sleep,

units.la: {a} Ex Ioranal. bibl. de stirpe Regia, (quæ prope extincta & deleta fuerat,) cogitatio, altius compressit somnus, in quo ubi visus est videre Petrum Apostolum, consecrare Edwardum Regem in Normanniatunc exulantem, ælibi vita, ac viginti quatuor annis regnaturum. Quæ tes nonob stupefecit, sed sic extulit Brithwoldum, ut percundaretur, quis esset in regno succelsurus. Cui hoc responsum est. Regnum Anglorum, Regnum Dei est. Et ipse sibi ptouidebit regem. Ac sane, ut nec eon cedendum, si nec detrahendum nimium somniis. Nam huius vaticinationis, qui peruersustos authores habet testes, cuentus ipse certus est. Quod admonet propheta oraculi instar esse diuini. Ipsi, ꝯ Gulielmo in somnis occurrebat, de sua in lõgæuum regnatura gente, & progenie. Quam cum videmus ea fœcilitate regnare, cur de huius Regis, aut illius Episcopi somnii veritate dubitamus? Sed ad 10 Stigandum reuertamur.
units.tr: {a} From the Ioranal, on the royal stock, in which, when he seemed to see the Apostle Peter consecrating Edward, then in exile in Normandy, as king, and that he would reign for twenty-four years. This did not frighten him, but so raised Brithwold up that he asked who would succeed to the kingdom. To him this answer was given: The kingdom of the English is the kingdom of God, and he himself will provide a king for himself. And indeed we should neither yield too much to dreams nor wholly despise them. For the outcome of this prophecy is certain, since it has trustworthy witnesses. This shows that the prophet's word is like a divine oracle. The same dream also came to William, concerning his own race, which was to reign for a long time. Since we see that they reign with such ease, why do we doubt the truth of this king's dream or that bishop's? But let us return to Stigand.

units.la: Certum est, Guilielmo Duci, cum Haraldum in acie prostrauerat, totam Angliam ei suam vim & potestatem concessisse, præter Cantium comitatum, in quo Stigandus, (siue belli renouandi causa: Siue ut æquiore alia & tolerabiliori subiectionis conditione se ac suos illius imperio subiicerei) deliuit. Id tamen effecit pro suis Cantiis, quod in sua patria nemo. Omnes enim inopinata cædè Haraldi, stupore & mœrore perculsi, in Gulielmi ditionem se dabant, præter Cantios. Qui consultore Stigando, sedomi, suisq; sinibus connibebant. Ad quos cum Gulielmus iter perrexisset, Stigandus, aducato sibi Egelsino Abbate Augustinensi, qui totius, suꝯ Cantii princeipatum tenebant, vniuersum Comitatus populum in vnum locū congregabant, quibus & miseram ac seruilem vicinorum conditionem, sub Normannorum iuga redaćtam, & sua pericnla, quæ ex Gulielmi aduenu imminebant, declarabant. Populus mori potius in acie voluit, quàm ab vsitata libertate ad incognitam & insolită seruitutē deduci. Itaq; dies statutus est, quo apud Stranefordhe Cantii oppidū instrucți armatiq; rursus eo uenirent. Stigandus & Egelsinus, (Machabæorum more) Duces exercituipraefecti, & vt auxilia sua geminarent, inito consilio decreuerunt, vt aduenient duce, & præoccupatis transitibus, singuli milites singulos ramos, ea (vt videtur) magnitudine, qua vnusquisq; se tegere possit, in manibus coràm gestaret. Postridie Gulielmus in campestribus prope Stranfcombe / totam Cantii multitudinem, tanquam nemus mobile se circumdantem, & paulatim moderato græssu approprinquantem, attonitus mirabatur. Cantii cum propius a Duce abessent, cū 50 umq; circumuallarum animadueruissent, ramos deiiciunt: arcubusq; tensis, gladiis euaginatis, & hastis vibratis, cæterisq; armorum generibus extensis, rubæ sono præli signum dant. Dux cum exercitu stupefactus est: vt poste qui superiori elatus victoria, tanquam in pugno continere se totam Angliæ existimaret: Nunc hoe subito Cantiorum motu perterritus, non de victoria solum, & amissione exercitus, sed de sua vita perielitabatur. Postulatum est itaque, vt colloquium prius haberetur, antequam initretur præliũ. Strigandus & Egelsinus Cantiorum Duces, mandati sunt eorundē ad Gulielmum legati, qui pro suis Cantiis hæc otatione vsi sunt. Occurrunt tibi, Dux Inelyte, Cantii, amici & tuæ ditioni pariturii, si æquissimis eorum postulatis concesseris, vt qui libertatem à maioribus acceptam, & leges ac consuetudines patrias retinere contendunt, nec in seruitutem inexpertam redigi, aut noua stura tollerare volunt. Regiam enim potestatem, non dominatum ferre possunt. Illibata itaq; libertate, referuarisq̄ue moribus, legibusq; pristinis, recipe Cantios, non seruos, sed side & amore in teaffectos subditos. Sin libertatem legumq; immunitatem auferre niteris, vi40 ita & vitam aufetes. Malint enim incerto Marte tecum dimicare, & sub eertis hostibus in acie succumbere, quàm in foro sub incertis legibus. Nam quanquam cæteri Angli serui- tutem pati possunt, Cantiorum tamen est propria libertas. Dux & hacoratione, & nonis angustiis perculsus, perplexo atque turbato animo, consilium cum suis habuit. Cumq; sibi venisset in mentem, quàm anciptti prælio dimicaturus esset, aut si infecta re discederet, quàm sibi, non modo ad infamiam ignominio- 30 sum, sed ad siaduram acquisiti nuper Regni periculosum foret, si Cantium totius Regni clauem, reliquo regno non adiungeret, & amicitia magis atque fœdere, quàm vi retineret, non necessitate magis, quàm voluntate, concetsit Cantiis, vt libere secundum veteraimstituta viuerent. Itaque inter Gulielmum & Cantios, initum fœdus fuit, & cobfides vtriuq; dati. Posteaq; depositis armis, læti Cantii, lætos Normannos Rosecefstriam deduxunt, vbi Duci Gulielmo, & Comitatum, & Douorense nobile castrum in deditionem tradunt. Hicautem vetus mos & consuetudo Cantiorum in legibus Anglorum muniscipalibus, appellatur, Gauelfinde: quæ intoto regno ante Ducis aduentum, frequens vsitata fuit: postea caeteris adempta, Cantiis solum ex hac Stigandi & Egelsini armata intercessione & instanna, integra & inuiolata remansit. Quae res, satis comprobatur ex antiquis scriptis de consuetudinibus Cantii, vbi inter caetera sic scribitur. Dicit Comitatus quod in Comitatu isto de iure debet de eiusmodi grauamine esse liber, quia dicit, quod Comitatus iste, vt residuum Angliae, nunquam fuit conquestus, sed per pacem facta se reddidit Conquestoris dominatui, saluis sibi omnibus libertatibus suis & liberis consuetudinibus primo habitis & vsitatis. Subacto igitur, seu potius conciliato Cantio, de quo maxime laborabat, quod illic regnum ingredientibus & exeuntibus, pontus aditulque esset maxime commodus ac opportunus, ad inaugurationem seu coronationem 10 proparauit Gulielmus. In quo quanquam moris est, Reges a Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo consecrari, tamen a Stigando vnctus non fuit, sed ab Aldredo Eboracensi Archiepiscopo: vel, quia Stigandus ab exercendo suo munere per sedem Romanam prohibebatur: vel, quia noluit viro sanguinolento, & per tam diram cladem atque eadem patriam suam occupanti munus consecrationis conferre: vel, quod est veritimilimum, quod Gulielmus a Stigando suspenso & interdicto, & multorum criminum a sede Romana postulato, atque reo, consecrari recusabat: sed quaecunque fuerit causa, certum est Gulielmum, omni externo cultu tractasse Stigandum perhonorifice, & comiter eum permulsisse, etsi pessime de eo senserat, quod tristis eius exitus declarabit. Namque finitis inauguratiomis solennibus, praesidiisque passim dispositis, omnibusque rebus secundis & pacatis in Anglia, Rex Gulielmus in Normanniam reuersurus, Stigandum etsi renitentem, secum vna cum aliis regni proceribus duxit, honoris, vt dixit, causa. Sed credibilius est, timuisse Gulielmum, eius tum versutam & callidum ingenium, suum gratiam & potentiam, qua valebat illi Cantio, ne eo absente nouos morus in Anglia concitaret, & defectionis author fieret. Nec passus est eum vsquam abs se discedere, ahtequam rediret in Angliam, etsi benigne atque blande in Normannia retentum. Namque eum patris nomine appellare solitus, occurrit ei ex pius cum illis (tamquam solutus) processionum pompis, longa serie ductis, domumque duxit atque reduxit, & in conuentibus cum magna veneratione assurrexit, neque quicquam non modo officii, sed ne obseruantiae in eum praetermisit. Sed postquam rebus in Normannia compositis in Angliam rediturn est, illa tam diuturna Ducis simulatio, reipsa in apertum prorupit odium, etsi id verbis adumbrauit Gulielmus, & facti inuidiam in Alexandrum Romanum Pontificem transtulit. Miserto enim Stigando structae ilico insidiae, & tacita Gulielmi interpellatione, missi ab eodem Alexandro, Hearmenfredus Sedunensis Episcopus, & Iohannes ac Petrus presbyteri, Cardinales Legati, vt de Stigando Archiepiscopo & Angliae Clero institurent & ordinarent iudicia, quibus hac illuc agitatus Stigandus, nunc in Scotiam cum Alexandro Lincolniensi Episcopo profugit: nunc Elienfe Coenobium latitandi, & se occultandi causa petiit. Tandem totius Cleri Synodus Winthoniae facta, vbi legati predicti, multus contra Stigandum obiectis criminibus, cum obtrectatio causas Archiepiscopatu & ordinibus abdicabant, primo quod Archiepiscopatum Cantuariensem Stigando tenere sit fuisset, non noui sane aut inusitati in Anglia tunc exempli, quod recenti ante cum aetate Dunstanus & Oswaldus, quos historiae inter sanctos & integerrimos patres referunt, in Episcopatibus plurales fuerunt, ille Wigorniensem simul cum Londinensi, hic Eboracensem Archiepiscopatum & Wigornicensem (vbi vt Ecclesia sanctae Mariae, quam ipse condidit, sepultus iacet) simul tenuerunt. Deinde quod Archiepiscopatum Robertio viuente, neque amoto possedisset. Ad extremum, quod Roberti pallium Cantuariae relictum (qui vi iniuste ab Anglia pulsus est) aliquandiu vsus est, & postea a Benedicto Papa, qui excommunicatus & sacris interdictus fuerat, eo quod pecuniis sedem Apostolicam inuasit, pallium accepisset. In eodem Cleri conuentu, multi alii a statu & dignitatibus non iure, sed regali Papalique authoritate pet legatos coacti recesserunt, videlicet frater eius Agelmarus Eliensis Episcopus est degradatus, Abbates etiam aliqui ibi degradati sunt, operam dante Rege, vt quamplures ex Anglis, suo honorepriuarentur, in quorum locum suae genti personas subrogaret, ad confirmationem scilicet Regni sui, quod uper acquisierat. Hinc & nonnullos, tam Episcopos quam Abbates quos sine vlla euidenti causa, nec leges seculi damnabant, suis honoribus priuauit, & vsque ad finem vitae, custodiae mancipatos detinuit, suspicione (vt diximus) tantum inductus noui Regni. Stigandus vero ad summum iam adductus discrimen, deprecatione nea Gulielmum, an iusta expostulatione veteratur, incertus, cum per fidem tam fimiter vtinque datam ac interpositam, instanter obsecrauit, ne se tam iniquis permittat calamitatibus. At Rex lenissimis, & manuductis verbis eiusrei authoritatem & atrocitate sibi derogauit, ac Papalibus mdatis attribuit: Verumtamen Stigandum exautoratum,bonisque ac fortunis spoliatum,carceribus perpetuis inclusit,ubique famelicum ex fisco pareissime alebat, vt extorqueret fortasse,quos thesauros condidisset.Id enim à Stigando quæsitum fuit, qui multis & magnis iuramentis asseruit,ne quicquam sibi aut æris, aut bonorû superesse: vel quia spes eum aliquate nuit libertatis,in quatam grandi thesauro aut ipse fruereur,aut ad perniciem Ducis veterrur: vel quia tam indignis modis a Duce tractatus, peierare & mori maluit, potius quàm tam insigni beneficio inimicum Ducem afficere.Ex fame enim interiit & ægritudine voluntaria, postquam Archiepiscopali sedi septendecim annis incubuisset.Eo autem morruo in examinati corporis collo, clauicula alligata repertaeft,quæ ingentis thesauri indicium dedit, & magnarum opum in subterraneis specubus occultarû: chariæque inuentæ,in quibus cõscriptæ sunt summæ thesauri ful, quibusque in prædiis latebant,cuiusque magnitudinis, ponderis, & qualitatis metalla fuerunt. Quæ omnia in lucrum Gulielmi, qui non modo non læsus,sed plurimum adiutus ab eo fuit,cesserunt.
units.tr: It is certain that after Harold had been struck down in battle, Duke William was granted by the English all their power and authority, except for the county of Kent. There Stigand, whether to renew the war or so that he and his people might submit to William's rule on terms more equitable and bearable, held out. Yet in this he did something for his Kentish people that no one did in his own country. For everyone else, stunned and overwhelmed by the unexpected death of Harold, surrendered to William's dominion, except the men of Kent. On Stigand's advice they stayed at home and kept within their own borders. When William marched against them, Stigand, having summoned Egelsin, abbot of St Augustine's, who together held the principality of Kent, gathered the whole population of the county into one place. He set before them the wretched and servile condition of their neighbours, brought under the yoke of the Normans, and the dangers that hung over them from William's arrival. The people preferred to die in battle rather than be led from their accustomed liberty into an unknown and unfamiliar slavery. So a day was appointed on which they would come again, armed and equipped, to Stranfordhe, a town in Kent. Stigand and Egelsin, like the Maccabees, were set over the army as leaders, and to double their forces they resolved, after consultation, that the soldiers should go forward with a leader and, having occupied the passes, each carry in his hands a branch of such size (as it seems) that each man could hide behind it. The next day, on the fields near Stranfcombe, William was astonished to see the whole multitude of Kent advancing slowly towards him, moving like a wood on the march. When the Kentish men were nearer the Duke, and had seen that they were surrounded, they threw down their branches. Then, with bows bent, swords drawn, spears brandished and other kinds of weapons raised, they gave the signal for battle with a blast of the trumpet. The Duke and his army were stunned. He who had lately been elated by victory, and who had thought he held all England in his fist, was now terrified by this sudden movement of the men of Kent, and feared for his life as well as for the victory and the loss of his army. It was therefore demanded that a parley be held before the battle began. Stigand and Egelsin, the leaders of the men of Kent, were sent as their envoys to William, and they spoke on behalf of their Kentish people in these words: "Illustrious Duke, the men of Kent come to meet you, friends who will submit to your rule if you grant their most just demands. They are determined to keep the liberty received from their ancestors and their native laws and customs, and they will not be reduced to an unknown slavery or endure new burdens. For they can bear royal power, but not domination. Therefore, with their liberty unimpaired and their customs and ancient laws preserved, receive the Kentish men, not as slaves, but as subjects bound to you by loyalty and affection. But if you seek to take away their liberty and the immunity of their laws, you will also take their lives. For they would rather fight with you in uncertain battle and fall in the field before enemies they can see, than live under uncertain laws in the marketplace. For although the other English can endure slavery, the freedom of the men of Kent is their own." The Duke, struck by this speech and by his own straits, deliberated with his men in a perplexed and troubled state of mind. He considered how doubtful the battle would be if he fought, or, if he left the matter unsettled, how dangerous it would be, not only for his infamy and disgrace, but for the security of the kingdom he had recently acquired, if he did not join Kent, the key to the whole realm, to the rest of the kingdom, and hold it by friendship and treaty rather than by force. Less from necessity than from choice, he granted the men of Kent that they might live freely according to their ancient institutions. So a treaty was made between William and the Kentish men, and hostages were given on both sides. Afterwards, with their arms laid down, the joyful Kentish men led the joyful Normans to Rochester, where they handed over to Duke William both the county and the noble castle of Dover. This ancient custom and usage of the Kentish men among the municipal laws of the English is called gavelkind. Before the Duke's arrival it was commonly practised throughout the whole kingdom; afterwards it was taken from the others, and through this armed intervention and insistence of Stigand and Egelsin it remained whole and inviolate for Kent alone. This fact is sufficiently confirmed by the ancient writings on the customs of Kent, where among other things it is written thus: "The county says that by right it ought to be free of this kind of burden, because it says that this county, unlike the rest of England, never complained, but surrendered itself to the Conqueror's dominion by a peace made, all its liberties and free customs previously held and used being saved to it." Therefore, with Kent subdued, or rather won over, which was what he was chiefly concerned about, since its shore and harbour for those entering and leaving the kingdom were most convenient and useful, William prepared for his inauguration or coronation. In this, although it is customary for kings to be consecrated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, he was not anointed by Stigand but by Ealdred, Archbishop of York. Either because Stigand was forbidden by the Roman See to exercise his office; or because he was unwilling to confer the rite of consecration on a bloodstained man who had seized his country through such a dreadful slaughter and so much destruction; or, which is most likely, because William refused to be consecrated by Stigand, who had been suspended and placed under interdict, and who had been accused of many crimes before the Roman See and was under indictment. Whatever the cause, it is certain that William treated Stigand with every outward mark of honour, and courteously flattered him, although he thought very badly of him, as his sad end will show. For when the solemn rites of the inauguration were over, the guards were posted everywhere, and all things in England were prosperous and peaceful, King William, about to return to Normandy, took Stigand with him, though he resisted, together with other nobles of the kingdom, as he said, for the sake of honour. But it is more credible that William feared Stigand's crafty and cunning nature, and the favour and power he enjoyed in Kent, lest in William's absence he should stir up new disturbances in England and become the author of a revolt. Nor did William allow him to leave his side at any point before he returned to England, although he was kept in Normandy with kindness and flattery. For William used to call him "father," and met him with processions, long in order, as if he were a free man; he took him along and brought him back, rose to him with great reverence at assemblies, and omitted nothing of courtesy or deference towards him. But after affairs in Normandy had been settled and he returned to England, that long pretence of the Duke at last broke out into open hatred, although William had veiled it in words and transferred the odium of the deed to Alexander, the Roman Pontiff. For when snares had been laid against Stigand, and with William's silent prompting, Hermenfrid, bishop of Sion, and the priests John and Peter, sent as legates by the same Alexander, were dispatched to institute and conduct judicial proceedings concerning Archbishop Stigand and the clergy of England. Harried this way and that, Stigand at one time fled into Scotland with Alexander, bishop of Lincoln; at another he sought the monastery of Ely as a hiding place and to conceal himself. At length a synod of the whole clergy was held at Winchester, where the aforesaid legates, with many crimes alleged against Stigand, deprived him of his archbishopric and his orders, on the ground, first, that he had held the archbishopric of Canterbury while holding another see. This was no strange or unusual precedent in England at that time, for in the recent past Dunstan and Oswald, whom the histories count among the saints and most upright fathers, held pluralities of bishoprics: the one held Worcester together with London, the other the archbishopric of York and Worcester together (where, buried in the church of St Mary which he himself founded, he lies). Secondly, that he had held the archbishopric while Robert was still living and had not been removed. Lastly, that he had used the pallium left at Canterbury by Robert, who had been violently and unjustly driven out of England, for some time, and afterwards had received the pallium from Pope Benedict, who had been excommunicated and placed under interdict because he had invaded the Apostolic See with money. In the same assembly of the clergy, many others were removed from their station and dignities, not by right, but by royal and papal authority, through the legates. His brother Agelmar, bishop of Ely, was deposed; some abbots were also deposed there, the King taking pains that many of the English should be deprived of their honours, so that he might put persons of his own race in their place, namely to secure the kingdom he had lately acquired. Hence he also deprived of their honours some bishops and abbots whom no evident cause, nor the laws of the state, condemned, and kept them in custody until the end of their lives, moved, as we have said, only by suspicion of his new kingdom. But Stigand, brought to the greatest peril, was uncertain whether to turn to William with entreaty or with a just complaint. Since the same faith had been given and pledged on both sides, he earnestly besought him not to subject him to such unjust calamities. But the King, with the gentlest and most soothing words, denied the authority and the severity of the matter to himself and attributed it to papal commands. Nevertheless, he deposed Stigand, stripped him of goods and fortune, and shut him up in perpetual prison, where he kept him starving and fed him very sparingly from the treasury, perhaps to extort from him what treasures he had hidden. For this was what was sought from Stigand, who asserted with many and great oaths that nothing of money or goods remained to him; or perhaps because some hope of freedom had moved him, so that he might either enjoy or turn against the Duke the great treasure in which he trusted; or because, treated so shamefully by the Duke, he preferred to perjure himself and die rather than bestow such a remarkable benefit on the enemy Duke. For he perished of hunger and self-imposed illness, after he had sat in the archiepiscopal see for seventeen years. And when he died, a small key was found tied around the neck of his body, which gave indication of an immense treasure and of great wealth hidden in underground caves; and papers were found in which the sums of the treasure were written down, and on what estates they lay concealed, and of what size, weight and quality the metals were. All these things passed to the profit of William, who was not only not harmed by him but was greatly helped by him.

units.la: XXXIII. Lanfrancus
units.tr: XXXIII. Lanfranc

units.la: Anfrancus natione Transalpinus, patria Papiensis (quæ civitas Mediolanensis est ditionis, a Mediolano x. mille passibus diisiuncta) ab ineunte ætate in literis educatus, & cum adoleuisset,progressus in Normanniam venit,fama & celebritate Elisini Abbatis Beccensis prouoeatus in itinere Rhotomagum profecturus, vesperi per fylaum tranluens, incidit in latrones,a quibus manibus ad tergum alligatis spoliatus,& in densum coiectus est. Mane à viatoribus transeuntibus opem clamore petiit, & solutus est.Inde ad Beccensem Coenobium se contulit, vbi ad inopiam rantam subleuandam, dialecticam stipendioprofessus,Monachus primum, deinde Prior Beccensis fuit: Postea Gulielmi Ducis dono, Abbas scil. Sancti Stephani Cadomensis coenobii, quod Dux erexerat. Deinde Gulielmus Angliæ regno potitus, Stigadotâ turpiter a sede quasi auulso, Lanfrancum omni literarum genere excultum,&in quo summam gerêdi regni ipsem & fidem collocarat,ad Archiepiscopatum Cantuariensem ex Normannia vocat: quem Lanfranus,& à Rege coactus, & à Papa Alexandro iussus suscepit. Celeberrima est autem huius ptæ cæteris electio & consecratio. Electus enim est a maioribus populi consensus in aula Regis: quod sane est instar Senatus seu Parliamenti Anglicani, Ad eum vero consecrandum omnes in Anglia Episcopi conuenerunt, seruato antiquo & veteri consecrationis more, & qui adesse non poterant, literis & legationibus excusabantur. Consecratio hæc tam nobilis & perunigata, Quarto Calendas Septembtis, An.1070 quatto anno Gulielmi Regis celebrata fuit Cantuariæ, cui interfuerunt Gulielmus Lordinensis, Siwardus Roffensis, Walchelmus Wentanus, Remigius Dorcensis, Horfaftus Helmanensis, siue Tbedfordensis, Stigerardus Selesiensis, Hermannus Sireburnensis, Gifo Welienfis. Hac tam insigni claritate electus & consecratus fuit Lanfrancus. Paulo post Thomas Eboracensis Archiepiscopus eius ad Lanfrancum sacrandus venit. Hora statura est, qua Thomas quæstionem seu examinationem subiret: qua Lanfrancus cum suis Suffraganeis in Choro lineis induti sbant,& Thomam expectabant.Quo aduenien te,Lanfrancus ei detulit subiectionis & obedientiæ professionem iureiurando confirmandam, Thomas respondit: Nõ se id factûrû,quod saluo iure,&maiorum suorum more & ptiuilegio suæ Ecclesiæ facere non possit.Itaq; nisi scriptis,authoritatibus & tabulis obsignatis,clarisque probationibus sibi de re tanti momenti liqueret, quianoluit exemplo suo Eboracensi Ecclesiæ quicquam prævidicit generari, fine sacratione discedere maluit, quam ignotam sibi sùæque Ecclesiæ obedientiam adiutamento prositeri. Et quanquam in ea suasione aperte monstrasset Lanfrancus, quod nihil à Thoma flagitaret, quam quod & Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ authoritati, & Eboracensis iuri, ac vtriusque consuetudini esser consenraneum, tamen Thomas minimè sacratus disceßit, & habita ad Regem querela eum in Lanfrancum irritauit. Lanfrancus contra expositá Regi tam probabili facti sui ratione, eoque pacato atque mitigato impetrauit, vt Thomas quod ante recusabat, Regis edicto coactus, iam obedientiæ professionem Lanfrancu ex scriptis cum iuramento recitaret, in qua se Lanfranco obtemperaturum in omnibus, quo ad Christianæ religionis cultum pertinent, absolute promisit. Posteaque Lanfrancus a reliquis Angliæ Episcopis, qui prius ab aliis faerant tuerant, subiectionis professionem vna cum cappis professionalibus petiit & accepit. Thomas vero Eboracensis Archiepiscopi professio verbatim sic descripta est.
units.tr: Lanfranc, a Transalpine by birth and a native of Pavia (a city in the territory of Milan, ten thousand paces from Milan), was educated in letters from his earliest years. When he had grown up, he came to Normandy, drawn by the fame and renown of Herluin, abbot of Bec. On a journey to Rouen he passed through a forest in the evening, where he fell into the hands of robbers. They bound his hands behind his back, stripped him, and threw him into a thicket. In the morning he called out for help to travellers passing by and was released. He then went to the monastery of Bec, where, to relieve his great poverty, he taught dialectic for a fee. He was first a monk and then prior of Bec. Afterwards, by the gift of Duke William, he became abbot of the monastery of St Stephen at Caen, which the Duke had founded. Then William gained the kingdom of England, and Stigand was shamefully removed from his see as if torn from it. William summoned Lanfranc from Normandy to the archbishopric of Canterbury. Lanfranc was a man trained in every kind of learning, and the King had placed in him his highest trust both in governing the kingdom and in matters of faith. Lanfranc accepted the office, both because the King compelled him and because Pope Alexander ordered him to. The election and consecration of this man were, however, among the most famous of all. He was chosen by the consent of the chief men of the people in the King's court, which is truly like the Senate or Parliament of England. For his consecration all the bishops of England assembled, observing the ancient and established manner of consecration; those who could not be present sent letters and envoys as their excuse. This consecration, so noble and well attended, was celebrated at Canterbury on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the year 1070, the fourth year of King William. Present were William of Lincoln, Siward of Rochester, Walkelin of Winchester, Remigius of Dorchester, Horsfast of Chelmsford or Thetford, Stigerand of Chichester, Hermann of Salisbury, and Giso of Wells. Lanfranc was elected and consecrated with this great distinction. Shortly afterwards Thomas, archbishop of York, came to Lanfranc to be consecrated by him. An hour was fixed at which Thomas would undergo the examination. Lanfranc and his suffragans were waiting in the choir, vested in linen, and expected Thomas. When he arrived, Lanfranc presented him with a form of submission and obedience to be confirmed by oath. Thomas replied that he would not do what he could not do without prejudice to his right, to the custom of his predecessors and the privilege of his church. Therefore, unless the matter of such importance were made clear to him by written documents, authorities, sealed records and clear proofs, he would not allow anything to be done that might prejudice the church of York by his example. Rather than promise by oath an obedience that was unknown to him and to his church, he preferred to depart without consecration. Lanfranc, in that exhortation, had plainly shown that he asked of Thomas nothing but what agreed both with the authority of the church of Canterbury and with the right of York and the custom of each. Nevertheless Thomas left unconsecrated, and, having lodged a complaint with the King, he stirred up feeling against Lanfranc. Lanfranc, however, set out to the King the very reasonable grounds for his conduct, and by this means he calmed and softened him. He obtained that Thomas, compelled by the King's edict, should now recite in writing and under oath the profession of obedience to Lanfranc which he had previously refused. In it he unconditionally promised to obey Lanfranc in all things that pertain to the worship of the Christian religion. Afterwards Lanfranc asked for and received the profession of submission, together with the professional copes, from the remaining bishops of England, who had previously been consecrated by others. The profession of the archbishop of York, Thomas, was recorded word for word as follows.

units.la: Decet Christianum quemque Christianis legibus subiacere, nec his, quæ à sanctis patribus salubriter instituta sunt, quibus liber rationibus contraire. Hinc namque ir, dissensiones, iniuriæ, contentiones, ceteraque procedunt, quæ amatores suos in poenas æternas demergunt. Et quanto quis altioris est ordinis, tanto impensius diuinis debet obtemperare præceptis. Propterea ego Thomas ordinatus Eboracensis Ecclesiæ Metropolitanus antistes, auditis cognitisque rationibus absolutam tibi Lanfranco Dotobernensi Archiepiscopo tuisque successoribus de canonica obedientia professionem sacio, & quidquid a te, vel ab eius iuste & canonice inibi iniunctum fuerit, seruaturum me repromitto. Dehac autem re, dum ate adhuc ordinandus essem, dubius fui. Ideoque ibi quidem sine conditione, sucessoribusve tuis conditionaliter me obrepetaturum esse promisi. Paulo post Lanfrancus cum Thoma Eboracensi, assoclato etiam Remigio Doceftrensi Episcopo, pallium ab Alexandro Papa receptuti Romam profecti sunt. Lanfranco pallia, vnum honoris, amoris alterum. Cui Lanfranci seu virtuti, seu fœlicitati Thomas inuidens, cepit coram Papalitem de subiectione & primatu antea Regio decreto sopitam redintegrare, tum prouinciæ suæ fines in Lieoln. Wigorn. & Lichefeld. dioceses dilatare, quas ex veteribus regni institutis suæ ditionis ambitu contineri asseuerabat. Quæ disceptatio quia ptiuilegiis & consuetudinibus, ac priuatis vtriusque Archiepiscopatus institutis certius quam iure scripto definiri posse videbatur, decretum est a Papa, vt a Rege & Regni proceribus diiudicaretur. Qui in Windosoriensi Castro, vt ex sequenti decreto apparet, contra Thomæ intensionem prouincias Humbro flumine sese parabat, & Eboracensem prouinciam seiunctis illis, quas Thomas vendicabat, diocæsis bus, & Cantuariensi prouinciæ a scriptis, perexiguis (si ad Cantuariensem referatur) sinibus concludebant.
units.tr: It becomes every Christian to be subject to Christian laws, and not to oppose those things that have been wholesomely instituted by the holy Fathers. From such opposition anger, dissensions, injuries, contentions and other evils arise, which plunge their lovers into eternal punishments. And the higher a man stands in rank, the more diligently he ought to obey the divine precepts. Therefore I, Thomas, ordained metropolitan bishop of the church of York, having heard and considered the reasons, make to you, Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and to your successors, a full profession of canonical obedience, and I promise that I will observe whatever is enjoined on me by you, or by your successors, justly and canonically. I was doubtful about this matter while I was still to be ordained. Therefore I promised that I would bind myself to you without condition, or, to your successors, only conditionally. Shortly afterwards Lanfranc, together with Thomas of York, and with Remigius, bishop of Dorchester, as companion, set out for Rome to receive the pallium from Pope Alexander. Two palls were given to Lanfranc, one of honour and the other of love. Thomas, envying Lanfranc either his virtue or his good fortune, began before the Pope to renew the dispute over subjection and primacy, which had earlier been laid to rest by a decree of the King. He also began to extend the boundaries of his province into the dioceses of Lincoln, Worcester and Lichfield, which he maintained were included within the bounds of his jurisdiction by the ancient institutions of the kingdom. Since this dispute seemed capable of being settled more certainly by privileges, customs and the private institutions of each archbishopric than by written law, the Pope decreed that it should be decided by the King and the nobles of the realm. They met in the castle of Windsor, where, as appears from the decree that follows, they divided the provinces on the Humber, contrary to Thomas's intention. They marked off the province of York from the dioceses which Thomas claimed, and they bounded the province of Canterbury by very narrow limits, as the records show, if they are referred to Canterbury.

units.la: CONSTITVTIO SVPER CAVSA DE PRIMATV, quem Dorobernensis Archiepiscopus super Eboracens. Ecclesiam iure sua Ecclesia proclamabat, ordinata de consensu Domini Wilhelmi, ad tunc Regis Angliæ & Archiepiscoporum Cant. & Eborac. & caeterorum qui interfuerunt, Episcoporum.
units.tr: THE DECREE CONCERNING THE CAUSE OF PRIMACY, which the Archbishop of Canterbury claimed over the Church of York by right of his own Church, ordained by the consent of Lord William, then King of England, and of the Archbishops of Canterbury and York and the other bishops who were present.

units.la: Anno ab incarnatione Domini nostri Iesu Christi. 1072. Pontificatus autem Domini Alexandri Papæ vndecimo, Regni vero Wilhelmi gloriosi Regis Anglorum & Ducis Normannorum sexto. Ex præcepto eiusdem Alexandri Papæ, animante eodem Rege in præsentia ipsius & Episcoporum atque Abbatum ventilata est causa de primatu, quem Lanfrancus Dorobernensis Archiepiscopus super Eboracen. Ecclesiam iure suæ Ecclesiæ proclamabat, & de ordinatione quorundam Episcoporum, de quibus ad quem specialiter pertinerent, certum minime constabat. Et tandem aliquando diuersis diuersarum scripturarum authoritatibus probatum atque ostensum est, quod Eboracensis Ecclesia Cant. debeat subiacere. Eiusque Archiepiscopi, vt primatis totius Britanniæ, dispositionibus, in his q. ad Christianam religionem pertinent in omnibus obedire, Subiectionem vero Dunelmensis, hocest, Lindisfarnensis Episcopi, atque omnium regionum aeterminis Licifeldensis Episcopi, & Humbræ magni fluuii vique ad extremos Scotiæ fines, & quicquid ex hac parte prædicti fluminis ad parochiam Eboracensem Ecclesiæ iure competit, Cantuariensis Metropolitanus Eboracensi Archiepiscopo eiusque successoribus in perpetum obtinere concessit. Ita vt si Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus concilium cogere voluerit, vbicunque visum eifuerit, Eboracensis Archiepiscopus fui præsentiam eum omnibus sibi subiectis ad nutum eius exhibeat, & eius Canonicis dispositionibus obdiens existat. Quod autem Eboracen. Archiepiscopus professionem Cantuariensis Archiepiscopo facere etiam cum sacramento debeat: Lanfrancus Dorobernensis Archiepiscopus,ex antiquo antecessorem consuetudine ostendit,ied ub a morem Regis Thomæ Eboracensis. Archiepiscopo sacramentum relaxauit, scriptamq; tantum professionem recepit, non prætermittens quod præsulcesoribus suis, qui sacramentum cum professione a successoribus Thomæ exigere voluerint. Si Archiepiscopi Cantuarienses vitam finierit, Eboracensis Archiepiscopus Dorobernium venit, & cum qui electus suerit, cum cæteris præfatæ Ecclesiæ Episcopis, vt primatem propriinmiure consecrabit. Quod si Eboracensis Archiepiscopus obierit, is qui ei successurus eligitur accepto a Rege Archiepiscopatus dono, Cantuariam, vel vbi Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo placuerit,accedet, & ab ipso ordinationem canonico more suscipiet. Huic constitutioni consenserunt præfatus Rex, & Archiepiscopi Lanfrancus Cantuariensis & Thomas Eboracensis, & cæteri qui interfuerunt Episcopi. Venitque aliter hæc causa prius apud Wentanam ciuitatem in Paschali solemnitate, in capella regia, quæ sita est in castello; postea in villa Regia, quæ vocatur Windsor, vbi & finem accepit, in præsentia Regis, Episcoporum, Abbatum dicentium quod congregati erant apud curiam infecstiuitate Pentecostes.
units.tr: In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1072, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander, and the sixth year of the reign of William, glorious King of the English and Duke of the Normans. By order of the same Pope Alexander, with the same King encouraging, the cause of primacy was debated in the presence of the King, the bishops and the abbots. Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, claimed this primacy over the Church of York by right of his own Church. Concerning the ordination of certain bishops, as to which of the two churches they specifically belonged to, nothing certain was established. At length, it was proved and shown by various authorities drawn from various Scriptures that the Church of York ought to be subject to Canterbury, and that its archbishop should obey the arrangements of the Archbishop of Canterbury, as primate of all Britain, in all matters pertaining to the Christian religion. The Metropolitan of Canterbury granted to the Archbishop of York and his successors forever the subjection of the Bishop of Durham (that is, of Lindisfarne), and of the Bishop of Lichfield, whose region extends over all the territory as far as the borders of Scotland, together with the Humber, a great river, and whatever on this side of that river belongs by right to the parish of the Church of York. So that, if the Archbishop of Canterbury wishes to convene a council wherever it seems fit to him, the Archbishop of York shall present himself at his command, with all who are subject to him, and shall be obedient to his canonical arrangements. As for the fact that the Archbishop of York ought also to make a profession with an oath to the Archbishop of Canterbury: Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, showed that this was the ancient custom of his predecessors, but on account of the custom of Thomas, Archbishop of York, he relaxed the oath and accepted only a written profession, without prejudice to what his predecessors might demand from the successors of Thomas, namely an oath together with the profession, if they wished. If the Archbishop of Canterbury ends his life, the Archbishop of York comes to Canterbury and, together with the other bishops of the said Church, consecrates the one who has been elected as primate by right of his own office. But if the Archbishop of York dies, the one elected to succeed him, having received the gift of the archbishopric from the King, shall go to Canterbury, or wherever the Archbishop of Canterbury pleases, and shall receive ordination from him in the canonical manner. The aforesaid King, the Archbishops Lanfranc of Canterbury and Thomas of York, and the other bishops who were present, agreed to this decree. The matter was otherwise taken up first at Winchester, at the Easter festival, in the royal chapel which stands in the castle; afterwards in the royal town called Windsor, where it also reached its end, in the presence of the King, the bishops and the abbots, who said that they had gathered at the court for the feast of Pentecost.

units.la: +Signum Gulielmi Regis. +Signum Matildis Reginæ. +Ego Lanfrancus Dorobernensis Archiepiscopus subscripsi. +Ego Thomas Eboracensis Archiepiscopus subscripsi, +Ego Gulielmus Londinensis Episcopus consensi, cum multis aliis Episcopis & Abbatibus, vt in Archiuis patet.
units.tr: + Sign of King William. + Sign of Queen Matilda. + I, Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, have subscribed. + I, Thomas, Archbishop of York, have subscribed. + I, William, Bishop of London, have consented, together with many other bishops and abbots, as appears in the archives.

units.la: Sed Romæ siue ob hanc motam controuersiam, siue ob indignitatē Thomæ & Remigii commotus Pōtifex, vt rumoʒ patorali baculo & annulo priuauit: illum quod sacerdotis esset filius: hunc quia multis opibus Gulielmum in Anglia superanda iuuit, & muneribus pactus de Episcopatu, si Gulielmum rerum potiretur, Lanfrancus tamen vt restitueretur intercessit, & summa gratia impetrauit. Lanfrancus & opinione sui, principisq; ac pontificis gratia elatus, cepit reliquos regni Episcopos præ se contemnere, ac imperiam exptobrate(licet moribus & vitæ sanctitate iudicio populi longe superiores) quæ res multum de fide sua, & ceteris Romæ, Gregorius, qui Hildebrandus dictus est. Qui coniugatos sacerdotes nouo exemplo a diuinis muneribus & officiis amouebat, & vt multis ac sanis videbatur, temerario & inconsiderato contra sanctorum patrum sententiam præiudicio. Quam de re Lanfrancus Synodo Wintoniæ habita statuit inter alia, vt nullus canonicus vxorem haberet. Extra vrbem in vicis & castellis sacerdotes non compellendos vxores dimittere. prohibendos autem ne inatrimonio contraherent, qui iam cælibes essent. Tum Episcopis iniunctum, ne quos ausint præsbyteros vel Diaconos ordinarent nisi calibatum profesos, vt mox indicabimus. Alia Synodus celebrata Londini, sub eodem Lanfranco, in quo decretum est, vt quædam sedes Episcopales, quæ in oppidulis ac pagis antea fuerant, in locis celeberrimis collocarentur. Quo factum est vt Lincolnia, Bathonia, Sarisburia, Exonia, Ceftria, atque Cisteria, ciuitates nouæ Episcoporum sede ac incolatu nobilitatæ sint. Elmhamensis vero Episcopatus sedes ad Thedfordiam deducta nigrauit. Quam illinc pustea Norduicum, translatum quidam Herebertus Losinga dictus. Extra ciuitatem Cant. in parte orientali erat Ecclesia sancti Martini, vbi sedes Episcopi erat, qui domi, vel in comitatu semper manebat, & vices Archiepiscopi. (qui Regis curiam frequentabat) per omnia gerebat. Monachos Ecclesiæ Christi (ac ipse monachus) in obsequium accipiebat: solennitates in Ecclesia Metropoli celebrabat, quibus peraētis ad suam ediebat. Hic & prior Ecclesiæ Christi (quem Decanum vocabat) in Synodis pariter ornatu considebant: Atque hic mos vsque ad tempora Normannorum perduraui, Eiusque Episcopi præsul extremus fuit Godwinus. Quo mortuo anno scilicet 1065. Lanfrancus Episcopū Ecclesiæ beati Martini sublituere renuit, dicens quod in vna ciuitate duo Episcopi esse non deberent, cū reuera in ciuitate Episc. non suit, sed extra ciuitatem. Is igitur loco Episcopi quendam Clericum suum Archidiaconum ordinauit, cuius si rei ante mortem eum pœnituit. Præterea Lanfrancus etsi aliis in rebus multa & præclara edidisset, pietatis simul & eruditionis indicia, Wulstanum tamen virum integerrimum, nec subiauit cuiquam pietate secundum, ab Episcopatu Wigorniensi exstudere nitebatur: sed siue totius populi, qua florebat Wulstanus, gratia impeditus, siue illo diuulgato miraculo, de Wulstani pastorali baculo, Edwardi Confessoris sepulchro infixo, nec cuiusquam manu aut potentia prætetquam ipsius Wulstani auulso, perterrirus, ab inepto nou sine magna infamia destitit. Lanfrancus non modo ob Ecclesiæ, sed ob Reip. administrationem spectaræ fuit angustes industrię. Absente enim Gulielmo, omnia Lanfranco mandabantur, qui summa prudentia cuncta moderatus proceres aræque plebeïn officio tranquille, sine vllo motu aut tumultu cōtinebat, adeo vt si quæ defectionis aut seditionis suspicio nascebatur, ad eam illico compescendā maximus & potentissimus quisque, opem & adiumentum illi imperanti præstitit. Cuius sapientiæ sic confilius Gulielmus, vt etiam ad Rhotomagense concilium eum accerfuit, cui Gulielmus præfuit. Interfuere autem Iohannes Archiepiscopus Rhotomagensis, Odo Baiocensis Episcopus, Hugo Luxouiensis, Michael Abrincensis, Gilbertus Ebroicensis, Robertusque Sagensis Episcopi. In hoc autem Rhotomagensis Coocilio, Gulielmus permulta, non minus de negociis Ecclesiasticis, quam de noui Angliæ regni vtilitatibus deerceuit. Sed inter alia Lanfrācus, cū Archiepiscopatus sui iura a sede diuulsa, ab aliis inuasoribus tenerinimadueneret, huic quoque malo sanando remedium adhibuit. Odoe nim quidam tunc Baiocensis in Normannia præsul, idemque Cantii Comes, plurima Archiepiscopatus prædia iniuste occupauit, quæ recuperauit & sedi restituit Lanfrancus. Et præter minuta illa prædiola viginti quinque muneris Archiepiscopali sedi illius o pera recuperata fuere. Totam autem suam Ecclesiam, atque territorium terra marique tā hbera & à vectigalibus, exactionibusq; ac seruitutibus immunia, atque ipsa regia de solla fuerit: deinde si succisa in suo prædio arborin regiam viam procliuis cecideritt: tertio si homicidium vel sanguinis effusio fiat. Idem & Ecclesiam Christi Cantuariæ caducam & partim ruinam minantem, partim magna ex parte combustam instaurauit, & xenodochia dun iuxta vrbem Cant. scil. Harbaldowne & S. Iohns, quorum alterum leprosis, alterum infirmis coustitutum erat, condidit, quibus de thesauro Archiepiscopi, 140. libras singulis annis dabat. Prætetea Ecclesiam Gregorii extruxit, in qua canonicos posuit, qui infirmis seruirent: aliam item Ecclesiam iuxta ædes leprosorum in qua Deo seruirent & sepeliebatur. Fuit etiam in pauperes munificentissimus, quibus quingentas libras quotannis Eleemosinæ loco erogauit. Cumque fames Angliam grauiter premeret, Loodinum misit, vbi vel mille pauperes pascebat. In consecratione eius repertum est scriptum super caput dum consedit, illud Euangelicum. Date Eleemosinam, & ecce omnia munda sunt vobis. Quod futurum tanti viri liberalitate antea declarauit. Ecclesiam Cathedralem Roffensein (veteri demolita) extruxit, eandemque plurimis opulentis donis affecit, & munerium Lamethæ cum patronatu Ecclesiæ, quam prius Goda Comitissa Ecclesiæ Roffensi dedit ante Normannorum aduentum, eidem sedia Rege adiungi libenter satagebat, sed postea permutatione seu excambio hoc Lamethe munerium, à Richardo Rege, Anno 1196. Cantuariensi sedi commodius, Huberto tunc Archiepiscopo concessum fuit, cuius loco munerium Darenta Roffensi Ecclesiæ obtigit, Gelbertus tamen tunc Rofsensis Episcopus consentire noluit, ante obtentam quandam aream iuxta Ecclesiam beato rum Martyrum Stephani & Thomæ, in qua sibi palatium (nuper muro lateritio per Io. Fisherum cinctum) extruxit. quod nunc vocatur Carlet place. Iremque annuū censum quinque marcarum de Ecclesia de Lamethe, quas Episcopus Roff. annuatim Archiepiscopo pendere cōsueuit. Episcopi n Roff. Londinū profectū in manetio de Lamethe hospitio excepti fuerunt ex eoque palcam, ligna, cæteraque ad rem familiarem opportuæ atque commodè percipere solebant. Id quod charta Huberti Archiepiscopi de rectore Ecclesiæ de Lamethe. An. 1196. per Priorē & Capitulum Cant. confirmata, (Godefredo tunc Winton. Episcopo testimonium ad id perhibente) manifeste declarat ur. In Monachos etiam Albanenses perliberalis fuit, in quos mille marcas contulit, & munerium de Rochbourne acquisiuit. Et quamuis summā gerebat Reipub. curam, tamen Theologiæ studio assiduè & incontinenter vacabat, nec minorem operam legendo quam scribendo dabat. In eo enim studio, simulatque adoleuisset, patr Haribaldus & mater Rosa eum diligenter instituit procurabant. Itaq; veteris atque noui Testamenti libros, à scriptoribus corruptos correxit, & emendatos atq; sinceros edidit. Acutissimae que contra Berengarium de Eucharistia in scriptis disseruit. In Paulinas Epistolas & Psalmos Dauidicos edidit Commentaria, & nonnulla alia opuscula quotannis diuulgauit. Archiepiscopalem iurisdictionem etsi leniter & sine aperta contentione, tamen seuerissimè exercuit. Nam fractis primùm viribus Thomæ Eboracensis, in ea controuersia, quæ antea de subiectione & primatu cōmemorata est, postea q. nutu rem gerebat. Nec tamen iniuriam cuiquā facere vnquam putabatur. Ad colloquium illius facilis ad itus cuiuis patebat, tristem à se neminem dimisit, sed si quem mærore affectum conspiceret, causa accurate indagata, medelam adhibuit.
units.tr: But whether at Rome, because of this controversy that had been stirred up, or because of the unworthiness of Thomas and Remigius, the Pontiff, as the rumour goes, deprived them of the pastoral staff and ring: Thomas because he was the son of a priest, and Remigius because he had helped William with much money to conquer England, and had bargained with gifts for a bishopric should William gain control of affairs. Lanfranc, however, interceded that Thomas be restored, and obtained this by great favour. Lanfranc, elated both by his own opinion and by the favour of the prince and the pontiff, began to despise the other bishops of the kingdom and to reproach them haughtily, although in morals and sanctity of life they were, by the judgment of the people, far superior to him. This matter greatly harmed his standing with the Fathers, and with the others at Rome, and with Gregory, who was called Hildebrand. Gregory, with an unprecedented measure, removed married priests from divine offices and duties, and, as it seemed to many, rashly and inconsiderately prejudged the matter against the opinion of the holy Fathers. Concerning this matter, Lanfranc, in a synod held at Winchester, decreed among other things that no canon should have a wife; that priests in villages and castles outside the city were not to be compelled to dismiss their wives; but that those who were already unmarried were to be prevented from marrying. Then it was enjoined on the bishops that they should not dare to ordain as presbyters or deacons any but those who had professed celibacy, as we shall shortly show. Another synod was held at London under the same Lanfranc, in which it was decreed that certain episcopal sees, which had formerly been in small towns and country places, should be placed in the most famous localities. As a result, the cities of Lincoln, Bath, Salisbury, Exeter, Chester and Chichester became noble by the new residence and dwelling of bishops. But the see of Elmham, moved to Thetford, lost its lustre; from there it was afterwards transferred to Norwich by one called Herbert Losinga. Outside the city of Canterbury, on the eastern side, was the church of St Martin, where the seat of a bishop was. This bishop always remained at home or in his retinue, and in all things performed the functions of the archbishop, who frequented the royal court. He took the monks of Christ Church into his service (he himself being a monk), celebrated the solemnities in the metropolitan church, and when these were finished went back to his own church. Here also the prior of Christ Church (whom he called dean) sat in the synods with equal dignity. This custom lasted until the times of the Normans, and the last bishop of it was Godwin. On his death, in the year 1065, Lanfranc refused to appoint a bishop to the church of St Martin, saying that two bishops ought not to be in one city, when in truth the bishop had never been in the city but outside it. Instead of a bishop, he therefore ordained a certain clerk of his as archdeacon, a step he afterwards regretted before his death. Moreover, although Lanfranc had produced many distinguished works in other matters, evidence both of piety and of learning, he nevertheless tried to expel from the see of Worcester Wulstan, a most upright man, second to no one in piety; but he was either hindered by the favour of the whole people, in which Wulstan flourished, or was terrified by that widely publicised miracle, when Wulstan's pastoral staff, fixed in the tomb of Edward the Confessor, was pulled out by no hand or power except Wulstan's own. So he gave up the unseemly enterprise, not without great infamy. Lanfranc was remarkable for his diligence not only in the administration of the Church but also in that of the realm. For while William was absent, all affairs were committed to Lanfranc, who, with the greatest prudence, governed everything and kept the nobles and the common people quietly in their duty, without any movement or tumult. So if any suspicion of revolt or sedition arose, each of the greatest and most powerful men at once gave help and assistance to him in suppressing it. William so relied on his wisdom that he also summoned him to the council of Rouen, which William presided over. Present there were John, Archbishop of Rouen, Odo, Bishop of Bayeux, Hugh of Lisieux, Michael of Avranches, Gilbert of Évreux and Robert of Sées. In this council of Rouen, William settled many matters, no less concerning ecclesiastical affairs than concerning the advantages of the new kingdom of England. But among other things, when Lanfranc saw the rights of his archbishopric torn away from the see and held by other usurpers, he also applied a remedy to heal this evil. For Odo, then Bishop of Bayeux in Normandy and also Earl of Kent, had unjustly seized many estates belonging to the archbishopric; these Lanfranc recovered and restored to the see. And besides those small farms, twenty-five manors of that archbishopric were recovered through his efforts. He also restored the whole church of Christ at Canterbury, which had been falling down and was partly threatening ruin and partly largely burned, and he made it renewed. He founded two hospitals near the city of Canterbury, namely Harbaldown and St John's, one of which was for lepers and the other for the sick, and from the treasury of the archbishop he gave them 140 pounds every year. Moreover, he built the church of St Gregory, in which he placed canons to serve the sick; likewise another church beside the house of the lepers, in which they might serve God and be buried. He was also most generous to the poor, to whom he gave five hundred pounds yearly as alms. And when famine severely pressed England, he sent to London, where he fed as many as a thousand poor people. At his consecration, it was found written above his head, while he sat, that Gospel saying: Give alms, and behold, all things are clean to you; which had earlier shown forth the future liberality of so great a man. He built the cathedral church of Rochester (having pulled down the old one), and enriched it with many generous gifts. He also gladly sought to have the manor of Lambeth, with the patronage of the church, which Countess Godgifu had earlier given to the church of Rochester before the coming of the Normans, joined to that see by the King. But afterwards, by exchange, this manor of Lambeth was granted by King Richard, in the year 1196, to Hubert, then Archbishop, as more convenient for the see of Canterbury; and in its place the manor of Darenth came to the church of Rochester. Gilbert, however, then Bishop of Rochester, was unwilling to consent until he had obtained a certain area beside the church of the blessed Martyrs Stephen and Thomas, on which he built a palace for himself (recently enclosed by a brick wall by John Fisher), which is now called Carlisle Place. And he also took from the church of Lambeth the yearly rent of five marks, which the Bishop of Rochester was accustomed to pay the archbishop each year. When the bishops of Rochester went to London, they were received in the lodging at Lambeth, and from there they were accustomed to take firewood, wood, and other things suitable and convenient for their household. This is clearly declared in the charter of Archbishop Hubert concerning the rector of the church of Lambeth, of the year 1196, confirmed by the Prior and Chapter of Canterbury, with Godfrey, then Bishop of Winchester, bearing witness to it. He was also very generous to the monks of St Albans, to whom he gave a thousand marks, and he acquired the manor of Rochbourne. And although he bore the chief care of the commonwealth, he nevertheless devoted himself assiduously and without intermission to the study of theology, and he gave no less effort to reading than to writing. For from the time he had grown up, his father Haribald and his mother Rosa had diligently arranged his education in this study. Thus he corrected the books of the Old and New Testaments, which had been corrupted by copyists, and published them emended and pure. He also disputed most acutely in writing against Berengar concerning the Eucharist. He published commentaries on the Pauline Epistles and on the Psalms of David, and each year he issued several other short works. He exercised the archiepiscopal jurisdiction, although gently and without open contention, yet most strictly. For, first, having broken the strength of Thomas of York in that controversy about subjection and primacy which was mentioned before, he afterwards managed the affair by his own will. Yet he was never thought to have done injury to anyone. Access to him in conversation was easy for anyone, and he never sent away a sad person; but if he saw someone affected by grief, he carefully inquired into the cause and applied a remedy.

units.la: Anno post suscepturn Archiepiscopatum tertio, Monachi Cant. secularibus omnibus W. Malmuf.
units.tr: In the third year after he took up the archbishopric, the monks of Canterbury, unlike all the secular clergy, (W. Malmesb.)

units.la: {a} Sigebt. Gemblac. no similes, venari, aucupari & genio indulgere consueuerunt, vt illos conisles magis qui Monachos, ob seruorum ingentem cateruam censeres, quorum insolentia Lanfrancus austeritate sua paulatim repressit & extinxit. Eodem etiam anno Lanfrancus Petrum quendam Lichefeldensem seu Ceftrensem Episcopum Colceftriæ consecrauit, & anno sequenti Patricium Dublinensem, in Hibernia Episcopum Londini.
units.tr: Sigebert of Gembloux: they were accustomed to hunt, to fowl and to indulge their appetites, so that one would have judged them more like laymen than monks, because of the huge crowd of their servants. Lanfranc gradually repressed and extinguished their insolence by his severity. In the same year Lanfranc consecrated a certain Peter, bishop of Lichfield or Chester, at Coventry, and in the following year he consecrated Patrick, bishop of Dublin in Ireland, at London.

units.la: Sexto anno celebrabatur Concilium apud Winton. in hæc verba anno ab incarnatione Domini. 1076. Indictione. 14. regnante in Britannia gloriosissimo Rege Wilhelmo, Præsidente Cantuariæ Lanfranco totius Britanniæ Primate, in Eboraco vero Thoma Archiepiscopo, eo inquam Anno in Kalend. Aprilis habita est Synodus Wintoniæ conuocata ab eode Cant. Ecclesiæ Primate. In qua fratris nostri Ailrici Cicefi quodam Episc. causa canonice definita, & ad certum finem perducta est. Decretumque est vt nullus Canonicus vxorem habeat. Sacerdotum verò in castellis vel in vicis habitantium habentes vxores non coguntur vt habeant, & deinceps caueant Episcopi, vt sacerdotes vel diaconos non præsumant ordinare, nisi prius profiteantur, vt vxores non habeant. Nullusque Clericus aut Monachus in Episcopatu alicuius iuscipiatur, absque Episcopi sui literis. Si quis vero Monachus etiam Canonice susceptus fuerit, non permittatur Ecclesiis publice dicseruire, &c. Statutum est etiam ne aliquis Clericus ciuilis vel Rusticus, de beneficio Ecclesiæ aliquod seruitium reddat præter illud quod fecit tempore Regis Edwardi. Laici vero si de crimine suo accusati fuerint, & Episcopo suo obedire noluerint, vocentur semel, & iterum, & tertio. Si post tertiam vocationem emendarinoluerint, excommunicentur. Si autem post excommunicationem ac satisfactionem venerint, foris factuam suam quæ Anglice vocatur ofterpomeffic fcu lafeltte, pro vnaquaque vocatione Episcopo suo reddant. Præterea statutum est, vt nullus filiam suam, vel cognatam det alicui absque benedictione sacerdotali. Si alter fecerit, non vt legitimum coniugium, sed vt fornicatorium iudicabitur. Supplantationes vero Ecclesiarum omnibus modis interdicimus.
units.tr: In the sixth year a council was held at Winchester, in these words: in the year of the Lord's incarnation 1076, in the fourteenth indiction, while the most glorious King William reigned in Britain, with Lanfranc presiding at Canterbury as primate of all Britain, and Thomas being archbishop at York. In that year, on the first day of April, a synod was held at Winchester, convened by the same primate of the Church of Canterbury. At it the cause of our brother Ailric, a certain bishop of Chichester, was canonically decided and brought to a definite end. It was decreed that no canon should have a wife. Priests who live in castles or villages and have wives are not to be compelled to put them away; but from now on the bishops are to take care not to presume to ordain priests or deacons unless they first promise that they will have no wives. No clergyman or monk shall be received into any bishop's diocese without the letters of his own bishop. If any monk has been received canonically, he is not to be permitted to serve publicly in churches, etc. It was also decreed that no clerk, whether civil or rustic, should render any service for a church benefice beyond what he rendered in the time of King Edward. As for laymen, if they are accused of a crime and refuse to obey their bishop, they are to be summoned once, a second time and a third time. If after the third summons they will not amend, they are to be excommunicated. If after excommunication and satisfaction they come back, they are to pay their bishop, for each summons, the fine for their offence, which in English is called ofterpomeffic or lafeltte. Moreover it was decreed that no one may give his daughter or kinswoman to anyone without a priestly blessing; if anyone does so, the union will be judged not a lawful marriage but fornication. We forbid by all means the supplanting of churches.

units.la: Eodem anno Hernosto Cantuariensi Monacho Roffensem Episcopatum dedit, & Londini consecrauit.
units.tr: In the same year he gave the Roffen bishopric to Hernost, a monk of Canterbury, and consecrated him at London.

units.la: Anno 11. mortuo Hernosto Episcopatum Roffensem in Gundolphum alium Cantuariensem Monachum contulit, quem Cantuariæ consecrauit.
units.tr: In the eleventh year, after Hernost died, he transferred the bishopric of Rochester to Gundulf, another monk of Canterbury, whom he consecrated at Canterbury.

units.la: Eodem anno Thomas Eboracensis per literas eum rogauit, vt duos ex Cantuariensi prouincia Episcopos ad consecrandum quendam in Orchadibus, iuxta Scotiam Insulis postulatum Episcopum mitteret. Qui Wulstanum Wigorniensem & Petrum Ceftrensem ad hoc munus legauit.
units.tr: In the same year Thomas of York asked him by letter to send two bishops from the province of Canterbury to consecrate a man who had been nominated bishop of the Orkneys, islands near Scotland. He sent Wulstan of Worcester and Peter of Chester for this task.

units.la: Octauo anno publico Cleri concilio Londini inito, Ailnodum Glastinensem Abbatem deposuit.
units.tr: In the eighth year, after a public council of the clergy had been held at London, he deposed Ailnoth, abbot of Glastonbury.

units.la: Vndecimo, Wilhelmum Dunelmensem Episcopum in quadam Claudiæ ciuitate, ad Eboracensem Archiepiscopatu visitato ritu transtulit, iubente id Regc, & sc consentiente, eo quod a Scotorum Episcopis, qui subiecti sunt, habere sibi adiutorium non potuit.
units.tr: In the eleventh year, following the ritual that had been observed, he translated William, bishop of Durham, to the archbishopric of York in a certain city of Clavia; this was done by the king's command and with William's own consent, because he could not have help from the bishops of the Scots, who were subject to him.

units.la: Decimo sexto anno donatum Monachum suum Cantuariensem Dublinia Episcopum solitis sacris instituit.
units.tr: In the sixteenth year he installed with the usual sacred rites a monk of his own of Canterbury, who had been given the bishopric of Dublin.

units.la: Eodemque anno Concilio Deuceftriæ habito Wlfleceteu Exulandensis cœnobii Abbatem priuauit, & Robertum Ceftrensem, Willielmumque Helmeancnsem vno die Cantuariæ consecrauit, & paulo post Mauricium Londinensem Episcopum Wintoniæ similibus sacris firmauit.
units.tr: In the same year, at a council held at Dorchester, he deprived Wulfsige, abbot of the monastery of Exeter [Exulandum], and on one day at Canterbury he consecrated Robert of Chester and William of Hereford; shortly afterwards he confirmed Maurice, bishop of London, at Winchester with similar rites.

units.la: Decimo octauo anno mortuo Willielmo Rege in transmarinis partibus, filiu eius Willielmum iuxta patris institutum in Regem elegit, quem in Ecclesia Petri in occidentali parte Londoniæ sita sacrauit & coronauit. Quo etiam anno Godfredum Ciceftrensem, Iobannem Wellensem Episcopos, & Guidonem Ecclesiæ Augustinensis Abbatem Cantuariæ sacrauit. Monachi vero huic Guidoni valde restiterunt, vt necesse Lanfrancus postridie fuerat, adiuncto sibi Odone Baiocensi Episcopo Regis fratre, qui tunc è Normannia Cantuariam venerat ad Augustinense cœnobium, sacratum nuper Abbatem ducere, & Monachis acriter imperare, vt eum suscipferent, eique obtemperarent, iussis his qui obstare vellent, ilico exire, & Monasterio cedere : Paucis itaque reliftis reliquì dicedebant. His qui remanserant præsentibus, Lanfrancus Abbatem honorifice in sede locauit. Quod ipse facere coactus est, quia Elwicini Prioris operatune interalios contumaces ad id haberi non poterat. Quem cum nonnullis aliis delicti authoribus Cantuarienf. carcerihus custodiri iussit Lanfrancus. Quo facto nuncl tum est ei cæteros abire iussos, sub castro (ad Ecclesiam Sanctæ Miltrudis posito) con-sedisse. sedisse. His nunciatum ab eo est, si delicti veniam petituri ante horam nonam ad Monasterium sponte redirent, impunitos fore. Ea vero bora praeterita,non vt liberos sed vt fugitiuos reducendos.Itaque dubii & suspensi animis,irent an redirent,seu fame coacti, seu sponte adducti maior eorum pars pettunaeiæ pertæsa,obedientiam Abbati promisit. Qui reuersi super Augustini rumulũ(quod sacramẽti loco babebatur)Guidoni obedientia iureiurãdo profesi sunt reliquos vt trâsfugas cepit,& huc illuc in Ecclesiis sparsos ac diffusos vinculis coppedibusq; tenuit, donec ad subiectionẽ iurãdâ eogeretur, postea§ locis separatos reduxit Caor. Sed b uius differentionis semitula postbas sumptas poenas in cineribus permansit.Columbanus enim Monachus mortem Abbatis clam mioatus,deprebenssus & ad Lanfrancum adductus est.Is in quaestione rogatus,an Abbatem voluerit interimere, respondit,id te praesto facturum,si in sua esset potestate. Quo audito ante Monasterii portas, populo inspectante ligarus, flagellis caesus, ac abrasis & amputaris crinibus, Monasterio & vrbe exclusus, ignominiose dimissus. Huius vindicta caeterum audacia repressa est.Verum post Lanfranci obitum, qui illico, vt videtur, post hanc remgestam contigit,Monachi cum ciuibus quibusdam coniuncti & conspiraniei,Guidonem domi interficere tentabant. Cuius familia cum defensionem pararet, pluribus vtrinque vulneratis,&aliquibus caesis,Abbas in Ecclesiam aegre profugit.Quod facinus cum percrebuisset,missi sunt à Rege Cantuarium,Willelmus Wentanus, & Gundolphus Rofsensis Episcopi,cum aliis regni proceribus de eo cogniturj, & supplicia de reis sumpturi. Monachi rei reperti & iudicati sunt. Quos maioribus criminis reos, cum legati publica poena,iuxta delicti qualitatem corrigere vellent, prior & caeteri Monachi qui in eulpabiles fuerunt restituere & inercesserent,ne ratione buiusmodi infames, populoq; desipicabiles haberentur. Itaque occultis poenis teortum a populo plectebantur, & ex Augustinensi Monasterio eiecti, & viritim in singula Monasteria dispersi,eorum loco xxiiij. noui Monachi suffecti sunt. Ciues vero armata manu Monasterium ingressi effossis oculis exciaiaem poeam tulerunt.
units.tr: In the eighteenth year, after King William died in the transmarine parts, he chose his son William as king, according to the father's appointment, and he anointed and crowned him in the church of St Peter in the western part of London. In the same year he consecrated Godfrey, bishop of Chichester, John, bishop of Wells, and Guy, abbot of the church of St Augustine at Canterbury. The monks, however, strongly resisted this Guy, so that Lanfranc was obliged the next day, with Odo, bishop of Bayeux and the king's brother, who had then come from Normandy to Canterbury, to lead the newly consecrated abbot to the Augustinian monastery and to command the monks sharply to receive him and obey him, and to order those who wished to oppose him to leave at once and give up the monastery. Few therefore resisted, and the rest withdrew. Lanfranc seated the abbot honourably in his chair in the presence of those who had stayed. He was forced to do this because Elwin, the prior, could not be found among the other obstinate men. Lanfranc ordered him to be kept in the Canterbury prison, together with some other authors of the offence. Then the others who had been ordered to leave were told that they should withdraw under the castle, at the church of St Mildred. It was announced to them that if they came back of their own accord to the monastery before the ninth hour, to ask pardon for their offence, they would go unpunished; but after that hour had passed they would be brought back not as free men but as fugitives. Torn and uncertain in mind whether to go or return, and partly driven by hunger, partly by their own will, the greater part of them, weary of the wandering, promised obedience to the abbot. Returning, they swore an oath of obedience to Guy upon the mound of St Augustine, which was held to be in the place of a sacrament. Those who had not returned he seized as deserters, and he kept them scattered and dispersed through various churches, in chains and fetters, until they were forced to swear submission; afterwards he brought them back, separated by places. But the traces of this dispute remained in the ashes of the punishments taken afterwards. For the monk Columbanus, who had secretly threatened the abbot's death, was caught and brought to Lanfranc. Under questioning, when asked whether he had wished to kill the abbot, he answered that he would have done it immediately if it had been in his power. Upon hearing this he was bound before the gates of the monastery, in view of the people, beaten with whips, shaved and stripped of his hair, shut out of the monastery and the city, and dismissed in disgrace. The vengeance on him repressed the boldness of the rest. But after Lanfranc's death, which came, as it seems, shortly after these events, the monks, joined with certain citizens and in conspiracy, tried to kill Guy in his house. When his household prepared to defend him, many were wounded on both sides and some were killed, and the abbot barely escaped into the church. When this crime had become widely known, William of Winchester and Gundulf of Rochester, bishops, were sent by the king to Canterbury with other nobles of the realm to inquire into the matter and to take punishment from the guilty. The monks were found guilty and condemned. When the legates wanted to correct those who were charged with greater crimes by public punishment, in proportion to the nature of the offence, the prior and the other monks who had been most at fault resisted and interceded, lest they be held infamous and despicable to the people on account of such a judgment.
