So they were punished with hidden penalties, as if by the people, and, cast out of the monastery of St Augustine and scattered one by one into single monasteries, twenty-four new monks were put in their place. The citizens, however, entered the monastery with armed hands, put out eyes, and bore the other punishment.

units.la: Incertum est,quid Monachorum & ciuium odium in Guidonem cogitauerat. Sed verisimile est,Lanfrancum contra illos, quieì, cuius studuerat resisterant, nimis a erem & vehementiùs fuisse,vt ne repulsam quidem æquo animo ferre potuisset. Nam que Scollando quodam Abbate Augustineofi mortuo , summa ope & contentione nitebatur, vt Monachus quidam sibi charus eligeretur ,quod cùm authoritate nec precibus obtinere poterat,rem (quod turpe dictu est ) tentauit pecunia, vt Monachos corrumperet . ad extremum aggressus magna interceßione Regem, nihil profecit. Sed eius mandato alium doctrina celebrem ,à Monacbis electum inuitus sacrauit. Regi nihilominus intimus & charissimus, populoque gratiosus , de Willielmo Rufo(quem in militia educauerat) Rege post patrem creando, etsi fratri minor natu esset,suasit,de quo pariter & iniuria Wulftano illata, etsi caetera cunÊta fœlicit er gessisset, male audiebat. Itaque Gulielmo conquestore moriuo Rufus successit, & à Lanfranco Cantuariensi, Thoma Eboracensi Archiepiscopis, nec nona Londinensi Episcopo vnctus & creatus est. Sed Lanfrancus ab hoc Rufo aduersi aliquid sensit, fortasse quod ituenilem eius animum in armis & re militari ante sub eo exercitatum, iam Regem, fano consilio ad amorem & timorem Dei, virtutemq; vehementius hortatus sit. Nam in exilium actus Romam profectus est , & varias regiones in exilio peragrans , charta no de quadam quali diuinitus lapsa est in manus Clerici, in qua scriptum erat: Gulielmus Rufus occisus est: quod postea contigit. Namque baud ita multo post allatum nuncium est et de Russi morte,qua intellecta. ad sedem Cantuariensem reuersus est,ibi que cum annis nouendecim sedisset,Archiepiscopatus muneribus,& huius vitæ molestiis perfunctus, febri quemadmodum optauerat laboransobiit,4.Iunii, Anno Domini 1088.vacauit sedes 4.annis.
units.tr: It is uncertain what hatred of the monks and citizens was directed against Guy. But it is likely that Lanfranc was too harsh and too vehement against those who resisted what he had wished, so that he could not bear even a refusal with an even mind. For after the death of Scolland, abbot of St Augustine's, he strove with the greatest effort and contention that a certain monk dear to him should be chosen; when he could not obtain this by authority or prayers, he tried the matter with money, which is shameful to say, to corrupt the monks. Finally, having made a great intercession with the king, he gained nothing. By his command, however, he unwillingly consecrated another man, famous for learning, chosen by the monks. Nevertheless, dear and most intimate with the king and gracious to the people, he persuaded the king, after the father, to appoint William Rufus (whom he had brought up in the military life), though he was younger than his brother; for this, and for the wrong done to Wulfstan, though he had otherwise managed everything happily, he was ill spoken of. So when William the Conqueror died, Rufus succeeded, and he was anointed and created king by Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas, archbishop of York, and also the bishop of London. But Lanfranc sensed some hostility from this Rufus, perhaps because he had exhorted more vehemently, with sound counsel, to the love and fear of God and to virtue, the king's spirit, which was fierce and had been trained in arms and the soldier's life under him. For Lanfranc was driven into exile, went to Rome, and while wandering through various regions in exile, a certain paper fell by some divine chance into the hands of a clerk, on which was written: William Rufus has been killed; which later came to pass. For not long afterwards news was brought of Rufus's death; when this was known, he returned to the see of Canterbury, and after sitting there for nineteen years, having finished the labours of the archbishopric and the troubles of this life, he died of a fever, as he had wished, on 4 June, in the year of the Lord 1088. The see was vacant for four years.

units.la: XXXIV. ANSELMVS.
units.tr: XXXIV. Anselm.

units.la: Nselmus ex Augusta Burgundiæ ciuitate ad Alpium radices positaoriundus, ac illustribus parentibus,Gundulfo patre,ac Heinebergamaire prognatus,& a puericia ingenuè, liberaliterque instituturus, ad Beccense Coenobium, permotus Lanfranci fama, discendiqueꝛ studio venit: Ibi ætatis suæ anno 17. primum fit Monachus, deinde Lanfrancο ad Cadoniensem Abbatiam præfectο, in Beccensi prioratu successit, in quo ordine quindecim annis fietit. Tum Eluino Beccensi Abbate mortuo, Anselmus Abbas creatur: quem gradum quindecim etiam annis gessit. Tandem ab Hugone Cestriæ Comite graviter ægrotante, ecclesiæ britate sui nominis peruulgata, in Anglia accersitus venit, vt quædam illius Comitis negocia procuraret, & Ceitrenlis Monasterii cœtum, exclusis sacerdotibus Monachis compleret. Dequo cum Wilhelmus Rufus accepisset, cum Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum nominauit. Omnes autem Archiepiscopatus proventus toto quadriennio Rex perceperat, plurimasque Ecclesias venales habuerat, & triginta Cæmeteria in feramrum pascua redegerat, & Ecclesiarum vacantium fructus sibi reseruauerat. Cuius lucri suauitatem, cum vel prorsus amittendam, vt valde minuendam ex Archiepiscopatus concessione senserat, pœnituit eum illico huius tam promptæ & propensæ in Anselmum beneficentiæ. Itaque vt eius animum a suscipiendo oblato Archiepiscopatu auerteret, simulate primo expositi: etsi amore & meritus eius ductus Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum ipsi contulisset, tamen se iam cernere, grauitatem & magnitudinem Prouinciæ Cantuariensis maiorem esse, quam quæ ab homine Monasticis occupationibus, vigiliis, lucubrationibusq; diuinis dedito, perferri ac sustentari posset. Sed cum neq; hac suauione quicquam protecisset, prouque certo comperisset, Proceres, populumque Angliæ aduersos, aut minus fidos sibi, Anselmo fauere, eumque ad Archiepiscopi munus iam oblatum flagitare, aperte contradicere noluit: verumtamen excepit possessiones rerum Ecclesiasticarum, quas illo vocationis quadriennio fecerat, vt Anselmi quoque authoritate & sententia ratæ essent. Ad quæ Anselmus nolle se dixit illi Ecclesiæ nocere, in quam officii nihil contulisset. Itaque eum Archiepiscopatum deferre noluit, Abbatiam Beccensem, obtenta Rothomagensis Episcopi licentia (in cuius dioecesi fuit) sponte sed non sine vberioris spei causa deserens, Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis à Walkelino Wintoniensi tum Episcopo confirmatur, fidelitatemque Rufo Regi de more fecit. Tum vero in ea sede locatus & constitutus cepit Regem liberius atque ieuctius de tam nexplebili cupiditate, & rapina bonorum Ecclesiasticorum admonere, qua nihil post se esse certius, quod tot cœmiteria feris ipsis ob ruinam Ecclesiarum compascua fecisset. Sed cum suis precibus & exhortationibus de Regis animo spem nullam concipere potuit. Set, veniam petiit Romam eundi pro obtinendo ab Vrbano Papa pallio. Qua sive petitione, siue nominatione turbatus & accensus vehementer Rex asseruit & acriter contendit, hoc Anselmum contra suæ fidelitatis promissæ fœdus fecisse: fuisse enim a patre suo decretum, ne quisquam quia a Rege nuncupatus non esset, in Anglia regno eo Papæ nomine censeretur: & qui secus fecisset, læsæ maiestatis reum Regiqueinimicum, quod regni consuetudinem violaret, iudicandum. Huius vero rei veritatem Edmerus his verbis describit. Regè de transmarege regressum Anselmus adiit, & vt sibi Romæ ad Papam Vrbanum pro stola sui Archiepiscopatus eundi licentiam daret, humiliter petit. At ille ad nomen Vrbani turbatus, dixit se illum pro Papa non tenere, nec suæ consuetudinis esse, vt absque sua electione alicui liceret in regno suo Papam nominare. Hinc igitur orta quæ40 dam grauis dissensio est, sed in aliud tempus disicutienda est dilata. Iubet ergo vt totius Angliæ Episcopi, Abbates & Principes ad diffusionem diuisi huius apud castrum quod Rochingam dicitur, vna veniant: factum est: & terria septima quadragesimæ iuxta edictum conuenerunt. Causa in medium ducitur, & Anselmus diuersis quærelis hinc inde concutitur. Siquidem multi, sed maxime Episcopi, Regii voluntati fauere volentes spreto æquitatis iudicio, id probare nitebantur: quod Anselmus salua fide quam Regi debebat, nullatenus posset in Regno ipsius, Vrbanum sedis Apostolicæ præsumsulem pro Papa tenere. Quibus cum plura, quæ ratio tulerat, obiecta fuisset, & Anselmus eos ex vetibus Domini; Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari, & quæ sunt Dei, Deo: aliiisque nonnullis, quæ ratio nulla refellere posset, penitus in fronnasset, illi e con50 tra quod dicere non habentes, cum in Regem blasphemare vno strepitu clamauere quadduplicē ausus erat in regno eius (nisi eo cœdente) quieq̃ vel Deo ascribere. Igitur ad vnam regiæ indignationis vocem, quidam ex Episcopis Archiepiscopo suo atque primatì, omnem subiectionem atque professam obedientiam, vno impetu abnegant, eique vnitatem fraternæ societatis pari voto miserandi abiurant. Quidam vero in eis tantum quæ ex parte Vrbani Papæ præciperet, illi se negant obedituros Episcopi. Itaque omnes (Roffensi solo excepto) aut vnoaut alio modo debitam illi subiectionem & obedientiam abnegarunt. Rex etiam ipse cunctam ei confidentiam & securitatem in suis ombib. ademit, nec se illum pro Archiepiscopo vel patre amplius habituram iurat, nihil ipse Vicario beatt beati Perti vterius obediturum statim deneget. Tres dies in isto negocio clamoribus in Anselmium & coutumeliis grauidi expensi sunt, tandem in hoc fine concluduntur.
units.tr: Anselm, born in the city of Aosta in Burgundy, which lies at the foot of the Alps, was of illustrious parents, Gundulf his father and Ermenberga his mother. From boyhood he was given a free and liberal education, and, moved by the fame of Lanfranc and by his desire to learn, he came to the monastery at Bec. There, in his seventeenth year, he became a monk. Later, when Lanfranc was made abbot of Caen, Anselm succeeded him as prior of Bec, a position he held for fifteen years. Then, after the death of Herluin, abbot of Bec, Anselm was created abbot, an office he also held for fifteen years. At last Hugh, Earl of Chester, fell seriously ill. Anselm's name had become widely known in the Church, and he was summoned to England to manage some of the Earl's affairs and to fill the community of the monastery of Chester, from which secular priests were to be excluded and monks installed in their place. When William Rufus heard of this, he nominated Anselm to the see of Canterbury. The King had received all the revenues of the archbishopric for the whole four years of its vacancy. He had also kept many churches for sale, had turned thirty cemeteries into pasture for wild beasts, and had kept for himself the revenues of vacant churches. When he realised that the sweetness of this gain would be entirely lost, or greatly reduced, by granting the archbishopric, he regretted at once his prompt and eager generosity towards Anselm. So, in order to turn Anselm's mind away from accepting the archbishopric that had been offered him, he first pretended that, although he had conferred the see of Canterbury on him out of affection and because of his merits, he now saw that the burden and greatness of the province of Canterbury were too great to be borne and sustained by a man devoted to monastic duties, to vigils and to divine studies. But when he had gained nothing by this pretence, and had learned for certain that the nobles and people of England, who were hostile to him or less loyal to him, favoured Anselm and demanded that he accept the archbishopric now offered to him, he did not wish to oppose them openly. Nevertheless, he kept the possessions of Church property that he had acquired during those four years of vacancy, so that they would be confirmed by Anselm's authority and consent as well. To this Anselm replied that he was unwilling to harm that Church, to which he had contributed nothing by his service. So he chose not to accept the archbishopric, and, having obtained the permission of the Bishop of Rouen, in whose diocese Bec lay, he left the abbey of Bec of his own accord, though not without greater hope of gain. The Archbishop of Canterbury was then confirmed by Walkelin, Bishop of Winchester, and did homage to King William Rufus in the customary manner. Then, once settled and established in that see, he began to admonish the King more freely and more sharply about his insatiable greed and his plundering of Church goods. He said that nothing was more certain than that the King, by ruining the churches, had turned so many cemeteries into pasture for wild beasts. But by his prayers and exhortations he could conceive no hope of changing the King's mind. Instead, he sought leave to go to Rome to obtain the pallium from Pope Urban. The King, disturbed and greatly inflamed by this request, or rather by this nomination, insisted sharply that Anselm had acted against the covenant of loyalty he had promised. For his father had decreed that no one who had not been named by the King should be recognised in the kingdom of England as Pope, and anyone who acted otherwise was to be judged guilty of treason and an enemy of the King, because he violated the custom of the realm. Edmer describes the truth of this matter in these words: "Anselm, having returned from overseas, went to the King and humbly asked for permission to go to Rome to Pope Urban, to receive the pallium for his archbishopric. But the King, troubled at the name of Urban, said that he did not acknowledge him as Pope, and that it was not the custom of his realm for anyone to name a Pope without his election." From this a serious dispute arose, but since it had to be discussed at another time, it was postponed. The King therefore ordered all the bishops, abbots and princes of England to come together at the castle called Rockingham, to deal with the matter. It was done, and on the seventh day of the fortieth (fourth) week of Lent, in accordance with the edict, they assembled. The case was brought before them, and Anselm was assailed on all sides by various complaints. Many, and especially the bishops, eager to favour the King's will, disregarding the judgement of justice, strove to prove that Anselm, without breaking the loyalty he owed the King, could not in the King's kingdom hold Urban, the bishop of the apostolic see, as Pope. When many arguments that reason suggested had been put to him, Anselm refuted them from the words of the Lord: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's," and from several other points that no reasoning could overturn. They, having nothing to say in reply, cried out with one voice that he had dared, in the King's kingdom, to ascribe anything to anyone except the King, and so they blasphemed against the King. At the single voice of royal indignation, some of the bishops, with one impulse, renounced all subjection and the obedience they had professed to their archbishop and primate, and with equal eagerness they abjured the unity of fraternal fellowship with him. Some of them, however, declared that they would not obey him in matters that came from Pope Urban. Thus all the bishops, except the Bishop of Rochester alone, in one way or another renounced the due subjection and obedience owed to him. The King himself took away from him all trust and security in his affairs, and swore that he would no longer regard him as archbishop or as a father, and at once declared that he would no longer obey him in anything, nor the vicar of the blessed Peter. For three days this business was spent in clamour against Anselm and in insults, and at last the matter was brought to this conclusion.

units.la: At Anselmus in suo proposito constans, postulat à Rege, vt tutus Regno discedat, quo sibi negato, factæ sunt utrinque induciæ ad Pentecosten, & plena pax & tranquillitas promissa. Nihilominus Anselmus, hominibus suis captis & spoliatis, terrisque vastatis in immensum afflictus est. Post hæc tamen Vrbanum per Walterum Albanensem Episcopum (qui pallium Anselmo à Roma Cantuariam detulit) pro Papa susceptus. Cuius stilus etsi Vrbano & Anselmo aduersus Regem & præla-tos benignior est, tamen oste ndit nō esse nouum, Papalem iurisdictionem ab Angliæ Regibus recusari. In hac autem tractanda controuersia, Rex cum Vrbano Papa priuatim egit de Anselmo ab Anglia penitus abducendo. Sed cum obeximiam viri doctrinam, morumque probitatem id efficere non poterat, Anselmus accepto iam pallio Archiepiscopalem curam & authoritatem Regę conniuente exercuit, & Samuelem quendam Dublinensem Archiepiscopum, Malchumque Waterfordiensem primum Episcopum, ad Regis Muriercdach populique in Hibernia petitionem, aliosque Episcopos, accepta subiectionis prosessione Lamethi consecravit. Sed post Cambrensem expeditionem reuersus Rex expostulari cum Anselmo cepit, de militibus ab eo missis, ad tantum gerendum bellum parum idoneis, & nova crimina inferre de his, quæ Anselmus de Ecclesiastica libertate recuperanda atq; retinenda, nec no de vastitate & ruina Ecclesiarum quæ Regis inuasione acciderant, liberius & palam & secum priuatim egisset. Quibus suis factis recessit is, datur illico Anselmo vtriusque rei facultas atq; optio, suae manendi in Regno Angliæ, cum ea præstatione fidelitatis & obsequii Regi, quam iurisiurandi sacramento promiserat, & a superioribus Archiepiscopis præstari consuevit, & ne quacunque de re ad Papam de Rege prouocaret, & ad sedem Apostolicam appellaret. vel ex Angliæ regno discedendi. (quod homini peregrino atq; adueuę difficile non fuerat.) Itaque Anselmus constitutis sibi vndecim dierum induciis, intra quos confectis rationibus suis transferretur. ego (in quit Regi & Proceribus) vado, vobis tamen benedictionem meam, si non contemnitis, impertior. Quam cum le Rex non spreturum dixit. Anselmus ei leuata dextra benedixit, & Cantuariam discessit, ibi quatuordecim dies manst. Et postridie nauem Doueri conscensurus (tanquam insignis alicuius criminis reus,) à quodam Wilhelmo Clerico Regis ad nuncio detinctur, donec magna plebis astante corona, supellectilę fuatota petitrutata, bonis omnibus exutus, superato mari, alieno littori nudus expositus est. Post eius discessum, Rex proscripsit omnia, quę Anselmi iuris erant, & in sunm dominium transtulit, & quæcunque statuerat, irrita pronunciauit. Anselmus autem Lugdunum perrexit. Inde Romam à Papa accersitus, qui perbenigno eum hospitio accepit. Inter Romam venit Wilhelmus, qui Anselmum in littore discedentem scrutatus est, Regis ad Papam legatus, vt de Anselmi causa inducias ad sequentem Michaelis Archa- gelì festum impetraret. Quo concesso, Anselmus id ægrè ferens, Lugdunum reuertit constituit. sed à Papa ad Concilium, quod tum conuocatum fuit, retentus est. Inter cæteras illius Concilii sanctiones, excommunicationis sententia lata est, tam in laicos Ecclesiarum inuestituras dantes, quàm in Clericos easdē à laicis accipientes. Et pendētibus de Anselmi causa inducijs obiit Papa, & paulò post Rufus Rex, qui se viuente nec Synodos Ecclesiasticas ad vitia corrigenda celebrari, nec plurimas Ecclesias a Clericis possideri permisit, sed earum fructus percepit, iocosé semper hoc vetsuilludens toti clero. Panis Christi, panis piuguis est. Rufo autem mortuo, successit frater eius Henricus, à Mauricio Londinensi Episcopo consecratus, qui calamitosum & disceptatum à fratre Ecclesiæ statum refarciuit, Anselmum ab exilio reuocauit, eique procurationem Ecclesiasticam commisit. Quantum autē Anselmo fauerit, ex suo ad Londinenses de Anselmi seruorum & famulorum immunitate, eosque bene humaniterque tractando misso diplomate, quo petit vt Anselmus ac sui tam liberi & quieti esse possint, ac Lanfrancus eū suis fuerit, vt è concessione Wilhelmi Conquestoris intelligi potest. Et vt perspiciamus quam fuerit illa etsa aperta & simplex, minimeque prolixa & curiosa verbis, non erit alicunum ipsum diploma latinè Anglicèque scriptum verbatim insercre, quod totum in vtraque lingua comprehensum, ne palmæ latitudinem attingit. Magnum autem Regis sigillum, quod nunc in fine diplomatum appendi solet, in hoc antiquo diplomate ad modicam membranæ partem paulatum extensam & excisam ex diplomatis sinistra latere adhærebat. Sigilla vero antiquitus diplomatibus Regis non appendebant, quod tamen ab Edwardo Regum Angliæ primo inductum fuit, qui chartis suis adueritatis testimonium ceram impreslam appendebat.
units.tr: But Anselm, steadfast in his purpose, asked the king that he might leave the kingdom in safety. When this was refused, a truce was made on both sides until Pentecost, and full peace and tranquillity were promised. Nevertheless, Anselm, his men having been seized and robbed and his lands laid waste, was reduced to immense distress. After this, however, he was received as pope by Urban, through Walter, bishop of Albano, who brought the pallium from Rome to Canterbury for Anselm. Although this letter of Urban's is more kindly towards Urban and Anselm, and against the king and the prelates, it shows that it was not new for the papal jurisdiction to be refused by the kings of England. In handling this dispute, the king dealt privately with Pope Urban about removing Anselm from England altogether. But since he could not bring this about through the learning and integrity of the man, Anselm, having now received the pallium, exercised the archiepiscopal care and authority, the king connivingly allowing it. With the consent of King Muirchertach and the people of Ireland, he consecrated Samuel, a certain archbishop of Dublin, and Malchus, the first bishop of Waterford, and other bishops, at Lambeth, after receiving their profession of subjection. But after the Welsh expedition the king, on his return, began to complain to Anselm about the soldiers he had sent, who were little fit for waging so great a war, and to bring new charges about what Anselm had said more freely, openly and privately to the king himself, concerning the recovery and retention of ecclesiastical liberty, and also concerning the devastation and ruin of churches which had come about through the king's invasion. When the king had said these things and withdrawn, Anselm was at once given the choice of two things: either to remain in the kingdom of England, with that profession of fealty and obedience to the king which he had promised under oath, as the earlier archbishops were accustomed to make, and not to appeal to the pope or to the apostolic see concerning the king on any matter; or else to leave the kingdom of England (which for a foreigner and newcomer would not have been difficult). So Anselm, given eleven days' truce, within which he might settle his affairs and be transported, said to the king and the nobles: "I am going, but to you I impart my blessing, if you do not despise it." When the king said that he would not spurn it, Anselm lifted his right hand and blessed him, and he left for Canterbury, where he stayed fourteen days. On the following day, as he was about to go on board ship at Dover, he was detained as if guilty of some notable crime by a certain William, a clerk and messenger of the king, until, with a great crowd of people standing around, all his goods were taken away, and he, stripped of everything, was carried across the sea and set down naked on a foreign shore. After his departure, the king proscribed all that belonged to Anselm's rights, transferred it to his own lordship, and declared null whatever he had decreed. Anselm, however, went on to Lyons. From there he was summoned to Rome by the pope, who received him with the most kindly hospitality. Meanwhile William came to Rome, the king's envoy to the pope, who had watched Anselm departing from the shore, to obtain from the pope a postponement concerning Anselm's case until the following feast of Michael the Archangel. When this was granted, Anselm, taking it badly, resolved to return to Lyons. But he was detained by the pope for the council which was then convened. Among the other decrees of that council, a sentence of excommunication was pronounced against laymen who gave investitures of churches, as well as against clerics who received those investitures from laymen. While the postponement of Anselm's case was pending, the pope died, and shortly afterwards King William Rufus, who during his lifetime allowed neither ecclesiastical synods to be held for correcting vices, nor most churches to be held by clerics, but took their revenues, and always jested about this, saying to the whole clergy: "The bread of Christ is fat bread." But when Rufus died, his brother Henry succeeded him. He was consecrated by Maurice, bishop of London, and he repaired the church's state, which had been made wretched and disputed by his brother. He recalled Anselm from exile and committed the ecclesiastical administration to him. How much he favoured Anselm may be understood from his charter sent to the Londoners concerning the immunity of Anselm's servants and attendants, and from his treating them well and kindly, by which he asks that Anselm and his people may be free and at peace, and that Lanfranc may be with them, as can be understood from the grant of William the Conqueror. And so that we may see how plain and simple that document was, and very brief and not elaborate in its words, it will not be out of place to insert the charter itself verbatim, written in Latin and English, which, all contained in either language, does not fill a palm's breadth. The great seal of the king, which is now usually appended at the end of charters, was attached in this old charter, having been partly drawn out and cut from a small part of the parchment, on the left side of the charter. Seals, however, were not appended to royal charters in ancient times; this practice was introduced by Edward, the first king of the English, who appended a wax impression as a witness of truth to his charters.

units.la: HRex Anglorum, Huge de Boclande, & W. Baignardo, & omnibus ministris meis Londoniæ.sal. Præcipio & volo vt omnes homines Anglinii Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi quos in Londonia habet, & omnes qui in ea villa esse & iacentes ... ea melius & quietius habuit tempore patris mei, & videte ne eis vllam iniuriam faciatis. Teste Hug Comite de Cestra apud Westmonster.
units.tr: Henry, King of the English, to Hugh de Boclande, W. Baignard, and all my ministers in London, greeting. I command and wish that all the men of the Archbishop of Canterbury at Lenham [Anglinii] whom he has in London, and all who are in that town and lying there, shall have and hold it better and more quietly than they did in the time of my father; and see that you do them no injury. Witness Hugh, Earl of Chester, at Westminster.

units.la: Anselmus vero Ecclesiasticam suâ procurationem diligenter exercens totius Cleri Synodum Londini conuocauit, in qua plurimi ab Ecclesiasticis dignitatibus ob Simoniacas pactiones, aliaq; flagitia deiecit: Guidonem Abbatem Winmondensem, Eldwinumq; Ramsensem Symoniacos: Galfricium Petriburgensem, Haymonem Ceruellensem, Egelricum Midletonensem, quòd in clero non essent ordinati, Richardum Eliensem, & Robertum Sancti Edmundi, ob varios defectus & excessus. Huius autem Synodi, quæ anno tertio Henrici primi celebrata fuit, constitutiones sunt hæc.
units.tr: Anselm, however, diligently exercising his ecclesiastical office, called a synod of the whole clergy at London, in which he deposed many from ecclesiastical dignities on account of simoniacal bargains and other scandals: Guy, abbot of Winchcombe, and Eldwin of Ramsey, for simony; Galfrid of Peterborough, Haymo of Cerne, and Egelric of Middleton, because they had not been ordained in the clergy; and Richard of Ely and Robert of St Edmunds, for various defects and excesses. The decrees of this synod, which was held in the third year of Henry I, are these.

units.la: I. VT Episcopi seculares officia ne suscipiant, nec sint sicut laici, sed ordinatas vestes, vt religiosas personas decet, habeant, vt semper & vbique honestas personas testes habeant iuxte conuersationis.
units.tr: 1. That bishops shall not take up secular offices, nor be like laymen, but shall wear ordained garments, as befits religious persons, so that they always and everywhere have honest persons as witnesses of their conduct.

units.la: 2. Vt Archidiaconatus ne dentur ad firmam.
units.tr: 2. That archdeaconries shall not be given out to farm.

units.la: 3. Vt Archidiaconi ad minus sint Diaconi, & vt nullus Archidiaconus præsbyter, Diaconus canonicus vxorem ducat, aut ductam retineat.
units.tr: 3. That archdeacons shall be at least deacons, and that no archdeacon, presbyter, deacon or canon shall take a wife or keep one whom he has taken.

units.la: 4. Subdiaconus fi post professionem castitatis vxorê duxit, eadem lege cõstringatur.
units.tr: 4. If a subdeacon has taken a wife after making a profession of chastity, he shall be bound by the same law.

units.la: 5. Præsbyter quam diu illicitam conuersationem mulierum habuerit non sit legalis, nec missam celebret, nec ab aliis audiatur.
units.tr: 5. A presbyter who has had an unlawful relationship with women shall not be lawful [in office], nor shall he celebrate mass, nor be heard by others.

units.la: 6. Vt nullus ad Subdiaconatum vel supra ordinetur sine professione castitatis.
units.tr: 6. That no one shall be ordained to the subdiaconate or above without a profession of chastity.

units.la: 7. Vt filii Præsbyterorum non sint hæredes patrum suorum.
units.tr: 7. That the sons of presbyters shall not be heirs of their fathers.

units.la: 8. Vt Clerici ne sint Secularium præpositi, seu procuratores aut iudices sanguinis.
units.tr: 8. That clerics shall not be placed over secular affairs, nor act as stewards or judges in cases of blood.

units.la: 9. Vt præsbyteri ne eant ad potationes.
units.tr: 9. That presbyters shall not go to drinking parties.

units.la: 10. Vt vestes Clericorum sint vnius coloris, & calciamenta ordinata.
units.tr: 10. That the garments of clerics shall be of one colour, and their footwear fitting.

units.la: 11. Vt Clerici qui ordinem suum abiecerunt, aut redeant, aut excommunicentur,
units.tr: 11. That clerics who have cast off their order shall either return to it or be excommunicated.

units.la: 12. Vt Clerici patentes Coronas habeant,
units.tr: 12. That clerics shall wear open crowns [tonsures].

units.la: 13. Vt decimæ non nisi Ecclesiis dentur.
units.tr: 13. That tithes shall be given only to churches.

units.la: 14. Vt Ecclesiæ aut præbendæ ne emantur.
units.tr: 14. That churches or prebends shall not be bought.

units.la: 15. Ne noua Cepella fiat sine consensu Episcopi.
units.tr: 15. That no new chapel shall be built without the bishop's consent.

units.la: 16. Ne Ecclesia sacretur, donec prouideantur necessaria & Præsbytero & Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 16. That a church shall not be consecrated until what is necessary for both the presbyter and the church has been provided.

units.la: 17. Ne Abbates faciant milites, vt in eadem domo cum Monachis suis manducent aut dormiant.
units.tr: 17. That abbots shall not make knights, so that they may eat and sleep in the same house as their monks.

units.la: 18. Ne Monachi compatres, aut Monachæ commatres fiant.
units.tr: 18. That monks shall not become godfathers, nor nuns godmothers.

units.la: 19. Ne Monachi teneant villas ad firmam.
units.tr: 19. That monks shall not hold estates at farm.

units.la: 20. Ne Monachi Ecclesias nisi per Episcopos accipiant, nequé sibi datas ita spolient suis redditibus, vt Præsbyteri ibi seruientes in aliquo penuriam patiantur,
units.tr: 20. That monks shall not accept churches except through the bishops, nor so strip the revenues given to them that the presbyters serving there suffer any want.

units.la: 21. Vt fides inter virum & mulierem occulta, & sine testibus de coniugio data, si ab alterutro negata fit, irrita habeatur.
units.tr: 21. That a secret pledge of marriage between man and woman, given without witnesses, shall be held void if either party denies it.

units.la: 22. Vt criniti sic tondeantur, vt pars aurium appareat, & oculi non tegantur.
units.tr: 22. That long-haired men shall be cut so that part of the ears shows and the eyes are not covered.

units.la: 23. Vt cognati vsque ad septimam generationem ad coniugium copulentur, vel copulati simul permaneant, & si quis huius incestus conscius fuerit, & non ostenderit, eiusdem criminis participem se esse cognoscat.
units.tr: 23. That relatives up to the seventh degree shall not be joined in marriage, or, if joined, shall not remain together; and if anyone knows of such incest and does not reveal it, he shall recognise that he is a sharer in the same crime.

units.la: 24. Ne corpora defunctorum extra parochiam suam sepelienda portentur, vt presbyteri paroc: hinc perdant, quod inde illis debeatur.
units.tr: 24. That the bodies of the dead shall not be carried for burial outside their own parish, so that the presbyters of the parish do not lose what is owed to them from there.

units.la: 25. Ne quis temeraria nouitate corporibus mortuorum, aut fontibus, aut aliis retibus, (quod contigisse cognouimus) siue Episc. authoritate, reuerentia aut sanctitate exhibeat.
units.tr: 25. That no one shall, out of rash novelty, show honour to the bodies of the dead, or to springs or other relics (which we have learned has happened), whether by the authority, reverence or sanctity of a bishop.

units.la: 16. Nequis illud nepharium negocium excerceat, quo hactenus homines in Anglia solebant veluti bruta animalia venundari.
units.tr: 26. That no one shall carry on that nefarious trade by which, until now, men in England were accustomed to be sold like brute animals.

units.la: Synodus ista Londinensis Synodi appellatione etiam vulgo ferebatur, cuius constitutiones statim spretæ atque contemptæ fuerunt. Nam Girardus Eboracensis Archiepiscopus, cum illos Canones edixisset feruandos, totus illius provinciæ clerus recusauit, unde Anselmo scripsit:
units.tr: This synod of London was also commonly called by the name of the Council of London, and its decrees were at once scorned and despised. For Girard, archbishop of York, when he had decreed that those canons were to be observed, found that the whole clergy of his province refused, and so he wrote to Anselm:

units.la: Sitio Cleticorum meorum integritatem. Sed præter in paucis admodum vel aspidis surditatem, vel fabulosi cuiusdam Prothei mutabilitatem inuenio. Varns linguarum acúleis modò minas, modò conuicia inflignt. Professiones verò mihi penitus 10 abnegant Canonici illi, qui sine professione ad sacros ordines inordinabiliter sunt prouecti. hi etiam qui in presbyterio vel Diaconatu constituti, & vxores siue concubinas in publico habentes habuerunt, & ab altari nulla seruire ecclesia continuerunt. Cùm vero ad ordines aliquos inuito, dura cervice renitentur, ne in ordinando callitate proficerent.
units.tr: I thirst for the integrity of my clergy. But I find, apart from a very few, either the deafness of the asp or the changeableness of some fabled Proteus. With the various stings of their tongues they now hurl threats, now insults. Those canons, who were advanced to holy orders without profession in a disorderly way, utterly refuse their professions to me; also those who have been placed in the priesthood or diaconate and have kept wives or concubines openly, and have continued to serve no church at the altar. When I summon some of them to orders, they resist with stiff necks, so that they make no progress in becoming fit for ordination.

units.la: Obstitit etiam ne Canones huius Synodi legum vim & potestatem sortirentur, ingens inter Regem & Anselmum discordia, & contentio de Ecclesiarum inuestituris orta. Nam toto illo triennio quo abfuerat Anselmus, sedibus Episcopalibus & Ecclesiis vacantibus, Rex arbitratu suo viros Ecclesiasticos præposuit, earumque possessionem per inuestituram, & baculi pastoralis, & annuli donationem tradidit. Quod quidem inncstiendi ac in possessionem inducendi ius, Christiani principes tunc temporis sibi 20 vendicarunt atque reseruarunt. Ex his igitur qui authoritate Regia Episcopatibus & Ecclesiis inducti fuerunt, petiit Rex, vt qui sacratim non essent, ab Anselmo consecrarentur. Eorum qui vero absentes ea ab aliis Episcopis consecrati essent, in consortium & consuetudinem suam & Episcoporum cæium permitteret. In vtroque horum Anselmus Regi restitit, tum quod cæteri Laici Regis exemplo, authoritate priuatâ præsbyteros sine legitima Episcoporum approbatione sacerdotiis præficerent, tum quod Vrbanus Romanus Pontifex superiori concilio statuisset, Nequis de manu Regis aut laici Ecclesiæ aliquius inuestituram acciperet. aut laicali authoritate potestàt apprehenderet. At Rex, Regni proceres, Episcopi, & cuiuscunque generis aulici, hoc præter regni consuetudinem ab Anselmo factitatum indigne ferentes, asserebant asseruros se nunquam tam ini30 quo Papæ decreto: & potius tam Anselmum regno exterminaturos, & ab Ecclesia Romana penitus discessuros, quàm hanc Papæ sententiam à iure regio, regnique consuetudine prorsus alienam, ratam haberent. Quem procerum & Episcoporum secu confirmante & congruente sensum cum animaduertisset, Rex Girardo Eboracensi Archiepiscopo suasit & mandauit, vt ipse hoc consecrationis munus suscipiet & absolueret. Girardus hoc oneris in se assumpsit diemque ad consecrationis huius celebrationem Londini in Paulina Ecclesia præscripsit. Quò cùm plures conuenissent, Wilhelmus Wintoniensis Episcopus tunc sacrandus, baculu pastorale & annulû (quæ a Rege acceptisset) iterū Regi tradidit: dixitq, quæ iniuste accepisset amplius se non posse retinere. Cuius 40 factî nouitate, quòd præter omnium expectationē tam subitò & inopinatò accidit, perculsus Rex, Wilhelmi bona proscripsit, eumq; regno eiecit. Poëtea mulris in vttáq; partem, sicut in quoniam dissidio fieri solet, huc illuc inclinantibus, ad discordiâ tantâ quæ Regi recentis regni victoris filio periculosa foret sedandâ, conuentum est vt ad icicitandû Papæ (tanquâ Apollinis) oraculû, Anselmus & Wilhelmus Werelast Regis legatus, qui semper Anselmi partibus aduersus fuit, Româ proficiscerétur. His Romæ ante Papæ tribunal hanc causam agentibus, Anselmus Papæ causam, coram Papa præsente & iudice: Wilhelmus Regis sui absentis nec iudicis causam tractauit. Cumq; Wilhelmus vehementius in Regis propositum affectus dixisset: Regem suû, ne pro Regni Angliæ amissioneius Ecclesias donandi, & earù possessione tradendi amissuum. Respondit Paschalis Papa: (v: verbis Edmeri authoris vrar.) Si quemadmodum dicis, Rex tuus nec proRegni 50 sui amissione parietur Ecclesiarum donationes amittere, scias, ecce corâ Deo dico, quia nec pro sui capitis redemptione, eas illi aliquando Paschalis Papa impunè permitteret, habere. Hoc itaq; Papæ tam excelso & magnifico responso, causa secundum Anselmum contra Regem definita est. Alii scribunt Anselmum audiuisse Paschalem Papam illam diram & cruentam excommunicationis sententiam in Laicos inuestituras dantes, & Clericos eas à laicis capientes fulminantem, eaqù perterritum Principi suo a maioribus suis visitatum iuris vendicanti, consentire non aulum. Nam in illa excommunicatione Papa huiusmodi verbis vsus est. Execrabile videri manus, quæ in tantam eminentiam excreuerant: vt quod nulli Anglorum concessum est, Dominum cunctæ creantem suo ministerio creent, & eundem ipsum pro redemptione & salute totius mundi, summi tamen de inuestitura inre quicquam dissederet, mediam quandam in huius causæ decisione viam sequutus est: vt Episcopi a Rege ante inuestiri, quos Paschalis excommunicauerat, ab illa sententia soluerentur, & in sedibus suis confirmarentur: sed nerale quid in posterum a Rege aut Laico quocunq; fiat, cauit atque statuit. Quo Papæ decreto Rex acquiescit, & Anselmum omnibus bonis & fructibus exilii tempore a se perceptis & restentis plenè restituit. Reditigitur in Angliam Anselmus summo totius populi applausu, a Regina & optimatibus perhonorifice in regnum acceptur. Rex enim Normannico motu deterrens erat, quo sedaro Normanniam iterum suo subiecit imperio. Reuersusque Concilium Regni publicum Londini indixit, in quo statuum fuit, Non licere Regi vel cuicunq; laico per baculum & annulum Episcopum vel presbyterum quemcunque investire, tatisesse vt homagium ab Episcopis Regi fiat pro possessionibus temporalibus. His ex Anselmi sententia gestis, cepit prioris illius Londinensis à se celebratæ Synodi decreta executioni mandare, & sacerdotum legitimas nuptias prohibere atque disfoluere: sed cum Rex animaduertisset maiorem mel.oremq; Cleri partem, aut esse maritos, aut filios sacerdotum coniugatorum, illosq; Londinensis Concilii Canones, de vxoribus renunciandis, & vouenda continentia plurimis displicere, permisit Clericis matrimonia, sicut patris fratrisq; sui temporibus sub Lanfranco Archiepiscopo erant permissa. At Anselmus tunc Regis obstitit indulgentiæ, & sacerdotes vxorum consuendus habentes Ecclesiasticis beneficiis spoliauit, cuius proiectæ præfractaeque perinaciæ cessit tandem Rex. Quiquod authoritate potuisset efficere, maluit Anselmi importunitati cedere. Sub hæc tempora, mortuo Girardo Eboracensi Archiepiscopo, Thomas (Samsonis Wigorniensis Episcopi filius,) Archiepiscopus electus est, qui cum ab Anselmo consecrandus esset, prouinciæ suæ Clero eum pellente & instigante, subiectionem Cantuariensi sedi debitam, & a prioribus Eboracensibus Archiepiscopis præstitam profiteri recusauit. Ob quam contumaciam Anselmus nec eum consecrare voluit, & ne ab alio quoque Episcopo sacrarerur, per literas vetuit. Itaque Thomas sine consecratione, toto Anselmi tempore vitæ, electus tantum modo rletit: eo vero mortuo Rex, regni proceres atque Præsules, ad inundum de Ebotacefis Archiepiscopi consecrationem Concilii Londinensis conuocauit. Episcopi enim ab Anselmo prohibiti consecratæ illum oluerunt. Quod cum Thomas Comes Meletensis, cuius tunc fuit cum Rege intima maximaque gratia, sensisset, vultu sermoneque sæuiori quæsiuit: An quisquam huiusmodi literis parere auderet, sine Regis authoritate & scientia. Quo perterriti & stupefacti Episcopi, Samsone Wigorniensi Episcopum, Thomæ Eboracensis Archiepiscopi patrem accersitum rogarunt, vt filium suum consecraret, Qui id se facturum negauit, nisi Thomas Cantuariensi sedi iubitionem ex more profiteturum promitteret. Cui & Rex assensus est, iuffitq; vt quinto Kal. Iulii prox. in Ecclesia Paulina præstitutus Episcopus Thomas sacraretur, & præstita superiorib. Archiepiscopis professione faceret: quo tempore conuenientib. Episcopis, qui sacras ceremonias absoluerent, porrigitur Thomæ professio sigillo obsignata iam ohimà suis præscriptib. legi solita, quam cum summa gratiuate & reuerentia, qua decuit, aperte legisset, Episcopo Londinensi (Ecclesiæ Cant. Decano, Priore etiam eiusdem Ecclesiæ præsente) tradidit. Professionis forma hæc erat.
units.tr: Another obstacle to the canons of this synod gaining the force and authority of law was a great discord and contention between the King and Anselm over the investiture of churches. For the whole of those three years during which Anselm was away, the episcopal sees and churches stood vacant, and the King, at his own pleasure, appointed ecclesiastical men to them and handed over possession by investiture, through the giving of the pastoral staff and the ring. Christian princes at that time claimed and reserved for themselves this right of investing and inducting into possession. Of those who had been installed in bishoprics and churches by royal authority, the King asked that Anselm consecrate those who were not yet consecrated, and that he permit those who had been consecrated elsewhere by other bishops to be admitted to his company and fellowship, and to that of the bishops. Anselm resisted the King in both matters: partly because the other laymen, following the King's example, were setting presbyters over priesthoods on their own private authority without the lawful approval of the bishops; and partly because Pope Urban of Rome had decreed at an earlier council that no one should receive an investiture of any church from the hand of a king or a layman, or grasp the power of it by lay authority. But the King, the nobles of the realm, the bishops, and all the courtiers of every rank took it badly that Anselm had done this contrary to the custom of the kingdom. They declared that they would never confirm so unjust a decree of the Pope; they would rather drive Anselm out of the realm and break entirely with the Roman Church than hold this sentence of the Pope, which was wholly alien to the royal right and the custom of the realm, as valid. When Anselm perceived that the sense of the nobles and bishops was of one mind and agreed with this, the King persuaded and commanded Gerard, Archbishop of York, to take up this office of consecration himself and to perform it. Gerard undertook this burden and appointed a day for the celebration of this consecration in St Paul's Church in London. When many had gathered there, William, Bishop of Winchester, who was to be consecrated, returned the pastoral staff and the ring (which he had received from the King) to the King again, and said that he could no longer keep what he had received unjustly. The King, struck by the novelty of this deed, which happened so suddenly and unexpectedly beyond everyone's expectation, proscribed William's goods and drove him out of the realm. Afterwards, since many leaned to one side or the other, as is usual in such disputes, it was agreed, in order to settle so great a discord, which would be dangerous to the King, the son of the recent conqueror of the realm, that Anselm and William Warelwast, the King's envoy, who had always been opposed to Anselm's party, should set out for Rome to seek the oracle of the Pope (as if of Apollo). When they pleaded this cause before the Pope's tribunal at Rome, Anselm argued the Pope's cause in the presence of the Pope as judge, while William handled the cause of his absent king and not of a judge. And when William, pressing the King's proposal more vehemently, had said that his king would not, even for the loss of the kingdom of England, give up the donation of churches and their transfer into possession, Pope Paschal replied (to use the words of the author Eadmer): "If, as you say, your king will not suffer the loss of his churches' donations even for the loss of his kingdom, know that, behold, I say before God that Pope Paschal will never allow him to keep them, not even for the redemption of his own head." With this lofty and magnificent response of the Pope, the cause was decided in Anselm's favour against the King. Others write that Anselm heard Pope Paschal thundering that dreadful and bloody sentence of excommunication against laymen who gave investitures and against clergy who received them from laymen, and that, terrified by it, he would not consent to his prince's claim to the right handed down by his ancestors. For in that excommunication the Pope used words such as these: "It seems detestable that hands which have grown to such a height of pride should presume to create by their ministry the Lord who created all things, and to offer that same one for the redemption and salvation of the whole world, which has been granted to no Englishman." Yet on the main question of the investiture, the Pope, though he had made some concession, followed a middle course in deciding the cause: the bishops whom Paschal had excommunicated for having been invested by the King were absolved from that sentence and confirmed in their sees, but he laid down and decreed what should be done in future by the King or by any layman. The King acquiesced in this decree of the Pope and fully restored to Anselm all the goods and revenues which had been received and retained by the King during the time of exile. Anselm therefore returned to England to the great applause of the whole people, and was received with great honour into the realm by the Queen and the nobles. For the King was then detained by a Norman disturbance, which he quelled, and by which he again brought Normandy under his rule. On his return, Anselm called a public council of the realm at London, in which it was decreed that it was not lawful for the King or any layman to invest any bishop or presbyter whomsoever with the staff and the ring, and that homage should be made to the King by the bishops for their temporal possessions. After these things had been done at Anselm's instigation, he began to put into execution the decrees of the earlier London synod which he had held, and to forbid and dissolve the lawful marriages of priests. But when the King perceived that the greater and better part of the clergy were either married or the sons of married priests, and that the canons of the London council about renouncing wives and vowing continence displeased very many, he permitted the clergy to marry, as marriage had been permitted in the times of his father and brother under Archbishop Lanfranc. But Anselm then resisted the King's indulgence and stripped of ecclesiastical benefices the priests who kept wives, and at length the King yielded to his obstinate and stubborn perseverance. What he could have accomplished by his authority, he preferred to yield to Anselm's importunity. About this time, after Gerard, Archbishop of York, had died, Thomas (son of Samson, Bishop of Worcester) was elected archbishop. When he was to be consecrated by Anselm, at the urging and instigation of the clergy of his province he refused to profess the subjection owed to the see of Canterbury, which had been rendered by the earlier archbishops of York. On account of this obstinacy Anselm would not consecrate him, and by letter forbade him to be consecrated by any other bishop. And so Thomas, without consecration, remained merely elect for the whole of Anselm's lifetime. But when Anselm had died, the King, the nobles of the realm and the prelates called a council at London to consider the consecration of the Archbishop of York. For the bishops whom Anselm had forbidden were eager to consecrate him. When Thomas, Count of Meulan, who then enjoyed the greatest and most intimate favour with the King, perceived this, he asked with a harsher look and tone whether anyone would dare to obey such a letter without the authority and knowledge of the King. Terrified and astonished by this, the bishops asked Samson, Bishop of Worcester, the father of Thomas, Archbishop of York, to come and consecrate his son. He refused to do so unless Thomas promised that he would make the customary profession of subjection to the see of Canterbury. The King also agreed to this and ordered that the bishop-elect Thomas should be consecrated in St Paul's Church on the fifth day before the Kalends of July next, and should make the profession of the earlier archbishops. At that time, with the bishops assembled to perform the sacred ceremonies, Thomas's profession, already sealed and drawn up in the form customarily prescribed by his predecessors, was presented to him; and after reading it openly with all the grace and reverence fitting, he handed it to the Bishop of London (the Dean of the Church of Canterbury and the Prior of the same church being present). The form of the profession was as follows.

units.la: Ego Thomas Eboracensis Ecclesiæ consecrandus Metropolitanus profiteor subiectionem & Canonicam obedientiam sanctæ Dotouernensi Ecclesiæ, & eiusdem Ecclesiæ primati canonice electo & consecrato, & succesforib. suis canonice inthronizatis, salua fidelitate Henrici Regis, & salua obedientia mea Romanæ Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: I, Thomas, to be consecrated Metropolitan of the Church of York, profess subjection and canonical obedience to the holy Church of Canterbury, and to its primate canonically elected and consecrated, and to his successors canonically enthroned, saving the fealty owed to King Henry, and saving my obedience to the Roman Church.

units.la: Anselmus vero Cantuariæ, 4. Idus Augusti, Wilhelmum Wintonien sem, Rogerum Salisburien sem, Raynelium Herefordensem, Vrbanumq; Glamorganensem Episcopos consecrauit, præsentibus Gerardo Eboracensi Archiepiscopo, & aliis Cantuariensis provinciæ suffragantibus. Multum autem & operæ & sumptus contulit, in ornando & instaurando Ecclesiam Christi Cantuariensem, & in instituendo Cestriæ Monachorum Coenobio, ab Hugone Comite prius extructo, cuius Richardum Capellanum suum Abbatem fecit. Inscribendis Epistolis frequens & assiduus fuit, quarum 367. ad nostram tempora referuntur. Scripsit tractatus varios. 1. de veritate. 2. de libertate arbitrii. 3. de casu diaboli. 4. de grammatico & disciplina. 5. vocatur monologion: multas dialecticas quaestiones propositas & solutas: Scripsit etiam Libellum Sententiarum Profologion: librum Epistolarum ad diuersos: librum de Incarnatione verbi: librum, cur Deus homo: adhæc de conceptu virginali: de orationibus contemplatiuis, & de processione spiritus sancti. Et biennio post secundum in Anglia ab exilio redieruntransacto in Abbatia Sancti Edmundi grauissima febri correptus Cantuariam festinauit, ibique diu lecto decumbens, vndecimo Kal.Maii. An 1109.xatis suæ.76.& Pontificatus An.16.obiit, tumulo〔que〕 ad capus Lanfranci sepultus & conditus iacet.
units.tr: Anselm at Canterbury, on 4 Ides of August (10 August), consecrated the bishops William of Winchester, Roger of Salisbury, Rainelm of Hereford and Urban of Glamorgan, with Gerard, archbishop of York, and other suffragans of the province of Canterbury present. He also devoted much effort and expense to adorning and restoring the Church of Christ at Canterbury, and to founding a monastery of monks at Chester, which Earl Hugh had built earlier; he made his chaplain Richard its abbot. He was frequent and diligent in writing letters, of which 367 are reckoned to survive from our times. He wrote various treatises: (1) on truth; (2) on freedom of the will; (3) on the fall of the devil; (4) on the grammarian and on discipline; (5) the work called the Monologion; and he proposed and resolved many questions in dialectic. He also wrote the Book of Sentences, the Proslogion, a book of letters to various people, a book on the Incarnation of the Word, a book Why God Became Man, and besides these a work on the virginal conception, one on contemplative prayers, and one on the procession of the Holy Spirit. Two years after returning to England from exile, he was seized by a severe fever in the abbey of St Edmund and hurried to Canterbury. There, lying ill for a long time, he died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, 1109, in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the sixteenth of his pontificate, and he lies buried and laid to rest beside Lanfranc's tomb.

units.la: Hic Anselmus etiam dustus & inomni vita constmens habebatur, tamen in sua sententia perunax a ventare & doctrina Christiana Lepe deflexit, Christianaq; laudis gloriulam & inanem famam,potius quam virtutem iplam adamauit. Nam & de se lupra Christianam modestiam iactitare solitus est, & in hac facetdotum coniugia vehementius & fuperstitiuius,quam humani doctoris Christianopai fuit,incalu it. Ipfeenim de se dixit. Nullum fe vnquam verbum voce protulisse, cuius recordatione grauari posset conscientia,& tamen cum pisciculum crudum incautus in coenacomedillet, ingemuit & deflevit tantum peccatum,quod contra Dei tanctionem de crudo lumpfisset. Cuius autem spiritus est ista simulatio & iactantia: vt le perhiberet,nc verbo vnquam etrasse, tum vt in cruditcumestione quæ casu contigit,tantum delictum agnosceret.
units.tr: Anselm was also regarded as learned and blameless in every part of his life; nevertheless, stubborn in his own opinion, he departed from the truth and from Christian teaching, and he loved the empty fame and glory of Christian praise rather than virtue itself. For he was accustomed to boast about himself beyond Christian modesty, and in the matter of priests' marriages he grew more vehement and superstitious than was fitting for a Christian teacher of humankind. For he said of himself that he had never uttered a word with his voice of which his conscience could be burdened by the memory; yet when, carelessly, he ate a small raw fish at supper, he groaned and wept over the sin he had committed in taking something raw, contrary to God's command. But what spirit is this pretence and boasting, to present himself as one who had never spoken a word amiss, and yet to acknowledge such a great offence in an accidental eating of something raw?

units.la: At in dissolucndis sacerdotum lege diuina permissis nuptiis,ne obsirmatum setsi sum deponeret,scuus & supra omnem modum attox esse putuit. Hic enim primus nuptias sacordotibus omnino interdixit.Nam priores,Dunstanus,Æthelwoldus,& Oswoldus,qui Monachorum patres dicti sunt, coniugatos Clericos ab vxoribus non separabant,sed Monasterus solum excludebant, neque hos solum,sed quoscunq; seculares,s Monachatum non suscipercnt.
units.tr: But in dissolving the marriages of priests, which divine law permits, he was, lest he lay down the obstinacy he had taken up, thought to be too severe and beyond all measure. For he was the first to forbid marriage to priests altogether. For earlier men, Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald, who are called the fathers of the monks, did not separate married clergy from their wives, but only excluded them from monasteries; and not only these, but any laymen who did not take up the monastic life.

units.la: Scribit de Anselmo his verbis Historiographus. Anselmus Archiepiscopus ad se-stnm S.Michaelis Concilium tenuit apud Londoniam, in quo prohibuit vxores sacerdotibus Anglorum (antea non prohibitas) quod quibusdam mundi stimum vitum est, quibusdam periculosum, nedum munditiasvitiosiass mirori appeterent, in immundi nas horribiles ad Christiani nominis summum dedecus inciderent. Sed quem affecdum sortita fit hæc Anselmi prohibitio,perinde eo viuu atque mortuo videamus. Tribus enim existii sui annis irritam fuisse declarauimus.Reuersus autem tanta eam seuerit exercuit,vt & coniugatos beneficiis amauerit, & vxores non deserentes proscripserit,eorumque buna Diocesis Episcopoadiudicarit, & eos cum vxoribus adulteriidamnarit. Quo suo exemplo permouit,vt diximus,Regem præteresuam consuetudinem, exhaustiss suis in Normannico bello facultatibus, ex Clericorum coniugis quæ prius approbauerat,& de quibus ipsum Anselmum,etsi frustra interceslerat, pecuniarum quastum facere,& pensionibus ad retinendam illius Anselmi constitutionis penam ,& retinendas vxores,Clericos supra suas vires onerare:quas tandem & remisit, & sacerdotum coniugia permisit,vt ducendi: pene post Anselmi coństitutionem annis rata manerent : etsi frequentia sequentium Cantuariensium Archiepiscoporum editaprohibitoria promulgabantur.
units.tr: The historian writes of Anselm in these words: "Archbishop Anselm held a council at London at the feast of St Michael, in which he forbade wives to the priests of the English (who had not been forbidden before). This seemed to some a light matter of the world, but to others a dangerous one, since men who sought cleanness by an unclean way fell into horrible uncleanness, to the greatest disgrace of the Christian name. But whatever effect this prohibition of Anselm had, let us see it as if he were both alive and dead. For we have shown that it was void for three years. But on his return he enforced it with such severity that he both lost his affection for the married clergy and proscribed those who would not give up their wives, and he had their goods adjudged by the bishop of the diocese and condemned them with their wives as adulterers. By this his example he moved the King, as we said, to set aside his former custom, which he had approved, of taking money from the wives of the clergy, a practice in which Anselm himself had tried, though in vain, to intervene. Exhausted of his resources in the Norman war, the King burdened the clergy beyond their means with payments to keep the penalty of Anselm's constitution and to keep their wives. At last he remitted these payments and permitted the marriages of priests to be entered upon, and these remained in force for almost as many years after Anselm's constitution, although the successive archbishops of Canterbury repeatedly published prohibitions."

units.la: Nec multus esse volo in eo,quod multis admirabantur , cum nephandum il-lud prætet naturam vitium,ita tunc temporis in Monachis & religiosis inoleuerit,quo aliquo aut proposito nuptias Anselmus vetuerit.Id quod Sanctus Bernhardus vbericus testatur.Tolle,inquit,de Ecclesia honorabile conuigium & thorum immaculatum, nonne reples eam concubinariis,incæstuosis,feministuis,mollibus masculorum concubitoribus & omni denique genere immundorum ? Sed Anselmus præterquam quòd abeo, quod semel apud se statuerat&addixerat,siue id æquum siue iniquum fuerat,auelli nulla ratione potcrat Fuit etiam in Principes Regnique procerescaduerusa,pene què imperiosus, quod ex multis suis contumaciis leuissimis de rebus Regibus appositus facilime cernimus.Nam cum,vt diximus,de inucstituris controuersiam Regi Henrico,(qui eum vnicè dilexerat, & ab exilio reuocauerat,)mouisset ,nec morem vssum Regi, proceribus,atque Præsulibus gerere vellet, (ponte nullo pentuo cogente (vt ait Edmerus )Rex gno Romam discessit. Quo exemplo,quod a pluribus reprehensum tum fuit,animauit succellores suos Regibus aduersos esse, & querelas de illis Romano Pontifici deferre, Regnumque sacris interdicere,vt populum Romanæ superstitioni dedicum,ad intellinos tumultus prouocarent. Deinde Romam profectus,cum rogaretur,vt Regis ad Papam legatum vnà secum in itinere proficisci permiscerat, elatus nimium & inhumanus,scilicet multorum exhortationibus & precibus petitus noluit:sed affirmato animo ne-fpondit.Quod dixi,dixi. Adhæccum à Regeipso Henrico rogaretur,vt Thomæ Eboraeensi Archiepiscopu sacrado dclibcrādi inducias daret de prosessione subiectionis,pro-struc & iracunde respondit.Satius esse sibi viuo in srutta discerpi,quàm vniushoræ moram ad eam deliberationem,quæ conuellat præcedcssorum suorum instituta capiédam indulgere. Itaque in ipso semio,cum iam haud pruculabesset ā morte, obstinatiæ & iracundiæ cunditæ calore ductus ad Thomam scripsit arrogantius. Priuare se eum omni sacerdotali ordine, quem ab aliquo suorum Suffraganeorum accepisset, interdixitque oe pastoralis securæ villatenus immisceret, donec subiectionem profiteretur, his verbis. Tibi quoque Thomae interdico sub anathemate, ex parte Dei, ut nunquam Episcoparus Eboracensis benedictionem suscipias, nisi prius professionem facias. &c. Atque harum literarum copiam singulis Angliæ Episcopis misit, quibus sub eodem anathemate præcipit, ne quisquam ei manus imponeret. Atque hæc sanè Anselmi & Archiepiscoporum similis cœtumacia Regibus causam iustam præbuit, cur illis mortuis tam multis annis penes se Archiepiscoporum tenuissent, ut de moderato aliquo & pacifico viro, qui permanisicia sua hos tumultus in regno permisere noluit, ad tantum eos suscipiendum prouideret. Sed oon tam durum & iniquum in his Anselmus se ostendit, quàm facilem & proclivem in gratioribus scelerib. tolerandis: pto pluribus enim Simoniacis intercessit, de quo lepide Matth. Paris. Anselmus Archiepiscopus pro Episcopis & Abbatibus degradatis, multa precum iostantia Papam rogare cœpit, ut cum illis misericorditer dispensaret, ut posset amissas recipere dignitates. Tum sedes clementissima, quæ nolli deesse confuerit (dumodo albi aliquid vel rubei intercedat) præscriptos Pontifices & Abbates ad priscos dignitates revocauit. &c. Hic igitur tam constans & pius pater ob castitatis ardorem incensus contra coniugaros, ob Papæ lucrum Simoniacis, (quos omnia diuina humanaq; iura detestantur,) æquabilis & benignus fuit.
units.tr: I do not wish to dwell long on what many admired: that unspeakable vice, against nature, had then grown so strong among monks and religious men that Anselm forbade marriages with some purpose. Saint Bernard bears witness to this at length: "Take away from the Church," he says, "honourable marriage and the undefiled bed, and does it not fill it with concubinaries, incestuous persons, adulterers, the soft lovers of men, and in short with every kind of uncleanness?" But Anselm, apart from the fact that he could by no means be turned from what he had once decided and resolved, whether that was just or unjust, was also harsh and almost domineering toward princes and the nobility of the kingdom, as we can very easily see from many of his small acts of obstinacy toward kings. For when, as we said, he had stirred up a dispute over investitures with King Henry, who had loved him above all and had recalled him from exile, and when he would not observe the custom used by kings, nobles and prelates, and no one compelled him (as Eadmer says), the King went over the sea to Rome. By this example, which was then much criticised by many, he encouraged his successors to be hostile to kings, to carry complaints against them to the Roman Pontiff, to lay the realm under interdict, and so to stir the people, devoted to Roman superstition, to internal tumults. Then, having gone to Rome, when he was asked to set out on the journey together with the King's legate to the Pope, he, too proud and inhumane, refused, even though he was urged and begged by many; but with a firm mind he answered, "What I said, I said." Moreover, when King Henry himself asked him to grant a delay to Thomas of York, who was to be consecrated, to deliberate on the profession of subjection, he replied harshly and angrily that it would be better for him to be torn to pieces alive than to grant even one hour's delay for that deliberation, which would undermine the institutions of his predecessors. So, at the very end, when he was not far from death, led by the heat of obstinacy and anger, he wrote to Thomas more arrogantly: he deprived him of all sacerdotal order which he had received from any of his suffragans, and forbade him to meddle in any way with the pastoral care until he made profession of subjection, in these words: "To you also, Thomas, I forbid under anathema, on God's behalf, that you ever receive the blessing of the bishops of York unless you first make profession, etc." He sent copies of these letters to each of the English bishops, commanding them under the same anathema that none of them should lay hands on him. Certainly this stubbornness of Anselm and of the archbishops like him gave kings a just cause why, after their deaths, they kept the archbishoprics in their own hands for so many years, rather than let the see be filled by some moderate and peaceable man who would not allow such disturbances to continue in the kingdom. But Anselm showed himself not so hard and unjust toward these things as he was ready and inclined to tolerate more serious crimes. For he interceded for many simoniacs, about which Matthew Paris wittily writes: "Archbishop Anselm, with great urgency of prayer, began to ask the Pope for the bishops and abbots who had been deposed, that he might mercifully dispense with them so that they could recover the dignities they had lost. Then the most merciful see, which is never wanting to anyone (provided that something white or red intercedes), recalled the named bishops and abbots to their former dignities, etc." Thus this so constant and pious father, inflamed with zeal for chastity against married clergy, and for the Pope's gain toward simoniacs (whom all divine and human law detests), was equable and mild.

units.la: Anselmo mortuo Elienfis Episcopatus ab Henrico Regè a Lincolniensi diocesi sumptus, erectus est, quo Herusæus tunc Banchorensis Episcopus primus functus est. At Rex post Aolselmi obitum, patris fratrisq; sequutus vestigia, cum præter suum institutum iam ad quæstum animum iotenderat, tam Cantuariensis Archiepiscopatus, quam aliarum Ecclesiarum vacantium emolumenta atque iura in suos vsus contulit. Et illa rigida Londinensis Synodi de prohibitis Clericorum coniugiis decreta seruari mandauit, illiusq; reos pecunia mulctauit: tandemq; generalem & lucrosam mulctam omnibus indifinctè Clericis, siue cooiugatis, siue solutis indixit: & Episcoparus quoscunque vacantes pacto & recepto precio concessit. Episcopatum Dunelmensem Ranulpho Capellano suo mille libris donauit: & Therfordensem Roberto Lofango muneribus interuenientibus contulit: qui illam sedem ad Noruicensem ciuitatem, in qua nunc permanet, primus traduxit.
units.tr: After Anselm's death, the bishopric of Ely was taken from the diocese of Lincoln by King Henry and erected, and Herbert was its first bishop, then bishop of Bangor. But the King, after Anselm's death, following the footsteps of his father and brother, had now turned his mind to gain, contrary to his own rule, and he applied to his own uses the revenues and rights both of the archbishopric of Canterbury and of other churches that were vacant. He ordered the harsh decrees of the London synod on forbidden marriages of clergy to be kept, and he fined the offenders in money; and finally he imposed a general and profitable fine on all clergy without distinction, whether married or unmarried. He also granted vacant bishoprics for a stipulated and received price. He gave the bishopric of Durham to his chaplain Ranulf for a thousand pounds, and he conferred Thetford, through the intervention of gifts, on Robert Losinga, who first transferred that see to the city of Norwich, where it now remains.

units.la: XXXV. RODVLPHVS.
units.tr: XXXV. RODULPHUS

units.la: Odvlphvs patria Normannus, Monachus Benedictinus, auditor Lanfranci in Cœnobio Cadomensi quondam fuit. Sagacientis primò Abbas, inde ab Anselmo ad Roffensem Episcopatum deductus est. Cumq; Archiepiscopatum Cant. multaque alias sedes & Ecclesias vacantes tenuisset, continua procerum atque Præsulum interpellatione tandem superatus, mutasque ad eas cathedras Windefor conuocaris, deliberauit de dignis Præsulibus sedibus vacantibus præficiendis, inter quos Fareeium Abindoniæ Abbatem Rex ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum designauit, virum spectatæ grauitatis & prudentiæ. E magnatibus autem complures, qui Monachos odisse coeperunt, aliquem è Regis Capellanis aut secularibus Clericis ad Archiepiscopalem dignitatem fumi volebant. Cùm ecclesiam est, quòd à prima sedis illius institutione, quam Augustinus posuit, secularis ordinis (ut asserebant) nemo eam sedem tenuisset, præter Stigandum, cuius infœlix exitus tam sanguinis & institutionis violatæ signum ostendit. Itaque ab omnibus penè Rodulphus ad Archiepiscopalem Celsitudinem postulatus, à Rege mutata sua de Farecio sententia probatus, & in frequenti Episcoporum conuentu ab Wilhelmo Winton. Episcopo Cantuariæ consecratus est, Anno Pas. halis 15. & Henrici primi 14. pallium quoque quinto Kal. Iulii proximo, à Paschali missum per Anselmum (Sanctæ Sabinæ Abbatem, Anselmi Archiepiscopi Cant. nepotem,) Cantuariæ magnifico quodam & instructo apparatu, frequentique populi corona accepit: quo die etiam Teolsum Wigornienses Episcopum Cantuariæ consecrauit. His temporibus, sue Anglorum astutia dignitas, siue Regum in peregrinos potius & Normannos propensio, sine quòd sæpe in usu est, eorum quos domi nouerimus, ertsi multò digniores sunt, fastidium tulit, vt Episcopatibus gerendis Angli non censerentur idonei, Normannique quantumuis indigni iudicarentur apti. Ex quo paucis annis euenit, vt eminentiores Ecclesiasticas dignuates quasq; Normanni possiderent. Namque hic Rodulphus (senex valetudinarius, paralyticus & pedibus aeger fuit, praeterea difficilis ac morosus ad ex temum in Regem ipsum, a quo promotus fuit, ingratus. Cum enim Henricus Normannam tubiug.dLet, reuersus ad Windeforienses castrum, Regni proceres deliberandi & consilii capiendi causa conuocauit, ibique nuptias cum Adelina Godefredi Lotharingiae Ducis filia celebrauit, Sarisburiensis tunc Episcopus ad depositionis munus a Rege & Regina expetitus, & vestibus sacris indutus ac paratus, à Rodulpho Archiepiscopo deesitere iussus est, illudque negotii ab eodem Rodulpho Wintoniensi Episcopo committitur. Deinde cum Rex apud Barkleiam tempore Paschae fuisset, & poit Pentecosten Londinum rediens corona insignibus in chrono sederet, & tum Regina consecranda & coronanda esset, Rodulphus Archiepiscopus tunc missam celebrans ad Regem, (quòd sciente, vt supra diximus, Anselmo, a Thoma Eboracensi Archiepiscopo, in consecratione diadema imposituum ei est) accessit. Cui accedenti Rex comiter assurrexit. Quaerinit Archiepiscopus, quis eius capiti diadema imposuerit Mea, inquit Rex, haud inter tebasit, ideoque mea ex illius memini. At Archiepiscopus atra bile percitus inquit: nullo id iure fecit, quisquis ille fuerit: proinde aut tu a gerenda corona cessabis, aut ego ab admissione missa. Ad haec Rex nihilo turbatus vultu placido & modesto respondit. Si, vt ais, hoc diadema capiti meo nonire imponitur, tu id facias, quod iuri censeas consentaneum, ego non refragabor. Quo dicto accessit propitius Archiepiscopus manusque ad diadema Regis capiti detrahendum attollens, cum Rex etiam fibulam sub mento ligatam, qua diadema capiti vinciretur, soluerer, Procerus Regis modestiam & Archiepiscopi iracundiam admirantes, vna voce an Archiepiscopum ferebantur, instabantque, ne in tam solemni Reginae coronatione Regi Diadema aufer- ret Quorum clamoribus actus Rodulphus acquieuit, & Regi astans canticum, Gloria in excelsis, exortus est, & subsequente, vt confuerit, choro musla illa quiete peracta est. Ex quo perspici posset, quàm intempestiue & impudenter lenitatem Principis illius generis hominus abusi sunt, qui Monachali sanctitate & dignitate reliquii, & in Principes habere imperium putabant. Henricus enim Rex vrbanitate, comitate, assabilitate, lenitate, iustitia & fortitudine omnes sui temporis Principes anteire putabatur. Huc etiam accessit, quod omni literarum genere Cantabrigiae, Lutetiaeque instructus a pueritia atque profecit, vt Willielmus eius pater cum Episcopali munere aptum censuerit.
units.tr: Rodulphus, a Norman by birth, was a Benedictine monk and once a pupil of Lanfranc in the monastery of Caen. He was first abbot of Sées, and was then promoted by Anselm to the bishopric of Rochester. When he had held the archbishopric of Canterbury along with many other vacant sees and churches, he was at last worn down by the constant importunity of nobles and prelates. Then the king summoned a meeting of the bishops at Windsor to deliberate on filling the vacant sees with worthy prelates. Among those named, the king designated Faricius, abbot of Abingdon, a man of proven gravity and prudence, for the archbishopric of Canterbury. Several of the nobles, however, who had begun to hate the monks, wanted one of the king's chaplains or a secular clergyman raised to the archiepiscopal dignity. They argued that since the first founding of that see by Augustine, no one of the secular order (as they claimed) had held it except Stigand, whose unhappy end showed the sign of a violated blood and institution. So Rodulphus was demanded for the archiepiscopal dignity by almost everyone. The king, changing his opinion about Faricius, approved him, and in a full assembly of bishops he was consecrated by William, bishop of Winchester, in the fifteenth year of the Paschal (Pope's) ... and the fourteenth year of Henry I, in 1115. The pallium, sent from Paschal through Anselm (abbot of Santa Sabina, nephew of Archbishop Anselm of Canterbury), he received at Canterbury the following fifth day before the Kalends of July, with a magnificent and well-appointed ceremony and a crowd of people. On the same day he also consecrated Theulf, bishop of Worcester, at Canterbury. In these times, whether from the cunning of the English or from the king's inclination towards foreigners and Normans rather than towards men whom he knew at home, though they were far more worthy (as often happens), a distaste arose, so that the English were not thought fit to hold bishoprics, while Normans, however unworthy, were judged apt. From this it came about, within a few years, that the more eminent ecclesiastical dignities were possessed by Normans. For this Rodulphus, an old man, infirm, paralysed, and sick in his feet, was also difficult and peevish, and at last ungrateful towards the king himself, by whom he had been promoted. For when Henry had gone over to Normandy and returned to the castle of Windsor, he summoned the nobles of the kingdom to deliberate and take counsel, and there celebrated his marriage with Adeliza, daughter of Godfrey, duke of Lorraine. Then Osmund, bishop of Salisbury, was sought by the king and queen for the office of deposition; he was clothed in sacred vestments and made ready, but was ordered by Rodulphus, the archbishop, to desist, and that business was entrusted by the same Rodulphus to the bishop of Winchester. Next, when the king had been at Berkeley at Easter, and after Pentecost, returning to London, sat in the choir wearing the crown insignia, and the queen was then to be consecrated and crowned, Archbishop Rodulphus, who was celebrating mass at that time, approached the king (since, as we said above, the diadem had been placed on him by Thomas, archbishop of York, at his consecration, with Anselm's knowledge). As he approached, the king rose courteously to greet him. The archbishop asked who had placed the diadem on his head. "I," said the king, "did not ask anyone's advice, and so I remember that it was mine." But the archbishop, stirred by black bile, said: "He had no right to do it, whoever he was; therefore either you will cease from wearing the crown, or I will cease from admitting you to mass." To this the king, not at all disturbed, replied with a calm and modest countenance: "If, as you say, this diadem is wrongly placed on my head, do what you think is consistent with right; I will not oppose you." With these words the archbishop approached kindly and, raising his hands to take the diadem from the king's head, while the king was loosening the clasp tied beneath his chin by which the diadem was fastened to his head, the nobles, marvelling at the king's moderation and the archbishop's anger, cried out with one voice against the archbishop and urged that he should not snatch the diadem from the king at so solemn a coronation of the queen. Moved by their cries, Rodulphus yielded, and standing by the king he began the canticle "Glory to God in the highest," and, with the choir answering as usual, the mass was completed in quiet. From this it can be seen how untimely and shamelessly they abused the gentleness of a prince, men who, having left behind the holiness and dignity of the monastic life, thought they had rule over princes. For King Henry was thought to surpass all the princes of his age in courtesy, affability, gentleness, justice and courage. To this was added that, having been trained from boyhood in every kind of learning at Cambridge and Paris, he was so advanced that his father William thought him fit for the episcopal office.

units.la: Qui doctrinae praesidio & salutberrimas multas leges ipse condidit, & Papales technas & saepe olfecit, & caute vitauit, vt si cam opportunitatem, quam Henricus obtauus nactus fuisset, & Papalem iurisdictionem extermina set, & praefraeum, ac a Papa concitatum in se Clerum in officio tenuisset. Hoc autem Rodulphi factum, non modo Regi & proceribus, sed ipsis Episcopis, tonèque Clero tam inuisum & indignum fuit, vt aperto ore omnes dicetent se hunc quam permittiuros vt Monachi amplius Archiepiscopatus gerent, nec eorum imperium aequo animo laturos; quorum consensum Rex laudauit, & turer ratum statuit.
