In Elphegi vita supra descriptum est, ut ab Episcopatibus Monachos praefuisse, & quòd ad Edgari Regis petitionem Iohannes Papa sub anathemate statuisset; Wintoniensem Episcopum neminem nisi Monachum instituendum. Nunc videmus eodem mana hemate spreto & contemptor, tam Regio quàm Episcoporum consensu & decreto detrusos ad infetiora clausitra rursus Monachos, & ab Archiepiscopali Cleri feudine, & Episcopali dignitate deiectos. Quod tamen primo illo decreto non praeuaduit: nam duo tunc sequuti Archiepiscopi Monachi fuerunt, tertius Beckettus primus post Stigandum Canonicus, Archiepiscopus Cant. factus. Huius etiam Archiepiscopi temporibus denuo repetita fuit illa totius de Archiepiscopi Eboracensis prosessione Canonicorum fedi moratio. Nam mortuo Thoma Eboracensi Archiep. scopo successit Thurstinus, qui & mollicus fuit, ac imprudentia tum tam pertinax atque strenuus, vt Archiepiscopatum illum tanta sua ac amicorum opera expetitum ambitum maluit deserere, quàm debitam subiectionem profiteri.
units.tr: He also himself, with the protection of learning, drew up many wholesome laws, and both smelled out and cautiously avoided the papal wiles, so that if he had seized the opportunity which Henry had obtained, he would have destroyed papal jurisdiction and kept in check a clergy that was unruly and stirred up against him by the Pope. But this act of Rodulphus was so hateful and unworthy not only to the king and nobles but to the bishops themselves and to the whole clergy, that all openly declared they would never allow the monks to hold the archbishopric any longer, nor would they bear their rule with equanimity. The king approved their consent and decided that it should be firmly maintained. It was described above in the life of Elphege that, at the request of King Edgar, Pope John had decreed under anathema that no one but a monk should be appointed bishop of Winchester, and that monks should be excluded from bishoprics. Now we see that, with that anathema despised and scorned, monks were again thrust down into lower positions by the consent and decree of both the king and the bishops, and were cast out from the archiepiscopal chair of the clergy and from episcopal dignity. Yet this did not prevail against that first decree, for the two archbishops who followed were monks, and the third, Becket, was the first after Stigand to be made archbishop of Canterbury who was not a monk, but a canon. In the time of this same archbishop, that old dispute over the profession of canons in the archbishopric of York was again revived. For after the death of Thomas, archbishop of York, Thurstan succeeded, who was both effeminate and at that time so imprudent, yet so stubborn and strenuous, that, though he had sought that archbishopric with great effort and that of his friends, he preferred to give it up rather than profess the due subjection.

units.la: Hic cum omnia Romae venalia sciuisset, & quòd ab vno Papa decretum est, ab alero preciorecisindi posse sperabat, cum Calixtorum Papa egit, vt ab eo Romae consecraretur. Et quanquam in illo publico Regni coetu, quod Salisburiae de Matilda Regis filia Henrico Imperatori nubenda celebrabatur, multum de hac contouersia altercatu fit, Thurstanustamen eo se retrocedit Regi iudicius in hac causa facile vinci posse ptexisset, ne illo concilio de causa iudicaretur procuraruit, posteaq; Romam profectus, consecrationem a Calixto inuito Rege & Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi obtinuit. Quo audito Rodulphus in ipso senio & infirmissima valetudine Romam etiam properar. Expositaq; Papæ aduentus sui causa, cum de sedis suæ prærogatiua (per hanc Thurstini surrepta clam sine Dauid ica a Papa consecrationem) multum violata egisset, verbis sanè benignis & perhumanis permullus est. Responsa verbi in vtramq; partem ambigua Apollinis oraculis similima accepit. Papam nihil contra Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ priuilegium facturum, vtrique sedi pariter fauere & indulgere, sed omnia iura Episcopalia in Papæ sinu recondita esse, eaque Papæ cum sibi licuerit, licitum exercere: vt hoc consecrationis negocium Archie10 piscopo Cantuariensi non posset iure displicere. Quæ quam in partem Rodulphus acciperet incertus, in Angliam re Principi nunciata reuersus est. Rex huno Thurstini morem indignè ferens, edixit, hęc in Angliam redire. Papa horrenda excommunicationum fulmina in Regem & Rodulphum iaculatus, coegit eos Thurstanum saltem in Eboracensem prouinciam recipere, hac lege, ne extra propriam diocæsin quicquam administraret, Ecclesiæq; Cantuar. sedi dubitam subiectionem profiteretur. Ad hanc rem multa ex Ecclesia Cant. vetera monumenta eruta & depromptæ sunt, quæ causæ finem imponebant: quæ ab Edmero verbatim descripta sunt. Calixtus sub hæc tempora Petrum quendam Monachum ad Regem misit, quem suum in Anglia moratorum legatem statuit. At Rex nonse permissurum vllum in suo regno Papæ legatum respondit. Id 20 enim & contra morem regni & Regis priuilegium esse, Calixtumq;e Papam summam sibi & Cantuariensi sedi in conseerando Thurstano iniuriam fecisse. Ostensa igitur illa veteta monumenta Petro legato fuerunt, quibus perspectis Petrus, Papam illud Cătuariëfi sedi illatum prærudicium correcturum, & priuilegia pristina restituturum spofpondit. Sed Rodulphus ad firmam iam senectutem proucctus, & paralisi perpetuo triennio laborans, non tam corpore quam animo æger, postquam 8. annis sedilset, 13. Kalend. Nouembris Anno Domini 1122. obiit, mortuusque triduo in media parte nauis Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis sepultus iacet. Vir fuit affabilitate præstans, nullo delicto notabili suspectus, misi quòd ad locos & risus inclinatior erat, quàm gradum & ætatem suam decebat, ideoque Nugax dicebatur.
units.tr: When he had learned that everything at Rome was for sale, and believed that what had been decreed by one pope could be undone for a price from another, he dealt with Pope Calixtus, so that he might be consecrated at Rome by him. And although in that public assembly of the kingdom which was held at Salisbury, concerning Matilda, the king's daughter, to be married to the Emperor Henry, much argument was made about this controversy, Thurstan nevertheless took care that the matter should not be judged in that council, having foreseen that he could easily be defeated in this cause by the king's judgement. Afterwards he set out for Rome and obtained consecration from Calixtus, against the wishes of the king and the archbishop of Canterbury. When this was heard, Rodulphus, though in his old age and in very weak health, also hurried to Rome. Having set out the reason for his coming, he complained at length about the violation of the prerogative of his see by Thurstan's consecration, which had been secretly obtained from the Pope without his knowledge. He was received with quite kind and very courteous words. He received answers that were ambiguous in either direction, most like the oracles of Apollo: that the Pope would do nothing against the privilege of the church of Canterbury, but would favour and indulge both sees equally, yet that all episcopal rights were laid up in the bosom of the Pope, and that he could lawfully exercise them as far as he was permitted; so that this business of consecration could not rightly displease the archbishop of Canterbury. Uncertain in which direction Rodulphus should take this, he returned to England, having reported the matter to the prince. The king, taking ill this custom of Thurstan, issued an edict that he should not return to England. The Pope, hurling terrible thunderbolts of excommunication against the king and Rodulphus, compelled them at least to receive Thurstan into the province of York, on this condition: that he should administer nothing outside his own diocese, and should profess due subjection to the church of Canterbury. For this matter many ancient records of the church of Canterbury were brought out and produced, which put an end to the dispute; these were copied word for word by Eadmer. About this time Calixtus sent to the king a certain monk, Peter, whom he appointed his legate for staying in England. But the king replied that he would never allow any legate of the Pope in his kingdom, for this was contrary both to the custom of the kingdom and to the king's privilege, and that Calixtus had done a great injury to himself and to the see of Canterbury in consecrating Thurstan. Those ancient records were then shown to the legate Peter, and when he had examined them he promised that the Pope would correct the prejudice done to the see of Canterbury and restore its former privileges. But Rodulphus, having advanced to a firm old age, and suffering from paralysis for three years, sick in mind rather than in body, after he had sat for eight years died on the 13th day before the Kalends of November, in the year of the Lord 1122. He was buried three days after his death in the middle of the nave of the church of Canterbury, where he lies. He was a man outstanding in affability, suspected of no notable offence, except that he was more inclined to jests and laughter than his rank and age befitted, and for this reason he was called "the Trifler."

units.tr: XXXVI. William

units.la: E huius Archiepiscopi ortu, & iuuenili institutione nihil comperimus, cognomento autem Corbel vel Corbois dictus est, quidam Willielmum de Turbine eum nominant. Primò Clericus secularis, deinde Monachus Benedictinus, post Sanctæ Olithæ de Chiche Prior fuit. Annoque 22. Henrici primi, tertioque Ca40 lixti Papæ in Purificationis festo tam huius Archiepiscopatus ab Henrico Rege, quàm legatinæ authoritatis à Calixto Papa munus suscepit, consecratus à Willielmo tunc Winton. Episcopo, Londinensi Episcopatu vacante, peractoque sacrationis ritu Romam profectus est, vt pallio donaretur. Ibi tum Thurstinus Eboracensis Archiepiscopus (de quo in Rodulphi vita antea diximus) nactus, vt putabat, tempus idoneum, instabat iterum Calixto Papæ ne sua sedes Cantuariensi subdatur, sed quia Calixtus Regis, procerumque ac Præsulum animos ad Cantuariensis sedis dignitatem minuendæ prorsus alienos & auersos commouere in se noluit, veritusque ne quod ante senserat, si præter eorum mentem & expectationem quicquam statueret, ad dedecus & ignominiam Papalis authoritatis penitus relcinderetur, eam litem æse penitus amouit & abdicauit. 50 Etsi Chronica Petriburgensis Saxonica diserte testatur his verbis. Quòd aurum & argentum hanc controuersiam diremit. Itaque eam Gulielmus quam Thurstinus vna redeuntes ad Henricum Regem in Normannia tunc agentem accedunt, eoque salutato veniunt in Angliam. Rebus sic compositis Gulielmus Archiepiscopale munus iam gerere & excercere cepit: ac primum Episcopatum Roffensem vacantem Iohanni Archidiacono suo Cantuariensi dedit. Deinde Alexandrum Lincolniensem Episcopum Cantuariæ, & Godefridum regni Cancellarium Bathoniëfem Episcopū Lódini consecrauit. Quarto suæ consecrationis anno frequentem Cleri Synodum in Monasterio S. Petri Londini celebrauit, cui Iohannes Cremensis Honorii secundi tum Papæ legatus
units.tr: We have found nothing about this archbishop's birth or his early education. He was called by the surname Corbel or Corbois, though some name him William de Turbine. First he was a secular clerk, then a Benedictine monk, and afterwards prior of St Olave's at Chiche. In the twenty-second year of Henry I, and the third of Pope Calixtus, on the feast of the Purification, he received the office of this archbishopric from King Henry, and the legatine authority from Pope Calixtus. He was consecrated by William, then bishop of Winchester, since the see of London was vacant. When the rite of consecration was done, he set out for Rome to receive the pallium. There Thurstan, archbishop of York (of whom we spoke earlier in the life of Rudolph), seized what he thought was a suitable moment and again pressed Pope Calixtus that his see should not be made subject to Canterbury. But Calixtus did not wish to stir up against himself the minds of the king, the nobles and the prelates, who were wholly opposed to, and averse from, diminishing the dignity of the see of Canterbury. He feared that if he decided anything contrary to their mind and expectation, his earlier decision would be utterly annulled, to the disgrace and shame of papal authority. So he quite removed and dismissed that dispute with money. Indeed the Peterborough Saxon Chronicle clearly bears witness to this in these words: "Gold and silver settled this controversy." Accordingly William and Thurstan, returning together, came to King Henry, who was then in Normandy, and after greeting him they came to England. With matters thus settled, William began to discharge and exercise the archiepiscopal office. First he gave the vacant bishopric of Rochester to John, his archdeacon of Canterbury. Then he consecrated Alexander as bishop of Lincoln, Godfrey, the king's chancellor, as bishop of Bath, and John of Crema as bishop of London. In the fourth year of his consecration he held a well-attended synod of the clergy in the monastery of St Peter at London. At this synod John of Crema, then legate of Pope Honorius II, was present.

units.la: {y} Ex Archiepiscopo; cf. Eadmer. interfuit. Quod cum acerbissimis contumeliis Clericorum coningia exagitasset, sequenti nocte in propatulæ meretricis sinu & amplexibus, fœdissimaque voluptate deprehensus est. Cutus rei turpitudine & infamia coactus, legationis suæ infectis negotiis, nullisque faluratis aut reuisis clam discessit. Post hanc Synodum cum & nupriæ iam essent Clerici iterum interdictæ, & Clerici adillius impuri cœlibatus iuga per Willielmum humilis & pusilli animi virum arceri non poterant, egit cum eo Rex, vt eorum corrigendorum authoritatem atque ius sibi permitteret. Quod Willielmus facile concessit ex quo Rex quæstum magnum consllauit, quòd sacerdotalia coniugia venditia fecerit. Hæc Synodus Willielmi Synodus dicta est. Eodemque anno Henrico primo mortuo, cum Henricus secundus diadema Regio sacrandus esset, Thurstinus nullam veteris suæ simultatis & querelæ occasionem prætermittens, contempto ob animum pusillum atque modicum Gulielmo Regis capitis diadema imponere nitebatur, sed tam à Rege quàm à magnatibus Præsulibusq; ignominiosè turpiterque repulsam pariter ac ludibrium tulit, rū Crucigerr eius vna cum cruce, quæ ante Thurstinum gestabatur prostratus, cum risu & cachinnis è Regis capella probrosè eiectus est, et coronationis ceremonia à Londinensi ecclesia lebrabatur. Huius Archiepiscopi tempora insignia calamitate & incendio Londinensis vrbis & Paulini templi commemorantur. Vrbs enim ab Ecclesia S. Clementis, (quæ Danorum Ecclesia dicebatur,) ad Pontem exusta & vastata fuit An. Dom. 1130. quod etiam fuit consecrationis suæ anno. Eodemque anno Ecclesia Christi Cantuariæ similiter flagravit incendio atque concidit, quam Gulielmus iterum extruxit, & splendido ac magnifico apparatu dedicavit, Rege, Regina, ac Davide Scotorum Rege, & vtriusque tegmi proceribus præsentibus. Huic Ecclesiæ iam sacratæ Rex donavit Ecclesias S. Martini Doucrensis. Neque quicquam præter hoc à Gulielmo munere suo dignum gestum est. Animi tam angusti & debilitari fuit, vt ab Henrico de Bleise Wintoniensi Episcopo, Stephani Regis fratre, qui hospitium S. Crucis prope Wintoniensem civitatem condidit, fuligationis iure quod tacite obtinere conabatur, superatus penè cessit. Primum eniam Henrico pro legationis munere Romam petiit, hunc Gulielmus sequutus est, vt Henrico resisteret. Sed ita valuit Henrici authoritas vt Cardinalis creatus Gulielmo mortuo in legatione succederet. Declarauit etiam inconstantiam Gulielmi Stephani Regis coronatio, quam primus contra iutiiurandi fidem in Londinensi concilio à se primum, deinde ab omnibus optimatibus Præsulibusque Matildæ Augustæ eiusque hæredibus regni fucoessione promissi celebrauerat. Cui vnà cum Guhelmo Henricus Wintoniensis, & Rogerius Sarisbuciensis, cum nonnullis Abbatibus, proceribus vero quàm paucissimis interfuerunt. Gulielmo autem periurii conscientia tremenți atq; paruido in ipsa coronationis ceremonia & missa celebranda è manibus excidit hostiae posteaque Anno 1136. ægritudine mæstitiaque concubuit, cum 9. Annis & 9. mensibus sefdiffet moritur, in Ecclesia Cantuariensi humatus. Quo anno obierunt etiam Episcopi Exon.& Roffen. & statim postea obiit Thurstanus ille prædictus Eborac. Archiepiscopus, qui iussu & admonitione suaexcitauit Boreales regni proceres vt resisterent Scotis, quì se crudeliter, cum innumerabili exercitu in Northumbriam induerunt. Ipse verò Archiepiscopus, cum ægritudinis causa hinc pugnæ interesse non posset, misit loco suo Rodulphum Dunelmensem, siue (vt alii volunt) Otcadensem Episcopum ad populum exhortandum.
units.tr: {y} From the Archbishop; cf. Eadmer. When he had assailed the wives of the clergy with the most bitter insults, on the following night he was caught in the embrace and bosom of a common harlot, in the most foul pleasure. Compelled by the shame and infamy of this deed, he abandoned the business of his legation unfinished, and secretly left without greeting or taking leave of anyone. After this synod, when marriages of clergy had again been forbidden, and the clergy could not be restrained from the yoke of that impure celibacy by William, a man humble and of small spirit, the king dealt with him to grant the king authority and right to correct them. William readily agreed to this, from which the king gathered a great sum of money, since he sold clerical marriages. This synod was called William's Synod. In the same year, King Henry I having died, when Henry II was to be crowned with the royal diadem, Thurstan, not letting slip any occasion of his old rivalry and quarrel, tried to place the crown on the king's head, despising William as small-spirited and of mean character. But he was repulsed by the king, the magnates and the prelates alike, shamefully and disgracefully, and suffered this mockery. Prostrate, together with his cross-bearer and the cross which had been carried before Thurstan, he was shamefully thrown out of the king's chapel with laughter and jeering, and the coronation ceremony was celebrated in the London church. The times of this archbishop are remembered for notable calamity and the fire of the city of London and of St Paul's church. For the city was burnt and laid waste from the church of St Clement (which was called the Danes' church) as far as the bridge, in the year of our Lord 1130, which was also the year of his consecration. In the same year the church of Christ at Canterbury was likewise destroyed by fire and fell down, and William rebuilt it and dedicated it with splendid and magnificent ceremony, the king, the queen and David, king of the Scots, being present, with the nobles of both realms. To this church, now consecrated, the king gave the churches of St Martin of Dover. Nothing worthy of his office was done by William beyond this. He was of so narrow and feeble a spirit that he was all but worsted, and yielded, to Henry de Blois, bishop of Winchester, brother of King Stephen, who founded the hospital of the Holy Cross near the city of Winchester, over the right of visitation which he tried to secure tacitly. For first Henry set out for Rome on the business of his legation, and William followed him in order to resist Henry. But Henry's authority was so strong that he was made cardinal and succeeded William as legate when William died. The coronation of King Stephen also revealed William's inconstancy. In the council of London, against the faith of his oath, he had first celebrated it himself, and then all the nobles and prelates had done so, for the succession of the kingdom promised to Matilda the Empress and her heirs. With William, Henry of Winchester and Roger of Salisbury took part, with some abbots, but very few nobles. William, however, trembling with a conscience of perjury and quivering, let the host fall from his hands during the very ceremony of coronation and the celebration of mass. Afterwards, in the year 1136, he took to his bed through sickness and sorrow, and died after holding the see for nine years and nine months, and was buried in the church of Canterbury. In that year the bishops of Exeter and Rochester also died, and shortly afterwards that Thurstan, archbishop of York, mentioned above, died. At his command and urging he had roused the northern nobles of the realm to resist the Scots, who had invaded Northumbria cruelly with an innumerable army. The archbishop himself, because of his sickness, could not take part in the battle, and sent in his place Rudolph, bishop of Durham, or (as others will have it) of Orkney, to exhort the people.

units.la: Hic Thurstinus non tam iuris alieni oppugnator in detrahenda sedi Cantuariensi pristina subiectione, quàm sui strenuus asserror & vindicator fuit. Nam coram Papa præsentibus Scotiæ Regis oratoribus accrrimè vindicauit, Scotiam & suæ Eboracensis esse Prouinciæ, & Scotiæ Regem Angliæ Regis vasallum. Posteaq; de hac quæstione cū Davide Scotorum Rege armis & prælio dimicauit, eumq; superanit. At animo æger cum se frustra toties ac tam diu contra Cantuariensis sedis dignitatem contendisse vidisset, spote dimisso Archiepiscoparu. ad Monasterium Pontis fracti recessit, ibiq; Monachismo induto reliquam vitam peregit.
units.tr: This Thurstan was less an assailant of another's right in trying to remove the former subjection of the see of Canterbury than a vigorous asserter and defender of his own. For in the presence of the pope, with the envoys of the king of Scots present, he most vehemently claimed that Scotland belonged to his province of York, and that the king of Scots was vassal of the king of England. Afterwards he fought with David, king of the Scots, over this question, with arms and battle, and defeated him. But when he saw that he had so often and for so long contended in vain against the dignity of the see of Canterbury, sick in spirit, he voluntarily laid down the archbishopric, withdrew to the monastery of Pontefract, and there, having taken the monastic habit, spent the rest of his life.

units.la: XXXVII. Theobaldus.
units.tr: XXXVII. Theobald.

units.la: Vlterior successit Theobaldus, cuius etiam origo & institutionis ignota est historia. Sed ex Monacho Benedictino, Abbas Beccensis fuit: deinde anno 2. Regis Stephani in Londinensi Concilio (per Albertum Hostiensem Episcopum Romani Pontificis Legatum coacto,) à Suffraganeis electus est Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus, præsente Ieremia Cantuariensi. Ecclesiæ priori, ab eodem ctiam Legato, eodem in concilio consecratus est. Ac Romæ ab Innocentio. 1. pallium accepit, à quo etiam legati nati titulo donatus est, qui sedi & successioni suæ attributus ab omnibus Cantuariensibus Archiepiscopis inde usque retinetur. Parum eruditus, sed moribus commodis, ingenioqs miti ac mansueto fuisse perhibetur, ut tà regibus quàm procerinbus populoqs gratiosus fuerit. Huic Monachi omnia sua prædia permiserunt, & ab ipso foti ac nutriti fuerunt, sed postea liberam cis rerum suarum possessionem restituit. Consecrauit primò Walterum Dant. Atchidiaconū in Roffensem Episcopum, à Monachis Roffensibus fibus tussu suo electum. Roffensis enim Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi primi ordinatores & patroni deinceps semper fuerunt. Deinde Rogerum Cantuariensem Archidiaconum ad Eboracensis Archiepiscoparus eulmen cuexit, eumqs (acceptò obedientiā iuramento) consecrauit. Archidiaconatū autē Cant. Thomæ Becket, de quo primo loco dicendum est, contulit, quem tanta gratia Regi conciliauit, ut regni Cancellarius, quod maximæ dignitatis est officiū, à Rege constituetur. Siluestro deinde Priori Augustinensi à Monachis Abbate electo, consuetamb cnedictionem denegauit, quod esset infamis, is prouocauit ad Papam, qui crebris eum interpellauit pro Siluestro benedicendo literis. Diu rem difficilem Theobaldus, sed papalii literarum multitudine & instantia coactus, Pontificalē benedictione in Augustinensi Cænobio, Syluestro tandē imperatum est. Ieremiam autē priorem, qui sua electioni interfuit, summa sibi fide & beneuolentia coniunctum, diu, ut ei crebro vices suas committeret, occulta intercrueniente simultate, quæ firmissimas amicitias dissoluit, tandem infestauit, & loco mouit. Sed appellatione ad Papam interpostia Ieremias per Henricum runc Wintoniensem Episcopum, & Papæ legatum eius mandata peragentē restituitur. Quod Theobaldus præter suam confuetudinē indignē ferēs, iureiurado affirmauit se ab omni sacrorū administratione cessaturū, quamdiu Ieremias præsset Ecclesiæ. Iraq; Ieremias metuens ne sua eaufa Monasterium grauc aliquid ab Archiepiscopo, tamgrauiter sibi infenso patetetur, Monachorū odia in se concitaret, acceptis 100. marcis quibus creditoribus satisfaceret, prioratu sponte cessit, & totā reliquā vitā in Augustinensi Cænobio priuatus delituit. Anno huius Archiepiscopi cōsecratio tertio, Eugenius Papa generale Concilii indixit Remis, ad quod Theobaldus accitus est. Iraq; Henricus tum Winton. Episcopus, Papæ Legatus, qui in eo munere fræpe cū Theobaldo contendebat, ut Theobaldū vitum apertū, simplicē ac fidelem in Regis aut Papæ odium traheret, veršitissimē egit cum vtroq; cum Papa, ut Theobaldum ad concilium vocaret, cum Rege, vt eum in Anglia retinereret, ut si Papæ non pareret, censuram Ecclesiasticam, si Regi proscriptioncm & ciuilem pœnam timeret. Rex Henrici consilio Theobaldo interdixit ex regno exitū, omnesq; maris portus obseruari præcepit, ne exiret. Sed vt illa cæca & misera tulerunt tempora, Papis magis est quàm principibus, præsertim à clero obsequuti. Iraq; omniū custodum atq; vigilum manus euasit Theobaldus, transfretauit, ac Remensi Concilio interfuit. Regis postea mandato proscriptus est: isq; Regem atq; tegnū vitiffim intetdicti sententia percussit. Concilio a. dimisso rediit in Angliam, & in Norfolcia aliquantisper resedit, & Episcoporum intercessione Regi conciliatus, interdictum telaxatuit. Posteatantum valuit in Anglia anthoritas eius atque gratia, ut Stephanum Regem & Henricum Matildæ Augustæ filium pro iurc Regni Martē dimicaturos, sua opcta & diligentia Wallingfordiæ conciliauerit quo& bellū atrox ac interstinū auertit & patriæ tranquillitatē incolumitatēq; peperit. Reuersus autē Theobaldus exegit modicā argenti summā à S. Augustini Monachis pro datione chrismatis, quinquaginta cantūm solidos & 7. denarios solutionem Monachincgabant, Theobaldus censuriseos coegit. Res per appellationem ad Papam delata est. Is rescripsit ad Henricum Wintoniensem Episcopum & Robertum Hereford. 50 Episcopum, ut de causa cognoscerent eandemqúe definirent, qui sententiam contra Monachos secundum Theobaldum tulerunt. Pacatis in Anglia rebus Concilium Romæ iterum indictum est. Ad quod Thenbaldus cum Waltero Roffensi Simeone Wigorn. Rogero Couentrensi, Roberto Exceftren. Episcopis, cum totidem Abbatibus vocatus accessit, eoq; finito omnes comiter nulla litcaut discordia mota reuersi sunt. In hoc quieto & tranquillo Reipub. statu Theobaldus frequentem eleri Synodum habuit Londini, An. Dom. 1172. qui fuit suæ consecrationis decimus quartus. Huic Concilio intect fuit Rex Stephanus cumEnstachio suo filio, cuius, vt est vetisimile, prouocatione cōuenerunt. Postnlaut enim vt Eustachlo Regi creando consentirent, ad q. Papæ literisac mādato veriti adducinō poterāt. Iraq; Rex & Euftach. ira peciti oës eos Synodoinclusos,
units.tr: Next came Theobald, whose origin and early career are also unknown to history. From a Benedictine monk he became abbot of Bec. Then, in the second year of King Stephen, at the London council convened by Albert of Ostia, bishop and legate of the Roman Pontiff, he was chosen Archbishop of Canterbury by the suffragans, in the presence of Jeremiah, prior of the Church of Canterbury. He was consecrated at the same council by the same legate. At Rome he received the pallium from Innocent II, who also granted him the title of Legate by birth. This title was attached to his see and its successors, and all the Archbishops of Canterbury have kept it ever since. He is said to have been little learned, but of pleasant manners, gentle and mild in disposition, so that he was popular with kings, nobles and people alike. The monks gave him all their estates, and he was cherished and nourished by them, but later he restored to them the free possession of their property. He first consecrated Walter, archdeacon, as bishop of Rochester, having been chosen at his command by the monks of Rochester. For the Church of Rochester had always been the ordainers and patrons of the Archbishops of Canterbury. Then he raised Roger, archdeacon of Canterbury, to the summit of the Archbishopric of York and consecrated him, after receiving his oath of obedience. He conferred the archdeaconry of Canterbury on Thomas Becket, of whom we must speak first in due place, and he won such favour with the King that Becket was appointed Chancellor of the realm, an office of the greatest dignity. Then, when Sylvester, prior of St Augustine's, was elected abbot by the monks, Theobald refused him the customary blessing, on the ground that he was infamous. Sylvester appealed to the Pope, who repeatedly pressed Theobald by letters to bless him. For a long time Theobald resisted, but, compelled by the multitude and insistence of the papal letters, he at last ordered Sylvester to be blessed with the pontifical blessing in the monastery of St Augustine. Jeremiah, the prior, who had taken part in Sylvester's election, had been joined to Theobald by the greatest trust and goodwill, so that for a long time Theobald often entrusted his duties to him. But secret enmity intervened, which dissolved the firmest friendships, and at last Theobald harassed Jeremiah and removed him from office. Jeremiah, however, appealed to the Pope, and through Henry, then Bishop of Winchester and papal legate, who carried out the Pope's commands, he was restored. Theobald, bearing this indignantly and contrary to his custom, swore an oath that he would abstain from all administration of sacred rites as long as Jeremiah presided over the Church. Jeremiah, fearing that on his account the monastery would suffer something grievous from an archbishop so bitterly hostile to him, and that he would stir up the monks' hatred against himself, accepted 100 marks with which to satisfy his creditors. He resigned the priorate of his own accord and spent the rest of his life in private, hidden away in the monastery of St Augustine. In the third year of this archbishop's consecration, Pope Eugenius indicted a general council at Reims, to which Theobald was summoned. Henry, then Bishop of Winchester and papal legate, who often contended with Theobald in that office, wished to draw the simple and faithful Theobald, who was open-hearted, into the hatred of either the King or the Pope. He very cleverly dealt with both: with the Pope, that he should summon Theobald to the council; with the King, that he should keep Theobald in England, so that if he did not obey the Pope he would fear ecclesiastical censure, and if he did not obey the King he would fear proscription and civil punishment. By Henry's counsel the King forbade Theobald to leave the kingdom, and ordered all the harbours on the coast to be watched so that he could not go out. But as those blind and wretched times bore, men obeyed the Popes more than princes, especially the clergy. So Theobald escaped the hands of all the guards and watchmen, crossed the sea, and attended the council at Reims. Afterwards he was proscribed by the King's command, and he struck the King and the kingdom with the sentence of interdict. When the council was dismissed, he returned to England and stayed for a while in Norfolk. Reconciled to the King through the intercession of bishops, he lifted the interdict. Afterwards his authority and favour in England were so great that, by his effort and diligence, he brought King Stephen and Henry, son of the Empress Matilda, who were about to fight a battle over the right to the kingdom, to an agreement at Wallingford. By this he turned away a fierce and internecine war and secured peace and safety for the country. On his return, Theobald demanded a modest sum of silver from the monks of St Augustine as payment for the giving of chrism. The monks were paying fifty shillings and seven pence, and Theobald compelled them by censure. The matter was carried by appeal to the Pope. He rescripted to Henry, Bishop of Winchester, and Robert, Bishop of Hereford, to hear the case and settle it; they gave sentence against the monks in Theobald's favour. With affairs in England settled, a council was again indicted at Rome. Theobald was summoned to it, and he went, together with Walter of Rochester, Simon of Worcester, Roger of Coventry and Robert of Exeter, bishops, and as many abbots. When the council was finished, all returned amicably, without any quarrel having been stirred. In this quiet and tranquil state of the commonwealth, Theobald held a frequent synod of the clergy at London in the year of our Lord 1172, which was the fourteenth year of his consecration. King Stephen was present at this council with his son Eustace, whose coming, as is likely, was by summons, for they had come together to consent to the creation of Eustace as king, which they feared to bring about by the letters and command of the Pope. Therefore the King and Eustace, thus angered, shut in all those assembled at the synod

units.la: ac obsequios minis excogitabant, ut metu ac terrore efficerent id, quod authoritate atque gratia non poterant. Ac pserim, ad Regis voluntatem ac nutum redacti sunt. At Theobaldus Synodo elam ac cautissime egressus, cymba per Thamesim ad ostium maris vectus, nauiculam conscendit, & ad tranimarinas oras traiecit. Cuius discessione Rex multo turbatiot eum iterum proscripsit, eiusque bona fisco adiudicauit. In eodem etiam Concilio, multa friuolarum appellationum genera prohibita sunt, quae ab Henrico Winton. Episcopo, Regis fratre & Papae Legato, viro robusto atque strenuo, suam potentiam supra Archiepiscopalem dignitatem efferenti, omnesque causas ad suam tribunal trahenti, iustitia citata fuerunt. Quam diu enim ita elati & insuperabilis animi vir, Papali legatione fungebatur, infinitae ac inusitatae appellationes vndiq; ad eum adferebantur. Graues idcirco inter Theobaldum & Henricum Wintonien sem inimicitias gerebantur. Nam Cantuariensis in Wintonien sem ordinariam, & Wintonien sis in illum legatinam potestatem exercuit. Quibus duabus potestatibus inuicem collidentibus, & fracta Ecclesiae pace ad Romanum pacificatorem conuolarunt, cui quaestionem eo grauiorem quo ponderosiorem attulerunt: Et altercare caus a potior, sed neuter in exhausto saeculo reuertere est. Mortuo Stephano ab exilio reuocatus est Theobaldus, ac Henrico. 2. ob morum placabilitatem atque constantiam, multo maiori gratia quam Stephane fuit. Thurstinus seu Gulielmus eius successor iterum elam & ambitiose tentauit, ut Henricus a se Eboraci coronaretur. Sed Rex contra Cantuarienses dignitatem nihil fieri passus, non nisi ab eo, aut eius mandato coronari voluit, ut ex litteris eius constat, quas hic inteximus.
units.tr: and devised threats and menacing measures, so that by fear and terror they might bring about what they could not by authority and favour. Indeed, the bishops were reduced to the King's will and nod. But Theobald left the synod very secretly and most cautiously. He was carried by boat down the Thames to the mouth of the sea, boarded a small ship, and crossed to the lands beyond the sea. At his departure the King, much more troubled, proscribed him again and adjudged his goods to the fisc. In the same council, many kinds of frivolous appeals were forbidden, which were brought against Henry, Bishop of Winchester, the King's brother and papal legate, a robust and vigorous man who raised his power above the archiepiscopal dignity and drew all cases to his own tribunal. Such appeals were cited before the justice of the council. For as long as this man of such a proud and invincible spirit held the papal legation, endless and unusual appeals were brought to him from everywhere. Hence grave enmities were waged between Theobald and Henry of Winchester. For the Archbishop exercised ordinary power over Winchester, and the Bishop of Winchester exercised legatine power over the Archbishop. These two powers clashed, the peace of the Church was broken, and they flew to the Roman peacemaker, bringing him a question the more grave because it was weightier. The cause was the more powerful in argument, but neither party could return in an exhausted age. After Stephen's death, Theobald was recalled from exile, and with Henry II he was in much greater favour than he had been with Stephen, because of his gentle and steadfast character. His successor, Thurstan or William, again rashly and ambitiously tried to have Henry crowned by himself at York. But the King, allowing nothing against the dignity of Canterbury, would be crowned only by Theobald or by his command, as is clear from his letter, which we have inserted here.

units.la: HEnrieus Rex Angliae & Dux Normanniae, & Aquitaniae, & Comes And. Theobaldo Cantuar. Archiepiscopo salutem. Super hoc quod mihi mandastis, quod audieratis me coronandum, ad natale ab Archiepiscopo Eborac. apud Lincoln. in provincia vestra. Sciatis quod nullo modo me ibi coronabit, nec alibi contra dignitatem vestram. Ibi enim me coronabit, sicut mandastis, Lincoln. Episcopus, si praesentiam vestram haberem non potero, quam multum desideratam. Sed hac vice parco labori vestro, & cum Dominus Lincoln. Episcopus possit modo supplere vices vestras, nolo, quod ad me veniendo tanto labore vexemini. Et hoc pro eorum scitis, quod nec in his nec in aliis, quaediu coronam portabo, vestram offendam gratiam, nec diuinam dignitatem. Teste T. Cancellario apud Nottingham.
units.tr: Henry, King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, greeting. Concerning what you ordered me, because you had heard that I was to be crowned at Christmas by the Archbishop of York at Lincoln in your province: know that he will in no way crown me there, nor anywhere else against your dignity. For the Bishop of Lincoln would crown me there, as you commanded. If I had your presence, which I greatly desire, I could not be there. But this time I spare your labour, and since the Lord Bishop of Lincoln can now fill your place, I do not want you to be worn out with such labour in coming to me. And let them know this: neither in this nor in other matters, for as long as I bear the crown, will I offend your grace or the divine dignity. Witnessed by T., the Chancellor, at Nottingham.

units.la: Idem vero Gulielmus cum a Rege tepulsam tulisset, rem Romae tentauit, vbi cum nihil profecisset, reuersus in Angliam, in missa hausto ex calice veneno expirauit. Et tamen Rex a Theobaldo postea coronatus anno. 1155. qui fuit consecrationis fuit 17. eius consilio in maximis rebus, regnique administratione semper assensus est. Theobaldus placidam & hilarem, concordem cum Henrico Rege senectutem produxerat: sed languente valetudine, ipsaque senectute, (quae morbus est,) infirmus, suas vires indies sine labore ac maestitia, ipso die atque tempore tolli ac labefactari sensit. Itaque de piis acquisitis piè testari voluit. Testamentum condidit, in quo singula quae superfuerant illis bona pauperibus & in pios vsus contulit. Huius tempore Roffensis Ecclesia atque ciuitas combusta est, fere queque Cantuaria tota, & Ecclesia Cathedralis Eboracensis. Tum Nordouiei ad contemptum & ludibrium saluatoris nostri Iesu Christi affixus cruci puerulus a ludaeis fuit. Nouusitidem nummus vniformis pertotum regnum pereffusus fuit. Sed fuit tandem senectutis & languidae vitae molestia pertaesus Theobaldus bene, (vt fuerunt illa tempora) anteactam vitam morti persoluit An. Dom. 1160. cum 22. annis sedisset, ac in Ecclesia Christi Cant. sepultus in puluere dormit.
units.tr: When William had been rejected by the King, he tried the matter at Rome. There he achieved nothing, and on returning to England he died after drinking poison from the chalice at Mass. Yet the King was afterwards crowned by Theobald in the year 1155, which was the seventeenth year of Theobald's consecration; in all the greatest affairs and in the administration of the kingdom, the King always agreed with his counsel. Theobald had passed a calm, cheerful old age, in harmony with King Henry. But as his health declined, and old age itself, which is a sickness, made him feeble, he felt his strength ebbing day by day, without labour or sadness, on that very day and at that very hour. So he wished to bear piously witness to the pious goods he had acquired. He made a will, in which he gave to the poor and to pious uses whatever goods remained to him, one by one. In his time the church and city of Rochester were burned, and almost all of Canterbury, and the cathedral church of York. Then at Norwich a little boy was fixed to a cross by the Jews, to the scorn and mockery of our Saviour Jesus Christ. A new coinage, uniform, was likewise spread throughout the whole kingdom. But at last, weary of the burden of old age and of a languishing life, Theobald departed this former life, as good a death as those times allowed, in the year of the Lord 1160, after he had sat for 22 years, and he sleeps in the dust, buried in the church of Christ at Canterbury.

units.la: XXXVIII. Thomas Bscket.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Thomas Becket.

units.la: EHoc Thoma multa varie magis quam vere scribuntur. Itaque danda nobis opera est, vt veritate diligenter indagata, in lucem ea proferamus, quae certissimae fidei esse possint. Patria & ciuitate Londinensis fuit, patre Gilberto Becket mercatore, matre peregrina, nepe Syria prognatus. Pater a priore Mertonensis Coenobii primis literis imbutus, cum & sedulus & docilis, zelatoque prouectior fuerat, ad Academiam Parisiensem missus est, ibi cum & doctrinam vberiorem, & linguam Gallicam ealleret, Londinum reuersus iuftitiarii munus aliquandiu administrauit. Sed eius pertæsus, in Theobaldi (de quo antea diximus,) tum Cantuar. Archiepiscopi familiam & clientelam irrepsit, ab eoque ob ingenium & doctrinam vnice dilectus in Italiam missus est, vrius Ciuile perdisceret, ne quid in eo desiderari possit, quod ad administrationem Reip.(ad quam Theobaldus eum iam antea destinarat,) pertineret. Itaque iuris ciuilis scientiam coniequutus ad Theobaldum redit, à quo Archidiaconatu Cantuariensi præpositura Beuerlacensi, & Rectoria de Bromfeld donatus est. Deinde eiusdem Theobaldi commendatione in Regis familiam acceptus, totius regni Cancellarius, (quifummuset in Anglia magistratus,) constituitur, opimis tam spiritualium quam secularium
units.tr: Many things are written about this Thomas, variously and more than truly. We must therefore take care, having carefully investigated the truth, to bring forward into the light those things which can be most certain. He was born in the city of London, the son of Gilbert Becket, a merchant, and of a foreign mother, a Syrian by birth. His father was given his first schooling by the prior of the monastery of Merton. Being diligent, teachable and advanced beyond his years, he was sent to the University of Paris, where he acquired both a fuller learning and the French tongue. On returning to London he held the office of justiciar for some time. But growing weary of it, he crept into the household and following of Theobald (of whom we spoke earlier), then Archbishop of Canterbury. Theobald, who loved him above all for his talent and learning, sent him into Italy to learn the civil law thoroughly, so that nothing might be lacking in him that pertained to the administration of the commonwealth, for which Theobald had already destined him. Having gained knowledge of the civil law, he returned to Theobald, who gave him the archdeaconry of Canterbury, the provostship of Beverley and the rectory of Bromfield. Then, through Theobald's recommendation, he was received into the king's household and appointed chancellor of the whole kingdom, which is the highest magistracy in England, and was enriched with the ample revenues of both spiritual and secular dignities.

units.la: 10 dignitatem reditibus locupletatus. Quem tanta fide prudentiaq; gessit, vt Regis erga se benevolentiam indies cumularet. Theobaldus, vt diximus, sub haec tempora, cum senio confectus & infirma valetudine esset, quo minus Reip. operam nauare potuisset, eo plus authoritatis ad Thomam accessit. Idque eo quidem consilio fecisse Theobaldum scriptores tradunt, quod cum Thomam in consiliis fidum: diligentem & cautum, in dubiis prouidum & intrepidū, in aduersis fortem & magnanimum comperisset: Regem vero etsi adolescentem, sapientem tamen & argutum cognouisset, veritus ne Rex procerum atque laicorum contuetudine & consilio ab Ecclesiastica iurisdictione tuendā se ad latcam augendam inclinaret, in hoc Cancellariatus munere Thomam Regi coniungeret, vt aduersa Clero consilia labefactaret, & regiorum ministrorum audaci-
units.tr: 10 He discharged this office with such fidelity and prudence that he daily increased the king's goodwill towards him. Theobald, as we have said, at this time, worn out with age and in poor health, could no longer labour for the commonwealth as he had, and so much more authority came to Thomas. Writers relate that Theobald did this with the following purpose: he had found Thomas faithful in counsel, diligent and cautious, provident in doubtful matters, bold and magnanimous in adversity. He also knew the king, though young, to be wise and shrewd. Theobald feared that the king, swayed by the custom and counsel of the nobles and laymen, would be inclined to extend secular power at the expense of ecclesiastical jurisdiction. So he joined Thomas to the king in this office of chancellor, to weaken the plans hostile to the clergy and to curb the boldness of the royal ministers, who under the pretext of public power and right had conspired to plunder the properties of the Church as well as those of the provinces.

units.la: 20 am reprimeret, qui publicæ potestatis iurisque præterxu, tam Ecclesiæ quàm prouincialium facultates diripere conspirauerant. Itaque Thomas Aulam ingressus quò gratior Regi & Proceribus atque Aulicis haberetur, clericalem aructum, consuetudinemque depositi, & aulicum splendorem ac magnificentiam induit. Ac vt Regi sein omnibus aecòmo daret, eosdem pene mores, eandèq; vitæ degendæ rationem sibi finxit, easdem epulandi, atque dormiendi horas statuit, vna siue in seriis siue in iocosis rebus semper adfuit, in omni enirali lepore festiuus & concinnus fuit, gloriam, auram popularem, & multorum clientelam ambiuit. Præterea aucupio, venatione, vestium splendore, ec gregiocq; corporis cultu, copioso frequentēq; famulatu; equis generosis, argentearatiliq; ornamentis, epularum & conuiuiorum crebra lauitie, omnia aulico nitore tam profuse vtebatur, vt multi dicerent, ei Archidiaconatus ful, quem refitiuit, & ordinis Clericalis(Diaconus enim iam fuit) sibi in mentem non venire. Adhaec papalia atque clericalia iura tanta seueritate defendit, vt multorum procerum à se voluntates alienaret, & Regi ipsi nonnunquam resisteret. Quod ex quiori animo tulit Rex, quia in exteris cundis rebus gerendis vtilem sibi fuisse eius operam experiretur. Non minus enim domi, quàm militiæ Regi magna admiratione laudequè profuit. Gilbortum & alia quaeque loca munitissima, quæ in Gallia ad Regem pertinebant, enim à Gallo oeruptarentur, recuperauit. Eas vrbes quas Rex in agris Tolofanis vltra Guafconam bellum gerens cepit; dum Rex in bello progrederetur, Thomas militibus instructus donec Rex redirect eonfensuit, aliquatiam castellaipse oppugnauit. Sed in hac tanta gratia & potentia mul-
units.tr: 20 Thomas entered the court, and to be more pleasing to the king, the nobles and the courtiers, he put off clerical dress and manners and put on courtly splendour and magnificence. So that he might accommodate himself to the king in everything, he took on almost the same manners and the same way of life; he fixed the same hours for eating and sleeping. He was always present with the king, whether in serious or in playful matters, and was cheerful and witty in every pleasant conversation. He sought glory, popular favour and the following of many. Moreover, in falconry, hunting, the splendour of his clothing, the elegance of his personal grooming, a large and frequent retinue, fine horses, silver and gilded ornaments, and frequent lavish feasts and banquets, he used everything with such courtly lavishness that many said that he had the archdeaconry which he had given up, and that he did not think of the clerical order at all (for he was already a deacon). Besides, he defended papal and clerical rights with such severity that he alienated the goodwill of many nobles and sometimes resisted the king himself. The king bore this with an even mind, because he found Thomas's work useful to him in all the other affairs he conducted. For Thomas served the king with great admiration and praise, no less at home than in war. He recovered Gisors and other very strong places in Gaul which belonged to the king and had been seized by the French. Thomas, equipped with soldiers, while the king pressed on in the war, waited until the king returned and in the meantime himself attacked a castle in the territory of Toulouse, beyond Gascony, which the king had taken.

units.la: 40 torum qui occultas in eum struebant insidias inuidia conflagrauit. Quæ eò vehementius exarsit, quod eum Matia Regis Stephani filia, Abbatissa de Rummesia Mattheo Boloniæ Comiti nupsisset, duasq; filias ei peperisset, Thomas hoc tanquam ingens & indignum facinus protius aperteq; damnauit, quod Comitis thultorum; procerum in eum odia accendit.
units.tr: 40 But amid this great favour and power, many who secretly laid snares for him burned with envy. The envy blazed up the more fiercely because Matilda, daughter of King Stephen and abbess of Romsey, had married Matthew, Count of Boulogne, and had borne him two daughters. Thomas openly and fully condemned this as a great and unworthy deed, and by doing so he kindled the hatred of the count and of many nobles against him.

units.la: Quz tamen non minus cantè vixauit quàm despexit, Regis tantagratiâ fretus, vt magno peneque regio apparatu, vt Margaretam Galli filiam trienhem, Henrico Regis filio septenni sponsam acetpere, Parrisios mitteretur: Hæc sponsalia Henrico Pisano, & Wilhelmo Papiensi in Burgo Cardinalibus, & Papæ Legatis sacra ministrantibus celebrata Anno. 1160. quarto nonas Nouembr. omniaq; inter Regem atque Gallum odia dissidiaq; pacata, pacisq; diuturnæ fœdera pacta sunt: Obiit paulò ante Adrianus Papa qui in natione Anglus fuit, & Hyberniam Insulam Regi Henrico. 1. subiugandam papali diplomate concessit, ea conditione vt pro singulis eius Insulæ domibus denarium annuum beato Petro soluerer. Sed eo mortuo Cardinales qui diuersarum partium & factionum fuerunt (quidam enim Cæsarem, quidam Regem & Gallum sequebantur) duos Antipapas elegerunt. Cæsariani videlicet Octauianum, alteri Alexandrum, inter quos durante (vt dicemus) schismate diuturno, Alexander tandem potior, & superior euasit. His gestis Theobaldus Cantuariensis (vt diximus) Archiepiscopus lothagæua ætate, vitaq; functus est. Cuius mors in Archiepiscopis ingressum tanquam in perpetuæ cum Rege dissensionis seminarium, & ad propriam ruinam ac perniciem aditu Thomæ patefecit. Rex enim et si totis suis viribus pro Thoma vt Archiepiscopatu potiretur contendit, tamen tanto, tam assiduo ac tam vili eius semper obsequio quinque continuis annis in quibus Cancellariatum gessit, visus, exsistimare non potuit Thomæ studium in Reip. praesertim causa iam aucta sua dignitate sibi aduersum esse potuisse. Itaque Theobaldi morte per nuncios in Normanniam vbi Thomas secum tunc egit, cognita, Rex cui maximæ curæ fuit, vt is Theobaldo in Cantuariensi sede succederet, ne Monachi Cantuarienses (quos satis praefractos & pertinaces cognouerat) alterum eligendo suum propositum & desiderium anteuerterent, primùm Thomam ad se vocauit, ei & Cambrorum infestationes, & sein Normannia, atque Gallicanis prouinciis occupato Anglorum ad deficiendum mobilitatem facilitatemque indicauit. Quæ mala eò se magis dixit periclitari, quòd Theobaldus prudentissimus & fidissimus sibi praefuit nuper obiisset, cuius mors se absente perturbationis ac nouorum in Rep. motuum cupidos citius excitare posset, ea vero antequam nascerentur, & in apertum discrimen erumperent, cohiberi sine tumultu atque suspicione vlla posse, si Thomas in Angliam properaret, & authoritate atque praesentia sua regni subditos ad fidem Henrico Regis filio iureiurando praestandam adduceret.
units.tr: He, however, lived no less cautiously than he despised them, relying on the king's great favour. With a great, almost royal, retinue he was sent to Paris to receive Margaret, the three-year-old daughter of the French king, as the bride of Henry, the king's seven-year-old son. This betrothal was celebrated in the year 1160 on the fourth of the nones of November, the cardinals Henry of Pisa and William of Pavia, at the Burg, and the Pope's legates performing the sacred rites. All hatreds and disputes between the king and the French were laid to rest, and treaties of lasting peace were agreed. Shortly before this, Pope Adrian, who was English by birth, had died, and by papal bull had granted the island of Ireland to King Henry II to be subdued, on condition that he pay an annual penny to blessed Peter for each house on that island. But after his death the cardinals, who were divided into different parties and factions (some followed the emperor, others the king and the French), elected two antipopes. The imperialists elected Octavian, the others Alexander. During the long schism which we shall describe, Alexander at last prevailed and came out on top. With these things done, Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury (as we said), departed this life in his seventies. His death opened the way for Thomas to the archbishopric, a seedbed of perpetual dissension with the king and of Thomas's own ruin and destruction. For although the king strove with all his might to have Thomas obtain the archbishopric, still, having seen in him for five continuous years, during which he held the chancellorship, such great, such constant and such humble obedience, he could not think that Thomas's zeal for the commonwealth could be turned against him, especially now that Thomas's dignity had been increased. So when Theobald's death became known through messengers in Normandy, where Thomas then was with the king, the king, who took the greatest care that Thomas should succeed Theobald in the see of Canterbury, lest the monks of Canterbury (whom he knew to be rather stubborn and obstinate) should forestall his purpose and wish by electing someone else, first summoned Thomas to him. He pointed out to him the raids of the Welsh, and the instability and readiness of the English to revolt, while Normandy and the French provinces were occupied. He said these evils were the more dangerous because Theobald, the most prudent and most faithful man who had stood by him, had recently died, and his death might quickly rouse those eager for disorder and for new upheavals in the commonwealth during the king's absence. But these things, before they could arise and break out into open danger, could be restrained without tumult or any suspicion, if Thomas hastened into England and, by his authority and presence, brought the subjects of the realm to swear the oath of allegiance to Henry, the king's son.

units.la: Quod simul atque perfecisset, Rex ei Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum promisit, vt filio suo etsi minori in regno, & Thoma in sacerdotio collocato ipsi erutius ac sine vllius perturbationis, aut defectionis metu & discrimine externa bella gerere posset. Ad haec Thomas fertur respondisse. Ea quoque Rempe componendam, ius regium, fidemque filio suo publice dandam spectarent, se ex animo Regis curaturum, sed de Archiepiscopatu Cantuariensi cum meminisset quàm difficilis sibi ab aulica vita institutendæ ratio suscipienda sit, dixisse Regi: si id contingat, tantam Regis gratiam quæ suo diuturno & continuo obsequio collecta fuisset, non esse duraturam. Quod in sacerdotio tanto positus à quo detrahere studerent nobiles atque Curiales, non modo morem in omni re perinde ac in Cancellariatu solebat, Regi gerere non posset, verumetiam fide regni & Ecclesiæ dignitate atque iuribus contentio nascceretur, in eius partibus tuendis atque conseruandis ita Regi refutaret, vt haec iam summa gratia in atrox & exitiale aliquod odium verteretur. Verùm Rex qui iam de vtriusque tam Regiæ quàm Ecclesiasticæ Iurisdictionis certis finibus statuendis sentit, Thomam ad id commodissimum ratus, cum rem perfici sine mora voluit, intimum sibi ac fidissimum Consiliarium Richardum de Lucy vocauit, ei narrat perinde sibi curæ fore vt Thomas in Archiprælulatu Cantuariensi, ac vt filius suus Henricus in Regni Angliæ solio collocaretur, proinde eum vna in Angliam proficisci iussit operam daturam vt res ad eum quem Rex proposuit, exitum perduceretur. Accum in Angliam Thomas, Richardus Lucy aliique Regis legati venisset e primò praesules atque proceres, deinde reliquos speciatim conditionis (subditos Henrico Regis filio fide iureiurando publice praestare adegerunt. Hoc iuramentum quod Fidelitatis dicebatur, Thomas primus iuravit, salua fide Regi patri quamdiu viueret ac regno praeesse vellet, & reliqui ordine secuti eodem modo iurarunt. Hac itaque iuratoria securitate praestita, totius Cantuariensis prouinciæ Clerus edicto Regis Westmonasterii conuenit, ac Thomam (Rege per nuncios acriter solicitante) Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem nemine (praeterquam Londinensi Episcopo) contradicente summa conspiratione & consensu elegit. anno domini. 1162. regni Henrici secundi 7. Pontificatus Alexandri tertii 2. ac aetatis ipsius Thomæ electi 44. Deinde Presbyter ab Waltero Roffensi Episcopo (ante enim Diaconus tantum fuit) Sabbato Pentecostes ordinatus, postridieque ab Henrico Wintoniensi Episcopo solenniter consecratus, & in Throno Archiepiscopali Cantuariae collocatus est. Qui primus post Normanorum victoriam Anglus Cantuariensem dignitatem occupauit. Consecrationi huic tam illustri interfuit Henricus Regis filius cum plerisque Regni proceribus, & quadraginta Cantuariensis prouinciæ Episcopis, innumerâque plebis multitudine atque copia. Ea peracta Adamus Abbas Conchamensis ad Alexandrum Papam, qui rebus nouo schismatae Romæ turbatis in monte Pesulano in Alpibus morabatur, pro pallio missus est. Quod simul atque Thomas accepisset, tam dissimili & immutato genere vitæ à priori illa curiali fuit, vt Monachalem superstitionem sub vestitu clericali exerit. Nam vt scribit Triuetus, post suscep-tum pastoris officium supra humanam aestimationem fa-ctus est Deo devotus. Consecratus enim cilicium clam induit foemoralibus, & vsus est visu: ad poplices alicinis, sub vestis clericalis honestate habitû colės Monachalé. Et Wil. Cant. paucis conscius sub lorica fidei militabat, gaudens quia in triplici veste triplicem personam gerere, exterioriClericum exhiberet, interiori Monachum occultaret, & intima Eremitæ moles-tias sustineret. Ex quo quidem exsistimare facile est quamuis Monachum, namachorum sibi stondla hac dissimulatione adiunxerit, quantum tamen Regis praesulum, atque procerum animos abalienauerit, si quis ea quae de communi omnium voto, de Monachis ab Episcopali dignitate deinceps repellendis in Rodolphi vita antea scriptis, animaduerterit. Atque haec prima esse poterat offensionis & dissensionis regiae causa, quod cum antea politius vrbaniusque vixisset, iam odiosam illam Monachalem institutionem suscepisset, siue sponte sua, siue quodillam obsoletam papalis excommunicationis sententiam in Elphegi vita antea descriptam timuerit. Quae noua religio eti tamen subito Thomae incestit Archidiaconatum, tamen Cantuariensem suscepto Archiepiscopatu (etiam Rege acerrime post ulante,) diutius distulit dimittere. Ideoque Regis gratiam hoc sibi merito ademptam primo, postea tamen redintegratam non agnouit ad plenum. Itaque cum antea Thomas & Regis gratia & authoritate in Rep. quam maximam floreret, ex hac commutatione vitae dignitate maximae & sine villa reconciliatione perpetuae dissensionis tempora subito inciderunt. Cuius rei veritatem vt ab ipsis Monachis copiosissimis Thomae praeconibus accepimus, ita declaratum, ne (quod ab historia nostra alienum esse voluimus,) ad alteram partem nimio motu ac fetnote rapi videamur. Ad summum iam apicem & fastigium ascenderat authoritas Papalis, contra quam etiam principes luctarentur, tamen a praelatis atque clero, qui omnes Papae nexibus, non tam conciliorum & rescriptorum papalium decretis, quae pro legibus seruabantur, quae super fictione, & teligionis inicitia, mentisque caecitate & cauteriata conscientia, astrictae fuerunt, dum Ecclesiae suae dignitatem, immanitatem que defenderent, coram Romani, pontificibus sacerdotali Regali authoritate propensioribus superabantur. Itaque Thomas etiam ante semper Regi assensus fuit, & in singulis deliberationibus, concilii, capiendi congressibus a Regni iure, Regiaque dignitate vtiquam dissenserunt, tamen (cum animo semper elato, excelsoque fuerat,) Archiepiscopus tam Cantuariensis sacerdotali magis quam regiae dignitati amplificandae studuit, & ex occulta Papae Cleticque fuisse totus ac supra modum Ecclesiasticis priuilegiis incubuit, a quibus ne digitum vnquam, vt aiunt, latum recessit, quin pro illis augedis ius omnereliquum tam Regni quam Regis extenuaret. Ac Archiepiscopatu suscepto vt a inundantis rebus totus ad Ecclesiasticas traductus videretur, Cancellariatu sciens abdicauit, nuncque ad Regem tunc in Normannia detentum, cum regni sigillo misit, nec posse se scripsit cuius & Ecclesiae simul vacare. Rex qui Thomae operam in regni administratione cum sua filiuque sui adhuc minoris coniunctum esse voluit, iam suifacti quod eum ad Archiepiscopatum extulisset, persuasit, simulque pertimuit, quorsum haec praepopera Thomae abdicatio, cuius elationem magnificentiam cognouit, euaderet. Itaque magnam ex hac re aegritudinem (cuius tamen saufam in te retorsit) atque animi perturbationem Rex alta mente reposuit. Deinde Thomas cum Ecclesiae suas Cantuariensis iuribus angendis & conseruandis tanquam adaras sese deuouisset, multos plebeios atque nobiles pro praedijs quae Cantuariensis Ecclesiae fuisse propria asserebat, in ius vocauit, & authoritate, iurisque scientia potior ea recuperauit.
