units.tr: As soon as he had done this, the King promised him the Archbishopric of Canterbury, so that with his son, though still a minor, set up in the kingdom and Thomas placed in the priesthood, the King could wage foreign wars more easily and without fear of disturbance or revolt. To this Thomas is said to have replied that settling the commonwealth, the royal right and the public oath of loyalty to his son were matters he would take up from his heart as the King wished. But when he recalled how hard it would be for him to adopt the manner of life of a courtier as Archbishop of Canterbury, he said to the King: if that happens, the great favour of the King, gathered by Thomas's long and constant service, will not last. Placed in so high a priesthood, he would be disparaged by the nobles and courtiers, who would strive to pull him down. He could not in every matter follow the custom he had observed as Chancellor in obeying the King. Indeed, a dispute would arise over the faith of the kingdom and the dignity and rights of the Church, and in defending and preserving these he would refuse the King in such a way that this high favour would turn into bitter and deadly hatred. But the King, who already intended to fix certain limits to royal and ecclesiastical jurisdiction, judged Thomas the most suitable man for this. Wishing the matter carried out without delay, he summoned his most intimate and most trusted counsellor, Richard de Lucy, told him that it would be as much his care that Thomas be placed in the archiepiscopal see of Canterbury as that his son Henry be placed on the throne of England, and therefore ordered him to set out for England with Thomas and to take pains that the matter reached the outcome the King had proposed. When Thomas, Richard de Lucy and the other royal envoys came to England, they first compelled the prelates and nobles, and then the rest of the people according to rank, to swear publicly the oath of fealty to Henry, the King's son. Thomas swore this oath, called the oath of fealty, first, saving his fidelity to the King his father as long as he lived and wished to rule the kingdom, and the rest followed in order and swore in the same way. With this oath given as security, the whole clergy of the province of Canterbury assembled at Westminster by the King's edict, and, with the King pressing hard through messengers, chose Thomas Archbishop of Canterbury with the greatest unanimity and agreement, no one opposing except the Bishop of London. This was in the year of the Lord 1162, the 7th year of Henry II, the 2nd of Pope Alexander III, and in Thomas's own age of 44 as elect. Then he was ordained priest by Walter, Bishop of Rochester (for before this he had been only a deacon) on the Saturday of Pentecost, and the next day was solemnly consecrated by Henry, Bishop of Winchester, and placed on the archiepiscopal throne at Canterbury. He was the first Englishman to hold the Canterbury dignity after the Norman conquest. Henry, the King's son, attended this so illustrious consecration with many of the nobles of the kingdom, forty bishops of the province of Canterbury, and a countless multitude of people. This done, Adam, Abbot of Conches, was sent for the pallium to Pope Alexander, who was staying on Mount Pesulanus in the Alps, since Rome was disturbed by the new schism. As soon as Thomas received it, his way of life changed so completely from his former courtly one that he practised monkish superstition under clerical dress. For, as Trivet writes, after taking up the office of shepherd he became devoted to God beyond human estimation. Once consecrated, he secretly put on a hair shirt under his clothes and used it, keeping the monastic habit hidden beneath the decency of clerical dress. William of Canterbury, who knew few of these things, tells that he fought under the breastplate of faith, rejoicing that in a threefold garment he bore a threefold person: outwardly he showed the cleric, within he concealed the monk, and inwardly he endured the hardships of a hermit. From this one may easily judge how much, though by this dissimulation he won the monks to himself, he alienated the minds of the King, the prelates and the nobles, if one considers what was written earlier in the Life of Rudolph about the common vote of all to remove monks from episcopal dignity. This could be the first cause of the King's offence and dissension: having lived more politely and courteously before, Thomas now took up that hateful monastic way of life, whether of his own accord or because he feared that obsolete sentence of papal excommunication described earlier in the Life of Elphege. Although this new religious practice had at once befallen Thomas as archdeacon, he nevertheless, after taking up the Archbishopric of Canterbury (the King objecting most bitterly), delayed for a long time to lay it aside. Hence the King's favour, which he had rightly lost by this, was at first not acknowledged in full, though later it was restored. And so, whereas Thomas had before flourished in the greatest favour and authority with the King and in the commonwealth, from this change of life the greatest and perpetual dissension, without any reconciliation, suddenly set in. We have related the truth of this matter as we received it from the monks, Thomas's most copious heralds, lest (which we wished to be foreign to our history) we seem to be carried away with excessive zeal to the other side. The papal authority had now risen to its highest peak and summit, against which even princes struggled. Yet the prelates and clergy, all bound by the bonds of the Pope, were overcome by the Roman pontiffs, who were more inclined to sacerdotal than royal authority, while the clergy defended the dignity and immunities of their Church. They were bound not so much by the decrees of councils and papal rescripts, which were kept as laws, as by fiction and religious ignorance, blindness of mind and a seared conscience. Thus Thomas too had always before assented to the King, and in individual deliberations, councils and assemblies had by no means dissented from the right of the kingdom and royal dignity. Yet, since his spirit had always been lofty and elevated, as Archbishop of Canterbury he strove to enlarge the sacerdotal rather than the royal dignity. From a secret favour toward the Pope and clergy he devoted himself wholly, and beyond measure, to ecclesiastical privileges, from which, as they say, he never moved a finger's breadth, and for their increase he diminished all the rest of the right of both the kingdom and the King. Once he had taken up the archbishopric, so that he might appear wholly turned to ecclesiastical affairs, he knowingly gave up the Chancellorship and sent the seal of the kingdom to the King, then detained in Normandy, writing that he could not hold both that office and the Church at once. The King, who wished Thomas's service in the administration of the kingdom to remain joined with that of his still minor son, now persuaded himself that he had raised Thomas to the archbishopric; and at the same time he feared where this over-hasty resignation, which revealed Thomas's pride and grandeur, would lead. So the King laid deep in his mind a great distress from this matter (which he later turned back against Thomas) and a perturbation of mind. Then Thomas, having devoted himself as a sacrifice to maintaining and defending the rights of the Church of Canterbury, summoned many commoners and nobles to court over estates which he claimed belonged to the Church of Canterbury, and by his authority and superior skill in law he recovered them. Concerning these claims at length brought forward, he entered into a confer-

units.la: tim multi Regem in Normannia adierunt, ac de Thoma grauiter conquaesti sunt, quod praetextu Ecclesiae in omnium pene bona posse filiones, & inuolaret. Quibus de eatis a Monachis propugnator atque vindex iurium Ecclesiasticorum, sed a caeteris rerum aliarum expilator atque praedo dicebatur. Paulo post redilte Normannia in Angliam Rex vt effrenem Thomae cleticque potentiam exiguis magis certis, finibus coerceret: Cui vna cum Regis filio occurrit obuiam Southamptonae Thomas, quia Rege in osculo, sed non in gratiae plenitudinem receptus est, sicut vultus eius statim auersus omnibus qui aderant, palam indicauit, animitamen motum adhuc repressit atque cohibuit. Hic Regis reditus ex translatione corporis Edwardi Regis atque confessoris quam Thomas Westmonasterii peregit, celebris ac insignis habebatur. Eodemque etiam anno Alexander Papa Turonense Concilium celebrauit, cui Archiepiscopi & Praelati Angliae Regis permisione ac licentia interfuerunt, ac a dextris Papae Thomas cum suis suffraganeis, a finistris vero Eberacensis Archiepisc. cum solo Dunelmensi Episcopo fecerunt, ibi capto de Ecclesiastica quadam supra regiam libertate petitionem retinenda consilio a papae oustoniis dimissi & in Anglia reuerti sunt. Post hoc Turonense Concilium omnibus pene in rebus Clerus se a populo diffunxisset, cepit in Anglia de regni atque facetdotii auctoritate atque vi multo vario sermone disceptari, factaque perturbatio grauis de praerogatiua aut priuilegiis ordinis clericalis. Regi n. in regni tranquillitate custodienda, quietisque ac pacis perturbatoribus exterminandis occupato a iudicibus ac ministris suis nuciatu est, furta, rapinas, homicidia, & eiusmodi delictorum genera a clericis frequentius quam a laicis perpetrari, quos a seculari brachio atq; gladio tuebatur & vendicabat excommunicationis Ecclesiasticæ fulminatio. Quam præiatorum & Cleri licentiam vt repri-merer, & seculáris regiæque potestatis ius a sacerdotali distingueret, Rex consuetudines quaidam, quas regni vocauit, ab Henrico primo Rege auo suo delectas, sed non dum editas statuit promulgare. Quod vt tutius faciliusque facere posset, nuncios ad Papam misit, vt abeo prius confirmarentur, ne Præsati, ac maxime Thomas Cant. Arch. qui fetam amerceam Celsitudinem efferre cepit, reluctari possint. Sed in Turonensi priori Concilio inter Papam & Angliæ præsatos interuenisse tam occulta federa verisimile est, vt suam magis quam Regiam dignitatem extollere conspiraverint. Nàq; illarū consuetudinum capitulis a Papa retedis, Regii Legati re infecta reuersi sunt. Hoc ita Regem commouit, vt quia Præsatos atque Clerum Duce Thoma in vnam sententiam contra se coiffe animaduenerat, toto iam animo a Cleto aucrius, & in omnibus causis atque pri-uilegiis laicalem ordinem contra Clerum adiuuaret. Thomas vero Regis offensam & ægram mentem vno amplius iam obsequio leniuit, sed maiori pertinacia irritauit. Nam cum Rex vedigal quoddam a singulis terræ hydis ad regni defensionem tunc pendi cōsuetum in sicum quotannis suum deferri iussit, Thomas obstitit, eamq; pensionem arbitrariam atq; liberam cuique debere esse dixit, non alteram quique aut coactam. Tum in atrocissimis facinoribus per laicos iudices ac Regios ministros deprehensi quidam Clerici, in quos rex a suis iudicibus pœnas legitimis animadverti maxima seueritate voluit, à Thoma tanquam patrono seruati, mituisq; quam deliciis par erat castigati, omnes quæ sequebantur tragœdias excitarunt. In his vnus in Sarisb. diocæsi a regiis Iudicibus pro homicidio ad Episcopum ductus est, Regis officialibus & intempti propinquis atq; necessariis instanter vt de eo iudicium fieret & supplicium sumeretur fla-gitantibus. Ei vero acriter inficianti cum testibus & probationibus luculentis (iuxta iuris in causis criminalibus exigentiam) conuinci non poterat, canonica purgatio indicta est, in qua cum defecisset, Episcopus Archiepiscopum de pœna imponenda in iure consulit. Arch. autem consultus mandauit vt omni priuatus ecclesiastico beneficio exauthoraretur, & in monasterio ad agendam angustisśimæ vitæ perpetuam pœnitentiam recluderetur. Quo quidem supplicio Rex contentus non fuit, sed vt ad mortem subeundā produceretur, & seculari potestati (cum le coram iudice Ecclesiastico purgare non poterat,) punicendus traderetur, flagitauit. Sed Thomas iam dux & author Clerinę id fieret restituit. Haud ita multo post cum papalis Clerus hac Thomæ ferocia animum exultaret, Philippus quidam Brois Canonicus ad Regiū tractus Tribunal, Iudiciarios Regis in iure sedentes multis probris contumeliisq; affecit, cuius audacia Regem non modo in ipsum sed in totum Clerum commouit, & quanquam Thomas iam sero Regem placare studens cum virgis publice cæsim, ab omni Ecclesiastico beneficio muneréq; suspenderit, tamē Regis indignatio ita creuit, vt occultos Clericorum inquisitores per Regnum collocarit, quibus singula clam iustitiam tantas tantam facinorum copiam in Ecclesiastico ordine deprehendit & conquisiuit, vt quia leuibus præiatorum castigationibus augeretur indices Clericorum flagitia, ad ea corrigenda regia & atroci animadueritione opus iam elle ccernetur. Itaque dum Rex populi pacem, Arch. Cleri libertatem tueretur, præsulum processumque concilium Westmonasterii conuocatum est. In eo facinorosissimos Clericis scatere iam regnum vbique conquenitur, qui in talibus denique ceps flagitiis deprehensi vel conuicti nisi suis lictoribus (Ecclesiæ præsidio ac patrocinio destituti) tradantur, Ecclesiā breui nihil aliud quam Latronū asylum, regnumque ei prædam esse futuram. Nam parum curare eos Ecclesiasticum adimi sibi ordinem, ut quibus venerationem a tam granibus deliciis nollent continere: didicisse præterea se dixit Rex ab vtriusque iuris peritis Clericos facinorosos ranquam infames ab Ecclesiæ corpore amputandos, & ad Laicalem animadueritionem detrudendos, proindefe cum Rex esset, & gladiū ad facinorosos coercendos a Deo datum gereret, non magis Clericorum deinceps scelera quam Laicorum impunita patiturum. Ad quæ Thomas cum suis suffraganeis & præsatis respondendi diem postera petit. Eo die multa pro Ecclesiæ libertate ac immunitate, ne ad alia quam ad sua tribunalia pro quibuscunq; rebus ducerentur, protulit. Regem rogauit ne nouas leges aut nouaexempla in Cleri præiudicium aut grautamen ederet, quod si faceret senec debere sustinere, nec posse. Rex cum omnes reliquos præiatos in Thomq; sententiam consprasse cerneret, se nec legibus nec exemplis nouis vfuturum, sed pristinas Regni regiaq̄ue consuetudines ab Henrico primo auo suo collectas & repetitas, ab omnibus regni incolis teneri præceptum respondit, rogauitq; an illi cas essent seruaturi. Ad quod Arch. & confratres suos illas obseruaturos esse dixit, saluo
units.tr: Meanwhile many went to the King in Normandy and complained bitterly of Thomas, that under pretext of the Church he seized and plundered almost everyone's goods. To these complaints the monks replied that he was the champion and defender of ecclesiastical rights, but by others he was called a plunderer and robber of other men's property. Shortly afterwards the King returned from Normandy to England, intending to restrain Thomas's and the clergy's unbridled power within narrower and more certain limits. Thomas met him with the King's son at Southampton and was received with a kiss, but not into full favour. As soon as his face was turned away from all who were present, it plainly showed that his mind was still stirred, although he held that feeling back and checked it. This return of the King was regarded as famous and remarkable, because of the translation of the body of King Edward the Confessor, which Thomas carried out at Westminster. In the same year Pope Alexander held a council at Tours, which the archbishops and prelates of England attended with the King's permission and licence. Thomas with his suffragans sat at the Pope's right hand, and the Archbishop of York with only the Bishop of Durham at his left. There, after a petition was taken up concerning certain ecclesiastical liberties above royal liberty, they were dismissed by the Pope's kindness and returned to England. After this Council of Tours, when the clergy had separated themselves from the people in almost every matter, a debate began in England, in many and varied speeches, about the authority and power of the kingdom and of the priesthood, and a grave disturbance arose over the prerogative or privileges of the clerical order. For while the King was occupied in keeping the kingdom tranquil and in driving out the disturbers of quiet and peace, his judges and ministers reported to him that thefts, robberies, homicides and crimes of that kind were committed more often by clerics than by laymen, and that these clerics were protected and defended from the secular arm and sword by the thunderbolt of ecclesiastical excommunication. To curb this licence of the prelates and clergy, and to separate the right of royal and secular power from the priestly, the King resolved to promulgate certain customs, which he called the customs of the kingdom, chosen by Henry the First his grandfather but not yet published. So that he might do this more safely and easily, he sent envoys to the Pope, so that the customs might first be confirmed by him, lest the aforesaid men, and especially Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, who had begun to exalt his own greatness, should resist. But it is likely that in the earlier Council of Tours such secret agreements were made between the Pope and the aforesaid English prelates that they conspired to exalt their own dignity rather than the royal one. For when the chapters of those customs were rejected by the Pope, the royal legates returned having achieved nothing. This so moved the King that, having perceived the prelates and clergy to have combined against him in one opinion under Thomas's leadership, he now with his whole mind began to favour the lay order against the clergy more fiercely, in all causes and privileges. Thomas, however, soothed the King's offence and sick mind by one more act of obedience, but he provoked it with greater obstinacy. For when the King ordered that a certain tax, customarily paid for the defence of the kingdom, be brought to him yearly from each hide of land, Thomas resisted, saying that this payment ought to be voluntary and free for each person, neither imposed nor compelled. Then certain clerics, caught by lay judges and royal ministers in the most atrocious crimes, and whom the King wished to be punished with the utmost severity by his judges according to law, were protected by Thomas as their patron and punished more lightly than their deserts required. These set off all the tragedies that followed. Among them, one from the diocese of Salisbury was brought before the bishop by the royal judges for homicide, the King's officials and many relatives and kinsmen urgently demanding that judgement be given and punishment exacted. He stoutly denied the charge, and since he could not be convicted by witnesses and clear proofs (as the law in criminal causes requires), canonical purgation was appointed. When he failed in it, the bishop consulted the archbishop on the law about the penalty to be imposed. The archbishop, so consulted, ordered that he be stripped of every ecclesiastical benefice and shut up in a monastery to perform lifelong penance in the narrowest of lives. The King was not content with this punishment, but demanded that the man be brought forth to face death and handed over to the secular power to be punished, since he could not clear himself before an ecclesiastical judge. But Thomas, already the leader and author of the clergy's resistance, prevented this from happening. Not long afterwards, when the papal clergy were exulting in Thomas's ferocity, a certain Philip of Broi, a canon, was dragged before the royal tribunal and heaped many insults and abuses on the royal judges sitting in court. His audacity moved the King against not only him but the whole clergy. Although Thomas, now too late and seeking to appease the King, had him publicly beaten with rods and suspended from every ecclesiastical benefice and office, the King's indignation grew so much that he placed secret inquisitors of the clergy throughout the kingdom. Through them he secretly investigated and gathered such a quantity of crimes within the ecclesiastical order that, since the light castigations of the aforesaid men only increased the clerics' wickedness, it was judged that these crimes now needed to be corrected by royal and severe punishment. Therefore, while the King was guarding the peace of the people and Thomas the liberty of the clergy, a council of prelates and leading men was convened at Westminster. In it, it was complained that the kingdom now swarmed everywhere with most criminal clerics, who, if caught and convicted of such shameful crimes and not handed over to the King's officers (the Church having withdrawn its protection and patronage), would soon make the Church nothing but a refuge for robbers and the kingdom their prey. For they cared little that the ecclesiastical order was taken from them, since they would not refrain from such grave crimes out of reverence for it. Moreover, the King said he had learned from experts in both laws that criminous clerics, as infamous, ought to be cut off from the body of the Church and thrust down to lay punishment. Therefore, since he was king and bore the sword given by God to restrain wrongdoers, he would no longer allow the crimes of clerics to go unpunished any more than those of laymen. To this Thomas, with his suffragans and the aforesaid men, asked for a day to reply, and the next day he put forward many arguments for the liberty and immunity of the Church, namely that clerics should not be led before any tribunal but their own, whatever the cause. He asked the King not to issue new laws or new precedents to the prejudice or burden of the clergy, saying that if he did, they ought not and could not endure it. The King, seeing that all the other prelates had conspired in Thomas's opinion, replied that he would use neither new laws nor new precedents, but that the old customs of the kingdom and of the royal office, gathered and revived by his grandfather Henry the First, were ordered to be held by all the inhabitants of the kingdom. He asked whether they would observe them. To this the archbishop replied that he and his fellow bishops would observe them, saving

units.la: {y} Ioan. 3. saluo ordine suo: reliquique omnes tanquam in eius verba iurassent à Rege sigillarim interrogati eodem modo responderunt, præter vnum Hilarium Cicestrensem Episcopum qui cum Regem ea adiectione turbarum perpexerat, se Regias & regni consuetudines bona fide seruaturum promisit. Sed Rex cum ira excandescente mitigari non poterat, paratam vidisse contra se Clericorum instructam sub Thoma duce aciem dixit quam alio remedio disiiparet, ac denuo iussit vt absolute & sine conditione vllas eas se consuetudines obseruaturos promitterent. Archiepiscopus non alia se ratione hoc permissuros quæ de membro & honore terreno iurarent. i. saluo ordine suo. Ita cum longa altercatione penè aduesperasset, à Rege insalutati omnes discesserunt, à quibus Cicestrensis Episcopus quod à conceptis Thomæ verbis recedere præsumpsegit, singulorum conuitiis exagitatus est. Postridie Rex accitum Thomam omnibus quibus eum in Cancellariatu muneribus auxilset præterquam Archiepiscoparu amouit, & crastino clam ante lucem Londino Oxonium discessit. Interea Thomas cum ita intercessisset & quasi tribunitiam potestatem interposuisset Regiis consuetudinibus, Clericos etiam facinorosissimos à regni iure & potestate Regia vendicauit & ad suum Tribunal tam ipsos quam Laicos illos accusantes compellere ituduit. Qui conatus & Reip. perniciosus & ad Regiam Maiestatem amplitudinem que minuendam spectare ab omnibus putabatur. Rex è contra commotus permissam fuisse Clericis Ecclesiasticæ iurisdictionis prætextu tam impie nequiterque delinquendi licentiam, graues pœnas sanxit quibus Clerus perinde atque populus teneretur. In qua tam acerba (quali inter regnum atque sacerdotium) digladiatione etsi Thomas pertinaciter aliquandiu perstitisset, tamen eius suffraganei (Luxoniensis Episcopi Normanni interuentu) ad Regis sententiam adducti, cum parari sibi aliquam exitiosam machinam à Rege formidarent, Thomam deseruerunt. Paulò etiam post Thomas (eiusdem & Herefordensis Episcopi suasu, Robertiique Venduniæ Comitis, nec non Abbatis de Elcemosyna, qui se à Papa missum ad Thomam dicebat vt Regi obtemperaret,) Oxonium ad Regem profectus (ea quæ Regem tantopere offendebat clausula de tractatu,) se pure & absolute obseruaturum Regias consuetudines promisit. Quo facto exhilaratus Rex diem, quo ea de re vltra deliberaturi secum adessent, Clarendoniæ statuit. Cumque eò conuenissent (præsidente Iohanne de Oxonia) coram omnibus Prælatis & proceribus Regni facta est recognitio consuetudinum siue libertatum Regiarum proptere as distinctiones, quæ inter Clerum, & Regis iusticiarios, regniq; magnates tum frequentes inciderunt. Quas singuli bona fide in verbo veritatis obseruaturos spoponderunt. Deinde Rex has consuetudines Regni (populo iam conuocato) in Tripartitis & indentatis membranis tribus copiis describi mandauit, quas Archiepiscopi & Episcopi ram iuramento quam sigillis & chirographis suis communirent, & se pro iure culmnos promitterent quarum vnam penes Arch. Cant. alteram penes Eboracensem, tertiam penes se in Regiis Archiuis reponendam voluit perinanere. Sed cum descriptas consuetudines perlegissetThomas, dubitare se dixit an illarum quædam inter consuetudines est sint habendæ, itaque diem deliberandi antequam sigillum & chirographum adhiberet periit. Eo concesso Wintoniam profectus cum esset in itinere ex necessariis suis quidam eum liberius increparunt, quòd tanta facilitate Regiis consuetudinibus assensus sit, quorum sermone variè & inconstanter a priori assensione lapsus, abstinuit (quasi sua conscientia suspensus) à diuinis, donec promisso atque iuramento Regi præstito authoritate Papæ soluerentur. Papa ad soluendum quam confirmadam fidem promptior huius promissi liberationem indulsit Thomæ, damnauitque eas quas Rex ratas esse voluit consuetudines, quia Ecclesiasticam iurisdictionem quam dilatari voluit, coercebant. E quibus vna fuit ea quæ de Ecclesiarum iure patronatus describita, ab eodem Alexandro Papa In rescripto, quod iam inter decretales extat, reprobatur. Postea Thomas cum Regem in se hostiliter affectum cognouisset, quod à Papa fide Regi data liberatus esset, apud Rumenel nauem consendit ad Papam profecturus, sed reflante vento In Angliam reiectus est. Concilium tum Rex Northamptoniæ tenuit, eò à hictoribus Regiis tractus Thomas repetrundarum, peculatus, periurii, proditionis, falsi, pro his quæ in Cancellaria Regis gesserat, tam à Rege ipso, quam à Præsulibus & proceribus impetitur. Et Episcopi Regi permittebant se Thomæ eorū criminum reum coram ipso Papa doctoros. At Thomas quia ab Henrico Regis filio, eiusque in absentia suffitiario liber & absolutus ab omni anteacti Magistratus ratiocinio Arch. Cant. designatus fuit, (ne eorum quæ runc gessit iudicium paterertur) ad Papa appellauit, & sub pœna Anathematis Suffraganeis suis Episcopis, exteritisq; præcepit, ne in se patrem suũ atq; iudicē sententia vllã promulgaret. Qui appellatione sua reiecta, & spreto Anathemate sententiam nihilominus prolulerunt.
units.tr: John 3. saving his own order. The rest, questioned one by one by the King as if they had all sworn to his words, answered in the same way, except for one man, Hilary, Bishop of Chichester, who, when he saw the King's anger at that qualification, promised to observe the royal and national customs in good faith. But the King, inflamed with anger, could not be pacified. He said he had seen the clergy drawn up against him in battle array under Thomas as their leader, and that he would scatter them by some other remedy. He again ordered them to promise absolutely and without condition to observe all those customs. The Archbishop said he would permit this only in the form in which they swore concerning their temporal member and honour, that is, saving their order. So, after a long dispute, as evening was nearly come, all departed without a word of farewell from the King. The Bishop of Chichester, because he had dared to depart from the words Thomas had framed, was assailed with abuse by each of them. On the next day the King summoned Thomas and removed him from all the offices in the Chancery which he had held under the King, except the archbishopric. The following day, before dawn and in secret, he left London for Oxford. Meanwhile Thomas, having thus interposed himself and, as it were, a tribunician power against the royal customs, also claimed the most criminal clergy from the law and royal power of the realm, and tried to compel them, and the laymen who accused them, to appear before his own tribunal. Everyone thought this attempt both harmful to the commonwealth and aimed at diminishing the majesty and authority of the King. The King, on the other hand, was moved to indignation that under the pretext of ecclesiastical jurisdiction the clergy had been granted licence to offend so impiously and wickedly, and he decreed heavy penalties, by which the clergy, just like the people, were to be bound. In so bitter a contest, such as is waged between kingdom and priesthood, Thomas held out obstinately for some time. Nevertheless his suffragans, brought round to the King's judgment through the intervention of the Norman Bishop of Lisieux, and fearing that the King was preparing some deadly engine against them, deserted Thomas. Soon afterwards Thomas went to the King at Oxford, on the advice of the same bishop, of the Bishop of Hereford, of Robert, Count of Vendôme, and of the Abbot of Elcemosyna, who said he had been sent by the Pope to Thomas to urge him to obey the King. He there promised purely and absolutely to observe the royal customs, leaving out that clause about deliberation which had so offended the King. Having done this, the King, delighted, appointed a day at Clarendon on which the bishops and nobles were to meet with him to deliberate further on the matter. When they had assembled there, with John of Oxford presiding, before all the prelates and nobles of the realm, the customs or royal liberties were recognised, with regard to those distinctions which then often arose between the clergy and the King's justices and the great men of the kingdom. Each of them promised to observe them in good faith, on the word of truth. Then the King, with the people now assembled, ordered these customs of the realm to be written out in three copies, on tripartite indented parchments. The archbishops and bishops were to confirm them with their oaths, their seals and their signatures, and promise to keep them as law. One copy he wished to remain with the Archbishop of Canterbury, another with the Archbishop of York, and the third with himself, in the royal archives. But when Thomas had read through the written customs, he said he doubted whether some of them ought to be counted among the customs, and so he asked for a day to deliberate before he would affix his seal and signature. This was granted. As he set out for Winchester, some of his own household reproached him rather freely for having assented so readily to the royal customs. He, wavering in his words, varied and inconstant in his earlier assent, abstained from divine services, as if held back by his conscience, until the promise and oath he had given the King were released by the authority of the Pope. The Pope, readier to release a pledge than to confirm one, granted Thomas release from this promise. He condemned the customs which the King wished to be ratified, because they restrained the ecclesiastical jurisdiction that he wished to extend. Among them was the one describing the right of patronage over churches, which Pope Alexander himself rejects in a rescript that now stands among the decretals. Afterwards Thomas, learning that the King was hostilely disposed towards him, and that by the Pope's release he was freed from the faith he had given the King, embarked at Rumenel for a ship to go to the Pope. But a contrary wind drove him back to England. Then the King held a council at Northampton, to which Thomas was drawn by the King's officials, and he was attacked, for extortion, embezzlement, perjury, treason and forgery, on account of what he had done in the King's Chancery, by the King himself and by the prelates and nobles. The bishops allowed the King to have Thomas shown guilty of these crimes before the Pope himself. But Thomas, because he had been released and absolved by Henry, the King's son, and by his deputy during the King's absence, from all accounting for his past magistracy, and had been designated Archbishop of Canterbury, appealed to the Pope so that he would not have to suffer judgment on what he had then done. Under penalty of anathema he ordered his suffragan bishops and others not to pronounce any sentence against him, their father and judge. They, however, rejected his appeal, scorned the anathema, and nevertheless pronounced sentence.

units.la: M lantur ... [illegible, ~20 letters] Cardinalium legationem nouam à Papa potestatem quoscunque in Anglia sibi aduersos habuerat (Rege Regina, Regisque liberis proximisque cognatis solummodo exceptis) excommunicandi, quasi iam cum Gallo Regis inimico coniunctus nimis insolenter abusus est. Itaque Rex Alexandrum Papam promissi per Cardinales nuncios suos sibi haud ita pridem factis admonet. Papa se illius antiquae authoritatis Thomae (ariete Cardinalium adiuentum concessa sed nuper reuocata) praetextu excusauit, Gallus legatos ad Papam atque Cardinales misit, vt Thomae causam contra Regem tuerentur, eumque tanquam oculi sui pupillam defenderent. Papa in his difficultatibus inter Regem atque Gallium positus quid ageret, aut cui magis obsequeretur, incertus fuit. Tandem vt vtrique inuidiam vitaret, Regem rogauit vt cum Gallo de hac re communicare dignaretur, Gallum enim monuit ne Regem in ea re commoueret propter eam cum Caesare coniunctionem, quaeque Regem in priori amicitia, foedereque retento auerti posset, eo vero offensione & alienato Romanae curiae ipsiusque Galli detrimento maximo futura sit. Atque hoc in loco admirari libet varietatem & inconstantiam Monachorum, qui ipsum Papam atque Cardinales quod in hoc discrimine Regi propensiores fuerint tantis insectentur opprobriis, Gallum autem (eum bella & apertas inimicitias contra Regem gessit,) quod Thomam contra Regem atque patriam tibi coniunctum dilexerit, pietatis virtutisque laudibus ornent: adeo prodiciones omnes & scelera probant: quaecunque pro Ecclesiasticae pietatis ambitione & libidine suscipiuntur. Verum inter Regem atque Gallum reconciliationem (ex Papae consilio) antefractis foedenbus, Rex ex Anglia in Normanniam, indeque ad inuitendum Gallum Parisios venit, vbi (exteris rebus transactis,) de Thoma eum Rege conciliando colloquio agi coepit. Atque aderat in aula Thomas sed in Regis conspectum nondum venit, ideoque ea quae ad concordiam inciendam necessaria putauit, in scripta redacta ad Regem misit. In his erat vt Archiepiscopatum Cant. omniaque ab eo receptaplene restituerat, tum alias possessione (postquam Archiepiscopus fuit) ablatas redderet. Quibus postulatis Rex respondit, restituere se nihil ei posse qui sponte Ecclesiam deseruerit, itaque cum e tegni consuetudine, Regisque dignitate Cantuariensis Ecclesiae quam Thomas fuga voluntaria pro derelicta habuit, fructus vacantes certis iam personis contulisset, nolle se dixit ea, quae prout iure regni potuit contulisset, in irritum 30 dubiumque reuocari, si paratum se Thomae satisfacere vel coram ipso Gallo, vel senatu Parisiensi, aut si id Thomas mallet coram diuersarum prouinciarum in Lutetia Academia studentibus Scholaribus. Quo dicto omnium animi Thomae simulatione ante a Regeaurefi conciliati ei iunt, statimque intromissus Thomas ad pedes Regis Angliae his verbis procidit. Domine Rex totam causam unde inter nos orta est dissensio, tuo commitio arbitrio, sed in Rege Vi quae adiectione grauiter communis Rex, Regiae dignitatis munificentiaeque immemorem, & ingratum eum appellauit, & ad Gallum conuenius. Quicquid isti inquit, displicuerit, dicet honori Dei esse contrarium, sed ne videar vel Dei, vel suo honori in aliquo velle resistere, hoc tantum potest Multi in Anglia extitere Reges, quorum quidam maiori, quidam minori auihoritate atque ditione fuerunt 40 quam ego sum. Multi rursus Archiepiscopi Cant. praeter hunc magni atque sancti viri. Itaque quod officii sui eorum antecessorum maximus meorum minimo praestiit, hoc mihi Thomas praester, atque aequiescam. Quae cum dixisset Rex, ab astantibus vndique acclamatum est, Rex satis se humiliat. Cumque Thomas aliquantisper siluisset, Gallus, Quid, inquit, Domine Archiepiscope, viselle maior sanctis viris, vel maior Petro? Quid dubitas? Ecce pax pro fonibus. Ad haec respondit eallide satis & elate Thomas, illorum temporum atque hoc horum non fuisse rationem eandem, illos pedetentim Reges ad Christum obsequio alieniste, cum omnia quae ad religionem spectarent vno momento petisse non poterant, se ab his non esse tecesserunt quae iam Ecclesiae acquisita atque lucrifacta sunt. Praeterea lapsos illos in multis, vt homines ipsumque Petrum singulos fuisse, 50 quorum exempla sequi necesse non haberet, ereuisse Ecclesiae facultates semper constantia Praelatorum, qnas sua iam acquisitas Ecclesiae vt diminuantur nunquam esse passurum. Quibus respondis cum pertinax & morosus fuisset, vtriusque Regni proceres impedimentum pacis arrogantiae Thomae imputabant, indignumque esse aiebant, vt quia patria fugit, alterent in Gallia, Et tamen intetededentibus vtrisque multis ad conceordiam vtcunque reducti esset Rex & Archiepiscopus, nisi tam temere emisisset eam adiectionem Thomas, salue honore Dei. Omnem enim aliam securitatem promisit illi Rex, praeter osculum Pacis, Archiepiscopus autem omnes alias concordiae conditiones repudiauit. Cum itaque discessissent, Rex eo die satis vlam proditoris sui dixit superbiam, Praesulesque atque proceres concordiae mediatores, multa recedentes Archiepiscopo iri os obiecerunt.
units.tr: M [illegible] the new legation of the Cardinals. From the Pope he had obtained the power of excommunicating whomsoever in England were hostile to him (only the Queen, the King's children and his nearest kin being excepted), and, as though he were now allied with the Frenchman, the King's enemy, he abused this power too insolently. So the King reminded Pope Alexander of the promise made through the Cardinals, his envoys, not long before. The Pope excused himself on the ground that the former authority granted to Thomas, aided by the Cardinals' battering-ram, had been conceded but was lately revoked. The Frenchman sent envoys to the Pope and the Cardinals to defend Thomas's cause against the King, and to guard him as the apple of their eye. The Pope, placed between the King and the Frenchman in these difficulties, was uncertain what to do, or whom to obey more. At last, in order to avoid unpopularity with both, he asked the King to deign to confer with the Frenchman on this matter. He warned the Frenchman not to stir up the King over this, on account of that alliance with the Emperor, since the King, if the former friendship and treaty were kept, might be turned away; and if he were offended and alienated, it would be the greatest loss to the Roman court and to the Frenchman himself. Here it is worth wondering at the fickleness and inconsistency of the monks, who denounce the Pope and the Cardinals with such great insults because they were more inclined to the King in this crisis, yet praise with the glory of piety and virtue the Frenchman, who waged wars and open enmities against the King, because he cherished Thomas, who was allied against the King and his country. So fully do they approve all treacheries and crimes that are undertaken for the ambition and lust of ecclesiastical piety. But after the treaties had been broken, a reconciliation between the King and the Frenchman was brought about on the Pope's advice. The King came from England to Normandy, and from there to Paris to visit the Frenchman, where, once other business was settled, a conference about reconciling Thomas with the King began. Thomas was at court, but had not yet come into the King's sight, and so he sent to the King in writing the things he thought necessary for bringing about concord. Among them was that the King should fully restore to him the Archbishopric of Canterbury and everything received from it, and should also return the possessions taken from him since he became archbishop. To these demands the King replied that he could restore nothing to one who had voluntarily abandoned the Church. Since, by the custom of the realm and by the dignity of the King, he had already bestowed the vacant revenues of the Church of Canterbury, which Thomas had treated as abandoned by his voluntary flight, on certain persons, he said he was unwilling that what he had lawfully conferred under the law of the realm should be called back into question and annulled. He would, however, satisfy Thomas, either before the Frenchman himself, or before the Parisian senate, or, if Thomas preferred, before the scholars studying at the University of Paris, students from the various provinces. At these words the minds of all were won over to reconciliation with the King, since Thomas's pretended change of heart had been brought about earlier. Thomas was at once admitted and fell at the feet of the King of England with these words: "Lord King, I put the whole cause from which our dispute arose under your authority and judgment, but..." The King, however, was gravely offended by the addition, and called him ungrateful and forgetful of royal dignity and generosity, and went off to the Frenchman. "Whatever these men may say," he said, "will be called contrary to the honour of God. But so that I may not seem to resist either God's honour or his own in any way, this only can he do: there have been many kings in England, some of whom had greater authority and dominion than I have. Likewise there have been many Archbishops of Canterbury besides this great and holy man. So let Thomas render to me, the least of them, what the greatest of his predecessors rendered to my predecessors, and I will acquiesce." When the King had said this, acclamations rose on all sides from the bystanders: "The King humbles himself enough." When Thomas had kept silent for a while, the Frenchman said: "What, my lord Archbishop? Do you wish to be greater than holy men, or greater than Peter? Why do you hesitate? Behold, peace is at your feet." To this Thomas answered rather cunningly and loftily that the reasoning of those times was not the same as that of these, that those men had by degrees alienated kings to obedience to Christ, since everything relating to religion could not be sought in a single moment; he said that he had not given way to those things which were already acquired and gained by the Church. Moreover, he said, those men had fallen in many things, being men like others, and Peter himself singly was not an example they needed to follow; the constancy of the prelates had always preserved the Church's possessions, and he would never allow those possessions, now acquired by the Church, to be diminished. When he had answered thus, and was stubborn and difficult, the nobles of both kingdoms blamed Thomas's arrogance for the hindrance to peace, and said it was unworthy that, because he had fled his country, he should cause changes in France. And although many were working on both sides to bring the King and the Archbishop back to concord in some way, it would have succeeded, had Thomas not so rashly added that qualification, "saving the honour of God." For the King promised him every other security except the kiss of peace, but the Archbishop rejected all the other conditions of concord. So when they had parted, the King said that day that he had sufficiently seen the pride of his traitor, and the prelates and nobles who were the mediators of concord, as they withdrew, heaped many reproaches on the Archbishop's face. [He was] always proud, haughty, and wise in his own eyes, and truly always a follower of his own will, through whom the Church, already partly ruined, would soon be utterly destroyed. Driven by these shouts and those of the courtiers, Thomas left the court, and did not know for certain where he should betake himself, but the King...

units.la: Quòd semper superbus, elatus, sapiensque in oculis suis fuisset, proprièque semper sectator voluntatis, quod per ipsum ex parte iam destructa, penitus cito destrueretur Ecclesia. Quorum atque aulicorum clamoribus actus Thomas Aula discessit, nec quò se reciperet certò cognovit, sed Regè in Angliam reuerso iussit sua perfidia Gallus Thomam iterum per nuncios ad se vocauit, cumque omnibus rebus abunde instructum misit ad Senones. Rex deinde ne intestini in Anglia motus ex hac Thomæ turbatione nascerentur, cum Galli mobilitatem verlutiaque perspexisset, filium suum Henricum Angliæ Regem corona sacrare decreuit, vt ipse transmarinas suas provincias, de quibus à Gallo timebat, securè administrare posset. Itaque omnes Regni Præsules atque Proceres Idibus Iulii. 1170. Westmonasterij iussit convenire. Quod cum Thomas accepisset impetrauit à Papa literas ad Eboracensem Archiepiscopum reliquosque Angliæ Episcopos, ne fine suo mandato, & Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis consensu quis Regem sacrare praesumat. Sed antequam hæc promulgatæ essent, hæc regalis coronatio à Rogerio Eboracensi Archiepiscopo in Ecclesia S. Petri Westmonasterij peracta est, Londinensi, Sarisburiensi, & Roffensi Episcopis praesentibus, qui de iure Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis, ad cuius dignitatem atque ius Regum Angliæ coronatio ab antiquo pertinere dignoscitur, protestati sunt. Perfectisque coronationis solennibus Rex traiecit in Normanniam, atque Gallum adiens de Thoma tantis ab eo officiis culto, tantaque liberalitate subleuato acerbius expostulauit. Is cum & ius Regni firmatum filio, & res in Angliam sedatas atque compositas cognouisset, Regis iam praesentia nonnihil perterritus, folumnodo de reconciliatione procurandâ se studuisse dixit, petiitque à Rege vt id suo interuentu fiat, Thomam enim iam eius diuturno suafuad omnem obseruantiam Regi deferendam esse parare. Quæ Galli oratio Regi non displicuit, itaque accepitus Thomas cum nihil ad summam reconciliationem præter osculum defuisset, in ipsum amplexu atque osculo, *in honore(inquit) Dei vos oscalor. Quibus verbis turbatus iterum Rex ab osculo recessit, nihil præter occultam dissimulationem sub his consuetis Thomæ clausulis, Nunc saluo ordine meo, nunc saluo honore Dei, nunc saluâ fide Dei, & similibus abscondıtam esse suspicans. Sed paulò post Rhotomagensi atque Senunensi Archiepiscopis atque Niuernensi Præsule Papæ nomine procuratoribus, Rex Gallum in die Mariæ Magdalenæ ad fraudu valentiorum conuenit, quo adductus Thomas cum Regè hoc modo in gratiam rediit. In quando planitiem equis vectis vt priuata inter se colloquia conferrent, feceliserunt, factaque reconciliatione Archiepiscopus se ab equo demisit, & ad pedes Regis se proiecit, Rex verò inclinato Archiepiscopo ab equo descendens, eum medius vnus eleuauit, atque equum ascendenti frenum & ascensorium aptauit atque tenuit, quæ curiositas duobus tribusue spacijs factis iterum repetita est, omnibus qui aderant cernentibus & admirantibus, sed causas nescientibus. His gestis cum à Rege restitutionem petiisset, iussit Rex vt prius perinde atque vellet & optaret rediturum.
units.tr: That he had always been proud, haughty and wise in his own eyes, and always a follower of his own will, so that through him the Church, already partly destroyed, would quickly be utterly destroyed. Driven by the outcry of these men and of the courtiers, Thomas left the court, not knowing for certain where he should go. But when the King had returned to England, the Frenchman, faithless as he was, again summoned Thomas through messengers and sent him to Sens, fully supplied with everything. Then the King, fearing that domestic disturbances in England would arise from this trouble with Thomas, and having observed the fickleness and cunning of the Frenchman, whom he feared for his overseas provinces, resolved to have his son Henry crowned King of England, so that he himself could administer those provinces safely. Accordingly, on the Ides of July 1170, he ordered all the prelates and nobles of the realm to assemble at Westminster. When Thomas heard of this, he obtained from the Pope letters addressed to the Archbishop of York and the other bishops of England forbidding anyone to presume to crown the King without his mandate and the consent of the Church of Canterbury. But before these were published, the royal coronation was performed by Roger, Archbishop of York, in the church of St Peter at Westminster, in the presence of the bishops of London, Salisbury and Rochester, who protested concerning the right of the Church of Canterbury, to whose dignity and right the coronation of the Kings of England is known to have belonged from of old. When the solemnities of the coronation were complete, the King crossed into Normandy and, approaching the Frenchman, complained bitterly about Thomas, whom he had cherished with such great services and raised with such great generosity. The Frenchman, having learned that the right of the kingdom had been confirmed for the son and that affairs in England were calmed and settled, and somewhat alarmed by the King's presence, said only that he had striven to bring about a reconciliation and asked the King that this be done through his intervention, since Thomas was now preparing, through his long persuasion, to show every deference to the King. The King did not dislike this speech of the Frenchman, and so Thomas was received; since nothing was lacking to a full reconciliation except the kiss, he embraced him and kissed him, saying: "In the honour of God I kiss you." Disturbed by these words, the King again drew back from the kiss, suspecting nothing but hidden dissimulation under Thomas's customary formulas: "saving my order," "saving the honour of God," "saving the faith of God," and the like. But shortly afterwards, the Archbishops of Rouen and Sens and the Bishop of Nevers, acting as procurators in the Pope's name, brought the King together with the Frenchman on the feast of Mary Magdalene, at a place on the border between the two realms, to the more powerful party's advantage. Thomas, thus brought there, returned to favour with the King in the following manner. They met on horseback on a level plain so that they might hold private conversation together; when the reconciliation was made, the Archbishop dismounted and threw himself at the King's feet, and the King, bowing to the Archbishop, got down from his horse, and one of those present lifted him up and held the bridle and stirrup for him as he mounted. This courtesy was repeated two or three times, with all who were present watching and wondering, though not knowing the reasons. After these things were done, when he had asked the King for restitution, the King ordered that he should return as soon as he himself wished and desired.

units.la: Acad filium suum Henricum nuper coronatum Regem scribitur, reconciliatum esse ex Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo Thomæ, proinde sibi atque his qui secum Angliam exiissent, restituat ea quæ tribus ante eorum discessum menibus habuerunt. Thomas cuius animus sola elatione & vindictæ cupiditate saucius fuit, ante quam redirét Cantuariam, quasdam excommunicationis & Anathematis sententias à Papa diu ante latas, & suo arbitrio permissas in Angliam praemisit. In quibus Eboracensem Archiepiscopum, Londinensem, & Sarisburiensem Episcopos, aliosque nonnullos qui Regis minuris coronationem celebrauerunt, nominatim ferit. Quo facto maiori fastu atque arrogantia post septem annorum exilium reuersus est quàm aufugit. Illi ad Regem in Normanniam transiciunt, quaeruntur omnia rursus à Thoma nouis Papalibus censuris esse perturbata, se quia in filii coronatione obtemperabant Regi, à Papa atque Thoma quasi aqua & igni interdictos. Rex renouatum sibi ex hac iterata Thomæ pertinacia dolorem continere non potuit, illi ... quia ex Anglia venerant Episcopisad filio Regè remissis, caeteris aûr audientib. famulis acerbissimas & graues contra Thomam voces & querelas emisit. Non posse se amplius ab illo homine fidè & obseruantia sperare, quì vix diu restitutus, oes nouarum offensionum, & Reip. perturbationum causas conquireret, execrandum sibi esse illum diem quo Thomam ad Archiepiscopatum extulerit, aut restituerit, qui ob tumaciam Maiestatem violat Regiam, totumque sine vindice conculcat regnum: omnes quos putriverant beneficiis affecerat ita maledictos, si aliquis de sacerdotio qui ipsum atque Regnum indesinenter perturbat, dignam poenam non sumat. Huic funestae Regis execrationi insecuti sunt quatuor Milites Reginaldus filius Vrß, Hugode Mortuilla, Gulielmus de Tracy, & Richardus Brito, qui ex tam tristi Regis sermone collegerunt gratissimum seilli obsequium præstaturos si Thomam interficerent. Interea Thomas maximo equitatu atque famulatu stipatus Cantuariam veniit, ibi à Monachis summo gaudio receptus, Papales illas censuras in suos Suffraganeos promulgauit: deinde eadem magnificentia atque pompa venit Londinum, & in Londinensem iterum Episcopum tumulumque suæ diocesis Clerum eas diras Papales sententias repetit. Inde cum ad Regem silium qui tum apud Woodstoock prope Oxonium egit properaret, Regis nomine à Militibus Regis Cantuariam reuerti, easque sententias quas in Episcopos atque Clerum denunciasset reuocare iussus est. Quo accepto nuncio ad munerium, siue munimentum quoddam suum de Harwel, quod septem miliaribus à Cœnobio Sancti Albani distabat duxerit. Venitque ad eum postridie de reditu ab exilio gratulatum Abbas Sancti Albani, quem rogauit Thomas vt Regem silium adiret, eisque vt Thomæ aduentum ad se admitteret molli aliquo sermone suaderet. Sed cum Rex offensus per Thomam fuisset, quod suam coronationem à suspensis Episcopis, & administrationem sui officii non habentibus, celebraretur, fuisse vbique præditaret, ne ipsum Abbatem à Thoma accedentem admisit. Reuerso Abbate, Thomas etsi irritatum vtriusque Regis animum, commotosque cunctos in se suos Suffraganeos cerneret, elatos tamen spiritus non remisit, sed cristas erigens rediit tumens & superbus Cantuariam, à multis tamen spretus & contemptus, qui eum à Rege in irinere repulsum reieCtumque cognouerant. In his erat quidam Robertus Brook, eius Ranulphi frater consanguineus qui Thoma prius(vt diximus) proscripto Regis mandato Cantuariensis Archiepiscopatus fructus percepit. Hic cuiusdam iumenti quod Thomæ fuit & culinæ necessaria vehebat, caudam amputauit, illudque mutilatum ludibrii causa duxitante Thomam. Postridie qui dies Christo nato festus fuit, Thomas è suggesto in Regis clientes atque famulos nimis intemperanter inuectus est. & Ranulphum de Brook qui Cantuariensis Archiepiscopatus prædia Regio iussu se absente tenuit, eiusque consanguineum Robertum cum multis aliis maligno spiritu perpetuo perculsit Anathemate. Et quia Natalis Christi dieseo anno in diem Veneris incideret, etsi ex publico more sescebantur cæteri vescebantur carnibus, is tamen (qui solus omnibus religiosior videri voluit) à carnium esu abstinuit. In qua tamen præscripta sibi à carnibus continentia in Eboracensem Archiepiscopum & Episcopum London. reliquosque Episcopos Regisque Clericos ac ministros qui ex Regis voluntate & mandato quicquam gessissent, nunquam destitit contumeliosè debacchari. In quibus insolentiæ ac elationis suæ furis, die Lunæ, (qui innocentibus in Bethlehem Herodis crudeli iussu trucidari sunt, sacer habebatur, ) è Normannia Cantuariam in Angliam secundis ventis appulerunt illi quos antea nominauimus Regis execrationi præsentes quatuor milites, qui postridie ad Thomam ingressi nunciarent ei mandasse Regem vt silium suum Regem, cutus coronationi apertis salumnis detraxerat, reuerenter adeat , eique homagium atque fidelitatem pro Archiepiscopatus sui Baronia in tramento præsteret , tum vt Clericos quos ab exilio peregrinos in Angliam secum duxerat, si hic remanere volunt, de Regis atque regni securitate iurent, tertio vt Episcopos cæterosque excommunicationis & Anathematis sententia irrititos absolutione laxaret. His Thomas respondit. Regem vel à se vel ab aliquo suorum Clericorum iuramentum quod exigere iure non possit, nulla vi, ratione neque extorturum. Episcoposautem aliosque qui coronationem Regis minoris celebrantes, sibi & Ecclesiæ suæ Cant. manifestam iniuriam insulssent à Papa non à seexcommunicatos, qui(si resarcire damnum atque præiudicium iuramento promitterent) cosabsoluerat. Ipsum enim Regem voluisse dixit, vt hanc Ecclesiæ suæ factam ab Eboracensi & Episcopis contumeliam, authoritate Ecclesiastica reformaret. An igitur, inquiunt enistes, Regem silii sui designas prodiorem, vt is suam coronationem ratam non haberet, aut infectam esse vellet? Quonam animo si sta scitent vtrosque, tatuoros putas? Mea inquit, Thomas haud referi, nam si mihi meesue Cantuariensi Ecclesiæ à Regibus aut alio quoconque fiat deincepsiniuria, in promptu est remedium. Quod de regni inserdicto, a Papa diuanteinterdicto distrimus acceperunt Milites Iesque multis minis vitrinque datis ac relatis, discedentes Milites Monachis à Rege præceptum sunt, vt Thomam ne exiret intus seruarent, atque hora vesperitina armati in Thomam atque Monarhos sacra facientes irruentes exclamarunt, vbi est regni Regisq; prodior Archiepiscopus? Illæ tertio quartoue presbyteril gradu quem ascenderat eis obniam regressus ab vnoquoque Militum gladio capite vno ictu percussus, atq; trucidatus, gradibus cecidit. Cuius Cadauer cum Militès aut in mare, vel amnè aliquem proiiceret, vel in minuta fru-
units.tr: It is written that the King, having been reconciled with Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, on account of his son Henry, lately crowned king, should restore to himself and to those who had gone into England with him what they had possessed three months before their departure. Thomas, whose spirit was wounded by pride alone and by the desire for revenge, before he returned to Canterbury sent ahead into England certain sentences of excommunication and anathema, long before pronounced by the Pope and left to his own discretion. In these he struck by name the Archbishop of York, the bishops of London and Salisbury, and several others who had celebrated the coronation of the King's son. Having done this, he returned after seven years' exile with greater pride than when he fled. Those men crossed over to the King in Normandy and complained that all things had again been thrown into disorder by Thomas with new papal censures: they, because they had obeyed the King in his son's coronation, had been banned by the Pope and Thomas as though by water and fire. The King could not contain the grief renewed in him by this repeated obstinacy of Thomas. He poured out bitter and grievous words against Thomas, both to the bishops who had come from England and had been sent back to the King's son, and to the other attendants who were listening: that he could no longer hope for faith and obedience from that man, who, scarcely restored, was seeking out every cause of new offences and disturbances of the commonwealth; that the day on which he had raised Thomas to the archbishopric, or restored him, was accursed to him, since Thomas, out of arrogance, violated the royal majesty and trampled the whole realm without a champion; and that all whom he had enriched with benefices, however they might have rotted, were thus cursed, if someone from the priesthood, who constantly disturbs both him and the kingdom, did not take a fitting punishment. Following this deadly curse of the King, four knights, Reginald fitz Urse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy and Richard le Breton, gathered from so sorrowful a speech of the King that they would render him the most welcome service if they killed Thomas. Meanwhile Thomas came to Canterbury, surrounded by a great retinue of horsemen and servants, and was received there by the monks with the greatest joy. He published those papal censures against his suffragans; then with the same magnificence and pomp he came to London, and once more in London, before the clergy of his diocese, he repeated those dire papal sentences against the bishop and the clergy. Then, when he hastened to the King's son, who was then staying at Woodstock near Oxford, he was ordered, in the King's name, by the King's knights to return to Canterbury and to revoke the sentences which he had pronounced against the bishops and clergy. On receiving this message, he went to a country house or fortified residence of his at Harrow, which was seven miles from the monastery of St Albans. The Abbot of St Albans came to him there the next day to congratulate him on his return from exile, and Thomas asked him to go to the King's son and persuade them, with some gentle speech, to admit Thomas's arrival to his presence. But since the King, offended by Thomas, had been told everywhere that his coronation had been performed by suspended bishops who did not hold the administration of their office, he would not admit the Abbot himself, who was coming from Thomas. When the Abbot returned, Thomas, though he saw that the minds of both kings were roused and that all were stirred against him and his suffragans, did not relax his proud spirit, but returned to Canterbury puffed up and haughty, raising his crest, although he was despised and scorned by many who had learned that he had been repulsed and rejected by the King on the road. Among these was a certain Robert de Broc, cousin of that Ranulf who, as we have said, had received the revenues of the archbishopric of Canterbury by the King's command while Thomas was proscribed. This man cut off the tail of a beast of burden which belonged to Thomas and carried the necessities of his kitchen, and led the maimed animal about as a mockery of Thomas. On the following day, which was the feast of the birth of Christ, Thomas, from the pulpit, inveighed too intemperately against the King's clients and servants, and with a malignant spirit he struck Ranulf de Broc, who had held the lands of the archbishopric by royal command during his absence, and his cousin Robert, together with many others, with perpetual anathema. And because Christmas Day fell that year on a Friday, although by public custom the others ate meat, he alone, who wished to seem more religious than all, abstained from eating flesh. Yet even in this self-prescribed abstinence from meat he never ceased to rage insultingly against the Archbishop of York, the Bishop of London and the other bishops, and against the King's clerks and ministers, who had done anything by the King's will and command. In the midst of this madness of his insolence and arrogance, on Monday, which was held sacred because the innocents were slaughtered at Bethlehem by Herod's cruel command, the four knights mentioned before, who had been present at the King's curse, sailed with favourable winds from Normandy to Canterbury in England. On the following day they went in to Thomas and reported that the King had ordered him to approach reverently his son, the King, whose coronation he had openly disparaged; to swear fealty and homage to him for the barony of his archbishopric; then, that he should absolve from the sentence of excommunication and anathema the bishops and the others whom he had condemned, and that the clerks whom he had led with him from exile as pilgrims into England, if they wished to remain here, should swear concerning the security of the King and the realm. Thirdly, they told him to absolve the bishops and the others who had been struck by the sentence of excommunication and anathema. To these things Thomas replied that he would never extort from the King, either by himself or by any of his clerks, an oath which he could not demand by right, by no force, reason or means. But the bishops and the others who had celebrated the coronation of the younger King, having inflicted a manifest injury on him and on his Church of Canterbury, had been excommunicated not by himself but by the Pope; and if they promised by oath to make good the damage and the prejudice, he had absolved them. For he said that the King himself had wished that the insult done to his Church by the Archbishop of York and the bishops should be remedied by ecclesiastical authority. "Do you then," said the knights, "mark the King your son out as a traitor, so that he would not hold his coronation valid, or would wish it to be void? With what mind do you think the two of them would take this if they knew it?" "It is no concern of mine," said Thomas, "for if from now on an injury is done to me or to my Church of Canterbury by kings or by anyone else, the remedy is at hand." When the knights heard this, and with many threats given and returned on both sides concerning the interdict of the kingdom and the interdict of the Pope, they departed. The monks were ordered by the King to keep Thomas from going out. Then, in the evening hour, armed men rushed in upon Thomas and the monks who were performing the sacred rites, and shouted: "Where is the archbishop, the traitor of the kingdom and of the King?" Thomas, returning to meet them, went up three or four steps of the presbyters' rank which he had ascended, and was struck on the head with one blow of a sword by each of the knights, and slain, and fell down the steps. When the knights wished to throw his corpse into the sea or some river, or to tear it into small pieces, it was at once buried in the ground without any delay by the Prior and the monks.

units.la: M . 3 sta discerpere vellent à Priore atque Monachis sine ulla dilatione mox humi conditum est. Papa omnes generaliter qui Thomæ (quemadmodum Martyres (suoque sanctos retulit) necis rei conscisque fuerunt, excommunicavit. Rex ipse per legatos iuramento le purgare coactus est. Absolutus tamen non poterat nisi certis poenarum generibus peractis. In his erant ut in Anglia reuertetur ad Thomæ tumulum flexis genibus devote oraret, &in Monachorum capitulo a singulis ordine fraterbus uno virgæ ictu percuteretur, cum decentis multitudinis Hierosolymis alendis trecentos aureos uno anno praberet, potremò ut consuetudines quas sanxit Clarendoniæ revocaret, atque facere irritas. Thomas etiam celebri testimonio Martyrii à Papali clero pro Ecclesiæ suæ Cant. privilegiis candidatus, &in Ecclesia Christi humili primum, &in cripto positus, deinde sublimiori &excelso ac sumptuoso delubro conditus fuerit, in quo caput eius seorsim a cadavere situm, Thomæ Martyris corona appellabatur, ad quod peregrinantes undique confluerent, munerâque preciosa deferrent, stupendaque edita miracula, quæ ab Anglicis Latinisque scriptoribus eius laudes celebrantibus commemorantur, utque perenni gloria, nullaque obliuione intercitura sloteret, horis matutinis atque vesperitinis precesab acutissimo Theologo Thoma Aquinate, elegantiori stylo, tanquam rythmo composita atque concinnatâ, quibus auditorum aures mulcerent, in eiusque stuporem raperentur, quotidie ei fuit fuerint tandem tamen (seculis aliquot labentibus) diligencia ac sedula indagatione, adhibitis iotius regni præsulibus ac procerbibus, Rex & quoties Thomas fuerit, certò comperit, quàm nephandâ gesserat, quanìasque turbas & tragædias in regno concitauerat. Ideoque nomen eius in publicarum precum libris ut sanctum vbiuis decanatum deleri penitus & abradi præcepit. Intolerabili enim arrogantia & supra regiam authoritatem iuraq; publica, magisque quam Christianæ aut Ecclesiasticæ libertatis immuniras diuino iure postulat, se extulerat. Tanta autem fama & celebritate adumbrat sanctitatis suæ nomen petrebatur, ut Cant. Ecclesiam in qua delubrum eius situm erat, quæ vt diximus Christi seruatoris Ecclesiæ x prima institutione dicebatur, id nomen amiserat, & in S. Thomæ Ecclesiæ nomen fere transfiterat. Sed hic semper est adulterinarum & fucatarum rerum exitus, vt veritate tempore probata, hypocrisis patefiat, & in nihilum concidat.
units.tr: The monks of the priory, without any delay, buried him at once in the ground, before the soldiers could tear the body into pieces and throw it into the sea or some river. The Pope excommunicated generally all who had been guilty of, or party to, Thomas's death, just as he had counted him among the martyrs and saints. The King himself was compelled to clear himself by oath through legates, but he could not be absolved unless he first performed certain kinds of penance. Among these, he was to return to England and kneel devoutly at Thomas's tomb and pray; in the chapter house of the monks he was to be struck with a rod, one blow from each of the brothers in order; he was to provide three hundred gold pieces a year for one year for the support of a decent number of men in Jerusalem; and finally he was to revoke the customs he had sanctioned at Clarendon and render them void. Thomas, too, was enrolled as a martyr by the papal clergy, on the strength of the famous testimony of his martyrdom, for the privileges of his church of Canterbury. He was first laid humbly in Christ Church, in a crypt, and then buried in a higher, more splendid and costly shrine, in which his head, set apart from the body, was called the crown of the martyr Thomas. Pilgrims flocked to it from everywhere, bringing precious gifts, and the stupendous miracles recorded by English and Latin writers in praise of him were commemorated. So that his glory might be everlasting and never be lost to oblivion, the most acute theologian Thomas Aquinas composed hours of prayer for morning and evening in an elegant style, as if in rhythm and harmony, to soothe the ears of the hearers and carry them away in wonder; these were sung to him every day. Yet at last, after some centuries had passed, the King, by diligent and careful inquiry, with the bishops and nobles of the whole kingdom summoned, found out for certain what a wicked man Thomas had been, and what great disturbances and tragedies he had stirred up in the realm. Therefore he ordered his name, which had been sung as holy wherever it was used, to be wholly deleted and erased from the books of public prayer. For Thomas had raised himself, with intolerable arrogance, above royal authority and public law, and beyond the immunities that Christian or ecclesiastical liberty demands by divine right. Indeed, the fame and celebrity of his supposed sanctity became so great that the church of Canterbape in which his shrine stood, which, as we said, had been called Christ the Saviour's church from its first foundation, lost that name and well-nigh passed over into the name of the church of St Thomas. But this is always the outcome of counterfeit and feigned things: when the truth is proved by time, hypocrisy is laid bare and comes to nothing.

units.tr: XXXIX. Richard

units.la: Ost Thomæ cædem mensem februario proximo, Robertus quidam Beccensis Abbas Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus electus est, qui tranquilla & placabili vita delectatus, pcellas, quibus Thomas exagitatus fuerat, meruens, id merentis confuso vitauit. Egit deinde cum Priore & Monachis Cant. Rex, vt præterntarum turbarum & contentionum memores, sedatum aliquem & quietu virú suo consensu ptobandum eligerent, ne in turbulentum & seditiosum rursum inciderent. Respondit illi Regi, eidem factum. Itaq; Richardus Monachus Benedictinus S. Martini Douerensis Monasterii Prior abillis electus, ab Henrico Rege Cant. Archiepiscopus appellatus, ab Alex. 3. Anaginio his verbis consecrabatur. Tabi Richardi tuisq; fuceesfor ibus Cant. Ecclesiæ primatum, ita plene concedimus, sicut à Lanfranco & Anselmo aliisq; ipsorum praedecessoribus quondâ Cant. Archiepiscopis fuisse possessum constat. Et paulo post Archiepiscopus primas & Romanæ sedis legatus cum pallio in Angliam redit. Hic electus Regi fidelitatem iuravit, saluo ordine suo, nulla prioris facta mentione de prioribus regni côsuetudinibus obseruandis. Causa fuit ad Papâ profectionis hæc esse poterat, si credendum sit Cant. Gervasio, cum procuratione Henrici Regis maioris, vt diximus, esset electus, Rex filius electionis reliturus, itaq; cû Cantuariæ celebrandus esset; dilata eius literis confirmatio & consecratio fuit, q. eo inficio electio interuenisset. Iam enim ceperat Patri Regi adueritus esse Rex filius. Sed Richardus etiam facili atq; simplici ingenio fuerat, nec aperte audere coercendo, cum tamen videret Enderitco Imperatore & Henrico Rege Papæ coepimus, quantis interuallis Papalis authoritas in illa Cæsaris Regis Regis lucratione iam tunc regiam superassent, litteris & nunciis elam Romam prætnissis, ipse celerrime subiectus est. Eo cum veniset, sensis sibi acerrem contentionem contra grauissimos aduersarios sub nomine dignitatio iudice futuram, quotum potentiam formidans in apertam actione prodire noluit, sed pecuniarii iudicis benignitati confisus, quod virtute efficere debuit, id tentauit pecunia. Clam enim teste Gervasio immensam pecuniâ prosudit. Habebat enim
units.tr: After Thomas's murder, in the following February, a certain Robert, abbot of Bec, was elected archbishop of Canterbury. He loved a calm and peaceable life, and, dreading the storms with which Thomas had been harassed, he avoided the office out of embarrassment. The king then urged the prior and monks of Canterbury that, mindful of the past troubles and disputes, they should choose some calm and quiet man, acceptable to himself, so that they would not fall again into turmoil and sedition. They answered the king that the choice was left to him. So Richard, a Benedictine monk and prior of the monastery of St Martin at Dover, was chosen by them, named archbishop of Canterbury by King Henry, and consecrated by Alexander III at Anagni, with these words: "To you, Richard, and to your successors of the Canterbury church, we grant the primacy in full, just as it is established that it was possessed by Lanfranc and Anselm and their other predecessors, formerly archbishops of Canterbury." A little later the archbishop, primate and legate of the Roman see, returned to England with the pallium. This elect swore fealty to the king, saving his own order, and made no mention of observing the customs of the realm handed down from earlier times. The reason for his journey to the Pope could have been this, if one believes Gervase of Canterbury: since he had been elected through the procuration of the elder King Henry, as we said, the young king was to leave the election, and so, when it was to be celebrated at Canterbury, his confirmation and consecration were put off by letters, because the election had taken place against the young king's wishes. For the young king had already begun to be opposed to his father the king. Richard, however, was of a rather easy and simple disposition, and did not dare to resist openly; yet, seeing how the Emperor Frederick and King Henry had yielded to the Pope, and how far papal authority had by then outstripped royal authority in that struggle, he sent letters and messengers to Rome ahead of him and submitted himself very quickly. When he arrived there, he perceived that a very fierce contest lay ahead, under the name of dignity, against very grave adversaries. Fearing their power, he was unwilling to come forward in open action, but, trusting in the goodwill of a judge who could be bought, he tried with money what he ought to have achieved by his own merit. For, according to Gervase, he secretly poured out an immense sum of money.

units.la: Gervas. Radulphus de Diceto. enim grauissimos aduersarios, infectos[?] negocio domum redire simulabat, sed cum iam iter parauerat, a Papa reuocatus subito confirmatus consecratur, & more maiorū Anglię Legatione & priuilegiis munitus est. Liberalis, affabilis, prudensque fuisse dicitur, obsequio cam in Papam, quam in Regem ptoculuis, quorum neutrius animum voluit in se seu pertinacia seu constantia vila commouere. Nam Episcoporum electiones ad voluntatem nutumq; Prioris sine inquisitione legitima in Camera Regis confirmare consueuit, de quo ab Alexandro Papa reprehensus erat, Papalem autem amicitiam pecunia sibi colligauit. Primo suæ consecrationis anno, quatuor Episcopos Richardum Winton. cum Eliensi, Herfordensi & Cicestrensi Lamethi consecrauit totamque Prouinciam suam, legatinam vbiqué exercens poreitatem frequenti equitatu ac famulatu stipatus, nimio apparatu atque sumptu Ecclesias & Coenobia onerans, & in plurimorum maleuolentiam incurrens peragrauit. Cumque Gloecestriam peruenisset, in Ecclesia Sancti Oswaldi (quæ Eboracensis Archiepiscopi iuri suberat,) Clericos Rogerium hunc Eboracensis Archiepiscopi, qui cum alterius iuris esset, nolebant Cantuariensi iuri esse subiecti, omnibus pene censuris percussit. Ex hoc omnia discordiarum ac turbarum, de quib. inter Archiepiscopos mox diceadum est, seminarium profluxit. Reliquis duobus annis res Ecclesiasticæ ex intestinis Patris, filiisq; Anglię Regum bellis conticuere. Sed illis biennio post iranquilla pace Concilatis Richardus concilium Westmonasterij celebrauit. Cui Rogerus Eboracensis Archiepiscopus nō interfuit, sed suæ Prouinciæ Clerus quedam relam de sui Archiepiscopi ioruce in Cant. prouincia gestanda renouauerunt, ac etiam Lincolniensem, Gestrensem, Wigornienses & Herefordensem diocæses sui Archiepiscopi prouinciæ ac iurisdictionis iuree esse debere asseuerabant. Tum nouam quæstionem edunt de iniuria & Anathematis sententia, quam Clerici Eboracenses in Ecclesia S. Oswaldi Gloecestrenli ministrantibus, & ad illum accedere vt suæ prouinciæ Clerici monitis, sed recusantibus intulerat. Super quibus interposita tanquam a grauaminib. appellatione Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum ad Papam prouocabant. Quo accepto Rex hanc lite in Wintoniæ his condicionibus diremit. Vt S. Oswaldi Ecclesia Eboracensi Archiepiscopo ex Dominio & concessione Regia iudicaretur, eiusque ibi ministrantes Clericos iure & sententia Archiepiscopi Cant. soluerentur ab reliquis ferendæ crucis ac Prouinciarum ambitus contrauersus, vt Rotomagensis Archiepiscopi iudicio starēt. Sequenti anno, qui fuit suæ consecrationis quintus in Cantuariensi diœcesis ferendæ Archidiaconatus, quæ vno ante comenta fuerat, ordinauit. Eodem anno Rex concilia Northamptoniæ indixit. Iamq; Scotorum Rege Regi Angliæ subiecto & de fidelitate iurato, ceperunt in hoc concilio Archiepiscopi, vtrum Cantuariensis an Eboracensis Prouincia Scotia subdatur litigare, multaq; aliæ suscitatæ lites, quas in adiuentum Papalis legatū a accersiti & expectati Rex dimissò eo concilio distulit. Ipsetamen ne ob occupatos a Episcopatus rain diu vacantes male audiret, Lincolniensem Episcopatum xvii. annis vacuum Galfrido notho suo contulit. Qui Regis mandato electus, cum tamen natalium ordinum quæ defectum, quamaliæ causas confirmari consecrarique domi non poterat, Romam peregrinaturus abiit, ibique nullis suscepti ordinibus largitione Episcoporum obtinuit. Iamque Legatus in Angliam à Papa venit nomine Hugocio (Hentico Rege id postulante,) tam vt Reginam Blenoram a se diuortio separaret, quàm vt primatus inter Cant. & Eborac. Archiepiscopos controuersiam componeret. Hic concilium Westmonasterij in ædibus Monachorum Ecclesia coegit, quo ab vtriusque Prouinciæ Cleru confertim consuetum est. Cumque dies inchoandi concilii aderat, Legatus in sublimi sedens solio dextras Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo concessit. Sed Eboracensis Regem sibi quam Cantuariensi propriorem spernans sinistras respuit, & impudentissime inter Legatum & Cantuariensem natibus innitens sedere, tandem in primatis sui gremio reiectus. Vix tandem vmbone suo, quo ad medium locum obtinentibus decertauit,Cantuar. attigerat, cum à plurimis tam Episcopis quàm Clericis atq; laicis turpiter reprehensus esset.
