Ministri Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi facinoris indignitate, & iustæ correctionis veritate ita incitati Eboracensem & Domini sui gremio creptū, & humi deiectum prædictum conculcarent, & Archiepiscopalib. insignib. cōsumeliosissime deiectis atq; lacerati pugnis concudunt. At Cantuariensis suos fratres parcitos auocare & continere non poterat, sed tam vt discessu suo secum abduceret, concilio exiuit. Ministri Dominium sequuti Eboracensem humi prostratum, vestibusque discerpti obstum relinquunt. Tandem Rhoracensis amhelius frequenti respirans semianimis surgit. Ad Regem qui eum filio suo concilio interesset, horridus squalidusque accedit, querelam contra Cantuariensem exponit. Rex accepto Eboracensis tantum nuncio in Cantuariensem M 4 primò incensus est, postea temeritatis & impudentiæ propriæ patefacta veritate, eam tam ridiculum ludibrium & cachinnis affectum dimisit. Cum iam a Rege Ebora-censis cum ignominia discederet, plerique cum eiamonibus infequuti, vade, vade, inquiunt, tradiror Sancti Thomæ, manus tuæ adhuc fætant sanguine. Ille autem miser non iam Thomæ, sed proprio macebat sanguine. Sed quia Regem minorem sine Thomæ mandato coronauerat, quod ut ante diximus redintegrauit discordiæ ac Thomæ necis causam dedit, existimauit vulgus eum eius rei conscium & auctorem fuisse. Inter hos turbas Hugonio metu perplexus, data benedictione concilium iam infaustum subito difsoluit, & Cantuariensem tanquam huius pulsationis reum ad Papam appellauit, quod & Ebotacensis fecit. Cantuariensis quoque neappellationibus vtrioque obruertur, se suosque Papali protectioni tam Legatum quam Eboracensem ad Romam appellando subiecit: ita ab omnibus appellarum est. Sed postridie Cant. qui Pontificii morem nouerat, muoetibus legatum sedauit: illi itaque conciliati virtinque appellationes remiserunt: Eboracensis autem suæ adhæsit. Legatus Cantuariam profectus in Archiepiscopi palatiofe occultauit, nec sui eopiam vllis fecit, teste eq; Honendeno, abscondit se a facie illorum. Ipsoque pafchate cum omnes expectarent vt ad missarum solennia prodiret, mare celeritèr & elam petiit atq; traiecit. Postea Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis & Gaudfridus Elienfis à Rogero Ebor. iterum coram Rege accusati sunt, quod in concilio Westmonasteriensi violentas ei manus attulerant, qui cum delato iuramento id negassent, seq; purgassent, Rege mandante reconciliati sunt. Eodem anthore inter Cant. & Eborac. Archiepiscopos quinque annorum inducias fecerunt. Qui iurato inuicem promiserunt, tam de illa verberatione quam de cæteris motis cõtroversiis fe Rhotomagensis & Franciæ Episcoporum arbitrio firmiter statuerunt. Mortuo iam Henrico Regis filio Richardus Archiepiscopus Regi maiori charus (Provincia sua Gilberto Londoniens. Episcopo fe absente, commissa) ad Siciliæ Regem proficiscitur Angliæ Regis Legatus, cum Iohanna Regis filia eandem Siciliæ Regi cupiis coniunctus. Eodemq; anno reuersus Willielmum quendam de Watermilla Abbatem Sancti Petri de Burgo tam gradu quam dignitate detexit.
units.tr: Gervase; Ralph of Diceto. For he had very grave adversaries, and, pretending that the business was unfinished, he made as if to return home. But when he had already prepared his journey, he was recalled by the Pope, and was suddenly confirmed and consecrated, and fortified with a legation and privileges in the manner of the English forebears. He is said to have been generous, affable and prudent, showing compliance both toward the Pope and toward the King; by neither obstinacy nor any firmness did he wish to stir the mind of either against himself. For he was accustomed to confirm the elections of bishops according to the will and nod of the prior, without lawful inquiry, in the king's chamber, for which he was rebuked by Pope Alexander; but he bought papal friendship with money. In the first year of his consecration he consecrated four bishops at Lambeth: Richard of Winchester, with those of Ely, Hereford and Chichester. Exercising his legatine power everywhere, attended by a crowd of horsemen and servants, he travelled through his whole province, burdening churches and monasteries with excessive display and expense, and incurring the ill will of many. When he came to Gloucester, in the church of St Oswald (which was subject to the jurisdiction of the archbishop of York), he struck with almost every kind of censure the clerks there who served under Roger, the archbishop of York; since they were under another jurisdiction, they were unwilling to be subject to the Canterbury jurisdiction. From this came the seedbed of all the discords and troubles about which we must soon speak between the archbishops. For the remaining two years ecclesiastical affairs fell silent because of the wars between the father and the sons of the English kings. But after the peace was restored two years later, Richard held a council at Westminster. Roger, archbishop of York, did not attend it, but the clergy of his province renewed certain matters concerning the rights of their archbishop in the province of Canterbury, and asserted that the dioceses of Lincoln, Chester, Worcester and Hereford ought to be under the right of their own archbishop's province and jurisdiction. Then they raised a new question about the injury and the sentence of excommunication which the clerks of York had inflicted in the church of St Oswald at Gloucester on those who ministered there and on those who, as clerks of his province, had gone to him for admonition but refused it. On these matters they appealed against the grievances, and summoned the archbishop of Canterbury to the Pope. When the King received this, he settled the dispute at Winchester on these terms: that the church of St Oswald should be adjudged to the archbishop of York by royal grant and concession; that the clerks ministering there should be released by the law and sentence of the archbishop of Canterbury from the rest of the controversies about the carrying of the cross and the bounds of the provinces; and that they should abide by the judgment of the archbishop of Rouen. In the following year, which was the fifth of his consecration, he set in order an archdeaconry in the diocese of Canterbury, which had been devised the year before. In the same year the King called a council at Northampton. Since the King of Scots was now subject to the King of England and had sworn fealty, the archbishops began in this council to dispute whether the province of Scotland should be subject to Canterbury or to York, and many other disputes were raised. The King, having dismissed that council, deferred them until the arrival of the papal legate, who had been summoned and was awaited. Yet, lest he be ill spoken of for keeping bishoprics vacant for so long, he gave the see of Lincoln, vacant for seventeen years, to his bastard son Geoffrey. Elected by the King's command, but since he could not be confirmed and consecrated at home because of defect of birth and other causes, he went off to Rome as a pilgrim, and there, having received none of the orders, he obtained it through the largesse of bishops. And now a legate came from the Pope into England, named Hugo (King Henry requesting it), both to separate Queen Eleanor from himself by divorce and to settle the controversy over primacy between the archbishops of Canterbury and York. He called a council at Westminster in the buildings of the monks of the church, to which the clergy of both provinces were accustomed to flock together. When the day for beginning the council arrived, the legate, seated on a raised throne, gave the right-hand place to the archbishop of Canterbury. But the archbishop of York, scorning the left-hand place, which he considered more proper to himself than to Canterbury, rejected it, and most shamelessly, pushing in between the legate and Canterbury with his buttocks, tried to sit down; at last he was thrust back into the lap of his own primate. Scarcely had he, by pushing with his shoulder to get to the middle place, reached Canterbury, when he was shamefully rebuked by many bishops, clerks and laymen alike. The servants of the archbishop of Canterbury, roused by the indignity of the deed and the justice of the correction, trampled the archbishop of York, who had been snatched from his lord's lap and thrown to the ground, and, most insultingly stripping him of his archiepiscopal insignia, tore and beat him with their fists. But the archbishop of Canterbury could not call back and restrain his men, and so he left the council, taking them away with him. The servants followed their lord, leaving York prostrate on the ground with his garments torn. At length the archbishop of York, gasping heavily, rose half-dead. Filthy and squalid, he went to the King, who had been present at the council with his son, and set out his complaint against the archbishop of Canterbury. The King, at first inflamed against Canterbury when he heard only York's messenger, afterwards, once the truth of York's own rashness and impudence had been revealed, dismissed the whole affair as a ridiculous joke and treated it with laughter. As York was leaving the King in disgrace, many pursued him with shouts: "Go, go," they said, "traitor to St Thomas; your hands still reek with blood." But that wretched man was bleeding not Thomas's blood, but his own. Yet because he had crowned the young king without Thomas's mandate, which, as we said before, renewed the discord and gave cause for Thomas's death, the common people thought he had been privy to that matter and its author. Amid these tumults Hugo, perplexed with fear, gave his blessing and suddenly dissolved the council, already ill-omened, and appealed the archbishop of Canterbury to the Pope as the one responsible for this blow; the archbishop of York did the same. The archbishop of Canterbury too, lest he be overwhelmed by appeals from both sides, placed himself and his men under papal protection, appealing both the legate and York to Rome; thus everyone appealed. But the next day Canterbury, who knew the custom of the Papists, calmed the legate with warnings; being thus reconciled, both sides withdrew their appeals, but York stuck to his. The legate, having gone to Canterbury, hid himself in the archbishop's palace and made himself available to no one; as Hoveden testifies, he hid himself from their sight. On Easter itself, when everyone expected him to come out for the solemn Mass, he secretly and quickly made for the sea and crossed over. Afterwards the archbishop of Canterbury and Geoffrey of Ely were accused again before the King by Roger of York, because at the council of Westminster they had laid violent hands on him. When they denied it under the oath that was offered, and cleared themselves, they were reconciled at the King's command. In the same year the archbishops of Canterbury and York made a truce for five years. Under oath, they promised one another that they would firmly abide by the arbitration of the bishops of Rouen and of France, both regarding that beating and regarding the other disputes that had arisen. Henry the young King having now died, Archbishop Richard, dear to the elder King (his province being entrusted to Gilbert, bishop of London, in his absence), set out as legate of the King of England to the King of Sicily, to whom Joan, the King's daughter, was to be united in marriage. In the same year, on his return, he deposed one William of Watermill, abbot of St Peter of Burgh, from both rank and dignity.

units.la: Sexto consecrationis suæ Anno Guidonem Banehorensem Episcopum consecrauit. Eodem anno Rogerus Augustinensis Cœnobii electus Abbas Archiepiscopum benedicendus adiit. Id iubedictione & obedientia sibi vicissim promissa paratum se facere dixit. Hoc Monachi sc immunes afferentes recusabant. Sed postea quam accepissent Abbatem suum id munus fine benedictione administrare non potuisse, his conditionibus consenserunt, ne id in Cant. Ecclesia fieret. Et vt professionis schedulam adderentur (saluis virtusq; Ecclesiæ Priuilegiis) cui respōfum est, Abbatem debite debere professionem facere, aenon ex scripto sed a corde dicere: salua sanctaparens, vel salue festa dies, vel saluis priuilegiis. Id Abbas & Monachi se factur negabant, nec verbo sed scriptura professuros aiebant. Itaq; reiecta eorum petitione Rogerus Papam adiit, eiq; cœnobium suum reddidit vt digale. Papa itaq; ad Archiepiscopum rescripsit, vt omni exceptione & mora sublata eum sine professione in Ecclesia sua Augustinensi benedictione sacraret. Quo mandato pertinetur Archiepiscopus venit ad Augustinensi cœnobium secundum Papæ monita facturos. Sed interuentu Prioris Cant. Ecclesiæ, qui multis Ecclesiæ Metropoliticæ dignitatem esse arguebat, cessauit ab eo quod facere occeperat Archiepiscopus, Romamq; profecturus traiecit in Normanniam. Ibi Regi exponit iniurias & contumelias, ab Augustinensi Abbate Ecclesiæ suæ factas. Rex tam infelicitè temporis morem aliquatenus gesturus Archiepiscopum secum retinuit, ipse rem authoritate Papæ compositurum promisit. Romanos enim aiebat, muneribus magis & lucro inhiare quam iustitiæ studere, ideoque malores inter eos seditiones & litigia commoturos. Itaq; Archiepiscopus Regi obsequuturus rediit. Sed Rogerus Papam iterum adiit, ab eoque tam benedictione quam immunitate atque priuilegiis decoratus, cum rescripto in quo Papa Cœnobium Sancti Augustini Cantuariens. suæ tantum iurisdictionis, & ab omnibus aliis adem prum affirebat, rediit. Quofacto incertius est statuere, vtrum Papæ cupiditatem auri, an suam honoris & ambitionis magis expleuerie. Sed Anno sequenti Papa ne Archiepiscopum, quem etiam ante emunxerat, penitus à se ihaiuria alienaret, perhumanis eum literis vtro scriptis permulsit, in quibus eum certiorem fecit de concordia cum Frederico Imperatore conciliata. Eodemq; anno Episcopos S. Dauid in Wallia consecratus, professionem manu suâ scriptam & one prolatam Richardo tradidit. His temporibus Lateranense Concilium 25. Canonibus inclusum & compre-
units.tr: In the sixth year of his consecration he consecrated Guy, Bishop of Bangor. In the same year Roger, elected Abbot of the monastery of St Augustine, came to the Archbishop to be blessed. He said he was ready to do this, since they had promised him blessing and obedience in return. The monks of St Augustine's, claiming their exemption, objected and refused. But after they learned that their abbot could not receive his office without a blessing, they agreed on these conditions: that it should not take place in Canterbury Cathedral, and that a written form of profession should be added, with the privileges of both churches preserved. To this it was answered that the abbot ought to make his profession properly, not from a written text but saying it from the heart: "saving the holy parent", or "saving the feast day", or "saving the privileges." The abbot and monks refused to do this, saying they would profess in writing and not in words. Their petition being rejected, Roger went to the Pope and surrendered his monastery to him, as was fitting. The Pope therefore wrote back to the Archbishop that, with every objection and delay removed, he should bless Roger without any profession in his church of St Augustine's. When this mandate was shown to him, the Archbishop came to the monastery of St Augustine's to do as the Pope had advised. But at the instance of the Prior of Canterbury Cathedral, who argued that the dignity of the metropolitan church was being diminished by it, the Archbishop stopped what he had begun, and set out for Rome, but crossed into Normandy. There he complained to the King of the injuries and insults inflicted on his church by the abbot of St Augustine's. The King, since the times were so unhappy, kept the Archbishop with him for a while, and promised that he himself would settle the matter by the Pope's authority. For he said the Romans were more intent on gifts and profit than on justice, and that for this reason greater seditions and quarrels would be stirred up among them. So the Archbishop returned to obey the King. But Roger went to the Pope again, and, honoured by him with the blessing, immunity and privileges, returned with a rescript in which the Pope affirmed that the monastery of St Augustine's at Canterbury was under his jurisdiction alone and free from all others. After this deed it is uncertain whether one should judge that the Pope's love of gold or Roger's love of honour and ambition was more fully satisfied. But in the following year the Pope, so that he might not wholly alienate the Archbishop, whom he had already offended, soothed him with very courteous letters written in his own hand, in which he informed him of the concord brought about with the Emperor Frederick. In the same year the Bishop of St David's in Wales, consecrated, handed to Richard a profession written in his own hand and spoken. In these times the Lateran Council, comprising twenty-five canons, was held by the same Alexander.

units.la: {y} Ebor. comprehensum beneficiorum & decimarum iura statuens ab eodem Alexandro celebratum est.
units.tr: ...comprehending and settling the rights of benefices and tithes, was held by the same Alexander.

units.la: Huius Alexandri rescripta extant in Gregoriano Decretalium Codice plura quàm cuiusquàm Papæ, quorum pleraque ad Episcopos & Clerum Angliæ data sunt. Richardus morem Papæ pariter ac Regi gerens, multis benignus ac munificus, cum tam decem annis,octo mensibus, in summa Papæ Regisque gratia sedisset, parum vnquàm incommoditulisset, improuisa morte migrauit è vita. Scribunt enim cum in praedio suo Wrotham sommo alto compressus esset, humanam personam terroris ac authoritatis plenam ei adfuisse & dixisse. Tu quis? Cùmq; Archiepiscopus paucùe expergefactus haud respondheret, subiunxisse. Tu es qui dissipasti bona Ecclesiæ tibi cominissa, & ego dissipabo te de terra. Quo dicto cuanuit. Diluculo itaque surgens Archiepiscopus Rofsam perrexit, stupidusque familiari cuidam suo in itinere narrauit quid sibi in omnis occurrisset.
units.tr: The rescripts of this Alexander survive in the Gregorian Decretals more than those of any other Pope, most of them addressed to the bishops and clergy of England. Richard, obliging the Pope as well as the King, was kind and generous to many; having sat in the highest favour of Pope and King for ten years and eight months, and having scarcely ever been ill, he departed this life by an unforeseen death. For they write that while he was asleep in his manor at Wrotham, a human figure full of terror and authority stood beside him and said: "Who are you?" When the Archbishop, half awake, did not answer, the figure added: "You are the one who squandered the goods of the Church entrusted to you, and I will drive you from the earth." With these words it vanished. So, rising at dawn, the Archbishop hurried to Rochester, and in a stupor told a certain familiar of his on the journey what had befallen him.

units.la: Cumque finem narrandi fecisset, tanto frigore, horrore & mentis ægritudine confectus est, vt vix ad villam Ecclesiæ Rofensis quæ Halinga appellatur perduci poterat. Ibi lecto decumbens colica passione aliisque morbis vehementer affictus, postridie 15. Kalend. Martii nocte exhausi-ravit. Cadauer eius Cantuariam postea delatum in Ecclesia Christi in oratorio sanctæ Mariæ sepulchro honorificè conditum est.
units.tr: When he had finished the telling, he was so overcome by cold, shivering and sickness of mind that he could scarcely be brought to the village of the Church of Rochester called Halling. There, lying in bed and sorely afflicted by colic and other illnesses, he breathed his last the night after the 15th day before the Kalends of March. His body was afterwards carried to Canterbury and honourably buried in the Church of Christ, in the chapel of St Mary.

units.la: Huius Archiepiscopi tempore Cant. Ecclesia iusta est, Anno Dom. 1177. & Roffensis cum urbe tota Anno 1178. Nummusq; uniformis iterum in regno percusus est. Hoc quoq; tempore nix ita valles impleuit, dumos cooperuit, pressit; arbores, vt infinita pecorum turbaniue resoluta, in aquis perierint. Anno Domin. 1177. in Waltamense coenobium quod Heraldus extruxerat, (exclusis clericis secularibus) primò inducuntur Monachi.
units.tr: In this Archbishop's time the Church of Canterbury was burnt, in the year of the Lord 1177, and the Church of Rochester together with the whole city in 1178. A uniform coinage was also struck again in the kingdom. At this time too the snow filled the valleys, covered and pressed down the thickets and trees, so that countless herds and flocks, released, perished in the waters. In the year of the Lord 1177 monks were first installed in the monastery of Waltham, which Harold had built, the secular clergy having been excluded.

units.la: XL. BALD- WINUS.
units.tr: XL. BALDWIN.

units.la: ALDWINUS Deuoniensis patria, ignoti parentis filius, Exoniæ natus, & literis constitutus, paucis annis eos fecit progressus, vt ipse schola ampertit, publicèque docuit. Inde in clericali ordine cōstitutus moribus vitaq; tā cōspicuus, vt populi lucerna diceretur, Archileuita creatus est. Quem honorem sponte deserens, inter cādidos Monachos seu Cisterciensis ascriptus, transfaxus in eo ordine aliquot annis, Fordiensis Abbas in Deuonia creatur, inde ad Wigorniensem Episcopatum traductus, & demum ad Archiepiscopalem celsitudinem, ex sui ordinis Monachis primus euectus est. In quo eligendo inter Cantuarien. Ecclesiæ Monachos & Prouinciæ Suffraganeos, magna discordia (breuiter perstringenda) commota est. Electionis ius clero populoq; olim commune, clerus tandem penes se retinuit, exclusō populo. Quod etiam non plebeianis clericis permissum, sed in Ecclesiis Cathedralibus ad Conuentus & Capitula redactum est. Archiepiscopi verò à totius Prouinciæ Episcopis eligi solebant.
units.tr: Baldwin, a native of Devon, the son of unknown parents, born at Exeter and educated in letters, advanced in a few years to such a point that he opened a school himself and taught publicly. Then, being established in the clerical order, he became so conspicuous for his morals and way of life that he was called the lamp of the people, and was made archdeacon. Giving up this office of his own accord, he was enrolled among the white monks, that is, the Cistercians; after spending some years in that order he was made Abbot of Ford in Devon, then transferred to the bishopric of Worcester, and finally raised to the archiepiscopal dignity, being the first of his order's monks to be so raised. In his election a great discord arose between the monks of the Canterbury Church and the suffragans of the province (which must be briefly described). The right of election, once common to clergy and people, was at last kept by the clergy alone, the people being excluded. This was not even permitted to the ordinary clergy, but was confined to the chapters and convents of the cathedral churches. The archbishops, however, used to be chosen by the bishops of the whole province.

units.la: Sed & in Archiepiscopalibus sedibus ita se tandem permisceabant cum Suffraganeis Conuentus & Capitula, vt interdictis & prohibitis tandem illis, eligendi sibi solis vendicarint.
units.tr: But the convents and chapters so mixed themselves at last with the suffragans even in the archiepiscopal sees that, when those others were barred and excluded, they claimed the right of electing for themselves alone.

units.la: Quod in Baldwini electione clarissimè patuit. Primùm enim egit Rex cum Priore & Monachis Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ, vt de moderato aliquo arq; pio viro ad id muneris aptò deliberarent.
units.tr: This was most clearly shown in the election of Baldwin. For first the King dealt with the Prior and monks of the Canterbury Church, that they should deliberate about some moderate and godly man fit for that office.

units.la: Deinde cum Episcopis, vt neminem eo munere dignum censerent, qui non prudens, doctus, moribus, tantæ dignitati commodis aptissimus fuerit, ne (quod ante senserat) rebus sedatis nona Reip. perturbatio contingat.
units.tr: Then he dealt with the bishops, that they should judge no one worthy of that office who was not prudent, learned, of good character, and most suited to so great a dignity, lest (as he had feared before) once things were quieted some disturbance of the commonwealth should follow.

units.la: Episcopi Regi parentes agunt cum Monachis Cantuariensibus nouo Thomæ Martyri oelatis, & præfiatis, vt in Archiepiscopo eligendo secum consentirent. Hi non se permissuros respondent, vt ei rei Episcopi se interponant, suum esse ius peculiare atque proprium, quo si cedant, Ecclesiæ Christi iniuriam se facturos timent.
units.tr: The bishops, obeying the King, dealt with the Canterbury monks, who had lately been pressing the new martyr Thomas, and asked them to agree with them in electing the Archbishop. They replied that they would not allow the bishops to interpose themselves in that matter, since it was their own peculiar and proper right, and they feared that if they yielded they would be doing an injury to the Church of Christ.

units.la: Regires nunciata est, is precari ab his quibus imperare debuerat coactus, vt in electione concuenirent cum Episcopis, nec obtinuit. Multa vtrinque dicta, respon&s, scripta, rescripta, sunt. Ad Papam multis Regis, Episcooporum, Priorisac Monachorum nunciis literisq; crebris itineribus, itum reditum est. Obtento tandem, Episcopis Cant: Prouinciæ, & priori Ecclesiæ Cant: Papali rescripto, vt de Archiepiscopo idoneo prouideant & eo consentiant: Londinenlis Episcopus qui sensum Monachorum perpulchre calebat, Priore & Episcopis ad colloquium congregatis, rogauit Priorem aliquem ad huc eligissent. Is papalium literarum ignarus, negauit. Quas Londinensis illico proculit, earumque authoritate coniunctum Episcopis cum Monachis eligendi facultatem a Papa concessam ostendit. Itaque dicm statuit, quo electioni adesset. Eo die abfuit Prior. Quo contumace & absente, Episcopi vnanimes ac concordes eligunt Badwinum Wigorniensem Episcopum: quo nihil opinatus Regi fuit. Ante enim in Thomæ vita diximus, Thomam ab Anglia profugum in Pootiniacenti in Gallia cœnobio delituisse, indeque Cicestrensium fratrum decreto, id exigente Rege, eiectum, quorum numero venisimile est hunc Badwinum fuisse, Regique co nomine charum, quæ ab intestina & ciuili dissensione abhorruerat. Sed quocunque nomine Regi placuerit, certum est quorumcunq; scriptorum testimonio, cum pium, doctum, prudentem, & moderatum fuisse. Quem Giraldus suis etiam tam in peragranda Wallia quam inexpeditione Hierosolymitana Comes Archidiaconus Brec: sic describit: Colore fusco, vultu simpliciac venusto, statura mediocri, habitudine corporis boua, sed ienui non erasa. Morib... ...istrum ausa fuisset fama prætumere: sermone parcus, ad iram tardus. Literarum studiis à pueritia imbutus, iugum dominiab adolescentia portans. Hoc igitur ab Episcopis e'ecto, fremuerunt Monachi, & minarum appellationum q; arrocitate ateq; vinon Regem solùm, sed Episcopos id deterruerunt, vt Regi Papales insidias & amicitias experto, necesse fuit Cantuariam proficisci, obnixeq; a Priore atq; Monachis petere ac instare, nè hanc querelam ad Papam deferant, quibusfuis se ab illis conditionibus datis contentum, si in Baldwinum consentiant. Quid multa: Res aliter tranfiginon poterat, nisi & Baldwinus Episcoporum eligioni renunciaret, & Episcopi eandem electionem cassarent. Ex lege se Baldwinum electuros promitunt. Cesserunt Monachis & Rex & Episcopi, priorem si ac electionem irritam statuerunt. A priore igitur & Monachis denuo Badwinus eligitur, & Episcoporum omnium consensu confirmatur. Hæc eligendi discordia novem mensibus duravit, quatransasta, per Legatos Regis & Conuentus Cant. nunciata Papæ resest Is qui nihil lucri a concordi regno sperabat, pallium & veterem Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ dignitatem facile concessit, & per legatos impertiuit. Quibus reuersi & a Conuentu honorificè receptis Baldwinus pallio donatus, & in Archiepiscopali throno locatus est Cantuariæ 14. Kalend. Iunii. Anno Regis Henrici 31. Toto reliquo Anno Rex Baldwino coniunctissimus Monachis eius voluntati tam strenuè resistentibus speciem quandam beneuolentiæ præ se ferebat, omniaque tum tranquillafuere, vt sine vlla perturbatione ac tumultu deliberandi ac consilii capiendi opportunum tempus daretur. Itaque ea concilii ratio Regi cum Baldwino habita est, cuius exitus Cantuarienses Monachos ob eorum insolentiam Regi & Episcopis exosos honore consueto, & eligendi facultate priuasset. Thomæ Martyrium per totum orbem Christianorum à Pontificiis scriptoribus diffusum tam illiustre habebatur, vt qui eius nomini aliquid concillisset vel condidisset sanctis ipsius pares atque similes viderentur. Itaq; Baldwinus ex Regis proposito & consilio D. Thomæ Martyri nouum templum Hackingtoniæ in Ecclesia S. Stephani, quæ à Cantuaria ad Aquilonem posita tribus distat stadiis, extruere & dedicare statuit. In hac Ecclesia ad exemplum & similitudinem S. Thomæ, qui ipse sæcularis fuit, sæculares Clerici, Canonici & Præbendarii instituendi e numero, Numerusque præbendariorum æqualis Suffraganeorum Cantuariensis prouinciæ numero constitutus fuit: vna præbenda Regiis sumptibus ordinanda, & Regi, eiusq; successoribus Angliæ regibus cooperanda fuerat, vt perenni quadam & longæua per hæredes ad finem sæculi ducta pœnitentia cædes Thomæ penitus expiaretur, reliquæ præbendæ Suffraganeis concedendæ eorumq; sumptibus erigendæ erant. Ad hoc opus, quod summa religionis tantiq; colendi Martyris laude omnium ore ferebatur, accessit Papæ authoritas & licentia Baldwino concessa, quarraquè pars omnium oblationum, quæ ab illo die Thomæ delubro deferrentur. Inceptaresest, omneq; tigrii genus vndiq; conqnisitû, ad cumq; locum deportatum fuit, sed Monachi omnibus callidiores, omnium etiam astutiam olfecerunt. Quibus cum Baldwino simulatas semper intercessit, inuicemq; inuisi ac infesti erant, omniaq; Baldwini institura & consilia suspecta habebant, nec eos opinio fefellit. Destinarat enim ex Regis instinctu Baldwinus, frequentes Episcoporum coetus ibi celebrare, quibus Rex quoties vellet, cum ex eorum numero atque grege esset, interesse poterat. Operecq; perfecto & absoluto in eadem Ecclesia Episcopos consecrare, Synodos habere, oleum cum lacte ad cōfandum chrismapermiscere, singulaque quaeordini suo incumbebant facere, & paulatim non eligendi solum sed quaecunq; alia Monachorum Cant. iura eo deducere, Monachi haec quae certò statuebantur, tanquam vaticinantes, suspicabantur & praedicabant euentura, modisque omnibus auertere nitebantur: vt Iuno, quae Imperii sui locum Carthaginis statuit praeter voluntatem Iouis:
units.tr: When the king was told of this, he was forced to beg those whom he ought to have commanded that they would meet with the bishops for the election, but he did not prevail. Much was said on both sides; answers, writings and replies were exchanged. Many messengers of the king, the bishops, the prior and the monks, and many letters, went back and forth, and there were frequent journeys to and from the Pope. At last the bishops of the province of Canterbury and the prior of the church of Canterbury obtained a papal rescript that they should provide a suitable archbishop and agree to him. The Bishop of London, who was very warm in support of the monks' feelings, gathered the prior and the bishops for a conference and asked whether they had yet chosen a prior. The prior, who was ignorant of the papal letters, said no. The Bishop of London at once produced them and, on their authority, showed that the Pope had granted the bishops the power to elect jointly with the monks. He therefore fixed a day on which the prior should be present at the election. On that day the prior was absent. In his stubborn absence, the bishops unanimously and harmoniously elected Baldwin, Bishop of Worcester, which the king had not at all expected. For we said earlier in the life of Thomas that Thomas, when he fled from England, had hidden in the monastery of Pontigny in France, and was from there expelled by a decree of the brothers of Chichester, at the king's demand; and it is likely that this Baldwin was one of those brothers, and for that reason was dear to the king, who had shrunk from internal and civil discord. But whatever the king's reasons for favouring him, it is certain, on the testimony of all writers, that he was pious, learned, prudent and moderate. Giraldus, Archdeacon of Brecon, who went with him both through Wales and on the Jerusalem expedition, describes him thus: of a dark complexion, with a simple and pleasant face, of medium height, of a good but lean body, not unwashed. ... fame would have dared to presume ... sparing in speech, slow to anger, imbued with the study of letters from boyhood, bearing the yoke of the Lord from youth. Therefore, when he had been chosen by the bishops, the monks raged, and with the harshness of threats and appeals they so frightened not only the king but the bishops that the king, having experienced the papal snares and friendships, had to go to Canterbury and earnestly beg and urge the prior and the monks not to carry this complaint to the Pope, and he would be content with whatever conditions they gave, if they agreed to Baldwin. In short, the matter could not be settled otherwise unless Baldwin renounced the election by the bishops and the bishops annulled that same election. They promised to elect Baldwin according to law. The king and the bishops yielded to the monks and declared the prior's election void. Therefore Baldwin was elected again by the prior and the monks, and was confirmed by the consent of all the bishops. This dispute over the election lasted nine months; the matter was reported to the Pope through the legates of the king and the convent of Canterbury. He, who hoped for no profit from a peaceful kingdom, readily granted the pallium and the ancient dignity of the church of Canterbury, and sent them through legates. On their return, and after being received with honour by the convent, Baldwin was invested with the pallium and placed on the archiepiscopal throne at Canterbury on the 14th day before the Kalends of June, in the thirty-first year of King Henry. For the rest of that year the king was most closely united with Baldwin, and while the monks strenuously resisted his wishes, he showed a certain semblance of goodwill, and all things were then so calm that an opportune time was given for deliberating and taking counsel without any disturbance or tumult. Thus the king took counsel with Baldwin in such a way that its outcome would have deprived the monks of Canterbury, hateful to the king and the bishops on account of their arrogance, of their customary honour and of the power of election. The martyrdom of Thomas, spread throughout the whole Christian world by the Papist writers, was regarded as so illustrious that whoever had added or composed anything in his name seemed to be like and equal to the saints themselves. Therefore Baldwin, by the king's plan and counsel, resolved to build and dedicate a new temple to St Thomas the Martyr at Hackington, in the church of St Stephen, which lies three furlongs north of Canterbury. In this church, after the example and likeness of St Thomas, who was himself a secular priest, secular clerks, canons and prebendaries were to be established, and the number of prebendaries was fixed equal to the number of the suffragans of the province of Canterbury. One prebend was to be endowed at the king's expense, and was to be maintained by the king and his successors, the kings of England, so that by a lasting and long-enduring penance, continued through heirs to the end of the age, the slaying of Thomas might be wholly expiated; the remaining prebends were to be granted to the suffragans and established at their expense. To this work, which was spoken of on everyone's lips with the highest praise of religion and of honouring so great a martyr, was added the authority and licence of the Pope granted to Baldwin, and a part of all the offerings brought to the shrine of Thomas from that day on. The work was begun, and every kind of marble was sought out from everywhere and carried to that place; but the monks, more cunning than all, sensed the cunning of all. With them, Baldwin always had a pretended intercourse, while they were mutually hostile and enemies, and they regarded all of Baldwin's plans and counsels with suspicion, and their suspicion did not deceive them. For Baldwin had intended, at the king's urging, to hold there frequent assemblies of bishops, at which the king, whenever he wished, since he was of their number and flock, could be present. And once the work was finished and completed, to consecrate bishops in that same church, to hold synods, to mix oil with milk for the consecration of the chrism, and to do each of the things that belonged to his office; and gradually to bring under that place not only the election but all the other rights of the monks of Canterbury. The monks, as if prophesying, suspected and foretold that what was being firmly decided would happen, and they strove by every means to avert it, just as Juno, who set up the seat of her empire at Carthage against the will of Jupiter:

units.la: Hic currus fuit, Hoc Regnum Dea gentibus esse,
units.tr: "Here was her chariot; here she wished this to be the kingdom of the goddess for the nations,

units.la: Si qua fata sinant, iam tum tendit, fouetq;
units.tr: if the fates allowed it; already then she strove for it and cherished it."

units.la: Sed Æaex aduentu perterrita, ne mutaretur Imperii locus, exclamat.
units.tr: But Juno, terrified at the coming of Aeneas, lest the seat of empire be changed, cries out:

units.la: —Mene incepto desistere victam?
units.tr: "Am I, defeated, to desist from my undertaking,

units.la: Nec posse Italia Teucrorum auertere Regem?
units.tr: and not be able to turn away the king of the Trojans from Italy?"

units.la: Sie Monachi Cantuarienses illam Hackingtonensis Ecclesiæ fabricam fore sui fuit di calamitatem praescientes ad Romanum Æolum accedunt.
units.tr: So the Canterbury monks, foreseeing that the building of the church at Hackington would be the calamity of their own side, go to Aeolus, the Roman king of the winds:

units.la: Æole, nam tibi Diuum pater, atque hominum Rex,
units.tr: "Aeolus, for to you the father of gods and king of men has given

units.la: Et mulcere dedit fluctus & tollere ventos.
units.tr: both to calm the waves and to raise the winds.

units.la: Gens inimica mihi.
units.tr: A people hostile to me

units.la: Incute vim ventis.
units.tr: strike force into the winds.

units.la: Sunt mihi bis septem praestanti corpore Nymphae.
units.tr: I have fourteen nymphs of outstanding beauty,

units.la: Effectricem auri. Quarum quae forma pulcherrima Chrysopeprum.
units.tr: maker of gold; of whom the most beautiful in form, Deiopea,

units.la: Connubio iungam stabili, &c.
units.tr: I will join to me in lasting wedlock, etc."

units.la: Hunc Æolum si Neptunus aliquis compelcuisset, Regis & Baldwini consilium ad foedicem exitum perduxisse. Sed minarum & ceniuarum eius tutbines atque flatus ita omnia permiscebant, vt eo commodo nec gerinec petfici quicquam potuerat. Iam enim paratis ad extuendam hanc Thomae Martyri dedicandam Ecclesiam cunctis necessariis, venit Cantuariam Baldwinus, introductus quosdam saecularis clericos a tribus Monachis obuius sit in itinere, qui Priorem suum nomine Cant. Ecclesiæ ab eius institutio ac proposito Romam appellasse denunciarunt. Verumtamen pergit Baldwinus, ad S. Stephani Ecclesiam accedit, percrebuit eum nouos clericos ibi instituturum. Missi rursus a Priore Monachi, qui appellatione prænissa, inhibitisq; tam Archiepiscopo quam clericis institutendis, ac Rectore Ecclesiæ S. Stephani, negotii progressum impediant. Baldwinus prohiberi noluit, sed petactis sacris clericos institutiuat inducit, Priore administratione sua remouet, appellatibus altari interdicit, eum qui appellationem recitauit Conuentu exclusit. A iantoribus exigit iureiurando fidem, hec in iscio Monachotum quempiam foribus exire permittant. Prior ipse qui Honorius dicebatur exiens, Romam magnis itineribus contendit. Corruscationes Papales expectantur. Interea Rex hos nouos motus metuens, legauit ad Monachos Cesterensem Episcopum electū, Iohannem Nordouicensem, & Willielmum Wigernicensem, qui multis rationibus, blandoque sermone, permixtis interdum minis, suaserunt vt de his controuersiis de quibus ad Papam prouocassent, Regis atque praesulum iudicia subirent. Illi appellationem eum suam ab Honorio suo Priore iam ad Papam perlatam aiunt, nec posse eo absente statui quicquam. Episcopi ad Regem redeunt, & illa referunt. Turbatus hoc responso Rex, Cantuariam ipse venit, Archiepiscopum & Monachos ad se vocauit, litemque dirempturum ptomisit. Monachi tenaces propositi, tam ad Papam delatam esse aiunt, ideoque se alterius iudicio eam causam non permissuros. Itaque infecta pace Rex rediit. Missi a Rege & Baldwino ad Papam legati, & a singulis Cantuariensi, prouinciae Episcopis datae literae. Papae legatis suo more salutatis, lectisque literis Regis & Baldwini, Episcoporum literas ad sen eitram reiecit. Diem statuit, quo de causa cognoscere voluit, eo die ab utraque parte re expostta, Papa secundum Priorem & Monachos iudicauit. Ad Archiepiscopum scripsit, & serio imperauit, vt Priorem ac Monachos a se amotos, prohibitos vel exclusos, in integrum restituat. Diximus ante ipsum Papam Baldwino operi suo aggrediendo authoritatem dedisse. Sed Papis semper fuit libertum tamen sua quam aliorum decreta rescindere. His literis Baldwinus non destitit, nec Monachos restituit, & quo magis eos irritaret ac incenderet, Chrismat Londini consecrauit. Illi Romam recurrunt, se restitui per legatos procurationouas a Papa Baldwino literas referunt, quibus ei multis minis iniunctū est, vt nouam Ecclesiam q post Monachorum densiationem constructus demoliret, nec in opere incepto amplius pergeret. Iraq; ab operaꝰ destitut Baldwinus cum Rege & totius suæ Proninciæ prælulibus, petulantissimis Monachis Papæ iudicio succumbens. Sed cum tam contumeliose superari a Monachis nolent, nouum consilium initum est, quod ille Romanus Æolus reficriptorum suorum procellis iterum disflauit. Dirui iam ex Papæ mandato Baldwinus iusserat omnia, quæ Hackingtonæ constructerat. Ea iussu suo solo ²quata subito sunt. Sed terrarum permutatione acquisiuit abEpiscopo & Monachis Roff. prædium quoddam in villa Lametha, quæ interfluente Thamesi è Regione Westmonasterii ad orientem posita est. Ad hoc prædium lapides, cæmenta & tigna, omniaq; qnæ ad Hackingtonensem Ecclesiam erigendam parauerat deferri iussit. Redintegratum opus est Vrbano Papa mortuo, qui summa ope Monachos iuuit. Et successit Gregorius 8. Regis & Baldwini fautor. Qui animos iam erigunt, & Monachi deponendent, ut contrariarum rerum interuentu qui studenti partibus, hilariores aut tristiores esse solent, sed Gregorius secundo Papatus mense fatis concessit. Durauerat iam quatuor amplius annis sub quatuor Papis, Lucio, Vrbano, Greg. Clementeque, hæc Hackingtonensis extruendæ & diruendæ, & mutandæ Ecclesiæ controuersia. Quo spacio infinitum esset Monachorum querelas & eiaculationes, Baldwini seueritates, Regis ipsius dissimulationes, excusationes, & actorum suorum renouationes omnesipsa temporis necessitate coactas recensere. Quæ breuitati studentes omisimus, ab hac enim Ecclesia tanquam à fonte manarunt omnia. Sub hæc tempora Prior Cant. Honorius ex pestæ interiit, quem cum suis affectis Cantuarienses Monachi inter sanctos venerari voluerunt. Cuius loco Regis & Baldwini authoritate & gratia successit Rogerius. Iamque Henrici secundi prudentissimi principis aderat mors. Quæ illi obrigit, ut existimare conuenit, celerius, quòd tam indigna Regi atque patri à Monachis atque liberis tulisset. Quæ tamen forti Regio<q;> animo toleravit, & prudenti vitauit. Huius inclytissimi Regis obitu, quæ de Hackingtonensis siue Lamethensis negocii exitu dicenda sunt, ad suum locum reiicientur, sed inter illas turbas, alia quædam à Baldwino gesta sunt pertransfeunda. Anno consecrationis suæ quarto Monachos Cant. tanto odio habuit, ut deturbatis S. Trinitatis Cœnobio Monachis, authoritate regia feculares induxerit. Sed cum ad Papam itum esset, Rex maluit controuersiam sopiri, & Monachos restitui. Eodemq; anno Westmonasterii Baldwinus Richardo Regi diadema imposuit, 3. Nonas Septembr. præsentibus Rhotomagensi, Treuerensi, & Dublinensi Archiepiscopis. Ptolemaeo, Tiuton. & Hubertus Sarisburiensis Westmonasterii in sacello S. Katarinæ, & paucis post diebus Richardus Londinensis, & Willielmus Elienfis Lamethæ ab eodem Baldwino consecrari sunt. Eodem etiam anno Rex Richardus Archiepiscopatum Eboracensem, Godefrido fratri suo notho, qui ante nullis sacris initiatus Lincolniensis Episcopus fuerat, contulit. Quo electo intercessit pro sedis Cantuarien sis dignitate coram Rege Baldwinus, eaque de re Williclmi Normanni decreti protulit, & tam Godefrido electo q omnibus aliis Episcopis Angliæ appellatione ad Papam promulgata interdixit, ne à quocunque quàm à Cant. Archiepiscopo ordinaretur atq; sacraretur. Iohannes Regis frater Dorseti atq; Somerseti Comes ad Iohannem Anagninæ Cardinalem in Angliam appulsum, & Clementis Papæ Legatum Baldwinum appellauit, quod Comitatum suum interdicto suppositum ob nuptias, qnas cum filia Comitis Glouerniæ tertio sibi gradu iuncta conciliaret, appellatione sua ad Papam refutata. Hanc appellationem Legatus ratam habuit, & Baldwini interdictum aboleuit. Idem Legatus sacellum Hackingtonensem in Monachorum gratiam, esti iam dirutam soloque æquatam, attoci sententia prophanauit. Sed intercessione Regis ne Baldwinus Monachorum calumniis infestaretur, consensum est vt modica in eo locoi capella, sine Lauacro & cæmiterio, vnius sœcularis clerici ministerio contenta extrueretur. Rogerius etiam qui Honorio Priori successit, Monachorum odia sustinere non potèrat, itaq; sub hoc Legato Cant. Mohachis cessit & ad Euesham Cœnobium & Regis & Baldwini gratia Abbas migrauit. Richardus Rex patris sui seditionibus & coniurationibus suis ⅓ memor peccatum quod desleuit, expeditione ierosolymitana abolere se posse putauit. Quam quidem ad rem omnia inquirit atq; parat, & ad grandem pecuniam conflandam tributa populo scit, regias possessiones vendit, locat, pignoriq; dat. Inter alia Hugo de Pufez vir gloriosus & multis criminibus infamis, cum Episcopatum Dunelmensem 40. annis sine ordine clericali tenuisset, Northumbriæ Comitatu à Rege preclo acquisiuit. Cumq; ex more accingendus Comitatus gladio, Comitisque homine appellandus à Rege esset, subridens Rex: Eu, inquit, ego mirus artifex ex veterano Episcopo Comitem feci innenem. Multi crucis & illius expeditionis votum cum Rege suscepserunt. Inter quos Baldwinus, phus Hubertus Sarisburgensis & Ranulphus de Glandfeld totius regni sub Rege procurator, & Hugo Dunelmensis fuêre, Verùm Ranulphus illo munere procurarono le abdicauit, vt ad profectionem Ierosolymitanam commodius sese præpararet. Sed Hugo Regi iam ad iter patato 1 0 0 0. marcas obtulit, vt absente Rege in Ranulphi locum, Regni procurator designaretur, domiq; a militia vacaret atque maneret. Quod datis summis impetrauit, sed postea ob voti sui redemptionem Romanæ fedi, quæ nulli deesse petitioni arg̃ gentì, infinitam pecuniam largitus est.
units.tr: If some Neptune had calmed this Aeolus, the plans of the King and of Baldwin would have reached a happy end. But the whirlwinds and gusts of his threats and censures so disturbed everything that nothing could be accomplished at that opportune moment. Now that everything needed for dedicating this church of Thomas the Martyr was ready, Baldwin came to Canterbury. On the way he was met by three monks, who announced that their Prior, in the name of the Church of Canterbury, had appealed to Rome against his installation and his purpose. Nevertheless Baldwin pressed on, came to the church of St Stephen, and it was rumoured that he would install new clergy there. The monks were sent again by the Prior. Having lodged their appeal, they forbade both the Archbishop and the clergy to proceed with the installations, and also the rector of St Stephen's church, and so they tried to block the progress of the business. Baldwin did not wish to be stopped. He consecrated the altar, installed the clergy, removed the Prior from his administration, placed an interdict on the altar, and shut out of the convent the man who had read out the appeal. He demanded an oath from the sponsors that they would not let any of the monks leave by the doors without his knowledge. The Prior himself, whose name was Honorius, went out and hastened to Rome by long journeys. The papal thunderbolts were awaited. Meanwhile the King, fearing these new disturbances, sent to the monks the bishop-elect of Chester, John of Norwich, and William of Worcester. By many arguments, with smooth speech and at times mixed with threats, they urged the monks to submit the controversies for which they had appealed to the Pope to the judgement of the King and the prelates. The monks replied that their appeal had already been carried to the Pope by their Prior Honorius, and that nothing could be decided in his absence. The bishops returned to the King and reported this answer. Upset by the reply, the King came to Canterbury himself, summoned the Archbishop and the monks before him, and promised that he would settle the dispute. The monks, holding firmly to their purpose, said that the case had been carried to the Pope and that therefore they would not allow it to be decided by any other judgement. So the King returned, the peace having come to nothing. Envoys were sent to the Pope by the King and by Baldwin, and letters were given by each of the bishops of the Canterbury province. When the Pope had greeted the legates in his customary manner and read the letters of the King and Baldwin, he cast the letters of the bishops aside. He set a day on which he wished to hear the cause. On that day, after the matter had been laid out by both parties, the Pope judged in favour of the Prior and the monks. He wrote to the Archbishop and seriously commanded him to restore the Prior and the monks, whom he had removed, forbidden or excluded, to their full position. We have said before that the Pope himself had given Baldwin authority to undertake his project. But it has always been the practice of the Popes to annul their own decrees as well as those of others. Baldwin did not desist because of these letters, nor did he restore the monks; and in order to provoke and inflame them the more, he consecrated the chrism at London. The monks hurried back to Rome, and reported that they had been restored through the agents of the Pope, and letters of procuration from the Pope to Baldwin, by which he was sternly ordered, under many threats, to tear down the new church which had been built after the expulsion of the monks, and not to proceed any further with the work begun. Thereupon Baldwin desisted from the work, together with the King and all the prelates of his province, yielding to the judgement of the Pope, against the most insolent monks. But since they were unwilling to be so shamefully defeated by the monks, a new plan was devised, which that Roman Aeolus again scattered by the storms of his rescripts. Baldwin had already ordered by the Pope's command that everything he had built at Hackington should be pulled down. At his command those buildings were suddenly levelled to the ground. But by an exchange of lands he acquired from the Bishop and monks of Rochester a certain estate in the village of Lambeth, which lies on the opposite side of the Thames from Westminster, to the east. He ordered the stones, mortar and timbers, and everything else he had prepared for erecting the church at Hackington, to be carried to this estate. The work was renewed after Pope Urban died, for he had helped the monks with all his might. Gregory VIII succeeded him, a supporter of the King and Baldwin. They now raised their spirits, and the monks lost heart, as is usual in the interplay of opposing circumstances, when people become more cheerful or more gloomy according to the party they support. But Gregory died in the second month of his papacy. The controversy over building, pulling down and moving the church at Hackington had now lasted more than four years, under four Popes: Lucius, Urban, Gregory and Clement. To recount over that span all the complaints and outbursts of the monks, Baldwin's harshness, the King's own evasions, his excuses and renewals of his own acts, all forced by the necessity of the time, would be endless. Since we are aiming at brevity, we have passed these over, for all these things flowed from this church as from a fountain. About this time the Prior of Canterbury, Honorius, died of the plague, and the Canterbury monks wished to venerate him among their saints along with his supporters. In his place, by the authority and favour of the King and Baldwin, Roger succeeded. And now the death of Henry II, the most prudent prince, was at hand. It came upon him, as we may reasonably suppose, more swiftly, because he had suffered such unworthy treatment from the monks and from his sons, things unworthy of a King and a father. Yet he bore these with a brave royal spirit and avoided them with prudence. At the death of this most renowned King, what is to be said about the outcome of the Hackington or Lambeth business will be reserved for its proper place. But among those troubles some other acts of Baldwin must be passed over. In the fourth year of his consecration he hated the Canterbury monks so intensely that, having driven the monks out of the monastery of the Holy Trinity, he brought in secular clergy by royal authority. But when an appeal had been made to the Pope, the King preferred that the dispute be settled and the monks restored. In the same year at Westminster, Baldwin placed the diadem on King Richard, on the 3rd of the Nones of September, in the presence of the Archbishops of Rouen, Trier and Dublin. Ptolemy of Tiverton and Hubert of Salisbury were consecrated at Westminster in the chapel of St Catherine, and a few days later Richard of London and William of Ely were consecrated at Lambeth by the same Baldwin. In the same year King Richard conferred the Archbishopric of York on his half-brother Geoffrey, who had been Bishop of Lincoln though he had never been ordained to any sacred office before. When Geoffrey had been chosen, Baldwin interceded before the King on behalf of the dignity of the see of Canterbury, and produced a decree of William the Norman on this matter. He also, by a proclamation of appeal to the Pope, forbade both Geoffrey, the elect, and all the other bishops of England to be ordained and consecrated by anyone other than the Archbishop of Canterbury. John, the King's brother, Earl of Dorset and Somerset, appealed against Baldwin to John of Anagni, the Cardinal who had landed in England and was the legate of Pope Clement. He did so because his county had been placed under an interdict on account of his marriage, which he had arranged with the daughter of the Earl of Gloucester, though she was related to him within the third degree; his appeal to the Pope had been rejected. The legate approved this appeal and annulled Baldwin's interdict. The same legate, for the sake of the monks, profaned with a solemn sentence the chapel at Hackington, although it had now been pulled down and levelled with the ground. But through the intercession of the King, so that Baldwin should not be harassed by the calumnies of the monks, it was agreed that a modest little chapel should be built on that spot, without a baptistery or a graveyard, to be content with the ministry of a single secular cleric. Roger, too, who succeeded Honorius as Prior, could not endure the hatred of the monks. Therefore under this legate he yielded to the Canterbury monks, and by the favour of the King and Baldwin he moved on as abbot to the monastery at Evesham. King Richard, mindful of the sin which his father had lamented, namely his own seditions and conspiracies against him, believed that he could atone for it by an expedition to Jerusalem. For this purpose he made every preparation and arrangement, and to raise a great sum of money he imposed taxes on the people, and sold, leased and pledged the royal possessions. Among other things, Hugh de Puiset, a glorious man infamous for many crimes, who had held the bishopric of Durham for forty years without clerical orders, acquired the county of Northumberland from the King at a high price. When the custom was that the county should be girded with a sword and named by the King as earl, the King smiled and said: "Well, I am a wonderful craftsman: out of an old bishop I have made a young earl." Many took the vow of the cross and of that expedition along with the King, among them Baldwin, together with Hubert of Salisbury, Ranulph de Glanvill, who was procurator of the whole kingdom under the King, and Hugh of Durham. But Ranulph gave up that office so that he might prepare himself more conveniently for the journey to Jerusalem. Hugh, however, offered the King, who was already ready for the journey, a thousand marks, so that in the King's absence he might be appointed procurator of the kingdom in Ranulph's place and remain at home, free from military service. He obtained this by paying the sum; but afterwards, to redeem his own vow, he gave an enormous sum of money to the Roman see, which never refuses anything to anyone who offers silver.

units.la: Baldwinus cum Rege profecturus Concilium Westmonasterii habuit, ibi rebus ordine compositis, maioris excommunicationis sententiam in omnes pronunciauit, qui peregrinationis suæ tempore Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis iura perturbarent, vel minuerent. Inde Cantuariam profectus eandem sententiam promulgauit. Posteaque acceptis baculo & pera, fidoque comitatu Huberto, Duuoria traiecit. Et ad Syriam, itinere multis regionib. terra marique superatis, prouectus Aconem ad exercitum Regis peruenit, cuius pars fame & inopia grauiter laborabat, pars aeris inclementia morbum contraxerat, alii diuturnitate temporis, tam longe a patria distracti, fatigati sunt quos omnes Baldwinus, verbo, vitæ claritate, & sumptibus suis consolatus, tandem læthali morbo correptus, in obsidione vrbis Aconobiit postquàm sedisset annis sex, mensibus vndecim, diebus quinque. Ibi testamento militibus, omnia legauit, bonaque sua Huberti fidei intereos diuidenda commisit. Is tam piam testationem non minori fide in omnibus executus est, mortuumque honorifice humauit. In hunc Baldwinum etiam mortuum Cantuarienses Monachi fœuiebant. Osbertum enim Bristoliensem, quem ex Baldwini consilio Richardus Rex S. Trinitatis Coenobii priorem constituerat, mortuo Baldwino Regeque absente eiecerunt. Deinde ex oprimi hominis bonitate ac virtute calumnias fabricarunt. Nam quia natura mitis ac lenis fuit, torpentem ac tepidum vocante. Et quia Regi obsequutus est, ab Vrbano Papa Monachorum fautore in Epistola his verbis reprehensus est. Vrb. P p. seruus seruorum Dei, Monacho feruentissimo, Abbati calido, Episcopo tepido, Archiepiscopo remisso, ex quo Monachi affirmant, quòd melior Monachus simplex quàm Abbas, melior Archiepiscopus, melior Episcopus quàm Archiepiscopus fuerit. Sed facile est tam Papalem quàm Monachorum in bonum virum inuidiam & maledicentiam animaduertere, quorum hi inuisum eum habebant, ille placabilem & moderatum Archiprɛsulem nõ tulit, sed tumultuosum aliquem (qualis Thomas fuit) optauit. Hic Baldwinus legatina authoritate Walliam primus visitauit, & in singulis cathedralibus Walliæ Ecclesiis solennes missas Pontificalibus indutus ornamentis, celebrauit. Primusque illam totam prouinciam in Cantuariensi statuit. Erfi quidem Wallenses Episcopi etiam subiectione profesSa à Cantuarientibus Archiepiscopis ante sacrati fuerunt. In qua peregratione complures Wallenses cruce signatos militiæ Christianæ asseripsit, secumque ad bellum Ierosolymitanum perduxit.
units.tr: Baldwin, about to set out with the King, held a council at Westminster. There, once affairs were put in order, he pronounced the sentence of greater excommunication on all who, during his pilgrimage, should disturb or diminish the rights of the Church of Canterbury. He then went to Canterbury and published the same sentence. Afterwards, having taken up the staff and wallet and with his faithful companion Hubert, he crossed to Dover. Passing through many regions by land and sea, he came to Syria and reached Acre, where the King's army was. Part of it was suffering badly from famine and want, part had caught sickness from the harshness of the air, and others were worn down by the long time they had spent so far from home. Baldwin comforted them all by his words, the brightness of his life and his own expense. At last, seized by a deadly illness during the siege of the city of Acre, he died, after he had sat as archbishop for six years, eleven months and five days. There, by his will, he left everything to the soldiers and committed his goods to be divided by the good faith of Hubert. Hubert carried out this pious charge with no less faithfulness in all things, and buried the dead man with honour. The monks of Canterbury raged even against this Baldwin after his death. For they drove out Osbert of Bristol, whom King Richard had appointed prior of the convent of the Holy Trinity on Baldwin's advice, when Baldwin was dead and the King was absent. Then, from the goodness and virtue of this excellent man, they fabricated slanders. For because he was of a gentle and mild nature, they called him sluggish and lukewarm; and because he had obeyed the King, Pope Urban, a champion of the monks, rebuked him in a letter in these words: "Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to a fervent monk, a warm abbot, a lukewarm bishop and a slack archbishop," from which the monks maintain that a simple monk is better than an abbot, and an archbishop better than a bishop. But it is easy to see the envy and slander against a good man, both of the Papal party and of the monks: the latter held him in hatred, while the former could not bear an archbishop who was peaceable and moderate, but wished for some turbulent man (such as Thomas was). Baldwin, by legatine authority, was the first to visit Wales, and in each cathedral church of Wales he celebrated solemn masses, vested in pontifical ornaments. He was also the first to place that whole province under Canterbury. Indeed, the Welsh bishops had earlier been consecrated by the archbishops of Canterbury, having professed subjection to them. On that journey he enrolled many Welshmen who had taken the cross into Christian military service, and he led them with him to the war for Jerusalem.

units.la: XL. REGINALDVS.
units.tr: XL. Reginald.

units.la: EGINALDVS etsi post electionem improuisa morte absorptus caruit consecratione, tamen omnino non est prætereundus silentio, quoniam & prætet voluntatem Regis electus est, & Monachi elatos animos adhuc non demittentes, in eo eligendo non arrogantiam solum, sed & virulentiam suam prodiderunt. Baldwino iam mortuo datæ sunt ilico à Rege ad Priorem & Conuentum Cant. literæ quibus eos rogauit, vt aliquem suo iudicio probandum eligerent.
units.tr: Although Reginald, carried off by a sudden death after his election, never received consecration, he must not be passed over in silence. He was elected against the king's will, and the monks, not yet lowering their proud spirits, revealed in that election not only their arrogance but also their venom. Baldwin being now dead, the king immediately sent letters to the Prior and Convent of Canterbury asking them to choose someone whom he might approve.

units.la: Acceptis his cum tam læto nuncio literis, incredibile dictu est, quantùm Monachi gestiebant. Sed, vt in improuisa penitus accepta nouirate esse solet, dubitabant Monachi, an ea quæ acceperant, quæque vera esse maximè optabant, certa ne an secus essent. Hac incertitudine perplexi atq; sui spensi de tegiis literis deliberaturi conuenerent, anteaquàm certi quicquam statuissent. Interea Rhotomagensis Archiepiscopus, qui post Elienfis Episcopi fugà à Rege absente præfectuvregno fuit, de Regis voluntate agit cum Episcopis. Hi Londinensis Episcopi mandato, qui Decanus habetur Cantnariensis sedis, Cantuariam conuenerunt. Quorum aduentu inter Monachos suspicio orta est, eos ex Regis voluntate rem acturos. Clam itaque de Reginaldo Bathoniensi Episcopo (qui Monachis confoederatus priuati Monachi habitum sumpsisset) consenserunt. Cum Episcopis aderat Cantuariæ Rhotomag. Archiepiscopus præfectus regno, venerunt-que ad Priorem & Monachos Regis mandatum exposituri. Priorin Episcoporum & conuentus sui præsentia Regis per Rhotomagensem voluntate prius declarata, Ecce, inquit, authoritate regia ex mandato vestro parata sunt omnia. In nomine Sanctæ Trinitatis Regnaldum eligimus Bathoniensem. Quem præsentem pronunc apprehendunt Monachi, etsi (vt atunc) inuitum, renitentem, plorantem, & clamantem, in Ecclesiam violenter trahunt, & in sede Metropolitana quasi re bene gesta atque rata statuunt. Sedata aliquantulum hac Monachorum in solentia atque turba, Rhotomagensis Regis nomine appellationem ab his Monachorum gestis interposuit, pauculque inde diebus conuocatis Londini Episcopis & regni proceribus, Bathoniensis a Rhotomagensi interrogatus est, An Monachorum de se electioni consentiret. Bathoniensis de sua in Regem fide atque obseruantia præfatus. Monachi, inquit, matricis Ecclesiæ ad quos specialiter spectat electio, personam nostram elegerunt renitentem & reclamantem, vt ipsi vidistis: nunc autem quia quæritis, quid sentiam, dico vobis mente mea ab omni contagione ambitionis, quod si sua electioni stare voluerint Monachi, anxius & inuitus consentiotiss vero respuerint, gratulabundus cedo. Verumtamen quia contumelias quorundam & minas audiuimus, prohibemus ex parte Dei & authoritate Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ, sub appellatione sedis Apostolicæ, & anathematis interminatione, ne Cantuariensi Ecclesiæ vel Bathoniensi aliqua præsumptis inferre grauamina. Dixitque Prior Cantuariensis: Ab electione quam tam iuste & legitime fecimus non resipiscimus, sed vnanimi consensu firmiter stamus, & ne quolibet molimine præpediatur, sedem Apostolicam appellamus.
units.tr: When they received these letters, which brought such welcome news, it is hard to say how eagerly the monks rejoiced. But, as is usual with news received unexpectedly, the monks doubted whether what they had received, and what they most wished to be true, was certainly so. Perplexed by this uncertainty, and eager to deliberate on the king's letters, they met before deciding anything for certain. Meanwhile the Archbishop of Rouen, who had been put in charge of the kingdom in the king's absence after the flight of the Bishop of Ely, dealt with the bishops about the king's wishes. At the command of the Bishop of London, who is regarded as the dean of the see of Canterbury, these bishops came together at Canterbury. Their arrival raised suspicion among the monks that they would act according to the king's will. Secretly, therefore, they came to an agreement about Reginald, Bishop of Bath, who had joined the monks' cause and had put on the habit of a private monk. The Archbishop of Rouen, acting as governor of the kingdom, was present at Canterbury with the bishops, and they came to the Prior and the monks to set out the king's command. When the Prior and his convent had first been told the king's will through the Archbishop of Rouen, the Archbishop said: "Look, by royal authority, at your request, everything is arranged. In the name of the Holy Trinity we choose Reginald of Bath." The monks then seized him, though he was present and unwilling, resisting, weeping and crying out, and dragged him violently into the church, and set him in the metropolitan see as if the business were well done and settled. When this tumult of the monks had calmed somewhat, the Archbishop of Rouen, in the king's name, lodged an appeal against the monks' proceedings. A few days later, with the bishops and the nobles of the kingdom summoned to London, the Archbishop of Rouen asked the Bishop of Bath whether he consented to the election of the monks. The Bishop of Bath, after professing his loyalty and obedience to the king, said: "The monks of the mother church, to whom the election specially belongs, chose my person, though I resisted and protested, as you yourselves saw. But now, since you ask what I think, I tell you, with a mind free of all taint of ambition, that if the monks are willing to stand by their election, I consent, anxious and unwilling; but if they reject it, I yield gladly. Nevertheless, since we have heard the insults and threats of certain people, we forbid, in God's name and by the authority of the Church of Canterbury, under appeal to the Apostolic See and on pain of anathema, that any injury be inflicted on the Church of Canterbury or on the Bishop of Bath." The Prior of Canterbury then said: "We do not retract our election, which we made so justly and lawfully, but stand firmly in unanimous agreement, and so that it may not be hindered by any device, we appeal to the Apostolic See."

units.la: Veloces hac de re nuncii ad Papam ab Archiepiscopo electo & Priore missi aduolauerunt. Quibus sine mora traditum illico pallium, & satis benigne confirmata est electio. Nulla res vnquam à Monachis fœlicius atque celerius Romæ peracta est. Quæ sanè Romanæ fœcis atque αἰσχροκερδὴς suspicione non caret, quod infimæ & abiectæ conditionis hominibus, cum Regibus, totiusque regni magnatibus non modo contendi audacia, sed & vincendi ipes ingenita fuerit. Sed ipse Deus omnis vltor contumaciæ atque maliciæ, hanc Monachorum cum Bathoniensi coniurationem in ipso iam electo vindicauit. Interea enim dum Romæ de mutendo Pallio, & electione stabilienda agebatur, Reginaldus Bathoniam proficiscens obiit in itinere Dogmerssfeldiæ (quæ in Southamptonnensi comitatu (pagus est) decimo quinto die, postquam electus fuerat, ipsoque Christi Natiuitatis festo cadauer eius Bathoniam vectum, & sepultura conditu est. Cuius inexpectata mors tanto luctu à Monachis plagebantur, vt si Dominus Thomas iam eorum preces exaudiret, aliquidue tanto numine dignum præcipere poterat, dubium non est, quin Reginaldus ad vitos à mortuis redüsset. Sed credibilius est Reginaldum eodem sanctitatis præmio cum Thoma affectum, viuorum consortia penitus deseruisse, & mortuorum latebras sempiternas sectari. Hoc tempore Hugo Episcopus Ceftrensis è Conuentrenfi Ecclesia exclusit Monachos eorumque loco introduxit clericos seculares: Sed Hugone mortuo eiectis rursus Clericis Monachi recepti ac restituti 40 sant.
units.tr: Swift messengers were sent from the Archbishop-elect and the Prior to the Pope about this matter, and they flew to Rome. Without delay the pallium was handed over at once, and the election was confirmed quite graciously. Nothing was ever done by the monks more happily and quickly than this at Rome. Indeed, this surely does not lack the suspicion of Roman greed and sordid profit, since men of the lowest and most despised condition were not only bold to contend with kings and all the magnates of the kingdom, but also had an innate hope of winning. But God himself, the avenger of all obstinacy and malice, punished this conspiracy of the monks with the Bishop of Bath in the man already elected. For while at Rome the exchange of the pallium and the confirmation of the election were being arranged, Reginald, setting out for Bath, died on the journey at Dogmersfield, a village in the county of Southampton, on the fifteenth day after his election. His body was carried to Bath and buried on the very feast of Christ's Nativity. His unexpected death so grieved the monks that, if Lord Thomas were now hearing their prayers and could command anything worthy of so great a divinity, there is no doubt that Reginald would have been brought back to life from the dead. But it is more credible that Reginald, having been honoured with the same reward of holiness as Thomas, wholly abandoned the company of the living and sought the everlasting hiding places of the dead. At this time Hugh, Bishop of Chester, drove the monks out of the church of Coventry and put secular clergy in their place. But after Hugh's death, the clerics were thrown out again, and the monks were received and restored, and there are forty of them.

units.la: XLII. HVBERTVS.
units.tr: XLII. Hubert

units.la: Nter has domi factiones atque partes, quas tanto studio & sedulitate sectabantur Monachi, Richardus Rex multis præliis fœlicitèr gestis, Cypro & Aconæ captis: totaq; Syria superata, dum ad hos no uos Monachorum motus compescendos in Anglia properaret, ex Philippi Regis Galliæ, & Henrici Imperatoris coniunctis & occultis insidiis, ab Austriæ Duce in quadam ciuitatula, quæ Gynacia nuncupatur, captus, 5 & Imperatori traditus est. Quibus conflictus difficultatibus, de Anglia tamen, quæ iam tam Regali quam sacerdotali potestate careret, suspensus magis & solicitus quam de se su it. His tot simul congruentibus malis existimauit Rex neminem citius facilius{que} succurrere posse, quam Hubertum. Cuius & erga se fidem, & in rebus agendis solertiam, tam ex illa veteri cum Baldwino necessitudine, quàm ex multis aliis argumentis domi militiæ que perspectam & cognitam habebat. Hic Hubertus in villa Westdcrehamiæ in Norfolcia natus est. Educatus vero à Ranulpho de Glandsfeld, præclaræ prudentiæ viro lurisperito, regnique generali Procuratore: Decanus primo Boracensis, deinde An. t. Richardi Regis a Baldwino (vt ante diximus) Sarisburensis Episcopus sacratus, eiusque lerosolymitani itineris
units.tr: Amid these factions and parties at home, which the monks pursued with such zeal and eagerness, King Richard had fought many battles successfully, taken Cyprus and Acre, and subdued all Syria. While he was hurrying back to England to put down these new disturbances of the monks, he was seized by the Duke of Austria in a small town called Gynacia, through the joint and secret plots of Philip, King of France, and the Emperor Henry, and was handed over to the Emperor. Amid these difficulties he was more anxious and troubled about England, which now lacked both royal and priestly authority, than about himself. Seeing so many evils converge at once, the king thought that no one could bring help more quickly or effectively than Hubert. He knew Hubert's loyalty to himself and his skill in managing affairs, both from that old friendship with Baldwin and from many other proofs of his service at home and in war. Hubert was born in the village of Westdereham in Norfolk. He was brought up by Ranulf de Glanville, a man of notable prudence, a lawyer, and the kingdom's chief justiciar. He was first dean of York, then, as we said above, was consecrated bishop of Salisbury by Baldwin, and he had accompanied Baldwin on his journey to Jerusalem. He was also the executor and heir of Baldwin's will, and had been the king's closest confidant after Baldwin's death, through whom all military and camp business had been conducted.

units.la: {y} Florilegium In Vienna contaert 13. Cal. Lam. Wul Nub. Lib. 4. cap. 3 tuneris comes, ac testamenti hæres fidei Commissarius, mortuoq; Baldwino Regi intimus (pet quem omnia militaria & cafirenfia negocia gerebantur) fuerat.
units.tr: Florilegium, Vienna, Lib. 4. cap. 3. Hubert was the companion of Baldwin's journey, executor of his will, and after Baldwin's death the king's intimate, through whom all military and camp business was carried on.

units.la: Cumq; Decanus esset Eboracensis, emit à Galfrido Galfridi filio de Westderchâ quicquid terrarum in eadem villa & pertinentiis habuit, vel habere potuit cum pertinentiis, cum aduocationibus Ecclesiarum, & omnibus libertatibus, &c. ex quibus Præmonstratensis Ordinis Monasterium, pto suæ (vt ait) patriæque ac matris, & Ranulphi de Glanfeld & Bertæ vxoris eius animarum salute (à quibus inqnit, nos nutriti sumus) fundauit atque condidit. Quam concessionem eisdem pene verbis cum esset Episcopus Saritb. postea renouauit.
units.tr: When he was dean of York, he bought from Geoffrey, son of Geoffrey, of Westdereham, all the lands he had or could have in that village with their appurtenances, together with the advowsons of the churches and all the liberties, and so on. With these lands he founded and established a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order, for the salvation of his own soul (as he says), of his country and mother, and of the souls of Ranulf de Glanville and of his wife Berta, by whom, he says, we were brought up. Later, when he was bishop of Salisbury, he renewed this grant in almost the same words.

units.la: Hunc igitur literis ad Reginam Elnorem matrem suam, & Rhotomagensem Archiepiscopum, quem Regno præfecerat, expeditum in Angliam, quam celerrime proficisci iussit, vt eurbulentium rerum statum pacaret, & se redemisquam citissime curaret. Quam quidè adremetsi virtute singulari ingenioque polleret, tamen ne authoritas illi tam grauis & difficilis muneris obeundi deesset, Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem eum cteati voluit. Quod vt fieret & matrem Elnoram & Rhotomagensem literis instanter rogauit. Ab hijs Episcopi Regionomine solicitati fidem dederunt, se hoc negotium inuitis Monachis curaturos. Scripserat eodem tempore ad Monachos Rex, vt de pio Antistite Cantuariensi Ecclesiæ præficiendo conuenirent, nec de Huberto mentionem vllam fecit. Id illi in eam partem interpretabantur, ac si eis Rex libera electionis iura sine quacunque intercessione aut nominatione permisisset. Sed Rex qui hoc inuitis illis perfice renitebatur, rogare eos amplius noluit à quibus prioribus literis repulsam tam indignam tulisset. Regina iam & Rhotomagensis conuocatis Londini Episcopis, Prioris & conuentui Cantuariensi nunciarunt, vt iv. Calendas Iunii ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum eligendum adessent. Illi cum de tacita Regis voluntate suspicarentur, veriti quid in tanto rerum discrimine contingere posset, Hubertum (insignem prudentia & pietate virum) eligunt. Dieq; statuto Prior in Episcoporum concione Londini Hubertum (quo non viderent aliquem in Anglia præstantiorem) electum declarat. Res præter Reginæ & Episcoporum expectationem accidit, vt eorum de Huberto eligendo conatus à Monachis (quos solos obstaturos putabant) iuuarentur. Itaque Londinensis Episcopus stupore affectus, hene (inquit) fecistis qui præsentastis nobis nostrum electum. At Prior, Nos, inquit, ad quos de iure spectat eligendi potestas, Regiæ curiæ nostrum præsentamus electum, Qua re tam feliciter ex omnium votis perfecta, missi sine mora Romam pro pallio & legatina potestate legati. Hubertus interea in Mertonensi coenobio Monachatu initiatus est, quo Monachos Cantuarienses Baldwino familiari suo ob illius ordinis contemptum infensos commodius sibi res grandes molienti deuinciret. Postea de Rege tedimendo agit. Ad eam rem ex quadrante prouentuum totius Regni, rebusq; saeris ac Ecclesiis dedicatis venditis, tum Cistercensium Monachorum exactalana, centum 50. marcarum millia congerunt. Quæ æquissimis omnium animis tam Inclyto Regi liberando persoluta sunt. Richardus Rex (tedemptionis precio, & certarum conditionum obtidibus Imperatori) datis captiuitatis nexu solutus, in Angliam festibat.
units.tr: Therefore the king sent him to England as quickly as possible, with letters to Queen Eleanor, his mother, and to the archbishop of Rouen, whom he had put in charge of the kingdom, ordering him to settle the disturbed state of affairs and to take care that the king be ransomed as soon as possible. Although Hubert was outstanding in courage and talent, the king wished to make him archbishop of Canterbury, so that he would have the authority needed to carry out so heavy and difficult a task.
