To bring this about, he urgently asked his mother Eleanor and the archbishop of Rouen by letter. Urged by these letters, the bishops and the rest of the nobility gave their word that they would arrange this business even against the wishes of the monks. At the same time the king had written to the monks that they should meet to choose a godly prelate to govern the church of Canterbury, and he made no mention of Hubert at all. The monks interpreted this as if the king had granted them the free right of election without any intervention or nomination. But the king, who was opposed to their carrying this out against his wishes, did not wish to ask them again, since he had suffered such an unworthy rejection from their earlier letters. Now the queen and the archbishop of Rouen, having summoned the bishops to London, informed the prior and convent of Canterbury that they should be present on the fourth day before the Kalends of June to elect an archbishop of Canterbury. Suspecting the king's unspoken will, and fearing what might happen in so great a crisis, the monks chose Hubert, a man distinguished by prudence and piety. On the appointed day the prior, in an assembly of the bishops at London, declared Hubert elected, since they could not see anyone in England more outstanding. The matter turned out contrary to the expectations of the queen and the bishops, since the monks, whom they had thought alone would be obstacles, supported their efforts to elect Hubert. The bishop of London, astonished, said: "You have done well in presenting to us our own candidate." But the prior replied: "We, to whom the power of election properly belongs, present our candidate to the royal court." When the matter had been brought to such a happy conclusion by the votes of all, messengers were sent at once to Rome for the pallium and the commission of legate. Meanwhile Hubert was initiated into monastic life at the monastery of Merton, so that he might bind the monks of Canterbury more closely to himself, since they were hostile to Baldwin, his associate, because of his contempt for their order, and he was planning great things. Afterwards he turned to ransoming the king. For this purpose they collected from a quarter of the revenues of the whole kingdom, from the sale of sacred things and dedicated churches, and also from the tax levied on the Cistercian monks, one hundred and fifty thousand marks. This sum was paid with the greatest goodwill of everyone toward liberating so renowned a king. Richard the king, freed from the bonds of captivity by the price of his ransom and by hostages given to the Emperor under certain conditions, was hastening to England.

units.la: Interea à Cœlestino Papa nuncii cum Pallio & Legatinæ authoritatis mandato redeunt. Quibus Anno Domini 1194. solenniter suscepti, vna cum Archiepiscopali & legatina potestate totius regni administrationem gessit, & tam foro Ecclesiastico Archiepiscopus, quam laicali Cancellarius, & criminalibus atque capitalibus iudiciis summus Angliæ Iusticiarius præsidebat. Neq; enim vnquam in Anglia quisquam tanta atque hic imperandi coercendique potestate præditus fuit. In qua tamen non modo moderatus atque pius fuit, Regis gratiam, populiq; benevolentiam conciliauit, sed etiam facinorosos actiter castigauit, tumultus prudenter sedauit, seditiosos atque conspiratos fortiter restituit ac tepugnauit. Vt difficile dictu sit, quanta temperantia lenitatem cum seueritate permisceret. Willielmum quendam Longobardum legulcium atque factiosum (qui in pendendo illo pro Rege captiuo redimendo tributis, Londinensibus atque plebem ad tumultum pene concitauerat) capite punit. Hic Willielmus cum ea suasione populi seditionem commouere non poterat, capefcedam à vulgo æqualem atque patrem cum superioribus libertatem, & a ceruicibus suis deiiciendam illam locupletum potentiorumq; authoritatem omni secutus intolerabilem sæpius pro concione præcidauit. Huic ingens plebis multitudo adhæsit, quæ eum vbique sequuta est. Vt ipsi summi iudices, regnique eosliseritm ad se vocatum tanta multitudine deterriti dimittere cogerentur. Hinc tantos tibi spiritus, arrogantiamque sumpsit, vt eiusem Londinensem tibi occurrentem trucidaret. Quo per vrbem cognito Willielmus vndique armis petitus, & multitudine suâ diffusa atq; dissipata cum concubina & orto socius in Arcuatum templum actus est. Ibi secanquamin æde sacra, vndequnquam vi eximi nefas esset, diu continuit, donec Huberti mandato flammis templo admbitis vltro exiuit. Tum deprehensus, & tam atrocis concitationis reus iudicatus per plateas ciuitatis equorum caudis ligatus &ad London turrim tractus laqueo gulæ circumductò a furca paululum pendebat, ilico præcisolaqueo semiuiuus demissus, viscera ei & intestina euulsa sunt, capiteque amputato corpus in quatuor partes dissectum est. Qui cum eo ad arcuatum templum confugerunt laqueis a patibulo gula pendentes suffocati sunt. Hunc tam graui supplicio damnatum inlana plebs vt Martyrem diu colebat, corporisque membra atque ossa vt sanctas reliquias venerabatur. Coniuratorum cum eo numerus multorum millium fuit, quihuberti moderatione & prudentia depolitis armis pacati sine supplicio ad sua secesse runt. Ita c coniuratione delata, de ducibus sumpta poena, & multitudo seruata est. Nec minus solerssatque sagax Hubertus fuit, in Iohannis Comitis contra Regem fratrem iam captiui fenuendis & anteuertendis insidiis. Nam rege capto Iohannes (contra fratrem necessitudinem & fidem datam) cum Philippo Gallia Rege fœdus idque iurato iniit. Quo nequiter stabilito, Philippus Regi (in Imperatoris itudia Vigilantissimi seruato) sine villa causa bellum denunciauit. In illa impia confœderatione pactum est, vt suscitatis vna & vndique ad bellum inferendum copiis Gallus Normanniam, Iohannes Angliam subito occuparent, vt nulla respiratione aut inteicapedine data, captiuum adhuc Regem & Angliæ regno, & Galliærum regionum Dominio prorsus exuerent. Sed tam scelerati inceptis obstitit, Regemque abscentem iuuit summa subditorum per Hubertum conciliata retentaq; fides & obseruantia. Iohannes castrum Windesur eiecto Elienfi Episcopo, regnique Cancellario, tenuit id militibus, copiisque clam instruxit suis, eas copias post bellum in Syria gestum dolose subtraxit fratri, auxilia à Belgis, Cambris, & Scotis expectauit. Belgæ iam copiosa classe ad Angliæ oras appulerant ipsis pascha libus feriis, ied confluente omnium ordinum nobilium pariter & ignobilium infinita multitudine atque turba à littore prohibentur. Itaq; mutata vehiculatione, & conuersa puppi discedunt. Cambri Kingstoniam præter gressi cum ad castrum appropinquarent, annonę caritate prædæ sedabant, agrosvaftabant, iamque fame pene cnecti sine ordine palantes à populo fugati & exacti sunt. Scotus auxilium plane denegauit. Hubertus interea quamcunque cogere potuisset pecuniam ad Reginam mitit, qua excercitum instruere et. Ipse Westmonasterū cum Episcopis & Præla-tis consilium iniuit, in quo Comitem Iohannem Anathema pronunciauit, nisi hostilitate aduersus Regem deposita delictum agnosceret, & in Regis gratiam supplicirer redire studeret. Regina iam copiosum excercitum parauerat, ei Rhotomagenfem ducem præfecit. In Castium Windsor (quod vincere potuisset) longiore obsidione tenere fuipicabatur quòd Normannis quibusdam in eo militibus pepercit. Præterea parum Regi fidus putabatur, quòd post Huberti aduentum regni admiistratione motus fuerit. Itaque regni Procères fide in Regem integri, animisque infracti, abiecta Rhotomagensis procrastinatione & tarditate se accingunt, &lobannem hac conditione ad castri dedtionem compellit, 40 vt milites salui discedant. Quo concesso ipse in Gallias profugit, & Philippo Regi turpiter adbzlit. Philippus interea Gisortium in Normannia prodidione magis quam virtute cepit. Deinde Rhotomagum accelerauit. Sed aduolans citius Leycestrius Comes Regem anteuertit, ciuiumque animos firmauit. Regique aduenienti paresiunt portæ ciuitatis, quas cum ingredi velles, fundis & sagittis ex vrbe iactis, rum aqua feruenti immunda atque turbida ab ipsis mulierculis ciuitatis (marnia in viriliamictu tenebutus) in milites effusatam ignominiosam & turpem repulsam perpeslus est. vt deserta penitus Normania ad suam regionem cum infamia festinaret. His itaque duobus interfitiis tumultibus periculi atque discriminis plenis prudenter auersis & profligatis, Regeque liberato primus Huberti consecrationis annus optimis auspiciis iranfactus est. Iamque Regis 50 aduentus a Regina matre, & Regina sponsa, ab Huberto(omnia moderata & iecunda iuxta Regis desiderium gerente)& a cunctis ordinibus Regi obsequentibus, auide expectatur. Interea perfectis istis feriis ante Regis aduentum (inter ponamus iocofa). Omnes iam ordines aduentanti Regi occurrunt. Inter quos Godefridus Eboracensis Archiepiscopus Regis ( vt ante diximus) ex illicito coitu frater, cum in itinere cruce anta se lata Cantuariensem prouinciam attingeret, Regia via progredi cum cruce metuit. Itaq; ne crucé videretur deponere, per deuia atq; dumos progressus crucè magnifice gestans Sandwici quo Rex appulerat, omnesque concurrebant, ei obuiam dat. Id Hubertus ægre tulit, & de iniuria illa cum Rege conquestus est. Rex has siue nugas, sine minutas controuersias a se ad Papam transtulit. Idem Godefridus in Episcoporum conuentum, qui de Huberti electione Londini habitus est, ante cum cruce gloriosius venerat. Cui a Roffensi Episcopo grauiter & acute reprehenso, omniumque clamoribus cum cruce exploso, a nemine adiuuari potuit. Tum vero in plateis incessit cum cruce magnificentius, adu'terina sua nobilitate & cognatione fretus. Sed minis ciuium quos saltu suo incenderat, & consilio Magnatum (qui Regis causa ei prosperexerant) crucem depulsit & ne vi rumperetur aurea ... Controuersiam inter Londinensem & Roffensem Episcopos, cum Hubertus Pallium Crucemque suscieperet, de intronizatione motaeft. Intronizandi enim tius Londinensis vrde canus,
units.tr: Meanwhile the messengers came back from Pope Celestine with the pallium and the mandate of legatine authority. Hubert received them solemnly in the year of the Lord 1194, and together with his archiepiscopal and legatine power he administered the whole kingdom. As archbishop he presided over the ecclesiastical courts, as chancellor he presided over the lay courts, and as chief justiciar of England he presided over criminal and capital trials. Indeed, no one before him in England had held so great a power of command and restraint. Yet in exercising it he was not only moderate and pious, winning the king's favour and the goodwill of the people, but he also punished wrongdoers energetically, quelled disturbances wisely, and resolutely put down and crushed rebels and conspirators. It is hard to say how he mingled gentleness with severity in such measure. A certain Lombard, a litigious and factious man (who, in the matter of the tax levied to ransom the captive king, had almost stirred the Londoners and the common people to riot), he had put to death. This William, since he could not stir up sedition by the persuasion that the common people should seize equality and their former liberty and throw off the intolerable authority of the rich and powerful, kept preaching such things in public. A huge crowd of the common people clung to him and followed him everywhere. So the chief judges themselves were forced to dismiss the case, being frightened by so great a multitude that had been summoned to his side. From this he took such spirit and arrogance that he killed a Londoner who met him. When this became known in the city, William was attacked on all sides with weapons, and his followers, scattered and dispersed by the crowd, were driven along with his concubine and a few companions into the church of St Mary-le-Bow. There he kept them for a long time, since it would have been a crime to drag them out by force from a sacred building, until at Hubert's order the church was set on fire and they came out of their own accord. Then he was seized and, judged guilty of so atrocious an uprising, was dragged through the streets of the city, tied to horses' tails, to the Tower of London, where he was hanged by the throat from a gallows for a short time. Then the rope was cut, and he was let down half alive, his bowels and entrails were torn out, his head was cut off, and his body was divided into four parts. Those who had fled with him to the church were hanged by the throat from the gallows and suffocated. The common people, mad with grief, venerated this man, condemned to so severe a punishment, as a martyr, and worshipped the limbs and bones of his body as holy relics. The number of his conspirators was many thousands, and they were pacified by Hubert's moderation and prudence, laid down their arms, and withdrew to their homes without punishment. Thus the conspiracy was disclosed, the leaders were punished, and the multitude was spared. No less watchful and shrewd was Hubert in forestalling and frustrating the plots of Count John against his brother the king, who was now a captive. For when the king was taken, John, against the bond of brotherhood and the faith he had pledged, made an alliance with Philip, king of France, and confirmed it with an oath. When this wicked pact was firmly settled, Philip, without any cause, declared war on the king, who was kept in the emperor's custody. In that impious confederacy it was agreed that, once they had gathered forces from everywhere for the attack, the Frenchman should suddenly seize Normandy and John England, so that, allowing no breathing space or interval, they might strip the king, still a captive, of both the kingdom of England and the dominion of the French lands. But Hubert stood in the way of this wicked scheme, and the king, though absent, was helped by the great loyalty and obedience of his subjects, which Hubert had secured and maintained. John, having ejected the Bishop of Ely from the chancellorship, held Windsor castle, equipped it secretly with soldiers and supplies of his own, and then treacherously withdrew those forces from his brother after the war waged in Syria. He looked for auxiliaries from the Flemings, the Welsh and the Scots. The Flemings had already landed on the English shores with a large fleet on the very days of Easter, but with the vast crowd of nobles and commoners of every rank gathering, they were kept from the shore. So they changed course, turned their stern about, and departed. The Welsh advanced as far as Kingston, and when they came near the castle they were calmed by the scarcity of plunder; they laid waste the fields, and now nearly dying of hunger, wandering without order, they were put to flight and driven out by the people. The Scot flatly refused help. Meanwhile Hubert sent to the queen as much money as he could raise, with which she was to equip an army. He himself held a council at Westminster with the bishops and prelates, in which Count John was pronounced anathema unless he abandoned his hostility to the king, acknowledged his offence, and strove to return to the king's favour. The queen had already prepared a large army and placed the Duke of Rouen in command of it. It was thought that the siege of Windsor castle, which she might have conquered, would be prolonged, because she spared some Norman soldiers who were in it. Moreover, the queen was thought to be little trusted by the king, because she had been moved to take the government of the kingdom after Hubert's arrival. And so the nobles of the realm, faithful to the king and with their spirit unbroken, cast aside the procrastination and delay of the Duke of Rouen and armed themselves, and they compelled John to surrender the castle on the condition that the soldiers might leave safely. When this was granted, John himself fled to Gaul and shamefully went over to King Philip. Philip meanwhile took Gisors in Normandy more by treachery than by valour, and then hastened to Rouen. But the Earl of Leicester, riding ahead more swiftly, got there before the king and strengthened the spirits of the citizens. The gates of the city opened to the king when he arrived; but when he tried to enter, stones and arrows were thrown at him from the town, and boiling, foul and muddy water was poured over the soldiers by the very women of the city, who had tucked their skirts up into their men's clothing. So he suffered an ignominious and shameful repulse, and hurried back in disgrace, leaving Normandy wholly abandoned for his own region. Thus these two disturbances, full of peril and danger, were wisely averted and crushed, and with the king freed, the first year of Hubert's consecration passed under the best auspices. And now the king's coming was eagerly awaited by his mother the queen, by his bride the queen, by Hubert (who was managing everything in moderation and prosperity according to the king's wishes), and by all the orders obeying the king. Meanwhile, before the king's arrival, those holidays having been completed (let us put in some jests here), all the orders went out to meet the arriving king. Among them was Godfrey, archbishop of York, the king's brother by an illicit union, as we said before. When he reached the province of Canterbury, carrying his cross before him on the journey, he feared to proceed along the royal road with his cross, so, lest he seem to be laying the cross aside, he went through byways and thickets, carrying the cross with great show, to Sandwich where the king had landed, and there met him, while everyone came running together. Hubert took this badly and complained to the king about the injury. The king referred these trifles, or petty disputes, to the Pope. The same Godfrey had come more proudly with his cross to the meeting of bishops that was held in London about Hubert's election. When he was sharply and grievously rebuked by the Bishop of Rochester, and hooted down by the shouts of everyone with his cross, no one could help him. Then indeed he strode through the streets with his cross more ostentatiously, relying on his illustrious birth and his kinship. But, frightened by the threats of the citizens whom he had inflamed by his arrogance, and by the counsel of the magnates (who had been favourable to him for the king's cause), he put the cross away; and lest it be broken by force, [it was taken?] of gold ... The controversy between the bishops of London and Rochester, when Hubert received the pallium and the cross, arose over the enthronement. For the Bishop of London claimed the right to enthrone him, and the Bishop of Rochester, as the archbishop's chaplain, claimed it for himself.

units.la: 10 Roffensis vt Capellanus Archiepiscopi sibi vendicauit. His aurem litigantibus interponunt se Monachi, suumque ius asseruerunt esse. Tum totus Episcoporum coetus instabat, & ad ie tam intronizationem quam consecrationem spectare affirmabant. Hac dissensione turbata aliquantulum pallii suscipiendi ceremonia fuit. Tandem sic compositia est, vrin throno sedentis Episcopus Londinensis, pallium autem suscipientis, Episcopus Roffensis Archiepiscopi dextras occupauet. Sed his omissis ad Regem redeamus.
units.tr: 10 Since these two were disputing, the monks intervened and asserted that the right was theirs. Then the whole company of bishops insisted and affirmed that both the enthronement and the consecration pertained to them. Amid this dissension the ceremony of receiving the pallium was somewhat disturbed. At last it was settled in this way: the Bishop of London was to sit on the throne, and the Bishop of Rochester, who received the pallium, was to occupy the archbishop's right hand. But let us set these matters aside and return to the king.

units.la: Paulo ante Regis aduentum misse a Comite Iohanne ad confederatos literæ, quibus interceptis Hubertus castrum Marleburgense (quod erat Comitis) obsidione cepit excercituque dispositio & ad obsidendam Nottinghamiam locato Regi occursum redit. Qui Roffæ obuii mutuis se amplexibus lachrymantes tenuere. Tum Nuting-
units.tr: Shortly before the king's arrival, letters sent by Earl John to the confederates were intercepted. Hubert then took the castle of Marlborough, which belonged to the earl, by siege, and after posting his army to besiege Nottingham, he returned to meet the king. They met at Rochester and, weeping, held each other in a mutual embrace. Then they hastened to Nottingham,

units.la: 20 hamiam properant, urbemque ac castellum ceperunt. Conciliumque totius regni co Regis iussu coacti sunt, in quo Hubertus dextras, & Godefridus Eboracensis sinistras Regis tenuerunt. In eo consilio amputatis omnium dissensionum causis, motibusque pacatis, omnia quæ Rex vendiderat, aut leuiter concessera ante bellum Syriacum restituta fuot. Hugoque Dunelmensis, (de quo in Bald. vita antea diximus) Northumbriæ Comitatu reddio, Comes esse desiit, & in Episcopatu reuersus est. A Rege autem postulatum est, vt quoniam captiuitate (quæ seruirutiaequiparatur) regalia iura videbatur amisisse, diadema sibi imponi, sceptrumque tradi denuo permittere. Cui libenter assensus est. Ad eam rem Wintoniæ ab omnibus ordinatus, diadema atque sceptrum iterum suscepit. Post-
units.tr: 20 and took the city and castle. By the king's command, a council of the whole kingdom was convened, in which Hubert held the king's right hand and Geoffrey of York his left. In that council the causes of all disputes were removed, the disturbances were calmed, and everything the king had sold or lightly granted before the Syrian war was restored. Hugh of Durham (of whom we spoke earlier in the life of Baldwin) gave up the county of Northumberland, ceased to be earl, and returned to his bishopric. The king then requested that, since by captivity (which is equated with servitude) he seemed to have lost his royal rights, the crown be placed on him again and the sceptre be handed back to him. He gladly agreed. For this purpose, at Winchester, he was ordained by all and received the crown and sceptre again.

units.la: 30 ea Reip. cura illi commissa, naeum Hamptoniæ conscendit, & in Normanniam traiecit. Hubertus Londinum reuersus est, ibique Hubertum (Cantuariensem Archidiaconum) Sarisburiensem Episcopum ordinauit. Paulo post Hugo Dunelmensis obiit, cui mundus non crucifixus, sed infixus fuit. Huic Philippus successit, (vt aiunt) accinctus gladio (vt Eboracensis saltum & arrogantiam minueret) venit Eboracum. Ibi tamEcclesiastica quam temporalia excercuit iudicia, totamque Eboracensem prouinciam ad nutum redegit suum. Sed Godefridus Eboracensis Archiepiscopus Romam adueniauit, vt se suam quæ prouinciam ab Huberti potestate eximeret, ibi nihil profecit. Tum ad Regem fratrem in Normanniam venit, cuius aures nunquam cuiquam contra Hubertum querenti patefactæ sunt. Itaque (in ani labore, sumptuque sustentato) domum reuersus est.
units.tr: 30 After this, the care of the commonwealth was entrusted to him again. He embarked at Hampton and crossed over to Normandy. Hubert returned to London and there ordained Hubert, archdeacon of Canterbury, as bishop of Salisbury. Shortly afterwards Hugh of Durham died, to whom the world was not crucified but fixed. Philip succeeded him and, as they say, came to York girded with a sword, to diminish the pride and arrogance of the York men. There he exercised both ecclesiastical and secular jurisdiction and reduced the whole province of York to his nod. But Geoffrey, archbishop of York, came to Rome to free his province from Hubert's power, and there achieved nothing. Then he went to his brother the king in Normandy, whose ears were never opened to anyone complaining against Hubert. So he returned home, his labour and expense spent in vain.

units.la: 40 Hubertus eodem anno Glocestriam visitauit. Ibi Robertum Abbatem de Tornay (in sua praefentia constituendo) dignitate priuauit. Is prouocauit ad Papa. Sed spreta appellatione Hubertus legatinæ & Metropolitanæ sue iurisdictioni adhibens seculari, eum anno & semestri tempore carceribus & vinculis Glocestriæ tenuit. Huberto iam omnes tanquam Regis & Papæ vicario parebant. Itaque nefide erga Regem deesset, nouam iuramenti formam deprinxit, qua in toto Regno peruulgata cunctos astrinxit, vt pacem Regis-toris viribus seruarent. Sub hæc tempora Cambri refertis agminibus erumpuntin Angliam, prædisque ac incendiis agros & oppidula vastant. Hos Hubertus collectis quis celerrime militibus in suas Regiones fugauit & coegit. Tum castellum de Poelobsidione cepit, & instruxit militibus. Ab hac aurem Cambrorum fuga rediens Iohannem
units.tr: 40 In the same year Hubert visited Gloucester. There, in his presence, he deprived Robert, abbot of Tewkesbury, of his dignity. Robert appealed to the Pope. But Hubert spurned the appeal, invoked the secular arm in support of his legatine and metropolitan jurisdiction, and kept him in prison and chains at Gloucester for a year and a half. Now everyone obeyed Hubert as the vicar of both king and Pope. So that he might not be found lacking in loyalty to the king, he devised a new form of oath, which was widely published throughout the kingdom and bound everyone to keep the king's peace with all their strength. About this time the Welsh poured into England in crowded bands and laid waste fields and small towns with plunder and fire. Hubert quickly gathered soldiers, drove them back into their own regions and forced them to stay there. Then he besieged and took the castle of Poel and garrisoned it with soldiers. On his return from this flight of the Welsh,

units.la: 30 de Constantiis Wigorniensem Episcopum electum Stratfordiæ consecrauit. Hubertus totoq; biennio summos tam in Ecclesia quam in Rep. Anglicana gerens magistratus, inuidia iam (quæ secundarum rerum comes est) multorum cœpit flagrare. Ad eam vitandam callide hac dissimulatione Regis de se sensum tentauit. Egit cum Rege nunciis atque literis defessum se iam esse atque imparem tanto oneri ferendo, nec valere regnum simul cum Ecclesia administrare, ideoque se vehementer cupere ut regni negucia alteri delegarentur, vt Ecclesiæ guberatione diligentius possit prospicere. Rex hoc primo tulit grauatè, quia nemo similis eiusregni iure desc̄ndendu& conseruando fuerat, sed tamen precibus tanta ratione nixis Rex concessit, multum laudata illius diligentia & fide in administrando officio, quod corpore debili & valetudinario fuisset. Hubertū iam suus dolus fefellit, qui expectauit vt Rex inuitti cum in regni administratione retineret. Itaq; poenituit cum huius tam facile circumuentus imperatri postulati. Expertus enim est quod in custodiedis illius est tetribuitio multa. Vt igitur quod imprudenter fecerat consultius vitaret, antequam administrationem deponeret, collectis iam suis rationib. quas Regi reddere parauerat, ad Regem scripsit seillo biennio ad opus Regis ex Angliæ regno acquisiuisse vndecies cert. n. millia marcatū. Itaq; ipsa diuturnior sua Regi placere possit, non se laborem recusaturum, seq; curaturum vt ne seneceftus sua quanquam ingrauescens impedimento sibi in huiusmodi negocio fiat. Hubertus etsi prudens atque placabilis, hoc tamen iudicio ambitionem & cupiditatem ostendit suā. Nequeenim nostri fuit instituti in Huberto describendo, virum bonum, sanctum aut Euangelicū, sed prudentem vtilemq; Regi ac Reipublicæ Magistratum proponere. Qui longo maiori vsu & peritia in Aula, foto atque caetera pacis in Ecclesiis fuerit.
units.tr: 30 he consecrated John de Constantiis, the bishop-elect of Worcester, at Stratford. Hubert, holding the highest offices for the whole of these two years both in the Church and in the English commonwealth, now began to be inflamed with the envy (which is the companion of prosperity) of many. To avoid this, he cunningly tested the king's feeling about himself by a pretended show of weariness. He told the king by messengers and letters that he was now worn out and unequal to so great a burden, that he could not manage the kingdom together with the Church, and that he therefore earnestly wished the affairs of the kingdom to be handed over to another, so that he could give closer attention to the government of the Church. At first the king took this badly, since no one of similar right of descent and similar ability to preserve the kingdom existed. Nevertheless, moved by prayers resting on such reasons, the king gave way, greatly praising Hubert's diligence and fidelity in discharging an office he had carried out with a weak and infirm body. Hubert's own cunning now deceived him, for he had expected the king would unwillingly keep him in the administration of the kingdom. He therefore repented of having so readily yielded to this request, for he found that there was much to answer for in keeping that office. So, to avoid more prudently what he had done rashly, before laying down the administration, he gathered the accounts he had prepared to render to the king and wrote to the king that in these two years, for the king's business, he had acquired from the kingdom of England eleven hundred thousand marks. He added that, so that he might please the king more by a longer service, he would not refuse labour, and that he would take care that his old age, though growing heavier, should not become a hindrance to him in such business. Hubert, though prudent and placable, showed his ambition and greed in this judgement. For it was not our purpose in describing Hubert to set forth a good, holy or evangelical man, but a prudent magistrate, useful to the king and the commonwealth, who had far greater experience and skill in the court, in state affairs, and in the other arts of peace in the Churches.

units.la: Id quod ex Giraldi (de qno in Baldwino antea diximus) testimonio satis liquet. Qui cum in eam ante scripsisset acerbius, & tam latinæ linguæ quam lncrarum inscitiam, varias mercaturas, Regiique sigilli cui profuit abulum, liberius merito taxauisset, ea cuncta potius malignitate famæ confida, quam à veritate profecta reuocauit, his verbis.
units.tr: This is sufficiently clear from the testimony of Giraldus (of whom we spoke earlier under Baldwin). He had written more bitterly against Hubert before, and had rightly censured more freely both his ignorance of Latin and of letters, his various trades, and the abuse of the royal seal from which he profited. Later, however, he retracted all these things, trusting rather to the malice of reputation than to what proceeded from the truth, in these words.

units.la: "Vt enim ea quæ de ipso vere dici ac scribi potuerant paucis aperiam. Erat itaque vir ille, "vir animosus ac strenuus, & intet virtutes varias incomparabiliter daplilitate conspicu"us, vnde vt ad animi magnitudinem res illi suppeterent & facultates, fuit in accquiren"do domodis omnibus solicitus nimis & curiosus. Attamen erat hic Principis frenum, & "tyrannidis obstaculum, Populi pax & solacium, maiorum pariter & minorum suis die"bus contra publicæ potestatis oppressiones in necessitate refugium. Hæc ille.
units.tr: "To set out briefly what could truly be said and written about him: he was a man of spirit and energy, and among his various virtues he was incomparably conspicuous for his prudence. Hence, so that the means and resources for his great spirit were available to him, he was too anxious and too curious in acquiring them by all means. Yet he was a curb on the prince and a check on tyranny, a peace and comfort to the people, and an equal refuge for greater and lesser men in their days of need against the oppressions of public power." So far he.

units.la: "Neque enim si verum indicare volumus, in Republica Christiana quicquam sani atque integri seculum illud tulit. Fictaque & adumbrata religionis specie proposita, totus Clerus in sceleribus, muneribus, honoribus & rapinis neglecto penitus verbo impunè volutabat. Huius mali otigo ab hoc profluxit, quod contra Orthodoxorum patrum decreta, Clerus nimium mundanis se negociis immisceuit. Nam & eodem tempore Ecclesiæ Paulinæ London. Decanus æraru Regii custos fuit, siue vt vocant thesauratius. Is cofungens officio ingentem clam thesaurum coacernauit, tandem in lethalem morbum incidit, cumque iam valetudinis nulla spes esset, ab Episcopis & magnatibus admonctur de sumendo corpore Christi, quo audito cohorruit, remque consultò distulit. Quod illi mirari Regem rogant, vt ad sacramenti perceptionem cum compelleret. Accedens Rex cū rogauit, monuit, atq; iussit. Is eid factuum crastino promisit. Interea ad testamentū condendū monitus est. Ad quod paratus, exire præter vnū scriptoræ czeros voluit. Is testamentum scripturus expectans quid Decanus dictaret, ex more testamentorum sic orsus est. In nomine patris, & filii. &c. Quod cum Decanus comperisset, iratus iussit id deleri, & hæc verba tantū scribi. Lego omnia bona mea Domino Regi, corpus sepulturæ, & animam Diabolo. Quod dicto exprauit. Rex cadauer illius iussit cutru exportari atque in amnem proiici & demergi. Cuius generis exemplia idcirco "proferenda sunt, vt deterrentur à vectigalibus Regiis exigendis & ciuibus publicis"què occupationibus Clerus. & Euangelio propagando præcipue studeat ac incum"bat. Huberti autem seculo omnium pene rerum potestas penes clerum fuit. Nec ciuitas solum sed & bellica officia sæpe gerebant. Hinc & illud scitum dictū est, quod cum in bello eum Gallis gesto Richardus Rex Beluacensem Episcopum tanquam exercitus ducem cepisset, cum din compeditum tenuit, ne armis quidem quæ in bello geserat exutum. proquo Papa intercessit, ac mirari se scripsit eum tam durier & acerbe dilectū suum filium Beluacensem Episcopum tractauerit. Richardus ilico detracta Beluacensi Episcopo Lorica, & missa per legatos, interrogauit Papam, nūquid hæc est vestis filii tui?
units.tr: "For, if we wish to speak the truth, that age produced nothing sound or whole in the Christian commonwealth. With a feigned and shadowy show of religion put forward, the whole clergy wallowed with impunity in crimes, bribes, honours and robberies, the Word being utterly neglected. The origin of this evil flowed from this: contrary to the decrees of the orthodox Fathers, the clergy mixed themselves too much in worldly affairs. For at the same time the dean of St Paul's in London was also keeper of the royal treasury, or, as they call it, treasurer. Discharging this office, he secretly heaped up a huge treasure. At last he fell into a deadly sickness, and when there was no hope of recovery, the bishops and great men urged him to receive the body of Christ. On hearing this he shuddered and deliberately put the matter off. The bishops asked the king to compel him to receive the sacrament. The king came, asked, admonished and ordered. He promised to do it the next day. Meanwhile he was urged to make his will. Ready to do so, he wished everyone to leave except one scribe. The scribe, about to write the will and waiting to see what the dean would dictate, began in the customary way of wills: In the name of the Father and of the Son, etc. When the dean found this out, he was angry and ordered it erased, and only these words written: I leave all my goods to my lord the King, my body to burial, and my soul to the Devil. He carried out what he had said. The king ordered his corpse to be put in a chest, carried out, thrown into the river and sunk. Examples of this kind are to be brought forward, so that the clergy may be deterred from collecting the royal revenues and from public occupations, and may chiefly devote their zeal and effort to spreading the Gospel. In Hubert's age the power over almost everything lay in the hands of the clergy. They often performed not only civil but also military duties. Hence also that witty saying: when King Richard, in the war waged against the French, had captured the bishop of Beauvais as leader of the army, he kept him in fetters for a long time, and did not even strip him of the armour he had worn in the war. On this the Pope intervened and wrote that he marvelled that his beloved son, the bishop of Beauvais, had been treated so harshly and bitterly. Richard at once stripped the bishop of Beauvais of his breastplate, sent it by envoys, and asked the Pope: 'Is this the garment of your son?'"

units.la: Atque hoc in loco cutiosis & nimis exquisitis Clerī iam censoribus commodè respondere possumus. Quæ runtur abesse eos à iudicijs consiliisque Regni publicis, tum à negociis manentibusque Reip. abstinere. Olim verò cum Episcopi & viri Ecclesiastici Rempub. capescebant, & Collegia extructa & vberiora ab his mentia in laicos longe quā tam profecta fuisse. Quibus de rebus vt æquiores Cleri iudices esse possint, in eligendum est hæc de quibus nunc tractamus tempora, in Cleri conditione atque statu ab his nostris longe alienâ & diuersa fuisse. Ecclesiastici cum viri administrabant omnia non Ecclesiastica solum sed ciuilia, sæpe etiam ipsa bellica officia. Cum Vrbanus quintus Papa tempore Sim. Langham Cant. Archiepiscopi mandaret, vt de his qui plura Ecclesiastica beneficia contra canonica decreta simul possiderent, inquisitio in Anglia habe得retur, compertum est Clericos fere omnibus curis & tribunalib. Regiis fuisse præfectos, inter
units.tr: And at this point we can fittingly answer the over-curious and overly exacting critics of the clergy. They say that the clergy keep away from the public judgments and councils of the realm, and abstain from affairs of state and the business of the commonwealth. But formerly, when bishops and churchmen took part in government, the colleges they founded and the far richer benefactions they bestowed on laymen were far greater. So that these critics may be fairer judges of the clergy, we must understand that the times we are now discussing were very different from ours, and that the clergy's condition and standing were far removed from our own. Churchmen then administered everything, not only ecclesiastical but civil affairs, and often even military offices. When Pope Urban V, in the time of Simon Langham, Archbishop of Canterbury, ordered an inquiry in England into those who held several ecclesiastical benefices at once contrary to the canonical decrees, it was found that clergymen had been put in charge of nearly all royal offices and courts, among

units.la: {y} Vide Regis Langham. sol. 115. inter quos fecularia Regis munera distributa fuerunt, his Ecclesiastica beneficia, quibus animarum cura annexa non fuit, confertim & cumulatim accessere. Ex quibus cum quidam Cancellarii, quidam iusticiarii, quidam thefaurarii Regni essent, alii in fingulis foris Regiis alia Regis munera negociaque procurarent, percipiebant ex prebendis, dignitatibusq; Ecclesiasticis quibus animarum cura uon imminebat proventus annuos ducentarum, trecentarum, aut quingentarum, sæpe etiam mille librarum. Alii etiam beneficia ipsa curata (vt aiunt) coaceruabant, & sæpissime quinque, decem, viginti, ac nonnunquam plura tenebant. Vt in veteribus monumentis in quibus tam Clericorum quam ipsorum beneficiorum nomina, vnacum eorum locis atque parochiis sigillatim Sed vt cuiuis si libeat, liceat plebeianz ac vulgaris 20 orationis inconstantiam & mutabilitatem admirari. His ipsis præsentis argumenti temporibus extiterunt ex singulis ordinibus nonnulli, qui Clerum tum hoc nomine acerrime taxarunt, quod qui ad illum diuinitatis gradum, quo nihil in humaoa vita sanctius censeri debet, euectiessent, secularibus negociis tanquă seruilibus operis impedirentur, & in pecuniariis ac hiscalibus à suæ vitæ dignitate alienissimis rebus, à diuinis abducti hærerent. Ex quibus quædam (vt ex Decani illius Paulini exemplo patet) conscientiæ atque animæ iacturam naufragiumque passi sunt. Cuius generis exempla etsi repeti ex monumentis multa possent, silentio tamen ne histotiâ multitudine ac prolixitate turbemus, prætereamus. Cuiusdam saltem authoris verba (qui, cum omnium rerum tam ciuilium quàm Ecclesiasticarum potestas penes Clerum erat, scripsit) recennon de panis astimatione quam Assisum vocant, statuta promulgata fuerunt. Nec aliud in eo vitiũ(praeter ea quæ illa tulerat tépora in quibus religionis sensus exinctus fuit, regnabat, quam quæ maxima plerum que occupat ingenia, ambitio, honoris, cupiditas cuius sane studio vt ne populi preconio careret, nihil humile aut minutum cogitas Turrim Londinensem & ingenti inuro, & fossa qua aqua vndique ducereretur cinxit. Dominum Præmonstrentium dictum Derham construxit, Cœnobium Ciccestensis ordinis Wulferhamptoniæ inchoauit, quod morte abductus non absoluit. Archiep. si copatoris autem & magnificis ædificiis decorauit, & multis proventibus ac prædus locupletauit. Præterea amplissimis & securitlimis priuilegiis (quæ pristinis antiquis Anglicanus iuris vocabulis Geld, Dengeld, Hidagium, Pecunia pro murdro, opus pontium, Castelorum, 10 Porcorum, Clausurarum auxilium, Pecunia pro exercitu, Warpon, Bloodwhit, & Childwhit, & Villenagia nuncupantur,) non sinas tantum possessiones & prædia sed & Monachorum firmauit. In familiæ autem copia, & splendore iptos Regios tumptus pene adæquauit. Ad quæ tot tantaque tam publica quam priuata negotia, Ecclesiastica sua munera sufficere haud potuissent nisi & ciuilia adiunxisset. Nactus est præterea ex concessione Regis, impuberum eorumque qui in minori essent curationes ac tutelas. Quos a rerum suarum administratione & aggnatorum hæreditatibus diutius abstinere fecit vt fructus medii in suam commoditatem luctumque cederet. Sed hunc tanta Regis, Papæ, præsulum, magnatum, omniumque ordinum gratia, & fœlicitate fluentem & abundantem soli Cantuarienses Monachi comprehenserunt. 20 Quorum dolus peritissimos, audacia potentissimos superauit. Quod vt intelligatur, ad illam Hackingonensi Ecclesia narrationem in Baldwino commemoratam, & hunc in locum reiectam redeundum nobis est. Hubertus ad Regem in Normanniam profectus est, ibi de Regni negociis sermone secreto habito, & exigui temporis mora ducta redit in Angliam. Post reditū illico ad Cantuarienses Monachos tam Regio quam suo nomine misit Waltamense, Redingen s, & Chertense Abbates. Hi molli sermone tã Regis quã Archiepiscopi in Cantuariensem Ecclesiam merita exponunt, optandum esse aiunt vt Monachi, vtrique suam vicißim obseruantiam ostendant, vnam rem esse eamque facilem in qua de Rege & Archiepiscopo optime mereri simul possint, si Ecclesiam a Baldwino Lamethæ institutam, eiusque morte ac temporum difficultate in- 30 termissam, iam sine controuersia perfici & ad exitum perduci sinant: cupere enim valde tam Regem quam Archiepiscopum s omnibus tam secundis sibi & regno a 'cœlesti numine præsitus) vt aliquod opus insigne atque celebrandum Deo sanctis- que dedicaretur. Hoc acceptonuncio Monachi vix datoresponso(tanquam rerum fortunarumque suarum omnium occasus & interitus imminetet,) ad suriis, illico capitalcs suscipiunt cum Huberto inimicitias, & in coniugiem lissimam appellationem ernpunt. Eamque ad Papam quam celerrime delatam huiusmodi calumniis referrant consereinaruat. Omnium iam ealliditates & in Ecclesiam Cant. iniuirias etiam ipsius Baldwini, huc Huberti conatum anteire. Ciuilibus illis officiis & muneribus a discipliua & cuta Ecclesiæ abduci eum penitus & auocati. Eius rei argumento esse quod con- 40 ira iura Ecclesiastica, & immunitatem Ecclesiæ ciuilia & crimnalia iudicia in Ecclesia Catholica Eboracensi excesserunt, quod Willielmum Longobardum ex arcuato templo vi eximi mandant, cumque capitali sententia damnauit, quod in militia & cafris Duxauthor Christiani sanguinis fundendi sæpe fuerit Non esse sperandum vt is rei Ecclesiassica suprofpiciat, nisi authoritate Papalis se abdicare omnibus ciuilibus Magistratibus compellatur, & Ecclesiastica iurisdictione fungenda septus conclusulq; teneatur. Hacappellatione prouocatus Papa ad Regem & Archiepiscopum sub Anathematis interminatione scripsit, vtram Cancellaria Regia quam criminali capitaliue tribunali moneatur. Tu vt Ecclesia Lamethæ inchoata penitus expensis Archiepiscopi dirurtur, & si qui ibi diuina celebrauerint Clerici, ab officio Clericali suspendantur. Quod Papæ re50 scripto inter decretalia iura retulit Gregorius. Ita Regeo Archiepiscopo inuitis, Archiepiscopus ciuilibus magistratibus exuitur. Sed de Ecclesia Lamethana instabat. Ad Papā veloces ab omnibus ta Rege quæ Episcopis nucii literæque mãdantur, Monachis cõditiones ꝛquissimas offeruntur. Nihil acturum Archiepiscopũ quod Cantuariensi Ecclesiæ præiudicium possit generare. Quorum petitio neque a Monachis accepta, neque a Papa audita fuit. Ditus inuisam hanc Monachis capellam necesse est. Nouum constitutum initum est vt ex huius destructæ Ecclesiæ puluere altera Maidstoniæ suscitaretur: Id etiam a Monachis anteuersum est. Quitanta vehementia & ardore hanc litem persecuti sunt, vt hoc ad suum exitium inceptum opus ita deleretur, vt nullam non modo memoriam, sed ne suspicionem sui relinquere possit. Hubertus (imurid lanimi peneque iniustæ authoritatis vir) Monachorum pressus angustiis cessit. Monachi etsi Romæ tam Regem quam Archiepiscopo potiores fuerant, tamen cesserunt tandem aliquantulū de iure suo. Itaque arbitrario positea his conditionibus concentum est, ut Ecclesia Lamethæ extrueretur, quæ tamen iacemda non erat super fundamenta operis demolati. Eius Ecclesiæ redditus & proventus annuus nō amplius quam centum libratum censeretur, in ea Canonici viginti instituendi. Sed in ea Sacros ordines, Episcoporum consecrationes, Abbatum benedictiones, Chrismatis confectiones Archiepiscopus non celebraret. His itaque tam indignis modis Hubertus a Monachis victus & deiectus est.
units.tr: {y} See Regis, Langham, p. 115. Among them the secular offices of the King were distributed, and to these men ecclesiastical benefices to which no cure of souls was attached came in heaps and piles. Some of them were chancellors, some justices, some treasurers of the realm, and others in the various royal courts managed other royal duties and business. From prebends and ecclesiastical dignities to which no cure of souls was attached, they drew annual incomes of two, three or five hundred pounds, often even a thousand. Others, as they say, piled up benefices with cure of souls, and very often held five, ten or twenty, and sometimes more. As in the old records, where the names of the clergy and of their benefices are listed one by one together with their places and parishes... but let anyone who wishes marvel at the inconsistency and fickleness of common speech. In these very times of our subject there arose from every order some who sharply censured the clergy on this count: that those who had been raised to that degree of divinity, than which nothing in human life should be deemed holier, were hindered by secular business as if by servile labour, and, drawn into monetary and fiscal matters most alien to the dignity of their calling, were kept away from divine things. Some of them, as the example of that Dean Paulinus shows, suffered the wreck and shipwreck of conscience and soul. Although many examples of this kind could be drawn from the records, let us pass them over in silence, lest we clutter the history with their number and length. Let us at least quote the words of one author, who wrote when the power over all affairs, civil as well as ecclesiastical, lay with the clergy, and the statutes promulgated concerning the assessment of bread, which they call the Assize. Nor was there any other fault in him, apart from those that the times had brought, when the sense of religion was extinguished and reigned, than that ambition for honour and desire which most often occupies the greatest minds. Out of zeal for it, lest he lack the praise of the people, he thought nothing humble or small, and he girded the Tower of London with a huge wall and a moat drawn with water on all sides. He built the Premonstratensian priory called Dereham; he began a Cistercian monastery at Wolverhampton, which death, carrying him off, did not let him finish. He adorned the archbishopric with magnificent buildings and enriched it with many revenues and estates. Moreover, by the most ample and secure privileges, which under their old English legal names are called Geld, Dengeld, Hidage, murder-money, bridge-work, castle-work, pig-money, help for enclosures, money for the army, Warpenny, Bloodwite, Childwite and Villenage, he strengthened not only the possessions and estates but also those of the monks. In the number and splendour of his household he nearly matched the royal expenses themselves. For so many and so great affairs, public as well as private, his ecclesiastical offices could not have sufficed unless he had added civil ones. Moreover, by the King's grant he obtained the wardships and guardianships of minors and of those who were under age. He kept them for a long time from managing their own affairs and from the inheritances of their kinsmen, so that the intervening profits went to his own advantage and gain. But this man, flowing and abounding in such great favour and good fortune from the King, the Pope, the prelates, the magnates and all orders, was caught only by the monks of Canterbury. Their craft outdid the most skilful, and their boldness the most powerful. To understand this, we must return to that account of the church of Hackington, recorded under Baldwin and put back here. Hubert went to the King in Normandy, held a private conversation there about the affairs of the realm, and after a short delay returned to England. After his return he at once sent to the Canterbury monks, in the name of both the King and himself, the abbots of Waltham, Reading and Chertsey. In smooth words these men set out the services of both King and Archbishop to the church of Canterbury, and said it was to be wished that the monks in their turn would show their regard. There was one thing, and an easy one, in which they could at once deserve well of both King and Archbishop: if they allowed the church at Lambeth, founded by Baldwin and interrupted by his death and the difficulties of the times, now to be completed without dispute and brought to its end. For both King and Archbishop greatly desired (since heaven had granted them all such prosperity for themselves and the realm) that some notable work be dedicated to God and the saints. On receiving this message, the monks, hardly giving an answer as though the collapse and ruin of all their fortunes were at hand, at once in furious rage took up deadly enmity with Hubert, and broke out into a most sworn appeal. They carried it to the Pope as quickly as possible, stuffed with such calumnies. They claimed that the tricks of all, and the wrongs done to the church of Canterbury even in Baldwin's time, went before Hubert's present attempt. That he had been wholly drawn away from the discipline and care of the Church by those civil offices and duties. The proof of this, they said, was that contrary to ecclesiastical law and the immunity of the Church he held civil and criminal trials in the Catholic church of York; that he ordered William the Lombard to be dragged by force from the vaulted church and condemned him to death; and that in the army and camps he was often the leader and author of shedding Christian blood. It was not to be hoped that he would attend to ecclesiastical affairs unless he were compelled by papal authority to renounce all civil magistracies and be confined to the exercise of ecclesiastical jurisdiction alone. Moved by this appeal, the Pope wrote to the King and the Archbishop, under threat of anathema, that Hubert be warned to give up either the royal chancery or the criminal and capital court. Also, that the church at Lambeth, begun at the Archbishop's expense, be utterly demolished, and that any clergy who had celebrated divine service there be suspended from clerical office. Gregory included this papal rescript among the decretal laws. Thus, though the King and Archbishop were unwilling, the Archbishop was stripped of his civil offices. But the matter of the church at Lambeth pressed on. Swift messengers and letters were sent to the Pope from all, both the King and the bishops; very fair terms were offered to the monks, with the assurance that the Archbishop would do nothing that could prejudice the church of Canterbury. Their petition was neither accepted by the monks nor heard by the Pope. Hence this chapel, hateful to the monks, had to be dealt with. A new arrangement was made that from the rubble of this destroyed church another should be raised at Maidstone; this too was forestalled by the monks. They pursued this quarrel with such vehemence and ardour that the work, begun to their own ruin, was so wiped out that it could leave no memory of itself, not even a suspicion. Hubert, a man of weak spirit and of almost unjust authority, pressed by the monks' distress, gave way. Though the monks at Rome were more powerful than both King and Archbishop, they nonetheless in the end yielded somewhat of their right. So by arbitration terms were agreed on: that the church at Lambeth should be built, though it was not to be laid on the foundations of the demolished work. Its revenue and annual income was not to be assessed at more than a hundred pounds, and twenty canons were to be installed in it. But in it the Archbishop was not to celebrate holy orders, the consecrations of bishops, the blessings of abbots, or the making of chrism. By such unworthy means, then, Hubert was beaten and cast down by the monks.

units.la: Postea Gaufridus filius Petri Filexiæ Comes, funimus iusticiarius Angliæ qui criminalia & capitalia (ut diximus) moderatur iudicia a Rege institutus est. Impetrauit hoc ienopore Hubertus muneris de Lamethā, quod ab Episcopo & Monachis Roff. (vt in Baldwino ante diximus) tertarum permutationem acceperat, sibi & successoribus suis a Richardo Rege confirmari in perpetuum. Eandemque postea confirmationem a Ioanne Rege obtinuit. Hubertus depositio magistratu ciuili, Ecclesiæ curæ totus vacabat. Consecrauitque postea Robertum de Salopesby Episcopum Banchorensem, & Eustachium qui in Cancellarij munere ei successit Eliensem Episcopum Westmonasterii, debita accepta ab utroq; subiectionis professione. Postea q. G. Conuentrensem Cantuariæ similiter professus. Interea inuidus & pius Rex Richardus a Pictauiensibus in Gallia 20 ictus balista, moritur. Et Iohannes frater successit, & ab Huberto diadema suscepit Londini. 10. Kal. Iunii 1199. Sub haec tempora scripsit ad Hubertum Eugenius Papa de decimis (quæ ante ind. stinctæ ex voluntate laicorum quibusius clerici pendebantur) ne fraus vlterius fiat, soli parochio, in cuius parochia prædia possident, integre persoluendis. Quo etiam anno Gulielmus genere Normannus, Ecclesiæ S. Pauli Canonicus Westmonasterii ab Huberto London. Episcopus consecratus est. Hubertus etsi iam tunc publico magistratu essent, tamen ob antecedta in Rep. merita nō minus fuit populo quā ante gratiosus. Sed a Rege alienior, quod illius in fratre & Rep. conatus (ut ante diximus) fortuter prudentereq; fregerat. Sequenti autem anno Iabella, quā Rex Iohannes uxorem duxerat, Reginā Westmonasterii consecrauit, ac paulo post Maugerium Wigorniensem Iohannem 30 Norwicensem, & Ægydium Herefordensem, Episcopos Westmonasterii sacrauit. Eodem etiam anno Iohānes Rex Christi die natalē magno apparatu Guilfordiæ celebrauit multaq; ministris ac militib. suis munera distribuit, & spiendidis indumentis, quib. ab eis dignoscī poterāt, ornauit & quibusdam distinxit. Quod & Hubertus, cuius (ut diximus) familiæ lautitiæ à pari cū Rege contendebat, Cantuariæ fecit. Id Rex in suam contumeliā factū esse putauit. Itaq; inuisum Archiepisc opū atq; suspectū habuit. Sed postea Rex ab itinere borcali q. in Northumbriā suscepératque reuertus, cum Isabella regina venit Cantuariā, ad Hubertum Archiepiscopum, ibi in festo Paschæ diademata regia solenniter gestarunt, quibus Archiepiscopus Hubertus copiosas (ne dicam superfluas) minstrauit expensas. Cum tamen perspexisset quanta fides, & in regiis procurandis negociis industria cum animi magnitudine coniuncta in illo fuerat, tum quanta autoritate cunctis regni ordinibus eminerēt, conciliatum ad se vocauit, & in Normanniam properans custodem regni reliquit. Deinde ad Ecclesiam de Feuersham Rex præsentauit Archidiaconum Wellensem. Sed intercedebant Abbas & Monachi Cœnobii de Feuersham eam Ecclesiam suæ donationis atque collationis esse. Itaq; Monachi manu militari seruata Ecclesiæ custodia Archidiaconum ingressu prohibent, tum appellatione querelam ad Papam deferunt. Rex ad Archiepiscopum scripsit. Is cum Abbate & Monachis vehementer agit vt Regi parerent. Monachi Cantuariensium Monachorum exemplo incitati, eo duriores fuerunt quo magis ab Archiepiscopo rogati fuerunt. Spes illos certis.tenuit, Regē & Archiepisc. Papalib. mandatis in hac causa sibi cessuros.
units.tr: Afterwards Geoffrey, son of Peter Fitz Eve, Earl, was appointed by the King as chief justiciar of England, who (as we said) presides over criminal and capital cases. At this time Hubert obtained from King Richard that the office of Lambeth, which he had received from the Bishop and monks of Rochester in exchange for lands (as we said earlier, in the account of Baldwin), be confirmed to him and his successors in perpetuity. He later obtained the same confirmation from King John. After laying down civil office, Hubert devoted himself wholly to the care of the Church. He afterwards consecrated Robert de Salopesby as Bishop of Bangor, and Eustace, who succeeded him in the office of Chancellor, as Bishop of Ely at Westminster, each having made the due profession of obedience. Afterwards G., Bishop of Coventry, likewise made his profession at Canterbury. Meanwhile the much-envied and pious King Richard was struck by a crossbow bolt by the men of Poitou in France, and died. His brother John succeeded him and received the crown from Hubert at London on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, 1199. Around this time Pope Eugenius wrote to Hubert concerning tithes, which had formerly been paid, without distinction and at the will of laymen, to whichever clergy they chose; so that fraud might not occur further, they were to be paid in full solely to the parish priest in whose parish the estates lie. In the same year William, a Norman by birth and canon of St Paul's, was consecrated at Westminster by Hubert as Bishop of London. Although Hubert had by then laid down public office, he was no less popular with the people than before, on account of his earlier services to the commonwealth. But he was more estranged from the King, because he had bravely and prudently thwarted the King's attempts against his brother and the realm (as we said above). In the following year he crowned Isabella, whom King John had married, as Queen at Westminster; shortly afterwards he consecrated Mauger as Bishop of Worcester, John as Bishop of Norwich, and Giles as Bishop of Hereford, at Westminster. In the same year King John celebrated Christmas at Guildford with great display, distributed many gifts to his officers and soldiers, and adorned some of them with splendid robes by which they could be recognised, and distinguished others with honours. Hubert did the same at Canterbury, for, as we said, his household vied in magnificence with the King's. The King thought this was done as an insult to himself, and so he regarded the Archbishop as hateful and suspect. Afterwards, however, the King returned from his northern journey into Northumbria and came with Queen Isabella to Archbishop Hubert at Canterbury, where at Easter they solemnly wore the royal crowns; Archbishop Hubert provided lavish (not to say superfluous) expenses for this. Yet when the King had seen how great was the faithfulness and diligence Hubert showed in managing royal business, joined with greatness of spirit, and how much authority he held above all the orders of the realm, he summoned the council to meet him, and, hastening into Normandy, left Hubert as guardian of the realm. Then the King presented the Archdeacon of Wells to the church of Faversham. But the Abbot and monks of the monastery of Faversham intervened, claiming that the church was of their gift and conferment. So the monks, keeping guard over the church with armed force, forbade the Archdeacon entry, and then by appeal brought their complaint to the Pope. The King wrote to the Archbishop, and he strongly urged the Abbot and monks to obey the King. The monks, spurred on by the example of the monks of Canterbury, became the more stubborn the more the Archbishop begged them. Hope held them that, by papal mandates in this cause, the King and the Archbishop would yield to them.

units.la: Rex incensus mandat Monachos ē templo flammis exigi. Sed postea mitigato hoc præcepto iussit eos à Vicecomite Cantii manu militari vi abstrahi. Is iussum Regis peregit, & armato milite complet Ecclesiam. Archidiaconus etiam Cantuariensis Monachos vi tenentes Ecclesiam excommunicauit, arafaque tanquam hac vi exsecratas diruit, Ecclesiam diuinis vsibus interdixit. Iterum ad Papam Monachi appellant.
units.tr: The King, inflamed with anger, ordered the monks to be driven out of the church with fire. But afterwards, this command having been softened, he ordered the Sheriff of Kent to drag them out forcibly with armed men. The Sheriff carried out the King's order and filled the church with armed soldiers. The Archdeacon of Canterbury also excommunicated the monks who held the church by force, pulled down the altars as if they had been defiled by this violence, and forbade the church to be used for divine services. Again the monks appealed to the Pope.

units.la: Quo audito Hubertus ita perterritus est, ne rei euentus in se recideret vt Regem obnixe rogaret, ne cum Monachis amplius contenderet, vtque omnia obliuia restituerat; quod Rex Huberti suasu concessit. Tum Archidiaconus sua decreta laxauit, & reuocauit. Ita Monachi omnium pene iurisdictione, legeque soluti animos extulerunt. Huberus postquam vndecim annis vixit mensibus sedisset, cum Roffam ad conciliandos cum Episcopo Monachos proficisceretur, gemina febri percitus est, diuertitque ad Manerium de Tenham, ibi aeger quatriduo animam efflauit. Sed corpus eius gritudo, nec animi pietatem, nec memoriam labefactauit. Cuius rei fuit indicium in summa aegritudine, de bonis suis legitimam pietatis testatione. Motte tamen eius nuncia ta, Rex Guifus, arrepto Cantuariam itinere, in hac ciuitate eius innuit, bonaque omnia cepit: Summinquit, nunc tandem Rex Angliae. Cadauereius Cantuariam traductum, & in Choripariete ad Austrum politia conditum est Anno 1105. Id. Iulij.
units.tr: On hearing this, Hubert was so frightened that the outcome of the affair might fall back upon himself that he earnestly begged the King not to contend any further with the monks, and that everything be restored to oblivion; the King granted this at Hubert's urging. Then the Archdeacon relaxed and revoked his decrees. So the monks, released from almost all jurisdiction and law, grew proud. Hubert, after he had held the see for eleven years and some months, set out for Rochester to reconcile the monks with the Bishop, when he was seized by a double fever. He turned aside to the manor of Teynham, where, sick, he breathed his last after four days. But the sickness of his body did not weaken the piety of his mind or his memory. Evidence of this was that, in his extreme sickness, he made a lawful testament of his goods, a witness of his piety. Yet as soon as news of his death was announced, King John, taking the road to Canterbury, seized all his goods in that city, saying: "Now at last I am King of England." His body was carried to Canterbury and laid in a polished tomb in the south wall of the choir, in the year 1205, on the Ides of July.

units.la: XLIII. Stephanus Langton.
units.tr: XLIII. Stephen Langton.

units.la: Ontificiam potentiam & donationem superbam atque fastidiosam nulla ratione se Regibus extulisse magis, quam Monachorum insolenti pertinacia ex hac historia verissime constabit. Nam Huberto mortuo Cantuariensis Monachi Regis naldum quendam suum Subpriorem Archiepiscopum media nocte elegerunt, veriti ne sua contumacia, quam ipsorum perturbaret, coerceretur a potestate regia. Itaque Rege inconsulto huic suum electum intronizari, & cum literis expeditum miserunt ad Papam, iuramento prius praestito se hanc electionem nulli pareficuturum, aut se palam pro electo gestuum sine Monachorum licentia. Sed ille simulatque tuetraiecisset, & venisset in Flandriam, elatus gloria, quodq; suae electionis famam ante suum adventum Romam perferri voluit; id suae cautae multum exstitimans profuturum Monachorum litteris: Tolaris & ostensis hoc promulgauit. Monachi tandem ... nec ita pro mortuo elegerunt.
units.tr: That the papal power and its proud and overbearing grants could raise themselves above kings in no way more than through the insolent obstinacy of the monks will be clearly established from this history. For when Hubert had died, the monks of Canterbury secretly elected at midnight a certain Reginald, their subprior, as archbishop, fearing that their own stubbornness, which he had disturbed, would be restrained by royal power. So, without the king's knowledge, they had their chosen man enthroned and sent him off to the Pope with letters. First, however, they swore an oath that they would not submit this election to anyone else, nor openly act on behalf of the man chosen without the monks' permission. But as soon as he had crossed the sea and come into Flanders, he was elated by glory and wanted news of his election to reach Rome before his own arrival. He thought this would greatly help his cause through the monks' letters, so he made it public by showing them. The monks at last ... and so they did not elect him as one already dead.

units.la: Matth. Paris. Chron. maj. ... Stephanus Langton. Archiepiscopus.
units.tr: Matth. Paris. Chron. maj. ... Stephen Langton, Archbishop.

units.la: aliorum suffragia non videntur nobis necessaria, in virtute obedientiæ & sub Anathematis pœna præcipimus, vt illum eligatis quem nobis damus vobis in pastorem animarum vestrarum. Monachi perplexi, & Regi ne an Papæ obtemperaret hæsitantes, magis tamen Papalem quam Regium iram ac iniuriam expauescentes, Stephano Langton coacti & inuiti cum tacito fremitu, murmureque consensum præbuerunt. Solus Helias quidam de Brantefeld Monachus (qui Regis & Iohannis Gray electi causam summa fide atque opera procurauit) assensus non est, Qui Papæ metuës iniurias, Romam clam & celeriter decessit in Angliam. reliqui Romæ præsentes Monachi psallentes TE DEVM Stephanum electum possessionis loco ad altare duxerunt. Qui postea 15. Cal. Iulii Viterbii ab ipso Papa consecrationem accepit. Deinde Monachis Cantuar. in Angliam dimissis, quibus omnem Papalem benignitatem Papa promisit, quòd Stephanum ereaturam suam elegissent, vt Iohannem Regem nutigaret, ipsorum Monachorum rogatu scripsit literas plenissimas flagitiosæ ac astutæ assentationis arq; blanditiæ. Quibus rogauit Regè vt Stephanû Lögton virum facûdia, doctrina, vitæque bonitare nemini secundum iam electum & consecratum, virtute & authoritate sua regia in Cantuariësem Archiepiscopatum acciperet. Sed Rex his Pontificiis dolis, iustoque dolore turbarus atq; percitus, Monachos qui Romæ essent & hanc in suum contemptum atque præiudicium electionem celebrauerant, lxsæ maiestatis reos publicauit, cæteros qui Cantuariæ in Monasterio latuissent, proscripsit, & tam suis elaustris quam Regni finibus in exilium eiecit, omnia tam Archiepiscopatus quam Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis bona atque prædia sisco & ztario suo adiudicauit. Stephano Langton ingressum in Angliam sub lxsæ maiestatis pœna interdixit. Hic motus a Papa, Stephano, & Monachis Cant. concitatus tantas inuexit in Angliæ Regi atque regno contumelias atque strages, quantas ab hostili inuasione vix vnquam accepisse videatur. Stephanus Langton si hæc Pontificia fraus & calliditas ab fuisset, ne indignus quidem Archiepiscopali Celsitudine existimari à quopiam rite potuit. Erat enim tam corporis quam animi atque morum constitutione & dignitate, omnisque doctrinæ ac humanæ institutionis præsidio administrandæ Ecclesiæ iuxta illa tempora ita compositus, vt omnium iudicio Anglicanæ regendæ Ecclesiæ aptissimus iudicaretur. Nam Parisiis educatus sub optimis Magistris fuit, Regiqué Franciæ ac proceribus familiaris & acceptus, Academiæ Parisiensis Cancellarius constitutus est. Deinde à Papa qui se iure posse id affirmar, quod dolo sæpissime fecit(quorumque hæreditates atque regna a iustis dominis transferre ad alienos) æcitus Romam & S. Chrysogoni Cardinalis creatus est Itaque Rex hunc quem elegerunt Monachi patriam deserentem, Parisiis instructum, Regi & magnaribus Galliæ familiarem, inde a Papa ad Romanum gerendum Cardinalatum, non minus Regni atque fui inimicum publicum iudicauit, quàm Papam atque Monachos, qui hunc se infeio(ersi contradicere secretè electioni potuisset, & inuito in sui atque regni lcsionem eligi curauissent. Atque illius Subpriorisi tam astute & clanculum electi querela renouata Regi est, vt nihil à Monachis amplius quâ simulatas atq; fraus speranda aut expectâda fit. Ad extremù suptus regi, regnique thefanri ad confirmationem Iohannis Gray a Monachis in Papam & illum sordidû Cardinalium cœtum (è quibus ipse Stephanus vnus erat) profusi atque consumpti satis argumento esse Regi omnibusque potuit, quam exigua fides versutiæ Monachali, atque deuotio Romanæ auaritiæ cupiditatique adhibenda sit. Itaque eiectis Monachis cum quibus sibi Regnoq; suo commercium deinceps esse noluit, ad Papam, cuius è re gesta, literisque sermonem blandum summæ fraudi adhibitû perspexisset, cum comminatione & exprobratione rescripsit, non posse se tam in singulas sedeiniuriani pati, quæ permulti ab Angliæ regibus assecta beneficiis tam indecenter se iam gesserit, vt mala pro bonis reddidisset. Papa qui cœsurarum suarum fulmine totius Angliam terruisset, Regisque res in Normania & transmarinis prouinciis aliquantulum labefactari senserat, hunc Stephanum ex ordine Cardinalium Romanæ sedi contra suam patriam addistum & conserderatum(vt ipse putabat)nactus accingit se iam ad inferendum huic regno vulnus illud, quo etsi diu saucium sanari non poterat, tandem tamen ipso Papismo veluti totius mali morbo abiesto & ꝓ stossigaro, diuinas vires tanquam valetudinem pristinam recuperauit. Interea dum de his motibus elam a Papa consilium capitur, in Angliam venit Iohannes quidam Florentinus cum Papali legatione huc missus, humilis quidem duobus tantum equis, tertioque claudo sine equite sed duũtore, ac tribus famulis Regnum intrauit, sed totam perlustrans regionem, congessit grandem & copiosam pecuniam. Deindeue coaceruandis tantum copiis, non dandis huic regno sanis conciliis operam dedisse videretur, Cleri concilium Radingham eouocauit, quo congregato & aliquandiu celebrato (onustis illis suis sarcinulis secure cauteq; disposuit) festinans repente ad mare propetat, & transuectus Angliam salutauit a tergo. Misit etiam eodem tempore ad perturbandum Reip. Anglicæ iam vacillantis statum a Papa Innocentio inauditæ fraudis & malitiæ homines qui Minores fratres vel prædicatores dicebantur, Hi sub extetna & adumbrata humilitatis specie hypocrisin summam occultabant, victutenues, & vestitu non obstinted humiles fuerunt. Pedibus nudis, grisei tunicis, funiculis nodosis cinti incedebant. Diebus festis populo semper prædicabant, quod quia ab Episcopis Monachatu, & reliquo tuin clero factitatum non erat, odium summum ab eis creatum illis fuit. Exortique sunt alii qui hanc fidem & vitæ sine necessitate suscepta egestate damnabat, neq; ex Christi aut Apostolorum & dilecipulorum exemplo, quos mandata ipsa prælii inopia, sed ex proprii sensus vanitate instituta docebant. Verum bi fratres vulgari atque popolari aura tantopere florebant, ut breui acquisitis facultatibus, etiam ex profesto nihil sui possidere statuebant, quasi nihil habentes omnia possidebant, & ædificia splendida, quæ fraternitates vocabant, extruebant, vicinaque his adiecta prædia comparabant. Historia tellus Anglicæ referta subito & repleta est, & non modo vrbes atque ciuitates sed ipsi vicus & pagi frequentari. Horum prædicatio cum hypocrisi coniuncta concitauit Papæ, à cuius dolo fraudeq; meditara profecti sunt, magnam Anglorum bencuolentiā. Vt ex hac improba caterua coniunctis & concilatis sibi subditis, liberius audaciusque in Regem id moliri & perficere posset, quod in Angliæ Regem regnumq; se facturum cum Cardinalibus deereuiffet. Hoc enim astu collecta populi beneuolentia scripsit ad Regem Papa, vt omnia sua tam in Cantuariensis Monachos quam in Stephanum Langton acta, gesta, seu decreta rescinderet, eosque suo in omnibus iuri fine damno aut amissione quacunq; restitueret. Mandat negocium Willielmo Londinensi, Eustachio Eleusini & Maugero Wigorniensi Episcopis, vt si suasionibus adducere Regem ad ea quæ Papa imperauit non posset, totum Angliæ regnum Ecclesiastico interdicto supponerent. Qui Papæ in omnibus etiam contra Regem atque suum patriam obsecuti, cum Regem in eo quod statuerat fortiter stantem auertere, uec minis nec blanditiis Pontificiis a sententia potuissent, ex Papæ mandato interdicti censuram per totum regnum denunciarunt, eaque denunciata mox cum lofelino Bathoniensi, & Ægidio Herefordensi Episcopis à regia vindicta se fuga tuebantur. Omnis iam diuinorum celebratio in Ecclesiis vbique esse cessauit, paruulorum baptismate, & auricularis confessione, & Eucharistiæ communicatione è vita migrantibus solummodo retentis. Quod ex callida indulgetia Papæ concessum est, vt abalienatis à Rege, sibi& conciliatis regni subditis tam regnum quam Regem sibi subiiceret. Quo etiam consilio Stephanus Langton paulo post impertrauit, vt iis Ecclesiis saltem conuentualibus septimanatim liceret diuina celebrare. Rex Ecclesiarum omnium prouentus edicto in fiscum distringit. Monachorum, fratrum & sacerdotum impura & infinita turba regno auolant. Tumultuari populus & magnates non modo deficere, sed resistere coeperunt his quæ legitime Rex imperitauit. Itaque metuens ne Papa subditos suos a parendi necessitate, & magnates à iurisdictione religione absoluetet, eos quos suspectos habebat pecunia, libertatibus & possessionibus multauit, vel obsidibus datis coercuit, & in officio continuit. Eorum Episcoporum consanguineos & familiares (qui Papale interdictum promulgarunt) bonis summa securitate & æquitate ductus priuauit, quia regni hostes & profugos ex reliquis sibi facultatibus in transmarinis regionibus lautius exhibuissent, qui omnibus affluentes deliciis, cum Lupum viderunt venientem, diuinorum oues, & fugerunt, splendidecq; quoridie ac bilariter conuiuati sunt. In hoc tanto motu ductus est ad Regem homicida quidam, qui sacerdotem in via publica trucidasset, quem Rex impune absolui & dimitti iussit quod inimicum suum interfecisset. Papa cum Iohannem regio pectore tam firmiter in sententia iudicatoq; perseuerasse intellexerat, cum prius iniquo illo interdicto suo contra ipsa sua pontificia iura alto totam Anglorum gentem ob vnius tantum culpam (si modo regalis in iure suo tuendo cōstantia culpa dicenda) sit biennio toto afflixisset, actioni censura Regem ipsum solum ferire statuit. Itaq; Papalis excommunicationis fulmina in eum nominatim cum Cardinalium consilio iaculatus est. Eam sententiam Londinensi, Elienfi, & Wigorniensi Episcopis, qui post interdicti publicationem aufugerunt, iamq; laute & delicate in exteris nationibus vixerunt, in omnibus Angliæ Ecclesiis proponendam committit. Illi à tam suaui molliq; ocio ad periculosum negocii auellinc papali præcepto potuerit. Sed his quæ in Anglia manserunt Episcopis atq; prælatis, impositu sibi onus delegarūt. Qui regē timentes obedire domino suo Papæ non audent, vt à Monachis his verbis taxentur. Effecti sunt vniuersi metu Regio vel fauore canes multi, non audentes latrare. Verumtamen ex more atque dolo Pontificio illius excommunicationis literæ per plateas & vias publicas per totum regnum dissipatæ ad singulorum notitiam peruenerunt, multoq; secreto murmure omnium occupauit ora atque colloquia. Inter quos eum ad fidcum Regium Gaufridus Noruicensis Archidiaconus negociis regiis intendens sedisset, cepit assidentibus exponere excommunicationis sententiam in Regem iam latam, affirmauitque non effectuum Capellanis, & Ecclesiasticis dignitatibus, beneficiisque affectis seruireRegi amplius. Ideoque aulam deferens, ad Ecclesiastica beneficia quæ Regis seruitio acquisierat, secessit. Rex huncta pro-
units.tr: We do not think the votes of others are necessary. In the virtue of obedience, and under pain of anathema, we command you to elect the man we give you as minister of your souls. The monks, perplexed and unsure whether to obey the King or the Pope, but fearing the Papal wrath and injury more than the royal, were compelled and unwilling; with silent grumbling and murmuring, they gave their consent to Stephen Langton. Only one monk, Elias of Brantefield, who had promoted the cause of the King and of John Gray the elect with the utmost loyalty and effort, did not assent. Fearing the Pope's injuries, he quickly and secretly left Rome for England. The rest of the monks present at Rome, singing the Te Deum, led the elect Stephen to the altar as a sign of taking possession. He afterwards received consecration from the Pope himself at Viterbo, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July. Then the Canterbury monks were sent back to England, to whom the Pope promised every papal kindness because they had chosen Stephen, his own creature, to thwart King John. At the monks' own request, he wrote letters full of shameful and crafty flattery and blandishment, in which he asked the King to receive Stephen Langton, a man second to none in eloquence, learning and goodness of life, already elected and consecrated, into the archbishopric of Canterbury by his royal virtue and authority. But the King, disturbed and roused by these Papist tricks and by just grief, declared guilty of treason the monks who were at Rome and had celebrated this election to his contempt and prejudice. He proscribed the others who had lain hidden in the monastery at Canterbury, and drove them into exile both from their cloisters and from the borders of the kingdom. He adjudged all the goods and estates of the archbishopric, as well as of the Church of Canterbury, to his fisc and treasury. He forbade Stephen Langton to enter England on pain of treason. Stirred up by the Pope, Stephen and the Canterbury monks, this man (the Pope) inflicted on the King and kingdom of England such insults and ruin as England seems hardly ever to have suffered from a hostile invasion. Had this Papal fraud and cunning been absent, no one could rightly have thought Stephen Langton unworthy even of archiepiscopal dignity. For he was so formed, in body, mind, character and standing, and so equipped with all the resources of learning and human training for governing the Church in those times, that by the judgement of all he was considered the most fit man to govern the English Church. For he was educated at Paris under the best masters, was familiar and welcome to the King of France and his nobles, and was made Chancellor of the University of Paris. Then he was summoned to Rome by the Pope, who claimed the right to do what he very often did by fraud, namely transfer inheritances and kingdoms from their rightful lords to strangers, and was created Cardinal of St Chrysogonus. Therefore the King judged this man, whom the monks had chosen, to be as much a public enemy of the kingdom and of himself as the Pope and the monks. He had deserted his country, been trained at Paris, was familiar with the King and the great men of France, and was then made a Cardinal at Rome by the Pope. The monks could have secretly opposed the election without his knowledge, yet they had him chosen against his will, to the injury of himself and the kingdom. And the complaint about the election of that sub-prior, made so craftily and secretly, was renewed to the King, so that nothing but pretence and fraud was to be hoped for or expected from the monks.
