Finally, the King's money and the treasure of the kingdom, poured out and squandered by the monks on the Pope and that filthy college of Cardinals (of which Stephen himself was one) to secure the confirmation of John Gray, could be proof enough to the King and to everyone how little trust is to be placed in monkish cunning, and how much devotion is to be given to Roman greed and avarice. So, with the monks expelled, and with them no longer willing to have any dealings with himself or his kingdom, the King wrote back to the Pope. He had seen that the Pope's letters used a bland style as a cover for the greatest fraud. His reply was full of threats and reproaches: he could not suffer such an injury to his realm, since a man who had received many benefits from the kings of England had now behaved so shamefully that he had returned evil for good. The Pope, who had terrified all England with the thunderbolts of his censures, and who had sensed that the King's affairs in Normandy and the overseas provinces were somewhat weakened, got hold of this Stephen from among the Cardinals, who were devoted to the Roman see against their own country, as he himself thought. Now he prepares to inflict on this kingdom that wound which, though it could not be healed while it had long been open, was at last recovered, when Popery itself, as the disease of all evil, was cast off and thrown away, and the kingdom regained its divine strength like its former health. Meanwhile, while the Pope was taking counsel about these movements, a certain John of Florence came into England, sent here with a papal legation. He was indeed humble, with only two horses, a third lame one without a rider but carrying baggage, and three servants. He entered the kingdom, but while travelling through the whole region he amassed a great and abundant sum of money. Then, as though he had devoted his efforts only to piling up resources and not to giving sound counsel to this kingdom, he summoned a council of the clergy at Reading. When it had met and been held for some time, having arranged his little bundles securely and carefully, he suddenly hurried to the sea, crossed over, and bade England farewell from behind. At the same time, to disturb the already tottering state of the English commonwealth, Pope Innocent also sent men of unheard-of fraud and malice, who were called Minor Friars or Preachers. Under an outward and feigned appearance of humility they concealed the greatest hypocrisy; they lived on slender fare and were humble in dress without display. They walked barefoot, in grey tunics, girt with knotted cords. On feast days they always preached to the people. Because the bishops, the monks and the rest of the clergy did not practise this, the greatest hatred was stirred up against them. Others arose who condemned this faith and this poverty undertaken without necessity, and who taught that these practices did not come from the example of Christ, the Apostles and the disciples, but were devised from the vanity of their own opinion. But these friars flourished so greatly in popular and common favour that, having soon acquired wealth, they resolved to possess nothing of their own, as though having nothing they possessed all things. They built splendid buildings, which they called friaries, and bought up the estates adjoining them. The land of England was suddenly filled and crowded with them, and not only cities and towns but even villages and hamlets were frequented by them. Their preaching, joined with hypocrisy, stirred up great goodwill among the English for the Pope, who had sent them out from his guile and fraud. So that, with his subjects united and won to himself from this wicked band, he might more freely and boldly carry out against the King of England and his kingdom what he had decided with the Cardinals to do. For by this stratagem, having gathered popular goodwill, the Pope wrote to the King that he should rescind all his acts, deeds and decrees, both against the Canterbury monks and against Stephen Langton, and restore them to their rights in all things, without loss or forfeiture of any kind. He committed the business to William of London, Eustace of Ely and Mauger of Worcester, bishops, with orders that if they could not by persuasion bring the King to what the Pope commanded, they should place the whole kingdom of England under ecclesiastical interdict. They, obedient to the Pope in everything, even against the King and their own country, could not turn the King from his purpose, for he stood firmly by what he had decided, whether by threats or Papal flatteries. So, by the Pope's command, they proclaimed the censure of interdict throughout the kingdom. Once it was proclaimed, they soon sheltered themselves in flight from royal vengeance, together with Jocelin of Bath and Giles of Hereford. All celebration of divine services in churches everywhere now ceased, only baptism of infants, auricular confession, and communion for those departing this life being retained. This was conceded by the Pope's crafty indulgence, so that by winning the subjects of the kingdom, now estranged from the King, to himself, he might subject both kingdom and King to his own rule. By this same counsel, shortly afterwards, Stephen Langton obtained that in those churches, at least the conventual ones, divine services might be celebrated weekly. The King, by edict, seized the revenues of all churches into the treasury. A foul and endless crowd of monks, friars and priests fled out of the kingdom. The people and the great men began not only to fail in obedience to what the King had lawfully commanded, but to resist it, and they began to murmur tumultuously. So, fearing that the Pope would absolve his subjects from the necessity of obeying, and the great men from their allegiance on grounds of religion, the King punished those he held suspect with fines, loss of liberties and estates, or restrained them by taking hostages and kept them in their duty. Led by the utmost security and fairness, he deprived of their goods the kinsmen and household of those bishops who had published the papal interdict, because these had been lavishly supporting the enemies and fugitives of the kingdom in foreign lands out of their remaining means. These men, abounding in every luxury, when they saw the wolf coming, fled like sheep of the divine flock, and every day they dined splendidly and cheerfully. In the midst of this great commotion, a certain murderer was brought before the King, who had slain a priest on the public highway. The King ordered him absolved and dismissed with impunity, because he had killed his enemy. When the Pope learned that John had persevered so firmly in his royal resolve and in the judgement he had given, he resolved to strike the King alone with censure. Earlier, with that unjust interdict of his, contrary to the Pope's own pontifical rights, he had afflicted the whole English nation for two full years for the fault of one man alone (if indeed the constancy of a king in defending his right is to be called a fault). So he hurled the thunderbolts of papal excommunication against the King by name, with the advice of the Cardinals. He committed the publication of this sentence in all the churches of England to the bishops of London, Ely and Worcester, who had fled after the interdict was published and were now living sumptuously and luxuriously in foreign nations. They could not be dragged from so pleasant and soft a leisure to this dangerous business except by papal command. But they delegated the burden laid on them to the bishops and prelates who had remained in England. These, fearing the King, did not dare to obey their lord the Pope, so that the monks rebuked them in these words: "Through fear of the King, or through favour, many have become dogs, not daring to bark." Nevertheless, in the customary Pontifical manner and by guile, the letters of that excommunication were scattered through the squares and public roads throughout the kingdom and came to everyone's notice, and with much secret murmuring they occupied the mouths and conversations of all. Among them, when Geoffrey, Archdeacon of Norwich, who was attending to the King's business, had sat down beside the royal exchequer, he began to explain to those sitting by him the sentence of excommunication now pronounced against the King. He affirmed that chaplains and those holding ecclesiastical dignities and benefices should no longer serve the King. So, leaving the court, he withdrew to the ecclesiastical benefices he had acquired through the King's service. The King had this man, who had deserted him treacherously, seized by William Talbot, a knight, and brought back to him. He kept him in public custody until, wearied either by his punishment or by his conscience, he came to the end of his life and died.

units.la: ditorié à se deficientem per Willielmum Talbot militem prehendi & ad se reduci fecit, eumque in publica custodia seruatum, donec siue pœnæ, siue conscientiæ tædio perixsus vitæ fuit, & exspirauit, desinuit. Interea Iohannes Rex ne his Papalibus perterrefactus diris, Regia multa exantlauit, Wallos & Hybernos subiugauit, Scotos suis conditionibus ad concordiam redegit, Clericos Romanos exterminauit, ne Romæ aut extra Regnum causæ quæcunque tractarentur, edixit. Rebellesin regno compescuit, Orhoni Imaperatori consanguineo suo grandem ex Anglia pecuniam conflauit, mutuoq; dedit, nec Papam, nec Stephanum, nec illius sectæ quæcunque formidauit. Cuius rei certissimum est argumentum, quod cum Hugo Lincolniensis Episcopus ex Regia licentia ele&us, Regiqué pollicitus esset se ad Rhotomagensem Archiepiscopum profecturum ad sacrationem obtinendam, isque more Pontificio callide ad Stephanum Langton confugisset, factaqi ei subiectionis cum iuramento professione ab eo sacrationem accepisset, eum vt proditorem merito proscripsit, & Episcopatus Lincoln. bona suo fisco detulit. Papa non minus in Angliæ Regem quam in ipsum Imperatorem Othonem elatus, eum etiam singulari excommunicatione ferit, vtrisq; sane(vt ea fuerunt tempora) gladio Papali nec diuina nec humana acie prædito percussi, attonitimagis & stupefacti quam vulnerati fuerunt. Vulnus.n.illehebes Papalis gladius infligere nö potuit, probatis sed imperitis, nec sensuacri pditis stuporé intulit. In quo tamé vt diximus inuictam Regiamq; animi magnitudinem lohannes declarauit, quod nunquam defecit antequam Stephano Langton cum illis profugis Episcopis Papam solicitantibus, Papa inauditam à seculis rulit de Rege regno abdicando sententiam. Cuius impii decreti executionem Philippo Francorum Regi(Iohanni totiq; Angliæ regno inimicissimo) in remissionem omnium anteactorum suorum scelerum atque criminum commisit ac mandauit. Pandulphus Cardinalis Legatus Papæ, vir ex illa Pontificia institutione satis callidus & versutus, hoc negocium ex Papæ & Cardinalium sententia tractauit commodè. Legatione & procuratione Papali primò Gallie Regem Philippum instigauit ad arma. Quem cum non modo propensum sed paratum & incitatum ad bellum pro regno acquirendo genium admaduerteret, astu paulatim sedauit. Nolle se dixit, neque ipsum Papam velle in Angliæ Regem hostilia denunciari, antequam in eo desperatio quædam totiusq; volutaris à Romana sede abalienatio cerneretur. Hoe plane præsighioso Pandulphi consilio Gallie Rex ab armis contra Iohannem suscipiendis continebatur. Interea Iohannes ad bellum, quod satis feliciter administrauit, sirpe contra hos hostes quorum coniurationem acceperat, se accinxit, nauem & exercitum copiosé parauit ac instruxit, ipseq; lacessere suum hostem maluit, quam ab eo prouocari. Itaque classem & exercitum eduxit in Galliam, & cum classe fuisset in Oceano, Stephanus Langton cum suis sece profugis & exulibus rediit in Angliam, ac Papalem sententiam, qua Rex amotus regno fuit, promulgauit. Rex tam domi quam foris inter hostes vndique intentis, subditorum fide Pontificia inperfitione sibi detracta, regnoque per proditores occupato, ad Papales conditiones per Pandulphum coactus non sine magno discrimine fuit. Alioquin ne coniunctis vnà Papæ atque Regis Gallie copiis superari potuit. Pandulphus, cum Gallie Rex exercitum atque classem 50 traduceret, misit ad Regem Iohannem Legatos qui eum de tanto periculo imminente admonerent, eiusq; vitationem ex Pandulphi consilio habendam docerent. Nihil autRegem magis ad tam turpes Papales conditiones adegit, quam quod ne à magnatibus populoq; suo desereretur, pertimuit. Itaq; Pandulphi aduentum per eosdem legatos optauit. Is tam atrox instanti, periculum omni oratione exaggerauit, vitariq; vno tátum modo posse docuit. Si Papæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ se submittens reciperet ab eo regnū vellet à quo priuatus est, qui eodem spiritu sorbere ac flare, soluere ac ligare poterit. Rex his quasi copeditus difficultatib. Pandulphe assensus, regna sua Papæ resignauit, ab eoq; eadem recepit, pollicita & ei scriptis confirmata annua mille marcarû pensione. Deinde Rex absolutus, interdictu relaxatu, exules reuocati, Ecclesiisq; ablata restituta sunt.
units.tr: ...deserting him, was seized by Sir William Talbot and brought back to him. He was kept in public custody until, worn down by either the punishment or the torment of conscience, he lost his life and breathed his last. Meanwhile King John, not terrified by these papal curses, accomplished many royal feats. He subdued the Welsh and the Irish, brought the Scots to agreement on his own terms, and drove out the Roman clergy, ordering that no causes be tried at Rome or outside the realm. He suppressed rebels within the kingdom and lent a large sum of money from England to his kinsman, the Emperor Otto. He feared neither the Pope, nor Stephen, nor any of that faction. The clearest proof of this is that when Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln, was elected with the king's licence and had promised him that he would go to the Archbishop of Rouen to obtain consecration, he instead, in the papal manner, craftily fled to Stephen Langton. After making a profession of subjection with an oath, he received consecration from him. The king therefore rightly proscribed him as a traitor and transferred the goods of the see of Lincoln to his own treasury. The Pope, no less elated against the King of England than against the Emperor Otto himself, struck the king with a special excommunication. Both of them, to be sure (such were the times), were struck by a papal sword endowed with neither divine nor human edge, and they were more astonished and stupefied than wounded. For that blunt papal sword could not inflict a wound: it was tried but unskilled, and it brought stupor rather than pain to men whose sense was keen. In this, as we have said, John showed his unconquered and royal greatness of spirit, for he never gave way until, with Stephen Langton and those exiled bishops soliciting the Pope, the Pope pronounced a sentence against the king, deposing him and renouncing the kingdom, such as had not been heard of in any age. He committed and ordered the execution of this impious decree to Philip, King of the French, the most bitter enemy of John and of the whole kingdom of England, in remission of all his former sins and crimes. Pandulph, the cardinal legate of the Pope, a man sufficiently crafty and wily by that papal training, handled this business skilfully according to the judgment of the Pope and the cardinals. By papal legation and agency he first incited King Philip of France to arms. But when he noticed that the king's spirit was not merely inclined but ready and roused to war for the sake of gaining the kingdom, he cunningly calmed him little by little. He said that he was unwilling, and that the Pope himself did not wish hostile war to be declared against the King of England, until some despair of him and a general alienation of the will from the Roman see could be seen. By this most far-sighted counsel of Pandulph, the King of France was restrained from taking up arms against John. Meanwhile John girded himself for war, which he conducted quite successfully, often against these enemies whose conspiracy he had learned of. He copiously prepared and equipped a fleet and an army, and he preferred to attack his enemy himself rather than be provoked by him. So he led his fleet and army into France, and while he was at sea with the fleet, Stephen Langton returned to England with his fugitive and exiled companions and proclaimed the papal sentence by which the king had been removed from the kingdom. The king, with enemies threatening him on every side at home and abroad, his subjects' loyalty drawn away from him by papal superstition, and his kingdom seized by traitors, was forced by Pandulph to accept papal terms, and not without great peril. Otherwise he could not have been overcome by the combined forces of the Pope and the King of France. When the French king was leading his army and fleet across, Pandulph sent legates to John to warn him of the great danger that was impending and to teach him that he must seek to avoid it on Pandulph's advice. Nothing moved the king more to accept such shameful papal terms than his fear of being deserted by his nobles and his people. So he wished for Pandulph's arrival through the same legates. Pandulph magnified the imminent peril with every speech, and taught that it could be avoided in one way only: if the king, submitting himself to the Pope and the Roman Church, would receive back from him the kingdom from which he had been deprived, since he who can swallow and blow with the same breath can also loose and bind. The king, as if hemmed in by these difficulties, assented to Pandulph, resigned his kingdoms to the Pope, and received them back from him, with an annual pension of a thousand marks promised and confirmed to the Pope in writing. Then the king was absolved, the interdict was lifted, the exiles were recalled, and what had been taken from the churches was restored.

units.la: Sed Stephanus Langton eisi havimiurias & calamitates tam Regi quàm regno conflauit, tamen cum tobus compositis in Cantuariensi Archiepiscopatu cum Regis beneuolètia sedisset quietus, victus amore atq; charitate patriæ, cùm Iohannes Rex in Pandulphi manus sceptrum & diadema Regium concessisset, iniquissimo id animo ferens, accedens ad altare ob tam indignam Papæ facinus continere se non potuit, quin in appellationis vocem a tam indignam grandi illaro Angliæ prænuncio prorupit, & in reliquis vitæ gestis amætem patriæ, doctumq; ac prudentem patrem semper se declararit. Pandulphus rebus sic ad Papæ voluntatem in Anglia perductis, osto librarum millibus onustus lætus reuer- sus est.
units.tr: But Stephen Langton, although he had suffered wrongs and calamities at the hands of both the king and the kingdom, nevertheless, when everything had been settled, sat quietly in the Archbishopric of Canterbury with the king's goodwill. Overcome by love and affection for his country, when King John had handed over the sceptre and the royal diadem into the hands of Pandulph, he took it very ill. Approaching the altar because of so shameful a deed of the Pope, he could not restrain himself from bursting out into a cry of appeal, as the herald of England, against so unworthy a deed. In the rest of his life he always showed himself a lover of his country, and a learned and prudent father. With affairs in England thus brought to the Pope's will, Pandulph returned joyfully, laden with eight thousand pounds.

units.la: Hæc de historia, reliqua de Stephano Langton ut de vtili patriáque amanti, 10 eodem tamen viro, dicenda sunt. Anteactum septennium fuit regni Tragœdia, sequitur iam ex sequuto Pontificatu Comœdia. Nam cum Papa Iohannes ad sui regnique deditionem ascenso omnia atque liberrima iura Regia, (quod in illius tunc dixit suisse potestate) concessisset, Rexq; auferendis priuilegiis atq; libertatibus coercere magnates a se prius desicientes volunt, Regi adhærere Papa, Baronibus Stephanus. Exhac Regis & Baronum discordiá, ingens regni pertubatio sequuta multis duraturanensis. In qua Rex pene vitus atque superatus de regno Papali ditioni tradendo sugitauit. Nouerat enim, quod Papa super omnes mortales ambitiosus erat & superbus, pecuniæq; sititor insatiabilis, & ad omnia sceleta pro præmiis datus vel promissis aprus & prochuus. Hunc itaque muncribus, regnique spe solicitauit Rex, vt authoritate sua Archiepiscopum & Barones sibi ad- 20 uersos comprimeret atq; coerceret. Multa sane atq; æqua iura post crebras altercationes . Baronibus ipso Marte instantibus Rex concessit, & à Papa confirmari procurauit. Quibus cum sedari non potuissent, Papa illis iuribus priuilegiisq; rescisilis Barones in Regem rebelles excommunicauit. Hanc sententiam Stephano denunciandam atq; publicandâ commisit. Is iam ad generale concilium quod PapaRomæ celebrandam statuerat, Win- toniensi Episcopo , & Panoulpho Papæ nuncijs , qui mandatum scriptum de Baronibus excommunicandis attulerant (respondit, hanc Papæ sententiam fuisse tacita veritate in Barones latam, ideoq; nolle eandem executioni mandare, antequam Papam ipse consuluisset. Atilli ex Papæ præcepto cum Stephanum Archiepiscopum mandatu Pa- pæ exequi tardantem ab Ecclesiæ ingressu & celebratione diuinorû suspendebant, qui 39 Barones excommunicabant. Itaq; Stephanus Romam properat, ibi ab Abbate de belli loco, & Thomade Huntindonâ atq; Godefrido de Croucomb militibus, Regis nuncii & procuratoribus coram Papa est accusatus, quod opera & consilio suo Barones Angliæ Regem asolio deiicere molirentur, cumq; a Papa literas accepisset vt eos Ecclesiastica sententia a Rege persequendo refrenaret, ipse a sacris prohibens atq; suspeddi quàm id exequi mallet. Stephanus his criminationibus victus & percutbatus nulla excusatione vsus est, sed humiliter petiit à suspensione absolui. Cui Papa cum indignatione respondit. Frater, per sanctum Petrum nó ita facile beneficium absolutionis impetrabis. Itaq; eius- dem suspensionis sententiam noua fulminatione duplicauit, denunciariq; per Angliam totius Cantuariensis prouinciæ Suffraganeis mandauit. Inrerea Eboracensis Ecclesiæ Ca- 40 nonici Simonem Langton Stephani fratrem Eboracensem Archiepiscopum elegerunt, quem Papa iam incensus contra Stephanum in eodem concilio ad se prærcentarum confirmari atq; sacrari Canonicis seniorius obiurgans prohibuit, sed paulo post Stephanus à dicta suspensione sententia hac stipulatione conditionéq; interposita, quòd de bis controuerisis quæ inter Regem & Baronem exortæ essent, Papæ arbitrio staret, quod s ante casdem finitas & pacatas in Angliam non rediret, absolutus est. Concilium autem illud generale quod more Papali grandia prima fronte præ se tulit, in risum & scòmma quo Archiepiscopos, Episcopos, Abbates, Decanos, Archidiaconos, omnesq; ad id cócilium accedentes artificiose ludificatos est, desiit. Illi enim cum iam nihil geri in tanto negocio cernerent, tedeundi ad sua cupidi veniam sigillatim petierant. Quibus Papa non cócef- 5 sit, antequam sibi grandem pecuniam promisissent, quà à mercatoribus Romanis prius acciperet mutuo Papæ, qui soluere coactisunt, anteq; discedere Roma potuissent Papaiam accepta pecunia questuosam hoc concilio dissoluit graris, totusq; Clerus abiit tristis, Papa si lohann Regi coniunctissimus quod se suumq; regnũ sibi permisset, Barones Angliæ contra Regè quicquà molientes prius generaliter excommunicatos ad Regis rogariũ ieorsim & nominatim excommunicauit. Quilhac vsi sunt in Papa execratione. Exhaustorem pecuniæ Anglicanæ, & exactotem nobilitatis Britanniæ tibi inclinantem defendis, vt in barathrum Romanæ auaritiæ omnia demergantur. Papa præterea statuit ipsum Stephanum Langton Regis intuitu depriuare, nisi Cardinales restituissent. Cum itaque amoutre eum Rex ne Papa adiuuante potuit, fingunt Monachi eum in agritudinem lethalem & ineuitabilem incidisse, ex eoque contabuisse, etsi verius est eum ex veneno à Monacho sibi in quo delituit, Coenobio ministrato interisse, ipsorum Monachorum intestino odio, qui neque Regem neque Papam, neq; quenquam aduersos sibi, tolerare atque ferre poterant. Paulo ante Iohannis mortem, Papa interdicentea acerrimeq; minante & excommunic.telo fulminitante, inuito à Monachis & Baronib. instigatus intrauit hanc gentem superaturus Lodouicus Philippi Gallorum Regis filius, qui asseruit tam esse sibi quàm Papæ liberum Angliam in suam ditionem vendicare, neque in cuiusquam Regis aut Principis esse potestate Regnum sua voluntate in alium transferre, aut alteri vectigale reddere. Proinde inquit Regnum Angliæ patrimonium beati Petrinec erat necesti, nec vnq; erit. Post hasturbas Lodouicus magnos in Anglia motus excitauit Papali omni iurisdictione contempta, donec post Iohannis Regis mortem Henrico 3. Iohannis filio natu maximo regnante, cum tam Barones miserum suum statum deflentes resipuissent, & Henrico adhæsissent, de acquirendo regno desperauit, & in suas oras Gallicanas reuersus est. Sed ante decessum absolutus à Papæ legato tum Angliæ regno quàm à Papali sententia fuit. Sed ab illo absolutionis & pacis beneficio excepti omnes Episcopi, Abbates, Priores, & Prælati, qui quacunque opera aut consilio, etsi coacti fuissent, Lodouicum iuuerunt, vt legati faucibus quasi deuorandi exponerentur. Simon autem de Langton & Gerualius de Hobrugg. omnibus beneficiis bonisq; spoliati, Romam profecti sunt. Papalem misericordiam (quæ parua fuerat,) experturi. Hugo autem Lincoln. Episcopus (de quo ante diximus) cum in Angliam rediisset, qui auri argentique locupletes habebatur, pro Episcopatu recuperando ad curandam intercurem seu hydropsin Papæ, mille marcas, & ad extinguendam sitim Legati centum ex probatissima moneta numerauit. Rex Henricus iam decem annis natus in hac minori ætate in Willielmi Pembroki Comitis, Regni Marisicalci tutela custodiaq; positus, à Petro Wintoniensi & Iohanni Bathoniensi Episcopis absente Stephano Cant. primo vndus & suratus fuit, deinde Lodouico cum suis Gallis strenuè penitusq; electo, dictoque Comite Pembrook mortuo, Henricus Rex in tutela Petri Wintoniensis Episcopi positus fuit, denuoque à Stephano Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo in frequentissima Cleri populiquæ frequentia Westmonasterii coronatus, eiusque concilio crucis signo suceptus in Christianam militiam adscriptus est. Post Iohannis Regis & Innocentii Papæ obitus, transactis compositisque omnibus inter Regem & Barones controuersiis, Stephanus tandem ... cepit. Concilium prouinciale Oxonii in Ecclesia de Osney statuit. In quo inuenis quidam qui se Iesum Christum nominauit, & in manibus pedibusque atque lateree confossa vulnera ostendit, damnatus, mortequecrucis affectus est. Cum eo pariter mulieres duæ, quarum vna se Mariam virginem, altera Mariam Magdalenam nuncupauit damnatæ, & Diaconus Apostasiæ conuictus, omni Clericali gradu amotus, flagellisque absumptus est. Leges Ecclesiasticas eodem concilio 46. tulit, quarum permultæ in prouinciali constitutionib. typis expressæ sunt, reliquæ in Arctiuis custoditæ manent. Quæ quo statu atque conditione Anglicana tunc fuerint Ecclesia apertissimè demonstrant. Huiusque concilii tempore, Epistolæ decretales quæ sus Pontificium continent, ab Innocentio nono edite atque publicatæ sunt.
units.tr: These matters concern history; the rest about Stephen Langton must be told as about a man useful to his country and a lover of it, yet the same man. The seven years before were a tragedy of the kingdom; now a comedy follows from the pontificate that came after. For when Pope John, having submitted himself and his kingdom to the Pope, had granted up all the royal rights and most liberal powers (which at that time he said were in his power), the King wanted to curb the magnates by taking away the privileges and liberties which they had previously held. The Pope adhered to the King, and Stephen to the barons. From this discord between King and barons there arose a great disturbance in the kingdom, lasting for many years. In it the King, almost conquered and overcome, fled to hand the kingdom over to papal authority. For he knew that the Pope was more ambitious and proud than all mortals, an insatiable thirster after money, and ready and eager for every crime in return for rewards given or promised. So the King sought him out with gifts and the hope of the kingdom, so that by his authority he might restrain and check the Archbishop and the barons opposed to him. After frequent disputes, and with the barons pressing him by force of arms, the King indeed granted many fair and just rights and procured their confirmation by the Pope. But when the barons could not be pacified by these, the Pope annulled those rights and privileges and excommunicated the barons who were rebels against the King. He committed this sentence to Stephen to be announced and published. Stephen, however, replied to the Bishop of Winchester and to Pandulf, the Pope's envoys, who had brought the written mandate for excommunicating the barons, that this sentence of the Pope had been passed against the barons without due hearing of the truth, and therefore he was unwilling to put it into execution before he had consulted the Pope himself. Then the envoys, by the Pope's command, suspended Stephen, the Archbishop, from entering the church and celebrating divine services, since he was delaying to carry out the Pope's mandate, and they excommunicated the barons. So Stephen hastened to Rome. There he was accused before the Pope by the Abbot of Battle, and by Thomas de Huntingdon and Geoffrey de Croucombe, knights, envoys and agents of the King, that by his work and counsel the barons of England were striving to depose the King from his throne; and when he had received letters from the Pope ordering him to restrain them by ecclesiastical sentence from persecuting the King, he had refused, preferring to be suspended from sacred duties rather than carry this out. Stephen, overcome and disturbed by these accusations, made no excuse, but humbly asked to be absolved from the suspension. The Pope answered him with indignation: "Brother, you will not easily obtain the benefit of absolution by Saint Peter." And so he doubled the sentence of suspension with a new thunderbolt, and ordered it to be announced throughout England to the suffragans of the whole province of Canterbury. Meanwhile the canons of the church of York elected Simon Langton, Stephen's brother, as Archbishop of York. The Pope, already inflamed against Stephen, forbade that Simon be confirmed and consecrated, which he had summoned to himself at the same council, rebuking the senior canons. But shortly afterwards Stephen was absolved from the said suspension, on this stipulation and condition interposed: that concerning the controversies which had arisen between King and barons he would abide by the Pope's judgment, and that he would not return to England before these were settled and pacified. That general council, however, which at first sight had displayed great things in the Papal manner, ended in laughter and mockery, by which the archbishops, bishops, abbots, deans, archdeacons, and all who came to that council were cunningly deceived. For when they saw that nothing was being accomplished in so great a matter, they, eager to return home, asked for leave individually. The Pope did not grant this until they had promised him a large sum of money, which he obtained as a loan from Roman merchants, and which they were compelled to repay before they could leave Rome. Having received the money, the Pope dissolved the council, profitable to himself and burdensome to others, and the whole clergy departed sad. The Pope, being most closely allied with King John, and because he had handed over himself and his kingdom to him, excommunicated generally and then specifically at the King's request those barons of England who were planning anything against the King, who had previously been excommunicated in general. They used this curse of the Pope against... the exhauster of English money and the extorter of British nobility, who bent down to them, so that all things might be sunk into the abyss of Roman avarice. Moreover, the Pope decided to deprive Stephen Langton himself of his office, unless the cardinals had restored him, out of regard for the King. When the King could not drive him out, with the Pope's help, the monks pretended that he had fallen into a deadly and unavoidable sickness, and had wasted away from it; yet it is truer that he died from poison administered to him by a monk in the monastery where he was hiding, from the monks' own internal hatred, since they could endure neither the King, nor the Pope, nor anyone opposed to themselves. Shortly before the death of John, while the Pope was thundering interdicts and excommunications, Louis, son of Philip, King of the French, was stirred up by the barons and the monks, against their will, and entered this nation intending to conquer it. He asserted that it was as lawful for him as for the Pope to claim England for his own dominion, and that it was not in the power of any king or prince to transfer a kingdom to another at his pleasure, or to make it pay tribute to another. Therefore, he said, the kingdom of England was not, and never would be, the patrimony of blessed Peter. After these disturbances Louis stirred up great movements in England, with all papal jurisdiction despised, until after the death of King John, when Henry III, John's eldest son, was reigning, the barons, lamenting their wretched state, came to their senses and adhered to Henry; then Louis despaired of acquiring the kingdom, and returned to his shores in Gaul. But before his departure he was absolved by the Pope's legate, from the kingdom of England as well as from the papal sentence. Yet all bishops, abbots, priors, and prelates who had helped or advised Louis in any way, even if they had been compelled, were excluded from that absolution and peace, so that they were exposed to be devoured, as it were, by the jaws of the legate. Simon de Langton and Gerald de Hobrugg, stripped of all benefices and goods, went to Rome to experience the papal mercy, which was small. But Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln (of whom we spoke earlier), when he returned to England, who was considered rich in gold and silver, paid a thousand marks to cure the papal intercourse or dropsy, and a hundred of the most approved coin to quench the thirst of the legate, in order to recover his bishopric. King Henry, already ten years old, was placed in his minority under the guardianship and custody of William, Earl of Pembroke, Marshal of the kingdom; he was anointed and crowned by Peter, Bishop of Winchester, and John, Bishop of Bath, in the absence of Stephen of Canterbury. Then, when Louis, with his Frenchmen, had been vigorously and thoroughly defeated, and the said Earl of Pembroke had died, Henry the King was placed under the guardianship of Peter, Bishop of Winchester; and again he was crowned at Westminster by Stephen, Archbishop of Canterbury, in the presence of a very great crowd of clergy and people, and by his council he was received under the sign of the cross and enrolled in Christian warfare. After the deaths of King John and Pope Innocent, with all controversies between King and barons settled and composed, Stephen at last ... began. A provincial council was held at Oxford in the church of Osney. In it a certain young man who called himself Jesus Christ, and who showed wounds pierced in his hands, feet and side, was condemned and suffered the death of the cross. Together with him two women were condemned, one of whom called herself the Virgin Mary, the other Mary Magdalene; and a deacon convicted of apostasy was deprived of every clerical rank and beaten with whips. At the same council he enacted 46 ecclesiastical laws, of which very many were printed in the provincial constitutions, and the rest remain preserved in the archives. What the English Church was like in that time and condition these clearly demonstrate. And at the time of this council, the decretal letters which contain the papal law were published and issued by Innocent III.

units.la: Ex quo colligi potestiura huius regni Ecclesiasticæ illis Pontificiis esse priora. Stephanus Archiepiscopus gloriolæ atque pompæ suæ adaugendæ studens institutionem Thomæ Becket Cantuariæ, cui tam stupendæ ceremoniæ maximatotius Cleri, nobilitatis, populiquæ frequentia cum ipso Rege interfuit, qui illud cadauer è marmoreo lapide sublatum, & in novo phetero ex auro gemmisq; constructo collocari videtur. Et vt multitudinem copiosam congregaret, Londino Cantuariam itinerantib. ea ceremonia durante fœnum & equinum pabulum exhibuit. Tunc ipso translationis die vinum è canalibus ad hoc fabrefactis per varia urbis loca iugiter distillare fecit. Sumptus quos in hac celebritate immensos fuitinuit, sic Archiepiscopatus non modo Thesaurus, sed facultates exhausit & labefactauit, vt ne à quatuor deinceps ordine species Archiepiscopi refici ac recolligi potuissent, sed quaedam huius Thomae; quem tam pompose sanctificauit, reliquias Romam ante transportauerat, ob quas honorifice suscepturus est. Cum autem omnes regni tumultus essent sedati, Stephanus Archiepiscopus pro his libertatibus intercesserat, de quibus tanta contentione inter Iohannem Regem, atque proceres non modo ad amissionem regni, sed ad internecionem gentis digladiatum est. Cui Willelmus Briewer Regius quidam consiliarius. Haud (inquit) concedendæ, necisure obseruandæ sunt illæ consuetudines quas subditorum in Regem vibratus gladius impetauit & extorsit. Hunc liberius increpauit Archiepiscopus. Si inquit Regem diligeres, pacem regni non impedires. Et ad Regem conuersus admonuit eum iuramenti de concedendis illis libertatibus, quas discedente ex Anglia Lodouico Baronibus praestitisset.
units.tr: From this it can be gathered that the ecclesiastical authority of this kingdom was earlier than those Papal claims. Archbishop Stephen, eager to increase his own glory and pomp, arranged the translation of Thomas Becket at Canterbury. The King himself attended this stupendous ceremony, together with a great crowd of the whole clergy, the nobility and the people, and the King is seen to have had the body lifted from its marble tomb and placed in a new shrine made of gold and gems. To gather a large crowd, Stephen provided hay and horse fodder for those travelling from London to Canterbury for the duration of the ceremony. On the very day of the translation he had wine made to flow continually from conduits built for the purpose in various parts of the city. The expenses he incurred in this celebration were so immense that they drained and weakened the archbishopric, not only its treasury but its resources, so that the four archbishops who followed him could not restore or recover its condition. Some of the costs went to the relics of this Thomas, whom he had so pompously sanctified and had earlier sent to Rome, and for whose sake he was to receive them with honour. When all the disturbances of the kingdom had been calmed, Archbishop Stephen had interceded on behalf of those liberties over which King John and the nobles had contended so fiercely that the struggle threatened the ruin not only of the kingdom but of the nation. To him William Briewer, a certain royal councillor, said: "These customs, which the sword brandished by the subjects against the King has wrung out and extorted, are not to be conceded at all, but must be observed by necessity." The Archbishop rebuked him more freely: "If you loved the King," he said, "you would not hinder the peace of the kingdom." Turning to the King, he reminded him of his oath to grant those liberties which he had sworn to the barons when Louis had left England.

units.la: Rex constantia & gravitate Archiepiscopi, nec non iuramenti religione ac recordatione superatus, dignam Rege sententiam emisit. Decere se & iuramentum memorem esse, & eas consuetudines atque libertates ad quas astrictus tanta religione esset obseruare. Itaque edicta per totum regnum proposuit, ut ex singulis Angliae comitatibus duodecim milites vel ingenui atque legalis status homines ad se protinus convenirent, quos omnes iuramento onerauit, ut summa fide ac diligentia inuestigarent & inquirerent, quae ac cuiusmodi libertates tempore Henrici aui sui in Anglia obseruatae fuerunt. Hi inquisitione habita ea quae verissima certissimaque compererunt, miserunt ad Regem scripta. Ex quibus Rex fundamentum iuris Angliae muniepialis, quod iam magna charta nunc sumpsit, conflauit. Quo facto sedidiones omnes compescuit, suamque Remp. liberrimis institutis & legibus decoranit. Eodemque anno ob tantum eonecessum regno beneficium quasi aiuhro ad facultates augendas Regias, quas Iohannes Rex in illis externis & intestinis tumultibus exhausisset, omnium haereditum minorum donec ad legitimam haereditatem peruenissent, tutelas ac custodias quas in iure municipali Guardias appellamus, concesserunt. Stephanus Archiepiscopus in hac concordia regni Cleri Synodum habuit Westmonasterii. In qua is diuinam concionem ad populum habiturus cum illo scripturarum loco e suggestis exorsus est. In Deo sperauit cor meum, & adiurus sum, & refloruit eo mea. Cui hic incipienti e concione plebeius quidam alta voce exclamauit. Per mortem Dei inquit, mentiris, eorum nunquam in Deo, nec refloruit carorua. Qui mox a reliqua conciione deprehensus, eductus templo dimissa eocione diginas tanti sceleris & audaciae poenas dedit. In hoc etiam concilio constitutiones nonnullas prouinciales edidit. Sub haec quoque tempora fratres Minores dicti Franciscani, qui eredecim tum tantum fuerunt, in Anglia ingressi sunt, & capella S. Mariae Virginis a Rege Henrico tertio illius fundamentum eum lapidibus & cementis manibus suis ponente extruxit. Romanus Helluo Lupina voracitate lucro inhians misit Ottoni quendam suum in Anglia nuncium, eique hoc in mandatis eum suis ad Regem Henricum literis dedit, vt ab Ecclesiis in Anglia Cathedralibus, dnas praebedas quarum vna ab Episcopo, altera de capituli portione sumenda fit, duaque ex singulis ecenobiis ex Abbaris similiter Connenrufq; portionibus Ecclesiae Romanae exhiberi procuraret. Is Regi Papales tradidit literas. Rex qui a Papae petitione etiam animo toto abhorruit, tamen quia irritare illum noluit, lectis et occultaris literis respondit, quod solus negocium tanti momenti expedire non potuit. Ita consilio Stephani Cant. Archiepiscopi eonitutus Ottonii dies est in octauis Epiphaniae, vt in totius Cleri popnlique consensu postulatum Papae tractaretur. Westmonasterii. Eo die adfuit Otto, cui Rex Papae literas recitandas reddidit. In quibus idem Papa allegauit scandalum Romanae Ecclesiae, & opprobrium vetustissimum, notam scilicet coneupeientiae, quae radix dicitur omnium malorum, & in hoc praecipue quod nullus potest aliquod negocium in Romana curia expedire, nisi eum magna effusione pecuniae, & donorum exhibitione. Sed quoniam scandali buius & infamiae Romana pauperias causa est, debent Angli matris inopiam subleuare vt filii naturales. Quia nisi a vobis & ab aliis viris bonis & honestis dona receperem, defecerit nobis necessaria vitae, quae esset omnino Romana ineongtuu dignitati. Ad istud itaq; scandalo penitus eradicadis, ver cofilius fratrum nostrorum S. Romanae Ecclesiae Cardinalium, quanda prouidimus formam, cui si voluerint consentire, a scandalo matrem vestram poteritis liberare, & in curia Romana finedonorum obsequio exhibitionem iustitiae obtinere. Forma autem prouisa haec est. Petimus inprimis ab omnibus Ecclesiis Cathedralibus, duas nobis praebendas exhiberi, vna de pomone Episcopi, & alteram de Capitulo. Et similiter de ecenobiis, vbi dinerfae sunt portiones Abbatis & Conuentus, a Conuentibus quantum pertinet ad vnum Monachi aequali factae distributione bonorum suorum, & ab Abbate tantundem. Haec quae direétis & adumbrantibus sanctitatem verbis Papa postulauit, non minus salubri quam prudenti consilio vitauerunt Angli conedere, etsi nec expresse negarunt, priores Papae insidias & securitam experti. Rex ipse simulata valetudine concilio decessit. Episcopi muti & filies, ne noui tumultus oriantur, ad diocaeses & ciuitates suas discedere iussi sunt.
units.tr: The King, overcome by the constancy and gravity of the Archbishop, and also by the force of his oath and the recollection of it, gave a sentence worthy of a king: he should be mindful of his oath, and he must observe those customs and liberties to which he was so solemnly bound. Accordingly, he published edicts throughout the whole kingdom, ordering that twelve knights or freemen of lawful standing from each county of England come to him at once. He bound all of them by oath to investigate and inquire with the utmost fidelity and diligence what liberties, and of what kind, had been observed in England in the time of his grandfather Henry. Having held the inquest, these men sent the King in writing what they had found to be most true and certain. From these writings the King laid the foundation of the municipal law of England, which has now taken shape as Magna Carta. Having done this, he quelled all sedition and adorned his commonwealth with the most free institutions and laws. In the same year, in return for so great a benefit to the kingdom, and as a kind of aid to replenish the royal revenues which King John had exhausted in those foreign and domestic tumults, they granted the wardships and custodies of all minor heirs until they came of age to their lawful inheritance; in municipal law we call these Guardias. In this agreement of the kingdom, Archbishop Stephen held a synod of the clergy at Westminster. There, about to deliver a divine sermon to the people, he began from the pulpit with the verse of Scripture: "My heart trusted in God, and I was helped, and so my flesh has flourished again." As he began, a certain commoner shouted loudly from the congregation: "By the death of God, you lie! Your heart never trusted in God, and your flesh has not flourished again." He was at once seized by the rest of the congregation, led out of the church, and, the sermon being broken off, paid the penalty for so great a crime and audacity. In this council the Archbishop also issued several provincial constitutions. Around this time the friars called Minorites, or Franciscans, who then numbered only thirteen, came into England, and the chapel of St Mary the Virgin was built by King Henry III, who laid its foundation with his own hands, setting stones and mortar. The Roman glutton, gaping for gain with wolfish greed, sent a certain Otto to England as his nuncio, and gave him instructions, with letters to King Henry, to procure from the cathedral churches of England two prebends for the Roman Church: one to be taken from the bishop, the other from the portion of the chapter. Similarly, from each monastery, two portions were to be given to the Roman Church from the shares of the abbot and the convent. Otto handed the Papal letters to the King. The King, who in his heart wholly abhorred the Pope's request, nevertheless, not wishing to provoke him, read the letters, kept their contents to himself, and replied that he alone could not settle a matter of such importance. Thus, by the counsel of Stephen, Archbishop of Canterbury, a day was fixed for Otto in the octave of Epiphany, so that the Pope's demand might be considered with the consent of the whole clergy and people. At Westminster, on that day, Otto was present, and the King handed him the Pope's letters to be read aloud. In them the same Pope alleged the scandal and the ancient reproach of the Roman Church, namely the mark of covetousness, which is called the root of all evils, and especially the fact that no one can get any business done in the Roman curia without a great outlay of money and the offering of gifts. But since the cause of this scandal and infamy is Roman poverty, the English ought to relieve their mother's want as natural sons. For unless she received gifts from you and other good and honourable men, she would lack the necessities of life, which would be wholly unworthy of Roman dignity. Therefore, to root out this scandal completely, we have, with the counsel of our brothers the Cardinals of the holy Roman Church, devised a plan; if you are willing to agree to it, you may free your mother from scandal and obtain in the Roman curia the administration of justice without the obligation of gifts. The plan is this. We ask first that two prebends be given to us from all cathedral churches: one from the bishop's portion and the other from the chapter. Likewise from monasteries where the shares of abbot and convent are separate, we ask from the convents as much as falls to one monk, made by an equal distribution of their goods, and from the abbot as much. The English, with no less wholesome than prudent counsel, avoided conceding what the Pope demanded in words that were phrased to seem holy and reasonable. They did not expressly refuse, yet they had learned from earlier experience to beware of the Pope's snares and insecurity. The King himself, feigning ill health, withdrew from the council. The bishops were ordered, lest new tumults arise, to depart to their dioceses and cities, mute and silent.

units.la: Ottoni pro Papa totis ingenii ac orationis suae neruis instanti a quodam Iohanne Archidiacono Bedfordiensi responsum est. Quia haec res quae Regi valetudinis causa iá absentem maxime tangit, & Episcopos ad sua loca abire iussos, nec non quosquunque Ecclesiarum patronos, his absentibus, non esse reliquis tutum si in absentium praeiu-
units.tr: To Otto, who was pressing the Pope's cause with all the strength of his talent and his speech, a certain John, Archdeacon of Bedford, gave answer: since this matter touches the King, who is already absent for reasons of health, and the bishops who have been ordered to go to their own places, and likewise all the patrons of churches, and since these are absent, it is not safe for those who remain to answer, should they presume anything to the prejudice of the absent.

units.la: dicium quicquam præsumerent respondere. Nec dum Bedfordiensis perorauit, quin Iohannes Marescalcus Regis nuncius in Ottonis præsentia præcipit prætatis, ne laicum suum feudum obligarent Papæ. Itaque Otto pene stupefactus, his qui aderant alium deliberandi diem statuit, nempe mediam quadragesimam, ac in se suscepit Regis & absentium prælatorum aduentum procurare. Sed illi Regem non iubente ne diem illum admittere voluerunt, itaque singuli sine legati venia ad sua recesserunt. Interea alius Papæ legatus hanc causam a Gallicanis Episcopis solicitauit, eadem ad verbum visu oratione atque suasione, cui Archiepiscopi Lugdunensis procurator respondit. Fieri non posse vt hac concessione ille gurges atque fons Romanæ eupiditatis explearur. Diuturnum enim copiam redegisse semper Romanos ad insaniam. Quo peroranre a reliquo Gallicano concilio his verbis Legato Romano respondum atque conclusum est. Domine, moueat vos zelus hanc causam Ecclesiæ, & sanctæ sedis Romanæ: quia si omnium esset vniuersalis oppressio, posset timeri, ne immineret generalis decessio, quod Deus auertat. Quo responso Legatus Romanus ipsa mente & conscientia attonitus respondit, secum in Romana est curia nunquam huic exactioni consensisse, huius autem Papalis mandati literas ad eum postquam in itinere multum progressus esset peruenisse, quod quidem pergere etsi necessarium, tamen molestum & odiosum fuit, & ad extremum addidit non se amplius in tam callido negocio antequam reliquæ Christianæ gentes consenserint, progressurum. His in Angliaperceptis suasit Stephanus Archiepiscopus Cant. Papæ & Cardinalibus tantum negocium non esse Ottoni aut externo cuidam, sed sibi qui & Ecclesiæ Romanæ Cardinalis, & Anglis ac Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus esset committendum. Itaque Papa consilius Stephano (qui autem eum iusst,literas tam ad Stephanum de illo negocio gerendo & suscipiendo, quam ad Ottonem, vt eo omisso sine vlla mora & procrastinatione Romam rediret, decit. Literæ Ottoni iam in Scotiam, vt ex ea prouincia aliquid emungeret, properanti, cum in itinere Northamptonam peruenissent, (procurante Archiepiscopo) redditæ sunt. Quibus obliquo oculo & demissio vultu perlectis eas proiecit in ignem, sed Dominum suum Papam veritus, proposito mutato cum nihil ex Anglia aut Scotia congessisset, vacans, inanis, maestitiaque consufus ex Papæ mandato (tanquam obtotto collo) Romam ex Anglia retractus est. Cumque iam Otto discessisset, Stephanus Papæ mandatum satis versute tractauit. Conuocari à Rege procurauit Episcopos & magnates ad hanc rem antea satis instructos. Coram his Stephanus Papales literas recitauit, quibus auditis singuli singulos quasi risus mouebant de inexplebili auaritia Romana, quæ cupiditate excæcata hos versus nunquam intellexit.
units.tr: Before the Archdeacon of Bedford had finished speaking, John the Marshal, the King's messenger, in Otto's presence ordered the prelates not to pledge their lay fiefs to the Pope. Otto, almost stunned, then fixed another day for deliberation for those present, namely mid-Lent, and undertook to procure the arrival of the King and the absent prelates. But they, the King not ordering it, refused to admit that day, and so each withdrew to his own home without the legate's leave. Meanwhile another Papal legate pressed this cause upon the Gallican bishops, with the same words and the same persuasion word for word. To him the procurator of the Archbishop of Lyons replied that it could not be that this gulf and fountain of Roman greed should be filled by such a concession, for the Romans, once they had gathered abundance, always rushed on to madness. When he had finished, the rest of the Gallican council replied to the Roman legate in these words, and concluded: "Lord, may zeal for this cause of the Church and of the holy Roman See move you; for if it were a universal oppression, one might fear that a general defection was impending, which God forbid." At this reply the Roman legate, astounded in mind and conscience, answered that he knew the Roman curia had never consented to this exaction, and that the letters of this Papal mandate had reached him only after he had travelled a long way on his journey. To continue was necessary, yet troublesome and hateful, and at last he added that he would proceed no further in so delicate a business until the other Christian nations had agreed. When these things were learned in England, Archbishop Stephen of Canterbury advised that so great a business should not be entrusted to Otto or some foreigner, but to himself, who was both a Cardinal of the Roman Church and Archbishop of Canterbury for the English. The Pope therefore followed Stephen's counsel, and sent letters both to Stephen, concerning the conduct and undertaking of that business, and to Otto, ordering that, the matter being set aside without any delay or procrastination, he return to Rome. The letters reached Otto as he was hastening into Scotland to squeeze something out of that province; they were delivered to him at Northampton, when he had got that far on his journey, through the Archbishop's arrangement. Having read them with a sidelong glance and a downcast face, he threw them into the fire, but fearing his lord the Pope, he changed his plan, since he had gathered nothing from England or Scotland. Empty, vain, and confounded with sadness, he was dragged back from England to Rome by the Pope's order, as if with his neck bent. When Otto had departed, Stephen handled the Pope's mandate rather shrewdly. He had the bishops and magnates, already sufficiently instructed in the matter beforehand, summoned by the King. Before them Stephen read the Papal letters, and when these were heard, each man, as if laughing, remarked on the insatiable Roman avarice, which, blinded by its greed, had never understood these verses:

units.la: Quod uirtus reddit, non copia, sufficientem,Et non pauperas, sed mentis hiatus, egentem.
units.tr: What virtue gives, not abundance, makes a man sufficient; and it is not poverty but the gaping of the mind that makes him needy.

units.la: Tum Rex anteptouisus & meditatus respondit. Hæc quæ nobis Papa suadet, totum orbem tangunt Christianum. Nos itaque qui à reliquo orbe diuisi atque separati sumus, & ab ipsa Roma maximis interuallis diuncti, cum inrellexerimus quid cæterae gentes de bis exactionibus statuerint, earum exemplo ad Papæ obsequendum erimus promptiores. His dictis dimissum est concilium, & Papa frustratus magna spe. Huic autem Pontificiæ fraudi, quæ omnes sibi per orbem Christianum Ecclesias reddere vt legales censuit, videmus quam aperte ingenuæque Gallis, quam occulte & insidiose Anglia, quæ à Papa tot calamitatibus afflicta fuit, restitit. Stephano iam senio confecto instabat summa huius zui dies.
units.tr: Then the King, after a pause and reflection, answered: "What the Pope urges upon us touches the whole Christian world. We, therefore, who are divided and separated from the rest of the world and far removed from Rome itself, when we have learned what the other nations have decided about these exactions, will be readier to comply with the Pope on their example." With these words the council was dismissed, and the Pope's great hope was disappointed. As for this Papal fraud, which thought to make all the churches of the Christian world its own by legal right, we see how openly and nobly the French resisted it, and how secretly and insidiously England resisted it, though England had been afflicted by the Pope with so many calamities. Stephen, now worn out with age, faced the last day of his life.

units.la: Sed anno antequam decessit Cantuariensem Archidiaconatum Simoni fratri suo, qui à Papa Innocentio de Archiepiscopatu Eboracensi repulsam passus est, reliquisque suis bonis orbato postea contulit. In cuius etiam gratiam in concilio statuit, vt quæcunque Cantuariens. diœcesis Ecclesiæ, siue in suis feudis atque muneriis, siue in Monachorum essent sitæ, quo ante immunes erant atque liberæ Archidiaconali iurisdictioni subesserunt. Ipse cum 22. annos sedisset, & posterioribus annis se vtilem atque charum patriæ ciuem declarasset, in quodam suo munerio quod Stindonam in Suffexiæ comitatu appellant, 7. Idus Iulii obiit, atque Cantuariæ pridie nonas eiusdem deductus, & in capella S. Michaelis sepultus est. Cum autem corpus eius coram altari Cant. Ecclesiæ, sepultura tradendum iaceret, Monachi eiulantes in magna Cleti populiq; corona appellationem ad Papam alta voce eiecerunt, Ecclesiam suam, personas Ecclesiæ, iura & libertates eiusdem, terras & possessiones & homines suos, sub protectione Domini Papæ, & Romanæ curiæ subdicientes, & interdicentes ne aliqua Ecclesiastica vel seculars persona aliquid attentare præsumat in iudicium Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis. Multa scripsit cloganter & erudite Biblie sacra hiscapitibus, quibus hunc in Christianis Ecclesiis distinđta sunt separavit. Richardi Regis vitam & historiam descripsit. Huius tempore vicus seu Burgus de Southwerk cum Ecclesia Sanctæ Mariæ incendio consumpta est. Quod quidem incendium Londinum Pontem usque ad Turrim & Vinetariam plateam pertransiit.
units.tr: But in the year before he died, he conferred the Canterbury archdeaconry on his brother Simon, who had suffered rejection by Pope Innocent from the archbishopric of York and, later, deprived of his other goods, had been left destitute. In Simon's favour he also decreed in the council that whatever churches of the Canterbury diocese were situated either on the fiefs and offices of others or on those of the monks, which before had been immune and free, should now be subject to archidiaconal jurisdiction. Having sat for twenty-two years, and having shown himself in his later years a useful and dear citizen of the country, he died on one of his estates, which they call Stindon, in the county of Sussex, on 9 July. He was brought to Canterbury on the day before the Nones of the same month and buried in St Michael's chapel. While his body lay before the altar of the Canterbury church, ready to be laid in the tomb, the monks, wailing, with a great crowd of clergy and people around them, loudly lodged an appeal to the Pope. They placed their church, its persons, rights and liberties, its lands, possessions and men, under the protection of the Lord Pope and the Roman court, and forbade any ecclesiastical or secular person to presume to undertake anything against the jurisdiction of the church of Canterbury. He wrote many things, elegantly and learnedly, on the holy Bible, and he divided the sacred text into those chapters by which it is now distinguished in the Christian churches. He described the life and history of King Richard. In his time the village or borough of Southwark, together with the church of St Mary, was consumed by fire. This fire passed from London Bridge as far as the Tower and Vintry street.

units.la: XLIV. Richardus Magnus.
units.tr: XLIV. Richard the Great.

units.la: EPULTO Stephano, Cantuariensis Monachi quidem suo gremio foetum aliquè tot annis parturiebant, Regem prius de facultate eligendi rogantes, elegerunt quendam ius societatis insignem, alienæ infamem, Walterū de Hemesham 3. Nonas Augusti. Hunc electum ad Regem præsentarunt, qui habita cum Episcopis deliberatione deiecit tam celebri electioni eundem: quòd & eligentes virum despicabilem, sibique ac regno inutilem elegissent, & quòd electos duplici infamia laboraret. Pater enim eius furti postulatus ac convictus fuit, ideoque gula suspensus patibulo.
units.tr: When Stephen was dead, the monks of Canterbury, who for so many years had been in labour with a child in their bosom, first asked the King for permission to elect. They then chose one Walter of Hemsham, a man distinguished by his standing in the community but infamous through another's crime, on 3 August. They presented this man-elect to the King, who, after deliberating with the bishops, rejected so notable an election, on the grounds that the electors had chosen a contemptible man, useless to himself and to the kingdom, and that the man chosen was burdened with a double infamy. For his father had been prosecuted and convicted of theft and had therefore been hanged on the gallows.

units.la: Ipse autem contra Regem Iohannem interdicti tenipore litent. His Regiis criminationibus adiecerunt Cantuarienses protuncia Suffraganei, quòd sanctimonialis cuiusdam consuetudine visus esset, ex eaque sepius compressa suscepisset virili fortitudine atq; sexu puetos. Renouabant praeterea causam contra sententiam Romæ ab ipso Innocentio contra ius omne definitam, quòd hunc Suffraganeis non adhibitis vocatisve elegissent. Electus autem hic Walterus, etsi in Anglia de his criminibus & antea actâ sua vita inquisitionem habere nolunt, Romæ tamen, ubi omnia tam essent venialia, de nullo flagitio desperauit. Eò itaque festinat, sed Regii & Episcoporum nuncii eum antegressi praeoccupauerunt Papam. Qui nihilominus inueterate Papali assuetus seu natus aestua, negocium proeraftinauit, & in aliud tempus reiecit. Crastinum Cinerum definiendi diem statuit. Interea tam nuncii Regis quam Walterus multa pollicitando Papæ & Cardinalium animos lacebant, (qui quasi sub hasta & auctionis causa venditionis atque licitationi traderetur,) a quapatte plurimum exigi posset, expectabant. Gregorius tum Papa, eum F. Ederieum Imperatorem excommunicationis gladio dissecare & perimere non poterat, sumptus armis indixit illi bellum Itaque Episcopus Cesterensis, & Episcopus Couentensis Legati Regii, cum Papam & Cardinales motosos & difficiles in respondendo inuenissent, veritate Rex desideri suo fraudaretur, & Monachi vincerent, consilio inter se perniciosò atque detestabili habito, Papae promiscerunt ad bellicos suos contra linpetatorem sumptus omnium mobilium rerum in Angliæ & Hyberniæ Regnis decimatione. Quo promisso exhilerius Papa sine mora aut vlla suatione venit in eorum tutelam. Itaq; crastino eiusdem die statuto ipse in consistorio & pro tribunali sedens, pronunciauit Walterum à Monachis electum, à duobus suis Cardinalibus scilicet Petro & Albanensi de quibusdam Christianæ religionis dogmatibus examinatum, nō modo malè sed pessimè tractum; quod pronunciare illumque electum proriuus esse indignum, ac fide rigore iuris procedere veller, aliud dicere cogerentur. Itaque eam electionem cassauit, & tam ob electiquam ob eligentium indignitatem atque culpam prouisionem Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ sibi reseruauit. Qua tefatuatione Regiam causam non minus periclitari meiuerunt Regis nunci, quam electione Walteri: ne quod in Stephano Cant. Atchiepiscopo ab Innocentio constituto contigit, in alio ex Romano gremio atque sinu à Papa praeficiendo iam rursus tuentiat. Itaq; magna celeritate ab Hentico Rege ad Papam literas impetrabant, vt sua tam ampla promissa rata haberet, & Richardum Lincolniensis Ecclesiæ Cancellarium virum & scientia & fama atque vitæ inuiolata clarum, ad Atchiepiscopatum Cantuariensem promouerent. Papa tanta largitione delinitus Regi concessit quod optauit, literisq; ad Suffraganeos Cantuariensis, punctiæ datis ostedit, quo numine inspirans, nobilissimus sedis Apostolicæ membrum, atq; ipsam terrestre in Anglia paradysum, in qua lignū boni & mali satū est, & à quaprofluunt quatuor torrentes, quæ virâ mortuis, sanitatem ægrotis, libertatem servis, & audaciâ timidis conferunt, nëpe ex Thomæ Martyrio & miraculis. In hac autem paradyso collocandum Richardum Lincolniensem Cancellarium, in quem vitæ spiraculum inspirauit. Præcepitque omnibus Suffraganeis Clericisque totius prouinciæ, vt huic suæ dignissimæ creaturæ in paradyso constituere in omnibus pareant & obtemperent. Erat hic Richardus statura elegantì, erecto & procera, oratione facunda atque dulci, in omni genere literarum scientia recondita, vitaque non reprehendenda sed inculpata. Hic sine pallio ab Henrico Roffensi Edifcopo consecrationem Cantuariensem accepit, cui Rex Henricus interfuit in festo S. Trinitatis, insigni (vt tunc solitum est) luxu atque pompa: quo etiam die Londinensis & Elienfis Episcopi ab eodem Henrico consecrati fuerant. Papa cum Regis votis atque precibus in hoc Archiepiscopo creando satisfecisset, promissam retributionem expectabat. Misit itaque in Angliam Stephanum quendam suum capellanum. Is postquam Rex omnes cleri atque populi ordines congregasset, expulsur domini sui Papæ postulatum. Bellum ei atrox contra Fredericum pro Ecclesia Romana, quam caeterarum diceret matrem, suscipiendum, æquum autem esse afflictam & despicientem matrem à filiis subluuari. Itaque decimam omnium bonorum petiit ex Anglia, Cambria, & Hybernia Papæ sine moratribui. Rex quod ante promiserat etsi iam præstare nollet; silentio tamen assensisse visus est. Barones expresse negarunt. Episcopi tridui aut quatridui deliberationem petierunt, postea timentes ne Papa vim sui fulminis coruscam in illos mitteret, assensi sunt. Tum Stephanus præl atis ostendit literas Papæ procuratorias, in quibus ei potestas data est has decimas taxandi & recipiendi. Ad quod in singulis regni comitatibus procuratores subsitituit, publicata prius excommunicationis sententia contra omnes, qui hunc vbertimum Papæ illico persolui quæcumque quocunque modo impedirent. Quæstores autè suos in singulis comitatibus constitutos sub excommunicationis, aut interdicti pœna monuit, vt certo statuto die optimi ponderis, nuperrimeque percussam monetam ex his exactis decimis collectam, qua Papæ creditoribus possit satisfacere, mitterent. Qui duriflimè à clero populoquè hanc decimationem flagitarunt, vt illi Ecclesiastica vasa vendere vel pignori dare, hi futuram etiam mulierem credirorbus obligare cogerentur. Aderant vna fœneratores ex Italia permulti, qui illum abrasorem Stephanum vbique comitati, his qui papali exactioni soluendo non essent, pignoribus & hypothecis capris mutuum pecuniam dabant. Ita cum magno regni detrimento & calamitate exactissime hæc decima à Stephano Papæ perceptæ est. Solus Ranulphus Ceftrensis Comes restitit, qui generosè & magnanimo pectore suum comitatum in papalem redigi seruitutem, populumque ac clero eiusdem tantam patifolutionem non permisit. Quem tamen Papa satis aliunde locupletatus fulgure & censuris suis nominatim non læsit.
units.tr: Walter himself was at that time in dispute with King John during the interdict. To these royal charges the Canterbury men and their suffragans added that he had been seen to keep company with a certain nun, and had often had intercourse with her, and had fathered sons and daughters by her. They also renewed the case against the sentence, which Innocent himself had decided in Rome against all law, because they had elected him without summoning or consulting the suffragans. Walter, although in England they did not wish to inquire into these crimes or into his earlier conduct, nevertheless despaired of no disgrace at Rome, where, as everything there was regarded as pardonable, he thought all things could be excused. So he hurried thither, but the King's and the bishops' messengers, having gone ahead, forestalled him with the Pope. The Pope, however, accustomed and born to Papal delay, put off the business and postponed it to another time, and fixed the day after Ash Wednesday for deciding it. Meanwhile both the King's messengers and Walter, by promising many things, tried to move the minds of the Pope and the Cardinals, and waited to see how much could be extracted from each side, as though the see were being put up for sale by auction and handed to the highest bidder. Pope Gregory, since he could not cut down and destroy the Emperor Frederick with the sword of excommunication, took up arms and declared war on him. Therefore the Bishop of Chichester and the Bishop of Coventry, the royal legates, finding the Pope and the Cardinals hesitant and difficult in their reply, and fearing that the King would be defrauded of his desire and the monks would prevail, took a counsel between themselves which was pernicious and detestable: they promised the Pope, for his war against the Emperor, a tithe of all movable goods in the kingdoms of England and Ireland. With this promise the Pope was more cheerful, and without delay or any hesitation he came to their protection. So on the appointed day, sitting in consistory and on the judgement seat, he pronounced that Walter, chosen by the monks, had been examined by two of his Cardinals, namely Peter and the Cardinal of Albano, on certain doctrines of the Christian religion, and had not merely been ill-treated but most wretchedly handled; that he should declare him at once unworthy, and that, if he wished to proceed by the strict rigour of law, they would be compelled to say otherwise. And so he annulled that election, and reserved to himself the provision of the Church of Canterbury, both on account of the election and on account of the unworthiness and fault of the electors. The King's messengers feared that the King's cause was in no less danger from this decision than Walter's election, lest what had happened to Stephen, the Archbishop of Canterbury appointed by Innocent, should again happen in another man appointed by the Pope from the Roman bosom and lap. So with great speed they obtained letters from King Henry to the Pope, that he would hold to his own great promises, and they asked that Richard, Chancellor of the Church of Lincoln, a man distinguished for learning, fame and an unblemished life, should be promoted to the archbishopric of Canterbury. The Pope, soothed by such great largesse from the King, granted what he desired, and by letters sent to the suffragans of Canterbury he showed by what authority he was inspired, a most noble member of the Apostolic See, and, as it were, the earthly paradise in England, in which the tree of good and evil was planted, and from which flow four streams which bring life to the dead, health to the sick, liberty to slaves and boldness to the timid, namely from the martyrdom and miracles of Thomas. In this paradise he decided to place Richard, the Chancellor of Lincoln, into whom he breathed the breath of life. He also commanded all the suffragans and clergy of the whole province to obey and submit in all things to this most worthy creature of his in paradise. This Richard was of elegant stature, upright and tall, eloquent and sweet in speech, learned in deep knowledge of every kind of letters, and of a life not reprehensible but blameless. Without the pallium he received consecration as Archbishop of Canterbury from Henry, Bishop of Rochester, at which King Henry was present on the feast of the Holy Trinity, with the splendour and pomp customary at that time; on the same day the Bishops of London and Ely had been consecrated by the same Henry. When the Pope had satisfied the King's wishes and prayers in creating this Archbishop, he waited for the promised repayment. He therefore sent into England a certain chaplain of his, Stephen. After the King had gathered all the orders of clergy and people, he demanded on behalf of his lord the Pope that they should undertake a fierce war against Frederick on behalf of the Roman Church, which he called the mother of all the others, and that it was right for the afflicted and despised mother to be supported by her sons. Accordingly he demanded without delay a tenth of all goods from England, Wales and Ireland for the Pope. The King, although he was unwilling now to grant what he had earlier promised, seemed nevertheless to assent by silence. The barons expressly refused. The bishops asked for three or four days' deliberation, and afterwards, fearing that the Pope would hurl the bright force of his thunderbolt at them, they assented. Then Stephen showed the prelates letters of procuration from the Pope, in which power was given to him to assess and receive these tithes. For this he appointed agents in each county of the kingdom, after first publishing a sentence of excommunication against all who by any means should hinder this tenth from being paid to the Pope at once. He also warned his collectors, appointed in each county, under penalty of excommunication or interdict, that on a fixed day they should send to him coin of the best weight, lately struck and collected from these exacted tithes, with which he could satisfy the Pope's creditors. These men demanded the tithe from the clergy and people so harshly that the clergy were compelled to sell or pledge the Church's vessels, and the people to pledge even their wives and children to the creditors. At the same time very many moneylenders from Italy were present, who followed that extortioner Stephen everywhere, and lent money at a price, on pledges and mortgages, to those who were not able to pay the Papal exaction. Thus this tithe was most rigorously collected by Stephen for the Pope, with great loss and calamity to the kingdom. Only Ranulf, Earl of Chester, resisted, who with a noble and magnanimous heart did not allow his county to be reduced to Papal servitude, nor did he permit the people and clergy of it to suffer such a drain. Yet the Pope, enriched sufficiently from elsewhere, did not harm him by name with his lightning and censures.

units.la: Richardus autem compositis multis Prouinciæ suæ negociis, Prouinciæ suæ Synodum Westmonasterii congregauit, in qua tredecem salubertimas prouinciales leges tulit, quæ tam æquabiles & temperatæ sunt, vt suæ manuetudinis specimen præbere ac indicare possint. Sed etsi natura mitis ac manuetus fuit, in vendicandis tamen Ecclesiæ suæ iuribus acris atque fortis. Quod ex ea controuersia, quæ inter eum & Hubertum Cantii comitem, exercitata diu fuit, facile constat. Hic Hubertus vir tam authoritate sua, quia Regis gratia potens in Rep. fuit, belli pacisque negocia feliciter sub Rege Iohanne & Henrico co gessit, vnde & Iustitiarius criminalis fuit regni, & quòd castrum Douieri obsidione Gallorum à Lodouico ex pugnatum fortiter defendit, Comes Cantii creatus est. Huius etiam filium Richardum Henricus. 3. militari cinxit cingulo. Hic primus Ecclesiasticà inuasit atque depraedatus est iura. Itaque Richardus Cantuariensis deo conquestus est Regi, quòd Tunebrugensè castellum cum tota villa & vicinis rusticeis prædiis, aliàsque Clarensis Comitis terras, quæ durante minori ætate hæredis eius ad Ecclesiam Cantuariensem spectab ant, ab Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis iure possessioneq; detinuit. Rex verò nullius querelam contra Hubertum admisit, sed Archiepiscopo respondit. Hubertum hæreditatem de se Rege, vt principali Domino tenere, quod iure municipali dicitur, in Capite tenere. Minorum autem hæredum tutelas & custodias ad regiam coronam pertinere.
units.tr: Richard, having settled many matters of his province, called a synod of his province at Westminster, in which he enacted thirteen most salutary provincial laws, which are so fair and moderate that they can show and display a specimen of his gentleness. But although he was by nature mild and gentle, yet in claiming the rights of his Church he was keen and strong. This is easily established from the long dispute which was carried on between him and Hubert, Earl of Kent. This Hubert, a man powerful both through his authority and because he was in favour with the King, conducted the affairs of war and peace successfully under Kings John and Henry; hence he was also Chief Justiciar of the kingdom, and, because he bravely defended the castle of Dover against the siege of the French by Louis, he was created Earl of Kent. King Henry III also girded his son Richard with the knightly belt. This Richard was the first to invade and plunder the rights of the Church. Therefore Richard of Canterbury complained to God and to the King that he had seized the castle of Tonbridge with the whole town and the neighbouring rustic estates, and other lands of the Earl of Clare, which during the minority of his heir belonged to the Church of Canterbury, from the right and possession of the Church of Canterbury. But the King admitted no complaint against Hubert, and answered the Archbishop that Hubert held the inheritance from himself the King as principal lord, which in municipal law is said to be held in chief, and that the wardships and custodies of minor heirs pertained to the royal crown.

units.la: Hoc Regis responso repulsam immotam ferens Archiepiscopus, omnes dictarum possessionum inuasores aliosque qui cum his commercium haberent, præter ipsum Regem excommunicauit. Hæc prima Ecclesiastico tum iurium à laicis occupatio, primiaque ob tantam iniuriam excommunicatione sumpta vindicta fuit. Deinde Archiepiscopus Romam profectus est. Rex discessu eius cognito ad Papam Rogerum de Cantelupo cum aliis nuncijs legauit; qui quærenti Archiepiscopo contradicerent, & regia inta defenderent. Romam venit Archiepiscopus, querelam coram Papa tam contra Hubertum Ecclesiasticorum iurium prædonem, quam contra Regè illius soliùs consilio & prorutatione Remp. administrantem, Episcopos Cant. prouinciæ Suffraganeos in Fisco sed Sic volo sic iubeo, sit pro ratione voluntas.
units.tr: Archbishop Edmund bore this refusal of the King's with an unbroken spirit, and excommunicated all the invaders of the said possessions, and any others who had dealings with them, except the King himself. This was the first occupation of Church rights by laymen at that time, and the first excommunication taken as vengeance for so great an injury. The Archbishop then set out for Rome. When the King learned of his departure, he sent Roger de Cantelupo and other envoys to the Pope, to oppose the Archbishop's complaint and defend the royal cause. The Archbishop came to Rome and laid his complaint before the Pope, against Hubert, the plunderer of ecclesiastical rights, and against the King, who administered the commonwealth on Hubert's counsel and by his persuasion alone, and against the suffragan bishops of the province of Canterbury in the Exchequer, but thus I will, thus I command; let my will stand in place of reason.
