units.la: Veruntamen quia nullum fuit siue postulatione siue postulati vinum, concessa Monachis facultas est eligendi alium. Illi igitur Iohannem Subpriorem suum eligunt, cui & Rex assensus est. Sed cum Romæ literas suæ electionis exhibuissset Papæ, Cardinalibus quibusdam, qui de doctrina eius atque moribus exquirerent, traditus est. Hitriduo post retulerunt Papæ se iustam in eo recusationis causam inuenire non posse. Papa tamen cuius sola voluntas vim legis habuit, eum non aliam ob causam repulit quàm propter senectutem, senioq; bono congruam simplicitatem atque integritatem, eique suasit tantam dignitatem à sene tam miti simpliciq; ingenio prædito sustineri non posse, proinde consultius facturum eum si Monachorum electioni renunciaret. Is Papæ oblecutus facile ac sine mora eessit, veniaque impetrata discessit in Angliam. Monachis a papa denuo imperatum est vt virum aliquem strenuum & valentem, qui prouinciam totam fortiter administrare posset, eligerent. Tertiò itaque Blunduoi à Rege probarum qui Oxonii cum studuit elegerunt. Hunc etiam reiecit Papa, quòd familiaris Petro Wintoniensi Episcopo abeodem duo marcarum millia accepisset, quibus vt suspicabatur Cantuariensis Monachos se eligentes muneribus & Simoniaca prauitate corrupit: deinde quòd duo beneficia Ecclesiastica ad curam animarum destinata, contra consilii præscriptum simul tenuisset. His Simoniæ & ambitionis notis Iohannis Blundi electio reprobata à Papa est Iamq; Monachos Cantuarienses præsentes Romæ Papa
units.tr: Yet since there was no agreement, either in the petition or in the one petitioned, the monks were granted the right to elect another. They therefore chose their sub-prior, John, to whom the King also gave his assent. But when he had presented the letters of his election at Rome to the Pope, he was handed over to certain Cardinals, who were to inquire into his learning and character. Three days later they reported to the Pope that they could find no just cause for refusing him. The Pope, however, whose will alone had the force of law, rejected him for no other reason than his old age, and the simplicity and integrity that befit an old man. He persuaded him that so great a dignity could not be borne by one of such a gentle and simple disposition, and that he would therefore act more wisely by renouncing the monks' election. John, yielding to the Pope, withdrew at once without delay, and having obtained pardon, went back to England. The Pope again ordered the monks to choose some vigorous and capable man who could administer the whole province firmly. Thus, for the third time, they chose John Blund, a man of proven worth whom the King had approved, who had studied at Oxford. The Pope rejected him too, because he had been a familiar of Peter, Bishop of Winchester, and had received from him two thousand marks, by which, as he suspected, he had corrupted the Canterbury monks who were choosing him, with gifts and simoniacal wickedness; and further, because he had at the same time held two ecclesiastical benefices destined for the cure of souls, contrary to the prescribed rule. On these marks of simony and ambition, the Pope set aside the election of John Blund. And now the Canterbury monks who were present at Rome were asked by the Pope,

units.la: (Ut strictus supplicus esse potens) rogat, vt Cantuariensi Ecclesiæ tribus electionibus rescissis, exemplo Saræ vxoris Tobiæ paerore tantum maritò destitutæ, Edmundum Ecclesiæ Sarisburiensis Cannnicum atque Thesaurarium, virum pium atque doctum suis notis atque suffragiis designarent. Hic Edmundus Abindoniæ in Barkeria natus est patre Edwardo, matre Mabella cognomento Diuiue, (quia mercaturam eopiosam Abindoniæ exercebant.) Parentes hunc Edmundum in Oxoniensi Academia, quæ quinque passuum millibus abest Abindonia, bonis literis ab incunte ætate educari curarunt. Quit u. diligenter exculcus in virili ætate Theologiæ se suaponte dedit. In eaque progressus & in ordinem clericalem ascriptus verbum diuinum in Oxonii, Glocestriæ, & Worcestriæ comitatibus passim & aliisque prædicauit. Deinde in Canonicatum in Sarisburiensi Ecclesia assumptus est. Edwardus huius patèr a coniugio cum vxoris consensu se diuunxit, & vitam Monasticam in Cœnobio Euesham ingressus est. Sed hunc Edmundum tam spectatum prudentia, moribus & doctrina virum, instante ne Papa quidem, Cantuariensis Monachi qui Romæ fuerunt, sine Regis & sui conuentus assensu eligere voluerunt. Papa ei tanquam ex taciturnitate Monachorum qui aperte conitadicere non audebant electo, transmisit pallium, quo ductus in absentem, peregrinum, & ignotum motu laud scimus ex historiis. Satis autem constat cum à Rogero Londinensi Episcopo sacratione accepisse Cantuariæ. An. Dom. 1234, eodemq; die induisse pallium tempore missæ, quæ celebrauit ipso Rege cum 13. Episcopis magnaque multitudine præsente, sacratus autem & in Archiepiscopalium iurium possessione positus, Angliam ioriestino motu turbatam hoc consilio iuuit. Regi suasit vt à consiliis suis Petrum Wintoniensem Episcopum & Petrum de Riuallis viros ambitiosos, totiusq; ciuitis discordiæ authores seperegaret. Ipse cum Cestrensi & Roffensi Episcopis in Walliam profectus, inter Regem & Leolinum aquilonaris Walliæ principem, ac Richardum Comitè Marisfalcum (qui coniunctis copiis bellum in Regem parabant,) pacem conciliauit. Regni Comites qui à Rege defecerant, in gratiam Regis, & pristinos honores reduxit. Petro Wintoniensi Episcopo Rex præcepit, vt ad Episcoparus sui sedè ab aula prorsus recederet, ibique animarum curæ vacaret. Petrum autem de Riuallis contumeliosissimè, ex Aula eiecit, minatus quòd nisi in clericali forte esset, suis manibus oculos illi effodere vellet. Hæc autem per Archiepiscopum conciliata pax fœderibus fractis in bellum iterum prorupit. Edmundus autem pacifudiens eleri Synodum Londini congregauit, in qua 36. prouinciales leges tulit, quarum plerasq; pontificia superstitione refertæ atque plebes sunt, reliquæ æquitate atque ratione nituntur. Edmundus enim æquabilis & temperatus atque instus fuit, tum ab omni populari atque ciuili discordia, hisque rebus quibus ea concitatur, inferendis iniuriis, & rapinis muneribusq; extorquendis animo toto semper abhorruit. Quæ hominis virtus atq; cōstantia pontificiorum odium (quod eum optime de patria meritum in exilio egit) comparauit. Quod tamen cōmode vitare atq; adeo cōtēnere potuisset, si Regis à se animū & beneuolētia pro minuto & paruo pēdēdo iure quodā pontificio à se penitus nō alienassèt. Quæ quanq; prolixior narratio futura est, hoc tamen
units.tr: (As one able to be a close suppliant) that, with the three elections annulled, they should, after the example of Sarah, wife of Tobias, who was bereft only of her husband, designate for the Church of Canterbury Edmund, a canon and treasurer of the Church of Salisbury, a man pious and learned by his marks and votes. This Edmund was born at Abingdon in Berkshire, to his father Edward and his mother Mabel, surnamed Divine (because they carried on a considerable trade at Abingdon). His parents took care that Edmund should be educated in good letters from his earliest age at the Academy of Oxford, which is five miles from Abingdon. Having been diligently cultivated there, in manhood he devoted himself to the study of theology. Advancing in it, and enrolled in the clerical order, he preached the divine Word in the counties of Oxford, Gloucester and Worcester, and elsewhere. Then he was taken into the canonry of the Church of Salisbury. His father Edward, having separated from marriage with his wife's consent, entered the monastic life at the monastery of Evesham. But the Canterbury monks who were at Rome wished to choose this Edmund, a man so esteemed for prudence, character and learning, without the assent of the King or of their own convent, even though the Pope did not insist. The Pope sent him the pallium, as though the monks, who did not dare to contradict openly, had consented through their silence; the pallium was taken by him in absence, as a stranger and unknown, as we learn from the histories with a motion of laughter. It is quite certain, however, that he received consecration at Canterbury from Roger, Bishop of London, in the year of our Lord 1234, and on the same day put on the pallium at the time of Mass, which the King himself celebrated with thirteen bishops and a great crowd present. Consecrated and placed in possession of the archiepiscopal rights, he aided England, troubled by internal strife, with this counsel: he persuaded the King to separate from his counsels Peter, Bishop of Winchester, and Peter des Roches, men of ambition and the authors of discord throughout the whole state. He himself, with the Bishops of Chester and Rochester, went into Wales, and between the King and Llywelyn, prince of northern Wales, and Richard, Earl Marshal (who, with their forces joined, were preparing war against the King), he brought about peace. He restored to the King's favour and to their former honours the earls of the realm who had defected from the King. To Peter, Bishop of Winchester, the King commanded that he withdraw entirely from the court to his episcopal see and there devote himself to the care of souls. But Peter des Roches he thrust out of the court with the greatest insults, threatening that unless he were in holy orders he would tear out his eyes with his own hands. But this peace, brought about through the Archbishop, broke out again into war once the treaties were broken. Edmund, however, grieving at the peace's failure, called a synod of the clergy at London, in which he passed thirty-six provincial constitutions, most of which are filled with papal superstition and plebeian, while the rest rest on equity and reason. For Edmund was even-tempered, moderate and just; he always abhorred from his whole mind every popular and civil discord, the inflicting of injuries, the rapine, and the extortion of gifts, and the things by which such discord is stirred up. This virtue and constancy of the man won him the hatred of the papists (which drove him into exile, though he had deserved very well of his country). He could have easily avoided and utterly disregarded this, if he had not, by offering a small and trifling right of a papal kind, entirely alienated the King's mind and goodwill from himself. Although this narrative will be longer, it shall nevertheless be set out in this order: hoc tamen

units.la: ordine exponatur. Rex Willielmo Marescalco Glocestriæ Comite in Hybernia mortuo, sororem suam Elenoram eiusdem Comitis uxorem studuit nuptiis Simonis Montfort Leycestrensis postea Comitis coniungere. Sed illa sui ex animo, siue simulatæ, simulatq; Maresc alco maritoo rbata esset, angæ eastitatem vouerat. Itaq; Edmundus qui astringere illam ad votum conseruandum voluit totis viribus, his nuptiis restitit. Regég; acriter increpavit, quod hominini nuptiis conciliandis, Ecclesiasticâ iura dissoluendi authorfieret. Quæ in impediendis his a Rege constitutis nuptiis Edmundi operatæ oratio, Regem ab eo prorsus abalienauit atque seiunxit. Itaque non minus incensus quàm cautus Rex clam cum Papa egit, vt tam ad hunc Archiepiscopum quam alios tibi aduersos coercendos subditos aliquem strenuum & solcrte virum cum legatina potestate in Anglham mitteret. Papa ex sua Regisq; sententia delegit Ottonem S. Nicolai in carcere Tulliano diaconum Cardinalem. Hic instructus dolis & arte pontificia, Parisiis in itinere iam fuit, antequam de aduentu eius Archiepiscopus aut Magnates quicquam vel minimo signo aut suspicione vila accepissent. Hunc itaque aduenientem Magnates his maledictis execrantur. Immutatorem totius regni vocant. Qui oblata inæstimabilia munera accepit quidem palam aliqua, ne Romanam auaritiam indicaret omnibus, sed ea quæ inoculis coràm non accepit, callide sibi referuan iussit. Rex ipse ad locum marinima occurrit, suscepiq; inclinato ad genua capite, & ad mediterranea officiose deduxit. Episcopi & prælati muneribus plusquam decuit affecerunt. Legatus commodum ex hac Regis cum proceribus discordia ad regnum expilandum tempus nactus, primo suo aduentu, beneficiorum in Anglia vacantium reditus atq; fructus in Romanorum gregem stipatus. Edmundus Regem de huius Legati ingressu increpat, ipsumq; legatum Anglicani cleri per eum vexati & expilati, tantorumq; acceptorum munerū reprehendit. Rex & Legatus Egmundi orationem derisam & contemptam iusserunt. Sed Legatus eandem vt magnam iniuriam postea vitus est. Interea Simon Montfort muneribus obtinuit a Papa, vt sponsæ suæ Eleonoræ sororis Henrici Regis relaxato & remisso voto, progredi ad celebrandas nuptias iure pontificio illæso posset. Papa mandauit interedeunte hae autata intereessione Legato Ottoni, vt ( votonon obstante) pro matrimonio prædicto secundum Simonem & Eleonoram iudicaret. Is mandatum Papæ fine mora peregit. Ita Edmundo sprerto, nuptiæ factæ sunt. Hæc prima contemnendi, iudiblioq; afficiendi Edmundum Archiepiscopum causa fuit. Alia deinde his Regis & Legati acquisitis inimicitiis grauiorain hominem insontem atq; pium meditata malasunt. Romana iub hec tempora feruens & inexplebilis auaritia cuiusquam generis hominibus doctis ac Indoctissimis atque summis patefacta est. Mirum enim est, quibus artibus per orbem Christianū, in Anglia vero maximè expressit vndiquè pecunias. Decimajilla Stephano Langton Archiepiscopo paucis ante annis Papæ persoluta exhausta est, sed redintegrandus technis, redintegranda solutio est. Illa decima Romanum exercitum contra Fridericum Imperatorem alebat. Iam autem noua fraude excogitata pro terra sancta dimicandum est. Itaque destinati vndique à Curia Romana legati, qui prædicando, supplicando, præcipiendo, comminando, excommunicando atque exigendo innumeros regni subditos extorres & mendicos reddiderunt. Scripsit Papa & Angliæ Regi, populo atque clero liberas verborum adumbrato fuco, speciecq; sanctissimas, sed reipta omni pietati & iustitiæ Christianæ contrariae. In quibus dolere se aitamissionem illius sancti regni ex induciis breui inter Soldanum & Orientalem Cæsarem olim pactis breuiqué desituris immineret. Prouocandos itaq; ad id defendendum, aut sicamittatur recuperandum omnes Christianos. Itaq; sed ad tam pium facinus summa charitate motum ex plena sua indulgendi, soluendiq; atque ligandi potestate, qui aut ad illud bellum suscipiendum se inserbere, aut proficiscentibus largiri aliquid volunt, texta operæ aut datarum faciliatum modum peccatorum remissionem largiri & polliceri. Quin hanc militiam inscriptifunt, crucis Christianæ signo notandi fuerunt. Postulatum ad hoc non modò militare, sed & nauale subsidium fuit. Ad hanc rem suadendam ex fratrum Minorum ordine exorti Prædicatores per Angliam passim scatebat. His a Papa concessa potestas est huic militiæ se vltra scribentes cruce signare, postridieq; acceptis nummis ab eisdem voto soluere, veniamq; peccatorum in multos dies concedere. Hi e religiosis (etsi minimi) tamen hac accepta potestate populo plebiq; gratiosi, sed Monachis, quibus Papa hanc facultatē nō permisit, ædiofi fuerunt. Verū paulo post eū populus (etiā ipsis Monachis suadentibus) perspexisset, & accurato atq; vaferrimè fabricato dolo tāto cerrasa & collecta pecunia fuisset, infectoq; cōtra Imp. ii hostiliter vibrato bello, accepta ab Anglia tanta pecunia pacē illico sequuta. Nullumque in Terram sanctam apparatum, aut militum delectum haberi, ipsisque qui profectiones vouissent, vota sua pecunia redimere ab ipsis religiosis Papæ quæstoribus rogatos, ipsis animis & consentientia læsi atque saueiati eeperunt, tam insidiosam auaritiam papalem aperte atque passim reprehendere ac taxare. Itaque postea magis magisque cœperunt esse tam fraudulentis & iniquis pecuniarum expressionibus obstari, cum aperte cognitum & vulgatum esset Romanam ingluuiem atque sordem sanctitatis praetextu solum lucrum inhiare. Sed Legatus Otto vt hanc suæ curiæ infamiam & contumeliam cautius deuitaret, munera iam respnere contra consuetudinem Romanorum callidè eepit, vt gravioribus oneribus Angliam demum opprimeret, & affluentionibus largitionibus illam voraginem satiaret.
units.tr: Let it be set out in this order. When King William, Earl of Gloucester, had died in Ireland, the King eagerly sought to join his sister Eleanor, the Earl's widow, in marriage to Simon de Montfort, later Earl of Leicester. But she, whether from genuine feeling or pretence, as soon as she was separated from her husband, had vowed chastity. So Edmund, who wished to bind her with all his strength to keep that vow, opposed this marriage. He sharply rebuked the King for making himself an overturner of ecclesiastical law in order to arrange a marriage. The speech by which Edmund worked to hinder the marriage arranged by the King completely alienated and estranged the King from him. Therefore the King, no less inflamed than cautious, secretly dealt with the Pope, so that he would send into England some vigorous and skilled man with legatine power to restrain not only this Archbishop but the other subjects who opposed him. The Pope, by his own choice and the King's judgment, chose Otto, deacon-cardinal of St Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano. Equipped with the tricks and craft of the papacy, he was already on his way at Paris before the Archbishop or the magnates had received the slightest sign or suspicion of his coming. So when he arrived, the magnates cursed him with these abuses: they called him the changer of the whole realm. He did openly accept some offered gifts of incalculable value, lest he show Roman greed to everyone, but those things he did not receive in public he cunningly ordered to be kept back for himself. The King himself met him at the seacoast, received him with head bowed to his knees, and courteously escorted him inland. Bishops and prelates honoured him with more gifts than was fitting. The Legate, seeing in the discord between the King and the nobles an opportunity to plunder the realm, in his first arrival crammed the revenues and fruits of the benefices vacant in England into the Roman flock. Edmund rebuked the King for this Legate's arrival, and rebuked the Legate himself for harassing and plundering the English clergy through him, and for accepting such gifts. The King and the Legate ordered Edmund's speech to be mocked and scorned. But the Legate was afterwards punished for this, as for a great wrong. Meanwhile Simon de Montfort obtained from the Pope, by gifts, that the vow of his betrothed Eleanor, sister of King Henry, should be relaxed and remitted, so that he could proceed to celebrate the marriage without harm under the papal law. The Pope commanded Legate Otto, with this intervention brought in, that (the vow notwithstanding) he should give judgment in favour of the said marriage of Simon and Eleanor. He carried out the Pope's command without delay. So, with Edmund set aside, the marriage was made. This was the first cause of the contempt and disgrace in which Archbishop Edmund was held. Then, with these enmities gained by the King and the Legate, they plotted still graver measures against this innocent and pious man. At that time the Roman greed, seething and insatiable, was laid open to people of every kind, learned and most unlearned. For it is remarkable by what arts they drew money from every quarter of the Christian world, and especially in England. A tithe had been paid to the Pope some years before by Archbishop Stephen Langton, and it was exhausted; but by new contrivances the payment must be renewed. That tithe had fed the Roman army against the Emperor Frederick. Now, with a new fraud devised, the fight must be for the Holy Land. So legates were sent from the Roman Curia everywhere, who by preaching, supplicating, commanding, threatening, excommunicating and exacting, reduced countless subjects of the realm to exiles and beggars. The Pope wrote to the King of England, to the people and to the clergy, in free words coated with a veneer and in most holy appearances, but in fact contrary to all piety and Christian justice. In these letters he said he grieved at the loss of that holy kingdom, which was imminent because the truce, once agreed between the Sultan and the Eastern Emperor, would soon end. Therefore all Christians were to be stirred up to defend it, or to recover it if it was lost. And so, to so pious a deed, moved by the greatest charity, out of his full power of indulgence, absolution and binding, he granted and promised remission of sins, measured by the amount of works or of the sums given, to those who wished to enlist for that war or to give something to those setting out. Nay, those enlisted were to be marked with the sign of the Christian cross. The aid demanded was not only military but also naval. To urge this cause, preachers sprung from the order of the Friars Minor swarmed everywhere through England. The Pope granted them power to sign with the cross those who enrolled for this service, and the next day, having received money from them, to release them from their vows and grant forgiveness of sins for many days. These men, from among the religious (though the least of them), were agreeable to the people and common folk by this power received, but hateful to the monks, to whom the Pope had not granted this faculty. But soon after, the people (even with the monks themselves urging them) perceived that by a most carefully and craftily contrived trick so much money had been squeezed and collected; and when war was hostilely launched against the Emperor, the money taken from England was immediately followed by peace. No preparation for the Holy Land and no levy of soldiers was made; and those who had vowed the journey, asked by these same religious Papal questors to redeem their vows with money, began, their minds in agreement and their feelings hurt and wounded, openly and everywhere to reprove and censure such insidious papal greed. Therefore afterwards more and more they began to resist such fraudulent and unjust extortions of money, since it was openly known and talked of that Roman gluttony and filth, under the cover of sanctity, gaped for nothing but gain. But Legate Otto, so that he might more cautiously avoid this infamy and insult to his Curia, began cleverly, contrary to Roman custom, to refuse gifts, so that he might at last oppress England with heavier burdens and sate that whirlpool with abundant largesse.

units.la: Ac primum vt in omnem animos simulata sanctitate influeret, magnates diuturnâ discordia vindictam meditantes concilium Londini moduxit, cui Archiepiscopos, Episcopos cæterosque Prælatos, ac inferioris cleri procuratores adesse mandauit, vt de suæ legationis potestate cognosceret, & de Ecclesia Anglicana reformanda tractaret. Interim Episcopi & Prælati esculenta atque poculenta abunde largitos ministrabant. Petrus Wintoniensis à Rege (vt ante diximus) aula prohibitus, male sibi metuens, quinquaginta opimos boues, centum summas selectissimi tritici, & octo dolia vini generosissimi Legato misit. Hæc gratuito accepit Legatus quia à pastore locupletè profecta fuit, à exterorum accipiendis muneribus fuit temperantior, iuris ciuilis regulam secutus, vt neque passim, neque vbi neque ab omnibus acceptere videretur. Hoc concilium in Ecclesia Paulina celebratum est. Incepto exercitio misitad Legatum Rex, eiquè præcepit ne contra authoritatem potestatemque sitam regiam quicquam decerneret, aut tractaret. Vbi legatos Otto in occidentalitemph parte extrui mandauit sibi sedem fastigiosam, ad quam gradibus peruenire posset: ibi pristina inter Cant. & Ebor. Arch. de præeminentia retinuata contentio est, certabant enim vt solebant ad Papam appellando, vtri dextras aut sinistras legati sedentes tenerent. His altercantibus, Ea inquit Legatus (prolata Bulla Papali) videtis, hic depictum Christum crucifixum, eiquè a dextris Paulum, & sinistris Petrum astare, inter quos nunquam motæst de Christi dextris aut sinistris occupandis contentio, etsi ambo sint in gloria coæquali. Verumtamen propter Petri Clauigeri dignitatem, & Apostolatus principarum, merito à dextris erueis eius imagó collocanda videtur. Ita sedatis Archiepiscopis deinceps Cantuariensis a dextris; Eboracensis a sinistris legati sedebant. In hoc concilio Simon Langton Archidiaconus Cantuariensis (de quo in Stephani Archiepisc. vita antea dictum est) petiit vt Ottonis legationis authenticum Papæ mandatum publicè legeretur. Quo facto, Otto aduentus sui causam Papæ concilium declarauit. Deinde addidit ad suam notitiam peruenisse, multos in Anglia spurios & ex illegitimo eoitu natos beneficia Ecclesiastica, permultoq; plura quâ iure permissum esset possidere, quorum pleriq; nobiligenere orti, cum iam legibus amouendi essent, non modò insidias illi occultas sed vim apertam pararent. Itaque Archiepiscopos & Episcopos atque prælatos obsecrauit, vt hanc se vim prohiberent ac repellerent. Exortus deinde est Wigorniensis Episc. ex illustri progenie sanguine, mitraque deposita ita perorauit. Qui hæc beneficia (pater sancte) tenent nobiles sunt, aut ætate proueæa aut iuuenili. Senes per honorifice semper hucusq; vixerunt, familiam laetam administrarunt, eleemosynasq; foribus apertis abunde largiti sunt, hos iam ad pauperatem detrudi ignominiosissimum esset. Adolescentes autem feroces atque strenui sunt, quia armis dimicare potius quàm beneficiis cedere malint. Ego ipse in hac semper fui sententia, vt in diferimen omnium meorum beneficiorum venire malueri, quàm huiusmodi vestræ constitutionis ptextu vel vnū deposuere. Proinde rogamus vt nõu tibi minus in hoc negocio prospicias, quâ nobis qui contra tâ generosam multitudinem nos opponere in hac causa nec possumus nec audemus. Sed eo iam omisso, pro tua nostraq; incolumitate Papam cum Romam redieris, cautè prudenterq; consulas. Legatus hoc rerespondo deterritus, etsi aliis quos oratione sua deligauit amoris, prospicere ac prouidere ex vacaturis beneficiis Romanis suis voluit, tamen ab incepto destitit, & à Synodo peciit vt secum vnâ de hoc tanto incommodo communibus literis Papæ auxilium implorarent, quòd promissò pergit in concilio Legatus. Deinde constitutiones suas scriptas & in ordinem redactas legiac publicari fecit. Quæ etiam Legatiharum in Anglia constitutionum appellatione denotantur. Sed permulti (è quibus Archiepiscopus Cant. Edmundus primus atque author fuisse putabatur) finita Ottonis legatione omnia sua legatina decreta iuraretsciinderet irritaq; facere statuebant. Quòd ad Legatum delatum est, Iohanne à Papa in libello authenticô, In quo omnes illæ constitutiones exaratæ sunt decretalè de confirmandis inperpetuum Ottonis legibus Epistolam imperauit. Hanc decretalem in Papæ registro reconditam recitauit in concilio publicè Magister Eadmo, qui Ottonis constitutiones hisannotationibus quas iam habemus explanauit. His itaque constitutionibus promulgatis atque roboratis, hoc concilium tertio die dissolutum & dimissum est. Et data a Legato benedictione omnes cum paruo gaudio recesserunt.
units.tr: And first, so that he might flow into all minds under a pretended sanctity, he arranged a council at London, when the magnates, after long discord, were meditating vengeance. He ordered the archbishops, bishops, the other prelates and the proctors of the inferior clergy to attend, so that he might learn the extent of his legatine power and treat of reforming the English Church. Meanwhile the bishops and prelates supplied food and drink in abundance. Peter of Winchester, forbidden the court by the King (as we said before), fearing badly for himself, sent the Legate fifty fat oxen, a hundred quarters of the choicest wheat, and eight casks of the finest wine. The Legate accepted these as a free gift, since they came from a wealthy minister; he was more restrained in accepting gifts from foreigners, following the rule of civil law, so that he would not seem to accept them everywhere, nor from everyone, nor in every place. This council was held in St Paul's Church. When the business had begun, the King sent to the Legate and ordered him not to decree or treat anything against the authority and power of the Crown. Otto then ordered a lofty seat to be built for himself in the western part, to which he could ascend by steps. There the old contest over precedence between the Archbishops of Canterbury and York was revived, for, as usual, they were contending, appealing to the Pope, as to which of them should hold the right or the left when the legate sat. While they quarrelled, he said (producing the papal bull): "You see here Christ crucified, depicted, with Paul standing on his right and Peter on his left; between these two there was never any dispute over occupying the right or left of Christ, although both are in equal glory. Nevertheless, on account of the dignity of Peter, bearer of the keys and chief of the apostles, his image is rightly placed on the right of the cross." With the archbishops thus pacified, from then on the Archbishop of Canterbury sat at the legate's right hand, and the Archbishop of York at his left. In this council Simon Langton, Archdeacon of Canterbury (of whom we spoke earlier in the life of Archbishop Stephen), asked that the authentic mandate of the Pope for Otto's legation be read publicly. When this was done, Otto declared to the council the reason for his coming, on the Pope's behalf. Then he added that it had come to his knowledge that many in England, bastards born of illegitimate union, held ecclesiastical benefices, and far more than the law allowed them to possess; and that most of them, being of noble birth, since they were now to be removed by law, were preparing not only secret plots but open force. Therefore he begged the archbishops, bishops and prelates to forbid and repel this violence. Then the Bishop of Worcester, sprung from an illustrious family, rose, laid aside his mitre and spoke thus: "Those who hold these benefices, holy father, are nobles, some of advanced age and some young. The older men have always lived honourably up to now, have kept a generous household, and have given alms in abundance with open doors; for them to be thrust down into poverty would be most disgraceful. The young men, however, are fierce and vigorous, since they would rather fight with arms than give way in the matter of benefices. I myself have always held this view: that I would rather risk all my benefices than give up a single one on the pretext of such a constitution of yours. Therefore we ask that you look out for this business no less for yourself than for us, who can neither oppose so numerous and so noble a multitude in this cause, nor dare to. But, setting that aside, for your own safety and ours, when you return to Rome, consult the Pope cautiously and prudently." The Legate, deterred by this reply, although he wished to provide for those whom he had bound to himself by his speech with promises of affection, from the Roman benefices that were falling vacant, nevertheless desisted from the undertaking, and asked the Synod that together with him they seek the Pope's help by joint letters about this great inconvenience, which the Legate promised in the council to do. Then he had his constitutions, written out and arranged in order, read and published. These are also called the legatine constitutions in England. But very many (of whom Archbishop Edmund of Canterbury was thought to be the first and author) decided that, once Otto's legation had ended, they would tear up all his legatine decrees and render them void. When this was reported to the Legate, he obtained from the Pope, by an authentic document in which all those constitutions were written out, a decretal letter confirming Otto's laws for all time. Master Eadmer recited this decretal, which was kept in the Pope's register, publicly in the council, and explained Otto's constitutions with the annotations we now have. With these constitutions thus promulgated and strengthened, the council was dissolved and dismissed on the third day. And with the blessing given by the Legate, all departed, with little joy.

units.la: Hoc autem dissipato concilio, quia motus intestini fuit statim concitari, Papa litteris Ottonem Romam reuocauit. In quibus eum monuit tam populum quàm clerum ad grandem Romanæ sedis ignominiam oberatum eius aduentu, & ad pauperiatem exactum fuisse, proinde sibi omissis legationis negociis sine mora Romam redeundum. Sed legatus malens in Anglia remanere, & metere vbi non seminauerat, cauté procurauit, vt scriptum D. Papæ destinandum, Regis & Rich. eius fratris, ac Episcoporum sigillis firmaretur, in quo quàm vilis esset Regi, Regno atque Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ exponeretur. Qua fraude discessum hinc suum, diutius quàm vtile aut necesse Angliæ fuit, retardauit.
units.tr: This council being broken up, since internal unrest immediately broke out, the Pope recalled Otto to Rome by letter. In it he warned him that both the people and the clergy had been weighed down by his arrival, to the great disgrace of the Roman see, and reduced to poverty, and that he should therefore abandon the business of his legation and return to Rome without delay. But the legate, preferring to stay in England and reap where he had not sown, cunningly arranged for a letter to be sent to the Pope, sealed with the seals of the King, of the King's brother Richard, and of the bishops, which set out how worthless he was to the King, the kingdom and the English Church. By this trick he delayed his departure from here far longer than was useful or necessary for England.

units.la: Sub hæc tempora Hugone Wellensi Episcopi Lincoln. mortuo electus est à Capitulo Robertus cognomento Grosceeste, id est, Caput crassum, vir humilis quidem spirpe satus, sed virtute, prudentia, doctrinaq; insigni. Hunc cum Radinghi consocrare Edmundus voluit, Cantuariensiens Monachi pro iure suæ Ecclesiæ, extra quam non esse celebrandam cuiuscunq; Cantuariensi Suffraganei consecrationem se inuitis affirmabant, interceserunt.
units.tr: About this time, Hugh of Wells, bishop of Lincoln, having died, the chapter elected Robert, surnamed Grosseteste, that is, "Thick Head," a man of humble birth but of outstanding virtue, prudence and learning. Edmund wished to consecrate him together with Radingh, but the monks of Canterbury intervened, citing the right of their church, outside which they declared that no consecration of any suffragan of Canterbury should be celebrated against their wishes.

units.la: Tandem in huius consecrationem, de futura sua dissensione si alibi quam Cantuariæ deinceps consecrationes habeantur, protestati. Idem etiam Edmundus Radulphum de Madeneftane Episcopum Herefordensem consecrauit. Ac paulò post Henrico Rossenfi Episcopo mortuo, Monachi Richardum quendam de Wendouere suis suffragiis electum Edmundo consecrandum præsentarunt. Is eum vt iodignum reiecit. Hunc orta & exaggerata contentione Monachi appellando Romam volant. Edmundus eos pari celeritate sequutus est. Sed Otto Legatus, cum iam opportunitatem vindicatæ Edmundo sumendæ nactus esset, eam nulla ratione præterimisit. Primum ei iam naucam ascendenti vetuit discessum, veritus ne de semagis quàm de Monachis querelam iustiorem ad Papam deferret. Sed quia iam Ottonis à Papa reuocati, authoritas cessare Edmundo visa est, respondit eius iussu se retinere nolle, cuius non modo congressum, sed & expilationes direptionesq; fugeret, cuiusque iam reciffa nihil valeret authoritas. Ita Romam Edmundus properat. Ibi de suæ gentis atque prouinciæ Anglicanæ direptione insatiabili Ottonis impressa auaritia grauiter conquestus est. Multa etiam importunè dixit in Regem. Cuius tota criminatio in absentes emisia etiam veritissima fuit, tamen ab ipsis reis absentibus sic vitata, eorumq; intercessione atq; gratia sic ab ipso Papa reiecta est, vt in ceteris etiam suis iustissimis causis postulationibus q; succubuerit. Nam primum electio Richardi Roffensis Episcopi, quam Edmundus irritam pronunciauit, à Papaconfirmata est, & pro Monachis contra eum lata sententia. Deinde sententia quædam, quam Edmundus in Hugonem Arundellie comitem antea tulerat, alio Papæ decreta infirmata atque reuocata est, & in vtraque lite Edmundus a lexpensas mille marcarum aduersis partibus soluendas adiudicatus. Ita inglorius, tristis, nec itinere magis & longinqua prosectione lassus, quàm sumptibus defatigatus, & ad summam inopiam pulsus in Angliam vir pius reuersus est. Eum iam redeuntem excepit noua contumelia atq; calamitate Legatus hominemq; Romæ prostratum & deiectum, omniumq; rerum tædio afflictum atque miserum, maiori mærore ægritudineque confecit. Monachi enim Cantuarienses e legerunt, ubique præfecerunt Priorem inconsulto Archiepiscopo. Quod quia præter ius ac consuetudinem factum est, eos excommunicauit Edmundus, quos Legatus non minus cæca munerum cupiditate, quàm aperto Edmundi odio relaxauit, eorumq; electionem confirmauit.
units.tr: Finally, at this consecration they protested about their future dissent if consecrations were thereafter held anywhere other than Canterbury. Edmund also consecrated Ralph of Maidstone as bishop of Hereford. Shortly afterwards, when Henry, bishop of Rochester, died, the monks presented Edmund with one Richard of Wendover, whom they had chosen by their votes, for consecration. He rejected him as unworthy. The monks, with the dispute having arisen and been inflamed, fled to Rome by appeal, and Edmund followed them with equal speed. But Otto the legate, having obtained an opportunity to take vengeance on Edmund, let it pass by in no way. First, as Edmund was already going aboard ship, he forbade his departure, fearing that he might carry to the Pope a more just complaint about himself than about the monks. But since the authority of Otto, now recalled by the Pope, seemed to Edmund to have lapsed, he replied that he did not wish to be detained at the order of one whose company he shunned, and whose plundering and depredations he shunned even more, and whose authority, now cut off, counted for nothing. So Edmund hastened to Rome. There he bitterly complained of the insatiable plundering of his nation and of the English province, a plundering stamped with Otto's avarice. He also spoke many intemperate things against the King. The whole accusation, though launched against men who were absent, was entirely true; yet it was so evaded by the accused, who were themselves absent, and so rejected by the Pope through their intercession and favour, that Edmund gave way in his other most just causes and demands as well. For first, the election of Richard, bishop of Rochester, which Edmund had declared void, was confirmed by the Pope, and sentence was pronounced for the monks against him. Then a certain sentence which Edmund had earlier pronounced against Hugh, earl of Arundel, was annulled and revoked by another decree of the Pope, and in both suits Edmund was adjudged to pay the expenses of a thousand marks to the opposing parties. Thus the pious man returned to England inglorious and sad, worn out not so much by the journey and the long travel as by expense, and driven to extreme poverty. As he was returning, the legate met him with a fresh insult and calamity, and wore him down, a man prostrated and cast down at Rome, weary of everything, wretched, with greater grief and sickness. For the monks of Canterbury elected a prior and appointed him everywhere without consulting the archbishop. Because this was done against law and custom, Edmund excommunicated them; the legate absolved them, no less from blind greed for gifts than from open hatred of Edmund, and confirmed their election.

units.la: Eandem vero iterum Edmundus infirmauit, & Monachorum contumacium poenam auxit, eorumque Ecclesiam interdicto supposuit. Tandem crescente duo hoc, tumultu ne superior in hac controuersia Edmundus videretur, Legatusipse Cantuariam accedit, auditaque & repetita iterum causa, compertaque Monachorum fraude in quodam authentico scripto depraurando, Priorem amouit, Monachos acriter castigauit, é quibus quosdam perpetuæ penitentiæ damnauit, quosdam ardiori regulæ ordinique astrinxit.
units.tr: Edmund again annulled the same, increased the penalty of the obstinate monks, and placed their church under interdict. At last, as this dispute grew into a tumult, and lest Edmund seem the superior in this controversy, the legate himself went to Canterbury. Having heard the case again and gone over it, and having discovered the monks' fraud in corrupting a certain authentic document, he removed the prior, sharply rebuked the monks, condemned some of them to lifelong penance, and bound others to a stricter rule and discipline.

units.la: Verumtamen prorogato iam sibi Legationis tempore, & Edmundo Archiepiscopo ad hoc silentium coacto, vt neque responderet nec omnino hitcere auderet, tanquam callidus & clandestinus inuenerator qui so insinuauit dolo, iam tandem rebus ex sua sententia firmatis exactiones aperte cepit flagitare. Ac primum vt Monachos compesceret, authoritate Papæ Abbates regni in Ecclesiam S. Martini Londini conuocauit; his duras & tasque leges de ordine Monastico reformando dedit. Ita Regeipso, diuurnitate & obsequio, Archiepiscopis autem & Episcopis, Abbatibus totidemque Clerorum artificiose meditatis a se technis in sua potestate nutumq; deductis, impetrare exfitimauit sibi facile esse, quicquid rogaret, cum iam imperare potuisset. Ad hanc direptionem seu postulandam seu imperandam cogit Episcopos ad Synodū Londini, ab his nouas pecuniarias petit procurationes. Sed Episcopi iam praeter opinionem legati responderunt. Quod totics boni Ecclesiæ exhauiretur Romana importunitas, quod nullo modo amplius tolerarent, exhibeat vos qui inconsulte vos vocauit. Quo responso Henricum, qui Ottonem acceperat, & postea a Papa audacium detinuit, notarunt. Ac postea quam concedere nequicquam voluerunt, cum magno murmure frementes a concilio discesserunt. Hac tactus contumelia in Scotiam se actingit. Sed Scotorum Rex aducntu eius cognito occurrit ei suum regnum ingredienti, ingressumq; prohibet. Nunquam aliquem ante a Papa Legatum Scotiam intrauisse afferens. Satis enim recte & ex ordine religionis coponi posse in Scotia res Ecclesiasticas sine Papalis legati interuentu. Sed ille versutus Otto, ne cum tam insigni contumelia ac tepulsa in Angliam tepellerent, multis precibus ingressum saltem, & aliquam moram in Scotia his legibus imperrauit. Ne quicquam incolulto Rege moliretur, utque Chirographo suo authentico ante discessum patefacteret ac indicaret, illi ingressum non esse trahendum deinceps in consequentiam.
units.tr: However, his term as legate having been extended, and Archbishop Edmund having been forced into such silence that he neither answered nor dared to utter a word, the legate, a crafty and secret contriver who had insinuated himself by guile, at last, with affairs settled to his liking, began openly to demand exactions. First, to restrain the monks, he summoned the abbots of the kingdom by papal authority to the church of St Martin in London, and gave them harsh and burdensome laws for the reform of monastic order. Having thus brought under his power and nod the King himself, by flattery and obsequiousness, and the archbishops and bishops, the abbots, and as many of the clergy as he had skilfully ensnared in his own schemes, he thought it easy to obtain whatever he asked, since he could already command. To this plundering, whether it was to be requested or enforced, he compelled the bishops to a synod at London, and from them demanded new monetary procurations. But the bishops answered, contrary to the legate's expectation, that the Roman importunity should not drain the good of the Church so often, that they would by no means tolerate it any longer, and that he who had summoned them without consultation should provide for it himself. By this reply they reproached Henry, who had received Otto and had afterwards been held back by the Pope's audacity. And when they would in no way yield, they left the council fuming with loud murmuring. Stung by this insult, he turned to Scotland. But the King of the Scots, learning of his arrival, met him as he entered his kingdom and forbade his entry, declaring that no papal legate had ever before entered Scotland, and that church affairs could be settled rightly and in good religious order in Scotland without the intervention of a papal legate. But the crafty Otto, lest he return to England with so notable an insult and rebuff, obtained by many entreaties at least entry and some stay in Scotland, on these conditions: that he would undertake nothing without the King's knowledge, and that before his departure he would declare and make known, by his authentic written instrument, that his entry should not be drawn into a precedent in future.

units.la: Ingressus tandem his conditionibus Scotiam, Episcopos, & eos qui Ecclesiastica beneficia possidebant, ad se sigillatim vocauit, pecunias multas Papæ nomine colligit, tandem quasi de improuiso Regeque inconsulto recessit clam a Scotia, Chirographumque illud quo Regi oportuit testatum reliquisse, illum suum in Scotiam introitum non futurum deinceps praeiudicium & exemplum, iam simulate ut Regem falleret scriptum secum subduxit.
units.tr: Having at last entered Scotland on these terms, he summoned the bishops and those who held ecclesiastical benefices to him one by one, and collected much money in the Pope's name. Finally, as if unexpectedly and without the King's knowledge, he secretly left Scotland, and he took with him that written document, which he should have left attested for the King, declaring that his entry into Scotland would not be a prejudice or precedent in future. It had been drawn up in feigned terms, so as to deceive the King.

units.la: Reuertis iam Otto in Angliam Imperatorem Fredericum Papæ iussu, primum in Cœnobio S. Albani, deinde in Ecclesia Paulina Londini excommunicauit. Hinc rumores variis in plebe exorti atque sparsi de Papæ & Imperatoris meritis, veer religiosior iudicandus esset. Cuius tam varii omniumque pene vocibus frequentati sermonis cauam dederunt tam Imperatoris quam Papæ ad Regem & magnates Angliæ literæ eius excusatoriae, huius autem crimi inatoriae.
units.tr: Otto now returned to England and, by the Pope's order, excommunicated the Emperor Frederick, first at the abbey of St Albans and then at St Paul's in London. Hence various rumours arose and spread among the common people about the merits of the Pope and of the Emperor, as to which of them was to be judged more religious. The cause of this talk, so varied and so frequent on almost everyone's lips, was given by letters: the letters of the Emperor and of the Pope to the King and the magnates of England, the Emperor's apologetic, the Pope's accusatory.

units.la: Quibus in populum petiulgatis ipsi Romani Pontificis fautores solam execrabilem auarit am omnem fidem suis suasionibus abrogasse aiunt. In omnium ore haec voces iterare saepe sunt. Sentit Ecclesia Occidentalis praecipue Anglicana oppressiones Romanorum quotidianas, necadhuc vnquam vel minimas pressuras sentit Imperiales. Addidisque populus: Quid tibi vult hoc. In Epistolis suis humiliter de Deo scribit Imperator & Catholicè, nisi tantum quod hac victima, Papali personæ derogat, non officio, nec publicè praedicat, nec procaciter sustinet quicquam haereticum, vel prophanum, non vsurarios nobis imitit sicut Papa nec raptores reditum. Et sic est eorum schisma in populis formidandum.
units.tr: When these were published among the people, the Pope's own supporters said that only execrable avarice had destroyed all faith through their persuasions. On everyone's lips these words were often repeated: the Western Church, and especially the English, feels the daily oppressions of the Romans, and yet has never yet felt even the slightest pressures from the Imperials. And the people added: "What is this to you?" In his letters the Emperor writes humbly and catholically of God; he only detracts from the papal person in that he is not wanting in this victim; he does not preach publicly, nor insolently uphold anything heretical or profane; he does not send us usurers as the Pope does, nor extortioners of revenues. And so their schism is to be feared among the peoples.

units.la: Isdem temporibus manus cupiditatis Romanæ iniecta in Ecclesiam, quæ fuerat auris patronatus militis culifidam Aquilonaris Thomæ Tuing. Is Romanorum iuga cervicibus Anglorum depellere contendens cum procerum literis Romam profectus est. Quarum literarum summa erat haec. Demersam pene Romanis suis tibus, auctis eius sedis in eos procellis, Angliæ liberiatis manu cula, proinde coactos se exeunte è seminis. Dominum qui in Perri nauicula quieuit, vnaq; voce clamare. Dominè salua nos, quia perimus. Sed patronatus multarum in Anglia Ecclesiarum fuisse sibi suisque maiorius primus Christianæ religionis institutione haereditarium atque liberum, antequam nuper hoc libri a Papæ mandatariis & ministris admisi cepisse sit. Nescire se verum eius vocationem, ut cum intelligo ac, nisi fas, ac tum tum tegni auctorem. Vocunque fit, prosperacius illos, et hic extraordinarie tum fit, uerare, & erudiit ex destrutionem, ac tum prefatum. Cum tamen se iam ad praeiudicium Roberti Tuing militis renouatum ab Ebor. Archiepiscopo nolit ferendam exemplum. Timere se ex vicino incendio periculum suum, valdeq; mirari quod ab eodem fonte Romano, aquis dulcis & amara simul possit diffluere; petere se vt quod ab Eboracensi admissum contra Roberti ius fuit; authoritate Papæ refutatur.
units.tr: At the same time, the grasping hand of Rome was laid upon the Church. It had been the patronage of the knight Thomas Tuing, a loyal man of the north, which he now sought to lift from the necks of the English. He set out for Rome with letters from the nobles. The substance of those letters was this: the English Church, nearly sunk by the Roman storms, was being pressed in its own waters, and it was forced to cry out, as the disciples did in Peter's boat, "Lord, save us, for we perish." The patronage of many English churches had belonged to him and his ancestors, from the first institution of the Christian religion, as a hereditary and free right, and only recently had the mandataries and ministers of the Pope begun to take it away. He said that he did not know the true reason for this, and that he could not understand how such a thing could be done. Whatever the cause, he said, it had been brought about by an extraordinary act, and it harmed the Church and the realm alike. Since the precedent of Sir Robert Tuing had now been renewed by the Archbishop of York, he would not endure the example. He feared danger to himself from the nearby fire, and he was greatly surprised that from the same Roman spring sweet and bitter waters could flow together. He asked that what the Archbishop of York had done to the prejudice of Robert's right be annulled by papal authority.

units.la: P
units.tr: P

units.la: His literis ferocia Papalis aliquantulum domata est, qui eos lenissimis aequissimisque literis leniuit, & aliis ad Legatum datis imperauit, vt quod Eboracensi in praeiudicium Roberti Tuing perfecit irritum decernatur, nihilque deinceps contra Laicorum iura in Ecclesiarum patronatu Ratuarur. Sed quo magis sibi Papa in Laicos benignior esse visus est, eo atrocius in totum Clerum saeuit. Qui cum Laicos Papalibus nexibus lenaeri, seq; solos Papali crudelitati relictos viderent. Heu (inquiunt) soluum daze sunt in direptionem & praedam Romanam possessiones personarum Ecclesiasticarum, & imbellium religiosorum.
units.tr: By these letters the Pope's fierceness was somewhat tamed. He soothed the English with very gentle and fair letters, and by other letters sent to the legate he ordered that what the Archbishop of York had done to the prejudice of Robert Tuing be declared void, and that nothing further be attempted against the rights of laymen in the patronage of churches. But the more the Pope seemed to be kinder to the laity, the more savagely he raged against the whole clergy. The clergy, seeing that the laity had been bound by papal snares and that they themselves had been left alone to papal cruelty, cried out: "Alas, we alone are left to be plundered and despoiled by Rome, the possessions of ecclesiastical persons and of defenceless religious."

units.la: Legatus autem iterum congregauit Londini Episcopos. Qui sperabant tantz ac tam crebrae direptionis aliquam leuationem, sed legatus contra nummarias procurationes expectauit. Cui petenti vnanimes & concordes responderunt Episcopi. Quod toties & tam diuersis argumentis bona Ecclesiae exhauserat Romana semper hians importunitas, quod exhaustis iam fere omnibus, vix poterant respirare vel ad modicum tempus, nec vellent huiusmodi amplius extorsiones tolerare. Et adiderunt. Quid vtilitatis contulit adhuc regno vel Ecclesiae istius superstitiosa dominatio? Itaque Legatus ab istorum persuasione sibi tam inutili, ad humilitatem Monachorum & religiosorum soluto hoc concilio conuersus est, a quibus quicquid voluit impetrauit sine gratia. Ac paulo post quam hoc concilium dimissum est, ante Cleri dissessionem Willielmus Rale Episcopus Norwicensis ab Edmundo consecrationem accepit in Ecclesia Paulina Londinensi, infinita Praelatorum & magnatum turba praesente. Sed Papa cum Imperatore Frederico aduersus trocissimo bello persequi proposuisset, nouas vbique pecunias corradendi artes excogitat. Orsus semper versutias & dolos suos in Anglia, in hac praesertim Regis procerumque exitiosa penè regno discordia: quam is vt sibi commodissimam captauit, eamq; simultatibus clam per Ottonem interiectis, ne suo incommodo sedaretur, alterius. Ac primum cruce signaris (de quibus ad bellum Hierosolymitanum paratis sante diximus) per Ottonem Legatum imperat, ne se ad id iter ante aliud tempus a se staruendum parerent. Quos a voto postea nummis legato soluris liberauit. Deinde a fide a subditis Imperatori iuramento data omnes absoluit, praecepitq; vt tota vi in eum tanquam in Dei & Papae inimicum irruerent. Sed tantum promeruit Romanae Ecclesiae improbitas omnibus execrandis, quod a nullis, vel a paucis, meruit Papalis authoritas exaudiri. Alia deinde callidi tate rursus aggressus est Papam pecuniariam. Emisit per totum orbem Christianum infinitam scaturiginem fratrum minorum, quos vbiq; praedicatores ordinauit, vt Imperatori obliterarent, & singulis pecunias ad hoc bellum contra Imperatorem gerendum minis, blanditiis, indulgentiisq; ac peccatorum remissionibus imperarent. Huius ordinis viri cum ob voluntariam professionem eleemosynas depeciati ante collegium, iam auctoritate Papali ceteris Clericis ac religiosis elatiores, destinati ad Reges de Papae voluntate nuncii speciales, aulas intrabant.
units.tr: The legate then again assembled the bishops at London. They hoped for some relief from such great and frequent plundering, but the legate looked for money from them through procurations. To his request the bishops replied with one voice and in agreement: that the Roman greed, always gaping, had drained the goods of the Church by so many and such various pretexts, and that now, with almost everything exhausted, they could scarcely draw breath even for a short time, and were unwilling to endure such extortions any longer. And they added: "What advantage has this superstitious domination yet brought to the realm or to this Church?" So the legate, finding no use in their persuasion, turned to the humble monks and religious men, dismissed this council, and from them obtained whatever he wished, without any goodwill. And shortly after this council was dismissed, before the division of the clergy, William Rale, Bishop of Norwich, received consecration from Edmund in St Paul's Church in London, with a vast crowd of prelates and magnates present. But when the Pope had resolved to pursue the Emperor Frederick with a most bitter war, he devised new arts of gathering money everywhere. He always set his tricks and deceits to work in England, especially in that discord between the King and the nobles which was nearly fatal to the realm. He seized upon it as most convenient for himself, and he kept it alive by secretly stirring up quarrels through Otto, so that it should not be settled to his own disadvantage. First, through Otto the legate, he ordered those marked with the cross (of whom we spoke above, as made ready for the Jerusalem war) not to set out on that journey before another time appointed by himself. Later he released them from their vow for money paid to the legate. Then he absolved all the subjects from the oath of fidelity given to the Emperor, and ordered them to rush upon him with all their might as an enemy of God and of the Pope. But the wickedness of the Roman Church had earned all manner of execration, so that the papal authority earned to be heeded by none, or by very few. Next, with yet another cunning, he again turned to raising money for the Pope. He sent out through the whole Christian world an endless flood of Friars Minor, whom he appointed everywhere as preachers, to preach against the Emperor, and to order each person to contribute money for this war against the Emperor, by threats, flatteries, indulgences and remissions of sins. Men of this order, who had been regarded with esteem for their voluntary profession of poverty, were now raised above the other clergy and religious by papal authority; sent as special messengers to the kings at the Pope's will, they entered the royal courts.

units.la: Non secus quondam mollibus induti in domibus Regum erant; sed vilibus vestiti in domibus, cameris, & palatiis Principum, Regum consiliis secretioribus admitti bantur. Ex hac sordida labe Angliae Rex quendam Iohannem S. Ægidii fratrem ad suum consilium accciuit. Imperator de Regis Angliae ad Papae voluntatem inclinatione certior factus, degenerem eius timidumque animum arguit, quod se, qui sororis (quae coniugio nita sibi affinitate coniunctus esset, in suo regno excommunicari a Papa permitteret. Tum quod immemor nuptialis foederis & amicitiae, Papae Legatum exhaustorem atque vastatorem sui regni, ad Ythinque perniciem ac ruinam grassatin Anglia, indeque ad Papam regni sui Thesauros atque copias transferretam dui sitisset. Rex Imperatoris nam Papae diffluxerat dubius, scriptis tam ad hunc quam ad illum literis, Papam vt mittus cum suo affini, qui sororem suam duxisset, ageret rogauit. Imperatori, quod sibi tributarius atque vassallo Papae necesse esset in omnibus obtemperare Papae, se exoluisset. Sed tamen sibi conscius quod Ottonem occultum regni sui, & Imperatoris inimicum, nam a sibi familiaris tate coniunxisset, eamq; amicitiam vt sibi regnoque in fidelem amputare volusset, consuluit Ottoni bona fide vt Romam ocyus properaret, meanendum enim ei esse tam a Clero quam a populo Anglicano, sed morem hic diutius fecisset. Legatus hac Regis monitione perturbatus, nec moram hic diuturnam sperans, imitatus est medicos non indoctos, qui his quorum curationem suscipiunt, quoq; cito ac sine suspicione aeq; sensu perimere statuerunt, leuissimo mortis genere, sanguinis millione interimit. Sic legat ex Anglia ut suae expilarione exhausta & exangui noua non modo vitale sanguine, sed ipsam animam elicere tentabat. Primo nouas procurationes exegit, deinde omnes ad militiam Ierosolymitanam suo nutu ascriptos, exacta solutione, voto soluit.
units.tr: Just as in the past, they were clothed in soft garments in the houses of kings; yet, dressed in cheap clothing, they were admitted into the houses, chambers and palaces of princes and into the more secret counsels of kings. From this filthy taint, the King of England took a certain John, a brother of St Giles, into his council. The Emperor, having been informed of the King of England's inclination to the Pope's will, accused him of a degenerate and timid spirit, because he had allowed himself, who was bound to his sister by marriage and affinity, to be excommunicated in his kingdom by the Pope. Moreover, forgetful of the marriage covenant and of friendship, he had permitted the Pope's legate, the exhauster and despoiler of his kingdom, to rage through England to its ruin, and from there to transfer the treasures and resources of his realm to the Pope. The King, wavering between the Emperor and the Pope, wrote letters to both, asking the Pope to act through his kinsman, who had married his sister. To the Emperor he replied that, as a tributary and vassal of the Pope, he was bound to obey the Pope in all things. Yet, conscious that Otto, a secret enemy of his kingdom and of the Emperor, had been joined to him by intimacy, and wishing to cut off that friendship as disloyal to himself and his kingdom, he advised Otto in good faith to hasten to Rome, since he was to be awaited by both clergy and people of England, but here he had lingered too long. The legate, disturbed by the King's warning and hoping for no long delay, imitated those not unskilled physicians who resolve to kill their patients quickly and without suspicion, by the mildest kind of death, and so he destroyed him by repeated bloodletting. Thus the legate drained England, and, with his plunder exhausted and his victim bloodless, he tried to draw out not only fresh vital blood but the very soul. First he exacted new procurations; then, once payment had been extracted, he released from their vows all who had been enrolled by his nod for the Jerusalem campaign.

units.la: Hae hippo
units.tr: These things hitherto.

units.la: Hoc loppū & tamsoribus cum omni debacchatione notum est.
units.tr: All this, both in its places and its times, is known with every kind of raving.

units.la: Illas procurationes nullis minis obtinere poterat. Absurdum enim videbatur etiam simplicibus, quod simplicem Dei populum substantia sua moliebatur Romana curia priua re, nihil petens nisi aurum & argentum. Tandem vero in discriminePapa positus instante cum suis copiis Imperatore, mandat Ottoni vt quintam Anglieanorum prouentuum ad bellicos suos contra Imperatorem vsus sine mora cogeret. Otto nulla procrastinatio ne aur circuitione vsus hoc à Rege, Clero, populoq; flagitat. Ad Regem his verbis fideles sui accessere. Domine Princeps nominatissime, quare permittis Angliam fieri prædam & desolationem transeuntium, quasi vineam sine maceria communem omni viatori, ab apris exterminandā: cum habeas efficax priuilegium, vt non fiant tales in regno isto ex actiones: nec sir dignus priuilegio, quieo concessio abutatur. Quibus talia persuadenti bus, ait. Nec volo nec audeo Domino Papæ, in aliquibus contradicere.
units.tr: He could not obtain those procurations by any threats. Even simple people thought it absurd that the Roman curia, asking for nothing but gold and silver, was draining the substance of God's simple people for its own private ends. At last, however, the Pope was placed in danger, with the Emperor advancing against him with his forces, and he ordered Otto to collect the fifth of English revenues without delay for his warlike purposes against the Emperor. Otto, using no delay or circumlocution, demanded this from the King, the clergy and the people. His faithful men approached the King with these words: "Most renowned Lord Prince, why do you allow England to become the prey and desolation of passers-by, like a vineyard without a wall, open to every traveller and trampled by wild boars? You have an effective privilege so that such things do not happen in this kingdom, and he is not worthy of a privilege whose concession is abused." To men who urged him thus, he replied: "I neither wish nor dare to oppose the Lord Pope in anything."

units.la: Hoc Regis responso populus salutem desperauit, & Regis regniq; calamitatem deplorauit. Legatus vero Regis animo sic fracto & Papæ metu debilitato infolētior, Episcopos, Magnates, & Prælatos Radinghi congregat, Papæ mandata de colligenda prouentuum quinta exponit. Illi Regis formidine qui solus resistere debuit atque potuit attoniti, negare aperte noluerunt, deliberandi saltem inducias petierunt. Dies datus statuendi est. Eo dic cum Edmundus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus de quibusdam suis tam contra Regem ipsum, quam contra Cant. Monachos coram Papa expositis querelis, sententiam ex suo desiderio expectasset, (quanquam semper antea audacter restiterat) tamen ea fpenixus, (quæ vt postea dicemus, eum maxime fefellit, & in exilium ac è vita coegit,) Papæ postulationi concessit, & vt reliquus tam flagitiosæ solutionis exemplum præberet, octingentas marcas silico numeravit. Huius exemplo reliqui æquali solutioni inuiti afsensi sunt, promissamque pecuniam præstiterunt. Hanc executandam & vaferrimam Papæ rapinam, sequuta est altera grauior & callidior. Intrauit enim Petrus Rufus quidam clandestinus Papæ ad eruendam ex omnibus latebris pecuniam nuncius. Hic omnes locupletes Episcopos, & Prælatos sigillatim pertransiit; à singulis pecunias Papæ nomine exegit. Denegantibus & morosis, quid inquit? Hic atque Episcopus, Abbas, vel Decanus hoc idem sæpius factitauit. Demum adactos hac fraude solutioni iureiurādo astrinxit, ne cuipiam negocium Papæ ante sex menses indicarent.
units.tr: The people gave up hope of safety after this answer from the King, and lamented the calamity of the King and the kingdom. The legate, his spirit thus broken by the King's response and his strength weakened by fear of the Pope, grew more insolent. He gathered the bishops, magnates and prelates at Reading and set out the Pope's commands for collecting the fifth. Stunned by fear of the King, the one man who ought to have been able to resist, they did not dare to refuse openly, and at least asked for time to deliberate. A day was appointed for deciding. On that day Edmund, Archbishop of Canterbury, had laid before the Pope his complaints, some against the King himself and some against the monks of Canterbury, and he hoped for a judgment in his favour. Although he had always resisted boldly before, he now yielded to the Pope's demand, as we shall say later, the hope which mainly deceived him and drove him into exile and out of life. So that he might provide an example to the rest of so shameful a payment, he counted out eight hundred marks in silver. Following his example, the others, though unwilling, assented to the same payment and paid the promised money. After this rapine was carried out, the Pope's most cunning robbery was followed by another, heavier and more crafty. For a certain secret messenger of the Pope, Peter Rufus, came in to drag money out of every hiding place. He went through all the wealthy bishops and prelates one by one and demanded money from each in the Pope's name. When they refused or delayed, what did he say? He did the same thing repeatedly with every bishop, abbot or dean. At last he bound those brought to payment by this fraud with an oath not to tell anyone about the business for six months.

units.la: Tandē Pontificibus & Prelatis expilatis descendit Papa per legatum ad inferiores Clericos absorbendos. Hos, nempe parochos, legatus in Berksheria conuocat. Exponit bellum contra Imperatorem hæreticum à Papa fine mora gerenduin. Illi respondent Imperatorem nondum eo crimine condemnatum.
units.tr: At last, when the bishops and prelates had been stripped, the Pope went down through the legate to swallow up the lower clergy. The legate summoned these, namely the parish priests, in Berkshire. He set out the war against the heretical Emperor, which the Pope was to wage without delay. They replied that the Emperor had not yet been condemned for that crime.

units.la: Præterea Ecclesiam non vti bracchio seculari contra hæreticos. Deinde si se Papa defendere, aut Imperatorem oppugnare cupit, id ex suis Romanis facultatibus faciat. Anglicanas enim Ecclesiasticas possessiones non ex arca Petri sed ex Principum atq; magnatum domi concessione suppeditatas ad Anglicarum Ecclesiarum regimen, non ad Papalia præliafuisse. Hos parochos tandem ad se, dissensione interiecta, Legatus traxit.
units.tr: Moreover, the Church does not use the secular arm against heretics. Next, if the Pope wishes to defend himself or attack the Emperor, let him do so from his own Roman resources. For the ecclesiastical possessions of England were supplied not from St Peter's chest but from the grant of princes and magnates, for the government of the English churches, not for papal wars. At last the legate drew these parish priests to himself, after a dissension had arisen between them.

units.la: Paulò post Ecclesia S. Pauli Londini à Rogero Londinensi Episcopo titulo Cathedrali dedicata est. Cui rei gerendæ Rex cum Episcopis & magnatibus interfuit. Quibus omni bus Londinensis Episcopus, Decanus & capitulum eiusdem Ecclesiæ lautissimum conuiuium instruxerunt, Legatus vt aliquid pro suo iure in tanta solemnitate agere videretur, anteactorum in quatuordecim annis criminum in hoctempore dedicationis tempo re deuote orantibus remissionem edicto in templi valuis affixo tribuit.
units.tr: A little later the church of St Paul in London was dedicated as a cathedral by Roger, Bishop of London. The King attended this ceremony with the bishops and magnates. For all of them the Bishop of London, the dean and the chapter of that church provided a most lavish banquet. So that the legate might seem to do something by his own right in such a solemnity, he granted, by an edict fixed to the doors of the church, forgiveness of the crimes committed during the previous fourteen years to those who prayed devoutly at the time of the dedication.

units.la: Sed post has dedicatorias epulas, fnamque in delinquenti venia concedenda facilitatem, aliam iam tanquam vltimam manum Clericorum bonis adfertre à Papa cogitur.
units.tr: But after these dedication feasts, and after the readiness to grant pardon for wrongdoing, the Pope was compelled to bring against the goods of the clergy another attack, as if it were the final blow.

units.la: Qui in congregandā pecunia vigilantissimus pastor iubet ne omnē simul Clerū ad solutionē vrgeat, ne vna voce q; sæpe fecerunt contradicat, sed singulos seorsim artificiose iterū tractet, Rege tamē in eos prius cōmoto, quò toti deterriti atq; stupefacti facilius ci tiusq; soluant. Legatus vero, qui tam improbū magistrū habuit, de docto factus iā doctior ad nocendū, primū Regis animū in eos incēdit, deinde Londinum omnes concilii de re bus Ecclesiasticis ineundi prætextu congregat. Ibi nulla res,ppositae deliberationi fuit, sed legati astutia, Clerus totus à Rege præsente multis minis & conuitiis exagitatus, finitó mox concilio discessit. Legatus labefactatam & defesiam iam prædam ea ratione quam Papa præscripserat, inseqitur, eamque misere dilaniatam vorat. His factis cum omnibus iam inuisus maximo odio legatus flagraret, cum Oxoniensem Academiam visitare vellet, Abbatis Ofnei Coenobii hospitio vsus est, ibi perhonorifice à Scholaribus delicatissimis atque vberrimis esculentis poculentisque oblatis ab eoque acceptis inuitatus. Cum autem (vt in tam celebris & famosi viri aduentu fieri solet) Scholarium turba intrô-ire hospitium eius vellet, a ianitore ac legati famulis vi repulsi fuissent. Id aegrè tulerunt, eoque molestius quod tantis muneribus ipsum louem placari potuisse perabant. Itaque vim vi repellentes ad arma venerunt. Prodierunt conferrum Romanicum Oxonienbus dimicaturi, sed Coquo Legati in ea dimicatione trucidato superati recesserunt, & occlusis sordibus ingredi volentibus restiterunt.
units.tr: This most watchful minister in gathering money ordered that the whole clergy not be pressed for payment all at once, lest they contradict with one voice, as they had often done, but that he deal with each separately and artfully again, though first the King should be stirred up against them, so that all, terrified and stunned, might pay more easily and quickly. The legate, who had so wicked a master, having become more learned in harming by the teaching he had received, first inflamed the King's mind against them, then gathered them all at London under the pretext of holding a council on Church matters. There no business was put before the deliberation, but by the legate's cunning the whole clergy was harassed by the King, who was present, with many threats and reproaches, and when the council was soon ended they departed. The legate then pursued the prey, now weakened and exposed, in the manner the Pope had prescribed, and devoured it, wretchedly torn to pieces. After these things, the legate, now hated by everyone and burning with the greatest odium, wished to visit the University of Oxford. He used the hospitality of the abbot of the monastery of Osney, and there he was received very honourably by the scholars, who offered him and entertained him with the most delicate and abundant food and drink. But when the crowd of scholars, as usually happens at the arrival of so famous and celebrated a man, wished to enter his lodging, they were driven back by force by the doorkeeper and the legate's servants. The scholars took this badly, and all the more so because they thought the legate could have been appeased by such gifts. So, repelling force with force, they came to arms. They came out against the Roman company, ready to fight the Oxonians, but in that fight the legate's cook was slain, and they were beaten and withdrew, and when the gates were shut they resisted those who wanted to enter.

units.la: Legatus ipse horrore ac metu tremens in Ofnei templi Turri sen pinnacidio se occultat. Inuestigantes eum undique Oxonienses, & exclamant. Exi foras Ecclesie, expilator Angliae, Romanae cupiditatis gurges. Ille misso clam ad Regem, qui tum Wallingfordiae agebat nū. 10, eius praesidio a tanto periculo & Scholarium obsidione liberati petit. Rex missis satellitibus hominem eximit. Liberatus iam in Oxonienses fauit, omnes sacris interdicit, officiis & beneficiis praeditos priuat, Ecclesias interdicto reclusit, lectiones, disputationes ac quaecunque literarum exercitationes fieri vetat. Ab his censuris liberari & absolui nō poterant, antequam Abbas Ofnei, praefectiq; ac magistri capite pedibus, nudi, t ogis exuti, reliquiq; vestibus discinctis transeundo platea Ghepsidè ad domum legati accessissent, eique se supplicis obtulissent. Fabianus huius tam hostilis dimicationis causam docet, quod constitutiones in Presbyteros coniugatos, atque concubinarios absolui, nuuenili Clero parum gratas sanxiuisset.
units.tr: The legate himself, trembling with horror and fear, hid himself in the tower or pinnacle of the church of Osney. The Oxonians searched for him on every side and shouted: "Come out, Church's plunderer, gulf of Roman greed!" He secretly sent to the King, who was then at Wallingford, and asked to be freed from so great a danger and from the siege of the scholars by his protection. The King sent soldiers and drew the man out. Freed, he now turned against the Oxonians, placed all under interdict from sacred rites, deprived of offices and benefices those who held them, closed the churches under interdict, and forbade lectures, disputations and all exercises of learning. They could not be freed or absolved from these censures until the abbot of Osney, and the prefects and masters, with bare heads and bare feet, their gowns taken off and the rest of their clothing loosened, had walked through the street of Gepsid to the legate's house, and had presented themselves to him as suppliants. Fabian teaches that the cause of this so hostile conflict was that he had enacted constitutions against married and concubinary priests, which were little welcome to the young clergy.

units.la: Superest vt de exilio morteque Edmundi Cant. Arch. pauca dicamus. Inter caeteras querelas quas contra Regem Papae porrexerat, maxima fuit, quod Ecclesias tam Metropoliticas quam Cathedrales atque Conuentuales vacuas, & pastoribus orbatas ad suā vtilitatem & detrimentum Ecclesiarum diutius in sua custodia teneret. Itaque a Papa impetrauit, vt si Rex electione permissa de digno aliquo pastore Ecclesiae cuicunque vacanti intra semestre spacium non prouideret, iure perinde ac in parochialibus Ecclesiis deuoluto ab Archiepiscopo prouincia prouideretur. Quod Papae decretum magna pecunia data ab Edmundo obtentum, Rex ab eodem Papa rescindi ac in irritum reuocari procurauit, In quo sane Pohdorus ipse falsus decepit saepe multos, dum hoc a Rege ipso per Edmund, & aliquandiu seruatum seribiz, donec confuto lucro carens quod ante pro miserat, ipse reuocauit. Non enim a Rege sed a Papa, Regi damnosa protecta haec concessio est. Deinde nec vnquam receptum exemplo vllo aut vsu fuit. Rex enim accensus Bonifacium quendam Winton. Episcopum se ignaro electum, vt Regiam potestatem declararet, protinus amouit.
units.tr: It remains for us to say a little about the exile and death of Edmund, Archbishop of Canterbury. Among the other complaints which he had laid before the Pope against the King, the greatest was that the King kept in his own custody the metropolitan, cathedral and conventual churches, which were vacant and deprived of ministers, for his own profit and to the detriment of the churches. So he obtained from the Pope that if the King, with election permitted, did not provide a suitable minister to any vacant church within six months, provision should be made by the Archbishop of the province, by right just as in parish churches. The King arranged for this decree of the Pope, which Edmund had obtained by a large sum of money, to be rescinded by the same Pope and revoked as void. In this matter indeed the false Pandulph himself often deceived many, while this was observed for some time by the King himself and by Edmund, as written, until he himself revoked it when it no longer brought him the profit he had previously expected. For this concession, harmful to the King, was made not by the King but by the Pope. Moreover, it was never received by any precedent or practice. For the King, inflamed with anger, at once removed a certain Boniface, Bishop of Winchester, whom he had elected without his knowledge, so as to declare the royal power.

units.la: Deinde Edmundus patriam & Ecclesiam tot iniuriis vexatam & oppressam, Rege rolerante, & Papa exigente, se quae tot Pontificis dolis delusum, au hortatu atque suam Metropoliticas Legatiex safu & auaritia fabricati interuentu diminutam a gerrimè ferens, Regem salutans increpat, & profuse lachrymans, Nunquam, inquit, fa-cem mea videbis amplius, vitaque pertaesus, cum ea amplius cernere noluit, quae ne audire quidem sine dolore potuit, in voluntarium sededit exilium, marique traiecto venit in Gal. liam, & in Pontiniaco Coenobio in precibus ac iciuniis Deum assidue pro Angliae a Romanorum faucibus redimenda interpellans, tristissimam vitam aliquandiu produxit. Historia Paris. Historiae Histmepotibus Iudaei, qui Nordouicia duenae fuerunt, puerum quendam Christianum suo ritu circumciderunt, quem in Christi nostri saluatoris contumeliam cruci affigendum reseruarunt. Sed pater adolescentis eo diligenter exquisito, facinoreque comperto Iudaeos criminis reos ad supplicium postulat, qui equinis caudis distracti, patibulo; suspensi perierunt. Edmundus autem aegritudine & abstinentia in tabem, deinde in acutissimam febrim incidit. Mutatoque recuperandae tam afflictae imo desperatae valetudinis causa, a Pontiniaco ad Soisim loco obiit 16. Kal. Decemb. postquam octo annis in Archiprasulatu vixisset. Dissectoque a Medicis ventre euulsa cum corde viscera in Sorti sepulta sunt, eadauer Pontiniacum reductum Archiepiscopali tu\u0304 humatum fuit. Legatus Otto Edmundo iam mortuo etiam Cisterciensia Coenobia ab omni penitentione munitissimis Papae priuilegiis liberrima, mandato & authoritate ipsius Papae Legatus inuasit. Illi vero fortiter restiterunt, suisque priuilegiis coram Papa ostensis, si veteres vim non obtinerent, nihil deinceps ab Anglis ei iperandum edixerunt. Hoc Papa vergens rus ad Ottonem literis se excusauit.
