Non esse sua intentionis scripsit, vt pecuniarias a Cistercienfibus procurationes exigeret, itaque mandat si vilitationis aut quacunque alia causa ad eos accesserit, praeceptis illi ordini cibis tantum contentus sit, & a carnibus abstinere. Cicestrenfibus a faucibus Legati tam opportune erceptis, cum vastatis omnibus nullius depræda-tionis spes superesset, ex Angliaiam atida & exangui Romam festinat. Qui huc missus non erat ad oues quæ perierant protegendas , sed ad pecuniam quam inuenerat, vindemiandam. Hic autem prædator Angliæ quisquis. Ec-clesiastica beneficia Italis Romanisque suis in Anglia contulerat , à Rege, magnatibus & Præsulibus cum tubarum clangore ad litus maris deductus est, ibi Regem amplexus legatina insignia deposuit,nauemq; conscendit,non minus pecuniis quam singulorum diris & execrationibus onustus. Cum traiecisset,multaque itinera conficesset,à Prædonibus Imperatoris captus & spoliatus est. Factus præda de prædatore iuxta illud prophericum: Væ qui prædaris,nonne tu prædabeteris?
units.tr: Then Edmund, seeing his country and Church so harassed and oppressed by many wrongs, with the King tolerating them and the Pope demanding them, and himself deceived by the many tricks of the Pontiff, and his metropolitan authority diminished by the interference of legates produced by fraud and greed, took it very badly. Greeting the King, he rebuked him, and weeping profusely said: "You will never see my face again." Weary of life, since he no longer wished to see those whom he could not even hear of without grief, he went into voluntary exile, crossed the sea into France, and at the Cistercian abbey of Pontigny spent a very sad life for some time, interceding with prayers and fasts to God without ceasing for the rescue of England from the jaws of the Romans. (Paris, History.) Among the Jews who were at Norwich, they circumcised a certain Christian boy after their own manner, whom they reserved for crucifixion, in contempt of Christ our Saviour. But the boy's father, making careful inquiry and discovering the crime, demanded that the Jews be punished as guilty; they were torn apart by horses' tails and perished hanged on the gallows. Edmund, however, fell by illness and abstinence into a wasting, and then into a most severe fever. Changing his place to recover his health, which was so broken, indeed desperate, he died at Soissons on 16 November, from Pontigny, after he had lived eight years as archbishop. His belly was opened by the physicians, and his viscera with his heart were buried at Soissons; his body was taken back to Pontigny and buried in the archiepiscopal tomb. After Edmund was already dead, the legate Otto invaded the Cistercian houses, which by the most fortified privileges of the Pope were entirely free from all penalties, by the command and authority of the Pope himself. They, however, resisted bravely, and having shown their privileges before the Pope, declared that if the old privileges did not hold force, nothing further was to be demanded of them by the English. The Pope, inclining to this, excused himself by letter to Otto. He wrote that it had never been his intention to exact financial procurations from the Cistercians; therefore he orders that if Otto came to them for a visitation or any other cause, he should be content with the plain food of that order and abstain from meat.

units.la: Edmundum autem sex penè annis sepultum, Innocentius Papa veritus ne manes ipsius mortui Romanam sedem ob tot acceptas iniurias vindicarent,sanctorum tuorū Pontificio catalogo inscripsit. Cuius corpus anno sequenti translatū est à Lodouico Francorum Rege,iterumq; triennio post è sepulchro leuatū,nouoq; pheretro ex auro,argento,& Chrystallo fabricato inclusum fuit.
units.tr: Innocent, the Pope, fearing that the spirit of the dead Edmund might avenge the Roman see for the many wrongs it had received, enrolled him in the Papist catalogue of saints, though he had been buried for nearly six years. His body was translated the following year by Louis, King of the Franks, and three years later was again lifted from the tomb and enclosed in a new shrine made of gold, silver and crystal.

units.la: Huius Archiepiscopi tempore Gregorius Papa Decretales Epistolas ab Innocentio priuseditas reexuit, suo s nomine edidit,in quibus quædam non tam iuris quàm lucri causa innouauit. Hospitium item S. Katarinæ quod Turri Londinensi adiacet,ab Eleanora Regina filia Comitis Prouinciæ Gallicæ ad sustentandas debiles & pauperes fœminas extructum est. Nec non & Iudæis ad Christi fidem conuersis aliud hospitium(quod nunc rotulorum seu archiuorum Regiorum custodiæ destinatum est,) ab Henrico Rege(eius coniuge)dedicarum fuit.
units.tr: In this archbishop's time Pope Gregory republished the Decretal Epistles previously issued by Innocent, putting them out under his own name, and in them he renewed some things less for the sake of law than of profit. The hospital of St Katherine, next to the Tower of London, was built by Queen Eleanor, daughter of the Count of Provence, to support weak and poor women. Also another hospital, for Jews converted to the Christian faith (now set apart for the keeping of the Royal rolls or archives), was dedicated by King Henry and his consort.

units.la: XLVI. Bonifacius.
units.tr: XLVI. Boniface.

units.la: OMANA curia,mortuo iam tabeaque & mœrore confecto Edmundo, pio atque erudito viro, insatiabili duĉta pecuniæ cupiditate, vt effrontes & impudicæ meretrices abiecta verecundia exponere se venales solent, omnibus gentibus, & præsertim Angliæ se prostituit precio: exempliq̄ue suo assines Prouincias visura, (quam modicum,) & (Simonia, (quam nullum delictum putauit,) tanquam contagione fœdaut.
units.tr: The Roman curia, now that Edmund, a pious and learned man, was dead and worn out by sickness and grief, driven by an insatiable desire for money, offered itself for a price to all peoples, and especially to England, just as shameless and immodest harlots, casting off all modesty, are wont to put themselves up for sale. Intending to make the neighbouring provinces like itself by its example, it defiled them as with a contagion through Simony, which it did not think any crime at all.

units.la: Quæ quidem insignis & impudica impudentia Reges atque populum religionis prætextu atque specie diu deceptos & infatuatos, à suis dolis & præstigiis,quibus lucrum sine modo captabat,primùm auertere cepit.
units.tr: This remarkable and shameless impudence began first to turn away kings and peoples, long deceived and infatuated under the pretext and appearance of religion, from its tricks and deceptions, by which it grasped at gain without any limit.

units.la: Nam vt sicorta venuitio sa quam diu aliquam retinent verecundiam & ipsa retenta sunt, sin totam deserurint, simul deserta sunt. Sic Roma munetibus moderata procos multos amplexast,tandem verò cum supra modum saurie atque corrupta esse cepit, omnes abalienauit.
units.tr: For just as harlots, while they keep some modesty, are themselves kept; but if they abandon it wholly, they are abandoned together with it. So Rome, while moderate in its bribes, attracted many suitors; but when it began to be corrupted beyond measure, it alienated them all.

units.la: Post Ottonis discessum Rex qui non modo suspicari sed perspicere planè atq; cernere Papales fallacias cepit, Cursinos fœneratores Italos, qui mutuas pecunias his qui Papalibus exactionibus soluendo non essent,sub viuris credebant,quinque Papali astu vt Angliam obzaratent introducti fuerunt, regno eiecit.
units.tr: After Otto's departure, the King, who now began not merely to suspect but plainly to perceive and see the papal deceits, expelled from the kingdom the Italian Cahorsin moneylenders, who lent money at usury to those who could not pay the papal exactions, having been introduced by papal cunning to drain England.

units.la: Sed Papa Gregorius postquam nummis Angliam exinanisset, & ad grande æs alienum redegisset, noluam adhuc exhauriendi rationem excogitauit. Quosdam in Anglia sibi chaos atque fidos Abbati & Conuentui de Burgo cum suis mandatis misit. Hi Papæ nomine contendunt, vt Ecclesiam aliquam quæ suii iuris patronatus,eraz, & centum marcarum redditu annuo æstimandam ipsi Papæ conferrent.
units.tr: But Pope Gregory, after he had drained England of money and reduced it to a great debt, still devised a new way of draining it. He sent certain men to England, faithful and loyal to him, to the Abbot and Convent of Bourne, with his mandates. In the Pope's name they demanded that the Abbot and Convent confer on the Pope some church in their right of patronage, valued at one hundred marks a year.

units.la: Hanc alii 2 Papa rursus locationis titulo accepturi, Papæ annuum prouentum persoluerent, sesiduum suis visibus reseruarent. Papæ ad hoc impetrabum pactum man-darani potestatem habebant , Abbatem & Conuentum ad hoc per censuras Papales compellendi.
units.tr: Others, who were to receive this church by a pretended title of lease, would pay the Pope its yearly revenue and keep the surplus for themselves. The Pope's agents had authority to compel the Abbot and Convent to this pact by papal censures.

units.la: Sed Abbate absente respondit Conuentus hoc se sine Regispermisso, qui Patro-nus huius siuæ ac permutarum in Anglia Ecclesiarum sit, non posse licite concedere. Sed ui stant atque si agirant Papales mandatarii,vt inox atque clam hoc negocium transigatur. Sperare enim se in aliis Ecclesiis eadem perfeĉturos, si exemplum cæteris ab hac prima concessione proponatur. Circumuenti iam hac tam subita flagitatione Monachi non aliam tam importunam petitionem vitandi ratione inuenire potuerant, quam vt Abbatem abiicnem cuius necessarius fuit consensus, consulant. Abbas detam callido & clandestino consilio eccltior factus Regem clam instruxit. Is continuo tandemque Romanos laqueos atq; cupiditatem (cui modus nullus adhiberi poterat) exceratus, restituit, ac edixit ne quis deinceps huiusmodi Pontificia mandata exequeretur aut suscipere. Ita fraudis Pontificiæ ouentus innatis tandem sibi que ignominiosus fuit. Interea duo Clerici Romani, (Ottonis legati quasi Vicarii) in Angliam clam ingressi sunt Petrus Rufus de quo antea dictum est & Petrus Supinus, qui tamen sedulus fuit & inde festus extractor pecuniæ. Huic Hybernia, illi Anglia expilanda commissa est. Conuentus Cleri publicos non cogebant, etsi exigēdi, interdicendi, excommunicandi, & pecuniam variis modis à misera Anglicana Ecclesia extorquendi, vt huiusmodi rapinis Ecclesia Romana, ab his incommodis quibus ab Imperatore (vt illi dicebant) tam diu affecta & vexata est tandem respiraret. Maxima autem huius rei gerendæ potestas penes Petrum Rufum fuit, qui se alteri anteruit. Quofque illerin Hybernia ligaffet, hic Londinum prius appulsos relaxare solebat. Et ne authóritate sepernenda & pere xigua prædicta videretur, literis quasad linguulos dedit, quos ad „ soluendum non soliciatuit, scriptum nominis sui titulum sic præponere solebat. Magiller Pe- „ trus Rufus, Domini Papæ familiaris & consanguineus salutem. &c. Quo titulo à singulis multa exegit. Collega autem suus Supinus paucis mensibus mille libras collegit, quas ad Petrum Rufum Londinum salutis duxit. Cumque iam plurimis repetitis expilatio num generibus omnem auri argentique copiam ex Anglia, Scotia, & Hybernia exhauisset, nunciatum est Gregorium Papam mortifero & exitiali morbo laborare. Itaq; onusti iam atque referti Romam properant. Veritate Rege, si de tanta Papæ inualitu- dine cognosceret, retinerentur, colle&taque pecunias refundere cogerentur. Nec eos sane fefellit opinio. Mox enim atque Cantuariensium Monachorum ope transissent in Galliam, ad Regem cum literis in Angliam venit Walterus de Ocrâ Legatus Imperatoris. In illis literis nunciata est Regi moros Gregorii Papæ, deinde Rex admonitus vt tam Papales prædones, quam prædam caperet atque deuineret. Sed illis (vt diximus) iam claplis Waltherus iratus Regis ignauiam increpauit, & ipse Prædonum vt nasuti canes lolent, olfaciens vestigia, viarum quibus incedebant, diuerticula perscrutatus est. De quo Imperatorem quam citissime certiorem fecit.
units.tr: But with the Abbot absent, the Convent replied that they could not lawfully grant this without the King's permission, since he is patron of this and of all exchanges of churches in England. But the papal agents insisted and pressed that the business be concluded at once and in secret, for they hoped to obtain the same from other churches if this first concession were held up as an example to the rest. The monks, beset by so sudden a demand and unable to find any other means of avoiding so troublesome a petition, consulted the Abbot, whose consent was necessary. The Abbot, made more cunning by this crafty and secret counsel, secretly instructed the King. He at once, cursing the Roman snares and the greed that could never be restrained, put a stop to the matter and ordered that no one should thereafter carry out or accept such papal mandates. Thus the outcome of the papal fraud proved shameful to its own authors in the end. Meanwhile two Roman clerics, as it were vicars of Otto's legates, secretly entered England: Peter Rufus, of whom we spoke earlier, and Peter Supinus, who was diligent and a skilled extractor of money. Ireland was entrusted to the one and England to the other to be plundered. They did not summon public assemblies of the clergy, but although they exacted, interdicted, excommunicated, and extorted money from the wretched English Church in various ways, so that the Roman Church might at last breathe freely from these burdens, by which, as they said, it had so long been afflicted and harassed by the Emperor. The chief power in managing this business lay with Peter Rufus, who put himself before the other. While the other bound men in Ireland, he used to release those who first landed in London. And lest the aforesaid authority seem slight and trifling, he gave letters, as it were to small fry, whom he did not press to pay, and he used to put his title at the head of them in this form: "Master Peter Rufus, familiar and kinsman of the Lord Pope, greeting," and so on. By this title he extracted much from individuals. His colleague Supinus, in a few months, collected a thousand pounds, which he carried to Peter Rufus at London for safe keeping. And when they had now drained every store of gold and silver from England, Scotland and Ireland, by many repeated kinds of plunder, news came that Pope Gregory was suffering from a deadly and fatal illness. So they hurried back to Rome, already laden and stuffed full. Had the King known of the Pope's great weakness, they would have been detained and forced to refund the money they had collected. Nor indeed did that expectation deceive them. For as soon as they had crossed into France, with the help of the monks of Canterbury, Walter of Ocra, legate of the Emperor, came to England to the King with letters. In those letters the King was told of the death of Pope Gregory, and then the King was warned to seize and bind both the papal robbers and their plunder. But they had already slipped away, as we have said. Walter, angry, rebuked the King's sluggishness, and himself, as keen-nosed hounds do, sniffing out their tracks, searched out the byways by which they had gone. Of this he informed the Emperor as quickly as possible.

units.la: Itaque illi cum diuulgata iam Gregorii mors esset insidias veriti, abdiderunt se vna cum prædia in amicorum & consanguineorum ædibus, vt palam atque liquido deprehendi non poterant. Sed Imperator per singulas sua ditionis in Italia civitates de Iis Papalibus nuncijs, multarumq; Ecclesiarum & præsertim Anglicanæ mercatoribus indigari fecit. Eoíq; tandem captos carceribus atque vinculis coercuit. Eorum affines, familiares & consanguineos, quiuefhis opem villam dederant proscripsit, pecuniam omnem per tabellionés & scripta penes ciuitatum mercatores atque depositarios exploratam intis Dominis restituì curauit. His expilationibus quæ tam infelicitas cesserat, defessa tadem Romana curia. Quatores, vt deinceps ofiendemus huc non misit amplius, sed pecunias quas exegit, ad le perferri cauté voluit. Gregorius autem Papa qui bello in, Imperatorem motorum orbem Christianum tumultu permiscuit, Angliamque maxime perturbauit, ægritudine atque tabe confectus obiit, quòd Imperator Castellum in Campania, ad quod Papæ consanguinei confugerant, expurgatione cepit, ipsosq; captos pattbulis suspendit, & in huius vindicta memoriam turrim quandam semidirutam reliquit. Ac mortuo iam Gregorio dolore nemagis an hilaritate ingemuerit Rex, incertum est. Nam Incredibili ac intolerandum quadam seruitute, a quæ viuente illo se vendicare hoc poterat, liberatus esset iam, si regni Baronès in fide obsequio, steterunt. Sed reluctantibus sibi que aduersus illis, respublica per externos atque peregrinos administrata est.
units.tr: Therefore, when Gregory's death was already widely known, they feared ambushes and hid themselves and their plunder in the houses of friends and kinsmen, so that they could not be clearly detected. But the Emperor, through every city of his dominion in Italy, had inquiries made about these papal messengers, and especially about the merchants of many churches, above all the English. At last he seized them and restrained them with prisons and chains. He outlawed their kinsmen, household members and relatives who had given them any help, and he had all their money, traced through notaries and written records with the merchants and depositaries of the cities, restored to its rightful owners. Worn out by these plunderings, which had turned out so unhappily, the Roman curia at last gave up. It no longer sent collectors here, as we shall show later, but wished the money it exacted to be carried to it by safe means. Gregory the Pope, who had stirred the whole Christian world into tumult with his war against the Emperor and had especially troubled England, died worn out by sickness and wasting away, because the Emperor took by storm a castle in Campania, to which the Pope's relatives had fled, and hanged them on gallows, leaving a half-ruined tower as a memorial of this vengeance. Whether the King groaned more from grief or from joy now that Gregory was dead is uncertain. For he would now have been freed from an incredible and intolerable servitude, which he could not escape while Gregory lived, if the barons of the kingdom had stood firm in faith and obedience. But since they resisted him and opposed him, the commonwealth was administered by foreigners and outsiders.

units.la: Itaq; postquam de Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi iam diu deliberaffet, Eleonoræ Reginæ sunsu Bonifacium Petri Sabaudiensis in Provinciâ Gallia filium, Reginæ annuncutum, à Monachis Cantuariensibus eligi postulauit. Hi virum ignorum, tanta Regi affiniatate coniunctum etsi ab illa sede prohibere libentius quam eligere vellent, tamen cum Papæ querti nondum sedebat esse mortuo, omnia Regi indulgere & concedere ex tam multis argumentis accepissent, verùm ne si præter Regis sententiam quem elegissent, repellerentur, in Bonifacio eligendo Regi obsequuntur sunt. Acriter celebrata electione Rex illico membranam de laude & commendatione auctoritate sui Bonifacii ad Papam conscribi, & tam suo Regio quam Episcoporum & Abbatum sigillis appensis tanquam publico commu- niqué ntque omnium testimonio roboràri, inuitis quidem permultis sed perterritis atq; enervatis curauit. Bonifacius enim praeterquam quod nobili genere ortus, & corporis præceritate, atque vitiis personæ dignitate præditus fuerit, exterisin rebus indignus tamen gerendæ dignitati existimabatur: unde quidam Cantuarienses Monachi pudore atque moerore affecti quod eum elegissent. Cantuariensem Ecclesiam deseruerunt, & ad petruam agendam poenitentiam arctissimo ordini Carthusiano sese astrinxerunt. Veruntamen haud ita post Rex legatis ad Innocentium Papam, qui tum Lugduni fuit, cum illo suo atque Præsulum scripto atque sigillato testimonio missis facile impetrauit, vt in ea sui uitate sactationem ab ipso Papae ceciperet. Ae paulò post Petrus Sabaudiensis Comes in Angliam venit, qui illas snagnificas ędes quas Henricus septimus repararat, & pauperibus alendis destinauit, primus extruxit, quæ antiquum nomen the Saxon adhuc retinet. Incidit hic Bonifacius in tempora valde periculosa atque turbulenta, ob motus atque tumultus frequentes qui non modo ob papales exactiones (à Rege conniuentibus occullis permissas, ) sed etiam ob aduenarum peregrinorumq; aduentum, quorum consilio Rex omnia gessit, inter Regē & Barones concitati sunt. Ad quos sedandos in Parhamento Oxony celebrato statutum atque decretum fuit, vt vetera regni iura ante Gustelmi Normani vidtoriam vsitata, & vi magis quam desistetudine, abrogata regni incubi restituerentur. Ad quæ obseruanda tam Rex quam Barones mutuis iuramentis praetitiis sese astrinxerunt. Sed Rex rarus ea iura ad populi libertatem augendam, suamq; dignicatem minuendā esse remissiora, egit eum Papa postea vt eius authoritate à fatissiurandi religione absoluereatur. Papa hoc vt soletfecit, vtpote qui regibus & magnatibus dislidcntibus sibi vsu cepit potentiam Regemq; clam soluit iuramento. Ex quo ciuilis bella inter Regem ac Barones mox suscepta sunt. In hac ciuili discordia Papa qui occasione quaecunq; siue acquisitam, siue oblatam pecunias in Anglia colligendi praetermittere noluit, Martinum quendam nouum pecuniarum exhaustorē cum excommunicandi, interdeundi & quocunq; modo etiam arbitrario sibi repugnantes coercendi authoritatem in Angliam misit. Is dum Rex & magnates ciuili confliftatione impediretur, Praelatos Angliæ non minus hostiliter aggressus est, quos à beneficiorum fructibus percipiendis indicta causa seuerissimo decreto suspendit, donec Papali voluntati satisfacum suisset. Quibus de illa voluntate quaerentibus respondit Martinus ; vt permuttianui tedditus consanguineis atque clericis Papæ ab Angliæ praelatis contribuetentur. Se autem redditum nullum qui viginti Anglicas libras annuas non valeret admisfurum, ne quisquilias in Anglia colligere videretur. Equos praeterea elegantiores atque generosos (quorum tunc habebatur in Anglia copia) à praelatis exegit. Quos tamen suæ negociationes atque adeò maximè necessarias excustionum causas allegarent, tamen ad praestandum Papalium poenarum atrocistate compulit. His modis magnus Ecclesiassticorum beneficiorum, praebendarum, atque dignitatum numerus Romanis clericis abscentibus acquisitus, nec non equorum selecissimorum copia celeriter Romam traductaest. His tot iacturis labesacta à Papa Anglia, cepit totus populus atque clerus de Papali iugo suis ceruicibus penitus exeutiendo cum Rege conspirare. Qui quasi parturientes, conceperunt acretentum alta diu mente odium in apertas tandem querelas effundunt. Angliam tam varias tantasq; largiciones vlcertus ferre non posse, si suis consanguinicis clericisq; Romanis ex Ecclesiis prouentus prouidete cupiat, potestatem suiam vicinioribus Italicis Ecclesiis non Anglicanis, tam longe Romana distributis admoueat. Nam Ecclesiasticos in Anglia prouentus à Regibus ac magnatibus Ecclesiarum patronis ad continuum diuinum cultum in Anglia gerendum hospitalitatis munera, & alendos elemosynas pauperes, Ecclesiarumq; extrustiones atque reparationes fuisse suppeditatos. Quibus peractis, si ex Ecclesiasticis facultatibus supersit quicquam, id pontium, atelium, & viarum refectioni aliisque regni necessitatibus subleuandis; qtiām illi Romano sacerdotali luxui concedi est ac quius. Praeterea nec honestum hee tutum Angliæ esse potest Papam suis contra Imperatorem sistuere, qui & affinitatem cum Regenuptiis contraxit. Ex quibus liberi procreandi ex Anglica regia stirpe prouenhl tent. Deinde Imperatorem obesse atque inseommodare posse multum Angliæ, si aut vicinas metcaturas impediat, aut contra Ludouicum Francorum Regem ad eas provincias recuperandas quas armis cepit, auxilio suo non subueniat. His malis compulsus Henricus Rex ad Papam scripsit, & eum obnixè rogauit, vt miserae diuque assistat Angliæ, & à Romanis expilatoribus ad vitum atq; adeo ad ossa te secassatum scedee pluteset, laborare eam & interstinis & externis multis incommodis, quibus omnibus multo grauior & acerbior effet auari illa Romana manus. units.tr: Therefore, after the King had long deliberated about the Archbishop of Canterbury, at the urging of Queen Eleanor he asked that Boniface, son of Peter of Savoy in the province of Gaul and kinsman of the Queen, be elected by the monks of Canterbury. These men, though they would much rather have kept out a man unknown to them, so closely bound to the King, than elect him, nevertheless, since they had learned from many signs that the King would be granted and conceded everything, yielded to the King in electing Boniface, lest, if they chose someone against the King's wishes, they should be rejected. After the election was hotly contested, the King at once had a letter of praise and recommendation of Boniface's authority drawn up for the Pope, and, with his royal seal and those of the bishops and abbots appended, confirmed as a public record by the testimony of all. Many were unwilling, but they were terrified and enfeebled, and so it was done. For Boniface, though he was of noble birth and endowed with bodily stature and the dignity of his person, but with faults, was thought unworthy to bear the dignity in outward affairs. Hence some of the Canterbury monks, struck with shame and grief that they had chosen him, deserted the Canterbury church and bound themselves to the most strict Carthusian order to perform penance. Yet not long after, the King sent envoys to Pope Innocent, who was then at Lyons, with a written and sealed testimony of his own and of the prelates, and easily obtained that Boniface be consecrated by the Pope himself in that city. Soon after, Peter of Savoy, the Count, came to England, and he first built those magnificent houses which Henry VII had repaired and destined for feeding the poor, and which still keep their old name, the Savoy. Boniface fell upon very dangerous and turbulent times, because of frequent disorders and tumults, which were stirred up between the King and the barons not only by the papal exactions (permitted by the King, who connived at them in secret), but also by the arrival of foreigners and aliens, on whose counsel the King did everything. To quiet these, it was enacted and decreed in the Parliament held at Oxford that the ancient laws of the kingdom, used before the victory of William the Norman, and abrogated more by force than by disuse, should be restored. Both the King and the barons bound themselves by mutual oaths to observe them. But the King, who had been unwilling that those laws should be relaxed, to the enlargement of the people's liberty and the diminution of his own dignity, afterwards brought it about that the Pope should absolve him from the obligation of that oath by his authority. The Pope did this as he usually did, since he had made a practice of taking power while kings and magnates were at odds, and secretly loosed the King from his oath. From this, civil wars between the King and the barons were soon undertaken. In this civil discord the Pope, who was unwilling to let pass any occasion of collecting money in England, whether acquired or offered, sent into England a certain Martin, a new drainer of money, with the authority to excommunicate, to lay under interdict, and to coerce by any means, even arbitrary ones, those who opposed him. While the King and the magnates were hindered by civil strife, he attacked the prelates of England no less hostilely, suspending them from receiving the fruits of their benefices, without a hearing of the case, by a most severe decree, until they should satisfy the papal will. When they asked what that will was, Martin replied that they should grant the revenues of the Pope's relatives and clerics that were held in England, and that he would not admit any income which was not worth twenty English pounds a year, lest he seem to be collecting trifles in England. Besides, he demanded from the prelates the finer and nobler horses, of which there was then a plentiful supply in England. Although they alleged their own business, and especially the most necessary causes of their exemptions, he nevertheless compelled them to pay, by the severity of the papal penalties. By these means a great number of ecclesiastical benefices, prebends and dignities was acquired for Roman clerics who were absent, and a store of the choicest horses was quickly carried off to Rome. Under these many losses England, impoverished by the Pope, the whole people and clergy began to conspire with the King to shake off the papal yoke completely from their necks. Like women in labour, they brought forth at last in open complaints the hatred long hidden in their deep minds. They declared that England could not bear such varied and such great exactions, if the Pope wished to draw the revenues of the English churches for his relatives and Roman clerics; they said he should turn his power on the nearer Italian churches, which were not English and were so far distant from Rome. For the ecclesiastical revenues in England had been provided by kings and magnates, the patrons of the churches, for the continual divine worship to be performed in England, for the offices of hospitality, for feeding the poor with alms, and for the building and repair of churches. When these were done, if anything remained of the ecclesiastical resources, it was to be spent on the repair of bridges, roads and highways, and on relieving the other needs of the kingdom, rather than granted to that Roman priestly luxury. Moreover, it could be neither honourable nor safe for England for the Pope to set himself against the Emperor, who had also entered into a marriage alliance with the King, from which children might be born of the English royal stock. Further, the Emperor could greatly harm and inconvenience England, if he should either hinder the neighbouring trade, or not support it with his aid against Louis, King of the French, in recovering those provinces which he had taken by arms. Compelled by these evils, King Henry wrote to the Pope and earnestly begged him to help England, which was miserable and had long been afflicted, and to free it from the Roman plunderers, who had stripped it to the skin and even to the bones; it was labouring under many internal and external burdens, all of which were made far heavier and harsher by that greedy Roman hand. If he would give England at least a little relief from this, it could more quickly and easily free itself from the other evils. But the Pope, moved by the King's prayers rather than softened, not only did not relax at all from so harsh an exaction, but with a new kind of ambition sought to extend his power.

units.la: An.1244. Vetus Mat. Paris. ruret, ceteris malis se explicare citius ac facilius posset. At Papa regis precibus commotus magis quàm mitigatus, non modò de tam atroci explicatione nihil remisit, sed novo ambitionis genere potentiam suam dilatare studuit. Daudem enim Northwalliæ principem, qui fidedata se Angliæ Regi astrinxerat, ab ea fide liberare, iuoque domino mancipare voluit, vt Romanæ Ecclesiæ ex illa provincia quingentæ annuæ marcæ solverentur. Hac pollicitatione atque spe Daudem in Regem contumacem & rebellem protexit atque fovit, donec publicis instrumentis in iure probaretur princeps Walliæ Regis Angliæ vasallum atque subiectum fuisse. Deinde hac amota fraude pontificia cum ita exhaustæ essent Anglorum facultates, vt ne Regi auxilia praestare possent, Rex subsidio sibi a Clero denegato, a Papa petiit vt is ad eos monitorias atque adeo infligatorias literas daret. Cuius rei euentus in se posterea receidit. Cum enim ne Papa quidem intercedente impetrare aliquid a praelatis potuit, Papam tamen magna pecunia remunerare coactus est. Praeterea cum animadvertisset Papa Anglos authoritate sua magis quàm regia pecunias dandas impelli posse, prodesse tibi multo prudentius quamRegi decreuit. Cumq; iam tam praesules quàm Magnates pecuniario subsidio iuuare Regem gratis æquis conditionibus promisissent, venit in Angliam Martinus quidam ad exigendas pecunias Papæ Legatus, potestate quadam noua & inaudita praeditus, quàm is mira sedulitate & seueritate exercuit. Hunc tam improbum pecuniarum raptorem Anglimutata in eius nomine litera Martinum appellabant. Hic Romanis clericis Ecclesiasticha beneficia simulatq; vacarét scriptis (vt aiunt) bullatis, quorum infinitam secum adduxit copiam, contulit, Vt inomnium ore hoc esset, Martinum Schedulas multas non scriptas sed bullatas, in quibus quiequid vellet exarare poterat, secum in Angliam attulisse. Cum itaque Anglicanum clerum ad festinam deeem millium marcarum solutionem vrgeret, illi duabus istis a Rege & a Papa postulationibus tanquam inter incudem &malleum contriti. Heu inquiunt. Duplex instat petitio, vna Regis, altera Papæ, sed a Rege sperare aliquam retributionem possumus, a Papa vero nullam. Itaque cum Regem iam iuuassent, Martino, qui eos Londini conuocatos dilectissimos Ecclesiæ Romanæ filios, in quorum sinu reposita tota spes Papalis esset, Comites appellabat, respondent se nequitam frequentes contributiones, neq; Ecclesiarum Romanis concessiones vlterius esse laturas. Quam quidem ad rem Imperatoris ad Regem literis instigati facile fuerunt. In quibus Regem rogat, ne auxilia praestari Papæ ad suam perniciem diutius paterentur. Sed hic controversiis, de quibus tam grandis infamia papalibus calumniis inuffa sibi fit, Angliæ atq; Galliæ Regum procerum q; iudicio fl atorum. Nec nõ Angliam ab illo tributo quod Innocentius a Iohanne Rege exegit, aliisq; grauaminibus quibus quotidie afflicta est, ipsò Marte vindicatur. Martinus tamen vacantibus Ecclesiis auidas manus semper iniecit. Cum enim Rogerus quidam Praeceptor Ecclesiæ Saresburiensis Bathoniensis Episcopus fuit, omnes priores eius dignitates cuidam Papæ consanguineo contulit. Quo etiam tempore Robertus Passeleue qui in thesauris Regiis custodiendis & augendis totus versatus est, coq; nomine Regi charus, ab Ecclesiæ cathedralis Cicestrensis Canonicis, qui Regi placere studuerunt, Cicestrensis Episcopus electus est. Bonifacius Cantua. Archiepiscopus indigne tulit, & Episcopis provinciæ suæ conuocatis in difficilibus quibusdam & nodosis quæstionibus per Linbi.Inienfem Episcopum propositis sciò examinauit, deinde electione reiecta hunc Robertum repulit, & Richardò quandam de Wiz loco suo (inconsulto Rege) substituit. In qua curba atq; lite Martinus ille prouisor Romanus qui praesens atque promptus lucro inhiabat, Richardi vacantes reddituas bullato scripto sine mora contulit. Rex autem tantam contumeliam non laturus in Episcopatus Baroniam & posteriores seculares ingressum Richardo interdixit. At paulo post Bonifacius Cant. Archiepiscopus cum Wigorniensi & Herefordensi Episcopis qui Anglis inuisi, suspectiq; fuerunt , quod Papæ tantum tribuebant (Regeetiam inconsulto) Romam profecti sunt. Bonifacius hanc itineris sui causam commemorauit obseruatam iam esse suam Cantuariensem Ecclesiam in quindecim millibus Marcarum. Cuius aris alieni atraicitas & magnitudo sine Papæ auxilio dissolui haud poterat, sed tamen dilecdens a Cantiis multis & exquisitis rationibus, maximè verè cædendis vendendisq; nemoribus pecuniam magnam conflauit. Et per prouinciam Galliam & Allobroges, vt expugnaret militem quendam prouincialem qui Reimundi Comitis Prouinciae filium & haeredem ad coiugium raptauerat, transfit. Ad huns expugnandū thesaurus grandis in Anglia coaceruatus est, etiā hoc praetextu eximendi ecclesiam Cantuariensem ab aere alieno, hocfecisse visus est. Ad Papam deinde accedens precio impetrauit, vt Episcopatum in Prouincia Valen-tinum num aliasque commodas & optimas Ecclesias quas in illo itinere ac quifierat cum Cantuariensi Archiepiscoparu retineret.
units.tr: A.D. 1244. Old Matthew Paris. ...could free itself from its other troubles more quickly and easily. But the Pope, moved by the King's prayers rather than softened by them, not only relaxed nothing of so savage an exaction, but also sought to extend his power by a new kind of ambition. For he wished to release Dafydd, prince of North Wales, who had bound himself to the King of England by an oath of fealty, from that allegiance and hand him over to his own lordship, so that five hundred marks a year might be paid to the Roman Church from that province. By this promise and hope he sheltered and fostered Dafydd as a stubborn and rebellious man against the King, until, by public instruments, it was proved in law that the prince of Wales had been a vassal and subject of the King of England. Then, that papal trick having been exposed, the English resources were so drained that they could not even give the King aid. The King, refused a subsidy by the clergy, asked the Pope to issue monitory and even coercive letters to them. The outcome of this request turned back on him afterwards. For when, even with the Pope interceding, he could obtain nothing from the prelates, he was forced to reward the Pope with a large sum of money. Moreover, when the Pope saw that the English could be driven to hand over money by his authority more than by the King's, he decided that it would profit himself much more prudently than the King. And when both the prelates and the magnates had promised, on fair terms and freely, to help the King with a money subsidy, there came into England a certain Martin, a papal legate for exacting money, endowed with a new and unheard-of power, which he exercised with remarkable zeal and severity. The English, altering one letter of his name, called this most shameless plunderer of money "Martyr." Whenever Church benefices fell vacant, he conferred them on Roman clerics by written documents (as they say) under the leaden seal, of which he had brought an endless supply with him, so that it was on everyone's lips that Martin had brought into England many blank documents, sealed but unwritten, on which he could write whatever he wished. Since he pressed the English clergy to pay ten thousand marks in haste, they, crushed as between anvil and hammer by these two demands from the King and from the Pope, cried out: "Alas! A double demand presses us: one from the King, the other from the Pope. But from the King we can hope for some return, from the Pope none at all." So, having already helped the King, when Martin summoned them to London and addressed them as the beloved sons of the Roman Church, in whose bosom all papal hope lay, and called them his Counts, they replied that they would no longer bear frequent contributions or the Roman concessions of churches. Moved by letters from the Emperor, they were easily stirred to this; in those letters he urged the King not to allow aid to be given to the Pope to his own ruin any longer. But this matter, over which such great infamy is heaped upon the papal calumnies, was judged by the nobles of the Kings of England and France. Nor was England freed from that tribute which Innocent exacted from King John, and from other burdens by which it was daily afflicted, by any other means than by force of arms. Still, Martin always laid greedy hands on vacant churches. For when Roger, a certain teacher of Salisbury, was bishop of Bath, he conferred all his former dignities on a certain kinsman of the Pope. At this same time Robert Passelewe, who was entirely occupied with guarding and increasing the royal treasures and was dear to the King on that account, was elected bishop of Chichester by the canons of the cathedral of Chichester, who had sought to please the King. Boniface, Archbishop of Canterbury, took this badly. Having summoned the bishops of his province, he examined them on certain difficult and knotty questions proposed by the Bishop of Lincoln, and then, rejecting the election, he repulsed this Robert and substituted in his place a certain Richard of Wiz (without consulting the King). In this quarrel and strife, that Martin, the Roman provisor, who was present and eager for gain, promptly conferred Richard's vacant revenues by a sealed document without delay. The King, not willing to bear so great an insult, forbade Richard entry into the bishopric, its baronies and its secular revenues. But a little later Boniface, Archbishop of Canterbury, went to Rome together with the bishops of Worcester and Hereford, who were hateful and suspect to the English because they attributed so much to the Pope (even without consulting the King). Boniface gave as the reason for his journey that his Church of Canterbury was burdened with debts of fifteen thousand marks. Since the heaviness and magnitude of this debt could not be dissolved without the Pope's help, he nevertheless raised a large sum of money by many exquisite devices, chiefly by cutting and selling timber from the woods. And he passed through the province of Gaul and the Allobroges to subdue a certain provincial knight who had abducted the son and heir of Count Raymond of Provence for marriage. For the subduing of this man a great treasure was gathered in England, and he seemed to have done this under the pretext of freeing the Church of Canterbury from debt. Then, approaching the Pope, he obtained by payment that he might retain the bishopric in the province of Valence and other convenient and excellent churches which he had acquired on that journey, together with the archbishopric of Canterbury.

units.la: Interea Papacum ad colligendas in Anglia pecunias non multum se legatis prosiscere animadnerteret, callido nouoq; initocum Cardinalibus suis (qui soli erant amatores pecuniae) concilio ipse in regnum accedere statuit. Cardinales sub adumbrata & ficta in Regem amoris specie insidias suas occultantes ad eum communes literas dant, in quibus consilium se exponere amicum, Regi vtile, regnoq; honorificum exponunt, vt Rex per illustres aliquos nuncios Papam rogaret, vt Angliam (in qua ius quoddam proprium atque singulare tenet) dignaretur sua praesentia illustrare.
units.tr: Meanwhile, when the Pope perceived that he was not making much progress in collecting money in England through legates, he decided, with a clever and new plan, to come into the kingdom himself, in council with his Cardinals (who alone were lovers of money). The Cardinals, concealing their snares under a pretended and feigned show of love for the King, sent him joint letters, in which they set out a plan, friendly, useful to the King and honourable to the kingdom: that the King should, through some illustrious envoys, ask the Pope to deign to grace England (which holds a certain special and singular right) with his presence.

units.la: Nihil Regi fore gloriosius quàm vt id quod nullius Regis temporibus accidere, iam ad perpetuum sui regni, decus contingat, se operam sedulo daturos vt si Rex hoc peterer, a Papa impetrarer. Eoque paratiores futuros quod meminerint dixisse nuper Papam, quam grato animo delicias Westmonasterii, & diuitias Londini inuiscere cupiat. Rex his subdolis Cardinalium blanditiis facile primò irretitus, prudenter posteacōsilio auocatus est. Qui Regi suaserunt, Romanorum rapinis atque Simonia, nec non Gourlinorum ac Italorum qui vnà cum illis Angliam ingressi sunt visuris, integritatem & quasi pudicitiam Angliæ satis violari. Opusnon esse vt ipse Papa praesens praedatum accedat. Hanc autem improbam Cardinalium insinuationem, esse flagitationem callidam. Perisse enim Papam tam Franciam q; Aragoniam ingrediendi a Regibus potestatem, a quibus repulsam passus est. Id quod infamia Papalis curae promeretur, eius factor ad iubes fumum tetterrimū exhalabat. Papa cum intellexisser, quam ingratus suus in Angliam aduenuus foret, generale Concilium Lugduni indixit. Ad quod primo citat Regem & praesules Angliae, in quibus maximam se habere spem, maximumque percepisse solatium testatur.
units.tr: Nothing would be more glorious for the King than that what had happened in no king's time should now come to the perpetual honour of his realm; they would take pains to see that, if the King sought this, he would obtain it from the Pope. And they would be the more ready, since they remembered that the Pope had lately said how gladly he would like to enjoy the delights of Westminster and the riches of London. The King, at first easily ensnared by these crafty flatteries of the Cardinals, was afterwards wisely called away by counsel. Those who advised the King said that the integrity and, as it were, the chastity of England would be sufficiently violated by the plundering and simony of the Romans, and also of the Gascons and Italians who had entered England along with them to see what was there. It was not necessary for the Pope himself to come in person as a plunderer. They said that this wicked insinuation of the Cardinals was a cunning solicitation: the Pope had lost the power of entering both France and Aragon, from which Kings had repulsed him. Whatever the papal infamy deserved as its due, its author was breathing out the foulest smoke. When the Pope learned how unwelcome his coming to England would be, he summoned a general council at Lyons. To this he first cited the King and the prelates of England, in whom, he testified, he had the greatest hope and had received the greatest comfort.

units.la: Papae nuncius Nonis Martiis Regem & praesules ad hoc concilium citauit, Concilii dies dictus est Octauo Kalend. Iulii. Interea Rex misit ad Papam capellanum quendam suum Laurentium de S. Martino, vt pro absentia quorundam praelatorum a Cœcilio veniam peteret, & de iniuriis sibi a Bonifacio Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo illatis quererētur. Papa illud concessit, sed in altero cum Bonifacio (cuius largitione delinitus fuit) 30 contra Regem stetit. Rex etsi Papae resistere palam ausus non sit, tamen Magnates clam incitat. Illi portus omnes obseruari, & veloces Papae nuncios qui cum mandatis ad Martinum Papae proui forem quotidie ibant & redibant detineri, Papalesq; literas ad eiusferri praecipiunt, & paulo post Douerum applicuit Cursor papalis, onustus litteris & mandatis (vt aiunt) bullatis quae variis argumentis pecunias corradendi, potius quam dicendi aut orationis figuris erant refertae. Hunc Douerensis portus custos captum carcerिbus inclusit. Cuius rei fama ad Martinum illum citius quam ad Magnates ipsos perdūctaest: Is Regem adiit, rem indicat, Rex a dhuc Papam veritus, ad eusdem illico scripsit vt Cursorem illum liberaret. Ita ipse saluus ad Martinum suum papales chartas saluas perduxit. 40 Iam Lugdunensis illius concilii dies instabat. Papa ipse mense Maio aduenit. Cuius primo aduentu conclaue Papae subito combustum est. Hoc quidem callidè factum putabant vt incepto concilio causa Papae exigendi pecunias ministraretur. Sed vt multa asseberant, execrabilis in charta quam a Iohanne Rege de tributaria Anglia facienda extorsit, in eodem incendio periit. Papae ante inchoatum hoc concilium cepit illam authoritatem, quam vendicare rum in animo habuerat, in Lugdunenses Canonicos exercere. Itaque in praebendas quasdam vacantes inuasit, in aquam possessionem consanguineos & affines suos inisit. Cui in os restituerunt Canonici Lugdunenses, cum minis & iuramentis exelamantes, quod sitales Lugdunensem Ecclesiam ingrederentur, nemo eos seruando seruare possit, quin in Rhodanum vicinum amnem mergerentur. Quibus dictis 50 deterriti Papae consanguinei ne in aspectum quidem prodierunt, sed subito cuanuerunt. Ae in Anglia Magnates cum hoc concilium imminere ceruicibus suis animaduerterent, Rege in suam sententiam contra Papam clam adducto, miserunt Fulconeni quendam Warini filium totius Anglicani populi ad Martinum Praedonem nuncium, Martinus tum Lundinii in nouo templo fuit. Quem Fulco his verbis allocutus est. Recedens statim exi ab Anglia. Cui Martinus: Quis mihi hoc mandat? An tu exceipso hoc habes? Cui Fulco: hoc tibi per me mandat eorum qui armanuper Luitoniae & Dunestapliæ ceperunt vniuersitas (magnus enim in illis tum oppidis conuenerat gladiatorum numerus quos Rex ipse suspectos habebat) & si sano (inquit Fulco) cõsilio credis, ne moteris vsq; in diem tertium, ne tu in frusta concidaris cum omnibus tuis.
units.tr: The papal messenger, on the Nones of March, summoned the King and the prelates to this council; the day of the council was set for the eighth day before the Kalends of July. Meanwhile the King sent to the Pope a certain chaplain of his, Laurence of St Martin, to ask pardon for the absence of certain prelates from the council, and to complain about the injuries inflicted on him by Boniface, Archbishop of Canterbury. The Pope granted this, but in the other matter he took the side of Boniface against the King (by whose bribes he had been softened). Although the King did not dare openly to resist the Pope, he secretly incited the magnates. They ordered all the ports to be watched, and the swift messengers of the Pope, who went and came daily carrying the papal commands to Martin, to be detained; and they gave orders that the papal letters be carried to him. Shortly afterwards a papal courier put in at Dover, laden with letters and commands (as they say, under the leaden seal), which were full of various arguments for gathering money rather than of any eloquence or figures of speech. The custodian of the port of Dover seized him and shut him in prison. News of this reached that Martin more quickly than the magnates themselves. He went to the King and reported the matter; the King, still fearing the Pope, at once wrote to him to free the courier. So the courier himself brought the papal documents safe and sound to his Martin. Now the day of that council of Lyons was drawing near. The Pope himself arrived in May. On his first arrival the papal conclave was suddenly burned. People thought this had been cleverly done so that a cause for exacting money from the Pope might be supplied at the start of the council. But, as many asserted, the accursed charter which he had extorted from King John, making England tributary, perished in the same fire. Before this council began, the Pope assumed the authority which he had intended to exercise over the canons of Lyons. He therefore invaded certain vacant prebends and put his kinsmen and relatives into possession of them. The canons of Lyons, shouting threats and oaths, drove them back from the door, declaring that if they should enter the church of Lyons, no one could keep them safe unless they were drowned in the neighbouring river Rhône. Frightened by these words, the Pope's kinsmen did not even come into view, but suddenly vanished. And in England, when the magnates saw this council hanging over their necks, the King having been secretly brought over to their opinion against the Pope, they sent Fulk, son of Warin, as spokesman for the whole English people, to the messenger Martin, who was then in London, in the new temple. Fulk addressed him in these words: "Leave England at once, without delay." Martin replied: "Who orders me this? Do you have this from yourself?" Fulk answered: "This is ordered you through me by the united will of those who lately seized Lewes and Dunstable (for a great number of gladiators, whom the King himself held suspect, had gathered in those towns). And if you trust sound counsel, (said Fulk), do not stir until the third day, lest you be cut to pieces with all your men."

units.la: Verba Med. Parm. Recessit trepidus & suspiria ducens Martinus, Regem adiit. Commemorat quæ ei nũciata sunt, rogat an authoritate sua, vel subditorum temeritate fiant. Cui Rex. Ego, inquit, huius rei author non sum. Sed Barones mei vix fe continent quin in me arma capiant, quia deprædationes & iniurias tuas quæ modum omnem, iusque atq; fas superant tamdiu toleraui. Hoc responso perplexus Martinus petiit saltem exitum e regno facilem atq; tutum. Cui Rex commotus & iratus, Diabolus te inquit perducat & inducat in inferos, mandauitq; pallatii fui Marifcalcho cuidam Roberto Norifco, vt Martinum ad mare saluum perduceret. Cui pauidus iam Martinus tanquam ad latus adhæsit dum ad mare deduceretur, veritus omnes quos comfpexerat, ac quibus obuius effet, ne ab illis trucidaretur. Subinde Robertum rogauit supplex vt fe protegeret, his verbis. O mi amice, quem cupis in reddituc Ecclesiastico promouen? Cui Robertus. Absit inquit, vt aliquis meorum per te potiatur Ingressu in Ecclesiam. Et cum Doueram peruenissent, Vade inquit Robertus, ne si vel respicias saltem in Angliam, in frusta ab ipsis nautis disseceris, vel maris fluctibus obruaris. Ita fefitinanter traiecto Martino per lnque Itali Simoniaci, & Courfini vsurarii qui totam pene sua contagione contaminarunt Angliam, in latebris sese absconderunt, & repente discesserunt, Martinus qui magnis itineribus ad Papam contendit, quo furore exactus fit ab Anglia declaraut. Papa excanduit quod Franciæ & Aragoniæ Reges ingressum in suorum regna sibi prohibuissent, & quòd Angliæ Rex aduentum suum oblarum non acceptasset, ideo nuncium suum diris & execrationibus eieccisset. Et in voce susurra, oculos obliquando, & nares corrugando. Expedit inquit, vt hos regulos conteramus, & componamus cum Imperatore. Contrito. n. vel pacificato Dracone, cito serpentuli conculcabuntur. At Henricus Rex tandem & pene sera poenitentia ductus insatiabilem illam Romanæ curiæ cupiditatem abominari & detestari cepit, & post Martini discessum per singulos Comitatus inquisiuit, quantis ex Angl'ia Ecclesiasticis annuis prouentibus Romani atque Itali per Romanam curiam locupletati fuerint. Et repertus est annnus redditus sex aginta millia marcarum, quam summam ne regius quidem tum attigit redditus. Quare permotus Rex cum consiliariis suis deliberauit, de mittendis ad concilium legatis, qui publicam querelam de Papæ fuorumq; legatorum grauissimis exactionibus & rapinis proponerent. Nec non ab illo tributo quod Iohannes Rex sine consensu regni promiserat, liberationem postularent. Hi quarto die post inceptum concilium Regis regnique causam in concilio ostendunt, cum summa iniuria belli ciuilis tempore extortum ab Angliæ Rege multis calamitatibus oppresso, Romano Pontifici tributum, id remitti petunt, quia nobilitas atque populus nunquam assentire, nec vllis rationibus adduci possent, vt consentiant. Ad hoc Papa nec vultum, nec vocem extulit, sed murus contieuit. Tum interiecto silentio protulerunt totius Angliæ vniuersitatis literas summam omnium iniuriarum & calamitatum quas Papalis auaritia in Angliam inuexisset continentes. Quibus palam recitatis respondit tandem Papa, cum de responso diu vrgerent Legati. Tantum negocium moram in deliberando requirere. Cumq; ita dilatata & proreastinata res esset, addiderunt Legati nouam quandam impudentem, & intolerandam exactionem nuper a Romana curia inuentam esse. Dum quæ prius concessisset, ea commodi fui causa, cum hac clausula quas legulei, Non obstante &c. vocant, statim reuocaret. Ex quo nemo iuris sui diu certus esse queat. De his propositis atq; postulatis diu responsa expectabant legati quibus tandem expressum est, quod postulata ad votum non reportarent. Quare irati cum his minis atque diris discesserunt, se nunquam tributum seu quodcunque aliud deinceps Romanæ cupiditati soluturos, aut ex Anglia solui præstariue Romæ permissuros. Sed Papa callidus illis leniter & æquabiliter concilio dimissis, Episcopos atque Prælatos quos detinuit excommunicationem comminando coegit, vt signis & sigillis suis Iohannis Regis de tributo concessionem confirmarent. De quo Rex certior factus iuramento professus est se contra infirmos illos & timidos Episcopos pro regni libertate staturum, nec censum deinceps vllum Romanæ cutiæ præstiturum. Papa insignem sibi à Rege & proceribus Angliæ contumeliam factam putauit, quòd cum suosq; Legatos in Cocilio tantarū iniuriarū reos fecissent, vt nec à minis quidē apertis continere se poterat, quin aperte denunciaret, si Imperatore Fredericû superare poterat, proximum sibi fore contra reluctantes & deficientes Anglos de tributo negocium. Incitauit q; in Regē Angliæ Francorū Regem, qui tamen initas paulo ante inducias ne Paac Papa postulante frangere noluit. Lugdunensi autem Concilio iam finito in quo spontaneis donis, vel saltem clanculum postulatis Papa multas opes congessit. Bonifacius Papale rescriptum omnibus Cantuariensis Provinciæ clericis obtinuit, vt ex illius provinciæ beneficiorum vacantium vedigalibus septennio proximo ad illud æs alienum dissoluendum, quod in translatione Thomæ quam Stephanus fecerat, Cantuariensis Ecclesia contraxerat, decem millia marcarum collidere possit, præter duo millia marcarum annuatim ei ab Ecclesia Cantuariensi soluendarum.
units.tr: Martin, trembling and drawing sighs, withdrew and went to the King. He reports what had been announced to him, and asks whether these things were done by his authority or by the recklessness of his subjects. The King replied: "I am not the author of this business. But my barons can scarcely restrain themselves from taking up arms against me, because I have tolerated for so long your depredations and injuries, which exceed every measure, and every right and law." Perplexed by this answer, Martin sought at least an easy and safe departure from the kingdom. The King, moved and angry, said: "May the devil take you and lead you down into hell," and he ordered a certain marshal of his household, Robert Norwich, to bring Martin safely to the sea. Martin, already frightened, clung close to Robert's side as he was led to the sea, fearing all the men he had seen and whomever he met, lest he be slaughtered by them. Again and again he humbly begged Robert to protect him, with these words: "O my friend, what benefice in the Church do you wish me to obtain for you?" Robert replied: "God forbid that any of my people should obtain through you entrance into the Church." And when they had reached Dover, Robert said: "Go, lest, if you so much as look back toward England, you be torn to pieces by the sailors themselves, or overwhelmed by the waves of the sea." So Martin was hurriedly conveyed across the sea, and the Italian Simoniacs and Caursine usurers, who had contaminated almost all of England with their contagion, hid themselves in their lurking-places and suddenly departed. Martin, who hastened to the Pope by great journeys, was driven out of England with what fury they declared. The Pope flared up because the Kings of France and Aragon had forbidden him entry into their kingdoms, and because the King of England had not accepted his offered arrival, and therefore he had cast out his messenger with dire curses and execrations. And speaking in a whisper, with sidelong glances and wrinkling his nose, he said: "It is expedient that we crush these petty kings and come to terms with the Emperor. For once the dragon is crushed or pacified, the little serpents will soon be trampled underfoot." But King Henry at last, led by a repentance late and almost too late, began to abominate and detest that insatiable greed of the Roman court; and after Martin's departure he inquired through each county how great the annual revenues of ecclesiastical benefices in England were, by which the Romans and Italians had been enriched through the Roman court. And it was found that the annual return was sixty thousand marks, a sum which even the royal revenue did not then reach. Therefore the King, moved, deliberated with his counsellors about sending envoys to the council, who would lay before it a public complaint concerning the very grievous exactions and plunderings of the Pope and his legates. Also they should demand release from that tribute which King John had promised without the consent of the realm. On the fourth day after the council began, these envoys set forth the cause of the King and the realm in the council; since the tribute to the Roman Pontiff had been extorted from the King of England, oppressed by many calamities, in time of civil war, with the greatest injustice, they sought that it be remitted, because the nobility and the people had never assented, nor could they be brought by any arguments to consent. To this the Pope raised neither countenance nor voice, but remained silent like a wall. Then, after a pause of silence, they produced letters from the whole university of England, containing the sum of all the injuries and calamities which papal greed had brought into England. When these were publicly read out, the Pope at last replied, though the legates pressed him for an answer for a long time: such a business required delay in deliberating. And when the matter had been thus put off and postponed, the legates added that a new, shameless and intolerable exaction had lately been devised by the Roman court: whatever it had previously granted for its own advantage, it would at once revoke, with this clause, which the lawyers call "non obstante etc." From this no one can long be certain of his own right. The legates waited a long time for responses to these proposals and demands, until at last it was made clear to them that they would not bring back their demands as they wished. Therefore they departed in anger, with threats and curses, declaring that they would never again pay the tribute, or whatever else, to Roman greed, nor would they allow anything to be paid from England to be handed over at Rome. But the Pope, being crafty, dismissed them gently and evenly, and compelled the bishops and prelates whom he had detained, by threatening excommunication, to confirm with their signs and seals the concession of tribute made by King John. Having been informed of this, the King swore an oath that he would stand against those weak and timid bishops for the liberty of the realm, and would pay no census to the Roman court henceforth. The Pope thought he had been dealt a signal insult by the King and the nobles of England, because they had made his legates guilty of such great injuries in the council, so that he could not restrain himself even from open threats, but openly declared that, if he could overcome the Emperor Frederick, the business of the tribute against the resisting and defaulting English would be next for him. He also stirred up the King of the Franks against the King of England, though that king did not wish to break the truce he had recently made, at the Pope's request. But when the Council of Lyons was already finished, in which the Pope had gathered great wealth by voluntary gifts or at least by secret demands, Boniface obtained a papal rescript for all the clergy of the province of Canterbury, that from the revenues of the vacant benefices of that province, during the following seven years, he might collect ten thousand marks towards that debt which the Church of Canterbury had contracted in the translation of Thomas, which Stephen had made, in addition to two thousand marks a year to be paid to him by the Church of Canterbury.

units.la: Quæ Regem concessio primo valde commouit. Qui miror, inquit, si Bonifacius Cant. Archiepiscopus quem ego ad tantam dignitatem euexi, iam eiulmodi meo regno incômoda à curia Romana procurET. Sed Rex etsi aliquandiu restiterat, tamen vtrumque tam Papam, quam Archiepiscopum Cant. infestare noluit, sed precibus ac interce ssione victus tandem cessit. Verumtamen literis ac edictis iam tandem per totam Angliam præcepit, ne Papales nuncij ad pecunias siue clam siue palam petendas in portus reciperentur, aut vagari regnumque circumire permitterentur, si qui huiusmodi inuenti essent, carceribus inc ludi iussit. Quo facto subditorum animos multis Romanorum iniuriis demissos atque labefactatos extulit & exhilarauit. Et paulo post vt omnes vias papalibus in Anglia depredationibus intercluderet, præsules & Magnates regni ad concilium in Parliamento Londini celebrato conuocauit. In quo Rex abiectâ illa Papali formidine regiam & se dignam vocem extulit. Satis iam diu se ac subditos suos papalibus dolis ludificatos, se tam multis promissis deceptum fidem deinceps nullam habiturum. Quod & Legati ac procuratores tam sui quàm regni in Concilio Lugdunensi à Papa male aut nihil respondentes spteri contemptiq; discessissent. Et quanquam aliqua satis æque concesserit, eadem tamen indices reuocauerit, & vt vere dici possit, grauiores manus Angliæ quam vnquam antè attulerit, & quasi in suum regnique contemptum plus solito nuper seuierit. Quibus generaliter, regioque modo declaratis, adiunxit ilico & in specie explicauit papalia gravamina huic regno illata.
units.tr: This grant at first greatly moved the King. "I wonder," he said, "if Boniface, Archbishop of Canterbury, whom I have raised to so great a dignity, now procures such troubles for my kingdom from the Roman court." But although the King had resisted for some time, he did not wish to harass either the Pope or the Archbishop of Canterbury, and, overcome by prayers and intercession, at last gave way. Nevertheless, by letters and edicts he at last commanded throughout all England that papal messengers seeking money, whether secretly or openly, should not be received into ports, nor be permitted to wander and go round the kingdom; if any such were found, he ordered them to be shut up in prisons. By this act he raised and cheered the spirits of his subjects, which had been cast down and weakened by many injuries from the Romans. And a little later, in order to block all the ways of papal plunderings in England, he summoned the prelates and magnates of the realm to a council in Parliament held at London. In it the King, casting off that papal fear, raised a royal voice worthy of himself: he and his subjects had been mocked for long enough by papal tricks; deceived by so many promises, he would henceforth place no faith in them. Since both his own and the realm's legates and procurators had departed from the Council of Lyons with scorn and contempt, having received unfavourable or no answers from the Pope, and although the Pope had granted some things fairly enough, he had nevertheless revoked the same by his rescripts; and, to speak truly, he had lately laid heavier hands on England than ever before, and had raged more than usual, as if in contempt of his kingdom and of himself. When these things had been set out in general and in royal fashion, he at once added and explained in particular the papal grievances inflicted on this kingdom.

units.la: 1. Quod non contentus fuerit illo subsidio quod vocatur denarius S. Petri, sed mille indies modis & astutiis sine consensu regio, & contra antiqua iura, libertatef; regni, & contra appellationem Legatorum & procuratorum in Concilio Lugdunensi interposi-
units.tr: 1. That the Pope was not content with that subsidy which is called Peter's Pence, but by a thousand daily methods and tricks, without royal consent, and against ancient laws and the liberty of the realm, and against the appeal lodged by the legates and procurators at the Council of Lyons, drew money out of England.

units.la: tam in Anglia pecunias conficit.
units.tr: (continued) ...

units.la: 2. Deinde quòd Ecclesiæ & prebendæ in Anglia conferuntur Italis ac Romanis idiomatis regni neq; loqui neq; intelligere valentibus, à quibus Ecclesiasticæ regni facultates exhausta, & extra regnum ad peregrinos traductæ sunt in animarum periculum, & Ecclesiarum ruinam atque vastitatem.
units.tr: 2. Secondly, churches and prebends in England are conferred on Italians and Romans who can neither speak nor understand the language of the kingdom. Through them the ecclesiastical revenues of the realm are drained and carried abroad to foreigners, to the peril of souls and the ruin and devastation of the churches.

units.la: 3. Tum quod à cæteris Ecclesiis quibus exteros non præfecit pensiones exigit, etiam contra suas literas.
units.tr: 3. Then, from the other churches to which he has not appointed foreigners, he exacts pensions, even contrary to his own letters.

units.la: 4. Adhæc Italos Italo, Romanus Romano in Anglicanis beneficiis tanquam fixeditario iure succedant, & in omnibus pene causis Angli ad Romanum tribunal contraręgni consuetudines & iura scripta, nec non contra ipsa Papalia privilegia antiquitus constituta, cessa trahuntur.
units.tr: 4. Furthermore, Italians succeed Italians and Romans succeed Romans in English benefices as if by a fixed hereditary right. And in almost every case the English are dragged before the Roman tribunal, contrary to the customs and written laws of the realm, and also contrary to the papal privileges established of old.

units.la: 5. Præterea ille nouus & prioribus omnibus seculis inauditus Papalis nunciius & adiuena, qui NON OBSTANTE, dicitur. Quæ clausula nouis concessionibus atque induhgentiis prioribus semper derogat, per quam iuramenti religio, consuetudines antiquæ, scripturarum vigor, concessionum auctoritas, statuta iura & priuilegia debilitantur, plufes nuper in Anglia quàm ante vnquam afflixit & oppressit. In qua quidem plenitudine papalis potestatis exercenda immoderatius se Papagessit, quàm procuratoribus regni verbo tenus nupet dederat in promissis.
units.tr: 5. Besides, there is that new papal device, unheard of in all earlier ages, the so-called "notwithstanding" clause. This clause always overrides earlier concessions and indulgences. Through it the sanctity of oaths, ancient customs, the force of written instruments, the authority of grants, and statutes, laws and privileges are weakened. It has lately afflicted and oppressed England more than ever before. In exercising this fullness of papal power, the Pope has behaved more immoderately than he had promised in words to the procurators of the realm.

units.la: 6. His accedunt infinita collegendi, & e regno sine Regis consensu euehendi pecunias genera, contra quæ in eodem Lugdunensi Concilio aperta voce à Regis atque regni procuratoribus appellatum est.
units.tr: 6. To these are added the infinite kinds of money-raising, and the export of money from the realm without the king's consent. Against these practices the king's and the realm's procurators openly appealed at the same Council of Lyons.

units.la: 7. Ad extremum in beneficiorum & prebendarum Ecclesiis quas Itali, & Romani in Anglia possident, nec verbum diuinum enunciatur, necritus & cæremoniæ Ecclesiasticæ seruantur, nec pauperibus eleemosynæ conferuntur, sed hospitalitas, animarum cura, & diuina obsequia negliguntur, & ædificiorum tam parietes quàm tecta corruunt.
units.tr: 7. Finally, in the churches of the benefices and prebends which Italians and Romans hold in England, the divine word is not proclaimed, the rites and ecclesiastical ceremonies are not observed, and alms are not given to the poor. Hospitality, the care of souls and the divine services are neglected, and the walls as well as the roofs of the buildings are collapsing.

units.la: De his grauaminibus quibus tamdiu oppressa conticuit Anglia, tandem sui querelam erupit. Scriptæ sunt ad Papam de illis quaternæ literæ, vna ab Episcopis, alteræ ab Abbatibus, tertia à Baronibus, quartæ ab ipso Rege. Episcopi timere se scribunt ne regnum Angliæ à Papali sacerdotio pro his quas diu tulit calamitatibus, penitus seiugatur. Abbates commemorant minas magnatum atque procerum, se Ecclesias in suasa proprietatem reuocaturos, si exteris aut Romanis deinceps conferantur. Magnates atque populus exclamant quanta scandala de rapina & auaritia Romana non modò per Angliam, sed per totum orbem dissipata sint. Se non permissuros vt sua patria deinceps tam male tractetur, ne Rege quidem conniuente. Et nisi, inquiunt prædicta per vos citius corrigantur, pro certo teneat sanctitas vestra, non immerito timeri poterit, quod tam Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quàm Domino Regitale periculum immineb it, quod cidè remedium (quod absit) facile non poterit adhiberi. Rex obnixè Papam rogat vt procerum atque præsulum postulatis sine mora concedat. Ne si secus fiat, Romana, inquit, Ecclesia, & nos in tali simus periculo constituti, cui nos oporteat in perpetum subiacere.
units.tr: England, which had for so long been oppressed, at last broke into complaint about these grievances, and for a long time kept silent no longer. Four letters were written to the Pope about them: one by the bishops, another by the abbots, a third by the barons, and a fourth by the king himself. The bishops write that they fear the kingdom of England may be wholly cut off from the papal priesthood, because of the calamities it has long endured. The abbots recall the threats of the magnates and nobles, who say they will reclaim the churches into their own ownership if they are henceforth conferred on foreigners or Romans. The magnates and the people cry out at what scandals have been spread, through rapine and Roman greed, not only throughout England but throughout the whole world. They will not allow their country to be so badly treated from now on, even if the king should not object. "And unless," they say, "the aforesaid abuses are corrected by you quickly, let your holiness be assured that it may not unjustly be feared that a danger as great is hanging over the Roman Church as over the lord king himself, and that a remedy for it (which God forbid) will not easily be applied." The king earnestly asks the Pope to grant without delay the requests of the nobles and prelates. "Otherwise," he says, "if it is done otherwise, the Roman Church and we are placed in such danger that we must be subject to it forever."

units.la: His literis missis populus, ne Rex in Papam iam concitatus labasceret aut a proposito desisteret, nouas criminationes addidit. Prælatos Angliæ, Papa per suos internuncios clam petebat, militaria seruitia promisisse, quæ solì Regi ac belli administrationem, regnique defensionem debebant. Quoddam viginti, alios decem, nonnullos plures aut pauciores, fortissimos ex delectu habito milites equis armisq; instructos ad quæcunque Papa præscriperit loca missuros. Quæ fraus papalis vt Regem & magnates lateret, interminatum esse à Papæ mandatariis præsulibus sub excommunicationis pœna, ne ante sex menses commissa Papæ cuiquam enunciarent. Id etiam repetitum & exaggeratum est, quod de vacantibus beneficiis Bonifacio concessum paulo antea tediximus. His rebus turbatus Rex edixit, & proscriptione sanxit, si quis quodcunque militare auxilium sine suo iussu suppeditare Papæ audeat.
units.tr: After these letters were sent, the people, lest the king, now stirred up against the Pope, should waver or give up his purpose, added new accusations. The Pope was secretly seeking, through his go-betweens, that the prelates of England had promised military service, which was owed to the king alone, and to the conduct of war and the defence of the realm. Some twenty, others ten, some more or fewer, the strongest men chosen from a levy, equipped with horses and arms, were to be sent wherever the Pope should direct. So that this papal fraud might be hidden from the king and the magnates, the bishops who were the Pope's agents had been forbidden, under penalty of excommunication, to disclose to anyone what had been committed before six months. This too was repeated and exaggerated, the matter of the vacant benefices that we mentioned was granted to Boniface a little earlier. Troubled by these things, the king issued an edict and sanctioned by proscription that if anyone should dare to supply any military aid to the Pope without his command.

units.la: Papa his Anglorum literis non respondit, sed tem ad secundiora sibi magisq; opportuna tempora silentio reseruauit. Et vt opimam ouem cuius toties tondisset vellera, non modo excoriaret sed maetaret, & cuisceraret, sequeipsis intestinis fariaret. Nam cum Fredericus Imperator comperuisset Papam Anglico numismate ditatum Indiæ, in his portubus quibus commeantibus in Angliam sit transitus, custodes occultos & insidiatores posuit. Eius conatus cum præsciuisset Papa hoc dolo antecurrit. Instituit novos non conuentos, sed laicos, sub specie religionis prædicatores & minores fratres dictos. Hi amictus habitu mutato regnum clanculum ingressi sunt, Monachis præcipuè reclamantibus. Qui cum animadvertissent quantis priuilegiis ad electionyias imovo erius rapinas non pauperum, sed Papæ nomine collegendas esse muniti, quæ suæ fidei, id quod optabant, non committerentur, exclamabant Papam sui lucri causa Indiæ religiosorum novos ordines fingere ac formare. Nam Monachorum ordo qui strictissimus antea putabatur, iam præ his novis fratribus in contemptum abiit. His omnia indulsit Papa, vt quia peccantes clam sibi delicta confitentes audirent, eosque in poenis retinerent vel relaxarent, non modo ordinariorum præsulum loco, (præterquam in foris & criminalibus) in ligandi & absoluendi potestate esse nt, sed quæcunq; Papæ mandata & imperata peragerent. His itaque nouum & inauditum negotium in mandatis dedit, vt electorum ab intestato decedentium hæreditates atque bona ad Papæ commoditatem raperent. Obierant enim Lincolniensis, Bedfordiensis, & Northemptonensis Archidiaconi opulentissimæ tam in pecuniis quam in vasis preciosis, & copiosa suppellectile hæreditate sine testamento relicta, quæ ad laicorum cognatorum possessionem peruenit. Quam sibi adimi tanquam pinguem & dulcem bolum e faucibus eripi Papa molesté tulit. Quòd cum Regi denunciatum esset, non animo solum, sed & verbis execrari cepit tam varias & multiplices pecuniæ colligendæ artifidas. Quas tamen edictis per totum regnum propositis vetuit. Sed Romæ iam cum Papa multi Anglicani adorant clerici, qui cappis, vt aiunt chorealibus & infulis, ornamentisq; Ecclesiasticis ex Angliæ tunc more gentis ex lana tenuissima, & auro artificiose intexto fabricatis vterentur, huiusmodi ornamentorum aspectu & concupiscentia prouocatus Papa togauit cuiusmodi ecclesiæ. Responsum est Aurifrisia appellari, quia Aurum & eminens ex panno lana, quam Angli Gyrsiæ appellant, sicut contexta sunt: cui subridens & duleedine captus Papa. Vere inquit, hortus nostet delitiarum est Anglia, verè puteus est inexhaustus, & vbi multa abundant, de multis multa sumere licet. Itaque concupiscentia illedeus octilorum litteras suas bullatas sacras misit ad Cistercienses in Anglia Abbates, quorum orationibus se deuotè commendauerat, vt ipsi hæc Aurifrisia speciosissima ad suum ornandum chorum compararent. Hoc Londinensibus placuit, qui ea tum venalia habebant, tantique quanti placuit, vendebant.
units.tr: The Pope made no reply to these letters from the English, but reserved them in silence for more favourable and more suitable times. He acted like one who, having shorn a rich sheep's fleece so often, not only wishes to flay it but to slaughter it, and to cut it up, and to slice it apart even to its entrails. For when the Emperor Frederick learned that the Pope had been enriched with English money, he posted hidden guards and ambushers at those harbours through which passage into England was possible for those travelling there. The Pope, foreseeing these attempts, forestalled them by a trick. He set up new preachers, not monks but laymen, called Friars Minor under the appearance of religion. These men, with their dress changed, entered the kingdom secretly, the monks above all protesting. When the monks noticed with what privileges these new brothers had been fortified to collect, in the name of the Pope and not of the poor, the revenues that were to be gathered from the faithful, and that they were not entrusted to their own faith, as they had wished, they cried out that the Pope, for the sake of his own gain, was inventing and forming new orders of religious. For the order of monks, which had formerly been thought the strictest, now fell into contempt beside these new brothers. The Pope granted them all these things so that, since they heard the sins of those who secretly confessed their misdeeds to them, and could hold men in punishment or release them, they might have the power of binding and absolving not only in place of the ordinary bishops (except in external and criminal matters), but also to carry out whatever the Pope had commanded and ordered.
