So he gave them a new and unheard-of task in their commissions: to seize the inheritances and goods of those who died intestate among the clergy, for the Pope's advantage. For the archdeacons of Lincoln, Bedford and Northampton had died, and their very wealthy estates, in money, costly vessels and abundant household goods, had been left without a will, and passed into the possession of lay relatives. The Pope was troubled that these were taken from him, as if a rich and sweet morsel had been snatched from his jaws. When this was announced to the king, he began to curse, not only in his mind but in words, the many and varied devices for raising money. Nevertheless he forbade them by edicts posted throughout the kingdom. But at Rome, many English clergy were already present with the Pope; they wore choir copes, as they call them, and mitres and ecclesiastical vestments, made in the custom of the nation at that time from very fine wool and cloth worked with gold. Stirred by the sight and desire of these vestments, the Pope asked what kind of cloth they were. It was answered that the cloth was called orphrey, because gold is woven into it, and the wool that the English call gyrsiae stands out from the cloth. The Pope, smiling and captivated by its sweetness, said: "Truly, England is our garden of delights, truly it is an inexhaustible well, and where many things abound, many things may be taken from many." So, enticed by the bait of the eyes, he sent his sealed letters to the Cistercian abbots in England, whose prayers he had devoutly commended himself to, so that they would procure this most splendid orphrey to adorn his choir. The Londoners were pleased by this, since they then had it for sale, and they sold it at whatever price they pleased.

units.la: Vnde multi manifestam auaritiam Romanæ Ecclesiæ detestabantur. Sed his mitidis mūneribus satiari Papa non poterat, quin interea dum Legati regis eum mandatis supra scriptis essent Romæ, Papa cum in exiguo quæstu Anglicanum sibi Clerum flexibilem esse sensisset, scripsit Wintoniensi & Noruicensi Episcopis, vt sex marcarum millia à Clero suis vsibus persolui curarent. Illi mandatum Papæ occipiunt exequi, sed à Rege sub proscriptionis pœna prohibentur. Clerus inter Regem & Papam interpositus, ac vtriusque minis perterritus, quid ageret incertus fuit, sed quia in Rege constantiam desiderabant, veriti ne animo deficeret, & vt ante sæpe fecit, succumberet Papæ, permulti clandestina solutione tam Regis quàm Papæ indignationem vitabant. Nuntii deinde qui de Regis, procerum, Prælatorum, totiusque Anglicani populi æquissimis postulatis Romam missi sunt, redierunt. Illi Wintoniæ, vbi Parliamentum habirum est, exponunr quàm superba Papæ responsa tulerant. Se probris lacessitos, & repulsos ab omnibus tanquam schismaticos fuisse. Papam autem dixisse Rex Angliæ qui iam recalcitrat atq; Fredericus, suum habet consilium, ego verò meum habeo. Rex hoc allato nuncio commotus, vbiq; in Anglia per præcones edixit, ne à quoquam deinceps quicquam præstaretur Papæ. Sed Papa incensus iam iracundia asperius Prælatos sub omnibus suis poenis interminatus est, vt tandem dictam pecuniarum summam suo nuncio in nouo rum templo Londini comporante quàm citissimè persoluerent. Rex ipse minis fratris sui Richardi Cornubiensis Comitis qui sibi semper aduersus fuit, erfi idem acriter ante sæpe contra Papam cum magnatibus steterat atque scripserat, & Episcoporum cum eo conspirantium vt Regem huc illuc tam in Papæ quàm in populi suo odium traherent, inter quos præcipuus erat Wigornensis, cui concessa pœstas à Papa fuit regnum sacris interdicere, metu fractus & debilitatus succubuit. Hinc cunctis excidit resuperandæ libertatis spes dolorque cruentus, quòd Romanæ cupiditatis faucibus ac hiatibus Anglia sola devoranda permissa sit, omnium pene corda pertransiit. Papa cum tam dolo quàm minis Regem & Barones Angliæ compesceuisset, singulis vicibus singulas atque nouas se locupletandi ex Anglia fraudes excogitauit. Imperium Constantinopolitanum victis & repulsis eiusdem hostibus restaurare & Græcorum qui schismate à fide Romana se seiunxissent, insolentiam frangere se velle multis præconibus diuulgauit. Ad hos nouos conatus, nouis ex Anglia sumptibus opus est. Itaque instituit quendam quem Provincialem ministrum fratrum minorum & prædicatorum in Anglia appellauit, ad hunc sex literas dedit, quatum vnæ, de quibus vltimo loco dicendum est, sibi soli referuandæ, nec cum altero quoquam communicandæ essent. Reliquæ quinque cum fratribus & prædicatoribus communicandæ.
units.tr: Hence many detested the manifest greed of the Roman Church. But the Pope could not be satisfied by these small gifts. Meanwhile, while the king's envoys were at Rome with the aforesaid commissions, the Pope, having sensed that the English clergy would be pliable to him in a small matter of profit, wrote to the bishops of Winchester and Norwich, that they should see to it that six thousand marks were paid to him from the clergy for his own uses. Those bishops began to carry out the Pope's command, but were forbidden by the king under penalty of proscription. The clergy, placed between the king and the Pope and terrified by the threats of both, did not know what to do. But because they lacked firmness in the king, and feared that he might lose heart and, as he had often done before, give way to the Pope, very many avoided the anger of both the king and the Pope by secret payment. Then the messengers who had been sent to Rome with the most just requests of the king, the nobles, the prelates and the whole English people returned. At Winchester, where a parliament had been held, they explained how proud the Pope's replies had been. They said that they had been assailed with insults and rejected by everyone as schismatics. The Pope, they said, had declared: "The King of England, who now kicks back, and Frederick, have their own counsel, and I have mine." The king, moved by this news, had heralds proclaim throughout England that nothing was to be paid to the Pope by anyone from now on. But the Pope, already inflamed with anger, threatened the prelates more harshly under all his penalties, so that they should pay the said sum of money as quickly as possible to his messenger, who was collecting it in the New Temple at London. The king himself, broken and weakened by the threats of his brother Richard, Earl of Cornwall, who had always been opposed to him, and who had himself often stood sharply against the Pope with the magnates and written against him, and by the bishops who conspired with him to draw the king hither and thither into hatred both of the Pope and of his own people, among whom the chief was the bishop of Worcester, to whom the Pope had granted the power of interdicting the sacraments to the kingdom, gave way. From this came a despair and bitter grief at the loss of hope for recovering liberty, which passed through almost everyone's hearts, because England alone had been permitted to be devoured by the jaws and gaping mouths of Roman greed. The Pope, having restrained the king and the English barons as much by trickery as by threats, devised one new fraud after another for enriching himself from England, each time. He announced to many heralds that he wished to restore the Constantinopolitan empire, with its enemies defeated and driven off, and to break the insolence of the Greeks who had separated themselves from the Roman faith by schism. For these new attempts, new money from England was needed. So he appointed a certain man whom he called the provincial minister of the Friars Minor and Preachers in England, and to him he sent six letters. Of these, one, which must be mentioned last, was to be reserved for himself alone and was not to be shared with anyone else. The other five were to be shared with the friars and preachers.

units.la: Quarum primæ continebant, vt cum fratribus inquirat de vsurariis viuis, captatoq; ab his vsuras censuris Ecclesiasticis ad Imperii Constantinopolitani restaurandi necessitatem colligant & conuertant. Secundæ, vt qui militiæ sacramentum pro eodem imperio recuperando suscipere, aut aliquid ex suis bonis largiri velint, à peccatorum pluribus annis perpetratorum poenis relaxarentur. Tertiæ vt quæ sub vsuris acquisita, & in Testamentis ab vsurariis conditis legata, fidei commissa, seu quòcunq; modo relicta sint ad eiusdem imperii snbsidium colligantur. Idemvt quæcunque aut quocunque modo, à quibuscunque testatoribus male parta relicta sint, iisdem vtibus cedant.
units.tr: Of these, the first ordered the friars to inquire about living usurers and, by ecclesiastical censures, to extract usury from them and turn it to the necessity of restoring the Empire of Constantinople. The second granted that those who would take up the military oath to recover the same empire, or who wished to contribute some of their goods, should be relieved of the penalties for sins committed over many years. The third ordered that whatever had been acquired by usury and left in the wills of usurers, whether as bequests, trusts, or in any other way, should be collected for the support of the same empire. Likewise, whatever had been left in any way by any testators as ill-gotten property should go to the same use.

units.la: Quartæ, vt quæ à restatoribus in pios vsus distribuenda relicta sunt, huic vtì rei atque soli toto proximo triennio conferantur. Quintæ vt quæ viui patrationibus atque commerciis fraudulenter nequeuerunt acquisierint, cogantur ad Constantinopolitani Imperii restitutionem Papæ persoluere. Sed sextis illis literis inaudita quædam omnemque omnium malignitatem fuerunt ...
units.tr: The fourth ordered that whatever testators had left for pious uses should be devoted to this purpose alone for the whole of the next three years. The fifth ordered that whatever living people had acquired by fraudulent dealings and trade should be compelled to pay the Pope for the restoration of the Empire of Constantinople. But those sixth letters contained certain unheard-of things and all the malice of everyone...

units.la: Sed sextis illis literis inaudita quædam omnemque omnium malignitatem fuerunt ... Papæ mandata vbiq; publicè denunciantes, simul excommunicationis sententias frequentes in omnes contradicentes, reluctantes, & non parentes fulminarunt. Hi ab solui nisi ab hoc provinciali fratrum & prædicatorum Papalium ministerio ex Papæ præcepto non poterant.
units.tr: But those sixth letters contained certain unheard-of things and all the malice of everyone... They publicly proclaimed the Pope's commands everywhere and at the same time hurled frequent sentences of excommunication against all who contradicted, resisted, or did not obey. These men could not be absolved, by the Pope's order, except by this provincial minister of the Papal friars preachers.

units.la: Itaque huic illis sextis literis iri mandatis dedit Papa, vt recepta sibi, vel fratribus pro delicto atq; contumacia, congrua satisfactione, quæ in Papæ vsus conuersa est excommunicatione soluerētur. Nec minus industrii in occulta hac fraude fratres prædicatores, quà in illa altera aperta rapina Quæstores Papæ fuerunt, quibus cũRex nò minus Papales censuras, quâ fratris sui Comitis, & Prælatorum insidias cauens resistere verebatur, à Frederico Imperatore vt effœminatus ac mollis reprehensus est. Qua reptehensione impulsus cepit iterû erigere animũ, verbisq; sæpe in Pontificiâ cupiditate inuectus est. Quæ ad Papam petlata, ira sanctitatem suam commouebant, vt sutore pene perculsus aspectu torno in Cardinalium præsentia exclamaret, se Regnum Angliæ protinus omnibus sacris prohibiturũ. E Cardinaliũ tũ grege fuit quidam Monachus Cistercien-sis ordinis
units.tr: Therefore the Pope gave this man orders, by those sixth letters, that whatever was received, either by himself or by the friars, for crime and contumacy should be released upon suitable satisfaction, which was turned to the Pope's use, and by excommunication. The Preaching friars were no less diligent in this secret fraud than the Pope's questors had been in that other, open robbery. The King, who feared to resist them no less than the papal censures and the plots of his brother the Earl and of the prelates, was rebuked by the Emperor Frederick as effeminate and soft. Stirred by this rebuke, he began again to raise his spirit and often inveighed in words against papal greed. When these words were carried to the Pope, they so moved his holiness to anger that, almost struck dumb, with a grim look, he cried out in the presence of the Cardinals that he would at once forbid all sacred rites in the Kingdom of England. There was then among the Cardinals a certain monk of the Cistercian order

units.la: Q nis, Anglus nomine Iohannes. Is Papæ huiusmodi se oratione oppositit. Domine Papa huic iræ quæ sine causa concitata est, adhibe temperanter modum. Circumspiciamus & vos & nos qui culmen Ecclesiæ sumus, in quibus malis & discrimine versemur vndique. Terra sancta amissa est. Ecclesia Græca à nobis diuisa recessit. Imperator Fredericus qui potentia reliquos Reges, Principesque superat, aduersus nobis est. Nos ipsi non modo à sede Romana, sed ab vrbe, ipsaque Italia hucusque tanquam in exilium coacti sumus. Gentes autem Christianæ non minus bellis intestinis & exteris, quàm per nos affictæ sunt. Hungaria timet ne suæ indigenæ exterminentur à Tartaris. Germania bello ciuili per nos motoquassatur. Hispania in ipsos Episcopos sæuire incipit. Gallia quam aduentu & præsentia nostra ad magnam egestatem adduximus, cum hostibus nostris conspirat, & in nos meditatur insidias. Anglia nostris iniuriis toties lassa quasi Asina Balaam, calcaribus & fustibus cæsa, tandem loquitur & obloquitur, & se nimis & intolerabiliter conquerit fatigatam. Itaque ita igitur modo omnibus odiosi, omnes ad odium prouocamus.
units.tr: named John, an Englishman. He opposed the Pope with this speech: "Lord Pope, moderate the measure of this anger, which has been stirred up without cause. Let us, both you and we who are the summit of the Church, look around at the evils and dangers in which we are everywhere involved. The Holy Land is lost. The Greek Church has withdrawn, separated from us. Emperor Frederick, who surpasses the other kings and princes in power, is set against us. We ourselves have been driven, not only from the Roman see, but from the city and from Italy itself, into what is almost exile. The Christian peoples have been afflicted no less by internal and external wars than by us. Hungary fears that its native people will be exterminated by the Tartars. Germany is shaken by civil war stirred up by us. Spain has begun to rage against the bishops themselves. Gaul, which we have reduced to great poverty by our coming and presence, conspires with our enemies and plots snares against us. England, so often worn down by our injuries, like Balaam's ass beaten with spurs and clubs, at last speaks and complains back, and protests that it is weary beyond measure and intolerably so. And so, by these means, we make ourselves hateful to all and provoke all to hatred."

units.la: Quatamen verissima & æquissima oratione præfractus & pertinax Papa mitigari non potuit, antequam per suos nuncios certior factus fuerit, Regem etsi tam diras contra se voces emiserit, omnem tamen expilandi potestatem suis quæ storibus re ipsa permisit se. Cuius reigaudium, vultum & animum Papæ mirificè serenauit. Ex hac Regis & Anglorum facilitate, cum quicquid voluit aut impetauit, Papa tam facile, aliqua nonnunquam, sæpe etiam cum nulla contradictione impetrauit, ad grauissimam totius Cleriopresionem se accinxit. Iussit vt in beneficiis & dignitatibus Ecclesiasticis residentes tertiam, absentes autem dimidiam prouentuum partem sibi præstarent. Cumque antea sæpe literis ad Regem & Clerum datis policitus esset se deinceps ab his tam grauibus exactionibus abstenturum, in hoc nouo & tam attocimandato inseruit illam nouam & inauditam à seculis clausulam de qua antea diximus (non obstante) quæ omnem æquitatem & iustitiam ante concessam abolet & extinguit. Hoc negocium Londinensi Episcopo iniunctum est, qui cum in Ecclesia Paulina multos Prælatos conuocasset, & Papæ mandatum demonstrasset, à Rege nuncii interuenerunt distrincte prohibentes ne tam diræ & in totius regni vastitatem solutioni consentirent. Qui læti concilio interrupto ab inceptis destiterunt. Et ne sine causa id fecisse viderentur, collectis multis necessariis argumentis & rationibus, quibus probant Papæ mandatum non modo inutile sed impossibile & intolerabile Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ futurum, omnes una voce non modo contradixerunt, & ad sententiam D. Iesu Christi, & concilii vniuersalis quandoque per eius gratiam conuocandi appellatunt.
units.tr: Yet the Pope, stubborn and obstinate, could not be softened by this most true and just speech, until his envoys informed him that the King, although he had uttered such dire words against him, had nevertheless in fact granted his courtiers full power to plunder. At this news the Pope's joy, face and mind were wonderfully brightened. From this readiness of the King and the English, since the Pope obtained whatever he wished or sought so easily, sometimes in part and often even without any opposition, he girded himself for the most grievous oppression of the whole clergy. He ordered that those residing in benefices and ecclesiastical dignities should pay him a third of their revenues, and absentees half. Although earlier he had often promised the King and the clergy, in letters, that he would henceforth refrain from such heavy exactions, he inserted into this new and so vexatious mandate that new and unheard-of clause, unknown for ages, of which we spoke earlier: "notwithstanding" (non obstante), which abolishes and extinguishes all the equity and justice previously granted. This business was enjoined on the Bishop of London, who, having summoned many prelates to St Paul's and shown them the Pope's mandate, was interrupted by messengers from the King, who strictly forbade them to consent to a payment so dire and ruinous to the whole kingdom. Glad of this, they broke off the council and desisted from their undertaking. And so that they should not seem to have acted without cause, they gathered many necessary arguments and reasons by which they proved that the Pope's mandate would be not only useless but impossible and intolerable for the English Church. They all, with one voice, not only contradicted it but appealed to the sentence of Lord Jesus Christ and to a universal council, to be convened by His grace at some time.

units.la: Cum tantis iniuriis regnum à Papa pressum esset, Rex aliquo remedio succurrendum putauit. Itaq; Parliamentum Londini habuit, in quo decretum est legatos à Rege & toto regno ad Papam cum literis mittendos. Literarum summa fuit. Anglos etsi maxime vellent atque cuperent, non posse tam immensas & infinitas pecuniarum largitiones Papæ præstare. Angliam suæ sanctitatis pedibus obuolutam obnixè supplicare, vt sibi totiestöse, & ad viuum refecatæ tandem parcat. Sed Papa hoc accepto nuncio, vt Regem vetius blanditiùs pe[r]meeret, nec tamen à proposito declinaret, per curiales quosdam Regi familiares quos corruperat, fuisse Regi, ieiam tandem Regis precibus, quemRomanæ curiæ tam diu semper intellexit, adducum, vt Regi quæ voluit concederet.
units.tr: Since the kingdom was so oppressed by the Pope's wrongs, the King thought it must be helped by some remedy. So he held a Parliament at London, in which it was decided that envoys should be sent to the Pope from the King and the whole kingdom, bearing letters. The sum of the letters was that the English, however much they might wish and desire it, could not pay such immense and infinite largesses of money to the Pope; that England, prostrate at the feet of his holiness, earnestly begged him to spare her, now cut back to the quick and well-nigh flayed. But the Pope, having received this message, wished to flatter the King more and yet not to depart from his purpose. Through certain courtiers familiar with the King, whom he had corrupted, he was at last, by the King's own prayers, induced to grant the King what he wished, as the Roman court had long understood.

units.la: Itaque & remittere se illam decimarum petitionem, & præterea prouisiones pro Italis deinceps non facturum, fine hac verborum formula. Rogamus Dominum Regem cum instantia magna, quod placeat Domino Regi, vt huic vel illi prouideatur de tali beneficio. Hac fraude non magis pacauit quam illaqueauit Regem. Qui quandoque rogatus à Papa esset, nunquam contradixit. Cumque sopita & sedatatam tempestas esset, prodeunt duo minores in Anglia fratres tanquam ex antris Lupi incautum gregem insuafuri. Hi mandata Papæ feorfim Episcopis & Prælatis cum pœnis & censuris horrendis exponunt. Primò Lincolniensem Episcopum cuius dioecesis latissima est, aggrediuntur, ab eo mandatis Papalibus ostensis sex marcarum millia popoficunt. Quibus Lincolnienfis. Fratres, inquit, Hæc exactio salua Papali authoritate inexcusabilis, & inhonesta est, nec minus ad implendum impossibilis, nec me continget solum, sed Regem & vniuersitatem regni, quibus inconsultis mihi neque consentire, neque respondere fas est.
units.tr: And so he both remitted that petition for tithes and promised that he would make no further provisions for Italians, in this form of words: "We ask the Lord King with great urgency that it may please the Lord King that provision be made for this or that man with such a benefice." By this fraud he did no more to pacify the King than to ensnare him. Whenever the Pope asked him, the King never refused. And when the storm had subsided and calmed, two lesser friars came forward in England, as if from the dens of wolves, to creep upon the unwary flock. These expounded the Papal mandates separately to bishops and prelates, with penalties and dreadful censures. First they attacked the Bishop of Lincoln, whose diocese is very extensive, and having shown him the Papal mandates, demanded six thousand marks from him. To them the Bishop of Lincoln replied: "Brothers, this exaction, even with Papal authority behind it, is inexcusable and dishonourable, and no less impossible to fulfil. It will concern not only me but the King and the whole community of the kingdom, and it is not right for me to consent to it or to answer it without their consultation."

units.la: Eodem etiam modo singulos Anglia perlustrata tentabant, à quibus cum eadem responsa tulissent, cum diris execrationib. & minaci murmure secesserunt. Et interea dum hi sigillatim omnia scrutarentur, ingreditur Angliam Capellanus & familiaris Papæ quidam nomine Marinus, cum Legatina quidem authoritate etsi ornamentis & inlustris careret. Hic Marinus alter ab illo Marino auidissimo Papæ quæstore fuit, de quo paulo antea dictum est. Et nominis similitudinem sequutus, dum alii venatum, iste piscatum pecunias a Papa missus est. Has largitiones cum Anglis audacter imperaret, à Gallicano Clero mutuam saltem sibi modico tempore præstari pecuniam argutus scilicet & callidis rationibus per diuersos legatos petiit. Sed Galli multo in ea re quam Angli prudentiores cum comperissent nullam sibi iure contra Papam actionem competere, qua mutuam pecuniam recuperarent, ne teruncium ei credere voluerunt. Itaque legati per Galliam non modo inanes atque vacui, sed risu & cachinnis delusi redierunt. Interea dum Papæ nuncii tam cupidè grassarentur in Anglia, Episcopi Cantuariensis prouincique qui Papæ amplius qd præstare aperte sæpe recusassent, etiā illi, quam diximus, Bonifacii Arch. Cantuar. concessioni testiterunt, quos ille authoritate Papali ab Ecclesiasticis muneribus suspendit, eosdemque à Papa Romæ excommunicari, ac quoscunque alios Bonifacio propolito telucantes, detrahentes, vel fraudem quouismodo facientes impetrauit. Hæc excommunicatio per Decanum Beluacensem Papæ mandatarium Episcopis & Clero Cantuariensis prouinciæ denunciata est, qui tam diris censuratum teste confessi, inuiti Bonifacio assensi sunt. His igitur qui tam fortiter primò restiterant tam citò labefactatis, Papa vt confuerit non destitit ad se quæcunque potuit ex Anglia rapere. Itaque Abbati Abendoniæ scripsit, vt cuidam Romano de fructuosa aliqua & opulenta Ecclesia prouideret. Romanus vt aquila muscas non captauit, & cum multæ vacarent, de Papæ mandato statim non instabat, sed expectauit vbetrimam. Tandem Ecclesia S. Helenæ in Abindonensi villaque maxime optima fuit, rectore caruit. Hanc Romanus ex Papæ mandato petiit. Eandemque Rex fratri suo vterino Æthelmaro, qui tot Ecclesias posiederat vt earum numerum ignoraret, conferri voluit. Abbas perplexus & tanquam inter duos molares lapides conterendus, quid ageret statuere nō potuit, Conuentum & amicos consuluit. Illi Regi gratificandum censent, magis quam Romano, quem insidiatorem penes se vigilem ac perpetuum experiretur. Abbas ex eorum consilio concessit illam Ecclesiam Æthelmato. Papa Abbatem hunc infirma valetudine senem Romam citauit, vbi conuitiis multis exagitatus, de contemptu iudicium subire debuit, nisi quinquentas annuas marcas Romano illi se folututum obligassest. Præterea cum Bonifacius S. Edmundi mortuus esset, Monachi alium eligerunt. Quem vt Papa confirmaret, miserunt ex fratribus sui ordinis tres Romam, qui electione Papæ præsentata, cum sine vlla contentione aut contradictione celebrata esset, expectabant vt sine controuersia confirmaretur. Sed Papæ fictis in electum querelis sine vlla inquisitione ex potestatis suæ plenitudine electionem cessauit, & electum reiecit. Monachi tristes discedere parati sunt. Quos tanta mœstitia affectos, & abeuntes Papa reuocauit. Cum inquit, miseri misericordia indigeant, ex mera gratia nostra vobis electum vestrum concedimus. Verumtamen respiciat in octingentis marcis, quas tali mercatori, cui nos tantum debemus, soluat.
units.tr: In the same way they went through England, trying each of the bishops singly, and having received the same answers from them, they withdrew with dreadful curses and threatening mutterings. Meanwhile, while these men were examining everything one by one, there entered England a chaplain and familiar of the Pope, a certain man named Marinus, who had legatine authority, though he lacked distinction and ornaments. This Marinus was a second to that Marinus, the most greedy questor of the Pope, of whom we spoke a little earlier. Following the similarity of their names, while the others hunted, this one fished for money, sent by the Pope. When he boldly demanded these largesses from the English, he sought, by shrewd and clever arguments and through various legates, that the Gallican clergy lend him at least some money for a short time. But the French, having learned that in this matter they were far more prudent than the English, found that they had no lawful action against the Pope by which they might recover the money lent, and they would not trust him a penny. So the legates returned through Gaul not only empty-handed but mocked with laughter and jeers. Meanwhile, while the Pope's messengers were so eagerly raging in England, the bishops of Canterbury and of its province, who had openly and often refused to give the Pope anything more, even those who had witnessed the concession of Archbishop Boniface, were suspended from their ecclesiastical offices by him by papal authority. He obtained from the Pope that they and all others who opposed Boniface's proposal, who slandered him or in any way committed fraud, should be excommunicated at Rome. This excommunication was proclaimed to the bishops and clergy of the province of Canterbury by the Dean of Beauvais, the Pope's mandatary, and they, struck by such dire censures, reluctantly assented to Boniface. With these men, who had at first resisted so strongly, thus quickly shaken, the Pope, as was his custom, did not cease to snatch to himself whatever he could from England. So he wrote to the Abbot of Abingdon that he should provide some Roman with a fruitful and wealthy church. The Roman, like an eagle that does not catch flies, did not press immediately for the Pope's mandate although many churches were vacant, but waited for the richest. At last the church of St Helen in Abingdon, a very excellent village, fell vacant of its rector. The Roman sought it by the Pope's mandate, but the King wished it to be conferred on his uterine brother Æthelmar, who had held so many churches that he did not know their number. The abbot, perplexed and as if to be ground between two millstones, could not decide what to do, and consulted the convent and his friends. They advised that the King should be gratified rather than the Roman, whom he would find a watchful and perpetual plotter at his side. By their advice the abbot granted that church to Æthelmar. The Pope summoned this abbot, an old man in weak health, to Rome, where, harassed with many insults, he was to undergo judgment for contempt, unless he bound himself to pay that Roman five hundred marks a year. Moreover, when Boniface of St Edmund's had died, the monks chose another abbot. To have him confirmed by the Pope, they sent three of their order from Rome. Having presented the election to the Pope, since it had been carried out without any contention or contradiction, they expected that it would be confirmed without dispute. But the Pope, on fictitious complaints against the elected man, without any inquiry, by the fullness of his power ceased the election and rejected the one elected. The monks were ready to depart in sorrow, but the Pope, seeing them so affected and leaving, recalled them: "Since wretched men need mercy," he said, "from our mere grace we concede to you your elect. Yet let him pay eight hundred marks to such a merchant, to whom we ourselves owe so much."

units.la: Monachi ex impudenti auaritia tantam ægritudinem conceperunt, vt cœrum vnus Lugdunj, alter Doueri cum essent in itinere ex tanto dolore interierunt. Tertius æger & ægrotus superstes fuit vt tam indignum Papæ facinus breuiter fratribus suis referret.
units.tr: The monks, from shameless greed, were so overcome with grief that one died at Lyons and another at Dover while they were on the journey. The third, sick himself but surviving, lived to report briefly to his brothers this shameful deed of the Pope.

units.la: Bonifacius autem Cantuariensis tandem è prouincia, vbi non sub Christi, sed mundi vexillis militauit, in prouinciam Cantuariensem quam absens (vt diximus) expilauit, rectius imitatus Papam nouas pecunias conficiendi rationem sequutus est. Visitare prouinciam totam, Episcopos, Abbates, Clerum, atque populum voluit. Ab Ecclesia sua Cantuariensi exortus est. Quam tam duris legibus & institutis vt ad soluendum cogeret, tractauit, vt omnes exclamarent præcium sum Mõbachos suæ stultitiæ & improbitatis ferre, quod peregrinum indoctum, & Martj potius quam religioni intentum elegissent. Cuius rei fama cum eum visitantem vbiqeue præcurreret, ingratus & inuisus ad singula loca accesit.
units.tr: Boniface of Canterbury finally came out of the province where he had fought under the banners not of Christ but of the world, and entered the province of Canterbury, which he had plundered while absent (as we have said). Imitating the Pope more closely, he followed the method of minting new money. He wished to visit the whole province: bishops, abbots, clergy and people. He set out from his own church of Canterbury. He handled it with such harsh laws and regulations, forcing payment, that everyone cried out that the monks deserved to suffer for their folly and wickedness in choosing a foreigner, untaught and more devoted to Mars than to religion. When the report of this ran ahead of him everywhere he visited, he came to each place hated and unwelcome.

units.la: Cum iam Londinum venisset Episcopi Cicestrensis magnificas ædes Londini positas occupauit, cibariaque Londinensibus nullis adhibitis sibi conuiuis exegit. Fulconem virum pium & eruditum Londinensem Episcopum contra Clericalem verecundiam in ea visitatione contumeliis palam oneraruit. Et postridie cum Decanum & capitulum S. Pauli visitaturus, accessisset, ab his ad Romanum Pontificem appellantibus exclusus est. Quos nihilominus excommunicauit. Deinde inflatus atque tumens & castra redolens induit se lorica, ad Priorātū S. Bartholomæi accessit. Cui intranti occurrunt Subprior cum Conuentu cappis chorealibus amicti. Quos honorem ei summum exhibentes elata fronte despexit, & futm aduentum visitandi causa fuisse denunciauit. Cui vnus ex coeonuentu alta voce respondit. Habere se Episcopum doctum & vigilantem, curas munus esse, cum necesse sit, eos visitare, ab alio autem non velle, nec iure oportere se visitari. Quo responsoria percitus Bonifacius non in loquentem, sed insano more in Subpriorem, qui proximus sibi fuit, senem & infirmum quanta vi potuit, crudeliter irruit, pugno ad terram cecidit, in pectus senile, faciem senis venerandam, & canum caput pedibus insequit, cappam pretiosissimam ex auro & gemmis contextam discerpsit, & a iergo senis detraxit, eam in multas minutas partes lacerataam concuicuit, quae famulus suis in reliquum confuerunt pari dementia saeuientibus praedae fuit. In illa confusione Bonifacius rerorum cecidit, in quo casu eum vestimenta sua dissiparentur loricacius 3 multis conspecta est. Qui praedicabant eum eastris potius quam Ecclesiis administrandis esse aptiorem, & ad pugnandum, quam visitandum, ad ius vendicandum, quam alios corrigendum paratorem. Post hanc pugnam Canonici Londinenses Episcopum at dierunt, illi eos rem Regi prout gesta sit, narrare voluit. Ad aulam cum veniisset, Regem nec alloqui, nec conspicere potestas eis fuit, neque quisquam eorum querelam deferre Regi voluit. Qui Reginae intercessione ne aures de Bonifacio quicquam conquerentibus patefacere potuit.
units.tr: When he had now come to London, he seized the splendid house of the Bishop of Chichester in London and demanded food from the Londoners for himself, with no guests invited. Against all clerical decency, during that visitation he openly loaded Fulco, the pious and learned Bishop of London, with insults. The next day, when he came to visit the Dean and Chapter of St Paul's, they shut him out and appealed to the Roman Pontiff. Nevertheless he excommunicated them. Then, puffed up and swelling and smelling of the camp, he put on a breastplate and went to the Priory of St Bartholomew. As he entered, the subprior came out to meet him with the convent, clothed in choir copes. Although they showed him the highest honour, he looked down on them with a haughty brow and declared that he had come to visit them. One of the convent answered him in a loud voice: they had a learned and vigilant bishop, whose duty it was, when necessary, to visit them, but they did not wish to be visited by another, nor ought they by right to be. Provoked by this reply, Boniface did not turn on the speaker but, in a mad fashion, savagely attacked the subprior nearest him, an old and feeble man, with all the force he could muster. He knocked him to the ground with his fist, trampled on the old man's aged chest, his venerable face and his grey head with his feet. He tore the most precious cope, woven of gold and jewels, and dragged it from the old man's back, ripped it into many small pieces and flung them about. His servants, raging with the same madness, shared the plunder among themselves. In the confusion Boniface himself fell headlong, and in that fall his garments were torn apart, and he was seen by many in his breastplate. Those who had said that he was better suited to camps than to governing churches, readier to fight than to visit, and more prepared to claim rights than to correct others, now had their say. After this brawl the London canons went to their bishop, and he wished to tell the King exactly what had happened. When he came to court, neither could they speak to the King nor even see him, and none of them wished to lay the complaint before the King. Through the Queen's intervention he could not open the King's ears to anyone complaining about Boniface.

units.la: Interea Cines Londinenses ad arma connolant, Bonifacium in frusta distracturi, nisi Regio iussu & edicto pacati & compressi essent. Bonifacius interim eloquentiam periit, & Lametham deductus est per Thamesim. Canonici ad Papam appellarunt. Bonifacius 2 cum sam Lamethi secutus esset, excommunicationis sententiam in D. Pauli, & S. Bartholomaei capitulum & conuentum fulminauit, in qua etiam Fulconem Londinensem Episcopum tanquam eorum fautorem innodauit. Post has rixas pene digladiationes Decanus D. Pauli, vir grauis atque prudens cum nonnullis aliis literas Episcoporum & Praelatorum Cantuariensis Prouinciae certam praemissorum fidem continentes Romam ad Papam pertulerunt. Hoscum aliis Regis literis, & nobilitati suae gentis confisus iniecutus est cum magna pompa & apparatu Bonifacio. Sed cum esset Romae ac verissimas contra se criminationes paratas intelligeret, aduersarios tam Regis ae Reginae, quam suo nomine partim minis partim blanditiis compescuit. Deinde vi prouinciam Cantuariensem ad nutum suum in perpetuum profitaret, egit cum Papa de visitationis fuziure eius 30 authoritate fimando, quod cum in ellexissent Suffraganei, pecuniam grandem ad suppeditandos in iure fumprus in curia Romana, quae pecunia interuc nienre more arundinis ventis agitatae, huc illuc flectu confuerit, conflabant. Graue enim omnibus vitum est Bonifacium nec moribus nec doctrina excultum. post quam 11.marcarum millia absens e sua sola pronuncia hausisset, iterum visitationis praetexu prouinciam exhaurire statuisse; sed cum Rex Papam iterum literis instanter rogasset, vt Cantuariensi Bonifacio in omnibus contra Suffraganeos subueniret, Fulco Londinensis Episcopus primus annum defecit, submisit se Archiepiscopali iurisdictioni & iuramento se astrinxit ita rarurum cuius arbitrio. Post cuius defectionem reliqui coniunctam causam defecerunt. Sed Papa qui perceptis vtrinque a litigantibus vt aequus index videretur, quanquam caetera indulsit, 40 Bonifacio tamen Londinensem Episcopum, Decanum & Canonicos S. Pauli, Subpriorem & Canonicos S.B rtholomaei, aliosque nonnullos, quos Bonifacius tam temere excommunicauisset, absolui praecepit. Sed Bonifacius Decanum & Capitulum D. Pauli iterum aggressus est. Officialem in Anglia discedens Romam Eustachium de Leir constituit. Huic mandauit vt Decani & Canonicorum Londinensium viuendi consuetudinem, & delicta obseruaret, is eos in nouo crimine deprehensos, simulaque a priori excommunicatione absoluti essent, iterum excommunicauit. Huius rei indignitas iterum concitauit Cantuariensis prouincia Clerum, vt mutua deliberatione, coniunctis facultatibus, huius Bonifacii qui vindictam & potentiam tantam sectatur, tyrannidem a se quantocunque dato precio auerterent. Itaq; Dnmestapliae conuenerunt, vbi deliberatione habita decreuerunt procuratorem suo nomine generalem cum hac authoritate mittendi, vt quatuor millia marcarum pro redimenda desiderata sua libertate Papae promitteret, simulque de multis aliis Bonifacii iniuriis in Cantuariensem prouinciam illatis Papa rediderat certiorem. Papa huius lucri spe Episcopis rescripsit, se Bonifacii in eos imperium mitius redditurum, citpeteantem se, vt omnium rerum quae perperam in Anglia gestisset, notitiam ad se perferri curarent. Nec minus Episcopis & Praelatis, quam Regi & Archiepiscopo Papa moderationem & aequitatem sui iudicii decretis pollicitus est. Sed quotidianis vtriusq; partis donis locupletarus sententiam diu distulit diffinitiuam.
units.tr: Meanwhile the citizens of London took up arms, about to tear Boniface to pieces, unless they were pacified and restrained by the King's command and edict. Boniface, meanwhile, lost his power of speech and was taken by the Thames to Lambeth. The canons appealed to the Pope. When Boniface had followed them to Lambeth, he hurled a sentence of excommunication against the Chapter and convent of St Paul's and of St Bartholomew, in which he also bound Fulco, Bishop of London, as their supporter. After these quarrels, almost duels, the Dean of St Paul's, a grave and prudent man, together with some others, carried letters from the bishops and prelates of the province of Canterbury, containing a certain proof of the aforesaid facts, to the Pope at Rome. Relying on other royal letters and on the nobility of his race, he set out with great pomp and display against Boniface. But when he was at Rome and learned that the most true charges against himself were being prepared, he restrained his adversaries, both those of the King and Queen and those acting in his own name, partly by threats and partly by flattery. Then, to bind the province of Canterbury to his will for ever, he dealt with the Pope about confirming the authority of his visitation. When the suffragans learned of this, they melted down a large sum of money to supply funds for the lawsuit in the Roman court. This money, like a reed shaken by the winds, was carried hither and thither in the Roman court, for it was grievous to all that Boniface was cultivated neither in morals nor in learning. After he had drawn 11,000 marks from his province while absent, he resolved to drain it again under the pretext of a visitation. But when the King again urgently asked the Pope by letter to support Boniface of Canterbury in everything against the suffragans, Fulco, Bishop of London, first deserted the cause, submitted himself to archiepiscopal jurisdiction, and bound himself by oath to Boniface's will. After his defection the rest abandoned the common cause. But the Pope, who had received gifts from both litigants so that he might seem a fair judge, although he indulged them in other matters, ordered that Boniface absolve the Bishop of London, the Dean and canons of St Paul's, the Subprior and canons of St Bartholomew, and some others whom Boniface had so rashly excommunicated. But Boniface again attacked the Dean and Chapter of St Paul's. Departing for England, he appointed Eustace de Leir as his official at Rome, and ordered him to observe the way of life and the offences of the Dean and canons of London. If he caught them in some new crime, then, as soon as they had been absolved from the earlier excommunication, he was to excommunicate them again. The indignity of this matter again roused the clergy of the province of Canterbury, so that by mutual deliberation and pooled resources they might ward off, at whatever price, the tyranny of this Boniface, who pursued vengeance and such power. So they met at Dunstable, where, after deliberation, they decided to send a general proctor in their name, with the authority to promise the Pope four thousand marks for the redemption of their longed-for liberty, and at the same time to inform the Pope of the many other injuries Boniface had inflicted on the province of Canterbury. The Pope, hoping for this profit, wrote back to the bishops that he would make Boniface's rule over them milder, and asked them to see that a full account of everything wrongly done in England was brought to him. He promised the bishops and prelates, no less than the King and the Archbishop, moderation and fairness in his judgment. But, enriched by the daily gifts of each party, he long delayed his final sentence.

units.la: Papa tandem sumpta hinc inde pecunia visitationem Bonifacio, adhibito in procuratio-
units.tr: At last the Pope, having taken money from either side, granted Boniface the visitation, to be carried out with the use of proctors in

units.la: Vera Matt. Paris.
units.tr: True account: Matt. Paris.

units.la: An. 1252. curationibus exigendis modo, concessit. Et utriq; parti contra se inuicem muneribus quæ ipse percepit collucanti, huius sententiæ moderatione & æquabilitate satisfecisse sibi visus est. Hac sententia lata rediit in Angliam Bonifacius, cuius aduentus omnium diris execratus est. Propositaq; illi aduenienti contra eo omnium ordinum querelæ insurgere fuerunt. Quibus non mitericordia fedtra permotus respondit. Hi sunt dulci tumores in primo aduentu nostro. Diem edixit callidus & versutus quo in Ecclesia arcuata Loudini solenniter sederet, his quicq; die adesset peccatorum triginta annis perpetratorum remissionem promisit. Huius indulgentiæ spe magnus populi numerus confluxit.
units.tr: An. 1252. ...only with the procurations to be levied did he grant it. And he seemed to himself to have satisfied both parties, having shone, by the moderation and evenness of this sentence, with the gifts he had received from each side against the other. After this sentence was pronounced, Boniface returned to England, and all cursed his arrival. Complaints from every order of men rose up against him on his arrival. Moved by no mercy, he replied to them: "These are the sweet swellings of our first arrival." The cunning and crafty man set a day on which he would sit solemnly in the arched church at London, and he promised remission of the sins of the past thirty years to everyone who attended on that day. A great crowd of people flocked together in hope of this indulgence.

units.la: Qui cum magna quædam & expectanda cuperent, non aliam quam tetram quandam & cruentam excommunicationis sententiam sine omni exceptione in omnes, (pteterquam in Regem, Reginam, Comitem Richardum, & Comitissam eorum; liberos) qui quocunq; nomine in Bonifacium, eiusque conatus aliquid dicere, cogitare, vel perpetrare auderent, excaudire potuerunt. Hanc sententiam Wintoniensis Episcopus electus Æthelmarus frater Regius veterinus in sua diœcesi vt nullam declarauit. Sed Bonifacius eandem Oxonii iterum promulgauit. Iamque itetum hanc suam visitationem inchoauit Bonifacius, sed ex altuo Papæ præscripto & consilio moderatius. Nam in prouincia, vtriusque dolis & euisceratinibus pene deleta & extincta quid in ipsa moderatione moderatum esse potuit? Sed tamen visitationem suam in Roffensi pulila diocæsi inceptam & repetitam gessit sine muneribus, vt facilior sibi ad alias Cant. prouinciæ diœceses adirus patefierent. Ad reliquas tamen cum accessit, turbas magnas fecit, ita vt hęc visitatio multuosa passim dicta sit. Nam in Lincolniensem Ecclesiam mortuo iam Episcopo ius conferendi præbendas & Ecclesias, quod antea capitulo vacante sede competebat, vendicauit, contradictores omnes excommunicauit. Restitit summa vi Willielmus Lupus Archidiaconus Lincolniensis appellatione ad Papam emissa. Hunc non solum excommunicatione, sed omni alia afflictione Bonifacius infequitus est. Itaque latebras quæsiuit in quibus cum ne tutus delitescere posset. Romam pergit, Papam adit, qui exulis aliq; profugi pro suæ Ecclesiæ iure miserit suum absoluit, & a Bonifacio protegit, simulque ipsum deresituendo Lincolniensis Ecclesiæ in ea controuersia iure ei defendendi dedit. Sed cum in utriq; esset molestiis & laboribus toto antedicto triennio defatigatus, efflauit animam. Deinde Roffensem Ecclesiam, in qua iu visitationis exordio fuit moderatus, ademptis quibusdam tertis pro spreto quodam sibi (vt asseruit) impendendo seruitio, diu vexauit. Cantuariensis Monachi qui in eo nihil tamen aut moderatum animadvertebant, a Papa priuilegium obtinuerunt, ne vilitando, suspendendo, vel excommunicando se aut Ecclesiæ suæ statum turbarent. Sed ille Papales de eo priuilegio litetas sibi, cum in Monasterio S. Albani esset, traditas igni cremauit, eatum latores excommunicauit. Ad Regem & Papam de hac immoderata atque sæua crudelis hominis potentia conquestum est. Rex coniugis suæ gratia, cuius auunculus Bonifacius erat, displicere ei noluit. Papa ob gentis suæ in prouincia nobilitatem sibi vicinam, tum ob diuisam intet eos Anglicanam prædam, cum pessimè meritus esset, tamen blandè comiterque affari 40 semper coactus est. Nam q...um facinus est commune, eorum quoq; præda debet esse communis. Itaq; his turbis in prouincia, quam toties detractis facultatibus eneruauit, commotis ad liberandum fratrem suum Thomam Sabaudiensem quondam Comitem, qui à ciuibus vrbis Taurinæ carceribus inclusus & detentus fuerat, & bellumque re- rendum, ex Anglia iam locuples in prouinciam profectus est. Ibi ne Papa quidem adiuuanie, & censuras omnes in Thomæ inimicos fulminante quicquam profecit, sed copiis consumptis ignis & ingloriis reuersus est. Interea dum aberat Henricum Lexinter Lincolniensem Episcopum electum in transmarinis partibus consecrauit. Et Rex Henricus, motus ac defectionem in Guasconia timens, cum ad eos compescendos maturè proficisci cuperet, pecuniæ nerui scilicet belli defuere. Nec in regno toties & tam miserè 50 permissu suo à Papa & Bonifacio expilato vndequaque possit, sciebat. Itaque ad Papam pecuniam accepturus mutuam confugit. Papa non alia ratione quam sub vsuris, iisque grauissimis, tum toto Angliæ regno sibi sub pignore & hypotheca constituto, pecuniis credere voluit. Rex vt pecuniarum copiam haberet, se suum regnum sub pœna exhæreditationis si pecunia statuto die non redderetur, illico obligauit. Cuius facti temeritas & imprudentia omnium pene animos à Rege abalienauit. Papa hanc pecuniam a feneratoribus suis Italis sumpsit. Ac Rege in Guasconia occupato, novam & execrandam viam excogitauit, qua & fœneratoribus suis ex Anglorum pecuniis solucret, & Rex hypotheca & obligatione commissa regnum amitteret. Ruftandum quendam Italum cum Herefo rdensi Episcopo potestate & calliditate instruxit sua ad comparandas pecunias, lite-
units.tr: Though they wanted great and long-awaited things, they could obtain nothing but a foul and bloody sentence of excommunication, without exception, against all who dared to say, think or do anything against Boniface or his undertakings. The exceptions were the King, the Queen, Earl Richard, their countess and their children. Æthelmar, the bishop-elect of Winchester and the King's uterine brother, declared this sentence null in his own diocese. But Boniface promulgated it again at Oxford. He now began his visitation again, though more moderately, following the Pope's instructions and counsel. But in a province almost destroyed and exhausted by the tricks and plundering of both, what moderation could there be? Still, he carried out his visitation, begun and repeated in the small diocese of Rochester, without gifts, so that easier access to the other dioceses of the Canterbury province might be opened to him. When he came to the rest, however, he caused great disturbances, so that this visitation was commonly called troublesome. For at Lincoln, after the bishop had died, he claimed the right of conferring prebends and churches, which had previously belonged to the chapter while the see was vacant, and he excommunicated all who contradicted him. William Lupus, archdeacon of Lincoln, resisted with great force, having sent an appeal to the Pope. Boniface pursued him not only with excommunication but with every other kind of affliction. So he sought hiding-places, and since he could not safely lie hidden, he went to Rome and approached the Pope. The Pope, who had absolved the exiled fugitive and protected him from Boniface, and at the same time, by restoring him, gave him the right to defend the Lincoln church in that dispute. But since he had been worn out by troubles and labours in both places throughout those three years, he breathed his last. Then Boniface harassed the church of Rochester for a long time, in which at the start of his visitation he had been moderate; he took away some tithes on account of a service, as he alleged, that had been spurned by its people. The monks of Canterbury, who however saw nothing moderate in him, obtained a privilege from the Pope that he should not disturb them or their church by vilifying, suspending or excommunicating them. But he burned the papal letters containing that privilege, which had been handed to him while he was in the monastery of St Albans, and he excommunicated the men who had brought them. Complaints of this immoderate, savage and cruel power of the man were made to the King and to the Pope. The King, for the sake of his wife, whose uncle Boniface was, did not wish to displease him. The Pope, because of the nobility of Boniface's family near to him in the province, and because of the English spoil divided between them, though Boniface had deserved very badly, was always forced to speak to him smoothly and courteously. For since the crime is shared, the spoil too must be shared. So, with these disturbances in the province, which he had so often weakened by draining its resources, Boniface roused himself to free his brother Thomas, formerly Count of Savoy, who had been shut up and held in prison by the citizens of Turin, and to wage war. He set out from England, now rich, into the province. There not even the Pope helped him, and though he hurled every censure against Thomas's enemies, he achieved nothing; he returned with his forces spent and without glory. Meanwhile, while he was away, he consecrated Henry of Lexington, bishop-elect of Lincoln, in the lands beyond the sea. King Henry, fearing a movement and revolt in Gascony, wished to set out quickly to put it down, but the sinews of war, namely money, were lacking. He knew that there was no money to be had anywhere in a kingdom so often and so wretchedly plundered on all sides by the Pope and Boniface. So he fled to the Pope to receive a loan of money.

units.la: ris suo homine feorum singulis Ecclefiis Cathedralibus & conuentualibus fcriptis, vt quadam quingentas,quaedam fexcentas,quaedam feptingentas,quaedam mille Sterlingorum marcas(ficenim vetus illè nūmus Angliæ appellabatur)Papæ mutuas darent. Si pecuniias paratas non haberent, indicauit a quibus mercatoribus fub vfuris poffint fu- mere. Poteftatem Ruftando & Herefordenfi Epifcopo, qnos huius mutuandæ pecuniæ conftituit quæftores, veniam his Ecclefiis quæ mutuari pecuniias vellent,terras & Ecclefias ipfas fi vellent pignoridandi. Omnes Angliæ Præfulari hac de re Londinum conuocati funt,propofita hæc caufa eft. Quæ tam inaudita quæftura cum omnes ahrœdas expllationes fuperafiet, Londinenfis Epifcopus exclamauit. Potius quàm confentiam huic extremæ feruituti & iniuriæ Ecclefiæ,capite plectar. Hunc fequutus Wigornienfis;& ego inquit,fufpendio mallem & cruce perire quam hanc non modo feruiuutem,fed euerfionem & ruinam Ecclefiæ eernere. Horum conftantia reliqui In vna fententia contra Ruftandum confpiantes foriter fteterunt. Quos ita cohaerentes cum à Ruftando diftrahi non potuiffent, Ruftandus eis iterum conuoeatis caufabatur Bonifacii Cant. Archiepifcopi pluriumque aliorum Epifcoporum ahfentiam,& Eboracenfis Archiepifcopi mortem Papæ negocio impedimento effe,itaque eos a conuentu illo demiffi. Interea Papa à Ruftando de his quæ in Anglia gererentur, certior factus, nec turpem & ignominiofam repulfam pateretur,per nuncios verfuie confuluit,fe hanc pecuniam petere, vt Regem fibi fub regni hypotheca obaxatum illo xre eximeret. Si igiturauthoritate Regiam fuæ Papali adiungerct,fe eoxre Regem facile foluturum. Quæ omnibus feculis commemoranda fraus Papalis Regem anteaclis suis dolis ad eam inopiam coaætum in tam odiofam traxit fententiam,vt a cunctis Ecclefiafticis viris in Anglia diceretur. Papam & Regem velut paftorem & Lupum in ouium exterminium effe confœderatos.
units.tr: Letters written by the Pope's agent were sent to each of the cathedral and conventual churches, ordering some to give five hundred, some six hundred, some seven hundred and some a thousand sterling marks (for that old coin of England was so called) to the Pope as a loan. If they did not have the money ready, he indicated from which merchants they could borrow at interest. He gave power to Rustand and the Bishop of Hereford, whom he appointed as collectors of this loan, to grant pardon to those churches that wished to borrow money, and to pledge their lands and the churches themselves if they wished. All the prelates of England were summoned to London on this matter, and the case was laid before them. When this unheard-of collection surpassed all previous extortions, the Bishop of London cried out: "Rather than consent to this extreme servitude and injury to the Church, I will suffer beheading." Following him, the Bishop of Worcester said: "I would rather perish by the rope or the cross than see not only this servitude but the overthrow and ruin of the Church." Through the constancy of these men, the rest, agreeing in one opinion against Rustand, stood firm. When they could not be separated from one another by Rustand, he summoned them again and pleaded, as impediments to the Pope's business, the absence of Boniface, Archbishop of Canterbury, and of many other bishops, and the death of the Archbishop of York. So he dismissed them from that assembly. Meanwhile the Pope, informed by Rustand of what was happening in England, and unwilling to suffer a shameful and ignominious rebuff, sent messengers to ask that this money be given to him, so that he could free the King, who was bound to him under a pledge of the kingdom. If, therefore, the royal authority were added to his papal authority, he would easily pay off the King with it. This papal fraud, to be remembered for all ages, drove the King, who had been reduced to such want by his earlier tricks, into so hateful a judgment that all the ecclesiastical men in England said that the Pope and the King had allied themselves like shepherd and wolf for the destruction of the sheep.

units.la: Itaque cum tertio conuoniffent hoc Ruftando imperitante Præfati,compofita eiusdolo fcriptura in membranis fuit,in qua fing■li Præfati faterentur fe a mercatu ibus imo potius nummulariis & fceneratoribus tranfalpinis grandem quandam pecuniarum fummam ad fuam & fingulorum vtilitatem conuerfam accepiffe mutuam. Cui Leonardus quidam doctus atque prudens omnium confenfu contradixit. Ruftandus vir & doctus & verfutus nolle fe dixit ex vnius fermone fingulorum colligere fenfus, itaq; iuffit vt ordine feorfimac figillatim finguli ore fuo affenfum præberent,aut diffentirent. Quæ inopinata doctihominis aftutia attonitos omnes ftupefecit. Vfi itaque longo filentio neque contradixerunt,nec aflenfi funt.Tàdem Ruftandus gemitibus & filentio Anglicani Cleri motus fimulauit fe velle cum D. Papa de hoc negocio confulere. Illi inter gemitus anhelantes affirmabant,quod mori in hac caufa via fuifti.tMartyrii manifeftior, quàm fuerat caufa beati Thomæ Becket Martyris. Itaque Romam ad Papam Decanum D. Panli communemomnium nunciuns & procuratorem mifenunt,veriti ne hac Regis & Papæ confœderatione Ecclefia Anglicana in fetuitutem cuudtis feculis deplorandam veniret.
units.tr: So when the aforesaid men had gathered a third time under Rustand's command, a document was drawn up on parchment by his trickery, in which each of them would confess that he had received from merchants, or rather money-changers and usurers from beyond the Alps, a large sum of money as a loan for his own and each one's benefit. To this a certain learned and prudent man, Leonard, objected with the agreement of all. Rustand, a man both learned and cunning, said he was unwilling to gather each man's opinion from one man's speech. So he ordered that, one by one, in turn, each should give his assent or dissent with his own mouth. This unexpected cunning of the learned man astonished them all. So after a long silence they neither objected nor assented. At last Rustand, moved by the groans and silence of the English clergy, pretended that he wished to consult the lord Pope about this business. They, panting amid their groans, declared that to die in this cause would be a more manifest martyrdom than the cause of the blessed martyr Thomas Becket had been. So they sent to Rome, to the Pope, the Dean of St Paul's as messenger and procurator for them all, fearing that through this alliance of King and Pope the English Church would fall into a servitude to be lamented in all ages.

units.la: Papa non modo Clerũ er Ruftandõ,fed primatis literis nobiles & magnates regni ad pecuniam fibi mutuo dădam folicitauit. Inter quos à Richard o Cornubiz Comite quingentas marcas mutuas poftulauit. Sed Richardus uon fe contradicturum cum eo mutuum i efpondit cum quo iure contendere & experiri non poterat. Lanam item à Ciftercienfis ordinis Monachlis iantam flagitauit, quantam vno integro anno ad fui fuftentationem collegiffent. Decanus autem D. Pauli cum effet Romæ ab Alexandro Papa,qui Innocetio vaferrimo illo & inexplicabili Anglicani Thefauri heluoni fucceffferat, refponfum in tam arduo & perplexo negocio fatis æquum & henignum tulit. Vt quia Rex eum regni hypothecaalienigenis nempe Italis creditoribus fefe obligaffet , vt pro ea peeunia quam ad as Regium diffoluendum præftarent, deeimam honorum Ecclefiafticorum quam ad tertram fanctamrendendam polliciti eflent,retinerent.Ita regni hypotheca ab Angliæ Clero liberata & redempta eft.Iamque Bonifacius à hello Taurino in prouincia (vt diximus)reuerfus,ab Epifcopo Roffenfi,cuius iura & libertates aperte violauerat,ad Papam appellatione præmiffa citatus eft.Sed Regis affinitate,& nobilitate fua,tum Papæ coniunctione in anteactis rapinis fretus,quæcunque in fe fufcepta effent, contempfit & lucibrio habuit.Ita in fua prouincia Cantuariensi diutius in Clericorum bonis grassandio fium & occafionem vifitando atque corrigendo captans, aliquot annis fecuré permanfit. Hoc anno Ecclefia Cath.Sarum à Bonifacio in fefto S.Michaelis dedicata eft & Hugo de Balesham Collegii S.Petri Cantabrigiæ fundator, Epifcopus Elienfis confeeratus.Sed poft eaquâ Alexander Papa Regé ab eo iuramēto,q. de feruandis regni priftīnis iuribus atq; libertatibus cum Edwerdo fuo filio,Baronibus regni, (vt ante diximus) Oxonii
units.tr: The Pope urged not only the clergy and Rustand but also, by letters, the nobles and magnates of the kingdom to lend him money. Among them he demanded a loan of five hundred marks from Richard, Earl of Cornwall. But Richard replied that he would not refuse to lend, though he could not contend with him at law or bring a suit against him. He likewise demanded wool from the Cistercian monks, as much as they had gathered in one whole year for their own support. The Dean of St Paul's, however, while he was at Rome, received from Pope Alexander, who had succeeded that most crafty and inexplicable glutton of the English treasury, Innocent, a reply in so difficult and perplexing a matter that was quite fair and kind: since the King had pledged the kingdom as security to foreign creditors, namely Italians, the creditors should retain, for the money they would pay to discharge the King's debt, the tenth of ecclesiastical revenues which the clergy had promised for the Holy Land. Thus the pledge of the kingdom was freed and redeemed from the English clergy. And now Boniface, returning into the province from the Turin war (as we said), was cited by the Bishop of Rochester, whose rights and liberties he had openly violated, by an appeal sent to the Pope. But relying on his kinship with the King, his nobility, and his connection with the Pope through past plunders, he despised whatever had been brought against him and treated it as a joke. Thus he remained for some years secure in his Canterbury province, raging for a long time against the goods of the clergy, and seizing every opportunity of visiting and correcting. This year the cathedral church of Salisbury was dedicated by Boniface on the feast of St Michael, and Hugh de Balsham, founder of St Peter's College, Cambridge, was consecrated bishop of Ely. But afterwards Pope Alexander secretly absolved the King from the oath which he had sworn at Oxford in Parliament, to Edward his son and the barons of the kingdom, to observe the ancient rights and liberties of the realm (as we said before), at Oxford

units.la: {a} Verbo Mat. Paris. Oxonii in Parliamento praestiterat, secreto absoluisset, Rexq; ab eorum iurium obseruatione recessisset, nec pacta seruasset, ciuile bellum atrox inter Regem & Barones sitscepit ut est. Haec iura quae a Rege fracta sunt in legibus regni municipalibus Magnacharta dicuntur, quae Bonifacius antea cum omnibus Regni Episcopis potificalibus ornamentis induci in aula Westmonasteriensi sub excommunicationis latae poena, ex Regis praecepto ab omnibus seruanda praeceperunt. Itaque his a Rege iuribus violatis cum armae essent capienda, prospexit sibi Bonifacius discessione quae instar fugae fuit, & ne tam quaestoae prouinciae lucrum amitteret, vices suas Hugoni Mortimero viro tam in pecuniis congerendis scientissimo commisit. Quam quidem ad rem satis cautus atque
units.tr: {a} In Matthew Paris's words: at Oxford, in Parliament, he had sworn to these, and then secretly absolved himself from them. The King withdrew from observing their rights and did not keep his agreements, so a savage civil war broke out between the King and the barons, as is well known. These rights, which the King broke, are called in the municipal laws of the realm Magna Carta. Earlier, Boniface, vested in his pontifical ornaments in the hall at Westminster along with all the bishops of the realm, had under pain of the excommunication he pronounced, and by the King's command, ordered that they be observed by all. So when these rights had been violated by the King and arms had to be taken up, Boniface provided for himself by a departure that was like flight. Lest he lose the profit of so lucrative a province, he committed his duties to Hugh Mortimer, a man most skilled in collecting money.

units.la: 10 prouidus tam a Rege quam a Baronibus in ipso pene praecinctus atque castris anicquam discederet, veniam impetrauit. Ita in patriam Sabaudiam discessit. Hoc tempore Vrbanus Papa refecisset duabus electionibus quas Wintonensis Conuentus fecisset, Iohannem Oxon. Ebotacensem Cancellarium in Winton. Episcopum Romae consecrauit, qui Papae sex marcarum millia, totidemque Iordano Papae vicecancellario soluisset, & quanquam a Papa sacratus esset, tamen subiectione postea Bonifacio iureiurando promisit. Ac Vrbano Papa mortuo, magna inter Cardinales de alio oligendo contentio diu mota fuit. Qui tandem Guidonem Sabinensem Episcopum militem quondam uxoratum, tunc autem in Anglia Romanae sedis legatum elegerunt. Hic Clemens dictus est. Sed Angliae praesules ac Barones haud clementer tractauit, sed quamdiu vixit, sum-
units.tr: Being shrewd and prudent enough in this matter, and while almost surrounded and hemmed in by the camps of both the King and the barons, he obtained pardon from both before he left. So he departed for his homeland, Savoy. At this time Pope Urban, having rejected the two elections that the Winchester convent had made, consecrated John of Oxford, the chancellor, as bishop of Winchester at Rome. He paid the Pope six thousand marks, and as much to Jordan, the Pope's vice-chancellor. And although he had been consecrated by the Pope, he afterwards promised Boniface, under oath, submission. When Pope Urban died, a long and great dispute arose among the cardinals over choosing another. At last they chose Guy, bishop of Sabina, a former soldier and married man, who was then the Roman see's legate in England. He was called Clement. But he did not treat the English prelates and barons mercifully; as long as he lived he pursued them with the utmost

units.la: 20 mo odio persecutus est eo quod legationis tempore ingressus in Angliam ei prohibitus est. Interea bellum hoc procutante Vrbano Papa qui Alexandro successit, per Ottonem & Octobonum in Angliam missos legatos tandem transactum & pacatum. Postea Octobonus duas Cleri Synodos, vnam Northamptoniae, alteram Londini celebrauit; in quibus constitutiones multas prouinciales tulit, quae inter iura huius regni Ecclesiastica etiam nunc obseruantur. Bonifacius quoq; postquam quadriennio toto aberat Cantuariensis reuersus est, sed ante aduentu suum & ingressum, conditionem a Baronibus accepit, vt in sua prouincia non nouas turbas vt antea concitaret, sed se quieti ac pacifice gereret. Sed in hac absentia Walterum Gifford Bathoniensem Episcopum electum ab Episcopo Parisiensi mandauit consecrari. Et reuertus Hugonem de Sanwico Londinensem
units.tr: hatred, because when he had entered England on his legation he had been forbidden entry. Meanwhile, while Pope Urban, who succeeded Alexander, pursued this war, the legates sent into England, Otto and Octobonus, at last brought it to an end and restored peace. Afterwards Octobonus held two synods of the clergy, one at Northampton and the other at London. In them he enacted many provincial constitutions, which are still observed among the ecclesiastical laws of this kingdom. Boniface too, after he had been away for four whole years, returned to Canterbury; but before his arrival and entry he accepted a condition from the barons, that in his province he should not stir up new disturbances as before, but conduct himself quietly and peaceably. But during this absence he had ordered Walter Gifford, bishop-elect of Bath, to be consecrated by the bishop of Paris. And on his return he consecrated Hugh de Sanwich, bishop of London,

units.la: 30 Episcopum Cant. consecrauit. Walterum autem de Lauilla Sarisburiensem electum a Winton. Episcopo vicino mandauit consecrari. Cumq; rursus entus Reip. statu pacaruis esset, Rex ad eas controuersias quas Ecclesia Bonifacius disseminauerat, componendas adhibuit animum. Itaq; illae cum Episcopo & Ecclesia Roffensi, cum Episcopo & Ecclesia Lodinensi, cum Ecclesia Lincolniensi, Sarisburiensi, & cum Ecclesia sua Cantuariensi lites quas ante commemorauimus, ne aliqua veterum discordiarum scintilla in Rep. aut Ecclesia superesset, Rege ipso intercedente sopitae & extinctae sunt. Roffensem Episcopum & Ecclesiam feudalia sibi pro omnibus suis terris debere seruitia in iure vicit. Horum seruitiorum loco 12. annuas marcas stipulatus est. Douorensis autem Ecclesiae subiectio in illa pactione Episcopo Roffensi reseruata est. In Lincolniensi Ecclesia & de vi-
units.tr: as archbishop of Canterbury. He ordered Walter de Lavilla, the elect of Salisbury, to be consecrated by the neighbouring bishop of Winchester. When the state of the commonwealth was again peaceful, the King turned his mind to settling the disputes that Boniface had spread through the Church. So those quarrels which we mentioned before, with the bishop and church of Rochester, with the bishop and church of London, with the church of Lincoln and Salisbury, and with his own church of Canterbury, were calmed and ended, the King himself intervening, so that no spark of the old discords might remain in the commonwealth or the Church. He won a legal judgment that the bishop and church of Rochester owed him feudal services for all their lands. In place of these services he stipulated twelve yearly marks. The subjection of the church of Dover, however, was reserved to the bishop of Rochester in that agreement. In the church of Lincoln, winning by force, he obtained the whole episcopal right,

units.la: 40 cante totum ius Episcopale obtinuit, octo tantum Ecclesiis quae in ciuitate Lincolniensi sitae sunt, exemptis & capitulo retentis, Visitationem plenam summa vi & ope resistentibus omnibus Suffraganeis, ipsisq; inuitis compleuit, procuratione vnius cuiusq; diei in visitando consumptae ad quatuor marcas taxatae. Item cum Richardo Glocestriae Comite de his seruitiis militatibus quae Cantuariensi Ecclesiae pro munerius de Tunbridge, Bratford, Werlston, Horsmond, Reieston iure debentur, nec non de eiusdem Comitis ordine, loco, & stipendio in Archiepiscoporum Cantuariensium institutionibus pepigit. Cantuariensem Ecclesiam grandi aere alieno praedecessorum suorum Stephani, Richardi magni, & Edmundi immoderatis sumptibus deuinctam 12. marcarum mil- 50 libus liberauit. Aulam illam nobilissimam & amplissimam Cantuariensis palatii cuius sinus appenditiis quam Hubertus inchoauit ipse perfecit & absoluit. Vnde ioco inter familiares suos dicere solitus est. Maiores suos sibi aulam construendam locasse. Praedecessores inquit, mei istam aulam cum magnis expensis fecerunt, bene quidem fecerunt, sed expensas ad illam construendam nisi de pecunia mutua non inuenerunt, videlicet quidem mihi, quod ego illam feci: quia illorum debita persoluí. Quod, vt dixi mus, reuera praestitit. His perfectis Synodum ptouinciale in Londini ex Vrbani Papae mandato celebrauit. Huic Otto & Octobonus Legati interfuerunt. In ea prouinciali iura seu decreta 17. promulgata sunt. Paulo post cum sibi sanctior & moderatior, vtpote qui castris & tumultibus, quibus antea totus vacabat, relictis Ecclesiae curam gerere coepit, Regem cum Episcopis suis adit. Eum togat vt regni sui peregrinorum incursu qui praecipuas Eaclesiasticas dignitates & Ecclesias tenebant, labefactati memor, deinceps praficiat suae gentis atque nationis, inter quos optimus delectus haberi poterat, viros doctos atq; pios. Cui Rex, Hoc inquit libenter faciam. Proinde equidem censeo vt tu qui alienigena & indoctus is, meusq; frater Athelmarus Winton. Episcopus, quos non alia quam affinitatis & cognationis ratione praeficiendos tantis dignitatibus curaui, ad reliquorum exemplum vos abdiceris Ecclesiis, & prospiciam vt vobis eruditi atq; pii viri succedant. Hoc Regis responsum Bonifacium ita pugugit, vt molestam sibi vitam in Anglia deinceps ducere semper visus sit. Itaque cum icuisset se & Regi ipsi ingratum, & populo atq; eloroinuisum fuisse, redire poritus in suam patriam, quam Cantuariae manere voluit. Itaque memoribus succisis, locatis Archiepiscopus praediis, exactis a tenentibus variis tributis, permultifq; aliis Cleri & ptouinciae suae spoliis, ingenti confecta pecunia, abominibus pene execratus in suam patriam Sabaudiam profectus est: ibi in S. Helenae capella, postea quam 26. annis, & mensibus sex, ac 16 diebus a sua consecratione sedisset, a prima vero electione viginti nouem annis, 15. Kalend. August. obiit. Maidestoniae in Apostolorum Petri, & Pauli, necnon Thomae Cantuariensis honorem hospitale multis praediis instructum fundauit. Quod hospitale nouo operis vulgariter dictum est. Hoc postea Willielmus Courtney Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus in Collegium saecularium lacerdotum mutauit. Vulgus eum saepe vt vxoratum exprobrabat. Viuus multa magnificè magis quam piè gestit. Eodemq; modo moriens testamento singulis Abbatibus ad Cisterciii capitulum accedentibus decem marcas legauit. Vt proximo post eius mortem capitulo quadringenti plures Abbates conuenirent. Huius tempore Palatium Westmonasterii igne penè totum deletum est. Et ciues Norwicenses ob Monachorum odium Ecclesiam Cathedralem cum palatio incendunt. Annonae item caritas parentes in multis locis ad liberos suos deuorandos compulit. Modius enim trinici ra. solidis, intetdum etiam 16. aestimabatur. Prouidentia item Oxoniensis Academiae diplomate regio confirmata est. His igitur calamitatibus & cruentis Papae rapinis, cuius auctoritas iam tandem exosa Regibus atq; populo vacillare, & ad ruinam paulatim vergere coepit, Bonifacii Archiepisc. ignominiose & infeliciter gestus ac transfactus est. Quo mortuo Papa Simonem de Mountford Leycestriae Comitem, omnefq; qui cum eo occubuerant, quos ante excommunicauerat curia Romana, absoluit. Dicebat enim Romanam curiam in sententia contra eos lata fuisse deceptam.
units.tr: excepting only eight churches situated in the city of Lincoln, which were exempt and kept by the chapter. Against all the suffragans resisting with the greatest force and effort, and against their will, he carried out a full visitation, and the fee for each day spent on visiting was fixed at four marks. Likewise he agreed with Richard, Earl of Gloucester, about the military services owed by right to the church of Canterbury for the manors of Tonbridge, Bradford, Werlston, Horsmonden and Reigate, and also about the earl's rank, place and pay at the installations of the archbishops of Canterbury. He freed the church of Canterbury, bound by the heavy debts of his predecessors Stephen, Richard the Great and Edmund and by their immoderate expenses, from twelve thousand marks. He himself completed and finished that most noble and spacious hall of the archiepiscopal palace, with its adjoining wings, which Hubert had begun. Whence he was accustomed to say jokingly among his household that his predecessors had let him the building of their hall. My predecessors, he said, built this hall at great expense; they did well, but they could find the money for building it only by borrowing; so it fell to me, since I built it, to pay off their debts. And this, as we said, he in fact did. When these things were completed, he held a provincial synod at London by the mandate of Pope Urban. The legates Otto and Octobonus were present at it. In that provincial synod seventeen decrees or laws were promulgated. Shortly afterwards, becoming holier and more moderate, since he had left aside the camps and tumults to which he had previously devoted himself entirely, he began to attend to the care of the Church, and he approached the King with his bishops. He asked the King that, mindful of his kingdom's weakening by the inroads of foreigners who held the chief ecclesiastical dignities and churches, he should from then on appoint to these men of his own people and nation, from whom the best choice could be made, learned and pious men. To which the King replied: "I will gladly do this. Accordingly I think that you, who are a foreigner and unlearned, and my brother Aethelmar, bishop of Winchester, whom I placed in such dignities for no reason other than kinship and family ties, should, as an example to the rest, give up your churches, and I will see that learned and pious men succeed you." This answer of the King so stung Boniface that he always seemed to lead a troubled life in England from then on. So when he had perceived that he had become unwelcome even to the King himself, and hateful to the people and clergy, he preferred to return to his own country rather than remain at Canterbury. Accordingly, with the woods felled, the archiepiscopal estates let out, various taxes exacted from the tenants, and very many other spoils of the clergy and his province, having amassed a vast sum of money and almost cursed by all with abomination, he set out for his homeland of Savoy. There, in the chapel of St Helena, after he had sat as archbishop for twenty-six years, six months and sixteen days from his consecration, and twenty-nine years from his first election, he died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August. At Maidstone he founded a hospital in honour of the Apostles Peter and Paul and also of Thomas of Canterbury, endowed with many estates. This hospital is commonly called the New Work. Later William Courtney, archbishop of Canterbury, changed it into a college of secular priests. The common people often reproached him as a married man. While alive he carried out many things more magnificently than piously. In the same way, dying, he bequeathed in his will ten marks to each abbot who came to the chapter of the Cistercians, so that at the next chapter after his death four hundred more abbots might gather. In his time the Palace of Westminster was almost entirely destroyed by fire. And the citizens of Norwich, out of hatred of the monks, set fire to the cathedral church together with the palace. Likewise a dearth of grain drove parents in many places to devour their children. For a bushel of wheat was valued at twelve shillings, and sometimes even at sixteen. Also in this period the Academy of Oxford was confirmed by a royal charter. So, amid these calamities and the bloody plunderings of the Pope, whose authority, now at last hateful to kings and people, began to totter and gradually to tend towards ruin, the archbishop Boniface's career came to an end, shamefully and unhappily. After his death the Pope absolved Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester, and all who had fallen with him, whom the Roman court had earlier excommunicated. For he said the Roman court had been deceived in the sentence passed against them.
