units.la: Hic Bonifacius vt moribus gestufq; peregrinus, sic nomine ipso & appellatione reliquis omnibus tam prioribus quam eum sequuris Archiepiscopis fuit dissimilis. Id quod Radulphus de Diceto Ecclesiae quondam Paulinae Londinensis Decanus, vir in Anglicana historia sui temporis peritissimus, qui ad Hubertum Archiepiscopum scribens ex illa tam longa Archiepiscoporum Cantuariensium tot annis ducta serie, mirari se ait, nec duos vnquam vno eodemque nomine appellari. Quod quidem viique ad Huberti tempora, vt ipse annotauit, verum fuit. Nos vero qui 70. Archiepiscoporum vitas in hoc opere descripsimus multo magis mirari debemus, & animaduertendum esse diximus, praeterquam quod & hic Bonifacius, & quatuor post eum Archiepiscopi nominibus a caeteris omnibus distincti & discriminati fuerunt, ex illo toto septuagenario numero, ne media partem coniunctam Archiepiscopalem sedem tot annis occupasse, quot hic noster septuagesimus solus ad hunc annum Dom. 1372. tenuit. Quiquod deinceps annis eum locum tenebit, in eius solius est cognitione atque potestate, qui suo arbitrio regit & custodit singula.
units.tr: Boniface was as foreign in his conduct and deeds as he was different from all the earlier archbishops, and also in his very name and title. Radulph of Diceto, once Dean of St Paul's in London and a man most expert in the history of his own time in England, makes this point. Writing to Archbishop Hubert, he says that he marvels at that long succession of archbishops of Canterbury over so many years, in which no two were ever called by the same name. This was certainly true down to Hubert's time, as he himself noted. We who have described the lives of seventy archbishops in this work ought to marvel much more, and I have said that we must take note. Apart from the fact that Boniface and the four archbishops after him were distinguished and set apart from all the rest by their names, out of that whole series of seventy, not even half of the years in which the archiepiscopal see has been held together were occupied by them, as many years as this our seventieth alone has held it up to the year of the Lord 1372. How long he will hold that place from now on lies in the knowledge and power of Him alone, who rules and keeps each thing by his own will.

units.la: XLVII. Robertus de Kylwarbi, sive de Kylwerdeby.
units.tr: XLVII. Robert of Kylwarby, or Kylwerdeby.

units.la: ODEM anno quo Bonifacius Sabaudiensis Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus regno atque vita (vt diximus) cessit, tanti & tam copiose diffluentes imbres post fulgura atq; rutbines Cantuariae consecuti sunt, vt incredibilis & a fecuIis in illa ciuitate inaudira pluuia non modo ingros sed ipsam pene ciuitatem inundauit.
units.tr: In the same year that Boniface of Savoy, Archbishop of Canterbury, departed both his realm and his life (as we have said), such great and abundant rains followed the lightning and thunder at Canterbury, rains so incredible and unheard of in that city for ages, that they flooded not only the fields but almost the city itself.

units.la: Dic primum toto atque sequente nocte aere tonante, nimbi confertim collecti obduxerunt tenebris ciuitatem, a quibus profluens pluribus diebus pluuia, greges & armenta ex agris abduxit, præsepia subuerit, ipsas arbores vi sua prostrauit, sæpe etiam radicitus auulsit. Hoc diluuium fames & annonæ caritas occupauit, famemq; contagio & pestis. Vt vulgus dicere ac existimare solebat: hanc diuinam cladem & vltionem ob Bonifacii permissa & perperrata scelera Cantuariæ contigisse. Interea Henricus Rex Clemente Papa mortuo, Romanaq; sede triennio penè vacante, aliquam alleuationem intolerabilis illius iugi papalis senit. Itaque modica sibi a Papali exactione intercapedine concessa, tanquam respiratione & paucorum dierum ab hostili direptione indneiis datis, cepit illam excelsam & illustre Westmonasterierisem Ecclesiam fabricare. Postea Nordouicum ad sumendam de his pœnas, qui (vt in Boni-
units.tr: For the whole of that day and the following night, with the air thundering, storm clouds gathered thickly and covered the city in darkness. The rain that poured from them for many days swept away flocks and herds from the fields, overturned the cattle-sheds, beat down the trees with its force, and often tore them up by the roots. Famine and scarcity of provisions followed this deluge, and with the famine came contagion and plague. The common people used to say and believe that this divine calamity and vengeance had fallen upon Canterbury because of the crimes Boniface had allowed and committed (as we have said of Boniface). Meanwhile King Henry, with Pope Clement dead and the Roman see vacant for almost three years, obtained some relief from that intolerable and constant papal yoke. Having been granted a brief respite from papal exactions, like a breathing space of a few days from hostile plunder, he began to build that lofty and famous church of Westminster. Afterwards he set out, joined by the nobles, for Norwich, to take vengeance on those who had set fire to the cathedral church and the palace.

units.la: facio diximus) in Cathedralem Ecclesiam & Palatium incendium miserunt, magnatibus fisis sociatus profecturus est. Ibi facinoris tanti duces flammis deleuit, reliquos aut patibulis suspendit, aut equis distraxit. Qua peracta scrutate cum ad S. Edmundi Cœnobium diuertisset, lethali morbo correptus obiit, testamentumq; moriens nuncupauit, vt creditoribus solutis bonorum suorum reliduum distribueretur indigentibus. Paulo antequam è viuis excessit, licentiam Monachis Cantuariensibus eligendi Willielmum de Chillinden Conuentus sui Subpriorem in Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem fecit. Is electus Romam ad Gregorium decimum, qui Vrbano iam mortuo successit, vt electio firmaretur, profectus est. Sed Gregorius, vt maiorum suorum exemplo specimen aliquod in papatus sui primordiis illius (vt nuneupant) plenariæ potestatis ostenderet, hominem aperte, cum simplicem vt electioni cederet facilima non suasione sed oratione cogit.
units.tr: ...) There he destroyed the leaders of so great a crime with flames, and hanged the rest from gibbets or tore them apart with horses. When this was done and the inquiry finished, he turned aside to the monastery of St Edmund, was seized by a deadly illness, and died. Dying, he made his will, directing that after his creditors were paid, the remainder of his goods should be distributed to the needy. A little before he departed this life, he allowed the monks of Canterbury to elect William of Chillenden, subprior of their convent, as Archbishop of Canterbury. The elect went to Rome to Gregory X, who had succeeded the late Urban, to have the election confirmed. But Gregory, wishing to show some sample of his full power at the beginning of his pontificate, as they call it, after the example of his predecessors, compelled the man, who was plainly simple and easily yielded to the election, not by persuasion but by a peremptory word of command.

units.la: Hiusloco fine Monachorum consensu, simulans in Subprioris illius electione vitium manifestum, quod in suam potestatem ius conferendi transtulit, interuenisse Robertum de Kylwarby Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum pronunciauit. Hic Robertus gente Anglus, ab incunte ætate Parisiis educatus, artes illas ingenuas & liberales professus est. Quarum profitendarum gradu donatus in Angliam rediit, & fratrum Minorum, quique (vt supra in Bonifacio commemorauimus) cum prædicatoribus Roma missis occultam Papæ in Anglia quæsturam gerebant, ordinem ingressus est. Horum ille non miles Gregorius, sed Antelignanus fuit, nempe Prouincialis, cuius inter eos munus præcipuum & verberrimum fuit. Nam quos reliqui fratres prohibuissent à sacris, hic solus (vt diximus) ex Papæ mandato restituit.
units.tr: Thereupon, with the consent of the monks, feigning that there was a manifest defect in the election of that subprior, he transferred to himself the right of conferring the see, and declared that Robert de Kylwarby, Archbishop of Canterbury, had intervened. This Robert, an Englishman by birth, had been educated at Paris from his earliest years and had professed those noble and liberal arts. Having gained the degree of teaching them, he returned to England and entered the order of the Friars Minor, who (as we mentioned above in the life of Boniface) had been sent from Rome along with the preachers and secretly served as the Pope's questors in England. Among them he was not a soldier of Gregory's, but an Antelignanus, that is, the provincial, whose chief and most weighty office among them was this: those whom the other brothers had forbidden to exercise sacred functions, he alone (as we have said) restored by the Pope's command.

units.la: Quod munus vndecim annis gratissimus Romanæ curiæ quæstor gessit. Hunc cum cedente atque repulso Willielmo, Papa sua voce tanquam oraculo Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum declarasset, Monachi quorum insolentia Regibus sæpe (vt in Baldwino declarauimus) molesta, iam tandem ab ipso Papa quam contra Reges implorare cōsuenerunt, fracta est, ne ius eligendi amissile viderentur, hunc Robertum a Papa Antistitem declaratum, etiam & ipsi eligunt. Ad eumq; Lonrini cum illa fratrum minorum seu prædicatorum scaturigine agentem suum Subpriorem, qui electioni suæ coram Papa renunciauit, Priorem Douorensem, & Officialem Cantuariensem miserunt, qui eum Cant.
units.tr: He held this office for eleven years as a most acceptable questor of the Roman court. When William had yielded and been set aside, and the Pope had declared Robert Archbishop of Canterbury by his own voice as if by an oracle, the monks, whose insolence had often been troublesome to kings (as we showed in the life of Baldwin), and which they had customarily sought from the Pope himself against the kings, now at last laid aside that habit. Lest they appear to have lost their right of election, they elected this Robert too, since he had been declared bishop by the Pope. And they sent to him at Lyons, where he was engaged with that fountain of Friars Minor or preachers, their subprior, who renounced his own election before the Pope, the prior of Dover, and the official of Canterbury, to hail him

units.la: Conuentus nomine electum salutarent. At Robertus etsi Archiepiscoparum hunc Papæ acceptum tulit, vt Monachorum gratiam & beneuolentiam colligeret, perhumaniter eius accepit atq; tractault, secumq; de Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis negociis confisllum datos oco diebus retinuit. Inter alia, consecrationis suæ die prima quadragesimi dominicæ statuerunt, quæ illo anno in 4. Kal. Martii incidit. Eo die conueneruit vndecim Cantuariensis Prouinciæ Suffraganei, reliqui seprocuratoribus constitutis excusabant. In quorum præsentia à Willielmo Bathoniensi Episcopo (nam Londinensis aduersa valetudine impeditus abfuit) in ipsa Ecclesia Metropolitica Cantuariensi consecratus est. In ipsa consecratione Prior Cantuariensis exegit ab hoc Roberto tria millia marcarum, quæ Conuentus Cantuariensis in electione Willielmi de Chillindon Subprioris Cant. electione confirmasset, quæq; Papa eidem Willielmo electioni renunciante promisisset, proximum Archiepiscopum Cœuentui redditurum. Sed Robertus hac ab eo repetita petuniain Priorem motus, inquisitione habita de moribus eius atq; vita scrutatus est, vt eum Priorauitamouaret. Quod cum intellexisset Prior, indixit Conuentu, vt ex tam grandi debito nulle & ter centum marcas Archiepisc. remitteret. Quo concesso Archiepiscopus ab inquirendo destitit. Peracta consecratione redit Londinum. Ibi mortuo (vt diximus) Henrico Tertio, cum Edwardus eius primogenitus esset in Syria, multaq; in Sarracenos gessisset egregiè, Robertus Cantuariensis cum regni præsulibus & magnatibus in Nouo templo Londini congregatis, Edwardum absentem Dominum & Regem suū agnouerunt, eumq; paternæ dignitatis successorem populo toti per Angliam præconum vocibus declarari fecerunt. Et rarii custodes, regiique fisci procuratores & ministros, qui regni prouentus in visus regios conseruarent constituerunt. Interea Edwardus primus cum de patris obitu accepisset, dimissis Acone stipendiariis militibus in Angliam festinat, marique traiecto Siciliam applicuit. Ex Rex Carolus obuiam honoriffice dedit, eumque Romam comitatus est. Vbi Edwardus cum Gregorio. X. familiari suo multa communicabat. Nam cum post Papæ Clementis mortem, qui Vrbano successit Romana sedes peneannis Pontifice caruerat, Cardinales huncGregoriorum decimum (quitum cum Edwardo in castris & Christiana commilitia Acone fuit, & Theobaldus, Archidiaconus Leodiensis dicebatur) Henrici Regis Angliæ, & Edwardi filii sui gratia Romanum Pontificem elegerunt. Itaque magna ex illa militari familiaritate & coniunctione necessitudo atque amicitia inter Gregorium Papam & Edwardum Regem constata est. Itaq; Gregorius Edwardo ad eos sumptus quos in Sitia fecisset recuperandos potestatem concessit bonorum in Anglia quorumcunque tam temporalium quam spiritualium decimam partem à Clero percipere, Egregium scilicet munus, cum de suo "largiri nihil voluit, de alienis bonis sumendi veniam indulsit. Roma itaque huiusmodi "Papæ beneficio affectus Edwardus Rex discedens ab Italiæ ducibus cum tubis & tripudiis pet Hetruriam in Burgundiam ductus est. Ibi à proceribus Angliæ occursum eius fuit, qui Galliam magno honore & admiratione transeuntes tandem in Angliam appellunt. Cumq; iam paucis diebus in Reginæ matris, & Antistium procerumque suorum consuetudine ad deliberandum de publicis priuatisq; negociis suisset, in Angliam à Gregorio Papa missus venit Romanus quidam Clericus Raymundus natione Guascounus, cum authoritate viros Ecclesiasticos papalibus animaduertionibus compellendi decimam tam temporalium quam spiritualium Edwardo Regi soluere. Ex qua sine morocollecta pecunia Rex perexiguam tulit partem. Raymundus enim (qui nomine Regis huic conficiendæ pecuniæ præfectus fuit) Papalis potius & Romanæ cupiditatis, quam Regiæ necessitatis quæstor exi-stimari iure debuit. Qui cum rationes retulisset pro suis in hoc negocio expensis atque operarum modicam portionem detraxit, deinde Papæ Domino suo donum tanto Pontifice dignum exhiberi postulauit. Quæ duæ rationes, hanc tam copiosam pecuniam penè totam absorpsit, vt Regi ex præsulum beneuolentia vix aliquid Regiis dignum gratiis telictum sit. Cumq; hoc exemplo Gregorius Papa in Christianas Ecclesias Romano more grassandi occasionem nactus esset Concilium generale indixit Lugduni, vbi cum inutiliter de coniugenda Græca cum Romana Ecclesia multa actæ essent, illuisq; coniunctionis ex Paleogi Græcorum Imperatoris & Episcoporum Græcorum literis ad Papam datis spes inanis, aliu Gregorii totum concilium lactauisset, decretum fuit, vt toto proximo septennio & prouentum Ecclesiasticorum decima parsin icrræ sanctæ subsidium solueretur. Cuius (vt patebit postea) cum quæstores à Papa constituti essent, in Romanam auaritiam non illius negotii expeditionem aut curam tota conuersa est.
units.tr: as elected in the name of the convent. Robert, although he took the Pope's gift of the archbishopric as a great favour, nevertheless, to win the goodwill and kindness of the monks, received and treated them most courteously, and kept them with him for eight days to consult about the affairs of the Church of Canterbury. Among other things, they fixed the day of his consecration for the first Sunday of Lent, which that year fell on 4 Kal. March. On that day eleven suffragans of the province of Canterbury gathered; the rest excused themselves and appointed proxies. In their presence he was consecrated in the metropolitan church of Canterbury itself by William, Bishop of Bath, for the Bishop of London was absent, prevented by ill health. At the consecration, the prior of Canterbury demanded from Robert three thousand marks, which the convent of Canterbury had promised in the election of William of Chillenden as subprior, and which the Pope had promised to that same William when he renounced his election, namely that the next archbishop would restore them to the convent. But Robert, moved by the prior's demand for this repayment, held an inquiry into his morals and way of life, in order to find grounds for removing him from the priorship. When the prior learned of this, he summoned the convent, and the convent remitted to the archbishop one thousand three hundred marks of so great a debt. Once this was granted, the archbishop desisted from the inquiry. When the consecration was complete, he returned to London. There, with Henry III dead (as we have said), and his eldest son Edward absent in Syria, where he had fought splendidly against the Saracens, Robert of Canterbury, with the prelates and magnates of the realm assembled in the New Temple at London, acknowledged the absent Edward as their lord and king, and had heralds proclaim him throughout England as the successor to his father's dignity. They also appointed keepers of the royal treasury and procurators and officers of the royal fisc, who would keep the revenues of the realm for the royal use. Meanwhile Edward I, when he heard of his father's death, dismissed his mercenary soldiers at Acre and hastened to England; having crossed the sea, he landed in Sicily. King Charles met him there with honour and accompanied him to Rome. There Edward discussed many matters with Gregory X, his intimate friend. For after the death of Pope Clement, who succeeded Urban, the Roman see had gone almost three years without a pope, and the cardinals elected this Gregory X (who had been with Edward in the camp and the Christian army at Acre, and was called Theobald, Archdeacon of Liège) as Roman Pontiff, out of regard for Henry, King of England, and for his son Edward. Thus from that military familiarity and association a great bond of intimacy and friendship was established between Pope Gregory and King Edward. Accordingly, Gregory granted Edward the power, in order to recover the expenses he had incurred in Syria, to take from the clergy a tenth part of all goods in England, both temporal and spiritual. A fine gift indeed: since he was unwilling to give anything from his own, he granted leave to take from the goods of others. Thus favoured by this papal kindness, King Edward left Rome, and was led with trumpets and rejoicing, away from the Italian leaders, through Tuscany into Burgundy. There the English nobles met him, and passing through France with great honour and admiration, they at last reached England. When he had been a few days in consultation with his mother, and with his bishops and nobles, on public and private affairs, there came into England a certain Roman clerk, Raymond, a Gascon by birth, sent by Pope Gregory, with authority to compel churchmen by papal censures to pay King Edward the tenth of both temporal and spiritual goods. From this money, collected without delay, the king received only a very small part. For Raymond, who was put in charge of collecting it in the king's name, ought rightly to be regarded as a questor of papal and Roman greed rather than of royal need. When he had rendered his accounts of expenses in this business, he deducted a modest portion for his own labours, and then demanded that a gift worthy of so great a pontiff be presented to the Pope, his lord. These two items swallowed up almost all of this so abundant sum, so that scarcely anything worthy of royal thanks was left to the king from the goodwill of the prelates. And since Pope Gregory, with this precedent, had found an opportunity to rage against the Christian churches in the Roman manner, he summoned a general council at Lyons. There, after much had been done in vain about joining the Greek Church with the Roman, and the empty hope of that union, raised by letters sent to the Pope from the Greek emperor Palaeologus and the Greek bishops, had been cast aside, the whole council was persuaded by Gregory, and it was decreed that for the whole following seven years a tenth of ecclesiastical revenues should be paid as aid for the Holy Land. As will appear later, once questors had been appointed by the Pope for this, the whole business was turned to Roman greed, not to the carrying out or care of that undertaking.

units.la: Hanc decimâ cum Gregorius postulasset, deliberandi diem Arch.Episcopis, Prælatis statuit, quo vel consenserint vel dissenserint causas & rationes ostenderent. Adueniente die plerique contradicere non ausi aperte suffragiis assensi sunt. Inter quos Robertus Kylwarby Cantuar. Archiepiscopus ab ipso (vt diximus) Papa constitutus. Pater inquit sancte, Opus & cteatio manuum vestrarum ego sum, & Ecclesia mea Ecclesia vestra, bona mea, bona vestra sunt. Disponite ergo de Ecclesia mea, & de bonis meis, sicut de bonis propriis. Inter cæteros autem qui contradicere statuerunt, erat Simon quidam de Mepham Decanus Lincolniensis. Qui Papæ tradidit schedulam excusatoriam, Angliæ Ecclesiæ expilationes diuturnas & varias continentem, quibus ita deiecta & depressa, vt vix aut ne vix quidem alterfugere aut sc attollere possit. Cui perlecta schedula Papa. Dictasti schedulam hanc D. Decane: Et ille pater sancte ego dictaui & scripsi. Et "Papa. Numquid consentis & tu, vel contradicis? Et ille, Domine non contradico. Et Papa: aliud est nõ consentire, aliud nõ contradicere. Quid igitur, consentis? Eodemq; iterû modo respondit. Domine non contradico. Cumq; aliter non respondet, priuauit cum "dicto citius omnibus beneficiis Ecclesiasticis. Cuius metu cæteri sine contradictione assensus suos præbuere.
units.tr: When Gregory had demanded this tithe, he set a day for the archbishops and prelates to deliberate, on which they were to state whether they agreed or disagreed, and to show their reasons. When the day came, most of them, not daring to object openly, assented by their votes. Among them was Robert Kilwardby, Archbishop of Canterbury, appointed by the Pope himself (as we have said). "Holy Father," he said, "I am the work and creature of your hands, and my Church is your Church; my goods are your goods. Dispose, therefore, of my Church and of my goods as of your own." Among the others who had resolved to object was a certain Simon de Mepham, Dean of Lincoln. He handed the Pope an excusatory schedule, containing the long and various plunderings of the English Church, by which it had been so cast down and depressed that it could scarcely, or hardly at all, rise up or get free. When the Pope had read the schedule through, he said: "You drafted this schedule, Mr Dean?" And he replied: "Holy Father, I both drafted and wrote it." And the Pope: "Do you too consent, or do you object?" And he: "Lord, I do not object." And the Pope: "To not consent is one thing, to not object is another. What then, do you consent?" He answered in the same way again: "Lord, I do not object." And since he would answer in no other way, the Pope at once deprived him of all ecclesiastical benefices. Through fear of this, the others gave their assent without objection.

units.la: Tandem ipse Decanus ne solis dissentire videretur, & dignitates amitteret, vnà cum reliquis assensus est, & elapso triduo beneficiis suis restitutus. In hoc concilio Gregorius multas constitutiones, quas in certis Decretalium titulis digessit, quæq; Gregorianæ constitutiones appellantur, tulit.
units.tr: At last the Dean himself, lest he seem alone in dissenting and lose his dignities, assented together with the rest, and after three days was restored to his benefices. In this council Gregory issued many constitutions, which he arranged under certain titles of the Decretals, and which are called the Gregorian constitutions.

units.la: Hoc anno Thomas Aquinas, curiosus magis & subtilis quàm solidus Theologus in quodam Cisterciensium Monachorum Cœnobio, quod Noua fossa dicebatur obiit. Io eoque concilio Papa quo facilius in bppressos anteactis iniuriis Anglos sese insinuaret, Edwardum Regem ob terram sanctam sua præsentia & aduentu seruatum infinitis laudibus extulit. Huius decimæ solutione à Clero promissa Concilium statim à Gregorio dissolutum est, Iáţ in Anglia apparatus splendidi ad Regem & reginam Electorum regiis sacris initiando instituti sunt. Qui Westmonasterii à Roberto Cantuar. Arch.14. Kal.Septemb.regiis coronis insigniti, arq; faerari sunt.Interfuerunt his solemniis regina Mater Regis, Comitum præsulum nobiliumq; pariter & ignobilium copiosa frequentia.Ex alienigenis autem Alexander Scotorum Rex, & Dux Britanniæ.Quorum vtriq; in vxores suas suscèptis duabus Regis furoribus affines Regi fuerunt. Sed horum coniugibus subita ereptis morte accidit, vt nuptiarum gaudia lugubres exitus sortita sint. Posteaq; in vigilia S.Nicolai,terræmotus, fulgura, & tonitrua, Draceq; igneus & Cometa Anglos terruere,in qua tempestate Regis lusticiarii,dum ad tribunalia in aula Westmonasteriensi accederet,ad Crucem lapideam quæ Charing Crosse appellatur,confitere,ibique terrore perculsi confidere coacti sunt, sequutaq; hunc terrorem est lues ex oue morbida ex Hispaniis importata, quæ monstri similis, & ouium intusitata magnitudine instar biennalis bouiculi fuit, dum in Anglia cum ouibus gregibus permisceretur,eos illata contagione infecit. Hæc lues 18.annis duranit. Interea Robertus exacto iam primum sub confœrationis anno veteri Cantuariensis curiæ, quæ in aruano Lontuni templo celebratur,statuta à multis Cantuariensibus Archiepiscopis antiquitus sancita,desuetudine penè adumbrata renouauit,omniaq; breuiter quinq; articulis complexus est. Deinde suq; Prouinciæ Clerum ad nuuum templum conuocauit, cui concilio etiam Eboracēsis Archiepiscopus accersitus interfuit. In hoc Concilio Lewelyn Griffini filius Princeps Walliæ,quia mandatis Regis obtemperare recusauit, totius Synodi decreto excommunicatus est. Et cum ad pertinaciam dicti principis compescendam bellum Edwardo Regi necessariò suscipiendum esset, milirumque deletus habendus,ciuibus Cant. duodecim oquites imperauit. Illi Monachos rogant, vt ex suis bonis horum nullum sumptibus cōferrent Id Monachi sine Regis & Archiepiscopi sui authoritate & consensu factura negant.Itaq; commoti ciuesinierunt inter se iuramento fœdos se indignis modis Monachos mulctaturos.
units.tr: In this year Thomas Aquinas, a theologian more curious and subtle than solid, died in a monastery of Cistercian monks called Fossanova. At this same council, so that he might more easily insinuate himself among the English, who had been oppressed by earlier wrongs, the Pope extolled King Edward with endless praises for having been preserved for the Holy Land by his presence and arrival. Once the clergy had promised payment of this tithe, the council was immediately dissolved by Gregory, and in England splendid preparations were made for the consecration of the King and the Queen with royal rites. They were crowned with royal crowns at Westminster by Robert, Archbishop of Canterbury, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, and were anointed. Present at these solemnities were the Queen Mother, and a copious crowd of counts, prelates and nobles, both high and low. Of foreigners there came Alexander, King of the Scots, and the Duke of Brittany. Both of these had married sisters-in-law of the King, and so became related to him. But their wives were suddenly snatched away by death, so that the joys of their weddings had mournful endings. Afterwards, on the vigil of St Nicholas, earthquakes, lightning and thunder, and a fiery dragon and a comet terrified the English. In that storm the King's justices, as they were going to their tribunals in the hall of Westminster, were struck with terror at the stone cross called Charing Cross, and were compelled to stop there in fear. This terror was followed by a plague from diseased sheep imported from Spain, which was like a monster, and in size was unusual for sheep, like a two-year-old calf. When it was mingled with English flocks of sheep, it infected them with the contagion it carried. This plague lasted eighteen years. Meanwhile Robert, in the first year of his confirmation, renewed the ancient statutes of the Canterbury court, which are celebrated in the chapel of St Mary of Arches in London, which had been enacted anciently by many Archbishops of Canterbury and had been almost overshadowed by disuse; and he briefly embraced all of them under five articles. Then he summoned the clergy of his province to the New Temple, and the Archbishop of York, summoned to this council, attended as well. In this council Llywelyn, son of Gruffydd, Prince of Wales, because he refused to obey the King's commands, was excommunicated by the decree of the whole synod. And since war had to be waged against the obstinacy of this prince by King Edward, and a soldier was to be regarded as lost, he ordered twelve horsemen from the citizens of Canterbury. They asked the monks to contribute none of their goods to these expenses. The monks refused to do so without the authority and consent of the King and their Archbishop. Therefore the citizens, roused to anger, swore an oath among themselves that they would punish the monks by unworthy means.

units.la: Primò omnes Monachorum in vrbe Cantuariensi inquilinos ex omnibus vrbanis illorum prædiis proscriptione eiecturos, omnes eorum redditus perceptu ros, & datu ros pauperibus. Deinde edicturos ne quis Cantuariensis ciuis cum Monachis quocunque modo contraheret. Ad hæc se quæ euncq; in vrbem Monachorum causa importata aliunde essent distracturos. Monachis præterea quos cepissent detracturos ad corporis nuditatem & ignominiam vestes. Monasterium ipsum valle atque fossa profunda, vt ingressus & egressus omnis prohiberetur,circumseptures. Ad Thomæ delubrum peregrinantes iureiurando adacturos, ne pecunias offerrent. Ad extremum vt quietes ad Regem mittendi Thomæ delubrum inuaderent, & ex eo exquisitissimos annulos vt ablatos digitis gestarent. Hic autem ciuium Cantuariensium in Monachos fructus conatus à Roberto Ieni & benigna suasione repressus est. Ineratenim huiusmodi illa rutie temporis ignaris hominibus gratiæ superstitionis nugis dicendi suadela. Iamq; Monachi postfratrum & prædicatorum in Anglia aduentum ( vt ante diximus) Regi atque populo præ illis despectui esse ceperunt. Hoc pacato tumultu,totam Cant. Prouinciam visitationis iure peragrauit, sequè donis non impericando, sed artificiose vt sui ordinis fratres solebant suadendo locupletauit. In hac visitatione Academias ipsas Metropolitica authoritate ingressus est. Et Oxonii in scholis non modò de Theologia, sed de Philosophia, atque Logica argute disceptauit. In quibus artibus multas Oxoniensium opiniones & sententias tanquam minus probabiles reprehendit atq; reuellit.Quas opiniones Iohannes Peckam qui eum in Archiepisc. proxime sequntus est institutus Cleri Synodo,cuminania tantum & inepta Sophistarum essent deliria,tanquàm hæreticas & à fide Christiana abhorrentes condemnauit. Eodem anno fratrum Minorum Cœnobium ex veteri Londinensi Turri ad occiduam ciuitatis partem quondam posita,ipsaq; vetustate demolita,grandi à pronincialibus fratrum Miourum solicitatione collecta pecunia constructit.
units.tr: First, they would expel from their urban estates all the tenants of the monks living in the city of Canterbury, would take all their revenues and give them to the poor. Then they would decree that no citizen of Canterbury should have dealings with the monks in any way. Besides, they would seize whatever goods had been brought from elsewhere for the monks' sake into the city. Moreover, they would strip the monks they had captured of their clothes, to their bodily nakedness and shame. They would surround the monastery itself with a deep valley and ditch, so that every entrance and exit would be forbidden. They would force those on pilgrimage to Thomas's shrine, under oath, not to offer money. Finally, they would send the most exquisite rings, as if taken, to the King, and would invade Thomas's shrine and wear them on their fingers. But this violent attempt of the Canterbury citizens against the monks was checked by Robert by gentle persuasion; for in that rude age such eloquence of persuasion was effective with men ignorant of grace, and given to the trifles of superstition. And now, since the coming of the Friars Minor and Preachers into England (as we said before), the monks had begun to be despised by king and people in comparison with them. When this tumult was calmed, he travelled through the whole province of Canterbury by right of visitation, and enriched himself not by demanding gifts but by persuading, skilfully, as the brothers of his order were accustomed to do. In this visitation he entered the universities themselves with metropolitan authority. At Oxford, in the schools, he disputed keenly not only about theology but about philosophy and logic too. In these arts he rebuked and rooted out many opinions and judgements of the Oxford men as less probable. Which opinions John Peckham, who most closely followed him as Archbishop, condemned in a synod of the clergy, since they were mere empty and foolish delusions of the Sophists, as heretical and abhorrent to the Christian faith. In the same year the friary of the Friars Minor was built with money collected by the vigorous solicitation of the provincial friars, moved from the old Tower of London, which had once stood in the western part of the city, and which had been demolished by age.

units.la: Huius occidentalis turris reliquias, quæ in lapidibus & cæmento fuerunt,ad reparadam Templi Paulini Cancellam incendio deletam Londinensi quondā Episcopo Willelmus Normannus cōcessit. At Robertus hoc extructo & condito ad Minorū fratrum
units.tr: The remains of this western tower, which had been stone and mortar, Willelm Norman, once Bishop of London, granted for the repair of St Paul's church, which had been destroyed by fire, the chancel. But Robert, when this had been built and founded as a convenient habitation for the Friars Minor' monastery, now rich and wealthy,

units.la: commodam habitationem Coenobio, iam loeuples atque diues, à Nicolao tertio Papa, inter quem & Gregorium Aridanus quintus intercessit, Romam ad precium participandum accitus est, ab eoque Cardinalis Hostiensis, & Portuensis Episcopus creatus Qui Cantuariensis Archiepiscopatui non tam sponte cessit, quàm vt alium sui ordinis atque loci virum illius scaturiginis Minorum in Anglia fratrum, sicut ipse fuerat provincialem loco suo à Papa surrogari procurat. Scripsit in Theologia, Logica, atque Philosophia acute permulta, quibus de rebus viuus saepe eodem acumine differere consueuit, eoq; libros diuulgauit. Simulatq; ad Cardinalatum, & Episcopatum Romae gerendi accessit, correptus graui morbo fuit, ex eoq; paucis postea diebus Viterbii interiit, vbi homo conditus iacet.
units.tr: was summoned to Rome by Pope Nicholas III, between whom and Gregory there came Adrian V, to share in the counsel; and he was created by him Cardinal and Bishop of Porto and Ostia. He ceded the Archbishopric of Canterbury not so much willingly as he procured that another man of his order and place, from that spring of the Friars Minor in England, just as he himself had been provincial, be substituted in his place by the Pope. He wrote very many acute things in theology, logic and philosophy, on which subjects, while alive, he was often accustomed to debate with the same keenness, and so he published books. As soon as he came to the cardinalate and to the bishopric to be administered at Rome, he was seized by a grave illness, and a few days later died at Viterbo, where the man lies buried.

units.la: XLVIII. Iohannes Peckam.
units.tr: XLVIII. John Peckham.

units.la: V A M gratiosus fratrum Minorum & praedicatorum (quiin Anglia, sedentibus, vt diximus, Edmundo, & Bonifacio, à curia Romana nouae religionis praetextu missi sunt) ordo Papis habebatur, non modò ex antegresso Roberto Kylwarby, sed ex fratre Iohanne colligemus. Namque his fratribus praeualentibus, Monachi in quibus omnis vitae sanctitas & puritas Dei cultus ineße antea putabatur, hoc nouo à Papa suscitato religiosorum numero ignaui & desidiosi, ideoque inutiles atque putidi censebantur.
units.tr: How favoured the friars Minor and the friars Preachers were with the Papists (who, as we said, were sent to England by the Roman court under the pretext of a new religious order, while Edmund and Boniface were in office) can be gathered not only from the earlier Robert Kilwardby but from Brother John. For while these friars held the upper hand, the monks, in whom all holiness of life and purity of worship had formerly been thought to lie, were judged idle and sluggish by this new body of religious that the Pope had raised up, and therefore useless and foul.

units.la: Horum igitur aucta & illorum extenuata tam Regi quàm Papae gratia, eum Robertus ex illo fratrum grege primus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus, Cardinalis & Portuensis Episcopus à Nicolao Papa creatus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopatui cessisset, Papa eundem Archiepiscopatum Iohanni Peckam, Monachis Cantuariensibus non modo non requisitis, sed etiam inuitis contulit, eumq; sine Suffraganeorum praesentia Romana in curia consecrauit. Nam Monachi Robertum Burnel Bathoniensem Episcopum Regni Cancellarium postulauerunt, qua postulatione spreta & contempta Iohannes Peckam, Monachis Cantuariensibus, non modo non requisitis, ...
units.tr: So, with the favour of both the King and the Pope increasing for these friars and declining for the monks, Robert, the first archbishop of Canterbury from that band of friars, was made cardinal and bishop of Porto by Pope Nicholas. When he gave up the archbishopric of Canterbury, the Pope conferred that archbishopric on John Peckham. The Canterbury monks had not asked for him, and indeed they opposed him, and the Pope consecrated him at the Roman court without the presence of any suffragans. For the monks had nominated Robert Burnell, bishop of Bath and Wells and the King's chancellor. When this nomination was scorned and rejected, John Peckham, not requested by the Canterbury monks but even against their will, ...

units.la: Ioan. 3. omnipotentia exištimabatur, šcripsit. Ecce me creastis, & quanto creatura à šuo naturaliter appetit perfici creatore, šic in meis oppressionibus censeo per vos recreandum. Sane nuper ad me peruenit cuiusdam executionis litera horribilis in aspectu, & audiri terribilis, quod nisi infra mensem a festo Beati Michaelis mercaturibus Lucanensibus cum effectu de quatuor millibus marcarum quae in Romana curia contraxi, satisfaciam, ex tunc sim excommunicationis sententia innodatus, & in Ecclesia mea, & alus maioribus, pulsaris campanis, accensis candelis, excommunicatus denuncier singulis diebus Dominicis & festiuis. Hanc tamen grandem solutionem impossibilem sibi futuram rescribit. Quoniam & Robertus Kylwarby discedens Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis bona secum abstulit, & anteeum Bonifacius archiepiscopalia caduca & ruina reliquisset, & Rex vniusanni redditus retinuisset, & sibi ad vnius anni sumptus sustinendos mutua sumenda esset pecunia. Quz in Anglia tam crebris solutionibus exhausta haberi vix aut ne vix quidem poterat. Et ad Gétilem quendam suum in Romana curia familiarem scribit, se coactum ad accipiendum mutuo duo millia marcarum pro intronizationis suæ sumptibus octauo Idus Octob. proximi faciendis. Illa autem Papalis cautela, vt hi, quib. pecunias mercatoribus suis soluendas imperaret, agnoscerent se eas ad suos vsus mutuos priusaccepisse, non noua iam fuit, sed à Rustando quondam(vt in Bonifacio antea diximus) Papæ in Anglia quæstore calliidissimo in vsum, nouo exemplo introducta est. Io-hannes sæpe atque multa non modo Papæ, sed Cardinalibus, suoque quondam confraci atque prædecessori Roberto Kylwarby vt ab hac solutione libe ràrentur scripsit, quod enim impetrare non poterat, data ei est post diuturnam intercessionem ægre tandem vinius anniad soluendum dilatio. Interea Robertus Kylwarby Anglicanus (vt diximus) spoliis locupletes indignitatis suæ culmine positus, cuius vsuram petexiguo percepit tempore, Romæ vita functus est. Quo mortuo atque intestato frater Iohannes Peckam ad Papam qui intestatorum bona, pauperibus & piis vsibus ipso iure Pontificio concessabi reseruauit, de restituendis Cantuariénsi Ecclesiæ 5000 marcis, quas Robertus Romani discedens ab eadem Ecclesia iniuste abstulisset, literas dedit. Ad quas etiam repetendas procuratorem Anselmum quendam suum constitutum ̄ multis ad Cardinales mandatis misit. Etsi mirum videri possit hominem satis astutum atque callidum, quinque ipsos 30 Romanas versutias longè edoctus tempore cognouisset, eiusmodi expectatione atq; spe decipi voluisse. Præsertim cum suo exemplo ex antedictis quatuor marcarum millibus Papam non reddendis, sed exigendis rationibus assiduam dare operam intellexisset. Sed dum hac petitione liberari se saltem ab illa 4000. marcarum præstatione sperabat pro isdem soluendis, literis nouis Papales execrationes minantibus illico interpellatus est. Quo quasi imperato sibi silenuo re perinde atque ipse exci dens deinceps conticuit. Iamq; ad prouinciam regendam conuersus Concilium Cleri Lamethi celebrauit. In quo non EuAn.1280 angelii prædicationem, sed Lugdunensis Concilii à Gregorio decimo sancita, & Othonis atque Octoboni Romani Pontificis Legatorum decreta (de quibus in Edmundo & Bonifacio antea diximus) religiosissimè obseruanda præcepit. Præterea leges Ecclesiasti40 cas sexdecim nouas condidit, quæ inter prouinciales constitutiones continentur. Hoc concilio durante Ebotacensis Archiepiscopus dum vt Regem adiret. Cantuariensem prouinciam cruceante se gestata ingressus est. Ea res(vt sæpe antea diximus) magnarum inter Archiepiscopos contentionum causa sæpe fuit. Itaque lohannes Cant.edictis per totam suam prouinciam promulgatis sub excommunicationis pœna iussit, ne quis Ebotacensi aut suis famulis esculenta, poculenta, scu. quæcunque ad victum necessaria ministraret, vllusue publici aut priuati negotii commercium cum illis haberet. Cuius rei seueritate cum aut prouincia infestis negotiis exeundum, aut fame pereundum esset Ebotacensibus, crux illa tanto fastu erecta, humiliter deposita & deiecta fuit. In eodem Concilio exemptos quos vocant, qui Metropolitani iurisdictione conti-nineri, eiusque iussu ad concilium accedere recusarunt, excommunicationis atque suspensionis pœnis afflixit. Inter hos Westmonasteriĭ, S. Albani, S. Edmundi, & Waltami Cœnobiorū Abbates tanquā reliquorū duces prouocabant ad Papā, quibus magnus per Cant. prouinciam exemptorū numerus adiundus adhæsit. Sed cū Cătuariensis Arc hiepiscopi vim ac potentiá sustinere nō poterāt, appellatione deserta in eius potestatē& misericordia sese cōmittebant. Cōclu so aūt & dimisso illo Cōcilio prouincia tota visitando perlustrauit, magis vt de singulis Ecclesiis totiusque prouinciæ statu certior fieret, quàm vt seueritate aut Ecclesiastica disciplina vteretur. Cuius lenitatis atque moderatio-An. 1281 nis causæ perhibentur, quod primo ingressu prouincialium suorum beneuolentiam captauit,ideoque durius adhuc cum eis agere noluit. Deinde quod bello à Cambris in RegeEdwardum moto,Iohannes in Cambriam vt sederet tumultum Regepsfo (vt alleruit)insidio secessit.Hoc bellum à Leolino Criffini filio Wallię Principe fratre suo Dauidem infligante,nec non ariolis quibusdam Cambrensibus,qui Principi suasserunt iam iam fore vt Bruti diademate,prout Merlinus quondam vaticinatus est,insigniretur,totamq; Britanniæ Insulam regeret,iusceptum est.Etsi Leolinus eiusque frater Dauid scri- ptis ad Iohannem Cant. cum in Cambriam venissetliteris, affirment se arma sumere, quòd contra inita fœdera Regii Iusticiarii & Balliui Cambrosiniustis non tolerandis toties affecissent,vt mori,& in acie perire malint quàm vitam in seruitute atque tyrannide molestam ducere. Itaque cum Iohannes de pace concilianda in Snowdonia Cambriæ provincia diu sed frustra tractaniffet,in Angliam rediit;excommunicationisque sententiam Oxonii , vt in Bonifacio ante dixit mus, in pacis Regiæ violatores latam contra Leolinum & Dauidem, eorumq; milites promulgauit. Sed antequam in Cambriam pedem intulisset,veritus ne vt retineretur,nec redire facile cum vellet posset,R.Burnell. Bathonien sem Episcopum,quem(vt ante diximus)Cant.Monachi In Archiepiscopum postulauerunt, Vicarium suum, & admin istratorem suæ prouinciæ generalem constituit, Et vt Cambros aliquo merito deuinciret, multos ex ea prouincia Clericos indoctos,egentes,atque peregrinos nouo superstitionis modo insti tuto,in Angliam misit. Codices enim Euangeliorum omnes & curiose in membranis ligatos singulis dedit,his qui inscitia literarum pronunciare aliquid ex illis non poterant vt saltem quarundam instar reliquiarum manibus gestarent populoque ostenderent,præcepit. Tum literas ad multos dedit,in quibus rogauit, vt hos Cambrenses Clericos Euangellum non ore proferentes, sed digitis baiulantes reciperent, & ad eleemosynas percipiendas circumire permitterent.Illitaque Codices Euangelii scripti circumducentes,eos insano & amenti sine doctrina vulgo non sine admiratione,& stupore,idiomate suo Euangelion Euangelion clamantes ostendebant. Qua superstitione Angliæ delusa plebs signatus & ignotos homines multis donis affecit.Rebus his in Cambria gestis, Edwardus Rex armata & militari manu Cambriam inuadit.Ibi tum Edmundus quidam strenuus miles cum Leolino subito confixit,eumque fuso exercitu trucidauit.Fraftiquecambrorum iam animis Dauid , qui suis imposturis has turbas concitauit, paulo post à Regiis satellitibus captus,& Regitradictus est. Amborum capita palis longis superposita, & in altitudinem erecta supra Pontem Londinensem more proditorum fuerunt. His superaris ducibus tota Cambria in Regis Angliæ ditionem se protinus dedit.Cuius rei euentus suæ spei, & expectationi quam ex Merlini vaticiniis colligebant,planè contrarius accidit. Vt victoria quam sibi statuerunt euenturam à Deo concederetur Anglis. Post banc victoriam Cambri quandam partem ligni eius crucis , cui seruator nostrer Iesus Christus affixus fuit, Regi obtulisse pethibentur.Subiugata itaque Wallia Rex Nonhamptonæ Parliamentum tenuit,ad quod Cambriæ Baronesaccesserunt,Regique fidem & homagium iureiurando dederunt.
units.tr: ...was thought to be omnipotent, he wrote [Ioan. 3.]. "Behold, you have created me, and just as a creature naturally desires to be perfected by its creator, so in my oppressions I think I am to be recreated by you." Indeed, a letter of a certain execution, dreadful to look upon and terrible to hear, has lately come to me, saying that unless within a month from the feast of St Michael I satisfy the Lucca merchants with the four thousand marks which I contracted at the Roman court, I shall then be bound by the sentence of excommunication, and my churches and other greater churches, with bells rung and candles lit, will have me proclaimed excommunicate every Sunday and feast day. He writes back, however, that this great payment will be impossible for him to make: since Robert Kilwardby, on leaving, carried off the goods of the Church of Canterbury, and Boniface had left behind the archiepiscopal revenues in ruin and decay, and the King had kept one year's income, he would have to borrow money to meet the expenses of a single year. In England, drained by such frequent payments, that money could scarcely, or hardly at all, be had. He writes to a certain Gentile, his familiar at the Roman court, that he has been compelled to borrow two thousand marks to meet the costs of his enthronement, to be paid on the eighth day before the Ides of October next. That Papal cautela, by which those on whom he ordered the money to be paid to his merchants should acknowledge that they had first received it as a loan for their own use, was not new, but had been introduced in a novel way, as the Papal collector Rustand, the most crafty of men, had formerly used it in England (as we said earlier under Boniface). John often and at length wrote not only to the Pope but to the cardinals and to his former brother and predecessor Robert Kilwardby, that he might be freed from this payment. What he could not obtain, however, was granted to him, after long intercession, with difficulty: a delay of one year for paying. Meanwhile Robert Kilwardby, the Englishman (as we said), enriched with spoils and raised to the height of his unworthiness, died at Rome after enjoying the revenues only a short time. When he had died intestate, Brother John Peckham wrote to the Pope, who by Papal right reserved the goods of the intestate for the poor and for pious uses, about restoring to the Canterbury Church five thousand marks which Robert had unjustly taken from that Church when leaving Rome. To demand these back he also sent many instructions to the cardinals through a proctor he had appointed, a certain Anselm, his own man. Although it may seem strange that a man quite shrewd and crafty, who had learned at length the Roman tricks, should have wished to be deceived by such an expectation and hope, especially since he knew from his own example that the Pope was intent on exacting the accounts of the four thousand marks, not on repaying them, yet while he hoped by this petition to be freed at least from that payment of four thousand marks, he was at once challenged by new letters threatening Papal curses. As if commanded by this, he fell silent, and afterwards kept quiet about the matter, as if he himself were being cut off. Now turned to governing his province, he held a Synod of the Clergy at Lambeth. In it he ordered that not the preaching of the Gospel, but the decrees of the Council of Lyons, sanctioned by Gregory X, and those of Otto and Ottobono, the Roman Pontiff's legates (of which we spoke earlier under Edmund and Boniface), be observed most scrupulously. Besides this, he drew up sixteen new ecclesiastical laws, which are contained among the provincial constitutions. While this council was in session, the Archbishop of York entered the province of Canterbury, having a cross carried before him as he went to see the King. That affair (as we have often said before) was often the cause of great contentions between the archbishops. So John of Canterbury, having published edicts throughout his whole province under pain of excommunication, ordered that no one should supply food, drink, or anything else necessary for life to the Archbishop of York or his servants, nor have any dealings with them in public or private business. By the severity of this order, since the people of York had either to leave the province with their business in ruin or perish by hunger, that cross, raised with such pride, was humbly laid down and cast aside. In the same council he afflicted with the penalties of excommunication and suspension those whom they call exempt, who refused to answer to the Metropolitan's jurisdiction and to attend the council at his command. Among these, the abbots of Westminster, St Albans, St Edmunds and Waltham, as leaders of the rest, appealed to the Pope, and a large number of exempt persons throughout the province of Canterbury joined them. But when they could not withstand the power and might of the Archbishop of Canterbury, they abandoned their appeal and committed themselves to his power and mercy. The council concluded and dismissed, he toured the whole province on visitation, more to be informed about the state of each church and of the whole province than to use severity or ecclesiastical discipline. The causes of this gentleness and moderation are said to be that at his first entry he sought the goodwill of his provincials, and therefore did not wish to deal more harshly with them. Then, when war was stirred up against King Edward by the Welsh, John withdrew into Wales to calm the disturbance, as he himself alleged, on the King's behalf. This war, stirred up by Llewelyn, son of Gruffydd and Prince of Wales, with his brother David urging it on, and also by certain Welsh soothsayers, who persuaded the Prince that it was about to come to pass that he would be crowned with the diadem of Brutus, as Merlin once prophesied, and would rule the whole island of Britain, was undertaken. Although Llewelyn and his brother David, when John of Canterbury had come into Wales, affirmed in letters written to him that they were taking up arms because the King's justiciars and bailiffs had repeatedly inflicted unjust and intolerable wrongs on the Welsh contrary to the agreements made, and that they preferred to die and perish in battle rather than lead a life made wretched by slavery and tyranny. So when John had long but fruitlessly laboured to make peace in Snowdonia, the province of Wales, he returned to England, and at Oxford he published the sentence of excommunication, as we said above under Boniface, against Llewelyn and David and their soldiers, as violators of the King's peace. But before he had set foot in Wales, fearing that he might be detained and could not easily return when he wished, he appointed Robert Burnell, bishop of Bath, whom the Canterbury monks had nominated as archbishop (as we said before), his vicar and general administrator of his province. And, to bind the Welsh to him by some kind of favour, he sent many unlearned, needy and foreign clergy from that province into England, by a new institution of superstition. For he gave to each of them the Gospel books, all carefully bound in parchment, and ordered them, since they could not pronounce anything from them through ignorance of letters, at least to carry them in their hands as relics of a kind and show them to the people. Then he wrote letters to many, asking that these Welsh clergy, who did not utter the Gospel with their mouths but carried it on their fingers, should be received and allowed to go round collecting alms. So they carried about the written Gospel books, and showed them to the foolish, mad and untaught crowd, who cried out "Efengyl, Efengyl" in their own tongue, not without wonder and amazement. By this superstition the common people of England were deluded, and they bestowed many gifts on these marked and unknown men. These things being done in Wales, King Edward invaded Wales with an armed and military force. There a certain valiant soldier, Edmund, suddenly ran through Llewelyn with a lance and slew him after routing his army. Then David, who had stirred up these disturbances with his deceptions, was seized a little later by the King's soldiers and handed over to the King. The heads of both were set on long stakes, raised high above London Bridge in the manner of traitors. With these leaders thus removed, all Wales at once surrendered itself to the rule of the King of England. The outcome of this affair was plainly contrary to their hope and expectation, which they had drawn from Merlin's prophecies, since the victory they had thought would come to them was granted by God to the English. After this victory, the Welsh are said to have offered the King a piece of the wood of that cross on which our Saviour Jesus Christ was fixed. With Wales thus subdued, the King held a Parliament at Northampton, to which the barons of Wales came and gave the King their fealty and homage under oath.

units.la: In hoc Parliamento illa de Manu mortua lex,ne omnes soli possessiones in Ecclesiastandem transferantur lara est.Cuius ferendæ legis fratrum & prædicatorum auaritia,qui possessiones ac quirere contra suum institutum cœperunt,causam dedit. Deinde Aimarus quidam de Monte forti Clericus,quem Rex Cambrensis beli reum suspicabatur,& carceribus inclusit, intercedente Cant. Archiepiscopo cum suis Suffraganeis, simulque fideiubente ne quid detrimenti ab eo Reipublicæ inferatur, liberatus est. Is Romam sed Papam contulit,& abiecto Papæ authoritate Clericatu se addixit virtutis militiæ.Paulo enim postquam se armis ensèque cinxisset,nullo gestoaut suscepto discrimine obiit.In hoc Parliamento Iohannes Cant. Archi. cum Rex à Clero decimam prouentuum Ecclesiasticorum ad sumptus in Cambria factos recuperandos toto proximo triennio sibi solui petiisset, vicissim petiit vt iura & priuilegia vetera pro Ecclesiastica immunitate a Britannorum,Saxonum,& Dacorum Regibus antiquitus tributa,quæ in S. Edwardi & Canuti Regum Legibus descripta,ab Willielmo Normanno approbata , ab Henrico primo in conrouerfiam vocata, sed ab Henrico secundo reiectæ posthabita fuerit,iamtandem authoritate Regia,omnium que in eo Parliamento consensu firmarëtur. Cuius rei deliberatio decima ita concessa in aliud tépus dilatata est. Hoc itaq; dimisso Parliamento,Iohanes Cant. Arch. provincia diligentius q̄ ante fecit visitari, criminaq; ac delicta provincialia accuratius explorare,feueriusq; animadvertere statuit. Visitatione hanc suscepturus, prospiciendum sibi maxime putauit, vt Papæ ne ab eo turbaretur in quibuscunque mandatis obiceretur. Diximus ante inRoberto Kylwarby, Papæ Gregorio X. concessum in Lugdunensi Concilio decimale subsidium ad recuperandam terram sanctam. Hanc decimam in Anglia Edwardus I. collegit. Papa id ægre tulit ab aliquo quàm à seaut à suis collectoribus hanc pecuniam perceptam fuisse. Iraq; ut constaret omnibus posset, qua dominatione ac potentia non modo in Clerum, sed in Reges ipsos Romanus Pontifex elatus sit, & quibus obsequiis ipsos Episcopos sibi arctavit, ut sua mandata in ipsos Reges peragerent, ex vnis literis hic insertis à Papa ad hunc Iohannem scriptis, quibus imperat ut Regem sub interdicti poena, cuius atrocitatem Anglia Iohanne Rege (ut diximus) regnante ante senserat, à dicta solutione cessaret. Quod mandatum Iohannes celeriter & ex præscripto, Papale imperium magis quam regale metuens exequutus est.
units.tr: In this Parliament the statute of mortmain was at last passed, forbidding that all lands be transferred to the Church. The greed of the friars and preachers, who had begun to acquire possessions contrary to their rule, gave cause for this law. Then a certain Aymer de Montfort, a clerk whom the King of Cambria suspected of being guilty of war, was thrown into prison, but at the intercession of the Archbishop of Canterbury with his suffragans, and with a surety that no harm would come to the commonwealth from him, he was released. He went to Rome to the Pope, and, abandoning the authority of the Pope and his clerical office, devoted himself to the valour of soldiering. For shortly after he had girded himself with arms and sword, he died without having undertaken or faced any danger. In this Parliament, when the King had asked the clergy for a tenth of ecclesiastical revenues, to be paid to him over the whole of the following three years to recover the costs incurred in Wales, John, Archbishop of Canterbury, in turn asked that the ancient rights and privileges of ecclesiastical immunity, granted of old by the kings of the Britons, Saxons and Danes, written into the laws of Kings Edward the Confessor and Canute, approved by William the Norman, called into question by Henry I but set aside by Henry II, should at last be confirmed by royal authority and with the consent of all in that Parliament. The deliberation on this matter was postponed to another time, the tenth having been granted. This Parliament being dismissed, John, Archbishop of Canterbury, resolved to have his province visited more diligently than before, to investigate the provincial crimes and offences more carefully and to punish them more severely. Undertaking this visitation, he thought it most necessary to take care that he should not be hindered by any mandate of the Pope. We said before, in the account of Robert Kilwardby, that Pope Gregory X granted at the Council of Lyons a tenth as a subsidy for recovering the Holy Land. Edward I collected this tenth in England. The Pope took it badly that this money had been received by anyone other than himself or his own collectors. So that it may be clear to all by what domination and power the Roman Pontiff has exalted himself not only over the clergy but over kings themselves, and by what obedience he has bound the bishops to himself so that they carry out his commands against the kings, here is inserted one letter written by the Pope to this John, in which he orders him to make the King, under penalty of interdict (whose atrocity England had already felt in the reign of King John, as we said), cease from the said payment. John carried out this command quickly and exactly, fearing the Papal rather than the royal power.

units.la: LITERÆ DIRECTÆ D. PAPÆ ET CARDINALIBUS.
units.tr: Letters Directed by the Lord Pope to the Cardinals

units.la: An. Dom. 1283. Edwardi primi. II.
units.tr: A.D. 1283. Edward I, year 2.

units.la: ANCTISSIMO patri ac Domino Martino Dei gratia sacrosanctæ Romanæ ac vniuersalis Ecclesiæ summo Pontifici. Fratet Iohannes permissione diuina sacerdos Cantuar. inutilis, cum omni reuerentia & honore pedum osculà beatorum. Sanctitatis vestræ literas dudecimo Kal. Nouemb. recepi London. sub forma inferius annotata.
units.tr: To the most holy father and lord Martin, by the grace of God supreme Pontiff of the holy Roman and universal Church: brother John, by divine permission priest of Canterbury, unworthy, with all reverence and honour, kissing your blessed feet. I received your Holiness's letters at London on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the form noted below.

units.la: Martinus Episcopus seruus seruorum Dei venerabili fratri Archiepiscopo Cantuar. Salutem & Apostolicam benedictionem. Intellecto nuper quod charissimus in Christo filius noster (Edwardus) Rex Angliæ illustris pecuniam decimæ in regno Angliæ per Lugdunen. Concilium terræ sanctæ concessæ subsidio, quæ per Collectores à sede Apostolica deputatos in sacris & rutis locis deposita, sub fide iugique custodia seruabatur, de locis ipsis sigillis serisque violenter effractis, quibus loca eadem firmabantur, motu proprio, pecuniæ præfatæ custodibus renitentibus & inuitis totaliter amouerit, & ad certum locum pro suæ voluntatis libito, non absque magna dolo uinæ Maiestatis offensa, multoque Apostolicæ sedis contemptu, ac eiusdem terræ graui dispendio fecerat asportari: mirati fuimus non modicum & turbati, cum sine nostra & ipsius sedis licentia speciali attentare talia minimè debuisset. Vndè nos præfato Regi nostras sub certa forma dirigimus literas, inter alia continentes, ut ipse diligenti meditatione considerans, quantum in hoc suum offenderit creatorem, cuius in hac parte negocii agitur, quantum Romanam Ecclesiam perturbarit, quàotumuc læserit famam suam, pecuniam ipsam in locis de quibus excitit, dem mandato Dominici Regis amota faciat, sublata difficultate qualibet, excusationibus seu rationibus in literis Regiis nos super hoc transmissis, expressis nequaquam obstantibus, quas omnino frivolas duximus reputandas, cum integritate restitui seu reponi, ulterius a similibus abstinendo, ac etiam Ecclesiasticas aut alias quascunque personas, penes quas prædicta pecunia èst deposita, vel eam deponi contigerit per Apostolicam sedem, pro terræ iam dictæ commodis disponendam, per se vel per alium seu alios nullis impetendo molestiis, vel vexationibus perturbando, illam in hoc efficaciam & solicitudinem impensuram; ut debitæ restitutionis celeritas asportationis indebitæ ausum redimat, & sedis prædictæ gratia quam libenter ad filios deuotos extendimus, circa eum non immerito augeatur. Nec ipsum latere volumus, quod quantumcunque personam eius sinceris affectibus prosequamur, Regioque libenter deferamus honori, nequaquam pati poterimus, cum non sit deferendum homini plus quàm Deo, quin super hoc iu opus exciterit, aliud remedium apponamus. Volumus igitur, & fraternitati tuæ per Apostolica scriptam in virtute obedientiæ districtè præcipiendo mandamus, quatenus ad eundem Regem te personaliter conferens ipsum iuxta datam tibi à Deo prudentiam, ex parte nostra diligenter moneas & inducas, ut infra vnius mensis spacium post monitionem tuam, prædictam pecuniam in locis eisdem iuxta literarum ipsarum tenorem, cum integritate restituì faciat seu reponi; aperté prædicens eidem quod cùm tantum & tam graue dictæ terræ sanctæ dispendium nolumus, sicuti nec debemus, aliquatenus sustinere, nisi buiusmodi monitioni parere curauerit, tam contra eum quam terrami suam prout qualitas facti exegerit, & expedire videbimus procedemus.
units.tr: Martin, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother the Archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing. It has lately come to our knowledge that our most beloved son in Christ, Edward, illustrious King of England, has, on his own initiative, violently taken away from the places in which it was kept under faithful and constant guard, the money of the tenth in the kingdom of England, granted to the Holy Land by the Council of Lyons, which had been deposited in holy and secure places by collectors appointed by the Apostolic See. He broke open the seals and locks by which those places were secured, and against the reluctance and will of the custodians of the said money, he removed it entirely and had it carried off to a place of his own choosing, not without great contempt for the majesty of God, great offence to the Apostolic See, and serious loss to that Holy Land. We were not a little astonished and disturbed, since he ought by no means to have attempted such things without the special licence of ourselves and of that See. Wherefore we send to the said King our letter in a fixed form, containing among other things that he, considering with careful thought how greatly he has offended his Creator, in whose cause this business lies, how greatly he has disturbed the Roman Church, and how much he has harmed his own reputation, should restore the money to the places from which it was taken, by the command of the Lord King, and should do so in full, removing every difficulty and by no means being hindered by the excuses or reasons expressed in the royal letters sent to us on this matter, which we have judged to be wholly frivolous. He should also abstain from similar acts in future, and should not molest or vex with any troubles, by himself or through another or others, the ecclesiastical or other persons in whose keeping the said money is deposited, or may be deposited by the Apostolic See for the advantage of the aforesaid land. He is to apply such effort and diligence to this that the speed of due restitution may redeem the daring of the unlawful removal, and that the favour of the said See, which we willingly extend to devoted sons, may rightly be increased toward him. Nor do we wish him to be unaware that, however much we cherish his person with sincere affection and gladly pay honour to the King, we cannot allow this, since what is due to God is not to be yielded to a man above God; and unless he takes care to obey this admonition, we shall apply another remedy. We therefore wish, and by these apostolic writings we command your fraternity in virtue of obedience, strictly enjoining, that you go in person to the said King and, according to the prudence given you by God, diligently admonish and persuade him on our behalf, that within the space of one month after your admonition he cause the aforesaid money to be restored in full, or placed back, in the same places according to the tenor of those letters, openly declaring to him that since we do not wish, and indeed ought not, to suffer so great and so grave a loss to the said Holy Land in any way, unless he takes care to obey such an admonition we shall proceed against him and against his land as the nature of the deed shall require and as we shall see fit.

units.la: Et quia huiusmodi negocium potissimè incidet cordi nostro, volumus ut de monitione tua, & ipsius Regis responsione, acaliis quæ super hoc egeris cum eodem, conficiet facient duo publica familia instrumenta, quae nobis per latorem praesentium mit- tere non postponas. Nihilominus significaturus nobis plenarie quicquid super permissis duxeris faciendum, vt per te super his informati plenius & instructi, tutius & efficacius in hac parte procedere valeamus. Dat. apud urbem veterem. 3. Non. Iulu. Pont. nostri An. 3.
units.tr: And because a matter of this kind will very much weigh upon our heart, we wish that you should make two public instruments, in the form of a family record, of your admonition, of the King's reply and of whatever else you do with him on this matter, and that you not delay in sending them to us by the bearer of these presents. Nevertheless, you are to inform us fully of whatever you think must be done in these matters, so that, being fully informed and instructed by you, we may proceed in this affair more safely and effectively. Given at Orvieto, on the third day before the nones of July, in the third year of our pontificate.

units.la: Hvic igitur sanctitatis vestrae mandato vires & vota subiicien reuerenter requisitę Hdilate Regę praedicto repertoque in finibus Walliae, post literas vestras eidem dd restas, quas ipsius inuli manibus, literas etiam vestrae beneficiatio mihi missas, coram ad, pso & magnatibus suis tunc praesentibus exposui vulgariter & aperte, tandemq; exposiui authoritate mandati Regem ipsum monui super tribus.
units.tr: Therefore, submitting strength and will to this mandate of your Holiness, I reverently sought the aforesaid King and found him on the borders of Wales. After your letters had been delivered to him, I showed the originals in his hands, together with the letter sent to me by your beneficence, and I set them forth openly and in the vernacular before him and his magnates then present. Finally, by the authority of the mandate, I admonished the King on three points.

units.la: Primo vt pecuniam decim a suis iussionibus asportatam faceret integraliter infra mensem ad pristinam loci custodiam reportari, tanta deuotionis promptitudine, quae po sset asportationis maculam explare.
units.tr: First, that he should cause the tithe carried off by his officials to be wholly restored within a month to its former place of custody, with such readiness of devotion as might wipe away the stain of the removal.

units.la: Secundo vt de cetero a talibus ausibus penitus abstineret, adiungens quod licet ipsum Apostolica clementia in chanslimbrum filiorum numero complecti., tamen ipsum contingeret in talibus offensionibus de caetero inueniri, nec posset eam nec velle virgam eii correctionis subtrahere, ne parcendo hominiu, diuinis iniuriis quas non corrigeret, assentiret.
units.tr: Second, that from now on he should utterly abstain from such rash acts. Adding that although the apostolic clemency embraces him among the number of its most beloved sons, yet he might be found again in such offences, and that she could neither nor would withhold from him the rod of correction, lest by sparing men she should assent to wrongs against God which she did not correct.

units.la: Tertio ne custodib. vel depositariis pecuniae memoratae aliquid huius occasione molestiae vel grauaminis irrogaret. Quibus silenter ac reuerenter audiens, tandem cum su s deliberatione praehabita ad sibi proposita sic respondit.
units.tr: Third, that he should not inflict any molestation or grievance upon the custodians or depositaries of the said money on account of this matter. Listening to these things silently and reverently, and at length, after prior deliberation, he answered the points put to him as follows.

units.la: Ad primum inquiens, quoniam non fuisset necessarium pro hac causa summum pontificem nobis suas literas destinasse, nec Archiepiscopum ad Regiam accessisse praeterea cum penè duobus elapsis mensibus pecuniam praedictam iusserimus restitui cum effectu.
units.tr: Replying to the first point, he said that it would not have been necessary for the supreme pontiff to send us his letters about this matter, nor for the Archbishop to have come to the King. Moreover, almost two months having passed, we have ordered the said money to be restored in full.

units.la: Ad secundum subiungens, quod nihil indebitum intendebat de cetero contra Ecclesiam attentare.
units.tr: To the second point he added that he intended to attempt nothing undue against the Church from now on.

units.la: Ad tertium, miramur afferens, quare ad illos custodes inbemur specialiter innocentiam custodire, cum nostri sit propositi immobilis conceptio, sicut & debitum Regiae dignitatis nullum tale laedere pro viribus innocentem. Demum iuxta mandati vestri beneplacitum pater sancte feci fieri publica instrumenta, praecepta vestra reuerenter & diligenter sicut potui in omnibus executus. Adhaec nouerit vestra prouidentia sanctitatis, quod licet communiter fidedignis testimonis astruatur, quod praedicta pecunia sit mixta iussionem Regiam suis custodiis restituta, huius tamen praesentia veritas sciti non potuerit, nisi per illos qui ipsius nouerunt pondus, nomerum, & mensuram. Custodiat Dominus incolumitatem vestram Ecclesiae suae sanctae per tempora longiora. Scriptum penultima die Nouembr.
units.tr: To the third point he replied with surprise: why are we ordered to guard the innocence of those custodians in particular, when our purpose is a fixed resolve, just as it is the duty of royal dignity to harm no innocent person as far as it can help it? Finally, holy father, in accordance with the pleasure of your command, I have had public instruments made, and I have carried out your precepts reverently and diligently in all things, as far as I was able. Furthermore, let your holy providence know that although it is commonly asserted by trustworthy witnesses that the said money was sent back to its custodians by royal order, the truth of its presence could not be known except through those who knew its weight, number and measure. May the Lord keep your health for his holy Church for many years. Written on the penultimate day of November.

units.la: In visitatione autem quam peractis Papae mandatis exotsus est, primum Iudaeos in perpetuum exilium aduerit scripsit Episcopo Londinensi, vt eorum omnes Synagogas cuerfas & demolitas solo adaequaret. Quod decretum paulo post Rege procurante mitigatum est, ac Iudaeis permissum vnum templum in publico aliquo ciuitatis loco, in quo suos ritus amputata tamen ceremoniarum multitudine celebrarent. In hac visitatione crimina & excessus pulmonum Clericorum atque laicorum acriter castigauit. Primum quia plura beneficia retinendi licentia in Anglia impune contra iura permissa Clericis fuit, eam non ab infimis modo, sed a summis iumpto supplicio eradicauit. Nam Richardum More sacrae Theologiae professorem Episcopum Wintoniensem electum, nec non Iohannem Kyrkey capellanum Regis ad Lichefeldensem Episcopatum etiam electum, quia in beneficiis plurales ante fuerant, confirmare noluit sed reiecit. Quorum utrique cum ad Papam appellassent, appellationes longo tempore prosequuti eas tandem tandem tedio deferre, & iudicatz a Iohanne contra se sententiae stare inuiti coacti sunt. In huius autem locum Iohannes Pontifarius ab ipso Papa Wintoniensis Episcopus creatus est, qui Wintonienses Monachos grauissime infecstauit, & Episcopatus iura atque praedia mitum in modum ex Monachorum spoliis auxit, vt ex illius Ecclesiae monumentis apparet. Cumque hos in iure vicisset, inferiores cleticos qui plura beneficia simul tenebant, aggressus est. Quos omnes uno beneficio contentos esse compulit. In quo proposito sterit durior, quod Romae Cardinales quidam, vt ex eius literis intelligi posset, cum coram papa accusassent, quod hunc Anglicani cleri excessum mitius tolerasset. Quam iniquam criminationem vt vitaret, plures non modo beneficiis amouit, sed huiusmodi maledic-tis. ðis, Filios Belial, contemptores Canonum, vsurpatores, & beneficiorum sacrilegos appellat. Nec minus in plurales quam in abientes & non residentes acris iudex fuit, à primis & elatissimis exorsus. Episcopum Lichefeldensem peregrinum & Anglicanæ linguæ ignarum, ideoque extra suam diœcesin commorantem edicto publicato monuit, vt sub annotionis pœna ad Episcopatum rediret, ibique resideret. Cumque ideo venisset, eum acerrime increpauit, quod etsi idiomatis in scius pascere suæ Diœcesis gregem verbi prædicatione nequiisset, præsentia tamen sua eleemosynis & liberalitate alere debuisset. Cuique Collegium Wolverhamptoniense in Lichefeldiensi diœcesi, cuius ius patronatus ad Cant. Ecclesiam olim spectabat, vitare voluisset, iure & priuilegio exemptionis quam vendicabat, Concanonicis veritus & exclusus est. Cuius rei controuersiam cum Romam delata penderet, Iohannem Theodosium de Camilla litem hanc Romæ persequentem duabus rectoris in quibus non relidebat, spoliauit. His diebus fatetur in literis suis Regiæ Fraciæ scriptis, expendisse in refectione ædificiorum in muneris suis plusquam duo millia marcarum.
units.tr: In the visitation he undertook after receiving the Pope's mandates, he first wrote to the Bishop of London that the Jews were to be exiled forever, and that all their synagogues were to be overturned, demolished and levelled with the ground. This decree was soon softened through the King's intervention, and the Jews were permitted one temple in some public place in the city, where they might celebrate their rites, though with the multitude of ceremonies cut back. In this visitation he sharply rebuked the crimes and excesses of clergy and laity alike. First, since in England the holding of several benefices had been allowed to clerics with impunity, contrary to the laws, he uprooted this practice, not only among the lowest but among the highest, adding punishment. For he refused to confirm Richard More, professor of sacred theology and elected Bishop of Winchester, and likewise John Kirkby, the King's chaplain, elected to the bishopric of Lichfield, because they had previously held several benefices; he rejected them. When both appealed to the Pope, he prolonged their appeals for a long time until at last, worn out by the tedium, they were forced, unwillingly, to abide by the sentence John had pronounced against them. In their place John Pontoise was created Bishop of Winchester by the Pope himself. He very grievously harassed the monks of Winchester and increased the rights and estates of the bishopric in a remarkable way from the spoils of the monks, as the records of that church show. Having won these cases in law, he went after the lesser clergy who held several benefices together, and compelled them all to be content with one benefice. He was harder in this purpose because certain cardinals at Rome, as could be understood from his letters, had accused him before the Pope of having tolerated this excess of the English clergy too mildly. To avoid this unjust charge, he removed several men not only from their benefices but also called them, with such curses, sons of Belial, contemners of the canons, usurpers and sacrilegious holders of benefices. He was no less a stern judge of pluralists than of absentees and non-residents, beginning with the highest and most exalted. By published edict he warned the Bishop of Lichfield, a foreigner ignorant of the English tongue who therefore stayed outside his diocese, that under penalty of censure he must return to his bishopric and reside there. When he came, John rebuked him severely: although, owing to his ignorance of the language, he could not feed his diocese's flock by preaching the word, he ought at least to have nourished it by his presence, with alms and generosity. When the Bishop wished to avoid the college of Wolverhampton in the diocese of Lichfield, whose patronage once belonged to the church of Canterbury, on the ground of the right and privilege of exemption which he claimed, he was opposed and shut out by his fellow canons. While the dispute over this matter was pending at Rome, he stripped John Theodosius of Camilla, who was pursuing this suit at Rome, of two rectories in which he did not reside. In these days he confesses in his letters, written to the King of France, that he had spent more than two thousand marks on repairing the buildings of his office.

units.la: Et An.1284. dicit se expendisse circa 3. millia marcarum in ædificiis necessariis.
