Hoc tempore causa quædam inter Archiepiscopum Eboracensem, & Dunelmenses Monachos controuersia ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum per tutoriam appellatione deducta est. Archiepiscopus autem aliis impeditus negociis causam Priori de Southwerke, Decano de Archubus, & Canonico cuidam Ecclesiæ Paulinæ delegauit, quibus etiam mandauit, vt iuditiones euentum de causa principali cognosceret. Similiter inter Dunelmensem Episcopum, & Eboracensem Arch. controuersia Archidiacono Cantuariensi appellationis tuitoriæ iure comissa est, in qua Archidiacono Cant. de ea lite cognoscendi data est Eboracensem Archiepiscopum suum; Officialem inhibendo à gerenda in Dunelmensis Episcopi prætudicium quacunque iurisdictione comprimendi potestas. Adulteria & stupra non minori seueritate vendicauit, cum Cicestrensem diœcesin visitaret, Rogerum Ham Presbyterum fornicarium ad triennalem pœnitentiam iureiurando adegit. Quod temporis in ieiuniis, orationibus, & longinquis ad Romam, Coloniam, & Compostellam peregrinationibus contereret, beneficiorum suorum redditibus sibi prohibitis, & in pauperum vsus sequebatur. In Sarisburiensis etiam parochiæ visitatione compertum fuit Osbernum Gifford militem Monialesduas ex Wiltoniensi Cœnobio abduxisse. Quem Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus excommunicatione primò percussit. Deinde sub his duris conditionibus relaxauit, Primo ne in tota reliqua deinceps vita vllum monialium Cœnobium ingrederetur, aut monialis cuiusquam consortio vteretur.
units.tr: And in the year 1284 he says he spent about three thousand marks on necessary buildings. At this time a certain dispute between the Archbishop of York and the monks of Durham was brought before the Archbishop of Canterbury by an appeal in tutory. The Archbishop, however, being occupied with other business, committed the case to the Prior of Southwark, the Dean of the Arches and a certain canon of St Paul's, and ordered them also to examine the outcome of the principal cause and to pass judgement. Similarly, a dispute between the Bishop of Durham and the Archbishop of York was entrusted to the Archdeacon of Canterbury by right of an appeal in tutory, and the Archdeacon was given authority to hear that suit, while their Official was forbidden to exercise any jurisdiction to the prejudice of the Bishop of Durham. He punished adultery and fornication with no less severity. When visiting the diocese of Chichester, he compelled Roger Ham, a priest guilty of fornication, to undergo a three-year penance under oath: during that time he was to spend his days in fasting, prayers and long pilgrimages to Rome, Cologne and Compostela, with the revenues of his benefices forbidden to him and assigned to the use of the poor. In the visitation of the parish of Salisbury it was also discovered that Osbern Gifford, a knight, had carried off two nuns from the convent of Wilton. The Archbishop of Canterbury first struck him with excommunication, and then released him on these harsh conditions: first, that for the rest of his life he should never enter any convent of nuns, nor keep company with any nun.

units.la: Deinde veteribus diebus Dominicis in Ecclesia parochiali Wilton exutus vestibus virgis verberarer tur. Eandemque posteaпœnam tam in foro, quam in Ecclesia parochiali de Eschatiebus publice subiret. Adhæc multorum mensium ieiunium etinunciatum est. Præterea omnibus milit: aribus insignibus detractis priuatus, nec calcaria deaurata, nec gladium, nec cellam militarem, aut deauratas phaleras habiturus. Ad extremum vt nec vestes coloratas sed tantummodo de rosco, cum agninis pellibus vel ouinis, nec vtatur camisia posteaquam fuerat castigatus per tres annos, ordinem suum inuitare non rediret antequam tres continuos annos in terra sancta exegisset. Ante omnia vt moniales Cœnobium simili pœna mulctandas restitui atque remitti curaret. Hæc omnibus se iureiurando factorum spoponderit, ieiuniorum nihilominus ab Episcopo Sarisburiensi illi præscribendo modo. Nec minorem in reprimendis iurisdictionem suam contemnebat, tibus seueritatem Petrus quidam de S. Marco Decanus de Arcubus exercuisse fertur, qui Herefordensis Episcopi Officialem suis monitis non parentem 1. decem, deinde auctam & persequentem contumaciam 40. marcis tanquam rebellem & potestatis suæ contemptorem mulctauit, nec non Episcopum ipsum Herefordensem, quod Officialis sui partes audacius tueretur, excommunicauit, eiusque capellum interdixit Ecclesiastico supposuit.
units.tr: Then, on successive Sundays, stripped of his clothes, he was to be beaten with rods in the parish church of Wilton, and afterwards he was to undergo the same punishment publicly, both in the market place and in the parish church of Eschatiebus. Moreover, a fast of many months was also imposed on him. Furthermore, deprived of all military insignia, he was to have no gilded spurs, no sword, no military saddle and no gilded trappings. Finally, he was not to wear coloured clothes but only russet, with lambskin or sheepskin lining, nor to use a shirt. After he had been punished for three years, he was not to return to his order until he had spent three continuous years in the Holy Land. Above all, he was to see to it that the nuns of the convent, who were to be fined with a similar penalty, were restored and pardoned. He promised all these things under oath, the fasts nevertheless being prescribed to him in the manner laid down by the Bishop of Salisbury. Nor was he less severe in curbing those who despised his jurisdiction. Peter of St Mark, Dean of the Arches, is said to have exercised the same severity: when the Official of the Bishop of Hereford did not obey his admonitions, he fined him ten marks, and then, as the contumacy grew and persisted, forty marks, as a rebel and contemner of his authority. He also excommunicated the Bishop of Hereford himself, because he defended his Official too boldly, and placed his chapel under an ecclesiastical interdict.

units.la: Hoc etiam tempore lis quædam inter Lincolniensem Episcopum & vniuersitatem Oxon. aliquot annis de iurisdictione Episcopi in Scholares vniuersitatis agitata est. De qua Iohannes Cantuariensis cum Scholariorum tam causam vacillare, nec iure fitare posse intelligerat, Scholaribus rescripsit. Si in iure contenderent vinci eos ac superari necesse esse, præsertim cum his quibus niterentur priuilegiis à iurisdictione Episcopali iure communi habilitatio eximi nequaquam potuissent. Ipsaque perlustrata reliqua prouincia Oxoniensem Academiam iure Metropolitico visitaturus adiit. In qua visitatione quasdam Philosophicas opiniones, quos errores & à Roberto Kylwarby ante reprehensos docuit, tanquam hæreses & à fide Christiana abhorrentes suggestu Latine refellit. Inter has vna erat in homine esse tantummodo formam vnam. Quam frater Iohannes non concoxit,
units.tr: At this time, too, a certain dispute between the Bishop of Lincoln and the University of Oxford over the Bishop's jurisdiction over the scholars of the university had been argued for some years. John of Canterbury, when he understood that the scholars' case was wavering and could not be defended in law, wrote back to them: if they contended at law, they must necessarily be conquered and overcome, especially since the privileges on which they relied could not by common law exempt them from episcopal jurisdiction. Having toured the rest of the province, he went to visit the Academy of Oxford by metropolitan right. In this visitation he refuted from the pulpit, in Latin, certain philosophical opinions, which Robert Kilwardby had earlier condemned as errors, and which he treated as heresies abhorrent to the Christian faith. Among these was the view that there is only one form in a man. Brother John did not accept this.

units.la: R. ş neque elligeretur inde corpus Christi non fuisse vnum numero viuum & mortuum, nec sanctorum corpora eadem tota vel secundum partes in orbe existere vel in vtbe, leq alia quaedam quae non peperierunt matres, sed de nouo peperit phantasia. Sed iste haereses Philosophicae ab Oxoniensium Scholis in praedicatorum & fratrum turbas profecti & disseminati fuerunt. Inter quos Richardus Knapwell doctor ordinis praedicatorum octo opiniones contra Iohannis Peckam asserriones defendit. Hunc itaque Iohannes Peckā ad suum tribunal vocauit, coque non accedente, eum sualiq; opiniones cum suo Clero damnauit. Sed Hugo de Mancestria cuius ordinis Prouincialis intercessit, & Cant. restituit. Allegauitque neminem in sui ordinis fratres, praeter solum Papam potestatem habere.
units.tr: Nor, it was said, would it follow from this that the body of Christ was not one in number, living and dead, nor that the bodies of the saints, whole or in part, could exist in the world or in the city, and certain other things which mothers did not bring forth but which fancy has newly engendered. But these philosophical heresies, having set out from the schools of Oxford, were spread among the troops of the Preachers and Friars. Among them Richard Knapwell, a doctor of the Order of Preachers, defended eight opinions against the assertions of John Peckham. John Peckham therefore summoned him to his tribunal, and when he did not appear, condemned him and his opinions together with his clergy. But Hugh of Manchester, provincial of that order, interceded and restored him to the Archbishop of Canterbury. He also alleged that no one has power over the brethren of his order except the Pope alone.

units.la: Itaque appellatione interposita superdeinde negocio Cantuariensis atque continuit. Nec quicquam deinceps in homunculum fratrem valuit eius authoritas, qui in Regem & Episcoposomnia potetat. Idem acutus frater & Theologus, cum è sacris scripturis, probare vellet, non esse permissum Clericis duo beneficia Ecclesiastica retinere, protulit hanc ex Euangelio sententiam: qui habet duas tunicas, vnam tribuat non habenti, & qui habet escas similiter. Richardus ille frater inter alia quae de nugis Philosophicis scripsit, edidit vnum de Formarum vnitate libellum, vt omnibus liquido constate posset eum nullis Cantuariensis minis deterritum in sententia sua perseuerasse. His in prouincia visitanda gestis, scilicet ad plerosque Suffraganeorum literis, ne se, suos officiales, & tribunalia muneribus (quae cum insigni Praelatorum opprobrio diu nephariae percipi in visitatione intellexerat) deinceps inquinari permitterent, admonuit. Quod si fuit monitioni non parerent, se adinisse deineeps in muneribus percipiendis scelera seuerius animadueturum. In literis etiam ad Ordonicum Cardinalem Tufculanum Episcopum scriptis quaeritur de quodam, quem remigem, suam nauem atque puppim subuertiurum nominat, qui muneribus moueri, ac duas pelues aureas plenas Florenis accepisse ait. Idem ad Romanae curiae Vicecancellarium scribit, comperisse fuisse in Anglia multa priuilegia per falsarios fabricata. Sed commoti Suffraganei, quod non modo tam erebris visitationibus, sed etiam quotidiana iurisdictione partes suas in eorum dioecesibus tam saepe interponeret, querelam 25. articulis comprehensam in eum proponent. Cuius querelae viin & cuentum cum in seipsos recidisse intellexissent, ea omissa luctari amplius cum Metropolitano noluerunt. Inter hos Suffraganeos Londinensis cum Episcopus grauaie tulit quendam Henricum de Stookes suae London. dioecesis Rectorem, de beneficiorum pluralitate coram Decano de Arcubus in iuis vocatum fuisse. Qua de re scripsit Iohannes Peckam se id non laturum, sed nisi desistat tam in hac quam in aliis cauiss de suis Clericis subditisue cognoscere, se appellationis ad curiam Romanam sacram anchoram petiturum. Cui Iohannes stupuisse se scribit de illa minaci & praeiudicialisua pagina. Sane inquit, duo per nos vobis illata fuisse grauamina causamini. 1. quod Henricum Stookes de pluralitate beneficiorum ad nostrum euocauimus examen. 2. quod ipsum per Decanum de Arcubus citari feci mus, adiungentes quod sub ditus Suffraganei Metropolitano non subest, quasi velitis iura Cantuariensis Ecclesiae quae tueri & defendere iuraftis, ad simplices Metropolitani limites coartare. Decani autem de Arcubus processibus cofuetis paces obicem nullatenus praesumatis. Pro certo sciturs, quod iura Ecclesiae Cant. partim scripta, partim à doctoribus authenticis notata, partim pacifice obtenta longo prouinciae usu intendimus conta omne hominum genus quantum poterimus constante animo defensare. Subacta sibi tam his modis prouincia Clerum suum Redinghi eongregauit. In eo Concilio quinque leges tulit. Propositi cognitionem de patronatu Ecclesiarum multis annis ad Regium tribunal spectantem indeat Ecclesiasticum forum traducere, tum prohibitiones Regias in litibus de bonis & catallis prorsus rescindere, & ne deinceps Ecclesiasticos iudices à iure reddendo retardarent vetare, Sed Rex inecpto hoc audito nuncius ad Concilium destinatis multis, tam Archiepiscopum quā totī Clero minis praecepit vt de50 sisterent. Vnde factum est vt sua praesumptione Archiepiscopus penitus transfiliret. Ita dissoluto Concilio omnes Praelati ipse inanes recesserunt.
units.tr: Therefore, an appeal having been lodged, the Archbishop of Canterbury postponed the matter. Afterwards his authority prevailed for nothing against this little friar, who could do everything against the King and the bishops. The same keen friar and theologian, when he wished to prove from Holy Scripture that clerics were not permitted to hold two ecclesiastical benefices, brought forward this saying from the Gospel: "He who has two coats, let him give one to him who has none, and he who has food, let him do likewise." That friar Richard, among other things he wrote about philosophical trifles, published a little book on the unity of forms, so that it might be clear to all that he, not deterred by any threats of the Archbishop of Canterbury, had persevered in his opinion. With these things done in the visitation of the province, he admonished several of the suffragans by letter not to allow themselves, their officials and their courts to be defiled thereafter by bribes, which, as he had learned during the visitation, had long been taken in a nefarious manner, to the notable disgrace of the prelates. If they did not obey this admonition, he said he would thereafter punish with greater severity the crimes committed in receiving bribes. In a letter also written to Ordonius, the Cardinal Bishop of Tusculum, he complains of a certain man whom he calls the oarsman who would overturn his ship and stern; this man, he says, was moved by bribes and received two golden purses full of florins. He writes to the Vice-Chancellor of the Roman curia that he had discovered many privileges to have been forged in England by counterfeiters. But the suffragans, moved because he interposed himself so often in their dioceses, not only by such frequent visitations but also by daily jurisdiction, drew up a complaint against him comprising twenty-five articles. When they understood that the force and outcome of this complaint would rebound upon themselves, they dropped it and would not struggle any further with the Metropolitan. Among these suffragans, the Bishop of London took it badly that a certain Henry de Stookes, rector in his diocese of London, had been summoned before the Dean of the Arches on a charge of pluralism of benefices. On this matter John Peckham wrote that he would not put up with it, but unless he desisted from taking cognizance of his clergy and subjects in this cause as well as in others, he would seek the sacred anchor of an appeal to the Roman curia. To him John wrote that he was astonished at that threatening and prejudicial letter of his. "Indeed," he says, "you complain of two grievances brought against you by us: (1) that we have summoned Henry Stookes to our examination concerning the pluralism of benefices; (2) that we have had him cited by the Dean of the Arches, adding that a subject of a suffragan is not subject to the Metropolitan, as if you wished to confine within the narrow limits of the Metropolitan the rights of the Church of Canterbury, which you have sworn to protect and defend. Do not presume to place any obstacle in the usual proceedings of the Dean of the Arches. Be assured that the rights of the Church of Canterbury, partly written down, partly noted by authentic doctors, and partly peacefully obtained by the long custom of the province, we intend to defend with constant mind against every kind of men, as far as we can." Having thus subdued his province, he assembled his clergy at Reading. In that council he passed five laws: first, to transfer to the ecclesiastical court the cognizance of advowsons, which for many years had belonged to the royal court; then to abolish entirely the royal prohibitions in suits concerning goods and chattels; and to forbid ecclesiastical judges to delay the administration of justice. But the King, hearing of this undertaking, sent many messengers to the council and by threats ordered both the Archbishop and the whole clergy to desist. Thus it came about that, through his own presumption, the Archbishop overreached himself completely. So the council was dissolved, and all the prelates withdrew empty-handed.

units.la: In eo etiam Concilio fama publica id exigente perquisuit de Episcopo quodam concubinario. De quo ad Matthaeum quendam Romanae Ecclesiae Cardinalem scripsit, sed de eius nomine mentionem nullam fecit. Id enim, vt ait, nuncio suo proferendum commisit. Petiit in illis literis à Cardinali Matthaeo, vt de eo corrigendo Papam secreto sermone consuleret, neque res enunciaretur. Multos enim ei in Romana curia amicos & exploratores fuisse, potiissimum autem mercatores Lucanenses, quorum (vt diximus) opera in expilationibus & vsutis Papa saepe vsus esset. Hunc autem non nominatum Episcopum cum secreto conuenisset, atque quæsiuisset, an vera essent quæ de eius concubinatu fama retulisset, testes quos Archiepiscopus expectabat & adesse iussit metuens, tandem turpia narrasse, & ipsius turpitudinis diem fatum fuisse, scribit. Deinde eadem sepimana cum Mortlaci moreretur, venisse ad cum fœminam quandam Iulianam de illius Episcopi factis quæsam narraturam. Eaiuramento eoacta peperisse se quinque libros ex code Epist. adhuc superstites falsa est. Hunc cum coercere vellet, metuens ne le muneribus ad papam fundendis defenderet, per hunc Cardinalem præoccupauit Papam. Propono, inquit, cum adhuc aggredi iterato. Sed scio quòd conatus meus parum proderit, nisi me litera iuuet Apostolica. Mox enim vt cum retigeret, appellationis aliis falsidicæ rete meum effugiet, infinitam pecuniam effusurus. Peto autem vt in omnibus aliis mihi per vos adsit adminiculū Papæ, per quod mea crescat authoritas, & timor incutiatur rebellibus, meaque iurisdictio excitetur, vt constantius noua inchoem, & inchoata authoritate maiori valeam confirmare.
units.tr: In that same council, since public report demanded it, he made inquiry about a certain bishop who kept a concubine. He wrote about him to a certain Matthew, a Cardinal of the Roman Church, but made no mention of his name, for he said he had entrusted that to his messenger to declare. In those letters he asked Cardinal Matthew to consult the Pope in private about correcting him, and that the matter should not be made public. For he had many friends and informers in the Roman curia, especially the Lucchese merchants, by whose work (as we have said) the Pope had often made use in his extortions and usury. Having met this unnamed bishop in secret and asked whether the reports of his concubinage were true, he writes that the bishop, fearing the witnesses whom the Archbishop was expecting and had ordered to be present, at last related shameful things, and that the day of his disgrace had come. Then in the same week, when he was dying at Mortlake, a certain woman, Juliana, came to him to tell certain things about the deeds of that bishop. Compelled by oath, she testified that she had borne him five children, still surviving. When the Archbishop wished to restrain the bishop, fearing that he would defend himself by pouring out bribes to the Pope, he forestalled the Pope through this Cardinal. "I propose," he says, "to attack him again. But I know that my effort will avail little unless an apostolic letter helps me. For as soon as I touch him, he will escape my net by a lying appeal, pouring out infinite money. I ask, however, that in all other matters the Pope's support be given me through you, by which my authority may grow, fear may be struck into rebels, and my jurisdiction be roused, so that I may more steadfastly begin new things and confirm those begun with greater authority."

units.la: Superiori anno annonæ maxima fuit copia, ita vt frumeti modius tribus denariis Londini venderetur, sed ex imbrium boc proximo anno tam abunde fluentium copia, quæ non modò ptata, sed ipsa segetu arua obruit & inundauit, ea caritas coœcuta quadraginta annis duravit, vt idem modius qui paulò antea tribus denariis iã duobus solidis væniret. Eodem anno Carolus princeps Achaiæ, Regis Aragonix subditus, ob proditionis metu vel suspicionem carceribus inclusus, gratia Regis Angliæ interposito de integra in Regem Aragonix habenda fide, & obsidibus datis liberatus est, à quo iuramento execrandaet detestabili authoritate Nicolai quarti Papæ postea absolutus, regnum Siciliæ contra fidem & religionem inuasit atque tenuit. Iohannes Peckam Cantuariensi Archiepiscopus cum tredecim annis sedisset, adesse sibi huius vitæ senit exitum: testamentum itaque condidit, cuius executores Nicolaum de Knouile Rectorem de Wilmington & Simonem de Greille constituit. Hi post mortem Guakeri Reynolds sede Archiepiscopali vacante ad reddendam executionis suæ testamentariæ rationem à Priore Cant. in ius vocati sunt. Rationibus exactis compertum est ex inuentario præter legata in specie relicta, superfuisse ex Iohannis Peckam bonis f 305. libras, 17. solidos, 2. denarios & quadrantem monetæ Anglicanæ. Hanc summam ad defecti funera, suasque expensas hi callidi executores sibi penè totam à Priore decetni obtinuerunt. Vt reddita ratione non amplius quinque solidis sex denariis in pauperum & pios vsus distribuendis remanserint. Hinc videmus quibus artibus tam occultam auaritiam hic bonus virtexit.
units.tr: In the previous year there was the greatest abundance of grain, so that a bushel of wheat was sold in London for three pence. But from the rains which fell so abundantly in the following year, which not only soaked the meadows but flooded and buried the very fields of grain, that scarcity, once begun, lasted forty years, so that the same bushel which a little before had sold for three pence now sold for two shillings. In the same year Charles, prince of Achaea, a subject of the King of Aragon, was shut up in prison on account of fear or suspicion of treason, and was freed through the favour of the King of England, who interposed his guarantee of perpetual faith toward the King of Aragon, and hostages were given. Afterwards, by the accursed and detestable authority of Pope Nicholas IV, he was absolved from that oath, and he invaded and held the kingdom of Sicily against faith and religion. John Peckham, Archbishop of Canterbury, having sat for thirteen years, sensed that the end of this life was at hand. He therefore made his will, and appointed as its executors Nicholas de Knowle, rector of Wilmington, and Simon de Greille. After the death of Walter Reynolds, the archiepiscopal see being vacant, they were summoned before the Prior of Canterbury to render an account of their executorship. When the accounts had been audited, it was found from the inventory that, apart from the legacies specifically bequeathed, there remained from John Peckham's goods £305, 17 shillings, 2 pence and a farthing of English money. These crafty executors, for the expenses of his funeral and their own outlay, obtained almost all of this sum from the Prior by decree, so that when the account was rendered, no more than five shillings and six pence remained to be distributed for the use of the poor and for pious purposes. From this we see by what arts this good man concealed so hidden an avarice.

units.la: Quia pauperi atem & inopiam Archiepiscopatum suum ingressus deplorabat (vt diximus) suam. Idem paucis annis tanta abundantia copiaq; repletus est, vt Cardinalibus & curialibus Romanis grandia stipendia annua decerneret, & quod laudi verti debet, pauperibus muneriorum suorum 770. marcas distribuit mandauit. His tam immensis summptibus non obstantibus, consanguineos suos multos mirum in modum pluribus præsidiis locupletauit, aliosq; ad equestrem, alios ad generosum ordinem euexit, quorum de stirpe nonnulli in Cantio, atque aliis Angliæ comitatibus veterem tunc institutum & ab eo acceptum splendorem retinent. In omnibus quas frequenter scripsitauit literis, hoc titulo exorsus est. Iohannes Frater Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ sacerdos humilis. Regi suiq; ministris pro Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis prædiis atq; iuribus sæpe audacter restitit, vt irato & offenso sæpe Regedę exilio subinde excogitaret. Ideoque multis prædicandum quam (vtdiximus) Lugduni babuit patentibus responder solitus est. Sedeim illam videre & expectare, quo hinc abiens ibi residderet. Quanquam ex fratrum & prædicatorum ordine prodiit, iuris tamen ciuilis & pontificij quàm sacrarum scripturarum fuit peritior, etsi librospermultos in illa rixosa, garrula, & digladiatoria frattū theologię conscripsit. Quorum mendicitatem Euangelicam perfectionem nominabat, ciusq; oppugnatores hereticos esse dicebat. Cum annis 13. 24. septimanis, & biduo Cantuariensem prouinciam rexisset t 3. mense Ianuario obiit, & Cantuariæ in Ecclesia Christi sepultus est.
units.tr: Since he had entered his archbishopric in poverty and want, as we have said, he lamented it. Within a few years he was so overflowing with abundance and wealth that he assigned large yearly stipends to the Cardinals and Roman officials, and, what ought to be counted to his praise, he ordered 770 marks distributed to the poor from his revenues. Despite these immense expenses, he enriched many of his relatives in a remarkable way with several benefices, and raised others to the rank of knights and others to the gentry. Some of their descendants in Kent and other English counties still keep the old standing and the splendour that they received from him. In all the letters he wrote frequently, he opened with this style: "John, Brother, humble priest of the Church of Canterbury." He often boldly resisted the King and his ministers on behalf of the estates and rights of the Church of Canterbury, so that the King, angry and offended, repeatedly devised exile for him. Therefore, when many asked him about the exile he had at Lyons, as we have said, he was accustomed to answer openly that he was waiting to see that see, to which he would withdraw from here and reside there. Although he came out of the order of friars and preachers, he was nonetheless more skilled in civil and papal law than in the Holy Scriptures, although he wrote very many books in that quarrelsome, chattering and combative theology of the friars. He called their mendicancy evangelical perfection, and said that its opponents were heretics. After he had ruled the province of Canterbury for 13 years, 24 weeks and two days, he died in January and was buried in Christ Church, Canterbury.

units.la: LIX. ROBERTVS WINCHELSEE.
units.tr: LIX. ROBERT WINCHELSEY.

units.la: AGNAS varietates atque mutationes perferre eorum dignitas atque status, qui in summis Reip. aut Ecclesiæ muneribus negociisq; gerendis, dum multis quorum sensus dispares & diuersæ
units.tr: Those who hold the highest offices and business of the Commonwealth or the Church must endure many changes and reversals of fortune, since they try to please many people whose feelings are at odds and whose opinions differ,

units.la: Florileg.
units.tr: Florileg.

units.la: Step. Byrth. sunt obsequi student, fluctuantur & distrahuntur, consiliis, nec in vna sententia persiueranter durant. Vt quod de fortunae inconstantia atque leuitate vet eres non magis imperitè quam impiè senserunt, nostris potius erroribus atque vitiis quam incertis casibus asscribatur. In quo quidam, qui mores vniuersiuiusq; sibi fortunam fingere affirment, rerumque humanarum euentus in humana potestate statuunt, etsi ab eo communi rece- pto & errore recedere, propiusq; ad veritatem se deduci putarunt, tamen dum à rerum humanarum gubernaculis temeritatem, ineonstantiam atque stultitiam, quarum humanae actiones plenae sunt, non seiungunt, in eundem quem reprehendunt, ac vitare vellent errorem incidunt de Fortuna. Quae a suis defensoribus non alia esse putatur quam huius vitae varia atque commutabilis ratio, cuius esse propriam & aqua seinngi 1 o non posse definiunt.
units.tr: Step. Byrth. and so they are tossed about and pulled apart and do not stand firm in one opinion. Hence what the ancients thought about the fickleness and inconstancy of fortune, not so much unwisely as impiously, should rather be ascribed to our own errors and vices than to uncertain chances. Some people, who claim that each man makes his own fortune and who hold that the outcomes of human affairs lie in human power, believe that they have departed from that common and received error and been led closer to the truth. Yet while they do not separate from the helm of human affairs the rashness, inconstancy and folly with which human actions are full, they fall into the same error about Fortune that they blame in others and wished to avoid. Its defenders hold that Fortune is nothing other than the varied and changeable course of this life, and they define that it cannot be separated from its own proper and inseparable disorder.

units.la: Quod si his viris Ecclesiasticis potestate praeditis, de quorum nunc gestis tractamus, iniediffet fixa dignitati & professioni congruens cogitatio, omnia summa ptouidentia, & incommunabili ratione ac sapientia administrari, non inanem necChristianis dignam laudem ex his rebus quaesuiffent, in quibus nec se interponere, nec contendere tantum debuerunt, nec eiuslium rerum atque mundanarum fluctibus se sece exposuissent, cum in Ecclesiae portu navigare potuissent. Sed omnis tum inter Pontifices atque Reges de Imperio magis atque dominatu, quam de Ecclesia ex diuini verbi praescripto gerenda fuit contentio. In qua eum acres dimiciationes non armorum, sed dirarum & execrationum essent concitatae, praesules inscitia verbiipsi caeci, ac coecorum duces 2 o Papis adhaerebant, & abiecta obedientia Regibus non parebant, quibus diuino humano- ique iure essent subiecti. Hanc illi contumaciam, constantiam, & Eeelesiae libertatem tunc appellabant. Quiq; in ea pertinacia vitas aut fortunas amisissent, Martyres ac Confessores appellabant. Quae nisi multis tunc anteactis ductaannis in hominum animis inueterasset fallacia, ac multos praeseriim praesules à fide, atque culpa, quem regibus tribuere debebant, ad Papam abduxisset, fatis bene & cum laude ab Archiepiscopis & E- piscopis gestos magistratus existimare conuenit, si quis eorum acta perpenderit. Sed quia ab illa sede Romana vel dolis infatuati, vel scelerubus & contagione inquinati fuerunt, & ab obseruantia Regibus debita recesserunt, sibi ex rebus gestis nō modo laudem detraxerunt, sed in vita moletias aetiaturas, & post mortem infamiam atque ignomi- 3 o niam pepererunt.
units.tr: If these churchmen, invested with power, whose deeds we are now discussing, had held a fixed thought suited to their dignity and calling, that all things are administered by the highest providence, by an unchangeable reason and wisdom, they would not have sought empty praise, nor praise worthy of Christians, from affairs in which they ought neither to have meddled nor contended so much, and they would not have exposed themselves to the waves of such worldly matters, since they could have sailed into the harbour of the Church. But at that time the struggle between the Pontiffs and the Kings was over empire and dominion rather than over how the Church was to be governed according to the prescription of the divine Word. In that struggle, when fierce conflicts were stirred up not with arms but with curses and execrations, the prelates, blind through ignorance of the Word, and blind leaders of the blind, clung to the Papists and, rejecting obedience, did not obey the Kings, to whom they were subject by divine, human and civil law. This obstinacy and steadfastness they then called the liberty of the Church. And those who lost their lives or fortunes in that stubbornness they called Martyrs and Confessors. Unless deceit had grown old in men's minds through many years before, and unless it had drawn many prelates, especially, away from the faith and from the duty they owed to kings, over to the Pope, it would be fitting to judge the offices carried out by the Archbishops and Bishops as fairly and creditably done, if anyone weighs their deeds. But because they were deluded by guile from that Roman see, or stained by crimes and contagion, and fell away from the obedience owed to Kings, they not only robbed themselves of praise from their deeds, but brought upon themselves troubles during life and infamy and disgrace after death.

units.la: Ex horum numero fuit Robertus Winchelsee Cantuariensis Archipraesul, cuius acta, si quo animo in patriam & Reipub. gesta sint, existimari debeant, recta iudicanda sunt, sin Romanam confuerudinem praeiutatemq; spectes, sceleratae atque impia. Et quia nonnunquam vir bonus & amator patriae, nonnunquam fraudis, proditionis, superbiae & rapinae plenus varie a scriptoribus perhibetur, sine noua aut calumnia, eaq; quapossumus breuitate scriptorum testimonio ostendamus, qualis ab adolescentia fuerit, qualemque se publice in muneribus gerendis ostenderit, adiunctis similium rerum quae suis temporibus contigerunt euentibus, vt lectori liberum sit de hominis Vita atque gestis pro arbitrio suo iudicare. Genem eius ae originem seniores nobis non prodiderunt. 4 o Sed in grammatica institutus puer Cantuariae fuit, non modo indole docilis, sed forma adeo liberali, moribusq; tam facilimis, atque commodis vt runc quasi vulgari varicinio praediceretur eum Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum olim enasuturum. Ac posteaquam puerilem aetatem & institutionem excessisset, Lutetiam profectus est, vbi liberalium artium peritia percepta, gradum Magistri suscepit. His postea artibus Theologiae studium adiunxit, in eo studio octo annis continuis cum summa norum, quam doctrinae ac literarum laudis celebrirate perseuerauit. Tum singulorum Parisius studentium suffragiis vniuersitatis illius Rector electus est. In quo magistratu integre prudentertque gerendo piorum laudem multis nominibus superauit. Eo magistratu perfunctus redit in Angliam, suiquepericulum in Oxoniensi Academia in Theologia atque his artibus, quas Lutetiae percepisset publice differendo atque concionando secit, acomnium iudicio probatus Doctoris gradum obtinuit. Paulo post cum non minus prudentiae & terum vsu quam literarum cognitione pollere cognicus esset, omnium suffragiis & precibus impositum sibi Cancellariatus munus suscepit. In eo admistrando multa in vtilitatem & honorem Academiae, eaque potissimum quae ad literarum studia amplificanda commodissima videbantur, statuit. Malasque & depravatas consuetudines quibus iuuenes á studiis abduei facile solent, aboleuit, atque sustulit. Ab hoc diuturno literarum otio maiuritatem suam assecutus adEcclesiae negociu traductus est,
units.tr: Among their number was Robert Winchelsee, Archbishop of Canterbury. His deeds must be judged rightly, if they are considered with regard to his country and the commonwealth; but if you look at Roman custom and its prejudice, they were wicked and impious. And since a good man and lover of his country is sometimes described by writers, and sometimes a man full of fraud, treachery, pride and rapine, I shall show, without novelty or slander, and as briefly as I can, by the testimony of writers, what he was like from youth, and how he showed himself in carrying out public duties, together with the events of similar matters that happened in his times, so that the reader may judge freely, as he pleases, of the man's life and deeds. Our elders have not handed down to us his family or origin. But as a boy, educated in grammar, he was at Canterbury, and was not only docile in disposition, but of such a gracious appearance and so agreeable and pleasing in manners that, as it were by common rumour, it was foretold that he would one day become Archbishop of Canterbury. When he had passed beyond boyhood and early education, he went to Paris, where, having acquired skill in the liberal arts, he took the degree of Master. After these arts he added the study of theology, and he persevered in that study for eight continuous years with great fame both for learning and for reputation in letters. Then, by the votes of the individual students at Paris, he was elected Rector of that university. In carrying out that office with integrity and prudence, he surpassed the praise of the pious in many respects. Having completed that office, he returned to England, and at Oxford University he gave public lectures and sermons in theology and in those arts which he had learned at Paris; approved by the judgment of all, he obtained the degree of Doctor. Shortly afterwards, since he was found to excel no less in prudence and experience of affairs than in knowledge of letters, he took up, by the votes and prayers of all, the office of Chancellor placed upon him. In administering it he decided on many measures for the benefit and honour of the University, especially those that seemed most suitable for extending the study of letters. He abolished and removed the bad and corrupt customs by which young men are easily drawn away from their studies. Having attained his full maturity from this long leisure devoted to letters, he was drawn into Church business.

units.la: Ste.Byrchre.
units.tr: Ste. Byrchre.

units.la: Walsing. est, donatus Archidiaconatu Essexiae & Prebenda in Ecclesia Cathedrali Londonensi. In ea Prebenda vefedit, quotidieq; in templo sanctas scripturas interpretaris est, tum in verbo e suggestu docendo atque declarando fuit assiduus. Archidiaconatum ipse quotannis visitavit, iurisdictione tam moderate ac prudenter vsus, vt summae doctrinae, prudentiae, & aequitatis fama vbique notus atque conspicuus fuerit. Ita erudinone ac intereritate tanta peripecta, quae cum xtare iemper in eo adoleuiflent a puericia, venit ut tantam Regis, praesulumq; procerum atque omnium ordinum gratiam & admirationem, vt mortuo Iohanne Peckam, cum eligendi potestas Monachis Cantuariensibus a Rege data esset, ex omnium votis & applausu Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus electus sit. Cuius
units.tr: Walsing. He was given the archdeaconry of Essex and a prebend in the cathedral church of London. He resided in that prebend, expounded the holy Scriptures daily in the church, and was constant in teaching and explaining the Word from the pulpit. He visited his archdeaconry himself every year, exercising jurisdiction so moderately and prudently that he became widely known and conspicuous for his reputation for great learning, prudence and fairness. Since his learning and integrity, so thoroughly tested, had always flourished in him from boyhood, he won such great favour and admiration from the King, the bishops and nobles, and all ranks, that when John Peckham died and the King granted the monks of Canterbury the power of election, he was chosen Archbishop of Canterbury by the votes and applause of all.

units.la: 10 que Romani ad Coelestinum Papam confirmandus atque sacrandus venisset, Papam roi tamque Romanam curiam in tantam prudentiae doctrinaeque suae admirationem ac stupo rem traduxit, vt non cognouisse se in quocunq; dicerent, tantam morum animique mansuetudinem cum literis & prudentia comunctam. Itaque cum in Cardinalium gregem cooptare, Romaeq; secum retinere decreuerunt. Sed expoticis multis causis necessaris, cur a Cantuariensi Ecclesia abesse non poterat, aegre tandem obtinuit, vt sacratus in Anglia rediret, & Prouinciae suae gubernandae vacaret. Interea vero dum Archiepiscopus Stephanus Byrch. pus abesset, Edwardus Rex a Clero Westmonasterii congregato, postquam pecunia in bellicos vsus effusa esset, & nouum sibi bellum in instaret in Gallos suscipiendum, dagitque omnium tam spiritualium quam temporalium bonorum seruitium. Quod sic ut in
units.tr: When he had come to Rome to be confirmed and consecrated by Pope Celestine, he so astonished and amazed the Pope and the whole Roman court with his learning and prudence that they said they had never known in anyone such gentleness of character and spirit joined with learning and prudence. Accordingly, they decided to enrol him in the college of Cardinals and keep him at Rome with them. But for many necessary reasons why he could not be absent from the Canterbury Church, he at last, with difficulty, obtained leave to return to England once consecrated, and to devote himself to governing his province. Meanwhile, while the archbishop was away, King Edward, after the money had been poured out on warlike uses, and a new war was threatening to be undertaken against the French, summoned the clergy of Westminster and demanded the service of all spiritual and temporal goods.

units.la: 30 audita exactione Praelati stupidi timore diu obmutuere. Tandem praedictus Ioannes Contuli ba titespirantes delibrandi diem petierunt. Is perbreuis statutu elt. Interea Guilelmus quidam de Monte forti, Ecclesiae Paulinae Decanus, vt Regis animum a tam immenta & incoherabili exactione, suasione aliqua auerteret, ad curiam sanus & incolumis venit; & meditaram atque conceptam orationem coram Rege exortus repente concidit, & animam effauit. At rex nihilo turbatus die statuto mitrad Praelatos Westmonasterii congregatos Iohannem de Hauering militem. Is Regis nuncius alta voce edixit, vt suis petitioni regiae obstare aut contradicere vellet, in medium prodirer, vt eius pertorta po gnita violatae atque turbatae regiae pacis reus iudicaretur. Qua oratione perplexi & a 40 nituis Praelati Regis postulatis concessaerunt. Quae concessio totius inter Regem & praelas tos, maxime vero Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum dissensionis perpetuum (vti declarabitur) seminarium fuit. Hoc anno Coelestinus Papa, siue taedio siue conscientia motus, siue quod veri usus est Benedicti Caietani qui ei callide succesorit, inductus dolo sciens abdicauit papatu, edita prius constitutione de Cessione seu renunciatione Romanorum Pontificum, & acti habita admonitione vt sine dissensione atque intercapedine virum indu strum & solertem eligerent. Eo itaque renunciante in sinuauit sein Cardinalium gratiam summo dolo & calliditate Benedictus, qui postea Bonifacius octauus dictus est. Qui simulatque electus & coronatus essit constitutionem Coelestini rescidit, in Cardinales quos suis partibus aduersos putauit summa crudelitate laeuit, Episcopum & Cardinalem Oltieniem a quo coronatus fuerat, vsu Pallij priuauit. Annum lubilcum profusa magna indulgentiarum per orbem terrarum copia magnifice celebrauit. Librum sextum Decretalium edidit, de quo Coelestinus eius astuta suasione cum papatui cessisset, deceptus hoc verto vaticinatus est.
units.tr: 30 When the demand was heard, the stunned prelates were struck dumb with fear for a long time. At length the aforesaid John and the others, drawing breath again, asked for a day to deliberate. A very short day was fixed. Meanwhile William de Montfort, dean of St Paul's, came safely and unharmed to the court, to turn the King's mind from so immense and unbearable an exaction by some persuasion; but when he began the speech he had prepared and composed before the King, he suddenly collapsed and expired. Yet the King, unmoved, on the appointed day sent John de Havering, a knight, to the prelates gathered at Westminster. This royal messenger announced in a loud voice that whoever wished to oppose or contradict the King's request should come forward into the open, so that he might be judged guilty of breaking the king's peace, which had been violated and disturbed by his obstinacy. Confused and pressed by this speech, the prelates granted the King's demands. This grant was a perpetual seedbed of dispute between the King and the prelates, and especially the Archbishop of Canterbury, as will be shown. In this year Pope Celestine, either moved by weariness or by conscience, or because he feared Benedict Gaetani, who cunningly succeeded him, and, induced by deceit, knowingly gave up the papacy, after first issuing a constitution on the cession or renunciation of Roman pontiffs, and after holding a meeting in which he urged them to elect a diligent and skilful man without dissension or delay. When he had renounced, Benedict, who was afterwards called Boniface VIII, insinuated himself into the favour of the Cardinals with the greatest guile and cunning. As soon as he had been elected and crowned, he annulled Celestine's constitution; he raged with the greatest cruelty against the Cardinals whom he judged hostile to his party, and deprived the Bishop and Cardinal of Ostia, by whom he had been crowned, of the use of the pallium. He celebrated the jubilee year magnificently, with a great abundance of indulgences poured out throughout the world. He published the Sixth Book of the Decretals. Concerning this, Celestine, who had yielded the papacy through Boniface's crafty persuasion and been deceived, truly prophesied.

units.la: Ascendisti vt vulpes, regnabis vt Leo, & mortieris vt Canis.
units.tr: Thou hast ascended like a fox, thou shalt reign like a lion, and thou shalt die like a dog.

units.la: Cuius vaticinij veritatem euentus ipse (vt suo tempore postea diccimus) compre bauit Iamq; Robertus Winchelseeie in Angliam reuertus est, Rege Edwardo in Cambriam ad Walienses qui nouos tum motus fecerant, subiugandos profecto. Eum igitur Archiepiscopus adiit, eiusque ex vetero moreatque insituto fidem iureiurando dedit. Tum Madockum Lenlinum Cambrum qui bellum in Regem parauerat excommunicauit, eumque ex communicatum per totam Angliam & Cambriam denunciari mulcis pu 50 blicis edictis praecepit. Eoque pacato tumultu Archiepiscopus a Rege cum summa gratia Londinum recessit. Ibi cleri sui Synodum celebrauit. In qua cum praelati vno ore de expilatione & vastatione Ecclesiarum conquestiflent, cum Regis petitis ipsi ob stare aut resistere non audebant, Papam praetextu cuiusdam constitutionis in qua sancitum erat, ne quid inconsulto Papa Regibus a Clero soluerentur, opponebat Haec itaque constitutio renouata est in ea Synodo, alias; permultaeque latae, quarum plerae; inter iura prouinciali obseruanda describuntur. Hac Synodo perasta, descriptis aduocatis, iudicibus, & procuratoribus, aliisq; ministris almae curiae do Atcubus iura quaedam & statuta, quae ipse in templo arcuato sedens pro tribunali legit atque obligauit
units.tr: The event itself confirmed the truth of this prophecy, as we shall say in its place. Robert of Winchelsea returned to England, King Edward being about to subdue the Welsh, who had then stirred up fresh revolts. The Archbishop therefore approached the King and gave him his oath of fealty, according to the old custom and institution. He then excommunicated Madoc ap Llywelyn, who had prepared war against the King, and ordered that he be declared excommunicate throughout England and Wales by many public edicts. With this disturbance quelled, the Archbishop took leave of the King, who showed him the greatest favour, and went to London. There he held a synod of his clergy. In it, when the prelates had complained with one voice about the plundering and devastation of the churches, they did not dare to oppose or resist the King's demands. They put forward a pope's constitution, by which it had been enacted that nothing should be paid by the clergy to kings without the Pope's consent. This constitution was renewed in that synod, and very many other decrees were passed, most of which are listed among the laws to be observed throughout the province. When the synod was finished, advocates, judges, proctors and other officers of the venerable Court of Arches were appointed, and certain rules and statutes were read out and imposed by him, sitting in the vaulted church as on a tribunal, on the fifth of the Ides of November.

units.la: quinto Idus Nouemb. Deindevenit Cantuariam, ibique thronum Archiepiscopalem cum magna Pompa & solennitate ingressus est. Ipsoque consecrationis die Iohannem Monmuthensem sacrae theologiae professorem Landauensem Episcopum creauit atque consecrauit. Et decem theologiae professoribus decem opulenta beneficia curata, in eaque bacchalaureis dectem minora contulit. Subadis autem(vt diximus) Cambris Edwardus Rex à Scotis atque Gallis vndique bello pulsus est. Itaque ne tot ac tantorum hostium viribus & imperio obtrueretur, cum Romanorum Rege foedus iniit. Cumq; ad bellum in vtrosque tam Scotum quam Gallum accindus esset, Bonifacius Papa qui summum esse putauit, Regum lites mercede componere, ad Gallix & Angliæ Reges Albanensem atque Prænestinum Cardinales misit. Hi in Anglia nihil profecerunt, quia Edwardus inconsulto Rege Romanorum, cum quo medio iuramento confœderatus erat, quicquam aut de pace aut de induciis cum Rege Galliæ noluit decernere. Itaque Legatu Papales infecto negocio pro quo venerunt, in Galliam remearunt, præ exhausta pecunia multa nimis, & a viris religiosis duplam pecuniam extorserunt. In huius belliapparatu Rex à populo atque clero exegit opem pecuniariam. Populus illico concessit, sed Clerus suadente Archiepiscopo rem aliquandiu distulit, & habita deliberatione Papæ vices in Anglia gerens, nc in fraudem superioris (vt diximus) Londinensis Cœcilii quicquam agere videretur, Archiepiscopus indulta sibi conferendi cum Suffraganeis atque Clero licentia vnanimi consensu Regi obtulit decimam partem prouentuum Ecclesiasticorum. Hanc oblationem Rex (sprevit) atque respuit. Archiepiscopus & cum eo Clerus in decreta summa perseuerarunt, nec eam augere voluerunt, sed Regi iterum obtulerunt. Rex hanc Cleri & Archiepiscopi constantiam admiratus eos semel atque iterum monuit primum per Iusticiarium, deinde per quendam Cancellariæ suæ Clericum vt salvem trientem, aut quadrantem bonorum suorum offerrent. Stetit adhuc firmiter Clerus in proposito, & Archiepiscopo duce decimam iterum obtulerunt. Rex siue quod bellica cura negocia morari pati non potuissent, siue memoria prioris illius tam profundæ largitionis (superiori anno (vt diximus) à clero concessæ ductus hanc oblatam (summam æquo atque grato animo accepit. Eaque soluta ad bellum properans Clerum dimisit. Et ad Belgas profectus cum Rogerus Couentrensis atque Lichefeldiensis Episcopus excessisset è vita, Willielmum quendam de Langtona eligi procurauit, qui in paruis transfert marinis Regis instantia ab Albanensi Cardinali consecratus est, priuilegiorum Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ, in omnibus statu suo saluo. Interea verò dum Edwardus aberat in Belgia, Scotorum inuasione reuocatus est. Qua fortiter repulsa, Scotis superatis, & capto Berwico thesaurum in Gallicanum bellum parantem exhausit. Itaque Parliamentum in ipso Berwico tenuit, vbi Magnates Scotiæ in prælio victos atque deditios ad fidelitatem iuramento & in scriptis polliendam adegit. Rex ipse Scotiæ captus Londinum missus & Turri inclusus est. Postea ad reficiendas consumptas in eo bello pecunias nouum sibi perdituum tributum poscit. In quo ciues & mercatores octonarium, Coloni duodenarium persoluunt nemmum. Clerus ne quicquam vel obrulit, vel concessit, prætendens præfatam constitutionem Papæ, videlicet, non esse permissum quicquam de Ecclesiasticis facultatibus detrahere & conferre Regibus inconsulto Papa. Interim enim Robertus Archiepiscopus mandatum de ea re bullatum à Bonifacio Papa obtinuerat. Rex cōmotus Parliamentum Londinum prorogauit, ibi in festo Hilarii adesse Clerum suis postulatis benignius responsurum iussit. Interim omnia Cleri horrea frumento iam plena sigillis publicis obsignari & occludi præcepit. Hoc imperatum dum Regis ministri peragerent, Robertus Archiepiscopus lucta iam atque contentione cum Rege instituta, mandauit papalem constitutionem sub excommunicationis pœna inhibentem, ne ex prouentibus Ecclesiasticis Regi aut cuicunque principi seculari tributum pendatur, in Cathedralibus Ecclesiis diuulgari. Die statuta Parliamento inchoato Archiepiscopus cum Suffraganeis & Prælatis iniit Concilium in Ecclesia Paulina Londini, & decreuerunt in proloti sententia stare, nec quicquam Regi concedere. Quo accepto decreto misit Rex ex aula sua nuncios, qui suo nomine agerent cum Clero, quoniam eorum & tranquillitas maior, & fructus atque reddit us annui tunc esset longe vberiores quàm populi, vt ad Regem in his bellicis angustiis adiuuandum seostenderent promptiores.
units.tr: Then he came to Canterbury and entered the archiepiscopal throne with great pomp and solemnity. On the very day of his consecration he created and consecrated John of Monmouth, professor of sacred theology, as Bishop of Llandaff. He conferred ten rich benefices with cure of souls on ten professors of theology, and ten lesser ones on bachelors. Meanwhile, as we have said, while King Edward was engaged with the Welsh, he was attacked in war on every side by the Scots and the French. So that he might not be overwhelmed by the forces and power of so many great enemies, he made an alliance with the King of the Romans. And when he was girding himself for war against both the Scot and the Frenchman, Pope Boniface, who thought it his office to settle the quarrels of kings for a fee, sent the Cardinals of Albano and Palestrina to the Kings of France and England. They achieved nothing in England, because Edward, without the consent of the King of the Romans, with whom he was bound by a solemn oath, would not agree to any terms of peace or truce with the King of France. So the papal legates, having failed in the business for which they had come, returned to France, having spent far too much money, and they extorted double the amount from religious men. In preparation for this war, the King demanded financial help from the people and the clergy. The people granted it at once, but the clergy, on the Archbishop's advice, put the matter off for some time. After deliberation, and so that it might not appear that they were acting in fraud of the earlier London council of Cecilius (as we said), the Archbishop, who was acting as the Pope's vicar in England, with the unanimous consent of his suffragans and clergy, having been granted leave to confer with them, offered the King a tenth of ecclesiastical revenues. The King scorned and rejected this offer. The Archbishop and the clergy with him persisted in the same fixed sum and would not increase it, but offered it to the King again. The King, admiring the constancy of the clergy and the Archbishop, admonished them once and again, first through the Justiciar and then through a certain clerk of his chancery, to offer a third or a quarter of their goods. The clergy still stood firm in their resolve, and under the Archbishop's leadership offered a tenth once more. The King, whether because the cares of war would not allow him to delay his business, or because he was moved by the memory of that earlier and very generous grant made by the clergy the year before (as we said), accepted the offered sum with a fair and grateful mind. When it was paid, he hurried to the war and dismissed the clergy. Setting out for Flanders, and when Roger, Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield, had died, he arranged for one William de Langton to be elected. At the King's urging, William was consecrated overseas by the Cardinal of Albano, with the privileges of the Church of Canterbury preserved in every respect. Meanwhile, while Edward was away in Flanders, he was recalled by a Scottish invasion. Having repulsed it vigorously and defeated the Scots, and having taken Berwick, he exhausted the treasure that was being prepared for the French war. He therefore held a Parliament at Berwick itself, where he compelled the Scottish nobles who had been defeated in battle and surrendered to give their fealty by oath and in writing. The King of Scotland himself was taken, sent to London and shut up in the Tower. Afterwards, to make good the money used up in that war, he demanded a new tax. Citizens and merchants paid an eighth, and the farmers of the land a twelfth, of their goods. The clergy neither offered nor granted anything, pleading that papal constitution, namely, that it was not permitted to take anything from ecclesiastical property and give it to kings without the Pope's consent. Indeed, Archbishop Robert had already obtained from Pope Boniface a mandate on this matter, sealed with a bull. The King, moved to anger, prorogued Parliament to London and ordered the clergy to appear there on the feast of Hilary, to answer his demands more kindly. Meanwhile he ordered that all the clergy's granaries, now full of grain, be sealed with public seals and closed. While the King's officers were carrying out this order, Archbishop Robert, now engaged in struggle and contention with the King, ordered that the papal constitution, which forbade under penalty of excommunication that any tax be paid from ecclesiastical revenues to the King or to any secular prince, be published in the cathedral churches. On the day appointed for the opening of Parliament, the Archbishop with his suffragans and prelates held a council in St Paul's Church in London, and they decided to stand by their earlier decision and grant nothing to the King. When the King received this decree, he sent messengers from his court to deal with the clergy in his name, since their tranquillity and their annual revenues and returns were then far greater than those of the people, so that they might show themselves readier to help the King in these warlike distresses.

units.la: Quibus Archiepisc. Satis, inquit, constat, quod sub Deo vniuersali rerum Domino, duos habemus Dominos, (spiritualem D. Papam, & temporalem D. Regem. Et quanquà vtriq; obtemperandum est, (spirituali tamen magis quàm temporali Domino est obsequendum. Itaq; Legatos ad D. Papam mittere destinamus, vt eius venia obtenta id Regi largiri. giri possimus quod à nobis flagitat. Ad hæc Regis nuncii. Statuite aliquos ex vobis, inquiunt, qui hæc Regi referant. Nos enim experti sumus eius animum huiusmodi dictis ac responsis accendi & commoueri solitum. Accepto tandem hoc responso Rex indignè tulit his Papæ clericq; dolis sic in regno suo ludificari, exclusoq; è Parliamento Clero cõcilium eum solis Baronibus atq; populo habuit, rotumq; statim Clerum protectione sua priuauit. Tum capitalium criminum & maleficiorũ iudex edixit pro tribunali non esse Archiepiscopus, Episcopis, aut Clero quacunq; affectis iniuria in foro regio pro quibuscunq; iudibus, querelis vel negociis ius tribuendum. Quibuscunq; autem contra eos agere vel experiri volentibus Regis voluntate atque iure licere.
units.tr: To these the Archbishop replied: "It is well established that under God, the universal Lord of all things, we have two lords: the spiritual lord, the Pope, and the temporal lord, the King. And although we must obey both, we must obey the spiritual lord more than the temporal. Therefore we have determined to send envoys to the Lord Pope, so that, having obtained his leave, we may be able to grant the King what he demands of us." To this the King's messengers said: "Appoint some of your number, they say, who may report this to the King. For we have learned from experience that his mind is usually stirred and inflamed by such words and replies." When at last the King received this answer, he took it badly that he should be so mocked in his own kingdom by these tricks of the Pope and the clergy. Excluding the clergy from Parliament, he held a council with the barons and the people alone, and at once stripped the clergy of his protection. Then the judge of capital crimes and offences declared from the bench that no legal remedy was to be granted in the royal court to the Archbishop, bishops or clergy of any rank, for any suits, complaints or business, if they were wronged. And whoever wished to act or to bring suit against them was permitted to do so by the King's will and law.

units.la: Clerus tam atroci decreto percitus contumaciam remisit. Elegerunt Eboracensem Archiepiscopum & Dunelmensem, Elienfem, & Sarisburiensem Episcopos cum aliis, quibus vices suas commisserunt, ut remedium aliquod opportunum, quo & papalis excommunicatio & regia proscriptio simul vitari possint. Hi statuerunt deponendam in æde sacra quintam bonorum Ecclesiasticorum partem ad Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ tuitionem & defensionem vrgentissimæ necessitatis. Qua & à papali comminatione salui, & in gratiam protectionemq; iterum recipiuntur. At Robertus præfractus à sententia non destitit, ob quam contumaciam bona eius quæcunque in visus regios occupata sunt, domoque eiectus vix hospitio cuiusquam auxiliatur, protectatione semper bac visus, se nequicquam nihilo magis præstiturum, omnesque qui præter Papæ voluntatem Regi aliquid contulissent, bullata illa excommunicatione teneri. Snb hæc tempora cum Archiepiscopi & Episcopi de hac dubia & ancipitii inter Regem & Papam authoritate consulerent, suborti sunt duo fratres ordinis prædicatorum, qui argumentis probabant, subueniendum esse Regi a Clero in belli necessitatibus, non obstante prohibitione papali. Simulq; edictum est a Rege, ne quis sub incarcerationis poena in Regem, cosue qui iam priidem suam protectionem quæserant, illius papalis excommunicationis sententiam promulgaret. Quo facto dissipatum fuit Episcoporum concilium, qui vtriusq; gladii formidine perterriti, quid agerent, incerti fuerunt. Eoque magis quod Robertus concilio discedens. Saluet, inquit, vnusquisq; animam suam. Clerus autem & animam & bona simul seruare statuens, cum protectione carentes a nullius iniuria tuti esse poterant, super Ann. 1196 plices Regem eiusq; euriam adibant, & nunc quartam nunc quintam bonorum suorum partem non rogaui vltro offerebant, vt ablata Regia manu temporalia redimerent, & sub regia tutela defensioneq; secure viuere possent.
units.tr: The clergy, roused by so savage a decree, gave up their obstinacy. They chose the Archbishop of York, the Bishops of Durham, Ely and Salisbury, with others, to whom they committed their powers, so that some suitable remedy might be found by which both the papal excommunication and the royal outlawry could be avoided together. These men decided that a fifth part of the ecclesiastical goods should be deposited in a sacred building, for the protection and defence of the English Church in a most urgent necessity. By this means they were both kept safe from the papal threat and received again into favour and protection. But Robert, obstinate, did not desist from his opinion. On account of this obstinacy all his goods were seized for the royal use, and he was driven from his house and scarcely anyone gave him lodging. He always protested that he would not give anything, and that all who had given the King anything, except by the Pope's will, were bound by that bull of excommunication. At this time, while the Archbishop and bishops were consulting about this doubtful and double-edged authority between the King and the Pope, two friars of the Order of Preachers came forward and argued by reasons that the King should be assisted by the clergy in the necessities of war, notwithstanding the papal prohibition. At the same time the King issued an edict that no one, on pain of imprisonment, should publish that papal sentence of excommunication against the King, or against those who had long since sought his protection. By this act the council of bishops was broken up. Terrified by the fear of both swords, they were uncertain what to do, the more so because Robert, leaving the council, said: "Let each man save his own soul." The clergy, however, resolved to save both their souls and their goods. Lacking protection, they could not be safe from anyone's injury, so they went as suppliants to the King and his court, and now offered of their own accord a quarter, now a fifth, of their goods, so that by yielding their temporal possessions to the royal hand they might buy their safety and live securely under the King's protection and defence.

units.la: Rex cum necessario sibi & celeriter aggrediendos armis Gallos animadverteret, commodius esse duxit hanc Archiepiscopi inimicitiam dissimulare, donec bello confecto de eo poenas sumere superatis hostibus sine tumultu & discrimine posset. Itaque Parliamento Londini celebrator, Archiepiscopum in gratiam recepit, eiusque ablata restituit, tum vt populum discedens deliniret, adhibitis sibi Archiepiscopo & filio suo Edwardo principe, nec non Waruicensi Comite, in aula Westmonasterii in quam conueniri populum iusserat, oranonem flebilem habuit. In qua multis se rationibus excusauit quòd tanta tam grandem pecuniam tributis augendis & exigendis tam a Clero quam a populo confecissent. Ad id se inuitum coactum ne populum suum in hostes sanguinarios vndique infestantes permitteret. Se iam in Galliam pro eorum salute profecturum & suam vitam summo discrimine expositurum. Si vicor salvis rebus redierit, reddiurum se subditis ea quæ acceperat, si non redierit, vt filium suum Edwardum Wallie Principem Regem crearent, petiit. His dictis Archiepiscopus vt populum ad Regem flecteret, effundens lachrymas suscepit Regem ea quæ promiserat præstiturum, & illico populus extensis manibus vno ore fidem Regi stipulantur. Comites autem & Batones iam Rege in Flandriam festinare eo deferuissent, nisi libertatem Magna Charta & in Fotesta a patte suo, (vt in Bonifacio diximus) ratas confirmarct. Ad quod, netardaretur autimpediretur in hoc itinere inuito & reluctante animo ductus est. Quo concessio Coloni qui duodecimum denarium ante promiserant, iam libenter octauum obtulerunt. Rebus itaq; sic ex singulorum animis & sententia compositis, Rex secundis auris atq; velis in Flandriam applicuit. Interea dum Rex Gandaui in castris & exercitu instruendis occupareatur, Gallus vim eius primesfces biennales inducias obsecrabat. Quas non aliam ob causam fecit Rex, quam quòd de Comitum & Baronis domi in se confederatione accepit. Nã cum populi subsidium ad Regis qni tum aberat æ rarium esset soluendum, Comites, & Barones inter cesserunt, nec solui quicquam à populo aut à Regis quæstoribus recipi permiserant. Quoniam se consultis, sine quorum, vt asserebat, consensu tributum exigi aut imponi populo non debuisset, ea solutio concessa est.
units.tr: When the King saw that he must quickly take up arms against the French, he judged it more expedient to conceal his enmity toward the Archbishop until the war was finished and the enemy defeated, so that he could punish him without tumult or danger. Accordingly, at a Parliament held in London, he restored the Archbishop to favour and returned his confiscated property. Then, to placate the people as they dispersed, he gave a tearful address in the hall at Westminster, to which he had ordered the people to assemble, with the Archbishop, his son Prince Edward, and the Earl of Warwick at his side. In it he made many excuses for having raised and collected such a large sum in taxes from both clergy and people. He said he had been forced to this against his will, so that he would not allow his people to be attacked on every side by bloodthirsty enemies. He was now going to France for their safety and would expose his own life to the greatest danger. If he returned victorious with his affairs secure, he would give back to his subjects what he had received; if he did not return, he asked them to make his son Edward, Prince of Wales, king. When he had said this, the Archbishop, to bend the people to the King, shed tears and took the King's promise that he would fulfil what he had promised. At once the people, with hands raised, pledged their loyalty to the King with one voice. The earls and barons, however, would have hastened with the King into Flanders at once, had not the liberties of Magna Carta and of the Forest been confirmed by his father, as we said under Boniface. Because of this, lest he be delayed or hindered on his journey, he was led to it with an unwilling and reluctant mind. Thereupon the citizens, who had earlier promised a twelfth penny, now gladly offered an eighth. Matters having been settled in this way, to the minds and opinions of each, the King set sail for Flanders with favourable winds and sails. Meanwhile, while the King was busy at Ghent setting up his camp and army, the French begged for a two-year truce. The King granted this for no other reason than that he had learned of a confederacy of earls and barons at home against him. For since the money from the people, needed to pay the King's treasury in his absence, was to be paid, the earls and barons intervened and would not allow anything to be paid by the people or received by the King's treasurers. Since they had been consulted, and without their consent, as they claimed, no tax ought to have been levied or imposed on the people, that payment was conceded.

units.la: Quæ Magnatum interceßio populum à Rege ad eorum confœderationem conciliauit. Itaque plebe & Magnatibus vna conjunctis Edwardus filius Regis, qui patris absentis in regno vicarius fuit, concedendis his quas vendicabant libertatibus, periculum quod ad suum patrisq; exitium fuit meditatum prudenter auertit. Eodem etiam tempore Scoti fracta Berwici, (vt diximus) Regi data fide Northumbriam & regni finitima ibi loca armis invadunt, ratiRegem ad bellum Gallicum omnem opem multarem abduxisse, ad quorum audaciam reprimédam populus nonum. Clerus deinde nartum Comitibus absente Rege conceßit. Quod Regi magnopere displicuit, Clerum qui tam aduersus suis petitionibus fuit, iamabiente le Comitibus, qui suis a populo concessis tributis soluendis resistebant, tam facile concessisse. Hæres Archiepiscopum Regi su- ptum de procerum coniuratione fecerit, & indicias, quas aliquam rebus fie ad belluum inituit, & paratis noluissent, cum Gallo inire, & in Angliam quam celeriter redire Regem impulerunt. Igitur Kal. Aprilreuersus vindictam, quam in Archiepiscopum & proceres confœderatos meditabatur, celauit, donec inlis duorum annorum (vt dixi- ximus) cum Gallo inducit Scotos perfidos subrugasset, & rem suam periculis tantis ruittam fecisset, atq; roboraßet. Scotos primo aggressus est. Hos eomisso prope villam quaFrontrie appellatur, prælio superauit. Hoc anno Bonifacius Papa aliquandiu intermi- sum tuæ poße statis plenitudinem, ne in desuetudinem abiret, ecepit exercere. Nam Gulielmo Elienfi Episcopo mortuo, diuisio in duas partes capitulo, vna par Priore Elienfem; altera Iohannem de Langona Cancellarium Regis elegerunt. Hæc electionis dilenlio aliquandiu coram Roberto Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo agitata est, qui cum seeundum Priorem iudicasset Cancellarius ad Papam prouocauit. Ita ad curiam papalem vtriqué contendunt. Ibi à luc receßerunt, & suæ electionis ius Papæ arbitrio commisrunt. Qui virisque reiectis, iustit Procuratores Conuentus Elienfis vt ex aliis exemptis Cœnobijs videlicet, Westmonast. S. Edmundi, S. Augustini, vel S. Albani Abbatem eligerent, illi a priori electione non recesserunt, reprimendum. Commotus hac (vt dixit) contumacia, Papa pronunciauit ius conferendi Episcopatum Elienfem ob procuratorum improbitatem ad se pertinere. Itaq; ex mero proprio, suo motu Noruicensem Episcopum ad Elienfem transtulit, & Noruicensem Episcopatum Priori Elienfi contulit. Defuncto tunc temporis in sua curia Otionino Archiepiscopo Dublinenfi, Richardum Ferin. Archidiaconum Cantuariensem ad eum Archiepiscopatum promouit, & Archidiaconatum Cantuariensem Iohanni Cancellario Regis, qui de Elienfi Episcopatu conteneabat, contulit. Eodem etiam anno Minores qui deportata in Anglia fratres, quorum votum & institutum erat proprio carere, è cœno & mediocritate tam emersit Papæ obtulerunt in auro quadringenta milia Florenorum, & infinitam in argento pecuniam, ut eis terras, prædia, redditusq; annuos acquirendi atque possidendi more Monachorum venia suo diplomate fiue Bulla daretur. Quibus D. Papa. Vbi est inquit, illa vestr a pecunia ? Actilli, In manibus mercatorum. Quo audito cosiernio. iussit responsum accepturos. Interim mercatorem penes quos deposita effet pecunia, a depositi contractu, pecuniaq; fratribus reddenda absolut, & sub Anathematis pœna iussit, vt Romanæ sedis vibus eam reseraret. Fratrit ostentio die pa- pale diploma expectantibus, respondit. Regulam S. Francisci Canonizatam, se nullo sensu depraüare aut violare velle, nec permissuram vt fratres ab ea declinarent. Paulò ante (vt in Roberto Kylwarby diximus) lata est in Anglia illa Manus mortuæ lex, quæ prohibet Collegiis, Cœnobiis, fraternitatibus, atque religiosistis quiliam in infinitum creueisent, sine Regio consensu terrarum & prædiorum acquisitiones. Ea lex ab horum fratrum intemperanti hypocrisi & ingluuie nata est. Quo um mendicitatis speciè tectæ rapina, nisi illa lucrosa Papæ religione, & salubérrimis regni legibus coërcita fuisset, omnium hæreditates atque bona per breui deuorasset. Sed ab his quæ illis temporibus contingentia interposuimus, ad Regem & Archiepiscopum reuertamur, Rex Scotis s o in prælio (vt diximus) fusis, cum & intestina sibi & externa mala imminere sensisset, domestica simulans, prudenter primò caeuit de exterius. Cumq; se ad Scotos superiori vistos & examinatos prælio penitus debellando accinxisset, à Papa per Archiepiscopum Cæsuariensem, qui eius iussa sedulò exequutus est, satis pro impero prohibitus est, ne Scotos suæ protectioni submissos vlterius præsumeret debellare. Qua communicatione papali, cum Rex aliis permultis difficultatibus tenerctur, susceptoin Scoto negotio supersedit. Tum Bonifacio Papa prorsurante inter Angliæ & Franciæ Reges ima pacè & nuptiæ inter Angliæ Regem, & Margaretam Regis Franciæ sorotem Regali more atque magnificentia contractæ, & in Ecclesia Metropolitica Cantnarienfi, ipso Archiepiscopo diuina ministrante celebratæ sunt. Verum paulo post illa diu celata & occultara simultas quam Papa in Regem Franciæ altamente reposuerat, in apertum odium conuitiumque erupit. Nam dum Regis legatus cumPapa de niultis iniuriis in Regem factis ageret, Papa cum minis & superciliis contractis, Nos,inquit, habemus vtramque potestatem. Et ille pro domino suo respondit, vtique domine.Sed vestra est verbalis, nostra realis. Etin tantum excanduit ira domini Papæ, vt diceret moucre fe velle contra eum Cœlum & Terram. Sed has Papæ minas quas verbis emisit, postea vt dicemus re ipsa, quemadmodum Legatis edixit, Rex Franciæ vlrus est. Papa cum sibi a Gallo metuit,ne sibi deessent copiæ,decimam Ecclesiasticorum bonorum in Anglia triennio toto, concedentibus idlibenter Episcopis, qui Regi id ad bellicos vsus postulanti denegarunt, vsurpauit. Hoc anno Elienfis & Wigorniensis Episcopi obierunt, inquorum loca vtriusque Ecclesiæ Couentus Commonachos suos elegerunt, qui electi cum consecrationis gratiam a Cantuarienfi Archiepiscopo obtinere non poterant, ad Papam profecti sunt. Is perpenso rutfus electionis vtrufque ordine atque modo, Wigorniensem Monachum ab Episcopatu reiecit, sed Elienfem confirmauit. Deinde Wigorniensem Episcopatum cuidam Minorû fratrum iure(vt asseruit) ad fe devoluto contulit. Edwardus vero Rex pace cum Gallo nuptiis (diximus) interuenientibus & affinitate firmata, ad Scoros coercendos bellicas copias iterum parauit. Qui cum cognouissent omnia Romæ fuisse venalia opimis muneribus Papam ditarunt, vt sua proreclione Edwardi Regis vim hostilem prohiberet, & ab eius potestate eximeret, suaque conseruaret. Papa Lombardum quendam cum suis imperatis ad Cantuarienfem Archiepiscopum misit, qui Regem in expeditione fequuti cum ad eum venifient, exponunt Papæ mandata, nepe Scotos nulli prætercptâ sibi, Romanæq; capellæ subiici, proinde vt Rex suscepta in eos arma deponeret, Papæ nomen iubet. Fieri n.non posse quin ciuitas Hierufalè suos ciues protegeret. Quibus cômotus Rex. Ego, inquit, neq; proprer Hierusalem, nec Sionde sistam, quin ius meum in Scotos fœdifragos & periuros ipso Marte tueat. Mox Legatus Papæ reuertitur, ac Rex nihilominus ad bellum pergit. Sed ne videretur irritabilem Papam in fe rebus vix domi compositis concitare, misit Comites Lincolnienfem, & Hugonē Spenfer ad Papā qui multis monumētis & exēplis de iure suo in Scotos agerent. Quibus de rebus inter Papam & Regem ac proceres Anglię fcripras ac refcripras literas confulto omittimus. Sub hæc tepora Moniales Angliæ, cum eis egrediendi suas cellas&quocunque libuim fuerit, vagandi licentia permissa fuerat, nec iure vllo prohibita, lasciuire coeperunt, itaque Bonifacius Papa de eis cellis suis includendis ad Episcopum Cantuarienfem & suæ prouinciæ Suffraganeos decreralem fcripfit epistolam, in qua potestas eis factæ est Moniales visitandi, & circumseptos eorum cellis præscribere terminos quorum finibus contineri debeant.
units.tr: This intervention of the magnates won the people over from the King to their confederacy. Accordingly, with the commons and the magnates united, Edward, the King's son, who acted as his father's deputy in the realm while he was away, prudently averted the danger that had been plotted against his father and himself, by granting the liberties they claimed. At the same time the Scots, having broken the truce at Berwick (as we said), invaded Northumberland and the neighbouring parts of the kingdom with arms, supposing that the King had drawn off all his forces to the French war. To check their boldness, the people granted a ninth. The clergy then, in the absence of the King, granted a tenth to the earls. This displeased the King greatly, that the clergy, who had been so resistant to his demands, should so readily have granted it at the urging of the earls, who had themselves resisted the taxes granted by the people. Those who had made the Archbishop suspect to the King through the plot of the nobles, and who had not wanted to make a truce with the French on the terms that had been arranged for the war, pressed the King to return to England as quickly as possible. Therefore, on the first of April, he concealed the vengeance he planned against the Archbishop and the confederated nobles, until, after the two-year truce with the French had been concluded, he had subdued the treacherous Scots and had made his own position strong and secure against such great dangers. He first attacked the Scots, whom he defeated in battle near the town called Falkirk. In this year Pope Boniface, having been for some time in abeyance, began again to exercise the fullness of his power, lest it fall into disuse. For when William, Bishop of Ely, died, the chapter divided into two parts: one part chose the Prior of Ely, the other John of Langton, the King's Chancellor. This dispute over the election was for a time argued before Robert, Archbishop of Canterbury, who, judging the second choice (the Chancellor's) to be the valid one, the Chancellor appealed to the Pope. Thus both sides went to the papal court. There they withdrew from their own election and committed the right of choice to the Pope's judgment. He rejected both and ordered the proctors of the convent of Ely to elect an Abbot from other exempt monasteries, namely Westminster, St Edmund's, St Augustine's, or St Alban's. They did not give up their earlier choice. Moved by this stubbornness, as he called it, the Pope declared that the right of conferring the bishopric of Ely belonged to him, because of the proctors' wickedness. Accordingly, on his own authority and of his own motion, he transferred the Bishop of Norwich to Ely and conferred the bishopric of Norwich on the Prior of Ely.
