Then, when Archbishop Octavian of Dublin died in his court, he promoted Richard Ferings, Archdeacon of Canterbury, to that archbishopric, and conferred the archdeaconry of Canterbury on John, the King's Chancellor, who had been in line for the bishopric of Ely. In the same year the Friars Minor, who had been brought into England, whose vow and rule was to have no property, rose from their poverty and mediocrity and offered the Pope four hundred thousand florins in gold and an infinite sum in silver, so that they might be granted, by his letter or bull, the freedom to acquire and possess lands, estates and annual revenues in the manner of monks. To them the Lord Pope said: "Where is that money of yours?" They answered: "In the hands of merchants." Hearing this, he ordered them to await a reply. Meanwhile he released the merchant with whom the money had been deposited from his contract of deposit, and ordered, under pain of anathema, that he return the money to the friars, but to the treasury of the Roman see. When the friars were awaiting the papal bull on the appointed day, he replied that he would not in any way depart from or violate the Rule of St Francis, which had been canonised, nor would he permit the friars to turn aside from it. A little before this (as we said under Robert Kilwardby), the law of mortmain was passed in England, which forbids colleges, monasteries, fraternities, and religious bodies, lest they increase to infinity, to acquire lands and estates without the King's consent. That law arose from the immoderate hypocrisy and gluttony of these friars, for under the cover of a show of mendicancy they were plundering, and would soon have swallowed up everyone's inheritances and goods, had they not been restrained by that gainful papal religion and by the most salutary laws of the kingdom. But let us return from these matters, which we have inserted from those times, to the King and the Archbishop. The King, having routed the Scots in battle (as we said), when he perceived that both internal and external evils threatened him, feigning domestic concerns, prudently first kept his distance from foreign ones. When he had girded himself to crush the Scots utterly, whom he had examined and tested in an earlier battle, he was, through the Archbishop of Canterbury, who carried out his orders diligently, forbidden by the Pope, to a sufficient degree of authority, to presume to crush further the Scots who had been placed under his protection. With this papal intervention, while the King was held back by many other difficulties, he set aside the Scottish business. Then, while Pope Boniface was pressing for peace between the kings of England and France, a marriage was contracted between the King of England and Margaret, sister of the King of France, with royal custom and magnificence, and was celebrated in the metropolitan church of Canterbury, the Archbishop himself ministering the divine office. But soon afterwards that long-hidden and concealed enmity which the Pope had deeply stored up against the King of France broke out into open hatred and reproach. For when the King's envoy was dealing with the Pope about many injuries done to the King, the Pope, with threats and a frown, said: "We have both powers." And he replied on behalf of his lord: "Certainly, lord. But yours is verbal, ours is real." The Pope's anger so flared up that he said he would stir up heaven and earth against him. But these threats of the Pope, which he uttered in words, were afterwards, as we shall say, carried out in fact, just as he had told the legates; the King of France is the proof. The Pope, fearing lest he lack troops against the French, seized a tithe of ecclesiastical property in England for three whole years, the bishops gladly consenting, though they had refused the King when he asked for it for military use. In this year the Bishops of Ely and Worcester died, and in their places the convents of each church chose their own monks. When these elected men could not obtain the grace of consecration from the Archbishop of Canterbury, they went to the Pope. He, having again weighed the order and manner of both elections, rejected the monk of Worcester from the bishopric but confirmed the one of Ely. Then he conferred the bishopric of Worcester on a certain friar Minor, on the ground that (as he asserted) the right had devolved to him. King Edward, indeed, having made peace with France, with the marriage (as we said) acting as intermediary and the alliance confirmed, again prepared military forces to restrain the Scots. When the Scots learned that everything at Rome was for sale, they enriched the Pope with rich gifts, so that under his protection he would prohibit the hostile force of King Edward and free them from his power and preserve their own. The Pope sent a certain Lombard with his commands to the Archbishop of Canterbury, who, following the King on the expedition, when they arrived, set out the Pope's mandates: namely, that the Scots, being subject to no one but himself and the Roman chapel, should, at the Pope's command, lay down the arms raised against them. He said it was impossible that the city of Jerusalem should not protect its citizens. Moved by this, the King replied: "I will not stand on account of Jerusalem or Zion, nor will I fail to defend my right against the faithless and perjured Scots with Mars himself." Soon afterwards the Pope's legate returned, and the King nonetheless proceeded with the war. But so as not to seem to provoke the irritable Pope, while his affairs at home were scarcely settled, he sent the Earls of Lincoln and Hugh Despenser to the Pope to argue his rights over the Scots with many documents and examples. Of the letters written and answered between the Pope, the King and the nobles of England on these matters we deliberately say nothing. About this time the nuns of England, who had been granted permission to leave their cells and wander wherever they pleased, and were not prohibited by any law, began to behave wantonly. Therefore Pope Boniface wrote to the Archbishop of Canterbury and the suffragans of his province a decretal letter about enclosing them in their cells, in which power was given to them to visit the nuns, and to prescribe the boundaries within which they ought to be confined.

units.la: Iamque digladiari inter fe Rex Franciæ ,& Papa coeperunt. Hic verbalem, ille realem gladium, vt mutuis (sicut paulo ante diximus) conuitiis comminari inicem sunt, vaginis suis eduxerunt. Vter autem acurior & perniciosior fuerit, Papæ tristis exitus declarabit. Papæ excitaris illis in Franciæ Regem inimiciriis poenituit fe affinitatem & pacem eicum Angliæ Regecon ciliaffe. Itaque literis Regem Angliæ ad pactam pacem frangendam folicitauit,& fi Gallum Marte aggredi vellet, immensam pecuniam pul licetur. At Rex qui alias Papæ perfidiam sensisset, a Galli scedere nisi ab eo prouocatus recedere noluit. Tum Papa in Gallum excommunicationis sententiam fulminauit. Quam nemo ei nunciare aut in Gallia promulgare ausus est. Deinde omnes Gallię præ-latos, Theologos, iurisque canonici vel ciuilis peritos publico edicto monuit, vt coram eo Romæ in proximis Kalend. Nouemb. comparerent. Et Galliæ vicifim sub proscriptione edixit, ne quis suo regno aurum, argētum, vel merces quafcũque exportaret,&in Regni finibus exploratores constituit, qui Regno exeuntes scrutarentur. Quibus de caufis die staturo Clerus Galliæ fe per tres Episcopos nuncios excusauit. Itaque Papa Iohannem quendam Monachum præstyterum Cardinalem misit Lutetiam, qui Clerum papæ nomine feorsim & feeretò consuleret. In eo Conuentu milites quidam regii coram Clero& populo Parifienfi Papam Bonifacium de hæresi, Simonia,& homicidio poftularunt, Regisque nomine ab eo ad Concilium generale appellarunt. Tum Iohannem Cardinalem Papæ Legatum regno egredi iusserunt. Regem enim suum nullam in se authoritatem Papæ permissurum donec obiecta crimina in Concilio delcuisset. Papa subhæc tempora ad Anagniam Campaniæ ciuitatem vbi natus erat, venit. Ibi vim realis gladii a Rege Galliæ illati exitiosam sibi retundete non potuit. Proscripserat & excommunicauerat ante quosdam Cardinales Columpnenses Papa, quorum frater Scarra associato sibi Gulielmo de Longareto Regis Galliae Senescballo, aliisque Regis ministris & satellitibus, Papam copiosa manu militari subito obsessum tenet. Quo vis procurante Rege Franciae, Papaeque familiaribus ac vicinis vna conspirantibus in Papam motaest. Quiiam tantis praesidiis obsessus, cum necauxilium, nec euasionem sperare poterat, flagitat a Scarra pacis conditiones. Scarra nullas dare aut accipere condiuones volnit, nisi Papa fratres suos Cardinales Columnenses restitueret, & Papatui postea renunciaret, ac corpus suum dederet. Quibus auditis Papa ingemuit, animam effusurus potius quam papatui cessurus. In hacobsidioneMarchio Anagnienlis ciuitatis Papae nepos, acceptis de sua & filiorum atque famulorum vita conditionibus Papa inconsulto Scarrefe dedit.Quo cognito defleuit amare suam conditionem Papa. Nam post dediuonemMarchionis,Scarra irruptionein palatium factaPapam cepit,& peffimis probrisac maledictis oneraurt.Quibus Papa ne respondit,tandem Scarra ad renunciandum multis minis Papam voluit cogere, sed non potuit, omnibus autem indumentis, ornamentis,auro,argento,thesauroque adeo ingenti, vt omnium in orbe Christiano principum diuitias superare crederetur, eum spoliauit, eductumque palatio eque effreni conuersio ad caudam vultu imposuit, & per ciuitatis plateas ludibrio habendum circumduxit. Tandem cum militibus sociis,tantisque spoliis vrbe discedens papam nudum,egenum, fameque pene peremptum eiecit in plateas. Vbi gemitu & eiulatu famelicus sua voce, (nam praecones & nuncii,famulis suis trucidatis vel fugaris,ci defuerunt) coactus est indulgentiam,&omnium peccatorum veniam illis polliceri,quieum cibo&potu reficerent. Hac ore papali pro mulgata indulgentia, concurrunt aniculae & mulieres permultae superstitiosae, qui eum in palatium ductum fouent, & cibis ad saturitatem, replent,clamantes,viuas sancte pater. Cum ex hoc discrimine atque fame vires atque animum collegisset, Romam discessit totus lucuosus & squalidus, ibi aeger paucis post diebus periit. De quo iuxta Coelestini vaticinium mortuo haec carmina condita fuerunt. Vulpes intrauit,tanquam Leo Pontificauit. Exuit,vtque canis,de diuite factus inanis. Item,de vino. Are nomen habe,benedic,bene fac,Benedicte. Aut nomen perverte,maledic,malefac,Maledicte.
units.tr: Now the King of France and the Pope began to fight with each other. Each, as we said a little earlier, had threatened the other with insults, and they drew their swords from their scabbards: the one a verbal sword, the other a real one. Which was the sharper and the more destructive, the sad end of the Pope will show. The Pope, roused to anger against the King of France, regretted having arranged a marriage alliance and peace with the King of England. He therefore urged the King of England by letter to break the agreed peace, and promised him a huge sum of money if he would attack the Frenchman in war. But the King, who had already perceived the Pope's treachery, refused to withdraw from the Frenchman's side unless he himself was provoked by him. Then the Pope hurled the sentence of excommunication against the Frenchman. No one dared to announce it to him or to publish it in France. Next he issued a public edict warning all the prelates, theologians and experts in canon or civil law of France to appear before him at Rome by the first day of November. In turn he decreed under penalty of outlawry that no one should export gold, silver or any wares from his kingdom, and he set up spies on the borders of the realm to search those leaving it. For these reasons the clergy of France excused themselves on the appointed day through three bishops sent as envoys. So the Pope sent to Paris a certain John, a Cardinal and monk-priest, to consult the clergy privately and in secret in the Pope's name. At that gathering some royal soldiers, in the presence of the clergy and the people of Paris, charged Pope Boniface with heresy, simony and murder, and in the King's name appealed from him to a general council. Then they ordered John the Cardinal, the Pope's legate, to leave the kingdom, since their King would not allow the Pope any authority over himself until the charges brought against him had been settled by a council. At this time the Pope came to Anagni, a city of Campania where he had been born. There he could not ward off the violence of the real sword inflicted on him by the King of France. Earlier the Pope had proscribed and excommunicated certain Colonna cardinals, whose brother Sciarra, together with William of Longret, the King of France's seneschal, and other royal officers and henchmen, suddenly besieged the Pope with a large armed force. By the working of the King of France, and with the Pope's own household and neighbours conspiring together against him, a revolt was raised against the Pope. Beset by such forces, and able to hope neither for help nor for escape, he asked Sciarra for terms of peace. Sciarra would offer or accept no terms unless the Pope restored his Colonna cardinal brothers, renounced the papacy, and surrendered his person. Hearing this, the Pope groaned, ready to lose his life rather than yield the papacy. During this siege the Marquis of Anagni, the Pope's nephew, accepted conditions for his own life, and the lives of his sons and servants, and surrendered to Sciarra without consulting the Pope. When this was known, the Pope lamented bitterly his own wretched situation. For after the Marquis surrendered, Sciarra broke into the palace, seized the Pope, and loaded him with the foulest insults and curses. When the Pope made no reply, Sciarra with many threats tried to force him to resign, but could not. Instead he stripped him of all his vestments, ornaments, gold, silver and treasure, so vast that it was thought to exceed the riches of all the princes of the Christian world. He then led him out of the palace, set him backwards on an unbridled mule with his face to the tail, and paraded him through the streets of the city as a laughing-stock. At last, leaving the city with his soldiers and his great plunder, he threw the Pope out naked, destitute, and almost dead of hunger into the streets. There, since his heralds and messengers had been slaughtered or put to flight and were absent, he was forced to cry out hungrily in his own voice, groaning and wailing, and to promise indulgence and forgiveness of all sins to those who would refresh him with food and drink. When this indulgence had been proclaimed in the papal voice, old women and many superstitious wives gathered, took him into the palace, and filled him with food until he was satisfied, crying, "Long live the holy father!" When he had recovered strength and courage from this peril and hunger, he left for Rome, wholly filthy and squalid, and there, sick, he died a few days later. Concerning him, after his death, these verses were composed, in accordance with the prophecy of Celestine: "The fox entered, like a lion he played the pope; he stripped off, like a dog, and from rich became empty." And again, on wine: "Bless, do well, bless: have the name of Are [a]. Or pervert the name: curse, do evil, accursed."

units.la: Huic Papa ne mortuo quidem Gallus pepercit. Sed vt de haeresis, simoniae, & paricidii criminibus post mortem damnaretur, saepe institit. Cuius odio ducta tota Gallia ne sextum librum Decretalium ab eodem papa editum inter iura canonica admittere voluit. Quod si Iohannes quondam Angliae Rex huiusmodi gladio Papae censuris restituisset, nec senec regnum tot calamitatibus postea(vt commemorauimus) cofertim subsequutis exposuisset. Bonifacio tam ignominiosa morte sublato successit Benedictus, qui cum antecessoris sui cladem lugubri concione deploraffet, eiusque authores Anathemate feriiffet, & Columnensium fitirpem delere statuisset, Pincerna eius muneribus corruptus miscuit eius poculis venenū. Quo hausto 15.postea die obiit Perusii. Cui Berand Archiepiscopus Burdegalensis Clemens quintus vocarus successit. Hic duos Anglos Cardinales,& Episcopum Dunelmensem Hierosolymitanum Patriarchum creauit, nec non Guhelmum Grenefeld Archiepiscopum Eboracensem, & Rhadulphum Baldock Episcopum Londinensem electos confirmauit atque consecrauit Romae. Edwardus vero Angliae Rex Scotis superatis,cum neque de Gallo nuptiarum affinitate sibi iuncto,nec de Papa a quo a iuramenti fide qua se Baronibus obstrinxerat, absolutus est,obtinuit, opportunitatem nactus est illius in se absentem (vt diximus) coniurationis reos,inter quos Robertus Archiepiscopus Dux & Author fuisse suspicabatur, vindicandi.
units.tr: Not even when he was dead did the Frenchman spare this Pope. He persisted in seeking that after death he be condemned for the crimes of heresy, simony and parricide. Stirred by hatred of him, all France was unwilling to admit the Sixth Book of the Decretals, issued by that same Pope, among the canon laws. If King John of England had once restored the sword of censure to the Pope, the kingdom would not afterwards have been exposed, as we have recorded, to so many calamities following one upon another. When Boniface had been removed by so shameful a death, Benedict succeeded him. After he had lamented his predecessor's ruin in a mournful sermon, and had condemned its authors with anathema, and had decided to wipe out the family of the Colonnas, his cupbearer, bribed with gifts, put poison in his cup. Having drunk it, he died fifteen days later at Perugia. Bertrand, Archbishop of Bordeaux, called Clement V, succeeded him. He created two English cardinals and the Bishop of Durham Patriarch of Jerusalem, and at Rome he confirmed and consecrated William Greenfield, Archbishop of York, and Ralph Baldock, Bishop of London, who had been elected. But King Edward of England, having defeated the Scots, was not released from the marriage alliance joined to him with the French, nor from the oath by which he had bound himself to the barons, by the Pope who had absolved him from his fidelity. He obtained an opportunity, as we have said, to avenge the conspirators against himself who had been absent, among whom Robert the Archbishop was suspected to have been leader and author.

units.la: Nam quia huius intestinae seditionis causam,iuramentum Regni sui proceribus de obseruandis eorum priuilegiis ac immunitatibus a se praestitum esse senserat, eius religione amplius non teneri,sed papali authoritate solui voluit & obrinuit. Qua quidem in re Patris sui Regis Iohannis exemplum se imitatum ac sequutum affirmauit: qui instantia & necessitate procerum adductus facile iurare consueuit, vt eos concitatos sedaret, eamque facilitate refilerc a iuramento, quoties sibi tempus arrideret, praetendens semper papalem absolutionem a priori praestito iuramento. Qua Regum tam supina cacecitate, papalis iurisdictio ad eam magnitudinem creuit, vt Reges plusquam Aegyptiaca obscuritate inuoluti, Papae tantum authoritatis deferrentes quaecunque vel firmissima ac sanctissima iura atque foedera ea dissolui posse, saepe ad suam & regnorum perniciem credebant. Omnibus itaque firmatis ac dispositis a Rege adiumentis, de domestica fraude & conspiratione poenas tandem hoc ordine sumpsit. Comitem Marescallum, primo de hac coniuratione caute aggressus est, is nec contradicere, nec celare potest factam proditionem valens, Regis gratiam petiit, pro qua ubtinēda, vniuersorum suorum bonorum eum haeredem instituit. Quam conditionem Rex perbenigne accepit, & vt eum in officio fideique retineret, terras similmas mille libris annuireddidit Comiti ad vitam concessit. Reliquos quoque coniuratores eodem altu sigillatum periculit, & pecuniaria poena, quia capue, vt potuit, noluit, singulos multauit. Ad extremum conuenit Archiepiscopum, eumque huius cuniprationis tanquam ducem & autorem arguit, & de grauissimis criminibus postulauit, praecipue vero de proditione, & laesae Regiae Maiestatis crimine. Quod Rege multa causa absente eum Comitibus regniqne procedure dolosum iniciat consilium, de Rege a regni solio deiiciendo, perpetuoque carceribus mancipando, & filio suo Edwardo patris loco substituendo. Quicum multis conuictus agitatus a Rege, inficiari praedictanon poterat, in terram pronus ad pedes Regios cecidit, cum lachrymis & eiulatu, facinorum veniam obsecrans, Regemq; Dominum suum, quod nec voce, nec literis ante ea fecerat, appellans. Ita hic elatus, Deo & hominibus odiosus, qui per totum Anglorum orbem sua superbia & sacerdotum deturpauit & clerum, & tyrannidem in pupulum inauditam exercuisset, nunc scelere suo a Rege deprehensio, peccati conscientia, & metu poenae perterritus, deiectus & prostratus humi pro Rege iacet, ei pallium tendit, eiusque miserecordiae se suaque bona permittit. Cui Rex, Nos ego inquit, de te supplicium sumam, ne nec vindictae, quanquam iustissimae, magis quam tui ordinis rationem habere videar. Ac quanquam tu & illo ordine & gratia mea indignus iis, rem tamen ipsam Coepiscopis rius, ipsique, quae adiuncta Romano Episcopo, referant, vt a patribus tuis (ne me iniquum sententias, ipsius proditionis quod in subdito summum scelus est, quodque mecum auditioni & tribunali referuntur, haud dubie iudicem) in delicto tanto arguaris. Adiecit ad ista Rex. Non solum in maximis, sed etiam in minimis, paruique momenti rebus, simultatem & malitiam agnoui tuam, in quibus authoritate fretus tua, patientia mea animum abusus es. Quoties enim in prouincialibus tuis visitationibus te per literas interpellaui, ne meos, familiam in meo viuentes obsequio clericos vexares, aut quacunque ratione in ius vocares. Qui tamen omni illorum appellatione & mea intercessione posthabita, & regali authoritate coercitus, beneficiis suis spoliati sunt. Cui hoc dixisset Rex, Archiepiscopus denuo confusus & mente turbatus, ac his conuitiis dignissime affectus, nuntius quoque tantum leges exemplo, a Rege benedictionem petiit. Cui Rex, non te mea, sed me tua, decerat, inquit, magis benedictio. Rex itaque cum degenerem & conscium Archiepiscopi animum ex metu coniecisset, ad Papam querelam de eo instituit: Quod statum Regni sui aliquin tranquillum, & sua virtute ab externis hostibus tutum, se absente domini turbauerat, & proceres insidias & res nouas molientes defenderat atque fouerat. Rubertus Archiepiscopus ad Regis instantiam papali edicto ad Romanam curiam citatus est. Quo cum venisset, ab executione officii sui, & temporalium atque spiritualium administratione suspensus est, donec de accusationibus sibi impositis, & per Regem obiectis, legitime se purgaret. Cumque se a Regis praesentia subduxisset, antequam Romam proficisceretur inter Monachos Cantuarienses, quiaci iam egeno & proscripto nemo alimenta ministrate ausus est, aliquandiu deliruit, & ab his nutritus atque fotus est. Quo cognito eos quoque proscripsit Rex, vetuitq; edicto ne quis eis ad vsus vitae necessaria ministraret. Tum octoginta ac claustris Monachos praecipitauit. Praedia in fiscum contulit. Eiecti ad mendicitatem Monachi nec a fratribus quidem mendicantibus subleuati sunt, sed vicatim per singulas aedes cleemosynas petebat. Tandem Rex in exilium acto Roberto Monasterio bonisque restituit.
units.tr: For, since he had perceived that the cause of this internal sedition was the oath he had sworn to his nobles to observe their privileges and immunities, he wished, and obtained, that he should no longer be bound by its sanctity but released by papal authority. In this matter he affirmed that he had imitated and followed the example of his father, King John, who, driven by the urgency and necessity of the nobles, was accustomed to swear readily in order to calm them when they were stirred up, and, whenever the time smiled upon him, he would easily break away from the oath, always pretending a papal absolution from the oath previously sworn. Through such supine blindness of kings, papal jurisdiction grew to such a height that kings, wrapped in more than Egyptian darkness, attributing so much authority to the Pope that whatever even the firmest and most sacred rights and covenants could be dissolved by him, often believed it to their own and their kingdoms' ruin. Therefore, when all the aids had been secured and arranged by the King, he at last took vengeance for the domestic treachery and conspiracy in this order. He first cautiously approached the Earl Marshal about this conspiracy. He, being able neither to deny nor to conceal the treason committed, sought the King's favour, and to obtain it he made the King heir of all his goods. The King received this condition most graciously, and in order to keep him in duty and loyalty he gave back to the Earl for life lands worth a thousand pounds a year. He likewise examined the remaining conspirators one by one in the same way, and since he did not wish to take their lives, as far as he could, he fined each of them a sum of money. At last he summoned the Archbishop, charged him as leader and author of this conspiracy, and demanded an answer on the gravest crimes, especially treason and the crime of injured royal majesty. For while the King was far away, he had devised with the Earls and the realm a deceitful plan to depose the King from the throne of the kingdom, to consign him to perpetual prison, and to put his son Edward in his father's place. Confronted by the King with many proofs, and unable to deny these things, he fell prone to the ground at the royal feet, weeping and wailing, begging pardon for his crimes, and calling the King his lord, which he had never done before either by word or by letter. Thus he, once proud, hateful to God and men, who had through his arrogance disfigured the whole English world and the clergy with the priests, and had exercised an unheard-of tyranny over the people, now, caught by the King in his crime, terrified by consciousness of sin and fear of punishment, cast down and prostrated on the ground, lay before the King, stretched out his cloak to him, and committed himself and his goods to his mercy. To him the King said: "I shall exact punishment from you, lest I seem to have regard to vengeance, though most just, rather than to your rank. And although you are unworthy both of that rank and of my favour, nevertheless the matter itself is to be referred to your fellow bishops and to those who are joined with the Roman bishop, so that you may be accused of so great a crime by your fathers (lest I judge unfairly, since there is no doubt that treason against oneself is the greatest crime in a subject), and so that it may be referred to the hearing and tribunal of the court." The King added to these words: "I have recognised your hatred and malice not only in the greatest matters but also in the smallest and of little moment, in which, relying on your authority, you have abused my patience. For how often in your provincial visitations, when you were vexing my clergy who live in my household in obedience to me, or summoning them to judgement in any way whatever, did I intercede with you by letter, asking you to stop. Yet they, disregarding all their appeals and my intercession, and constrained by royal authority, have been stripped of their benefices." When the King had said this, the Archbishop, again confused and disturbed in mind, and most justly stung by these reproaches, and even the messenger having only the law as his example, sought a blessing from the King. The King replied: "It is not my blessing you should seek, but I should seek yours." So the King, perceiving from fear the degenerate and guilty mind of the Archbishop, brought a complaint against him to the Pope: that he had disturbed the state of his kingdom, otherwise peaceful and protected by its own valour from foreign enemies, in the King's absence, and had defended and fostered nobles plotting treachery and revolutions. Archbishop Robert, at the King's insistence, was summoned to the Roman court by papal edict. When he had come there, he was suspended from the exercise of his office and from the administration of temporal and spiritual affairs until he should lawfully clear himself of the accusations brought against him and laid by the King. And when he had withdrawn from the King's presence, before setting out for Rome, he for some time lost his wits among the monks of Canterbury, since no one dared to supply food to a man now needy and outlawed, and he was nourished and cherished by them. When this became known, the King proscribed them too, and by edict forbade anyone to supply them with the necessities of life. Then he cast out eighty monks from the cloisters. He transferred their estates to the treasury. The expelled monks, reduced to beggary, were not relieved even by the mendicant friars, but went from house to house begging alms street by street. At last the King, having driven Robert into exile, restored him to the monastery and his goods.

units.la: Franciae Rex a Papa Bonifacio (vt diximus) excommunicatus, hoc anno a Clemente Papa absolutus est, sed petiit vt Bonifacius mortuus haereticae prauitatis damnaretur, eiusque ossa exhumata igne cremarentur. Tum in Papa eligendo ius trium suffragiorum vendicauit, sed a Papa neutrum obtinuit. Roberto autem Archiepiscopo in exilium acto Wintoniensis Episcopus pro eo intercessit, eumque Dominum suum appellauit. Rex eo turbatus Episcopum Wintoniensem protectione sua priuauit, eiusque bona in fiscum deferri iussit, quod alium quam Regem Dominum agnoscerret, ac talem qui prouinciis & manifestae in Regem contumaciae reus, vel subditi ius in suo regno amisisset. In hoc Archiepiscopi exilio Clemens quintus Papa Cathuariensis sedis oeconomos constituit Gulielmum de Festa Archidiaconum Arrauensem, & Petrum Amalinum Canonicum Burgensem: qui authoritate nixi Papali Norwicensem Episcopum de primitiis,quasi a suæ dioecesis Cicero vendicauit in ius vocabant. Papa vero hoc motus exemplo qui ea quæ Episcopi in suis dioecesibus sibi arrogarunt, iure sive iniuria vlurpare, partasque ab aliis acquirere sibi solebat. popolcs & imperauit suæ camerae pr minus cultuque Ecclesiasticis in Anglia beneficiis trienuio proximo vacaturi, Archiepiscopalibus, Episcopalibus, & Conuentualibus Ecclesiis dumtaxat exceptis. Interea oum Robertus Archiepiscopus exul aberat, inclytus rex Edwardus primus qui Cambrios & Scotos imperio suo subiecit, & Gallos afflixit in tricesimo quinto octavo anno obiit. Quo mortuo Archiepiscopi ablentis & exulis siue metus, hue authoritas, atque gratia tantum valuit, vt cum duobus pene annis in exilio vixisset, Edwar. Rex e eius nominis primo mortuo, cum Edwardus secundus cotona regia coniectrandus esset, Winton. Episcopus, tunc Archiepiscopi vice eius absentis literis & speciali mandato in Rege coniectrando sunctus est.
units.tr: The King of France, excommunicated by Pope Boniface (as we said), was absolved this year by Pope Clement. But he asked that Boniface, though dead, be condemned for heretical depravity, and that his bones be dug up and burned. He then claimed the right of three votes in the election of a Pope, but obtained none of them from the Pope. When Archbishop Robert had been driven into exile, the Bishop of Winchester interceded for him and called him his lord. The King, angered by this, stripped the Bishop of Winchester of his protection and ordered his goods to be transferred to the treasury, because he acknowledged as lord someone other than the King, and because a man who was guilty of provisions and manifest contumacy against the King had, by that act, forfeited his rights as a subject in the kingdom. During this exile of the Archbishop, Pope Clement V appointed as stewards of the see of Canterbury William de Festa, archdeacon of Arrau, and Peter Amalin, canon of Bourges. Relying on papal authority, they summoned the Bishop of Norwich to court to claim the first-fruits, as though they belonged to the church of Canterbury and not to his diocese. The Pope, moved by this example, and accustomed to seize, rightly or wrongly, what bishops had claimed for themselves in their dioceses and to acquire for himself what others had gained, ordered that the first-fruits and the ecclesiastical benefices in England that would fall vacant during the next three years be paid to his chamber. Only archiepiscopal, episcopal and conventual churches were excepted. Meanwhile, while the Archbishop Robert was absent in exile, the illustrious King Edward I, who subjected the Welsh and the Scots to his rule and afflicted the French, died in the thirty-fifth year of his reign. On his death, the authority and favour of the absent, exiled Archbishop (whether from fear or from esteem) counted for so much that, although he had lived in exile for almost two years, when Edward II, the second of that name, was to be crowned, the Bishop of Winchester, acting in the Archbishop's place by his letters and a special commission, performed the coronation.

units.la: Cum enim Archiepiscopus Cant. vocatus fuisset ad curiam Romanam, respondit rusuper quibuldam rebus ei per legem Angliæ obiiciendis, iste Edwardus filius regis Edwardi post mortem patris sui, vt ius Ecclesiæ Cant. saluaret, domino Papæ Clementi scripsit, quod Archiepiscopum Cantuar. ad Ecclesiam suam mitteret, vt ab ipso Coronâ regni suscipere posset cum coronatio Regum Angliæ ad Archiepiscopos Cant. noscatur pertinere Restitutus igitur ad statum suum per dictum papam Archiepiscopus prædictus, cum præ debilitare corporis sui tantum sestinare non posset vt præfatæ coronationi interesset, fecit sub sigilio suo tribus Episcopis commissionem suam, vt vnus eorum quem Rex eligere vellet, ipsum Regë vice sua coronaret. nëpe Winton. Sarisburiensi, Sarisburiensi, & Ciceftrenfi. Et quia Episcopus Sarisburiensis, corpore debilis nimis erat, placuit domino Regi, quod Episcopus Winton, officium faceret & impleret Archiepiscopo vero Eborac. quia sine sua cruce venire noluit, non est permissum huic solennitati interesse.
units.tr: When the Archbishop of Canterbury had been summoned to the Roman court and had replied to certain charges to be brought against him under English law, this Edward, son of King Edward, after his father's death, wrote to Pope Clement, in order to preserve the rights of the church of Canterbury, asking that the Archbishop of Canterbury be sent to his church so that he could receive the crown of the kingdom from him, since it is known that the coronation of the kings of England belongs to the Archbishops of Canterbury. The aforesaid Archbishop, therefore, restored to his position by the said Pope, since he could not hasten, because of the weakness of his body, to be present at the said coronation, committed his commission under his seal to three bishops, so that whichever of them the King chose might crown the King in his place: namely the Bishops of Winchester, Salisbury and Chichester. And because the Bishop of Salisbury was too weak in body, it pleased the lord King that the Bishop of Winchester should perform and carry out the office. The Archbishop of York, however, because he refused to come without his cross, was not permitted to take part in this solemnity.

units.la: REVOCATIO CLEMENTIS PAPÆ.
units.tr: THE REVOCATION OF POPE CLEMENT

units.la: Lemens Episcopus seruorum Dei, venerabili fratri R. Archiepiscopo Cant. salutē, & Apostolicā benedictionē. Cum, sicut oblata nobis ex parte tua petitio cōtinebatur, coronatio Charissimi in Christo filii nostri Edwardi Regis Angliæ illustris, quæ in proximo imminet, sicut citer date domino faciendaad teratione tuæ Ecclesiæ pertinere noscatur, nos nolentes quod in hac parte officium tuum valeat impediri, tuis supplicationibus inclinati omnes literas, si quas super communione coronationis Regis ipsius alicui vel aliquibus forte direxerimus, cuiuscunque tenoris existunt, authoritate præsentium reuocamus. Nulli ergo omnino hominum liceat hanc paginam nostræ reuocationis infringere, vel ei ausu temerario contraire. Si quis autem hoc attentare præsumpserit, indignationem omnipotentis Dei, & Beatorum Petri & Pauli Apostolorum eius se noverit incurfurū. Datæ Pictauis II. Kalend. Februar. Pontificatus nostri anno tertio.
units.tr: Clement, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother R., Archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and the Apostolic blessing. Since, as the petition presented to us on your behalf stated, the coronation of our most beloved son in Christ, the illustrious Edward, King of England, which is at hand, is known without doubt to pertain to the office of your Church, we, unwilling that your office should be hindered in this matter, and inclined to your entreaties, by the authority of these presents revoke all letters, of whatever tenor they may be, which we may perhaps have addressed to anyone or to any persons concerning communion in the King's coronation. Let no one at all be permitted to infringe this page of our revocation, or to oppose it with rash daring. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Poitiers, on the second day before the Kalends of February, in the third year of our pontificate.

units.la: Posteaq; Regi nouo conciliatus, ab exilio reuocatus & restitutus est. Tum vero cum & Regis gratia & authoritate magna in Rep. floreret, Augustinensi Cœnobio redemit suâ temporalia 100. l'. & 100. summis grani, & prouinciales constitutiones celeberes noueque edidit, & perstrenuus Ecclesiæ Rector, regniq; iurium, libertatumquasserror ferebatur. Cuius rei laudem etsi sibi vendicauit, fuit tamen in illis asserendis nimius, & Regi semper aduersus, vt Papæ, cū quo coniunctissimus fuit, id tribuerer, quod Regi derogaret, nec tam libertatem regno, quam Papæ potentiam acquireret, Regis q; authoritatem minueret ac in Papam transferret. Diximus ante à Iohanne Peckam Cant. Archiepiscopo fuisse constitutum, vt Clerici plura beneficia non tenerent, sed vno conrenti sint, tum vt præsbyteri, vel ante adeptum beneficium, vel anno postea ordinarentur, deinde vt in beneficiis residerent. Huiusq; constitutionis hæc fuit sanctio: Quod secundi beneficii apprehensa possessione, vel perceptis fructibus, vacaret ipso iure primum, tum si posset presbyter non otdinaretur, vacaret etiam simili modo beneficium, & non residentes ad residendum moniti priuarentur, iusq; præsentandi denuo ad patronum rediret. Quæ Iohannis constitutio a Lugdinensi Concilio profecta est, sub Gregorio decimo celebrata, de quo Polychro. hoc versu affirmat. Gregorius denuo congregas congregas omne genus. Cui tamen Concilio quanq; generali Reges Angliæ intercesserunt, nec se teneri Conciliorum decretis amplius affirmabant, proferentes veterum ac maiorum suorū de ea immunitate priuilegia, vt quidam referunt, Edwardum primum in Robertum Winchelsey hac de causa primo commotum, quod in prouincialibus visitationibus, tantum pecuniæ à Clero, pluralitatum, ordinum, & residentiæ ratione, secundum prædecessoris sui Iohan. Peckam constitutionem, in quam virtuersus fere Clerus tum cōmiserat, exegisset. Qua in re tam acris fuit, vt ne Regiis rogatis pro suis Capellanis cesserit. Edwardus itaque secundus, quanquam multū tribuit Roberto iam ab exilio reuerso, fortiter tamen, tam in Concilio Lugdinensi, quam domi instabat, ne sibi ministrantes
units.tr: Afterwards, having been reconciled to the new King, he was recalled from exile and restored. Then indeed, when he flourished in the King's favour and great authority in the commonwealth, he redeemed the temporal goods of the Augustinian monastery for one hundred pounds and one hundred quarters of grain, and issued famous provincial constitutions, and was reported to be a most vigorous rector of the Church and a defender of the rights and liberties of the realm. Although he claimed the praise for this matter, he was excessive in asserting those rights, and always opposed to the King. Because he was most closely allied with the Pope, people attributed to the Pope whatever derogated from the King, and held that he sought not so much liberty for the realm as the power of the Pope, and diminished the King's authority and transferred it to the Pope. We said above that John Peckham, Archbishop of Canterbury, had enacted that clerics should not hold several benefices but be content with one; then that priests should be ordained either before obtaining a benefice or within a year afterwards; and finally that they should reside in their benefices. The sanction of this constitution was this: that if a clergyman, having taken possession of a second benefice or received its fruits, should not be ordained priest, the first benefice would become vacant by law; likewise, if a non-resident was warned to reside and did not, he would be deprived, and the right of presentation would return to the patron. This constitution of John's came from the Council of Lyons, held under Pope Gregory X, of whom Polychronicon affirms in this verse: Gregory, gathering the whole race of men again. Yet against this council, although it was general, the Kings of England interceded, and they affirmed that they were no longer bound by the decrees of the councils, citing the privileges of this immunity granted to their ancestors and predecessors. Some report that Edward I was first moved against Robert Winchelsey for this reason: in his provincial visitations he had exacted so much money from the clergy, on account of pluralities, orders and residence, under the constitution of his predecessor John Peckham, into which almost the whole clergy had then fallen, that he was as harsh in this matter as he refused the King's requests on behalf of his own chaplains. Edward II, therefore, although he gave much to Robert, now returned from exile, nevertheless strongly insisted, both at the Council of Lyons and at home, that his ministering chaplains

units.la: Capellani, aut Concilii decreto, aut Ottonis aut Ottoboni Papæ ad Angliam Legatorum aut Cant. Archiepiscopi constitutione ad sacros ordines, vel residentiam, vel cerium beneficiorum numerum astringerentur. Quod ex multis suis, tam ad Archiepiscopos Cant. & Ebor acensem, qui illius Concilii decretum in Anglia exequi nitebantur, quàm ad pluresptrones, qui huiusmodi constitutionis & decreti vi ad beneficia, quæ putabant vacua, præsentare alios volebant, rescriptis apparet. Quorum vnum tantum reliquorum indicium & exemplum inseruimus.
units.tr: should not be bound to sacred orders, or to residence, or to a fixed number of benefices, either by the decree of that council, or by the constitution of Otto or Ottobon, legates of the Pope to England, or by the constitution of the Archbishop of Canterbury. This appears from many of his rescripts, addressed both to the Archbishops of Canterbury and York, who strove to execute that council's decree in England, and to several patrons, who, by virtue of such a constitution and decree, wished to present others to benefices which they thought vacant. We have inserted one of these as an indication and example of the rest.

units.la: Edwardus Dei gratia &c. Abbati de T. salutem. Intelleximus vos ad Eccl. de M. quam quidam Clericus noster W. de C. est canonicè assequutus præsentasse de facto, ratione Concilii Lugd. Cum igitur Clericos nostros insistētes obsequiis statutum illud non liget,
units.tr: Edward, by the grace of God, etc., to the Abbot of T., greeting. We understand that you have, in fact, presented to the church of M. a certain clerk of ours, W. of C., who has canonically obtained it, on the ground of the Council of Lyons. Since, therefore, our clerks who are attending to our service are not bound by that statute,

units.la: eò quod clatæ memoriæ Reges & Principes Regni Angliæ, progenitores nostri, à tempo rehuius non extat memoria, ea immunitate & libertate hactenus gauisi sunt, quod Clerici dum eorum seruitiis intendebant, a nemine coarctabantur ad ordines suscipiendos, vel ad residentiam personalem in suis beneficijs faciendam, ac ad nos, in quem libertates seu immunitates huiusmodi deriuantur, spectare dignoscatur. Clericorū nostrorum indemnitati prospicere in hac parte, deuotionè vestram requirimus & rogamus firmiter iniungētes, quatenus præsentatione, quæ ad dictā Eccl. de M. à vobis minus prouidè, in ipsius Clerici, imo verius nullius præiudicij processisse dignoscitur: studeatis, pinde reuocare, præstatū à vobis ab incepta, psecutione desistere, faciētes taliter in isto negocio vos habere curetis. q nos nō oporteat super hoc manū apponere sollicitudinis ampliotis Dat.
units.tr: because the kings and princes of the realm of England, our ancestors of famous memory, from a time beyond recorded memory, have hitherto enjoyed that immunity and liberty, namely that their clerks, while attending to their service, should be compelled by no one to receive orders or to perform personal residence in their benefices, and because this immunity and liberty is known to derive to us, we ask and firmly urge your devotion to provide for the security of our clerks in this matter, requiring that you take care to revoke the presentation which was made to the said church of M. by you, too hastily and in truth of no force against the said clerk, and that you desist from the prosecution you have begun, acting in such a way in this business that we shall not need to put our hand to it with greater solicitude. Given, etc.

units.la: &c. Reuersus autem & restitutus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus Robertus ex Regis atque Papæ mandato omnes redditus, fructus, & prouentus qui se absente ab administratoribus Ecclesiæ suæ pereepti sunt, exquisitè sibi redditis rationibus accepit. Ita exilii sui calamitas summæ sibi vrilitati eessit. Namq; omnium qui ante cum Archiepiscopi Cantuarienses fuerant, ditissimus ex hoc euentu euasit. Vnde ipse adeo locupletatus se hoc versu de exilio suo sæpe narrans consolari solebat. Nihil nocebit aduersitas, vbi nulla iniquitas dominatur.
units.tr: Archbishop Robert, returned and restored, by the mandate of the King and the Pope, received from the administrators of his church, by strict accounting, all the revenues, fruits and profits which had been collected in his absence. Thus the calamity of his exile turned to his great advantage, for of all who had been Archbishops of Canterbury before him, he became the richest from this event. Therefore, being so enriched, he used often to console himself, speaking of his exile in this verse: Adversity will do no harm where no iniquity reigns.

units.la: Hoc anno Robertus Ratford, & Henricus Spigurnel, capitalium criminum in Cantio iudices, vt in illis iudiciis quę Assisas vocant, reis iuramenta tempore quadragesimæ defferent, ab Archiepiscopo facultatem impetrauerunt. Quæ quidem licentia à Papa ante concessa Stephano Langton Archiepiscopo Cant. Henrico Regè Regnante itinerantibus iudicibus ex publicis Regiis literis ab eodē Archiepiscopo impertita, his verbis dignoscitur. Henricus Dei gratia Rex Angliæ, Dominus Hiberniæ, Normanniæ, Aquitaniæ & Comes Andeg. vniuersis præsentes literas inspecturis S. Thomæ Apostoli, &c. Cum venerabilis pater Steph. Cant. Arch. authoritate domini Papæ, & de consilio fratrū suorū, fecerit nobis gratiam, de iuramentis præstandis coram iusticiariis nostris, de præcepto A. 1309. nostro itinerantibus, ab instanti aduentu Domini vsque ab vigiliam S. Thomæ Apostoli, & a principio septuagesimæ vsque ad dominicam qua cantatur. Isti sunt dies, duraxatin, causis subscriptis. nēpe in Assisis vlnimæ psentationis, de morte antecessoris, nouæ dissessinæ, de magna Assisa, & de inquisitionibus quæ de terris emergunt coram eisdem iusticiariis nostris vel, per iudicium, vel de consensu partium, quod hoc cunctessum iantu hoc anno durabit, vsque ad diem dominicum supradictum. Nos per has literas nostras patentes protestamur quod hæc concessio nobis de præsens scita vsque ad diem Dominicam prædictam non trahetur ad consequentiam post diem eundem. In cuius rei testimonium eidem Domino Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo dedimus has nostras literas patentes sigillo nostro sigillatas. Teste meipso apud West. 16. die mensis Octobr. An. Regi nostri decimo.
units.tr: In this year Robert Ratford and Henry Spigurnel, judges of capital crimes in Kent, obtained from the Archbishop the power to administer oaths to defendants in those trials called assizes, during Lent. This licence had earlier been granted by the Pope to Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, under King Henry, and was given by the same Archbishop to the travelling judges by public royal letters, in these words: Henry, by the grace of God King of England, Lord of Ireland, Normandy, Aquitaine and Count of Anjou, to all who shall inspect these present letters, greeting, etc. Since the venerable father Stephen, Archbishop of Canterbury, by the authority of the lord Pope and with the counsel of his brothers, has granted us the favour concerning the oaths to be taken before our justices, under our precept of the year 1309 (A. 1309.), to our itinerant justices, from the present coming of the Lord until the vigil of the Apostle Thomas, and from the beginning of Septuagesima until the Sunday on which is sung (Quasimodo?), these days only, for the causes written below, namely in the assizes of the last presentation, concerning the death of a predecessor, of novel disseisin, of the grand assize, and of inquests which arise concerning lands before the same justices of ours, either by judgment or by consent of the parties, which shall last only this year until the aforesaid Sunday. By these our open letters we declare that this concession, granted to us for the present, shall not be drawn into precedent after the same day. In witness of which thing we have given to the same Lord Archbishop of Canterbury these our open letters, sealed with our seal. Witnessed by ourselves at Westminster, on the sixteenth day of October, in the tenth year of our reign.

units.la: Sed euenit postea perpetui & incuitabilis luctus atque ægritudinis Archiepiscopo causa, quod Edwardus Rex Petrum de Gauetston qui omnium tam præsulum quam procerum odio semper flagrauit, &in Hiberniâ ab Edwardo patte suo Rege relegatus. gatus esset inuitis omnibus restituerit atque reuocauerit. Hic primo aduentu Couentrensem Episcopum Eboraci ex Regis praecepto carceribus ineludi procurauit. Vnde Archiepiscopus in Parliamento nullum negocii à prouincia suae Cleto tradari passus est, donec Couentrensis è publica custodia esset liberatus. Sub hac tempora Concilii generale Viennae celebratum est in quo multa & nepbanda crimina in celeberrimum & diffissimum Templariorum ordinem proposita fuerunt. Cuius accusationis author fuit rex Franciae, qui in eo Concilio filium suum Regem Hierofolymitanum create, & Templariorum bona atque praedia illi gerendo regno conuertere conatus est. Templarii itaque in eo Concilio instituta accusatione, quòd Christum Dominum diffiterentur, multaque horrenda nec suis nominibus designanda facinora assiduè perpetraren, damnati sunt. Omnesque ex edicto Regio Galliae finibus excedere illico capite iussi sunt, sed Galliae Rex spe frustratus est. Namque grandi interuenciente pecunia Papa Templariorum possessiones atque praedia Hospitalariis adiudicauit. Postea Robertus Archiepiscopus prouinciale Concilium Londini celebrauit, in quo Templarii de iisdem criminibus accusati fama publica, de qua se purgare non poterant, oppressi & damnati, & toto ordine dissoluto ad perpetuam poenitentiam peragendam per coenobia singuli distributi sunt. In Concilio autem Viennensi alterationem aquibusdam mota, nonnoporeretam celebrem ordinem totum ob quorundam confessionem damnari, Papa Clemens in Bullafua condemnatoria hanc adiecit clausulam; quanquam in rei non possumus, tamen in plenitudine nostrae potestatis dictum ordinem reprobamus.
units.tr: But afterwards there befell the Archbishop a cause of perpetual and inescapable grief and sickness, because King Edward restored and recalled Piers de Gaveston, who had always burned with hatred of all the prelates and nobles alike, and who had been banished to Ireland by his father King Edward, though all were opposed. On his first arrival he procured that the Bishop of Coventry be shut up in prison by the King's command. Hence the Archbishop, in Parliament, allowed no business to be handled by the clergy of his province until the Bishop of Coventry had been released from public custody. About this time the General Council of Vienne was held, at which many and unspeakable crimes were laid against the famous and most wealthy Order of the Templars. The author of this accusation was the King of France, who at that Council sought to have his son created King of Jerusalem, and tried to convert the goods and estates of the Templars to the support of that kingdom. Accordingly, at that Council, the Templars were condemned on the accusation, instituted there, that they denied Christ the Lord, and that they constantly committed horrible crimes that are not to be named by their names. All of them were ordered by royal edict to leave the borders of France at once, under pain of death, but the King of France was disappointed in his hope. For, through the intervention of a great sum of money, the Pope adjudged the possessions and estates of the Templars to the Hospitallers. Afterwards Archbishop Robert held a provincial council at London, at which the Templars, accused of the same crimes, were oppressed and condemned by public report, from which they could not clear themselves, and, the whole order having been dissolved, they were distributed singly among monasteries to perform perpetual penance. But at the Council of Vienne, since some were moved by the thought that the whole famous order should not be condemned on account of the confession of certain men, Pope Clement added to his condemnatory bull this clause: although we cannot in this matter, nevertheless in the fullness of our power we reprobate the said order.

units.la: Eodem anno Henricus Rex Alemanniae, creatus Imperator, tres coronas hoc ordine accepit, Aquisgrani argenteam, Mediolani ferream, & Romae aureum. Quicquenti anno in quodam Castello Pisanae ciuitati vicino cum à Romana curia rediret veneno extinctus est.
units.tr: In the same year Henry, King of the Romans, who had been created Emperor, received three crowns in this order: the silver one at Aachen, the iron one at Milan, and the golden one at Rome. In the following year, while returning from the Roman court, he was poisoned in a certain castle near the city of Pisa.

units.la: Eodem etiam anno Radulphus Bourn Augustinensis Ecclesiae Abbas electus, cum ad Papam Auinionij iam ageniem confirmandus accessisset, reuersus domum retatur se vidisse in itinere pisicinam in quadam Monialium Abbatia quae Prouines dicebatur. In qua cum educata aqua luto purgaretur, multa paruulorum ossa, ipsaque corpora adhuc integra reperiebantur. Vnde ad criminalia iudicia subeunda viginti septem Moniales Patisios ducta, & carceribus mancipatae fuerunt. De quibus quid actum fuerit, nescitur.
units.tr: In the same year also Ralph Bourn, elected Abbot of the Church of Augustine, went to Pope Clement at Avignon to be confirmed. On his way home he reported that he had seen a fishpond in a certain nunnery called Prouines. When its water was drained off to clear away the mud, many small children's bones were found there, and even whole bodies. Because of this, twenty-seven nuns were taken to Paris to undergo criminal trial and were committed to prison. What became of them is not known.

units.la: In superiori autem Londinensi Concilio Walderus Couentrensis, qui ab his carcerum angustiis in quas Petri de Gauerston odio ductus esset, solo Archiepiscopo interce- dente liberatus est, excommunicatus est. Quod Archiepiscopum & clerum per fide deferens Petro adhaesit, nec his constitutionibus feruandis quas in eo Concilio sanciuisset, vellet iurare. Abilla excommunicatione Walterus Couentrensis appellauit ad papam, & interim cum Petro coniunctus illius concilii constitutiones rescindi procurauit. Hoc annu Robertus Archiepiscopus Iohannem Heron equitem ob necem Rogeri Gracein arce Londinensi carceribus derentum, à Rege, vt clericum, & in furo spirituali iudicandum postulauit. Cui concessit Rex, Pe ftcaquecidem equeas a Londinensis Episcopi vicario teuocatio in Ecclesia Paulina per Decanum de Arcubus & Officialem Cantuariensem publicata fuit. Lis quaedam inter Priorem & Conuentum de Lanes. ac Episcopum Norwicensem in foro regio de iure patronatus , septem annis agitata, finem hoc modo sortita est. Prior & Conuentus praesentabant quendam Reginaldum Bedaling ad Ecclesiam parochialem de Gerel, quem Episcopus indignum Ecclesiasticis beneficiis pronunciauit, & reiecit de quo in foro Regio a Priore & conuentu petitus est. Quibus respondit: Admittere se Clericum praesentatum non potuisse, quem beneficiis Ecclesiasticis indignum pronunciauerat. Itaque iudices regii ab Archiepiscopo de indignitate clericorum ceteriores fieri voluerunt. Qui Noruicensis Episcopi factum comprobauit, iudicibusque regiis his verbis referipfit, Inuenimus quòd R.B. in breui mentionatus est, inhabilis ad omne beneficium Ecclesiasticum. Itaque secundum eius relationem & Norwicensis Episcopi decretum in foro Regio iudicatum fuit. Et ne iudices seculares Ecclesiasticam iurisdictionem prohibitionum regis nimium coercerent, obtinuit à Rege primum, vt causae prohibitionum à reis delatae diligentera Clericis ad id iuratis examinarentur, tum vt falsas causas deferentes carceribus & pecunia multarentur: deinde vt praelati iurisdictione praediti, omnes prohibitiones ex falsis & iniustis causis e foro regio ad se emissas, proximo quoquo Parliamento Regi proceribusque deferrent: Ad extremum vt utriusque fori iurisdictionem propriis cancellis terminaret, Ecclesiasticæ authoritatis iura conceptis verbis a Rege describi & prælatis exponiin articulis quos articulos Cleri vocant, procuravit. Iurisdictionem Archiepiscopalem tam severe exercuit, vt ne magnatibus delinquentibus parcetet. Iohannem enim Warren. Surriæ Comitem, a propria coniuge temere diuertentem, & domi suæ publice cum meretrice luxuriantem ab eiusdem consortio & præsentia, coacto iuramento abegit. Tum Comitem adhuc cum ea lasciuientem, liberosque ex adulteriis amplexibus procreantem edicto publico ad Synodum citauit, vbi tam periurii quam adulterii reus iudicatus, scortisque familiaritate iterum interdictus est. Regem Edwardum primum vnice adamauit, a quo Spensetos, aliosque Regis animum adulatione & facto obsequio, ad iniurias & libidines allicientes Parlamenti authoritate in exilium coegit.
units.tr: At the earlier London council Walter of Coventry was excommunicated. He had been freed from the narrow confines of prison, into which Peter de Gaveston had put him out of hatred, only through the intercession of the Archbishop alone. He had deserted the Archbishop and the clergy, clung to Peter, and refused to swear to observe the constitutions which that council had enacted. From that excommunication Walter of Coventry appealed to the Pope, and meanwhile, joined with Peter, he saw to it that the constitutions of that council were rescinded. In this year Archbishop Robert demanded that Sir John Heron, who had been held in prison in the Tower of London on account of the killing of Roger Gracein, be handed over by the King to be treated as a clerk and tried in the spiritual court. The King granted this. Afterwards, however, the excommunication was revoked by the vicar of the Bishop of London, and the revocation was published in St Paul's by the Dean of the Arches and the Official of Canterbury. A certain lawsuit between the Prior and Convent of Lanes and the Bishop of Norwich, concerning the right of patronage, was pursued in the royal court for seven years and ended in this way. The Prior and Convent presented one Reginald Bedaling to the parish church of Gerel, but the Bishop pronounced him unworthy of ecclesiastical benefices and rejected him. On this the Prior and Convent sued him in the royal court. They replied that they could not admit a presented clerk whom the Bishop had declared unworthy of ecclesiastical benefices. Therefore the royal judges wished to be informed by the Archbishop about the unworthiness of the clerks. He confirmed the act of the Bishop of Norwich and replied to the royal judges in these words: "We have found that R.B. was lately named as unfit for any ecclesiastical benefice." Therefore, according to his report and the decree of the Bishop of Norwich, the matter was decided in the royal court. So that secular judges might not overly restrain ecclesiastical jurisdiction by royal prohibitions, he obtained from the King, first, that the grounds of prohibitions brought by defendants should be carefully examined by clerks sworn to this task; second, that those who brought false grounds should be punished with imprisonment and fines; and third, that prelates endowed with jurisdiction should report to the King and the nobles at the next Parliament all prohibitions issued from the royal court to them on false and unjust grounds. Finally, so that the jurisdiction of each court might be bounded by its own limits, he procured that the rights of ecclesiastical authority be set out by the King in express words and explained to the prelates in articles, which they call the articles of the clergy. He exercised archiepiscopal jurisdiction so severely that he did not spare offending magnates. For he drove John Warren, Earl of Surrey, away from the company and presence of his own wife, after he had rashly deserted her and was openly indulging in lust with a prostitute in his own house, by forcing him to take an oath. Then, when the Earl was still carrying on with her and fathering children by adulterous embraces, he summoned him by public edict to the Synod, where he was judged guilty of both perjury and adultery and was again forbidden to keep company with harlots. He loved King Edward the Second alone, and by the authority of Parliament he drove into exile the Despensers and others who, by flattery and servile compliance, enticed the King's mind toward wrongs and lusts.

units.la: Vitia quæ in hoc Archiepiscopo deprehensa sunt, non tam hominis quam temporis propria fuerunt. Nam pro Ecclesiæ libertatibus cum Papa, & pro regni iuribus cum Batonibus aduersus Regif uit. In quarum vttaque causa Salomonis dictum verum expertus est. Indignationem Prineipis morti comparandam esse. Beneficia Ecclesiastica nunquam nisi doctis contulit. Ptecibus atque gratia nobilium fretos & ambientes semper repulit. Iuuenibus literarum studiosis ad Academias missis annua alimenta decreuit. In Eleemosynis & largitione quotidiana omnes ante se & sequutos Archiepiscopos anteire dicendus est. Pauperibusostiatim medicantibus præter quotidianas ex fragmentis largitiones quolibet die Dominico & feria quinta singulis pro Eleemosyna habenda ad loca vbi degebat venientibus panes frumentarios quadrante valentes dari præcepit. Horum panum numerus tempore caritatis annonæ quatuor, tempore copiæ trium milium fuit. His in illis festis solennioribus ceerarum quinquaginta denarios, totidem pauperibus in pecuniis numerandos addidit. Infirmis præterea, senioue confectis, puerperis & eiusmodi egenis prodite ad Eleemosynas petendas haud valentibus mittis singulos panes cum modica carnium, aut piscium, iuxta diei varietatem, quantitate iussit. Subleuabat insuper eos qui a secunda fortuna casu ad inopiam detrusi erant, quosque pudor a mendicitate prohibebat, quibus & vestes & pecunias misit. In mensa fuit inter conuiuas, lætus affabilis, iucundus. Detractores, adulatores, & seurtas a sua hilaritate & epulis seiunxit. A quibus & a consortio cum secretiora & interiora loca abduxisset, preclbus primum, deinde studiis incubuit. Postquam ab exilio reuertsus esset, sex annis in magna Edwardi secundi Regis gratia vixit. Quem cum adhibitis & restitutis Speuceris viris populo & magnatibus odiosis abalienasse a se optimum quemque vidisset, ægritudine contabuit, & Ottefordiæ obiit. 1313. quinto Idus Maii. Inde ad Ecclesiam Cantuariensem eadauer eius deductum, & prope altare Sancti Gregorii ad parietem austrum sepultum est. Sepulchrum eius, quia populus eum mortuum tanquam sanctum frequens adoravit, demolitum atque delectum est. Bibliothecam cum vestibus modicisque quæ superarant bonis, Ecclesiæ Cantuariensi donauit.
units.tr: The faults found in this archbishop were not so much his own as those of his age. For he fought for the liberties of the Church against the Pope, and for the rights of the kingdom against the barons, and in both causes he proved the truth of Solomon's saying that the anger of a prince is to be feared like death. He never conferred ecclesiastical benefices except on the learned. He always rejected those who relied on prayers and the favour of the nobility and sought them out. To young men devoted to letters who were sent to the universities he assigned yearly allowances. In alms and daily giving he surpassed, it may be said, all the archbishops who had gone before him and came after. Besides the daily largesse from leftovers, he ordered that on every Sunday and Thursday a wheaten loaf worth a farthing be given as alms to each of those who came to the places where he lived. The number of these loaves was four thousand in a time of dearth and three thousand in a time of plenty. On the more solemn feast days he added fifty pence, to be counted out in money to as many poor people. Moreover, for the sick, the aged and worn out, women in childbed, and other needy folk who were not able to go out begging, he ordered a single loaf to be sent, with a modest portion of meat or fish according to the variety of the day. He also relieved those who by chance had fallen from prosperity into poverty and whom shame kept from begging, sending them both clothes and money. At table he was cheerful, affable and pleasant among his guests. He kept detractors, flatterers and whores away from his good cheer and his feasts. Withdrawing from their company into more private and inner rooms, he devoted himself first to prayer and then to study. After he returned from exile he lived for six years in the great favour of King Edward the Second. When he saw that the King, by admitting and restoring the Despensers, was estranging from himself every good man, who were hateful to the people and the magnates, he was worn down by grief and sickness, and died at Otford on 11 May 1313. His body was brought to Canterbury Church and buried near the altar of St Gregory, by the south wall. His tomb was demolished and removed, because the people in large numbers worshipped him after his death as a saint. He gave his library, together with his clothes and the modest goods that remained, to the Church of Canterbury.

units.la: L. WALTERUS RAYNOLD.
units.tr: L. Walter Raynold.

units.la: Onachorum superstitiosam solitudinem, quæ cum Episcopis ipsisque Regibus toties luctabatur, iam tandem ab alia huiusmodi face, fratrum nempe & prædicatorum vulgari atque trita mendicitate superaram, & vtriusque ordinis profusionem, huiusmodi caruisse gratia in hoc Walterò ostensum est. Diuturnis altercationibus arque tixis se muiicem multis iam annis lacesserunt Monachi atque fratres, hi illis solitudinem & ignauiam, illi vicissim istis mendicitatem & petulantiam exprobrares. Sed superaris tandem Monachis a fratribus supplantatis, vtrique cum vulgo contemptui esse coeperunt, tandem Papæ atque Regi ludibrio fuerunt. Robertus Kylwarby ac Iohannes Peckam ex illa (vt diximus) mendicitate, quæ tam plebi, quoniam noua, Papæ quoniam quæstuosa, gratiosa fuit, ad Archiepiscopalem apicem ascenderunt. Quem nouum, & tanta paupertatis & religionis simulatione adumbratum quæstum, ac ad Romanam explendam cupiditatem traductum, cum Principes, præsules atque proceres offecissent, execrandam illam superstitionis sententiam abominati sunt. Papa cum hoc nouum a se instituto
units.tr: That the superstitious solitude of the monks, which had so often struggled with bishops and even kings, was at last overcome by another torch of the same kind, namely the common and worn-out begging of the friars and preachers, and that both orders, lacking the grace of this kind, were shown in Walter. For many years the monks and the friars had harassed each other with long and fixed quarrels: the friars reproached the monks with idleness and sloth, and the monks in turn reproached the friars with begging and insolence. But once the monks were overthrown and supplanted by the friars, both orders began to be held in contempt by the common people and at last became a laughing-stock to the Pope and the King. Robert Kilwardby and John Pecham rose to the archiepiscopal summit through that begging (as we have said), which was pleasing to the common people because it was new, and to the Pope because it was profitable. When the princes, bishops and nobles had found fault with this new profit, cloaked in such a pretence of poverty and religion and turned to satisfy Roman greed, they abhorred that accursed superstitious opinion. The Pope, with this new thing of his own devising...

units.la: chiepiscopus saepe contingebat, ut sua Archiepiscopalis iurisdictio proun̄ciatiū̄ appellationibus & querelis a Romana curia suscepris impediretur, huic tñ conatibus maxime obfuturo malo muneribus occurredū̄ putauit. Itaq; exeplo Iohannis Peckam (de quo ante dictum est) Papa, Cardin. atque Roic curialis aunus ltipedius, doniiq; plurimis affecit, de Papa expertus id quod Poetae de Ioue fingunt. Placatur donis Iupiter ipse dis. Quae largitio octo amplissimis Papae concessionibus atque priuilegiis remuneratae fuit. Prima, ut toto proximo triennio cohibita interim Suffraganeorum atque praelatorum iurisdictione rotam prouinciam Cantuariensem procuratoribus constitutis ibi uisitare liceat, & procurationes nihilominus integras percipiat. Secunda, ut tam locate{10}ligiota, quam alia quaecunque firmitimis exemptionis priuilegiis & iuribus iounicá a dia uisitatione se eximere atq; uendicare nequeant. Tertia ut irregulares ducentos, qui cum suspensi & excommunicati essent diuina celebrando irregularitatem contraxerunt, dispensando ad priorem statum, Regulamque restituat. Quarta, ut cum clerici aetate minoribus, ideoq; ad Ecclesiastica beneficia animarum cura praeditum inhabilibus super eo natalium defectu dispenset. Quinta, ut uiolentam manuū iniectionem in Clericos ipso iure excommunicatos dispensando absoluat. Sexta, ut quadraginta clericis plura Ecclesiastica beneficia curata simul retinendi facultatem concedat. Septima, ut quoniā quaecunque Ecclesiam aliquam Cathedralem uel Collegium uilitat, dignitatem, prebendam uel Ecclesiā aliquā sibi, cuicunq; uoluerit conferendā, referuet. {20}Octaua, ubicunq; ac quoniā quaecunq; praedicat, uisitat, uel transeuntes eleemosynas largitur, aut hospitalitatem edat, criminum certum retinentes diebus per petratorum ueniam fatentibus & contritis concedat. His auctus & locupletatus papalibus priuilegiis uisitatione exorsus est. Ad Lincoln. diocesim omniū (ut saepe diximus) maximā ipsē uisitatiū. Ac huic proximā Norwicē(em ingressus a Rege exorta a Baronibus motu auocatus est, eā iraq; impeditus alteri uisitandā cōmisit. Interea fratres praedicatores generale capitulū Londini celebrarūt, quo inito libellus facetus conuiris & ludibris plenus, & io appellationis more constitutus in eos editus, & Paulinae Ecclesiae ualuis affixus, magnū praeterueuntibus rīsum iocumque commouebat. Illa autem Vitaiia uisitatio mortuo Clemente Papa aliquandiu intermissa est. Cui in Papatu successit Iacobus Hafe Cardinalis {30}P ruentis, qui le Iohanem 22. nominauit. Hic Lugduni in Ecclesia Cathedrali coronatus est, Philippo Gallia Rege praesente, qui Papa equum inlidente frenum a loco coronationis ad domum fratrum praedicatorum ubi Papa hospitio acceptus est, manibus tenens incestit pedes. Quo etiam die non aliis quam Clericis Lugduni equitare permisum est. Huic Edwardus Anglia Rex opuleo- ta dona plurima doctis quibusdam uiris ex Academia Oxoniensi destinatis nunciis misit. Quae munera cum grauissime acceptasset, retinburionis loco ab Angliæ Clero uacantium toto proximo triennio beneficiorum primos fructus exegit. Eodem anno grauissimo inter Regem & Barones exorto (ut diximus) tumultu Cancellinus atque Lucas Romani Cardinales à Papa ad eam discordiam componendam in Angliam missi {40}sunt. Qui cum Dunelmum profecti essent, ut Lodouicum de Bello monte, nationē Gallum, indoctum, atque claudum eui papa Dunelmensem Episcopatum prouisionis titulo contulisset, in eiusdem possessione collocatent, à Iarronibus io itinere capti atque spoliati fuerunt. Quae quidem calamitas lucrosaillis fuit, quod reuersi cum hanc fibi factam iniuriam deplorassent, collectā ad hoc damnum resarciendum grandi a Clero pecunia, duplo plus repetierunt quam amisserunt. Deinde permultisisque selectissimis ex Episcoporum donationibus, beneficiis & dignitatibus Ecclesiasticis sese locupletaur, paeceque nequaquam inter Regem & proceres reconciliata Romam referri & opulenti reuersi sunt. His & similibus prouisionibus, tributis, ac impositionibus Anglis oppressit ac conetauit Papa. Quae in aliis regnis obtinere nulla fraude aut s uentate {50}potuit; Soli Angli, sicut boni Asini quicquid eis imponitur tolerantes, in his & aliis quam tumuis grauibus paruerunt. Ac paulo post idem Papa eam in plutales constitutionē edidit, quae in Extrauagantibus (quas aiunt) con stitutioibus immiscetur, & incipit. Execrabilis. Cuius constitutionis in quamplurimis a beneficiis amotis beneficia sub Clemente proximo Papa multo quam ante uendibiliora fuerunt. Nam dispensationes quas Iohannes decreto suo reseidisset, renouauit. Quidam tamen hanc fuisse Papae Iohannis eius constitutionis ferendę eaufam dixerunt, quod concessis ei (ut diximus) beneficiorum uacantium fructibus, ea constitutione pleraque in Anglia beneficia incumbentibus orbauit. Eodemq; anno Papa decretalium librum septimum edidit & festum Corporis Christi cum magna solennitate instituit. Illis autem a proceribus in Regem con-
units.tr: It often happened to the archbishop that his archiepiscopal jurisdiction was hindered by appeals and complaints taken up by the Roman court, and he thought that this evil, which would greatly hinder his efforts, had to be met with gifts. So, following the example of John Pecham (of whom we have spoken before), the Pope, the cardinals and the Roman courtiers, of whom there were many, were lavished upon with many gifts; the Pope, having experienced in himself what the poets feign of Jupiter, found that "Jupiter himself is appeased by gifts." This largess was rewarded with eight very generous concessions and privileges from the Pope: (1) that for the whole of the following three years, the jurisdiction of the suffragans and prelates being suspended in the meantime, he might visit the whole province of Canterbury through appointed proxies, and nevertheless receive the full procurations; (2) that neither the local nor any other persons, by the strongest privileges of exemption and rights, might be able to exempt or claim themselves from his visitation; (3) that he might dispense with irregular persons, who had incurred irregularity by celebrating divine offices while suspended and excommunicated, and restore them to their former state and rank; (4) that he might dispense with clerics who were under age, and therefore unfit for ecclesiastical benefices with the cure of souls, despite that defect of birth; (5) that he might dispense with and absolve those who had laid violent hands on clerics, who were excommunicated by law itself; (6) that he might grant to forty clerics the power of holding several ecclesiastical benefices with cure of souls at the same time; (7) that, since whatever person has a cathedral church or college in his power, he might reserve to himself the dignity, prebend or any church to be conferred on whomever he wished; (8) that, wherever and whenever anyone preaches, visits, gives alms to travellers, or provides hospitality, he might grant full pardon of sins to those who, confessing and contrite, had committed certain crimes. Enriched and made wealthy by these papal privileges, he began his visitation with the diocese of Lincoln, the largest of all (as we have often said). When he had entered Norwich, which was next, he was called away by the King, because a great uprising had arisen among the barons; hindered by this, he committed the other visitation to another. Meanwhile the friars preachers held their general chapter at London, at which a witty libel, full of jests and mockeries, was issued against them in the manner of an appeal, and affixed to the doors of St Paul's, causing great laughter and mirth to passers-by. But that visitation was for a time suspended after the death of Pope Clement. James of Cahors, cardinal of Porto, succeeded him as Pope, and named himself John XXII. He was crowned at Lyons in the cathedral church, with Philip, King of France, present, who, holding the bridle of the Pope's horse, which was stumbling, walked on foot from the place of coronation to the house of the friars preachers, where the Pope was received as a guest. On that same day no one but clerics was permitted to ride at Lyons. To him Edward, King of England, sent many rich gifts by envoys, certain learned men chosen from the University of Oxford. When he had accepted these gifts very gratefully, as a return he exacted from the clergy of England the first fruits of benefices falling vacant over the whole following three years. In the same year, when the very grievous tumult between the King and the barons had arisen (as we have said), the Roman cardinals Ceccano and Luke were sent into England by the Pope to settle that discord. When they had set out for Durham, to install in possession Lewis of Beaumont, a Frenchman, unlearned and lame, to whom the Pope had granted the bishopric of Durham under the title of provision, they were taken and robbed on the journey by robbers. This calamity turned out to their profit, for when they returned and had lamented the injury done to them, they collected a large sum of money from the clergy to make good that loss, and they took back twice as much as they had lost. Then, enriching themselves further with very many choice gifts, benefices and ecclesiastical dignities from the bishops, and the peace between the King and the nobles not at all being reconciled, they returned to Rome and went back rich. With these and similar provisions, tributes and impositions, the Pope oppressed and harassed the English. Such things the Pope could not get accepted in other kingdoms without fraud or violence; only the English, like good asses, bore whatever was laid upon them, and obeyed in these and other burdens, however heavy. And shortly afterwards the same Pope issued that constitution in several parts, which is inserted among the so-called Extravagants, and begins "Execrable." By this constitution many benefices were withdrawn, and under the next Pope, Clement, benefices became far more saleable than before, for he renewed the dispensations which John had annulled by his decree. Some, however, have said that the reason John issued that constitution was that, since the fruits of vacant benefices had been granted to him (as we have said), he had by that constitution robbed the incumbents of very many benefices in England. In the same year the Pope published the seventh book of the Decretals and instituted the feast of Corpus Christi with great solemnity.

units.la: {y} Ioan. 3. citatis turbis, Scoti Angliam inuaserunt ad Eboracum, & Lancastriam vbique praedati sunt. Ac Berwicum proditione coeperunt, sed conciliata cum proceribus pace Rex instructo exercitu Scotos in suos fines ex Anglia repulit, & Berwicum amissum recuperauit.
