Ad quod bellum administrandum, decimam a Clero postulauit, quod id sine Papae licentia concedere sibi ueri esse respondERUNT. Ita Adamus Murimuren. ad Papam a Rege missus est. Papa Regis causa hac solutione Cleri facile permisit, sed paulo post Episcopo Wintoniensi mortuo, Papa Episcopatus collationem sibi reseruauit, eumque Rigando cuidam suo in Anglia nuncio Regis inuito & itato cotulit. Qui a Londinensi Episcopo, quoniam Walterus Cantuariensis Regi fidus esse noluit, in Monasterio S. Albani conscreatus est. Interea Walterus illam celebrem visitationem quam Vrbano mortuo intermisit, iam accepta nona a Iohanne potestate peregit. Nam solus Londinensis Episcopus ei appellando restitit, quo eiusdem papae rescripto superato, & in potestatem Walteri remisso, reliqui humiliati sunt. In qua visitatione indulta sibi (quae ante commemorauimus) priuilegia a Londinensi Ecclesia exorsus in, qua capellano suo prouisionis titulo opimam praebendam contulit, per procuratores executus est. Multas item synodos, in quibus Regi subsidiariam a clero tribui opem popoficit, celebrauit. Sed Oxonii in quodam Concilio quod Concilium Oxoniense secundum appellatur, multa tulit, inter quae de appellationibus decreuit. Nullam appellationem a grauaminibus & interlocutoriis, sed a definitiua tantum sententia esse interponendam. Quam constitutionem Sithon Mepham ut iniquam, & multarum a Suffraganeis inferendatum subditis iniuriarum causam postea reuocauit. Idem Walterus in alia Synodo Lamethi celebrata ad appellationis vires in beneficiorum causis moderandas constitutionem tulit aequissimam Quomodo fructus beneficii lite pendente sequestrentur. In quo consilio Clerus pro salario publici praelectoris Hebraicarum literarum in Oxoniensi Academia quadrantem ex singulis libris Ecclesiasticorum prouentuum concesserunt. Ac paulo post Hugone Spefer, de quo in Rob. Spenf. Winckelsei ante a dicto est, Regi cociliato, vitio plebi pariter & procetibus inuiso, Barones atmis suscepti eius praedia & terras vbique diripiebant. Qui cum Regis edicto de armis deponendis non paruissent, proditores & lese maiestatis rei decreto pronunciati sunt. Ita bellum intestinum utrinque paratum est. Ad hoc sedandum bellum Cardinales Romanii ingressi Regnum cum nihil profecissent, commeatu exacto Romam teuerfi sunt. Sed superatis tandem Baronibus, eorumque quamplurimis capitalibus poenis affectis, Scoti, quia papae legatis quia bello desistere noluerunt, excommunicati fuerunt, crebro & confertim in Anglam praedatum irruerunt. Ad haec Franciae Rex Edwardum Regem Angliae in his turbulentissimis temporibus edicto ad reddendum sibi proGuascoma homagium in Galliam vocauit. Ad haec tot simul cogrunt ea mala vitanda Parlimentum Londini habitum est. In eo etiam de his qui illius belli Baronibus suscitati rei fuissent inquisitum est Inter quos Adam Herefordensis Episcopus a Regis lictoribus deprehensus, causam de proditione & lese Maiestatis crimine dicere iussus est. Ac obiectis criminibus multis, pulsatus contumelis & opprobriis cum diu stupidus obmutuisset, tandem sic ora resoluit. Domine Rex, vestram Regiae Maiestatis reuerentia semper salua. Ego S. Ecclesiae Dei minister humilis ac membrum, & Episcopus consecratus licet indignus, ad tam ardua neque respondere, nec debeo absque Domini Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi post summum pontificem meidirecti iudicis, & aliorum patrum Episcoporum, meorum parium consensu vel consensu. Quo dicto Archiepiscopi & Episcopi qui interfuerunt assurgentes Regi pro collega suo intercesserunt, cumque Rex exorari noluit, totus clerus Episcopum a Regis iudicio subeundo tanquam Ecclesiae membrum, vendicauit. Quorum actus clamoribus Rex cum Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo custodiendum aliàs de criminibus repsonfurum tradidit. Sed paulo post Regio iussu iterum captus & ad Regium tribunal ductus est. Quare Episcopis qui tum pencomnes Londini fuerant nunciata, Cant. Ebor. & Dublin. Archiepisc. crucibus erectis, dec eahis Episc. magna, huiusmodi caetera committi ad locum iudicii magna celeritate contendunt. Quorum aduentu fugatis ministris Regiis confratrem & Coepiscopum suum a cunctis derelictum atque solum in custodiam suam suscepit. Eoque abduco ilico sub Anathematis poena diuerunt, ne quis manus ei violentas adferre praesumat. Rex hac Cleri audacia commotus, eo absente inquisitionem de suis perpetrati legitimam instituit. Ita conuocatis Laicis (nam Clerici feculatibus praecipue capitalibus iudiciis adesse tum ne regia authoritate adduci aut cogi poterant) propof. crimina quae certis ia distincta formulis & articulis ante Herefordensi
units.tr: {y} Ioan. 3. While the crowds were stirred up against the King by the nobles, the Scots invaded England, and plundered Lancashire and York everywhere. They seized Berwick by treason, but when peace had been made with the nobles, the King, with an army in readiness, drove the Scots out of England back into their own borders, and recovered Berwick, which had been lost. To carry on this war he demanded a tenth from the clergy, and they answered that it was not lawful for them to grant this without the Pope's permission. So Adam of Murimuth was sent by the King to the Pope. The Pope, for the King's sake, easily allowed this payment by the clergy; but shortly afterwards, when the Bishop of Winchester had died, the Pope reserved the collation of that bishopric to himself, and conferred it, against the King's wish and against his will, on Rigaud, one of his own nuncios in England. He was consecrated in the monastery of St Albans by the Bishop of London, because Walter of Canterbury was unwilling to be faithful to the King. Meanwhile Walter carried out that famous visitation, which had been interrupted on the death of Urban, now with the authority granted him by John. For the Bishop of London alone resisted him by appeal; when this rescript of the Pope had been overcome and the matter returned to Walter's power, the others were humbled. In that visitation, beginning with the church of London, he used the privileges granted to him (which we mentioned before), and in it he conferred a rich prebend on his chaplain by provision, carried out through proxies. He also held many synods, in which he obtained from the clergy a subsidy to be given to the King. But at a council at Oxford, called the Council of Oxford, he proposed many things, among them a decree about appeals: that no appeal should be lodged from grievances and interlocutory sentences, but only from a definitive sentence. Simon Mepham later revoked this constitution as unjust and as the cause of many injuries inflicted by the suffragans on their subjects. The same Walter, in another synod held at Lambeth, passed a very equitable constitution for moderating the force of appeals in cases of benefices: that the fruits of a benefice should be sequestered while the suit is pending. In this council the clergy granted, for the salary of a public reader in Hebrew letters in the University of Oxford, a quarter from every pound of ecclesiastical revenues. Shortly afterwards, when Hugh Despenser (of whom we have spoken above under Robert Winchelsea) had become hateful to the King and equally to the common people and the nobles, the barons, taking up arms, plundered his estates and lands everywhere. When they did not obey the King's edict to lay down arms, they were pronounced traitors and guilty of treason by decree. Thus a civil war was prepared on both sides. The Roman cardinals entered the kingdom to quell this war, but when they had achieved nothing, they were paid their fees and returned to Rome. But when the barons had at last been overcome, and very many of them had been punished with capital penalties, the Scots, because they would not desist from war despite the Pope's legates, were excommunicated, and they repeatedly and in close formation poured into England to plunder. In addition, the King of France, in these most turbulent times, summoned King Edward of England by edict to render him homage in France for Gascony. Besides all these evils, so many at once, to avoid them a Parliament was held at London. In it inquiry was also made concerning those who had been implicated in the barons' war. Among them Adam, Bishop of Hereford, was seized by the King's officers and ordered to answer the charge of treason and lese-majesty. When many charges had been brought against him, and he had been assailed with insults and reproaches, he remained long dumbfounded; at last he broke his silence thus: "My lord the King, with the reverence due to your royal majesty always preserved. I, a humble minister and member of the holy Church of God, and a consecrated bishop, though unworthy, ought not to answer such grave matters without the consent, or assent, of the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, who is the judge appointed after the supreme pontiff, and of the other fathers, the bishops, my peers." At these words the archbishops and bishops who were present rose up and interceded with the King on behalf of their colleague, and when the King refused to be entreated, the whole clergy claimed for the bishop that he should not submit to the King's judgment, as a member of the Church. The King, moved by their clamours, handed him over to the Archbishop of Canterbury to be kept in custody, to answer the charges another time. But shortly afterwards, by royal command, he was taken again and led before the royal tribunal. Therefore, when the bishops who were then all in London had been informed, the archbishops of Canterbury, York and Dublin, with crosses raised and a great company of bishops, hurried with great speed to the place of judgment, that such matters should not be committed to others. At their arrival the royal officers were put to flight, and they took into their own custody their brother and fellow bishop, who had been abandoned by everyone and was left alone. And, carrying him away at once, they forbade under penalty of anathema that anyone should presume to lay violent hands on him. The King, moved by this boldness of the clergy, in his absence instituted a lawful inquiry into the crimes committed by them. Thus, with the laymen summoned (for the clerics, especially in capital trials, could not be brought or compelled to attend the secular courts by royal authority), he laid before them the charges which had been drawn up in certain articles and set forms before the Bishop of Hereford, and he ordered them, bound by oath, to hold the inquiry by lawful conjecture and by evidence of the fact according to the prescription of law, and, having weighed the whole matter among themselves and shared it, to report with a common answer what they believed concerning the truth of the articles. They, whether moved by fear of the King, or by hatred of the bishop, or by the truth or probability...

units.la: Hereforedensi Episcopo obiecisset,eos iureiurando astrictos inssiit, vt inquisitione per legitimas coniecturas, factiqúe euidentiam ex iuris præscripto habita, reque tota inter le perpensa & communicata,quid de articulorum veritate crederet,communi responso referrent.Illi siue metu Regis, siue Episcopi odio,siuerei veritate aut probabilitate ducti responderunt, Episcopum Herefordensem omnium crimioum in articulis comprehenso tum libi reum videri. Quo responso approbato Rex Episcopum proscripsit, prædia & terras in suam custodiam coepit, bonis omnibus spoliauit. Sed Episcopns ex omnium Archiepiscoporum & Episcoporum consensu sub tutela Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi qui Regi eum tandem reconciliauit, delituit. Hic post creatos in Anglia Episcopos primus laicalia iudicia subiit. Cuius rei atrocitas postea (vt in Iohaone Stratford dicemus) permixtis in criminalibus iudiciis Clericis atque laicis aliquantulum mitigata est. Cumque iam Walterus Archiepiscopus Regis animum multo obsequio, leniquè sermone placasset, quia is solus in tam tumultuosis temporibus summa fide Regis gratiam & beneuolentiam retinuit, & quicquid aliqua æquitate nixum postulauerat sine difficultate obtinere poterat,prouocatus est a toto Clero, vt cũ Rex peeuniariâ opẽ à Clero petiisser, pro restitucdis pristinis Ecclesiæ kbertatib.atq; iuribus,hisq; in perpetuũ confirmàdis cũ Regeageret. Archiepiscopus qui Regis animũ sensumq; ex longa consuetudine perpuls cbre cassuisset,conuenire eum de re tanta noluit, anteq̃ Clerus suam in Regem observantia aliquo beneficii signo declarasset. Itaq; Concilio Westmonasterti cũ Clero habuit.Ibi proposuit de Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ & Ecclesiasticarũ persoarum,rerumque suarum perpetua pace,securitate & immunitate proseguanda. Tum de Scotis interdicti & exeommunicationis sententias a Papæ Legatis promulgatas contemnentibus, & Anglis ...
units.tr: The Bishop of Hereford had brought these charges, and they were bound by oath to conduct the inquiry by lawful conjectures and by evidence of the deed, as the law prescribes. Having weighed the whole matter among themselves and shared their views, they were to report by a common answer what they believed about the truth of the articles. Whether moved by fear of the King, by hatred of the Bishop, or by their judgment of the truth or probability of the charges, they answered that the Bishop of Hereford seemed guilty of all the crimes contained in the articles. With this answer approved, the King outlawed the Bishop, took his lands and estates into his custody, and stripped him of all his goods. But the Bishop, with the consent of all the archbishops and bishops, went into hiding under the protection of the Archbishop of Canterbury, who at last reconciled him to the King. He was the first bishop, after bishops were established in England, to be brought before a lay court. The atrocity of this case was afterwards somewhat softened, as we shall say under John Stratford, when clerics and laymen were mixed together in criminal trials. Now Archbishop Walter, by great deference and gentle speech, had calmed the King's temper. He alone, in such turbulent times, kept the King's favour and goodwill by his sincere loyalty, and could easily obtain whatever he sought with some show of fairness. The whole clergy urged him that, when the King asked for money from the clergy, he should bargain with the King for the restoration of the Church's former liberties and rights and their confirmation for ever. The Archbishop, who from long acquaintance knew the King's mind and feelings well, did not wish to meet him on so great a matter before the clergy had shown their goodwill toward the King by some sign of kindness. So he held a council with the clergy at Westminster. There he proposed that the perpetual peace, security and immunity of the English Church, of ecclesiastical persons and of their property should be pursued. Next came the matter of the Scots, who despised the sentences of interdict and excommunication issued by the papal legates, and of the English...

units.la: Tertio de illis authoritate legitima puniendis atque corrigendis qui laicali vi ac potentia sine authoritate canonica in Ecclesiarum aut dignitarum possessionem Clericos inducunt aut eiiciunt. Quarto de nouo modo colligendi denarios Sancti Petri statuendo, & prouisione beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum persedem Romanam facienda,moderatione procurationum Cardinalibus Papæque Legatis adhibenda, nec non peregrinis ut residendum in his beneficiis quæ in Anglia tenent compellendis.
units.tr: Third, that those who by lay force and power, without canonical authority, install clerics in or eject them from churches or dignities should be legitimately punished and corrected. Fourth, that a new method of collecting Peter's pence be established, that provision of ecclesiastical benefices be made by the Roman See, that procurations for cardinals and papal legates be moderated, and that foreigners be compelled to reside in the benefices they hold in England.

units.la: Quinto vt Regi tot externis & totestinis bellis pecunia exhausto subsidii nomine Clero tribuatur. His postulatis respondit primo morose atq; duriter Clerus.Cum Ecclesiasticorum bonorum custodes essent, sæpe se auxilium regium sed stustra inuocasse,tum Regem non sua voluntate sed impiis laicorũ suasionibus a Clero auersum, ideoque canonicis remediis & censuris resistendum atque pugnandum vtEcclesia auitalibertate fruatur. Scotos vero laicorum opibus, & Clericonũ precibus esse repellendos, quibus orantibus, vt elevatis Moisis manibus vincebant hostes Israeliãe ita Anglos fore victores.
units.tr: Fifth, that aid be granted to the clergy's King, who was exhausted by money through so many foreign and domestic wars, in the name of a subsidy. To these demands the clergy first replied sullenly and harshly. Since they were the guardians of ecclesiastical goods, they had often sought royal help, but in vain. The King had been turned away from the clergy, not by his own will, but by the impious persuasions of laymen; therefore he must be resisted and opposed with canonical remedies and censures, so that the Church might enjoy its ancient liberty. The Scots, indeed, were to be repelled by the wealth of laymen and the prayers of clerics, just as, when Moses' hands were raised in prayer, Israel's enemies were overcome; so the English would be victorious.

units.la: De laicali autem potentia atque vi in inducendis & deturbandis Ecclesiastica possessione Clericis,adCanones atque Papam,quia alia deficiunt,nec spernantur remedia, esse recurrendũ. De aliis autem rebus Andreæ Bregges Romam profectò commissis sibi fas non esse ante eius reditum respondere. De subsidio concedendo statuere se nihil posse nec audete, quoniam suorum temporum malicia in tam immensum creuerat,& continua præstario decimarum, & beneficiorum vacantium Romaoo Pontificis fructus persoluti, & Cardinalibus ac legatis Romanis præstitæ procurationes, ita Ecclesiasticas opes exhauserat, vt Regiis subleuandis necessitatibus ne id tribuere possent quod libentissimis animis vellent. Sed paulo post expositis Cleto suis Regi semper ad eum finem, vt Ecclesia Anglicanæ tuendæ in tam perplexis temporibus vtilis esse possit,ministratis obseruantiis, tum quam procliuem & facilem Regem in Ecclesiæ vtilitatem sensisset, adduxit facile totum in suam ergo Regem de pecuniario subsidio senrentiamClerum.
units.tr: As for lay power and force in installing and deposing clerics from ecclesiastical possessions, recourse must be had to the canons and the Pope, since other remedies fail and must not be scorned. As for the other matters entrusted to Andrew Bregges, who had gone to Rome, it was not right to answer before his return. As for granting a subsidy, they could decide nothing and did not dare to. The malice of their times had grown so immense, and the continual payment of tithes and of the revenues of vacant benefices to the Roman Pontiff, together with the procurations paid to cardinals and Roman legates, had so drained the ecclesiastical resources that they could not grant to relieve the King's needs what they would most gladly have wished to give. But shortly afterwards, having explained their views to the King, always with the aim that the English Church might be able to defend itself usefully in such perplexing times, and having rendered their services, they saw how inclined and easy the King was to favour the Church's advantage. Thus they easily brought the whole clergy around to their own opinion of granting the King a money subsidy.

units.la: Qua ostensa & indicata Cleri in tam aduerso tempore benignitate, Rex non modo restituit Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ vetera & antiquissima Priuilegia, sed nouis, videlicet. De non exigendis a Clero in Regis hospitium esculentis, poculentis, & vesturis à Clero, acsimilibus immunitatibus auxit. Quæ quia typis expressa non sunt, authoritate ( quod dolendum est ) hoc rempore cacent sua.
units.tr: Having shown the clergy's kindness at such an adverse time, the King not only restored to the English Church its ancient and most long-standing privileges, but also increased them with new ones: namely, that food, drink and clothing should not be exacted from the clergy for the royal household, and other similar immunities. Since these have not been printed, they now lack their proper authority, which is to be lamented.

units.la: Idem Walterus, quod Regi gratiofisimus fuerit, Regis æqualissima responsa ad Prælatorum petita obtinuit. Quæ hodie sub hoc titulo, Articuli Cleri, in iuribus regni muncipalibus typis expressa feruntur. In hoc etiam Parliamento ad Walkeri & Episcoporum instantiam Rex concessit, vt nobilium corpora, quiob bellum antedictum morte crucis affecti sunt, sepulturæ traderentur. Ab hoc Archiepiscopo capitulum Exoniense veniam noui Decani eligendi petierunt, qui electus ante suam electionem ab Episcopo confirmatam, sibique datam ab eo potestatem Decanatum non suscepit.
units.tr: The same Walter, because he was most gracious to the King, obtained the King's most equitable replies to the prelates' petitions. These today, under the title Articles of the Clergy, are reported to be printed among the municipal laws of the realm. In this same Parliament, at the request of Walter and the bishops, the King granted that the bodies of nobles who had been put to death by the cross on account of the aforesaid war should be handed over for burial. From this Archbishop the chapter of Exeter sought permission to elect a new dean. The man so elected, before his election had been confirmed by the bishop and the power had been given him by the bishop, did not take up the deanery.

units.la: Subactis Baronibus omnia in Anglia pacata & tranquilla fuissent, nisi Hugonis Spenseri odio quem Rex Wintoniensem Comitem creauit, Regina cum ad pacem cum fratre suo Franciæ Rege componendam cum filio suo Edwardo missa esset, redire amplius negasset. Quam cum Rex cum filio nondum quatuordecim annis nato exhæreditasset ac proscripsisset, bellum Regi ipsi exitiosum exortum est. Nam Regina nuptiis inter Edwardum suum filium & Philippæ Ducis Hannoniæ filiam conciliatis, ad vindicta mde Rege marito sumendam ope Hannoniæ Ducis Angliam armis ingressa est. Cui plerique tam præsules quam proceres, quia Spenseros ferre non poterant, adhæserunt. Ipse Walterus semper animo pusillus & ignauus, in aduersissimis Regi rebus defecit, & Regem simulate colens clam pecunias Reginæ suppeditauit. Rex tot bellis & papalibus exactionibus ad eam inopiam redactus est, vt cum in tanto discrimine pecunia careret, a Papalibus denariorum Sancti Petri collectoribus ducentas sexaginta libras, cum ipse abundare debuerat, mutuari cogeretur. Iamq; exercitibus ex vtraque parte insistribus edicta etiam ab vtraque parte contraria promulgata sunt. Rex Reginam cum suis: Illa Spenseros, Robertum de Baldock Cancellarium, & Exoniensem Episcopum Thesaurarium proscribunt. In hoc tumultu Ciues Londinenses hos Cancellarium & Thesaurarium vi capiunt, illum carceribus ac vinculis in noua porta Londinensi constrictum fame, aegritudine interimunt, hunc captum secuti percutiunt, atque dilaniant. Spenseri tandem vtriq; comprehensi cum aliis nobilibus vltimo supplicio affecti sunt. Rex in Wallia pene profugus delituit. Interea ab Archiepiscopo Waltero qui Regem plane deseruit, Edwardus Regis filius Windsoriæ Rex creatus & coronatus est. Ac paulo post Iacobus Barkeley Exoniensis Episcopus electus Reginæ iussu ab eodem Waltero consecratus est. Papa qui eius Episcopatus collocationem sibi reseruauit, metu & iracundia perditus, hunc Archiepiscopum tanta acerbitate obiurgauiam reprehendit, vt vitæ iam pertæsus, postquam 13. annis, nouem mensibus, & viginti diebus sedisset, cum summa ægritudine animam efflauit, & Cant. in Australi cboro muri sepultus est. In rebus prosperis satis moderatus & æquabilis: sed in aduersis animo infirmissimo & abiecto peneq; nullo fuit. Munerium de Caldecote cum bosco de Thorlehot dedit conuentui Ecclesiæ Christi Cantuariæ Prohibitiones regias quæ tunc Regine inscio frequentes è regio criminali foro ab imperitis Iudicibus manabant, non tam authoritate quam iure ipso & æquitate babitis consultationibus deleuit atque fregit. In homine constantia, fides, & animi magnitudo desiderabantur.
units.tr: Once the barons had been subdued, all would have been peaceful and quiet in England, except for the hatred of Hugh Despenser, whom the King made Earl of Winchester. When the Queen was sent to make peace with her brother, the King of France, together with her son Edward, she refused to return again. When the King had disinherited and outlawed her and her son, who was not yet fourteen years old, a war broke out that proved ruinous to the King himself. For the Queen, after a marriage had been arranged between her son Edward and Philippa, daughter of the Duke of Hainault, entered England with arms, with the help of the Duke of Hainault, to take vengeance on her husband the King. Many prelates and nobles joined her, because they could not bear the Despensers. Walter himself, always timid and cowardly of spirit, deserted the King in his most adverse affairs, and, pretending to serve him, secretly supplied money to the Queen. The King, reduced to such poverty by so many wars and papal exactions, lacked money in such a great danger and was forced to borrow two hundred and sixty pounds from the papal collectors of Peter's pence, when he ought himself to have had plenty. Now, with armies on both sides ready to fight, contrary edicts were issued on each side. The King proscribed the Queen; she proscribed the Despensers, Robert de Baldock the Chancellor, and the Bishop of Exeter the Treasurer. In this tumult the citizens of London seized the Chancellor and Treasurer by force. They killed the former, shut up in chains in the New Gate of London, by hunger and sickness; the latter, once captured, they pursued, struck down and tore apart. The Despensers, both at last seized, were put to death with other nobles. The King, almost a fugitive, hid in Wales. Meanwhile, through Archbishop Walter, who utterly deserted the King, Edward, the King's son, was made king and crowned at Windsor. Shortly afterwards James Berkeley, the elect Bishop of Exeter, was consecrated by the same Walter at the Queen's command. The Pope, who had reserved to himself the appointment to this bishopric, consumed by fear and anger, rebuked this Archbishop with such bitterness that, weary of life after he had sat for thirteen years, nine months and twenty days, he breathed out his soul in great sickness, and was buried in the south choir wall at Canterbury. In prosperous times he was fairly moderate and even-tempered; but in adversity his spirit was very weak and abject, and almost nothing. He gave the manor of Caldecote, with the wood of Thorlehot, to the convent of Christ Church, Canterbury. The royal prohibitions, which then flowed frequently from the royal criminal court through inexperienced judges without the Queen's knowledge, he annulled and broke, not so much by authority as by law itself and by consultations held on the basis of equity. In the man, constancy, faith and greatness of spirit were lacking.

units.la: L. SIMON MEPHAM.
units.tr: L. SIMON MEPHAM.

units.la: Ortuo vt diximus Archiepiscopo Waltero, Ecclesiasticarum rerum potestas, & Archiepiscopalis authoritas, penes Priorem & Conuentum Cantuariensem remansit. Hi omnem iurisdictionem in vniuersam Cantuariensem prouinciam Commonacho cuidam suo Galfrido de Eton commiserunt. Sed Londinensis tunc Episcopus huic commissioni se acriter opposuit, quod ex veteris cuiusdam compositionis inter Conuentum Cantuariensem, & suffraganeos quondam initæ forma apparuit. Conuentum duos viros idoneos ad munieris designare, & Londinensi Episcopo Cantuariensis Prouinciæ decano præsentare debere, e quibus vnus a Londinensi Episcopo approbandus, & Priori atque Monachis iurisdictionem eorum authoritate suscipiendam remittendus fuerat. Itaque Conuentus duos nominabat, illum quem dixerat Galfridum, & Hugonem de sancto Iuone, Monachos Cantuarienses ambos. Ex his Galfridus a Londinensi Episcopo approbatus est, accepitque à Conuentu Cantuariensi Ecclesiasticam iurisdictionem plenam, præterquam in his rebus quæ Archiepiscopali sede plena, Archiepiscopi authoritati essent reseruatæ. Postea conuentus Cantuariensis in Episcopalibus sedibus vacantibus officiales seu spiritualitatis custodes collocauit. Sed Decanus & Capitulum Exoniensis Ecclesiæ aliquandiu restiterunt, donec minatoriis Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ literis pro sua Iurisdictione scriptis cesserunt, & Adamum Murimutensem ( de quo in Waltero antea diximus, ) gratis atque æquis animis Cantuariensi vacante tandem spirituali iurisdictionis in Exoniensi diœcesi vacante custodem admiserunt. Inde huc usque præsuluit Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis per totam Prouinciam Archiepiscopatu vacante æqualis ac par Archiepiscopali potentia. Erat eo tempore Prior Cantuariensis quidam Henricus, vir vt existimari conuenit, minus rerum viu, quam iure ipsoprudens, tutiusque Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ vacante sede quod ab antecessoribus suis neglecta videbatur, explorator sedulus atque sagax, tum in gerendis Ecclesiæ rebus assiduus atque solers. Hic paucis mensibus omnem illam intermediam iurisdictionem ante intermissam plene exercuit atque renouauit. De Clericis ad Ecclesiastica beneficia præsentandis & patronorum iure diligenter inquisiuit, electiones confirmauit, intestatorum bona administrandi commisit, prouocantium appellationes recepit, testamenta actis insinuauit, ab executoribus & administratoribus rationes exegit, inter quos maxime Episcoporum defunctorum testamentorum executores, aut bonorum administratores interpellauit. Ita vt Iohannis Peckâ (vt in eius vita diximus) testamentum exequetes ad rationes reddendas coegit. Adhæc visitauit, procurationes percepit, Synodu celebrauit, Clerum ex mandato regio ad Parliamentum citauit, contumaces & in suam iurisdictionem committentes pœnis coercuit, beneficiavacantiu sediu cotulit ad hæc capas choreales, annulos & sigilla a singulis Cant. provinciæ suffraganeis Cant. Eccl. vendicavit, omniaque ad Archiepiscopale iurisdictionem per singulas species tam exquisite exercuit, vt nihil fuerit prætermissum præter Episcoporum consecrationem, quam cum sua authoritate peragere non poterat, Episcopo Londinensi mandauit & iniunxit, vt is suffraganeis Cantuariæ in Christi Ecclesia die quodam statuto congregatis, Meneuensem & Bangorensem Episcopos tunc electos & sua authoritate confirmatos consecraret. Quibus sic consecratis in testimonium & fidem consecrationis literas conuentus sigillo sigillatas dedit. Exercitata hoc modo & agnita Cantuariensis conuentus sede vacante potestate scriptis ad Regem literis petierunt nouum Pontificem eligendi potestatem. Qua impetrata in patrem suum & Patriarchatus honorem elegerunt Simonem Mepham factæ Theologiæ professorem, canonicum Cicestrensem & in Ecclesia cathedrali Laudauensi præbendarium, nec non Rectorem de Tunstall. de cantio oriundum, virum sacrarum literarum in illo vt putabatur sœculo peritissimum. Cuius electionem cum Rex approbasset, Prior Henricus & Conuentus Cantuariensem veritine Papa electionem illam refermederet, prouisionisque titulo alium Archiepiscopum crearet, nuncios Auinionem, vbi Papa cum sua tunc curia mansit, mittunt. His ampla procuratoria suo nomine singula gerendi, & ne pecunia deficeret, quantumcunque vellent mutuum usque ad ducentas marcas sterlingorum Romæ sub Hypotheca omnium suorum bonorum contrahendi dederunt, ea lege & conditione vt electionem Simonis Mepham à Papa coroborari obtinerent. Is tandem donis superatis electionem confirmauit, & Simonem Auinione consecrauit. Accepta autem à Papa consecratione ad Prouinciam regendam reuersus est.
units.tr: After Archbishop Walter died, as we have said, the power over ecclesiastical affairs and the archiepiscopal authority remained with the Prior and Convent of Canterbury. They entrusted all jurisdiction over the whole province of Canterbury to a certain monk of theirs, Geoffrey of Eton. But the Bishop of London at that time strongly opposed this commission, on the ground that the form of an old agreement, once made between the Convent of Canterbury and the suffragans, showed that the Convent ought to nominate two suitable men for the office and present them to the Bishop of London, as dean of the province of Canterbury. One of them was to be approved by the Bishop of London and then returned to the Prior and monks, to receive their jurisdiction by his authority. Accordingly the Convent nominated two men: the Geoffrey already mentioned, and Hugh of St Ives, both monks of Canterbury. Of these, Geoffrey was approved by the Bishop of London and received from the Convent of Canterbury full ecclesiastical jurisdiction, except in those matters which were reserved to the authority of the archbishop when the archiepiscopal see was filled. Afterwards the Convent of Canterbury set up officials, or keepers of the spiritualities, in the episcopal sees that were vacant. But the Dean and Chapter of Exeter resisted for some time, until they yielded to threatening letters written by the Church of Canterbury concerning its jurisdiction; and they at last admitted, with good grace and fair minds, Adam of Morimuth (of whom we spoke earlier under Walter) as keeper of the spiritual jurisdiction in the diocese of Exeter, which was vacant. From then until now the Church of Canterbury has presided throughout the whole province, with power equal and on a par with that of an archbishop while the archbishopric is vacant. At that time there was a Prior of Canterbury named Henry, a man who, it was thought, was more skilled in the law than in practical affairs, but a diligent and sagacious guardian of the Church of Canterbury's interests during a vacancy, which his predecessors seemed to have neglected; and he was also busy and capable in managing the affairs of the Church. In a few months he fully exercised and revived all that intermediate jurisdiction, which had been dropped for some time. He diligently inquired into the presentation of clerics to ecclesiastical benefices and into the right of patrons; he confirmed elections; he committed the administration of the goods of those who died intestate; he received appeals from those who brought them; he had wills entered in the acts; he exacted accounts from executors and administrators, and above all he called to account the executors of the wills of deceased bishops, or the administrators of their goods. Thus he compelled those who were executing the will of John Pecham (as we said in his life) to render their accounts. Besides this, he made visitations, received procurations, held a synod, summoned the clergy to Parliament by royal command, punished by penalties the contumacious and those who trespassed on his jurisdiction, and conferred the benefices of vacant sees. In addition, he claimed for the Church of Canterbury the copes, the choir vestments, the rings and the seals from each of the suffragans of the province of Canterbury. He exercised the archiepiscopal jurisdiction in every particular so carefully that nothing was omitted except the consecration of bishops, which he could not perform on his own authority. He instructed and ordered the Bishop of London to gather the suffragans of Canterbury on a fixed day in the church of Christ, and there to consecrate the Bishops of Menevia and Bangor, who had been elected and confirmed by his authority. When they had been consecrated, the Convent gave them letters of testimony and proof of consecration, sealed with the convent's seal. Having thus exercised the power of a vacant see of Canterbury and recognised it as the Convent's, they petitioned the King in writing for the power to elect a new archbishop. This was granted, and they elected, as their own father and the honour of the Patriarchate, Simon Mepham, professor of theology, canon of Chichester and prebendary of the cathedral church of Llandaff, and also Rector of Tunstall, a native of Kent, a man who, as was then thought, was most learned in the sacred letters of that age. When the King approved this election, Prior Henry and the Convent of Canterbury, fearing that the Pope might reject that election and create another archbishop by provision, sent envoys to Avignon, where the Pope then remained with his court. They gave these envoys ample powers to act in their name in every matter, and, lest money should run short, authority to borrow at Rome as much as they wished, up to two hundred pounds sterling, pledging all their goods as security, on the condition and agreement that they should obtain the Pope's confirmation of Simon Mepham's election. At last the Pope, overcome by their gifts, confirmed the election and consecrated Simon at Avignon. Having received consecration from the Pope, Simon returned to govern his province.

units.la: Ac primum cum (vt in Ioanne Peckam antea diximus) canonicatus præbendain Ecclesia Lugdinensi Cantuariensi sedi Archiepiscopali fuerat in perpetuum asscriptus, ad eius fructus percipiendos procuratorem Richardum quendam de Solbury Eboracensis diœcesis Clericum constituit, sicut ex infra scripto procuratorio, quod vt de iure dicti canonicatus liquere posset inseruimus, patet.
units.tr: And first, since (as we said under John Pecham) a prebend in the Church of Lyons had been assigned in perpetuity to the archiepiscopal see of Canterbury, he appointed as procurator to receive its fruits a certain Richard of Solbury, a clerk of the diocese of York; as is clear from the following letter of procuration, which we have inserted so that the right of the said canonry might be made plain.

units.la: Omnibus ad quos præsentes literæ peruenerint, Simon permissione diuina Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus totius Angliæ Primas, salutem in Domino sempiternam. Noueritis vniuersitas vestra quod nos facimus & constituimus procuratorem nostrum nostrum dilectum nobis in Christo M. Richardum de Solbury Eboracensem diœcesis Clericum, ad petendum & recipiendum fructus, redditus, prouentus, & obuentiones quascunque munerii nostri de Quinceraco Lugdunensis diœcesis, aulam etiam, ædificia siue munerium nostrum infra claustrum Ecclesiæ Lugdunensis situata, necnon emedas & satisfactiones debitas pro damnis datis in eisdem, & tractandum & componendum & transigendum super eisdem fructibus, redditibus, damno, & emendis, & ad agendum & defendendum pro eisdem, & ad locandum & arredandum dicta munera, & ædificia & pensionem recipiendum pro eisdem, & ad liberandum & acquietandum soluentem, necnon adiurandum de calumnia & veritate dicenda, & omnia facienda quæ de iure necessaria fuerint in præmissis vel opportuna, etiam si mandatum exigant speciale. Dantes eidem Procuratori potestatem alium procuratorem substituendi, & eundem revo-
units.tr: To all to whom these present letters come, Simon, by divine permission Archbishop of Canterbury and Primate of all England, sends eternal greeting in the Lord. Know, all of you, that we make and appoint as our procurator our beloved in Christ, Master Richard of Solbury, clerk of the diocese of York, to demand and receive the fruits, rents, revenues and all dues of our manor of Quincey in the diocese of Lyons, and also the hall, buildings or manor of ours situated within the cloister of the Church of Lyons, and likewise the fines and satisfactions due for damage done in them; and to treat, compound and settle concerning those fruits, rents, damage and fines; and to sue and defend on their behalf; and to let and lease the said manors and buildings and receive the rent for them; and to release and acquit the payer; and also to require the oath of calumny and of telling the truth, and to do all things which by law shall be necessary or fitting in the premises, even if they demand a special mandate. We give the same procurator power to substitute another procurator and to revoke him whenever it seems expedient to him. For the same procurator and for any substitute of his we promise that the matter shall be held valid and the judgment paid, with all its clauses, as a guarantee to all whom it concerns. In witness of this matter our seal is appended to these present letters. Given at Wingham, on the sixth of the Ides of March, in the year of the Lord 1328.

units.la: T candi quotiescunque sibi videtur expedire. Pro eodem etiam procurat. & substituen do ab eodem rem ratam haberi & iudicatum solui cum omnibus suis clausulis promitti mus, omnibus quorum interest cautionem. In cuius rei testimonium sigillum nostrum praesentibus est appensum. Datum apud Wingham vi. Idus Martii. Anno Domini, Millesimo Trecentesimo Vicesimo Octavo.
units.tr: ...as often as it seems expedient to him. For the same, we also promise, for all whom it concerns, that the procurator and the substitute be held valid and the judgment be paid with all its clauses. In witness whereof our seal is appended to these presents. Given at Wingham, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the year of our Lord one thousand three hundred and twenty-eight.

units.la: Postea Londini Regina m Philippam Edwardi iii. coniugem coronauit, deinde Concilium prouinciale reuniuit, in quo iura quaedam vt a seruitibus uperis in diebus Paraseceues, animarum, & Conceptionis ceflaretur, & de iurisdictione, ac bannorum matrimonialium editione condidit. Inter quae Oxoniense illud de appellationibus adhenditis tantum sententiis interponendis decretum tanquam inuanum fuisse.
units.tr: Afterwards, at London, he crowned Queen Philippa, wife of Edward III. Then he reassembled the provincial council, in which he drew up certain laws: that works and services should cease on the days of the Parasceve (Good Friday), of the Souls (All Souls), and of the Conception; and laws concerning jurisdiction and the publication of matrimonial banns. Among these, the Oxford decree that appeals be lodged only against definitive sentences was treated as useless.

units.la: Haec iura in Prouincialibus singulae constituti onibus adhuc descripta feruantur. In eodem Concilio totius Cleri consensu excommunicati sunt omnes, qui Walteri Stapleton Exoniensis Episcopi trucidationis, (de qua in Waltero Archiepiscopo antea diximus) operam vel consilio rei fecerunt. Id quod Polidorus a Iohanne Stredford factum esse incerte autumat, dum plus aequo hilaris ac facetus Simonem Mepham Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem fuisse oblitus sit. Hic annus Papas congeminauit. Nam dum curia papalis esset Auinione, exortus est Romae Antipapa Petrus de Corbario ordinis minorum fratrum. Qui instigante & adiuuante Lodouico Bauariae Duce in Regem Romanorum electo, sed a Papa repulso, a Romanis ciuibus receptus, Cardinales, ac eiusmodi Romanae curiae ministros creauit. Deinde Lodouicum contra alterum papam interdictum Regem Romanorum in ipsa Romana ciuitate, a qua alter papa diu exulauerat, coronauit.
units.tr: These laws are still preserved in the Provincials, under their individual headings. In the same council, with the consent of the whole clergy, all were excommunicated who had a hand in or gave counsel to the murder of Walter Stapleton, Bishop of Exeter (of which we spoke earlier, under Archbishop Walter). Polydore uncertainly asserts that this was done by John Stratford, a claim made with more than due cheerfulness and wit, since he forgot Simon Mepham, Archbishop of Canterbury. This year doubled the Popes. For while the papal court was at Avignon, the antipope Peter of Corvara, of the order of Friars Minor, arose at Rome. At the instigation and with the help of Louis, Duke of Bavaria, who had been elected King of the Romans but was rejected by the Pope, he was received by the Roman citizens; he created cardinals and such ministers of the Roman curia. Then he crowned Louis King of the Romans in the Roman city itself, against the other pope, whom he placed under interdict, and from which that other pope had long been exiled.

units.la: Ideoque alter alterum maledictis, & dirs illis iolitis censuris fulminaris exceratus est. Tandem hic Romanus Papa potentia & viribus impar, ab illo Aumionensi vi pote valentiori superatus, deliciis sui veniam petiit, Papatu se abdicauit, & absolutus ad fratres in gnominiose recessit. Paulo post Rogerus Sarisburiensis & Iohannes Ba honiensis Episcopi in Anglia iuorui sunt. Ac Sarisburiensis Eccl. Praesulem Papa Roberto quendam de Wimbledon, virum non modo indoctum, sed inuenustum prouisionis praetextu creauit.
units.tr: Hence each cursed the other with curses and with the dire censures customary for such matters. At last this Roman pope, unequal in power and strength, was overcome by that Avignon pope, the stronger. He sought pardon for his offences, abdicated the papacy, and, absolved, withdrew ignominiously to the friars. Shortly afterwards, the bishops Roger of Salisbury and John of Bath died in England. And to the church of Salisbury the Pope, under the pretext of provision, appointed one Robert of Wimbledon, a man not only unlearned but also unattractive.

units.la: Sed in Bathoniensi Episcopatu Radulphus quidam de Salopia electione asumptus, citoque antequam Papa de vacatione compertum, per Simonem Archiepiscopum confirmatus & consecratus est. Quod cum Papa cognouisset citationibus & edictis Rhodulphum, longe ex sua curia dilationibus vexauit. Tandem tamen de curia Romana se redemit, vt rata essent facta de ipso non fine magna pecunia quantitate. Iam enim illa de Episcopatibus prouidendis Papalis consuetudo ad immoderatam licentiam excrescebat.
units.tr: But in the diocese of Bath, a certain Ralph of Shropshire was chosen, and before the Pope learned of the vacancy, Archbishop Simon confirmed and consecrated him. When the Pope found out, he harassed Ralph with summonses and edicts, and with long delays away from his court. In the end, however, Ralph bought his way out of the Roman court, so that what had been done concerning him might stand, at no small cost in money. For already that papal custom of providing to bishoprics was growing into unrestrained licence.

units.la: Vt Episcopatus in Anglia nullus vacaret, cui ille ante prioris Episcopi mortem de successore longe ante non prouidisse contenderet. Ita & eligendi iura violauit, & Episcopatus pro suo arbitrio imperitioribus plerumque conluit. Ac priores Papae modum fa lem in hac prouidendi iniuriosa licentia aliquem retinuerunt. Sed isti pollerioresiustitiae finibus ab Anreceforibus suis semel violatis, modum in iniuria nullum probant, sed de omnibus fine discrimine prouidere coeperunt. Atque vt plerumque euenire solet, vt omniatum ad ruinam vergant, cum ad summum perducta sunt: hic haec Papalis prouidendi impetas quae omnem iam modum excesserat, legibus (vt post dicetur) a Rege Eduardo Tertio laris tandem repressa & coercita est. Ipsumque Pontificale culmen quod supra Deum honesque eleuatum est, iam tandem ( vt ex sequenti historia patebi:) ad exitium paulatim inclinare & deduci labentibus annis coepit. Sed vt de his, pulsionibus dicamus, quae tum importune sibi Papa vendicauit, simul atque hic Simon Mepham Archiepiscopatum ingressus est, Thomas Cobham Episcopus Wigorniensis (de quo in Waltero antea diximus) obiit, ad quem Episcopatum Adamum Herefordensem prouisionis praetextu transtulit, tum Herefordensi Ecclesiae de quodam Thoma Charleto prouidit. Quid enim in transferendis & conferendis Ecclesiis prouisionis vsurpato titulo Papa, si ei permissa diuinus libere facultas fuisset, efficere in quocunque regno non potuisset. Literas autem ad Simonem de illa prouisione scriptas duximus inserendas, vt liquere omnibus possit, quanta impudentia eam sibi vendicauit.
units.tr: So that no bishopric in England should be vacant, he claimed to have provided a successor long before the death of the previous bishop. Thus he violated the rights of election and largely gave bishoprics to the less capable, as he pleased. The earlier popes did retain some moderate limit in this injurious licence of providing. But these later ones, once their predecessors had broken through the bounds of justice, show no limit in wrongdoing, and began to provide to everything without distinction. And, as usually happens, when things have reached their height they tend towards ruin. Here this papal assault of providing, which had now exceeded every limit, was at last checked and restrained by laws (as will be said later) enacted by King Edward III. And the papal pinnacle itself, which had been raised above God and honours, now at last (as will appear from the following history) began gradually to lean towards destruction and to be brought down as the years slipped by. But to speak of these provisions, which the Pope then claimed for himself without any right: as soon as this Simon Mepham entered the archbishopric, Thomas Cobham, bishop of Worcester (of whom we spoke earlier in the account of Walter), died. To that bishopric he transferred Adam of Hereford under the pretext of provision, and then to the church of Hereford he provided one Thomas Charlton. For what could the Pope not bring about in any kingdom in transferring and conferring churches, under the usurped title of provision, if the divine permission had freely granted him that power? We have thought fit to insert the letters written to Simon about that provision, so that it may be clear to all how shamelessly the Pope claimed it for himself.

units.la: EX REGISTRO CANTVARIENSI EPISTO- LARVM ECCLESIAE TEMPORE Simonis Mepham. Fol. 46.
units.tr: FROM THE CANTERBURY REGISTER OF LETTERS OF THE CHURCH IN THE TIME OF SIMON MEPHAM. Fol. 46.

units.la: Iohannes Episcopus, Seruus seruorum Dei, Venerabili fratri Archiepisc. Cantuariensi salutem & Apostolicam Benedictionem. Ad cumulum tuae credit salutis & famae, si personas Ecclesiasticas praesertim Pontificali dignitate praeditas diras diuinæ propitiationis intuitu opportuna præsidii & fauoris gratia prosequaris. Nuper siquidem vacante Ecclesia Hereford. pro eo quod nos Venerabilem fratrem nostrum Adamum Wigornienfem,olim Herefordenfem Episcopum,tunc & adhuc apud sedem Apostolicam constitutum, à vinculo quo eidem Herefordensi Ecclesiæ tenebatur, de fratrum nostrorum consilio,& Apostolicæ potestatis plenitudine absoluentes,ipsum ad Ecclesiam Wigornienfem tunc vacantem duximus transfetendum, præficiendo eum illi in Episcopum & Pastorem. Nos itaque attendentes quod nullus præter nos de ordinatione ipsius Ecclesiæ Herefordensis poterat, pro eo quod nos diu ante huius vacationem Ecclesiæ Herefordensis prædictæ prouisiones omnium Ecclesiarum Cathedralium tunc vacantium & vacaturarum in posterum, per translationes per nos tunc temporis factas, & ex tunc faciendas de Prælatis eorum ad alias Ecclesias tunc vacantes & non antea vacaturas dispositioni nostræ duximus reseruandas. Decernendo extunc irritum & inane, si secus super his per quoscunque quauis auctoritate scienter vel ignoranter contingeret attentari. Depræsiciendo eidem Herefordensis Ecclesiæ, ne prolixæ vacationis expendetur incommodis, personam valentem ac etiam fructuosum per cuius industriam studiosam salubriter posset regi ac dirigi, & etiam feliciter ac vtiliter adaugeri, cogitare cœpimus diligenter, & post deliberationem quam cum eisdem fratribus nostris super hac detentam habere curauimus in dictum filium Thomam de Charleton electum Herefordensem Canonicum Eboracensem in sacerdotio constitutum, luris ciuilis professorem, virum quidem pruit ex testimoniis fide dignis accepimus vitæ munditia redimicum, decorum, elegantia morum, discretionis, & consilii maturitate conspicuum, aliarumque multiplicium virtutum vtilis insignitum, aciem direximus nostræ mentis, quibus omnibus debita meditatione pensatis de persona eiusdem Thomæ electi eidem Herefordensi Ecclesiæ de fratrum prædictorum consilio authoritate Apostolica duximus prouidendum,ipsumq; illi perfecimus in Episcopum & Pastorem, curam & administrationem illius sibi tam in spiritualibus quàm in temporalibus plenariè committendo. In eo,à quo vniuersorum charismatum donaperueniunt confidentes, quod prædicta Ecclesia Herefordensis per ipsius electi diligentiæ studium fructuosum, clementia sibi opitulante diuina votiua honoris & commodi suscipiet incrementa. Vt igitur idem electus in commissio prædictæ Herefordensi. Ecclesiæ sibi facilius proficere valeat, tuus fauor eidè fore nosca[n]tur plurimum opportunus fraternitatem tuam rogamus & hortamur attente, per Apostolica tibi scripta mandantes quatenus prædictos electum & Ecclesiam Herefordensem habens pro nostra & dictæ sedis reuerentia propensius commendatos, in ampliandis & conseruandis iuribus suis & ipsius Ecclesiæ eundem electi tui fauoris præsidio prosequaris, quod ipsetuo fultus auxilio in commisso sibi Ecclesiæ Herefordensis prædictæ regimine se posse vtilius exercere, tuq; diuinam misericordiam & beneuolentiam dictæ sedis exinde valeas vberius promereri. Dat. Auinion. vii. Kal. Octobris pontificatus n ostri anno 12.
units.tr: John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the Archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing. It adds greatly to your salvation and reputation if, for the sake of divine mercy, you show timely protection and favour to ecclesiastical persons, especially those endowed with pontifical dignity. Recently, when the church of Hereford was vacant, we absolved our venerable brother Adam, formerly bishop of Hereford and then bishop of Worcester, who was then and still is at the apostolic see, from the bond by which he was tied to the church of Hereford. With the counsel of our brothers and the fullness of apostolic power, we decided to transfer him to the church of Worcester, which was then vacant, and placed him there as bishop and pastor. Therefore, considering that no one but ourselves could dispose of the church of Hereford, since long before this vacancy we reserved to our own disposition the provision of all cathedral churches then vacant or to become vacant in future, through translations of their prelates to other churches made by us at that time and to be made hereafter, and decreed that anything attempted otherwise in these matters, by anyone and under any authority, knowingly or ignorantly, shall be void and null: wishing to provide the church of Hereford, lest it suffer the inconveniences of a long vacancy, we began carefully to consider a person who was strong and also fruitful, through whose zealous diligence it might be healthfully ruled and directed and also happily and usefully increased. After deliberation, which we took care to hold with our said brothers on this matter, we turned the eye of our mind to our son Thomas de Charlton, elect of Hereford, canon of York, a priest, a professor of civil law, a man whom we have learned from trustworthy testimonies to be adorned with purity of life, decorous, elegant in manners, conspicuous for discretion and maturity of judgement, and distinguished by many other useful virtues. Having weighed all these things with due reflection, we decided, by apostolic authority and with the counsel of the aforesaid brothers, to provide this elect Thomas to the church of Hereford, and we made him its bishop and pastor, committing to him the full care and administration of it, both in spiritual and temporal matters. Trusting in him from whom all gifts of grace come, we hope that the church of Hereford, through the zealous diligence of the elect and with the help of divine clemency, will receive fruitful increases of honour and advantage. So that the said elect may the more easily make progress in the charge committed to him over the church of Hereford, we attentively ask and exhort your brotherhood, commanding you by these apostolic letters, that you hold the said elect and the church of Hereford more favourably commended to you for the reverence due to us and to the said see, and that you support the elect with the protection of your favour in extending and preserving his rights and those of the church itself, so that, aided by your help, he may be able to exercise more usefully the governance of the church of Hereford committed to him, and you may thereby deserve more abundantly the divine mercy and the goodwill of the said see. Given at Avignon, 7 before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth year of our pontificate.

units.la: Necminus in Episcopatibus quam in pecuniis prouidendis sedulus hic Papa suit.Cum enim in Lodouicum Imperatorem electum, & Romanam Regem ab Antipa (vt diximus) coronatum, bellum suscipiendum decreuerat, fructus beneficiorum vacantium quadriennio sibi reseruauit. Quos cum in Anglia iuflu nutuque suo, vt solebat obtinere non poterat, saltem vt prædam cum Rege participaret, eos Regi vit perbenignus & liberalis concessit. At Simon Mepham Archiepiscopus, in cuius tempora hæc & eius generis alia inciderunt, cum mitem, & benignam naturæ (vt existimabatur) suæ indolem quam siue sibi simulate finxerat, siue origine sua acceperat, penitus deposuerat, iam in Monachos Cantuarienses quorum gratiam ex humili loco in Archiepiscopatum prouectus est, & in totam Cantuariensem prouinciam, iurisdictionis suæ vi ac potestate fretus, nimium elatus tandem excidit. Monachos Cantuarienses de terris aliquis prædictis suis primum lacessiuit. Ab his ad Papam prouocatus est. Papa vt ex minimis tunc solebat notiore negociis eo tempore Lehetium quendam de Concoreto suum in Angliam Wallia Hibernia, atque Scotia non Legatum (Id enim Reges se inconsultis antea vetuere,) sed nuncium misit, illiique hanc litem inter Archiepiscopum & Monachos definiendam commisit. Ille suscepta cautæ cognitione suæ iure, siue iniuria Archiepiscopum in causa principali damnauit, deinde expensas litis septingentis libris eadem sententia æstimauit, quas comminatis illis soluere die perbreui statuto, nisi eas ipso facto subire velit, mandauit ac præcepit. Hanc diram sententiam ab illo Papæ nuncio nequam, hic noster Mepham haud satis æquo animo ferre potuit. Sed quid aut contra Papæ nuncii, aut contra Monachos qui præualuerunt ageret. Ab hisitaque fractus & debilitatus, multo maiora amens adortus est. Namqueab infirmis victus voluit cum valeotioribus contendere. More antecessorum totam Cantuariensem prouinciam statuit visitare. In qua incepta visitatione Parlamentum à Rege convocatum est. Eoque inchoato Cleri Concilium sub Archiepiscopo celebratum Londini. Aquo Concilio spreto Archiepiscopo ilico decessum est, rebus nullis nea Rege quidem imperatis aut solicitatis gestis. Hoc finito Cócilio visitationem Metropoliticam iterum suscepit. Ab ea Iohannes Grandisonus tunc Exoniensis Episcopus ad Papam, vt eius visitationem saltem aliqua mora retardaret, appellauit. Erat hic quoque Iohannes Grandisonus origine Caotius, & familiaris Simonis Mepham, sed eius iurisdictionem vel spreuit, vel formidauit, cui cum iure noo potuit, tamen vt potuit ad Papam appellando obstitit. Cum itaque in illa visitatione Simon Mepham Roffensem, Cicestrensem, Sarisburiensem, & Bathoniensem Wellensemque diocæses Metropolitica visitatioe secutus transfisset, & Exoniensem visitaturus, ogredi vellet, Iohannes Exonienfis eum militari manu prohibuit. Cumq; Archiepiscopus armis cum Exoniensi congregati statuit, re Regi nuciaia literis Regiis reuocatus, infecto visitationis negocio ex illa dioecesi turpiter & ignominiose recessit. Ex hac visitationis repulsa, & superiori illa Monachorum in iure victoria animo deiectus iocidit in ægritudinem. Et cum domi rediens esset in itinere in oppido quodam Magfeld febri letali coniracta. 12. Octobris obiit. Sedit annis quinque, mensibus sex, diebus 12. Habuit hic Archiepiscopus in Cantuariensi prouincia ex sua patria, nempe Cantio sex suffraganeos Episcopos. Nempe Iohannē Grandisonum Exoniensem, qui eum ægritudine & furore ad mortem (ut dixi-mus) perculit. Stephanum Gravesend Londinensem, Henricum Borowashe Lincolniensem, Thomam Cobham Wigorniensem, Richardum Swinfeld Herefordensem, & Hamonem Roffensem. Corpus autem Simonis. 7 kal. Nouemb. Cantuariam deductum, & marmorea tumba inclusum sepulchro traditum est, ex parte aqnilonari Capellæ Anselmi quondam Cant. Archiepiscopi.
units.tr: Nor was this Pope less zealous in providing money than in providing bishoprics. For when he had decided to undertake war against Lewis the Emperor, elected, and King of the Romans, crowned by the antipope (as we said), he reserved to himself for four years the revenues of vacant benefices. When he could not obtain these in England by his command and nod, as he was accustomed to do, he at least, so as to share the spoil with the King, most graciously and liberally conceded them to the King. But Archbishop Simon Mepham, in whose time these and other things of that kind happened, had entirely cast off the mild and kindly disposition of his nature (as was supposed), which he had either feigned for himself or received from his origin. Now he turned against the monks of Canterbury, by whose favour he had been raised from a humble position to the archbishopric, and against the whole province of Canterbury, relying on the power and force of his jurisdiction; and at last, too elated, he fell. He first attacked the monks of Canterbury over some of their lands, and from them he was called to the Pope. The Pope, as was then customary even in rather minor matters, sent to England, Wales, Ireland and Scotland a certain Lehetius of Concoret, not as legate (for the kings had earlier forbidden this without consultation) but as a messenger, and committed to him the decision of this dispute between the Archbishop and the monks. He, having taken up the cognizance of the case, whether rightly or wrongly, condemned the Archbishop in the principal matter; then by the same sentence he assessed the costs of the suit at seven hundred pounds, which he ordered and commanded to be paid within a very short fixed time, under threat, unless the Archbishop were willing to incur them by the very fact. Our Mepham could not well bear this harsh sentence of the Pope's messenger with composure. But what could he do against the Pope's messenger, or against the monks who had prevailed? Broken and weakened by these, he madly attacked much greater matters, for, overcome by the weaker, he wished to contend with the stronger. Following the custom of his predecessors, he resolved to visit the whole province of Canterbury. In the course of this visitation, which was begun, a Parliament was summoned by the King; once it had begun, a council of the clergy was held at London under the Archbishop. The Archbishop, scorning this council, at once withdrew, nothing having been done either at the King's command or at his solicitation. When this council was finished, he again undertook the metropolitan visitation. From it John Grandisson, then bishop of Exeter, appealed to the Pope, in order to delay at least somewhat his visitation. This John Grandisson was also a Kentishman by birth and a familiar of Simon Mepham, but he either scorned or feared his jurisdiction; and since he could not resist it by right, he resisted as far as he could, by appealing to the Pope. So when, in that visitation, Simon Mepham had passed through the dioceses of Rochester, Chichester, Salisbury, Bath and Wells, and wished to go into Exeter to visit it, John of Exeter forbade him with an armed force. When the Archbishop decided to come against the Exeter men with arms, he was recalled by royal letters, the King having been informed; and, the business of visitation left undone, he withdrew shamefully and ignominiously from that diocese. From this rebuff of his visitation, and from that earlier victory of the monks in law, he was cast down in spirit and fell into sickness. While returning home, in a town called Mayfield, he contracted a deadly fever and died on 12 October. He sat for five years, six months and twelve days. This archbishop had in the province of Canterbury six suffragan bishops from his own country, namely Kent: John Grandisson of Exeter, who struck him down to death with sickness and rage (as we said); Stephen Gravesend of London; Henry Burghersh of Lincoln; Thomas Cobham of Worcester; Richard Swinfield of Hereford; and Hamo of Rochester. The body of Simon, brought to Canterbury on 7 before the Kalends of November and enclosed in a marble tomb, was laid in the sepulchre on the north side of the chapel of Anselm, formerly Archbishop of Canterbury.

units.la: LII. Iohannes Stratford.
units.tr: LII. John Stratford.

units.la: Æpè vsu venire solet, vt hi quorum vita recta & cum virtute maxime coniuncta, & laude illustris, & præmiis honoribusque aucta, periculisque aditis, laboribusque multis suscepti optimè de Republica merita fuerit, dum in suspiciosa ac maledica multitudine insidias quæ ab obtrectatoribus intenduntur, vitare non possunt, extrema discrimina ac dimicationes fortunarum atque vitæ sentiant. Huiusrei conspicuum speculum vt aliquam præbuit Iohannes Stradford, cuius solida cum virtute parta laus, in Aula, loco sane lubrico & fallaci, inuidiæ, criminationibus quæ obiecta, nisi cum summa tolerantia, prudentiaque sæpè cautissel, summum sibi exitium interitumque attulisset. De cuius gente atque patria nihil accepimus. Ideoque ab ipsa institutione, primo in Rempublicam & Ecclesiâ ingressu demonstrandus nobis est. Iuri ciuili atque Canonico adolescens operam dedit. In quibus paucis annis doctus atque prudens euasit. deinde famæ celebritate notus, ad Lincolniensem Archidiaconatum spirauit, quum iurisdictionem cum prudenter diligenterque aliquandiu administrasset, a Waltero Archiepiscopo, de quo antea diximus, Almæ curiæ Cantuariensis de Arcubus London. Decaous & officialis præfectus est. In quo gerendo Magistratu non minus iuriperitiam, quàm rerum multarum intelligentiam, & acrem atque acutam in diiudicandis & definiendis litibus perspicaciam declarauit. Ita ingenio in eo tam fœlici, & tam singulari doctrina exculto cognito, Regis Edwardi 2. intimis consiliis adhibitus, eiusque Secretarius fuit. Cuius legatione, cum ad Iohannem Papam Romæ fungeretur, & Wintoniensem Episcopatum morte vacantem, Rege inconsulto Waltcri Archiepiscopi intercessione atque gratia prouisionis titulo ab eodem Papa adeptus est. Quæ res ei magnas molestias atque turbas primò generauit. Namque Robertus Baldock Regni (vt diximus) Cancellarius, Regi Edwardo 2. charus, Wintoniensem episcopatum tunc ambiuit. Quo à Iohanne Stratford intercepto, confingere atque comminisci omnes rationes cœpit, quibus Iohannem Stratford Episcopum Wintoniensem in omnium odium atque inuidiam traduceret. Ipse Iohannes Strarford, quodam die dominico, in cuius missa (vt ex more pontificio consuetum est) cantabatur versus, Atul-
units.tr: It usually happens that those whose lives are upright, closely joined with virtue, distinguished by praise, enriched with rewards and honours, and who have undertaken dangers and many labours and deserved very well of the commonwealth, nonetheless suffer the gravest perils and the greatest struggles for their fortunes and their lives, because among a suspicious and slanderous crowd they cannot avoid the snares laid by their detractors. A conspicuous mirror of this was John Stratford, whose solid praise, won by virtue, was indeed exposed at court, a slippery and deceitful place, to envy and to accusations. Unless he had often been very careful, with the greatest patience and prudence, this would have brought him the utmost ruin and destruction. We have received nothing about his family or his country. So we must set him out from the very beginning, from his first entry into the commonwealth and the Church. As a young man he devoted himself to civil and canon law. Within a few years he became learned and prudent in these. Then, known for his widespread reputation, he aspired to the archdeaconry of Lincoln. After he had administered that jurisdiction prudently and diligently for some time, Walter the Archbishop, of whom we spoke before, appointed him dean and official of the Court of Arches of Canterbury in London. In carrying out this office he showed not only his skill in law but also his understanding of many affairs, and a keen and sharp insight in judging and deciding suits. Thus, his talent being so happy and his learning so singular and cultivated, he was known to King Edward II, who admitted him to his innermost counsels and made him his secretary. While he was acting on an embassy at Rome to Pope John, the bishopric of Winchester fell vacant by death. Without the king's consultation, through the intercession and favour of Archbishop Walter, he obtained it from the same Pope under the title of provision. This matter first brought him great troubles and disturbances. For Robert Baldock, the chancellor of the realm (as we said), dear to King Edward II, was then seeking the bishopric of Winchester. When John Stratford had got it before him, Baldock began to invent and contrive every scheme by which he might bring John Stratford, bishop of Winchester, into the hatred and odium of everyone. One Sunday, while the verse was being sung in his mass (as is customary in the papal manner), John Stratford himself, struck as if by a prophecy, said that nothing remained for him in the rest of his life but troubles. (The text breaks off at the opening word of the verse.)

units.la: Ex Epist. Rich. Dun. te tribulationes inflorum &c. consecrationem Episcopalis muneris pethibetur accepit fe. Eo que quasi vaticinio pereulsum dixisse: Nihil sibi praeter molestias in reliqua vita superesse. Necfallus quidem est. Nam praedictus Robertus Baldock, qui non minus gratia, quam suatione Regem hue illuc Bedere atque impellere solebat, simulatque Iohannes episcoporum getere coepit, eum proscribi, & episcopatus praedia in Rogis custodiam tradi, ac ab eius visibus sequestrati procurauit. Tum variis cum edictis in ius vocauit, quibus propositis cum Iohannes metu delituisset, nec in ius venisset, novo & atrocissimo edicto promulgarunt, ne quis Iohannem aedibus aut hospitio exciperet, eiue alimenta ministraret, aut quocunque homine aut commercio cum eo contraheret. Has extrumnas anno toto satis moderate tolerauit. Tandem Walterus Archiepiscopus cum l'apaleueris Iohannis causam deprecantibus Regem adiit, & fuit in Iohanneim tantopere commouit animi, tantaque seuitiae causas requirit. Rex omnia se Roberto Baldock Cancellario suadente statuisse respondit, quoniam Wintoniensis Episcopatus, qui peuerat, & ad Papam pro Roberto scripserat, Iohanni se ignaro collatus esset. At Walterus eam tum fuisse Papam in prouidendis episcopatibus consuetudinem multis exemplis docuit, quae si Regi non probaretur, tamen quia tam diu impune a Rege tolerata sit, vt in totum denceps edicto aut lege vetaretur, nec tam graviter in Iohannem viro docto & prudenti sine exemplo animadverteretur, periit. Itaque Walteri oratione Rex Iohannem in gratiam recepit, & iuramento ab eo de fide in Regem gerenda praestito, praediaEpiscopatus exteraq; ablata iura restituit. Non ei tam amplius in Regis gratiam reducto Cancellarii aut cuiusuis maleuolentia potuit obesse. Nam Rex perspecta eius in quibusdam quas obierat legationibus gratitate atque prudentia, & inimis iuis consiliis adhibuit, & iummis gerendis Regni negotiis praepositus: quae tanta fide & solertia administrauit, vt Regem in maxima & exiuola, sicut in Walterò ante diximus, pericula atque discrimina adducto, & a suis Consiliarius, ipsoque Walterò Archiepiscopo, cui piurimum considebat deserto, Iohannes tamen ab eo non discederet, nec adueric parti adhaereret, donec tacito quodam Reginae & Rogeri Mortimeri sui Consiliarii iudicio neci adiudicatus, atque huc illuc ad latebras quaerendas diu actus est. Tandem Edwardo secundo mortuo, & Spenseris ac Reginae adueriariis supplicio delectis cum mihi in Iohanneim Strafford criminari potuissent, praeterquam quod cum Edwardus secundus à suis Consiliariis proditus ac proiectus esset, hic solus summo studio & integritate fidus permansit, non modo in magnam Reginae, & Edwardi Tertii Regis gratiam receptus, sed Regio summo tribunali Cancellarius praefectus est. Deinde Simone Mephà Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi mortuo, Rex Papam literis rogauit, vt Archiepiscopatum Iohannis Stratford conferret. Quo cognito Prior & conuentus Cantuariensis eundem in suo Archiepiscopum postularunt, de necessitate facientes virtutem. Papa cum Edwardi Regis desiderio in Iohannem Stratford concessisset, in rebus alienis pluribus gratificandi voluntatem Romano exemplo declarauit. Nam cum ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum Iohannem a Wintoniensi Ecclesia transtulisset, Adamum de Orleton Wigorniensem Episcopum, intercedente Rege Franciae, ad Wintoniensem Episcopatum tradu40 xit. Id quod Edwardum Regem Angliae, qui literis proaio interceffetat, nec ferre poterat, vt Franciae Rex quem suspectum habebat, in sui regni obtinendis Episcopatibus tantum proficeret, temporalia omnia huic papali Episcopo Wintoniensi detrahere mouit: eoque magis quod hic Adamus in legationibus quas ad Regem Franciae subiisset, Franciae magis quam Angliae Regi obsequendo maiorem dedisse operam suspicabatur. Sed paulo post in Parliamento Londini habito, Rex ei Clero petente reconciliatus temporalia restituit. In quo Parliamento Rex obtenta ope pecuniaria à Clero atq; populo expeditionem in terram sanctam vnà cum Rege Galliae se suscepturum promisit. Ad eam rem Iohannes Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus ad Papam & Franciae regem, vt certus illius suscipiendae militiae dies statueretur, missus est. In eo itinere a Iohanne Papa pallio 50 um sibi Hammone Roffensi Episcopo nuncio missum accepit. Tum eiusdem Iohannis Papae ad quem missus erat, morte nuciata, illius in terram sanctam expeditionis infecto negocio rediit Cantuariam, vbi in festo Dionysii solita specie atque pompa intronizatus est. Deinde Cantuariensem Ecclesiam, ciuitatem, atque diocesim visitauit. Hierofolomitana autem expeditio quae ab Angliae, Franciaque Regibus coniunctis copiis erat capessenda, à Franciae Rege tes novas in Angliam moliente impedita est. Itaque Benedictus papa illas sexennales decimas in eum vsum à Clero ante concessas percipi vetuit, perceptas autem restitui his qui eas soluissent mandauit. Verum in Anglia cum bellum à Gallo, expectaretur, ea decima in cathedralibus Ecclesiis reposita, Regi ipsi ad sum-
units.tr: From the letter of Richard of Dunstable: when he had received the consecration of the episcopal office, he is said to have declared, as if by a prophecy, that nothing remained for him in the rest of his life but troubles. Nor was this a false prophecy. For the aforementioned Robert Baldock, who was accustomed to drive and push the king hither and thither no less by favour than by persuasion, as soon as John began to exercise the functions of a bishop, arranged for him to be proscribed, for the episcopal estates to be handed over to the king's custody, and for him to be cut off from his revenues. Then he summoned him to court by various edicts. When John, through fear, went into hiding and did not appear, they issued a new and most savage edict forbidding anyone to take him into their house or lodging, to supply him with food, or to have any dealings or contact with him. He bore these hardships for a whole year with fair moderation. At last Archbishop Walter, with the prelates pleading John's cause, went to the king, and with great difficulty he moved the king's mind and asked the reasons for such cruelty. The king replied that he had decided everything on the advice of Robert Baldock the chancellor, since the bishopric of Winchester, which had fallen vacant, and for which Robert had written to the Pope, had been conferred on John without his knowledge. But Walter showed by many examples that it had then been the Pope's custom to provide bishoprics in this way; and even if this did not please the king, yet since it had been tolerated with impunity by the king for so long, it should not be forbidden altogether from now on by edict or law, nor should a man learned and prudent be punished so severely as John without precedent. Accordingly, at Walter's plea the king received John back into favour, and, once John had sworn an oath of loyalty to the king, he restored the estates of the bishopric and the other goods that had been taken away. Once he was restored to the king's favour, no malice of the chancellor or of anyone else could harm him any more. For the king, having observed his integrity and prudence in certain embassies he had undertaken, both took his counsel and placed him over the highest affairs of the realm. He administered these with such loyalty and skill that, although the king had been brought into the greatest and most dangerous perils and difficulties, as we said above with respect to Walter, and although the counsellors and Archbishop Walter himself, on whom he had relied most, had deserted him, John nevertheless did not leave him, nor did he join the opposing party. Until, by the tacit judgement of the queen and of Roger Mortimer, her counsellor, he was condemned to death and was driven for a long time hither and thither seeking hiding places. At last, when Edward the Second was dead and Spenser and the queen's adversaries had been chosen for execution, they could bring no charge against John Stratford, except that, when Edward the Second had been betrayed and cast off by his counsellors, he alone remained loyal with the greatest zeal and integrity. He was therefore received not only into the great favour of the queen and of King Edward the Third, but was also appointed chancellor of the supreme royal tribunal. Then, when Archbishop Simon Mepham of Canterbury had died, the king asked the Pope by letter to confer the archbishopric on John Stratford. When the prior and convent of Canterbury learned of this, they demanded the same man as their archbishop, making a virtue of necessity. The Pope, granting John Stratford at King Edward's desire, showed his willingness to oblige in other people's affairs after the Roman example. For when he had transferred John from the Church of Winchester to the archbishopric of Canterbury, he moved Adam de Orleton, bishop of Worcester, to the bishopric of Winchester at the intercession of the King of France. Edward, King of England, who was already angry at the letters that had intervened, could not bear that the King of France, whom he regarded with suspicion, should gain so much influence in securing bishoprics in his own kingdom; so he moved to strip this papal bishop of Winchester of all his temporal goods, the more so because he suspected that Adam, in the embassies he had undertaken to the King of France, had shown more zeal in obeying the King of France than the King of England. But shortly afterwards, in a Parliament held in London, the king was reconciled to him at the request of the clergy and restored his temporalities. In this same Parliament, having obtained a financial contribution from the clergy and the people, the king promised that he would undertake an expedition to the Holy Land together with the King of France. For this purpose John, Archbishop of Canterbury, was sent to the Pope and to the King of France, so that a definite day for undertaking that campaign might be fixed. On this journey he received from Pope John a pallium, sent to him through Hamo, bishop of Rochester, as nuncio. Then, when the death of Pope John, to whom he had been sent, was announced, and the business of the expedition to the Holy Land had come to nothing, he returned to Canterbury, where on the feast of St Denis he was enthroned with the usual display and pomp. Then he visited the Church of Canterbury, the city and the diocese. The expedition to the Holy Land, which the Kings of England and France had been going to undertake with their forces combined, was hindered by the King of France, who was planning new wars against England. Accordingly Pope Benedict forbade that those six-year tithes, previously granted by the clergy for that purpose, should be collected, and ordered that those already collected should be returned to those who had paid them.
