But in England, since war with the French was expected, that tithe was deposited in the cathedral churches and was given to the king himself, for warlike purposes, with the consent of the clergy. For when the Frenchman had interceded for the Scots, whom King Edward had recently attacked, he secretly plotted with them, having made an agreement, to make war on the King of England. units.la: An.1335 ptus bellicos Cleri consensu donata est. Nam Gallus cum pro Scotis ab Edwardo Rege iàpe oppugnatis intercessisset, clam sedere cum illis inito, bellum Angliæ Regi inferre itaque. Cuius sedens & apparatus suspicione olfacta, Edwardus ob pacem confirmandam Episcopum I. inculentiem multis comitatum proceribus, ad Gallum legavit. Cuius mandatis dedit, ut Gallum a pace auersi insequitur, adiret Lodovicum Imperatorem, ut cum eo, aliisque Germaniae principibus summæ coniunctionis foedera paciscerentur. Lincolnensis autem Episcopus ex Regis præcipitio, simulatque Galli simulatem perspexisset, sue ius cum Lodovico & Germanis fecit. Hoc pacto foedere, Rex cum Iohanne Stradford Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo quem prudentiæ & fidei plenum cognouerat, de hoc bello Gallico consilium capit. Is quia Gallus eum indicta causa ro sa prouocauerat, nec oblatas pacis æquissimas conditiones accipere voluerat, suadet vt in hoc bello ad quod lacessitus erat, gerendo Regnum Franciæ iure hæreditario, & cognationis proximitate ad se spectare vindicaret. Itaque vt ad perpetuum huic administrando bello suppeditandum subsidium Clerum, populum, omnesque sui Regni ordines summa alacritate excitaret. Deinde ut in militum delectu copiosum exercitum ex viris ad pugnam valentioribus, & Ducibus in re militari peritioribus confiaret. Quo comparato & cum omni militari copia instructo, ut fœcialibus ad Gallum missis Regnum Franciæ ubi reddi peteret, aut bellum denunciaret. Tum vt sine mora traiecto exercitu Gallum aggrederetur, monuit. Sese enim curaturum, vt absente Rege Reipublicæ recte administraretur, & neque pecunia nec alia quacunque ad belli 10 cos visus necessaria Regi in castris in pscindi occupato defuit. Quo consilio nihil tam illustri & magnifico Regi optatius esse potuit. Missi iheo fæciales, & bellum indictum est. Totaiam Anglia atque Gallia magno tumultu laborabant: aliaque regna fama & celebritate tanti belli in variis expectationes adducta sunt. Papatam bello quam pace recipecuniariæ studens, ad Angliæ Franciæque Reges misit duos Cardinales. Hi virtusque Regnis peragratis cum pacem cociliare nequiuissent, amplissimam procurationem percipendarum a Papa sibi in utroque Regno datam potestatem ostenderunt. Cuius vi cum multis execrationibus atque diris de singulis libris solidum extorserunt. His legatis iam ditatis atque saturis, Poeta quidam Anglus tunc temporis, hæc carmina de Romana cupiditate lepide confinxit:
units.tr: An. 1335 ...ptus bellicos: with the consent of the clergy it was given. For the Frenchman, having interceded for the Scots, whom King Edward had earlier attacked, secretly made an alliance with them and prepared to make war on the King of England. When this plotting and preparation was smelled out by suspicion, Edward, to confirm the peace, sent the Bishop of Lincoln, accompanied by many nobles, as envoy to the Frenchman. He instructed him that, while urging the Frenchman to withdraw from the peace, he should go to Emperor Louis so that they might make a most close alliance with him and the other princes of Germany. The Bishop of Lincoln, by the king's command, as soon as he had seen through the Frenchman's pretence, made his own treaty with Louis and the Germans. By this agreement the king, having found in John Stratford, archbishop of Canterbury, a man full of prudence and loyalty, took counsel with him about this French war. Since the Frenchman had challenged him without cause and had refused to accept the most equitable terms of peace offered, Stratford advised that in this war, into which he had been provoked, he should claim the kingdom of France as his by hereditary right and by proximity of kinship. Therefore, to furnish a permanent supply for carrying on the war, he should rouse the clergy, the people, and all the orders of his realm with the greatest eagerness. Then, in levying soldiers, he should form a large army of men most fit for battle and of commanders most skilled in war. When this had been arranged and the army fully equipped, he should send heralds to the Frenchman demanding that the kingdom of France be surrendered, or else declare war. Then he advised him to cross over with the army without delay and attack the Frenchman. For Stratford himself would see to it that, while the king was absent, the commonwealth was properly administered, and that neither money nor anything else necessary for the conduct of war would be lacking to the king, who was occupied in the camp. Nothing could have been more desired by the king than this plan, so splendid and magnificent. Heralds were therefore sent, and war was declared. All England and France were in great turmoil, and other kingdoms were stirred into various expectations by the fame of so great a war. The Pope, being more eager for money than for war or peace, sent two cardinals to the Kings of England and France. When these had travelled through both realms and could not bring about peace, they showed that the Pope had given them very ample authority to collect procurations in each kingdom. By virtue of this, with many curses and dire threats, they wrung a full pound from each book. Now that these legates were enriched and sated, a certain English poet of that time wittily composed these verses on Roman greed:

units.la: Roma capit marcas, bursas exhaurit & arcas.
units.tr: Rome takes marks, empties purses and chests.

units.la: Vt tibi tu parcas, fuge Papæ & Patriarchas.
units.tr: That you may spare yourself, flee the Pope and the Patriarchs.

units.la: Edwardus autem Angliæ Rex paratis iam copiis antequam exercitum traiecisset, Parlamentum tenuit in quo Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis Concilio Cleri celebrato Regi decimam triennalem a Clero concedi obtinuit. Subsidio iam comparato Rex exercitum in Flandriam classe deduxit. Omnemregni curam & gubernationem Archiepiscopo commisit. Ad Imperatorem Lodouicum Coloniæ agentem tendit. Ibi renovatum fœdus nuper ictum fuit, & Edwardus totius Impetu Vicarius a Ludouico subsitutus est. In primo horum principum conspectu mirari se dixit Lodouicus, cur Edwardus Angliæ Rex cæterorum Regum more non se prostraret ad sui Imperatoris pedes. Cui 30 responsum est. Angliæ Regem cæteros in hoc anteire Reges quod in sacratione vnctus sit. Renouata itaque & confirmata tam honorifica pactione Edwardus ad exercitum quem Antuerpiæ locauit, redit. Franciam hostiliter inuadit, ad Papam cum a bello revocantem deiure suo in Francia hæreditario scribit. Interea in Anglia Rep. negocia a Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo, bellica vero a Sarisburiensi Comite qui Scotis strenue resistit, gerebantur. Sub quæ tempora Stephanus Londinensis Episcopus obiit, in cuius locum Richardus de Bintworthe electus est, qui Ottefordiæ Iohanne Archiepiscopo confirmarus, eiusque iussu a Ciceftrensi Episcopo Lamethei consecratus fuit. Deinde duobus tributis suæ annis in hoc Gallico bello transfactis euenit vt Rex pecunia celeritet egere cœpit. Qua destitutus, & pene in ipso Martis discrimine enerustus Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum de sua pollicitatione qua se de nummis toto bello parandis prouisurum promisserat, interpellat, Archiepiscopus mirari se aut tantam pecuniam quæ in multos annos suffecturaesset, vno aut altero anno obliguriri posse. Tum hortat literis Regem vt malos consiliarios, thesauri sui exhaustores, & pecuniarum profusores a se remouevet. Intantis enim hisque bellicis negociis adhibendos Regi viros assiduos, frugi, atque cautos, pecuniamque nisi modus & summa cautio adhibeatur, facile dissipari solere. Eodemque tempore Lodouicus Imperator fœdifragus ad Edwardum Angliæ Regem imperiose scripsit, vt litem & controuersiam de posito bello suæ dilucidationi diffudicatione permitteret. Quod cum Edwardus renuisset, Lodoulcus Imperii Germanici Vicarius munus violatis & spretis fœderibus reuocauit. Sed Edwardus nihilominus in bello contra Gallum suscepto acriter & animose perstitit, donec Papa, quem Gallus huius belli exitum sibi perniciosissimum fore perumelcens muncrib. præoccupauit, internecio suasionibus & minis tam ad Regem ipsum quam ad Archiepisc. Cantuariensem ictipiisset, vt a bello desisteret, iisque iudicio non vi atque Marte componeret. Archiepiscopus qui huius belli suasor fuerat, cum & tributis & Romanis depraedationibus exhaurirt atque labefactari Regni vires perspexerat, vt tunc in illa Pontificia dominatione Pontificibus magis quam Regibus parebant, & Papæ sententia iam pa-
units.tr: King Edward of England, with his forces now ready, before he had crossed over with his army, held a Parliament. In it the Archbishop of Canterbury, after a council of the clergy had been held, obtained for the King a triennial tenth to be granted by the clergy. With this subsidy now secured, the King led his army by ship into Flanders. He committed the whole care and government of the kingdom to the Archbishop, and went to meet the Emperor Louis, who was staying at Cologne. There the covenant lately struck was renewed, and Edward was appointed Vicar of the Empire by Louis. At their first meeting Louis said he wondered why King Edward of England did not, as other kings did, prostrate himself at the feet of his Emperor. To this it was answered that the King of England surpassed the other kings in this respect, that he had been anointed at his consecration. So, with that honourable compact renewed and confirmed, Edward returned to the army he had stationed at Antwerp. He invaded France by force, and wrote to the Pope, who was calling him back from the war, asserting his hereditary right to France. Meanwhile in England civil affairs were managed by the Archbishop of Canterbury, and military affairs by the Earl of Salisbury, who vigorously resisted the Scots. About this time Stephen, Bishop of London, died, and Richard de Bintworth was elected in his place. He was confirmed at Otford by Archbishop John, and by his order was consecrated at Lambeth by the Bishop of Chichester. Then, after two years of this French war had passed, it happened that the King began to run short of money. Lacking it, and almost worn out at the very crisis of war, he called the Archbishop of Canterbury to account for his promise that he would provide the money needed for the whole war. The Archbishop replied that he was surprised that so great a sum, which should have sufficed for many years, could be squandered in a year or two. Then he urged the King by letter to remove from himself bad counsellors, the exhausters of his treasury and the squanderers of his money. For in such serious military affairs the King ought to employ men who are diligent, thrifty and cautious, since money, unless measure and the greatest caution are applied, is wont to be easily dissipated. At the same time the Emperor Louis, a breaker of covenants, wrote imperiously to Edward, King of England, ordering him to submit the dispute and controversy over the war he had begun to his judgement. When Edward refused, Louis, as Vicar of the German Empire, revoked the office, the covenants having been violated and scorned. But Edward nonetheless persisted fiercely and resolutely in the war he had undertaken against the French. Then the Pope, whom the French, fearing that the outcome of this war would be most ruinous to them, had anticipated with gifts, sent exhortations and threats to the King himself and to the Archbishop of Canterbury, urging them to desist from the war and to settle the matter by judgement rather than by force and arms. The Archbishop, who had been the adviser of this war, when he saw that the kingdom's strength was being exhausted and weakened by taxes and Roman plunder, and since in that papal domination men obeyed Pontiffs rather than kings, the sentence of the Pope had now begun to become the author of

units.la: cis auhor esse coepit. Id non minus Rex indigne tulit, quam regni procerescet cum Marte lupetior esse posset, iâ Archiepiscopo deficiete, & cessante abeo quod proniserat à leguma Gallicanæ hæreditatis vendicatione, ad inquisitionem cum Gallo pacem initus & inglorius cogeretur. Omnium iam oldium Archiepiscopus ex hac inconstantia, & mutatione consilii incurrit. Intet hos Henricus Lincolniensis Episcopus & Galfridus Scroope miles, Regis iustitiarius, occulto quodam diuque simulato in Archiepiscopum odio, Regem atrocius incendunt, eum prodictionis, & cum Gallis coniuratio-nibus, leisque maeleatis insimulant. His criminationibus, & rerum in castris necessariarum inopia motus Rex Angliam clam ingreditur, mediaque nocte in turrim Londinensem ne minimo quidem de aduentu eius rumore sparso deductus est. Ibi confiiunt inititum est, tandemque definitio ut Archiepiscopus, & Episcopus Cicestrensis Regni Cancellarius, & Couentrensis Thesaurarius, vna cum aliis a satellitibus & hostibus deprehensi ad pubhcam cultodiam rerum a Ie abiene Rege gestarum rationem reddituri ducerentur. Mane accedunt Satellites Lamechum. Sed Archiepiscopo ea prodicte decesserat, tum Londinii rcuerti Couentrensem & Cicestrensem Episcopos cum aliis designatis capiunt. Captos ad turrim deducunt. Hoc peruulgato Archiepiscopus Cantuariam feitinat. Eum Nicolaus Canielupo miles à Rege missus sequitur, qui adducto secum quodam lohane Farindon Notario publico, vt gesta cum Archiepiscopo in actainferret, Archiepiscopus Regis nomine monuit, vt quoniam is tantinarinis mercatoribus sub bonorum suorum hypotheca atq; pignore sese obligassit, de peeunijs reddendis quas Rex ad bellicos vsus mutuos lumpliset: Cumque Rex pecuniis de quibus perceperat in eo summam fidem collocauerat frustratus negocia bellica intermisisset, Regiusque exercitus cum Regni proceribus in castris, rebus in militia necessariis egerent, vt pecuniam illam aut statim creditoribus in foro transmarino respondurus in Flandriam traiceret, & sese in ipsorum custodiam traderet, donec totum aeris pro quo se obltrinxerat, esset dissolutum. Hoc explicato nuncio Milesprælicate tabellione responsum petiit. Archiepiscopus deliberandum detanius rebus antequam respondetur, ait. Discedit illico Miles. Iam Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus cum nou modo fortunarum ied vitæ atque capitis obiectum sibi crimen animadvertisset, cum Rege multis 40 hinc inde scriptis literis egit, vt consiliatios sibi faniores adhiberet, vt ab adulatoribus, & alienæ vitæ detractoribus caueret, nec bellum foris gesturus pacem domi perturbaret. His literis aliisque suasoriis modis, cum Regem pacare non potuisset, coepit de integritate atque fide tam in Regem quam in Regnum sua populo efugsgestu prædicare. Itaque Cantuariæ in Ecclesia Metropolitica conuocata Cleri, populique concione, hoc Themaex scripturis propositum. Non permittit Principem & potentia nemo vicit illum. &c. In ealongo variogo sermone, Thomam Cantuariensem quondam Archiepiscopum qui à secularibus negocijs ad Ecclesiæ regimè sese traduxisset, laudauit. Ipse autem ie vituperauit, quod omissa Ecclesiæ cura, in rebus Regiis procurandis totus & assiduus fuerat. Guius rei precium seob suaïn Regem & Regnum metita in inuidiam & capitis discri20 men adducto iustissime pertulisse, cum lachrymis testatus est. Deinceps autè in Ecclesia regimine se vigilantiorem fore promisit. His peroratis Articulos quosdam excommunicationum, quibus à se viim Regiam prohibere voluit, illo tetro & immani more Pontificio accensis & extinctis candelis, campanisque pulsatis edidit. In his articulis excommunicati sunt omnes qui pacem & tranquillitatem Regis aut Regni periurbarent, laïci qui violentas manus Clericis attulerint, qui in eorum prædia, ædes aut bona inuaderint, qui immunitatem Ecclesiasticam violauerint, qui libertates in magna charta Baronibus concessas aliquamac hinatione detraxerint, qui crimina falla in quempiam confinxerint, maxime vero quicunque Archiepiscopum vel suæ prouinciæ Episcopum quemcunque in Regis odium aut iram traxerint, cùm vel eos proditionis aut culpa quam famosi & capitalis iudicii reos falso dixerit. His in Ecclesia Cantuariensi publicatis articulis, mandauit Episcopo Londonensi, cuncti-sque Provinciae suae fidelibus, ut in suis ecclesiis atque diocesibus eosdem promulgarent. Rex vt Archiepiscopum fulminantem compesceret, Londinensi Episcopo scripsit, de bellum tam anceps atque varium Archiepiscopo suadente pro iure suo & haereditate suscepisse, eum tam qui author belli fuerat, cum hostes suos Franciae Regi conspiralle, ac vt tantis tot tamque tam varius ratis fuit vt vt iure...
units.tr: peace. The King took this no less ill. Since he could have had the upper hand in the war, the Archbishop was failing him and withdrawing from what he had promised about the claim to the French inheritance, the King was forced to make an inglorious peace with the French king. Now the hatred of everyone fell upon the Archbishop because of this inconstancy and change of plan. Meanwhile Henry, Bishop of Lincoln, and Sir Geoffrey Scrope, the King's justiciar, who harboured a secret and long-feigned hatred of the Archbishop, inflamed the King still more savagely, accusing him of treason, of conspiracy with the French, and of other crimes. Moved by these accusations and by the lack of necessary supplies in the camp, the King entered England secretly and, with no rumour of his arrival spread, was brought in the middle of the night to the Tower of London. There a plan was made, and at last it was decided that the Archbishop, the Bishop of Chichester, the Chancellor of the realm, the Treasurer of Coventry, and others should be seized by the henchmen and enemies and led into public custody, to render an account of the affairs conducted while the King was absent. In the morning the henchmen came to Lambeth, but the Archbishop had already left, so they seized the Bishops of Coventry and Chichester, with others who had been designated, in London, and led them to the Tower. When this became widely known, the Archbishop hurried to Canterbury. Sir Nicholas Canteloupe, sent by the King, followed him, bringing with him one John Farindon, a notary public, so that he might record the proceedings with the Archbishop. In the King's name the knight warned the Archbishop that, since he had bound himself, with the mortgage and pledge of all his goods, to certain merchants, he was to repay the money the King had borrowed for warlike purposes. Since the King, disappointed in the money on which he had placed full trust, had suspended the business of war, while the royal army and the nobles of the realm in camp lacked what the campaign required, the Archbishop was to either pay that money at once to the creditors in the foreign market, or cross over to Flanders and surrender himself into their custody until the whole debt for which he had bound himself was discharged. When this message had been set out, the knight asked the notary for a reply. The Archbishop said that the matter must be considered before he answered. The knight immediately departed. Now the Archbishop, perceiving that the charge laid against him concerned not only his fortunes but his life and his head, wrote many letters back and forth with the King, urging him to take wiser counsellors, to beware of flatterers and of detractors of other men's lives, and not to disturb the peace at home while waging war abroad. When he could not pacify the King by these letters and other persuasions, he began to proclaim, with an effusive gesture before the people, his integrity and loyalty both to the King and to the realm. And so, in the metropolitan church at Canterbury, a sermon was convened for the clergy and people, and this theme was taken from the Scriptures: "He does not allow a prince..., and no one has overcome him by power," etc. In this long and varied sermon he praised Thomas, formerly Archbishop of Canterbury, who had turned himself from secular affairs to the governance of the Church. He himself, however, blamed himself, because, neglecting the care of the Church, he had been wholly and constantly occupied with managing royal affairs. With tears he testified that he had most justly borne the price of this, since, on account of his loyalty to the King and the realm, he had been brought into odium and into danger of his head. Thereafter he promised that he would be more vigilant in governing the Church. When this peroration was finished, he published certain articles of excommunication, by which he wished to forbid violence against royal authority, with that foul and savage Papal custom of candles being lit and extinguished and bells being rung. In these articles were excommunicated all who disturbed the peace and tranquillity of the King or the realm; laymen who had laid violent hands on clergy; those who had invaded their estates, houses, or goods; those who had violated ecclesiastical immunity; those who had in any way withdrawn the liberties granted to the barons in Magna Carta; those who had fabricated false charges against anyone; and, above all, whoever had drawn the Archbishop or any bishop of his province into the hatred or anger of the King, by falsely calling them guilty of treason or of some fault of notorious and capital judgment. When these articles had been published in the Canterbury church, he ordered the Bishop of London and all the faithful of his province to proclaim them in their own churches and dioceses. To restrain the thundering Archbishop, the King wrote to the Bishop of London that he had undertaken so doubtful and changeable a war, at the Archbishop's urging, for his own right and inheritance; that he who had been the author of the war had conspired with the King of France, his enemies; and that, since so many things had been so variable... so that by right...

units.la: Poster venit ad Archiepiscopum Radulphus Baro de Stafford. Missus a Rege, qui adductus secum Iohanne Button aduocato & Iohanne Farrendon Notario publico, qui Regis nomine Archiepiscopum monuit, vt ad Regem sine more accederet, vt de hoc bello rebusque tam Angliam quam Galliam tangentibus vna cum exteris praelatis & magnatibus deliberare posset.
units.tr: Afterwards Sir Ralph Stafford, a baron, came to the Archbishop, sent by the King. He brought with him John Button, an advocate, and John Farrendon, a public notary. On the King's behalf he told the Archbishop to come to the King without delay, so that they could deliberate about this war and about affairs touching both England and France, together with the foreign prelates and nobles.

units.la: Cantuariensis autem de hac re deliberatorum respondit. Paulo post a Duce Brabantiae ex Flandria Legati Cantuariam venerunt, quibus cum Archiepiscopus sui copiam non fecisset, causam suae legationis in scriptis ad crucem excelsam extra portam Prioratus Cantuariensis affixis a meridie proponunt. Citati ac in ius vocati a Duce Brabantiae Iohannem Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum in Flandria de debitis Regis Angliae pro quibus obligatus extiterat, in iure responderet, ibidem moratus iuxta iuramentum in ea parte praestitum, donec Dominica debita plene fuerint persoluta.
units.tr: The Archbishop of Canterbury replied that he would deliberate on the matter. Shortly afterwards, envoys came to Canterbury from the Duke of Brabant in Flanders. Since the Archbishop would not give them an audience, they posted the reason for their embassy in writing, at noon, on the high cross outside the gate of the Priory of Canterbury. They also declared that the Archbishop of Canterbury, John, had been cited and summoned to court in Flanders by the Duke of Brabant, concerning the debts of the King of England for which he had become surety. He was to answer in law there, and was to remain in that place, according to the oath he had sworn on that point, until the debts owed to his lord had been paid in full.

units.la: In hac turba Rex dedit ad Priorem & Conuentum Cantuariensem literas, ad earum exemplum quas prius ad Londinensem Episcopum dederat scriptas, mandauit, vt publice coram populo atque Clero in Cant. recitarentur. Quibus allatis Prior & Conuentus Archiepiscopum certiorem faciunt, literas apertas ostenderunt. Is die cinetum aduocato populo atque Clero in Cant. Ecclesia fugge stum ascendit. In ea condicione de sua fide & integritate in regiis rebus gerendis multa dixit. Regis literas in quibus cum Rex multis probris exagitauit, publicari mandauit, cum singula crimina & conuicia diluit. Postea hanc ore editam responsionem in scriptis concepta per totam Cantuariensem provinciam publicauit. Ad eas tres replicauit, quas literas ex Stephano Byrchington qui solus eas commemorat, hic inserimus.
units.tr: In the midst of this turmoil, the King sent a letter to the Prior and Convent of Canterbury, a copy of the one he had earlier written to the Bishop of London, and ordered that it be read publicly before the people and clergy in Canterbury. When it was brought, the Prior and Convent informed the Archbishop and showed him the open letter. On that day, with the people and clergy of Canterbury gathered, he mounted the pulpit of the church. In that position he spoke at length about his loyalty and integrity in carrying out the King's affairs. He ordered the King's letter, in which the King had lashed him with many reproaches, to be published, and he refuted each charge and insult. Afterwards he had the answer he had given orally written out and published throughout the whole province of Canterbury. He replied to those letters three times. Stephen Birchington, who alone records them, is the source from which we insert them here.

units.la: EDwardus Dei gratia Rex Angliae & Franciae, & Dominus Hiberniae, Prior & Capitulo Cantuariensi salutem. Veteribus probatur historiis, & ex his quae quotidie geruntur clarius elucescit, quomodo multi bonitate Principum & honore qui in eos collatus est in superbia abutentes, nituntur interdum malitiae suae commentis Regum studia laudabilia depravare. Et vt manifestius quod dicimus cunctis fidelibus innotescat, vestra & eorum memoria non credimus exciditse, quod nos dudum in annis adolescentiae ad Regni solium exaltati, in eiusdem suscepto regimine, sanis consiliis dirigi cupientes, quia Iohannem tunc Wintoniensem, nunc veto Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum ... ximus onera debitorum: & sic retardata expeditione vlteriori coacti sumus ab inchoatis magnanimiter hostium aggressibus ea vice desistere & in Anglia remeare. Vbi expositis praefato Archiepiscopo nostris aerumnis multiplicibus, & infortuniis memoratis, conuocatoque super hoc Parlamento, Praelati, Proceres, caeteriqoe fideles eiusdem regni nostri, nonae partis garbarum, agnorum, & vellerum suorum, praeter decimam nobis a Clero concessam, tale nobis dedere subsidium, quod si fideliter collectum suisset congruo tempore, & obtentum ad expeditionem dictae guerrae, debitorum solutionem, & inimicorum confusionem, non modicum adminiculum praestitisset: & forte secundum moltorum opinionem verisimiliter suffecisset, Idem Archiepiscopus ad dicti subsidii culleCtionem & aliorum nobis necessariorum subministrationem iterum promisit interponere efficaciter partes suas. Vnde eius promissionibus inhaerentes, resumptis viribus nauigio ad hoc congregato versus Flandriam nauigantes, commisso graui bello nautico cum hostibus qui in nostram & totius gentis Anglorum perniciem procurauerant, misericordissima illius clementia qui ventis & mari imperat, non nostris meritis obtinuimus de tantorum hostium inumerosa multitudine victoriam & triumphum. Quo peracto cum pergrandi exercitu pro iurium nostrorum recuperatione progredientes exiode castrametati fumus prope ciuitatem fortissimam Tornacem, in cuius obsidione aliquandiu iugiter occupari, & continuatis expensis, & laboribus fatigati, praetolantes in silentio nobis promissum adiutorium. Sperabamus indies minister
units.tr: Edward, by the grace of God King of England and France and Lord of Ireland, to the Prior and Chapter of Canterbury, greeting. Ancient histories prove, and what happens every day makes it clearer, how many men, abusing the goodness of princes and the honour bestowed on them in pride, sometimes strive by the contrivances of their malice to corrupt the praiseworthy endeavours of kings. And so that what we say may become more plainly known to all the faithful, we do not believe that you or they have forgotten that we, raised to the throne of the realm in the years of our youth, and wishing to be guided by sound counsel in the government we had taken up, because John, then Bishop of Winchester but now Archbishop of Canterbury ... [the rest of the sentence is lost in the scan] ... we were compelled, with our expedition further delayed, to give up for that time the attacks on the enemy we had begun, and to return to England. There, after we had set out to the aforesaid Archbishop our many hardships and the misfortunes already mentioned, and a Parliament had been summoned on this matter, the prelates, nobles, and the other faithful of our realm gave us such an aid, over and above the tenth granted to us by the clergy, of a ninth part of their sheaves, lambs and fleeces, that if it had been faithfully collected in good time and obtained for the expedition of the said war, for the payment of debts and the overthrow of enemies, it would have given no small help; and perhaps, as many believed, it would have been sufficient. The same Archbishop again promised that he would effectively employ his efforts in collecting the said aid and in supplying us with other necessities. Relying therefore on his promises, we resumed our strength, sailed to Flanders in a fleet gathered for this purpose, and, after a great sea battle with enemies who had plotted the destruction of ourselves and of the whole English nation, we obtained a victory and triumph over their countless multitude, not by our merits but by the most merciful clemency of Him who commands the winds and the sea. When this was done, we advanced with a very large army to recover our rights, and encamped near the very strong city of Tournai. While we were kept for some time continually occupied at its siege, and worn out by continual expenses and labours, we waited in silence for the help promised to us. Day by day we hoped that the assistance of the said Archbishop would be revealed in such great and pressing needs of ours. At last, our hope having been frustrated, although we had fully made known through several messengers and various letters to the aforesaid Archbishop, and to our other councillors who adhered to him, our needs and the various dangers to which we were exposed on account of the lack of ...

units.la: rio dicti Archiepiscopi in tot & tanta nostris necessitatibus reuelari. Tandem spe concepta frustrati, licet per plures nuncios & diuersas literas plenc significaimus praefato Archiepiscopo, & aliis Consiliariis nostris sibi adhaerentibus, nostras indigentias & pericula varia quibus exposiri propter defectum promissi subsidii memorati vtilitatem semper & honorem quos ex successu pecuniae conspeximus, nos posse faciliter obtinere, nullum tamen ab eis emolumentum recipere potuimus, quia sua non nostra negocia curantes, & commoda propria procurantes friuolis excusationibus, & fucatis verborum phaleris suam desideriam (ne dicamus fraudem seu maliciam palliabant, similes illusoribus, qui (vt Esaias ait) deridendo ludificari diicentes. Mandas remanda, manda remanda, expectas recepetas, expectas modicum ibi, modicum ibi. Vnde proh dolor factum est vt dum triumphandi super inimicos nostros arridetur nobis gratiosissime spes prospiaqua, praeualente penuria cogeremur inuiti treugis inuitis consentire, cum verecunda nostrae expeditionis retardatione & exultatione non modica aemulorum. Reuersis igitur nobis in Flandriam, cum essemus pecunia vacui, & aeris alieni mole pressi, nec superesset quicquam in nostris vel nostrorum Marsupiis vnde possemus necessitatibus nostris consulere, & debita stipendia nostro obsequio militantibus erogare, compulsi sumus vsuraram voraginc nos immergere, & humeros supponere cumulatis oneribus debitorum. Tandem conuenerunt ad nos amici fideles peregrinationis nostrae comites, & tribulationis participes, cum quibus tractatum habuimus diligenter super optaris remediis, quibus a tanta infortunioram tempestate possemus commodius respirare. Visum est omnibus praefatae retardationis euentum tristabilem & egestatis nostrae incommoda multiplicia culpa vel desidia, ne dicamus malicia, praefati Archiepiscopi de cuius discretione tota Regni nostri dispositio pendete videbatur, & caeterorum officialium quos eius Consilio super Regni negocia constituimus accidisse, & vehementer iniuriantes, accusatis nostris mursuratis, super eo quod dictorum Archiepiscopi & officialium insolctiam Regia manstuetudo tanto tempore voluit incorrectam, suot publice protestati, quod nisi super his faceremus, congruum remedium celeriter adhiberi, oporteret eos le nostris obsequiis subtrahere, & ab limito foedere retroire. Et hoc vtiq; in regni nostri subuersionem, & nostram perpetuam ignominiam, & nationis Anglicanae perpetuum opprobrium redundare: quod anterat nostris temporibus Clementissimi patris benignitas, in cuius soliditate fixa est inniolabiliter anchora nostrae spei. Vnde nos addiciplinam & correctionem habuimus nostrorum Officialium mentis acie dirigentes quod sda ex eis quos ex causis probabilibus de mala administratione, iusticiae subuertione, ac subdiiorum nostrorum oppressione, acceptorum munerum corruptione, ac aliis offensis grauibus suspectos habuimus: a suis officiis fecimus prout nobis licuit amoueri: allos quoque inferioris gradus in praemissis culpabiles sub tua custodia detineri, ne illibertate solita potirentur, supplantaretur eorum afturia iusticiae executio, & deludereter callide inquisitio veritatis: quam cum ex dicti Archiepiscopi animi latebris eo certius & plenius elicere crederemus, quo nihil eorum quae ad informationem nostram in hac parte conferre poterant, ipsum verisimiliter latere debuerat, cuitotius Reipublicæ nostræ administrationem, & summam terum gerendarum à multo tempore duximus committendam, sibi per si-lelem nostrum Nicolaum de Cantelupo ad hoc specialiter destinarum mandauimus, quod ad nostram præsentiam, qui eius personali colloquio pertrui videbamur, Lon dinum venire maturius non tardaret. Ipse vero semper timidus in prosperis,& tumidus in aduersis, trepidus timore vbi non erat timor, mortis sibi periculum per aliquos nobis insistentes intentatum & comminatum, si ab Ecclesia Cantuariensi recederet immunere:minus veraciter allegauit: quia hoc teste Deo ex pura conscientia nunquam in mentem nostram cecidit: nec aliquis nobis insidentis vt credin us tetigit cogitatum, quanquam Clero & populo Regni nostri malignitatis suæ se merito reddidit odiosum. 10 Nos autem qui cundtos ad nostram præsentiam accedere volentes, piccipuè nostris ob hoc literis vel nunciis conuocatos plena volumus saturitate gaudere: ad conuincendā eius maliciam dilectum & fidelem nostrum Radulphum de Stafford hospitii nostri Senefchallum, ad ipsum destinauimus, vt ei securum conductum offerret, & faceret Regias nihilominus literas patentes sigillo nostro consignatas ei secimus præsentari, iteraro mandantes quod ad nos personaliter accederet, solicitudinem nostram informaturus super nostris negociis,quæ longo tempore gesserat, vt verò præcum & mandatorum nostrorum lenitate contempta, vultus& animo indignatio rispondit,quòd se nostris conspectibus seu colloquiis nequaquam conferret,nisi in pleno Parliamento,quod his diebus ex causa rationabilibus nullatenus expedit conuocari. 20 Sed quia idem Archiepiscopus quem Regalis benignitas beneficiis & honoribus magnificis ampliauit, & in suæ familiaritatis sacratiũ & vnanimitatem amicitiæ,& vinculum fœderis accersuit, super quem sicut patrem charißimum totus noster spiritus & animus requieuit. qui euam dum eius volũtatibus per omnia acquieuimus, sophisticæ dilectionis faciem suæ mendacis beneuolentiæ palliatam in ore patris amabilis nobis prætendere consueuit, subiro in vtrumonerofum grauem & crudeliter est conuersus: & beneficiis acceptis ingratus, timoris arrogantia benefactorem persequitur: & illam nobis retributionem impendit quam vulgariter proverbium dicit. Mus in pera. Serpens in gremio: Ignis in sinu,suis consueuerunt hospitibus exhibere. Nam licet in no 30 bis ad Regale fastigiũ iure hæreditario diuina cooperante gratia sublimatis detestabile semper sit & fuerit abuti potentiæ magnitudine, qui summis desideriis affectamus clementia & lenitate cum moderamine iusticiæ gubernare subiectos, vt oprara cundis mortalibus pace fruantur,opem tamen nostram innocentiam,ac consiliarium, & officialium nostrorum Regalem iusticiam persequentium fidelitarem & diligentiam conutitis lacerat publice prædicando: & suis literis parentibus in diuersis partibus publicari mandando,quod potestate Regia modernis temporibus cõtra iusticiam opprimitur populus,Clerus confunditur,& Ecclesia varijs exactionibus colleciis, & tallijs pregrauatur. Et quia nomen boni pastoris quo hactenus semper caruit,cum sit reuera iuxta communem opinionem & confessionem propriam (vt publice ferrur) emissam notorie mercenarius,fallaciter vsurpare. Fucaium zelum vulpinæ callidit atis fuco perizomare palliatum,ad liberationem Ecclesiæ cuius vexationis si quas in rebus vel personis nostro tempore sustinuit præsati Archiepiscopi duntaxat remissioni & callidis adinuentionibus, ac reprobris consiliis sunt veraciter ascribenõr, nequiter simulat se habere, & quasdam excommunicationis sententias in libertatis Ecclesiasticæ,& magnę chartæ violatores in genere dudũ latas, ad sigillandũ opiniõne Regiã & præfatos ministros, Regios defamandos, ac seditionem in populo nobis commisso proditorie suscitandum, & deuotionem comitum,procerum,& magnatum Regni nostri, Maiestati Regiæ subir.hedum, specificatis nonnullis articulis propter & contra solitum modum in consilio prouinciali traditum mandauit per suas litteras in locis pluribus insignibus publicari. Quamobrem nos 50 volentes ( vt tenemur ) tamen statu famæ nostræ prospicere , & prafati Archiepiscopi maliciæ obuiare, parauisque nobis & nostris ab ipsis laqueis cautius declinare prouidimus , propter ea quæ superius expressa sunt. Vt ad præsens de multis eius peruersis actibus taceamus aliqua deducere in publicum nomionem: nempe eius improuiso consilio & suasu in iunjore grate costituti,tot donationes prodigas ac alienationes prohibitas ac gratias fecimus excessiuas,q.per eas ꝗ ariũ nostrũ totaliter est exhaustũ,&hicales redditus sunt enormiter diminuti,ipũsq̃ muneri ac ceptione consuptum, magnas pecuniarũ summas nobis debitas quibusdam sine rationabili causa cũ id nulla necessitas vel vtilitas exposcebat cõperimus remississe,&plurimos prouεtus & rd. dinus ditas qui pro nostris vtilitatibus & necessitatibus conseruari debuerant, suis suorumque vibus applicasse, & aliis personis male meritis erogasse, quae etiam nedum munetum sed & personarum acceptorum cōtra vorum nostrum, & praeticum nobis hdcitati solirum iuramentum ad officia publica in terris nostre diuoni subiedis, dignis & enemeritis propositis & repulsis, indignos admisit, multaque alia animo inaligno temere attentare praesumplit, initatus nostri detrimentum, & dignitatis Regiae laesionem, ac populi nobis subditi damnum non modicum & grauamen, potestate sibi tradita, & omnimodo sibi officio abutendo, quae si violata obstinatione & obstinata rebellione, & continuata praesticerit, congruis loco & tempore intendimus declarare, vobis firmiter iniungendo mandantes, quod haec omnia singulatim clare in locis quibus expedire videritis publicetis,&faciatis, per alios publicari piam intentionem quam habemus ad tubducēdam nicommodā & promouenda commoda subditorum, ipsis iuxta datam vobis a Deo sapientiam efficaciter commendantes & in taliter vos habentes quod vestram debeamus solicitudinem providam merito commendare. Teste meipso apud Westm. 13.die Febr. Anno Regni nostri Angliae. 15. Regni vero nostri Franciae secundo.
units.tr: ...of the said Archbishop, in so many and such great necessities of ours, should be revealed. At length, frustrated in the hope we had conceived, although we sent word by several messengers and by various letters to the aforesaid Archbishop, and to the other councillors of ours who adhered to him, and fully signified to them our needs and the various dangers to which we were exposed through the failure of the promised aid, and the advantage and honour which we had seen would easily be obtained from the success of the money, we could nevertheless get no benefit from them. For, caring for their own affairs and not ours, and seeking their own advantage, they covered over their indifference, not to say their deceit or malice, with frivolous excuses and painted rhetorical flourishes, like mockers who, as Isaiah says, deride and trifle with us: "Command upon command, command upon command; wait for the line, wait for the line; a little here, a little there." Hence, alas, it came about that, while the hope of triumph over our enemies was smiling most graciously upon us, want prevailed and we were forced, against our will, to consent to a truce that was disadvantageous to us, with the shameful delay of our expedition and no small rejoicing of our rivals. Therefore, when we had returned to Flanders, empty of money and weighed down by the burden of debt, and nothing remained in our own purses or in those of our people from which we could provide for our needs and pay the wages owed to those serving us in our campaign, we were compelled to plunge into the whirlpool of usury and to put our shoulders under the piled-up burdens of debt. At last there came to us our faithful friends, companions of our journey and sharers of our tribulation, with whom we held a careful discussion about the best remedies by which we might more conveniently recover breath from so great a storm of misfortunes. It seemed good to all of them that the sorrowful outcome of the said delay, and the manifold troubles of our want, had come about through the fault or negligence, not to say the malice, of the aforesaid Archbishop, on whose judgement the whole disposition of our realm seemed to depend, and of the other officials whom we had appointed under his council to handle the affairs of the realm. And, greatly outraged, our nobles openly protested, on account of the insolence of the said Archbishop and officials, which our royal gentleness had for so long chosen to leave uncorrected, that unless we acted on these matters, a fitting remedy must quickly be applied, or they would be obliged to withdraw from our service and to go back from the sworn covenant. And this, surely, would redound to the overthrow of our realm, to our perpetual shame, and to the perpetual reproach of the English nation, which in our times the kindness of a most merciful father has gone before, in whose firmness the anchor of our hope is fixed unshakeable. Hence we turned our attention, with a keen mind, to the discipline and correction of our officials: and we removed from their offices, as far as we lawfully could, those whom we had for probable reasons held suspect of bad administration, the subversion of justice, the oppression of our subjects, the corruption of received bribes, and other grave offences. We also ordered that others of lower rank who were guilty in the aforesaid matters be kept under your custody, lest they enjoy their accustomed liberty, lest the execution of justice in their case be frustrated, and lest the inquiry into the truth be cunningly eluded. We believed we could draw out this truth from the hidden recesses of the said Archbishop's mind all the more surely and fully, because nothing of those things which could contribute to our information in this matter could reasonably have been concealed from him. Since we had for a long time judged that the administration of our whole commonwealth and the chief direction of affairs should be entrusted to him, we sent a command, through our esquire Nicholas de Cantilupe, specially appointed for this purpose, that he should not delay in coming to London more promptly to our presence, where we seemed to be able to enjoy his personal conversation. But he, always timid in prosperity and proud in adversity, trembling with fear where there was no fear, pleaded untruthfully that danger to his life had been threatened and menaced against him by certain persons who beset us, if he withdrew from the Church of Canterbury without a guarantee: for, God is witness, this never came into our mind from a pure conscience, nor did any thought of plotting against him, as we believe, touch anyone of us, although he had by his own malice deservedly made himself odious to the clergy and people of our realm. We, however, wishing all men to come to our presence, and especially those summoned by our letters or messengers for this purpose, wish them to rejoice in full satisfaction; and to convict his malice, we sent to him our beloved and faithful Ralph de Stafford, seneschal of our household, that he might offer him a safe conduct; and we caused royal letters patent, sealed with our seal, to be presented to him, again commanding that he should come to us in person, to inform our anxiety about the affairs of ours which he had managed for a long time. But, his prayers and our commands having been scorned, indignation answered from his face and mind, so that he would in no way present himself to our sight or conversation, unless in a full Parliament, which for reasonable causes in these days it is in no way expedient to summon. But because this same Archbishop, whom royal kindness had raised with benefits and magnificent honours, and had summoned into the sacred intimacy of his familiarity, the unity of friendship and the bond of covenant, upon whom, as upon a most dear father, our whole spirit and mind rested; who, while we had in all things yielded to his wishes, was accustomed to put before us, in the mouth of a lovable father, the counterfeit face of a sophistical affection covered over with his lying goodwill, has now been turned into a heavy and cruel burden for us, and, ungrateful for benefits received, under the arrogance of fear persecutes his benefactor, and repays us with that recompense which the common proverb describes: the mouse in the bag, the serpent in the bosom, fire in the lap, which such men are accustomed to show to their hosts. For although in us, raised to the royal dignity by hereditary right, under the cooperating grace of God, it has always been detestable to abuse the greatness of power, we who with the highest desire aim to govern our subjects with clemency and gentleness, tempered by the measure of justice, so that all mortals may enjoy peace, nevertheless he rends our innocence in public, and the loyalty and diligence of our councillors and officials who pursue royal justice, by preaching publicly and commanding that his letters be published in various parts, that under royal power in these modern times the people is oppressed against justice, the clergy is confounded, and the Church is burdened with various exactions, collections and tallages. And because he has falsely usurped the name of good shepherd, which he has hitherto always lacked, since he is in truth, according to common opinion and his own confession (as is publicly reported), notoriously a hireling; and because he pretends, with a feigned zeal cloaked over with the cunning of a fox, to be the liberator of the Church, whose vexations, if any she has suffered in her goods or persons in our time, are truly to be ascribed to the remissness and crafty devices and shameful counsels of the aforesaid Archbishop alone; he has, under pretext of excommunication, issued in general against the violators of ecclesiastical liberty and of Magna Carta certain sentences of excommunication long since pronounced, in order to stir up the royal opinion and to defame the aforesaid royal ministers, and treacherously to excite sedition among the people committed to us, and to alienate the devotion of the counts, nobles and magnates of our realm from the royal majesty; and, with certain specified articles, contrary to the customary mode delivered in the provincial council, he has ordered by his letters to be published in many notable places. Wherefore we, wishing (as we are bound to do) to provide for the state of our good name and to withstand the malice of the aforesaid Archbishop, and have provided that we and ours should more cautiously avoid his snares, because of the things expressed above, and so as not to bring to public notice at present many of his perverse acts, namely: when he was made treasurer, at his unforeseen counsel and persuasion, we made so many prodigal gifts, forbidden alienations and excessive grants that by them our treasury has been wholly exhausted and our revenues enormously diminished, and the money has been consumed by gifts and bribes; we have discovered that he remitted large sums of money owed to us by certain persons without any reasonable cause, when no necessity or advantage demanded it; and that he applied very many revenues and rents which ought to have been preserved for our advantages and needs to his own and his kinsmen's uses, and bestowed them on other ill-deserving persons; he also presumed, not only in the matter of offices but also of persons, against the oath which we and our people have customarily sworn to us, to admit unworthy men to public offices in the lands of our realm, while worthy and deserving men were set aside and rejected; and he has rashly dared to undertake many other things with a malicious mind, abusing the power and the whole office entrusted to him, to the no small detriment of our state, the wounding of royal dignity, and the damage and burden of the people subject to us. If he persists in these things with obstinate violation, obstinate rebellion and continued practice, we intend to declare it at a fitting place and time. Therefore we firmly enjoin and command you that you publish and cause all these things to be published singly and clearly in whatever places you judge fitting, and commend to them, efficiently, the pious intention we have to remove what is harmful and to promote the advantage of our subjects, according to the wisdom given you by God, and so conduct yourselves that we may rightly commend your careful foresight. Witness myself at Westminster, 13 February, in the fifteenth year of our reign in England, and the second of our reign in France.

units.la: EXCVSATIO ARCHIEPISCOPI.
units.tr: The Archbishop's Apology

units.la: Euerendo Domino suo Edwardo Dei gratia Franciae & Angliae Regi Illustrissimo Iohannes permissione diuina Ecclesiae Cantuariensis humilis minister suus olim temporaliter, nunc autem magis in Domino animae corporisque salute & omni tempore perleuerare in bono ac remiti viriliter suggestionibus malignis & prauis quae cortumpunt faciliter bonos mores. Duo sunt quibus principaliter regitur iste mundus: sacra pontificalis auctoritas & regalis ordinata potestas, in quibus est pondus tanto grauius & sublimius sacerdotium. quanto & de ipsis Regibus in diuino reddituri sunt examine rationem. Et ideo scire debet Regia Celsitudo ex illorum vos dependere iudicio, non illos ad vestram posse dirigi voluntatem. Quis enim dubitat sacerdotes Christi Regum & principum, omniumque fidelium, patres & magistros censeri? Nonne miserabilis infamiae dignoscitur fi filius patrem, discipulus magistrum sibi subiugare conetur? plurimique pontificum aliiRegues, alii Imperatores, excommunicatione testatur auctoritas canonica scripturarum. Et in speciale aliquid de personis principum inquiratis, beatus Innocentius Archadium Imp. excommunicationis murerone percussit, quia consensit sanctum Iohannem Chrysostomum a sede sua violenter expelli. Sanctus etiam Ambrosius Mediola. Archiepiscopus pro culpa quae aliis sacerdotibus non adeo videbatur enormis, Theodosium magnum Imperatorem excommunicationis vinculo innodauit. Qui postea praetita primitus satisfactione condigna moeruit ab eodem absolui, & tempore certiori & loco vicinior, de eonfimilibus exempla plurima possunt poni. Ideo qualescunque pontifices & si errore humanitus accidente, non tamen contra Religionis fidem vllatenus exceedente nullatenus videntur a potestate seculari posse vel debere percelli. Boni siquidem & religiosi principis est contritas & concussas ecclesias restaurare, novas aedificare, sacerdotes Dei honorare & cum reuerentia summa tueri, adinstar fidelissimae recordationis & pii principis Constantini decentis: cum ad eum fuisset delata quaestio Clericorum. Vos a nemine iudicari potestis seculorum, scilicet iudicum qui estis solus Dei iudicio reseruati iuxta assertionem Apostoli dicentis. Spiritualis homo a nemine iudicatur. Consideret igitur vestra serenitas quanta & qualis sit filii poena diuino iure & humano debita & inflicta patris verenda inhumaniter detegentis, patremque innocentem nequiter diffamantis, cui filius vt praemittitur renetur impendere reuerentiam & honorem. Paganorum enim Principes, templorum & Idolorum suorum Pontificibus quos flaminines appellarunt, non modicum honorem exhibuerunt & exhibent suo more. Quanto magis Christi Ministros & Pontifices reuereri tenentur Christianorum Principes veri Dei, fideique Christianae cultores. Sed proh dolor, ordine praeposterro & turbato, honor nobis occasione dignitatis, cui praefidemus, licet indigni tanquam patri vestro exhibendus conuersus est in opprobrium deuorio iu blaiphemiā, & reuerentia in contemptum. Dum vestras regias patentes regio annulo signatas Epistolas, quin verius libellos famosos per aemulos & inimicos nostros amare dictatos & scriptos, crimina varia & multa enormia contra nos in nostri infamiam & falso fabricata conuitia continentes, sicut ex ipsorum lectione luculenter poterit apparere suffraganeis omnibus nostrae prouinciae Cantuar. Decanis, Abbatibus,
units.tr: To his reverend lord Edward, by the grace of God most illustrious King of France and England, John, by divine permission humble minister of the Church of Canterbury, formerly his servant in temporal matters but now rather in the Lord, wishes for the salvation of soul and body, and that he may always persevere in good and resist manfully the malignant and wicked suggestions which easily corrupt good morals. There are two things by which this world is chiefly governed: the sacred pontifical authority and the ordained royal power. In these the priesthood carries the greater and more sublime weight, in proportion as kings themselves will render account to the divine judgment. Therefore Your Royal Highness ought to know that you depend upon their judgment, and that they cannot be directed to your will. For who doubts that the priests of Christ are reckoned the fathers and masters of kings and princes and of all the faithful? Is it not a matter of wretched infamy when a son tries to subject his father, or a disciple his master? The canonical authority of the Scriptures attests that very many pontiffs have excommunicated kings, and others emperors. And if you inquire into something specific about the persons of princes: blessed Innocent struck the emperor Arcadius with the sword of excommunication because he consented to St John Chrysostom being violently expelled from his see. St Ambrose also, archbishop of Milan, for a fault which did not seem so enormous to other priests, bound Theodosius the Great with the chain of excommunication. Afterwards, having first made fitting satisfaction, Theodosius was absolved by the same man at a more opportune time and place. Many examples of this kind can be given. Therefore, whatever bishops they may be, even if they have erred through human frailty but in no way gone against the faith of religion, they seem in no way able or bound to be struck down by secular power. For it is the duty of a good and religious prince to restore ruined and shaken churches, to build new ones, to honour the priests of God and to defend them with the greatest reverence, after the example of the most faithful and pious prince Constantine, when the question concerning the clergy was brought before him. You can be judged by no one of the secular order, that is, by judges, since you alone are reserved for the judgment of God, according to the saying of the Apostle: "The spiritual man is judged by no one." Let your serenity therefore consider how great and what sort of punishment is due, by divine and human law, to a son who inhumanly uncovers his father's shame and wickedly defames an innocent father, to whom, as has been said, the son is bound to show reverence and honour. For the princes of the pagans have shown, and still show in their own fashion, no small honour to the pontiffs of their temples and idols, whom they called flamens. How much more are Christian princes, worshippers of the true God and cultivators of the Christian faith, bound to revere the ministers and pontiffs of Christ! But alas, in a disordered and perverted order, the honour which ought to be paid to us, unworthy as we are, as to your father, on account of the dignity over which we preside, has been turned into reproach, into blasphemy, and reverence into contempt. Your royal letters, sealed with the royal ring, or rather defamatory libels dictated and written by our rivals and enemies, containing various crimes and many enormities and slanders falsely fabricated against us to our infamy, as can clearly be seen from reading them, have been ordered to be published to all our suffragans in the province of Canterbury, deans, abbots,

units.la: Prioribus & ipsorum Capitulis aliisque vitiis ecclesiasticis publicandos, seu publicandum in nostram vtinam & non diuinam iniuriam demandaltus. Vt tic ipsorum subditorum nolitotum erga nos devotio tepesceret & veiteretur obedientia in contemptum, ex quo inopinabili ne dicamus facto detestabili, cunctis intuebubus ostendit maiufeste, quod Regia potestas quae a Domino procedit secundum dicta Salomonis Regis sapientis. Audite Reges & intelligite, discite iudices finium terrae, quoniam data est a Domino potestas vobis, & virtus ab altissimo est infusa, ipsum Dominū Deum in personas ministrorum & sacerdotum suorum non solum in diuinae legis iniuriam iudicare praetumūt, sed coutra Dei, legis humanae & rationis naturalis ordinem, patrem spiritualem suum & parem terrae maiorem, illis non vocatum, non conuictū,per recordum vestrum, vt vulgaribus verbis vtamur, condemnare videmur, inauditum in animae vestrae periculum, in diuinum nostrum omnium parium & Regnicolarum terrae praeiudicium, manifestuin ac perniciosum exemplum. Nec quisquam calumniando causetur quod propter criminis conscientiam quaeramus subterfugia, ne per vos obiiciendorum incaumus certamen. Nouit enim altissimus quod praecunctis mortalibus vos videre corditer affectamus, vt vestri regnique pericula subditorum vestrorum affectionis & corda adulatione omnimoda circumcipta vestrae Celsitudini intimemus, & vt gesta vestra vtinam laudabilia alijs cederent in decorem iuxta illud sapientis, componitur orbis Regis ad exemplum, & etiam vt vera facie nostra reduceretis ad memoriam seruitia, quae dum in vestris egerimus obsequiis, deuote & fideliter iuxta animi nostri conscientiā. Sic Deus nos aduuet in examine vltimo quando omnes astabunt ante tribunal ipsius recepturi prout gesserint in suo corpore bonum siue malum, & maxime vt coram vobis, Praelatis procetibus & paribus Regni famam nostram epistolis & libellis vestris praedictis turpiter laceraram, ac etiam suggillatam, purgatam, veram, & puram sicut est Deo teste, duceremus in publicā notionem. Sed propter noticiani quorundam principalum consiliatorum vestrorum vobis assistentium motorias nobis minas mortis illatas, qui in terra ista non sicut Iosephin Aegypto, sed sicut tyranni dominantur in ľoblo his diebus iuxta dictum sapientis. Multi tyranni sederunt in solio, & insuspicabilis portauit diadema existente sic gladio in manu furiosorum non superba elatione vel inobedientia ducti, sed currenti cedendo furori ipsorum hucusque ad vos nostrum accessum distulimus, nos iusto metu qui in conftanuffimum caderet excusante parati tamen parere vestrae in omnibus Maiestati, honoreDei & Ecclesiae sanctae statu & ordine nostris in omnibus semper saluis. Sane ne medii temporis interualio huius tyrannorū potestate durante ad quam euellendam oriens exaltovosiuuare dignetur, vt impleatur dictū sapientis. Oportebat enim illis sine ceflatione quid superuenire interitum exercētibus tyrannidem, infamiae nostrae clamor ampliusinualefcat ad detegendam innocentiā nostram singulis articulis in ipsis epistolis seu libellis famosis contentis, non sophistice sed veraciter in forma quae sequitur respondemus. Continent siquidè epistolarum vestrarū praedictarū seu libelli famosi praedicti primordia probris plena, quod vobis dndū in annis adolescentiae ad Regni solium exaltatis, in eiusdem suscepto Regimine sanis consiliis dirigi cupientes nostro consilio super his quae animae vestrae saluti expediebant & Regni vestri augmentum & conseruationem spiritualiter ac temporaliter vsi fuistis, quod quae postmodum Regno Francie ad vos iure successorio deuoluto & à Domino Philippo de Valesio de facto notorie occupato, Regiae maiestati persuasimus, importune foedus nostrum cum Alemannis & aliis pro recuperando iure vestro, quod quae solummodo de petfonis ad arma doctis & strenuis cogitaretis. Quia nos pecuniam necessariam pro vestris vestrorumque necessitatibus & stipendis efficaciter prouideremus, & quia huius subsidio caruistis ex toto vos debito, grauissimo supponere oportuit vsurarum. Ad haec serenissime Princeps nobis tacentibus & linguaminimo palpitantibus facti ettotorietas congruum nouit dare responsum In principio enim regiminis vestri, dum Ecclesiae Wintonien sis praefuimus, quorum consilio regebatur Maiestas regia regno constat. Nouit enim qui nihil ignorat quod cùm quaestio Regni Franciae post mortem Regis Caroli fratris serenissimae matris vestrae in parliamento tuncapud Norhampto celebrato, tractata discussaque fuisset, quodqne idem regnum ad vos haereditario iure extiterat legitime deuolutum, & superhoc fuit ordinatum quod duo Episcopi Wyngorn.tunc, nunc autem Wintoniensi.Couentren.& Lych. in Franciam dirigerent grefus suos, nomineque vestro Regnum Franciae vendicarent, & praedicti Philippi de Valesio coronationem pro viribus impedirent, qui iuxta ordinationem praedictam legationem eis iniunctam tunc assumentes gressus suos versus Franciam direxerunt, dit exerunt, quę quidem legatio maximam guerrę præsentis materiam ministrauit. Nulla fuit tunc disputatio nostra penes vos & adolescentiam vestram vt alios in spiritualibus & temporalibus vos regentes accepta, quia nec tunc de Regiis negociis nos intromisimus quouismodo, sed in curia Regia qua de causa, nouit Deus, omnibus fuimus Regiis odioti. Postmodum vero vnitatis remporibus ex quo placuit vestrę Maiestati quòd vestra negocia vna cum aliis vestris secretariis tractaremus pro pace inter duo regna Angliæ scilicet & Franciæ facienda, considerando animarum corporum rerumque periculā ex guerrorum voragine imminentia, instituimus toto posse pluriesq; mare propterea transeuntes non absq; periculis multis, laboribus, & magnis expensis cum Prælatis variisque proceribus Regni vestri ipsius Philippi quæsiuimus præsertim per sonalem mensuramq; omnem non dicimus sufficientem sed superhabundantem ante. hæc rempora satis publicatam pro pace habenda obtulimus cum effectu. Ipso vero Philippo obturante more aspidis aures suas & nosaudire nolente missi fuerunt ad eundem ex parte vestra duo legati Episcopi spirituales Dunelm. scilicet & nunc Winton. pro pace huius procuranda, & ex alio latere bonæ memoriæ Domini H. Lincoln. Episcopus & Wilhelmus de Monte acuto. & Wilhelmus de Clynton, nunc Comes Sarum & Hunter qui nec pacem poterant procurare nec guerræ dilationem aliquam obtinere, sed ipsis nunciis ad hunc in transmarinis partibus constitutis dictus Philippus de Valesio commissiones varias ad omnes partes suas maritimas mox transmisit ad interficiendum & destruendum homines & naues Angliæ vbicunq; in mari poterant inuenire, manum armaram nouimus ad inuadendum terram vestram Vasconiæ cum omni festinatione mittendo. Sieq; per ipsum Philippum & non per vos guerra inchoata iuxta deliberationem & consensum parliamenti vestri apud Westm. tunc ea occasione convocati & non soliùs nostri oeca fione grauis sœuitiæ & obstinationis animi indurati Philippi prædicti Anglicos inuadētis & mensuram omnimodam recusantis, & pro iure vestro in regno Franciæ adipisecendo per dictum Philippum nequiter occupato cum Alemannis & aliis fœdus inire ordinatum extitit & consensum, pro vestris vero & vestrorum stipendiis in hac parte soluendis in consilio quodam apud Staunford tunc propterea conuocato cùm certis mercatoribus terræ vestræ nobis præsentibus conuentiones certæ factæ fuerunt: de quarum forma in Cancellaria vestra apparere poterit satis clare, quæ fi obseruatæ fuissent vna cum aliis subsidiis per Clerum & populum in subsidium guerræ vestræ & magnis lanarum custumis, non solum nostro sed omni consiliatiorum vestrorum arbitrio pro tota guerra huius suffecissent. Et satis nouit vestra Maiestas quod conuentiones prædictæ per nos nec violatæ nec immutatæ fuerunt, quodq; ad manus nostras subsidia nullarenus deuenerunt. Si ergo infortunium aliquod propter defectum pecuniæ contigerit quod nos tædet, hoc illis qui dictas conuentiones fregerunt & dicta subsidia male expenderunt & dilapidaucrunt, & non nobis qui portauimus pondus diei & æstus est totaliter imputandum, ex eo maximè quod post primum vestrum transitum non remansimus in hoc regno.
units.tr: to the priors, their chapters, and other ecclesiastical officers, to be published, or to be published by them, to our injury (would that it were not also to God's). The result was that the devotion of their subjects toward us grew cool and their obedience was weakened into contempt. By this unexpected, I might even say detestable, deed, it was made plain to everyone that the royal power, which comes from the Lord, is being disregarded. According to the words of Solomon, the wise king: "Hear, O kings, and understand; learn, you judges of the ends of the earth, for power is given you by the Lord and strength is poured into you by the Most High." They presume to judge the Lord God himself in the persons of his ministers and priests, and not only against the law of God. Against the order of God, of human law, and of natural reason, we seem to condemn our spiritual father and the greater peer of the land, who was neither summoned nor convicted, by your record, to use common words. This is an unheard-of danger to your soul, a prejudice against all the peers and subjects of the realm, and a manifest and pernicious example. Nor let anyone slander us by claiming that, because we are conscious of guilt, we seek evasions so as not to meet the charges before you. The Most High knows that we earnestly desire above all mortals to see you, so that we may make known to your Highness the dangers to you and your realm, and so that your subjects' hearts, freed from all flattery, may speak their affection. We also wish that your deeds, which I would they were praiseworthy, might become an ornament to others, according to the saying of the wise: "The world is set in order by the example of the king." And we wish that, with our true face, you might recall the services we have rendered in your obedience, devotedly and faithfully, according to the witness of our conscience. So may God help us at the last judgment, when all shall stand before his tribunal to receive what they have done in the body, good or evil. Above all, we wish to bring our reputation, which your letters and the libels mentioned above have shamefully torn and also defamed, before you, the prelates, the nobles and the peers of the realm, to be cleared, vindicated, and set forth as true and pure, as God is our witness. But because of the notice of certain principal counsellors of yours who attend you, and because death has been threatened against us, who in this land rule not as Joseph in Egypt but as tyrants, according to the saying of the wise: "Many tyrants have sat upon the throne, and one who was unknown has worn the crown." While the sword is in the hand of madmen, we have deferred our coming to you until now. We were not moved by proud arrogance or disobedience, but by yielding to their rage. We offer as excuse a just fear, which might fall even upon a constant man, yet we are ready to obey your Majesty in all things, always saving the honour of God and the state and order of the holy Church. Indeed, lest in the meantime, while this tyranny endures, the one who rises in the East should deign to help in tearing it up, let the saying be fulfilled: "For it behoved them, without ceasing, to face whatever destruction might come upon the exercisers of tyranny." Let the cry of our infamy grow stronger, so that our innocence may be revealed. We answer each article contained in those letters or infamous libels, not sophistically but truthfully, in the form that follows. For the beginnings of your letters and of the said infamous libels are full of reproaches: that when you were raised to the throne of the realm in your boyhood, wishing to be guided by sound counsel in governing it, you made use of our advice on those matters that were expedient for your soul's salvation and for the increase and preservation of your realm, both spiritually and temporally. As for what followed, that when the kingdom of France had passed to you by right of succession and was notoriously and unlawfully seized by Lord Philip of Valois, we persuaded your Royal Majesty to make a covenant, unseasonably, with the Germans and others to recover your right, and that you thought only of men skilled and bold in arms: we on our part took care to provide the necessary money for you and your needs and soldiers' pay, and because you lacked this help altogether, you were obliged to take on most heavy usury. To these charges, most serene Prince, while we keep silent and our tongues barely move, the facts themselves and the whole of history may give a fitting answer. For at the beginning of your reign, when I was bishop of Winchester, it is well known by whose counsel your royal Majesty was governed. For he who knows nothing ignores that, when the question of the kingdom of France was treated and discussed in parliament, after the death of King Charles, your most serene mother's brother, held at Northampton, and when that kingdom had lawfully passed to you by hereditary right, it was ordained in this matter that two bishops, then of Worcester (now of Winchester), of Coventry and Lichfield, should send their envoys into France, claim the kingdom of France in your name, and oppose, as far as they could, the coronation of the said Philip of Valois. Those who undertook the embassy enjoined upon them under the said ordinance then set their steps toward France, and that embassy supplied the greatest matter for the present war. There was then no dispute of ours with you or your youth, who had been received as regent of others in spiritual and temporal affairs, for we did not then meddle in any way with royal business. Rather, in the royal court, for a reason God knows, we were hated by all the king's men. Afterwards, in times of truce, when it pleased your Majesty that we should treat your affairs, together with your other secretaries, for making peace between the two kingdoms of England and France, considering the perils to souls, bodies and goods that threatened from the whirlpool of war, we undertook, with all our power and many times, to cross the sea, not without many dangers, labours and great expenses. With the prelates and various nobles of your realm, we sought Philip himself, by personal visit, and we offered, with effect, a peace which was not merely sufficient but more than abundant, and which had been fully made public before this time. But Philip, stopping his ears like an asp and unwilling to hear us, sent to him from your side two legates: the spiritual bishops of Durham (namely) and now of Winchester, for procuring this peace. On the other side came the late Lord H., bishop of Lincoln, William de Montacute, and William de Clinton, now Earl of Salisbury, and Hunter. They could neither procure peace nor obtain any delay in the war. Yet while these envoys were still in the transmarine parts, the said Philip of Valois immediately sent various commissions to all his maritime regions, to kill and destroy the men and ships of England wherever they could be found at sea. We know that he sent an armed force with all speed to invade your land of Gascony. Thus the war was begun by Philip, and not by you, in accordance with the deliberation and consent of your parliament held at Westminster, convened for that purpose. It was not begun on our account alone, nor because of the great cruelty and hardened obstinacy of the said Philip, who attacked the English and refused all moderation. And for recovering your right in the kingdom of France, which the said Philip had wickedly seized, it was ordained and agreed to make a covenant with the Germans and others. For paying your soldiers and yours in this matter, certain agreements were made at a council then convened for this purpose at Stamford, in the presence of certain merchants of your land and ourselves. The form of these may be seen quite clearly in your Chancery. If they had been observed, together with other aids granted by the clergy and people for your war, and with the great customs on wool, they would have sufficed for the whole war, not only at our discretion but at that of all your counsellors. Your Majesty knows well that the said agreements were neither violated nor altered by us, and that the aids never came into our hands in any way. If therefore some misfortune has occurred because of a lack of money, which grieves us, it must be imputed entirely to those who broke the said agreements and spent and squandered the said aids badly, and not to us, who have borne the burden of the day and its heat, especially since, after your first crossing, we did not remain in this kingdom.

units.la: Sed cum Reuerendis patribus Dominis Cardinalibus & Dunelmēn. Episcopo pro pacis reformatione prædictæ in Franciam præcessimus ad vos tunc in Brabantia moram facientes occasione prædicta eundo & redeundo vicibus iteratis. Et demum dicto pacis negocio tanquam desperato totaliter derelicto vobiscum in Brabantiam per aliquam temporam traximus, nobis vtiq; satis grauem. Vestræq; necessitatis participes effecti pro debiris grauissimis sub vsurarum quantitate contractis, de quibus in epistolis vestris prædictispleniori fir mentio, vnà vobiscum & aliis Prælatis ac proceribus rertæ vestræ, & pro vobis diuersimodas vtinam non in præiudicium status vestri affectione paterna quocūque periculo circumscripto obligationes fecimus valde graues. Sieq; serenissime Princeps non in illusoris baeculo arundineo spem vestram nostris confideratis operibus posuistus, sicut in epistolis vestris memoratis, sed in hacculo firmissimo illi simili in quo lacob Iordanem transiuit, & cum duabus turmis est gloriosè reuersus. Cum quâta ei gloria vice secunda vestra deeotata est reuersio, nouit mundus, vtinam continuetur ad Dei laudem honoremq; vestrum temporibus secuturis.
units.tr: But when we went into France with the reverend fathers, the lords Cardinals and the Bishop of Durham, to arrange the aforesaid peace, we then stayed with you in Brabant, going and returning many times on that pretext. At last, with the peace business given up as hopeless, we dragged on with you in Brabant for some time, a burden quite heavy for us. Having shared your necessity, we entered, together with you, with other prelates and nobles of your realm, and on your behalf, very grave obligations, for the heaviest debts contracted at a great rate of interest, of which fuller mention is made in your aforesaid letters. We did this out of paternal affection, and at whatever risk, I wish it had not been to the detriment of your state. So, most serene Prince, you did not place your hope in the reed of an illusory staff, in our works, as your letters recall, but in that most firm staff like the one by which Jacob crossed the Jordan and returned gloriously with two companies. The world knows with how much glory your second return was made; I wish it may continue to the praise of God and your honour in times to come.

units.la: Subsequenter etiam mirabile manus nobis imponitur in epistolis antedictis, quod retardara expeditione vestra vlteriori eoādi fuistis ab inchoatis magnanimiter hostium aggressibus ea vice desistere & in Angliam remeare conuocatoque parliamento præfati proceres caeteriqueFidelesei usdem regni vestri nonæ partis garbarum, agnorum & vellerum suorum præter decimam vobis à Clero concessam pro expeditione guerræ vestræ subsidium concesserunt. Ad cuius subsidii collectionem & aliorum vobis neceffariorum submi-nistrationem efficaciter permisimus interponere partes nostras. Cuius permissionis occasione post gloriôsam victoriam vobis in mari à Deo concessam capstrametati iuxta ciuitatem Tornacen.
units.tr: Next, a strange charge is laid against us in the aforesaid letters: that, because your further expedition was delayed, you were bravely forced to desist from the attacks you had begun on your enemies and return to England; and that, when Parliament was summoned, the aforesaid nobles and the other faithful subjects of your realm granted you a ninth of their sheaves, lambs and fleeces, in addition to the tenth granted you by the clergy, as a subsidy for your war. We effectively allowed our own efforts to be interposed in the collection of this subsidy and the supplying of your other needs. On the occasion of that permission, after the glorious victory God gave you at sea, you encamped beside the city of Tournai.

units.la: In eâius obsidione per aliquatempora fatigari spe recipiendi subsidium memoratum cogente penuria cogebamini inuiri treugis inuitis consenture. Serenissime Princeps vt cum Reuerentia devota loquamur. Vestra non ignorat Maiestas quod subsidium rotius nonæ partis vobis vt permittitur concessum ante transitum vestrum secundum, vestris creditoribus variis pro primo anno de consensu vestro ac totius consilii vestri extitit totaliter assignatum prout ex ipsis assignationibus luculenter poterit apparere. Et vt assignationes prædictæ firmiter seruarentur pluries post transitum vestrum secundum 10 lictoratorie præceptis.
units.tr: During the siege there, when you were worn down for some time by hope of receiving the aforesaid subsidy, and pressing want compelled you, against your will, to agree to a truce. Most serene Prince, let us speak with devoted reverence. Your Majesty is not unaware that the subsidy of the whole ninth, granted to you as is said, was before your second crossing wholly assigned, with your consent and that of your whole council, to your various creditors for the first year, as can plainly appear from those assignments themselves. And that these assignments might be firmly kept, several times after your second crossing they were enforced by writs of the king's bench.

units.la: Ex quo poterit manifeste liquere quod ad obsidionem prædictam cuius etiam obsidionis initium ignoramus, nihil Deo teste transmittere potuimus nec promisimus destinare. Nec imputari nobis potuit dicti subsidii retardata solutio cuius terminorum satisfactio in pleno Parlamento extitit ordinata.
