Et ideo his & aliis causis nosaliiqui consiliarii vestri præmissa plenè pensantes, vestræ nunciauerunt Maiestati quod sine præsentia vestra personali vobis subuenire minimè potuerunt. Non ergo dici poterunt illusores consiliarii vestri prædicti dicentes. Manda remanda &c. Sed seruì perfectiô&veracesDomino. Non ficta sed verissima nunciantes, secundum illud Euangelii. Cognoscetis veritatem & veritas liberabit vos. Et sic fiet Domino concedente. Modicum etiam vel nihil 20 de subsidio prædicto ante vestram secundam reuersionem extitit persolutum, sed omnia ad ministrorû vestrorû præsentiû manus deuenient. Vtinam ad honorem vestrû bene inposterum disponantur. Ad hæc Domine metuende, in vestris inseritur epistolis memoratis quod reuersis vobis in Flandriam post obsidionem prædictam non fuit aliquid in vestris vel vestrorum marsupiis vnde potuistis necessitatibus vestris consulere,& debita stipendia vestro obsequio militantibus erogare. Compusi fuistis vsuragini vos immergere, versumq; fuit amicis vestris fidelibus & peregrinationis vestræ participibus huiusmodi incommoda & infortunia, culpa, desidia, & vt præstenditur malitia nostra & aliorum vestrorum Officialium contigissent quorum ducti consilio ne à vestro recederent iuuamine remedium volentes opportunum apponere in præmissis quosdam vestros Officiales amouistis. Alios sub ruta custodia detineri fecistis. Credentesq; per informationem de commissis per eosdem plenius informati per Dominos Nicolaum de Cantilupo primò & Radulphum de Stafford hospitii vestri senec allum nobis postmodum demandastis, quod ad vestram personalem præsentiam ea occasione maturius accedere curaremunobis non minus propter timorem variû à nobis præstensum salui & securi coductus literas Regias destinando. Nos tamen precum & Regiorum mandatorum lenitate contempta vultu & animo indignato præstendituritale dedille responsum, quod nos vestris aspectibus seu colloquiis nequaquam offerremus nisi in pleno Parlamento coram proceribus & paribus vestri Regni. Quod Parlamentum vt testantur epistolæ memoratæ certis de eaufis non expedit facere ista vice, Reuerende Domine veritate confidcrata 40 perspicua prædictorum leuis est responsio ad eadem. Non enim iusto iudicio nobis imputari potuit in Flandriam vestra reuersio, cum nulla vt præmittitur nostra præcesserit permissio &per consequens de fraudis vel negligentiâ nostro commento conqueri non poterunt vestro obsequio militantes: nouis enim altissimus qu od tunc & omni tempore quo vestro operam dedimus officio fideliter & diligenter vestra prosecuti sumus vt præmisimus negocia & mandata: & iuxta vulgare dictum: vltra posse viri non vult Deus vlla requiri. De eo verò quod fideles amici & vestræ peregrinationis Comites similiter his affectant congruum adhiberi remedium, credendum est prout verba sonant quod iusto præcedente processu non voluntario sed maturo vt culpabiles pro culpa poena legitima percellantur.
units.tr: From this it can be clearly seen that, for the aforesaid siege (whose beginning we do not even know), God is our witness that we could send nothing, nor did we promise to send anything. Nor could the delayed payment of the said subsidy be imputed to us, the terms of whose payment were ordained in full Parliament. And so, for these and other reasons, we and certain other of your counsellors, weighing the aforesaid matters fully, reported to your Majesty that without your personal presence we could by no means help you. Your aforesaid counsellors therefore cannot be called deceivers, saying "Send, send back," etc. Rather, we report things that are complete and true, not feigned but most true, according to the words of the Gospel: "You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." And so it will be done, by the Lord's permission. Little or nothing of the aforesaid subsidy was paid before your second return, but everything has come into the hands of your present ministers. I wish it may be well disposed for your honour in future. Moreover, most dread Lord, your aforesaid letters insert that, when you returned to Flanders after the aforesaid siege, there was nothing in your purse or those of your followers from which you could provide for your needs and pay the due wages to those serving in your household. You were compelled to plunge yourself into usury, and these troubles and misfortunes befell your friends and the companions of your journey, through the fault, negligence, and, as is alleged, malice of ourselves and other of your officials. Led by their counsel, you were unwilling to be left without help, and wishing to apply a fitting remedy to these matters, you removed certain of your officials. You had others kept in close custody. And believing, from information better informed about the offences committed by them, which you received from the lords Nicholas de Cantilupo first, and Ralph de Stafford, of your household, you afterwards demanded of us that we should hasten to your personal presence on that account. You sent us royal letters of safe conduct, partly because of various fears you expressed to us. We, however, despising the gentleness of your entreaties and royal commands, gave an answer with a face and mind showing indignation, that we would not present ourselves to your sight or conversation except in full Parliament before the nobles and peers of your realm. As your aforesaid letters testify, for certain reasons it is not expedient to hold Parliament at this time. Most reverend Lord, when the truth of these matters is considered, the reply to them is plainly slight. For your return to Flanders cannot justly be imputed to us, since, as has been said, no permission of ours went before it; and consequently those serving in your household cannot complain of fraud or negligence on our part. For the Most High knows that at that time, and at every time when we devoted our labour to your service, we faithfully and diligently pursued the business and commands you gave us, as we said; and, as the common saying goes, God requires nothing beyond a man's power. As for the fact that your faithful friends and companions of your journey similarly seek a fitting remedy, it must be believed, as the words sound, that by due process not voluntary but mature, the guilty will be struck with the lawful penalty for their guilt.

units.la: Quodautem Clerici à indicio secularis potestaris exempti laiciq, liberi contra leges & regni cosueru dines ac contra formam magnæ chartæ capiantur & detineantur inuiti, quantùq; sit eorum facinus qui hæc agunt, nonpotest esse ignoratum Regiæ Maiestati, cum periculaanimarum ex his contingentia non solum sacris constitutionib. sint expressa, sed per nos & Suffraganeos nostros per totam nostrâ prouinciam Cantuar. diuulgata sint, & tam clero quàm populo publicata. Et certe serenissime Princeps multum nimemus quod processus in terra vestra factiò & habiti his diebus vtinam legitimi & maturi populi vestri corda (quod absit) à vobis auertent nisi celerius adhibeatur remedium opportunum.
units.tr: As for clerics exempt from the jurisdiction of the secular power, and free laymen, being seized and detained against their will, contrary to the laws and customs of the realm and against the form of Magna Carta, the greatness of the wrong done by those who act thus cannot be unknown to your royal Majesty, since the dangers to souls arising from these things are not only expressed in sacred constitutions, but have been published by us and our suffragans throughout our whole province of Canterbury, and proclaimed to clergy and people alike. And truly, most serene Prince, we greatly fear that the proceedings carried on in your land these days, would that they were lawful and mature, may (God forbid) turn the hearts of your people away from you, unless a fitting remedy is applied more quickly.

units.la: Nunciĩ
units.tr: Messengers.

units.la: Nuncii verò vestri prænominati qualia ex parte vestra nobis nunciauerunt & prout cis placuit, innunxerût, non possunt esse tacita vel occulta vt puta coram Notariis & hominum multitudine publice nunciata. Quorum primus Dominus videlicet, Nicolaus de Cantilupo literas Regias credentiæ sub secreto sigillo secum deferens, credentiamq; suam exponens. Nobis iniunxit, Nosq; citauit, vt in Brabantiam infra octo dies tunc immediate sequentes pro certis vestris Regiis debitis quibus extitimus obligati transfretando dirigeremus celeriter gressus nostros, illuc continuè moraturi donec plenè soluerentur debita supradicta. Sane verò nuncius Dominus scilicet, Radulphus de Stafford quasi peregrè proficiscens & nullam secum omnino literam deferens nobis dixerat nudo verbo. Cito te quod te trahas versus Regem asserens, similiter nudo verbo quod minantium insidias non oportuit nos timere. Si ergo nunciata huiusmodi inserris in epistolis vestris in ea parte clausulis consonantia fuerunt, iudicet iustus iudex. Videbuntur cuiq; circumspecto repugnantia continere in Brabantiam statim diuertere, in Angliam pro informationibus præmissis obtinendis iugiter permanere. Sciatq; vestra serenitas quod non timor vanus, superbia, inobedientia, contemptus, vel criminis cōscientia a faciei vestræ visione delectabilis nos retraxit. Sed causa iustissima superius allegata, equo libramine ponderata, & vt cum renerentia debita & devota loquamur, licet literæ Regiæ conductus ad consilia vestra veniendi, morandi & reuertendi sufficientes prima facie viderentur, si ad vestra consilia fuissemus vocati sicuti non fuimus. Eodem tum die quo portèctæ nobis fuerant literæ memoratæ directum fuit Breue Regium Vicecomiti Cāt. quod nos venire faceret coram vobis & consilio vestro London. ad respondendum super contemptu certo in eodem Breui contento. Quo tamen zelo iustitiæ vestræ memoratum conceptum fuerat, nouit Deus. Licet ergo Regius conductus in suo casu liberam nobis recedendi tribueret facultatem, naturatamen Breuis prædicti coactam nobis imposuit necessitatem inimicorum nostrorum manibus remanendi. Quod non decuit nec decuisset Regiam Maiestatem. Semper tamen vt prædiximus parati fuimus & erimus in præsentia vestra Præsulatorum & procerum ac parium terræ ad obiiciedum nobis singula respondere, pariumque iudicio per omnia sine contradictione parere. Statu nostro & ordine semper saluis.
units.tr: Your aforesaid messengers, however, what they reported to us on your behalf, and what they pleased to enjoin on us in whatever way, cannot be secret or hidden, since it was publicly declared before notaries and a crowd of people. The first of them, namely Lord Nicholas de Cantilupo, carrying with him royal letters of credence under a secret seal, and setting out his credentials, enjoined on us and summoned us to set our steps quickly across the sea into Brabant, within eight days immediately following, to make payment for certain of your royal debts to which we were bound, and to remain there continually until the aforesaid debts were fully paid. Indeed, the second messenger, namely Lord Ralph de Stafford, as if setting off abroad and carrying no letter with him at all, had said to us only by word of mouth: "Hurry, get yourself moving towards the King," likewise saying by word alone that we ought not to fear the snares of those threatening us. So if the messages of this kind inserted in your letters agree in that part with the clauses, let the just judge decide. It will seem to any prudent person contradictory that we should at once turn aside into Brabant, and yet continually remain in England to obtain the aforesaid information. And let your serenity know that it was not vain fear, pride, disobedience, contempt, or consciousness of crime that drew us back from the pleasing sight of your face. Rather, the most just cause alleged above, weighed in an even balance, and, to speak with due and devoted reverence, although the royal letters of safe conduct, sufficient on their face, seemed to allow coming to your counsels, staying, and returning, we would have come had we been summoned to your counsels, as we were not. On the same day on which the aforesaid letters were brought to us, a royal writ was directed to the Sheriff of Canterbury, ordering him to bring us before you and your council at London, to answer for a certain contempt contained in the same writ. With what zeal for your justice that charge was made, God knows. So although the royal safe conduct, in its own case, granted us free permission to withdraw, nevertheless the aforesaid writ forced upon us the compelled necessity of remaining in the hands of our enemies. This neither became nor would have become Your Royal Majesty. Yet, as we have said, we have always been and shall be ready in your presence, and in that of the prelates, nobles and peers of the land, to answer each charge laid against us, and to submit in all things to the judgement of the peers, without contradiction, our state and order always being preserved.

units.la: Illi autem qui Parlamenti conuocationem impedire niteantur, occasionem nō causam legitimam prætendentes, declarationem conantur effugere veritatis, testante veritate quæ dicit. Omnis enim qui male agit, odit lucem.
units.tr: Those who strive to prevent the summoning of Parliament, pleading an occasion rather than a lawful cause, try to escape the declaration of the truth, and Truth itself bears witness, saying: "For everyone who does evil hates the light."

units.la: Ad illud autem quod inseritur in epistolis memoratis videlicet nos Regalis benignitatis beneficiis & honoribus magnificis ampliatos, super quem vt patrem charissimum veneraturs requieuit, nosque vobis in virum onerosum crudeliter esse conuersum, beneficiorum acceptorum immemorem & ingratū, benefactoremq; persequente, illamque vobis retributionem impendimus quam mus in pera, serpens in gremio, & ignis in sinu suis consueuerunt hospitibus exhibere. Tacita veritate falsitate expressa ad ingratitudinem huius nobis salua Reuerëtia vestra minus veraciter impositam, magis ex odio diantis epistolam quàm mitrentis raliter respondemus: voce namq; dicitur veritatis. Omnis qui reliquerit propter me patrem vel matrem, vxorem aut filios, domum vel agros, centuplum accipiet & vitam possidebit æternam. Præmissa dic entem inuocamus in tempus, quod à tempore illo quo vestris spiritualiter insudauimus obsequiis, in ratum iuxta scientiam ab altissimo nobis datam cum omni fidelitate, devotione, & diligentia sicut præmisimus, negociorum vestrorum expeditioni pro honore vestro & saluatione Regni vestri animum nostrum dedimus adeo integrum ad eadem, quod non solum patrem & parentes, vxorem id est, Ecclesiam nostram & filios spirituales, domuum & agrorum nostrorum emendationem & culturam reliquimus atque curam nostram, sed die noctèque de vobis & negociis vestris soliciti multoties transiuimus noctes infomnes, nostris laboribus transmarinis & cismarinis aliqualiter non parcentes, vtinam nō in periculum animæ nostræ corpusque exinaniuimus, & bona nostra temporaliaexpendimus quasi pauperes facti fumus, amoremque Cleri & populi Regni vestri vestra procurando commoda perdidimus, sicut nouit mundus.
units.tr: As for what is inserted in the aforementioned letters, namely that we have been raised to honours and magnificent benefits by the royal kindness, that on us as on a most dear father he rested and was to be venerated, and that we have cruelly turned into a burdensome man towards you, forgetful and ungrateful of the benefits received, persecuting our benefactor, and that we repay you with that return which the moth in the purse, the serpent in the bosom and the fire in the lap are accustomed to show their guests: with truth passed over and falsehood expressed, we answer (saving your reverence) the ingratitude imposed on us less truthfully than the letter's writer, prompted by hatred, than its sender. For the voice of truth says: "Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall inherit eternal life." We call on him who has spoken these things to witness, that from the time when we laboured spiritually in your service, we have given our mind so wholly, in accordance with the knowledge given us by the Most High, to the carrying out of your affairs, for your honour and the safety of your kingdom, with all faithfulness, devotion and diligence, as we have said before, that we have left not only father and kin, and a wife (that is, our Church) and spiritual children, and the improvement and cultivation of our houses and fields, and our own cares; but also, day and night, anxious about you and your affairs, we have passed many sleepless nights, not sparing our labours in any measure, across the sea and on this side of it. Would that we had not, to the peril of our soul, spent our body and our goods, and had not been made as poor men; and that we had not lost the love of the clergy and people of your kingdom by promoting your interests, as the world knows.

units.la: Et si ista sunt facta vitrici vel parentis iudicet qui mentiri nescit Omnipotens verax Deus: vobis enim semper fuimus pater gratus, filiis autem nostris spiritualibus quod dolentes referimus, occasione vestri vitricus onerosus. Mus in pera vestra non fuimus, quia in vestris obsequiis non vestra sed nostra corrosimus, quod sentimus serpentis prudentiam exercendo, non veneni malitiam effundendo in gremio. Ignemque diuini amoris & chatitatis in sinu vestro non comburentem sed iuxta nobis datum à Domino intellectum illum summantem effectu sedulo accendendo. Pro quibus exquo deest humanae retributio, nobis retributionem impendat qui est bonorum omnium retributor.
units.tr: If these things have been done, let the Omnipotent and true God, who cannot lie, judge whether we have been a stepfather or a parent. For to you we have always been a grateful father; but to our spiritual sons we report with sorrow that, because of you, we have become a burdensome stepfather. We have not been a moth in your purse, because in your service we have spent not your things but our own; this we feel, exercising the prudence of the serpent, not pouring out the venom of malice in your bosom. Nor have we set fire to the fire of divine love and charity in your bosom so as to burn it, but, according to the understanding given us by the Lord, we have diligently kindled it so that it might bring the sum to effect. For which, since human repayment is lacking, may He who is the rewarder of all good things repay us.

units.la: Nec nostram apud altissimum minuere potest retributionem Regalium beneficiorum amplatio nobis impolita ex malitia ut conuicimus dictatoris, praesertim cum Regiam Magnificentiam non decet talia improperiari recitare. Non enim per Priocipuum secularium quorumcunque collationes vel procurationem beneficiis & honoribus magnificis quibus hactenus potiti sumus, aliqualiter ampliamur, sed per gratam Dei munificentiam qui de bonis collatis nulli improperat & omnibus tribuit affluenter.
units.tr: Nor can the enlargement of royal benefits, imposed on us by the malice of this (so-called) dictator, as we say, diminish our reward with the Most High, especially since it does not befit royal magnificence to recite such reproaches. For we are not enlarged in any way by the bestowals of secular princes, or by the procuring of benefices and magnificent honours which we have hitherto obtained; but by the grateful bounty of God, who reproaches no one for the good things bestowed and gives abundantly to all.

units.la: De illo vero quod nobis velamioe quodam impingit, Regis nos innocentiam, totum suorumque consiliariorum & Officialium Regalem iustitiam proiecquentium fidelitatem & diligentiam lacerare publice praedicando & literis demandando, quod potest state Regia modernis temporibus contra iustitiam populus opprimitur, Clerus cunsunditur & Ecclesia variis exactionibus & tallijs praegrauatur. Si praemissa veritate nitaotur altissimus bene novit, vestram namque innocentiam conseruare & aliis publice praedicare mente & spiritu ludimus incessanter utmini portposita fictione, pro qua conseruanda Deum hactenus deprecati sumus & quotidie deprecamur, ut subdito nostri pro statu vestro incolumi conseruando & feliciter dirigendo orationum suffragia effunderet nostris patentibus literis pluries direximus & in posterum faciemus.
units.tr: As for what he charges us with under a kind of veil, namely that we tear to pieces the innocence of the King and of all his counsellors and officials, who cast off royal justice, by publicly preaching and committing to writing that in the present state of the King the people is oppressed contrary to justice, the clergy is consumed and the Church is weighed down with various exactions and tallages: if they strive for this with the truth set aside, the Most High knows it well. For we incessantly, with mind and spirit, labour to preserve your innocence and to proclaim it publicly to others, without any feigned pretence; for its preservation we have hitherto prayed to God and daily pray. That our subjects might pour out the help of their prayers for the safe preservation and happy guidance of your state, we have sent our open letters many times, and will do so in future.

units.la: Si tamen quorundam Officialium vestrorum praesumptione damnabili abiso vestra ut credimus conniuentia contra iustitiam populus plus solito sit oppressus, Clerus & Ecclesia variis taxationibus & tallijs praegrauentur, singulae cuidam apparent cum iam a viris Ecclesiasticis exigatur quod nullatenus concederunt. Nuuis enim legibus vinam non voluntariis & iniustatis sic populus vester regitur his diebus, quod ipsius substantia vix ad victum sufficiens ad vltimam (nisi Deus auertat) pauperta-tem in vestrum opprobrium deducetur.
units.tr: If, however, through the damnable presumption of some of your officials, and, as we believe, with your connivance, the people has been oppressed beyond its usual burden against justice, and the clergy and the Church are weighed down with various taxes and tallages, then each single one is evident, since such things are now being demanded from churchmen, which they have in no way granted. For by such new and unwilling and unjust laws your people is now governed, so that its substance, scarcely sufficient for sustenance, will be brought down to final poverty (unless God forbid it), to your shame.

units.la: Nec talia ad vestram vestrorum Officialium cum in specie nullum nominauerimus, innocentiam lacerandam dixi mus, proposuimus, seu publicauimus iotentione nostra, sed vt per ea Regia mota Maiestas remedium apponeret eo citius opportunum, ne per illicitagrauamina populi vestri traffectio deuotionem consuetum quod abiit, aucter am amorem in odium duerterido.
units.tr: Nor did we, in naming no one in particular, say, propose or publish such things about your officials with the intention of tearing apart their innocence; but so that, His Royal Majesty being moved by them, he might apply a remedy the sooner, lest, through unlawful burdens on your people, their affection, turning away the customary devotion that has gone, should change an increased love into hatred.

units.la: Et quia Screnitas Regia impoocre nobis pro suae literae dictatoris maleuola voluntate videtur, quod nomen boni pastoris quo semper arumus iuxta communem opinionem & confessionem propriam, qua nos mercenarium nominauimus, nitimur vsurpare, factum zelum vulpinae calliditatis fuco perizomate palliatum ad liberationem Ecclesiae, cuius vexationes si quas in rebus vel personis vestri tempore sustinuit nostris, dumtaxat remissiones & callidis adinuentionibus ac reprobis conuiliis suot tantummodo ascribendae.
units.tr: And since Your Serene Majesty seems to impute to us, from the malevolent will of the dictator of that letter, that we strive to usurp the name of good shepherd, which we have always borne according to common opinion and our own confession, by which we called ourselves a hireling; the zeal shown for the liberation of the Church, covered with the veil of fox-like cunning, is to be ascribed merely to remissness, to crafty inventions and to wicked counsels. If any vexations have been suffered by the Church in its goods or persons in your time through us, they are to be attributed only to these.

units.la: Ad quae respondemus sicut materia subiecta permittit. Nam veritas bonum pastorem se nominabat dicens.
units.tr: To these things we reply as far as the subject matter permits. For Truth itself called itself the good shepherd, saying:

units.la: Ego sum pastor bonus. Nullusque alius dicere se poterit pastorem bonum testante ipsa veritate quae dicit, Nullus est bonus nisi solus Deus. Si ergo praedicando publice diversimus nos bonum pastorem non esse sed mercenarium iuxta doctrinam diximus Salvatoris dicentis. Cum omnia praecepta fecerimus, dicite vos seruos inutiles. Et ipsa novit veritas quod nunquam fallaciter ceualio quaelibet suo colore boni pastoris nomen vsurpare coegitatum, sicuti nec fumus nec esse possumus, sed reiectis calliditate vulpina & petitiomate antiqui peccati velamento tales quales fumus pro necessitatis vestrae releuamine & Regni vestri vtilitate, quo potius saluatione, q occultata fide innumeris infperimus existi positu periculis cum ceteris Praelatis & Cleri nostrae prouincie procuratoribus interposuimus iugiter partes nostras & concedi procurauimus tallias & subsidia quamplurima in Cleri praedictionus maximum & grauamen, vt ipsorum subditorum succurfu hostes Regis, Regni & Ecclesiae pellereotur, Ecclesia & Regnum pacis suauitate gauderent, pro quibus vt videtur quod per vos nulla culpa pollet rationabiliter oobis impingi, communi prouerbio attestante. Si culpeor alius te laudare necesse est.
units.tr: "I am the good shepherd." And no one else can call himself the good shepherd, Truth itself bearing witness, which says: "None is good but God alone." If therefore by preaching publicly we have said that we are not the good shepherd but a hireling, we have spoken according to the teaching of the Saviour, who says: "When you have done all the commandments, say: We are unprofitable servants." And truth itself knows that we have never, by any deceit or under any colour, been compelled to usurp the name of good shepherd, nor are we, nor can we be, such. But, casting off fox-like cunning and the veil of the petticoat of ancient sin, we have been such as we are, for the relief of your necessity and the advantage of your kingdom, and rather for its salvation; having placed ourselves in countless dangers, together with the other prelates and the proctors of the clergy of our province, we have continually interposed our efforts and procured that very many tallages and subsidies be granted, to the great burden and oppression of the clergy, so that by the succour of those subjects the enemies of the King, the kingdom and the Church might be driven away, and the Church and kingdom might rejoice in the sweetness of peace. For these things, as it seems, no fault can reasonably be imputed to you by us, as the common proverb attests: "If you are free of blame, someone else must praise you."

units.la: Super eo vero quod nobis imponitur quod quaedam excommunicationum sententias in libertatis Ecclesiasticae & magnae chartae violatores in genere dudum latas ad sugillandum opinioem Regiam, & praefatos ministros Regios diffamandos, ac seditionem in populo Regi comillo, pditorie fufciuandi, & deuotionem Comirū, procerū, & Magnatum Regni vestri Maiestati Regiae subtrahendam, mandauimus per literas nostras inloin locis pluribus insignibus publicari. Quia præmissa proditionis crimen in caput nostrum retorquere videntur, quo casu Rex nullus vel Dominus temporalis iudex nolter competens esse poterit, sicut satis supenus est ostensum, protestamur palam & publicè per præsentes, quod per dicta vel dicenda in nullo statu nostro præiudicare intendimus in hac parte, sed iudicis cuiuscunque secularis examen totaliter declinare. Extra iudicialiter tamen ad nostram innocentiam detegendam bene fatemur nec possumus dißiteri quod excommunicationum quasdam sententias in libertatis Ecclesiasticæ & magnæ chartæ violatores, & alias aliquas à sanctis patribus olim latas in genere denunciauimus & per alios fecimus nunciari. Regiam tamen personam Reginæ & liberorum suorum quatenus potuimus excipiendo specificè atque clarè, quibus neminem disfamauimus cum nullum in nominauerimus in eisdem, nec per hoc in populi, salua dictantus Rouereatia, sedinonem proditorie procuauimus, qui vobis in omnibus est in præsenti obedientia iuxta subtrahi fecimus, qui vobis intendunt per omnia sicut decet prout mundus totus poterit intueri, sed nobis ille qui novit omnia testis erit quod Maguares & populares Regni vestri quatenus nobis fuit possibile semper induximus publice & privatim, vt vos intime diligerent, & vobis in vestris agendis promptius assisterent, & vos toto posse iuuare-rent, sicut toti Regno vestro satis est notum. In fine verò epistolarum vestrarum prædictarum multa videntur contra nos ad suggillationem famæ nostræ dicta, proposita, & generaliter recitata, videlicet quod vos in minori ætate constituti improuido nostro consilio donationes prodigas, alienationes prohibitas, gratiasque fecistis aliquas excessiuas, ita quod per eas erarium vestrum totaliter est exhaustum, vtetius afferentes quod munerum acceptione corruptos magnas pecuniarum summas vobis debitas quibusdam sine causa rationabili remisisse, plurimoque vestros fiscales redditus & prouentus nostris nostrorumq; vsibus applicasse & aliis personis malemeritis erogasse, quodque non solum munerum sed & personarum acceptor existens contra votum vestrum & præstitum vobis fidelitatis iuramentum ad officia publica, in terris vestræ ditionis subiectis, dignis & benemeritis postpositis & repulsis, indignos admisimus, multaque alia animo indignato tenere attentate præsumptimus in statu Regii detrimentum, & dignitatis Regiæ læsionem, in damnum populi & grauamen, potestate nobis traditâ & commisso officio abutendo. Præmissa iterum protestatione prædicta, quia Regia Maiestas in præmissis periurium per viam eriminis nobis vt videtur imponit, qua causa iudex noster non citius licet necesse potestis. Ad generalia tamen generaliter respondemus, quod iuxta distinctionem nobis à Deo concessam in vestris existentes officiis, vestræ Regiæ Maiestati semper fideliter deseruiuimus, sanaq; consilia iudicio nostro vobis dodimus in agendis, donationibus prohibitis, gratiis ve exceßiuis, seu magnarum pecuniarum summarum vobis debitarum remissionibus, siue tam rationabili per vos factis, munerû corruptione, odio, amore vel fauore: nullum fallaciter prebentes assensum, sed honorem vestrum & commodum in præmissis & aliis omnibus pro viribus conseruando. Et quia donationibus variis & remissionibus aliquoties viriliter restitimus, à Regiis seruitoribus & aliis reportauimus sæpius malas grates. Et in specie conflituerit de præmissis tangulis congruum secundum Deum & veritatem daremus speciale responsum. Nostræ enim memoriæ non occurrit ad præsens quod donationes magnas aliquas nobis prætentibus & scientibus Regia fecerit Celsitudo. His dumtaxat exceptis quas certis Comitibus per vos nuper de novo creatis ex consensu Parlamenti solennius in Regio vestro palatio tunc apud Westm. celebrati, largitione Regia coniunctis, quas tunc credidimus & adhuc credimus, non in præiudicium Regium factas esse, sed & in vestri cederecommodum & honorem. Docet enim rerum experientia qualem locum pro vobis & regno hactenus tenuerunt, quantaq; pro vobis passi sunt & patiuntur ad præsens. Decrecessiuis vero gratiis seu remissionibus Regia libertate factis non recolimus in præsenti nisi de remissione debitori toti populo vestro Anglicano, in vltimo Parlamento vestro vobis tunc præsentibus apud Westm. cōuocato, intelligere voluerit vestra serenitas quæ ea occasione ex consensu Regio & totius Parlamenti concessa fuerat vestra maiori viIi ate pensata, vt terræ communitas nonam concederet supradictam, nec alio modo cōsentire voluit dicta communitas ad nonæ prædictæ subsidium faciendum, quod nobis ratione præuia non poterit imputari, Dictis vero generalibus iuxta iuris exigentiam specialibus declaratis, ad declarata responsa dabimus satis clara, vnum tamen non omittimus de quo miramur nobis obiectum, quod nostris & nostrorum vlibus Regios applicauimus redditus & prouenrus, quia nouit in coelo residens iustus iudex, quod nec erras Regias prouentus vel redditus aliquos nobis vel nostris hactenus applicauimus, nec vnquam applicare voluimus, sed in vestris & parentum vestrorum negociis pro quibus 30. duabus vicibus mare transfuimus, & versus Scotiam eundo multories & redeundo, aliisque variis vestris agendis in tantum de nostro expendimus, quod de marsupiis nostris dici potuit sicut superius in vestris epistolis recitatur. Modicum ibi, modicum ibi. A principio enim guerrae vsque in diem praesentem ab aerario Regio nihil omnino recepimus 300. librisexceptis, sicq; malum contra nos excogitatum proponitur, laborum, expensarum, & nostrae gratitudinis nullus memoriter recordatur. Ideo dicere poterto cum Iob, vtinam appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram merui, & calamitas quam patior in statera. Certe quasi arena maris haec grauior appareret. Personarum acceptores vero Domino teste nunquam fuimus, sed Regiam voluntatem semper praeponere cupientes, ad officia publica quibuscunque terris & locis Regiae ditioni subiectis dignos praefecimus & praefici procuravimus, quatenus humana conditio mores hominum scire permisit tuata scientiam & possibilitatem nobis desuper datam, dona vel munera propterea a nemine admittentes. Et si quis dicere volu erit & probare quod munera vel pecuniam ab aliquibus recepe rhnus, occasione praemissa parati erimus quaerelantibus omnibus & etiam impetificandis quandocunque Regiae placuerit Maiestati secundum legem Regni & consuetudinem respondere. Honore Dei statu & ordine nostris in omnibus semper saluis. Scientes seuerissime Princeps pro constanti quod si sana conscientia vestri consilii arcana vobis reuelare liceret, oftendermus apertissime toti mundo quibus omnium praemissorum defectus iusto Dei ac hominum veracium iudicio imputari deberet. Haec ad libellum famosum praedictum responsa sufficiant in praesenti, & vtinam propter honorem Regium nunquam scriptus & publicatus fuisset. Qui licet famam nostram sugillare & lacerare prima facie videatur, consideratis iamen intime consideran dis & scriptis in illo, non sine proditionis Regis & Regni macula & animae suae periculo iusto iudicio euadere poterunt qui libellum huiusmodi dictauerunt, seu in his praebuerunt consilium vel consensum, vel in eo contenta ad nostram iniuriam recitarunt, seu ad nostram infamiam publicarunt.
units.tr: As for the charge that we have caused certain sentences of excommunication, long since pronounced in general against violators of ecclesiastical liberty and of Magna Carta, to be published in many notable places, in order to disparage the royal reputation, to defame the royal ministers named, to stir up sedition among the people against the King, to betray him, and to withdraw from Your Royal Majesty the loyalty of the Earls, nobles and Magnates of your realm: since the charge of treason seems to be turned back upon our own head, in which case no king or temporal lord can be a competent judge over us, as has been sufficiently shown above, we protest openly and publicly by these presents that by what has been said or may be said we intend no prejudice to any of our rights in this matter, and that we wholly decline the examination of any secular judge whatsoever. Nevertheless, outside of judicial proceedings, to lay bare our innocence, we freely confess, and cannot deny, that we did pronounce in general, and have caused others to proclaim, certain sentences of excommunication against violators of ecclesiastical liberty and of Magna Carta, and some others once pronounced by the holy fathers. But we have specifically and clearly excepted the royal person, the Queen and her children, as far as we could; we have defamed none of them, since we named none of them in those sentences. Nor have we by this procured sedition against the King treacherously among the people, saving the due reverence of your Royal Majesty. We have caused the people to be withdrawn from obedience to you, which is in every way fitting for them to render to you, as the whole world can see. But he who knows all things will be witness for us that we have always, as far as was possible for us, persuaded the Magnates and commons of your realm, both publicly and privately, to love you heartily, to assist you more readily in your affairs, and to help you with all their power, as is well known to your whole realm. At the end of your aforesaid letters, many things are said, proposed and recited in general against us, to disparage our good name: namely, that when you were in your minority, through our improvident counsel you made prodigal gifts and forbidden alienations, and some excessive grants, so that your treasury has been wholly drained by them; and they further allege that, corrupted by the receipt of bribes, we remitted large sums of money owed to you, without reasonable cause, to certain persons; that we applied a great part of your fiscal revenues and income to our own uses and to those of our kin, and bestowed them on other ill-deserving persons; and that, being an acceptor not only of bribes but also of persons, we admitted unworthy men, against your will and the oath of fidelity sworn to you, to public offices in the lands subject to your dominion, while worthy and well-deserving men were set aside and rejected. They add that we presumed to hold many other things with an indignant mind, to the detriment of the state and the injury of royal dignity, to the loss and burden of the people, abusing the power entrusted to us and the office committed to us. Again, with the aforesaid protest made, since Your Royal Majesty seems to impute to us perjury by way of crime in these matters, for which cause our judge is not bound to answer more quickly, we nevertheless answer the general charges in general terms: that, according to the distinction granted us by God, while we held our offices we always served your Royal Majesty faithfully, and gave you sound counsel in your affairs, whether concerning forbidden gifts, excessive grants, remissions of large sums of money owed to you, or the remissions made by you on whatever ground, whether reasonable or not, through the corruption of bribes, hatred, love or favour. We have never deceitfully given assent to any such matter, but have preserved your honour and advantage in these and all other matters with all our strength. And because we have several times strenuously opposed various gifts and remissions, we have often received from the royal servants and others bad thanks in return. And as to the specific points, we would give a proper and specific answer to each, according to God and the truth. For it does not occur to our memory at present that Your Highness made any great gifts while we were present and aware of them, except those granted by royal bounty to certain Earls newly created by you, with the consent of Parliament, solemnly celebrated at that time in your royal palace at Westminster. Those we then believed, and still believe, were made not to the prejudice of the Crown but to your advantage and honour. For the experience of affairs teaches what place they have held for you and the realm up to now, and what they have suffered and still suffer for you. As to the excessive grants or remissions made by royal liberality, at present we recall nothing except the remission of debts to your whole English people, which in your last Parliament, convened at Westminster while you were present, was granted on that occasion by royal and general consent of Parliament, your serenity having weighed it with your greater wisdom, so that the commons of the land would grant the aforesaid ninth. Nor would the said commons otherwise consent to make the aid of the said ninth; this cannot rightly be imputed to us. Having declared the general charges in the specific manner required by law, we shall give sufficiently clear answers to the particular points. There is one thing, however, which we do not omit, and at which we wonder that it is objected to us: that we applied the royal revenues and income to our own and our kin's uses. For the just judge who dwells in heaven knows that we have never applied to ourselves or our kin any royal revenues or income, nor ever wished to apply them; but in your affairs and those of your parents, for which we twice crossed the sea and travelled to Scotland many times, going and returning, and in your various other affairs, we have spent so much of our own that it might be said of our purses what is recited above in your letters: "A little here, a little there." For from the beginning of the war to the present day we have received nothing at all from the royal treasury, except 300 pounds. And so the evil device is put forward against us, while no one at all remembers our labours, expenses and gratitude. Therefore I may say with Job: "Oh that my sins, for which I have deserved wrath, and the calamity which I suffer, were weighed in the balance! Surely they would appear heavier than the sand of the sea." But we have never been acceptors of persons, the Lord being witness. Desiring always to prefer the royal will, we have set over public offices, in all lands and places subject to royal dominion, men who were worthy, and have procured that they be set over them, as far as human nature allows us to know men's characters, and as far as the knowledge and ability given us from above permit; and we have accepted no gifts or bribes from anyone for this reason. And if anyone wishes to say and prove that we received bribes or money from any persons, we shall be ready, on the aforesaid ground, to answer to all complainants, and even to those who are to be impeached, whenever it shall please Your Royal Majesty, according to the law and custom of the realm. Saving always the honour of God and our state and office in all things. Most severe Prince, know for certain that if it were lawful for a sound conscience to reveal to you the secrets of your counsel, we would show most plainly to the whole world to what defects of all these matters should be imputed, by the just judgment of God and of truthful men. These answers are sufficient for the present to the aforesaid defamatory libel; and would that it had never been written and published, for the sake of Royal honour. Although it seems at first sight to slander and tear our good name, nevertheless, when the things inwardly considered and written in it are weighed, not without the stain of treason against King and realm, and not without peril to their own souls, those who composed such a libel, or gave counsel or consent to it, or recited its contents to our injury, or published them to our infamy, will be unable to escape the just judgment.

units.la: Quod corde perfecto Maiestas Regia considerare dignetur quam incolumem & sibi placabilem conseruare Rex illic dignetur per quem Reges regnant & Principes dominantur. Amen.
units.tr: May Your Royal Majesty deign to consider this with a perfect heart; and may the King there, through whom kings reign and princes rule, deign to keep you safe and well disposed toward him. Amen.

units.la: LITERÆ EXCVSATORIÆ DOMINI REGIS CONTRA ARCHIEPISCOPUM.
units.tr: THE KING'S LETTERS OF EXCUSE AGAINST THE ARCHBISHOP.

units.la: DWARNVS Dei gratia Rex Angliæ & Franciæ & Dominus Hiberniæ Episcopis &c. Cicatrix cordium superbia quæ semper ascendit, plerumque generat morbos ex remediis & ex medicina languorem. Et hoc probat Iohannes Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi praesumptio fastuosa, qui cum pridem de nobis & nostris quaedam sinistra, sicut in literis nostris excusatoriis super hoc vobis & aliis nuper directis plenius continetur publicè praedicasset, & ea mandasset in pluribus locis insignibus publicari, iam prioribus iniurijs iniurias cumulans grauiores, excusationes nostras veras, quas ad medelam laxare dignitatis & famæ Regiæ proudimus, nostris fidelibus inumari: nititur exquisitis machinationibus impugnare, & per nouas literas vobis & aliis noniter destinatas calumnioso eloquio. Licet fit de more summorum Pontificum, Cardinalium, & Praelatorum inferiorum affatus & literas Regias Reuerenter & benignè suscipere, ipse tamen dicas excusatorias nostras iusta & vera, quod congruis loco & tempore clare probare proponimus continentes, de eftabiles & libellos famosos intitulat in nostro nomine macularam falsam ponens, quia si quis gerens salutis publicae custodiam, scripta probare erimus, na sit paratus, si assertionibus suis opitulata fuerit vera fides, a culpa famosi carminis excusatur, & habetur ex hoc laude dignus. Ipse etiam non seruato more maiorum qui Principes suos colere solent & diligere, & pro eis obseruationes, orationes, postulationes, ac gratiarum actiones a se & aliis fieri, facere, & ipsos instruere in spiritu lenitatis, contra nos & larerales nostros in elationis spiritu temeritate factionis & inuentionis peruerse telam orditur, iniquitatem suam prolongando, & quaerens solatium miserorum plu-res vi. res, videlicet habere confortes in poena, & quod deterius est in peccato suffraganeos suos & alios devotos, & fideles nostros mendacij sermonibus in nostros præcipitare satagit irreverentiam & contemptum, & quamuis apud Deum non gradus elongatiorum, sed vitæ melioris actio comprobetur, glorians in alitudine status sui sibi tanquam Christo legato reverentiam exigit, quam nobis a se debitam non impendit, quin imo cum ipse & alij præstati Regni qui de nobis Ecclesiarum suarum temporalia recipiunt ex debito fidelitatis iuratæ, fidem, honorem & reverentiam debeant exhibere, solus ipse pto fide perfidiam, pro honore contumeliam, & contemptum pro reverentia reddete non vel ctur. Vnde & si parati sumus & semper fuerimus patres spirituales vt eouenit tcuereti, eorum tamen ostensas quas in nostri & regni nostri periculum redundare conspicimus, non debemus continuebitus oculis praeterire. Conqueritur autem idem Arch. contra se absentem inauditum, & indefensum etiam quam praefatis literis nostris excusatoriis obiecta fuisse, & se tetum capitalium sceleratum iudicatum, aci nos vt fatuè præcedit profeorum criminalitate ad summam contra cum, quod vtique non est verum, cum sollus excusatoris vices dumtaxat impleuimus necessitate compulsi, ne fami nam nostram negligere videremur. Sed videat calumniosus reprehensur si in caput suum haec quaerela iuste valeat retorqueri, qui nos Regem suum & consiliarios nostros absentes, inauditos, indefensos, ne coniunctos opprefores & transgressores iurium falso & malitiose verbis assertiuis deseriptit, cum neque metu culpa redarguit, quit erprobatum a se crimen incurrit, & in quo alium iudicat seipsum condemnat, dum in eodem ipse reprobus inuenitur. Ad hoc licet non nostris voluntatis sed propriis cupiditatibus studuerit inseruire, improperatatamen & iadat se Regijs negocijs, vt verbis eius vtamur, laborum fallhigo desudasse, vnde Dei & hominum timet grauissimas offensas multipliciter incurrille, & hoc iuste timere poterit, cum in illorum sorte censeatur, qui iuxta Prophetiam improperium docuerint linguas suas loqui mendacium: & vt inique agerent, laborarunt. Ceti runad alia quaedam fabulosa & fucata verba in ipsius Arch. literis comprehensa, licet ea posse- mus rationibus luce clarioribus cofutare, ne sermonem protrahamus, duximus ad praesens non dare responsum. Sed quia non decet cum homine contentioso funem trahere, & nec eius peruersitatibus consentire, vobis in fide & dilectione qua nobis tenemini, firmiter iniugendo mandamus, quod non obstante quocunq; mandato ipsius Archiepiscopi, cui in derogationem honoris Regij contra fidelitatis iuramentum nobis praestitum obedire non debetis, ad publicationem eorum quae in praefatis literis nostris excusatoriis continentur, iuxta ipsarū setiem proceedatis. Et qui de consecratione iurium & praerogatiuarum nostrarum Regalium quae progenitorum nostrorum Regum Angliæ dignè reco- lenda prioritas magnificè defenduit, fumus vt debemus summè solicitì, ac idem Archiepiscopus ad concitandum contra nos Clerum & populum, & ad impediendum expeditionem guerræ nostræ quam perceius consilium principaliter assumpsimus, quaiedam denunciationes & publicationes sententiarum excommunicationum, ac monitio nes iniuriosas, ac iuri cotonz & Regiæ dignitatis nostræ praeiudiciales cum per eas nitacui simus Rex inuictus, capaces esse dignosciimur, & qua nos & progenitores nostri scie tibus & tolerantibus summis pontificibus ac praelatis & Clero Regni nostri vt sumus pacifice ab antiquo, fecit & petalios fieri & publicari mandauit, in Maiestatis nostrae lesionem & iurium ac praetogatiuarum nostrarum Regalium derogationem manifestam, vobis destrictè & sub incumbenti periculo probibemus, ne publicationes, denunciationes seu monitiones hufusmodi indebitas, & iuribus ac praerogatiis nostris Regiis derogatorias & praeiudiciales, vel alia per quae fideles nostri contra nos concitari, vel expeditioni guerræ nostræ in fiubertionem nostri & fidelium nostrorum posuit, quod absit, aliquâliter impediri ad mandatum ipsius Archiepisc. vel alterius cuiuscunq; quomodo libet per vos & alios faciatis, vel quantum in vobis est ab aliis fieri permittatis. Et si quid per vos in hac parte actum fuerit, celeriter revocetis. T. meipso apud turrim London. 31. die Martij. Anno. &c. Hisita cedentibus, Rex edicto Archiepiscopum in ius vocauit, Archiepiscopus non esse sibi tutum, nisi in Parlamento coram praesulibus & procerebus Regni se de tantis criminibus purgare respondit. Parlamentum itaque conuocatum & protectio Regia Archiepiscopo vt tutè accedere possit, data est. Cum Londinum venisset, Londinensem & Ciceftensem Episcopos fecerunt coenit. Ab hiscum magna Clericorum & armigerorum multitudine ad Regis palatium, vbi Parlamentum indictum fuit, ductus accedit. Cui ingredienti occurrunt senescallus & Camerarius Regis, qui cū Regis nomine Parla lamen um intrare prohibebant, donec in scaccario Regis de eremiinibus obiectis iudicium subiisset. Cantuarienfis ne Regem conuocaret, venit in scaccarium, ibi articulorum de quibus accusatio inftituia fuit, copiam accepit, quibus fe habita deliberatione matura responsurum prominit. Tum eum Regis venia Parlamentum ingressus est. Ibi coram cunctis praesulibus & procerebus Regni fui ad Parlamentu aduentum causas exponit. Pro honore, iuribus & libertatibus Ecclesiae, pro commodo & vtilitate Regni, pro emolumento & honore Regis: ad extremum vt de diuersis criminibus sibi impositis, & per totam Angliam publicatis in Parlamento fe purgarer. Eo die mihil actum est sed Regie iubente dimisso Concilio singulì receffsrunt. Alio die cum Archiepiscopus ingredi arlam mentum veller, a quodam Wilhelmo Aitew oode farellite Regio Regis nomine prohibitus est, quo facto Archiepiscopus astantes sic affatur est. Amici, Rex mead hoc Parlamentum scripto suo vocauit. Et ego tanqua maior par Regni, post Regem & vocem primam in Parlamento habere debens, iura Ecclesiae mex Cantuarienf. vendico, & ideo ingressum in Parlamentum petio. Et cum ingredi a satellitibus exclusus non potuit, crucé propriis manibus apprehendit, ac firmiter asseruit fe ab eo loco non recessurum, donec Parlamentum ingrediendi potestas ei a Rege fiat. Acceffierunt ad Archiepiscopum de inde alii minis & maledictis Archiepiscopum insectantes. Quibus Archiepiscopus, Maledictio inquit Dei omnipotentis & beatissimae matris suae, & Sancti Thomae, & mea super capita eorum qui ipsum Regem taliter impediunt, veniat, Amen, Amen. In hac turba proceres aliquot a Parlamento prodeunt. Quos Archiepiscopus obsecrauit, vt Regem pro suo & Cant. Ecclesiae iure exorate vellent, illi feid factúros humaniter pollicentur. Interim articuli quidam callide fabricati, & vt Archiepiscopo populare odium genonerarent, vbiq; publicati sunt. Huius in Archiepiscopum conflictationis authores cenfebantur Wintonienfis Episcopus, D. Darfi, & Wilhelmus de Kyllesby. Sed Wintoniensis rem callidè diffimu!auit. Hi aperti in inimicitiis fuerunt. Tandem Magnatum in tercefsione atq; gratia Archiepif. Regis venia Parlamentum ingressus, de omnibus tibi criminationibus impositis legitimè fe in Parlamento purgaturum obtulit, vnde electi fuerunt duodecim pares Regni Anglie, videlicet London, Hereforden, Bathonen. & Exon. Episcopi. Tum Arundel, Sarisburiensis, Huntingdonensis, & Suffolcien fis Comites, & Henricus Percy, Thomas Wake, Radulphus Baffet, & Radulphus Neuil Barones, vt hi de criminibus Cantuarienfi obiectis deliberarent, Regique referrent quid confulmum factum fit.
units.tr: James, by the grace of God King of England and France and Lord of Ireland, to the Bishops, etc. Pride, which always rises up, usually brings forth diseases from the remedies, and the cure becomes a sickness. John, Archbishop of Canterbury, proves this by his arrogant presumption. Having lately publicly preached certain unfavourable things about us and our people, as is more fully set out in our letters of excuse recently sent to you and others on this matter, and having ordered them published in many notable places, he now heaps greater wrongs upon earlier wrongs. He strives by exquisite contrivances to attack our true excuses, which we have decided to publish for the healing of the dignity and reputation of the Crown, and to commend them to our faithful subjects. He does this by new letters lately sent to you and others, in a slanderous manner. It is customary for the chief Pontiffs, Cardinals and lesser prelates to receive and welcome the words and letters of kings reverently and kindly. Yet he calls our letters of excuse unjust and false, and publishes them as infamous libels in our name, staining them with falsehood. We intend to prove this at a suitable place and time, with clear reasons. For if anyone who keeps watch over the public safety is ready to prove his writings, and if sound faith supports his assertions, he is excused from the blame of a defamatory poem and thereby deserves praise. He also, not keeping the custom of our ancestors, who were accustomed to honour and love their princes, and to make observances, prayers, petitions and thanksgivings for them, and to instruct others to do the same in a spirit of gentleness, instead weaves a web against us and our subjects in a spirit of pride, with the rashness of faction and perverse invention. He prolongs his own iniquity, and seeking the comfort of the wretched, he tries to have more companions in punishment, and, what is worse, in sin, his suffragans and other devoted and faithful subjects of ours. By lying words he strives to cast down upon our people disrespect and contempt. Although before God it is not the height of rank but the good conduct of life that is approved, he glories in the loftiness of his station and demands reverence for himself as the legate of Christ, while withholding the reverence that he owes to us. Indeed, although he and the other prelates of our realm, who receive the temporal goods of their churches from us, owe us faith, honour and reverence by the oath of fidelity they have sworn, he alone returns perfidy for faith, insult for honour, and contempt for reverence. Hence, although we are, and always have been, ready to regard them as spiritual fathers as is fitting, we must not pass by with closed eyes the dangers that we see are likely to fall upon us and our realm. Moreover, the same Archbishop complains that charges were laid against him in the aforesaid letters of excuse while he was absent, unheard and undefended, and that he has been judged a guilty and condemned man. He says that we, foolishly, have rushed to the greatest criminal accusation against him. This is certainly not true, since we only performed the duty of excusing ourselves, compelled by necessity, lest we seem to neglect our good name. But let the slanderer see whether this complaint can justly be turned back upon his own head. He describes us, his King, and our councillors, as absent, unheard and undefended, and falsely and maliciously in his words calls us oppressors and violators of rights, when he himself is convicted by his own culpability. He incurs the very crime he has proved against others, and in the matter in which he judges another, he condemns himself, since he is found equally reprobate. In this matter, although he has sought to serve not our will but his own desires, he says, to use his own words, that he has laboured and sweated in the King's affairs with a falsely fawning zeal. Hence he fears that he has incurred the gravest offences against God and men in many ways, and he may justly fear this, since he is counted among those who, according to the prophecy, have taught their tongues to speak lies, and have laboured to act unjustly. As for certain other fabulous and disguised words contained in the Archbishop's letters, although we could refute them with reasons clearer than light, we have decided, so as not to prolong the discourse, not to give a reply for the present. But since it is not fitting to pull a rope with a contentious man, nor to consent to his perversities, we firmly enjoin and command you, in the faith and love by which you are bound to us, that, notwithstanding any command of the Archbishop himself, to whom you ought not to obey in derogation of the King's honour and contrary to the oath of fidelity sworn to us, you are to proceed to publish those things which are contained in our aforesaid letters of excuse, according to their tenor. And since we, who have magnificently defended the preservation of the rights and royal prerogatives of our Kings of England, which ought to be worthily honoured by our ancestors, are, as we ought to be, most solicitous, and since the same Archbishop, to stir up the clergy and people against us and to hinder the expedition of our war, which we have principally undertaken on the advice of our council, has been found capable of certain denunciations and publications of sentences of excommunication, and injurious admonitions, prejudicial to the right of our crown and royal dignity, which were made and ordered to be published, though we, and our ancestors, have been peacefully accustomed to this from ancient times, with the knowledge and toleration of the chief pontiffs, prelates and clergy of our realm, we strictly and under threat of penalty forbid you to allow those publications, denunciations or admonitions of this kind, which are undue and derogatory and prejudicial to our royal rights and prerogatives, or any other things by which our faithful subjects might be stirred up against us, or by which, God forbid, the expedition of our war, for the defence of us and our faithful subjects, might in any way be hindered, to be done by you or others at the command of the Archbishop or of any other person whatsoever. And if you, or anyone acting through you in this matter, have done anything, you are to revoke it quickly. Given by our own hand at the Tower of London, 31 March, in the year, etc. Matters proceeding in this way, the King summoned the Archbishop to court by edict. The Archbishop replied that it was not safe for him unless he might clear himself of such great crimes in Parliament, before the prelates and nobles of the realm. Therefore Parliament was summoned, and royal protection was given to the Archbishop so that he might come safely. When he came to London, he took with him the Bishops of London and Chichester. Accompanied by a great crowd of clergy and armed men, he came to the King's palace, where Parliament had been called. As he entered, the Steward and the Chamberlain of the King met him, and in the King's name forbade him to enter Parliament until he had submitted to judgment in the Exchequer concerning the charges laid against him. The Archbishop of Canterbury, so that he would not seem to refuse the King, went into the Exchequer. There he received a copy of the articles on which the accusation had been brought, and promised that he would reply to them after mature deliberation. Then, with the King's permission, he entered Parliament. There, before all the prelates and nobles of the realm, he set out the causes of his coming to Parliament: for the honour, rights and liberties of the Church, for the advantage and usefulness of the realm, for the profit and honour of the King, and finally so that he might clear himself in Parliament of the various crimes laid against him and published throughout England. On that day nothing was done, but by the King's command the council was dismissed and each departed. On the next day, when the Archbishop wished to enter Parliament, he was forbidden by a certain William Aylesworth, a royal officer, in the King's name. When this was done, the Archbishop addressed those standing by in this way: "Friends, the King has summoned this Parliament by his writ. And I, as the greatest peer of the realm, who ought to have the first voice in Parliament after the King, claim the rights of the Church of Canterbury, and therefore I ask to enter Parliament." And when, being shut out by the guards, he could not enter, he seized the cross with his own hands, and firmly declared that he would not leave that place until the power to enter Parliament was granted to him by the King. Then other men came to the Archbishop and attacked him with threats and curses. To them the Archbishop said: "May the curse of almighty God and of his most blessed mother, and of Saint Thomas, and mine, fall upon the heads of those who thus hinder the King himself. Amen, Amen." In this uproar some of the nobles came out of Parliament. The Archbishop begged them to pray to the King for his right and that of the Church of Canterbury, and they promised humanely that they would do so. Meanwhile certain cunningly fabricated articles were published everywhere, so as to produce popular hatred against the Archbishop. The authors of this attack upon the Archbishop were considered to be the Bishop of Winchester, Sir Dars, and William de Kyllesby. But the Bishop of Winchester cleverly dissembled the matter. These men were open in their enmity. At last, through the intercession of the magnates and the favour of the Archbishop, the King allowed him to enter Parliament, and he offered to clear himself lawfully in Parliament of all the charges laid against him. Hence twelve peers of the realm of England were chosen, namely the Bishops of London, Hereford, Bath and Wells, and Exeter; then the Earls of Arundel, Salisbury, Huntingdon and Suffolk; and Henry Percy, Thomas Wake, Ralph Basset and Ralph Neville, barons, so that they might deliberate on the charges laid against the Archbishop of Canterbury and report to the King what had been decided.

units.la: Ac paulò post purgatione nulla indicta aut recepta omnibus pene Parlamenti ordinibus pro Archiepiscopo deprecantibus, Rex eum sua sponte legitimè purgaui & excusatum pronunciauit, eumq; multò magis charum quam ante habuit, omnibus q; gerendis in Anglia rebus fe in militia absente praefecit. Hoc dissoluto Parlamento Rex iubditis hac in Archiepiscopum declarata beneuolentia ar Actiffime deuincitis in militiapergit. At Archiepiscopus postquam has deleuisset innocentia sua calumnias, in Arcuata sua Londini curia statuta ab aduocaris & procuratoribus aliifq; obseruanda edidit. Tu Clerifynodus duas in Ecclesia Paulina Londini celebrauit in quibus aequifimas multas coftitutiones, quae bodie obseruantur, tulit. Rex Gallum feroci Marte expilans postquam biennio belli gessisset, exercitu in castris relicto in Angliam reuersus est, & Weftmonafterii Parlamentum tenuit. In eo Clerusei concessit decimas triennales, & Rex Clero viciffim concessit, quòd nullus Archiepiscopus vel Episcopus coram iuftitiariis Regis iudicium subeat, nisi Rex hoc nominatim & specialiter praeceperit. Tum quod nullus Clericus coram iufticiariis Regis iudicium sustineat, siue ad ipsius Regis, siue alicuius partis instantiam, fi fe submittat Clericarui, & dicat fe membrum Ecclesiae sanctae, nec debere ipsius iuftitiariis respondere. Quod fi quis Clericus de Bigamia accusetur, de eo non fore permissum iuftitiariis inquirere, sed mittatur Curiae Christianae. Iohannes autem Archiepiscopus postquam quindecim annis fedifiet apud Magfeld in morbum lethalem 50 incidit, ibi condito testamento omnia in famulos distribuit atq; obiit. Monens Simonè Islepe sibi in Archiepiscopatu successurum praedixit. In Eleemosynis assiduus fuit, singulis diebus fummomane. 13. pauperibus. 13. d. tum hora nona aliis. 13. singulis panem & carnes cum olere coctas, & hora pomeridiana aliis. 13. singulos panes & denarios largitus est. In subditos benignus & misericors fuit. Cum nemine summo iure agere voluit, fi qui in leges commisissent, cum his dispensare, magis quàm poenas exigere folebat. Ecclesiae Cantuarienfi cappam preciofiffimam, & mitram peroptimam & libros Decretalium aliq; decretorum dedit Conuentui Cantuarienfi annuam pensionem centum solidorum de Ecclesiis Preston & Bocton monasterio de Feuerfam appropriatis assignauit. Corpus eius in Crastino beatæ Mariæ Cantuariam deductum & in Ecclesia Christi ad summum altare in australi parte, ad gradus altaris Dunstani in tumba alabastri honorifice sepultum est.
units.tr: And a little later, when no inquiry had been held and no evidence received, and almost all the orders of Parliament interceded for the Archbishop, the King of his own accord pronounced him lawfully cleared and acquitted. He held him even more dear than before and placed him in charge of all affairs in England while the King was absent at war. After Parliament was dissolved, the King, with his subjects bound even more closely to him by this declared goodwill towards the Archbishop, went back to the war. The Archbishop, having wiped away the false charges by his innocence, issued in his court at London, the Arches, statutes to be observed by advocates, proctors and others. Then a synod of the clergy held two sessions at St Paul's in London, in which it enacted very fair constitutions, which are observed today. The King, plundering France with fierce warfare, after waging war for two years, returned to England, leaving his army in camp, and held a Parliament at Westminster. In it the clergy granted triennial tenths, and in return the King granted the clergy that no Archbishop or Bishop should submit to judgment before the King's justices unless the King had expressly and specially commanded it. Likewise, that no cleric should submit to judgment before the King's justices, whether at the King's suit or at the instance of any party, if he submitted himself to the clergy and declared himself a member of the holy Church, and that he ought not to answer to the justices. And if any cleric were accused of bigamy, the justices were not to be allowed to inquire into it, but he was to be sent to the Christian court. John the Archbishop, however, after sitting at Mayfield for fifteen years, fell into a deadly sickness, and there, having made his will, distributed all his goods among his servants and died. Admonishing Simon Islip, he had foretold that Islip would succeed him in the archbishopric. He was constant in almsgiving: every day early in the morning he gave thirteen poor people thirteen pence; then at the ninth hour to others thirteen each a loaf and meat cooked with herbs; and in the afternoon to others thirteen loaves and pence each. He was kind and merciful towards his subjects. He never wished to press the strict rigour of the law against anyone who had broken it, but was accustomed to deal leniently with them rather than to exact penalties. To the church of Canterbury he gave a most precious cope, an excellent mitre and books of Decretals and other decrees. He assigned to the convent of Canterbury an annual pension of one hundred shillings from the churches of Preston and Bocton, appropriated to the monastery of Feversham. His body was carried to Canterbury on the day after the feast of St Mary, and was honourably buried in Christ Church, before the high altar on the south side, at the steps of Dunstan's altar, in an alabaster tomb.

units.la: LIII. Iohannes Vfford vel Offord.
units.tr: LIII. John Ufford or Offord.

units.la: OSt Iohannes Stratford mortem, etsi Rex Edwardus in castris & Gallico bello detentus in Angliam redire sine suo & exercitus incommodo non potuisset, tamen omnia pacis atque belli negotia, tam prudenter à Iohanne Stratford profuta fuerunt, ut nihil Regi domi forisque pertimescendum fuit. Id iudicabatur Rex qui simulatque audiisset Papam conciliatum Lodouico Imperatori fuisse qui seinuito Imperium gessisset, ac virosque a Gallo seductos contilium iniisse, quomodo Regem ad pacis conditiones cogerent. Incant, inquit, inter se quascunque volunt conditiones, ego enim cum utroque dimicare valeo. Quo quidem tempore cum Papa suam in Gallum beneuolentia, a quo multis donis muneribusque iam effectus est, nouo quodam & insigni, sed inani titulo declarauit. Nam quoddam virum nobilem Lodouicum de Hispania Galli legatum in hoc pacis ac inducratum procurando negocio creauit in publico consistorio earum Insularum Principem, quæ in Oceano vicinæ Hispaniæ fortunatæ dictæ sunt. Earum incolæ tunc Barbari, quidam feri & immanes nulla religione aut diuino cultu imbuti fuerunt. Lodouicus autem hunc Regium titulum laude gratiosq; dignum futurum dixit, cum Papa earum Insularum possessionem pacificam sibi traderet. Nam in Episcopatibus & Ecclesiasticis dignitatibus conferendis possessionem simul atque titulum concessit. Quod ius cum in Regnis sibi vendicauit, merito lusus & contemptus est. Ac in Episcopatibus prouidendis reuiteri iam primum Papæ proceres Regni cum Rege ceperunt. Namq; Richardo Bury Episcopo Dunelmensi mortuo Rex ad Papam pro quodam Thoma Hatfeld suo Secretario intercessit. Quem cum pleriq; indoctum laicum, & gradu Episcopali indignum ad Papam criminabatur. Papa, si Rex, inquit, pro alino supplicaret, obtinuisset ad votaista vice. Pap. lis huius vox obsequii causa haec fuit. Rex cum proceribus paulo ante ad Papam scripserat non literæ de Episcopatibus & Ecclesiasticis beneficiis in Anglia amplius prouidere. Rex ipse secretarii sui gratiam primus à proposito, in quo se contra Papam cum proceribus statutum promisisset, recessit. Id indigne tulerunt proceres ac Papalico Regi illa (vt dixit) vice esse finius est, veritus ne si contradixisset vsurpatæ, puisionis iura amitteret. Namq; paulo ante cum Clemes Papa duobus suis Romæ Cardinalibus duo milliannuarum marcarum de beneficiis Ecclesiasticis proxime vacantibus (episcopalibus & conuentualibus Ecclesiis dumtaxat exceptis) promisisset, nec Clerus palam contradicere, vix autem occulte hisce reaudiret, Rex cum magnaribus sibi iunctis, has papales exactiones amplius pati noluit, sed Papæ puisores Regno discedere sub carceris poena sine mora mandauit. Quibus exactis à Papa litteris obiurgatus est, ad quem vicitem literas de libertate Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ Regia magnificentia & authoritate dignas dedit. Quibus à Papa & Cardinalibus perlectis obstupuerunt, nec literis tanta dignitate ac ratione plenis respondere potuerunt. Quas vt scriptæ atque rescriptæ fuerunt, vitaliq; inseruimus.
units.tr: After the death of John Stratford, although King Edward, detained in camp and in the French war, could not return to England without his own and his army's loss, yet all the affairs of peace and war were so prudently handled by John Stratford that the King had nothing to fear at home or abroad. The King judged this, who, as soon as he heard that the Pope had been reconciled to the Emperor Lewis, who had ruled the Empire against his will, and that the men seduced from the French side had entered a council as to how they might force the King to accept terms of peace, said: "Let them agree among themselves on whatever terms they like; for I am able to fight against both." At that time, too, the Pope declared his goodwill towards the French by a new and remarkable but empty title, since he had already been won over by many gifts and presents. For he created a certain noble man, Lewis of Spain, envoy of France in the business of procuring this peace and truce, in a public consistory, Prince of those islands in the Ocean near Spain which are called the Fortunate Isles. Their inhabitants were then barbarians, some wild and savage, imbued with no religion or divine worship. Lewis said that this royal title would be worthy of praise and favour, since the Pope was handing him peaceful possession of those islands. For he granted possession together with the title, in order to confer bishoprics and ecclesiastical dignities. When he claimed this right over kingdoms, he was rightly mocked and despised. And in providing bishoprics the nobles of the realm first began to protest, together with the King, against the papal authority. For when Richard Bury, Bishop of Durham, died, the King interceded with the Pope on behalf of one Thomas Hatfield, his secretary. When many accused him to the Pope as an unlearned layman unworthy of episcopal rank, the Pope said: "If the King had petitioned on behalf of someone else, he would have obtained it this time." This answer of the Pope was given out of compliance. The King, with the nobles, had a little earlier written to the Pope that he should no longer make provisions for bishoprics and ecclesiastical benefices in England. But the King himself was the first to depart from the purpose in which he had promised, together with the nobles, to stand against the Pope, out of favour to his secretary. The nobles took this ill, and the King, as he said, yielded on this occasion, fearing that if he contradicted them he would lose the rights of provision which he had usurped. For a little earlier Pope Clement had promised two of his Roman cardinals two thousand marks a year from ecclesiastical benefices next falling vacant (bishoprics and conventual churches alone excepted). The clergy did not openly object, though they hardly dared to, and murmured about it only in secret. But the King, with the magnates joined to him, was unwilling any longer to bear these papal exactions, and ordered the papal provisors to leave the realm without delay, under penalty of imprisonment. Having taken these measures, he was rebuked by letters from the Pope; to whom in return he sent letters on the liberty of the English Church, worthy of royal magnificence and authority. When these were read by the Pope and the cardinals, they were astonished, and could make no reply to letters so full of dignity and reason. We have inserted them here as they were written and answered.

units.la: Epistola Regi directa pro Cardinalibus, quibus prouisiones prius fuerat, expulsis de suis prouisionibus.
units.tr: Letter addressed to the King on behalf of the Cardinals, whose provisions had previously been made, when they were expelled from their provisions.

units.la: LEmens Episcopus seruus seruorum Dei charissimo in Christo filio, Domino Edwardo Regi Angliæ illustri salutem & Apostolicam benedictionem. Dudum post creationem nouorum sacrosanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ Cardinalium, prouida & matura deliberatione præuia per nos facta honoribus Dei & Ecclesiæ suæ Sanctæ, ac vtilitati Reipublicæ conuenire quod Cardinales ipsi qui super expediendis negociis ad aluum Apostolicæ sedis Vndiq; confluentibus nobilcum labores & onera patiuntur, & habeuerint congrue vnde suis valerent necessitatibus secundum statum sui decentiam prouidere.
units.tr: Clement, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved son in Christ, the illustrious Lord Edward, King of England, greeting and Apostolic blessing. Some time after the creation of new Cardinals of the holy Roman Church, after prudent and mature deliberation previously made by us, for the honour of God and of his holy Church, and for the good of the commonwealth, it was fitting that the Cardinals themselves, who bear labours and burdens in dispatching business at the court of the Apostolic see, gathering from every quarter around us, should have means sufficient to provide for their needs in keeping with the dignity of their station.

units.la: Demum excogitatis & mediis licitis, quibus ahsq; minori Ecclesiarum & personarum Ecclehasticarum grauamine huius prouisio sequi posset, de beneficiis Ecclesiasticis tunc in diuersis regnis in partibus Christianitatis vacantibus & in antea vacaturis vsque ad certam summam pro singulis eorundem nouorum Cardinalium, & sub certis formis & limitationibus praefatis Cardinalibus distinctis eis prout expedire videmus prouinciis gratias fecimus speciales. Cum a duobus ex eis de ducatu Aquitaniae oriundis, videlicet dilectis filiis nostris Adimaro tituli Sanctae Anastasiae & Gerardo tituli sanctae Sabinae, Presbyteris Cardinalibus, de huiusmodi beneficiis in regno & terris tuis fili charissime constitutibus in forma pro ipsis & aliis praedictis Cardinalibus cum magna deliberatione Concilii ordinata gratias huiusmodi prouiderimus faciendas, ipsiq; pro eis consequendis gratiis certos procuratores ac nuncios suos Ecclesiasticos viros idoneos, qui pro deutes & literatos ad partes regni tui Angliae destinarent. Ipsi procuratores & nuncii postquam ad regnum peruenientes praedictum, inceperunt ibidem dominorum suorum praedictorum negocia prosequi supradicta, per gentes & officiales regios non solum impediti super eis, quinimo captiuati, & tandem de regno praedicto expulsi cum ignominia (sicut infestis nimii relatibus percepimus) exiterunt. Profecto filii dilectissime si praemissa quae de procuratoribus praedictis praemittimus veritate nitantur, attenta devotione sincera quam ad dominum & sacrosanctum Romanam Ecclesiam Matrem tuam gerere dignoscens, sicut clara memoria progenitores tui Reges Angliae gesserunt dum in humanis agerent, eadem tua profecisse conscientia facile credere non valemus. Certum est autem quod non solum in regno & terris tuis praedictis, imo quasi in omnibus regnis ex partibus tam propinquis quam remotis, vbi catholicae fidei vrget cultus aliis nouis Cardinalibus consimilem gratiam fecimus, in quibus rebellionem aliquam praeter praedictam, quam si vera sit cum dolore cordis referimus, factum nullatenus audiuimus vsque quaque, satis namq; honoribus & commodis regis credebamus & credimus expedire quod Cardinales & illi maxime qui naturaliter ad iuncti ut ad honores & commoda regia in regno & terris suis beneficia obtineant ecclesiastica, quia ex hoc prouenit dubio libentius & frequentius ad promouendos profectus regios inducuntur, & vrinam illi qui nutriti de micis eiusdem Romanae ecclesiae, & ad bonores & status exaltati per eam, impedimenta & alia praedicta procurasse non absque magna ingratitudinis vicio, & aliis suis periculis verisimiliter exsistimantur. Ex quibus praeter hoc excommunicationis & aliis poenis & sententiis promulgatis aduersus tales a canonibus sepericulose animum subiecerunt, quae saluti famae, & honoris Regii felicia respiciunt incrementa, fidelibus intenderunt studiis & contrarium acceptando nequaquam lucra propria sub manu regia venarentur.
