Demum Regia rogamus Excellentiam, & in Domino attentius exhortamur quatenus his quae praemissa & aliis quae in hac parte circumspectioni Regiae possunt occurrere, diligenti praemeditatione intra pectoris regii clausitra discussis, ea quae contra dictos procuratores & quosdam alios praefati Adamari Cardinalis ministros qui postmodum in eodem regno capti & detineri dicuntur, facta fuerit reparari & renouari decentur & benigne faciat, ipsosq; procuratores Regio fauore suffultos circa prosequenda in eodem regno supradicta negocia, plena securitate gaudere pro diuina & nostra dictaq; sedis reuerentia faciat Regia Celsitudo, aures non accommodando regias illis aliquam in Dei offensam, Ecclesiae praedictae contumeliam, ac honoris salutis & famae tuae culminis laesionem, possent quomodolibet redundare, vt Dominum tibi semper propitium, & sedem praedictam super tuis opportunitatibus constitutas promptiorem, rescripturus nobis fili dilectissime quae tua Regalis circumspectio circa haec prouiderit ordinanda. Data apud villam nouam Auinion. dioc. quinto Kalendas Septembris pontificatus nostri Anno secundo.
units.tr: At length, having devised lawful means by which this provision could be made with less burden to the churches and ecclesiastical persons, we granted special favours, under certain forms and limitations set down for the said Cardinals, distributed among the provinces as we judged fitting, concerning ecclesiastical benefits then vacant in various kingdoms in parts of Christendom, and those to fall vacant in future, up to a certain sum for each of the said new Cardinals. Since we, with great deliberation of the Council, ordained that such favours be granted for two of them, who are natives of the duchy of Aquitaine, namely our beloved sons Adimar, Cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, and Gerard, Cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina, concerning such benefits established in your kingdom and lands, dearest son, and for the others, the aforesaid Cardinals, we also sent, to obtain these favours, certain procurators and nuncios of ours, fit ecclesiastical men, both learned and experienced, to the parts of your kingdom of England. When these procurators and nuncios, arriving in the said kingdom, began there to pursue the aforesaid business of their lords, they were not only hindered in these matters by royal people and officials, but were even taken prisoner, and at last, as we have learned from troubling reports, were driven out of the said kingdom with disgrace. Truly, dearest son, if what we have set forth about the said procurators rests on truth, we cannot easily believe that your conscience has advanced in that sincere devotion which you are known to bear toward the Lord and the holy Roman Church your Mother, as your illustrious forefathers, the kings of England, bore while they lived. It is certain, however, that we have made similar grants to the other new Cardinals not only in your kingdom and lands, but in almost all kingdoms, from regions both near and far, where the worship of the Catholic faith prevails; and in these we have never at all heard of any rebellion beyond the one mentioned, which, if it is true, we report with grief of heart. For we believed, and still believe, that it is sufficiently for the honour and advantage of the king that Cardinals, and especially those who are naturally joined to you, should obtain ecclesiastical benefits in your kingdom and lands, because by this they are more willingly and frequently induced to promote the king's advancement. Would that those who were nourished on the crumbs of the same Roman Church, and raised by her to honours and standing, were not thought likely to have procured these impediments and the other aforesaid things, and that not without a great vice of ingratitude and other perils to themselves. Besides this, the excommunications and other penalties and sentences issued against such persons by the canons have likewise been directed, which look to the safety, the good name and the happy increase of the royal honour; let them apply themselves to faithful pursuits, and by no means, by accepting the contrary, seek their own gains under the royal hand. Finally, we ask Your Royal Excellence, and earnestly exhort you in the Lord, that, having carefully considered in the inmost recesses of your royal heart the things premised and others which may occur to royal prudence in this matter, you will kindly and graciously make amends for and renew what was done against the said procurators and certain other ministers of the aforesaid Cardinal Adimar, who are said to have been afterwards seized and detained in the same kingdom. Let Your Royal Highness, for the sake of divine reverence and of ours and of the said see, allow the procurators, supported by royal favour, to rejoice in full security in pursuing the aforesaid business in the same kingdom, and do not lend royal ears to anything which could in any way redound to an offence against God, an insult to the aforesaid Church, or an injury to the summit of your honour, safety and fame; so that the Lord may ever be propitious to you, and the said see more ready to serve your opportunities. Write back to us, dearest son, what your royal prudence has decided to ordain concerning these matters. Given at the new town of Avignon, in the diocese [of Avignon], on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the second year of our pontificate.

units.la: EPISTOLA REGIS ANGLIAE MISSA PAPAE CLEMENTI PRO LI- BERTATE ECCLESIAE ANGLICANA, PLENA FRUCTU, CUM PRO TUNC PAPAE AUT CAR- DINALES RESPONDERE RATIONABILITER NE FECERUNT.
units.tr: The letter of the King of England sent to Pope Clement concerning the liberty of the English Church, which bore full fruit, since at that time neither the Pope nor the cardinals replied reasonably.

units.la: MANTISSIMA in Christo patri ac Domino Domino Clementi, diuina prouidentia sacrosanctae Romanae ac vniuersalis Ecclesiae summo pontifici Edwardus eiusdem gratiae Rex Franciae & Angliae & Dominus Hiberniae devota pedum osculas beatorum. Pensata sedis apostolicae clementia quae de fomento deuotionis Christi fidelium ac animarum salute, solet essefummè folicitâ non querens quæ sua sunt, sed quæ sunt potius Iesu Christi, tenet probabiliter nostra fiducia q; vestra maturitas in specula Celsitudinis Apostolicæ præclaritate meritorum & scientiæ diuinitus iam erecta, ea quæ decus Ecclesiæ & denotionem plebis attenuát, ac animarum & rerum periculà comminantur, curabit misericditer reformare. In publicam autem non ambigimus notitiam peruenisse, qualiter ab exordio nascentis Ecclesiæ in regno nostro Angliæ progenitorum nostrorum Regum Angliæ procerum ac fidelium dicti regni digne recolenda, prioriscs præter diuini cultus augmentum construxit Ecclesias, & ipsas amplis dotauit possessionibus & priuilegiis communiuit, ponens in eis ministros idoneos qui fidem Catholicam in subiectis sibi linguis & populis fœliciter peragrarùt, per quorum curam & solicitudinem vinea Domini Sabaoth in cultu & fructu ibidem mirificè fæcundauit, sed quod dolendum est, ipsius vineæ propagines degenerant in labruscas, & exterminant eam apri de sylua, singularesq; ferè depasciit eam, dum per impositiones & prouisiones sedis Apostolicæ, quæ solito grauius in ualescunt, ipsius peculium contra piam voluntatem, & ordinationem donatorum manus occupant indignorum, & præsertim exterorum, & eius dignitates & beneficia conferuntur pinguia personis alienigenis plerumq; nobis suspectis, qui non residentin dictis beneficiis, & vultus commissorum eis pecorum non agnoscunt, linguam non intelligunt, sed animarum cura neglecta, velut mercenarii, solummodo i emporalia lucra quærunt, & sic diminuitur Christi cultus, animarum cura negligitur, subtrahiturq; posfitalitas, Ecclesiarum iura depereunt, ruunt ædificia Clericorum, attenuatur deuotio populi. Clerici dicti regni viri magnæ literaturæ & conuersationis honestæ qui curam & regimen possent sibi salubriter peragere, & forent pro nostris & publicis confiliis opportuni, studium deserùt, propter ptomorionis congruę spem ablatam, quæ diuinæ simus non esse placita voluntati. Quinimo graue nostrum & fidelium nostrorum versatur præiudicium, ac ineffabile periculum, nisi super hoc citius & consultius caueamus. Nam ius patronatus quod nos & fideles nostri in talibus obtinemus beneficiis, eneruatur. Curia nostra in qua dumtaxat causæ super iure patronatus dictorum beneficiorum tractari debent, deluditur, & ficlura coronæ nostræ tam prodrosè quam damnosè depereunt, & regni thesaurus ad extraneos, ne dicamus nostros maleuolos asportatur, subtili forsan coniectura, vt Regni deptesso sacerdotio & eius exlvausto thesaurus, reddatur regnum debilius in aduersis, quæ singula & alia quæ ex præmissis sequuntur incommoda fuerunt nuper coram nobis in Parlamento nostro generali pro communitate dicti Regni palam expósita, vnanimi & feruenti petitione subiuncta, vt prædictis dispendiis quæ dictæ communitati videntur intolerabilia, celeriter occurramus. Nos autem Anglicanæ depressionem Ecclesiæ, & exbæreditationem coronæ nostræ ac mala prædictæ quæ dissimulata diutius afferrent verisimiliter grauiora patulo ternentes intuitu, ad vos successores Apostolorum principis, qui ad pascendum non ad tondendum oues Dominicas, ac ad confirmandum non ad deprimendum fratres suos mandatum à Christo suscepit, ista deferimus votiuis affectibus supplicantes, quatenus præmissis debitè ponderatis, ac consideratis, quod de iure creandi sunt de vico populi magistratus & iuxta dictum prophetæ, dandi sunt de eodem loco populi vinitores, quod per beatos apostolos legitur esse factum, dum gentibus viros linguarum suarum habentes notitiam transumpserunt.
units.tr: To the most mighty in Christ, the father and lord, Lord Clement, by divine providence supreme pontiff of the holy Roman and universal Church: Edward, by the same grace King of France and England and Lord of Ireland, sends devout kisses on the feet of the blessed (father). Considering the clemency of the apostolic see, which is wont to foster the devotion of Christ's faithful and the salvation of souls, seeking not its own things but rather those of Jesus Christ, our trust holds that your maturity, already raised by divine gift to the watchtower of apostolic eminence through the brilliance of its merits and learning, will mercifully take care to reform those things which diminish the honour of the Church and the devotion of the people, and which threaten dangers to souls and property. We do not doubt that it has come to public knowledge how, from the beginning of the infant Church in our kingdom of England, our forebears the kings of England, and the nobles and faithful of that kingdom, worthy of remembrance, built churches before the increase of divine worship, endowed them with ample possessions, and fortified them with privileges, placing in them suitable ministers who happily spread the Catholic faith among the tongues and peoples subject to them; through whose care and solicitude the vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth was wondrously made fruitful there in worship and fruit. But, which is to be lamented, the shoots of that vineyard degenerate into wild grapes, and the boar out of the wood lays it waste, and almost entirely grazes upon it. For through the impositions and provisions of the apostolic see, which prevail more heavily than usual, its property is seized by unworthy hands, contrary to the pious will and ordinance of the donors, and especially by foreigners; its dignities and rich benefices are conferred on alien persons, often suspect to us, who do not reside in the said benefices, do not know the faces of the flocks committed to them, and do not understand their language; but, with the cure of souls neglected, like hirelings they seek only temporal gain. Thus Christ's worship is diminished, the care of souls is neglected, hospitality is withdrawn, the rights of the churches perish, the buildings of the clergy fall into ruin, and the devotion of the people is weakened. The clergy of the said kingdom, men of great learning and honest conduct, who could healthfully carry out the cure and government of souls, and would be fit for our and the public counsels, abandon their study, because the hope of suitable promotion has been taken away, which surely is not pleasing to the divine will. Indeed, a grave prejudice to us and our faithful is at stake, and an unspeakable danger, unless we take earlier and more deliberate precaution in this matter. For the right of patronage which we and our faithful hold in such benefices is weakened. Our court, in which alone causes concerning the right of patronage of the said benefices ought to be tried, is mocked, and the rights of our crown perish as shamefully as they do harmfully, and the treasure of the kingdom is carried off to foreigners, not to say to our ill-wishers, perhaps by a subtle calculation, so that with the priesthood of the kingdom depleted and its treasure exhausted, the kingdom becomes weaker in adversity. All these and the other inconveniences that follow from the premises were lately laid openly before us in our general Parliament on behalf of the commonalty of the said kingdom, with a unanimous and fervent petition added, that we should quickly remedy the losses which seem intolerable to that commonalty. We, indeed, fearing the depression of the English Church and the disinheriting of our crown, and the evils mentioned, which, if dissembled any longer, would probably bring graver harms, bring these matters before you, successor of the prince of the apostles, who received from Christ the commission to feed, not to shear, the Lord's sheep, and to strengthen, not to crush, his brethren, supplicating with heartfelt desire that, these matters having been duly weighed and considered, since by right magistrates are to be created from the people's own community, and, according to the saying of the prophet, vinedressers are to be taken from the same place among the people, as is read to have been done by the blessed apostles when they took men from among the nations who knew their tongues.

units.la: Pensata etiam deuotionis plenitudine, qua domus nostra Regia & Clerus & populus dicti regni perstiterunt, hactenus in obedientia dictæ sedis, propter quod non haberet paternus affectus eis onera & graiamina cumulare, & pater filiis thesaurizans, alleuians dictarum impositionum & prouisionum ac onerum tam per sedem Apostolicam inualescentiam grauitatem, permittentes vlterius, ut patroni patronatus sui solatium non amittant, Ecclesiæ, Cathedrales & aliæ dicti regni liberas electiones, & earum essectum habeant, quas quidem Ecclesias dicti progenitores nostri dudum singulis vacationibus earundem, personis idoneis iure suo Regio liberè conferebant, & postmodum ad rogatum & ad instantiam dictæ sedis, sub certis modis & conditionibus concesserunt, quod electiones fierent in dictis Ecclesiis per capitula earundem quæ concessio fuit per sedem Apostolicam ex certa scientia confirmata, sed contra formam concessionis & confirmationis prædictarum, dicta sedes per reseruationes & prouisiones suas, ditus Capitulis electiones adimit prædictas, & nobis ius & prærogatiuam, quę iuxta formam dictæ concessionis nobis competunt in hac parte, propter quod iuxta legem dicti Regni nostri ex quo lex in concessione positanon obseruatur, concessio reuoluitur, & rei status reuertitur in primæuum.
units.tr: Considering also the fullness of the devotion by which our royal house, and the clergy and people of the said kingdom, have hitherto persisted in obedience to the said see, on account of which a paternal affection would not wish to heap burdens and grievances upon them, and, as a father storing up treasure for his sons, we would lighten the said impositions, provisions and burdens which the apostolic see has made more violent and heavy. We further permit that the patrons do not lose the comfort of their patronage, and that the churches, cathedrals and others of the said kingdom have free elections and their effect, which our forebears formerly, at each vacancy, freely conferred by their royal right on suitable persons, and afterwards, at the request and instance of the said see, granted under certain modes and conditions, that elections should be made in those churches by their chapters; which grant was confirmed by the apostolic see from certain knowledge. But contrary to the form of this grant and confirmation, the said see, by its reservations and provisions, takes those elections away from the chapters, and takes from us the right and prerogative which, by the form of the said grant, belong to us in this matter. Therefore, according to the law of our said kingdom, since the law placed in the grant is not observed, the grant is revoked and the state of the matter returns to its first condition.

units.la: Super praemissis itaque digne quaesumus vestram benignitatem ad honorem Dei & ad salutem animarum, nec non ad tollendum scandala & praeiudicia praelibata, festiuum & salubre temperamentum apponere, vt nos & nostri qui personam vestram sanctissimam ut dictum, nam & sanctam Romanam Ecclesiam reuereri cupimus (vt debemus) ceterosque discis malis intolerabilib' in paternae vestrae dilectionis dulcedine quiescamus, reuerefcar; vestraque deuotio per ostensam nobis piae moderationis vestrae clementiam recreata. Conseruet vos altissimus ad regimen Ecclesiae suae sanctae per tempora prospera & longa. Datum apud Westmon. 15. die Sept. Anno Regni nostri Franciae quarto, Regni vero nostri Angliae 17.
units.tr: On the premises, therefore, we humbly beg your benignity, for the honour of God and the salvation of souls, and also to remove the scandals and prejudices mentioned, to apply a festive and wholesome moderation, so that we and our people, who desire (as we ought) to revere your most holy person, as said, and also the holy Roman Church, may rest from the other intolerable evils in the sweetness of your paternal love, and that your devotion, refreshed by the clemency of your holy moderation shown to us, may be restored. May the Most High preserve you for the governance of his holy Church through prosperous and long times. Given at Westminster, 15 September, in the fourth year of our reign of France, and in the seventeenth year of our reign of England.

units.la: In his literis si Rex perseuerasset, prouisiones omnes ei ademisset. Sed in tanti belli strepitu permulcere ram irritabilem patrem aliqua tolerantia confulinus fuit quam incendere.
units.tr: If the King had persisted in these letters, he would have taken from him all the provisions. But amid the din of so great a war, we thought it better to soothe with some tolerance a father so irritable than to inflame him.

units.la: Papa his temporibus cum Regis procerum, consensu a prouisionibus quas sine modo fecit in totum prohibendus esset, a Rege tamen rogatus Dunelmensem Episcopatum Thomas Hatfeld Regis secretarius conulit. Id quod iniquissime tulerunt proceres, Regem tanta inconstantia a tam sano proposito deflexisse. Papa vero quamuis sui Cardinales, Regis secretarium indoctum, laicum, & Episcopatui indignum censerent, tamen vt suae vsurpationis consuetudine vsumque reinueret, Vere, inquit, si Rex Angliae pro Alfonso supplicasset, obtinuisset ad vota ista vice. Quae sane non iam noua incessit Papae religio. Nam ante hunc Lodouicum quendam de Bellomonte Gallum quadragesimum exrum Episcopum Dunelmensem Regem atque Franciae precibus adductus, quia latine vix legere poterat Episcopum creauit. Monachi Dunelmenses Henricum Stamford Priorem de Finchall elegerunt, qui cum Romam confirmandus venisset accepit illum Gallum ante suum aduentum iam ad Episcopatum admissum, sed tamen Papam adiit, sibique non displicuisse dixit quod Dunelmensem Episcopatum quosfe indignum fuisse fatebatur, alteri contulisset. Cui Papa. Fili mi inquit. Neque odio personae tuae, nec vitio aut quocunque in te defectu sed magna Regum atque Reginarum instantia alterum admisimus, tibique deinceps de aliis prouidebimus. Hac verborum lenitate cum Priorem electum dimisisset, Lodouicum Chirographis ad tantam Romanae curiae solitum ... pecuniam obligauit quantam quatuor decim millia 30 fecratione sua literarum infcni iam legendo prodidit. Vt authoris verbis vtar. Erat autem Lodouic. de sanguine Regum Franciae & Siciliae. Facie venustus erat, sed vtrobique pede claudicans, dapsilis valde vt a multis dicerentur prodigus, ad habendum cupidus, sed de modo acquirendi non curans, tanta cupiditate excaecata fuit animae eius vt nihil dimisit q. conlorate habere potuit. Sed causam Ecclesiae suae viriliter defendebat. Ad sequelam eius de claratu fuit in Parliamento Regis, q. Episcopus Dunelmensis debet habere forisfacturas guerrarum infra libertates Episc. sicut Rex habet extra. Laicus erat latinum non intelligens, & cum difficultate pronuncians. Vnde cum in consecratione sua, phiteri debuit, quamuis permultos dies ante instructore habuisset, legere nescuit, & cum auriculantibus aliis cum difficultate ad illud verbum Metropolitica puenisset, diu, anhelans pronunciare non posset dixit in Gallico. Soit pour dit: i. dictum puta. Et cum semel celebraret ordines, neq; pronunciare posset, In zniqmate, dixit circumstantibus. Per Sains Lowys il n'est pas courteys que ce-fte parolle yce efcrit. i. Per Sanctum Lodouicum parum humanus fuit qui hoc verbum hic scripsit. Semper studuit quomodo de Priore & Conuentu pecuniā extorquere posset. Bullā habuit ad praeficiendū in Priorem, quēcunq; de domo vellet. Et ad allam ad habendū quartam partem bonorum prioratus, durante guerra Scoriae. Hoc ipsius authoris verba inseruit mus vt mos Papalis in conferendis sub puisionis suae titulo beneficiis, a lectore intelligatur. Mortuo Iohanne Stratford cum Prior & Conuentus Cantuarienis Thomam Bradwardin sacrae Theologiae professorem vnanimes elegissent, Rex qui Iohanni Vfford multo magis quam alteri promouendo fauit ad Papam scripsit, vt Iohannem Vfford prouisionis titulo spreta Monachorum Cant. electione Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum creauerit. Id Papa celeriter effecit, cuius viua voce creato tantas ei Romanas gratias, concessiones, & priuilegia indulsit, quantas vnquam nemini. Hic Iohannes Vfford in iure ciuili & canonico Cantabrigiae institutus primo legum doctor, deinde Decanus Ecclesiae Cathedralis Lincolniensis fuit. Et quia nobili genere ortus est (Suffolciensis enim comitis fuit filius) rūq; nobiliratī singularem iuris prudentiam & eloquentiam adiunxisset, ad Regis consilia vocatus, & Regni Cancellarius constitutus est. Cuius tantae amplitudinis ac honoris perbrenem vsurā morte, vt dicemus, extinctus accepit. Hoc reporte aris ex bello Gallicomagna in Anglia fuit inopia, cuncq; ibico sequuta tāta annonae copia, vt frusvt frumenti modius tribus denatis & bos pinguis sex solidis octo denariis Londini vaenerint. Sed hanc panis saturitatem pestis, omnium quae vnquam Angliam infecerunt gravissima occupavit. Ea statim post Natiuitatis Dominicae celebratum festum, ipsa nimirum hyeme, & rerum omnium ad victum necessariarum copia cum vix villa contagionis suspicio oriri mortalibus potuit, incepit. Nec ita longo quidem tempore, quinque tantum mensibus durauit. Nam ad finem mensis Maii opedivina citra hominum spem extincta est. Sed interim dimidiam penè hominum multitudinem deleuit atq; continuo, tum in Monachorum, religiosorum, & presbyterorum impurum turbam tanto surore, tanquam diuina vindicta sæuit, vt ne decimum quoque illorum superstitem reliquerit. Ipsaque vnda illa scaturigine ad tantam paucitatem redacta, beneficia atq; coenobia pene deserta sunt. Ipsæ Ecclesiæ parochiales pene omnes inofficiatæ fuerunt. Namque earum rectores gregè relicto aufugerunt, nec vlla mercede parochos conducere ad mortuos sepeliendos, aut diuina ministranda potuerunt. Nemo fere certa fede manere voluit, sed vnusquisque mortis formidine, cum tamen nullus locus rutus esset, (pestis enim haec tam dira omnes pariter invasit,) hunc illuc vagabatur. Presbyteri atq; sferui oppidatim mendicare, potius quam mercede victum acquirere malebant. Quae mendicitas & vagandi licentia huius contagionis orta meiu, cessante peste effraenata postea libidine magis quam necessitate durauit. Ad quam coercendam lata tunc primum lex fuit. Vt quicunq; viribus valens, si nec mercaturam, nec certum artificium nec agriculturam exercere, nec praedia, possessionesue, redditus aut prouentus quibus se commode sustentare non possit haberet, alicuius Mercatoris, Artificis, vel Agricolæ seruitio si sponte noluerit requisitus datis fideiussoribus inuitus manciparetur. In quaetiam lege seruorum, artificum & operariorum metecedes oe nimium parumue exigendo atq; soluendo iniuria cuiquam fieret æquabili summa moderatæ atq; taxatæ sunt.
units.tr: At this time the Pope, with the consent of the King's nobles, ought to have been wholly restrained from the provisions he made without limit. Yet at the King's request he conferred the bishopric of Durham on Thomas Hatfield, the King's secretary. The nobles took this very unjustly, that the King had turned aside from so sound a purpose through such inconstancy. The Pope, although his own cardinals judged Hatfield, the King's secretary, to be unlearned, a layman and unworthy of the bishopric, nevertheless, to keep up the custom of his usurpation, said: "Truly, if the King of England had petitioned for Alfonso, he would have obtained these wishes in the same way." This was not a new practice of the Pope's. For before this man, the Pope had made Lewis of Beaumont, a Frenchman and the fortieth bishop of Durham, at the urging of the King and of France, though Lewis could hardly read Latin. The monks of Durham had elected Henry Stamford, prior of Finchale. When he came to Rome to be confirmed, he learned that the Frenchman had already been admitted to the bishopric before his arrival. Yet he went to the Pope and said that he was not displeased that the bishopric of Durham had been given to another, whom he confessed to be unworthy. The Pope replied: "My son, we did not admit another out of hatred for your person, nor because of any fault or defect in you, but because of the great insistence of kings and queens. We will provide for you with others in future." With these gentle words he dismissed the elected prior. Lewis then bound himself by his bonds to so great a sum of money, which I now reveal by reading his letter of obligation, as fourteen thousand (marks). I use the author's own words here. Lewis was of the blood of the kings of France and Sicily. He was handsome, but lame in both feet, and so lavish that many called him a prodigal. He was eager to acquire and did not care how he acquired, and his soul was so blinded by greed that he let go of nothing he could possibly get hold of. Yet he defended the cause of his Church manfully. As a consequence, it was declared in the King's Parliament that the Bishop of Durham ought to have the forfeitures from wars within the liberties of the bishopric, just as the King has them outside. Lewis was a layman who did not understand Latin and spoke it with difficulty. So at his consecration, when he had to make the profession, he could not read it, although he had had an instructor for many days beforehand. When, with others whispering to him, he came with difficulty to the word "Metropolitical," he panted and could not pronounce it, and said in French: "Soit pour dit," that is, "let it be said." And once, when he was conferring orders and could not pronounce the word "aenigmate," he said to those standing round him: "By Saint Louis, it is not courteous that this word was written here," that is, "By Saint Lewis, the man who wrote this word here was not very civil." He always strove to find how he could extort money from the prior and convent. He had a bull allowing him to appoint as prior whomever he wished from the house, and another allowing him to have a fourth part of the goods of the priory during the Scottish war. We have inserted the author's own words so that the reader may understand the Papal custom of conferring benefices under the title of provision. When John Stratford died, the prior and convent of Canterbury unanimously chose Thomas Bradwardine, professor of sacred theology, as archbishop. But the King, who favoured John Offord far more than anyone else for promotion, wrote to the Pope asking him to disregard the election of the monks of Canterbury, to make the title a provision, and to create John Offord archbishop of Canterbury. The Pope quickly did this, and when Offord was created, granted him by word of mouth as many Roman thanks, concessions and privileges as he had ever granted to anyone. John Offord had been educated in civil and canon law at Cambridge. He was first a doctor of laws and then dean of the cathedral church of Lincoln. Because he was of noble birth (for he was the son of the Earl of Suffolk), and had joined to his nobility a singular knowledge of law and eloquence, he was called to the King's councils and made Chancellor of the realm. He enjoyed such great eminence and honour only for a very brief time, for death carried him off, as we shall say. At this time there was a dearth in England because of the French war, and this was followed by such an abundance of grain that a bushel of wheat and a fat ox were sold in London for three pence and six shillings eight pence respectively. But this plenty of bread was seized by the plague, the gravest of all that ever infected England. It began immediately after the feast of the Lord's Nativity had been celebrated, in the very winter, when there was an abundance of all things necessary for living, and when scarcely any suspicion of contagion could arise among mortals. Nor did it last long, only five months. For by the end of May, by a divine work beyond human hope, it was extinguished. In the meantime, however, it destroyed almost half the multitude of men. It raged continuously through the impure crowd of monks, religious and priests with such fury, like divine vengeance, that it did not leave even one in ten of them surviving. Reduced to such a small number, benefices and monasteries were almost deserted. Almost all the parish churches were left without services, for their rectors fled and abandoned their flocks. No one could be hired, for any wage, to bury the dead or to minister divine services. Hardly anyone wished to remain in a fixed place, for fear of death, but each wandered here and there, though no place was safe, since this dreadful plague attacked everyone alike. Priests and servants preferred to beg from town to town rather than to earn their living by wages. This begging and freedom to wander, which arose from fear of the contagion, continued after the plague ceased, through unbridled lust rather than necessity. To restrain it, a law was then passed for the first time: whoever was able-bodied, and did not practise trade, a certain craft or agriculture, and had no estates, possessions, rents or revenues by which he could decently support himself, should, if he would not serve when asked by a merchant, craftsman or farmer, be bound against his will by sureties to that service. In the same law the wages of servants, craftsmen and labourers were fixed at moderate and assessed sums, so that no one would be wronged by paying or receiving too much or too little.

units.la: Atque haec pestifera stragcs non modo Angliam, sed alias gentes Regionesque vastauit. Cuius causa perhibetur annus ille lubileus omnibus Christianis gentibus Romæ vndiq; confluentibus, & temissionem peccatorum spectantibus celebratus. Hunc annū Bonifacius octauus ita instituit, vt qui centesimo quoque anno Romam visitarent, his omnium scelerum atq; impietatum expiatio concederetur. Idem enim Bonifacius, quisè tam in diuinis quam humanis iuribus totius orbis Dominus appellasset, & Imperatoris Constantini donationem Syluestro Papæ factam, potius rei alienae vero Domino restitutionem quam legitimam concessionem fuisse dixisset. Hunc Jubilaeum annum vt Romanæ curiæ limina tanquam totius orbis oraculum à cunctis gentibus vno tempore frequentaretur, primus induxit.
units.tr: This pestilent slaughter devastated not only England but also other nations and regions. Its cause is said to have been that jubilee year, celebrated for all Christian nations, when people came flocking to Rome from every side, seeking the remission of sins. Boniface VIII instituted this year so that whoever visited Rome in every hundredth year would be granted the expiation of all their crimes and impieties. This same Boniface, who had called himself lord of the whole world in both divine and human law, and who had said that the donation of Constantine to Pope Sylvester was less a lawful grant than a restitution of another's property to its true lord, was the first to introduce this jubilee year, so that the thresholds of the Roman court, as the oracle of the whole world, would be visited by all nations at one time.

units.la: Sed hunc centesimum annum Clemens sextus ad quinquagesimum, ac post eum Paulus secundus ad vicesimum quintum, vt gentes humanæ sæpius Romæ convenirent, reduxit, in fauorem vt ipsi dicebant, animarum, sacratum scripturarum auritoritate atq; Maiestate ad suum quæstum & libidinem nefarie abutentes. Vt quia abundavit iniquitas, superabundaret & gratia. Quam Papæ impietatem atq; faustum gentium quæ superstitionem atq; coecitatem Deus hac per totum orbem Christianum in ipso anno lubileo dilatata peltilentia vindicauit. Iudicauit ergo iustis precibus atque pietate non peregrinationibus & contaminata superstitione, quæ nunc omnium gentium mentes quasi obligatas occupaverat sè placari, aut mortalium crimina expiari posse. Unde facete quidam cum ad animarum salutem instituto annos lubileos diceretur, id ita esse posse respondit, vt animabus sanitatem adferant. Nam corporibus eximiu sæpe attulerunt. Namque in hoc pestifero lubileo cuius cõtagio omnes gentes infecit, quinquaginta hominum millia Parisiis pestæ eneêti sunt, & in vicina finitimaque ciuitate quæ sancti Dionifii nuncupatur quatuordecim. In Anglia vero (vt diximus) innumeri perierunt. Londini coemeteriis sepultorum multitudine completis, in vnoCarthufianorum coemiterio quinquaginta hominum millia inhumata sunt. Noruicique præter Clericorum, Monachorum, & huc illuc vagantis populi turbam quinquaginta septem ipsorum ciuium millia sepulta Catalogus quidam recēset. Non iam extare in ea ciuitate aut vicinis ruribus ad quinque millia proximis tantam multitudinem multi autumant, quanta in illa pestilentia deleta fuit. Yarmuthi maritimo oppido tanta mortalitas fuit, vt incredibile penè sit tantam multitudinem eo oppido continere potuisse. Et tamen in tantum funesta contagione quae tantā hominum vastitatem atque cladem vbique gentium peperit, Edwardus Rex qui Calectum maririmum Gallia portum suis victoriis opportunum atque commodum cepit, quaque multitudine prælirorum cum multis simul gentibus Scotis, Gallis, & Hispanis dimicabat, ciusque totus exercitus qui illa Romana limina non adibant, non modo incolumis sed indies auctus fuit. Quo tempore nauali pugna Hispanorum ingenti elassi restitit. Tum ad bellum in Gallum motum persequendum filium suum primogenitum Edwardum cum copioso & optimo delectu instructo exercitu in Gallias misit. Is Guasconiam, Tholousam, & Notbonam incendiis atque spoliis neque hostibus quidem repugnantibus depopulatus est. Quem Rex ipse sequutus in Gallias transiit, multaqz in praeliis facinora praeclarè gessit. Et cum audisset Scotum periutum fracta pace atque fide se absente Anglia innatile, & Beruicum oppidum in vtriusqz Regni finibus situm cepisset, ac castellum militibus omnibus ope bellica munitum oppugnasse rediit, Scotumqz bello aggressus Berwicum recuperauit, eumqz in mediterranea Scotiae perlecutus ad deditionem regi suum tradi cogit. Interim Edwardus Regis filius multas Gallicanas prouincias bello ac incendio diripuit, captiuos multos eosqz opulentos crebris dimicationibus & confliagationibus cepit. Burdeacum maximam Guasconiae ciuitatem cum exercitu saluus peruenit. Eodemqz tempore Dux Lancastriae alio Anglorum exercitu alias Gallix prouincias vastauit. Quos illa pestis in Papae Iubileo exorta quae vbique pene singulos afflixit nunquam attigit. Ita vt cum nunciis, Legatis, litteris, omnibusqz modis ad pacem ineundam a Papa sepe solicitarentur victoriae tam gloriosae quae postea consecuta est, Ipse, nec Papae mnis, nec hostium potentia, nec illius pestis contagione deterriti ab armis discedere voluerunt, vt in ipsa acie motuqz bellico militibus maior, quam in tam infinito lubrico peregrinantibus sanitas atqz securitas adfuerit. Has lugubres strages Iohannes Vfford Archiepiscopus paucis mensibus vidit, qui eum sex mensibus & sex diebus pallium expectaret, neqz conseceratus, nec pallio donatus vnaeum illa funesta pesti septimo die mensis Iunii in villa dicta Totenhall extinctus est. Corpus eius proximo summo mane Cantuariam secreto ductum, & sine Archiepiscopali magnificentia & ad patrem aquilonarem iuxta murum Thomae Becket sepultum est. Huius bona quoniam intestatus obiit Andreas Vfford Archidiaconus Midlesexiae consanguinitatis iure administrauit, qui a Simone Islip Cantuariensi (vt postea docemus) Archiepiscopo in ius vocarus, etsi Iohannes Vfford tam paucis mensibus Archiepiscopatum tenuisset, & Thomas Bradwardyn ei proximus ac inter Simonem & Iohannem interiectus fuisset, in mille & centum libris triginta quinque solidis duobus denariis obulo & quadrante ob dilapidata & caduca zdificia damnarus est.
units.tr: But Clement VI reduced this centenary year to fifty years, and afterwards Paul II reduced it to twenty-five, so that the nations of mankind would gather at Rome more often. They said this was for the welfare of souls, and in doing so they wickedly abused the authority and majesty of the sacred Scriptures for their own profit and lust. "Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound." God punished this impiety of the Pope, and the superstition and blindness of the nations, by a plague spread across the whole Christian world in that very jubilee year. He judged, therefore, that by just prayers and piety, and not by pilgrimages and a polluted superstition, which now held the minds of all nations as if bound, God could be appeased and the sins of mortals expiated. Hence someone wittily replied, when it was said that jubilee years were instituted for the salvation of souls, that this might be so if they brought health to souls; for they have often brought destruction to bodies. Indeed, in this pestilent jubilee, whose contagion infected all nations, fifty thousand people died of the plague at Paris, and fourteen thousand in the neighbouring and adjacent city called Saint-Denis. In England, as we have said, countless people perished. At London the cemeteries were filled with the multitude of the dead, and fifty thousand people were buried unburied in the one Carthusian cemetery. At Norwich, besides the crowds of clergy, monks, and people wandering hither and thither, a certain catalogue records that fifty-seven thousand of its own citizens were buried. Many affirm that there are not now, in that city and in the neighbouring villages within about five miles, as many people as were destroyed in that plague. At Yarmouth, a maritime town, the mortality was so great that it is almost incredible that the town could have held so many. And yet, although this deadly contagion caused such devastation and slaughter of men everywhere, King Edward, who took Calais, a maritime port of France convenient and advantageous for his victories, and who fought with a multitude of battles against many nations at once, Scots, French and Spanish, and whose whole army did not visit those Roman thresholds, was not only unharmed but grew daily. At that time he also withstood a huge Spanish fleet in a naval battle. Then, to pursue the war against France, he sent his eldest son Edward into France with a large and carefully chosen army. He laid waste Gascony, Toulouse and Narbonne with fire and plunder, though the enemy did not even resist. The king himself followed and crossed into France, and performed many notable deeds in battles. And when he heard that the Scot, having broken peace and faith, had attacked England in his absence and had taken Berwick, a town situated on the borders of both kingdoms, and had assailed a castle fortified with all military supplies, he returned, and attacking the Scots in war, he recovered Berwick, and pursuing them into the midland of Scotland, compelled their king to surrender. Meanwhile Edward's son plundered many provinces of Gaul by war and fire, and by frequent battles and burnings took many prisoners, wealthy ones among them. He came safely with his army to Bordeaux, the greatest city of Gascony. At the same time the Duke of Lancaster, with another English army, laid waste other provinces of France. That plague which arose in the Pope's jubilee, and which afflicted almost everyone everywhere, never touched these men. So although they were often urged by the Pope, by messages, legates, letters and every means, to make peace, neither the Pope's threats, nor the power of their enemies, nor the contagion of that plague deterred them from laying down their arms. Thus in the battle line and in the movements of war there was greater health and safety for the soldiers than for those wandering about in such an infinite peril. John Offord, Archbishop, saw these dismal slaughters in a few months. He waited six months and six days for the pallium, and, neither consecrated nor given the pallium, he died on the seventh day of June, together with that deadly plague, in the village called Tottenhall. His body was taken secretly to Canterbury the next morning, early, without archiepiscopal pomp, and buried on the north side, next to the wall of Thomas Becket. Since he died intestate, his goods were administered by Andrew Offord, Archdeacon of Middlesex, by right of kinship. He was summoned to court by Simon Islip, Archbishop of Canterbury (as we shall show later). Although John Offord had held the archbishopric for so few months, and Thomas Bradwardine, who came next after him and was placed between Simon and John, had held it, Andrew was condemned to pay one thousand one hundred pounds, thirty-five shillings, two pence, a halfpenny and a farthing, on account of dilapidated and falling buildings.

units.la: LIV. Thomas Bradwardyn.
units.tr: LIV. Thomas Bradwardyn.

units.la: Homas Bradwardyn, cuius vt ante dixImus electio Rege interdente a Clemente Papa Iohanne Vfford in Cantuariensem Archiepiscoparum recepto, reprobata fuit Hartfeldiae in Sussexia natus est. Post puerilem institutionem adolescens disciplinarum litterarum studio operam dedit. In eo studio vitae quae sanctitate ab adolescentia conspicuus ad Regem Edwardum Tertium per Iohan. Stretford Arch. Cant. dedustus est, vt Regis confessor fieret. In quo munere a regni negociis atqz curis vacuus sine honoris aut praemii petitione, Regi bello militaqz assiduus fuit. Quem eriam increpare atqz redarguere simulatqz eum a recto deflectere aut aberrare sensetur, liberius quae quisquam nullo metu detegatus solebat. In bello aut Gallico longo atqz diuturno, magnaqz varietate terra mariqz iactato, illaqz multitudine praeliorum in quibus vt praedixi Galli fusi sunt, non modo sectetius Regem admonere solebat, sed frequentes totius exercitus conciones habuit; in quibus sanctissima dissertissimaqz sacnndia, appositisqz exemplis ex Theologia libaris, Regi & exercitui langvenires excitavit, vt victoriae ferocitate nimium exultantes ne modo transiliorent, cohibuit. Vt illas nobiles & gloriosas victorias quib. Galli debellaci, & in Regis Angliae dinione adductae sunt, permulti nullius potestiae aut prudentiae magis quam huius diuini simplicitas viri sanctitati & moderationi asseruerunt. Cui cum faciliter, quia Rege impetrare aegre tamen adductus vt in Lincolnensi, Canonicaru, & in Londinensi Ecclesia canonicatu simul teneret. Hic qui ante Iohannem Vfford a Monachis Cantuariensibus tola virtutis fama sine ambitione & ambitione electus est, etsi Regis praecibus repulsam indignam a Papa tulit, animo tamen motus aut offensus iudicio videbatur. Quod cum Regi vitio a multis versum fuerit, Rex se excusavit quod tam sancti viri confusurudine in castris & manis discrimine commode carere non potuisset. Itaque sepulto Iohanne Vfford, Monachi Cantuarienses hunc Thomam Bradwardyn interim elegerunt, electum vero summo studio Regi instanter atque vrgent vt admittat. Rex Monachorum importunitate & contentione ductus suo confessore viro integerrimo carere, eumq; Cant. Ecclesiæ ac Prouinciæ præficere coactus est. Clemētem autem Papam ferunt simulatq; de morte Iohannis Vfford accepisset antequam Cantuariensium monachorū electio cuiuserat ignarus, ibi præsentaretur suo more proprioque motu atq; sponte huic de Archiepiscopatu prouidisse.
units.tr: Thomas Bradwardyn, whose election, as we said above, was rejected after the King had forbidden it, and who had been replaced by John Offord, whom Pope Clement received, was born at Hartfield in Sussex. After a childhood schooling he devoted himself as a young man to the study of the liberal arts. Being conspicuous from youth for the holiness of his life in that study, he was brought by John Stratford, Archbishop of Canterbury, to King Edward III to become the King's confessor. In that office, free from the affairs and cares of the realm, and seeking no honour or reward, he was constantly at the King's side in war. He used to rebuke and correct the King more frankly than anyone else dared, whenever he perceived that the King was turning aside from what was right or going astray. In the long and protracted war with France, tossed about by great changes on land and sea, and through the many battles in which, as I have said, the French were routed, he not only admonished the King more earnestly, but also gave frequent sermons to the whole army. In these he delivered very holy and eloquent discourses, drawing on examples from theology, and he roused the King and the army, who were languishing, so that, exulting too much in the fierceness of victory, they might not break out beyond bounds. Many men attributed those noble and glorious victories, by which the French were defeated and brought under the rule of the King of England, to the holiness and moderation of this godly man, rather than to the power or prudence of anyone else. When he had been admitted with some difficulty, and only after the King had been persuaded, to hold a canonry in the church of Lincoln and at the same time one in the church of London, he (who, before John Offord, had been elected by the monks of Canterbury, with the whole reputation of his virtue and without any ambition or canvassing) bore with rejection by the Pope, though it was unworthy, despite the King's entreaties. Yet he seemed to be moved in spirit, or offended in judgement. When many blamed this as a fault in the King, the King excused himself by saying that he could not reasonably do without a man of such holiness in the camp and in the peril of the hand-to-hand fighting. So, when John Offord had been buried, the monks of Canterbury chose this Thomas Bradwardyn in the meantime, and they urged and pressed the King with the greatest zeal to admit the man they had chosen. Overcome by the importunity and insistence of the monks, the King was compelled to forgo his confessor, a man of the most upright character, and to set him over the church and province of Canterbury. They say that Pope Clement, as soon as he had heard of the death of John Offord, and before he knew of the election of the monks of Canterbury, then present there, provided him to the archbishopric of his own accord, by his own custom and on his own initiative.

units.la: Hoc itaq; modo à Monachis electus, à Rege permissus, & à Papa ipso expetitus Thomas Bradwardyn ad Papam confirmandus atq; sacrandus Auinionem inuenit. Vbi Monachorum electione corroborata sacrationis suæ ritus atq; cæremonia in Ecclesia fratrum minorum à Bertrando quodam Ebredunensi præsbyrero atque Cardinali in ipsorū Cardinalium corona solenniter celebrabatur. In ipso autem consecrationis conuiuio Hugo Turclensis Cardinalis, Papæ consanguineus, vir fastu inanis, Thomæ Cantuariensis iam sacrati humilitate & simplicitate despecta, vt ei conuiuium faceret, vilem quendam & abiectum homunculum asino insidentem & Archiepiscopatum petentem induxit, qui à toto Cardinalium cœtu reprehensus & stultitia notatus discessit. Peractis autem consecrationis ritibus Thomas Bradwardyn Papa & Cardinalibus salutatis rediit in Angliā. Ac primò Regem adiit à quo nomine patris salutarus Archiepiscopatus Cantuariensis temporalia accepit. Abeo mox Lametham discessit vt longinqui itineris lassitudinem aufferet. Ibi Roffensis Episcopi hospitio aliquot septimanis vius corpore ex illa lassitudine quassato incidit in febrem, ex ea quinque septimanis, & quatuor diebus postquam à Papa consecratus fuerat, antequam Cantuariæ introinizaretur, è vita migrauit. Postea Cantuariæ in Capella Anselmi Archiepiscopi ad parietem austtralem humo cōditus est. Ita vno anno res orbitates ac vacationes Cantuariensis Ecclesia passa est. Hic vltra multos alios libros per eum scriptos, vnum magnum opus scripsit cui titulum fecit de causa Dei contra Pelagium, qui liber adhuc extat.
units.tr: Thus Thomas Bradwardyn, chosen by the monks, permitted by the King, and sought after by the Pope himself, went to Avignon to be confirmed and consecrated by the Pope. There, after the monks' election had been confirmed, the rite and ceremony of his consecration was solemnly performed in the church of the Friars Minor by Bertrand, a certain priest and Cardinal of Embrun, in the presence of the whole college of Cardinals. In the banquet following the consecration, Hugh Turclensis, a Cardinal and kinsman of the Pope, a man vain in his pride, held in contempt the humility and simplicity of Thomas, who had now been consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury. In order to make a mockery of him at the feast, he brought in a certain vile and abject little fellow, mounted on an ass and claiming the archbishopric. This man was rebuked by the whole company of Cardinals and left, marked as a fool. When the rites of consecration were completed, Thomas Bradwardyn took leave of the Pope and the Cardinals and returned to England. He first went to the King, from whom he received the temporalities of the archbishopric of Canterbury, in the name of his father's kin. Soon after, he went to Lambeth to relieve the weariness of his long journey. There, while staying for some weeks in the house of the Bishop of Rochester, his body, shaken by that weariness, fell into a fever; from this, after five weeks, and four days after he had been consecrated by the Pope, and before he had been enthroned at Canterbury, he departed this life. Afterwards he was buried at Canterbury, in the chapel of Archbishop Anselm, against the south wall, in the ground. Thus the church of Canterbury suffered for one year the upheavals and vacancies of its see. Besides many other books written by him, he wrote one great work, which he entitled On the Cause of God against Pelagius; this book is still extant.

units.la: LV. Simon Islippe.
units.tr: LV. Simon Islippe.

units.la: Imon Islippe ex iuris peritorum etiam Schola adhunc Archiepiscopatum ascendit. Cuius ex Scholis primus gradus fuit in Ecclesia Paulina Canonicatus. Deinde sub Iohanne Stratford Archiepiscopo, Ecclesiastico tribunali in Arcuata Londini curia præfuit. Postea Edwardi Regis Tertii consiliarius, secretarius, & priuati sigilli custos fuit. His muneribus cum laude atq; fide gestis, mortuo (vt diximus:) Thoma Bradwardyn, Monachi Cantuariensis hunc Simonem quem Regi ac plerisque gratiosum fuisse cognouerant summa consensione elegerunt. Sed Papa vt prouidendi morem quem vsurpatione non iure diu iam cepisset, retineret, Monachorum electione spreta Simonem in Archiepiscopatu non electionis, sed suæ prouisionis titulo collocauit. Eadem re bullata sua diplomata in templo Arcuato Londini quarto die Octobris publicata sunt. Deinde mense Decembri proximo à Radulpho Stratford Londinensi Episcopo in Ecclesia Paulina consecratus est, assistentibus Willihelmo Edindon, Wintoniensi, & Iohanne Therisby Meneuensi Episcopis. Postea Michaelem Northburg legum doctorem ad pallium Romæ petendum, & Rogerum Dorking ad illius præbendæ, quam iure (vt diximus) Cantuariensis sedis in Ecclesia Lugdunensi Cant. Archiepiscopi tenebat, fructus percipiendos, procuratores constituit. Palliumq; obtentum à Wintoniensi Episcopo in munerio de Esher accepit. Doriatusq; pallio Cantuariæ secretò ad vitādam iumptuum immoderatam luxuriam, & profusas epulas intronizatus & parcissime conuiuatus est. Nam vir in omnibus frugi, sed nimium seuerus fuit. Cantuariensem dioecesin ea summa animadueriose visitauit, & in subditorum excessibus criminibus solers, multos Clericos loeis & beneficiis amouit. Tum Roff. & Cicestrensem dioecesses quasi transiens, omniaq; conniuentibus oculis præteriens perfunctorie visitauit. Id illi lenitati & moderationi ascribebant sue. Sed postea cum demi suæ sedens plures de quorum criminibus cognouissat ad pœnas subeundas è dioecesibus euocassent, compertum est eum non lenitate, sed seueritate Archiepiscopatū gestur. Hæc cepta asperitas Iohanne Buckingham Lincolniensem Episcopum impulit, vt se suoque Papali priuilegio, quod Auinione à Papa Clemente magnis munetibus impetrauit, ab huius Archiepiscopi iurisdictione defenderet. Quod priuilegium postea Archiepiscopo id Romae flagitante rescissum atque reuocatum est. Namque Oxoniensis Vniuersitatis Scholares Cancellarium suum quendam Wilhelmum de Palmorna elegerunt. Qui cum ad Lincolniensem Episcopum in cuius Dioecesi tunc esset, Oxonium confirmandus veniret, erebris procrastinationibus in aliud tempora ab Episcopo reiectus est. Id tam vniuersitas Oxoniensis quam ipse Cancellarius electus indigne tulit. Quj facti querela coram Archiepiscopo declarata abeo opem & remedium ad tam diutinam & voluntariam fine causa tollendam moram petierunt. Archiepiscopus edicto Lincolniensi praecepit vt Cancellarium electum die quodam statuto confirmaret, aut coram se compareret, dicturus causam cur admitti & confirmari non deberet. Interea Archiepiscopus eaufam Iohanni Caulton Cancellario suo & Ecclesiae Cathedralis Wellensis Decano committit. Die statuto aderant Cancellarius electus & Oxoniensis Vniuersitatis procuratores qui confirmationem & conseceratio nem instanter petierunt. Lincolniensis autem Episcopus non comparuit in cuius absentis eo tumaciam Cantuariensis Cancellarius in negotio electionis legitime procedens, eam legitime riteque celebratam, ac Canonicam esse pronnneiauit. Quo facto Archiepiscopus Cancellarium confirmauit & eundem ad vniuersitatem Oxoniensem regendam admit fit, gregiq; Seholarium scripsit, vt ei iam admisso iuxta Vniuersitatis iura & statuta obtemperent atque pareant. Ab hac admissione Lincolniensis Episcopus priuilegio suo ante dicto fretus ad Papam appellauit. Archiepiscopus autem reiecta appellatione, eum vt suę Iurisdictionis & Archiepiscopalis authoritatis contemptorem ad sui tribunal vocauit, &c non accedentis proteruiam interdictis Ecclesiasticis in eius terras praediaque latis mulctauit. Multa deinceps in hac lite coram Papa agitanda controuersia sunt, in quibus Lin colniensis reuocato suo priuilegio à Cantuariensi victus succubuit Cantuariensis autem Lineolniensi superato, Andreaum Vfford Archidiaconum Midlesexiae administratorem bonorum Iohannis Vfford Cantuariensis (vt diximus) Archiepiscopi pro his acdificiis quae caduca atque ruinosa Iohannes Vfford in Archiepiscopatu Cantuariensi reliquerat, injure conuenit, & grandem illam pecuniam, quam (vt in Iohanne Vfford antea dixi mus) ab eodem executore tecuperauit, in Palatio Cantuariensi reparando erogauit. Idemq; totum munerium de Wrotham demolitus aedificia quae Iohannes Vfford M.i denstonię inchoauit, ex demolitis tignis, lapidibus, & cocemento eo traduetus decimam. His 30 sumptibus factus à Papa impetrauit, vt sibi liceret à prouincie suae Cantuariensis Clero tantis Archiepiscopalibus ferendis oneribus subsidium comparare. Id ita ratum est vt à singulis Mareis quatuor denariosexigat. Sed eius praetextu quaestores totam decimam, Papales literas aliter ac concessionis verba fuerunt interpretates, à Clero extorserit. Cu ius tamen hoc astu & non modo indebite, si d praeter ipsius Papae concessionem soluta pecuniae repetitionem in curia Romana quae alienae sibi asciscere, non refundere solebat, tunc locus non erat.
units.tr: Simon Islippe rose to the archbishopric from the school of the lawyers as well. The first step of his career in that school was a canonry in St Paul's church. Then, under John Stratford, the archbishop, he presided over the ecclesiastical court at the Arches in London. Afterwards he was counsellor, secretary and keeper of the privy seal to King Edward III. Having carried out these offices with praise and fidelity, and after Thomas Bradwardine had died (as we said), the monks of Canterbury, with the greatest unanimity, elected this Simon, whom they knew to be acceptable to the king and to most others. But the Pope, wishing to keep the custom of providing bishops, which he had long since seized by usurpation and not by right, set aside the monks' election and installed Simon in the archbishopric under the title not of election but of his own provision. With this matter sealed by bull, his letters were published in the church of the Arches in London on 4 October. Then in the following December he was consecrated in St Paul's by Ralph Stratford, Bishop of London, with William Edington, Bishop of Winchester, and John Thoresby, Bishop of St Davids, assisting. Afterwards he appointed Michael Northburgh, doctor of laws, to seek the pallium at Rome, and Roger Dorking to receive the revenues of that prebend in the church of Lyons which, by right (as we said), the archbishop of Canterbury held. The pallium, once obtained, he received from the Bishop of Winchester at his manor of Esher. Then, invested with the pallium at Canterbury in private, so as to avoid immoderate expense, extravagance and lavish feasting, he was enthroned and entertained very sparingly. For the man was frugal in all things, but far too severe. He visited the Canterbury diocese with great diligence, and was shrewd in detecting and punishing the offences and crimes of his subjects, removing many clergy from their places and benefices. Then he visited the dioceses of Rochester and Chichester in passing, overlooking everything with closed eyes, and did so perfunctorily. They ascribed this to his gentleness and moderation. But later, when he sat in his own see and summoned from the dioceses many whose crimes he had learned of, to undergo their penalties, it became clear that he governed the archbishopric not with gentleness but with severity. This harshness, once begun, drove John Buckingham, Bishop of Lincoln, to defend himself and his diocese from this archbishop's jurisdiction by his papal privilege, which he had obtained at Avignon from Pope Clement with great gifts. That privilege was afterwards rescinded and revoked at the archbishop's demand in Rome. For the scholars of the University of Oxford had elected their chancellor, one William de Palmorna. When he came to Oxford to be confirmed by the Bishop of Lincoln, in whose diocese it then lay, he was repeatedly put off by the bishop to other times. The University of Oxford and the chancellor-elect himself took this badly. They declared their complaint before the archbishop and sought his help and a remedy to remove so long and wilful a delay without cause. The archbishop, by edict, ordered the Bishop of Lincoln to confirm the chancellor-elect on a set day, or to appear before him and state why he ought not to be admitted and confirmed. Meanwhile the archbishop committed the case to John Caulton, his chancellor and dean of the cathedral church of Wells. On the appointed day the chancellor-elect and the proctors of the University of Oxford were present, and urgently sought confirmation and consecration. The Bishop of Lincoln did not appear. In his absence, the archbishop's chancellor, proceeding lawfully in the matter of the election, pronounced the election lawfully and duly held and canonical. Upon this the archbishop confirmed the chancellor and admitted him to govern the University of Oxford, and wrote to the body of scholars that, now that he had been admitted, they should obey and submit to him according to the laws and statutes of the university. The Bishop of Lincoln, relying on his aforesaid privilege, appealed to the Pope against this admission. The archbishop rejected the appeal, summoned him to his tribunal as a contemner of his jurisdiction and archiepiscopal authority, and, since he did not come, punished his contumacy by ecclesiastical interdicts laid on his lands and estates. Many disputes afterwards arose in this suit, to be pursued before the Pope. In these the Bishop of Lincoln, his privilege revoked, was defeated and gave way to the Canterbury archbishop, and the archbishop, having overcome Lincoln, sued at law Andrew Ufford, archdeacon of Middlesex and administrator of the goods of John Ufford, the former archbishop of Canterbury (as we said), for the buildings which John Ufford had left in the archbishopric in a decayed and ruinous state. From the great sum which (as I said under John Ufford) he recovered from the same executor, he spent money on repairing the palace at Canterbury. He also pulled down the buildings of the manor of Wrotham, which John Ufford had begun at Maidenstone, and from the timbers, stones and cement so demolished he was...taxed a tenth. With these expenses incurred, he obtained from the Pope that he might raise from the clergy of his province of Canterbury a subsidy to bear such archiepiscopal burdens. This was ratified so that he could exact four pence from each mark. But under the pretext of this, the questors extorted from the clergy the whole tithe, interpreting the papal letters otherwise than the words of the grant. Yet at that time there was no room for recovering, in the Roman court, money paid beyond the Pope's own grant, by that trick, and not merely unduly; those who took it for themselves were accustomed not to refund it.

units.la: Quis me vestigia terrent Omnia.
units.tr: What terrifies me? All these footprints.

units.la: Archiepiscopus deinde à Rege & proceribus in Parlamento obtinuit, vt legum atq; 40 libertatis Ecclesiasticae oppressiones, quibus Clericorum statvs diu afflictus fuit, fltatuta tollerentur. Quo impetrato cum Clerici permulti priuilegio Clericali abutentes quam plurima flagitia perpetrarent, Rege & proceribus id flagitantibus ab Archiepiscopo, suif que Suffraganeis statutum est vt Clerici de capitalibus criminibus, testibus, probationi nibus, suaue confessione conuicti Episcopalibus perpetuo earcerit usmancipati, ad pristinum locum aut ordinem nnnquam restituantur, ne deinde Clerica' scandalum gene retur. Sed perpetuam agentes poenitentiam, quarta & sexta feriis & in sabbathis pane do loris, & aqua angustiae semel in die, exetetis diebus pane & tenuissima cereuisia. Domini eo autem die pane, cereuisia, & legumine tantummodo nutriantur. Huie simiiem c 6fti tutionem antea ediderat Bonifacius quondam Cant. Archiepiscopus, quam Gulielmus 50 Linwoode inter Cantuariensium Archiepiscoporum constitutiones, quas ipse notis interpretatus est, diuulgauit. Noua in superiori Parlamento inter Cantuariensem & Ebora censem Episcopos de illa toties repetita gestandę Crucis altercatione, quęstio mota est quam Rex ipse tandem tota lite ab Archiepiscopis eius arbitrio compromissa hoc modo compositu. Vt alterius Prouincia crucem suam liberę ante se ferre possit. Sed Ebo racensis in subiectionis signum & singuli eius successores secundo mense postquam de inceps Cantuariensem prouinciam ingressi fuerint, pro pacifica crucis delatione nun ciumaliquem solennem videlicet Vicarium suum in spiritualibus generalem, vel causarum auditorem, vel aliquem legum doctorem, vel Militem ad Ecclesiam Cathedralem Cantua-
units.tr: The Archbishop then obtained from the King and the nobles in Parliament that the laws and the oppressions of ecclesiastical liberty, by which the condition of the clergy had long been burdened, be abolished by statute. Once this was granted, many clerics abused their clerical privilege and committed a great many crimes. At the demand of the King and the nobles, the Archbishop and his suffragans then decreed that clerics convicted of capital crimes, whether by witnesses, by proofs, or by their own confession, should be handed over by the bishops to perpetual imprisonment and never restored to their former place or order, lest scandal arise from the clergy. But they were to perform perpetual penance: on the fourth and sixth days of the week and on Saturdays, on bread and water, and once a day in narrowness; on other days on bread and very thin beer; and on the Lord's Day they were to be nourished only with bread, beer and pulses. Archbishop Boniface, formerly of Canterbury, had earlier issued a similar constitution, which William Lyndwood published among the constitutions of the Archbishops of Canterbury, which he himself interpreted with notes. In the previous Parliament a new question was raised between the bishops of Canterbury and York concerning that oft-repeated dispute over carrying the cross. The King himself finally settled the whole quarrel, the archbishops having submitted it to his judgment, in this way: that the cross of each province may be carried freely before the other. But the Archbishop of York, as a sign of subjection, and each of his successors within two months after entering the province of Canterbury, shall send for the peaceful carrying of the cross some solemn messenger, namely his Vicar-General in spiritual matters, or an auditor of causes, or some doctor of laws, or a knight, to the cathedral church of Canterbury.

units.la: Ad. Mon. imp. Ex Ex. 40. Cantuariensem cum vna imagine aurea valoris xl.l.sterl.sculpta ad similitudinem Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis, Arch. Byr. chiepiscopi crucem in manu sua deferentis, vel altero locali aureo praedicti valoris mitatur.
units.tr: …with a golden image worth forty pounds sterling, sculpted in the likeness of the Archbishop of Canterbury holding his cross in his hand, or with another golden cross of the aforesaid value.

units.la: Cumque huiusmodi nuneius ad Ecclesiam Cant. accesserit imaginem illam vel localem ad delubrum Thomæ Beckeri in præsentia prioris, supprioris, vel alterius præsidentis offerat publicè ac devote. In Parlamentis autem, tractatibus, & consiliis Regis cum Cantuariensis & Eboracensis Archiepiscopi simul intersint, quia Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ antiquior & præminentior esse dignoscitur, Cantuar. Archiepiscopus dextras, & Eboracensis sinistras Regis occupabunt, eorum crucibus eodem modo a dextris ac sinistris sepositis. In consiliis etiam, conuocationibus, synodis ac huiusmodi congregationibus quibus utriq; intersunt, primus locus Cantuariensi, secundus vero Eboracensi tribuatur. Tum crucigeri cum in via ampla atq; lata conueneriat, cruces simul deferat, sed in portarum introitu atq; exitu loci, angustioribus Cantuariensis crucifer præbit, & Eboracensis sequetur. Hanc compositionem Rex sigillo suo roboratam in palatio suo Westmonasterii venit promulgauit vicesimo decimo mensis Aprilis: Quâ Innocentius sextus Papa quinto Kal. Martii ex sua certa scientia, non obstante quod tunc in compositione huiusmodi Suffraganeorum, Præsulatorum, Conuentuum, & capitulorum virtutiq; prouincæ consensus iuxta requisitus non accesserit, omniq; alium iuris quam facti defectum supplens confirmauit. Hæc crucis gerendæ controuersia recentis pene annis duranit. Etsi enim Alexander 3. Rogerum quondam Eboracensem Archiepiscopum cruce in Cantuariensi provinciæ ferre vetuisset, tamen Eboracenses cum aliis Papis contrarias literas, vt de primatu cum Cantuariensibus contenderent accepisset, omniaq; iura pecuniarum interueniua a Papis dissoluta atq; rescinda posset peterent, in hac contentione, donec Rex decretum suum interposuisset petiuerabant. Nihil enim a Papa, qui vnò (vt Sanctus spiritu sorbere atque flare poterit, ita constitutum vnquam fuit, quod cuiusque illa chasula Non Obstante facilime non derimeret.
units.tr: When such a messenger has come to the Church of Canterbury, he shall offer that image or cross publicly and devoutly at the shrine of Thomas Becket, in the presence of the prior, the sub-prior or another presiding officer. In Parliaments, treaties and councils of the King where the Archbishops of Canterbury and York are both present, because the Church of Canterbury is recognised as the older and more pre-eminent, the Archbishop of Canterbury shall occupy the King's right hand and the Archbishop of York his left, their crosses being likewise placed on the right and the left. In councils also, convocations, synods and such assemblies which both attend, first place is to be given to Canterbury and second to York. When the cross-bearers meet on a wide and open road, they shall carry the crosses together; but at the entrances and exits of gates, and in narrower places, the cross-bearer of Canterbury shall go first and that of York shall follow. The King published this settlement, confirmed by his seal, in his palace at Westminster on the twenty-ninth day of April. Pope Innocent VI, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, from his certain knowledge, confirmed it, although in making this composition the consent of the suffragans, prelates, convents and chapters of the province, as required, had not come; supplying every defect of law other than of fact, he confirmed it. This controversy over carrying the cross lasted for nearly recent years. For although Alexander III had forbidden Roger, formerly Archbishop of York, to carry the cross in the province of Canterbury, nevertheless the men of York, having obtained contrary letters from other popes so that they might contend with Canterbury about primacy, and seeking that all the rights and payments in between be dissolved and rescinded by the popes, persisted in this contention until the King interposed the decree they had sought. For nothing could be so easily undone by the Pope, who alone (as the Holy Spirit can swallow and breathe, so it was never decreed) could annul whatever such a clause "Notwithstanding" had covered.

units.la: Hanc Regiam compositionem præualuisse, & in actum atque consuetudinem trasfisse constat.
units.tr: It is established that this royal composition prevailed and passed into practice and custom.

units.la: Quod Iohannes Turtel miles centum annis postea, videlicet Anno Dom. 1452. Ioacalequoddam aureum quadraginta librisæstimatum tum Arch. Eborac. ad portam Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ splendide receptus Thomæ Delubro prædicti compositionis authoritate obtulit. Post hæc grauis inter Scholares & oppidanos Oxonienses vtri imperarent contentio commota est, in qua enim ad arma ventum esset aliquibus vtrinq; casus Scholares oppido actii sunt. Ehenlis autem Episcopus cuius tum lurisdictioni subest Oxoniu, pœnas oppidanis infliturus oppido Ecclesiastico interdicto supposuit. Deinde eo pautatim relaxato parochis omnibus præcepit, vt sim diuinorum administratione oppidani interuenirent, aut interesserint sacrorum celebratione, tamusper cessarent, donec oppidani discederent. Huic aliam nempe excommunicationis poenam Archiepiscopus adiunxit. Sed Scholaribus hæc illuc dissipauit Rex cum de literarum interitu atque clade doleret, tota controuersiam ad seaduocauit. Qua audita cum de oppidanis supplicium sumpsisset, Scholaribus tota seditionis noxa ea lege remisit, vrad Vniuersitatem redirent, & abecedia iam ac intermissa litterarū studia recolerent. Id eis ab Archiepiscopo nunciari voluit.
units.tr: A hundred years later, namely in the year of the Lord 1452, Sir John Turtel, a knight, offered to the shrine of Thomas, on the authority of that composition, a certain golden jewel valued at forty pounds, and it was splendidly received by the Archbishop of York at the gate of the Church of Canterbury. After this, a grave contention arose between the scholars and the townsmen of Oxford over who should rule; when it came to arms, some on each side were killed, and the scholars were driven out of the town. The Bishop of Lincoln, under whose jurisdiction Oxford then lay, placed the town under an ecclesiastical interdict to inflict penalties on the townsmen. Then, as this was gradually relaxed, he ordered all the parish priests that the townsmen should not attend the divine services or take part in the celebration of the sacred rites, and that these should cease until the townsmen departed. The Archbishop added to this the further penalty of excommunication. But the King, grieving over the scattering of the scholars and the loss and ruin of learning, called the whole controversy before himself. Having heard it, and having exacted punishment from the townsmen, he remitted to the scholars all the guilt of the sedition on this condition: that they return to the University and renew their studies of letters, the rudiments of which had been interrupted. He wished this to be announced to them by the Archbishop.

units.la: Deinde vt Scholares ab Oppidanorum iniuriis atque videinceps securi esse possint, pro damnis in ea conflictatione Scholaribus illatis in CC L. l. Scholaribus reddedis condemnati sunt, deinde sub graui poena obligati ne vim deinceps vllam Scholaribus inferrent. Tum totius Oppidi Regimen Cancellario Vniuersitatis, exclusis penitus & in perpetuum abdicatis oppidanis, à Rege comissum est. Cuius etiā auditioni cognitio de panis, potus, vini, omniumq; victualium ponderib. ac mensuris coercenda est. Præter has pubhcas opidanorum multas permissum est Scholaribus iure priuato de singulis iniuriis singulis actionib, oppidanos coram Cancellario coaenite. Dū hæc Oxonii gerebantur, Catabrigiæ reb. pacatis, Collegiū q; Aula S. Trinitatis de Norwico nuncupatur iuris studio addictū & cōsecratū a Willihelmo Bateman Norwicensi Episcopo extructū est, cui decimas atq; rectoriasassignatas Arch. & cōuentus Cant. sigillis suis ratas fecerūt Historiator Rogerus Northburgh Couētrēsis & Lichefeld. Episcopus obiit. In eius locū Robertus Stretton Canonicus Lichefeld. Edwardo Regis filio Walliae Principe interceédēte electus est. Hunc Papa veniuit, ne se p electo gerere et antequā in Romana curia de moribus, suis ac doctrina, nec nō de ordine atque iure electionis examinatione subiisset. Is Auinione a Papa primo quau indoctus repulsus est, deinde precib. atq; gratia Principis Walliae murata sententia, Papae ad Archiepiscopum Cant. & Episcopum Roff. scripsit, ab his examinatus si dignus videretur ad Episcopatum admittatur, cum quibus etiam sulicitè egit Princeps Walliæ, ut cum humanitate ac fauore, non ad amussim (vt aiunt) tractaretur. Cantuariensis & Roffensis cum summo gratificandi studio Walliæ Principi obsequi voluerunt. Verum ea fuit hominis electi insticia & indignitas, vt nefas esse iudicarent cuiuscunque gratia atque precibus virum tam imperitum in tanta dignitate locare. Electi Principi vtcunque satisfactum est quod vir tam indignus Episcoparu reiectus & repudiarus non erat, sed causa tota abdicata, integra ei reseruata est. Itaque Papam Principes iterum inuocat, qui vices suas tam Londinensi Episcopo commisit. A quo Principis gratia, & Papae authoritate, quomnes in homine imperitissimo defectus supplerent, legitimè electus, &Episcopatu dignus pronunciatus atque consecratus est. Hoc tam infulo & imperito viro ad Episcopatû promoto Thomas de Lyld Elienfis Episcopus vir doctus atque pius aulicorum inuidia, quodque Regem minus prudenter verbo Vno aut altero temere emissò provocassEt, in capitis discrimen venit. Comitissa Marischalla Domina Wake Regis consanguinea, quæ in Huntingdonensi Comitatu vicina prædia Elienfi Episcopo possidebat, multis sulcitatis de agrorum finibus controuersiis Episcopi potentiam non ferebat. Hinc incendiarij quidam qui Comitissæ ædes inflammauerunt deprehensi, Elienfem Episcopum & suos famulos suos auctores, & incendij illius reos criminantur. De quo ignorante Episcopo, instante Comitissa, & mandante Rege instituta subito de illius incendij authoribus & ministris inquisitio est. Iudicesque à Rege delegati, quibus more atque iure regni duodecim viris legalibus conuocatis iuramento delato mandauerunt, vt de criminé, & de reis inquirerent, & eos quos ex inquisitione reos comperissent ad se deferrent. His duodecim iuratis, illos incendiarios nominatum incendium illud perpetrasse, ac Episcopum in facinus cuius his consensisse retulerunt. Quo dicto iudices irrogata incendiaris poena Episcopum Elienfem in 9. C. libris Comitissæ pro incendij iactura reparanda soluendis condemnarunt. Quam summam statim ac sine mora ex Regis edicto atque præcepto soluit. At Elienfis Episcopus cuius animus nec in secundis rebus elatus, nec in aduersis deiectus aut demissus fuit, nouam de hoc tam famoso sibi indicio litem inchoauit. Impetrauit a Rege post multas preces, vt de testium fide, & tam iniqui testimonii falsitate & periurio inquisitio Huntingdoniæ haberetur. Dies taruto prioris illius testimonii inquisitionis, & iudicij copia a iudicibus postulata haberi non potuit, quia it. Itaque & proficiscente Comitissa Miles quidam Regius in cuius tum custodia fuit, exhibere illam iudicibus noluit, sine qua cum iudicesin causa progredi nequiuissent, re infecta discessere runt. Elienfis autem hanc sibi contumeliam non a iudicibus sed a Comitissa ne Rege quidem iniciò factam existimauit. Itaque Regem temerè ac iracundus adiit, acriter qui iustitiâ sibi ministrari petiit. Cui Rex, quisque inquit prohibet in regno nostro legem habere vel iustitiam? At ille inaniter & inconsideratè effutiens respondit. Domine sic est quod in causa mea ius obtinere nequeo potestate vt credo Regia impeditus. Quo audito Rex accensus: certè inquit tu Thoma de Lyld falsum dicis, nunquam a me impeditus fuisti, pinde ius tuo merito congruum tibi reddetur. Ita offensionis commoto Rege Elienfis Episcopus discessit. Paulo post Parlamentum Westmonasterii celebratum est. Ac eo durante Cleri Synodus habita Londini, in qua Cleri nullam suam opem aut operam in bellicis negotiis Regi defuturam promisit. Sed in Parlamento illius iniuriæ quam ab Elienfis Episcopi verbis acceperat memor, illum de iniuria postulauit, Elienfis verba quæ Rex recensuit, negauit. Rex testes produxit. Quibus testimonium secundum Regem ferentibus Elienfis attonitus obstupuit. Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus caeterique suffraganei cum Elienfem temeritate magis quam propositio in Regem deliquisse animaduerterent, flexis genibus & egemitibus obsecrabat. At Rex exorari noluit Episcoporû cum egressus, Elienfis Regem postea nunquam conspexit, super huenit. Eius hac quasi contumacia discedenti noua calamitas. De hac offensa Regis ira inter suos & Comitissæ famulos orta est, in ea Radulphus quidam genere Normannus Elienfis Episcopi Camerarius interfecit Willihelmum Holm. Comitissæ familiarem, & in Normanniam aufugit. Quo accepto Episcopus ad Somersham festinauit. Initinere occurrum ei est confestim a rustici per famulos Comitissæ concitatis. Quos cautè deuitans ad domum suam saluus Somersham peruenit. Ibi quid è re sua maxime fit statuès cum Regis ira & superioris iudicii iniuriam considerare tur, fore vt de hoc homicidio perinde ac de illo incendio ædemmonarerur, & agris bonisque suis direptis proscriberetur, omnia sua pecora & mobilia illico venundari, precium que ad se perferri iussit. Id vt iussit peractum est.
