Interea iudices Regii inquisitione per duodecim legales homines habita Elienfem Episcopum illius homicidii eidii reum tanquam suasorem & homicidæ fautorem atque receptorem statuunt.
units.tr: Then, so that the scholars might be safe from the townsmen's injuries from then on, the townsmen were condemned to pay the scholars 250 pounds in damages for losses suffered in that clash, and were further bound under heavy penalty never to inflict violence on the scholars again. Next, the whole government of the town was committed by the King to the Chancellor of the University, the townsmen being utterly excluded and removed from office for ever. Under this authority the inquiry into the weights and measures of bread, drink, wine and all victuals was also to be enforced. Besides these public fines, the scholars were allowed, by private right, to bring separate actions against the townsmen before the Chancellor for each individual injury. While these things were happening at Oxford, and affairs at Cambridge had been settled, the college called Trinity Hall of Norwich, devoted to the study of law and consecrated, was built by William Bateman, Bishop of Norwich. The Chapter and convent of Canterbury confirmed under their seals the tithes and rectories assigned to it. The historian Roger Northburgh, Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield, died. In his place Robert Stretton, canon of Lichfield, was elected, through the intercession of Edward, the King's son and Prince of Wales. The Pope refused to let him act as elected until he had submitted to examination in the Roman court concerning his morals and learning, and also concerning the order and law of his election. At Avignon he was first rejected by the Pope as unlearned; then, by the prayers and favour of the Prince of Wales, the sentence was changed, and the Pope wrote to the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of Rochester that they should examine him and admit him to the bishopric if he seemed worthy. The Prince of Wales also urged these men earnestly that he be treated with kindness and favour, not strictly (as they say) by the rule. The Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of Rochester, with the greatest eagerness to oblige the Prince of Wales, were willing to comply. But the man's ignorance and unworthiness were such that they judged it wrong to place a man so unlearned in so great a dignity, whatever the favour or prayers behind him. The elect was somewhat satisfied with the Prince's help, in that a man so unworthy was not rejected and repudiated as a bishop, but the whole matter was set aside and his claim was kept whole for him. So the Prince called upon the Pope again, who committed his own authority in the matter to the Bishop of London. By his grace, and by the Pope's authority, the Bishop of London, so that the defects of this most unlearned man might be supplied, was lawfully elected, pronounced worthy of the bishopric, and consecrated. While this man so foolish and unlearned was promoted to the bishopric, Thomas de Lyld, Bishop of Ely, a learned and pious man, came into danger of his life, through the envy of courtiers and because he had rashly provoked the King by a word or two said imprudently. The Countess Marshal, Lady Wake, a kinswoman of the King, who held lands near the Bishop of Ely's in Huntingdonshire, and who had many disputes with him over the boundaries of their fields, could not bear the Bishop's power. Hence certain arsonists who had set fire to the Countess's house were caught, and they accused the Bishop of Ely and his servants as instigators and as guilty of that fire. The Bishop was ignorant of this, but at the Countess's urging and by the King's command an immediate inquiry was instituted into the authors and agents of the fire. The judges, delegated by the King, summoned twelve lawful men according to the custom and law of the realm, and having administered an oath, ordered them to inquire into the crime and the guilty and to bring before them those whom the inquiry found guilty. These twelve, having sworn, reported that the named arsonists had committed the fire, and that the Bishop had consented to the deed. On this statement the judges imposed the penalty on the arsonists, and condemned the Bishop of Ely to pay 900 pounds to the Countess to make good the loss by fire. He paid this sum at once and without delay, by the King's edict and command. But the Bishop of Ely, whose spirit was neither lifted up in prosperity nor cast down or dismayed in adversity, began a new suit over this so notorious accusation. After many prayers he obtained from the King that an inquiry be held at Huntingdon into the credibility of the witnesses, and into the falsity and perjury of so unjust a testimony. The day for the former testimony and inquiry, and the copy of the judgement demanded by the judges, could not be had, because the Countess was leaving. Thus a royal knight, in whose custody she then was, refused to produce her before the judges, and without her the judges could not proceed with the case, so they departed having accomplished nothing. The Bishop of Ely, however, judged that this insult had been offered him not by the judges but by the Countess, and not even without the King's knowledge. So he rashly and angrily approached the King and sharply sought that justice be done him. The King replied, "Who prevents justice or law in our realm?" But he, speaking vainly and thoughtlessly, answered, "Sire, it is so, that in my case I cannot obtain justice, being hindered, I believe, by royal power." Hearing this, the King, roused, said: "Certainly, Thomas de Lyld, you speak falsely; I have never hindered you, and so your right will be rendered to you as it deserves." Thus the Bishop of Ely departed, the King having been moved to offence. Shortly after, a Parliament was held at Westminster, and during it a synod of the clergy was held at London, in which the clergy promised that they would not fail the King in military affairs with any help or effort of theirs. But in Parliament the Bishop of Ely, mindful of the insult he had received from the King's words, charged him with the injury, and the Bishop denied the words which the King recounted. The King produced witnesses, and when they gave testimony in the King's favour, the Bishop of Ely was struck dumb with astonishment. When the Archbishop of Canterbury and the other suffragans saw that the Bishop had offended against the King more through rashness than by intention, they knelt and with groans begged for him. But the King would not be moved by the entreaties of the bishops; the Bishop of Ely, going out, never saw the King again, and he was soon overwhelmed. Upon his departure, after this so-called obstinacy, a new calamity followed. Out of this offence of the King's anger, a quarrel arose between his people and the Countess's servants; in it a certain Ralph, of Norman birth, chamberlain of the Bishop of Ely, killed William Holme, a familiar of the Countess, and fled into Normandy. On hearing of this the Bishop hastened to Somersham. On the way, he was at once met by peasants stirred up by the Countess's servants. Avoiding them cautiously, he came safely to his house at Somersham. There, considering what was most expedient for his position, while the King's anger and the injury of the earlier judgement were weighed, he ordered that, just as in the arson case, it would come about that he would be accused of this homicide too, and his lands and goods would be plundered and he would be proscribed; so he ordered that all his livestock and movable goods be sold at once, and the price brought to him. This was carried out as he ordered. Meanwhile the royal judges, having held an inquiry through twelve lawful men, declared the Bishop of Ely guilty of that homicide, as its instigator, abettor and harbourer.

units.la: Eo iudicio omnia eius bona atque prædia Regis fisco adiudicata sunt. Ipseque a Regis iudicibus citatus vt coram eis in Regio foro capitis causam diceret. Qua a Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo ac nonnullis Cantuariensis prouinciæ suffraganeis comitatus accessit ad tribunal Regium. Cumq; declinatoris exceptionibus subterfugere Laicorum iudicium non potuit, respondit se antedicti homicidii nequaquam conscium, nec contulisse...
units.tr: By that judgement all his goods and estates were adjudged to the King's treasury. He himself, summoned by the King's judges to answer the capital charge before them in the royal court, came, accompanied by the Archbishop of Canterbury and some of the suffragans of the province of Canterbury, to the royal tribunal. And since he could not escape the lay court by pleading objections to the judges, he replied that he was in no way aware of the aforesaid homicide, nor had he contributed...

units.la: {a} Ioan. 3.
units.tr: {a} Ioan. 3.

units.la: Sequenti anno obierunt Lincolniensis & Ciltrensis Episcopi, quibus etiam a Papa successores dati sunt. Sub haec tempora Edwardus Regis filius Princeps Walliæ Aluphensi Episcopo mortuo Episcopalia iura atque prædia Episcopatu vacante sibi vendicaunt Quæ ad Cantuariensem Metropolitan longa cōtuetudine acquisiia (quæ tamen omnium pene tam laicorum quam Clericorum in illa diœcesi testimonio, Archiepiscopus in iure aliquandiu cum Principe contendens probauit, causamque obtinuit. Paulo post Dunelmensis Episcopus obiit.
units.tr: In the following year the bishops of Lincoln and Chichester died, and successors were given to them by the Pope. About this time Edward, son of the King and Prince of Wales, on the death of the bishop of Aluphen, claimed for himself the episcopal rights and estates during the vacancy of the see. The Archbishop of Canterbury, contending with the Prince at law for some time, proved the rights which the Metropolitan of Canterbury had acquired by long custom, and which the testimony of almost all in that diocese, both laity and clergy, confirmed, and he won the case. Soon after, the Bishop of Durham died.

units.la: Ad eum Episcopatum Regis gratia Thomas Haisfeld Præbendarius de Oxgate in Ecclesia Paulina permotus est. Eam Præbendam Londinensis Episcopus cuidam Nicolao Stanwey contulit. Rex qui prioris Præbendarium suagratia ad Dunelmensem Episcopatum euexit sui iuris atque donationis eam Præbendam fore asseruit, qui per cessionem vtrumque incumbentis vacauit, & tam Episcopum quam Nicolaum in suum sorum traxit. Qui allegabant cognitionem de Ecclesiasticorum beneficiorum vacatione ad Ecclesiasticum forum non Regium spectare debere. Rogerus autem Hillarye, & Hericus Greene Iusticiarij Regis quod iniquit dilationibus litem procrastinabant, ad Romanam curiam citati sunt, qui cautum dico é Regio foro ad Ecclesiasticum remissi runt. Elizabetha nobilis fœmina post mortem Iohannis Comitis Cantii sui mariti monialium cultum & religionem professa est. In quo cum aliquot annis perseuerasset cuiusdam militis Eustatii Abricourts amore capta, egressa monialium domum contraxit contra votum nuptias, & manè ante incensum sine bannorum editione matrimonium solemnitatum est. His Archiepiscopus pœnas grauies pecuniarias inflixit, cosque obligauit vt duobus capellanis perpetua stipendia assignarent, & vt iciunijs orationibusque diu vacarent, matrimonij vinculo nomine dissoluto. Cantuar. Archiepisc. celebre Oxoniæ Collegium quod Cantuariense appellatur condidit, cui Magfeld atque Paghamrectoriis appropriauit. Idemque Ecclesias de Munketon & Estrey Cantuariensibus Monachis concessit. Sed in hoc male audiuit quod 16. damas atque cetuos quos Comes Arundelliæ annuam Cant. Archiepiscopo soluit, ducetis quadragintamarcis acceptis eidem Comiti, iuiisq; successoribus remiss in itinere cum Magnfeldiam profectus est equo in paludem decidit.
units.tr: Thomas Haisfeld, prebendary of Oxgate in St Paul's, was promoted to that bishopric by the king's favour. The Bishop of London conferred the prebend on one Nicholas Stanwey. The king, who by his favour had raised the earlier prebendary to the bishopric of Durham, asserted that the prebend was within his right and gift, since it had fallen vacant through the resignation of both incumbents, and he drew both the bishop and Nicholas into his own court. They argued that cognizance of the vacancy of ecclesiastical benefices belonged to the ecclesiastical court and not to the royal one. Roger Hillarye and Henry Greene, the king's justices, who prolonged the suit by delays, were summoned to the Roman court; they were sent back from the royal court to the ecclesiastical one. Elizabeth, a noblewoman, after the death of her husband John, Earl of Kent, professed the religious life and joined a community of nuns. After she had persevered in it for some years, she was captured by love for a certain soldier, Eustace Abricourt. She left the convent and, contrary to her vow, contracted marriage early in the morning, before the incense was lit, and without the publication of banns, and the marriage was solemnised. For this the Archbishop imposed heavy financial penalties on them and bound them to assign perpetual stipends to two chaplains, and to devote themselves for a long time to fasting and prayer, the marriage bond being dissolved in name. The Archbishop of Canterbury founded at Oxford the famous college called Canterbury College, and appropriated to it the rectories of Mayfield and Pagham. He also granted the churches of Monkton and Estrey to the monks of Canterbury. But in this matter he was ill spoken of, because, having received forty marks from the Earl of Arundel for the sixteen dams and ... which the Earl paid yearly to the Archbishop of Canterbury, he remitted them to the same Earl and his successors. While on his way to Mayfield he fell from his horse into a marsh.

units.la: In quo casu cum equus certaret, ac se recuperare vellet Archiepiscopus luto inuolutus ac totus madefactus est, ita madidus ac lutosus Magsfeldiam peruenit, vbi in somno antequam vestes exuissent incidit, ex eo paralysim contraxit, & postquam annis 16. mensibusque quatuor, & diebus 12. sedillet, Maghi Lloit obiit. Moriens Cantuariensi cœnobio mille oues legauit, & vestimenta sua aurea, cappam pretiosissimam & vasa argentea, videficet sex duodecim disconum argenteorum, tot salaria, quatuorque peluis argenteas armis suis insignitas. Sine populi frequentia, & quam minimis expensis humati voluit, omnibus in rebus (vt ex eius vita patear) magnificentiam, multitudinemque sumtuum vitans. Huius inter Prouinciales duæ tantum constitutiones exstant.
units.tr: In that mishap, while the horse struggled and the Archbishop tried to recover himself, he was enveloped in mud and wholly soaked. In that wet and muddy state he reached Mayfield, where, before he had taken off his clothes, he fell asleep, and from that he contracted paralysis. After he had sat in the see for sixteen years, four months and twelve days, he died at Maghi Lloit. Dying, he bequeathed a thousand sheep to the Canterbury monastery, together with his golden vestments, a most precious cope and silver vessels, namely six dozen silver dishes, as many salt-cellars, and four silver basins marked with his arms. He wished to be buried without a crowd of people and at the least possible expense, avoiding in all things (as may be seen from his life) magnificence and great expenditure. Among the provincial constitutions only two of his are extant.

units.la: LVI. SIMON LANGHAM.
units.tr: LVI. Simon Langham.

units.la: IMONE Islippe Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo mortuo Monachi Cantuarienses Willihelmum Edundon Wintonien sem Episcopum postulaverunt. Is autem eorum postulationi renunciauit.
units.tr: After Simon Islip, Archbishop of Canterbury, died, the monks of Canterbury nominated William Edington, Bishop of Winchester. He, however, renounced their nomination.

units.la: Deinde intercessione Regia Vrbanus quintus Papa Simonem Langham a sede Eliensi, ad Cantuariensem provisionis titulo translulit. Monachus hic primo Westmonasteriensis, deinde Prior, ac demum Abbas fuit.
units.tr: Then, by royal intercession, Pope Urban V transferred Simon Langham from the see of Ely to Canterbury by way of provision. This man was first a monk of Westminster, then prior, and at last abbot.

units.la: Quo etiam tempore Regi intimus totius Thesauri rarii, Regiotumq; reddituum custodiam & quæsturam habuit. A Westmonasterio deinde cœnobio ad Londinensem Episcopatum adductus est, sed ilico Eliensi per mortem (vt antea diximus) Thomæ de Lyld vacante, Regis & Papæ gratia eò tanquam ad pinguiorem provinciam missus est.
units.tr: At the same time he was intimate with the king, and held the custody and treasurership of the king's treasure and revenues. Afterwards he was brought from the monastery of Westminster to the bishopric of London, but when Ely immediately fell vacant through the death of Thomas de Lyld (as we said earlier), by the favour of the king and the Pope he was sent there as to a richer province.

units.la: Abeaq;, vt diximus Papæ prouisione deductus, pallium à Bathoniensi Episcopo quarto Nonembris in capella Sancti Stephani Westmonasterii accepit, deinde Cantuariæ in festo Annunciationis beatæ Mariæ intronizatus est.
units.tr: Then, as we said, he was brought to that see by papal provision, and on 4 November he received the pallium from the Bishop of Bath in the chapel of St Stephen at Westminster. Afterwards he was enthroned at Canterbury on the feast of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

units.la: Hic Archiepiscopus in tota vita, omnibusque quæ gessit muneribus non minus pronidus atq; sagax, quam beneficus ac liberalis fuit. Ipso autem consecrationis die Homagii, fidelitatisque seruitia a Comite Stratfordiæ, Thoma Rose, Iohanne Kyriel, Roberto Brokyl, Radulpho Senileger, militibus, aliisq; nonnullis pro his prædiis quæ de eis dominio possident, ei Cantuariæ præstita sunt. Id quod in singulis Archiepiscoporum consecrationibus, & intronizationibus cum magna solennitate hen consueuit. Primo suæ translationis anno Vrbanus Papa in eos qui plura ecclesiastica beneficia tenerent, seuerissimū edictum proposuit, ac Simoni Langham Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo mandauit, vt in sua prouincia suo iussu omnes suffraganei diligenter inquirerēt, quæ ac quot ecclesiastica beneficia atque dignitates in singulis dioecesibus à singulis tenerentur. Tū quænam alia vectigalia, munera, stipendia, vel salaria clerici præter ecclesiastica possiderent. In ea inquisitione compertum fuit nonnullos viginti Ecclesias & dignitates ipsius Papæ authoritate possidere, illisq; insuper iisdem priuilegiis indultum esse, vt sine modo atque numero qnalcunq; alias quocunq; modo nactas licitè retinere possint. E quorum numero præcipnos hic selectos inseruimus.
units.tr: This Archbishop, throughout his life and in all the offices he discharged, was no less prudent and sagacious than he was beneficent and generous. On the very day of his consecration, homage and fealty were rendered to him at Canterbury for the lands which they held of him by the Earl of Stafford, Thomas Rose, John Kyriel, Robert Brokyl, Ralph Senileger, knights, and some others. This is what has customarily been done, with great solemnity, at the consecrations and enthronements of each of the Archbishops. In the first year of his translation, Pope Urban published a most severe edict against those who held several ecclesiastical benefices, and he instructed Simon Langham, Archbishop of Canterbury, that in his province all the suffragans should, by his order, carefully inquire what and how many ecclesiastical benefices and dignities were held in each diocese, and by whom. Then, what other revenues, offices, pensions or salaries clergymen possessed besides ecclesiastical ones. In that inquiry it was found that some held twenty churches and dignities by the authority of the Pope himself, and that they had moreover been granted privileges by which they might lawfully retain, without limit or number, whatever others they had obtained in any way. From their number we have inserted here the chief ones, selected.

units.la: Quo quidem tempore omnia publica Regis regniq; munera à clericis administrata sunt. Nam Simon Langham Archiepisc. Cantuar. quod antecedentibus & subsequentibus temporibus in vsu plerumq; fuit, Cancellarius erat. Iohannes Barhoniensis Episcop. thesaurarius. Dauid Wollor Præsbyter custos rotulorum. Wilhelmus Wicham Archidiaconus Lincol. custos priuati sigilli. Iohannes de Troy Præsbyter thesaurarius Hiberniæ. Robertus Caldwel Clericus husþitû Regis. Wilhelmus Bugbrig generalis receptor ducatus Lancastriæ, Wilhelmus Asheby Cancellarius Scaccarii. Iohannes Newnebam Camerarius Scaccarii, vnusq; custodum thesauri & iocaliū Regis. Wilhelmus de Mulso alter Camerarius & receptor atq; custos thesauri ac iocalium. Iohannes Ronceby Clericus familiæ, & dispositor ac contrariator sumptuum & expensarum in operibus regiis. Rogerus Barnburgh, Wilhelmus Mirseld, Robertus Muskam, Wilhelmus Burtlall, Michael Rauendale, Thomas Nuby, Richardus Rydick, Wilhelmus Lound. Clerici in Cancellaria regia. Richardus Chesterfeld subthesaurarius Regis. Thomas Brantingham thesaurarius Regis in partibus Guines, Merk, & Calis. Qui omnes Clerici, Ecclesiastici beneficiis & dignitatibus abundabant. Inter hos Wilhelmus Wickam mortuo Wilhelmo Ëdindon Wintoniensi Episcopo ab Vrbano Papa eius Episcopatus administratione in temporalibus & spiritualibus impetrauit, annoq; sequenti Episcopus Wintoniensis & Cancellarius Regis creatus est. Cuius tota vita in pecuniis congerendis, studium in duobus nobilissimis Collegiis Oxonii & Wintoniæ extruendis ad finem Reip. vtilem, sibique gloriosum relatum est. Hoc anno Edwardus Regis filius prælio comissio fudit Hericum quendā Nothum Hispanū, qui coninnčto sibi quodā Bertrando magnoq; coparato exercitu Petronem Regem regno expulerunt, vertit in fugam, & exercitum eius totum fudit ac dissipauit, Regemq; in regnum restituit. Pro hac tam insigni victoria, eleemosinæ, orationes ac ieiunia ab Archiepiscopo per totam prouinciam publicantur. Fodemetiam anno prouinciam suam visitaturus, in Ecclesia & Dioecesi propria Cantuariensi exorsus est. In qua vix aliquid gessit memorabile, præterquam quod Londini Clerū & populum de decimis dissentientes magnaq; altercatione contendentes, hoc decimandi modo statuto. vt vt de singulis redditibus x.s. valoribus denarii quadrans parocho soluatur, præter oblationes atq; decimas personales. Ac paulò post orta inter eum & scholares Cantuariensis Collegii ab antecessore suo Simone Islippe (vt dixi mus) extructi, Oxonii cōroueršia. Archiepiscopus enim fructus rectoriæ de Pagham ad illud collegium à Simone Islippe concessæ sequestrauit. A qua sequestratione à scholaribus ad Papam appellatum est, sed Archiepiscopus appellationi non concedens Iuhannem Radingal Monachum Cantuariensem scholaribus durante beneplacito præposuit, quem etiam cito domum reuocauit, aliumq; Monachum Cant. Henricum Woodhil collegio præfecit. Hic rem strenuè ex animo & sententia Simonis Langhami Archiepiscopi gessit: Cuius hic fuit conatus vt secularibus eiectis Clericis introducerentur Monachi. In eo tū collegio educatus est Iohannes Wiclisse de quo deinceps plura dicenda sunt. Is summa ope Monachis restitit. Sed Archiepisc. potentia, & Papæ ad quem appellatum erat gratia Monachi superiores in causa fuerunt, quibus seculares Clerici cedere coacti sunt. His gestis Vrbanus Papa Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum Simonem Langham Romæ titulo Sancti Sixti Cardinalem creauit. Quo audito permotus Rex prædia Archiepiscopatus tanquam vacantis in suam potestatem recepit. At Archiepiscopus nihilo tu ba
units.tr: At this time all the public offices of the king and kingdom were administered by clergymen. For Simon Langham, Archbishop of Canterbury, was Chancellor, as was usual for the most part in the preceding and following times. John, Bishop of Bath, was treasurer. David Wollor, priest, keeper of the rolls. William Wykeham, Archdeacon of Lincoln, keeper of the privy seal. John de Troy, priest, treasurer of Ireland. Robert Caldwell, clerk of the king's household. William Bugbrigge, general receiver of the Duchy of Lancaster. William Asheby, Chancellor of the Exchequer. John Newnham, Chamberlain of the Exchequer, and one of the keepers of the king's treasury and jewels. William de Mulso, another chamberlain, receiver and keeper of the treasury and jewels. John Ronceby, clerk of the household, and manager and controller of expenses and outlays on the royal works. Roger Barnburgh, William Mirseld, Robert Muskam, William Burtlall, Michael Rauendale, Thomas Nuby, Richard Rydick, William Lound, clerks in the royal chancery. Richard Chesterfield, under-treasurer of the king. Thomas Brantingham, treasurer of the king in the parts of Guines, Merk and Calais. All these clergymen abounded in ecclesiastical benefices and dignities. Among them, William Wykeham, on the death of William Edington, Bishop of Winchester, obtained from Pope Urban the administration of that see in things temporal and spiritual, and in the following year he was created Bishop of Winchester and Chancellor of the king. His whole life was given to amassing money and to the building of the two most noble colleges at Oxford and Winchester, a work reckoned useful to the commonwealth and glorious to himself. In this year Edward's son, the king's son, routed in battle a certain Henry, a bastard Spaniard, who, having joined with himself a certain Bertrand and assembled a great army, had driven King Peter from the kingdom. He put them to flight, scattered and destroyed their whole army, and restored the king to his kingdom. For this so signal a victory, alms, prayers and fasts were proclaimed throughout the whole province by the Archbishop. In the same year, intending to visit his province, he began in his own church and diocese of Canterbury. In it he did scarcely anything memorable, except that at London, when the clergy and people were at odds over tithes and in great dispute, he settled the manner of tithing so that, from each income of ten shillings in value, a fourth of a penny should be paid to the parson, apart from oblations and personal tithes. Soon afterwards a controversy arose at Oxford between him and the scholars of Canterbury College, which had been built by his predecessor Simon Islip (as we said). For the Archbishop sequestrated the revenues of the rectory of Pagham, which Simon Islip had granted to that college. From this sequestration the scholars appealed to the Pope, but the Archbishop, not allowing the appeal, placed John Radingal, a monk of Canterbury, over the scholars for as long as it pleased him, and soon recalled him home, and set another Canterbury monk, Henry Woodhill, over the college. He carried the matter through vigorously and with the full mind and purpose of Simon Langham, Archbishop. His aim was that, the secular clergy being ejected, monks should be introduced. Under this college John Wycliffe was then educated, of whom more is to be said hereafter. He resisted the monks with all his might. But the power of the Archbishop and the favour of the Pope to whom the appeal had been made gave the upper hand to the monks in the case, and the secular clergy were compelled to yield. After these things, Pope Urban created Simon Langham, Archbishop of Canterbury, a cardinal at Rome with the title of St Sixtus. On hearing this, the king, moved by it, took the lands of the archbishopric into his own power as vacant. But the Archbishop, nothing daunted,

units.la: {a} Ann. 1367. tus aegrè randem a Rege impetrata Romam proficiscendi licentia è suo famulatu destitutus omnibus Archiepiscopatus inginibus exutus, omnium iurisdictione Priori & conuentui Cantuariensi dimissa ad Pontificem properauit. Ibi suscepto Cardinalatu in maxima Papae, Romanae curiae gratia vixit, posteaque a Gregorio Papa duodecimo Cardinalis Praenestinus episcopus creatus est. Neq; haud ita diu vixit, quin Auinioni vita functus atq; sepultus sit. Ac triennio post ossa eius exhumata & ad Westmonasteriense coenobium, quod (vt mox dicemus) maxime adamauit, plurimisq; donis ac ingenuibus affecit deducta, sepulchro⁣ honorifico condita sunt. In Ecclesiam Cantuariensem non ita liberalis ac munificus fuit, ad quam cum ab Eliensi traduceretur, haec carmina Poeta quidem composuit. Exultent caeli, quia Simon transiit ab Ely, Cuius vna aduenit um, flent in Kent millia centum.
units.tr: Ann. 1367. Not at all disturbed, he at length with difficulty obtained the King's permission to go to Rome. He was stripped of his household and of all the revenues of the archbishopric, and, having handed all jurisdiction over to the prior and convent of Canterbury, he hastened to the Pontiff. There he took up the cardinalate and lived in the greatest favour with the Pope and the Roman curia. Afterwards Pope Gregory the Twelfth made him Cardinal-bishop of Praeneste. He did not live much longer, and he died and was buried at Avignon. Three years later his bones were dug up and brought to the monastery of Westminster, which (as we shall soon say) he loved most of all and enriched with many gifts and benefits, and they were placed in an honourable tomb. He was not so generous and bountiful to the Church of Canterbury, to which he was transferred from Ely; the poet indeed wrote these verses on it: "Let the heavens rejoice, for Simon has passed from Ely; at his one arrival, a hundred thousand weep in Kent."

units.la: Eiusdem in Westmonasteriense coenobium inexhausta extitit & profusa liberalitas. In quo simulatque Abbas fuisset, quaecunque Monachus aut Prior ante comparauerat consumptsit, in ipso primo ingressu ex alienum Ecclesiae Westmonast. quod ab Antecessoribus suis contractum erat & ad summam duarum millium & ducentarum marcarum creuerat, dissoluit. Grandem insuper pecuniam quam Monachi mercatoribus sigillatim debebant, soluit. Quos vt filios semper fouit, monasteriosque continuit, nihil abhis vnquam ad se privatim abduxit, sed vt eorum portiones augeret de suo concessit.
units.tr: His liberality towards the monastery of Westminster was boundless and lavish. As soon as he became abbot there, he paid off, right at the start, all that the monk or prior had previously accumulated: the debt of the church of Westminster, which his predecessors had contracted and which had grown to the sum of two thousand two hundred marks, he discharged. He also paid the large sums that the monks owed individually to merchants. He cherished them as his own sons and kept the monastery together, and never took anything from them for himself privately, but rather gave from his own resources to increase their shares.

units.la: Deinde cum Regis esset Thesaurarius & Cancellarius permultis comparatis praediis illud coenobium locupletauit. Ex Anglia discedens libros. 830. lib. cappasque & vestimenta 437. lib. aestimata eidem monasterio donauit. Moriens etiam omnia sua nomina atque debita, tum vasa aurea ac argentea legauit. Debitorum summa trium millium nongenta quinquaginta quatuor libris. t.3.5.& quatuor denariis in Inuentario descripta fuit. Vasa vero duobus librarum millibus ac septingenta aestimata sunt.
units.tr: Then, while he was the King's treasurer and chancellor, he enriched that monastery greatly by acquiring very many estates. On leaving England he gave to the same monastery books valued at 830 pounds, and copes and vestments valued at 437 pounds. When he died, he also bequeathed all his goods, names and debts, and his gold and silver vessels. The total of the debts, three thousand nine hundred and fifty-four pounds, t.3.5. and four pence, was set down in the inventory. The vessels were valued at two thousand seven hundred pounds.

units.la: Praeterea Cardinalis Carthusianorum coenobium Auinioni condidit,& ad Conuentum Westmon. mille marcas misit ad annuum redditum quadraginta marcarum comparandum, ad augendas portiones quatuor Monachorum, qui perpetuas missas pro se & parentibus celebrarent. Pecuniae summa quae ex huius beneficentia ad Westmonasteriense coenobium peruenit, existimatur fuisse octoginta librarum millium. Vnde Monachus Westmon. carmina conscripsit. Res est de Langham tua Simon sunt data quondam Octingenta librarum millia dena.
units.tr: Moreover, the Cardinal founded a Carthusian monastery at Avignon, and he sent a thousand marks to the convent of Westminster to buy an annual rent of forty marks, to increase the shares of four monks who were to celebrate perpetual masses for him and his relatives. The sum of money that came to the monastery of Westminster through his generosity is reckoned at eighty thousand pounds. Hence a monk of Westminster composed verses: "The matter is, Langham, Simon, that once eighty thousand pounds were given to you."

units.la: Hunc itaq; multis encomiis monachi Westmonasteriensis celebrarunt, dignumq; esse dixerunt vt qui cum primo illius ecclesiae fundatore compararetur. Cuius tumulo hoc Epitaphium inscripserunt. Simon de Langham sub petrus his tumulatus Istius Ecclesiae monachus fuerat, Prior, Abbas, Sede vacante fuit electus Londiniensis Praesul, & insigni Ely, sed postea primas Totius Regni, magnus Regisq; minister. Nam Thesaurarius, & Cancellarius eius Ac Cardinalis in Roma praesbiter iste, Patria praenestinus est factus Episcopus, atq; Nuncius ex parte Papa, transfmittitur istue Orbe dolent pater quem nunc reuocare nequimus, Magdalena festo millenno septuageno Et tercentena sexto Christi ruit Anno, Hunc Deus absoluat, de cunctis quae male gessit, Et meritis matris sibi celsa gaudia donet.
units.tr: The monks of Westminster therefore celebrated him with many eulogies, and said that he was worthy to be compared with the first founder of that church. On his tomb they inscribed this epitaph: "Simon de Langham, buried under this stone, was a monk of this church, its prior and abbot. While the see was vacant he was elected bishop of London, and then of Ely, and afterwards primate of the whole kingdom, a great minister of the King. For he was treasurer and chancellor, and as cardinal priest in Rome, a native of Praeneste, he was made bishop, and he was sent here as the Pope's nuncio. The world grieves for the father whom we now cannot recall. He died in the year of Christ 1367, on the feast of Magdalene. May God absolve him of all the wrong he did, and by the merits of the Mother grant him high joys."

units.la: In hoc autem Cardinali catalogum Anglorum Cardinalium ex ipsa Romana curia desumptum descripsimus.

units.la: ICOLAVS cognomento Boso natione Anglus ex oppido S. Albani Bathoniensis dioecesis MonachusOrdinis S.Benedicti in Monasterio de Malmesbira in Anglia, &c. Fuit Abbas in Monasterio S. Rufi prope Valentinam in Galliis in eadem congregatione: quum ob Abbatiæ suæ negocia ad sedem Apostolicam sub Eugenio 3. Papa venisset, in eiusdem Pontificis notitiam venit, qui cognitâ eius virtute, doctrina, morum gravitate & sanctitate eum Episcopum Cardinalium Albanum creauit, licet invitum & renitentem, Legatumque sedis Apostolicæ creauit, mittens eum ad partes Norvegiæ & Sueciæ vt Christum gentibus illis barbaris prædicaret. Ipse autem in Legationem proficiscens sua prædicatione intra aliquot annorum spacium ita profecit, vt omnes gentes quarum gratia profectus fuerat, ad Christi fidem traduceret. Re bene gesta Romam reuersus Anastasium. 4. qui Eugenio 3. successerat mortuum inuenit Anno sui Pontificatus primo vix exacto, magni nominis vir iam factus. Q. Iamobremomnium Cardinalium Suffragiis. 3. Nonas Decembris aliquibus diebus ab obitu Papæ Anastasii. 4. iam elapsis in eius locum Pontifex Maximus renunciatus Hadrianus 4. appellari voluit, Anno Christi. 1154. Sedit annos. 4. & menf 9. Fridericum Imperatorem cognomento Barbarossam coronauit. Obiit Anagniæ An. Christi. 1159 K. Sept. Cadauer Romam allatum in Basilica S. Petri in pilo marmoreo juxta capellum Gregorii Papæ. 3. sepultum est.
units.tr: Nicholas, surnamed Boso, an Englishman by birth from the town of St Albans in the diocese of Bath, a monk of the Order of St Benedict in the monastery of Malmesbury in England, etc. He was abbot of the monastery of St Rufus near Valence in France, in the same congregation. When he came to the Apostolic See under Pope Eugenius III on business concerning his abbey, he came to the Pope's notice. Recognising his virtue, learning, seriousness of character and holiness, the Pope made him bishop and cardinal of Albano, though he was unwilling and resisted, and appointed him legate of the Apostolic See, sending him to the parts of Norway and Sweden to preach Christ to those barbarous peoples. He went on this legation and, by his preaching, within the space of some years he so prospered that he brought to the faith of Christ all the peoples for whose sake he had set out. Having done his work well, he returned to Rome and found Pope Anastasius IV, who had succeeded Eugenius III, dead, in the first year of his pontificate scarcely completed; by then he himself had become a man of great name. Therefore, by the votes of all the cardinals, a few days after the death of Pope Anastasius IV, on 3 December, he was proclaimed Supreme Pontiff in his place and wished to be called Hadrian IV, in the year of Christ 1154. He sat for four years and nine months. He crowned the Emperor Frederick, surnamed Barbarossa. He died at Anagni on 1 September in the year of Christ 1159. His body was brought to Rome and buried in the Basilica of St Peter, in a marble tomb beside the chapel of Pope Gregory III.

units.tr: John Morton, an Englishman, archbishop of Canterbury, priest cardinal of the title of St Anastasius, was created by Pope Alexander VI in 1493.

units.tr: Christopher Bainbridge, an Englishman, archbishop of York, priest cardinal of the title of St Praxedes, was created by Pope Julius II in 1511.

units.la: Thomas Wolsey ex oppido Suffolciensi Ipswichensis dioecesis Norwicensis, Archiepiscopus Eboracensis, presbyter Cardinalis, tit. S. Cæciliæ a Leonc. 10. creatus. Au. 1515.
units.tr: Thomas Wolsey, from the town of Ipswich in Suffolk, of the diocese of Norwich, archbishop of York, priest cardinal of the title of St Cecilia, was created by Pope Leo X in the year 1515.

units.tr: John Fisher, bishop of Rochester, priest cardinal of the title of St Vitalis. Reginald Pole, an Englishman, deacon cardinal of St Mary in Cosmedin.

units.la: Sunt & alii decem Cardinales Aogli vel plures, aote Innocentii quarti tempora, quorum cognomina & titulos ignoramus.
units.tr: There are also ten or more other English cardinals from before the time of Innocent IV, whose names and titles we do not know.

units.la: In hoc Catalogo hic Simon Langham non recensetur, sicut nec Stephanus Langton, nec Iohannes Kemp qui Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi fuerunt, quos verisimile ex illo omisso denario numero fuisse.
units.tr: In this catalogue Simon Langham is not listed, nor are Stephen Langton and John Kemp, who were archbishops of Canterbury; it is likely that they were left out of this count of the denarius.

units.la: Sed hæc nostrorum Cardinalium commemoratio non adeo admirabilis est atque illa Romanorum Pontificum computatio, quam Iohannes. 12. Papa de suis præcessoribus egregie collegit. Recensetur enim ex ordine S. Benedicti, cuius ipse fuerat. Papas 24. fuisse Cardinales 183. Archiepiscopos 1464. Episcopos 1502. Abbates iooumerabiles.
units.tr: But this record of our cardinals is not as remarkable as that count of the Roman Pontiffs which Pope John XII drew up excellently of his predecessors. For it lists, in the order of St Benedict, to which he himself belonged, 24 popes, 183 cardinals, 1,464 archbishops, 1,502 bishops, and countless abbots.

units.la: Hic Cardinalis Simon Langham, dum sedit in collatione sua post prandium, subito Paralisi percussus loquelam suam amisit, qui per tres vel quatuor dies superuiuens in festo S. Magdalenæ spiritã suo Deo reddidit. Cuius corpus apud Donezere iuxta Aiuionem inter fratres Cartusienses io Ecclesia noua, quam ipse à fundamentis fecerit construi, est sepultum, & post processum temporis ossa eius inde apud Westmonasterium vbi primitus fuerat Abbas in Anglia ordinauit deferri, cui Monasterio multa bona legauit. Hic duobus aonis paulo amplius sedit, cõstitutionem vnam aut alteram edidit, quarum vna in titulo de consuetudine inserta est.
units.tr: Cardinal Simon Langham, while sitting at his table after dinner, was suddenly struck by paralysis and lost his speech. Surviving for three or four days, he gave up his spirit to God on the feast of St Mary Magdalene. His body was buried at Donzère near Avignon, among the Carthusian friars, in the new church which he had built from the foundations. After the passage of time he ordered his bones to be carried from there to Westminster, where he had first been abbot in England, and he left many goods to that monastery. He sat for two years and a little more, and issued one or two constitutions, one of which is inserted under the title on custom.

units.la: LVII. Wilhelmus Wittlesey.
units.tr: LVII. William Wittlesey.

units.la: Ihelmus Witlesey consanguineus fuit Simonis Islippe Cantuariensis quondam Archiepiscopi, ab eoque oon modò educatus & liberaliter instructus, sed ad multos honoris gradus euectus. Adolescens ex auunculi ceosilio iuri operam dedit, ac vtriusque iuris doctor, eiusdem negocia in Romana curia procuravit. Quæ cum sedulitate atque fide ad exitum perduxisset in Anglia reuersus, fuit vicarius Archiepiscopi generalis neralis atque officialis, tum Decanus de Arcubus, quibus muneribus Archidiaconatū Hungtingdoniæ, & rectorias de Croidon atque Cliff adiunxit. Ab his Ecclesiis atque muneribus ad Roffensem Episcopatum, inde ad Wigorniensem, tum ad Londinensem, poltremò Simone Langham creato Cardinali, & ad Romanum pontificem abducto ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum ab Vrbano Papa quinto Idus Octobris translatus est. Archiepiscopatus autem temporalia ei Westmonasterii in festo Sancti Hilarii restituta sunt. Fuerunt tunc temporis Romæ Angli quidam Iuris ciuilis & pontificii periti. E quibus quatuor, videlicet Thomas Paxton, Robertus Strarton, Iohannes Shepdam & Simon Sudbury maximæ authoritatis in curia Romana & causarum in Rota au-
units.tr: William Wittlesey was a kinsman of Simon Islip, sometime Archbishop of Canterbury. He was not only brought up and generously educated by Islip, but was also raised to many high offices. As a young man, on his uncle's advice, he devoted himself to the law, and, becoming a doctor of both laws, he handled his uncle's business at the Roman court. When he had carried this through to a conclusion with diligence and loyalty, he returned to England. There he became vicar-general and official of the Archbishop, and then Dean of the Arches. To these offices he added the archdeaconry of Huntingdon and the rectories of Croydon and Cliff. From these churches and offices he was promoted to the bishopric of Rochester, then to Worcester, then to London. Finally, when Simon Langham was made a cardinal and taken to the Roman pontiff, he was translated to the archbishopric of Canterbury by Pope Urban V on 11 October. The temporalities of the archbishopric were restored to him at Westminster on the feast of St Hilary. At that time there were some Englishmen at Rome skilled in civil and papal law. Of these, four, namely Thomas Paxton, Robert Stratton, John Shepham and Simon Sudbury, were men of the greatest authority in the Roman court and auditors of causes in the Rota. To them the Archbishop gave authority as his proctors to ask the Pope for the pallium and send it to him. It was delivered to him by William Wykeham, Bishop of Winchester, at Lambeth on 1 April. On 16 June following he was enthroned at Canterbury, without the usual show and pomp.

units.la: ditores fuerunt, quibus Archiepiscopus authoritatem procuratoriam dedit à Papa petendi & ad se transmittendi pallium. Id quod ei à Willihelmo Wickam Wintoniensi Episcopo Cal. April. Lamethi traditum est. Et xvi. die mensis Iunii ptoximo Cantuariæ fine solita specie atque pompa intronizatus est. Anno sequenti, 21. videlicet Ianuarii celebrauit Cleri Synodum in Ecclesia Paulina Londini, in qua ipse latinè, doctèque ac diserè concionatus est. In qua Synodo Robertus Thorp, Iohannes Knenet, & Thomas Ludloe Regis iusticiarii Regis nomine triennales decimas à Clero concedi ad bellicos sumptus petierunt. Et multo sermone habito clerus biennales decimas ægrè tandem cōcesssit, ac postea enim ea concessione Rex contentus non esset, Dux Lancastriæ, Regis filius, Comes Arundellia, Comes Waruicensis, & dominus Guido Brianus Synodū ingressi instarunt Regi bellum tam diuturnum pro incolumitate atq; gloria patriæ tam præclaro fœliciterque gerenti triennales decimas à Clero qui ab omni opera & labore belli immunes fuerint, non esse denegandas. Quorum instantia atque præsentia, decimæ statim nullo contradicente concessæ sunt. Eodem anno Vrbanus quintus papa Willihelmo Archiepiscopo acriter præcepit vt vniones beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum & eorum impropriationes factas Monasteriis dissoluteret, eaque deinceps fieri haud permitteret, sed hoc Papæ præceptum eo mortuo obliuioni commissum, nunquam postea renouatum est. Carthusianorum item cænobium Londini sumptibus Michaelis Northburgh Londinensis episcopi, & Walteri Menny militis cum illa mortifera pestis (de qua in Iohanne Vfford antea diximus) in Anglia grassabatur inchoatum, Londinensi Episcopo mortuo ab eodem Waltero etiam hoc anno perfectum est. Edwardus Rex multis commissis præliis & hostibus sæpe suitis bellum paulatim intermittere, & ad pecunias exhaustas reficiendas in Angliam redire coactus est. Itaque Parlamentum Londini celebratum est. In quo de bellico sumptu, & Regiis opibus, Regnique facultatibus consumptis actum est. Tantæque ac tam atrocis criminationis inuidia in clerum quia omnia regia munera, ciuiliaque officia proceribus bellum cum Rege in militia gerentibus ab his administrata fuerint, conuerla fuit. Quo in clerum concitato motu, Proceres vt Clerum in Regis odium adducerent, & ab huiusmodi muneribus amouerent, Regi suadent multò sibi atque vniuersoRegno commodius magisque è re fore si clericis abdicatis in eorum loca laicos substituerent. Rex ex hac nouitate commodum speraus
units.tr: In the following year, on 21 January, he held a synod of the clergy in St Paul's Church in London, where he himself preached in Latin, learnedly and eloquently. In this synod Robert Thorpe, John Knyvet and Thomas Ludlow, the king's justices, sought on the king's behalf triennial tithes from the clergy for the expenses of war. After a long speech the clergy granted biennial tithes, though with difficulty. But the king was not content with this grant, so the Duke of Lancaster, the king's son, the Earl of Arundel, the Earl of Warwick and Sir Guy Brian entered the synod and urged that triennial tithes should not be refused by the clergy, who were free from all the work and labour of war, for the safety and glory of a country waging so glorious and successful a war. Through their insistence and presence the tithes were at once granted, with no one objecting. In the same year Pope Urban V sharply instructed Archbishop William to dissolve the unions of ecclesiastical benefices and their appropriations made to monasteries, and not to allow such to be made in future. But this papal command, on the Archbishop's death, was consigned to oblivion and was never renewed. Likewise the Carthusian monastery in London, begun at the expense of Michael Northburgh, Bishop of London, and Sir Walter Manny, while that deadly plague (of which we spoke earlier under John Offord) raged in England, was completed this year by the same Walter, the Bishop of London being dead. King Edward, having fought many battles and often faced enemies, was forced to gradually suspend the war and return to England to restore his exhausted finances. Therefore a Parliament was held at London, in which the expense of the war, the king's resources and the wealth of the realm, now used up, were discussed. And the odium of so great and atrocious an accusation was turned upon the clergy, because all royal offices and civil functions had been administered by them, while the nobles who were waging war with the king in the army had been kept from them. With the clergy thus stirred up, the nobles, in order to make the clergy hated by the king and to remove them from such offices, persuaded the king that it would be much more advantageous to him and to the whole kingdom if he dismissed the clergy and put laymen in their places. The king, hoping for advantage from this novelty,

units.la: exactis à clericis administrationum suarum rationibus hisque amotis, tam Cancellariæ, quàm Ærario suo aliisque officiis Regiis præposuit laicos. Quorum administratio tanto detrimento atque incommodo Regiæ Reip. fuit, vt ne quinque annis retinere officia sibi commissa potuerunt, quin Clericis restitutis cederent, vt in Simonis Sudburyi Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi vita in proximo loco dicetur. In hoc Parlamento cleri Synodus ab Archiepiscopo in Ecclesia Paulina Londini celebrata est 24. die Aprilis, ad quam à rege missi venerunt Robertus Thorp Cancellarius, & Thomas Scroope Thesaurarius Regis vtrique clericis nuper amotis succedentes. Hi subsidium quinquaginta millium librarum à Clero Regi exhiberi in tantis bellorum sumptibus & difficultatibus petierunt. Clerus hoc infinito sumptu bellico exhauriri iam Ecclesiam docent, nec sibi suisse tribuendi amplius facultatem. Eo itaque die Regis ministri discedunt vacui. Interieftis paucis diebus oratione magis instructa atque meditata redeunt, sed nihilo magis profecerunt. Archiepiscopus Regis & proceribus obsequutus synodum ad capellam in ædibus Ducis Lancastriæ sitam ab Ecclesia Paulina prorogauit. Eò adesse singulos iussit. Et quamuis statuto tempore abesseent plures, tamen Ducis Lancastriæ, Procerumque solicitatione, maxime vero Edwardi Regis filii oratione qui plurimas se promisit immunitates atque libertates à patre suo Clericali ordini concedi procuraturum, omnes qui aderant solutioni. 5ooo. li. concesserunt. Willihelmus autem Archiepiscopus iam senio confectus corpore fuit tam debili ac infirmo, vt nulla re gesta duos pene annos domi ær ageret acquieuit. Sexto autem translationis suæ anno Rege id procurante synodum in Ecclesia Paulina conuocauit. Ipse suggestum ascendens de hoc Thema- te. Veritas liberauit nos, latine praedicauit. Cumque perorauisset, inualetudinis infirmitate synodo discedere, & vices suas Londinensi Episcopo committere coactus est. In hac synodo iterum à Cleto Regis nomine petitum subsidium fuit. Clerus sic iam paucis annis Regius sumptibus exhaustum penitus & enectuatum conquetitur, eoque magis quod non minus à Rege quàm à Papa singulis pene annis interpellentur. Cuius intolerabile iugum si à suis ceruicibus depelli posset, subuenire se posse commodius Regius necessitatibus. Eaque tandem lege annalis decima concessa Regi fuit. Sed Willihelmus Courtney Herefordensis tunc Episcopus qui pustea vt dicemus, ad hunc Archiepiscopatum euectus est, nobilitate & genere suo fretus. Erat enim Comitis Deuoniae filius, medio synodo se animose exrulit, altaq; voce edixit. Nec seque suae Dioecesis Clerum quicquam datutos antequam Rex his calamitatibus quas Clerus tam diu passus est, tememdum adhibuerit. Hac transfacta synodomissi sunt ad Papam à Rege nuncii vt cum eo agerent, ne deinceps beneficiorum vacantium reseruationes & prouisiones facerent, & vt electi ad cathedrales vel conuentuales Ecclesias suis electionibus pleno iure gauderent, & à Metropolitanis ex veteri more & institutio firmarentur, aliaque exponerent papae in quibus Rex populusque atque clerus Angliae se nimis diu iam grauati ienferat. Quibus papa ref-ponsa in scriptis conclusa dedit, ad quae Rex ex praesulum procerumque iuorum sententia referibere vellet, papam de Regiis postulatis determinaturum. Hoc accepto responso in Parlamento decretum est, vt Cathedrales Ecclesiae suis liberè electionibus fruetentur, eaque Rex nec sua potentia, ucc intercessione ad Papam impediret, sed ope & autoritate iuuaret. Quod tamen saluberrimè conditum statutum denceps parum profuit, nec din seruatum est. Et si mox in consuetudinem vsumque receptum in exemplo Thomae Arundel à monachis Elienfibus electi Episcopi fuit. Quam electionem sexto die Aprilis Willihelmus Archiepiscopus in capella sua Ottefordiae confirmauit, ipsumque electum eodem die ibidem consecrauit. Quo Anno t. Idus Octob. in summa senectute & aegritudine Archiepiscopus Lamethi ex hac vita decessit, postquam annis sex, mensibus octo, & quaruordecim diebus sedisset. Sepultus iacet in nasi Ecclesiae Christi Cantuariensis, inter duas columnas è regione tumuli Simonis Islippe. Huius Archiepiscopi intercessione atque gratia Oxonienfis Academia à iurisdictione Lincolnensis Episcopi per Vrbanum quintum Papam exempta est, & tam libera potestas Cancellarium suum eligendi facta scholatibus, vt Cancellarius sine admissione quacunque simul atque electus sit, magistratum inire atque gerere posset.
units.tr: having demanded accounts of their administration from the clergy and removed them, set laymen over the Chancery, his Exchequer and his other offices. Their administration proved so great a detriment and inconvenience to the royal commonwealth that they could not keep the offices entrusted to them for even five years, but gave way, the clergy being restored, as will be told in the life of Simon Sudbury, Archbishop of Canterbury, in the next place. In this Parliament a synod of the clergy was held by the Archbishop in St Paul's Church in London on 24 April. To it the king sent Robert Thorpe, the chancellor, and Thomas Scrope, the treasurer, who had succeeded the two clerics recently removed. They sought a subsidy of 50,000 pounds from the clergy, to meet such great war expenses and difficulties. The clergy taught that the Church was now drained by such endless war costs, and that they no longer had the power to grant more. So on that day the king's ministers departed empty-handed. After a few days they returned with a speech more carefully prepared and rehearsed, but they made no more progress. The Archbishop, complying with the king and the nobles, prorogued the synod from St Paul's to the chapel in the house of the Duke of Lancaster, and ordered every member to attend there. Although many were absent at the appointed time, nevertheless, through the solicitation of the Duke of Lancaster and the nobles, and above all through the speech of Edward, the king's son, who promised that he would procure from his father many immunities and liberties for the clerical order, all who were present agreed to a payment of 5,000 pounds. But Archbishop William, now worn out with age and so feeble and infirm in body that he had accomplished nothing, rested content to spend almost two years at home, scarcely able to act. In the sixth year of his translation, with the king arranging it, he called a synod in St Paul's. Mounting the pulpit, he preached in Latin on the theme The truth has made us free. When he had finished his address, being compelled by his infirmity to leave the synod, he committed his duties to the Bishop of London. In this synod a subsidy was again sought from the clergy on the king's behalf. The clergy complained that they had already been wholly exhausted and worn down by the king's expenses in these few years, and all the more because they were pressed almost every year by the king no less than by the Pope. If that intolerable yoke could be removed from their necks, they could more conveniently help the king's needs. On that condition an annual tithe was at last granted to the king. But William Courtney, then Bishop of Hereford, who was afterwards, as we shall say, raised to this archbishopric, relying on his nobility and birth (for he was the son of the Earl of Devon), spoke out boldly in the middle of the synod and declared in a loud voice that neither he nor the clergy of his diocese would give anything until the king had applied a remedy to those calamities which the clergy had suffered for so long. After this business was done, envoys were sent by the king to the Pope to deal with him: that henceforth he should not make reservations and provisions of vacant benefices; that those elected to cathedral or conventual churches should enjoy their elections with full right, and be confirmed by the metropolitans according to ancient custom and institution; and to set out other matters in which the king, the people and the clergy of England had long been burdened. To these the Pope gave a written reply, on which the king was to write back, with the opinion of the bishops and nobles, and the Pope would then decide the royal demands. On receiving this answer, it was decreed in Parliament that cathedral churches should enjoy their free elections, and that the king should not hinder them by his power or intercession with the Pope, but should help them with his aid and authority. Yet this most wholesomely framed statute did little good afterwards and was not long observed. Soon after, the custom that had been received in use was followed: in the case of Thomas Arundel, a bishop was elected by the monks of Ely. William the Archbishop confirmed this election on 6 April in his chapel at Otford, and on the same day consecrated the man elected. In this year, on the Ides of October, the Archbishop of Lambeth died in extreme old age and sickness, after having sat six years, eight months and fourteen days. He lies buried in the nave of Christ Church, Canterbury, between two columns opposite the tomb of Simon Islip. Through this Archbishop's intercession and favour, Oxford University was exempted by Pope Urban V from the jurisdiction of the Bishop of Lincoln, and such free power of electing their Chancellor was granted to the scholars that the Chancellor, as soon as he was elected, could take up and exercise the office without any admission whatsoever.

units.la: LVIII. SIMON SUDBVRY.
units.tr: LVIII. SIMON SUDBURY.

units.la: Oftquam in superiori (vt diximus) Parlamento electionis libertas à Papis atque Regibus tot scculis impedita, renouata iam ac restituta visa fit, Monachi Cantuatienses quos libertas effrenatos & indomitos; seruitus autem moderatos (atisque tolerabiles sempet efficit, Willhelmo Witlesey Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo mortuo, votis & suffragus tuis Anglum quendam Romae Cardinalem qui patriam deseruisse ad Archiepiscopatum poscebant. Quod Monachorum ram aduersum Regno atq; peruersum studium, Regem tam iusto dolore assecit, vt de eis proscribendis, & tam Monasterio quàm Regno expellendis consilium habetet. Sed Gregorius vnde cimus tum Papa vt Regem Monachis conciliaret, eam poftulationem repudiauit, Regeque consentiente Archiepiscopatum Cantuarien fem Si- moni Sudbury Londinenii tunc Episcopo prouisionis titulo donauit. Hoc itaque tam recenti nouoque exemplo praefractorum Monachorum proteruia illius de liberis electionibus salubettimae legis vires fregit, & papalem authoritatem conseruauit.
units.tr: After the freedom of election, which had been hindered for so many centuries by Popes and Kings, seemed in the last Parliament (as we have said) to be renewed and restored, the monks of Canterbury, whom liberty makes unruly and untamed, while servitude makes moderate and always bearable, demanded by their votes and suffrages, after the death of William Whittlesey, Archbishop of Canterbury, that a certain Englishman who was a Cardinal at Rome, and who had deserted his country, be made Archbishop. This perverse and hostile zeal of the monks so provoked the King with just indignation that he resolved to proscribe them and expel them from the monastery and the realm. But Pope Gregory XI, wishing to win the King over to the monks, rejected that demand, and with the King's consent granted the Archbishopric of Canterbury, under the title of provision, to Simon Sudbury, then Bishop of London. Thus by this recent and novel example of the stubborn monks' insolence, the force of that most salutary law concerning free elections was broken, and papal authority was preserved.

units.la: Simon Sudbury alias TyboId dictus est, illudque nomen à patre, huc à patria seu ciuitate accepit. Nigello Tybold patte, stirpe genetosa Sudburiae Suffolciae oppido in patochia S. Gregorii natus est. Ab ineunte aetate in literis educatus cum adoleuisset ad Gallicas & Italicas Academias, ad Ciuilis & Pontificii iuris cognitionem habendam à patre missus Doctoris gradum suscepit. Romaeque Inuocentii sexti domesticus Capellanus, & causarum in Romana rota auditor fuit. Cui idem Innocentius Cancellariatum cellariatum Ecclesiæ cathedralis Saris burienfis provisionis titulo contulit. Mortuoque Michaele Northburgh Londinensi Episcopo eadem provisione ad Londinensem Episcopatum euexit. In quo cum multis annis quietus Regique Edwardo tertio obsequens sedisset, provisione Papæ Gregorii contra Monachorum postulationem translatus est. Cui in Londinensi Episcopatu Wilhelmus Courtney Herefordiensis tunc Episcopus, eoque mortuo (vt deinceps dicendum est) in Archiepiscopatu Cantuariensi successit. Translationis siue provisionis suæ bullas papales Londini accepit sexto die mensis Iunii. An.1375 Quibus publicatis ad Archiepiscopatum sese transtulit. Primo translationis suæ anno Angli atq; Galli longo Marte defessi ad pacis fœdera ineunda proclives esse coeperunt.
units.tr: Simon Sudbury was also called Tybold, and he received that name from his father and the surname from his homeland or city. He was born of Nigel Tybold, his father, a man of good family, in the town of Sudbury in Suffolk, in the parish of St Gregory. Educated in letters from his early youth, when he had grown up he was sent by his father to the academies of France and Italy to acquire knowledge of civil and papal law, and he took the degree of Doctor. At Rome he was domestic chaplain to Innocent VI and an auditor of causes in the Roman Rota. The same Innocent gave him the chancellorship of the cathedral church of Salisbury under the title of provision. Then, when Michael Northburgh, Bishop of London, died, by the same provision he was raised to the bishopric of London. In that see he sat for many years in quiet and obedient to King Edward III, until by the provision of Pope Gregory, against the monks' demand, he was transferred. William Courtenay, then Bishop of Hereford, succeeded him in the see of London, and after Courtenay's death (as shall be related hereafter) Sudbury succeeded him in the archbishopric of Canterbury. He received the papal bulls of his translation and provision at London on the sixth day of June, in the year 1375. When these were published he moved to the archbishopric. In the first year of his translation the English and the French, worn out by a long war, began to be inclined to make terms of peace.

units.la: De quare vtrinque Legati Bruxellas missi sunt. Ex Anglia Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus, & Dux Lancastriæ Legati Gallos Bruxellis conuenere. Ibi aliquot mensium facta mora transactum nihil est, ataque Mense Martio reuerti sunt. Et Archiepiscopus Domunica palmarum post reditum Cantuariæ cum solita magnificentia Comite Stafordæ Senescballo in epulis adhuc ministrante intronizatus est. Postea cum nec pacis effectus, nec ad bellum propagandum paratæ facultates, Parlamentum vtris angelus subuenirentur conuocatum est. Sit eo etiam habita Londini in Ecclesia Paulina synodus, in qua Archiepiscopus in concione hunc locum scripturæ latinæ tractauit. An.1376 Datum est vobis noscere mysterra. Concione finita, Regis nuncii synodum ingressi sunt, qui diuturnum belli, multas præclarę partas victorias, Regisque inopiam ac egestatem longa oratione commemorantes, opem pecuniariam a Clero flagitant. Reque expolita sine responso dimiserunt. Deinde Wilhelmus Courtenay Londinensis Episcopus, qui seantea (vt in Wilhelmo Witlefey dixnius) his solutionibus oppositi, iniurias multas sibi ac Wilhelmo Wickam Wintoniensi Episcopo factas in scripta tedactas exhibuit synodo. Petitque ne quid Regi concedatur, antequam ptoilis iniuris satisfiat. Synodus assensa constituit Archiepiscopum vt Regem conuiterct. Is prorogata synodo Regem adiit, Cleri offensas exponit, vt Episcopus Wintoniensis restituatur interceditur. Rex paulo antea leihalem morbum... Concione finita, Regis nuncii synodum ingressi sunt, quibus cum reliqua & spem inducit se omnes commemoratas iniurias ablaturum. Hac spe Archiepiscopus Clericorum animos erigens, modicū interim subsidiū obtinuit, vt singuli Clerici beneficiis aut dignitatibus prædiți. Curati autē 4.d. Regi soluit. Huic synodo Wickamus Wintoniensis Episcopus a Rege proscriptus, nondū tamen restitutus interfuit. Cui ingredienti a singulis honorifice assurrectum, locusque sedenti honori suo congruus delatus est. Lancastriæ Dux mortuo iam Edwardo Regis filio inuictissimo Principe, tū Rege ægroto Regnum pene solus administrabat. Qui in maximam affectati Regni suspicionem venit, quòd cum militibus atque Burgenibus Parlamentum egeret, vt lege Salicæ legi in Galliis similem conderent: Ne fœminis in Angliæ Regnum jus succesionis daretur. Quamimpia suasione populum quem lenire sibiqué verbis summa blanditie deiunxit, ut eum ab Edwardo ad Archiepiscopum... nobilissimum virum Edmundum Mortimer Marciæ Comitem, cuius filia proxima post Richardus Regis nepotem Re-
units.tr: For this purpose envoys were sent from each side to Bruges. From England the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Duke of Lancaster came as envoys to meet the French at Bruges. There, after a delay of some months, nothing was accomplished, and in March they returned. On the Sunday of Palms, after his return, the Archbishop was enthroned at Canterbury with his usual magnificence, the Earl of Stafford, the Steward, still serving at the feast. Afterwards, since neither peace was achieved nor means were at hand to carry on the war, a Parliament was summoned to see how the king might be helped. During it a synod was also held in London in St Paul's Church, in which the Archbishop, preaching, treated this text of Scripture in Latin: "It is given unto you to know the mysteries..." (Luke 8). When the sermon was finished, the King's messengers entered the synod, and, recounting in a long speech the length of the war, the many victories nobly won, and the King's poverty and need, they asked the clergy for financial aid. Having set out their business, they dismissed the synod without a reply. Then William Courtenay, Bishop of London, who earlier (as we said under William Whittlesey) had opposed these payments, presented to the synod in writing the many injuries done to himself and to William Wykeham, Bishop of Winchester. He asked that nothing be granted to the King before satisfaction was made for these wrongs. The synod agreed and resolved that the Archbishop should approach the King. He therefore adjourned the synod, went to the King, set out the grievances of the clergy, and pleaded that the Bishop of Winchester be restored. The King, a little before, had been seized by a deadly illness... When the sermon was finished, the King's messengers entered the synod, and with them he held out hope that he would remove all the injuries recounted. Lifting the spirits of the clergy with this hope, the Archbishop obtained a modest subsidy in the meantime: each cleric holding a benefice or dignity paid the King... and the parish priests paid fourpence. The Bishop of Winchester, William Wykeham, who had been proscribed by the King but was not yet restored, attended this synod. As he entered, everyone rose to honour him, and a seat fitting his dignity was offered to him. The Duke of Lancaster, Edward the King's son, the most unconquered prince having now died, and the King being sick, administered the realm almost alone. He fell under the greatest suspicion of aiming at the kingdom, because he sought to have Parliament, with the knights and burgesses, enact a law like the Salic law in France, so that the right of succession to the English realm would not be given to women. By this impious persuasion, he so drew away from himself, by the greatest flattery, the people whom he had tried to soothe with words, that he turned them against the most noble man Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March, whose daughter was to be the next heir to the realm after Richard, the King's grandson...

units.la: 40 gni hæres extitura fuit, infestauit. Clero tot iniuius ob multas iniurias, hic enim author fuit, cura Regiis muneribus (vt in Wilhelmo Witelessey antea dixinus) essent amoti, sed cum his nouis rebus tam occulte studerent, Regi suspectus in minori indies fuit gratia. Itaque eo inuito Wintoniensis Episcopus & suæ pristinæ dignitati, & omnibus Episcopalibus iuribus quibus diu caruerat, restitutus est. Tum D. Latimer Regis Camerarius Duci Lancastriæ coniunctissimus aula exclusus & eiectus, omnesque laici qui procerib. procurantibus amotis clericis, negocijs curiisque Regis præcienbantur, tanquam mali administratores abdicati, & Clerici iterum recepti sunt. Adam Hunton Meneuensis Episcopus Cancellarius, & Henricus Wakefeld Wigorniensis Thesaurarius suerunt. Iohanne Kneuet, & Thoma Scroope laicis, qui ea munera prius gerebant, turpiter & cum infamia deiecti.
units.tr: 40 ...against many injuries done to the clergy, for he was the author of them; the clergy, as we said earlier under William Whittlesey, had been removed from the royal offices. But since they were secretly pursuing these new schemes, he became less and less favoured by the King, who grew suspicious of him. Accordingly, against the King's will, the Bishop of Winchester was restored both to his former dignity and to all the episcopal rights of which he had long been deprived. Then Sir Latimer, the King's Chamberlain, most closely bound to the Duke of Lancaster, was shut out and ejected from the court; and all the laymen who, at the urging of the nobles, had been put in charge of the clergy's business and the King's courts, were removed and dismissed as bad administrators, and the clergy were received back again. Adam Houghton, Bishop of St Asaph, became Chancellor, and Henry Wakefield, Bishop of Worcester, Treasurer. John Knyvet and Thomas Scrope, laymen who had previously held these offices, were shamefully and disgracefully cast down.

units.la: Et quia rempus ipsum nos duxit in memoriam & recordationem fagacissimi & opulentissimi Præsulis Wilhelmi Wickam Wintoniensis Episcopi, breuiter commemoremus ea quæ à probatæ fidei scriptoribus de eo referuntur, non vt præconcs (celebrandi enim, eumque laudandi partes his concedimus qui ex collegiorum ejusdem profecti sparsis maiori & abundanti otio. & facultate præditi sunt) sed vt ex historiæ fide atque veritate perspiciamus quàm minimis initiis sexorsa grandia modicis paulatim incrementis ad tantam magnitudinem creuerunt. Genere infimo adeoque perobscuro ortus est, vt quidam seruili fuisse conditione ferant. Aliisque insuper nominibus Perottum & Longum appellatum scribunt. Et tamen quocunque modo in clericalem cenium tandem. Vix enim mediocriter eruditum, etsi in plerisque rebus peragendis folertem & perspicacem fuisse constat. Tum clericali ordine susceptò Windesoriæ vixit aliquandiu ignobilis & inter pauperiores clericos, sed eo tempore Rex Edwardus tertius multa ædificia in arce Windesoriæ demolitus eadem lapius & elegantiori structura ædificare statuit. In hoc novo opere Wickamus se primò interfabros & operarios (cum ibi in pauperrate, ordine tamen clericali egisset) intercepsuit, & assiduus fuit, sæpeque cum otiosus tantum spectator esset, & operam ac manum adhibebat, & de ordine modoque ædificandi sententiam dixit suam. Habuisse enim in Architectura peritiam, siue eam in seruilibus operis, antequam esset clericus, ac hæreli instituitione, siue instinctu, bonitatequæ ingenii accepit. Inductus enim hoc ab arte aliqua methodove habere non poterat. 10 Hinc constat, quod fama hominis Regi nuncia ta tanto open perficiudo præfectus fuit, & vt chronographus scribit, Willihelmum Wickam Rex de paupere clerico assumens constituit superuisorem operum suorum, & ad eius dispositionem omnia eius ædificia rune temporis erant peracta. Iamque vir in hoc artificio intelligentissimus, idemque assiduus atque frugi, atenuissima fortuna quam diu toleraret ad Regis seruitium deductus, non minus obsequendi Regique in omnibus satisfaciendi rationes quam ædificandi sequitur est. Neque enim commodius quicquam magisque opportunum ei ad Regis beneuolentiam captandum eucnisse potuit, quam illud tam accuratum in ædiū luxuriæ atque magnificentia studium, in quo Rex victoriis partis & obsenium a militia cessans maxime cepit delectari. Cumque omnia ad hoc ædificium ipse tanta Wickamo permissa essent, undique ex toto Regno conquisiuit omnis generis architectos, fabros, cæmentarios, & huiusmodi tam extruendi quam destruendi operarios. Quorum ad tantum opus tanta opificum multitudo requisita est, vt a Rege edictum sit per totam Angliam vt omnes upifices ad suum opus suscipiendum conuenirent, nec quisquam vllum penes se retineat nisi hoc novo opere perfecto & absoluto. Hic Wickamus summus Architectus non minori sedulitate quam intelligentia quotidie imperitabat. Quo obsequio & assiduitate in tantam Regis gratiam se insinuauit, vt in omni pene consuetudine ac colloquio familiarissimus esset. In qua opportunitate cum & pluralitas beneficiorum Anglicanis Clericis (sicut in Simone Langham antea diximus) in vsu maxime fuerit, & ei a Rege facile fuit impetrare, aliquam exemplo, Regisque concessione atque gratia beneficia Ecclesiasticæ atque dignitates coaceruauit. 30 Nam præter Archidiaconatum Lineolniensem, & Wellensem præpositurum, & illam uberimam rectoriam de Manihebt in Deuonia, duodecim prebendas incathedralibus Ecclesiis obtinuit. Quæ omnia coniuncta beneficia in Papali regioque censu octingenta septuaginta sex libris, tredecim solidis, quatuor denariis tunc æstimata fuerunt. His loculpeturus beneficiis eum & ingenio & rerum multarum vsu ac experientia valeret, regemque assiduo obsequio, Procerelque atque aulicos conirate, humanitateque leniter, generisignobilitarem, literarumque insicitiam ita adumbrauit vt eius gratiam, existimationemque non minuerent. Is autem nobilissimum doctissimumque quemque tam opibus quam dignitate anteiter. Nam eo Windesoriæ perfecto iam & fabricato ædificio Rex ei priuati sigilli custodiam committit, & quæ cunque consilia communicauit. Idem suaefor Regi fuit in Insula de Shepey castellum, ne portus & emporium mercatorum fieret, extruendi, etsi locusipsè parum commodus ei rei putaretur. Quidam narrant Wickamum extructa Arce Windesorina in interiori quodam pariete hæc verba(quæ latine tam apposite & facete exprimi nequeunt) insculpsisse. This made Wickam, i. Hoc fecit Wickam. Quæ locutio in Anglicana lingua quæ casibus ram diseriminatur, tam ambigua est, vt incertum sit, vtrum is arcem, an arx cum effecisset. Hoc Regi à calumniatoribus quibusdam in eius invidiam ita delatum est, vt quali Wickamus omnem extructi ædificii laudem sibi arrogauerer vindicarit. Quod cum Rex iniquo animo tulisset eique probrose obiecisset: non sibi tam magnificæ, regiæque structuræ laudes, sed structuræ suas dignitates, commoditateque aferripisse dixit. Nec ego (inquit) hanc arcem, sed hæc Arx me effecit, & ab ima conditione, ad Regis gratiam, opes atque dignitates euexit. Cum hoc responso aduersariorum calumniam vitasset, opibus & potentia creuit in dies. Vacanteque (vt diximus) episcopatu Wintoniensi cum Rex ad summum honoris apicem hominem infimum perducere studuisset: instituit eum Regni Cancellarium, & cum Vrbano Papa egit, vt Wintoniensis Episcopus crearetur. Sed Papa siue quòd inops literarum, siue quòd locuples pecuniarum Wickamus fuerit, etsi Rege instante à Wintoniensibus Monachis electus sit, confirmationem anno amplius distulit, commissa tamen ei spiritualium et temporalium rerum illius Episcopatus interim custodia. Cum Wintonien[s]em episcopatum cupide ambiret, quidam ferunt Regem ipsum doctrinæ exilitatem, tenuitatemque ei exprobasse, Wickamumque respondisse, etsi indoctus fuerit, se tamen secundum factum parturire qui doctorum hominum maximam copiam procrearet. Id de amplissimis illis collegiis quæ Oxonii ac Wintoniæ extruxit postea subintellectum est. Verum ei in summo iam honoris gradu collocato orta mox invidia est. Nam à Duce Lancastriæ Iohanne Gaunt qui (ut ante diximus) Regem in totum clerum concitaverat, repetundarum atque fraudis in omnibus quos gesserat magistratibus accusatus est. Eiusque potentia, cum ad Regem iam infirmum accederet ut solebat non potuit, tractus in Regium forum nulla sibi respondendi
units.tr: Since the times themselves bring to mind the shrewd and very wealthy prelate William Wykeham, Bishop of Winchester, let us briefly recall what writers of proven good faith report about him. I do not do this to praise him. Praising him I leave to those who have come out of his colleges and have plenty of leisure and resources for it. I do it so that, from the trustworthy record of history, we may see how great things grew to such magnitude from very small beginnings and slow increases. He was born of the lowest and very obscure stock, so much so that some report he was of servile condition. They also write that he was called by other names, Perottus and Longus. Yet however he came to the clerical state, it is agreed that he was scarcely moderately learned, though he was clever and sharp in carrying out most business. After he took holy orders at Windsor, he lived for some time unknown and among the poorer clergy. But at that time King Edward III decided to pull down many buildings in the castle at Windsor and rebuild them with a finer structure. In this new work Wykeham, while still in poverty though in clerical rank, put himself among the masons and workmen, was constantly present, and often, though he was only an idle onlooker, he lent his effort and hand and gave his opinion on the order and method of building. It is said that he had skill in architecture, whether he gained it in the servile work before he was a cleric, or by a natural instruction and impulse and the quickness of his wit. For he could not have had this skill from any art or method learned by instruction. Hence it is clear that the report of the man reached the king, and he was put in charge of so great a work. And as the chronicler writes, the king took William Wykeham from being a poor cleric and appointed him overseer of his works, and by his direction all his buildings of that time were completed. Now this man, most skilled in this craft, and also diligent and thrifty, was raised to royal service while his fortune was still very slender, and he was no less careful in finding ways to serve and please the king in all things than in building. Nor could anything more convenient or more timely have happened to him for winning the king's goodwill than that so exact a zeal for buildings, luxury and magnificence, in which the king, having ceased from war after his victories, took the greatest delight. And since the whole of this building had been entrusted to Wykeham, he sought out from every part of the kingdom every kind of architect, craftsman, mason and such workers, for building as well as demolishing. So great a multitude of craftsmen was needed for so great a work that the king issued an edict throughout England that all craftsmen were to gather to take up his work, and no one was to keep any of them for himself until this new work was finished and completed. Here Wykeham, the chief architect, gave orders every day with no less diligence than skill. By this service and assiduity he so insinuated himself into the king's favour that he became almost the most intimate in every custom and conversation.
