In this opportunity, since the holding of many benefices at once was especially common among English clergy (as we said earlier in the case of Simon Langham), and it was easy for him to obtain it from the king, he heaped up ecclesiastical benefices and dignities by the example and by the king's grant and favour. For besides the archdeaconry of Lincoln and the provostship of Wells, and that very rich rectory of Manaton in Devon, he obtained twelve prebends in cathedral churches. All these benefices together were then valued, in the papal and royal assessment, at 876 pounds, 13 shillings and 4 pence. He was to be scorned for these benefices, but since he was able by his wit and his use and experience of many affairs, he gently softened, by constant service to the king, by courtesy to the nobles and courtiers, and by kindness, the lowness of his birth and his lack of learning, so that they did not diminish his favour and reputation. He surpassed in wealth and dignity every man of most noble and learned rank. For when the building at Windsor was now finished and built, the king committed to him the keeping of the privy seal, and he communicated to him all his counsels. He was likewise the adviser to the king in building a castle on the Isle of Sheppey, so that it should not become a harbour and market for merchants, although that place was thought rather unsuitable for such a purpose. Some relate that when the castle at Windsor was built, Wykeham carved on an inner wall these words, which cannot be expressed in Latin so aptly and wittily: "This made Wickam," that is, "Wickam made this." This phrase, in the English language which distinguishes by cases, is so ambiguous that it is uncertain whether he meant that he made the castle or that the castle made him. This was reported to the king by certain slanderers to his discredit, as if Wykeham were claiming for himself all the praise of the building that had been erected. When the king took this badly and reproached him harshly, he said that he had sought not the praises of so magnificent and royal a structure, but the dignities and advantages of his own position. "I," he said, "did not make this castle, but this castle made me, and raised me from the lowest condition to the king's favour, to wealth and dignities." With this answer he escaped the calumny of his adversaries, and he grew daily in wealth and power. When the bishopric of Winchester, as we said, became vacant, and the king wished to raise this lowly man to the highest peak of honour, he appointed him Chancellor of the Kingdom, and dealt with Pope Urban that Wykeham should be created Bishop of Winchester. But the Pope, whether because Wykeham was lacking in learning or because he was rich in money, delayed the confirmation for more than a year, although he had been elected by the monks of Winchester at the king's urging, while the spiritual and temporal management of that bishopric was meanwhile committed to him. While he eagerly sought the see of Winchester, some report that the king himself reproached him for his shallow learning and meagre talents, and that Wykeham replied that although he was unlearned, he nevertheless gave birth, in the manner of a mother, to a great company of learned men. That was later understood in relation to those very large colleges which he built at Oxford and Winchester. But soon, once he had been placed on the highest step of honour, envy arose against him. For he was accused by John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, who (as we said before) had stirred up the king against the whole clergy, of extortion and fraud in all the offices he had held. Since his power, when he approached the king, who was by then ill, as he used to do, could not avail him, he was dragged before the royal court, given no delay and no opportunity to answer or clear himself of the charges, and was condemned, not without some violence on the part of a harsh judge, William Skipwith, then the king's justiciar. Then, with the same Duke working for it, his temporal possessions of the bishopric were taken from him, and to win the popular applause for which he was eager, he obtained that they be granted to Prince Richard, the king's grandson, Earl of Bordeaux and Chester, who had also then received the principality of Wales that had belonged to his father Edward. Thus Wykeham, bishop of Winchester, was deprived for a long time of the temporal revenues of his bishopric, and was sustained only by its spiritual part.

units.la: ro aut crimina diluendi concessa dilatione aut venia à violento quodam iudice Willihelmo Scipwit Regis tum iusfitiario condemnatus est. Tum eodem Duce procurante ablata sunt ei Episcopatus sui temporalia, quæ ut vulgarem plausum, cuius perfudiosus fuit, captaret, Richardo principi Regis nepoti Comiti Burdegaliæ atque Ceftriæ, qui tum etiam Walliæ principatum qui Edwardi patris sui fuerat acceptir, concedi impetravit. Ita Wintoniensis episcopus Wickamus spiritualibus Episcopatus sui sustentatus temporalibus diu caruit.
units.tr: ...or to answer or clear himself of the charges, and was condemned, not without some violence on the part of a harsh judge, William Skipwith, then the king's justiciar. Then, with the same Duke working for it, his temporal possessions of the bishopric were taken from him, and to win the popular applause for which he was eager, he obtained that they be granted to Prince Richard, the king's grandson, Earl of Bordeaux and Chester, who had also then received the principality of Wales that had belonged to his father Edward. Thus Wykeham, bishop of Winchester, was deprived for a long time of the temporal revenues of his bishopric, and was sustained only by its spiritual part.

units.la: Præterea Dux eidem Regis nomine præcepit, ne aulæ Regis intra vicesimum lapidem appropinquaret. Huius autem tam atrocis odii Ducis ac vindictæ causa fuit, quod Wickamus natiuum Ducis statum in controversiam vocaslet. Nam cum Dux (ut ante dixi[mus]) Regnum clandestinis & occultis modis quæreret, Wickamus eum supposititium non Regium partum fuisse dixit. Reginam enim grauidam, quæ Gandaui peperit, non filium sed filiam edidisse. Tum veritatem ne id Rex ægre ferret, qui masculum desiderabat, supponi sibi iussisse Flandrensis cuiusdam fœminæ filium eodem pene momento natum, & ita fouisse ac Regi exhibuisse partum quem non peperit, videlicet Iohannem de Gaunt Lancastriæ ducem. Et hæc omnia Reginam moribundam sibi secretissima confessione retulisse, obnixeque rogasse ut si Iohannes ille Gandauensis vel Regnum affectaret, vel deleta Regia sobole hæreditario iure capesseret, Wilhelmus Wickam hoc palam diuulgaret, ne hæreditas Regai ad alienum & suppositicium deueniret. At Wickamus etsi in hac Episcopali tantum vmbra atque specie, & bonis & Regis gratia suaque authoritate quibus ante floruit careret, tamen Ducis potentiam maleuolentiamque callido & astuto consilio, cum aperta vi non potuit anteuerti: Regi iam ægroto ipsaque senectute confecto semper aderat atque ministrabat quædam fœmina Alicia Perres. Hæc Regi languido & infirmo obsecuta maiorem quam ipse Dux cum Rege initiigratiam. Temporisque commodiatem commodis suis adiungens, de multorum causis muneribus præmiisque conducta solicitauit Regem. Hanc præsente mercede, & vberiori promissa spe Wickamus adduxit, vt a Rege restitui sibi oblata Episcopatus iura, tam ea quam ante percepta & in sifco reseruata esse[nt], quàm omnia prædia procuraret. Quod illa inuito Duce continuò impetrauit. Quod etsi Dux grauissimè tulerauit, tamen huic fœminæ ex gratiæ, Regi æque concessioni non repugnauit. Tanta tamen in eum iracundia Rex antequam Alicia Perres intercessisset, in Wickamum fauit, vt cum generali indulgentia atque remissione singulis subditis pene singula commissa flagitia condonassent, solum hunc Wickamum immunitate exemerit. Et quanquam clerus populusque assiduus Regi preces pro Wickamo funderent, omnium tamen intercessioni solus Dux restitit, antequam ab Alicia Perres vincereter, cum qua contendere & coram Rege decertarent e tutum quidem sibi esse ducit. Restitutus iam & mirum in modum locupletarus Wickamus omne suum studium atque curam ad præclara & magnifica illa Oxonii ac Wintoniæ condenda collegia converrit. Quæ constructa & absoluta, tam præclaris legibus statutisque fundauit, terrisque ac possessionibus ita locupletauit, vt cæteris literarum collegia postea statuentibus tanquam exemplar atque speciem quam imitarentur, propositum videatur. Id quod à præcipuis collegiorum Cantebrigiæ Oxoniiique patronis postea obseruatum est, vt in his quæ fundauerunt collegiis Wickami itura & statuta paucissimis verbis immutatis verbatim describerent. Quæ res prudentiam eius singularem, hisque quæ in Rep. gessit muneribus dignam iudicauit, quòd ad bonarū literarum incrementum in quibus ne mediocriter eruditus existimabatur, tam accommodata & apposita statuta exeogitauit. Præter hæc maximis sumptibus extructa collegia Ecclesiæ Cathedralis Winton. nauem fabricauit. Consanguineos permultos opibus præditosque ditauit. Multis Ecclesiis multa contulit. Qua tam larga immensaque munificentia non obstante, condito testamento legata ad summam 6270. lib. præter vasa, gemmas, libros, vestimenta & suppellectilē moriens in pecuniis reliquit. Inter quæ legata, too.li. Aliciæ Perot cōsanguineæ suæ concedūtur. Quæ an eadē fuerit quam Aliciam Perres historiographi nuncupant, cuius (vt diximus) gratia Regi reconciliarus fuerit, incertum est. Honestis artibus rantas congestas opes quæ tam laudabiliter vtiliterque consumptæ sunt existimare conuenit. Virtsemper frugi fuit, atque ipsa parsimonia quæstum fecit maximum. Simulatque episcopatum ingredi ius est Wilihelmi Edindon antecessoris sui executores coram Wilhelmo Witeley Cantuariensi (vt diximus) Archiepiscopo in iure conuenit. Ab his 127. afros. 1556. boues, 3876. multones. 4717. oues matrices. 3521. agnos, &c. 1662. libras. x. s. pro reparatione ædificiorum ad ruinas vergentium recuperanit. Sedit annis. 37. mortuusque in Eccl. fia Cathedrali Wintoniensi ad aufralem parietem in naui Ecclesiæ honorifico egregioque tumulo conditus est.
units.tr: Moreover, the Duke, in the King's name, ordered Wykeham not to come within twenty miles of the royal court. The cause of this bitter hatred and revenge was that Wykeham had called into question the Duke's birth. For when the Duke (as I said above) was seeking the kingdom by secret and hidden means, Wykeham said that he was not the true son of the King. He alleged that the Queen, who was pregnant, had given birth at Ghent not to a son but to a daughter. Then, so that the King would not be upset by the truth, since he longed for a male heir, he had ordered that the son of some Flemish woman, born at almost the same moment, be substituted for him. Thus he had nursed and presented to the King as his own the child she had not borne, namely John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster. He added that the dying Queen had told him all of this in a most secret confession, and had earnestly begged him that if this John of Ghent either aimed at the kingdom or, with the royal offspring destroyed, claimed it by hereditary right, William Wykeham should make this known openly, so that the royal inheritance would not pass to an alien and substituted heir. But Wykeham, although he now had only the shadow and appearance of his bishopric and had lost the goods, the King's favour and the authority he had once enjoyed, nevertheless could not forestall the Duke's power and ill will by open force, so he turned to a crafty and subtle plan. The King, now sick and worn out with old age, was always attended and served by a certain woman, Alice Perrers. She, complying with the weak and infirm King, had greater favour with him than the Duke himself. Joining the opportunity of the moment to her own advantage, she was hired with gifts and rewards by many people, and she urged the King on their behalf. With this woman, by a present reward and a more generous promise of hope, Wykeham brought it about that the rights of his bishopric, both those he had formerly enjoyed and those that had been kept in the treasury, should be restored to him by the King, and he obtained all his estates as well. She secured this immediately, against the Duke's wishes. Although the Duke took this very badly, he nonetheless did not oppose the concession made by the King to this woman as a favour. Yet before Alice Perrers had interceded, the King was so angry with the Duke that, when they granted a general indulgence and remission to individual subjects, they pardoned almost every single crime committed, but excluded this Wykeham alone from the immunity. And although the clergy and the people constantly poured out prayers to the King on Wykeham's behalf, the Duke alone resisted the intercession of them all, until he was overcome by Alice Perrers, with whom he thought it safer not to contend and fight before the King. Restored now, and wondrously enriched, Wykeham turned all his zeal and care to the founding of those splendid and magnificent colleges at Oxford and Winchester. Once they were built and completed, he endowed them with such excellent laws and statutes, and enriched them with lands and possessions, that for the other colleges of letters founded afterwards, his foundation seems to have been put forward as a model and pattern to be imitated. This was afterwards observed by the chief patrons of the colleges at Cambridge and Oxford, who, in the colleges they founded, copied the ordinances and statutes of Wykeham word for word, with very few words changed. This fact judged his prudence singular and worthy of the offices he held in the commonwealth, because he devised such fitting and appropriate statutes for the growth of good letters, in which he was himself thought to be more than moderately learned. Besides these colleges, built at very great expense, he also built the nave of the cathedral church of Winchester. He enriched very many of his relatives who were endowed with wealth. He gave much to many churches. Despite such generous and immense munificence, at his death he left in money, by a will he had made, legacies to the sum of 6,270 pounds, apart from vessels, gems, books, vestments and household goods. Among these legacies, 100 pounds were granted to Alice Perot, his kinswoman. Whether she was the same as the Alice Perrers whom the historians name, through whose favour (as we have said) he was reconciled to the King, is uncertain. It is fitting to think that such great riches, gathered by honest arts, were spent so praiseworthily and usefully. He was always thrifty in his habits, and that very economy brought him the greatest gain. As soon as he had entered upon the bishopric, the executors of his predecessor William Edington brought suit against him before William Whittlesey, Archbishop of Canterbury (as we have said). From these he recovered, for the repair of buildings tending to ruin, 127 acres, 1,556 oxen, 3,876 wethers, 4,717 ewes, 3,521 lambs, etc., and 1,662 pounds, 10 shillings. He sat for thirty-seven years, and when he died he was buried with an honourable and distinguished tomb in the cathedral church of Winchester, against the south wall of the nave.

units.la: Nunc ad Simonem Sudbury Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum reuertamur. Cuius translationis anno secundo Edwardus Rex ternus obiit, & Richardus secundus eius ex Edwardo principe ncpos Westmonasterii ab Archiepiscopo Cant. anno ætatis suæ 11. vndecim & sacratus est. Eiusque coronationis ritibus finitis constituit Archiepiscopus suum Cancellarium, qui Cleri synodo Londini congregata obrinuit duas decimas concedi Regi. Eodem anno Ioannes Wielyffe sacræ theologiæ professor, & Ecclesiæ parochialis de Lutterworthe in Leycestriæ Comitatu Rector multa in Romanam curiam, consuetudinemque Oxonii disputauit, eadem é suggestu coram populo ac proceribus sæpe prædicauit. Huic Lancastriæ Dux & é plebe permulti adhærere cœperunt. Gregorius autem Papa veritus ne eius suasione Angli deficerent, ad Regem, Archiepiscopum, Episcopos, & Oxoniensis Academiæ Cancellarium scriter iterpsit, vt eum aut coercerent, aut prorsus abscindetent. Hunc itaque captum & ad se adductum Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus in Ducis Lancastriæ præsentia iussit, ne huiusmodi dogmata deinceps diuulgaret. Sed Iohannes Wiclyffe etiam aliquandiu conticuit, tamen postea maiore feruore concitatus in apertas voces contra impios & superstitiosos Romanæ Ecclesiæ ritus erupit. Quem cum Episcopi Papæ iussa atque minas illis cæcis & periculosis temporibus metuenies seuerius castigare ex Papæ atque Regis præcepto voluissent, conuenerunt Lamethi. Eò Iohannes Wiclyf ductus est. Quotanta turba non modò ciuium sed rusticorum confluxit, & in ipsam capellam irruit, vt Episcopi subito stupore correpti suæ vitæ timebant. Quos metu tremētes atque fractos quidam Lodouicus Clifford generosus audacter monuit, ne quicquam contra Iohannem Wiclyffe præsumerent definire. Quo dicto Iohannes Wiclyffeab Episcoporum iudicio custodiaque liberatus discessit.
units.tr: Now let us return to Simon Sudbury, Archbishop of Canterbury. In the second year after his translation, King Edward III died, and his grandson Richard II, son of Edward the Prince, was crowned at Westminster by the Archbishop of Canterbury, in the eleventh year of his age. When the rites of the coronation were finished, the Archbishop appointed his Chancellor, who, at a synod of the clergy gathered in London, obtained that two tenths be granted to the King. In the same year John Wycliffe, professor of sacred theology and rector of the parish church of Lutterworth in Leicestershire, disputed at length against the Roman court and the custom of Oxford, and often preached the same doctrines from the pulpit before the people and the nobles. The Duke of Lancaster and very many of the common people began to adhere to him. Pope Gregory, however, fearing that the English would revolt through his persuasion, wrote to the King, the Archbishop, the bishops and the Chancellor of the University of Oxford, urging them either to restrain him or to cut him off altogether. Therefore the Archbishop of Canterbury, having had him seized and brought before him, ordered him in the presence of the Duke of Lancaster not to spread such doctrines from then on. But John Wycliffe kept silent for some time; afterwards, however, roused with greater fervour, he broke out into open protests against the impious and superstitious rites of the Roman Church. When the bishops, fearing the Pope's commands and threats in those blind and dangerous times, wished to chastise him more severely by the order of the Pope and the King, they met at Lambeth, and John Wycliffe was led thither. A great crowd not only of citizens but also of country folk gathered there and burst into the chapel itself, so that the bishops, seized with sudden astonishment, feared for their lives. A certain nobleman, Lewis Clifford, boldly admonished them, as they trembled and were broken with fear, not to presume to decide anything against John Wycliffe. At these words John Wycliffe was freed from the judgment and custody of the bishops and departed.

units.la: Postea Archiepiscopus perplexus synodum Londini conuocauit, in qua nonnulla de hoc euenturo schismate cauit, & constitutiones quatuor edidit, ac deinde in curia sua de Arcubus multa reformauit, & monumenta eiusdem curiæ publica, archiuosque cooseruandi modum, ordinemque descripsit. Cumque Rex priori à Clero concessa decima exhausta & consumpta iterum egere cepisset, Archiepiscopus alia institutit Londini Synodo de hoc themate Latine in suggestu peroraui.
units.tr: Afterwards the Archbishop, perplexed, convened a synod at London, in which he made some provisions concerning this schism that was to come, and issued four constitutions. Then in his court of the Arches he reformed many things, and he laid down the public records of that court and the manner and order of keeping its archives. And when the King, having exhausted and spent the tenth previously granted by the clergy, again began to be in need, the Archbishop arranged another synod at London, and on this theme made a speech in Latin from the pulpit.

units.la: Vigilate, & orate. Deinde inchoata Synodo ipse cum Cancellario 4o Regni ollet, exposuit Regis necessitatem, cui pecuniario subsidio eo suadente zquisimis animis à toto Clero subuentum est. Archiepiscopalem suam iurisdictionem à suffraganeis aurinferioribus prouinciæ prælatis contemni ac violari nunquam impune permisit. Iohannem Appleby Decatum Ecclesiæ Paulinæ, Rogerum Holmes eiusdem Ecclesiæ Cancellarium, tum Adamum Mottron Londinensis Episcopi Vicarii in spiritualibus generalem, quia decreto cuidam à Decano almæ curiæ de Arcubus non paruissent, sententia seuerissima lata, omni munere Ecclesiastico & authoritate priuauit, quam tamen illis pœnitentibus & supplicitur genibusque flexis delicti ac contumaciæ veniam deprecantibus, tum Iohanne Lancastriæ Duce, & Wilhelmo Wickam Winton iensi Episcopo vna exorantibus remisit atque relaxauit. Appellationes prouincialium 5o semper recepit, earumque cognitionem plurimus cōmisit, nec eas à quocunque impediri siuit. Walterum Asbury choralem Vicarium in Regia capella Windoforiæ ab initio Wilhelmi Mugg primi decani eiusdem capellæ appellantem in pristinum ius commissione aliis facta reiiciuit. Idquod in illa libera & ab omnia priuilegia prætereque Regis auctoritate illius capellæ institutione Cæcellariis regni principis vice ami horitatem, fundus est. Postquā sex annis, vno mense ac deeē diebus sedisset in populari seditione interēptus est. Hic popularis motus suasione cuiusdam Iohannis Bail seditiosi atque popularis Presbyteri concitatus est. Quumad Wtclisfianorum inuidiam, ex illa secta & institutio-
units.tr: "Watch and pray." Then, when the synod had been opened, he himself, with the Chancellor, in the fourth year of the reign, set out the King's need, and on their advice the whole clergy came to his aid with a most willing spirit by a money subsidy. He never allowed his archiepiscopal jurisdiction to be despised and violated with impunity by his suffragans and the other lower prelates of the province. John Appleby, Dean of St Paul's, Roger Holmes, Chancellor of the same church, and then Adam Mottram, general vicar in spiritual matters of the Bishop of London, because they had not obeyed a decree of the Dean of the Court of Arches, he pronounced a most severe sentence and deprived them of all ecclesiastical office and authority. Yet when they repented, and with bowed knees and suppliant entreaties begged pardon for their fault and obstinacy, he remitted and relaxed the sentence, at the joint request of John, Duke of Lancaster, and William Wykeham, Bishop of Winchester. He always received appeals from the provincial courts, and committed the hearing of them to very many judges, and he did not allow them to be hindered by anyone. He rejected Walter Asbury, choral vicar in the royal chapel at Windsor, who appealed from the beginning of William Mugg, the first dean of that chapel, and restored him to his former right by a commission given to others. This he did because that chapel, by its free institution and by its privileges and royal authority, was founded in place of the Chancellor of the kingdom. After he had sat for six years, one month and ten days, he was killed in a popular uprising. This popular movement was stirred up by the persuasion of a certain John Ball, a seditious and popular priest. Since [the ill will against the Wycliffites, from that sect and institution]...

units.la: one prodisse qnidam fingunt salso equidem & ignoranter, quemadmodum cum ad narrationis exitum peruenerimus mox declarabimus. Atque verum tamen est eodem penetempore huius insaniam, quo Wicliffi doctrinam vulgo spariam & propagatam fuisse. Sed vt in omni nonitate ac mutatione fieri solet, atque hodiernis his temporibus factiatum est, nnnciata luce Euangelii, & libertate Christiana, iissana plebs scelerum impunitatem & omnium in Ecclesiaatq; Republica ordinum perturbationem sperat. Quæ si duces aut authores immanitatis suæ nacta fit, nulla feraram ipsarum feritas tantacit, quæ possit cum illius feritate contendere. Cuius rei nunquam in Anglia conspicuum magis atq; euidens argumentum fuit, ex cuius antegressis colligere sequeria li-cet, quàm illius perditi & tumultuosi sacrificuli exemplum. Qui annis amplius viginti plebe plaudente vbique in latebris docuit, statum seruilem contra naturam & legem diuinam violenter à potentioribus institutum, & à Christianis ceruicibus depellendum, eosque qui nobilitate & diuitiis pollerent, aut plebem dignitate anteiritat æquabilitatem reducendos. Omnes enim homines gradu ac fortunis patesse voluit. Tum obedientiam magistratibus & præsertim Clero debitam, neenon decimas subtrahédas. Quibus nepharijs & popularibus opinionibus permiscuit quaedam Wicliffi doctrina; quæ à potentioribus tum atque doctrioribus recepta cognouerat. Hæc & similia vulgo plausibilia primò publicè prædicauit, deinde sacris interdictus in plateis, vicis, atque campis multitudine congregata disseminauit, Clerum in omni sermone maledictis &
units.tr: Some people foolishly and ignorantly pretend that this madness came forth from [Wycliffe], as we shall declare when we reach the end of the narrative. It is true, however, that this madness arose at the same time as Wycliffe's doctrine was commonly spread and propagated. But, as happens with every novelty and change, and as has happened in these present times, once the light of the Gospel and Christian liberty were proclaimed, the unruly common people hoped for impunity for their crimes and for the overthrow of every order in the Church and commonwealth. If such people find leaders or authors for their savagery, no fierceness of wild beasts is so great that it could compete with theirs. Never was there a more conspicuous and evident proof of this in England than the example of that ruined and tumultuous little priest, from whose earlier conduct one may infer what followed. For more than twenty years he taught everywhere in hiding, with the common people applauding, that the servile condition, imposed violently by the more powerful against nature and divine law, ought to be cast off from Christian necks, and that those who excelled in nobility and wealth, or who stood above the people in rank, should be brought down to equality. For he wished all men to be equal in rank and fortune. He also taught that the obedience due to magistrates, and especially to the Clergy, should be withheld, and that tithes should be withdrawn. With these pernicious and popular opinions he mixed some of Wycliffe's doctrine, which he had learned had then been received by the more powerful and more learned men. These and similar things, pleasing to the crowd, he first preached publicly; then, forbidden the sacred pulpits, he spread them abroad in streets, villages and fields, gathering great crowds, and in every sermon he burdened the Clergy with insults and slanders.

units.la: calumniis onerauit. Tandem excommunicatus cum in contumaeia perseuerasset, ab Archiepiscopo captus & carceribus inclusus est. Cumque ad carceres ducereatur, prædixit semanu militari & viginti armatorum millibus carceribus educendum. Id quod paulò post euenit. Namque rustici & coloni, qui serui ascripticii fuerunt iam confertim tumultuari & congregari ceperunt. Qui multitudine copiosa in campo Blackheathe collecta Iohannem Strawe, & Walterum Tiler, eiusmodi enim nomina consulrò, & in contumeliam ludibriumque militum & armigerorum sibi imponebant, furoris sui duces crearunt. Paucisque diebus ita adauctus est eorum numerus vt ne Regis vim aut potentiam perrimescerent. Ac primò in carceres frangunt, & reos eximunt suæ-q; turbæ adiungunt, inter quos tum fuit perditus ille ac sacrilegiosus presbyter Iohannes Balle. Hunc sibi pastorem & ministrum præficiunt. Qui concione habita de hoc vulgari metro & prouerbio perorauit. When Adam dalf, and Eue span, who was then a gentleman. In eo themate explicando omnes homines pares fuisse creatos, & æquali similique primæuo atque naturali iure vixisse dicebat. Illa honorum, graduum, dignitatum, & ordinum discrimina, vt ambitiosorum hominum & potentiorum inenta quibus plebem opprimerent, & in seruitutem cogerent, damnabat. Deinde suasit vt Archiepiscopum, Episcupos, Regni proceres, iuriperitos, iustitiarios, omnesque qui iudiciis, tribunalibus, aut consiliorijs præssent tanquàm plebeianæ libertatis inimicos trucidarent. His deletis & sublatis facile sibi fore seruitutem omnem atque paupertatem exterminare, eaque iura describere quibus simili potestate, & æquali dignitate ac fortuna omnes viuere possint. Hoc iam tempus eis diuinitus esse concessum in quo seruituris iugum deponere possint, quod si prætermittant non esse vnquam amplius pro libertate sperandū. Cum hæc & his similia plausibilia dogmata decantasset, magnis clamoribus à rota multitudine dictum est : Eum prophetam cœlitus missum esse, solumque dignum qui Archiepiscopus & Regni Cancellarius esset. Ac statim concilio capro decernunt, Archiepiscopum, & Regni Cancellarium aliosq; nonnullos simulatque deprehenderentur sine vllo iudicio vt Regni proditores & plebis inimicos plestendos capite. Deinde edicta sua publicè proponunt, quæ Regis & plebis sine eomunitatis nomine exclusis Episcopis & proceribus conceperunt. Rex legatis ad eos militibus quibusdà quæsiuit causas quaretata multitudineac frequentia eonspirarent. Illi Legatos ad Regem redire, eiq; nunciare iusserunt. Se pro magnis quibusdam Reip. negocijs conuenisse, de quibus cum ipso Rege comunicare vellent, proinde necesse ei esse si coniurationis suæ causas, propositaq; scire vellet, vt ad eos accedat. Hoc impudens atq; audax eohiuratorum responsum cum accepisset Rex, consilium cepit, eundum nesibi an manendū esset, tam quib. modis tumultus ille ant quiete sedandus, aut vt eospescendus sit. Multi suadent vt Rex eos adeat, fore.n.si Rege præsente verbis ac pmissis lenioribus permulceatur, depositis armis ad sua singuli secedant. Verum Archiepisc.Cant. & Robertus Hales Magister hospitalis S.Iohānis Regni Thesaurarius contra suadet, neq; dignum neq; tutum esse Regi tam abiectà & desperatà multitudinē adire, de quibus su mendū esse aperto Marte & vi militari supplicium dicebat. Quod cum plebi nunciarū est, exclamarunt se quasi futuros Archiepiscopum & Robertum Hales eoisque Regis atque plebis hostes morte affecturos. Ac proximus iter e Londinum arrepto, primum in Ducis Lancastriæ domum quæ tum Sauoia fuit inuadunt, ibi omnia diripiunt, vasa argentea atque aurea securibus minutatim proscindunt, pannos aureos & holosericos dilacerpunt atque lacerant, annulos, iocalia, gemmas malleolis conterunt, lupellectilem omnem conuulsam & contritam in profluentem Thamesim, aut cloacas proiiciunt, ad extremum æd es ipsas quæ pulchritudine atque magnificentia quasicunque etiam ipsas regias superabant, immissis ignibus & incendio flagrantes reliquunt. Cum ad bas Ducis ædes accessissent, vetabat edicto, ne quis clam subriperet, aut priuatis vi bus aliquid reseruaret ex illa tam ornata & sumptuosa supellectile, sed omnia deleri & vastari iubebat. Repertus est vnus qui in sinum multa preciosa clam cogessrat, quem cum ipsa domo ipsque quæ acquisierat, & cælauerat combusserunt. Eoad iurisperitorum domos quæ prope Temple bar tum sitæ fuerunt, & ad bospitium Sanctis Iohannis de Clerkenwell properant, odioque Roberti Hales pari incendio vastant. His gestis cum numerus eorum iam pene in infinitum creuisset, in tres partes se diuidunt, vna agros depopulabantur, & ex prada reliquos sustentabar, altera ineo loco qui Milesend, eo quod mille passibus Londino abest, dicitur, collocata est, vt Londinum proficiscentes obseruarent, quosiurare cogerunt vt Regi atq; plebi communitati semper sint fideles. Tertia pars in monte propeareem Londinensem quæ vulgariter Tower hill appellatur, castra posuit. Rex cum Archiepiscopo, Consiliariisque suis Arcem Londinensem sexcentis sagittariis, aliisque permultis militibus instructam tenuit. Qui tamen hanc infamam plebem multitudinemque metuentes animis conciderunt, & ingressum permiserunt. Illi confertim ingressi regiis militibus minantur eadem, Regem ipsum conuenient, libertatem & diuitias poscunt, Archiepiscopum & Robertum Halesad eedem postulant. Quid multa? impetrant quæcunque flagitant. Ac primum Archiepiscopum in missæ celebratione deprehensum cum Roberto Halas, & Iohanne Legg lictore quodam Regio arce educunt, & capitibus securi abscissis interimunt. Post hanc cladem nullis quos suæ dementiæ aduersos susp icabantur, pepercerunt, s. d indicta causa sine diserimine crudelissima permultos morte affecerunt. Rex eis quascunque peterent conditiones obtulit, si a cæde & incendiis abstinerent. Qua pollicitatione Regia mitigari multi, armis castrisque relictis defessi domum redeunt, reliqui vt concessiones regiæ in scripta publica redactæ sigillo confirmarentur, petierunt. Aliquot iam diebus de cundicionibus inter Regem atque bos rusticos actum & interdum variatum est. Walterus Tyler rusticorum tribunus petit sibi Regio diplomate fieri potestatem trucidandi omnes iurisperitos, omnesque qui ratione scientiæ, studii, vel officii quicquam negocii in iure municipali haberent. Eaque petitione exposita cum Regem (etsi deliberasset) concessurum puauit, rediit ad suos & digito labiis admoto. Ante quatridiu fore dixit, vt omnia Regni iura de ore suo manarent. Postridie Rex per militem Iohannem Newton eum de conditionibus oblatis actorum accersiuit, & vt ocyus accederet, rogauit. Is vero si tanta festinatione opus sit, properare, & ad Regem suum redire celeriter militem iussit, seenim gressu suo proprio arbitrioque venturum. Eumq; tardius equo insecutus Regi in campo ferrario obuiam dat. Ibi ante quam Regem conuenit, idem miles equo vectus rogauit eum quid de conditionibus a Rege oblatis censeret. At Rusticus Tribunus iam elatior. Decerent inquit, pedestrem magis quam equitem ei specie quimo te reprehensatfe. Cui miles veteris militiæ atq; probitatis memor: iniuriam inquit tibi non facio, quod equitem eques alloquor. Quo responsione nisus Rusticus eductu vagina pugionem in militem vibrat, cumque protudorem appellat. Miles vicissim suum eduxit ensem, & rusticum mentiri asseruit. Qui concitatus silico suis rusticis commilitonibus in militem se armis defendentem irruit. Rex cum exitium imminere militi perspexisset, iussit vt equo descendet, & ensem tradetet. Tum Maior Londinensis ciuitatis Wilhelmus Walwoor the, aliisq; milites & armigeri Regii indignum esse dicebant, vt Rex militem rustico cedere iuberet, aut rusticorum insolentiam impunitam ferret. Quibus auditis Rex etsi annis pene pueribus esset, tamen suscepta iam audacia Maiori imperauit, vt tribunum rusticum arrestaret. Maior Regis iussum fortiter executus, renitentem rusticum lictoris scepiro magno ictu in capite percussit, & ad terram dedit. Mox ministri Regii eum circumdederunt a quibus gladiis cœfossus & irucidatus obiit. Duce suo interepto, rusticia vt mortem eius vindicarent ad arma se accingunt. Hos Rex vt pacaret, magna voce clamauit. Cur adeo ob proditoris mortem qui vos seduxit sequitis. Sequimini me Regem vestrum qui quæ cunque petieritis concedam. Itaq; vt eos e suburbiis quæ incedere flarucbat, educeret in campos festinauit. Illicum conferrim sequuti sunt. Interea Wilhelmus Walwoorthe Maior Londinensis cum mille ciuibus armatis succurrit, qui turbam illam rusticam & inarmaram circumducunt, & aliquibus captis atque caesis, reliquos ad deditionem compellunt. Quorû multitudo tanta fuit vt ciû ad supplicia retineri nō possint, palantes & dispersi aufugerunt. Sed postea in Cantio & Eslexia redintegrare conirationem ceperunt. Quibus Rex de manumissione, libertate, atque venia, diplomata sigillata misit, ne concitarentur denuo. Hic itaque seruilis atque Rusticus rumultus impius praesbyteri suasionibus excitatus praeter hominum expectationem diuina solum potentia sedatus atque pacatus est.
units.tr: At last, when he persisted in his contumacy after excommunication, he was seized by the Archbishop and shut up in prison. As he was being led to prison, he foretold that he would be led out by a military hand and by twenty thousand armed men. This came to pass shortly afterwards. For the peasants and farm workers, who were bound as villeins, began to riot and gather together in a body. Assembling in great numbers on Blackheath, they made John Straw and Walter Tyler (for so they called themselves, and so they were named in mockery and derision of soldiers and gentlemen) the leaders of their madness. In a few days their number grew so much that they did not fear the power or force of the King. First they broke into the prisons, freed the prisoners and added them to their mob; among these was that ruined and sacrilegious priest John Ball. They set him over themselves as their minister and pastor. Having held a sermon, he expounded on this popular verse and proverb: When Adam dalf, and Eue span, who was then a gentleman? In explaining this theme he said that all men had been created equal, and had lived in the same and equal first state and natural right. He condemned those distinctions of honours, grades, dignities and orders as devices of ambitious and powerful men by which they oppressed the common people and forced them into servitude. Then he urged them to kill the Archbishop, the Bishops, the nobles of the kingdom, lawyers, justices, and all who presided over courts, tribunals or councils, as enemies of popular liberty. With these men destroyed and removed, they would easily be rid of all servitude and poverty, and would draw up laws by which all could live with equal power, equal dignity and equal fortune. He said that this time had been granted to them by God, in which they could cast off the yoke of servitude; if they let it pass, there would never again be hope of liberty. When he had sung these and similar pleasing doctrines, the whole crowd shouted loudly that this man was a prophet sent from heaven, and the only one worthy to be Archbishop and Chancellor of the kingdom. And at once they resolved in council that the Archbishop, the Chancellor and some others, as soon as they were caught, should be put to death without any trial as traitors to the kingdom and enemies of the common people. Then they published their edicts, which they had drawn up in the name of the King and the common people without the community, the Bishops and nobles being shut out. When the King asked some soldiers who came to them as envoys why they had gathered in such a crowd and in such numbers, they ordered the envoys to return to the King and tell him that they had come together for certain great affairs of the realm, about which they wished to confer with the King himself; therefore, if he wished to know the causes of their conspiracy and the things proposed, it was necessary for him to come to them. When the King received this shameless and bold reply from the conspirators, he took counsel whether he should go to them or stay where he was, and how that tumult was to be calmed, either by peace or by suppression. Many advised that the King should go to them, for if he were present, they would be soothed by gentler words and promises, and would lay down their arms and each withdraw to his own home. But the Archbishop of Canterbury and Robert Hales, Master of the Hospital of St John and Treasurer of the kingdom, argued against this, saying that it was neither fitting nor safe for the King to approach so abject and desperate a multitude, and that they must be punished by open war and military force. When this was reported to the common people, they cried out that they would seize the Archbishop and Robert Hales and put them to death as enemies of the King and the people. Then, seizing the road from London, they first attacked the house of the Duke of Lancaster, which was then called the Savoy. There they plundered everything: they cut silver and gold vessels into pieces with axes, tore and ripped golden and silken cloths, crushed rings, jewels and trinkets with hammers, and threw all the furniture, torn and broken, into the flowing Thames or into the sewers. At last they left the buildings themselves, which surpassed in beauty and magnificence almost even the royal palaces, burning and ablaze after setting fire to them. When they reached the Duke's house, they had issued an edict forbidding anyone to steal secretly or keep anything for himself from that rich and costly furniture, and ordered everything to be destroyed and laid waste. One man was found who had secretly gathered many precious things into his bosom; he was burned together with the house itself and with what he had acquired and hidden. They then hurried to the houses of the lawyers, which lay near Temple Bar, and to the hospital of St John at Clerkenwell, and out of hatred for Robert Hales they laid them waste with the same fire. When these deeds were done, their number had now grown almost to infinity, and they divided themselves into three parts. One part laid waste the fields and fed the rest from the plunder; another was stationed at a place called Mile End, because it is a thousand paces from London, so that they could watch those who were going to London, and they compelled those they met to swear that they would always be faithful to the King and the community of the common people. The third part pitched their camp on the hill near London commonly called Tower Hill. The King, with the Archbishop and his councillors, held the citadel of London, garrisoned with six hundred archers and very many other soldiers. But they, fearing that infamous multitude and mob, lost heart and let them in. Entering in a body, the rebels threatened the King's soldiers with the same fate, demanded to meet the King himself, asked for liberty and riches, and demanded the death of the Archbishop and Robert Hales. What more? They obtained whatever they demanded. First they led the Archbishop out of the citadel, having caught him while he was celebrating Mass, together with Robert Hales and John Legg, a certain royal sergeant, and killed them by cutting off their heads. After this slaughter they spared none whom they suspected of being opposed to their madness, and without any trial, with no distinction, they very cruelly put many to death. The King offered them whatever conditions they might ask, if they would abstain from slaughter and burning. Many were moved by this royal promise; wearied, they left their arms and camp and went home. The rest asked that the royal concessions be drawn up in a public document and confirmed by the seal. For some days the terms were discussed and sometimes altered between the King and these peasants. Walter Tyler, the tribune of the peasants, asked that he be given a royal warrant to kill all lawyers and all who had any business in municipal law by reason of their knowledge, study or office. When this demand had been laid out, and he was told the King would grant it (though he had considered it), he returned to his own men and, putting his finger to his lips, said that within four days all the laws of the kingdom would come from his mouth. The next day the King sent for him by the knight John Newton, to speak about the terms offered, and asked him to come more quickly. But he ordered the knight to hurry and return quickly to his king if such haste was needed, for he would come at his own pace and as he pleased. Then, following more slowly on horseback, the knight met the King in Smithfield. There, before he met the King, the same knight, mounted on his horse, asked him what he thought of the terms offered by the King. But the peasant tribune, now more arrogant, said that he ought to be addressed on foot rather than on horseback, and that he was being insulted by his appearance. To him the knight, mindful of his old soldiery and integrity, replied: "I am not doing you an injustice, for I am speaking to you as a horseman to a horseman." Provoked by this answer, the peasant drew a dagger from its sheath and struck at the knight, calling him a pimp. The knight in turn drew his sword and declared that the peasant lied. Roused by anger, the peasant rushed upon the knight, who was defending himself with his weapons, and his fellow peasants joined him. When the King saw that death was threatening the knight, he ordered Tyler to dismount and hand over his dagger. Then the Mayor of London, William Walworth, and the other royal knights and gentlemen said it was unworthy that the King should order a knight to yield to a peasant, or allow the insolence of peasants to go unpunished. Hearing this, the King, though he was almost a boy in years, yet, having taken up courage, ordered the Mayor to arrest the peasant tribune. The Mayor bravely carried out the King's command, and striking the struggling peasant on the head with a great blow of a sergeant's staff, knocked him to the ground. Immediately the King's servants surrounded him, and he was stabbed and hacked to pieces and died. With their leader killed, the peasants armed themselves to avenge his death. The King, to calm them, shouted in a loud voice: "Why do you follow so eagerly after the death of a traitor who led you astray? Follow me, your King, and I will grant whatever you ask." And so he hurried to lead them out of the suburbs, which they were setting on fire, into the open fields. They followed him at once. Meanwhile William Walworth, the Mayor of London, came to help with a thousand armed citizens, who surrounded that unarmed rustic mob, and after taking some and slaying others, compelled the rest to surrender. Their number was so great that they could not be held for punishment; wandering and scattered, they fled away. Later, however, they began to renew their conspiracy in Kent and Essex. The King sent them sealed charters concerning manumission, liberty and pardon, so that they would not be stirred up again. And so this servile and rustic tumult, impious, roused by the persuasions of a priest, was calmed and pacified beyond men's expectation, by divine power alone.

units.la: Paulo postquam Walterus Tyler interfectus est, Maior Londinensis vir strenuus atque sedulus Iohannem Straw alterum rusticorum Ducem Londini in cauponali perpotantem deprehendit, & capire damnauit, damnatumque multis modis solicitauit, vt finem & propositum huius vulgaris commotionis declararet. Iscum aliquandiu hasitasset, & contiuisset, subiunxit Maior. Certo scias nullam vitae superesse spem, sed celeremtibi adesse mortem, proinde consule animae tuae saluti. Et ti verum fateri vis, ego in adiutorium animae tuae irrenanales missas faciam celebran. Id quod ab aliis astabius ciuibus promissum ei est. Tum abiecta vitę ipse & re, cepto missarum solatio. Eo inquit tempore, quo in Blackeath conuenimus, Regemque accersiuimus, statuimus omnes quos adduxisset Milites, armigeros, & generosos subita morte interfecisse.
units.tr: Shortly after Walter Tyler was killed, the Mayor of London, a brave and diligent man, found John Straw, the other leader of the peasants, drinking heavily in a tavern in London. He had him seized and imprisoned, and pressed him in many ways to declare the aim and purpose of this common uprising. When Straw hesitated for some time and kept silent, the Mayor said: "Be certain that no hope of life remains for you, but death is close at hand. Therefore take thought for the salvation of your soul. And if you want to confess the truth, I will have requiem masses celebrated to help your soul." Other honourable citizens had promised him the same. Then, giving up life and everything, he turned to the comfort of the masses. "At that time," he said, "when we gathered at Blackheath and sent for the King, we resolved to kill suddenly all the soldiers, armed men and gentlemen whom he had brought with him."

units.la: Tum Regem in noltram potestatem cepisse, & cum eo totum regnum perluftrasse, eoque populo exhibito suasiue eum nostrae coniurationis Ducem fuisse. Illosque quos trucidassent proditores, & laesae maiestatis reos. Deinde conciliata vbique nobis plebe primo proceres, deinde Regem, postremò Episcopos, Monachos, Canonicos, & Ecclesiarum rectores deterrapla deleuisse. Soluque fratres & presbyteri mendicates sacra nobis celebrasset. Omnibusque iam qui aduersi nobis fuerunt extinctis atque sublatis legibus nouas condidisse, & Reges in vnoquoque regni comitatu creassemus, quibus tanquam Imperatorem Walterum Tyler Cantii Regem praepositumus. Quod propositum quia per Archiepiscopu impeditum est, ideo in eum niniuri furore quam in quemquam exaltimus, primumque morte mulEtauimus. Iohannes Ball popularis & seditiosus presbyter huius conuirationis suasor Couentriae captus, & ad Regem in monasterio Sancti Albani tunc agentem ductus eadem pene confessus, de Wiclyffo eiusque dogmatibus mentionem nullam fecit Cuius etiam literae astutae & seditionis plenae de religione nihil prorsus commemorant. Atq; huiusmodi quidem tumultus non modo in Cantio, & Eslexia sed in pletisque regni Comitatibus quasi vno tempore orti sunt.
units.tr: Then, he said, we took the King into our power and, with him, travelled through the whole kingdom, and having displayed him to the people, we persuaded them that he was the leader of our conspiracy, and that those whom we slaughtered were traitors and guilty of treason. Then, having won over the common people everywhere to our side, we first destroyed the nobles, then the King, and finally the bishops, monks, canons and rectors of churches, whom we ruined by plunder. Only the friars and begging brothers celebrated sacred rites for us. When all who opposed us had been killed and removed, we drew up new laws and set up kings in every county of the kingdom, and over them all we placed Walter Tyler as Emperor, king of Kent. Since this plan was hindered by the Archbishop, we resolved to vent our fury on him more than on anyone else, and first we punished him with death. John Ball, a popular and seditious priest and the instigator of this conspiracy, was captured at Coventry and taken to the King, who was then staying at the monastery of St Albans. He confessed almost the same things, but made no mention at all of Wycliffe and his doctrines. Nor do his cunning letters, full of sedition, record anything whatever about religion. Uprisings of this kind arose, as it were at one time, not only in Kent and Essex but also in most of the counties of the kingdom.

units.la: Eodem enim anno Cantebrigienses oppidani magno furore correpti, in collegia & scholares irruerunt. In praetorio suo (quod Tolbothe appellant) Maior & Burgenses conuenerunt die Sabbati post festum corporis Christi. Ibi de subdendis sibi in perpetuum scholaribus consilium ceperunt. Iacobum quendam Grancester insani sui stulticiae conatus Ducem & authorem creauerunt. Quem iuuitum atque relactantem, mortis metu, ad suscipiendas illas partes fidemque sibi iuramento dandam, de his omnibus perficiendis praestandisque quae illis mandarent, coegerunt. Et frattem suum Thomam Grandecester adiungunt, vtrosque villa: suę Burgenses seu municipes creant. Hos inuitos duces furiosi satellites sequuti primo collegium corporis Christi adeunt, ibi aedificia diripiunt, chartas, scripta, & monumenta incendunt, locula & bona collegii aufetunt. Collegiorum praefectos & magistros vi aggrediuntur, eos omnibus Academiae Regibus antea concessis immunitatibus & priuilegiis iure iurando renunciare, sibiq; & suis in perpetuum succesoribus obedientiam profiteri, mortis metu compellunt. Adhaec obligatorias exigunt literas qui ibus scholarium vniuersitas Maiori & municipibus Cantebrigiensibus in tribus librorum millibus deuincerentur, soluendis si vnquam ab illis iuratis pollicitationibus deinceps recederent. Nec non acquietancias seu liberationes quibus ab omnibus debitis, recognitionibus, obligationib. litibus, actionibus, quaerelis, & impetitionibus scholarium...
units.tr: In the same year the townsmen of Cambridge, seized with great fury, rushed upon the colleges and the scholars. In their own court-hall (which they call the Tolbooth), the Mayor and burgesses met on the Saturday after the feast of Corpus Christi, and there they took counsel about subjecting the scholars to themselves for ever. They made a certain James Grancester, the leader and instigator of their mad folly, their captain. Unwilling and reluctant, he was forced by fear of death to take on that role, to swear fidelity to them, and to carry out and perform all that they ordered. They also took in his brother Thomas Grancester, and made both of them burgesses or freemen of their town. Followed by these frenzied henchmen, under these unwilling leaders, they first went to Corpus Christi College, where they tore apart the buildings, burned charters, writings and records, and carried off the coffers and goods of the college. They attacked the heads and masters of the colleges by force, and by fear of death compelled them to renounce on oath all the immunities and privileges previously granted to all the rulers of the University, and to promise obedience to themselves and their successors for ever. Besides this, they demanded bonds by which the university of scholars would be bound to the Mayor and townsmen of Cambridge for three thousand pounds, to be paid if ever they should later withdraw from those oaths and promises. They also demanded acquittances or releases by which the scholars would be freed from all debts, recognizances, obligations, lawsuits, actions, complaints and claims...

units.la: Praeterea ciftas & Archiuos Vniuersitatis tam in Ecclesia beatae Mariae quàm in aedibus Carmelitarum inuadunt. Iude chartas, bullas, literas patentes Regias, scripta, & monumenta omnia eruta igne eremant. Tum media fere nocte campanam magnam in Ecclesia beatae Mariae pulsari iubent, cuius sonitu excitati in praetorium conuenient. Ibi praeconis voce dictum est vt in domum Wilhelmi Wigham Vniuersitatis bedelli seu viatoris ac praeconis impetum facerent, eumque qui primus comprehenderet trucidaret. Eius ædes ditipiunt, chartas omnes atque literas quia es as Vniuersitatis fuisse credebant,incendunt. In hac turba edictum Regis superuenit, quod & proclamatum est,ne quis delinceps sub pœna capitis & amissionis bonorum insultu aliquê faceret,aut scile cum armis telisue congregarêt.Oppidani nihilominus præcipiti & inflamato furore agitati,magna celeritate ad Prioratû de Bernwel q mille palfibus abest contendunt,ibi arbores in ambitu Prioratus positas succidûr.multaq; vastant, & diripiunt. Postea reuersi cum omnia sibi profrata existimarent vt aliquem modum finemque furori statuerent,omnes chartas reliquasque membranas & ordinariones,ac statuta Vniuersitatis in foro tanquam publico incendio atque strage consumûr. Adextremum cum ad cineres redactas esset omnia, dehinc quædam & infanaanus, nomine Margareta Stars collectos cineres in ventû manu proiecit atq; dissipauit,exclamas alta voce, Abscedat Clericorû peruna: Abscedat Clericorû perena:poftquâ oppidani depositis armis singuli discesserunt,Rex de tam seditioso & graui motu certior factus:luftitiarius quibufdam Eitrenarchis mandauit,vt inquisitionè Cantebrigiæ horum sceletum instituerent. Tum Rex Rogero cuidam de Scales militi, ac Vicecomiti Cantebrigiensi alias literis mandauit, vt Cantebrigienses Municipes singulos captis centum librarum recognitionibus, (quarum vna pars Regi, altera Cancellario vniuersitatis debeatur) ad parendum Regis lustitiarijs coercerent. Deinde Municipes Cantebrigienses in Parlamento de intestino tumultu & insurrectione accufatiatque victi omnes immunitates,libertates atque priuilegia, iplaq; adeo Municipij iura amisisse Regis sententia iudicati sunt. Rexque dissoluto prius Cantuarienfis oppidanorum Municipio, adempta illis priuilegia,Vniuersitati Cantuariensem quam Matricem & propagatricem scientiarum & doctrinæ appellauit, concessit, vt Cancellarius Vniuersitatis Cantebrigiensis,fuiq; successores ac vices eorum gerentes, soli & in solidum, habeant custodiam Assise panis, vini, & cereuisiæ, ac cognitionem & punitionem eiusdem ac etiam Assisæ & Assisæ,ac superusum mensurarum & ponderum in Dominica villa Cantabrienfis & suburbiis eiusdem. Nec non potestatem inquirendi & cognoscendi de forftallatoribus, tegradariis, carnibus, & piscibus, tam putridis, vitiosis, & aliis incompeten- tibus, quam aliis, & super his punitionem debitam faciendi. Et gubernationem, correctionem & punitionem præmissorum ac aliorum victualium quorumcunque simul cum finibus, fortisfacturis, amerciamentis inde prouenientibus, pro quadam firma decem librarum nobis & hæredibus nostris inde annuatim reddendis in perpetuum. Et quia iam posito in ipsorum Maioris, Baliuorum & Communitatis libera electione, ex præcepto nostro si ipsi reliduas liberates, & priuilegia in manu nostra raliter existentia, perquod annuo incremento vltra antiquam firmam quam ipsi pro villa & omnibus libertatibus & priuilegiis per ipsos prius obtentis recipere an relinquere voluerint. Nec non idem maior, Balliui, & Communitas restitutionem reliduarum libertatum, & priuilegiorum prædictorum cum incremento quatuor Marcarum nobis & hæredibus nostris pro eisdem in perpetuum vltra antiquam firmam suam prædictam reddendarum humiliter & instanter sibi fieri postularunt. Quare volumus & firmiter præcipimus quod idem Maior & Burgenses dictam villam cum suis pertinentiis. & habeant & teneant sibi & hæredibus suis in perpetuum adeo plane ac integrè sicut ea ante impetitionem, submissionem & decreta prædicta rationabiliter habuerunt & tenuerunt. Hactenus breue Regium. Ex quo perspicimus quam digne atque regie seditiosi vulgi in doctorum hominum etatum temeritas castigata & compressa fuerit. Atque hiusmodi initio atque causa illa priuilegia municipibusCantebrigenfibus adempta, in Scholarium iurisdictionem translata atque deriuata perucnerunt. Oppidani autem & municipes hoc ipso adhuc miseré plectuntur quod etsi detractæ eis & scholaribus concessa sunt illa insignia priuilegia, tamen pro iuribus & libertatibus reliduis quatuor marcas annuas vltra censum & tributum antiquum Regi pendunt. In his omnibus tumultibus nihil prius & antiquius fuisse videmus imperitæ plebi qnam literarum & doctrinæ interitum atque cladem, deinde deiectionem Cleri. Quibus obtentis, non modo iurium violationem, sed nobilitatis ac principatus euersionem, omniisque societatis & Reipub.Ordinarumque confusionem & perturbationem facile censent secuturam. Verùm non modò Anglia, sed & aliæ nonnullæ gentes Christianæ hac vulgi insania tunc turbatæ atque vexatæ fuerunt. Lutetia Parisiorum (cuius est præter cæteras maximè nobilitata crudelitas) tam frequentes & immanes stragcs edidit, vt ea cfuitas sub infælici quodam & ad reterrimam crudelitatè pro-
units.tr: Moreover, they attacked the chests and archives of the University, both in the church of St Mary and in the buildings of the Carmelites. From there they snatched charters, bulls, royal letters patent, writings and all records, and consumed them by fire. Then, at about midnight, they ordered the great bell in the church of St Mary to be rung, and roused by its sound they gathered at the court-hall. There, by the voice of a herald, it was announced that they should attack the house of William Wigham, the University's beadle or messenger and herald, and that whoever first seized him should kill him. They plundered his house and burned all the charters and letters which they believed belonged to the University. In the midst of this uproar a royal proclamation arrived, and it was also published, forbidding anyone from then on, under pain of death and forfeiture of goods, to make an assault on anyone, or to assemble with arms or weapons. Nevertheless, the townsmen, driven by headlong and inflamed fury, hurried with great speed to the priory of Barnwell, which is a thousand paces away. There they cut down the trees standing in the precinct of the priory, and laid waste and plundered much. Afterwards, when they returned, thinking that everything was now overcome, and wishing to set some limit and end to their fury, they consumed in a public fire and destruction in the marketplace all the remaining charters, parchments, ordinances and statutes of the University. At last, when everything had been reduced to ashes, a certain mad old woman named Margaret Starre gathered the ashes, threw them into the wind with her hand and scattered them, crying out in a loud voice: "Away with the plague of the clergy! Away with the plague of the clergy!" After the townsmen laid down their arms and went away one by one, the King, having been informed of so seditious and grave a disturbance, ordered certain justices of the peace to hold an inquiry at Cambridge into these crimes. Then the King, by another letter, commanded Roger de Scales, a knight and sheriff of Cambridge, to compel each of the Cambridge townsmen, by seizing recognizances of one hundred pounds (one part of which was due to the King, the other to the Chancellor of the University), to obey the King's justices. Then the Cambridge townsmen, accused and convicted in Parliament of internal tumult and insurrection, were judged by the King's sentence to have lost all their immunities, liberties and privileges, and indeed the rights of the borough itself. And the King, after first dissolving the corporation of the townsmen of Cambridge and taking away their privileges, granted them to the University of Cambridge, which he called the mother and propagator of the sciences and of learning. He granted that the Chancellor of the University of Cambridge, and his successors and deputies, should alone and entirely have the custody of the assize of bread, wine and beer, and the cognizance and punishment of the same, as well as the assize and the assize of the supervision of weights and measures in the lordship of the town of Cambridge and its suburbs. He also gave them the power to inquire into and judge forestallers, regrators, and those selling meat and fish, whether rotten, faulty, or otherwise unfit, and to impose due punishment for these things. He granted them the management, correction and punishment of the foregoing and of all other victuals, together with the fines, forfeitures and amercements arising from them, in return for a fixed farm of ten pounds, to be paid yearly to us and our heirs for ever. And because now, by our command, the Mayor, bailiffs and commonalty, by their own free election, wish to recover or to retain the remaining liberties and privileges, which are in our hand, for an annual increase above the old farm which they had previously paid for the town and all the liberties and privileges they had obtained, the same Mayor, bailiffs and commonalty have humbly and urgently requested that the restoration of the remaining liberties and privileges be made to them, with an increase of four marks to be paid yearly to us and our heirs for them, above their old farm. Therefore we will and firmly command that the same Mayor and burgesses shall have and hold the said town with its appurtenances for themselves and their heirs for ever, just as fully and wholly as they reasonably had and held it before the claim, submission and the aforesaid decrees. Thus far the royal writ. From this we see how worthily and royally the rash behaviour of the seditious common people against men of learning was punished and suppressed. And at the beginning and cause of this, those privileges taken away from the townsmen of Cambridge were transferred and passed on to the jurisdiction of the scholars. But the townsmen themselves are still wretchedly punished by this very fact: although those distinguished privileges were taken from them and granted to the scholars, yet for the remaining rights and liberties they pay the King four marks a year above the ancient rent and tribute. In all these tumults we see nothing that the ignorant common people desired more eagerly than the destruction and ruin of learning and doctrine, and then the overthrow of the clergy. If these were achieved, they easily judge that not only violation of rights but also the overthrow of nobility and government, and the confusion and disorder of all society, the commonwealth and its orders, would follow. Yet not only England but also several other Christian nations were then disturbed and troubled by this madness of the common people. Paris (whose cruelty is especially renowned above all others) produced such frequent and monstrous slaughters that that city, under some unhappy and most cruel star, is thought to be placed under a

units.la: penso & inclinato sidere sita existimentur. Id quod ex illa recenti nobilium plebisq; strage mense Augusto simulatis inter Nauarrę Regem, & sororem Regis Galliæ nuptiis edita nuper cernimus. In qua praeter decem millia virorum (vt fertur) trucidata quadringenta nobiles fœminæ primo milltum libidini prostratæ, deinde ab eisdem crudeliter interemptæ sunt, iubente id Papa, vt eos quos pontificii Hugonotos in Gallia vocant deleret. In quo tumultu etsi illos quos Hugonotos appellabant, trucidare tantum voluissent, tamen pontificii multi cecidere. Quæ enim insania est militari libidini ac vindictæ subditorum atque ciuium supplicia commirere, quæ nec modum seruare vllum, nec his qui omni culpa vacant parcere poterit, sed in eos sine discrimine ac delectu maxime saeuit, à quibus maximam prædam & rapinam sperat? Nec dubium est quin haec pontificiorum in concitando militari furore dementia, ac in pactis violandis perfidia in seipsos olim fit maximè recisura. Sed quoniam huius verbi Hugonoti, quo Pontificii ignominiose designant Euangelicos in Gallia, fecimus mentionem, videamus quo tempore atque causa ea appellatio exorta primo fit. Cum Iohannes Wiclyff (vt diximus) multa in Romanum Pontificem, eiusque curiam in Anglia docuisset atque prædicasset, qui eius doctrinam sequuti Romanam defetebant, Lollardi à vulgo dicebantur. Eodemque pene tempore, quia Wiclyffiana disciplina ex Auglia in exteras gentes peruenit, hi qui in Gallia aliquid in Pontificiam superstitionem dixissent, Hugonoti dicti sunt. Ac primum de probrosi illo Anglico nomine, tum de hoc Gallico dicamus. Plerique eos Lollardos appellari solitos putant qui in quadragesima, & diebus prohibitis vescebantur carnibus, sed errant. Nam à Lollio seu Zizania Lollardos primo dictos hinc colligimus. Cum Wiclyffiana dogmata in Anglia serpsissent latius, Fraterculus quidam ordinis meudicantium in concione pro Paulina cruce Londini habita in Wiclyffianos longo sermone inuectus est. In eo sermone explicuit Parabolam de inimico seminante lolium in agro boni patrisfamilias sumptam ex 13. capite Euangelii secundum Matthæum, & crebris conuiniis frequenter in Wiclyffianos interpositis eos lolio comparabat. Exqua frequenti appellatione, vocabulo in vulgus recepto & dissipato Lollardi deinceps appellati sunt. Quod etiam ex constitutione Thomæ Arundel Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi quam in Wiclyffianos edidit, atque conquerit ur Anglicana Ecclesiam multis haereticis opinionibus, & praesertim novo damnabili Lollardia nomine suo tempore inuectam. Quod verbum Willielmus Lyndewoode in illius constitutionis commentario à Lollio dictum ait. Quia sicut lolium (inquit) inficit bonas segetes, sic Lollardi inficiunt fideles simplices inter quos conuersantur. Atque hęc de Anglico, nunc de Gallico nomine pauca dicamus. Hugonotorū appellationē in Gallia, eodē pene tēpore quo Lollardorū in Anglia exorta fuisse, eoscq; qui à doctrina Pōtificia recesserunt, designasse existimandum est. Quæ ab Hugone Aubrioto Burgundione Parisiorum praeside hoc casu incepit. Carolus Q. apud Vicennas mortuus ad D. Antonium Campestrem delatus est. Ibi aliquot dies afferuratus, dum fratres eius adueniissent, dum ex aede diui Antoni funus effertur, scholastici studii Parisiensis, qui spectandi causa frequentes aderat, à seruientibus Hug. Aub. Parif. praesidiis, quia forte praecedeté pompa impedretunt, propulsi in eū eiusq; seruietes tumultuati sunt. Quorum aliqui qui deprehendi potuerunt in vinculis habiti sunt. Ab hoc seueroinitio ptogressus in nocturnis excubiis scholares Parisienses, siquos nocte urbem oberrantes deprehenderet, acriter castigauit. Ad quos etiam coercendos arcem Antonianam mœnibus fortissimis cinctam & pontem S. Michaelis, atque Castellum extruxit. Itaque cum summo Vniuersitatis Parisiensis odio flagraret, & à Pontificia doctrinatota mente & conscientia abhorreret, animadueteretur, de haeresi postulatus & condemnatus est Etnifi Gallice proceres pro eo intercessissent, perisset flamma. Hanc poenam septem pene annis sustinuit, donec difficilimis tributis impositis Parisiensis populus suscepit subito armis in Regem eiusque consiliarios repentinum impetum fecit. Eoque cum paucis ad Meldas fugato omnes illius exigendi tributi consiliarios & ministros interemit. In hoc tumultu carceribus fractis compeditu laxati sunt. Et Hugo Aubriotus Episcopalibus carceribus liberatus in Burgundiam discessit? De quo eadem pene verbatim natrat Nicolaus Egidius in suis Annalibus & Chronicis Gallice scriptis. Hugo Aubriotus Burgundiæ oriundus, qui in Gallorum controuersiis diiudicandis auctoritate atque gratia plurimum valebat, intercedente Duce Burgundiæ Parisiensis praepositus institutus est, in eoque Magistratu æquissime atque prudentissime Parisios rexit. Quo authore atque inceptore multa praeclara & sumptuosa aedificia Parisiis extructa sunt, videlicet, Pons S. Michaelis, eaque mænia quæ ad Arcis Antoninæ præsidium collocata, per Sequanam præterlabentem fluuium extenduntur. Tum paruum Pontem, atque Castellū Parrisiens. ædificauit, aliaque vrbis præsidia quibus Scholares Parisienses noctè armatos & obernantes vrbe prohiberet, & si quos deprehenderet, compeditos in eodem Castello teneret. Hic de multis criminibus accusatus est. Quoniam, vt permulto sermone percrebruit, Prælatos atque Clerum magnopere detexit, maximeque Parisiensis Vniuersitatis Scholaribus aduersus fuit. Quo odio in eum summo ducti, de suavita interiori inquisitiones multashaberi procurarunt. In quatuorpiis, inhonestus, & flagitiosus inuentus est. Diuulgatum etiam fuit, quòd cum Iudæis confuctudinem haberet, quòdque Altaris Sacramento fidem non haberet, nec sua delicta lacerdotibus fateretur, sed huiusmodi ceremonias derideret. His criminationibus victus in publica custodia in eodem Castello quod Scholarium Parisiensium coercendorum gratia extruxit, positus & detentus est. Deindeco eductus, Parisienti·Episcopi carceribus & custodiæ traditus, audita & publicata sua confessione hæreticus iudicatus, & combustioni atque flammis adiudicatus est. Sed Principibus Galliæ deprecantibus moderari fuit hæc tam grauis sententia, & pœnacapitalis. Et in Ecclesia beatæ Mariæ Parisiensi hæreticus, & Iudaicæ superstitionis sectator, atque sacrorum sacramentorum contemptor declaratus æternis carceribus pane atque aqua alendus adiudicatus, & vt aboleatur illius in perpetuum memoria Episcopali carceri inclusus est. Itaque huius Hugonis odio, quem Scholares Parisienses inuisum habebant, hi qui à Romana disciplina postea deleuerunt Hugonoti in Galliadicti sunt, vt vno pene tempore tam Gallis quam Anglis Romanam secem deserentibus nomina ignominiosa & probrosa à calumniantibus pontificiis imposita sint. Alii huius appellationis aliam causam statuunt, ac illud nomen in Turonensi ciuitate inuentum aiunt. Cuius ciuitatis vna porta ab Hugone quondam Rege extructa est. Itaque cum hi, qui nouam quam appellabant teligionem, in Turonensi ciuitate sequuti sunt, in locum Hugonis portæ vicinum ac propinquum orandi & ritus suę religionis celebrandi causa conuenire consueuerunt, à reliquis ciuibus tatione illius portæ Huguenots siue Huguenauds, id est, Hugonenses dicti sunt: verum, quæcunque fuerit ad eos designandos huc vsque retenti nominis origo prima, iussu tunc Regio multis pœnarum generibus afflicti, & crudeliter magnis catetuis Parisiis interempti sunt. Cuius tam atrocis sæuitiæ authores atque suasores ipsi plebi ac multitudini (quæ tam cruentam stragem ferre non poterat) mox pœnas dederunt. Namque opeè adiumento ciuium Parisiensium Burgundiones in ciuitatem intromissi Comitem Armanacensem, Regem Gallorum ab Anglia Rege in præliocapto, & captiuo Londinum duxto, rebusomnibus in Gallia præfectum comprehensum viuum quidem excoriauerunt, & excoriati cotpus sanguinolentum plumis inuoluerunt, tum in aerem ductum & aliquandiu per propriascorigias suspensum cum sanguine madido congelato plumæ infixæ duriusinhærerent, auulsis sigillatim plumis, tot mortis tormentis & cruciatibus afflocerunt, quot plumas detraxerunt. Ae praeter hunc in ista seditione rabie tam singulari & inaudito supplicio affectum Cardinalem de Baar, Atchiepiscopum Remensem, Episcopum de Meux, Episcopum Constantiensem, Episcopum de Liseaux, Abbatem Sancti Dionysii, Cancellarium Franciæ, Præpositum Parisiensem interfecerunt. Atque his casus quatuordecim millia popularium trucidarunt. Nec in viris satiari hæc dira strages poterat, antequam incrmium fœminarum quinquemillia interemisset. Nam qui iudiciorum atque legum pœnas vulgi furori ac temeritati exercendas permitunt, non modo eos sed infantes acerrimis suppliciis tradunt. His Parisiis gestis Henricus Angliæ Rex Rhotomagum longa obsidione tenuit. In ea ciuitate obsidionis tempore bis centum septuaginta personarum millia fuisse censita pehibentur. Ex his centum millia fame perierunt, super illum esca fuit, equinae et canina caro, mures item feles & foraces in deliciis habehantur. Canis pinguis, 10 s. vænit, equus macer viginti marcis, 50 oum. 1 s. d. Pomum 3 s. 4 d. Pirum 2 s. d. quarta pars lagenæ frumenti 10 s. Hac fame pene oes enecti reddiderunt ciuitatem, & inermes discedere permissi sunt præstito Regi iuramento, netoto deinceps anno conuiva scarna capiant. Quibus exemplo videmus quanto supplicio Christianorum macdationes non humana modo sed diuina viāione vindicentur. Sequenti anno fœdus inter Ducem Burgundiæ & Delphinatem Franciæ post diuturnas inimicitias atque simultates initum & iuramento firmatum est. Eo fæderere constituto Delphinas versus & fedifragus, cum ingenuitatem & apertam indolem Ducis Burgundiæ in conferendis pactis perspexisset, familiaritate & amicitia simulata eum ad colloquium inuitauit. Burgundiæ Dux sæderum fide & religione ductus, fine suspicione. {ß}ione incaute ad eum venit. Ac simulatque venisset militibus clam suppositis proditus & inieremptus est. Hanc tam vafrè atque simulatè à Gallo fabricatam patris necem ducis hæredis filius cum vicisci voluit, miliis ad Angliæ Regem, quitum cum Gallo de Regno bellum gerebat, nuncijs, in eius clientelam, amicitiam, fœdusipsamque militiam recipi petiit, ac iuramento de summa fide gerenda præstito subditus Regis Angliç. Acne Scotia quidem in periu lis, erudeliate, & perfidia dissimilis censetur Gallix. Ad quæ vitia illa atque sidera ex Astrologorum sententia regionibus dominantur, suo quodam dedita videri possit. Subest enim vt Astrologi censent verfutissimo & inconstantissimo sideri Scorpioni. Cuius mores in singulis pene Scotis exprimuntur.
units.tr: ...seem to lie under a hanging and inclined star. We have lately seen this in that recent slaughter of nobles and common people, carried out in August at the sham wedding between the King of Navarre and the French king's sister. In it, besides ten thousand men (so it is said) who were butchered, four hundred noblewomen were first given over to the lust of the soldiers and then cruelly killed by them, the Pope having ordered it, so that he might destroy those whom the Papists call Huguenots in France. In that uproar, even though they had wished only to slaughter those they called Huguenots, many Papists nonetheless fell. What madness it is to hand over the punishment of subjects and citizens to soldiers' lust and vengeance, which can keep no measure and will not spare even those who are free of all fault, but rages without distinction or choice against those from whom it hopes for the greatest booty and plunder! There is no doubt that this madness of the Papists in stirring up the soldiers' fury, and their treachery in breaking agreements, will one day cut most deeply against themselves. But since we have mentioned this word Huguenot, by which the Papists shamefully designate the Evangelicals in France, let us see at what time and for what cause that name first arose. When John Wycliffe (as we said) had taught and preached much against the Roman Pontiff and his court in England, those who followed his teaching and had fallen away from Rome were called Lollards by the common people. At almost the same time, since Wycliffite teaching passed from England to foreign nations, those in France who had said anything against Papist superstition were called Huguenots. Let us speak first of that disgraceful English name, and then of this French one. Most people think that they were customarily called Lollards who ate meat in Lent and on forbidden days, but they are mistaken. For from this we gather that they were first called Lollards from lolium, that is, darnel or tares. When Wycliffite doctrines had spread widely in England, a certain friar of a mendicant order, in a sermon preached at Paul's Cross in London, inveighed at length against the Wycliffites. In that sermon he expounded the parable of the enemy sowing tares in the field of the good householder, taken from the thirteenth chapter of the Gospel of Matthew, and, frequently interposing abuse against the Wycliffites, he compared them to the tares. From this frequent appellation, the word being taken up and spread among the people, they were thereafter called Lollards. This is also clear from the constitution which Thomas Arundel, Archbishop of Canterbury, issued against the Wycliffites, in which he complains that the English Church in his time had been assailed by many heretical opinions, and especially by the new and damnable name of Lollardy. William Lyndwood, in his commentary on that constitution, says that the word was derived from lolium: for just as darnel (he says) infects good crops, so the Lollards infect the simple faithful among whom they live. Now let us say a few words about the French name. It should be understood that the name Huguenot arose in France at almost the same time as Lollard arose in England, and that it designated those who had withdrawn from Papist doctrine. It began by chance with Hugh Aubriot, a Burgundian, provost of Paris. Charles V, having died at Vincennes, was carried to Saint-Antoine-des-Champs. There he was kept for several days until his brothers arrived. As the funeral was being carried out of the church of St Anthony, students of the University of Paris, who had come in large numbers to watch, were pushed back by the servants of Hugh Aubriot, provost of Paris, because by chance they were impeding the procession in front; they rioted against him and his servants. Some of those who could be caught were held in chains. Going on from this harsh beginning, Aubriot in his night watches severely punished any Parisian students he caught wandering the city at night. To restrain them he also built the Antonine fortress, girded with very strong walls, and the Bridge of St Michael, and the Châtelet. So, since he blazed with the greatest hatred of the University of Paris, and in mind and conscience utterly abhorred Papist doctrine, he was noticed; he was charged with heresy and condemned, and had the French nobles not interceded for him, he would have perished in the flames. He endured this penalty for almost seven years, until, with very heavy taxes imposed, the people of Paris suddenly rose in arms and made a sudden attack on the King and his counsellors. With the King put to flight to Meaux with a few men, they killed all the counsellors and agents who had levied that tax.
