In this uproar the prisons were broken open and the shackled were set free, and Hugh Aubriot, freed from the episcopal prison, withdrew to Burgundy. Nicolas Gilles tells almost the same story, word for word, of him in his Annals and Chronicles, which are written in French. Hugh Aubriot, born in Burgundy, who had very great authority and influence in deciding the disputes of the French, was appointed provost of Paris through the intercession of the Duke of Burgundy, and in that office he governed Paris most justly and prudently. Under his authority and initiative many splendid and costly buildings were erected in Paris: namely the Bridge of St Michael, and those walls, placed to guard the Antonine fortress, which extend along the Seine as it flows past. Then he built the Petit Pont and the Châtelet of Paris, and other city strongholds by which he kept Parisian students from roaming the city armed at night, and if he caught any, he held them shackled in that same Châtelet. He was accused of many crimes. For, as was widely spread in much talk, he greatly exposed prelates and clergy, and was especially hostile to the students of the University of Paris. Moved by the greatest hatred of him, they arranged for many inquiries into his private life. He was found to be dishonourable and shameful in four respects. It was also made public that he kept company with Jews, that he did not believe in the sacrament of the altar, did not confess his sins to priests, and mocked such ceremonies. Overcome by these accusations, he was placed and held in public custody in the same Châtelet which he had built to restrain the Parisian students. Then, brought out, he was handed over to the prison and custody of the Bishop of Paris, and after his confession had been heard and published, he was judged a heretic and condemned to the flames. But at the entreaty of the princes of France, this very grave sentence and capital penalty was moderated. In the church of Blessed Mary at Paris he was declared a heretic, a follower of Jewish superstition and a despiser of the holy sacraments; he was adjudged to be kept on bread and water in perpetual prison, and, so that his memory might be wiped out for ever, he was shut up in the episcopal prison. So, from hatred of this Hugh, whom the Parisian students held in loathing, those in France who afterwards fell away from Roman discipline were called Huguenots, so that at almost the same time, when both the French and the English abandoned the Roman see, shameful and disgraceful names were imposed on them by slandering Papists. Others assign a different cause for this name, and say that it was devised in the city of Tours. One gate of that city was built by a former king, Hugh. So, since those who followed what they called the new religion in Tours were accustomed to gather for prayer and for celebrating the rites of their religion at a place near and close to Hugh's gate, the other citizens called them, from that gate, Huguenots or Huguenauds, that is, Hugonenses. But whatever the first origin of the name, which has been retained down to this point for designating them, by royal command they were then afflicted with many kinds of punishment and cruelly slain in great throngs at Paris. The authors and instigators of such atrocious cruelty soon paid the penalty at the hands of the common people and the multitude themselves, who could not bear so bloody a slaughter. For with the help and aid of the citizens of Paris, the Burgundians, having been let into the city, seized the Count of Armagnac, who had been taken prisoner in battle by the King of England and led captive to London, and who had been put in charge of all affairs in France. They flayed him alive, wrapped his bloodied body in feathers, then led him into the open air and hung him for a while by his own thongs; when the feathers stuck more firmly to the blood that had soaked into him and congealed, they pulled the feathers off one by one, and inflicted as many torments and agonies of death as the feathers they tore away. Besides this man, who was subjected to such unique and unheard-of torture in that frenzied sedition, they killed the Cardinal of Bar, the Archbishop of Reims, the Bishop of Meaux, the Bishop of Coutances, the Bishop of Lisieux, the Abbot of Saint-Denis, the Chancellor of France, and the Provost of Paris. And in this disaster they slaughtered fourteen thousand commoners. Nor could this dreadful slaughter be satisfied with men until it had killed five thousand unarmed women. For those who allow the penalties of judgments and laws to be exacted by the fury and rashness of the crowd deliver to the sharpest tortures not only the guilty but infants too. With these things done in Paris, Henry, King of England, held Rouen under a long siege. In that city, during the siege, it is reported that two hundred and seventy thousand persons were counted. Of these, a hundred thousand perished of hunger. Their food was horseflesh and dog-flesh; mice, cats and rats were also counted as delicacies. A fat dog sold for 10 shillings, a lean horse for twenty marks, an egg for 1 shilling 4 pence, an apple for 3 shillings 4 pence, a pear for 2 shillings 4 pence, and a quarter of a flagon of wheat for 10 shillings. Starved almost to death, they surrendered the city, and were allowed to leave unarmed after swearing an oath to the King that for the whole of the following year they would not take up arms against him. From this example we see with what punishment the curses of Christians are avenged, not only by human but by divine retribution. The following year a covenant between the Duke of Burgundy and the Dauphin of France was made and confirmed by oath, after long enmities and quarrels. When the treaty had been concluded, the crafty and treaty-breaking Dauphin, having seen the frankness and open disposition of the Duke of Burgundy in dealing with agreements, invited him to a conference under a pretence of familiarity and friendship. The Duke of Burgundy, led by faith in treaties and by the sanctity of his word, came to him carelessly, without suspicion. As soon as he arrived, he was betrayed by soldiers secretly placed there, and was killed. The duke's heir, the son, wished to avenge this death of his father, so craftily and deceitfully contrived by the Frenchman; he sent envoys to the King of England, with whom the Frenchman was waging war over the kingdom, and asked to be received into his clientage, friendship and alliance, and into his military service; and having sworn an oath to serve with the utmost loyalty, he became a subject of the King of England. Nor is Scotland, indeed, thought unlike France in perjury, cruelty and treachery. To these vices, those stars and constellations which, according to the opinion of the astrologers, rule over regions may seem to have given a certain special bent. For, as the astrologers think, it lies under the most crafty and most inconstant constellation of Scorpio, whose character is expressed in almost every Scot.

units.la: Sunt enim crudeles, elati, intemperantiæ & libidini dediti, falsi atque vafri, pacis, inducie tamque fœdetum que fractores, naturaauiè tam fera & Indomita, vt etiam in bellis sæpe victi fuecubuerint, & subiectionem ut eiurando promiserint, redintegrare tamen contra fidem datam præstia, & mortis atque Martis discrimina subire, quam exiere cuiusquam gentis dominationem perferre malunt. Itaque cum Astrologi Martem scorpionis esse dominum eique præesse auiument, Scotiam crebris vastationibus, incendiis, stragibusque cruentis ex illa Martis & Scorpionis coniunctione perpetuo subesse statuunt. Hæc itaque sceleratissimorum similitudo morum Gallos atque Scotos semper inuicem conciliaut. Tantaenim vtriusque gentis feritas & immanitas in vindictis proditaest, quanta non modo inter Christianos, sed ne inter barbaros à scriptoribus vllis perhibetur. Et quanquam his enumerandis deflexisse aliquantulum ab historiæ præsentis tempore videamur, tamen ea quæ explicauimus, propositio ita coniuncta sunt, vt inserieè quodammodo necesse sit. Nunc ad Archiepiscopum mortuū, qui ab his tumultuolis rusticis interfectus est, reuertamur. Cuius corpus rebus postea pacatis ad Ecclesiam Cantuariensem delatum, & ex parte australi aliaris Dumitani sepultum est.
units.tr: For they are cruel, haughty, given to intemperance and lust, false and crafty, breakers of peace, truces and treaties. Their nature is so wild and untamed that even when often defeated in war they have sunk under it, and though they have sworn to submit, they have nonetheless been ready to renew hostilities against the pledge they gave, and to face the perils of death and of war rather than endure the rule of any foreign nation. Accordingly, since the Astrologers affirm that Mars is the lord of Scorpio and presides over it, they hold that Scotland has been perpetually subject to constant devastations, burnings and bloody slaughters because of that conjunction of Mars and Scorpio. This likeness of the most wicked morals therefore always draws the French and the Scots together. For the fierceness and savagery of each nation in revenge is so great that it is recorded by no writers, not only among Christians but not even among barbarians. And although in listing these things we may seem to have strayed somewhat from the time of the present history, nevertheless the matters we have explained and the proposition are so connected that, in a sense, the order requires it. Now let us return to the Archbishop who was dead, who was killed by these tumultuous peasants. After affairs were settled, his body was carried to the Church of Canterbury and buried on the south side of the altar of Dunstan.

units.la: Hic Archiepiscopus qui ab impia ingrataque multitudine tam diram cladem perpessus est in tota vita munificus ac liberalis fuit. Cantuarienses mutos vetustate collapsos redintegrauit, eamque portam quæ Westgate appellatur, primus ædificauit. Suburbium in Suffolciensi Comitatu vbi(vt diximus) natus est, Collegium secularium clericorum multis suis hæreditariis & emptis possessionibus, opibusque ditatum extruxit, antequam ad Archiepiscopalem sedem peruenit, cum Londinensis esset Episcopus.
units.tr: This Archbishop, who suffered such a dreadful slaughter at the hands of the impious and ungrateful crowd, was generous and liberal throughout his whole life. He restored the walls of Canterbury, which had collapsed with age, and was the first to build the gate called Westgate. In the suburb in the county of Suffolk where he was born (as we have said), he built, enriched with many of his hereditary and purchased estates and with considerable resources, a college of secular clergy, before he attained the archiepiscopal see, while he was Bishop of London.

units.la: LIX. WILHELMVS COVRTNAY.
units.tr: LIX. WILLIAM COURTENAY.

units.la: Ic nobilis Antistes ex gente illustri atque clara profectus est, patre natus Hugone Deuoniæ comite. Iuri ciuili & canonico adolescens assiduam operam dedit. In eo studio maturitatem suam assecutus, ordine clericali suscepit. In tribus deinde cathedralib. Ecclesiis Bathoniësi, Exoniësi, & Eboracësi tres Præbendas obtinuit. Postea non minus nobilitate quam doctrina prudetiaq; celebris. Tertio regnate Edwardo. Metropolitano vero Simone Islippe ad Hertfordensem Episcopatum electus est. Inde Simoni Sudbury a Londinensi Ecclesia ad Cantuariensem translato in Londinensi Episcopatu, eoque mortuo in Archiepiscopatu fuecessit. Monachi Cantuarienses in vno sensu congruentes eum postulaient, ac Vrbanus Papa sexius ignarus postulationis Monachorum prouisionis vsurpatione eum ante ad Archiepiscopatum transtulit, & Londinensem Episcopatum Braibrooke Roberto contulit. Translationis suæ diploma bullatum (vt aiunt) in Ecclesia Christi Cantuariensi publicatum est nono Ianuarii. Deinde a Rege acceptis temporalibus, & homagio præstito cotulit Lamethan. Eo venit Monachus quidam Cantuariensis à Priore & Couentu cum eruce Archiepiscopali missus. Eamque Archiepiscopo in capella sua Lamethæ sedenti his verbis xxi. Ianuar. tradidit. Patet Reuerende nuncius sum summi Regis qui te rogat, mandat, & præcipit, vt Ecclesiam suam regendam suscipias, eamque diligas & protegas. In cuius signum nuncii, summi Regis vexillum tibi tradò ferendum. Archiepiscopus autem accepta à Monacho cruce dubitatione ipse hanc iniecit. An crucem ante se perferre liceat antequâ à Papa palliū accepisset. Ex eaque quæstione alia dubitatio nata est. Regis Boemiæ sorot Regi Angliæ Richardo 2. nuptura in Angliam hoc tempore venit. Has Regias nuptias Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus iure (vt diximus) Metropolitico cele-
units.tr: This noble prelate came from an illustrious and famous family, the son of Hugh, Earl of Devon. As a young man he devoted close effort to civil and canon law. Having reached maturity in that study, he took holy orders. He then held three prebends, in the cathedral churches of Bath, Exeter and York. Afterwards he became distinguished no less for nobility than for learning and prudence. In the third year of King Edward, with Simon Islip as Metropolitan, he was elected Bishop of Hereford. Then, when Simon Sudbury was translated from the London Church to Canterbury, he succeeded him in the Bishopric of London, and on Sudbury's death he succeeded him in the Archbishopric. The monks of Canterbury, agreeing in one mind, asked for him, but Pope Urban VI, unaware of the monks' request, transferred him to the Archbishopric by usurping the right of provision, and gave the Bishopric of London to Robert Braybrooke. The bull of his translation, sealed (as they say), was published in the Church of Christ at Canterbury on the ninth of January. Then, having received the temporalities from the King and done homage, he went to Lambeth. A certain monk of Canterbury came there, sent by the Prior and Convent with the archiepiscopal cross, and on the twenty-first of January handed it to the Archbishop, who was sitting in his chapel at Lambeth, with these words: "Reverend father, I am the messenger of the Supreme King, who asks, commands and charges you to take up the governance of his Church, and to love and protect it. As a sign of this mission, I hand you the banner of the Supreme King to carry." The Archbishop, however, having received the cross from the monk, himself raised a doubt about it: whether it was lawful to have the cross carried before him before he had received the pallium from the Pope. From that question another doubt arose. The sister of the King of Bohemia came into England at this time to marry King Richard II. The Archbishop of Canterbury, by metropolitan right (as we said), was to celebrate these royal nuptials and crown the queen.

units.la: Z brate, & Reginam coronare debuit. De quo non minus ante acceptum pallium quam de cruce gerenda dubitauit. Quitam perplexus dubitationis fetupulus non à iureconsultis & caiusdicis, sed à Monachis Cantuariensibus, quia actus crebros & frequentes rerum similiter sine palliogestarum proferebant, & Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ consuetudinem allegabant, facile iublatus est. Et tamen Archiepiscopus etsi ex Monachorum assertione gesta ante se cruce ineffit, tamen protestationem caute interposuit. Non se id in Romanæ curiæ contemptum facere. Deinde regales illas & solennes nuptias Westmonasterii in celeberrimo ac frequentissimo procerum coetu paulò post festum Epiphaniæ celebrauit. Et ineunte postea vere Thomam Cheyney illustrem militem ad Papam legauit. Cui & Iohanni Trefnaul Anglo & Papalis palatii magistro authoritatem procurationem petendi ab Vrbano papa pallium. Quo impetrato Thomas Cheyney reuertitur, secumque adductum pallium Londinensi prius dedit Episcopo. Qui sexto die Maii magna astante populi clericque corona, Archiepiscopo in capella in munerio suo de Croidon sedenti, id tolita pompa & magnificentia tradidit. His solennitér peractis ritibus in Archiepiscopali administratione ita processit: Baliuos Cantuariensis, qui laica potestate adulteria & huiusmodi crimina, quæ a Prælatis erant corrigenda vindicauerunt, Ecclesiastica censura compescuit. Cleri Synodum in fratrum præcobrio Coenobio Londini habuit, in ea plurima Iohannis Wiclifi dogmata, quæ non modo inter doctos sed in ipsum vulgus late sparsa fuerunt quasi hæretica & errorum plena damnauit. Robertum Rugg Oxoniensis Academiæ Cancellarium, & Thomam Brighwell sacræ theologiæ professorem, quos Wiclifianæ hæresis suspectos habebat, eadem dogmata diffiteri, contrariisque chirographis suis assensum præbere coegit. Tum Nicolaum Hereford, Philippum Ripington sacræ theologiæ professores, & Ioannem Asheton in artibus Magistrum Wiclifo assentientes, cum ab ea assensione nollent auelli, lata sententia hæreticæ prauitatis condemnauit. A qua sententia illi ad Papam prouocabant. Archiepiscopus appellatione reiecta eos nihilominus excommunicauit. Tum illa Wiclifiana dogmata condemnata, ipsosque hæreticos & excommunicatos denunciari, tam Oxonii quam Londini mandauit. Rex huic Ecclesiastica seueritati adiungens suam literis ad Archiepiscopum, & eius Suffraganeos, nec nonad Cancellarium Oxoniensem scriptis authoritatem dedit apprehendi, & carceribus mancipandi quoscunque in dictis dogmatibus suspectos habebant. His gestis magna crudelitate in permultos de religione, fuoq; in rebus diuinis sensu vndique secuitum est. Alterauce cleri Synodus Oxonii convenit, in qua Regi concessum subsidium est, Hugone Segrave Regis thefaurario id Regio nomine petente. Tum Nicol. Hereford, Philippus Ripington, & Iohâ. Afpeton iureiurando prædictis Wiclifianis dogmatib. renunciarunt, & ab excommunicatione absoluti atque restituti sunt. Ipse Ioannes Wiclifiuhuc illuc deprehenderetur latebras quærens persequentium insidias vitauit, tandem in festo S. Thomæ paralysi correptus vitam aliquandiu in ægritudine vsque ad Sylueftri festum product. Tumque in his quæ diuulgarat dogmatibus constans motitur. Ea vero dogmata latius propagata in Galliam atque Flandriam peruenerunt. Itaq; Henricus Spencer Episcopus Norviciensis militiæ quam Theologiæ peritior, exercitu sibi à Regetradito, acceptaque ab Vrbano Papa ligandi soluendiq; potestate, traiecit in Flandriam. Dunkirke muro cinctam ac munitam ciuitatem oppugnauit. Ea capta permulras alias villas & castella prostrauit. Mox magnus ex Flandria Galliaque & Armorica Britannia militum coniunctus numerus exercitum triginta millium conflanit. His Episcopum quinque tanrum millium ducem magno impetu prope Dunkirk aggressi sunt. Sed inea dimicatione septendecim millibus cæsis reliqui fuga dispersi euaserunt. Ex Anglis septem rantum milites interempti sunt. Prohac victoria, & Norvicensi Episcopo, suoque exercitu frequentes publicæ preces in Cantuariensi prouincia ex Archiepiscopi mandato fusæ sunt. Interea in Anglia Richardus Scroope miles Regni Cancellarius eo munere abdicatus est, & Rex Robertum Braibrooke Londinensem Episcopum eius loco Cancellarium constituit. Hoc tempore Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus quendam Richardum Ifmonger de Ailsford in Cantio, quia criminosos a prælatis corrigendos authoritate laica castigauit, & iura libertatesque Ecclesiæ violauit, excommunicauit. Is humiliter petens, iureiurando se Ecclesiasticam iurisdictionem non violaturum, pœnamque quamcunque suæ contumaciæ ac temeritatis dignam & ab Archiepiscopo imponédam subiturum promisit. Pœnainiunda fuit haec, vt primo in foro de Westmalling in frequentissimo conuentu populi trinis diebus forensibus fustibus nudus cædereture tur, deinde tam Maidstonię q; Cantuariç eadem pœna atq; toties plectereretur. In vltima vero castigatione Cantuariæ Ecclesiam nudus ingrederetur, & Thomæ delubro cereum .f.lb.ceræ offerret. Quam iniunctam pœnam excommunicationis statum reincideret. Papa cuidam fratri Carmelitano Waltero Diis, qui Ducis Lancastriç fuerat confessor, potestatem plurima indulgendi priuilegia concessit. In his erat vt si quos Papæ capellanos ercaret, hi nullius iurisdictione, nulla Regula aut institu-ta disciplina tenereutur. Itaque Petrus de Pateshal Augustinensis, pecunia data in numerum papalium capellanorum ab illo Carmelitano ascriptus est. Itaque ab illo ardeo vitæ genere quo diu grauiter constrictus tenebatur, relaxatus omnē immunitatem atque impunitatem 10 propositum ac permissam sibi existimauit. Et illco omnes fratrum ordines abominans Wiclyffianis se adiunxit. His omnia clandestina & impura fratrum flagitia indicauit. Eorumq; suasu suggestus ascendens contra fœdissimos fratrū ordinesvbiq; prædicauit. Tūin scriptis valuis Paulinæ Eccles. affixis varia confratrū inter se homicidia, furta, rapinas, Regis atq; Regni prodiciones, adulteria, & nefandas contra naturam fœditates proposuit. Et vt vbi fides haberetur, occisorum & tortorum nomina commemoraret, diesque atque loca quibus illæ cædes perpetratæ sunt delignauit. Hæc patefacta nefanda frattum turpitudine multi indies à Romana superstitione desciuerunt, & Wielufi dogmaribus assensi sunt. Inter quos Wilhelmus Neuil, Lodouicus Clifford, Ioannes Clenbow, Richardus Stowry, Thomas Latimer. Ioannes Montagu, Laurentius de Sancto 20 Martino nobilissimi, & generosissimi Milites fuerunt. Quos pontificii Lollardos & Capuniatos siue Pileatos nominabāt, eo quod altaria prætergressi ex Pontificio instituto sacramēto pixidi inclusoleuatis pileis honorem non deferebant. Hi illum Augustinen. frattem, Papæ Capellanum à fratrum & Monachorum impetu tuebantur, eaque quæ de eis prædicarat ae prodiderat, verissima asserebant. Magna plebis multitudo his equitibus adhæsit, & papisimum exec-rata est. Pontificii hac indies adauctamultitudine quid agerent eo magis incerti fuerunt, quod Romæ sub Vrbano Papa quidam Antipapa exorsus est. Ipseque Vrbanus Papa in magnas ab aduersariis angustias coactus à Rege atque Clero Angliæ opem & adiumentum petiit. Tum Archiepiscopus qui in Wiclifianos ante vehementissimus erat, iam in Arundelliæ Comitem magnam con- 30 trouersiam instituit. Cuius seruuli piscinā in Archiepiscopi munerio de Southmalling Cicestrensis diocæsis sublatis piscibus euacuauerunt. Quo facto Archiepiscopus in magnam actus sæuitiam Cicestrensi Episcopo mandauit, vt piscinæ suæ prædones,quos, faerilegos & Canuariensis Ecclesiæ violatores nominauit, excommunicatione feriret. Comes autem Regem adiit, petiitque vt de ea controuersia, ne excommunicationem incurrat, in sua præsentia transigatur. Atque Archiepiscopus postquam Rex huius controuersiæ cognitionem suscepisset, ad Cicestrensem Episcopum scripsit, vt latas excommunicationes reuocaret, & ab excommunicando deinceps desisteret. Nonnulla his similia aliquot annis gesta sine commemoratione quidam commode prætermitti possunt. Rege vero & proceribus diffidentibus vt omnes lites sederentur, Parlamen40 tum Londini tentum est. Ibi Archiepiscopus Synodum celebrauit & in concione Cleri de hoc scripturarum themate perorauit. Super muros Ierusalem constituti custodes. Tum Regi decimam concedi impetrauit. In eo Parlamento cum proceres multos qui seditionis inter eos atque Regem authores fuerunt, ad supplicia poposcissent, & de vltimo plurimorum supplicio agerēt, Archiepiscopus cum suis Suffraganeis qui iure interesse caulis sanguinis tractandis non poterant, interea dum proceres reos neci adiudicaret, à Parlamento hac vsus protestatione recessit. PROTESTATIO FACTA PER DOMINVM IN PAR-lamento prose & Suffraganeis fais. 50 NDei nomine Amen. Cum de iure & cōsuetudine Regni Angliæ ad Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem, qui pro tempore fuerit, nec non cæteros suos Suffraganeos, Confratres, & Coepiscopos, Abbatesque &Priores, alioïque Prælatos quoscunque, per Baroniam de domino nostro Rege tenentes, pertineat in Parlamentis Regis quibuscunque vt pares Regni prædicti personalitet interesse, ibi, demque de Regni negoeiis & aliis ibidem tractari consueuit, cum cæteris dicti Regni paribus & aliis ibidem ius intetessendi habentibus consulere, & tractare, ordinare, statuere, & diffinire, ac caetera facere quae Parlamenti tempore ibidem imminent facienda, in quib. omnib. & singulis, nos Wilhelmus Caotuar. Achicpis opus, totius Angliae primas, & Apostolicae sedis legatus, pro nobis, nostrisque Suffraganeis, Coepiscopis, & Confrattribus, necnon Abbatibus, Prioribus, ac Praelatis omnibus supradictis protestamur, & eorum quilibet protestatur, qui per se, vel per procuratorem hic fuerit modo praesens, publice, & expresse, quod intendimus, & intendit, volumus ac vult quilibet eorum in hoc praesenti Parlamento, & aliis ut pares Regni praedicti more solito interesse, consulere, tractare, ordinare, statuere, & diffinire, ac caetera exercere cum caeteris ius interessendi habentibus in eisdem statu & ordine nostris & eorum cuiuslibet in omnibus semper saluis. Verum quia in praesenti Parlamento agitur de nonnullis materiis, in quibus nō licet nobis aut alicui eorum iuxta sacrorum canonum instituta quomodo libet personaliter interesse, ea propter pro nobis & eorum quoliber protestamur, & eorum quilibet hic praesens etiam protestatur, quod non intendimus, nec volumus, sicuti de iure non possumus, nec debemus, intendit, nec vult aliquis eorundem, in praesenti Parlamento duni de huiusmodi materiis agitur vel agetur quomodo libet interesse, sed nos & eorum quemlibet in ea parte penitus absentare, iure pariatis & cuiuslibet eorundem interessendi indicto Parlamento quoad omnia & singula mihi exercenda, nostris & eorum cuiuslibet statu & ordine congruentia in omnibus semper saluo. Ad haec insuper protestamur, & eorum quilibet protestatur, quod propter huiusmodi absentiam non intendimus, nec volumus, nec eorum aliquis intendit, vel vult, quod processus habiti & habendi in praesenti Parlamento super materiis antedictis, in quibus non possumus nec debemus vt praemittitur interesse, quantum ad nos & eorum quemlibet attinet, futuris temporibus quomodolibet impugnentur, infirmentur, seu etiam infringentur.
units.tr: Z brate, and was obliged to crown the Queen. He hesitated over this no less before he received the pallium than he had over bearing the cross. This perplexing scruple was easily removed, not by lawyers and canonists but by the monks of Canterbury, who said that similar things had often been done before the pallium was received and cited the custom of the Canterbury Church. Yet although, on the monks' assurance, the Archbishop had the cross carried before him, he cautiously entered a protest: he was not doing this in contempt of the Roman court. Afterwards he celebrated the royal and solemn wedding at Westminster, in the most famous and crowded assembly of nobles, a little after the feast of the Epiphany. Early in the spring he sent Sir Thomas Cheyney, an illustrious knight, to the Pope, and gave authority to Thomas Trefnaul, an Englishman and master of the papal palace, to seek the pallium from Pope Urban. When it was obtained, Thomas Cheyney returned, and he first gave the pallium he had brought back to the Bishop of London. On the sixth day of May, with a great crowd of people and clergy standing by, the Bishop handed it over with the utmost ceremony and splendour to the Archbishop, who was sitting in the chapel of his manor at Croydon. With these rites duly performed, he proceeded in his archiepiscopal office as follows. He restrained by ecclesiastical censure the bailiffs of Canterbury, who had used secular power to punish adulteries and crimes of that kind, which ought to be corrected by the prelates. He held a synod of the clergy in the Dominican friary at London, and in it he condemned as heretical and full of error very many doctrines of John Wycliffe, which had been spread widely not only among the learned but among the common people. He compelled Robert Rugg, Chancellor of the University of Oxford, and Thomas Brightwell, professor of sacred theology, whom he held suspect of Wycliffite heresy, to recant these same doctrines and to give their assent in written documents signed by their own hands. Then, since Nicholas Hereford and Philip Repyngton, professors of sacred theology, and John Ashton, Master of Arts, who agreed with Wycliffe, would not be torn away from that assent, he condemned them by a sentence of heretical depravity. From this sentence they appealed to the Pope. The Archbishop rejected the appeal and nonetheless excommunicated them. Then he ordered those Wycliffite doctrines to be condemned, and the men themselves to be declared heretics and excommunicated, both at Oxford and at London. The King, adding his own support to this ecclesiastical severity, by letters addressed to the Archbishop and his suffragans, and also to the Chancellor of Oxford, gave authority to arrest and consign to prison all whom they held suspect in the said doctrines. After these measures, with great cruelty, very many people concerned with religion were harassed on every side and their sense of divine matters was attacked. A second synod of the clergy met at Oxford, in which a subsidy was granted to the King, Hugh Segrave, the King's treasurer, asking for it in the King's name. Then Nicholas Hereford, Philip Repyngton and John Ashton renounced the aforesaid Wycliffite doctrines by oath, and were absolved from excommunication and restored. John Wycliffe himself, seeking hiding places here and there, avoided the snares of his pursuers. At last, seized by paralysis on the feast of St Thomas, he prolonged his life for some time in sickness until the feast of St Silvester, and he remained constant in the doctrines he had published. These doctrines, however, spread more widely and reached France and Flanders. Therefore Henry Spencer, Bishop of Norwich, who was more skilled in war than in theology, received an army from the King and, having obtained from Pope Urban the power to bind and loose, crossed into Flanders. He attacked Dunkirk, a town surrounded and fortified with walls. Having taken it, he laid waste many other towns and castles. Soon a great number of soldiers from Flanders, France and Armorican Brittany joined together and formed an army of thirty thousand. With these they attacked the Bishop, who had only five thousand men, with great force near Dunkirk. But in that battle seventeen thousand were slain, and the rest, scattered in flight, escaped. Only seven English soldiers were killed. For this victory, and for the Bishop of Norwich and his army, frequent public prayers were offered throughout the province of Canterbury by order of the Archbishop. Meanwhile in England Sir Richard Scrope, the Chancellor of the realm, was removed from that office, and the King appointed in his place Robert Braybrooke, Bishop of London, as Chancellor. At this time the Archbishop of Canterbury excommunicated one Richard Ismonger of Ailsford in Kent, because he had used secular authority to punish criminals who ought to be corrected by the prelates, and had violated the rights and liberties of the Church. Humbly petitioning, he promised under oath that he would not violate ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and that he would undergo whatever penalty for his obstinacy and rashness the Archbishop should deem fitting and impose. The penalty imposed was this: first, in the market at Westmalling, before a very crowded assembly of the people, he was to be beaten naked with rods on three market days; then the same punishment was to be inflicted, and as often, at Maidstone and at Canterbury. In the last chastisement, at Canterbury, he was to enter the church naked and offer a wax taper of one pound of wax at the shrine of Thomas. If he fell back into the state of excommunication after this penalty had been imposed, he would be punished again. The Pope granted to a certain Carmelite friar, Walter Diss, who had been confessor to the Duke of Lancaster, power to grant many privileges. Among them was this: that if he should enrol any as chaplains of the Pope, these men should be bound to no one's jurisdiction, to no rule or institution of discipline. Thus Peter de Pateshull, an Augustinian, was enrolled by that Carmelite among the papal chaplains for money paid. And so, released from that austere way of life by which he had long been strictly bound, he considered himself freed and granted complete immunity and impunity. Immediately he abhorred all the orders of friars and joined the Wycliffites. He revealed all the secret and foul crimes of the friars, and by their persuasion he mounted the pulpit and preached everywhere against the most foul orders of friars. Then he set out in writing, posted on the doors of St Paul's Church, the various murders, thefts, robberies, betrayals of the King and the realm, adulteries and abominable unnatural filthiness among the friars themselves. And so that where faith might be given, he recalled the names of the slain and tortured, and pointed out the days and places in which those murders had been committed. When these unspeakable shameful acts of the friars were exposed, many daily fell away from Roman superstition and assented to the doctrines of Wycliffe. Among them were William Nevill, Lodowick Clifford, John Clanvowe, Richard Stury, Thomas Latimer, John Montagu and Lawrence de Saint Martin, most noble and generous knights. The papists called them Lollards and Capuchins or Hooded men, because, passing by the altars, they did not show honour to the sacrament enclosed in the pyx, raised by papal institution, by lifting their hats. These men defended that Augustinian friar, the Pope's chaplain, against the assault of the friars and monks, and they asserted as most true those things which he had said and published about them. A great multitude of the common people joined these knights and execrated papistry. The papists, as this multitude grew daily, were the more uncertain what to do, because at Rome, under Pope Urban, a certain antipope arose. And Pope Urban himself, pressed by great difficulties from his opponents, sought help and assistance from the King and clergy of England. Then the Archbishop, who had before been most vehement against the Wycliffites, now began a great quarrel with the Earl of Arundel. The Earl's servants emptied of fish the fishpond at the Archbishop's manor of Southmalling in the diocese of Chichester. Upon this the Archbishop, in great fury, ordered the Bishop of Chichester to strike with excommunication the plunderers of his fishpond, whom he named sacrilegious and violators of the Church of Canterbury. But the Earl went to the King and begged that this controversy be settled in his presence, so that he might not incur excommunication. After the King had taken cognizance of this dispute, the Archbishop wrote to the Bishop of Chichester that he should revoke the excommunications pronounced and cease from excommunicating thereafter. Some similar things done over a number of years may conveniently be passed over without mention. But since the King and the nobles were anxious that all these disputes should be settled, a Parliament was held at London. There the Archbishop celebrated a synod, and in a sermon to the clergy he spoke at length on this theme of Scripture: Set as watchmen upon the walls of Jerusalem. Then he obtained a tenth to be granted to the King. In that Parliament, when the nobles had demanded the execution of many nobles who had been the instigators of sedition between them and the King, and they were discussing the final execution of very many, the Archbishop, together with his suffragans, who by right could not take part in matters that involved bloodshed, withdrew from Parliament while the nobles were condemning the accused to death, having made this protest. PROTEST MADE BY THE LORD ARCHBISHOP IN PARLIAMENT, ON BEHALF OF HIMSELF AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. In the name of God, Amen. Since by the law and custom of the realm of England it pertains to the Archbishop of Canterbury for the time being, as well as to his other suffragans, fellow brethren and fellow bishops, and to the abbots and priors and whatever other prelates hold by barony from our lord the King, to take part in the Parliaments of the King as peers of the aforesaid realm, and there, as is customary, to deliberate and treat of the affairs of the realm and other matters, and to consult, treat, ordain, establish and determine with the other peers of the said realm and others having the right to take part there, and to do the other things which are to be done during the time of Parliament: in all these things, and in each of them, we, William, Archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England and legate of the Apostolic See, protest for ourselves, our suffragans, fellow bishops and fellow brethren, and likewise for the abbots, priors and all the aforesaid prelates; and each of them who is present here, either in person or by proxy, protests publicly and expressly that we intend, and each of them intends, wills and desires to take part in this present Parliament, as the peers of the aforesaid realm customarily do, and to consult, treat, ordain, establish and determine, and to exercise the other things with the others having the right to take part, in the same state and order as ours and each of theirs, always saved in all things. But because in the present Parliament matters are being dealt with in which it is not permitted to us, or to any of them, to take part in person according to the institutions of the sacred canons, therefore for ourselves and each of them we protest, and each of them who is here present also protests, that we do not intend, nor do we wish, nor does any of them intend or wish, to take part in any way in the present Parliament while matters of this kind are being or shall be dealt with, since by law we cannot and ought not; but we and each of them absent ourselves wholly in that respect, the right of each of them to take part in the Parliament being preserved in all things, as to all and each of the things to be exercised by me, agreeing with the state and order of ours and each of theirs, always saved in all things. Moreover we further protest, and each of them protests, that because of such absence we do not intend, nor do we wish, nor does any of them intend or wish, that the proceedings held and to be held in the present Parliament concerning the aforesaid matters, in which we cannot and ought not, as has been said, take part, should in any way be impugned, weakened, or even infringed in future times, so far as concerns us and each of them.

units.la: Aliud deinde Cantabrigiae Parlamentum in coenobio Carmelitarum inchoatum est, ibique synodus Rege procurante in Ecclesia Beatae Mariae celebrata Regi a Clero hac collatione concessa decima est, si ipse ante Cal. Octobris prox. cum exercitu in Gallos mare traiicerer. Io eo Parlamento multa salubriter constituta sunt, lataque lex est. Ne quis sine Regis licentia aliquod beneficium provisionis papalis titulo sibi conferri procuraret. Qui secus fecerit ut Regis protectione excludatur.
units.tr: Next, another Parliament was begun at Cambridge, in the house of the Carmelite friars. There, with the King's encouragement, a synod was held in the church of St Mary, and the clergy granted the King a tenth, on condition that he cross the sea with an army against the French before the first of October next. In this Parliament many salutary measures were established and a law was passed: no one was to procure for himself any benefice under the title of a papal provision without the King's licence, and whoever acted otherwise was to be excluded from the King's protection.

units.la: Item statuta sunt de stipendiis famulorum, de publice mendicantibus, de armis non ferendis, de stabulis non exercendis nisi ad arcum, de itapula reuocanda de Middleborough ad Calesiam, de laboratoribus non recipiendis in aliena villa nisi sub sigillo Hundredi &c. Hoc anno Dominus Ioannes Triuet iustitiarius Regis supremus lapsus ab eo quo interiora sua dirupit. In hoc anno Scoti quietis nescii intrantes Angliam (io prouisis prouincialibus) agebant caedes & rapinas, multos captiuantes, & villas conflagrantes, duce eorum Willhelmo Comite de Douglas, qui statim peremptus est manu Henrici Percy in primo congressu, quem Comes de Dunbar cepit cum fratre suo Radulpho Perci vbi multi ex Anglis caesi sunt. Scoti nihilominus humiliari aduentum aliorum procerum non audentes expectare, fugerunt. In superioribus autem Parlamento cum laici subsidium sub hac conditione Regi concessissent, si Clerus decimam concederet, Archiepiscopus cum suis suffraganeis valde iniquum & pestimi asserebant Cleri in Regem donationes quae spontaneae gratuitaeque esse debent, a laicis tam strictis modis & conditionibus alligari. Proinde de se quacunque cleri concessione in Synodo non actutos, nisi illa laicorum conditione deleta. Itaque Rex qui eo die interfuit expunxit laicorum conditionem iustum, quod mox publice in Parlamento factum est. Post haec Archiepiscopus cum visitationem Metropoliticam in prouincia peragere constituit, vt maiori authoritate niteretur, impetrauit ab Vrbano Papa vt sine Romanae curiae impedimento visitationem totius prouinciae suscipiret. Itaque Roffensem, Cicestrensem, Bathoniensem ac Wellensem nec non Wigorniensem diocesin nullo resistente aut contradicente visitauit. Cum autem ad Exoniensem ventum esset, visitationemque inchoassent, eandemque saepius de die in diem ac de loco in locum prorogassent, & iurisdictionem tam Episcopi quam reliquorum in ea diocesi praelatorum durante sua Metropolitica visitatione suspensam tenuerat, ac impediret, Exoniensis Episcopus omnibus suae dioecesis praecepit ac mandauit, ne Archiepiscopo in visitatione parerent, tam vt beneficiorum institutiones, collationes & admissiones, tenementorum insinuationes, bona intestatorum administrandi commissiones, electionum confirmationes, causarum omnium cognitiones atque decisiones, criminum correctiones, omniaque iura ordinaria non aliunde quam a se suisue inferioribus in sua dioecesi praelatis peterent. Omnes qui secus fecerint eodem edicto sententia lata excommunicauit. Hoc prohibitorium atque censorium Exoniensis Episcopi edictum, Archiepiscopus contrario edicto suflulitae deleuit, & excommunicationis illius sententiam ac inanem pronunciauit. Exoniensis deinde quater ad papam appellauit, & appellationes suas in scriptis Ecclesiæ cathedralis Exoniensis valuis affixit. Eas omnes Archiepiscopus reiecit ac refutauit, & nihilominus in visitatione pergit. Ipsum Episcopum reiponsurum certis in visitatione propositis articulis variis edictis citat. Quidam Exoniensis Episcopi assecla Petrum Hill Archiepiscopi mandatarium in oppido Tap: ham comprehenderunt, maleq; multatum, mandarum in membranis scriptum & Archiepiscopi sigillo sigillatum quod in unu ad Episcopum citandum habuit dentibus cum cera mandicare, & deglutire coegerat, Ad quos tanquam rebelles & facinorosos coercendos Rex Edwardo Courtney, Devoniæ Comiti, aliisque mandauit ut eos inuentos ad Archiepiscopum ducerent. Capti tandem hanc pænam ab Archiepiscopo iniunctam subeunt. In Ecclesia Cantuariensi, Paulina London, & Exoniensi, diebus festis statutis, camisiis tantum induti crucem cereis accensis portatis in illa papali processione præcedant, tum missidicum præsbyterum qui quotidianas missas ad tumulum Comitis Deuoniæ celebret dato salario substentent. Postremo. 10s. singuli reficiendis Exoniæ ciuitatis muris municipibus soluant. De hac pæna Archiepiscopum testimonio trium Decanorum Londinensis, Cantuariensis & Exoniensis sigillis suis sigillato certiorem facinnt. Postea Archiepiscopus in visitationis negociis processit, & Willihelmum Byd legum doctorem aduocatum curiæ de arcubus, quia contra Cantuariensis sedis dignitatem consilium Episcopo Exoniensi dedisset, ordine atque loco mouit. Tum iuramentum præscriptis quibusdam verbis concepit, quod à singulis eiusdem curiæ aduocatis deinde admissis præstitum & obseruatum est. Exoniensis autem Episcopus appellationem suam quam ad Papam contra Archiepiscopum interposuit sedulo prosequuntus est. Sed cum suam conditionem non modo infentiorem sed duriorem esse perspexisset quòd Rex Archiepiscopo adhæserat, appellatione deserta ad Archiepiscopum supplex confugit, & tam delictum suum quam Archiepiscopi authoritatem, iurisdictionem & prærogatiuam agnoscens temeritatis & contumaciæ veniam, in quam conciliio potius quàm iudicio se dedutum fatebatur, impetrauit. Sarisburiensis autem Episcopus cum visitandus esset eosdem sibi spiritus animumque resistendi Archiepiscopo sumpsit, sed in iure ut sibi visus est, cautius prudentiusque egit. Cum enim Archiepiscopus sola Vrbani papæ authoritate ad visitandum suffultum putaret, Vrbano mortuo à Bonifacio suo successore prose ac suæ diœcesis subditis priuilegium ne Vrbani literarum authoritate visitarentur impetrauit, ratus Archeepiscopalem & Metropoliticam authoritatem atque iurisdictionem nisi Papa subueniente haud valere. Sed Archiepiscopus & in iure peritior, & vsu atque experientia certior, & in aula, Romanaque curia gratiosior, cum ad eum in muncrio de Croidon, cum Papali priuilegio quo se à visitationis iure eximi putabat, Sarisburiensis Episcopus venisset, statim decretum suum interposuit, ae coram tabellione actis insinuauit se Sarisburiensem Episcopum, eiusque totam diocæsim authoritate Metropolitica visitaturum. Deinde Episcopum edicto ac mandato suo publicomonuit, vt Metropoliticam visitationem, de Vrbani Papæ concessione nec verbum nec mentionem faciens in Ecclesia sua cathedrali Sarum statuto & præfixo die subeat. Eo die Episcopus inani priuilegio imprudenter securus abfuit, & ab inchoata Archiepiscopi visitatione tanquam ab illato sibi suisque subditis grauamine sæpius appellauit. Archiepiscopus non eadem moderatione huius contumaciam qua Exoniensis Episcopi reiurauit, sed statim eundem excommunicauit. Deinde eundem de periurio & contemptu postulauit, quòd à subiectione quam Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo in consecratione iureiurando promiserat, priuilegiis obtinendis & appellando recessisset. Sarisburiensis Episcopus hac assidua seuoritate, & recenti exemplo confratris sui Exoniensis Episcopi detectritus, cum in iure succumbendum sibi fuit, appellationibus renunciauit, & Clanis. viro Comite Satisburiensi alijsq; nonullis exorantibus, cum se subiecisset Archiepiscopi in gratiam receptus est. Tum visitatione Archiepiscopi quietus & pacatus subiit, necinde vsque quisquam suffraganeorum visitationis iure cum Archiepiscopo luctatus est. Reliquas tunc diocæses sine molestia visitauit. In Lincolniensi solumodo à visitatione quorundam Monachorum gratia & intercessione Abbatis Albanensis Oxonii cessauit. Ita visitatione peracta aliquantulum conquieuit.
units.tr: Statutes were also passed concerning the wages of servants, beggars who go about in public, the non-carrying of arms, the keeping of stables except for archery, the moving of the staple back from Middelburgh to Calais, and labourers not to be received in another town unless under the seal of the hundred, and so on. This year Sir John Trivet, the King's chief justice, fell from office, having burst his inward parts. In this year the Scots, who knew no rest, entered England (the provincial levies having been called out) and carried on slaughter and plunder, taking many captive and burning towns. Their leader was William, Earl of Douglas, who was at once killed by the hand of Henry Percy in the first encounter, and the Earl of Dunbar captured the Scots' force together with Percy's brother Ralph, where many Englishmen were slain. Nevertheless the Scots, not daring to await the arrival of other nobles who would humble them, fled. In the earlier Parliament, when the laity had granted a subsidy to the King on condition that the clergy would also grant a tenth, the Archbishop and his suffragans strongly maintained that it was most unjust and pernicious that the clergy's gifts to the King, which ought to be spontaneous and free, should be bound by the laity with such strict terms and conditions. Therefore they would not proceed with any grant of the clergy in synod unless that condition of the laity was struck out. The King, who was present that day, accordingly deleted the laity's condition, and this was publicly done in Parliament soon afterwards. After this the Archbishop resolved to carry out a metropolitan visitation of the province, and in order to rest on greater authority he obtained from Pope Urban that he might undertake the visitation of the whole province without hindrance from the Roman curia. So he visited the dioceses of Rochester, Chichester, Bath and Wells, and Worcester, with no one resisting or contradicting him. When he came to Exeter and had begun the visitation, he repeatedly postponed it from day to day and from place to place, and he kept the jurisdiction of both the bishop and the other prelates in that diocese suspended and obstructed during his metropolitan visitation. The Bishop of Exeter therefore ordered and commanded everyone in his diocese not to obey the Archbishop in the visitation, but to seek from himself or from his inferior prelates in the diocese all ordinary rights: institutions, collations and admissions to benefices, the insinuation of tenements, commissions to administer the goods of those dying intestate, confirmations of elections, the hearing and decision of all causes, and the correction of crimes. By the same edict he excommunicated all who acted otherwise. The Archbishop, by a contrary edict, quashed this prohibitory and censorious edict of the Bishop of Exeter and pronounced the sentence of excommunication void. The Bishop of Exeter then appealed four times to the pope, and posted his appeals in writing on the doors of the cathedral church of Exeter. The Archbishop rejected and refuted them all and nevertheless went on with the visitation. He summoned the bishop by various edicts to answer certain articles proposed in the visitation. Some followers of the Bishop of Exeter seized Peter Hill, the Archbishop's agent, in the town of Tavistock, roughly mauled him, and forced him to chew and swallow with wax the mandate, written on parchment and sealed with the Archbishop's seal, which he had carried to cite the bishop. The King ordered Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon, and others to seize these men, as rebels and criminals to be restrained, and to bring them to the Archbishop. Once taken, they underwent the penance imposed by the Archbishop: on set feast days, clad only in shirts and carrying lighted candles, they were to walk before the cross in a papal procession in the churches of Canterbury, St Paul's in London, and Exeter; and they were to maintain a priest, with a stipend, to celebrate daily masses at the tomb of the Earl of Devon. Lastly, each was to pay ten shillings to the citizens for the repair of the walls of the city of Exeter. The Archbishop was informed of this penalty by a testimony of the deans of London, Canterbury and Exeter, sealed with their seals. Afterwards the Archbishop proceeded with the business of the visitation, and he removed William Byd, doctor of laws and advocate of the court of Arches, from his office and place, because he had given advice to the Bishop of Exeter against the dignity of the see of Canterbury. Then he framed an oath in certain prescribed words, which was afterwards taken and observed by each advocate of that court who was admitted. The Bishop of Exeter, however, pursued his appeal to the pope against the Archbishop with great diligence. But when he saw that his position was not only less favourable but harder, because the King had attached himself to the Archbishop, he abandoned the appeal and fled as a suppliant to the Archbishop. Acknowledging both his fault and the authority, jurisdiction and prerogative of the Archbishop, he obtained pardon for his rashness and contumacy, confessing that he had submitted to a reconciliation rather than to a judgment. The Bishop of Salisbury, when he was to be visited, took up the same spirit and purpose of resisting the Archbishop, but he acted more cautiously and prudently in law, as it seemed to him. For when the Archbishop thought he was supported in visiting by the authority of Pope Urban alone, the Bishop, after Urban's death, obtained from his successor Boniface a privilege for himself and for the subjects of his diocese that they should not be visited by virtue of Urban's letters, thinking that archiepiscopal and metropolitan authority and jurisdiction could not stand unless the Pope gave help. But the Archbishop, more skilled in law, more certain from practice and experience, and more favoured at court and in the Roman curia, when the Bishop of Salisbury came to him at his manor of Croydon with the papal privilege by which he thought himself exempt from the right of visitation, at once put forward his decree and had it recorded before a notary that he would visit the Bishop of Salisbury and his whole diocese with metropolitan authority. Then by his public edict and mandate he warned the Bishop to undergo the metropolitan visitation in his cathedral church at Salisbury on the day fixed and appointed, making no word or mention of Urban's grant. On that day the Bishop, imprudently secure in his empty privilege, was absent, and he repeatedly appealed against the Archbishop's visitation, which he claimed had been begun as a grievance inflicted on himself and his subjects. The Archbishop did not treat this contumacy with the same moderation he had shown towards the Bishop of Exeter, but at once excommunicated him. Then he sued him for perjury and contempt, because he had withdrawn from the subjection to the Archbishop of Canterbury that he had promised by oath at his consecration, by obtaining privileges and by appealing. The Bishop of Salisbury, broken by this unrelenting severity and by the recent example of his fellow bishop of Exeter, and having to give way in law, renounced his appeals. At the entreaty of the most distinguished man, the Earl of Salisbury, and some others, he submitted himself and was received back into the Archbishop's favour. Then he underwent the Archbishop's visitation quietly and peacefully, and from then on no suffragan contended with the Archbishop over the right of visitation. He visited the remaining dioceses without trouble. Only in Lincoln did he cease visiting certain monks, through the favour and intercession of the Abbot of St Albans at Oxford. With the visitation completed, he rested somewhat.

units.la: Hoc anno exorti sunt efficænati quidam & audaciores clerici, qui sibi licere affirmabant nonos præsbiteros atque clericos more pontificum creare, & sacros ordines celebrare. Eademque ie in Ecclesiastica administratione, potestate prædictos assereb ant qua Episcopi. Itaque multis manus non dicam sacras sed temerarias imponebant, qui eodem factu arrogantiaque ducti eandem Ecclesiasticæ potestatis æqualitatem sibi cum summis pontificibus communem vendicabant. Anno autem sequenti illud cœtu papales prouisiones statutum tenuatum est, quod toties iarum & repetitum, quia siue Papæ dolo ac potentia, siue clericorum amentia obseruatum non est, grauiori pœna sancitum est, vt quihuiusmodi prouisiones procurarent, tanquam rebellionis tei caeteribus includantur. Tum Rex edictum in toto Regno propoluit vt Angli qui in curia Romana beneficia sibi a Papa conferri procurabant redirent. Quo accepto Romam deferunt atque reuertuntur. Papa verò cômotus quod ab Anglis qui sua limina maximè frequentabant, esset desertus, Abbatem quendam callidum in Anglliam ecleriter proficisci iussit, vt & causas Anglorum diseffionis exploraret, & Angliæ Regem in Gallium commoueret. Is subdolus Regem conuenit. Papæ salutem Regi dicit, eius benevolentiam exponit, mirari se multum ait cur illa iura de prouisionibus, quare Impedit, & præmunire facias, achuiusmodi in Romanæ Ecclesiæ præiudicium ac detrimentum lata permittantur, petit vt abrogentur. Si id proceres egre ferant, non de Rege sed de Papa quærantur. Tum Gallum Antipapæ fauere, & eodem fœdere iungi suadet vt Rex eum bello petat, fore vt Gallus succumbat, quia Papa cum excommunicaturus, eiusque Regnum interdicto suppositurus est. Hæc Abbas Papæ nuncius. Rex verò petiit vt donec Parlamentum conuocetur, in Anglia maneat. Id Abbas haud grauare fecit multis clericorum donis muneribusque definitus. Parlamento conuocato interrogatum est vt tela contra papales prouisiones & similia iura tollantur, cuitam militès Parlamentum rare sint. Circa hæc tempora mirum in modum creuit eorum numerus qui Wickliffo assensi sunt, vt non modo plebs sed nobiles proceresque Regni exi·stimabantur his opinionibus imbui, quas Wickliffiani prædicabant. Multaque in opprobrium & dedecus Episcoporum atque Cleri dicta, edicta, scripta ac diuulgata sunt, quæ vix comprimi authoritate regia potuerunt. Id scriptores Episcoporum ignauiæ atque socordiæ tribuuntquos sciunt quæ sua fuerunt, non quæ Iesu Christi quæsiuisse. Ipse Archiepiscopus etsi Ecclesiasticas opes annuis solutionibus indies exhauriri senserat, tamen obtinuit à papa vt suæ prouinciæ clerus de singulis, 2.o.s. quatuor denarios sibi soluant. Hancli centiam Papæ Archiepiscopus Eboracensis & Episcopus Londinensis executi sunt. Lineolniensis autem ab hoc tributo ad Papam appellauit. Qua appellatione pendente Archiepiscopus postquam quindecim annis. 11. mensibus & biduo sedisset pridie Cal. Aug. apud Maidestone obiit. Vbi demolito veteri opere collegium seculariū sacerdotum extruxit ac fundauit. Tum Ecclesiam de Mepham collapsam ad vsus infirmorum fratrum redintegrauit, iuxtaque eum quatuor nouas ædes extruxit. Ecclesiæ Cant. ad reparationem nauis Ecclesiæ, claustri, & murorum mille marcas legauit. Item imaginem argenteam & deauratam Trinitatis cum sex Apostolis circumstantibus pondëris. 160.li. Album vestimentum cum sex cappis, vitide vestimentum cum 7. cappis, libroque permultos. In ecclesia Cantuariensi iuxta feretrum Thomæ Becket ex australi parte sepultus iacet.
units.tr: This year some ambitious and bolder clergy arose, who claimed that they might create priests and clerks in the manner of the bishops and celebrate holy orders. They also asserted that they possessed the same power in ecclesiastical administration as the bishops. Accordingly they laid hands on many, not sacred but rash, and, led by this same act and arrogance, they claimed for themselves the same equality of ecclesiastical power that the supreme pontiffs shared. In the following year the statute concerning papal provisions, which had been often enacted and repeated but was not observed, either through the Pope's deceit and power or through the folly of the clergy, was sanctioned again with a heavier penalty: those who procured such provisions were to be counted among rebels, together with the others. Then the King published an edict throughout the whole realm that the English who were procuring benefices for themselves from the Pope in the Roman curia should return home. On receiving this, they went to Rome and came back. The Pope, moved that he had been deserted by the English, who had most often frequented his threshold, ordered a certain shrewd Abbot to set out secretly for England, both to explore the reasons for the English estrangement and to win the King of England over to France. This crafty man met the King. He conveyed the Pope's greetings to the King, set out his goodwill, and said he greatly wondered why those laws about provisions, about the right of presentation and the statute of praemunire were allowed to stand, to the prejudice and detriment of the Roman Church, and he asked that they be repealed. If the nobles took this badly, they should complain not of the King but of the Pope. He then urged that the King join France, favouring the antipope in the same alliance, so that the King might attack the Frenchman in war, and it would come about that the Frenchman would be overthrown, because the Pope was about to excommunicate him and place his kingdom under interdict. Such was the Abbot, the Pope's messenger. The King, however, asked him to remain in England until Parliament should be summoned. The Abbot, loaded with many gifts and bribes from the clergy, did not object to this. When Parliament was summoned, it was asked that the weapons against papal provisions and similar rights be removed. Around this time the number of those who had assented to Wycliffe grew wonderfully, so that not only the common people but the nobles and magnates of the realm were thought to be steeped in those opinions which the Wycliffites preached. Many things were said, edicted, written and published to the shame and disgrace of the bishops and clergy, which could hardly be suppressed by royal authority. The writers who favour the bishops attribute this to the idleness and sloth of the bishops, whose concern was for what was their own, not for what belonged to Jesus Christ. The Archbishop himself, though he perceived that the church's wealth was being drained away day by day by the annual payments, nevertheless obtained from the pope that the clergy of his province should pay him four pence from each two shillings. The Archbishop of York and the Bishop of London carried out this order of the Pope. The Bishop of Lincoln, however, appealed to the Pope against this tax. While this appeal was pending, the Archbishop, having sat for fifteen years, eleven months and two days, died at Maidstone on the day before the Kalends of August. There, having pulled down the old building, he founded and built a college of secular priests. He also restored the church of Mepham, which had collapsed, for the use of the sick brethren, and beside it built four new houses. He left a thousand marks to the church of Canterbury for the repair of the nave, the cloister and the walls; likewise an image of the Trinity, silver and gilt, with six Apostles standing around it, weighing 160 pounds; a white vestment with six copes, a green vestment with seven copes, and very many books. He lies buried in the church of Canterbury, on the south side, beside the shrine of Thomas Becket.

units.la: LX. Thomas Arundel.
units.tr: LX. Thomas Arundel.

units.la: Antuariensis Ecclesiæ monachis, fratribus, ac plebeiis Clericis tot seculis pene vsu capta, à nobilibus tandem & illustribus viris occupata est. Nam mortuo Willihelmo Courtenay cuius Archiepiscopatus tranquille & quiete transiatus est, Thom. Arundele origine ac generis clarissimo, Thomas Arundel. Hic patrem habuit Arundellia Comitem, & adolescens theologia deditus Clericali ordine initiatus gessit Archidiaconatum Taunton. Tum cum subdiaconus tantum esset ad Eliensem Episcopatum electus, inde ad Eboracensem Metropolim, ac demum ad Cantuariensem prouisione papali perueniit. Cuius prouisionis bulla 11. Ianuarii Cantuariæ publicata est. Deinde D. Henricus Chillinden Cantuariensis Prior crucem Archiepiscopalem in Ecclesia Westmonasterienſi Regę ac proceribus præsentibus vsitata illa & concepta verborum formula quam in Wilhelmo Courtnay supra retulimus, tradidit. Et decimo Februarii proximo ab Wilhelmo Wickam Wintoniensi Episcopo pallium accepit. Tum Cantuariensis profectus decimonono eiusdem mensis magnis sumptibus & solita magnificentia inthronizatus est. Eo die Cleri synodus Londini conuenit. Quam Edmundus Stafford Exoniensis Episcopus Regni Cancellarius ad finem eius mensis prorogauit. In hac synodo scholares Oxonienses querelâ contra Thomam Hyndman Vniuersitatis Cancellarium, & Nicolaum Faux eius commissarium proposuerunt.
units.tr: The church of Canterbury, held for almost so many centuries by monks, brethren and plebeian clergy, was at last seized by noblemen and illustrious men. For after William Courtenay died, whose archbishopric had passed peacefully and quietly, Thomas Arundel, of the most distinguished origin and birth, succeeded. He had as his father the Earl of Arundel. As a young man devoted to theology, he was admitted to the clerical order and held the archdeaconry of Taunton. While he was still only a subdeacon, he was elected to the bishopric of Ely, then moved to the metropolitan see of York, and at last reached Canterbury by papal provision. The bull of this provision was published at Canterbury on 11 January. Then Dom Henry Chillenden, prior of Canterbury, handed over the archiepiscopal cross in Westminster church, with the king and nobles present, using that customary and formulaic wording which we related above concerning William Courtenay. On 10 February following, he received the pallium from William Wickham, bishop of Winchester. Then, setting out for Canterbury, he was enthroned there on the nineteenth day of the same month, with great expense and his customary magnificence. On that day the synod of the clergy met at London, which Edmund Stafford, bishop of Exeter and chancellor of the realm, prorogued to the end of that month. In this synod the Oxford scholars lodged a complaint against Thomas Hyndman, chancellor of the University, and Nicholas Faux, his commissary.

units.la: Quod exemptionis iura quibus ab Archiepiscopali & Episcopali iurisdictione Vniuersitas fiat immunis a Papa impetrassent, non modo in Metropolitani & Ordinarii, sed in Ipsius Vniuersitatis prætudicium atque grauamen. Quod priuilegium seruitutis potius quam libertatis instar esse docebant.
units.tr: They complained that the rights of exemption, by which the University is made immune from archiepiscopal and episcopal jurisdiction, had been obtained from the Pope not only to the prejudice and burden of the metropolitan and the ordinary, but also to the prejudice and burden of the University itself. They taught that this privilege was more like a form of servitude than of liberty.

units.la: Cum enim antea si iniquis Cancellarij aut Procancellarij imperiis opprimerentur, aut iniuriis afficerentur, appellationibus & Archiepiscopali ac quitate subuenum eis sunt, nec in vnius potestatem redacti, à quo nec permissa esset prouocatio, nec superioris iurisdictione possit coerceri, quasi perpetuæ seruituti subiacerent. Itaque ab Archiepiscopo petierunt vt quoniam suam in eos iurisdictionem agnoscerent, & antecedess sui Wilhelmi Courtnay moderationem atque prudentiam, cum Academiam Oxoniensem tam in capite quam in membris visitaret expertiessent, vt ea à Cancellario eiusque Commissario procuras priuilegia rescinderet.
units.tr: For previously, if they were oppressed by the unjust commands of the chancellor or pro-chancellor, or wronged in any way, they had been helped by appeals and by the equity of the archbishop. But now, reduced to the power of one man, from whom no appeal was permitted and who could not be restrained by any higher jurisdiction, they were as if bound to perpetual servitude. Therefore they asked the archbishop that, since he acknowledged his jurisdiction over them, and since they had experienced the moderation and prudence of his predecessor William Courtenay when he visited the University of Oxford both in head and in members, he would rescind the privileges that the chancellor and his commissary had procured.

units.la: Quibus ipsi interposito ad id Michaele Sergeaux iuris utriusque Doctore legitimo procuratore expresse atque publice in synodo renunciarunt. Eam renunciationem Archiepiscopus ratam habuit, & exemptionis Oxoniensis priuilegia irrita & inania iudicauit.
units.tr: To this end they had appointed Michael Sergeaux, a lawful proctor and doctor of both laws, who expressly and publicly renounced these privileges in the synod. The archbishop approved that renunciation and judged the privileges of Oxford's exemption void and of no force.

units.la: Tum Cancellarius quasi furore actus, petulanter ac immodeste se abdicauit magistratu, synodoque sine venia discessit; sed Archiepiscopus eum edicto reuocauit, eiusque proteruiam atque audaciam repressit. In eadem synodo Doctores Oxonienses quasdam Iohannis Wiceleffi opiniones exposuerunt, quas synodus eosdem omisit.
units.tr: Then the chancellor, as if driven by fury, wantonly and shamelessly resigned his office and left the synod without leave. But the archbishop recalled him by edict and repressed his insolence and audacity. In the same synod the Oxford doctors set out certain opinions of John Wycliffe, which the synod passed over.

units.la: Londini veterem quandam de soluendis decimis constitutionem à Simone Nigro Londinensi quondam Episcopo latam renouauit.
units.tr: At London he renewed an old constitution concerning the payment of tithes, enacted by Simon Niger, formerly bishop of London.

units.la: Litera Regiæ ad Episcopum Romanum aduersus Thomam Arundel.
units.tr: A letter of the King to the Roman Bishop against Thomas Arundel.

units.la: Homas proditionis non expers nostræ Regiæ maiestati insidias fabricauit, pro cuius demeritis, imo potius inexplicabilibus maleficiis is æternum solum est pæs exilium, qui pati potius debuit & merito prodi toris supplicium, vnde Dei reuerentia suit propicia nostræ maiestas regia, de quo doleat eadem Regia Celsitudo, dolent etiam & mirantur omnes & singuli Regni nostri. Cum tam intellexissent eundem Thomam ad veltrae sanctitatis praesentiam evocarum, & talibus consolatoriis sermonibus ipsum ut dicitur animaftis, quod ad eadem beneficia vel maiora infra nostrum Regnum vel [?]altem in partibus nostris ditioni subditis se credit verisimiliter promoueri, & in his & in aliis sedis Apostolicae communiri. Quod quam directe & immediate contra statum nostrum & Regni nostri pacificam gubernationem, ac manifestum periculum quod silentio praeterimus tenderet, vita nostra comite nullatenus tolerabimus, & sicut mundus ad hoc quomodo libet confentiret. Nouimus etiam hunc hominem ad medullas, nouimus eius animum (impatiente quidem pacis cuiuslibet) qui ad inuerterias imaginationes nobis suspectissimus totam intentionis suae congeriem etsi non publice, tamen per fuisse velamina si liberum ad partes nostras poterit habere recursum inter nostros ligeos deriuabit. Praeuideat igitur sancti apostolatus veltri discretione hac in parte tale praeiudicium contra mentem praeferum nostram & conscientiam nobis quod tum vix credere possumus inferatur, per quod inter sacerdotium & Regnum scandalorum materia valeat exoriri, quae forsan tam leuiter sopiri non potent, sicut ex causa inhonesta inconsultius generari. Vt enim plano non scio sermone loquamur, amicus autem nobis beneuolus esse non poterit qui notoris in inimicis dextras exhibet siue confert. Alibi namque si vobis placuerit satis sibi prouidere poteris, dum tamen nostro manum non inniterit in catino. Quod enim in partibus a nobis distantibus & remotis sibi prout vobis placuerit prouidcatis, Regia maiestas aequanimiter poterit tolerare. Hanc quaesumus materiam cordi teneriter commendetis, prout voluntatis quod Regia deuotio ad veltrae voluntatis beneplacita vehementius accendatur. Et sic nec Papa nec Cardinales valebant Regiae maiestati consentire. Sed Thomas Waldane tunc London. Episcopo & thesaurario Angliae ad instantiam Regis concessi Papa successionem sedis Cantuariae.
units.tr: Thomas, not without guilt of treason, has laid snares against our royal majesty. For his demerits, or rather his inexplicable crimes, he deserves eternal exile, and he ought rather to suffer the punishment of a traitor, which he has rightly earned. Therefore our royal majesty has been merciful out of reverence for God, and that royal highness grieves over the matter, as do all and each of our kingdom, who also marvel at it. When they had learned that this same Thomas was being summoned into your holiness's presence, and, as is said, was being encouraged with such comforting words, that for the same or greater benefices within our kingdom, or at least in the parts subject to our dominion, he might reasonably expect promotion, and be strengthened in these and other things by the Apostolic See, they judged that this would tend directly and immediately against our state and the peaceful government of our realm, and would be a manifest danger, which we pass over in silence. While we live, we shall in no way tolerate it, though the whole world should consent to it in whatever way. We know this man to the marrow, and we know his mind, impatient indeed of any peace. Most suspect to us for his restless schemes, he will draw the whole heap of his purpose, though not openly yet under some covers, among our liegemen, if he can have free recourse to our parts. Let your holiness of the apostolate therefore foresee, in your discretion, that no such prejudice be inflicted on our mind and conscience, which we can scarcely believe, whereby matter for scandal may arise between the priesthood and the kingdom, which perhaps cannot be so lightly quieted, having been generated so ill-advisedly from a dishonourable cause. For, to speak plainly, one who shows or extends his right hand to notorious enemies cannot be a benevolent friend to us. Elsewhere, if it please you, you may provide for him well enough, provided only that he does not lean his hand upon our dish. What you may provide for him, as you please, in parts distant and remote from us, the royal majesty can bear with equanimity. We beg you to commend this matter tenderly to your heart, so that royal devotion may be more eagerly kindled to the pleasure of your will. And so neither the Pope nor the cardinals were able to agree to the royal majesty. But Roger Walden, then bishop of London and treasurer of England, at the king's instance obtained from the Pope the succession to the see of Canterbury.

units.la: Quibus litteris Papa deterritus, non modo Thomam Arundell non promouit, sed Rege postulante Rogerum Walden Eboracensem Decanum & Londinensem Episcopum Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum creauit. Hic toto tempore quo Thomas exilio multatus peregrinatus est, sepro Archiepiscopo gessit, synodos celebrauit, constitutiones nonnullas prouincialis tulit, inter quas vnade obseruandis feriis inter eas 3 edita est quas Wilhelmus Lyndwoode congessit & diuulgauit. Tum Papa postquam Regi in Rogero Walden promouendo placuisse atque gratum fecisse visus sit, coepit ptoulsotiam suam potestatem in creandis & transferendis Episcopis declarare. Iohannem Lincolniensem Episcopum ad Episcopatum Ceftriae tunc vacanem transtulit.
units.tr: Frightened by these letters, the Pope not only did not promote Thomas Arundel, but at the king's request he created Roger Walden, dean of York and bishop of London, archbishop of Canterbury. During the whole time that Thomas was wandering in exile, Walden held the see as archbishop, celebrated synods, and issued several provincial constitutions, among which one concerning the observance of holy days was edited and published by William Lyndwood. Then, after the Pope seemed to have pleased and gratified the king by promoting Roger Walden, he began to display his power in creating and transferring bishops. He transferred John, bishop of Lincoln, to the see of Chester, which was then vacant.

units.la: Lincolniensem Episcopatum Henrico Beuford Iohannis Lancastriae ducis ex Katharina Swinford filio vt sibi ducem deuinciret, contulit. Sed Lincolniensis cedere potius quam tam ambitiosam patitransitionem maluit. Itaque ea spreta ingressus Monasterium Cantuariensis cum Monachis reliquum vitae curriculum peregit. Eo itaque cedente frater quidam praedicatorum qui Regis confessor fuerat a Landauensi Episcopatu ad Ceftrensem translatus est. Rex cum animadverteret Papam absolutam quadam & ef fraenatam in sui Regni Episcopatibus disponendis vti potestate, clerum conuocauit, & ab his quaesiuit, An Papae liceret arbitrio atque voluntate sua quocunque vellet cteare atque transferre Episcopos. Clerus cui tum nephas fuit de Papae potestate detrahere aut dubitare, Regiis interrogatis directe non respondit. Sed fuaslit vt Rex quasi Cleri populique sui Regni supplicationibus instigatus papam suis literis rogaret, vt a talibus transllationibus, collatio nibusque pro commodo Ecclesiae Ciuitatis deliberet. At Rex accepto tam pusillo & inerti a clero responsio in papam motus iurauit. Quod si Papae in hoc negocio constanter Clerus resisteret, se in eorum auxilium Regiam manum admouisse. Venit ad Regem eo tempore Petrus de Bosco Aquensis Episcopus Papae nuncius, egitque vt Rex permitteret suis subditis a Papa beneficiorum prouisiones acquirere, & statuta contra prouisiones breuiaque de quare impedit, & praemunire facias retraucarent. Sed Rex ob populi procerumque potestatem qui contra vehementer niterentur, id ne suae quidem esse potestatis respondit. Itaque eum re infecta dimisit. Hoc anno Romae repertus est thesaurus Helenae matris Constantini primi Christiani Caesaris in numis auteis Helenae effigie percussus. Huius thesauri magnitudine Papa capitolium & castellum S. Angeli Romae construxit. Sub haec tempora Rex Iohannes Lancastriae duce mortuo Henricum eius filium ad haeredem, quem antea in Hiberniam relegatum, perpetuo damnatur exilio, & ipse multis pecuniis magnisque copiis collectis ad supplicium de Hibernis fumendum qui Marchiae Comitem trucidassent profectus est. Interea Henricus dux Lancastriæ se cum Thoma Arundell Archiepiscopo & eius nepote anteinterempti comitis Arundelliæ filio in mutuo exilio se coniunxit. Qui coniunctus & comparatis copiis Angliâ ingrediuntur, & primò Wilhelmũ Scroope I hefau ranum, aliosq; Regis cõsiliatios, quorum improbis tuatiionibus, & se proscriptos & multa à Rege perperam ac in Reip. detrimentum gesta coniuxerant, Bristoliæ captos securiferiunt. Rex nunciata hac turba in Angliam festinat. Interim dux Lancastriæ grādem exercitum sexaginta millium conflarat, & omnium pene animos à Rege tantis tributis alienatos, sibi conciliarat. Rex in his angustiis non minus armatam hostium vim quàm suorum fugam & defectionem pertimescens petiit cum Thoma Arundel Archiepiscopo quem in exilium miserat atque proscripserat, colloquium. In eo colloquio, Regno cedere se paratum ait, si vitæ securitas sibi fiat, victufq; reliquo vitæ spacio honorificus suppeditetur. Eaq; conditione se reddidit in Ducis Lancastriæ potestatē. Tum Bonifacius Papacū Regem à duce Lancastriæ superatum acceperat, Rogerum Walden tanquam inuasoré atq; prædonem de Archiepiscopali Celsitudine postquàm eam duobus annis occupasset, deiecit, eò quòd præsumpserat ascendere cubile viuētis patris sui, restituitq; per literas bullatas in Archiepiscopatum Thomam Arundell, totiusq; rei crimen atque odinm in Regem & Rogerum Walden à quibus deceptum se ac circumuentum conqueritur, conuertit. Postea cum Richardus Rex Eborac. Archiepiscopo & Herefordensi Episcopo procuratoribus suis constituris in Parlamento sese renogno abdicasset, eaque abdicatio omnium in Parlamento præsentium apertis votis ac suffragiis rata esset, Henricus Lancastriæ Dux regnum hæreditatis proximitate ilico in Parlamento vendicauit. Cui ab omnibus assensum est. Tuncab Archiepiscopo Thoma Arundell manum eius dextram tenente ad Regale solium ductus, in eoque collocatus est, & Archiepiscopus sumpto hoc scripturarum themate. Vir dominabitur in populo eius, magnanimitatem ac virtutem in Parlamenti concione laudauit. Deinde eundem Westmonasterii die Lunæ in quo Edwardi Regis confessoris commemoratio celebrabatur, in frequentissimo omnium ordinum vndiq; applaudentium cætu coronauit. Ac dum Parlamentum Westmonasterii habitum est, Thomas Archiepiscopus in Ecclesia Paulina Synodum celebrauit. Ad eam Northumbriæ & Westmerlandiæ Comites à Rege missi sunt. Qui Clero indicabant non se ad pecuniās exigendas à Rege venisse, sed vt Regis in Clerum & Ecclesiasticam libertatem beneuolentiam declararent. Qui omnes Ecclesiæ immunitates Regia potestate tuiturus est, & hæreticos sibiq; aduersos quorumcunque his quibus Clerus optaret suppliciis affecturus. Itaque petiit vt pro sua regnique salute preces assiduas effundant Domino. Archiepiscopus Cleri nomine magnas vicissim Regi reddit gratias, petiitq; vt autoritate Regia papales prouisiones & præsentiones tolleret, quibus effectum vt viri docti in Academiis studentes, cū præmia indignis & ambitiosis ea Romæ querentibus darentur, studia deserent, & infcitia doctrinam expelleret.
