Eius se mali remedium inuenturum Rex pollicitus est, Rogerus autem Walden sede Archiepiscopali motus in Episcopali ordine & charactere priuatus aliquandiu in luctu gemituq; sine Episcopatu vlloue publico administrando munere delituit. Tandem Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi benignitate ad Londinensem Episcopatum promotus primo suæ consecrationis anno obiit. Multi deinde vno alterdque anno in Regem inteştini motus facti sunt. Quibus sedatis Rex viduam Iohannis de Montefracto Ducis minoris Britanniæ quondā vxorem sibi matrimonio coniunxit. Ea à Cantuar. Archiepiscopo Westmonasterii Regi nupta & coronata fuit. Post quas nuptias ortæst alia noua quorundam procerum in Regem coniuratio, qui vt vulgus commouerent, & ad res nouas moliendas accenderent, Richardum Regem Regno inuitum & coactum cessisse, sed tamen superstitem esse, atque bellicas vbiq; copias ad recuperandum Regni ius parare fingunt. Quibus captis, vltimoque supplicio affectis, & depositio tumultu Parlamentum Londini congregatum est. Tum Clerus Archicpiscopo iubente in Synodum eodem conuenit. Inchoata Synodo Northumbriæ, Westmerlandiæ, ac Worcestriæ Comites, & Thomas Herpingham Camerarius Angliæ ingressi Synodum Regias angustias & necessitatem exponunt, opem à Clero postulant. Paucis inde diebus clerus bonorum decimam pollicetur, & à Rege in Parlamento pro Clericis laicali seu Regio foro conuictis statutum ferri obtinuit. Tum Archiepiscopus constitutionem Simonis Islippe de clericis conuictis ante commemoratam obseruari præcepit, & quosdā Londinenses Wiclifianas opiniones vt hæreticas detestari, atq; abiurare compulit. Conciliumq; statim dissoluit. Atq; anno sequenti repetita iterum synodo, akeraque decima à Clero Regi præstitaest. Sed Milites & Burgenses Parlamenti cum præstare iuxta suas copias atque facultates Regi nollent, clerum tanquam omniũ hæreditatum, bonorumq; inuatorem & posse ssorem accusarunt, a quibus nisi temporalia subtrahantur, non posse laicos Regis necessitatibus subuenire ostenderunt. Quibus respondit Archiepiscopus, clericos semper Regi amplius multo quã laicos, scepiuiq; Decimas quã hos, Quintasdecimas Regi pe ssoluisse. Tum etsi abessent Abbatiq; Cleriei, tamen suos colonos atque famulos Regi in omnibus bellis atque præliis pari aur maiori numero quam laicorum adesse, ac insuper ne domi ociosos esse cum pro Regis regnique sui socolumitate bello atque pace quotidianas preces agerent.
units.tr: The bishopric of Lincoln was bestowed on Henry Beaufort, son of John, Duke of Lancaster, by Katherine Swynford, in order to bind the duke to himself. But the Bishop of Lincoln preferred to withdraw rather than endure so ambitious a transfer. Rejecting it, he entered the monastery at Canterbury and spent the rest of his life there among the monks. When he had withdrawn, a certain friar of the Preachers, who had been the king's confessor, was translated from the bishopric of Llandaff to that of Chester. The king, observing that the Pope exercised an absolute and unbridled power in disposing of the bishoprics of his realm, summoned the clergy and asked them whether it was lawful for the Pope to create and transfer bishops at his own pleasure and whim. The clergy, for whom it was then wicked to detract from or doubt the papal power, did not answer the king's question directly. Instead they advised that the king, as though moved by the petitions of the clergy and people of his realm, should ask the Pope by letter to consider, for the good of the Church and the commonwealth, refraining from such translations and collations. But the king, receiving so feeble and spiritless a reply from the clergy, was roused against the Pope and swore that if the clergy resisted the Pope steadfastly in this matter, he would lay his royal hand to their aid. At that time Peter de Bosco, Bishop of Acqui, the Pope's envoy, came to the king and urged that the king permit his subjects to obtain papal provisions to benefices, and that the statutes against provisions and the writs of quare impedit and praemunire facias be repealed. But the king replied that this was not even within his own power, on account of the power of the people and the nobles, who strongly opposed it. And so he dismissed him with his business undone. In this year at Rome a treasure of Helena, mother of Constantine the first Christian emperor, was discovered, consisting of gold coins stamped with the likeness of Helena. From the great size of this treasure the Pope built the Capitol and the castle of St Angelo at Rome. About this time King John, after the death of John, Duke of Lancaster, condemned Henry, his son and heir, who had previously been relegated to Ireland, to perpetual exile; and himself, having gathered much money and great forces, set out to take vengeance on the Irish who had slain the Earl of March. Meanwhile Henry, Duke of Lancaster, joined himself in mutual exile with Thomas Arundel, Archbishop, and with the nephew of the Earl of Arundel, who had been executed, that is, the son of that earl. Joined together and having assembled forces, they entered England, and first seized at Bristol William Scrope, Earl of Wiltshire, and other councillors of the king, by whose wicked counsels they, having been proscribed and having been driven into exile, had been provoked to many things done wrongly by the king and to the detriment of the commonwealth; and they put them to the axe. When this disturbance was reported, the king hastened into England. Meanwhile the Duke of Lancaster had gathered a great army of sixty thousand men, and had won over to himself almost the minds of all, who had been alienated from the king by such heavy taxes. The king, in these straits, fearing no less the armed strength of his enemies than the flight and defection of his own men, asked for a conference with Thomas Arundel, the archbishop whom he had sent into exile and proscribed. In that conference he said that he was ready to give up the kingdom, provided that his life was secured and that an honourable maintenance was supplied to him for the rest of his life. On this condition he surrendered himself into the power of the Duke of Lancaster. Then Boniface the Pope, having received word that the king had been overcome by the Duke of Lancaster, cast down from the archiepiscopal dignity Roger Walden, as an usurper and robber, after he had occupied it for two years, because he had presumed to climb into the bed of his living father; and by bulled letters he restored Thomas Arundel to the archbishopric, and turned the whole blame and hatred of the matter upon the king and Roger Walden, by whom he complained that he had been deceived and circumvented. Afterwards, when Richard the king had resigned his realm in Parliament, through his proctors appointed for this purpose, the Archbishop of York and the Bishop of Hereford, and this abdication had been ratified by the open votes and suffrages of all present in Parliament, Henry, Duke of Lancaster, straightway claimed the kingdom in Parliament by right of hereditary proximity. To him assent was given by all. Then, led by Archbishop Thomas Arundel, who held his right hand, he was conducted to the royal throne and seated upon it; and the archbishop, taking this theme from Scripture, A man shall rule over his people, praised his magnanimity and virtue in a sermon to Parliament. Then on the Monday on which the commemoration of King Edward the Confessor was celebrated, he crowned him at Westminster in the presence of a very full assembly of all orders, who applauded on every side. And while Parliament was being held at Westminster, Archbishop Thomas held a synod in St Paul's church. To it the Earls of Northumberland and Westmorland were sent by the king. They told the clergy that they had not come to exact money from them on the king's behalf, but to declare the king's goodwill towards the clergy and ecclesiastical liberty; that he would, by royal power, defend all the immunities of the Church, and would visit heretics and those opposed to them with whatever punishments the clergy might wish. And so they asked that the clergy pour out constant prayers to the Lord for their own and the realm's safety. The archbishop, on behalf of the clergy, gave great thanks to the king in return, and asked that by royal authority he would abolish the papal provisions and presentations, by which it had come about that learned men studying in the universities, while rewards were given to the unworthy and the ambitious who sought them at Rome, abandoned their studies, and ignorance drove out learning. The king promised that he would find a remedy for this evil. But Roger Walden, moved from the archiepiscopal seat, was deprived of his episcopal order and character, and for some time lay hidden in grief and sighing, without a bishopric or any public office to administer. At last, through the kindness of the Archbishop of Canterbury, he was promoted to the bishopric of London, and died in the first year of his consecration. Afterwards, in one year or two, many seditious movements were made against the king. When these were quelled, the king married the widow of John de Montfort, formerly wife of the Duke of Lesser Britain. She was married to the king and crowned at Westminster by the Archbishop of Canterbury. After these nuptials there arose another new conspiracy of certain nobles against the king, who, in order to stir up the common people and kindle them to undertake new affairs, pretended that King Richard had been forced against his will to resign the kingdom, but that he was still alive, and that military forces everywhere were being prepared to recover the right of the realm. When these men had been seized and put to the last punishment, and the tumult was put down, Parliament was assembled at London. Then the clergy, at the archbishop's command, came together in synod on the same occasion. When the synod had begun, the Earls of Northumberland, Westmorland and Worcester, and Thomas Erpingham, Chamberlain of England, came in, set out the king's straitened circumstances and need, and asked the clergy for help. A few days later the clergy promised a tenth of their goods, and obtained from the king, in Parliament, a statute to be passed concerning clerics convicted in the lay or royal court. Then the archbishop ordered that the constitution of Simon Islip concerning convicted clerics, mentioned above, be observed, and compelled certain Londoners holding Wycliffite opinions to detest them as heretical and to abjure them. And he at once dissolved the council. And in the following year, the synod being reconvened, a further tenth was paid to the king by the clergy. But the knights and burgesses of Parliament, since they were unwilling to contribute to the king according to their means and resources, accused the clergy as the usurpers and possessors of all inheritances and goods, and showed that unless temporal goods were taken from them, the laity could not relieve the king's needs. To these charges the archbishop replied that the clergy had always paid to the king far more than the laity, and had paid tenths where the laity paid fifteenths. Moreover, although the abbots and clergy were absent, their tenants and servants were present in all the king's wars and battles in equal or greater number than the laity; and besides, they were not idle at home, since they offered daily prayers for the king's safety and for the security of his realm in war and in peace.

units.la: Et cum hæc prolocutor militum vultu voceque prætendisset publicè se preces Ecclesiæ paruipendere: iam, inquit Dominus Cantuariensis, video manifeste quorsum s teodit Regni fortuna, exclusis vilipensisque suffragiis quibus diuinitas placari solet. Certe nunquam fuit diu Regnum stabile quod vacauit a precibus & deuotione. Attamen tu qui vilipendis cleri religionem, ne tu putes impune direpturum Ecclesiæ possessionem. Erat autem prolocutor miles, dictus Iohannes Cleyne, qui vt fertur, militiam sortemque Christi deferens, in sortem Martis apostacando transierat. Nam, pro vt dicunt, Diaconus fuerat ordinatus, nulla tamen, vt resiliret dispensatione licentiatus. Archiepiscopus inter hæc Regem nutantem considerans, surrexit genusexo coram Rege, rogauit vt attenderet primitiũ am propositum suum, quod cuius bet seruaret iura propria proposse suo, attenderet & iuramentum quod non inuitus præstiterat, videlicet quod Ecclesiam ministrosque eius honoraret, foueret, & manu teneret, attenderet & periculum iuramenti siut, dedecus violati, & Ecclesiam gaudere permitteret suis priuilegiis & libertatibus quibus gauisa est antecessorum suorum temporibus, vereretur offendere Regem perquem Reges regnant, vereretur & censuras quas incurrunt qui res Ecclesiasticas depredantur, quo omnes constar excommunicationis sententia in nodari. His a Cantuariensi prolatis, Rex præcepit ei repetere sedem suam asserens voluntatis suæ sore, Ecclesiam in adeo bono statu dimittere sicuti eam inuenerat vel potius meliori. Archiepiscopus concionatus militibus dixit: vos inquit & vestri similes consiliũ dedistis domino nostro Regi Modernô, & antecessoribus suis vt confiscarent bona Cellarum quæ Gallici vel Normanni possederunt in Anglia, dicentes ei per hæc diuitias accumulandas in magna copia, & quidem pro vt valent multa fului metalli millia, sed tamen constat hodie Regem non esse ditiorem dimidia quidem marca, vobis vel extorquentibus vel emendicantibus de manu sua, & vobismet appropriantibus ducta bona, vnde potest conuinci vos non pro Regis utilitate, sed pro vestra cupiditate temporalia iura petere. Quia proculdubio si Rex (quod ab sit) vestro satisfaceret exerecando propositũ, non esset opulentior vno quadrante sequenti anno.
units.tr: When the prolocutor of the soldiers, with his face and voice, had publicly pretended to make little of the Church's prayers, the Lord of Canterbury said: "I see plainly where the fortune of the realm is heading, since the votes by which the Deity is usually propitiated have been shut out and despised. Certainly a kingdom that has been without prayer and devotion has never long been stable. But you, who despise the religion of the clergy, should not think you will plunder the Church's possessions with impunity." The prolocutor was a soldier named John Cleyne, who, as is reported, had deserted the warfare and lot of Christ and passed over to the lot of Mars by apostasy. For he had been ordained a deacon, yet was not released from that office by any dispensation to return to the world. Meanwhile the Archbishop, seeing the King wavering, rose on his knees before him and asked him to attend to his first purpose, namely that he should keep the rights proper to his own power; to attend also to the oath he had taken, not unwillingly, that he would honour, cherish and protect the Church and its ministers; to attend to the danger of breaking an oath and the disgrace of it; and to allow the Church to enjoy the privileges and liberties which it had enjoyed in the times of his predecessors. He should fear to offend the King by whom kings reign, and fear also the censures which those incur who plunder ecclesiastical property, by which the sentence of excommunication is hung over all of them. When these things had been put forward by the Canterbury man, the King ordered him to return to his seat, declaring that it was his will to leave the Church in as good a state as he had found it, or rather in a better one. The Archbishop, addressing the soldiers in a sermon, said: "You and men like you gave counsel to our lord the present King and to his predecessors, that they should confiscate the goods of the alien priories which the French or Normans held in England, telling him that by this means great riches would be heaped up, indeed many thousands of pounds of metal as you put it. Yet it is plain that today the King is not richer by half a mark, since you, either extorting or begging from his hand, have appropriated those goods to yourselves. From this it can be proved that you seek temporal rights not for the King's advantage but for your own greed. For undoubtedly, if the King (which God forbid) were to satisfy your proposal by following it, he would not be richer by a farthing in the following year."

units.la: Post hæc Archiepiscopus Cantebrigiensem Academiam iure Metropolitico visitauit, multaq; Collegiorum statura ordinauit, pranas consuetudines deleuit, faeinota scholarium castigauit, & cum visitationem remisit, omnia quæ sibi in visitatione detecta fuerunt, causasq; de quibus cognoscere ac inquirere cœpit, suę iurisdictioni reseruauit. Reliquos Archiepiscopatus sui annos in synodis celebrandis, hisque coercendis qui Iohannis Wiclyf dogmata sequuti sunt transegit. Neq; enim vllus eo Archiepiscopo sine synodo & cohæssione subsidii efflurit. Anno autem consecrationis suæ.10.cum & Regni Cancellarii constitutus & in Regis legatione missus esset, Henricum Bewford Wintoniensem Episcopũ qui Willihelmo Wickam successit, Vicarium se absente generalē cōstituit. Is co anno synodũ Lodini cōuocauit, Regiq; decimã & subsidiũ concedi impetrauit, postca eidem synodo papalis quidam quæstor accessit, multaque papæ tributi voluit, quæ a cleto denegata sunt. Proximo anno cum Gregorius duodecimus eleCtus esset Papa, eique, Petrus de Luna quibusdam Cardinalibus assentientibus se opposuisset, & Papa Benedictus dicerĕtur, Archiepisc. cleri um Londini Regeipso præsente conuocauit, suasitque vt dum confligerent ac digladiarentur inter se Papæ tributa Romano curiæ pendi solita in Regis custodia ac sequestro ponerentur. Cuiꝰ Rege atque Cleroassensum est. Illud decretum in populi concione proxima die dominico ad crucem Paulinam publicatum est, tum legati ad Romanam curiam missi sunt Wintoniēsis Episcopus, D.Scroope, & Cantebrigiensis atque Oxoniensis Academiæ Cancellarij, qui nunciarent colluctantibus Papis misi alterum papatum deponerent, neutri deinceps Anglos quicq; præstituros, Acnegemini papæ rem Romanam pessundarent, Concilij generale Pisis in Herturia conuocatum est ad quod à synodo Robertus Saris buriensis, & Henricus Chicheley Meneuensis Episcopi cum Priore Cantuariensi Cleri procurarotes constituti aū misi sunt. In eo Concilio Cardinales amotis consligentibus illis gannientibus papis nouum elegerunt, quem Iohannem 23. appellarunt. Iegatis autem adConcilium emissis Archiepiscopus in ea synodo iura quædam qnibus tam Cantabrigiensis quàm Oxoniensis Academiæ tenerentur condidit, quæ in publicatis constitutionibus continentur. Nam & Richardus Rex Thomæ Arundel Cantuariensis Archiepiscopo antequàm in exilium iret, vtrasque Academias (vt ante diximus) exemptionem priuilegiorum à Papa obtinuisset, subiecit, & obtenta priuilegia nõ minus Archiepiscopali quam Regiæ autoritati præindicialia, ideoque rescindenda decreuit. Wiclifiianorum numerus indies iam adauctus est in quos Archiepiscopus atque clerus summa crudelitate sæuire cœperunt. Quam quidem adrem totius cleri synodus Londini convenit, & Wiclyffiana dogmata iterum condemnauit. In eis dogmatibus Iohannes quidam Badby Wigornientis diocæsis sutor vestiarius suasus constanter perseueravit. Huic Wigornientis episcopus primò in sua diocæsi hæresis condemnauit, posteaque ad hanc synodum duxit. Ibi Archiepiscopus eum de dogmatibus an ea vera crederet, interrogauit. Is ingenne & audacter confessus, abduci ab eorum fide atque suasione noluit. Itaq; Archiepiscopus Wigornensis Episcupi sententiam in eum ante latam confirmauit. Eum Duci Eboracensi, & Wintoniensi Episcopo regni Cancellario, Dominoq; Roofe rotulorum custodi, qui Synodo interfuerunt, tradidit, a quibus ad Regem ductus eius præcepto carnificinæ commissus, & in fabrorum ferrariorum campo igne crudeliter crematus est. In hac Wiclyffianorum cæde atque vastitate Henricus Quartus obiit, eoqne mortuo Henricus quintus eius filius suscepto imperio Londini idibus April. ab Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi coronatus est. Posteaq; cum Episcoporum crudelitas mactatione atque clade infimorum satiari non poterat, in nobilibus potentioribusq; expleta est. Nam in hac immani atq; feta sæuitia creuit eorum numerus qui Wiclyffoa sicnsi sunt. Ex eo numero fuit vir nobilitate & ægnatione sua, atq; affinitate clarus Iohannes Oldcastell, quiq; cum Domini Cobham hæredc atque filia contraxit nuptias, ex eaque gente ac familia Dominus Cobham appellatus est. Wicliffiani quos tunc Lollardos appellabant iu libellis famosis, quos in valuis Ecclesiarum locisque publicis propositurit, affirmabant centum hominum millia suæ sectæ adhærere. Ex hoc facto cum motus & perturbatio Reip. timeretur, & de huius Wiclyffianæ multitudinis ducib. inquireretur, Iohannes D. Cobham qui fauerelllis plurimum vitus est, in discrimen atque dubitationem adductus est. Qui naturæ suæ ingenuitate causæque integritate fretus, cum de eo quæreretur, nihil celauit. Itaqne synodo Londini congregata Archiepiscopus confinum cum suffraganeis capit, quibus modis contra Iohannem D. Cobham in hoc negocio agere oportear. Regi enim non minus nobilitate quam virtute atq; probitate sua eharus fuit, & synodalia Archiepiscopi decreta quibus Wiclyffiana dogmata damnata fuerunt, contempsit atque derisit. Igitur Archiepiscopus Regê primò conenit, ei diserimen atque periculum huius euenturi mali exponit, Iohannem D. Cobham gratissime accusat. Rex virum nobilem sibique charissimum præsenti periculo exponere noluit, rogauit Archiepiscopum vt inquisitionem differret, sese enim cum eo actutum, vt ab illis opinionibus reuocaret, sed cum neq; proficere quicquam suadendo Rex potuit, & indies ab Episcopis interpellaretur, vitum clarum sibique familiarissimum Episcoporum potestati & carnificinæ permisit. Archiepiscopus itaque eum edicto in Ecclesia cathedrali Roffensi propositio ad synodum citauit. Qui cum comparere noluit, excomunicatus & Regis mandato Roberto Morley militi turris Londinensis custode apprehesus est ad carceres ductus est. Tum sæpius examinatus ab Archiepiscopo, Romatii pontificis potestatem, Romanaque institura, ritus & ceremonias execratus est, cumque in ea sententia constanter perstitisset ab Archiepiscopo tandem hæreticus pronunciatus atq; condemnatus est. Ac paulò post à patibulo carhenis pendens crudeli flamma suppositu crematus obiit. Multique eum sequuti similem necem fortiter pertulere. In ea etiam synodo multi falsarii qui papales bullas & sigilla confinxerunt, & adulterarunt, depreheni sunt. Clerus autem postquàm D. Cobham condemnassent, in synodo decreuerunt, ne sacræ scripturæ in Anglicanam linguam verterentur.
units.tr: After this the Archbishop visited the University of Cambridge by metropolitan right, and ordained many things concerning the statutes of the colleges, abolished wicked customs, and punished the crimes of the scholars. When he had dismissed the visitation, he reserved to his own jurisdiction all matters discovered in the visitation, and the causes which he had begun to hear and inquire into. He spent the remaining years of his archbishopric in holding synods and in restraining those who followed the doctrines of John Wycliffe. For no subsidy was ever granted in that archbishop's time without a synod and a collection of the subsidy. In the tenth year of his consecration, when he had been made Chancellor of the Realm and sent on an embassy for the King, he appointed Henry Beaufort, Bishop of Winchester, who succeeded William Wykeham, as his general vicar in his absence. In that year Beaufort summoned a synod at London, and obtained the King's consent to a tenth and a subsidy. Afterwards a certain papal collector came to the same synod and demanded many tributes for the Pope, but these were refused by the clergy. In the following year, when Gregory XII had been elected Pope, and Peter de Luna, with some cardinals assenting, had opposed him, and Benedict was being called Pope, the Archbishop summoned the clergy of London in the King's own presence, and advised that, while they were fighting and battling among themselves, the tributes for the Pope which were customarily paid to the Roman court should be placed in the custody and sequestration of the King. To this the King and the clergy agreed. That decree was published in a sermon the next Sunday at St Paul's Cross. Then legates were sent to the Roman court: the Bishop of Winchester, Dr Scrope, and the Chancellors of the universities of Cambridge and Oxford, to announce that, unless both contending popes were deposed, the English would henceforth pay nothing to either, and that by refusing obedience they would ruin the Roman see. A general council was summoned at Pisa in Tuscany, to which Robert Sarum, Bishop of Salisbury, and Henry Chichele, Bishop of St Asaph, together with the Prior of Canterbury, were sent as proctors of the clergy from the synod. In that council the cardinals, the two contending popes being set aside, elected a new one, whom they called John XXIII. Meanwhile, when the legates had been sent to the council, the Archbishop in that synod drew up certain laws by which both the University of Cambridge and the University of Oxford were to be bound; these are contained in the published constitutions. For King Richard, before Thomas Arundel, Archbishop of Canterbury, went into exile, had subjected both universities (as we said before) to his authority, although they had obtained exemption from the Pope; and he decreed that the privileges obtained, being no less prejudicial to the archiepiscopal than to the royal authority, should be rescinded. The number of the Wycliffites was now increasing daily, and against them the Archbishop and the clergy began to rage with the greatest cruelty. For this very reason a synod of the whole clergy met at London and again condemned the doctrines of Wycliffe. Among those who were persuaded of these doctrines, a certain John Badby, a cobbler and tailor of the diocese of Worcester, persevered steadfastly. The Bishop of Worcester first condemned him for heresy in his own diocese, and afterwards brought him to this synod. There the Archbishop asked him whether he believed those doctrines to be true. He confessed boldly and without hesitation, and refused to be drawn away from their faith and persuasion. So the Archbishop confirmed the sentence previously pronounced against him by the Bishop of Worcester. He handed him over to the Duke of York, the Bishop of Winchester, the Chancellor of the Realm, and Lord Roos, keeper of the rolls, who had attended the synod; by them he was taken to the King, who by his command committed him to the executioner, and he was cruelly burned with fire in the Smithfield field of the smiths. In this slaughter and devastation of the Wycliffites, Henry IV died; and on his death his son Henry V, having taken up the government, was crowned at London by the Archbishop of Canterbury on 15 April. Afterwards, when the cruelty of the bishops could not be satisfied by the slaughter and destruction of the lowly, it was fulfilled upon the nobles and the more powerful. For in this savage and monstrous cruelty the number of those who followed Wycliffe grew. Among that number was a man distinguished by his nobility, his kinship and his marriage connections, John Oldcastle, who had married the heiress of Lord Cobham, and from that family and line was called Lord Cobham. The Wycliffites, whom they then called Lollards, affirmed in defamatory pamphlets which they posted on the doors of churches and in public places that a hundred thousand men adhered to their sect. Because of this affair, and since a stir and disturbance in the commonwealth was feared, and inquiry was being made after the leaders of this Wycliffite multitude, John, Lord Cobham, who had been very favoured by the King, was brought into peril and doubt. Relying on the openness of his nature and the integrity of his cause, when he was questioned about it he concealed nothing. So, a synod having been gathered at London, the Archbishop took counsel with his suffragans as to what means should be employed against John, Lord Cobham, in this business. For he was dear to the King no less for his nobility than for his virtue and uprightness, and he had scorned and mocked the synodal decrees of the Archbishop by which the Wycliffite doctrines had been condemned. Therefore the Archbishop first met the King, set before him the danger and peril of the evil about to come, and gravely accused John, Lord Cobham. The King was unwilling to expose a man so noble and so dear to himself to present peril, and asked the Archbishop to put off the inquiry, for he himself would soon bring him back from those opinions. But since the King could achieve nothing by persuasion, and was daily importuned by the bishops, he handed over his famous and most intimate friend to the power of the bishops and the executioner. The Archbishop therefore cited him to the synod by an edict posted in the cathedral church of Rochester. When he refused to appear, he was excommunicated, and by the King's command was seized by Robert Morley, knight, keeper of the Tower of London, and led to prison. Then, examined several times by the Archbishop, he denounced the power of the Roman pontiff and Roman institutions, rites and ceremonies; and when he had stubbornly persisted in that opinion, he was at last pronounced and condemned by the Archbishop as a heretic. Shortly afterwards he died, hanging by chains from a gibbet, burned by a cruel flame placed beneath him. Many who followed him bravely endured a similar death. In that same synod many forgers who had counterfeited and adulterated papal bulls and seals were detected. But the clergy, after they had condemned Lord Cobham, decreed in the synod that the Holy Scriptures should not be translated into the English tongue.

units.la: Atque vtinam dum tam impiam legem generalem tulit Archiepiscopus Oxoniæ, meminisset saltem illius sermonis quem in Annæ Reginæ funere Westmonasterii de laudibus eius habuit, cum esset Cancellarius Regni & Archiepisc. Eboracensi, quæ regina obiit. Anno 1394. Quâ nonalio nomine magis laudauit, quam quòd quâuis advena esset atq; peregrina nempe Bohemica & sotot Wenceslai Regis Bohemiæ & confunx Ric. 2. tamen quatuor Euangelia in Anglicam linguam versa & doctorum commentariis declarata assiduè meditaretur. Vt quod in tam nobili fœmina, regiaque
units.tr: And would that when the Archbishop of Oxford passed that impious general law, he had at least remembered the sermon he preached at the funeral of Queen Anne at Westminster, in praise of her, when he was Chancellor of the realm and Archbishop of York. She died in 1394. He praised her for no other reason more than that, though she was a foreigner and an alien (a Bohemian, sister of Wenceslas, King of Bohemia, and wife of Richard II), she nonetheless diligently meditated on the four Gospels, translated into English and explained by the commentaries of learned men. So that what he judged worthy of commemoration and praise in so noble a woman and royal consort,

units.la: coniuge commemoratione ac præconio dignum duxit, in exteris tam executanda poena sententiaque non vetuisset. Sed cum in eadem concione funebri, a tam piæ Reginæ factis literis dedit laudibus ad reprehendendam Prælatorum atque clericorum scordiam & ignauiam in propagando Euangelio transfiillet, nec minus sequi tunc Regni Cancellarius fuit quam alios mundanis negociis deditos, & a pastorum vigilantia curaque auersos acerrime increparet. Multi hæc verba quæ ad speciem & viurpationem veritatis simulatè dixisset, faceté ludeotes affirmabat is Cancellarians munere, aulicisque ucgoiser. Ictis dare le totum Euangelio vellet, ac perinde faceret vt prædicaret, nunquam emisisset a quoquam sermonem meliorem. Sed quia ea dixit, a quibus eum finste alienissimum, & ambitiose actæ vitæ, & legum nefarie, crudeliterque latarum in constantia declarat, detraxit sibi suaque oratoni fidem, ideoque posteà cum peruenisset ad sedem Cant. iram dei in fine vitæ sensit: quippe (vt scribitur) lethali morbo cotreptus ita saucibus atque lingua ligatus est vt nec deglutire, nec fari poterat, atque tandem mutus, sameque enectus obiit. Quod diuinum ei illatum supplicium iustum fuit, vt qui verbum diuinum salutarem Christianorum etiam nunciari vetuisset, is elinguis & inedia periret. Annis septendecim, vnoquemensefedit. Sepultusque in boreali parte navis Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis iacet. Nulla in re magnificè se ostendit sed ingressus Archiepiscopatū campanile condidit Cantuariæ, & more rituque pontificio campanas quinque nominibus impositis consecrauit. Primam Sanctam & indiuiduam Trinitatem, alteram virginem Mariam, tertiam Angelum Gabrielem, quartam sanctum Blasium, 20 quintam Iohannem Euangelistam appellauit.
units.tr: he would not have forbidden in foreigners, nor visited with such punishment and sentence. But in that same funeral sermon, after he had turned from praising the pious queen's deeds and writings to rebuke the sloth and idleness of the prelates and clergy in spreading the Gospel, he was no less a follower of worldly ways than the others devoted to worldly business, and he most sharply denounced those who had turned away from the vigilance and care of pastors. Many, jesting, asserted that these words, which he had spoken with a pretence of the appearance and usurpation of truth, belonged to the office of a chancellor and to courtly affairs; if he had wished to give himself wholly to the Gospel and acted as one who preaches, he would never have delivered a better sermon. But because he spoke those words, his inconsistency, being very far from them in an ambitious life and in laws impiously and cruelly enacted, revealed him and took away credibility from himself and his speech. Therefore afterwards, when he reached the see of Canterbury, he felt the wrath of God at the end of his life. For (as it is written) seized by a deadly disease, he was so bound in throat and tongue that he could neither swallow nor speak, and at last he died mute and starved. This divine punishment inflicted on him was just: he who had forbidden the saving word of God to be announced even to Christians should perish speechless and by hunger. He sat for seventeen years, [and] one month. He lies buried in the north part of the nave of the Church of Canterbury. He showed himself in no matter magnificently, but on entering the archbishopric he built a bell tower at Canterbury and, in the papal manner and rite, consecrated five bells with names given to them. He called the first the Holy and Undivided Trinity, the second the Virgin Mary, the third the Angel Gabriel, the fourth Saint Blaise, and the fifth John the Evangelist.

units.la: LXI. Henricvs Chicheley.
units.tr: LXI. Henry Chichele.

units.la: Ege (vt diximus) atque sanctione iam diu ante contra Papales prouisiones lata, multisque Regum decretis, & Cleri intercessionibus, procerum atque populi minis interpositis ne impetrarētur à Papa Episcopatuum & beneficiorum prouisiones, ea ramè adhuc impunitate ac licentia per- 30 missæ atque obtentæ sunt, ac si nulloiure vetari putarentur. Quæ Regum conniuentia & permissio pontificiorum audaciam ita aluit, vt cum Monachi Cantuariensis auitam suam elegendi potestatem papalibus prouisionibus aliquot iam seculis suspensam & intermissam recuperare vellent, & à Rege accepta venia Henricum Chicheley Meneuensem Episcopum ad Metropolitanam sedem postulasset, is electioni neque consentire, neque dissentire voluit, sed Papæ arbitrio rem totam permisit. Papa verò Iohannes 23. vt prouisionis vsurpationem teneret mordicus, nec ab ea desuetudine vlla aut contrariis tolerandis actibus recederet, Monachis Cantuariensibus rescripsit Cantuariensis Archiepiscopatus collationem suæ prouisioni ante mortem Thomæ Arundel fuisse 40 reseruatam, ieque irritum ac inane decreuisse quicquid ab his, aut aliis quibuscunque, in suæ prouisionis præiudicium fieret. Tum Archiepiscopatum eidem Henrico Chicheley prouisionis suæ prætextu donauit. Qui Papæ prouisionem admisit, eoque titulo Archiepiscopatum ingressus est. Natus est Henricus Chicheley in oppido Heighamfeyris Northamptonensis Comitatus, & Oxonii in iure ciuili ac canonico in collegio nouo à Willhelmo Wickam Wintoniensi quondam Episcopo extructo institutus. Ibi Doctoratus gradu in vtroque iure suscepto Sarisburiensem Archidiaconatum ab Episcopo Sarisburiensi accepit. Tum multa regia negocia, munera, & legationes obiit, quibus prudenter & integra fide perfunctis, Regis gratia ad Meneuensem Episcopatum, deinde ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum ascendit. Cui Archiepiscopatum 50 gerenti Henricus Bewford Winron. Episcopus pallium à papa missum. 29. menss Iulii Regeac proceribus multis prætentibus honorifice tradidit. Deinde Archiepiscopus Archiepiscopatus prouentus semestri tempore quo Aichiepiscopatus fuisset vacuus Regi debitos, numeratis sex centum marcis redemit. Papa Meneuensem episcopatum, à quo Henricum Chicheley Cantuariam transtulerat, cuidam suo notario Anglo Archidiacono Surrey contulit, atque mox eundem notarium ad Lichefeldiensem transtulit, deinde Meneuensem anno sequenti Stephano Patringron Carmelitano fratri dedit. Omnesque adeo Episcoporum translationes & prouisiones authoritate Papæ, spretis adhuc legibus & Regum interdictis impune factæ sunt. Verùm Verum magna & inaudita pene iam accidit hnic Papæ calamitas. Nam Concilium generale in Constantia Germaniæ ciuitate, Imperatore electo & Cardinalibus id procuranribus ob dissidium inter duos (vt diximus) Antipapas quorum utrique Papatum vendicabant, componendum per orbem Christianum conuocatum est. Itaque synodus in 75 statuerentur. Comes Warwicensis, Episcopi Sarisburiensis, Bathoniensis, & Herefordensis, cum Abbate Westmonasterii, & Priore Wigorniæ hanc legationem obierunt. Ex his (vt diximus) Papis vnus Gregorius duodecimus dictus est. Is cum impar esset alterius potentiæ, Roma profugit, & in Aragonia delituit.
units.tr: Although statutes had been passed long before (as we have said) against papal provisions, and although many decrees of the kings, the intercessions of the clergy, and the threats of nobles and people had all forbidden that bishoprics and benefices be obtained by papal provision, such provisions were still allowed and obtained with such impunity and licence, as if they were thought to be forbidden by no law. This connivance and permission of the kings so nourished the audacity of the Papists that when the monks of Canterbury wished to recover their ancient right of election, which had been suspended and discontinued for some centuries by papal provisions, and had received the king's pardon, they asked for Henry Chichele, bishop of Menevia, to the metropolitan see. He chose neither to consent nor to dissent to the election, but left the whole matter to the pope's judgment. Pope John XXIII, however, in order to hold tightly to the usurpation of provision, and to permit no departure from that practice nor any tolerance of acts to the contrary, wrote back to the monks of Canterbury that the collation of the archbishopric of Canterbury had been reserved to his provision before the death of Thomas Arundel, and he declared null and void whatever was done by them or by anyone else to the prejudice of his provision. Then, under the pretext of his provision, he gave the archbishopric to the same Henry Chichele, who admitted the papal provision and entered the archbishopric by that title. Henry Chichele was born in the town of Higham Ferrers in Northamptonshire, and was educated at Oxford in civil and canon law in New College, which had been founded by William Wykeham, formerly bishop of Winchester. There, having taken the doctorate in both laws, he received the archdeaconry of Salisbury from the bishop of Salisbury. Then he undertook many royal affairs, offices and embassies, which he discharged prudently and with unimpeachable faith. By the king's favour he rose to the see of Menevia, and then to the archbishopric of Canterbury. To him, while he was archbishop, Henry Beaufort, bishop of Winchester, honourably delivered on 29 July the pallium sent by the pope, the king and many nobles being present. Then the archbishop redeemed, by paying six hundred marks, the revenues of the archbishopric for the half-year during which it had been vacant, which were owed to the king. The pope gave the see of Menevia, from which he had transferred Henry Chichele to Canterbury, to a certain English notary of his, archdeacon of Surrey, and soon transferred the same notary to Lichfield; then in the following year he gave Menevia to Stephen Patrington, a Carmelite friar. All such translations and provisions of bishops were thus carried out by papal authority, with laws and royal prohibitions still disregarded and going unpunished. But a great and almost unheard-of calamity soon befell this pope. For a general council was convened in the German city of Constance, with the elected emperor and the cardinals promoting it, to settle throughout the Christian world the schism between the two antipopes (as we have said), each of whom claimed the papacy. And so a synod was held in which it was to be decided what should be done. The Earl of Warwick, the bishops of Salisbury, Bath and Wells, and Hereford, with the abbot of Westminster and the prior of Worcester, performed this embassy. Of these popes (as we have said), one was called Gregory XII. Since he was unequal to the power of the other, he fled from Rome and hid himself in Aragon.

units.la: Hic in Concilio abdicauit se ea conditione Papatui, si Iohannes alter Papa perinde cederet. Iohannes autem qui Romæ permanserat, & se pro Papa palam gesserat, omnemque illam Papalem potestatem exercuerat, & emolumenta vberrima pereperat, ab Imperatore vt schisma tam diuturnum cesseret, ægre tandem inuitus & adductus abdicationem simulauit. Sed pridie quam cedendum & renunciandum fuit, clam nocte discessit, & in Austriam à Duce perfugium quæsiuit. Motus hac perfidia & eallidiate Imperator eum armis insecutus, venatorio & fero vestitu amicitum, & arcus ac sagittas breues gestantem tandem apprehendit. Eodemque habitu adductu, Concilio & frequentissimo Cardinalium cœtui exhibuit.
units.tr: Here, at the council, he renounced the papacy on condition that John, the other pope, would likewise withdraw. But John, who had remained in Rome, openly acted as pope, exercised all that papal power, and had gathered very rich profits, was at last, with difficulty, and reluctantly, brought by the emperor to feign abdication, so that so long a schism might end. But on the day before he was to yield and renounce his office, he secretly left by night and sought refuge with the duke in Austria. Moved by this treachery and cunning, the emperor pursued him with armed men, and finally seized him, clothed in a hunter's rough garb and carrying short bows and arrows. Brought in the same dress, he was presented to the council and to a crowded assembly of cardinals.

units.la: Qui pastorem suum ferino habitu mutatum, lupum & prædonem Ecclesiæ sententia iudicauerunt, & addixerunt carceribus. Vulgus eius bona tanquam proscripta Quibus auditis in Anglia collecta & in Paulina Ecclesia recōdita donec hæc inter Antipapas altercatio diiudicaretur, pecunia ruptis feris extracta, & Regi ad vius bellicos concessa est. In superiori autem Londinensi synodo Henricus Archiepiscopus postquam Legati ad Cōcilium decessissent, de priuilegiorum & exemptionum vitibus cepit diligenter explorare. Hoc a Monachis ita reprehensum est, vt
units.tr: They judged their pastor, changed into wild attire, to be a wolf and a plunderer of the Church, and by sentence condemned him to prison. When these things were heard, the money that had been collected in England and deposited in St Paul's Church, to be kept until this dispute between the antipopes was decided, was taken out after the locks were broken, and was granted to the king for military purposes. But in the earlier London synod, after the legates had departed for the council, Archbishop Henry began to inquire carefully into the abuses of privileges and exemptions. The monks reproved this so sharply that

units.la: Ac Rex Henricus iam pecuniis omnibus bellicis copiis instructus exercitum fortem & inuictum in Gallias traiecit, vbi multis celeberrimis partis victoriis tandem præliō acri commisso in loco qui Agincourt appellatur, Gallorum exercitus superbissimo deleatu, & diligentissima conquisitione collectus pene omnis interiit, Rege ipso cum septingenta proceribus captis, cæsis autem tribus Ducibus, quinque Comitibus, & centū proceribus, armigeris ac militibus quatuor millibus sexaginta nouem. Gregarii autem milites quorum numerus non est relatus tanquam peeora mactati sunt. Omnium quæ vnquam facta sunt præliorum hoc secundissimum & gloriosissimum Anglis, calamitosissimum & ignominiosissimum Gallis fuit. Nam ex Anglis Edwardus Dux Eboraci, & Michael Comes Suffolciæ, quatuor equites, & vnus armiger, militesq; viginti octo tantum cecidere. Captoque itaq; Gallo Rex inclytis nobilibusq; secum ducitis captiuis rediit in Angliam.
units.tr: King Henry, now furnished with all the money and military supplies, led a strong and unconquered army across into Gaul. There, after many famous victories, he at last joined a fierce battle at the place called Agincourt, and the French army was destroyed in a most proud defeat; almost all of it, sought out with great diligence, perished. The king himself took seven hundred nobles captive, while three dukes, five counts and a hundred nobles were slain, together with four thousand and sixty-nine men-at-arms and soldiers. The common soldiers, whose number was not recorded, were slaughtered like cattle. Of all the battles that have ever been fought, this was the most successful and glorious for the English, and the most calamitous and ignominious for the French. For on the English side only Edward, Duke of York, and Michael, Earl of Suffolk, four knights and one esquire, and twenty-eight soldiers fell. With the Frenchman thus defeated, the king returned to England, bringing with him his illustrious noble captives.

units.la: Et altera ab Archiepiscopo celebrata synodo duas decimas à Clero cū summa beneuolentia & gratificatione oblatas accepit. In hac synodo dies festus Iohannis Beuerlaco dedicatus est, & Abbates multi qui exemptionis ptæ textu abfuerunt, sacris ab Archiepiscopo interdicti, cum eius Iurisdictioni pariuisent, tandem restituti sunt. Sinodoq; finita Archiepiscopus Iohannem Wackering Nordouicensem, Edmundum Lacy Herefordensem, & Iohannem Chaundlet Sarisburiensem electos Episcopos, dum Papatu vacante prouisiones cessarent, Londinii confirmauit atq; consecrauit. Interea in Concilio Constantiensi Papis abdicatis Wiclyffiana dogmata condemnata sunt. Tum Iohannes Hus, & Ieronymus Praghe contra fidem eis datam, quam Concilium cum hæreticis non esse seruandam decreuit, crudeliter flammis combusti. Quæ quoniā satis fuse ab aliis explicata sunt, hic suo tempore obiter aggressi nobis sufficiet. His gestis longa deliberatione habita Cardinalis de Colona electus Papa prodiit. Cuius electioni Richardus Londinensis Episcopus, qui etiā dānato Iohanne Hus, antequā flammis traderetur coram Imperatore & Concilio Latine prædicauit, primū suffragiū dedit. Hic Papa in Sancti Martini festo electa, ipse Martinus dictus est. Ae postridie præsbyteratus, perendieq; Episcopatus charactere suscepto primā missam in Costantiensi Ecclesia celebrauit. Huic missæ 140 mitrati interfuerunt. Postea in coronationis suæ solennis Anglicis Clericis plurimus honos delatus est. Namq; Prior Sancti Iohannis de Clerkenwel in peragendo coronationis situ Papæ diadema tenuit. Deinde etiin prandio sedenti ab eodem priore, & Abbate Sancti Edmundi ministratum est. Post prandium Papa equo ornatissime phalerato vectus, Cardinalibus, Episcopis & Abbatibus phaleratis etiam equis insidentibus comitatus, cinitatem Constantiensem transiit. Imperator in illa equitatione equum Papæ fræno pedes duxit.
units.tr: Another synod, celebrated by the archbishop, received two tenths from the clergy, offered with great goodwill and thanks. In this synod the feast day of John of Beverley was instituted, and many abbots who had been absent under the pretext of exemption, and who had been forbidden the sacraments by the archbishop, were at last restored when they submitted to his jurisdiction. When the synod was ended, the archbishop at London confirmed and consecrated John Wakering, elected bishop of Norwich, Edmund Lacy of Hereford, and John Chaundler of Salisbury, since provisions had ceased while the papacy was vacant. Meanwhile, at the Council of Constance, with the popes deposed, the doctrines of Wycliffe were condemned. Then John Hus and Jerome of Prague, contrary to the faith given them, which the council decreed was not to be kept with heretics, were cruelly burned in the flames. Since these matters have been explained at length by others, it will suffice for us to touch on them here in passing, at their proper time. When these things were done, after long deliberation the Cardinal of Colonna was elected pope and came forth. Richard, bishop of London, who had preached in Latin before the emperor and the council even after John Hus was condemned and before he was handed over to the flames, gave the first vote for his election. This pope was elected on the feast of St Martin, and was called Martin himself. On the following day he received the priesthood, and on the day after that the episcopal character, and he celebrated his first mass in the church of Constance. One hundred and forty mitred prelates attended this mass. Afterwards very great honour was shown to the English clergy at his solemn coronation. For the prior of St John of Clerkenwell held the pope's diadem while the coronation rite was performed. Then, too, while he sat at dinner, he was served by the same prior and the abbot of St Edmund's. After dinner the pope, mounted on a most richly caparisoned horse and accompanied by cardinals, bishops and abbots, likewise on caparisoned horses, passed through the city of Constance. In that procession the emperor walked on foot, leading the pope's horse by the bridle.

units.la: Quem Reges, Duces, Nobiles, Proceres, cæteriq; laici pedites sequuti sunt. Eam Cleri elationem, & Principum populiq; demissionem tam cæca tempora tulerunt.
units.tr: Kings, dukes, nobles, magnates and other lay people followed him on foot. Such blind times endured that elation of the clergy and humility of princes and people.

units.la: Ac Martinus Papa in ipso Pontificatus ingressu iura sua prouisionem vsurpata ceperat exercere. Namq; Meneuen sem Episcopum Stephanum ad Cicestrensem, eiusq; loco Benedictum Bangotensem ad Meneuensem sedem transtulit. Tum eodem anno Henricus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus Londini synodum convocauit. In quam Dux Bedfordiæ qui Regæ in Gallico bello absente Reipublicam administrabat ingressus, literas de Martino Papa à Constantiensi Concilio missas ostendit. Quæ postquam essent publicè recitatæ hymnis & litaniis cantatis nouî Papæ commemoratio celebratur, Tum Regi bellum cum Gallis gerenti synodus decimas duas concessit. In hac Synodo Rob. Gilbert, sacræ Theologiæ professor Mertonensis collegii Oxon. præses, longa & diserta oratione egit ut Scholaribus, quorum in literarum studiis industria viguit, attribuantur & ad victum interim necessaria, & proponantur maturis præmia. Hunc sequutus Thomas Kington legum doctor, & aduocatus curiæ de Arcubus pari facundia pro Cantebrigiensibus interceßit. Quibus suadentibus decretum est, vt Ecclesiasticorum beneficiorum patroni, ea vacantia his qui graduum dignitatibus ab Academiis donati sunt, deinceps conferant, gradus & profeßionis ratione iuxta beneficiorum census & valores habita. Hoc saluberrimum decretū ab arctū magistris atq; professoribus, qui sua multitudine reliquos in Vniuersitatibus regentes superabant, cū in Scholariū congregatione de eo approbādo agerentur, temere tanquam iuuenili multitudine reiectum & repudiatum est, Nō alia sanè ratione quam quod doctoribus, aliisq; quibus ordine & loco essent inferiores, in adipisce dis beneficiis pares esse non poterant. Ad eam etiam synodum Bedfordiæ Dux misit quēdam à se Wiclyffianæ doctrinæ suspectum homunculum, quirob corporis breuitate lohannes Dwarfe dictus est, synodumq; ingressus risus & cachinnos omnibus pene cōmouit. Is dogmatib. quibusdam sibi obiectis renunciauit, & dimissus est. Quod quo eōdem Dux Fedfordiæ fecerit, iocone an serio difficile est iudicare. Exiuit. n. postquam omnia negßet bomuncio, ne tam despectus a Clero quam ipse Clerū despiciens atq; ludēs. Anno consecrationis suæ sexto Archiepiscopus alijs synodū Londini celebrauit, in qua cōcessa Regi est Ecclesiasticorum, puentium media decima. In hac synodo Richardus Walker Wigorniensis præsbyter maleficii reus eam fecit ad crucē Paulinā prædicante Lodinensi Episcopo postquā poenitentia egisset publicè execratus est. Ac suorum præstigiorum codices atq; instrumenta flammis deleuit publice. Iamq; multi Episcopi in Angliaobierunt, in quorū loca Martinus Papa prouisionis titulo substituit alios. Neq; enim quisquam tam immodica & effrænata conferendi atq; prouidendi licentia vsus est atq; hic Papa, qui in Constantiensi Concilio ingressus Papatū, omniū Ecclesiarū vacationes interposito decreto ubi reseruauit. Duobus his proximis annis tredecim Episcopatus in Catuarienfi prouincia transferēdo atq; prouidendo cōtulit. Cicestrensi Henricū, Sarisburiensi Iobannē, Wigorniensi Philippū, Roffensi Richardū, Lincolniensi Robertū, Exoniensi Edmundū, Herefordensi Thomā, ac Lichefeldiensi Thomā præfecit. Tum ad Londinensem sedem vacuā Episcopū Cicestrensem transtulit. Ad Cicestrensem rursus Episcopum Herefordensem, & ad eius sedē Roffensem traduxit. Ac in Roffensi demū Ecclesia Iohannem Langton Cantuariensem monachū Episcopū præfecit. In quo Episcopatu prouidendo Cantuariēsi Archiepiscopo ininriam fecisse Papa visus est, quod is Episcopatus à Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo primò erectus atq; stabilitus omnia tam spiritualia quam temporalia iura ab eodem accepit. Semperq; sub eius rurela atq; potestate fuit, &Roffensis Ecclesiæ Episcopus Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo pro temporalibus bomagium præstare eō sueuit. Cuius homagii verba à Iohanne Langton Gallicè prolata hic inseruimus.
units.tr: And at the very outset of his pontificate, Pope Martin began to exercise the rights of provision he had usurped. He transferred Stephen, bishop of Menevia, to Chichester, and in his place put Benedict of Bangor into the see of Menevia. Then in the same year Henry, archbishop of Canterbury, convened a synod at London. Into it entered the Duke of Bedford, who was governing the realm while the king was absent in the French war, and he displayed letters concerning Pope Martin sent from the Council of Constance. When these had been read publicly, and hymns and litanies had been sung, a commemoration of the new pope was celebrated. Then the synod granted two tenths to the king, who was waging war with the French. In this synod Robert Gilbert, professor of sacred theology and warden of Merton College, Oxford, in a long and eloquent speech urged that scholars, whose diligence flourished in the study of letters, should be given what was necessary for their living in the meantime, and that rewards be proposed for those who were mature. Following him, Thomas Kington, doctor of laws and advocate of the Court of Arches, with equal eloquence interceded for the Cambridge men. At their urging it was decided that the patrons of ecclesiastical benefices should henceforth confer any vacant benefices on those who had been granted degrees by the universities, with rank and profession taken into account according to the value and income of the benefices. This most salutary decree was rashly rejected and repudiated, as if it were the work of youthful impulse, by the older masters and professors, who outnumbered the others teaching in the universities, when its approval was debated in the congregation of scholars. And this was for no other reason than that they could not be equal in obtaining benefices to the doctors and to others who were inferior to them in rank and position. To that synod, too, the Duke of Bedford sent a certain little man suspected of Wycliffite doctrine, who was called John Dwarf because of the shortness of his body. On entering the synod he moved almost everyone to laughter and cackling. When some doctrines were put to him, he renounced them and was dismissed. Whether the Duke of Bedford did this in jest or in earnest is hard to judge. For after the little man had denied everything, he went away, not so much despised by the clergy as himself despising and mocking them. In the sixth year of his consecration the archbishop celebrated another synod at London, in which a tenth of the ecclesiastical revenues was granted to the king. In this synod Richard Walker, a priest of Worcester guilty of sorcery, after performing public penance, was made to stand at St Paul's Cross while the bishop of London preached, and was publicly execrated. And he publicly burned his books of spells and the instruments of his tricks. Now many bishops in England had died, and in their places Pope Martin substituted others by the title of provision. For no one ever used so immoderate and unbridled a licence in conferring and providing as this pope, who, on entering the papacy at the Council of Constance, reserved by an interposed decree the vacancies of all churches. In these last two years he transferred and provided thirteen bishoprics in the province of Canterbury. He set Henry over Chichester, John over Salisbury, Philip over Worcester, Richard over Rochester, Robert over Lincoln, Edmund over Exeter, Thomas over Hereford, and Thomas over Lichfield. Then he transferred the bishop of Chichester to the vacant see of London. Again he moved the bishop of Hereford to Chichester, and the bishop of Rochester to Hereford's see. And finally in the church of Rochester he set John Langton, a monk of Canterbury, over the see as bishop. In providing this bishopric the pope seemed to have wronged the archbishop of Canterbury, since this see had first been erected and established by the archbishop of Canterbury, and had received from him all its spiritual and temporal rights, and had always been under his guardianship and power; the bishop of Rochester was accustomed to render homage to the archbishop of Canterbury for temporal matters. The words of this homage, spoken in French by John Langton, we have inserted here.

units.la: leo lehan Langdon Euesque de Rocestre toure à les Saintz Euangelies qus de ce iour en auant serra fayal, & loial & foy porterai à vous trefreuerent pier en Dieu Henry par la grace de Dieu l'Archeuefque de Canterbury & primâ de toute l'Angleterre, & à vos successeurs, des terres & tenementes les quex vos clame tenir de vous, & loialment ferai & cannoisfreres les services qua Ieos doi fair à vous mon seigneur. si Dieu me aide & les saintes Euangiles.
units.tr: I, John Langton, Bishop of Rochester, swear on the holy Gospels that from this day forward I will be faithful and loyal, and will bear faith, to you, Henry, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all England, and to your successors, for the lands and tenements which I claim to hold of you. I will loyally perform the services I owe you, my lord. So help me God and the holy Gospels.

units.la: Verum Papa neq; modo neq; ratione vlla habita sine discrimine omnes iam in Anglia Episcopatus conniuente Rege & in bellis occupato prouisione sua contulit. In qua exerceda tatopere festinauit, vt simulatqueEboracensem Episcopatū fuisse vacuū accepisset, Richardum Lincolniensem Episcopum eò temere transtulit. Verùm cum Decanus & capitulum Eboracense authoritate legum contra Papales prouisiones sancitarum ei resti-tutissent, neque Richardum Lincolniensem Episcopum inanì Papæ titulo prouisum Archiepiscopatus & Ecclesiæ Eboracensis possessionem ingredi permisissent, coactus est Vid. sup. Papa contraria Bulla eum quem ad Archiepiscopatum promouere voluit,ad Episcopatum Lincolniensem tanquam à calce ad carcerem iterum revocare. Quo Eboracensium exemplo Papalis in Episcopatibus prouidendis authoritas contra quam nec leges Regni, nec edicta Regia, nec procerum populi{que} minæ valebant, primum fracta & debilitata fuit. Archiepiscopus deinde octavo suæ consecrationis anno synodum Londinensem habuit in Ecclesia celebrauit. In hac synodo primò concessa est à Clero Regi decimæ. Sed Clerus à Rege vicissim impetrauit.
units.tr: But the Pope, without any regard to right or reason, now filled all the bishoprics in England without distinction, while the king connived at it and was occupied in war. He hastened so eagerly to do this that, as soon as he heard the see of York was vacant, he rashly transferred Richard, Bishop of Lincoln, there. But when the dean and chapter of York, by the authority of laws enacted against papal provisions, refused him, and did not allow Richard, Bishop of Lincoln, provided by the Pope's empty title, to enter into possession of the archbishopric and church of York, the Pope was forced by a contrary bull see above to recall the man he had wished to promote to the archbishopric back to the bishopric of Lincoln, as if from the threshold back to the prison. Following this example of York, the papal authority in filling bishoprics, against which neither the laws of the realm, nor royal edicts, nor the threats of nobles and people had any force, was first broken and weakened. Then, in the eighth year of his consecration, the archbishop held a synod at London, in the church. In this synod the clergy first granted the king a tenth. But the clergy in turn obtained something from the king:

units.la: Ne hospitij sui pro victualibus prouisores Clericorum bona, aut possessiones attingerent. Deinde vt Clerici in foro Regio capitalium criminum postulati datis fideiussoribus iudicio sisti carceribus liberentur. Tertiò vt præsbyteri castrati felonum, id est, homicidarum pœnis afficerentur. Tum in eadem synodo Willihelmus Taylor liberalium artium professor qui in Wigorniensi dioecesi neque sanctos neque Christum Iesum rationem humanitatis esse pro salute Christiana innocentes docuit, quoniam eadem & similia dogmata ante coram Thoma Arundel Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo confessus & detestatus esset, tanquam in hæresim relapsus, Clericali ordine atque gradu priuatus, & laicali potestati traditus est. Ad hanc autem synodum Iohannes Rikinghal Cantebrigiensis Vniuersitatis Cacellarius quoniam abfuit ab Archiepiscopo citatus venit, qui se cum Iohanne Castel Oxoniensi Cacellario coniunxit, illudque conferendis beneficiis Cantebrigiensibus ut ...
units.tr: that the purveyors of his household should not seize the goods or possessions of clergymen for provisions; then that clerks accused of capital crimes in the king's court, on giving sureties, should be released from prison to stand trial; and thirdly that priests convicted of felony, that is, of homicide, should be subjected to penalties. Then in the same synod William Taylor, professor of the liberal arts, who in the diocese of Worcester taught that neither the saints nor Christ Jesus, in respect of his humanity, were innocent for Christian salvation, since he had previously confessed and abjured the same and similar doctrines before Thomas Arundel, Archbishop of Canterbury, and had relapsed into heresy, was deprived of clerical order and rank and handed over to the secular power. John Rikinghal, chancellor of the University of Cambridge, came to this synod, since he had been absent when cited by the archbishop. He joined himself with John Castel, chancellor of Oxford, and so that the decree concerning the conferring of benefices on Cambridge

units.la: ... Vniversitatis Oxonienses studentibus decretum quod ab artium (ut dixi-mus) professoribus ante ... receptum & admissum non fuit, renouari impetrauerunt. Huic autem doctissimo viro Cœceffo à synodo præmio impuri indoctiq; fratres dium restituerunt. Sed Henricus quintus Rex literarum studio ducus contra petulantem fratrum instantiam ad synodum de eo inrerponendo decreto scripsit, idq; in Parlamento postea confirmauit. Deinde constitutionibus quibusdam latis de inductionum ac institutionum feudis moderandis, hæc synodus finita & dimissa est. Sequenti autem anno altera in eodem loco incepta & inchoata est, in qua Henricus quidam Webbe qui ex illa licentiosa turba (de quæ in Thoma Arundel dicimus) profluxit, & in Wigorniensi dioecesi otdine Clericali legitimè non recepto diuina ministrare, & prædicare consuevit, pœnæ fustium adiudicatus est. Itaq; in tribus Cathedralibus Ecclesiis Paulina, Wigorniensi, & Bathoniensi nudus in processione virgis verberibusq; publice cæsus est. Hoc anno indictum est generale Concilium Basileæ, & Anglicani Cleri nuncius ac procuratoribus eò profecturis in hac synodo prouisum est subsidium. In huius synodus extremo Henricus Whit præsbyter quibusdam dogmatibus renunciare coactus est. Eodem etiam anno Katharina Angliæ Regina filium primogenitum die sancti Nicolai Episcopi in arce Windsorina peperit, eumq; Hericum sextum nominauit. Cui ab Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi cum summa populari lætitia ac solennitate baptisato testimonium fidei ex more perhibuerunt Iohannes Dux Bedfordiæ, & Hericus Wintoniensis Episcopus. Ac Regnam post hunc fœlicem partum & purificationem valens mense Aprili proximo ad Regem in Normanniam traiecit. Cuius secundus iucundusq; aduentus Regalibus amplexibus exceptus est. At Rex in hoc bello Gallico omni contentione, vigiliis, laboribusq; sudans, etsi omnia sibi prospera secundaq; euenerunt, tamen ex intemperata lassitudine fcebrem acutam contraxit. Cuius vi consumptis & exhaustis viribus à Medicis desperatus obiit penultimo Augusti. Cuius immatura mors non à suis modo sed ab exteris atq; peregrinis ob bellicam virtutem lugenda fuit. Qui nullum vnquam præliū sine parta victoria gessit. Mente benigna atq; pia, vultu modesto, sermone raro ac moderato fuit.
units.tr: ... and on Oxford students, which (as I have said) had not been received and admitted by the professors of the arts before, be renewed, they obtained it. But the synod restored to this most learned man, Coceffus, the reward, while the impure and unlearned friars... Yet King Henry V, a lover of literary study, against the petulant insistence of the friars, wrote to the synod about inserting that decree, and afterwards confirmed it in Parliament. Then, after certain constitutions were enacted to moderate the fees for inductions and institutions, this synod was concluded and dismissed. In the following year another was begun and commenced in the same place, in which Henry Webbe, who had sprung from that licentious crowd (which we mention under Thomas Arundel), and who used to minister divine things and preach in the diocese of Worcester without having been legitimately admitted to clerical order, was sentenced to the penalty of flogging. So in three cathedral churches, St Paul's, Worcester and Bath, he was publicly beaten with rods and whips, stripped naked, in procession. This year the general council of Basel was called, and provision was made in this synod for a subsidy for the English clergy's envoys and proctors who were to go there. At the end of this synod Henry Whit, a priest, was compelled to renounce certain doctrines. In the same year Queen Catherine of England bore her firstborn son in the castle of Windsor on the feast of St Nicholas, bishop, and named him Henry VI. At his baptism by the Archbishop of Canterbury, with great popular joy and solemnity, John, Duke of Bedford, and Henry, Bishop of Winchester, bore witness to his faith according to custom. And the queen, after this happy delivery and her purification, crossed over to the king in Normandy the following April. Her second and welcome arrival was received with royal embraces. But the king, sweating with every effort, sleepless nights and labours in this French war, although all things turned out prosperously and favourably for him, nevertheless caught a sharp fever from immoderate exhaustion. His strength was consumed and spent by it, and, despaired of by his physicians, he died on the penultimate day of August. His untimely death was to be mourned not only by his own people but by foreigners and strangers, on account of his martial valour. He never fought a battle without winning it. He was gentle and pious of mind, modest of countenance, and sparing and measured in speech.

units.la: At verò in consiliis sagacitatem, & prouidentiam, in indiciis æquitatem, in bellicis rebus agendis magnanimitatem & constantiam summam declarauit.
units.tr: Indeed, in counsel he showed sagacity and foresight, in judgements fairness, and in conducting war great magnanimity and the highest constancy.

units.la: Idem in rebus diuinis, tribuendisq; eleemosynis fuit assiduus. Cuius tota vita in Castrensibus expeditionibus penè contrita est. Moriensis Testamento præcepit vt Westmonasterii sepeliretur. Quod magna solennitate & publica moerore factum est. Iusta ei tribusin locis Cætuariæ, Londini & Westmonasterii celebrata sunt. Paulo post etiā Rex Galliæ cū de generi sui morte accepisset, luctus ei funebres decreuit, & proceres ac magnates suos iurare iurando constrinxit, ne se mortuo à fœdere de Regno Galliæ Angliæque Regi tradendo recederent, sed cum tam glorioso amisso genero consolationem nullam admisit ipse ægritudine, doloreq; confectus 12. postea diebus vita cessit. Iamq; virumq; Anghiæ quàm Galliæ regnum iure fœderis & hæreditatis ad Henricum sextum infantem & in incunabulis fotum obuenit. Cuius tutelæ ex partis Testamento Iohanni Bedfordiensi, & Humfrido Gloceftrenfi ducibus commissa est. Inter quos ita diuisa & dispertita regna fuerunt, vt Bedfordiensis Galliam, & Gloceftrensis Angliam administraret. In Gallia verò Carolo Regedefuncto Carolus Regis filius qui viuente patre inita fœdera rupit, regnum sibi vendicauit, proposituq; edictis se Carolum septimum Galliæ Regem nominauit.
units.tr: He was likewise assiduous in religious duties and in giving alms. Almost his whole life was spent in campaigns in the field. Dying, he ordered by his will that he be buried at Westminster, and this was done with great solemnity and public mourning. Funeral rites were celebrated for him in three places: Canterbury, London and Westminster. Soon after, when the King of France heard of the death of his son-in-law, he decreed funeral mourning and bound his nobles and magnates by oath not to withdraw from the agreement to hand over the kingdoms of France and England to the King of England after his death. But he himself, weakened by grief and sorrow for the loss of so glorious a son-in-law, admitted no consolation, and twelve days later he departed this life. Now both the kingdom of England and that of France fell by right of treaty and inheritance to Henry VI, an infant still in swaddling clothes. The guardianship of him was committed by the king's will to John, Duke of Bedford, and Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester. Between them the kingdoms were so divided and shared that Bedford administered France and Gloucester England. In France, when Charles VI was dead, his son Charles, who had broken the treaties made while his father was alive, claimed the kingdom for himself and, by proclamation, named himself Charles VII, King of France.

units.la: Ad quem comprimendum in Anglia militum delectus habitus, pecunia confecta & omnia bellica & adiumenta comparata sunt. Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis 12. Octob. Clerum in Ecclesia Paulina conuocauit. In ea Henricus Bewford Wintoniensis Episcopus regni Cancellarius, & Iohannes Stafford Bathoniensis electus Episcopus regni Thesaurarius ad bellum Gallicum opem à Clero petunt, & interposita paucorum dierū deliberatione Wilhelmus Linwood officialis curiæ Cantuariensis de Arcubus hoc respōsum ab inferiori Cleri synodo accepit: Episcopis declaruit. Non esse penes Cleri procuratores potestatem lubsidiū concedendi. Nam cum indicta synodo in singulis diocesibus constituti essent, Clerus his solutionibus cōsentiendi licentiā expresse ademit. Quia tantis tributis diu pendendis ad magnam inopiam & egestatem deuenit. Itaq; Cancellarius à superiori synodo ad inferiorem transiens longa & diserta oratione de Regis iā minoris necessitate, ac de instanti in Gallia bello egit, ac ne quicquam suasit Postridie adeuant & alii Conciliarij, atq; proceres. Sed inferioribus Prælatis atq; Clericis in priori sententia perseuerantibus nihil concessum est. Tum synodus superior cum inferiores Prælatos nulla ratione adduci posse cerneret, vt his bellicis negociis subuenirent, decreuit vitra decimam, statuitq; vt ea iniuita & reluctante altera synodo a toto Clero exigatur. In hac synodo Wilhelmus Ruffel Stamfordiensis frater Stamfordiæ publicè prædicauit. Religiosorū atq; fratrum cum fœminis concubitus licitos & sine peccati reatu permissos esse. Is à synodo damnatus tam nefandum & impurum dogma e suggestu retractauit. Eodem Anno 24. Aprilis alia synodus Londini instituta, & decima Regi concessa est. In ea multi fratres seditiosa quædam dogmata retractabant. Inter quos Wilhelmus Ruffel affirmabat decimas personales non cadere sub diuino præcepto. Hæc opinio vt ichismaticanon modo à synodo, sed ab utriq; Cantebrigiensi & Oxoniensi Academiis damnata est. Is autem frater in transmarinas Regiones profugit, ad eumq; persequendū & deprehendendū synodus perquisitorib.decreuit ex singulis libris quadrantem. Proximo autem anno proxima synodus sub eodē Archiepiscopo 15. Aprilis inchoata est. Quæ Iohanne Kemp Ebor acensi Archiepiscopo, & Waltero Hunger ford milite Regis consiliario, illo Cancellario, hoc Thesaurario Regni, Regis nomine postulantibus Regi decimam concessit. Ac iisdem his potentibus triennio post in recetu synodo media decima Regia Clero data est. In qua cū interuenissent a Papa nuncii & subsidiū sibi ac Imperatori contra Bohemos Wiclyffianam doctrinam sequentes præstari petiissent, inanes reuersi sunt.
units.tr: To suppress him, levies of soldiers were held in England, money was raised and all the war materials and supplies were got ready. On 12 October the Archbishop of Canterbury summoned the clergy to St Paul's. In it Henry Beaufort, Bishop of Winchester, chancellor of the realm, and John Stafford, elect Bishop of Bath, treasurer of the realm, asked the clergy for aid for the French war. After a deliberation of a few days, William Linwood, official of the Court of Arches of Canterbury, received this answer from the lower synod and declared it to the bishops: the proctors of the clergy had no power to grant a subsidy. For since they had been appointed in the individual dioceses for a summoned synod, the clergy had expressly withdrawn their licence to consent to these payments, because by long paying such great taxes they had come to great poverty and want. So the chancellor, passing from the upper synod to the lower, spoke at length and eloquently about the king's now lesser need and the imminent war in France, and he urged nothing less than... The next day the other councillors and nobles also addressed them. But since the lower prelates and clergy persisted in their former opinion, nothing was granted. Then the upper synod, seeing that the lower prelates could by no means be brought to help these military affairs, decreed a tenth beyond the usual, and resolved that it be exacted from the whole clergy, against their will and unwilling, by the other synod. In this synod William Russel, a friar of Stamford, publicly preached at Stamford that intercourse of religious men and friars with women was lawful and permitted without the guilt of sin. Condemned by the synod, he recanted that nefarious and impure doctrine from the pulpit. In the same year, on 24 April, another synod was held in London, and a tenth was granted to the king. In it many friars retracted certain seditious doctrines. Among them William Russel maintained that personal tithes do not fall under divine precept. This opinion, as schismatic, was condemned not only by the synod but by both the universities of Cambridge and Oxford. This friar fled to the regions beyond the sea, and to pursue and seize him the synod decreed a quarter from each pound of income for the searchers. In the following year the next synod was begun under the same archbishop on 15 April. At the request of John Kemp, Archbishop of York, and Walter Hungerford, knight, councillor of the king, the former chancellor and the latter treasurer of the realm, speaking on the king's behalf, it granted the king a tenth. And three years later, in the same synod, a royal tenth was given to the clergy in the middle of its proceedings. During it, when envoys from the Pope had come and asked that a subsidy be provided for themselves and for the Emperor against the Bohemians who followed Wycliffite doctrine, they returned empty-handed.

units.la: Papa autem vt huius Bohemensis belli prætextu, pecunias periode conflare posset, atq; olim in Ierosolymitano bello, in quo cruce signati primò instituti sunt (vt dixim°) cōsueuit, publicatis vbiq; omnium criminum atq; scelerum impunitatibus & indulgentiis, & si in Anglia obtinere nihil poterat, tamen in aliis Regnis tentauit quid facere posset. Vt exlitteris ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum missis hic verbatim inferuimus.
units.tr: The Pope, so that under the pretext of this Bohemian war he might be able to raise money, and as he had formerly done in the war of Jerusalem, in which those marked with the cross were first instituted (as I have said), published impunities and indulgences for all crimes and sins everywhere. Although he could obtain nothing in England, he tried in other kingdoms what he could do. I have inserted here, word for word, the letters he sent to the Archbishop of Canterbury.

units.la: Henricus permissione diuina Cantuar. Archiepiscopus totius Angliæ primas & Apostolicæ sedis Legatus dilectis in Christo filiis fratri Wilhelmo Molefsh Priori Ecclesiæ nostræ Cantuar. & Magistro Iacobo Burbaycb Archidiacon. nostri Cantuar. Officiali salutem, gratiam & benedictionem. Missis super per sanctissimum Dominum nostrum Papam Reuerendissimo in Christo patri, & Domino Henrico Dei gratia titulis S. Eusebii presbytero Cardinali de Anglia vulgariter nuncupato, in vniuersa Germania, ac Hungariæ, & Bohemiæ Regnis Apostolicæ legato literis Apostolicis bullatis. Idem Dominus Cardinalis literas ipsas veraciter transmptas sigillo suo ac signo & subscriptione Richardi Petterworth Notarii publici in fide etestimonium earundem munitas nobis iam pridie transmisit, in nostris ciuitate & diocesi sub gremio modo & forma inferius descriptis publicandas, diligenterq; & celerius exequendas. Quarum quidem literarum Apostolicarum tenor de verbo ad verbū sequitur & est talis. Martinus Episcopus seruus seruorum Dei dilecto filio Henrico tituli Sancti Eusebii presbytero Cardinali in vniuersa Germania ac Hungariæ & Bohemiæ Regnis, Apostolicæ sedis legato salutem & Apostolicam benedictionem. Saluatoris omnium Dominiqui se pro redemptione Dominici
units.tr: Henry, by divine permission Archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England and legate of the Apostolic See, to our beloved sons in Christ, Brother William Molash, Prior of our church of Canterbury, and Master James Burbage, Archdeacon of Canterbury, our official, greeting, grace and blessing. Our most holy Lord the Pope has sent to the most reverend father in Christ and lord, Henry, by the grace of God presbyter Cardinal of the title of St Eusebius, commonly called the Cardinal of England, legate of the Apostolic See in all Germany and the kingdoms of Hungary and Bohemia, apostolic letters under seal.
