Inter hos insignem doctrina & pietate virum Wilhelmum Waynslete mortuo Henrico Beuford creauit Wintonicensem Episcopum. Qui cum scholæ Wilhelmi Wikam Wintoniensis quodam Episcopi Ludimagister esset, ab hoc Rege Henrico sexto qui Scholam & Collegium Etone (vt diximus) stabiliuit Etonensis Scholæ primus Ludimagister constitutus est, deindeProfositus Collegio.
units.tr: Throughout the whole of this Archbishop's time the Pope still appointed bishops by provision. Among these, on the death of Henry Beaufort, he created as Bishop of Winchester William Waynflete, a man outstanding for learning and piety. Since he had been schoolmaster of William of Wykeham's school at Winchester, he was appointed by this King Henry VI, who founded the school and college at Eton (as we have said), the first schoolmaster of Eton School, and afterwards Provost of the College.

units.la: Aedemum in Wintonienfis Ecclesia à Papa Nicolao cellocatus extruxit Oxonii celeberrimum Collegium S. Magdalenæ dedicatum. Henricus autem Rex tanto religionis ardore atque zelo (exco tamen quod dolendum est) flagrauit vt multas peregrinationatationes in huius Archiepiscopi tempore ad Thomæ delubrum Cantuariæ pedes suscepperit. Archiepiscopus autem anno suæ translationis vltimo Synodum Londini celebrauit. In qua Richardus Waruicensis, & Iohan. Wigornensis Comes, Priot S. Iohannis & Ioan. D. Stowrton Barones, aliique milites à Rege missi expositis bellorum difficultatibus in Gallia, petierunt vt Ecclesiasticis prouentib. Regi subueniatur. Quibus Archiepiscopus cum suis Suffraganeis respondit se id sedulo curaturos. Itaque Concilionobiles discesserunt. Post hos insignis quidam Præsultus Decanus S. Seuerini prope Burdegalliam Aquitaniæ ciuitatem iynodum ingressus, polita & copiosa latina oratione declarauit Aquitaniâ deficientem, penes à Gallis recuperatâ prudêtia & magnanimitate Illustrissimi Comitis Salopiæ in officio & subiectione retineri. Ideo que a cunctis Regni subditis & præsertim à Clero his bellicis necessitatibus primo quoque tempore succurrendum. Quo suadente Clerus duas decimas sine mora aut difficultate quacunque concessit. Erat in Anglia eo tempore Romanus quidam Vincentius Clemens Papæ Subdiaconus atque quæstor, qui cum accepisset quanta benignitate Synodus in Regem fuisset, inclinare se posse tam propensam ad liberatem synodum sperabat vt Papæ perindeatque Regi opem ferret. Itaque prolixa & tragica narratione indicauit quanto periculo & discrimine nouus Papa Nicolaus cum toto Cardinalium cœtu insidias cuiusdam Stephani de Potchariis Militis Romani vitaffet. Qui Nebulonibus & Meretricibus quibus Romam seaurire docebat, consociatis, Papam, Cardinales, totamque curiam trucidare & abolere conabatur. Deprehensum autem illum Stephanum, & cum nonnullis suæ conjurationis reis condemnatum, ac patibulo suspensum. Tum Synodum rogauit, vt publicas per totam prouinciam preces pro Papæ, & suæ curiæ salute frequentes haberi decerneret, omnium autem gratissimum fore si synodus Anglicana in quam maximam spem Papa semper collocauit, scriberet. Vt Papa suæ saluti consuleret, & Romam tanquam Babyloniam, omniumque scelerum atque flagitiorum sententiam detestaretur, & sedem atque curiam suam in alia regione ac ciuitate statuerec. Ad quod si subsidium abunde promitterent, non esse dubium quin Roma Italiaque deserta Papa alio migrasturus, & Clerum Anglicanum in maximo honore deinceps habiturus sit. Verum hic Romanus callidus suasionum artifex, cuius doli sua multitudine & diuturnitate iam patidi in Anglia fuere, præter preces atque vota nihil impetrauit. Hac synodo durante Iohannes Stafford Archiepiscopus Lamethe febri correptus valetudinis causa recessit Maidestonam, ibi postquam annis 8. mensibus 10. diebusque 13. sedisset, obiit. Bidnoque post corpus eius Cantuariam à fratribus albo vestitis deducetur, & Episcopo Roffensi cum Priore & Monachis Cantuariensibus triduo missificantibus, ac funebres ritus Pontificio more solennitet peragentibus iuxta Thomæ martyrium ante nouam Capellam Mariæ Virginis sepultum est.
units.tr: Also, having been placed in the Church of Winchester by Pope Nicholas, he built at Oxford the famous College dedicated to St Mary Magdalen. King Henry, moreover, burned with such ardour and zeal for religion (though, which is to be regretted, not without fault) that in this Archbishop's time he undertook many pilgrimages on foot to the shrine of Thomas at Canterbury. In the last year of his translation the Archbishop held a Synod at London. In it Richard, Earl of Warwick, and John, Earl of Worcester, the Prior of St John's, John Lord Stourton, and other knights sent by the King, having set out the difficulties of the wars in France, asked that the King be relieved from the ecclesiastical revenues. To them the Archbishop, with his suffragans, replied that they would take care of this diligently. So the nobles departed from the Council. After them a certain distinguished prelate, the Dean of St Severin near Bordeaux, the city of Aquitaine, entered the Synod and declared, in a polished and copious Latin oration, that Aquitaine, which had been lost and then recovered from the French, was held in obedience and subjection by the prudence and magnanimity of the most illustrious Earl of Shrewsbury. Therefore, he said, all the subjects of the kingdom, and especially the clergy, must come to the aid of these warlike necessities at the earliest opportunity. At his urging the clergy granted two tenths without delay or any difficulty whatever. At that time there was in England a certain Roman, Vincent Clement, a subdeacon and questor of the Pope, who, having heard how generously the Synod had treated the King, hoped that a synod so inclined to liberality could be brought to help the Pope as much as the King. So with a long and tragic narrative he showed what danger and peril the new Pope Nicholas, with the whole college of Cardinals, had escaped from the plots of a certain Stephen de Porcari, a Roman knight. This man had allied himself with scoundrels and prostitutes, among whom he taught them to rage through Rome, and tried to slaughter and destroy the Pope, the Cardinals and the whole Curia. Stephen was caught, condemned together with some of the guilty partners in his conspiracy, and hanged on the gallows. Then he asked the Synod to decree that frequent public prayers be offered throughout the whole province for the safety of the Pope and his Curia, and he said that it would be most welcome if the English Synod wrote to the Pope, in whom he had always placed the greatest hope, that he should look to his own safety, should denounce Rome as another Babylon and the sink of all crimes and abominations, and should establish his see and Curia in another region and city. If they promised abundant aid for this, there was no doubt that, Rome and Italy being abandoned, the Pope would move elsewhere, and would thereafter hold the English clergy in the highest honour. But this Roman, a clever artificer of persuasion, whose tricks had long been known in England by their great number and long duration, obtained nothing beyond prayers and good wishes. While this Synod was in session John Stafford, Archbishop of Lambeth, was seized by fever and withdrew to Maidstone for the sake of his health, and there, after he had sat for eight years, ten months and thirteen days, he died. Soon afterwards his body was brought to Canterbury by the White Friars, and with the Bishop of Rochester, the Prior and the Canterbury monks celebrating Mass for three days and performing the funeral rites solemnly in the Papist manner, he was buried near the martyrdom of Thomas, in front of the new chapel of the Virgin Mary.

units.la: LXIII. Iohannes Kemp.
units.tr: LXIII. John Kemp.

units.la: OStquam Monachi Cantuarienses Iohanni Stafford sepulto aliquandiu iusta fecissent, Ioannem Waltham in sacra professione Baccalaureum, & Walterum Hereford muneriorum Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis custodem commonachos suos ad Regem Henricum sextum cum literis mittunt, in quibus licere sibi sua concessa venia petunt, Iohannem Kemp Eboracensem Archiepiscopum & Romanum titulo Sanctæ Balbinæ Ecclesiæ Cardinalem ad Cantuar. Metropolim postulare. Regeque annuente conspirantibus suffragiis in vigiliis Apostolorum Petri & Pauli enndem postulauerunt. Regemque ac postulatum Cardinalē de sua postulatione rite & legitime perac̈ta Richardo Grauen, & Waltero Hereford confratribus suis, destinatis ad eam rem nunciis certiores fecerunt. At Papa Nicolaus qui prouisionis sibi ab anterioribus papis traditæ vsucaptam poterat mordiens reminuit, cum ta. Aug. Monachorum electione neglecta prouisionis titulo ab Eboracensi Metropoli ad Cantuariensem transtulit. Id ea calliditate fecit, vt cum Regem & Clerum Anglicanum irritare non auderet, eodem tamen præsule quem ex Regis sententia Cantuariensis Monachi elegissent à se prouiso, & Regi obsequi & à suo iure nequicquam recedere videretur. Itaque sex bullis prima Archiepiscopo secunda Cantuariensi capitulo, tertia Prouincialibus suffraganeis, quarta Cantuariensis ciuitatis & Diocæsis Clero, quinta eiusdem populo, ac sexta Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ Vasallis missis, & in Ecclesia Christi Cantuariensi in festo Sancti Matthæi Euangelistæ per Thomam Athe eiusdem Ecclesiæ Monachum pro celeberrima concione publicatis Iohannes Kemp Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum derelictâ Eboracensi suscepit. Hæ Bullæ iam tot numeris diuisæ & multiplicatæ papalem censum qui decimis & prouisionibus sublatis imminutus fuit, adhuc Romana meditatione fraudeq; auxit. Hic Archiepiscopus Archiepiscopatum ingressus cruce Cant. in ædibus Thomæ Kemp Londinensis Episcopi, fuiconsan guinei 24. Septemb. accepit Fullamiæ, atque ibidem postridie, præsulibus ac proceribus multis præsentibus, induit à Nicolao Papa missum, & ab eodem Episcopo Londinensi traditum sibi pallium. Deinde alia Bulla, hic Iohannes Kemp Archiepiscopus atque Cantuariensis, sicut antea ab Eboracensi Archiepiscopatu ad Cantuariensem, itanunc à S. Balbinæ Cardinalatu ad Cardinalatum S. Ruffinæ titulo præsentiorem deductus est. Quarum tot ac tam magnificarum Bullarum sumptus hi fuerunt qui solverunt atque acceperunt. Cum vero ad huius præsentis binis Archiepiscopatus & Cardinalatus titulis insigniti intronizatione ventum sit, quid omittendum fuit, quod è tanta dignitatis ratione, Archiepiscopus tantus facere debuisset. Itaque vndecimo die mensis Decembris hac solennitate intronizatus est. In processione occurrunt ei Prior & Monachi Cantuarienses in albis Cappis clamantes. Pastor noster Cardinalis Sanctæ Russinæ, & Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis. &c. His obuiam facit Archiepiscopus Thoma Londinensi, Wilhelmo Waynflete Wintoniensi, & Iohanne Roffensi Episcopis illis à lateribus, hoc à tergo comitatus. Hos Episcopos Abbates ttes sequuti sunt videlicet Sancti Augustini Cantuariensem de bello, atque Feuersham. In tertio ordine collocati nobiles, Comes Wigorniensis, Vicecomes Lysley, Dominus Molenx, & Priot Sancti Iohannis. Vltimus autem ordo venetabilibus viris tam Clericis quam Laicis, Decano Lincolniensi, Archidiacono Elinensi, aliisque permixtus fuit. Iam omnibus ingressi Archiepiscopatus ritibus recensitis, breuiter ostendamus cuiusmodi à ptimo in Ecclesiam ingressu tam multis titulis hic celebratus Archiepiscopus fuit. Natus est Weiæ in Cantio, & in literis à pueritia, tum in iure ab adolescentia institutus suscepto Doctoratus gradu Dunelmensem Archidiaconatum adeptus est. A Dunelmensi Archidiaconatu Henricus Chicheley Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus eum ad Arcuatam curiam secundam Archiepiscopatus sui anno traduxit, aceiusdem curiæ Decanum, suumque in spiritualibus vicarium generalem creauit. Quæ munera cum præclarè gessisset Normanniæ Ducatus præfectus prætorio fuit. Ab eo munere ad Episcopatum Roffensem electus venit: Ibi cum tribus annis consedisset ad Ceestrensem Episcopatum translatus, inde proximo anno ad Londinensem deductus, tum quadriennio post ad Eboracensem Metropolim postulatus accessit. Diximus ante Richardum Lincolniensem Episcopum à Papa prouisionis titulo Eboracensem Archiepiscopatum accepisse, quia à Decano & Capitulo Eboracensi spreta prouisione papali reiectus est. Eodem enim tempore Iohannem Kemp elegerunt. Quem deinde Nicolaus Papa postquam Rege imperante à Monachis Cantuariensibus electus esset, fucata quadam & adumbrata (vt diximus) prouisionis specie, vt Præsulatum magnanimum sibi deuincirer, ad Cantuariensem sedem transtulit. Hic tot titulis decoratus Antistes non ita diu sedet. Sed primo suæ translationis anno synodum Londini celebrauit, in qua tributo à Clero Rege subsidio, de decimis à Londinensi populo Clero debitis acta multa, sed nihil transactum est. Eodem autem anno tantam vim Dominus Deus incussit ventis, vt ædes atque arbores excelsæ, templorumque turres corruerent. Quæ quidem exempla tanquam diuina supplicia quoniam in hac tanta temporum serie ducta historia occurrunt nobis in diuersis locis sæpius, eadem simul hic collectasub vno quasi oculorum obtutu atque sensu ponamus. vt quoniam Pontificii Paulini templi incendium religionis Euangelicæ à nobis receptæ atque cultæ vitio vertunt, perspiciant ipsi ex incendiis, vastationibus, & eiusmodi repentinis detrimentis clades multo grauiores suis illis cæcis temporibus euenisse, Anno enim Domini. 764. Lamberto Archiepiscopo sedente, cum pontificia superstitio vires iam maximas nactæ esset, non modo ædes, Monasteria, têpliç, oppida tota, atq; vrbes celeberrimæ, sed quod extremi diuini iudicii instar fuit regiones nonnullæ repentino incendio flagrauerunt. In quo Londinû & Eboracû maximæ Angliæ ciuitates, cum Donwico & Donaecastria, aliisq; nonnullis locis flammis con-sumptæ sumptæ sunt, similiq; ne incendio Monasterium de Burgh triennio post ea delerum est. Cuius diuinæ vindictę causam si quis requiratur, probabiliorem certe non possumus reddere, quam quæ ab ipso scriptore comuiemoratur, propter anglicum & christianum Monasterium quorum externa vita tanta sanctitatis specie populo fulgere videbatur. Idemque Monasterium quasi huius supplicii prænomitum hostilis Gallorum invasione anno pene ante hoc incendium direptum fuit.
units.tr: After the monks of Canterbury had for some time performed the funeral rites for the buried John Stafford, they sent John Waltham, bachelor in sacred theology, and Walter Hereford, keeper of the offices of the church of Canterbury, their fellow monks, to King Henry VI with letters. In them they asked that they be allowed, by the permission already granted, to nominate John Kemp, archbishop of York and cardinal of the Roman title of St Balbina, to the metropolitan see of Canterbury. With the king assenting, they nominated him by unanimous votes on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul. They informed the king, and the cardinal nominated, that their nomination had been duly and lawfully carried out, through Richard Graven and Walter Hereford, their fellow monks, who were sent as messengers for that purpose. But Pope Nicholas, who tenaciously kept hold of the right of provision handed down to him by earlier popes, disregarded the monks' election and, under the title of provision, transferred him from the metropolis of York to Canterbury. He did this with such cunning that, not daring to provoke the king and the English clergy, he might yet seem both to obey the king and not to depart at all from his own right, by providing as archbishop of Canterbury the very prelate whom the Canterbury monks had chosen, with the king's approval. So, by six bulls, the first sent to the archbishop, the second to the chapter of Canterbury, the third to the provincial suffragans, the fourth to the clergy of the city and diocese of Canterbury, the fifth to its people, and the sixth to the vassals of the church of Canterbury, and published in Christ Church, Canterbury, on the feast of St Matthew the Evangelist by Thomas Athe, a monk of that church, before a crowded sermon, John Kemp took up the archbishopric of Canterbury and left York. These bulls, now divided and multiplied into so many numbers, increased, through Roman scheming and fraud, the papal revenue, which had been diminished by the abolition of tithes and provisions. The archbishop, having entered upon the archbishopric, received the cross of Canterbury on 24 September in the house of Thomas Kemp, bishop of London, his kinsman, at Fulham. The next day, there, with many prelates and nobles present, he put on the pallium that had been sent by Pope Nicholas and handed to him by the same bishop of London. Then, by another bull, this John Kemp, archbishop and of Canterbury, was moved, just as before he had been transferred from the archbishopric of York to Canterbury, so now from the cardinalate of St Balbina to the more prominent cardinalate with the title of St Ruffina. The costs of so many and such splendid bulls were borne by those who paid for them and those who received them. When it came to the enthronement of this man, adorned with the twin titles of archbishop and cardinal, what was there to omit that, given such a rank, so great an archbishop ought to have done? So on 11 December he was enthroned with this solemnity. In the procession the prior and monks of Canterbury met him in white copes, shouting: "Our pastor, the Cardinal of St Ruffina and Archbishop of Canterbury, etc." The archbishop was met by the bishops Thomas of London, William Waynflete of Winchester and John of Rochester; the first two walked at his sides and the last behind him. Following these bishops came the abbots, namely those of St Augustine's, Canterbury, of Battle, and of Faversham. In the third rank were placed the nobles: the Earl of Worcester, Viscount Lisle, Lord Moleyns, and the Prior of St John. The last rank was mixed with venerable men, both clerical and lay, including the dean of Lincoln, the archdeacon of Ely and others. Now that all the rites of his entry into the archbishopric have been recounted, let us briefly show what sort of man this archbishop was, so celebrated with so many titles, from his first entry into the Church. He was born at Wye in Kent, was trained in letters from boyhood and in law from youth, and, having taken the doctorate, obtained the archdeaconry of Durham. From the archdeaconry of Durham, Henry Chichele, archbishop of Canterbury, brought him in the second year of his archbishopric to the Court of Arches, and made him dean of that court and his vicar-general in spiritual affairs. When he had discharged these offices with distinction, he was made praetorian prefect of the Duchy of Normandy. From that office he was elected bishop of Rochester. After sitting there for three years he was translated to Chester, the next year was moved to London, and four years later came to the metropolis of York by nomination. We said before that Richard, bishop of Lincoln, had received the archbishopric of York from the Pope by title of provision, but was rejected because the papal provision was spurned by the dean and chapter of York. For at the same time they elected John Kemp. Then Pope Nicholas, after Kemp had been chosen by the Canterbury monks under the king's authority, transferred him to the see of Canterbury, under a certain disguised and shadowy appearance of provision (as we said), in order to bind this magnanimous prelate to himself. This prelate, adorned with so many titles, did not sit long. But in the first year of his translation he held a synod at London, in which a subsidy was granted to the king by the clergy, and much was debated concerning the tithes owed by the London people to the clergy, but nothing was settled. In the same year the Lord God sent such violent winds that houses, lofty trees and church towers fell. Since these examples, as divine punishments, occur to us often in various places in the course of this long history, let us set them down here together, gathered as it were under one view and one sense. Since the Papists blame the burning of St Paul's on the religion of the Gospel that we have received and practise, let them see for themselves, from fires, devastations and such sudden losses, that far graver calamities befell in their own blind times. For in the year of the Lord 764, Lambert being archbishop, when papal superstition had already gained very great strength, not only houses, monasteries, churches, whole towns and famous cities, but also, as a kind of final divine judgment, some regions were set ablaze by a sudden fire. In this fire London and York, the greatest cities of England, together with Donwich, Doncaster and some other places, were consumed by flames, and in a similar fire the monastery of Burgh was destroyed three years afterwards. If anyone asks the cause of this divine vengeance, we certainly cannot give a more probable one than that mentioned by the writer himself: because of the English and Christian monastery, whose outward life seemed to shine before the people with such a show of holiness. And the same monastery, as a kind of forerunner of this punishment, had been plundered by a hostile French invasion almost a year before this fire.

units.la: Iuciya vero Londinensis ciuitas flamma cœlesti iterum icta. An. Dom. 1077. a primis suis iactis fundamentis similem cladem ac interitum nunquam passa est. Culus pter has, quatuor deinde aliæ flammæ vastationes contigerunt. Nam an. 1086. Paulinum 10 templum incendio fulguris percussum est, totaq; Ecclesia cobusta. Illudq; incendiu tota Angliam celeriter percurrens omnes pene cathedrales Ecclesias & præcipuas quasque ciuitates deleuit. Tum altera Londinensis vrbis conflagratio an. 1132. fuisse perhibetur. Tertia cum flamma cœlestis primo Templum Paulinum cepit, & viterius accessit ad Pontem Londinensem, & ad S. Clementis Ecclesiam Danorum peruenit. An. 1135. Quatuor vero cum vico de Suthwarke flagrante flammæ (quod mirum est) interfluentes Thamesis vndas transilientes tres Pontis columnas & magnam ciuitatis partem incenderunt, & magnum virorum, mulierum & paruulorum multitudinem subito quasi fatali vindicta interemerunt. Atque Eboracum consumpto prius Monasterio altero in incendio crematum est. 1153. Ipsam Cantuariam Metropolim tribus incendiis modicis temporum interuallis separatis ad ruinam atque cineres redactam legimus. t. cum Elphegus a Danis occisus est. 2. cum Lanfrancus insignis Papalis militiæ Dux Archiepiscopatum suscepit. 3. paulo post quam Thomas Becket papali martyrio candidatus fuit. 1174. Quos tam horribiles casus iusto sed occulto Dei iudicio Cantuariæ inflictos affert Gervasius Cant. Monachus. Præterea totam pene Cantuariam altero an. 1161. arsisse scribit Tho. Wiccius. Ecclesiamque Christi igne cœlitus immisso an. 1168. concidisse teste tur Thomas Sprottus, cuiusque causam censet Abbatum incuriam qui magnatum precibus victi infantes à nutricum uberibus vix dum ablactatos adductos Monachatu initiari solebant. Ciuitas Roffensis vt iam ciuitas Rofensis vt ciuitas. Ciuitas ter incensa fuit ecclitus annis. 1084. 1130. & 1136. Wintoniensis bis, annis. 1080. & 1101. Wigorniensis Ecclesia semel. 1202. Ciuitas ter 1, 30 cum totum Monasterium & Castellum consumpta sunt. anno 1113. 2. cum à Rege Stephano capta atque combusta fuit. an. 1150. Tertio 1202. Glocestrensis ciuitas quinquies. 1. an. 1102. Ecclesia S. Petri Glocestriæ vna cum ciuitate igne crematâ est, deindeque vno an. 1122. bis conflagrauit. Quarto, an Dom. 1300. in die Epiphaniæ iubitum incendium Monasterium circumdedit, atq; claustrum Campanile, & magnam cameram cum vicinis ac proximè adiunctis ædificiis consumpsit. Quinto anno sequenti qui fuit annus dom. 1301. aliud exortum incendium Ecclesiam parochialem Danton Glocestriæ munibus adiunctam totam ad muros combustum, & quatuor Campanilia ad terram percussit, campanas aut liquefactas fudit, aut vi sua confregit. Cicestria etiam bis combusta cum toto cœnobio fuit. 1. tempore Radulphi Cant. Arch. an. 1114. deinde sedente ibidem Seffrido Episcopo. Lincolniensis ciuitas. an. 1123. vnum incendium passa est, alterum villa Petriburgensis an. 1116. in quo sinperbum illud Monasterium solo æquarum est Noruicensis ciuitatis pars. 1413. repentinis ignibus conflagrauit. In Elienfi ciuitate tempore Hatuzi primi Elienfis Episcopi summum culmen campanilis Ecclesiæ S. Petri medianō teac censum ciues pertertrafactos ad extinguendum incēdium excitauit. Carliolensem ciuitatem, cum Monasterio, atque cunctis fratrum minorum ædibus. an. 1289. horribile incendium vastauit. Ab his ciuitatum incendiis ad Monasteriorum & Ecclesiarum trâseamus An. 1148. Monasteriu Glasconiense, & Ecclesia Iuliani Cenomanensis fulminę consumuntur, & 1178. villa de Beuerlaco cum Ecclesia Iohannis Archiepiscopi combusta est. Quoquidem anno Baldwinus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus, & Richardus Episcopus Wintoniensis Monachos ex Cantuariensi cœnobio expulerunt. An. 1261. campanile Ecclesiæ de Euesham fulgore accensum est. Ac Monasterium de Barnwell propeCantebrigiam fulgure eriam ictum flagrauit. an. 1282. Cœnobium Gisbornensean. 1289. combustum est. Mideltonensis Ecclesia in Dorcestrensi comitatu cum Monachi ad matutinas preces conuenissent, correpta fuit fulgure, quo Cœnobii campanile, cameræ, ornamenta, vasa, & instrumenta publica Monachorum combustione deleta sunt. Antiquissimum illud Edmundi de Bury cœnobium præterquam quod bis igne sacro deletum est. An. 1334. etiam ab oppidanis à quibus iterum incensum fuit, depræâatum est. an. 1370. Quo etiam anno Monasterium Abindonense quod quinquies mille passibus abest Oxonio, ab Oxoniensibus direptum est, Ducibus quidem ipsis Municipibus seu Burgensibus, militibus vero gregariis villæ Oxoniensis & Abindonensis artificib. affectis aliquibus scholaribus qui se libidinibus & flagitiis dediderunt. Omittoventos, fulmina, flumina, terræ motus, niues, glacies, grandines, quibus submersæ regiones, prostrata ædificia, agri inundati, denique arbores excelsæ, iuxta ipsi pene portus maris congelati, annis 1247, 1266, 1280 aliisque fuerunt. In Sarisburiensi ciuitate resolutus a gelu tenacissimo aquus, aquæ totam ciuitatem cum Edwardus Rex secundus secundo sui Regni anno Parlamentum ibi celebrare instituisset, ita inundarunt, vt in Missarum celebratione in Ecclesiam laberentur & Regios pedes ad occidentale chori ostium attingerent, ideoque a diuinis celebrandis in ea Ecclesia biduo cessatum est. Omitte etiam immanes & horrendas pestes. Londini triginta hominum millia vna cum ex peste consumpta sunt, an. 1407. Postea ex dissenteria occubuere 40. M. an. 1411. Quæ quidem tot tantaque strages diuinæ cum & frequentiores, & vehementiores multo in illis papisticis seculis fuerint quam nunc sunt, existimare sane possumus Dominum Deum misericordem obsoletis iam & abiectis illis Pontificiis sacris recepto suo sacratissimo Euangelio sua benignitate nobis esse magis propitium atque secundum.
units.tr: Moreover, the city of London was struck again by heavenly fire in the year of our Lord 1077. Since its first foundations were laid, it had never suffered such a disaster and destruction. Besides this, four other conflagrations followed. In the year 1086 St Paul's church was struck by a bolt of lightning and the whole church was burned. That fire swept quickly through the whole of England and destroyed almost all the cathedral churches and the chief cities. Then a second conflagration of the city of London is said to have occurred in 1132. In a third, heavenly fire first seized St Paul's, then spread on to London Bridge and reached the church of St Clement Danes. In 1135 a fire broke out in the village of Southwark, and the flames (which is remarkable) leapt across the waters of the Thames, set fire to three piers of the bridge and a large part of the city, and suddenly, as if by fatal vengeance, killed a great multitude of men, women and small children. York too was burned in 1153, after another monastery had first been consumed by fire. We read that Canterbury itself, the metropolitan city, was reduced to ruin and ashes by three moderate fires, separated by intervals of time: (1) when Alphege was killed by the Danes; (2) when Lanfranc, the distinguished captain of the Papal army, took up the archbishopric; (3) shortly after Thomas Becket was made a candidate for papal martyrdom. In 1174 Gervase, a monk of Canterbury, relates such terrible calamities as these, inflicted on Canterbury by the just but hidden judgement of God. Moreover, Thomas Wykes writes that almost the whole of Canterbury was set on fire in another year, 1161. Thomas Sprot testifies that Christ Church fell in 1168, when fire was sent down from heaven, and he thinks its cause was the negligence of the abbots, who, overcome by the entreaties of great men, used to have infants, scarcely weaned from their nurses' breasts, brought in and initiated into the monastic life. The city of Rochester was burned three times by fire from heaven, in 1084, 1130 and 1136. Winchester was burned twice, in 1080 and 1101. The church of Worcester was burned once, in 1202. The city was burned three times: (1) in 1113, when the whole monastery and castle were consumed; (2) when it was taken and burned by King Stephen, in 1150; (3) in 1202. The city of Gloucester was burned five times. (1) In 1102 St Peter's church at Gloucester was burned together with the city; then in 1122 it burned twice more. (2) In the year of our Lord 1300, on the day of Epiphany, a sudden fire surrounded the monastery and consumed the cloister, the bell-tower, a great chamber, and the neighbouring and adjoining buildings. (3) In the following year, 1301, another fire broke out. It burned the parish church of Danton at Gloucester, which adjoined the walls, entirely down to the walls, struck four bell-towers to the ground, and either melted the bells or shattered them with its force. Chichester too was burned twice, with the whole monastery: first in the time of Archbishop Ralph of Canterbury, in 1114, and then, while Seffrid was bishop there. The city of Lincoln suffered one fire in 1123. In 1116 another fire struck the village of Peterborough, in which that proud monastery was levelled with the ground, and part of the city of Norwich was burned by sudden fires in 1413. In the city of Ely, in the time of Hervey, the first bishop of Ely, a fire broke out at the top of the bell-tower of St Peter's church and at the middle of its roof, and roused the citizens, who were driven to extinguish it. In 1289 a horrible fire laid waste the city of Carlisle, together with its monastery and all the houses of the Friars Minor. Let us now pass from the fires of cities to those of monasteries and churches. In 1148 the monastery of Glastonbury and the church of St Julian of Le Mans were consumed by lightning. In 1178 the village of Beverley was burned, together with the church of John the Archbishop. In that same year Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, and Richard, bishop of Winchester, expelled the monks from the monastery of Canterbury. In 1261 the bell-tower of the church of Evesham was set alight by lightning. The monastery of Barnwell, near Cambridge, was also struck by lightning and burned. In 1282 the monastery of Guisborough, and in 1289 it was burned. The church of Milton in Dorsetshire, when the monks had gathered for morning prayers, was struck by lightning, by which the monastery's bell-tower, chambers, ornaments, vessels and the monks' common implements were destroyed by fire. Besides the fact that that most ancient monastery of Bury St Edmunds was twice destroyed by sacred fire, in 1334 it was also plundered by the townsmen, by whom it was set on fire again. In the same year, 1370, the monastery of Abingdon, five thousand paces from Oxford, was plundered by the men of Oxford. The leaders were the townsmen themselves, that is the burgesses, while the common soldiers were the craftsmen of the town of Oxford and Abingdon, with some scholars who had given themselves over to lusts and crimes. I pass over the winds, lightning, rivers, earthquakes, snows, ice and hailstorms, by which regions were submerged, buildings thrown down, fields flooded, tall trees uprooted, and harbours of the sea nearly frozen in the years 1247, 1266, 1280 and others. In the city of Salisbury, when the stubborn frost thawed and the waters were released, they flooded the whole city just as King Edward II, in the second year of his reign, had decided to hold Parliament there. So much did they flood it that during Mass people slid down into the church and reached the royal feet at the west door of the choir, and for that reason divine services in that church were suspended for two days. I pass over also the monstrous and dreadful plagues: in London thirty thousand people were carried off by plague in 1407, and afterwards forty thousand died of dysentery in 1411. Since such great and numerous divine judgements were far more frequent and violent in those papistical ages than they are now, we may certainly reckon that the merciful Lord God, now that those Popish rites are obsolete and cast off and his most holy Gospel has been received, has been more gracious and favourable to us in his goodness.

units.la: Iam ab his diuinis supplicijs & vindictis ad vltimum huius Archiepiscopi finem accedamus, cuius Archiepiscopatus acta non alia quam quæ recensuimus, & extrema nobis ex historiis, suisue Archiuis traduntur. Postquam anno vno xxv. leptimanis, ac sex diebus sedisset, ex hac vitam Lamethæ euanuit. xi. Kalen. April. Deindeipsis Kalend. cadauer eius Cantuariam traductum, funerumque suorum sacris a Londinensi & Rofsensi Episcopis, nec non Monachis Cantuariensibus pontificio more petactis inter sedem Archiepiscopalem & tumulum Iohannis Stratfort ad australem portam Presbyterii inbumatum est. In funerum clementosynis emulibet Ecclesiæ Cantuar. sacris ordinibus iniciato xiii. s. vt. d. caeteris iv. s. vtt. d. largitus est. Benignitas eius aliquid liberalitas nō alia in Arcbiuis Cant. commemoratur, quàm quod consanguineos suos his tam multis annis multisque sedibus acquisiuit diuitiis, mirum in modum locupletauit, & in Cantio quodam ad equestrem splendorem, quosdam ad alias dignitates euexit.
units.tr: Now let us come from these divine chastisements and vengeances to the final end of this archbishop, whose acts as archbishop are handed down to us only as far as we have recounted them, and the last matters from histories or from his archives. After he had sat for one year, twenty-five weeks and six days, he passed from this life at Lambeth on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. Then, on the Kalends itself, his body was taken to Canterbury. His funeral rites were performed by the bishops of London and Rochester, and likewise by the Canterbury monks in the papal manner, and he was buried between the archiepiscopal seat and the tomb of John Stratford, at the south door of the presbytery. For the funeral alms he gave to each of the clergy of the Canterbury church who were in holy orders 13s. 4d., and to the others 4s. 6d. His kindness and generosity are recorded in the Canterbury archives as nothing other than this: that he enriched his kinsmen wondrously with the wealth he had acquired over so many years and in so many sees, and raised some of them in Kent to knightly splendour and others to other dignities.

units.la: LXIV. Thomas Bovrgchier.
units.tr: LXIV. Thomas Bourgchier.

units.la: Ecundo nonas Aprilis Conuentus Cantuariensis Iohannem Goldwell sacristam, & Walterum Hertford muneriorum custodem ad Hericum sextum Regem cum litteris mittunt. In quibus de morte atque functe Archiepiscopi sui Iohannis Kemp certiorem eum faciunt, & libertatem eligendi pristinam petunt, quod a Rege concessum est, tantaque quidem facilitate, atque æquitate, vt electionis libertati nec precè nec intercessione quacunque præiudicaret. Itaque Cant. Monachis 9. Kalen. Maii in festo S. Georgii vnanimis suffragiis Thomam Bourgchier Elienensem Episcopum ad Cantuariensem Metropolim postularunt. Quæ quidem postulatio proprio quodam & peculiari encomio celebranda est, quod aliæ electiones aut Regum atque principum liberis a Monachis extortæ, aut Papæ prouisionibus impeditæ sunt, hæc sola suis viribus atque libertate stetit. Hæc postulatio ad Papam Nicolaum quartum Romæ Kalendis Iuniis perlata est, atque mox scriptis & sigillatis bullis confirmata. Quæ reuersis & expeditis nuncijs in Ecclesia Christi Cant. à quodam Wilhelmo Thornden Monacho Cant. xt. Calend. Septembr. proconcione publicata sunt. Tum Prior Cant. cruce velata ante se gestaad Archiepiscopum equitauit, eamque in Eliensi domo apud Syoborn Londini tradidit. Venit deinde in Angliâ à Papæ latere missus legatus Archiepiscopus Rauennæ v. Idus Decembr. ad antequam a Caleto traiiceret, accepit à Rege ingrediendi licentiam. Hic Legatus huic nouo Archiepiscopo nouum à Papa honoris inanis titulum detulit, cumque in primo congressu Reuerendissimum patrem Cardinalem Sancti Siriaci in Thermis appellauit. Hoc accepto titulo Intronizatio vii. Calendas Februarii Cantuariæ celebrata est. In huius festi eonuiuijs medius inter Episcopos Archiepiscopus sedebat, a dextris Londinensis cum Roffensi, a sinistris Wintonensis cum Roffensi collocati sunt. Occupabant in eadem camera proximam mensam Abbates, Augustini Martini de
units.tr: On the fourth of April the convent of Canterbury sent John Goldwell, the sacrist, and Walter Hertford, the keeper of the muniments, to King Henry VI with letters. In them they informed him of the death of their archbishop, John Kemp, and asked for their former freedom of election. The King granted this with such ease and fairness that it prejudiced the freedom of election neither by petition nor by any intercession. Therefore, on the twenty-third of April, the feast of St George, the monks of Canterbury by unanimous votes petitioned for Thomas Bourgchier, Bishop of Ely, to the metropolitan see of Canterbury. This petition deserves a particular praise of its own, because other elections were either wrung from the monks by the children of kings and princes, or hindered by papal provisions, whereas this one alone stood by its own strength and liberty. The petition was carried to Pope Nicholas IV at Rome on the first of June and soon confirmed by written bulls and seals. When the messengers returned and had finished their business, it was published in the church of Christ at Canterbury on the eighteenth of August by one William Thornden, a monk of Canterbury, during the sermon. Then the Prior of Canterbury rode before the archbishop carrying a veiled cross, and handed it over at the Ely house at Shoebury in London. Afterwards the Archbishop of Ravenna came into England as legate sent from the Pope's side, on the fifth of December; before he crossed from Calais, he received the King's licence to enter. This legate conferred on the new archbishop a new title of empty honour from the Pope, and at their first meeting he addressed him as the most reverend father, the Cardinal of St Siriacus in the Baths. Upon receiving this title, the enthronement was celebrated at Canterbury on the twenty-fifth of January. At the feast of this enthronement the archbishop sat in the middle among the bishops: the Bishop of London and the Bishop of Rochester were placed on his right, and the Bishop of Winchester and the Bishop of Rochester on his left. In the same hall at the next table sat the abbots of St Augustine's, St Martin's of Battle, and Faversham, and the priors of Canterbury, Dover and Cumbwell, with the monks of Canterbury.

units.la: Bello, de Feuersham, ac Priores Cant. Douor. Clumbwel cum Monachis Cant. In suprema aulæ quæ alba dicta est, sedebant Dux Buckinghamiæ, Comes Dorcestrensis, Comes Staffordiensis, Comes de Hew, Vicecomes Beamont, Vicecomes Fewarren, Dominus de Shrewsbury, Dominus de Barues, D. de Burgeuenny, D. de Say, D. de Clynton, D. de Ecchingham. In magna aula discumbebant primam mensam D. Richardus Ferrys, D. Rogerus le Coniers Barones, atq; Milites Suffexiæ: ad proximam D. Iohannes Cheiney Vicecomes Cantii, D. Thomas Kyriel, D. Thomas Brown cum Militibus & Generosis Cantii.
units.tr: In the uppermost hall, which is called the white hall, sat the Duke of Buckingham, the Earl of Dorset, the Earl of Stafford, the Earl of Eu, Viscount Beaumont, Viscount Fitzwarin, the Lord of Shrewsbury, the Lord of Bures, the Lord Abergavenny, the Lord Say, the Lord Clinton and the Lord Echingham. In the great hall, at the first table, sat Lord Richard Ferrers and Lord Roger Le Conyers, barons, and the knights of Sussex. At the next table sat Lord John Cheyney, Viscount of Kent, Lord Thomas Kyriel and Lord Thomas Brown, with the knights and gentlemen of Kent.

units.la: Hos excelsos & illustres viros innumera plebs sequuta est. Peracta autem intronizatione tam magnifica, visitauit Ecclesiam atq; diocesin Cantuariensem, in qua multa straruendo atq; sanciendo edixit. 1. vt religiosi qui abiecto suæ professionis habitu, secu-lari amictu vestiti beneficia acquirunt, beneficiis amoti Apostasiæ pœnis plectantur.
units.tr: Such noble and illustrious men were followed by an innumerable common crowd. When the enthronement, so splendid, was over, he visited the church and diocese of Canterbury, and in it he decreed many things by way of reform and enactment. (1) That religious who, having cast off the habit of their profession and clothed in secular dress, acquire benefices, be deprived of those benefices and punished with the penalties of apostasy.

units.la: 2. Ne Ecclesiastica beneficia sine Episcopi licentia locentur. 3. vt de filiis, arboribus, fasciculis & biletis soluatur decima quacunq; consuetudine non obstante. 4. vt nuptiis contrahendis, testamentis conficiendis duo pluresue testes adhibeantur. Præterea de variis Clericorum, atq; laicorum excessibus corrigendis multa decreta, quæ ad crucé Paulinam publicari pro concione mandauit.
units.tr: (2) that church benefices shall not be let without the bishop's licence; (3) that tithes shall be paid on the young of animals, on trees, faggots and billets, notwithstanding any custom to the contrary; (4) that two or more witnesses shall be present for contracting marriages and for drawing up wills. Besides these, he ordered many decrees for correcting various excesses of clergy and laity, which he commanded to be published from St Paul's Cross in sermons.

units.la: Erat hic Thomas Bourgchier illustri genere prognatus, frater Henrici Bourgchier Essexiæ Comitis, ac in Oxoniensi Academia institutus, ac eiusdem Cancellarius, & Decanus S. Martini London.
units.tr: This Thomas Bourgchier was born of an illustrious family, the brother of Henry Bourgchier, Earl of Essex. He was educated at the University of Oxford, where he became chancellor, and he was dean of St Martin's, London.

units.la: Deinde Wigorniensis Episcopus, ab eo quoq; ad Eliensem, tum demum ad Archiepiscopatum (vt diximus) translatus. In hoc anno Richardus Dux Eboracensis, adiunctis sibi Richardis duobus, vno Sarisburiæ, altero Waruici Comite, Edmundum Somersetti Ducem, Henricum Northumbriæ Comitem, ac D. Clyfford Henrico Rege præsente cum septem militum millibus ad Sanctum Albanum commisso prælio trucidauit. Totiusq; regni administrationem & protectionem sub eodem Rege suscepit, & Cancellariatus munus Sarisburiæ Comiti, ac Caleti portus custodiam Waruicensi commisit. Hæc rerum nouitas aliquot annis frequentes bellorum strages intulit Anglis, donec interfecto Richardo Eboracensi Duce, altero Prælio in Dominica palmarum Eboraci commisso inter Edwardum Ducis hærilem filium & Henricum sextum Regem Mars litem diremit. In quo superatus Rex amisit regnum quod Edwardus vendicauit. Quem Thomas Archiepiscopus Westmonasterii 4. Kal. Iulii Regem vnxit, & sacrauit. Celebrauit eodem anno Archiepiscopus Synodalem Cleri conuentum Londini, in qua concessa Regi decima, multaq; de arboribus decimandis acta sunt. Statutumq; præterea omniū Prælatorum cōsensu fuit: Ne inferiores Prelati in bannorū editione, aut vllis negociis matrimoniū tāgentibus dispensationes concederent. In eadem Synodo Galfridus Longbrooke procurator Magistri Petri Courtnaii Archidiaconi Exoniensis à Maioris Londinensis licitoribus ad instantiam Simonis Notingham de actione personali apprehensus, & violenter in ius obtorto (vt aiunt) collo ductus est. Quod cum Synodus accepisset, Prior Cătuariensis ad Maiorem, & Vicecomites missus est vt idem Galfridus durante synodo à custodia & iudicio dimitteretur, alioquin synodū contra Londinenses per Ecclesiasticas cēsuras ad grauiora processurā. Hoc nūcio Galfridus liberatus & synodo restitutus est. His tēporib. illa vilissima cudendi atq; imprimendi scientia Argentorati Germaniæ ciuitate inuenta est, etsi de aut horis, loci, anniq; certa veritate inter scriptores magna dissensio est, quam perpendant lectores. Hæc autem hoc anno in eius laudem edita carmina sunt. O felix nostrū memorandā impressio tecū Inuentore nitet vtraque lingua tuo. Deficrat quasi tetum quod fundis in orbem Nunc parno dectus quisbet esse potest. Omnes te summis igitur nunc laudibus ornent. Te Duce quando Ars hac mira reperta fuit:
units.tr: Then he was Bishop of Worcester, from there he was translated by the same route to Ely, and at last, as we have said, to the archbishopric. In this year Richard, Duke of York, having joined to himself two Richards, one the Earl of Salisbury and the other the Earl of Warwick, slew Edmund, Duke of Somerset, Henry, Earl of Northumberland, and Lord Clifford, at St Albans, where battle was joined with King Henry present, and with seven thousand soldiers. He took over the whole administration and protection of the realm under the same king, gave the office of chancellor to the Earl of Salisbury, and entrusted the custody of the port of Calais to the Earl of Warwick. This upheaval brought frequent slaughters of war upon the English for some years, until Richard, Duke of York, was killed; then in a second battle, fought at York on Palm Sunday between Edward, the duke's son, and King Henry VI, Mars settled the quarrel. In it the defeated king lost the kingdom, which Edward claimed. Archbishop Thomas anointed and consecrated him at Westminster on 28 June. In the same year the archbishop held a synodal convocation of the clergy at London, in which, after the tenth granted to the King, much was enacted concerning the tithing of trees. Moreover, with the consent of all the prelates, it was decreed that inferior prelates should not grant dispensations in the publishing of banns, or in any business touching marriage. In the same synod, Geoffrey Longbrooke, proctor of Master Peter Courtenay, archdeacon of Exeter, was seized by the sheriffs of London at the instance of Simon Nottingham, in a personal action, and was dragged violently into court, by the neck (so they say). When the synod heard of this, the Prior of Canterbury was sent to the mayor and sheriffs to ask that the same Geoffrey be released from custody and from judgment for the duration of the synod; otherwise the synod would proceed against the Londoners with ecclesiastical censures and more serious measures. On receiving this message, Geoffrey was set free and restored to the synod. In these times that most vile art of casting and printing was discovered in the German city of Strasbourg, although writers disagree greatly about the true place, hour and year, which readers should weigh for themselves. In this year verses were published in its praise: O happy printing, worth remembering, in you both languages shine through your inventor. It was as if you were pouring out the whole world; now any poor man can become learned. Let everyone now crown you with the highest praises, since under your leadership this wonderful art was discovered.

units.la: Et sane diuino beneficio hæc ars in hoc seculo hominibus patefacta est, ex cuius fœcundo quasi gremio omnes artes ac scientiæ caecitate & caligine abstersa tanquam è longæuis tenebris prodierunt.
units.tr: And indeed, by divine benefit, this art was opened to men in this age; from its fruitful bosom, as though from long darkness, all the arts and sciences have come forth, their blindness and gloom wiped away.

units.la: Nunc ad historiam reuertamur. Edwardus Rex duobus iam annis feliciter gesto regno Parlamentum Westmonasterii tenuit, quo etiam tempore Archiepiscopus & Clerus in synodo conuenerunt. In hac Synodo Iohannes Comes Wigorniæ, Henricus Comes Effexiæ, D. Edmundus Gray Thesaurarius Angliæ, D. Humfridus Cromwell, D. Wentlocke, D. Iohannes Prior S. Iohannis, & Robertus Stillington legum Doctor, Custos priuati sigilli Regis consiliarii allatis literis Regiis petierunt a Clero decerni Regi ad Scotos repellendos subsidium. Quod quidem gratissimis omnium animis tam munifico Regi concessum est, qui superiori anno Ecclesiæ immunitates atque iura iniquis (vt in Iohanne Strafford antea diximus) luridicorum calumniis conuulsa & labefactata diplomate Regio restaurauit.
units.tr: Now let us return to the history. King Edward, having now governed the kingdom happily for two years, held Parliament at Westminster, and at the same time the archbishop and clergy met in synod. In this synod John, Earl of Worcester, Henry, Earl of Essex, Lord Edmund Gray, Treasurer of England, Lord Humphrey Cromwell, Lord Wenlock, Lord John Prior of St John, and Robert Stillington, Doctor of Laws and keeper of the privy seal, councillors of the King, brought royal letters and asked that the clergy grant the King a subsidy to repel the Scots. This was granted, most gladly by all, to so generous a king, who in the previous year had restored, by royal charter, the immunities and rights of the Church, which had been shaken and weakened by the unjust calumnies of lawyers (as we said earlier, in the case of John Strafford).

units.la: In quo sanxit & decreuit, vt Clerus tam veteribus Ecclesiasticis iuribus quam novuis, si quæ condere vellent, malitiam eorum à quibus sua iura violantur compescant, tum in cauiis omnibus ad Ecclesiasticum forum spectantibus, etiam in maiorum arborū decrimis etiamsi viginti aut plures annos ætate excesserint sine metu aut pœna statutorum deprouisionibus, aut breuium seu actionum de Præmunire aut cuiuscunq; prohibitionis etiam nulla consultatione obtenta liberè procedant. Et si quis index Regius seu secularis aliquem Archiepiscopum, Episcopum, Archidiaconum, suosue Vicarios, officiales, commissarios, aut iudices Ecclesiasticos qnofcunq; breuibus, & processu aliquo impeditat aut deterreat, vt ad eiuldem Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, iudicisue Ecclesiastici impediti aut perterriti monitionem (quam Rex rataam fidemq; eidem habiturum dixit) in Carcerlaria statuto sibi ab eodem Ecclesiastico iudice die sub pœna duecentarum librarum compareat respon surus Regi de contemptu, suumque in Ecclesiasticum iudicem procesllum authoritate Regia rescindi & irritum ac inane pronunciari visurus.
units.tr: In that charter he sanctioned and decreed that the clergy might freely pursue both the old ecclesiastical rights and any new ones they wished to establish, and check the malice of those by whom their rights are violated. In all causes belonging to the ecclesiastical court, even concerning tithes on larger trees, even if they have reached the age of twenty years or more, they might proceed without fear of penalty under the statutes of provisors, or the writs and actions of praemunire, or any prohibition whatever, even if obtained without consultation. And if any royal or secular judge should hinder or deter any archbishop, bishop, archdeacon, or their vicars, officials, commissaries or ecclesiastical judges by writs or any legal process, then, at the admonition of the archbishop, bishop or ecclesiastical judge who has been hindered or terrified (which the King said he would hold valid and trustworthy), that judge shall appear in prison, on a day fixed for him by that same ecclesiastical judge, under a penalty of two hundred pounds, to answer to the King for contempt, and shall see his suit against the ecclesiastical judge rescinded and declared void and null by royal authority.

units.la: Cum itaq; omnis laicorum iudicum in Prælatos querimonia, tum cum Romanæ curiæ poteltas etiam Regibus ipsis terrorem incussit, sola hæc fuit, quod nisi plerzq; cancæ ab Ecclesiastico foro amputentur, appellationibus à Regia cognitione ad Papalem perferantur, quid nunc dicere possunt, cum Prælati Regiam authoritatem & diuino verbo sanctius, & sua iurisdictione multo pentius tueantur quam Causidici. An non quod à RegeEdwardo tunc impetratum est, id nunc Prælatorū pcibus côcedi multo est a quius? Sed de Synodo ista reliqua persoluamus, quæ grauem pœnam sanxit in eos quorū vi, aut præceptoaliqui coemiteris aut Ecclesiis locisue sacris in ius aut carceres duxit sunt.
units.tr: Since, then, every complaint of the lay judges against the prelates (and the power of the Roman court, which struck terror even into kings themselves, was the chief grievance) rested on this alone: unless many cases were cut off from the ecclesiastical courts, appeals would be carried from royal cognizance to the Pope's. What can they say now, when the prelates defend royal authority both more sacredly, by the divine word, and far more vigorously, by their own jurisdiction, than the lawyers do? Is it not far more unjust that what was then obtained from King Edward is now granted to the prayers of the prelates? But let us finish the rest of that synod, which laid a grave penalty on those by whose force or command any persons were dragged from cemeteries, churches or other sacred places into court or prison.

units.la: Tum alia constitutione de vestitu Clericorū edita synodus dimissa est. Post ista Edwar dus Rex Elizabetham filiam D. Richardi Wooduyle, D. de Reuers sibi matrimonio iuxit. Hæ nuptiæ Westmonasterii à Cant. Archiepiscopo celebratæ, atq; Regina coronata est vit. Kal. Iunii qui eo anno festus fuit dies dedicatus Augustino primo Cantuariensi Antistiti. Quibus nuptiis celebratis Rex & Regina peregrinantes ad Thomæ delubrum venerunt Cantuariā, & magnis Archiepiscopiac Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis sumptibus ibidem aliquandiu conuiuati sunt. Sequenti anno venit in Angliam Patriarcha Anliochiæ patria à Turcis capta profugus, secumq; duos Camelos & quatuor Dromedarios stupenda & inusitata magnitudine duxit. Cuius exulis inopia Archiepiscopi liberalitate & hospitio subleuata est. Nuptiis deinde inter Carolum Burgundiæ Ducem, & Dominā Margaretam Edwardi Angliæ Regis sororem contractis, altera peregrinatio a Rege & Regina, cum eadem D. Margareta, & Clarentiæ, ac Glocestriæ Ducibus Regis fratribus, aliisque inclyuis proceribus Cæsariam susceptat est. In qua multis muneribus ad Thomæ delubrum oblatis, atq; triduo in epulis lautioribus consumpto, Rex & Regina Londinum reuersi sunt. At D. Margareta maré traiecit, & ad maritimum portum de Scluce applicuit, vbi a Burgundiæ magnatibus recepta ad Ducē ducta est. Inter quos terniodie menis Iulii nuptiæ a Sarisburiensi Episcopo celebratæ sunt. Hæ nuptiæ summa prudentia conciliatæ, maximo deinde Regi in exilium profugo ad regnum recuperandum præsidio fuerunt.
units.tr: Then the synod was dismissed, after another constitution had been issued concerning the dress of the clergy. After this, King Edward married Elizabeth, daughter of Sir Richard Woodville, Lord Rivers. The wedding was celebrated at Westminster by the Archbishop of Canterbury, and the queen was crowned on 25 May, which that year was the feast dedicated to Augustine, the first bishop of Canterbury. After the wedding, the king and queen made a pilgrimage to Thomas's shrine at Canterbury, and were entertained there for some time at great expense to the archbishop and the church of Canterbury. In the following year the Patriarch of Antioch came to England as a fugitive, his country having been taken by the Turks, and he brought with him two camels and four dromedaries of astonishing and unusual size. The poverty of this exile was relieved by the archbishop's generosity and hospitality. Then, after a marriage had been arranged between Charles, Duke of Burgundy, and the Lady Margaret, sister of King Edward of England, a second journey was undertaken to Caesaria by the king and queen, with the same Lady Margaret, the Dukes of Clarence and Gloucester, the king's brothers, and other illustrious nobles. There, after many gifts had been offered at Thomas's shrine and three days had been spent in rather lavish feasting, the king and queen returned to London. But the Lady Margaret crossed the sea and landed at the port of Sluys, where she was received by the Burgundian magnates and led to the duke. Among these, on 3 July, the marriage was celebrated by the Bishop of Salisbury. This marriage, arranged with great prudence, later proved of the greatest help to the king, when he was an exile, in recovering his kingdom.

units.la: Eodem anno in maris Cantiani littore Cæte quoddam maximum captum est, cuius longitudo amplexus decem, latitudo quinque superabat, quod in varias partes diffeædum vix à viginti quatuor bigis a lirore ad portum delatum est. Archiepiscopus Eboracensis peregrinādi causa ad Thomæ delubrum sequenti anno accessit: sed quia ex veteri illa compositione (de qua in Henrico Chicheley antea diximus) pro cruce in Cantuariensi prouincia gestanda non obtulit iocale, coactus est peregrinationis suæ instituit ritusAugustino præstare, deinde quinto die mensis Iulii fexenubus Waruicēsi, & Oxoniensi Ducibus iocali oblato ad Thomæ delubrum peregrinando accessit. Idem postea cū magno Clericorum choro ad ingentem quandam nauem à Comite Waruicensi extructa Pontificalib. indutus cimba vectus est, ameq; missis & innumeris Pötificiis ritib. a summo manet ad vesperū, ductis sacrauit. & Trinitatē appellauit. In hac nauiComes Waruicēsis, Comes Clarātinus, & Archiep. Eborac. ad Caletū cui' portus (vt diximus) custodiā Waruicēsis renuit, postridie applicuerūt, ibi nuptiæ inter Clarentinū Cornīcē, & Annā Waruicēsis filiā cōtractæ,& abEborac. Archiepiscopo celebratæ sunt. His pactis nuptiis Waruicensis qui iam ab Edwardo Regæ animo defecit, Clarentinum suum generum ad fœdus secum contra Regem frarrem ineundum solicitanit, vt excusso illius iugo, Henricum sextum Arce Londinensi inclusum liberent,& Regno restituant. Fœdus hoc ipsi Waruicēsi tandē exitiosum inirum est. Hoc Edwardus ipsa suspicione olefecit,& Cantuariam cum Regina,atque Domina Elizabetha primogenita filia,stipatus quinque Episcopis multisq; proceribus properauit. Ibi oblatis multis Thomæ Delubro donis biduo consilium cum Episcopis & Baronibus secretissimum habuit, à quo Archiepisc. Cantuariensis immeritò suspectus exclusus est. Res actā sic est vt deducto Waruicensis manu Henrico sexto, necesse fuit Edwardo ad Burgundiæ Ducem à quo militare auxilium impetrauit aufugere. Cum quo reuersus capto Henrico sexto Waruicensem prælio Barneti commisso fugauit,& interfecit. Deinde alio prælio Tewkesburiæ superauit Henricum sextū, eiusq; filium Edwardū, quibus victoriis in Regno securus atq; stabilitus fuit.
units.tr: In the same year a very large ray was caught on the Kentish shore. Its length exceeded ten fathoms and its breadth five; it was cut into pieces and carried from the shore to the harbour by scarcely twenty-four wagons. In the following year the Archbishop of York came to Thomas's shrine on pilgrimage. But because, under that old agreement (of which we spoke earlier under Henry Chichele), he did not offer a jewel for the cross to be carried in the province of Canterbury, he was compelled to pay Augustine the customary dues for his pilgrimage. Then, on the fifth day of July, with the Dukes of Exeter and Oxford, he came to Thomas's shrine on pilgrimage after offering a jewel. Afterwards he went with a great choir of clergy to a huge ship built by the Earl of Warwick, vested in pontifical robes, and was carried in a boat. There, from morning until evening, he consecrated the ship with masses and countless Pontifical rites, and named it the Trinity. In this ship the Earl of Warwick, the Earl of Clarence and the Archbishop of York put in the next day at Calais, whose port (as we said) Warwick had refused to hold for the king. There a marriage was arranged between Clarence and Anne, daughter of Warwick, and was celebrated by the Archbishop of York. With these marriage terms settled, Warwick, who had now withdrawn his allegiance from Edward, sought to bring his son-in-law Clarence into a league with him against his brother the king, so that, having shaken off Edward's yoke, they might free Henry VI, shut up in the Tower of London, and restore him to the kingdom. This league proved in the end fatal to Warwick himself. Edward, suspecting it, went to Canterbury with the queen and the Lady Elizabeth, his eldest daughter, attended by five bishops and many nobles. There, after offering many gifts at Thomas's shrine, he held a most secret council for two days with the bishops and barons, from which the Archbishop of Canterbury was excluded, though he had done nothing to deserve suspicion. The affair turned out so that, once Warwick had taken Henry VI into his hands, Edward was obliged to flee to the Duke of Burgundy, from whom he obtained military aid. Returning with him, he took Henry VI, defeated Warwick in battle at Barnet, and put him to flight and killed him. Then, in another battle at Tewkesbury, he overcame Henry VI and his son Edward, and by these victories he was made secure and firm in the kingdom.

units.la: Posthæc quatuor annis proximis, quatuor synodus instituit,tor Regi subsidia præstiterunt. At Papa bellicosus per totum Christianum orbem edixit,à cunctis Christianis gentibus conflandus in Turcarum Imperatorem misit. ...
units.tr: In the four years after this, four synods were held, and they granted the king subsidies. But the Pope, warlike, issued an edict throughout the whole Christian world that ... [the text breaks off here] ...

units.la: Editorial note: several lines of the lower paragraphs are too small or faint to read reliably; see notes. . Quo concesso Archiepiscopus omnia Domini Regis bona atque iura sequestro & custodiæ Wilhelmi Dawbeney, Richardi Laurence, & Roberti Foster interim dum illi deliberarent committit, præsentibus omnibus pene præsulibus & proceribus Regni. Sigillum verò magnum, & priuatum, nec non annulum signatorium ad suam custodiam recepit, atq; penes ie retinuit. Sed qui sumptus funerales 1496. I exhauerant, data ab eodem Archiepiscopo potestas fuit exequendi bonis sub sequestro reseruatis.
units.tr: [Editorial note: several lines of the lower paragraphs are too small or faint to read reliably; see notes.] ... With this agreed, the archbishop committed all the lord king's goods and rights, meanwhile, to the sequestration and custody of William Dawbeney, Richard Laurence and Robert Foster, while they deliberated, almost all the prelates and nobles of the realm being present. He took the great seal and the privy seal, and also the signet ring, into his own custody and kept them with himself. But the funeral expenses of 1496 had used up the money, and the same archbishop gave power to pay them from the goods kept under sequestration.

units.la: Anno sequenti Richardus Dux Gloceftriæ horrenda cæde Edwardi & Richardi filiorum fratris sui Edwardi Regis perpetrata, simulans Edwardum fratrem nothum iniuste regnum tenuisse idem vt triennio occupauit, quia ab hoc Archiepiscopo Westmonasterii eoronatus & sacratus est, is in sacratione stipulanti Archiepiscopo omnes libertates & immunitates Ecclesiæ iuxta Canonum institutaq defensurum, omniaq; Regni iuraß. Edwardo Rege quondam deserpta seruaturum, totumq; populum atq; Clerum in pace protecturum iureiurando promisit. Verùm tam immanium scelerum terribili conscientia tanquam furiis exagitatus, neque somnos postea dulces, ne spiritum ducere tranquillum vnquam potuit. Sed in tertio vsurpatu à se Regni anno ab Henrico Richmondiæ Comite in acie ad 11. Cal. Sept. victus & trucidatus est. Tum Henricus rerum potitus eum Domina Elizabetha Edwardi Quarti Regis primogenita filia contraxit nuptias. His vnis secundissimis nuptiis duæ gentes & familiæ illustrissimæ quæ tot annis de Imperio dimicabant, Lancastrensis cuius Hæres fuit Henricus Richemondiæ Comes, & Ebnracensis quæ trucidatis (vt diximus) à Richardo tyranno duobus fratribus ad Dominam Elizabetham iure hæreditario obuenit vnitæ & inperpetuum coneiliaræ sunt. Archiepiscop* Cant. istas nuptias celebrauit, & vtrosq; paulo post, illum Regem Angliæ nomine Henricum septimum, hanc Reginam Westmonasterii coronauit atq; sacrauit, pridie Cal. Nouemb. Postea Rex Parlamentum Westmonasterii, Archiepiscopus Synodum Lödini ecclebrauit. In synodo Clerus Regi victori & tyrannotono pruoenmū suorum decimas vlire detulit. In Parlamento permissum fuit Episcopis Clericos adulteros atque fornicarios careeribus suis coercere. Proximo anno Thomas Bourgchier Archiepiscopus postquam triginta duobus annis sedisset obiit, & ab aquilonari latere summi altaris in Ecclesia Cant. sumptuoso tumulo conditus sepultus iacet. Hic dedit Vniuersitati Cantebrig. centum viginti libras, quæ permissa cum centum libris quas ante eum M. Billingforth quondam præfectus Collegii corporis Christi, dictæq; Vniuersitatis Cancellarius dederat, in eadem eista in ea domo vbi congregationes & ennuociones Scholarium ennuenut posita vtriusq; fundatoris nomine Cista Billingforth & Boufier appellata est, cuius conseruando thesauro custodes singulis annis depuantur.
units.tr: In the following year Richard, Duke of Gloucester, having perpetrated the dreadful murder of the sons of his brother King Edward, Edward and Richard, pretended that Edward (his brother) was a bastard and had held the kingdom unjustly, and so for about three years he seized the throne. Because he was crowned and anointed at Westminster by this archbishop, he promised on oath, when the archbishop asked him at the anointing, that he would defend all the liberties and immunities of the Church according to the canons and the institutes, would keep all the laws of the realm and the customs once observed under King Edward, and would protect the whole people and clergy in peace. Yet, driven as it were by the terrible consciousness of such monstrous crimes, he could never afterwards enjoy sweet sleep, nor draw a tranquil breath. But in the third year of his usurped reign he was defeated and slaughtered in battle on 21 August by Henry, Earl of Richmond. Then Henry, having gained power, married Elizabeth, the eldest daughter of King Edward IV. By this most fortunate marriage, the two most illustrious nations and families, which had fought for the empire for so many years (the Lancastrians, whose heir was Henry, Earl of Richmond, and the Yorkists, whose heir, after the two brothers had been slaughtered by the tyrant Richard, as we said, came to Lady Elizabeth by hereditary right), were united and joined together for ever. The Archbishop of Canterbury celebrated this marriage, and a little afterwards crowned and anointed at Westminster both him, as King of England under the name of Henry VII, and her as queen, on 31 October. Afterwards the king held a parliament at Westminster, and the archbishop a synod at London. In the synod the clergy offered to the victorious king and the tyrant's conqueror the tithes of their own goods. In parliament it was permitted to the bishops to restrain adulterous and fornicating clergy in their own prisons. In the following year Thomas Bourchier, Archbishop, having sat for thirty-two years, died, and he was buried in a sumptuous tomb on the north side of the high altar in the church of Canterbury. He gave the University of Cambridge one hundred and twenty pounds, which, together with the one hundred pounds that Master Billingford, formerly president of Corpus Christi College and chancellor of the said university, had given before him, was placed in the same chest, in the room where the scholars' assemblies and summonses were held. In the name of both founders this chest is called the Billingford and Bourchier chest, and to preserve its treasure, custodians are appointed each year.

units.la: LXV. Iohannes Morton.
units.tr: LXV. John Morton.

units.la: OHANNES Morton Beerę Dorcestrensis Comitatus nppido natus, adolescens Oxonii studuit, & eum in iure ciuili atq; pontificio prnfecisset, controuersis causis in Areuata curia patrocinatus aduocatus fuit. Tum beneficio atque gratia Thnmæ Bourgehier Cantuariensis Areh. cuiob iuris scientiam & prudentiam charus fuit, non mudò multis Ecclesiasticis dignitatibus auctus, sed summa fide Henrico Regi sexto commendatus est. Cuius consiliis adhibitus in durissimis illis & periculosissimis temporibus citam firmitet adhæsit, vt ne in castris, atque summo diserimine ab eo vnquam discederet. Hane hominis fidem & integritatem ipsius hostis Edwardus Rex quartus, etsi suis partibus aduersam tantopere tamen adamauit, vt victoria parta, lohanne Morton multis benefieiis ad suum seruitium alliceret, & secreris consiliis adhiberet. In quibus eum & quantum ingenio polleret, & quo erga se animo & industria singula tractaret perspexisset, ad Elienfem Episcopatum eum promouit. Nam erat tum quisquam in quo suarum rerum recte gerendarum fiduciam, aut posteritatis suæ tuendæ spem maiorem quam in hoc Episcopo Rex collocarat. Itaque moriens eum testamento vnum executorum ordinauit. Id quod Riehardus tyrannus, qui Edwardi suifratris masculinam prolem deleuit, veritus, eumque animadiuertisset tam fidem Episcopum ad suas nenefarias & sceleratas partes ab impuberibus Regiis filiis tuendis nullo modo adduci potuisse, proditionis, atque læsæ maiestatis insimulauit, & Turri Londinensi inclusit. Mox inde eductum cum intendere hominitam insonti nullam accusationem potuit, sceleris & parricidij tui socij Ducis Buckinghamiæ custodiæ tradidit. Sed cum horrendis atribus atque dolis, & ope Ducis Buckinghamiæ Richardus tyrannus in Regio solio positus esset, occulta quædam simultas odiumq; incredibile inter hunc Regiis ritibus inauguratum tyrannum, atque Dncem subito intercesit. Quod cum tanto feruore intimo Ducis pectore æstuaret, vt eelari diu non poterat, rem omnem Iohanni Morton Elinensi Episcopo quem arctiori adhuc custodia tenuit, indicauit. Quo quidem nemine se habere potuisse existimauit commodiorem ad id quod meditabatur vindictam, exitiumque tyranni. Cumque eum sponte in eundem secum sensum primo sermone incidere vidisset, laxauit ei duras custodiæ habenas, permisitque libertatem. At Iohannes Elienfis etsi valde recreabatur, Ducem tamen odio à tyranno defecisse, prospexit tamen id prudenter quod euenit, Deum de vtrisque tanti sceleris sociis supplicium sumpturum. Ideoque quanquam Ducis conatum probaret, adhærere tamen ei noluit, sed nactus ex hac indulta libertate tempus opportunum habitu & amictu mutato celeriter atque clam in Elienfem suam Insulâ profugit, indeq; traiecit in Flandriâ. Tum cadentibus literis atque nuncijs cum omnibus his egit quos Edwardi Regis stirpi fauere cognouerat, vt inter D. Elizabetham Edwardi primogenitam filiam, & Henricum Richemondiæ Comitem in exilio iam agentem procurarentur nuptiæ, tam ad deiiciendum tam sæuum & crudelem tyrannum, quod ad intestinas seditiones tollédas, quæ tam diu inter Lancastrensem & Eboracensem familias ad totius Regni perniciem ingruerunt. Hoc sanum consilium auspice Deo profectum, depulso(vt ante dixi mus) tyranno, victoriaque diuinitus Henrico Regi septimo delata Deo propitio secundum euentum habuit. Itaque Henricus Regno potitus Iohannem Morton secum in patriam reduxit Regni Cancellarium confituit. Deinde Thoma Bourgchier mortuo eundem ad Metropolim Cantuariensem à Monachis postulari, & confirmatione Innocentii Papæ ab Elienfi solui atque transferri procurauit. Hæc translatio perinde atq; illa Thomæ Bonrgchier qui ab Elienfi etiam sede ad Cantuariensem deductus est, sex distinctis bullis, etti minori compendio agere Papa potuisset, publicata est. Sed auctoritate prœcio, multiplicari etiam conuenit illa plumbea instrumenta. Mox ab Wilhelmo Selling sacræ theologiæ professore, & Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis Priore allatum est vexillum Archiepiscopo quod in munerio Elienfis Episcopi in Holborne accepit, atque osculatus est, ac deinde Crueigero suo tradidit. Sed nuptiis (vi dixi mus) inter Henricum Regem septimum celebratis, Papa ad confirmandum illud legitimum diuinitus conciliatum ac ad pacem & tranquillitatem Anglorum maxime necessarium matrimonij suis bullis minime necessarius opus esse putauit, quia quarto consanguinitatis gradu eo nunc. Quod quidem nullo neque diuino, neque ciuili iure sed pontificio tantum prohibetur. In quibus etiam ne authoritate carere videretur regnum accessum Regi confirmauit, illudque iure hæreditario, iure belli, iure coniugali, iure electionis, iure renatus seu Parlamenti Anglicani, nec non iure pōtificio atque suo ad Henricum Regem septimum, eiusque hæredes in perpetuum speculare debere pronunciauit. Quid iam amplius his iuribus à Papa addi potuit? Solum ius diuinum omisit, cuius etsi ipse expers fuit, tamen illæ ecclitus nobis datæ nuptiæ caret non potuerunt. Archiepiscopus autem primo suæ translationis anno synodum Londini celebrauit. In hac synodo quia Rex Francisculus Louellum cum Humfredo Stafford qui ad Colcestrensem asylum profugerant, eos ad nouos populi tumultus citandos exiissent, aliosq; rebelles in acie prostrauit, & conspirantium duces capite puniuit, omnesq; motus sedauit, impetrauit à Clero decimam. Verum eodem tempore Richardus quidam Simondus humilis quidem forte ac conditione, verum non indoctus nec doli fraudisque ignarus Præsbyter, puerum venusta facie, & versuto ingenio Lambertum Simenellum liberis institutit Oxonit. Cui simulatque diuulgatum esset Edwardum Ducis Clarentiæ filium à Rege nouos populi motus formidantes in Turri Londinensi seruatum, iam neci traditum esse, ilico mnat nomen, eumq; Edwardû appellat, & cum eo protinus in Hyberniâ traiecit. Ibi narrat se seruasse Edwardum Ducis Clarentiæ filium, & à mortis periculo eripuisse, ac Hybernef. pueri specie & similitudine deceptæ, facile veniunt in eius fidem, & tam Anglos, quam Margaretam Ducis Burgundiæ sororem Ducis Clarentiæ solicitant, vt hunc puerum auxilio militari iuuent, & in regno ponant. Ex hoc audaci sacrificuli & pueri facinore magna strages edita est, sed Hericus Rex Marte superior euasit, & fusis aduersariis puerum, eiusque præceptorem improbum in prælio cæpit,illum tci ulmariæ addixit, hunc quia Presbyter fuit, Archiepiscopo misit. Quia durante superiori synodo cum suis carceribus inandaut, statimque ob multitudinem Clericorum in delinquentium qui vix suis carceribus contineri poterant, coram Maiore & Senioribus Luodiosi ciujbus eduxit. Is fallax est fe oppidani cuiusdam Oxoniensis filium Lambertum Simenellum a patre abductum finxisse & mutasse in persoonam Edwardi Ducis Clarentii filii, eoque commeoro Hiberneuses & Anglos concitasse,ad eum modum qui super tam funestus fuit. Post quam confessionem tanquam ieiejeme ilatus & tanti homicidii ac Christiani effusi sanguinis reus Clericali ordine priuat*,Maiori & Vicecomitibus Lôdon traditus est. Deinde in eadem synodo eductus est ex Turri Londinensi Edwardus puer Ducis Clarentini filius hæredis, quem in synodo omnibus ostentum Archiepiscopus secum Lametham duxit. Multi ad quos superioris coniurationis crimen pertinebat, ipsi sibi conclusi asylia seu sanctuaria petebant, sed bulla Innocentii Papæ id priuilegium ademptum est hi qui ex locis sanctis ad perpetranda huiusmodi scelera exiunt, ad ea quæ redirent. Ioter hos Humfredus Stafford aliique qui cum co ante ad asylum (vt diximus) Colcestrense confugissent, & post hanc pugnam asylia repetebant inde extracti pœnas luerunt iungiuoe. Lataque exilia Papali bulla lex est, vt asylus inscripti, si homicidia, furta, inceodia, sacrilegia, depopulationes agrorum, Regni aut Regis proditiones postea commiserint, inde eiecti vi laica ducantur ad supplicia. In hac synodo coerciti sunt acribus minis inepti quidam prædicatores, qui in conciones populum præsentem & auditores nihil docent, sed cum plausu populari, eloquentia canioa, latrant immodestius in Episcoposabsentes. Tum Londinensis Clerus increpatus est quod vestibus molliter laficiuiret, & in cauponis frequentius perpotaret. His gestis dimissa synodus est. Ac sub initio proximi anni iterum inchoata. Iohac synodo Oxoniensis atque Derbiensis comites contra Gallorum paratam ad bellum potentiam iuuandum Clericorum bonis Regem suaserunt. Itaque eynodus concessit Regi subsidium xxv. M.l'. biois solutionibus eodem anno soluendum. Et si bellum illud biennio duraret alterum pari æstimatione subsidium decreuit, ea lege ut ea concessio ad consequentiam non traheretur, nec exemplo suo deinceps Clero prærudicaret. Ipsi etiam Archiepiscopo a tota prouincia haud modicum auxilium tributum est. Accepit enim 30 subsidia duo, in quorum utroque curati fixl.s. salario conducti essent iii.s.iiii.d. si septem maiorum vi.s.viii.d. si decem v.s.fi duodecim xii.s. si decem librarum xvi. s. viii. d. eademque deinceps portione si maiora salaria caperent, soluerunt. Ac similis pene ratio in Ecclesiis parochialibus, cantarius, hospitalibus, hiemque capellis habita est. Huius Archiepiscopalis subsidii prima solutio in sola Cantuar. Dioecesi summa iii.c.liiii.l'. excreuit. Hoc anno Innocentius Papa rebus omnibus in Anglia sedatis, & victis confœderatis, terribilem Bullam excommunicationes in rebelles ionantem ad Heoricum septimum misit, quam Archiepiscopus in tota sua prouincia denunciauit. Idemque Papa anno sequenti in bullis emittendis frequentior fuit. Nam cum apertis postulationibus obtinere oc quicquam amplius in Anglia potuisset, occultas quasdam acquirendi rationes sibi ioeundas putauit. Itaque insolita quadam & admirabili bulla Ioanni Giglis suo (vt in Thoma Bourgchier antea diximus) in Angliam Quæstori plenissimam & singularem authoritatem dedit, viuram, simoniam, furta, homicidia, spolia, rapinas, adulteria, fornicationes, & crimina quæcunque perpetrata, (præter Cleti percussiones, & in Romanum Pontificem coniurationes, ac certos quosdam suæ soli potestati casus reseruatos) a reorum conscientiis remittendi atque dissoluendi. Præterea indulgendi, atque dispeofandi, & tam bona aliena quam ea quæ fraude quacunque acquiruntur salua conscientia retinendi, solutis aliquæ eorundem parte Papa commissariis, seu earum vices gerentibus. Omnes denique excommunicandi qui huic Bullæ obstarent, qui vero iuuarent sedi Romanæ pro suis meritis commendandi. hanc bullam Archiepiscopus retento originali transcripsit, & ad singulos provinciæ suæ suffraganeos misit. Quem Innocentius Papa tanquam bene de semeritum Antistitem aliis bullis reformatorem & visitatorem Monasteriorum & locorum quorumcunque ab Archiepiscopali & ordinaria iurisdictione priuilegiorum antiquorum prædidio tutorum seu exemptorum ordinauit. Eodem Anno Roffensi Ponte rupto, & ad interitum ruinamque labente, omnibus suis prouincialibus quia liquid ei reparando legassent aut donassent, quorumcunq; scelerum quadraginta continuis diebus commissorum pœnam purgatoriam remisit.
units.tr: John Morton, born at Bere in the county of Dorset, studied at Oxford as a young man. After he had taken up civil and canon law, he pleaded controversial cases as an advocate in the Court of Arches. Then, through the favour and patronage of Thomas Bourgchier, Archbishop of Canterbury, who valued his legal learning and prudence, he was not only enriched with many ecclesiastical dignities but was also commended with the highest trust to King Henry VI. Employed in the king's counsels in those very harsh and dangerous times, he clung to him so firmly that he never left him, even in the camp and at the greatest peril. Edward IV, though this man's enemy and hostile to his party, nevertheless so esteemed his faith and integrity that, once victory was won, he drew John Morton into his service with many benefits and admitted him to his secret counsels. Having seen how much ability he had, and with what disposition and diligence he handled each matter, the king promoted him to the bishopric of Ely.
