For at that time there was no one in whom the king had placed greater confidence for managing his affairs well, or greater hope for protecting his posterity, than in this bishop. Accordingly, when he was dying, the king named him one of his executors by will. Richard the tyrant, who destroyed the male offspring of his brother Edward, feared this. Having observed that the bishop, a man of such faith, could in no way be brought to his wicked and criminal designs against the young royal sons, he accused him of treason and high treason and shut him up in the Tower of London. Soon afterwards he had him brought out, but since he could bring no charge against the innocent man, he handed him over to the custody of the Duke of Buckingham, the companion of his crime and parricide. But when Richard the tyrant had been placed on the royal throne through dreadful acts and deceits, and with the help of the Duke of Buckingham, some hidden rivalry and incredible hatred suddenly sprang up between this tyrant, inaugurated with royal rites, and the duke. Since this burned so fiercely in the duke's inmost heart that it could not long be concealed, he disclosed the whole matter to John Morton, Bishop of Ely, whom he still kept under closer custody. He thought that no one could be better suited to him for the revenge and destruction of the tyrant that he was planning. And when he saw that the bishop, of his own accord, fell in with the same feeling at the first conversation, he loosened the harsh reins of his custody and granted him liberty. But John of Ely, although he was greatly cheered, nevertheless wisely foresaw what in fact happened: that God would exact punishment from both companions in such a crime. Therefore, although he approved the duke's attempt, he was unwilling to join him. Instead, seizing an opportune moment from this granted liberty, he changed his clothes and appearance and quickly and secretly fled to his own Isle of Ely, and from there crossed over into Flanders. Then, by letters and messengers sent out in quick succession, he dealt with all those whom he knew to favour the line of King Edward, so that a marriage would be arranged between Lady Elizabeth, Edward's eldest daughter, and Henry, Earl of Richmond, who was already living in exile. The aim was both to depose so cruel and savage a tyrant and to put an end to the internal seditions which had for so long raged between the Lancastrian and Yorkist families to the ruin of the whole kingdom. This sound counsel, undertaken under God's guidance, had, as I said before, a favourable outcome: the tyrant was overthrown and victory was divinely granted to King Henry VII, with God's favour. Thus Henry, having gained the kingdom, brought John Morton back with him to his country and appointed him Chancellor of the realm. Then, when Thomas Bourgchier had died, he saw to it that the monks of Canterbury petitioned for Morton as metropolitan, and by the confirmation of Pope Innocent he was released from Ely and transferred. This translation, like that of Thomas Bourgchier, who was likewise moved from the see of Ely to Canterbury, was published in six separate bulls, although the Pope could have accomplished it in fewer. But with authority at a price, those leaden seals also had to be multiplied. Soon afterwards William Sellyng, professor of sacred theology and prior of the Church of Canterbury, brought the archiepiscopal cross-banner, which he received at the Bishop of Ely's residence in Holborn, and kissed it, and then handed it to his cross-bearer. But when the marriage (as I said) had been celebrated between King Henry VII and [Elizabeth], the Pope thought that his bulls were hardly needed to confirm that lawful union, brought about by God and most necessary for the peace and tranquillity of the English. This was because the couple were related in the fourth degree of consanguinity, which is prohibited by no divine or civil law, but by papal law alone. In these bulls, so that the kingdom might not seem to lack authority, he also confirmed the king's accession and declared that it ought to pertain to Henry VII and his heirs for ever: by hereditary right, by right of war, by right of marriage, by right of election, by right of the English Parliament, and also by papal right and his own. What more could the Pope have added to these rights? He omitted only divine right, which, although he himself lacked it, that marriage given to us from heaven could not do without. The archbishop, in the first year of his translation, held a synod at London. In this synod, because Francis Lovell and Humphrey Stafford, who had fled to the sanctuary at Colchester, had gone out to stir up new popular tumults, and because the king had routed other rebels in the field and punished the leaders of the conspiracy with death, quelling all the disturbances, he obtained a tenth from the clergy. At the same time, one Richard Simon, a man of humble rank by chance, but not unlearned and not ignorant of trickery and fraud, a priest, instructed at Oxford a boy of pleasing face and crafty wit, Lambert Simnel. As soon as it was rumoured that Edward, son of the Duke of Clarence, who was being kept in the Tower of London because the king feared new popular uprisings, had now been put to death, he at once changed the boy's name and called him Edward, and immediately crossed over with him to Ireland. There he claimed that he had saved Edward, son of the Duke of Clarence, and rescued him from danger of death. The Irish, deceived by the boy's appearance and likeness, readily put themselves under his authority, and they urged both the English and Margaret, Duchess of Burgundy and sister of the Duke of Clarence, to help this boy with military aid and set him on the throne. From this bold deed of the little priest and the boy a great slaughter followed, but King Henry prevailed in battle, put the enemy to flight, and captured the boy and his wicked tutor in the fight. He sent the boy to the kitchens, and since the tutor was a priest, sent him to the Archbishop. Because during the previous synod he had sent [the offenders] to their prisons, and because, on account of the number of clerics among the offenders, who could scarcely be held in their prisons, he at once led them out before the Mayor and aldermen of the city. The man confessed that he had pretended that Lambert Simnel, son of a townsman of Oxford, had been taken from his father, and had changed him into the person of Edward, son of the Duke of Clarence, and by this means had stirred up the Irish and English to so deadly a war. After this confession, as a robber and guilty of so great a homicide and shedding of Christian blood, he was stripped of clerical order and handed over to the Mayor and Sheriffs of London. Then in the same synod Edward, the boy and rightful heir son of the Duke of Clarence, was led out of the Tower of London. The Archbishop displayed him to everyone in the synod and took him with him to Lambeth. Many to whom the guilt of the earlier conspiracy pertained sought sanctuaries and asylums for themselves; but by a bull of Pope Innocent that privilege was taken away from those who go out from holy places to commit such crimes and then return to them. Among these, Humphrey Stafford and others who had earlier fled with him to the Colchester sanctuary, and who after this battle sought asylum again, were dragged out and paid the penalty. The law laid down by the papal bull is that those who, having been received into asylum, afterwards commit homicide, theft, arson, sacrilege, the plundering of fields, or treason against the realm or the king, are to be ejected from there and led to execution by secular force. In this synod certain foolish preachers were restrained by severe threats. In their sermons they teach the people present and their hearers nothing, but with popular applause and empty eloquence they bark more shamelessly against bishops who are absent. Then the London clergy were rebuked because they dressed effeminately in soft clothes and drank too often in taverns. With these matters done, the synod was dismissed, and early in the following year it was resumed. In this synod the earls of Oxford and Derby persuaded the king to draw upon the goods of the clergy to help against the power of the French, who were preparing for war. So the synod granted the king a subsidy of 25,000 pounds, payable in instalments in the same year. And if that war lasted two years, it decreed a second subsidy of equal value, on condition that this grant should not be drawn into a precedent, nor by its example prejudice the clergy in future. The archbishop himself also received no small aid from the whole province: under each of the two subsidies, curates hired at a salary of forty shillings paid 3s. 4d.; those with seven marks paid 6s. 8d.; those with ten pounds paid 12s.; and those with a larger salary paid in the same proportion. A similar scheme was applied to parish churches, chantries, hospitals, and collegiate chapels. The first payment of this archiepiscopal subsidy in the diocese of Canterbury alone came to 354 pounds. This year, with all disturbances in England quieted and the confederates defeated, Pope Innocent sent to Henry VII a terrible bull of excommunication thundering against the rebels, which the Archbishop proclaimed throughout his whole province. The same Pope was more frequent in issuing bulls the following year. For since he could obtain nothing more in England by open demands, he thought he should pursue certain hidden means of acquiring money. So, by an unusual and remarkable bull, he gave to John Gigli, his quaestor in England (as I said earlier in the case of Thomas Bourgchier), the fullest and most singular authority to remit and absolve from the consciences of offenders usury, simony, theft, homicide, plunder, robbery, adultery, fornication, and whatever other crimes had been committed (except laying violent hands on a cleric, conspiracies against the Roman Pontiff, and certain cases reserved to his own power alone). Besides this, he was to grant indulgences and dispensations, and to allow people to keep with a clear conscience both others' goods and those acquired by any fraud, the Pope assigning a part of the proceeds to the commissaries or to those acting in their place. Finally, all who opposed this bull were to be excommunicated, and those who supported it were to be commended to the Roman See according to their merits. The Archbishop kept the original, had a copy made of this bull, and sent it to each of his suffragans in the province. Innocent the Pope, regarding him as a prelate who deserved well, appointed him by other bulls as reformer and visitor of monasteries and of all places exempt from archiepiscopal and ordinary jurisdiction under the protection of ancient privileges. In the same year, the bridge at Rochester broke and was collapsing into ruin. To all the people of the province who had left or given anything towards its repair, he remitted the purgatorial penalty for whatever sins they had committed over forty continuous days.

units.tr: A.1489. Arch. It was confirmed by Richard Whittington and by himself, and was to be aided by money or any other work. In the same year, which was the fifth of his translation, he visited the diocese of Lichfield and Coventry, after its bishop, John Hales, had died there. He then visited, in turn, those dioceses whose bishops had either died or been moved to other churches: Bath and Wells, Winchester, Lincoln and Exeter. Richard Fox, bishop of Bath and Wells, was moved to Exeter, and William, bishop of Coventry and Lichfield, was twice nominated or elected to the see of Lincoln. He also visited Rochester, Worcester and Salisbury. In the eighth year of his translation, Pope Alexander VI created this archbishop a cardinal, with the title of St Anastasius. In that same year King Henry VII, moved no less by piety than by a zeal for empty superstition,

units.la: integerrimum Henricum Regem sextum, quam inanis superstitionis Zelo ductus optauit eum ab Alexandro Papa inter sanctos referri. Papa vt hoc negocii curiose tractaret,tam ordinem atqj modum quam sumptus, sanctos in suum Kalendarium seu Catalogum inscribendi primo acurate descripsit. Ac primo hoc sanctificandi tanquam priuilegium suæ solius authoritatis atque potestatis esse quinque rationibus probat.
units.tr: wished that Henry VI, a most upright king, be numbered among the saints by Pope Alexander. So that the Pope might handle this business carefully, he first set out exactly the order and manner of enrolling saints in his calendar or catalogue, as well as the expense. He first argues that this power of sanctifying is a privilege of his own sole authority and power, and proves it by five reasons.

units.la: 1. Quia cum sanctis adiungi Deo, maximum est hominis Christiani beneficium,maximaque causa quæ inter mortales possit proponi, itaque cum grauiores omnes causæ ad Papam referantur, hanc eius præcipuam esse debere. 11. quia Sanctimiraculis declarantur, miracula autem à fide proueniant, omnes autem controuersitas à solo Papa decidi. 111. quia solius Papæ est declarare dubia scripturarum, multò igitur magis declarare dubia sanctitatis. 1v. ne si id cuilibet Episcopo permittatur, & plerique Episcoporum indocti sint & simplices, populus credulus decipiatur. v. ne numerus sanctorum in infinitum crescat, nisi Papa modum statuat, eaque ratione frigeat deuotio, & sanctitas vilipendatur. His argutiis cum canonizationem (vt appellat) sanctorum in sua sola potestate restare vult euincere, proximo loco quæ ad sanctificationem requirantur ostendit,quæ duo esse debent,vitæ sanctitas & miracula:nam nec vita integrum nisi edat miraculā, nec miraculis clarū si. nec vita pura inter sanctos canonizandum,ac ab omnibus reputandum sit. Itaque vtrumque horum testibus probandum, anteauam quis inter sanctos habeatur. Longum esset enarrare singula, nisi historiam in qua breuitati studemus, multis paginis non necessariis compleremus. Sumptus autem qui Cantoribus, Campanariis, choristis, parafrenariis Ecclesiæ S. Petri, nec non commissariis, notariis, acPapæ seruientibus cubiculariis, ferratiis, ac huiusmodi turbæ in peragendis Romæ canonizationis ritibus fere atritingunt summam mille atque quingentorum aureorum ducatorum. Quæ Feuda eriam augeri ad extremum addit Papa fecundum canonizati potentiam. Cum itaque tam Henricus v 1.canonizandus, quam Henricus v i 1. qui officio quodam cæco ductus canonizationem voluit impetrare vtriquè Reges fuerint, existimare iure possumus Regem non Papam magnitudine sumptus huius canonizationis negocio supersedisse. Inceptum enim fuisse constat ex bulla Alexandri v 1. Papæ missa ad Iohanem Morton Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum,& Richardum Fox Episcopum Dunelmiensem, quæ in loco Registri memorato extat. Rex igitur contentus hoc solo fuit,vt cadauer eius Regium quod Richardus Tyrannus non religione aut inhumati honore,sed fratris sui Edwardi Regis quarti, cuius regnum proditorie cæsis hæreditbus viac dolo occupauerat, innidia atque calumnia, à Chertseiesi Cœnobio ad Arcem Windsorinam transtulerat, more solenni regio inde exhumatum,ad Westmonasterii cœnobium ducere et humaretur. Quodetsi sine auihoritate pontificia facere potuisset, tamen Rex ad Papam indignis modis supplicare coactus est.Incidit autem hoc anno inter Archiepiscopum & Londinensem Episcopum grauis quædam de iurisdictione controuersia. Ac lis prope eadem est quæ inter Wilhelmum Courtney Archiprætsulem & Exoniensem Episcopum quondam (vt diximus) intercessit, sed ad suæ prærogatiuæ curiæ propugnationem specialius propiusque accedit. Richardus quidam Bladiwel Londinensis Episcopi commissarius executores testamentorum Richardi Simpson,& Iohannis Erick ciuium Londinensium ad exhibenda eadem testamenta, & actis coram te insinuanda citauit.Eosdem rursus Archiepiscopus quia testatorum bona pluribus diocesibus diuisa erant,à Londinensis Episcopi iurisdiction vendicauit, & ad suum tribunal vocauit. Ita- que hi executores ab eo Cômissario excômunicati, & ab Archiepiscopo absoluti sunt. Londinensis Episcopus ad Papam prouocauit, & is Romæ de hac prærogatiua Cantu- ariensis sedis instituta est. Cômissa fuit ab Alexandro Papa hæc causa Petro de Acoltis Iuris vtriusque doctori & auditori causarum in Romana curia. Magna huius iudicii per totam prouinciam Cantuariensem expectatio suffraganeorum animos qui Londinensi Episcopo adhæserunt, dintenuit suspensos. Sed Archiepiscopus non modo primæuo Cantuariensis sedis prærogatiua, sed ipsa consuetudine, & temporis diuturnitate ex propris Archiuiis atque tabulariis euicit causam. Postea Alexander Papa iam hanc detestamentis insinuandis, bonaque intestatorum administrandi commissionibus prærogatiuam, quam vacantibus Episcopalibus Ecclesiis iurisdictionem, Archiepiscopo, nec non Ecclesiæ Metropoliticæ Cantuariensi ad æternam concordiam, omnesque de iurisdictione lites & altercationes in perpetuum tollendas quatuor bullis confirmauit. Dum hæc controuersia Romæ agitaretur, multi prouinciales ab infestionibus prælatis quia suam iurisdictionem in incerto versari discrimine cernebant, incitati, variasin Archiepiscopum calumnias in vulgus sparserunt, contra quos Alexander Papa bullam excommunicationis crudeliter fulminantem edixit. Atque hoc modo Ecclesiæ Cantuariensis iura sæpe in dubium atque controuersiam vocata, tandem sub hoc Archiepiscopo firmata & stabilita sunt. Papa vero Alexander, qui (vt paulo ante diximus) Iohannem quendam de Eiglis cum retinendi, remittendi, & indulgendi potestate quæstorem atque corraforem pecuniarum in Anglia constituit, aut insatiabilis fuit, aut profusus celeriter egere cepit, aut quod est verissimum ab Anglis tones papali fraude expilatis nihil percepit. Itaque Robertum Castellensem notarium suum cum nouis mandatis atque simili potestate misit in Angliam, vt à singulis curatis Aureum Anglicum exigeret, prælatorum autem erga Papam benignitatem non flagitaret, sed permulsis eorum animis, equis precibus impetraret. Quo anno Anselmum Cantuariensem quondam Archiepiscopum Ioanne Morton magnis id sumptibus procurante Canone suo inter sanctos retulit. Iohannes Morton postquam Cantuariensem prouinciam 13. annis rexisset, obiit. Delubrum ipse viuus sumptuosum in Ecclesia in subterraneo crypto extruxit, in quo humatus est. Vir fuit prudens, facundus, atque grauis, qualem Henricus 7. vitæ socium, morumque quasi magistrum plerumque penes se habuit. Tulit (vt diximus) sub Richardo tyranno vitæ discrimina, exilium atque carceres, atribus Regibus Henrico 6. Edwardo 4. & Henrico 7. probata integerrimi, prudentissimique patris fides nunquam in dubium venit. In condendis & reparandis plerisque ædibus & Archiepiscopatus ac Ecclesiæ suæ ædificiis magnificentiam, in pauperibus crebris eleemosynis refocillandis, indigentium liberis in literis studiisque alendis, noris atque familiaribus promouendis, propinquis & consanguineis quibus opimas & honorarias hæreditates acquisiuit, cuandis, pietatem, liberalitatem, & munificentiam summam declarauit, vt in testamento suo fuisus apparet. Prima inter hunc & Richardum Foxpostea Wintoniensem familiaritas in exilio conflata est, quos prudentiæ, integritatis, morumque piorum similitudo in fide atque amicitia tota reliqua vita de inceps semper retinuit. In testamento omnia pene ad pias causas reliquit. Regi Portiferium, Regina Psalterium, D. Margaretæ filiæ Regis primogenitæ quam filiolam, quia eius in baptismo compater fuit, appellat, Cyphum aureum & quadraginta libras, Ecclesiæ Elien si mitram, & crucem Archiepiscopalem, ceteris finis necessariis admodum parce legauit, quia eius liberalitatem in viuis vberrime senserant. Suppellectilé diuisit inter famulos. Heredes seu executores suos, vt Oxonii viginti, Cantabrigiæ decem scholares viginti annis continuis in literarum studiis exhiberent, iureiurando astrinxit. Eo vero mortuo Cantuariensis Monachi Regis impetrata licentia Thomam Langton Wintoniensem Episcopum ad Cantuariensem sedem postularunt, verum is pestę quæ eo anno triginta hominum millia in Anglia consumsit, rat, vna cum Thoma Rotheram Eboracensi Archiepiscopo antequam accepit à Papa confirmationem viuis sublatus est. Post quorum obitus Richardus Fox Wintoniensem, & Thomas Sauage Londinensis Episcopus Eboracensem Ecclesiam occupauere. Londinensis autem Episcopatus Wilhelmo Watham legum doctori delatus est.
units.tr: (1) Because to be joined to God among the saints is the greatest benefit for a Christian and the greatest cause that can be brought before mortals; since all weightier causes are referred to the Pope, this one ought especially to be his. (2) Because saints are declared by miracles, miracles come from faith, and all controversies are settled by the Pope alone. (3) Because it is the Pope's alone to declare doubtful passages of Scripture, and so much more to declare doubtful matters of sanctity. (4) Lest, if this were allowed to any bishop, and since many bishops are unlearned and simple, the credulous people be deceived. (5) Lest the number of saints grow without limit unless the Pope set a limit, and so devotion grow cold and sanctity be held cheap. With these subtleties, wishing to prove that the canonization (as he calls it) of saints rests in his power alone, he next shows what is required for sanctification. There must be two things: holiness of life and miracles. For a man whose life is not sound may not be canonized even if he works miracles, nor may one famous for miracles be canonized if his life is not pure. Each of these must therefore be proved by witnesses before anyone is counted among the saints. It would take long to recount each detail, unless we filled with many unnecessary pages a history in which we aim at brevity. The expenses, however, which for the singers, bell-ringers, choristers and grooms of the church of St Peter, as well as the commissaries, notaries, chamberlains serving the Pope, farriers and that sort of crowd, incur in performing the rites of canonization at Rome, come to nearly fifteen hundred gold ducats. The Pope adds that these fees also increase at the end according to the power of the one canonized. Since, then, both Henry VI, to be canonized, and Henry VII, who, led by a certain blind duty, wished to obtain the canonization, were kings, we may rightly suppose that the King, not the Pope, dropped this business of canonization because of the great cost. For it is established that it was begun by a bull of Pope Alexander VI, sent to John Morton, archbishop of Canterbury, and Richard Fox, bishop of Durham, which exists in the place of the Register mentioned. The King was therefore content with this alone: that his royal body, which the tyrant Richard had moved from the abbey of Chertsey to Windsor Castle, not out of religion or honour for the dead, but out of envy and calumny toward his brother, King Edward IV, whose kingdom he had treacherously seized after slaying the heirs by deceit, should be taken from there with the customary royal solemnity to the abbey of Westminster and buried. And although he could have done this without papal authority, the King was nonetheless forced to beg the Pope in unworthy ways. In this year a rather serious dispute over jurisdiction arose between the archbishop and the bishop of London. It is nearly the same case that once arose, as we have said, between William Courtney, archbishop, and the bishop of Exeter, but it comes closer and more particularly to the defence of his own court of prerogative. Richard Bladwell, a commissary of the bishop of London, cited the executors of the wills of Richard Simpson and John Erick, citizens of London, to exhibit those wills and have them registered before him. The archbishop, because the goods of the testators were spread over several dioceses, claimed them from the jurisdiction of the bishop of London and summoned them to his own tribunal. Thus these executors were excommunicated by that commissary and absolved by the archbishop. The bishop of London appealed to the Pope, and at Rome the case was put in charge of this prerogative of the see of Canterbury. Pope Alexander committed the case to Peter de Acoltis, doctor of both laws and auditor of causes in the Roman court. The great expectation of this judgment throughout the whole province of Canterbury kept in suspense the minds of the suffragans who had attached themselves to the bishop of London. But the archbishop won the case, not only by the ancient prerogative of the see of Canterbury, but by custom itself and the long passage of time, from his own archives and records. Afterwards Pope Alexander, by four bulls, confirmed this prerogative in probating wills and in granting administration of the goods of those dying intestate, which the archbishop and the Metropolitan Church of Canterbury held as jurisdiction while episcopal churches were vacant, in order to secure eternal concord and to end for ever all disputes and quarrels over jurisdiction. While this controversy was being pursued at Rome, many provincials, incited by prelates hostile to the archbishop because they saw their own jurisdiction hanging in an uncertain danger, spread various slanders about him among the people, against whom Pope Alexander issued a bull of excommunication thundering cruelly. In this way the rights of the Church of Canterbury, often called into doubt and dispute, were at last established and secured under this archbishop. But Pope Alexander, who (as we said a little before) appointed a certain John of Eiglis as quaestor and collector of money in England, with the power of retaining, remitting and granting indulgences, either was insatiable or was spendthrift, and soon began to be in need; or, what is most true, he received nothing from the English, who had been plundered by papal fraud. So he sent Robert of Castello, his notary, to England with new mandates and similar power, to exact an English gold coin from each parish priest, and not to demand the goodwill of the prelates toward the Pope, but, having soothed their minds, to obtain it by fair prayers. In that year, with John Morton procuring it at great expense, he placed Anselm, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, among the saints by his canon. John Morton, after he had ruled the province of Canterbury for thirteen years, died. While living he built a costly shrine in the church, in an underground crypt, in which he was buried. He was a prudent, eloquent and serious man, the kind of man whom Henry VII often kept near him as companion of his life and, as it were, teacher of his manners. As we have said, he endured under the tyrant Richard the perils of life, exile and prisons; under the kings Henry VI, Edward IV and Henry VII the faith of this most upright and most prudent father was never called into doubt. In building and repairing many houses and the buildings of his archbishopric and church he showed magnificence; in relieving the poor with frequent alms, in supporting the children of the needy in letters and studies, in advancing his servants and friends, and in enriching his kin and relatives, to whom he acquired rich and honourable inheritances, he declared his piety, generosity and very great munificence, as is plain from his will at length. The first familiarity between him and Richard Fox, afterwards bishop of Winchester, was formed in exile, and the likeness of their prudence, integrity and pious manners, joined in faith and friendship, kept them always close for the rest of their lives. In his will he left almost everything to pious causes. To the King he left a breviary, to the Queen a psalter, and to Lady Margaret, the King's eldest daughter, whom he calls his little goddaughter because he was her sponsor at baptism, a gold cup and forty pounds; to the church of Ely his mitre and archiepiscopal cross; the rest he left only very sparingly, since they had felt his generosity most abundantly while he lived. He divided his household goods among his servants. He bound his heirs or executors, under oath, to maintain twenty scholars at Oxford and ten at Cambridge in the study of letters for twenty years continuously. After his death the monks of Canterbury, with the King's licence obtained, nominated Thomas Langton, bishop of Winchester, to the see of Canterbury; but he was taken away by the plague, which in that year carried off thirty thousand people in England, together with Thomas Rotherham, archbishop of York, before he received confirmation from the Pope. After their deaths Richard Fox, bishop of Winchester, and Thomas Savage, bishop of London, occupied the Church of York. The bishopric of London was offered to William Warham, doctor of laws.

units.la: LXVI. Henricus Deneus.
units.tr: LXVI. Henry Deane.

units.la: Enrici Regis septimi tempora multis interstinis coniurationibus turbata sunt. Ex his vna eaque ultima reliquas omnes quas Rex, etsi summum pene discrimen adferebat, prudenter compescuit, dolis & furtunæ varietate superabat. Obscuro quidã ortu Petrus Vatbechus, iuuenis liberali forma
units.tr: The times of King Henry VII were disturbed by many conspiracies, one after another. Of these, the last one surpassed all the rest. Although it brought the King to almost the utmost peril, he suppressed it wisely, and he overcame it by guile and the shifting of fortune. Peter Warbeck, a youth of obscure birth but of pleasing appearance

units.la: & ingenio ad tractandos dolos apprimè composito Richardus Edwardi Quarti Regis secundus filius falsò creditus est. Hoc commentâ indelebili odio muliebri fabricatum est, nempe Margaretæ Edwardi Regis Quarti sororis, & vxoris Caroli Burgundiæ Ducis, quę omnes exquisiuit rationes quibus Henrico summum pararet exitium. Eadem (vt in Iohanne Morton antea diximus) Lambertum Simonellum Ducis Clarentini filium simili mendacio fictum in regno ambiendo iuuit.
units.tr: and of a wit exceptionally well suited to devising deceptions, was falsely believed to be Richard, the second son of King Edward IV. This fiction was devised out of an undying female hatred, that of Margaret, sister of King Edward IV and wife of Charles, Duke of Burgundy, who sought out every means by which to bring the greatest ruin upon Henry. The same Margaret (as we said earlier in the case of John Morton) helped Lambert Simnel, the son of the Duke of Clarence, in his bid for the kingdom, with a similar lie invented for him.

units.la: Itaq; huic Petro qui se Richardum Eboracensem Ducem appellauit adhæserunt hi qui ex rerum nouitate, & perturbatione Reip. præmia sperabant. Nonnulli etiam viri ciam atq; nobiles ea charitate & beneuolentia, qua Edwardi Quarti progeniem, aut odio quo Heroicum Septimum prosequuti, speciè veri facile decepti sunt, eius partes sequuntur.
units.tr: Accordingly, to this Peter, who called himself Richard, Duke of York, there attached themselves those who hoped for rewards from the novelty of affairs and the upheaval of the commonwealth. Some men of rank and nobility too, moved either by that affection and goodwill with which they regarded the offspring of Edward IV, or by the hatred with which they pursued Henry the Seventh, were easily deceived by the appearance of truth and took his side.

units.la: Sed Rex olfacta celeritèt & explorata coniuratione, vim omnem tanti incendii exeinxit, & tam exitiosam ac (vt putabatur) inextricabilem à Domina Margareta contexťam tela discidit. De Ducibus permultis capitis supplicium sumpsit. Petrus autem ex Hibernia fugatus in Scotiam, affinitatem ex nuptiis cum Scotorum Rege contraxit, deinde à Rege Gallorum accersitus, eiusq; promissis animatus tentauit anglicam, ac à Cantiis repulsus ad Cornubienses quos ob tributum exactum in Regem tum concitatos nouerat, properat. Tandem militibus suis cæsis & profligatis in Beudleicnsi cœnobio quod prope Southamptonam iacet sacra loca petit, sed ad extremum Regi deditus laqueo tulpensus est. Multis prolixè verbis hæc coniuratio quæ octo pene annis duravit, ab his qui res Regias in historiis tractant, explicatur. Nobis autem eam breuiter commemorare necesse fuit, quod Rex Henricus eum huius conspirationis reeens iacta semina in Hybernia vbi radices agebant, maturè vellet extirpare, hunc de quo nuncagendū est, Archiprætulem tunc Monachum & Langtonensis Cœnobii præfectum, virum bonæ frugi & officii plenum Hyberoiæ Cancellarium designauit. Qui cum Edwardo Poninghoinsulæ tum præfecto Petrum ex humanioti cultoriq; insulæ ditione cum Syluestribus Hybernensibus in paludes atq; nemora locaq; inaccessa compulit, & reliquam citius insulam ad officium fidemq; reduxit. In hoc munere soleter exequendo Bangorensis in Wallia Episcopus propter loci vicinitatem absens creatus est. Ac eum quidem Episco-patum, cuius iura à vicinis potentioribus in eolis Episcopis plerumq; absentibus cōuulsa, & vsucapione pene ad alienos Dominos translata sunt, recuperandis animis propè iuribus recuperauit. Solebant enim Angliæ Reges hunc Episcopatum tam exiguum atq; tenuem propter eius exilitatem in Abbatem aliquem loecupletem alterius Dioecesis conferre.
units.tr: But the King, having scented the plot quickly and uncovered the conspiracy, extinguished all the force of so great a fire and cut apart the weapons woven by the Lady Margaret, so deadly and (as was thought) so inextricable. He had many of the nobles put to death. Peter himself, driven out of Ireland into Scotland, contracted a kinship by marriage with the King of the Scots. Then, summoned by the King of the French and encouraged by his promises, he attempted England, and, repulsed in Kent, he hurried to the Cornish men, whom he knew to have been stirred up against the King at that time on account of a tax levied. At last, his soldiers having been slain and routed, he sought sanctuary in the monastery of Beaulieu, which lies near Southampton, but in the end, surrendering to the King, he was hanged. This conspiracy, which lasted almost eight years, is set out at length and in many words by those who treat the affairs of the kings in their histories. I have had to mention it briefly here, because King Henry wished to root out at once the seeds of this conspiracy, recently sown in Ireland, where they were taking root. He appointed as Chancellor of Ireland the man of whom we are now to speak, then an archpriest, a monk and prior of the abbey of Langton, a man of good sense and full of duty. Together with Edward Poynings, then governor of the island, he drove Peter out of the more civilised and cultivated parts of the island's dominion into the marshes, woods and inaccessible places, along with the wild Irish, and he brought the rest of the island back to duty and loyalty fairly quickly. While he was diligently carrying out this office, he was appointed Bishop of Bangor in Wales, though absent, on account of the nearness of the place.

units.la: Ifq; cum sui commodi & pinguioris fortunæ causa à Bangorensi Episcopatu abesse, & in Abbatiæ ocio atq; fructu delitescere soleret, & Episcopatum in quo vix aut ne vix quidem vnquam resideret, negligeret, ex generosis Wallis vicinis quisq; paulatim cepit aliquid eius Episcopatus proprium sibi vendicare. Quod sane nouum non est in Anglia. Videmus enim quàra semper cupiditate atq; ferocia cum supini atq; desides sint Episcopi, laici in eorum iura prædiaq; incurrant. Itaq; huius Bangorensis Episcopatus rebus, inter vicinos, ignaris episcopis, qui vices sepè suas ipsis prædonibus eòmiserunt, distractis, perexigua sane pars huic Episcopo Henrico reliqua fuit. Verum is non minus prudenter atque sedulo explorauit de his iuribus atque prædiis quæ sui Episcopatus antiquitus erant propria, tum qua ambitione & iniuria eadem inuasissent hi à quibus occupabantur, quam animi magnitudine & constantia summa disturbatis & eicitis illis malæ fidei possessoribus omnia pene clam aulalla iura recuperauit. Ac plebeii quidem Episcopum adiuuerunt: siue quod inconstans atq; mobile vulgus nouos indies optar Dominos, & rerum Dominia crebrò hue illuc transferri cupiat, siue quod Episcopalium prædiorū oblationem summū tum facilegiū putauit. Erat ad septentrionū Insulæ Monæ quam Anglis elam iam nuncupant, inter promontoria Cornēti, eiusq; q Caput sancti dicitur, interposita Insula, quam veteri Britannico vocabulo puisi, i. Moyr hounnicū. i. foetarum seu alitum Insulam vocant, quia ea marina animalia magno ibidem numero verno & autumnali tempore singulis annis capiantur. Hanc insulam antiquitus fuisse Bangorensis Episcopatus, & ab iniustis occupatoribus retentam ac possessam Henricus iam Episcopus accepit. Itaq; cum & iure concederet possessionē auitam suę Ecclesię nollent incolæ, sed vt resistebant, eis classe ac militibus aggressus recuperauit Insulā, & Bangorensi sedi restituit. Præterea in palatio & Ecclesia reparandis, quæ diu ante Henrico Regę Quarto regnante ab Owcno Gleindoore rebelle incendio vastatæ fuerunt sumptus multos fecit. Et ab hoc Episcopo Sarisburiensem reliquit, tamen discedens suo successuri Penco mitrā atq
units.tr: Since he was accustomed to be absent from the bishopric of Bangor for his own advantage and to live in the leisure and revenues of an abbey, and to neglect the see in which he hardly or scarcely ever resided, one by one the well-born Welsh neighbours began to claim for themselves some part of the property of that see. This is certainly not new in England. For we see how, wherever bishops are idle and sluggish, laymen with their greed and boldness encroach upon their rights and estates. So, with the possessions of this see of Bangor being torn apart among the neighbours, while the bishops, ignorant of their affairs, had often entrusted their business to the very robbers themselves, only a very small part remained for this Bishop Henry. But he investigated, no less prudently and diligently, the rights and estates which had belonged of old to his see, and by what ambition and wrong those who held them had seized them. With great magnitude of spirit and steadfast resolve, he drove out and dislodged those possessors of bad faith, and recovered almost all the rights, secretly or openly. The common people indeed helped the bishop: either because the fickle and changeable crowd desires new masters every day and wishes the ownership of things to be shifted often hither and thither, or because he thought that the taking of episcopal estates was then the greatest of crimes. To the north of the island of Anglesey, which the English now call Ely, between the headlands of Cornetum and the one called St Bride's, there lies an island which in the old British word is called Puffin, that is, Moyr hounnicū, which means the island of the young or of birds, because those sea creatures are caught there every year in great numbers in spring and autumn. Henry, now bishop, learned that this island had formerly belonged to the see of Bangor, and that it had been held and possessed by unjust occupiers. Since they would not yield possession, though by right it was the ancestral property of his church, and they resisted, he attacked them with ships and soldiers, recovered the island, and restored it to the see of Bangor. Moreover, he spent large sums on repairing the palace and the church, which long before, in the reign of King Henry IV, had been laid waste by fire from the rebel Owen Glendower. He left this bishopric and passed on to the see of Salisbury, yet on departing he handed to his successor, Penco, the mitre and

units.la: Ce baculum pastorale, ea lege vt in Ecclesiæ Bangorensis à se incepta reparatione pergeret. Quod quidem ab eo factum est. At Henricus, Henrico Regi septimo prudentia, animiq́ magnitudine notus in Sarisburiēsi Ecclesia haud diu sedit, verum Iohannes Morton mortuo ad Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum elatus est. Eo anno Alexander Papa annum Iubilæum Romæ celebrauit, quo Cæli portas omnibus Christianis regnum Dei ingressuris à se reseratas & patefactas edicit. Id omnibus Christianis gentibus, Legatis à Papa vndiq; missis nuncianum est. Si Romam eo anno Iubilatum veniât acceptures singulos peccatorum veniam. At verò ne his qui aut valetudine aut grauioribus negociis impedititam longiqui itineris molestiam commodè subire non poterât, tam benignus atq; Iubilæus pater non prospexisse videretur, fecit omnibus potestatem vota aut hanc in curiosam profectionem pecunia tediuendi. Atq; his qui id fecerint infernalia delictorum supplicia, perinde ac si Romam accessissent, remisit. Tum vt ad soluendum acrius vrgetet suscipiendum, illico in Turcam atrox bellum, seq; cum exercitu id strenuè gestuum prædicat.
units.tr: and the pastoral staff, on condition that he would carry on the repair of the church of Bangor which he had begun. This indeed he did. But Henry, known to King Henry VII for his prudence and greatness of spirit, did not sit long in the church of Salisbury, for after the death of John Morton he was raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury. That year Pope Alexander celebrated a jubilee at Rome, and he proclaimed that the gates of heaven, which he had unlocked and thrown open, were open to all Christians who were to enter the kingdom of God. This was announced to all Christian nations by legates sent from the Pope on every side. If they came to Rome that year for the jubilee, they would each receive the pardon of their sins. But lest the Jubilee father should seem not to have provided for those who, hindered either by ill health or by more pressing business, could not conveniently bear the trouble of so long a journey, he gave everyone the power to fulfil their vows, or to redeem this pilgrimage with money. And to those who did so he remitted the infernal punishments of their sins, just as if they had come to Rome. Then, so as to urge them more keenly to pay and to undertake it, he at once proclaimed a fierce war against the Turk, and declared that he himself would wage it vigorously with his army.

units.la: Quin tam feliciter in anno Iubileo, seq; præsertim Duce ac Imperatore auspicato sison posse non Christianis gentibus victoriam, & exitium Turcis euenire suadet. At nec Rex tantæ fraudi obstaret, permisit ei Papa suæ prædæ partem. Hoc Papæ negocium in Anglia procurauit Gaspar quidam Pows-Hispanus, vir doctus atq; elegans, cuius in rebus agendis solertiam expertus Papa, mandare ei tutò poterat ea quæ recte curari voluit.
units.tr: Indeed he persuades them that victory would surely come to the Christian nations, and ruin to the Turks, so fortunately in the Jubilee year, and especially with himself leading and commanding under good auspices. But neither would the King stand in the way of such a fraud; the Pope allowed him a share of the spoils. This business for the Pope in England was managed by a certain Gaspar Pows, a Spaniard, a learned and elegant man, whose skill in carrying out affairs the Pope had tested, so that he could safely entrust to him whatever he wished to be properly attended to.

units.la: Is pancis mensibus ingentem confluxit in Anglia pecuniâ. Quâ simul atq; hic magnanimus sic. Imperator Alexander Papa accepisset, abstinuit a bello, & reliquo vitæ tempore more Papali indulsit lætus & locupletatus genio. Atq; hic quidem annus Iubilcus omnia Papalium exactionum atq; expilationum Anglis otium (vt ex aniceacta historia patet) vexatis tandem finem attulit. Modica quædam ex Fumis vectigalia sibi adhuc reliqua tuere. Dignū sane suis mercibus precij, vt quia tot seculis fumum vendidist Romana curia, latur ipsa interim fumo, taudem seq; æterno Gehennæ incendio flagret.
units.tr: Within a few months he drew a great sum of money into England. As soon as this magnanimous man, Pope Alexander, had received it, he refrained from war, and for the rest of his life he gave himself up cheerfully and enriched, in the Papal manner, to his own pleasures. And this Jubilee year, at last, brought an end to the Papal exactions and plunderings which had harassed the English (as is clear from our earlier history). A few small revenues from smoke-money still remain to them. Surely a fitting price for its wares: since the Roman curia has sold smoke for so many centuries, let it for the time being lie hidden in smoke, and at last burn in the eternal fire of Gehenna.

units.la: Expleto autem hoc Iubileo Alexander Papa Pallium Archiepiscopatus videlicet insignæ per Adrianum quendam Castellensem suum secretarium misit. Quod Lichefeldensis atq; Couentrensis Episcopus qui authoritatem ad id à Papa acceperat, Archiep. scopo Lamethæ his conceptis verbis tradidit.
units.tr: When this Jubilee had ended, Pope Alexander sent the pallium of the archbishopric, through Adrian, a certain Castellan who was his secretary. Hugh, Bishop of Lichfield and Coventry, who had received the authority for this from the Pope, handed it to Archbishop Hubert at Lambeth in these words:

units.la: Ad honorem Dei Omnipotentis, & beatæ Mariæ virginis, ac beatorum Petri & «Pauli Apostolorū, & Domini nostri Alexandri Papæ 6. & sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ, nec «non & Cantuariensis Ecclesiæ tibi committæ tradimus Pallium de corpore beati Petri «sumptum, plenitudinem videlicet Pontificalis officii vt vtaris coinfra Ecclesiam tuam «certis diebus qui exprimuntur in priuilegiis eiab Apostolica sede concessis. Et mox accepto Pallio Archiepiscopus Papæ hoc præstitit iuramentum.
units.tr: "To the honour of Almighty God, of the blessed Virgin Mary, of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, of our lord Pope Alexander VI, of the holy Roman Church, and also of the Church of Canterbury committed to you, we deliver to you the pallium, taken from the body of the blessed Peter, that is, the fullness of the pontifical office, so that you may use it within your Church on certain days, which are set out in the privileges granted by the Apostolic See." Immediately on receiving the pallium, the archbishop made this oath to the Pope:

units.la: Ego Henricus Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis ab hac hora vt antea fidelis & obediens ero beato Petro, sanctæq; Apostolicæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ, & Domino meo Domino Alexandro Papæ 6. suisq; successoribus Canonicè intrantibus. Non ero in consilio aut «consensu vel factõ vt vitam perdant vel membrum, seu capiantur mala captione. Consilium vero quod mihi creditum fuerit per se aut nuncios ad eorum dampnum me sciente «nemini pandam. Papatum Romanum, & Regalia sancti Petri adiutor eis ero ad retinendum & defendendum saluo meo ordine côtra omnem hominem. Legatû sedis Apostolicæ in cundo & redeundo honorificè tractabo, & in suis necessitatibus adiuuabo vocatus ad synodum veniam nisi præpeditus fuero Canonica præpeditione. Apostolorum limina Romana curia existente citra Alpes singulis annis, vltra vero montes singulis bienniis visitabo aut per me aut per meum nuncium, nisi Apostolica absoluat licentia. Possessiones vero ad mensam mei Archiepiscopatus pertinentes non vendam, neque donabo, «neque impignorabo, neque de nouo infeudabo, vel aliquo modo alienabo inconsulto «Romano Pontifice. Sicut me Deus adiuuet & hæc sancta Dei Euangelia.
units.tr: "I, Henry, Archbishop of Canterbury, from this hour will be faithful and obedient, as before, to blessed Peter, to the holy Apostolic Roman Church, and to my lord, Pope Alexander VI, and to his canonically entering successors. I will not be party to any counsel, consent or deed by which they should lose their life or limb, or be seized by evil capture. Any counsel entrusted to me, whether by themselves or by messengers, to their harm, I will not disclose to anyone, knowing it. The Roman papacy and the regalia of St Peter I will help them to retain and defend, saving my own order, against every man. I will treat with honour the legates of the Apostolic See, going and returning, and will assist them in their needs. When called to a synod I will come, unless I am prevented by a canonical impediment. I will visit the thresholds of the Apostles (Rome) every year if the Roman Curia is on this side of the Alps, and every two years if beyond the mountains, either in person or through my messenger, unless I am released by Apostolic licence. The possessions belonging to the table of my archbishopric I will not sell, nor give away, nor pledge, nor newly enfeoff, nor alienate in any way without the consent of the Roman Pontiff. So help me God, and these holy Gospels of God."

units.la: Hoc iuramentum à singulis Episcopis Papæ præstari consueuit, ex quo perspicere possumus, eos qui tanta religione Papam colucrint, Regi si contra Papam quiequam egisset, haud fidos esse potuisse.
units.tr: This oath was customarily sworn by each bishop to the Pope. From it we can see that those who honoured the Pope with such great reverence could not have been loyal to the King, had he done anything against the Pope.

units.la: Nihil autem præter illum annum Iubileum Henrico Deneo Cantuariæ sedente memorabile interuenit.
units.tr: Nothing memorable happened during the reign of Henry Deane at Canterbury, apart from that Jubilee year.

units.la: Qui cum duobus annis sedisset 15. Februarii obiit Lamethæ. Inde cadaner eius per Thamefim fluuium à triginta tribus nautis nigro panno vestitis Feuershamiam in Cinnba funebri more ornata, cum cereis accensis dnᵗum est. Quo etiam ildem nautæ idem cadauer simili funebri ritu in fererro Cantuariam duxerunt. Sepeliri pelitri se per eum locum vbi Thomas Beckeerrtrucidatus est in testamento iussit. Cantuariensi Ecclesiae legauit imaginem Iohannis Euangelistae argenteam centum quinquaginta vnius vnciarum ponderis. Funeralibus item sumptibus quingentas libras destinauit. Ideo funus eius magnificè ac sumptuosè peractum est. In eo funere exequendo Thomas Wolceus qui Capellanus tum eius fuit, cum Richardo Gardiner altero Capellano ab executoribus Testamenti huius Archiepiscopi impendendis funerariis sumptibus praesectus est. De hoc Thoma Wolceo qui Henrico Regeo Octavo postea regnante Cardinalis & Archiepiscopus Eboracensis fuit, plura deinceps dicenda sunt.
units.tr: He had sat for two years when he died at Lambeth on 15 February. From there his body was carried along the Thames river by thirty-three sailors dressed in black cloth, to Feversham, in a funeral barge decorated in the funeral manner, with lighted candles. The same sailors then conveyed the same body in a hearse, with similar funeral rites, to Canterbury. He had ordered in his will that he be buried in the place where Thomas Becket was slain. He bequeathed to the Church of Canterbury a silver image of John the Evangelist, weighing one hundred and fifty-one ounces. He also set aside five hundred pounds for the funeral expenses. For this reason his funeral was conducted with great magnificence and expense. In carrying out this funeral, Thomas Wolsey, who was then his chaplain, together with Richard Gardiner, another chaplain, was placed by the executors of this archbishop's will in charge of the funeral expenses to be spent. More will be said later about this Thomas Wolsey, who afterwards, under Henry VIII, became Cardinal and Archbishop of York.

units.la: LXVII. GVILIELMVS WARHAMVS.
units.tr: LXVII. WILLIAM WARHAM.

units.la: Actanus quibus amibus atq; dolis Anglicana Ecclesia a Romanis Pontificibus oppugnata amplius annis tractata sit commemorauimus: nunc ad perspicua magis atq; clara exponenda in quibus fulgore Euangelii Pontificiae tenebrae effugiaerunt, eorumque ipsa vis ac potentia fracta penitus atque concussa concidit, appropinquatur ... In quo sane admirabile est in vindicanda atque prosternanda Romana superbia occultum consilium Dei, vt cum tanta tempotis diuturnitate vires acquisitas omni humana ope ac prouidentia ita firmasset, vt nulla pene vi debilitari aut prosterni posse putaretur, in summum tum exitium interitumq; ruerent, & tantorum flagitiorum perennes poenas daret.
units.tr: We have recounted the wiles and tricks by which the English Church was assailed and handled for many years by the Roman bishops. Now we come to set out more clearly and plainly the matters in which the Papist darkness fled before the brightness of the Gospel, and their power itself was utterly broken, shaken and collapsed. There is indeed something remarkable here: in vindicating and overthrowing Roman pride, God's hidden counsel was at work. For though Rome had, over so long a time, so firmly strengthened the power it had gained by every human resource and foresight that it seemed almost impossible to weaken or overthrow it by any force, it rushed at that very moment into its greatest ruin and destruction, and paid the everlasting penalty of such great wickedness.

units.la: Hanc diuinam vindictam hypocrisis, fraudes, expilationes, rapinae, libidines & nefandae foeditates, Regum & Regnorum proditiones, falsitates, periuria, fastus ac elatio, dirae; Mattyrum strages diu popoliscerunt. Ac Romanum quidem Imperium quod cruentum & omnium pene gentium sanguine madidum fuit, caedem & crudelitatem à Lupae nutricis Romuli Regis vberibus suxit, & mox interfecto Rhemo caementum ad condenda moenia fraterno sanguine permisicuit, iuxta illud Lucani. Fraterno primum maduerunt sanguine muri. Idem ab his funestus augurijs progressum caedibus indies auctum fuit, donec nõ alio magis morbo quàm magnitudine laborans suacum omnes pene gentes sua ditione tenetet, & non minus re militari, quam literis, & eloquentia, optimilibus, ingenio & institutis floreret, & clarissimis Ducibus, Oratoribus, ac Prudentibus firmissime stare putaretur, ciuilibus tandem bellis in se motum & conuersum de suis ciuibus sanguinem cedium sumpsit supplicium, ac totius orbis totq; armis retentum, ac tot cladibus acquisitum, bello q; captum Dominium amisit. Hoc enim caede atque vi semper sibi simile constabat. At illa prima sua institutione ad Euangelii amussim sancta & simplex, Deo devota atq; consecrata, crebris Martyriis castigata, vitaq; integritate & puritate ipsaque candidior atq; Sole illustrior fuit. Itaq; post longas persecutiones recepta à Regibus & Imperatoribus Romanis fide Christiana tanquam specimen & Idaea visibilis Ecclesiae omnibus Romani orbis gentibus exhibita & oltensa est & in magno à caeteris Ecclesiis honore habita atque culta, donec religionis atq; sanctitatis vero exemplo deposità dominationem & imperandi potestatem sibi vendicavit, partamq; vera religione gloriam in hypocrisin ac superstitionem commutavit.
units.tr: Divine vengeance was long ago brought upon the Roman people by hypocrisy, frauds, plunderings, robberies, lusts and unspeakable filthiness, betrayals of kings and kingdoms, falsehoods, perjuries, pride and haughtiness, and dreadful slaughters of martyrs. The Roman Empire, indeed, which was bloody and almost soaked in the blood of nearly all nations, sucked murder and cruelty from the udders of the she-wolf, the nurse of King Romulus; and soon, after Remus was killed, it allowed the mortar for building its walls to be mixed with brother's blood, in accordance with that line of Lucan: "First the walls were soaked with brother's blood." From these ominous beginnings it grew daily, increasing in slaughters, until it held almost all nations under its sway, suffering from no disease more than from its own greatness. It flourished no less in warfare than in letters and eloquence, and in the best arts, talent and institutions, and it was thought to stand firmly through its most famous generals, orators and wise men. At length, however, it was overtaken by civil wars, and the blood it had shed from its own citizens was turned back upon itself as punishment; it lost its dominion, which it had held by arms over the whole world and had gained by so many defeats, and was taken by war. For it had always been consistent with itself in being founded on slaughter and violence. But that Church, in its first institution, was holy and simple according to the rule of the Gospel, devoted and consecrated to God, chastened by frequent martyrdoms, and brighter than purity itself and clearer than the sun in the integrity and purity of its life. Therefore, after long persecutions, when the Christian faith had been received by the Roman kings and emperors, it was set forth and displayed to all the nations of the Roman world as a pattern and visible image of the Church, and it was held in great honour and reverence by the other churches; until, having laid down the true example of religion and holiness, it claimed for itself dominion and the power of ruling, and exchanged the glory it had won by true religion for hypocrisy and superstition.

units.la: Deinde pristinae & inuerse vitae commonitatio in fideles ita saeuit, vt nulla non modò Imperatorum Romanorum, sed ne tyrannorum Siciliae immanitas vnquam tanta fuit, quae potuisset cum Papali feritate crudelitateq; contendere. Nam ex hac Dominatione cupiditate, obsequentibus eorum flagitiosissimis, omniu scelerum impuritates, resistentibus verò maximè piis extrema atq; summa pernicies proposita fuit. Hinc tantae simultates, tantaq; periuria ingenuitatem Christianâ inuaserunt, vt nec inuicem haberi amplius pedes, nec vllius salus ab infidelis tuta esse posset. Et sane peroppopтuna atq; cõmodae est ea comparatio, qua fideles Romanam Ecclesiam designant, & meretrici similem ostendunt. Nam primo virgines pulchritudine atq; venustate praeditae, tum castae & ab omni libidinis sensu alienae, amore & beneuolentia non minus corporis quàm virtutis specie colliguant: sinad luxum & libidinem sint proeliues, incedunt amore suo fatuos, & singulorum libidini muneribus prostitutae, simulatq; forma cum aetate transierit, vestula quae maleficia & lenocinia exercent, aut despectae insaniunt. Sic Romana Ecclesia speciosa primò atq; integra floruit, deinde specie sua superba & delectata cum fronte impudenter extulisset, amore cepit insanos, atq; precio se venûdari passa est. Ad extremum cum tot commaculata sordibus amore putido foedaret, & contempta iam esset atq; spreta, in sextitiam tanquam in rabiem converla nullum genus maleficii aut crudelitatis praetermisit. De cuius Lupanaris exitio quia nunc dicendum est, ad historiam revertamur.
units.tr: Then the reminder of their former and perverted life was so fiercely applied to the faithful that no savagery ever shown by the Roman emperors, nor even by the tyrants of Sicily, could be compared with Papal ferocity and cruelty. For from this lust for domination, with their most shameless followers complying, came every kind of impurity of wickedness; while for those who resisted, especially the pious, extreme and utter destruction was prepared. Hence such enmities and such perjuries invaded Christian candour, that no one could any longer be trusted to the other, and no one's safety could be secure from the faithless. And indeed the comparison by which the faithful designate the Roman Church and show it to be like a harlot is most apt and fitting. For first, virgins endowed with beauty and charm, then chaste and free from every sense of lust, attract love and goodwill no less by the appearance of their body than of their virtue; but once they have become bold towards luxury and lust, they go on, foolish in their self-love, and, prostituted to the lust of each one for gifts, as soon as their beauty has passed with age, they become old women who practise witchcraft and procuring, or are despised and grow mad. So the Roman Church flourished at first, beautiful and unblemished; then, proud and pleased with its own beauty, it displayed itself shamelessly, with a brazen face, and captivated madmen with love, and allowed itself to be sold for a price. At last, when it had defiled itself with love that stank of so many stains, and was now despised and scorned, it turned into fury as if into madness, and overlooked no kind of wickedness or cruelty. Since we must now speak of the destruction of this harlot, let us return to our history.

units.la: Guilhelmus Warhamus in Southamptonensi Comitatu generosa stirpe natus est, literis quoque puer institutus in Collegio ab Wilhelmo Wickamo Wintoniensi (ut diximus) Episcopo prope Wintoniensem exstitutem extructo. Deinde ad alterum eiusdem Wickami Collegium Oxoniuth deductus incubuit adolescens iuri civili, cuius pentium affectus legum Doctor & causis in arcnata curia tractandis Iohanne Mortono Archiepiscopo adiuvatus fuit. Iuri autem civili etiam eloquentiam & humanioris artes adiunxit, et a Rege Henrico Septimo ad summam Cancellariae curiam vocatus, & Custos Archiotorum seu Rotulorum constitutus est. Idem tum cum Lincolniensi & Roffensi Episcopis, aliisque doctorum eodem gradu Cantebrigiae donari impetrabant, quo Oxonus affecti sunt.
units.tr: William Warham was born of a noble family in the county of Southampton. He was also educated in letters as a boy in the college founded near Winchester by William Wykeham, the bishop of Winchester, as we have said. Then he was taken to the other college of the same Wykeham at Oxford, and as a young man he applied himself to civil law. In this he was helped by the zeal of John Morton, the archbishop, a doctor of laws, in managing causes in the Court of Chancery. Along with civil law he also added eloquence and the humane arts; and called by King Henry VII to the high office of the Chancery court, he was appointed Keeper of the Archives or Rolls. At the same time, he obtained from the bishops of Lincoln and Rochester, and other doctors, that he should be given at Cambridge the same degree that the Oxford men had received.

units.la: Cum Edwardi Quarti progeniei in persona Petri Warbecki (ut diximus) à D. Margareta Burgundiae Ducissa esset fraudulata, hic Warhamus cum Rotulorum Custos ad Philippum Burgundiae Ducem ab Henrico Rege septimo in legatione missus est, in qua prudenter atq; fraudo perfunctus, ut fictiscac compositis à D. Margareta mendacius Dux fidem non haberet, nec firmitas acmeditaris in Henricum Regem insidiis opes ferret. Paulò post ab hac legatione reversus translato (ut diximus) Eboracum Thoma Sauage Londinensi Episcopo ipse Episcopos ibidem electus & consecratus est. In ea Ecclesia duobus vix annis sedit cum Henricu: Denique Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus (de quo antea diximus) obiit, in cuius locum procurante Rege Warhamus successit. Qui confirmationem & consecrationem, Pallium atq; legatinam porestatem à Iulio Papa ea multitudine bullarum accepit, quas priores (ut diximus) Archiepiscopi accipere soliti sunt. At vero in introinzazione quam Cantuariae celebrauit nono die Martii, quieo anno in quadragesima fuit, Regalem pene pompam & magnificentiam edidit. Venit enim pridie Cantuariam ut omnia solenniter praeparaaret Edwardus inclytus Buckinghamiae Dux 40. confirmatus praeparatus, quaesum Archiepiscopi Senefchallus & Pincerna. Ac Pincernae munus delegauit in eo festo Thomae Bourgchier militi. Ipse autem Senefchallus, omnia munerationc ad quaeque dicitate perfuncta esset, Sequenti die qui Dominicus fuit, cum toto famulatu obuiam fit Archiepiscopo Cant, civitatem ingressuro, eiq; se humiliter ad S. Andreae templum inclinauit. Tum Archiepiscopum pedibus nudum (ut mos erat) insequentem ad Pretatum Sancti Thomae praecessit. Vbi a Priore & Cōuentu honorifice receptus sunt, ac Archiepiscopus missam ex more celebravit. Ea peracta ingressus est Duce praecedente palatium, receptique primum in cameram interiorem. Inde paulo post in magnam aulam publice pransurus prodiit. Ibi edita sunt inter epulas in singulis patinis haec spectacula. Quia (ut diximus) hic Archiepiscopus ex Oxoniensi Academia profectus est, Cancellarius Oxoniensis (bedellis suis praecedentibus) cum toto Scholarium Oxoniensium cetu Regi cum procerihus in Parlamento sedenibus fingitur Wilhelmum Warhamum his carminibus exhibere. Dedit us à tenerts studiis hic nostes Alumnus Morum & doctrina, tantum profecit, ut Aulam Illustrare suam, curare negocia Regni (Rex Henrice) tui, possit honorificè.
units.tr: When the person of Peter Warbeck, of the line of Edward IV (as we have said), had been used as a fraud by the lady Margaret, Duchess of Burgundy, this Warham, being then Keeper of the Rolls, was sent by King Henry VII on an embassy to Philip, Duke of Burgundy. In this he acquitted himself prudently and skilfully, so that the Duke would not believe the lies and fictions devised by the lady Margaret, nor would the firmness and resolve of the plots against King Henry bear fruit. Shortly after returning from this embassy, and when (as we have said) Thomas Savage, bishop of London, had been transferred to York, Warham himself was elected and consecrated bishop of London there. He sat in that church for barely two years with Henry. Finally, the Archbishop of Canterbury (of whom we have spoken before) died, and Warham succeeded him in that office through the king's influence. He received his confirmation and consecration, the pallium and the legatine power from Pope Julius, by that great number of bulls which earlier archbishops (as we have said) were accustomed to receive. But at his enthronement, which he celebrated at Canterbury on the ninth day of March, in the year that was in Lent, he put on almost royal pomp and magnificence. For the day before, to arrange everything solemnly, came the illustrious Edward, Duke of Buckingham, the steward and butler of the archbishop, who had been confirmed. He delegated the office of butler for that feast to Thomas Bourchier, the knight. The steward himself, when he had completed all the duties of his office with the proper ceremonies, the next day, which was Sunday, met the Archbishop of Canterbury, about to enter the city, with his whole household, and bowed humbly to him at the church of St Andrew. Then he went before the archbishop, who followed barefoot (as was the custom), to the precinct of St Thomas. There they were received with honour by the prior and convent, and the archbishop celebrated mass as usual. When this was done, he entered the palace with the duke going before him, and they were first received into the inner chamber. Shortly afterwards he came out to dine publicly in the great hall. There, during the feast, these spectacles were presented at each of the dishes. Because (as we have said) this archbishop came from the University of Oxford, the Chancellor of Oxford, with his beadles going before him and the whole company of Oxford scholars, was feigned to present to the king and the nobles sitting in Parliament the following verses on William Warham: "He, a student from tender studies, a foster-son of ours, has made such progress in morals and learning that he can honourably adorn his own hall and manage the affairs of your kingdom, O King Henry."

units.la: His totidem à Rege carminibus respon sum est. Tales esse decet, quibus vis sacra Maiestas Regnum in tot annos debeat Imperio. Quare suscipiam quem commendasti Alumnum Dignu daturus ei pramia pro meritis. Deinde Rex eum S. Matiae Rotulorum, his versibus commendat, Est locus egregius tibi virgo sacrata dicatur Publica servari quo monumenta solent. Hic primo hunc situ dignabere, dignor, honore, Commendo fidei scrinia sacra sua.
units.tr: To these verses the king replied from the same number of lines: "Such are the men whom Your sacred Majesty ought to owe to the empire of the realm for so many years. Therefore I shall receive him whom you have commended as a foster-son, giving him rewards worthy of his merits." Then the king appointed him Keeper of the Rolls of the Holy Court, in these verses: "There is a distinguished place for you, a virgin consecrated, where public records are usually kept. Here you shall first be honoured with this position, I honour you, and I commend to your faith these sacred chests."

units.la: In tertia patina candidae columbae species pro sancto spiritu simulata à coelo in Archiepiscopum descendens ore tenet ista Carmina. Gratiae traxit domis coelestibus aptum, Perge, parat a montes uberrima tibi. Tum ad ferculorum appositionem ventum est. Quod solenne seruitium Edwardus Dux Archiepiscopi Senescballus, eqnes & capite nudus album dextra baculum ferens præcessit, & simul atque apponerentur fercula, caput Archiepiscopo humiliter inclinauit & in cameram pransurus secessit. In hac prima ferculorum appositione alia edita sunt spectacula. Rex Wilhelmum Warhamum Rotulorum custodem Sancto Paulo iuxta Turri quadam inter Sanctum Petrum & Erkenwaldum medio his Carminibus tradit.
units.tr: In the third course, a figure of a white dove, representing the Holy Spirit, was made to descend from heaven onto the Archbishop, holding these verses in its beak: "Having drawn from the heavenly dwellings what is fitting for grace, go forward; the most fruitful mountains prepare themselves for you." Then came the setting out of the dishes. The customary service was performed by Edward, the Duke, the Archbishop's steward, who rode in front bareheaded, carrying a white staff in his right hand. As soon as the dishes were set down, he bowed his head humbly to the Archbishop and withdrew to the chamber to dine. At this first setting out of dishes, other spectacles were presented. The King handed over to William Warham, Keeper of the Rolls, in the middle of St Paul's, near a certain tower between St Peter's and Erkenwald's, the following verses.

units.la: Vrbis Londinicaput & doctissime Paule Hic regat, & feruet pastor ouile tuum.
units.tr: Head of the city of London and most learned Paul, here let him rule, and let the shepherd cherish your fold.

units.la: Tum à magna sanctorum multitudine hæc prodeunt scripta Carmina.
units.tr: Then from a great multitude of saints these written verses came forth.

units.la: Hic nisi praclara morum indole praditus esset Haud peteretur et tantus honoris apex.
units.tr: Unless he were endowed with a distinguished character of morals, so high a summit of honour would not be sought.

units.la: Post consecratio, & institutio eiusdem Wilhelmi Warhami cum Londinensem Episcopatum suscepit, figuratæ fuerunt, & hæc dicto illustratæ.
units.tr: After the consecration and installation of this same William Warham, when he took up the Bishopric of London, these things were represented and illustrated by the following saying.

units.la: Auxilium meum à Domino.
units.tr: My help is from the Lord.

units.la: At hæc in prima ferculorum appositione, in secunda vero primo tria Theatra exhibita sunt, in primo Sanctus Paulus, Erkenwaldus & Rex Henricus Wilhelmum Warhamum Episcopum Londinensem, Alphego, Dunstano, & Thomæ Becket Cant. quondam Archiepiscopis his carminibus obtulerunt.
units.tr: These were shown in the first setting out of dishes; in the second, however, three scenes were first displayed. In the first, St Paul, Erkenwald and King Henry presented William Warham, Bishop of London, to Alphege, Dunstan and Thomas Becket, formerly archbishops of Canterbury, with these verses.

units.la: Est minor ista tuis sedes virtutibus, illa Thoma dignatuis est potius meritis.
units.tr: This seat is too small for your virtues; that one, Thomas, is rather worthy of your merits.

units.la: Quibus Archiepiscopi arridentes respondent.
units.tr: To which the archbishops, smiling, replied.

units.la: O Wilhelme, veni, Domini fis cultor agelli, Esto memor quia honor, quæ tibi cura datur.
units.tr: O William, come, become a cultivator of the Lord's little field; remember what honour and what care is given to you.

units.la: Tum iidem Archiepiscopi Wilhelmum summæ Trinitati infinita Angelorum, Prophetarum, & Patriarcharum multitudine circumseptæ offerunt, profcrentes ista carmina.
units.tr: Then the same archbishops offered William to the supreme Trinity, surrounded by an infinite multitude of angels, prophets and patriarchs, uttering these verses.

units.la: Non deerunt exempla tibi sanctissima patrum Sanctorum hoc ipso quos imitere loco.
units.tr: Examples will not be lacking to you, most holy of the fathers; the saints themselves whom you may imitate in this place.

units.la: Appositæ deinde ferculæ sunt. Ad extremum prodeunt alia tria Theatra, Primum Papam cum Cardinalibus in solio suo sedentem, & Archiepiscopale Pallium Archiepiscopo tradentem repræsentat his verbis.
units.tr: Then the dishes were set out. Finally three other scenes came forth. The first represented the Pope sitting on his throne with the cardinals, handing the archiepiscopal pallium to the Archbishop, with these words.

units.la: Amplior hic meritis similis positaturhonore, Suppleat & vestrum sede vacante locum.
units.tr: Here one more distinguished in merits shall be placed in honour, and shall fill your place while the see is vacant.

units.la: Secundum intronizationem in Ecclesiam Metropoliticam, & capescendæ possessionis ritum continebat. Tertium Ecclesiam Cantuariensem & chorum Archiepiscopis Clericis & Cantoribus repletum exprimebat, atque hæc omnia spectaculo ex cruflis saccaro & amigdalis commixtis & deauratis compositæ fuerunt, ut in roculo impresso fuisus apparet.
units.tr: The second showed the enthronement in the metropolitan church and the rite of taking possession. The third portrayed the church of Canterbury and the choir filled with archbishops, clerics and singers. All these scenes were made of sugar crusts and almonds mixed together and gilded, as the printed illustration shows.

units.la: Post hæc appositis delicatioribus placentis conuiuium hoc tam splendidum & magnificum peractum est. In quo assidebant à dextris Archiepiscopo Comes Esscxiæ, Episcopus Maionensis, & Prior Ecclesiæ Christi Cant. à sinistris vero Dominus de Burgauenie, Dominus de Brooke, & Abbas S. Augustini. Cum ipso Duce in camera distinte bant, Dominus Clinton, Edwardus Poninos miles, D. Phynocks capitalis Iusticiarius Regis, D. Wilhelmus Scot miles, D. Thomas Kemp miles, Magister Butler seruiens ad legem.
units.tr: After this, with more delicate cakes set out, this so splendid and magnificent banquet was completed. Seated at the Archbishop's right hand were the Earl of Essex, the Bishop of Maionensis, and the Prior of Christ Church, Canterbury; at his left were Lord Burgavenny, Lord Brooke, and the Abbot of St Augustine's. In the chamber, seated apart with the Duke himself, were Lord Clinton, Sir Edward Poynings, Sir Fyneux, the King's chief justice, Sir William Scot, Sir Thomas Kemp, and Master Butler, serjeant-at-law.

units.la: Proxima his erat Theologiæ atque iuris Doctorum mensa, tum Baronum atque Militum, tertio Generosorum. Interiores etiam loci conuiuiis repleti sunt, quorum atque fereulorum multitudinem enarrare vereor ne videatur lectori incredibile. Sed hanc tum conuiuandi plusquam Asiatieum luxum, ad nimiam iam parsimoniam redactum vulgus vbique conquiritur. Atqi id quidem falso de Prælatis, quibus crepat possessiones in laicos translatæ sunt. Sed ab his nugis ad seria transeamus, & de Wilhelmo Warhamo ia in possessione Archiepiscoparus collocato dicamus. Qui non minus lautus ac magnificus quam doctus ac facetus fuit. Idex ea legatione quam ad Philippum Burgundiæ Ducem a Rege Henrico Septimo missus obiit, & ex literis ad Erasmum Roterodamum scriptis licet intelligere. In literis Erasmum calculo affluentem facere ac libetaliter nec minus ioco quam serio consolatus est. Misit enim decem Angleis aureis. Quid sibi inquit volunt saxa in corpusculo tuo? Nö enim construendo es magnificas domos, vel eiusmodi quippiam opinor, quocirca cum non sint ére tua calculi, cures te quam primum superfluo onere li-
units.tr: Next to these was the table of the doctors of theology and of law, then that of the barons and knights, and third that of the gentlemen. The inner rooms too were filled with banquets, and I fear the number of these and of the dishes would seem incredible to the reader. But this feasting, more than Asiatic in its luxury, now reduced to excessive frugality, the common people everywhere complain about; and this is said falsely of the prelates, on whom they cry out that their possessions have been transferred to laymen. But let us pass from these trifles to serious matters, and speak of William Warham, already established in possession of the archbishopric. He was no less lavish and magnificent than he was learned and witty. This is clear from the embassy he undertook, sent by King Henry VII to Philip, Duke of Burgundy, and from the letters written to Erasmus of Rotterdam. In those letters he consoled Erasmus, who was troubled by the stone, generously and with jest no less than earnest. For he sent him ten English gold angels. "What," he says, "do these stones mean in your little body? For you are not building magnificent houses, I think, or anything of the kind; so since these stones are not yours, see that you free yourself as soon as possible from the superfluous burden,

units.la: {y} Cc berare, desq; pecuniam vt auferantur hi lapides secus quàm ego qui quotidie do pecuniam vt lapides adserantur ad meaʒ dificia. In legatione vero Margaretam Caroli quōdam (vt diximus) Burgundiæ Ducis vxorem, fœminam fadiosam & partibus deditam monstrum appellauit. Quod cum eateræ fœminæ nono aut decimo mense, idq; iuuenes pariant, illa iam vetula peneque sexagenaria duos monstrosos partus vnum centesimo, alterum octonagesimo mense edidisset, eosq; non pusillos atq; teneros, sed adeo robustos vt cum Rege potentissimo congredi ac præliofimicare potuissent. Erasmus etiam ignotus propter summam dodrinam tantoperè ab eo adamatus est, vt cum Basileæ ageret suā imaginem arte acuratiss. & ingeniosissimi pictoris (Hans Holby Flandrensis, què ob eximiam pingendi noticiam Henricus Rexapud se retinuit) quàm similimè depingi, & ad Warhamum per eundem pictorem in Angliam perferri curauit. Isque se aliis tabulis ab eodem pictore ad viuam similitudinem expressum & delineatum ad Erasmum vicifim misit.
units.tr: and give money so that these stones may be carried away, unlike me, who every day give money so that stones may be brought in for my buildings." In the embassy he called Margaret, the wife of Charles, Duke of Burgundy (as we said), a factious woman devoted to her party, a monster. Other women bear children in the ninth or tenth month, and young ones at that; but she, already an old woman, nearly sixty, had brought forth two monstrous births, one in the hundredth month and the other in the eightieth. And these were not small and tender, but so robust that they could have met the most powerful king and fought. Erasmus too, while still unknown, was so loved by him for his great learning that, when he was at Basel, he arranged to have his own likeness painted as accurately as possible by a most skilful and ingenious painter (Hans Holbein of Flanders, whom King Henry kept in his service for his outstanding skill in painting), and had it brought to Warham in England through the same painter. He in turn sent Erasmus other portraits drawn from life by the same painter.

units.la: Quæ excellentissimæ doctorum patrum figuræ Reuerendissimo Patre D. Matthæo Cant. Arch. antiquitatis Anglicanæ sedulo explotoreac Thesauro conseruatur. Erasmus autem eum cognitum in tanta admiratione habuit, vt cum multas Christianas Regiones peragrasset, ab eoq; imitatus in Angliam venisset, cum animaduertisset quantum inter Episcopos Angliæ & aliarum gentium interfuisset, scripsit solam Angliam doctos Episcopos habere. Et cum Nouum Testamentum in Latinum sermonem vertisset, statuit illud Wilhelmo Warhamo dedicare, sed postea per literas impetrauit ab eo veniâ, vtLeoni X. Romano tum Pontifici destinaretur. Atque hanc ardam necessitudinem doctrina conciliauit. Quæ similem in hoc Archiepiscopo ergaIohannem Coletum Ecclesiæ Paulinæ Londinensis Decanum virum itidem pium atq; doctum amorem ingenerauit. Hic Coletus in transmarinis Academiis diu studuit, acreuersus Paulinæ Epistolas Oxonii publicè inter pretatus est. Scotum, Thomam Aquinatem & eiusmodi curiosos ac inanes Theologomachos damnauit, ad scripturæ sacræ Regulam omnia reduxit. Similiq; scripturas declarandi institutum Cantebrigiæ tum sequutus est Doctor Warner, postea Rector Wintrontiæ in Norfolcia, qui etiam Thomæ Bilney flammis Norwici combusto supremum consilium adhibuit.
