Vir fuit Coletus tam Latino quam materno sermone facundus atq; copiosus. Vitæ prætereà integer, prudens, comis, atq; frugi. Cumq; Paulinum Decanatum Regis beneficio accepisset, in diuino verbo prædicādo assiduus fuit, & ad iuuenes primis literis & Grammatica instituendos Scholam illâ egregiam quæ Paulina dicitur, extruxit. Huc in concionibus sæpe populum bardos illos & stupidos Theologos, qui semper eundem meditarum sermonem Concioni adferebant, & ex legendis notas ac decantatas narrationes sæpius iterabant. Inter hos tum fuit Londinensis Episcopus qui Fishiamés appellabatur, atq; hoc odio motus Coletum de hæresi coram Warhamo Archiepiscopo postulabat. Quoniam (vt criminabatur) simulachrorum cultum damnabat: deinde cum de verbis Saluatoris nostri ad Apostolum Petrum ter repetitis, Pasce oues meas, prædicaret, de hospitalitate mentionem nullam fecisset, sed tertiam pascendi Christi ouës rationem aliò traduxisset. Postremo quod sermones studio longo pmeditatos reprehenderet. Verû Arcbiepiscopus cũ huic Londinensis Episcopi accusationi subesse odiû, ipsaq; accusationis capita inania atq; friuola iudicaret, & Colorũ ob Theologiæ aliarumq; scientiarũ peritiã vnicè diligeret, eũ iudicio soluit atq; liberauit. Coletus aũt iudicio d imisus, verbũDei frequétius & ardentius pdicauit. Cumq; ex more, Archicpiscopus designaret quod dâ pdicatores qui diebusDominicis Mercurii atq; Veneris in septimanis quadragesimâ malib. coràRege concionarentur, ꝓxima tunc sequeti quadragesima Coletus die Veneris ante Pascha, q à Pȯtificiis sanctus dicebatur, iussuArchiepiscopi concionè corâ Rege habens docuit, quomodo sub Christi vexillis militandum Christianis fuerit. Eotépore Rexin Gallos bellû parabat. Ac Coletus cum de sedidis Principû discordiis, Christianisq; à bello reuocandis multa, caq; mira facundia prolisset, subiuxit his qui sub Christi vexillis pugnât Christi humilitate, nõ Alexandri aut IuliiCesaris aut similium Imperatorû ferociam esse proponendâ. Rex aliquato turbatus ac veritusne suorũ Ducum atq; procerũ animos tam piæ ac disertæ orationis vi à bello in Gallos suscepto flecterêt ac auerteret, finita concione eũ accersiuit. Id Londinensis Episcopus suique asseclæ qui inuisum Coletũ habebant, in eam partem interpretabantur, ac si Coletus qui contraRegis sententiam atque mentem tam acriter prædicaret, veniret Regi in prodisionis suspicionem, & Regis iussu ad carceres ex Aula duceretur. Multaque in eum dum adhuc cumRege loqueretur, petulanter inuecti sunt. At vero præter illorum opinionem, Rex Coletum valde humaniter, comiterq; tractauit, eique suum de
units.tr: These most excellent likenesses of the learned Fathers are carefully preserved in the treasury by the most reverend Father, Lord Matthew, Archbishop of Canterbury, a diligent explorer of English antiquity. Erasmus held Warham in such admiration that, after he had travelled through many Christian regions and had come into England in imitation of him, he observed how much the bishops of England differed from those of other nations, and wrote that England alone had learned bishops. And when he had translated the New Testament into Latin, he decided to dedicate it to William Warham, but afterwards obtained by letter his permission for it to be sent to Leo X, then Roman Pontiff. Learning won this burning friendship. The same learning produced a similar affection in this archbishop toward John Colet, Dean of St Paul's in London, likewise a pious and learned man. Colet studied for a long time in the academies overseas, and on his return publicly expounded the Pauline Epistles at Oxford. He condemned Scotus, Thomas Aquinas and such curious and empty theologians, and reduced everything to the rule of Holy Scripture. A similar plan of explaining the Scriptures was then followed at Cambridge by Doctor Warner, afterwards rector of Winterton in Norfolk, who also gave his last counsel to Thomas Bilney, burned at Norwich. Colet was eloquent and copious in both Latin and his mother tongue; moreover, he was upright in life, prudent, courteous and frugal. When he had received the Deanery of St Paul's by the King's favour, he was assiduous in preaching the divine Word, and he built that famous school, called St Paul's, for instructing young people in the first letters and grammar. In his sermons here he often rebuked the dull and stupid theologians who always brought the same studied discourse to the pulpit and repeated stories worn out and stale from their reading. Among these at that time was the Bishop of London, called Fitzjames, who, moved by this hatred, accused Colet of heresy before Archbishop Warham, alleging that he condemned the worship of images. Then, when preaching on our Saviour's words to the apostle Peter, repeated three times, "Feed my sheep," Colet had made no mention of hospitality, but had turned the third reason for feeding Christ's sheep elsewhere. Lastly, he was accused of criticising sermons that had been long premeditated with study. But the Archbishop, judging that hatred lay behind the Bishop of London's accusation, and that the heads of the charge were empty and frivolous, and uniquely loving Colet for his skill in theology and the other sciences, freed him from the charge by his judgment. Colet, dismissed from the trial, preached the Word of God more often and more ardently. And since, as usual, the Archbishop appointed certain preachers to preach before the King on Sundays, Wednesdays and Fridays in Lent, in the following Lent Colet, on the Friday before Easter, which the Papists called holy, preached before the King by the Archbishop's command, and taught how Christians ought to fight under the banners of Christ. At that time the King was preparing war against the French. When Colet, speaking at length and with wonderful eloquence about the seditious discords of princes and about calling Christians back from war, added that those who fight under Christ's banners should set before themselves the humility of Christ, not the ferocity of Alexander or Julius Caesar or similar emperors, the King, somewhat disturbed and fearing that by the force of so pious and eloquent an oration he might turn and divert the minds of his nobles and commanders from the war undertaken against France, summoned him when the sermon was over. The Bishop of London and his followers, who held Colet in dislike, interpreted this in the worst light, as if Colet, who preached so vehemently against the King's opinion and purpose, had come under suspicion of treason against the King, and was to be led from the court to prison by the King's order. While Colet was still speaking with the King, they railed against him insolently in many ways. But, contrary to their expectation, the King treated Colet very kindly and courteously, and told him of his plan and purpose of waging the war against France, saying that he had not undertaken it of his own accord but had been provoked and compelled, and had taken on the protection of the kingdom. Therefore, although in the sermon he had spoken elegantly and piously about exercising Christian piety and laying aside all desire for vengeance, so that the King's own mind...

units.la: bello Gallicogorendo consilium & institutum indicauit, non fe id sponte sed lacceffitum & coactum acait. Regni tutelam suscepisse. Proinde quamuis in concione de Chriftiana pietate gerenda & omnis vindictæ cupiditate deponenda eleganter atq; pie dixisset, ita vt fnum ipsius animum in Gallos hostiliter affectum pene mutagaffet, tamen quia hoc bellum necessitatis non voluntaris, nec illatio belli sed Gallicanæ vis ac iniuriæ repulfio quædam effet, rogauit eum vt altera concione feæc Aulam suam de bello ad incolumitatem atq; defensionem Patriæ Christianis suscipiendo eadem orationis faculate qua de humilitate rum docuit, instituerat. In quo Coletus non minus Regi quam Christo ossicium atque obsequium præstitit. Nam de bello Christianis licito gerêdo tanta grauitate & eloquentia dixit, vt nonemodo Regem atq; procerès ad bellum iam propêfos, sed languentes atq; timidos contra Gallos tum incenderet. Rex finita concione eum in populi corona gratias egit, & proceribus suis astantibus: sequatur, inquit, quifq; illum quem maxime probat Doctorem, mihi enim solus Coletus arridet. Post hoc encomium RegaleColetus ab inimicorum inuidia securus atq; turus Euangelium indicis in conciouibus propagabat. Etiam Aulicis, quàm ciuibus Londinenfibus (quos orationis facundia allexit & deliniuit) auditoribus flotebat. Sed illa temporum exercitatis paucifimis adhuc Chriftianæ lucis radiis illustrabatur. Sequuta mox sunt magis lucida claraq; tempora quæ à Papalibus tenebris Christianos vendicabant. Ea in Anglia ab hoc initio inchoata, in Romanæ curiæ interitum & occasum paulatim ita (vt dicemus) progressa sunt. Henricus Rex septimus inter Arturum Walliæ principem filium suum primogenitum & Catharinam Ferdinandi Hispaniarum Regis filiam nuptias conciliauit. Ea in Anglium copiofa classe adducta cum ad portum appellare vellet, fluctuum ac ventorum vi sæpius reicta est. Id mali cuiufdam ominis instar esse aliqui censebant, nec forte has fecundas prædicebant.
units.tr: He explained to Coletus his plan and decision to wage war on France. He said that he did not undertake it of his own accord but had been provoked and forced into it, and that he had taken up the defence of the realm. Therefore, although Coletus had spoken elegantly and piously in a sermon on the practice of Christian piety and the renunciation of every desire for revenge, so that he had almost changed the King's own hostile attitude towards the French, nevertheless, because this war was one of necessity rather than choice, and was not an act of aggression but a repulse of French violence and injustice, the King asked him to preach a second sermon to his court on undertaking war for the safety and defence of the homeland as a Christian duty, with the same eloquence with which he had taught on humility. In this Coletus rendered to the King no less service and deference than he had to Christ. For he spoke about the lawfulness of waging war for Christians with such weight and eloquence that he inflamed not only the King and nobles, who were already eager for war, but also those who were sluggish and fearful against the French. When the sermon was over, the King thanked him in the presence of the people and, with his nobles standing by, said: "Let each man follow the teacher he most approves; as for me, Coletus alone pleases me." After this royal commendation, Coletus, secure from the envy of his enemies and confident, continued to spread the gospel in his sermons, drawing both courtiers and the citizens of London (whom the fluency of his oratory attracted and charmed) to hear him. But that age, still lit by very few rays of Christian light, was illumined thus. Brighter and clearer times soon followed, which were to rescue Christians from papal darkness. These began in England from this beginning and gradually advanced, as we shall relate, towards the ruin and downfall of the Roman Curia. King Henry VII arranged a marriage between his eldest son, Prince Arthur of Wales, and Catherine, daughter of Ferdinand, King of the Spains. When she was brought to England with a large fleet and tried to land at port, she was often driven back by the force of waves and winds. Some thought this was a sign of ill omen, and perhaps they did not foretell that these things would turn out well.

units.la: Sed postquam varios portus repulsa petiisset, tandem egressa nauem cum Regali magnificentia Londinum duêta, ibique in templo Paulino a Cantuarienfi Archiepiscopo 19. Episcopis assistentibus, Rege cum Regina proceribufq; præsentibus Arturo Principi nuptiaeft, verum huius matrimonialis gaudii vsura modica fuit. Nam nuptiis celebratis Arturus in Walliam a patre sibi datam prouinciam cum coniuge discessit, ibique quinto postea mense ex hac vita migrauit. Tum luctus atque moeror omnes aliquandiu occupauit. At funeri iustis peractis Henricus Dux Eboracenfis Arturi frater, postquam muliebri experientia compertû fuit D. Catharinam ex Arturo non concepisse, Princeps Walliæ a patre designatus est. Catharina vidua quia magna dote propter nuptias affecta fuit, remâfit in Anglia. His gestis cum Henrico Rege septimo mortuo & Weftmonasterio fepulto regnû Angliæ iure hæreditario HenricoOctauo Inclyfsimo Regi obuenirêt, egerunt cum eo quidam vt D. Catharinam Arturi fratris fui relictam viduam vxorem duceret. Tantimomenti negocium Consiliariorum deliberationi commissum est. Inter cofiliarios tum maximæ authoritatis fuerunt Warhamus Cantuar. Archiepiscopus, & Richardus Fox Wintonienfis præsul. Hic nuptias fuaftr, ille dissensit. Verum cum in confifilio quæreretur vtrum ille nuptiæ forent licitæ, Regiq; atq; Regno expediret, vicit in ea deliberatione vtilitas. Exiftimarunt n. D. Catharinam fi non ab Henrico Rege duceretur, propter dotis magnitudinem extero alicui fortasse etiam Gallo aut Scoto infensifimis Regni hostibus illico nupturam. Id quodRegi atq; Regno magnam calamitatê atq; detrimentû adferre possit. Tum illis nuptiis ad Regni præfidiû contra Gallos conciliari in perpetuû Anglis, fi fobolesinde proueniat, Hispanos. Rex qui octodecim tantum annos excessisset ad hoc illicitû connubium facile per tatem consiliarijs suadentibus ductus est. Sed quia iure diuino fratris fui relictam viduâ haud liceret ducere, iturad Papam Iulium, in cuius pectore omnis diuini atq; humani iuris scrinium latere putabatur. Is qui non vt Moses accipe leges à Deo sed dare cöfueuit, ex suo sacro videlicet scrinio, Theo-logis Cardinalibus etiâ dissentientibus, instante Ferdinando ad contrabendû iuter Henricum Octauû Regê, & D.Catharinam matrimoniû iuris diuini dispensatione produxit. Hæ nuptiæ Archiepifc. Weftmon. ministrante celebratæ fuerunt. Postea quam Rex q; D. Catharina abeodem Archiepifc. facrationem Regiam acceperunt. Hoc infaustum & authoritate Papali auspicatum connubium post viginti annos dissolutum ipsi Papæ atq; Romæ fuit exitiale. Sequenti autem anno exorta est grauis inter Archiepiscopum aceius Suffraganeos de prærogatiuæ Cant. inter altercatio. Eius Romæ instituendæ author fuit, Richardus Fox Wintonienfis Episcopus, qui cum opibus & authoritate atque gratia cnm Regæ summa valeret, tantæ potentiæ animi magnitudinem adiungens ferre non potuit Archiepiscopi prærogatiuam. Itaqi cum, antequâ de care lis villa moueretur, intet se primò communicarent, suamq; prærogatiuam & potentiam recentis amplius annis longæua consuetudine confirmatam Archiepiscopus ostenderet, nec falsaturû vt Winτtonien sis Episcopi pertinacia Ecclesiæ Cant.iura violarentur,seruidiusaffirmarent, Wintonien sis incensus fertur respondisse,qnamuis Archiepiscopus in altiori folio sederet, se tamen in pinguiori collocarum. Et ab ea contumelia statim transiit ad deferendam Papæ contra Archiepiscopum querelam. Wintoniensis Episcopo Londinensis, Lincolniensis, & Exoniensis Regii fut idem Rex postea affirmauit) confirmarit tanquam Duci adhæsenunt. Institutaautem litis capita fuerunt, quod cum (vt sepe antea diximus) siquis de vita decedens bona notabilia in diuersis diœcesibus possideat, eius testamentum ab Archiepiscopo infirmaretur, aut si intestatus decesserit, bonorum suorum administratio ab eodem peteretur: primò ne huiusmodi bonorum appellatione prædiorum atq; prouentuum hæreditates, nec debitæ nisi speratæ censeantur. Deinde nisi decedentiû bona quæ quis extra eam diœcesin possidet in qua moritur, summam decem librarum attingant, notabilia non dicantur, nec Archiepiscopali prærogatiuæ locus fiat. Tum vt boni viri æstimatores ab Archiepiscopo in Suffraganeorum diœcesibus non constituantur, sed ex executorum aut administratinum iuramentis de bonorum æstimatione ac valore fides habeatur. Postremò ne peculiares iurisdictiones diuersæ instar diœcesinum diuersarû reputentur. Papa hanc litem quam sibi lucrosam fore putabat, atque suscepit, & Suffraganeis contra Metropolitanum litigaturis decreuit edictum quo Archiepiscopum in ius Romam vocarent. Richardus Wintoniensis cum hoc edictum accepisset, virum generosum ac foletten Willihelmum Paullet nuper summum Angliæ thesaurarium prædiocû suorum Episcopalium Senefchallum accersuit, eiquè in mandatis dedit vt eo edicto Archiepiscopum citaret. Is mandatum peregit. Citatus itaq; Archiepiscopus & acris contruertia Romæ, vbi omnium pene gentium nuncii atque legati conueniebant, tantaque se acerbitate contenderent. Proinde statuere se ne Romæ deinceps litigarent; tum vt si decedentium bona minoris quam decem librarum æstimentur, vt ab Archiepiscopali prærogatiua non disponantur, præterea ne prædio, prouentus & bona immobilia, quæ iure Regni legari atq; sub testamenti factionem cadere non possunt, ad prærogatiuam suam exercendam præstarent authoritatem.
units.tr: But after she had sought various ports in vain, at last she disembarked and was conducted to London with royal magnificence. There, in St Paul's church, with the Archbishop of Canterbury presiding and nineteen bishops assisting, and with the King, Queen and nobles present, the marriage to Prince Arthur was celebrated. But the enjoyment of this marital joy was brief. For after the wedding Arthur left with his wife for the province in Wales given him by his father, and there, five months later, he died. Then grief and sorrow occupied everyone for some time. But when the funeral rites were duly performed, Henry, Duke of York, Arthur's brother, was designated Prince of Wales by his father, after it was discovered, through the experience of women, that Lady Catherine had not conceived by Arthur. Catherine, a widow, since she had been endowed with a great dowry on account of the marriage, remained in England. After these events, when King Henry VII had died and been buried at Westminster, and the kingdom of England came by hereditary right to the most illustrious King Henry VIII, some urged him to marry Lady Catherine, the widow of his brother Arthur. A matter of such weight was committed to the deliberation of the councillors. Among the councillors of greatest authority at that time were Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Richard Fox, Bishop of Winchester. The one favoured the marriage, the other dissented. But when the council asked whether that marriage was lawful and expedient for the King and kingdom, advantage won in that deliberation. For they judged that if Lady Catherine were not wed by King Henry, then on account of the size of her dowry she would soon marry some foreigner, perhaps even a Frenchman or a Scot, the most hostile enemies of the kingdom. That could bring great calamity and loss to the King and the realm. By that marriage, on the other hand, the Spaniards would be permanently allied with the English as a bulwark of the kingdom against the French, if offspring should come from it. The King, who had scarcely passed eighteen years, was easily led by his councillors' persuasion into this unlawful union. But because by divine law it was not permitted to marry his brother's widow, he went to Pope Julius, in whose breast the repository of all divine and human law was thought to lie. He, who is accustomed to give laws rather than receive them as Moses did from God, drew from his own sacred chest a dispensation from divine law, though the Cardinals and theologians dissented, at the urging of Ferdinand, for the marriage to be contracted between King Henry VIII and Lady Catherine. This marriage was celebrated with the Archbishop of Westminster officiating. Afterwards, when the King and Lady Catherine had received royal consecration from the same archbishop, this unlucky marriage, begun under papal authority, was dissolved twenty years later, and it proved deadly to the Pope himself and to Rome. In the following year a grave dispute arose between the Archbishop and his suffragans concerning the prerogative of Canterbury. Its instigator at Rome was Richard Fox, Bishop of Winchester, who, since he was very powerful in wealth, authority and the King's favour, and added to such power a greatness of spirit, could not bear the Archbishop's prerogative. So, before any lawsuit was started, they first conferred among themselves. The Archbishop showed his prerogative and power, confirmed by long custom in recent years, and asserted it with urgency, lest the rights of the Church of Canterbury be violated through the obstinacy of the Bishop of Winchester. The Bishop of Winchester is reported to have replied in anger that although the Archbishop sat on a higher throne, he himself sat on a richer one. From that insult he at once passed to lodging a complaint against the Archbishop before the Pope. The Bishops of London, Lincoln and Exeter (as the same King later affirmed) adhered to the Bishop of Winchester as to their leader. The heads of the suit were these: since (as we have often said before) if anyone who dies possesses notable goods in various dioceses, his will is invalidated by the Archbishop, or if he dies intestate, administration of his goods is sought from the same, first, that by the term "goods" of this kind, inheritances of estates and revenues that are merely hoped for, and not owed, are not to be counted. Second, unless the goods which someone possesses outside the diocese in which he dies amount to ten pounds, they are not called notable, and there is no place for the archiepiscopal prerogative. Third, that good men as appraisers should not be appointed by the Archbishop within the dioceses of the suffragans, but credence should be given to the oaths of executors or administrators concerning the valuation and worth of the goods. Last, that separate jurisdictions should not be regarded as different dioceses. The Pope, thinking this lawsuit would be profitable to himself, took it up, and for the suffragans litigating against the Metropolitan he decreed an edict by which they were to summon the Archbishop to judgment at Rome. When Richard of Winchester received this edict, he summoned William Paulet, a gentleman of noble birth, formerly Lord Treasurer of England, to be steward of his episcopal estates, and charged him to cite the Archbishop under that edict. He carried out the order. So the Archbishop was cited, and a bitter dispute arose at Rome, where messengers and envoys of nearly all nations gathered, and the parties contended with such bitterness. Therefore they resolved that they would no longer litigate at Rome; and that if the goods of the deceased were valued at less than ten pounds, they should not be disposed of under the archiepiscopal prerogative; moreover, that estates, revenues and immovable goods, which by the law of the realm cannot be bequeathed nor fall under the making of a will, should give authority for exercising his prerogative.

units.la: Ad extremum vt neq; ab Archiepiscopo neq; ab Episcopis viterius constituantur æstimandis defunctorum bonis iudices, nisi ab executoribus aut administratoribus requirantur. Quod suum arbitriû Rex triennio proximo obseruari præcepit, eo vero trâsacto si quæ litigantium pars se grauari sentiat, iure contra alteram experiri eodem decreto permisit. At verò Archiepiscopus referipsit. Etsi arbitrio ac decreto Regio obiecqui atq; parete paratus fit, salua tamen sua in Regem obseruantia, existimare se tam bona immobilia quam cætera, etsi summam quadraginta solidorum Anglicanorum non excedant, cætera, fi tamen extra eam diœcesin & iurisdictionem in qua defunctus moriatur, suam prærogatiuam fundare. Cuius rei longæuam ac probatam consuetudinem ex veteribus & antiquissimis Cantuariensium Archiepiscoporum monumentis prodaxit. De apparitoribus item bonotnmq; atque rerum hæreditariarum æstimatoribus si ab Archiepiscopo & Episcopis non deligentur, verendum esse ne si æstimandi potestas solis executoribus & administratoribus committatur, ex defunctorum bonis vilius æstimatis atque pensis, executorumq; atque administratorû ftaude non modò Archiepiscopo & suis Suffraganeis, verùm etiam quod multò grauius est, ipsis defunctorum creditoribus, sæpe etiam illorum liberis cum mortuis patentibus in tutela atque curatione huiusmodi executorum aut administrantium fuerint iniuria summa fiat. Quæ vitari nulla ratione commodius possit, quàm si bona ab Archiep. vel Episcopis eorumue commissariis æqua lance æstimata administranda committantur. Tandem Archiepiscopus vt iniret cum suis Suffraganeis concordiam, quod facere boni viri solent, cum agere summo iure potuisset, de suo iure multum remisit & suffraganeis concessit.
units.tr: Finally, that judges for appraising the goods of the deceased should no longer be appointed by the Archbishop or the bishops, unless they are requested by the executors or administrators. The King ordered that this his arbitration be observed for the next three years, and after that period, if either party of the litigants felt aggrieved, he permitted by the same decree that they might proceed against the other by law. But the Archbishop replied that, although he was ready to obey and submit to the royal arbitration and decree, saving his own observance toward the King, he judged that his prerogative extended to both immovable goods and the rest, even if they did not amount to the sum of forty shillings sterling, provided they lay outside the diocese and jurisdiction in which the deceased died. He set forth the long and approved custom of this matter from the ancient and most venerable records of the Archbishops of Canterbury. Likewise, concerning the summoners and the appraisers of goods and hereditary property: if they are not chosen by the Archbishop and bishops, there is reason to fear that if the power of appraisal is committed to executors and administrators alone, the goods of the deceased will be valued too cheaply and assessed low, and through the fraud of executors and administrators a great wrong will be done not only to the Archbishop and his suffragans, but, what is much more grievous, to the creditors of the dead themselves, and often also to their children, while the dead are under the guardianship and care of such executors or administrators. This could be avoided by no more convenient means than if the goods were committed to be administered after being valued with an even balance by the Archbishop or the bishops or their commissaries. At last the Archbishop, in order to make concord with his suffragans, as good men usually do, though he could have pressed his claim by the strictest right, remitted much of his right and conceded it to the suffragans.

units.la: Namq; pollicitus est in aliis defunctorum bonis, quàm quæ Anglicano veteri nomine Catalla dicerentur, prærogatiuam nullam vendicaturum, si modo Catallorum appellatione ea bona censerentur de quibus defunctus testari poterat. Tum de apparitoribus & æstimatoribus vt in bonis æstimandis & feudis exigendis sint deinceps moderatoriores tiores æquius statuendum. Præterea executorum atq; administratorum iuramentis de bonorum æstimatione fidem habituram, si contrarii probatio clici ac inuestigari non posset. Summam etiam decem librarum ad suam exercendam præroguatiuam extra eam diocæsin in qua defunctus moritur, satis æquam declarauit. Postremo etsi in diuersis peculiaribus parochiis defunctorum bona ad eam summam diuisa sint, nisi tamen ea bona in peculiaribus parochiis quæ in diuersis suæ proninciæ diocesibus Cantuarien. Ecclesiæ reseruantur sita sint, inter positurū non esse suam prærogatiuam. Atq; hæc inter Cantuarienfem Archiepiscopum ac proniciæ suæ fufftaganeos toties excitata de prærogatiua controuersia hac æquabiliter atque temperata Warhami moderationem in perpetuum tandem sopita est. Sed Richardus Foxus Wintoniensis Episcopus, cum ob conciliatas illas inter Regem Henricum octauum, & D. Catharinā, quæ omnia postea (ut dicemus) perturbarunt, maxima authoritate atq; gratia apud Regem ac reginam valeret, senioque & infirmis debilitatisq; viribus affectus tantorum regni negociorum magnitudinem abquc multitudinem obire non poterat, impetrauit a Rege vacationem, & ad gubernandam suam Wintoniensem diocæsin ex aula recessit. Sed vir aulicæ ambitionis atque simulatoris peritus, vetitus nec extenuaretur sua gratia, & ad aerfariorum inuidia absentid structuret insidias, duos suo famulatu claros & insignes viros Regi commendauit, quorum præsentia se absentem in Regis gratia retineri posse sperabar, Thomam Wolceum Capellanum, & Wilhelmum Paulet armigerum præliorum Wintoniensis Episcopatus Scncfcalli. Hic primo hospitij Regii thesaurarius fuit, & cumulata indies ac ad auctoritatem Regis in se gratia amplissimos honores gradatim consecutus est. Henrico 8. ac Edwardo 6. Regibus, nec non Mariæ ac D. Elizabethæ Reginis consiliarius fuit, Reginæ thesaurarius atque Marchio Wintoniensis, ætate longæua in aula honoribusq; prudenter decursa, & in magna fortunæ varietate iactata tandem obiit. Anno Dom. 1572. At Thomas Wolceus animo elato atque ferro, non generosò ae moderato fuit, humili loco ac obscuris ortus parentibus (etat enim lanii filius, ut quidam putant) & luxu, rapina ac ambitione picenus nobilium atque plebis omnium ordinum mimicis carnifex tandem deuenit. Cuiusmodi ingenia cum ab infima tenuiq; fortuna ad summam euectii sunt, honores tempera-ri ceree aut modi retincre non possunt. Hic socius fuit Magdalenensis Collegii ab Wilhelmo Wainflet (ut diximus) Oxonii extructi, eo excluso quod æratrum Collegij inuasisset, schoiam grammaticalem Rheadinghae aperuit, & modico interiecto tempore dunc fuerit cum infamia abolereturn, inuiuauit sein famulatum Henrici Denny Cat. Archiep. Eò verò mortuo venitad Richardum Fox Wintoniensem Episcopum, qui cū non animaduertiffer quantum nequitiæ atq; occultæ fraudis sub excellenti & commodo ingenio latere posset, eum Regi commendauit. Rex eum eleemosinarium suum ordinauit, Ac Wolceus, iam id nactus ad quod omnem ingenii vim & conatum diu intenderat, vt aliquo loco in aula hærerer apud Regem, obtendit se brcui qui vir in officio atq; magistratu esse posset, Regi obsequio, aulicos affabilitatem & comitate tractauit, in omnium gratiam & beneuolentiam irrepsit, nec quicquam aulicæ curiositatis præ-mifiit, quod ad magnificentiæ, & ingenii ostentationem, cuius fuit studiosior quam vllius sanctitatis; valere posse putaret. Rex ipse iuuenilibus iam annis per ætatem cos maximè adamauit qui præteringenii ac doctrinæ speciem (cuius ipse fatis guarum, utpote Cantabrigiæ primum nistitutum fuit) iuxta quorundam sententiam eleganter atque vitæ pompa edere ac declarare potuissent. In quo Woleeū nactus est ex sententia virum, qui & doctus & oratione dulcis, ingenio profundus, & corporis etiam gestu ac habitu tam concinnus erat, vt ei siccentia colloquio Regem deliniret, intimis Regni consiliis adhibitus est. Tum In Gallicana expeditione vna cum Rege fuit in castris, omnibusq; publicis Regis negociis tam domi quam militiæ solus Wolceus præfuit. Ab eaque expeditione cum Rege reuertit, eum Wathanus Cantuarien-sis Archiepiscopus per senilem ætatem vel inualitudinem 50 præsedere amplius Cancellariæ iudicis non poterat, Regiq; munus cum magno sigillo reddetur, Wolceus ei successit.
units.tr: For he promised that in the goods of deceased persons, other than those which in old English were called chattels, he would claim no prerogative, provided that those goods were counted as chattels in the sense of goods over which the deceased could make a will. Then it should be settled more moderately and fairly that the apparitors and appraisers, in appraising the goods and collecting the fees, should act with restraint. Besides this, he would give credit to the oaths of executors and administrators concerning the valuation of goods, unless proof to the contrary could be produced and investigated. He also declared a sum of ten pounds, for exercising his prerogative outside the diocese in which the deceased died, to be quite fair. Finally, although the goods of a deceased person were divided among several separate parishes up to that sum, he ruled that his prerogative would not extend to goods lying in separate parishes that belonged to the Church of Canterbury in the various dioceses of his province. And so this long-standing dispute over the prerogative between the Archbishop of Canterbury and his suffragans was at last settled in perpetuity, evenly and moderately, by the moderation of Warham. But Richard Fox, Bishop of Winchester, though he held great authority and favour with King Henry VIII and Queen Catherine, because of the agreements made between them, all of which afterwards (as we shall say) threw everything into confusion, was weighed down by old age, infirmity and failing strength, and could not bear the weight and multitude of such great affairs of the realm. He obtained leave from the King and withdrew from the court to govern his diocese of Winchester. But being a man skilled in courtly ambition and in dissimulation, so that his favour should not be diminished, and so that he might lay snares against the envy of his rivals while absent, he commended to the King two men distinguished and notable in his service, Thomas Wolsey, his chaplain, and William Paulet, esquire, steward of the lands of the Bishopric of Winchester. He hoped that by their presence he might be kept in the King's favour even in his absence. Wolsey was first treasurer of the royal household, and by degrees he obtained the highest honours, his favour with the King increasing daily. He was councillor to Kings Henry VIII and Edward VI, and also to Queens Mary and Elizabeth; he was treasurer to the Queen and Marquis of Winchester. Having prudently run through a long life at court, and been tossed about in great changes of fortune, he at last died in the year of the Lord 1572. But Thomas Wolsey, with a proud and fierce spirit, was not of noble or moderate character. Born of a humble and obscure family (for he was, as some think, the son of a butcher), and through luxury, rapacity and ambition, he became a hangman to the nobility and to the common people of every rank. Such natures, when they are raised from the lowest and meanest fortune to the highest, cannot restrain or moderate their honours. He was a fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, founded by William Wainfleet (as we said), but he was expelled for having embezzled the money of the College. He opened a grammar school at Radcliffe, and after a short interval, when that too was closed with disgrace, he entered the service of Henry Deane, Archbishop of Canterbury. When Deane died, he went to Richard Fox, Bishop of Winchester, who, not noticing how much wickedness and hidden fraud could lie beneath an excellent and agreeable wit, commended him to the King. The King appointed him his almoner. Wolsey, now having obtained that for which he had long directed all the power and effort of his mind, namely a place at court near the King, promised that he would soon be a man of influence and office. He served the King with devotion, treated courtiers with affability and courtesy, crept into the favour and goodwill of all, and left unattempted nothing of courtly display that he thought could serve the show of magnificence and of wit, in which he was more eager than of any holiness. The King himself, even in his youthful years, loved especially those who could display, elegantly and with a flourish of life, the appearance of wit and learning (of which he himself had enough, having first been educated at Cambridge), according to the opinion of some. In this respect Wolsey, in the opinion of many, found a man who was both learned and sweet in speech, profound in intellect, and so elegant also in bodily bearing and dress that by his pleasant conversation he could soothe the King; and he was admitted to the innermost councils of the realm. Then in the French expedition he was in the camp with the King, and Wolsey alone presided over all the public business of the King, both at home and in the war. When he returned from that expedition with the King, Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury, because of his old age or ill health, could no longer preside as Lord Chancellor, and the royal office was surrendered together with the Great Seal; Wolsey succeeded him.

units.la: Qui mox etiam Lincolniensis Episcopus sub ente Rege electus est. In eo Epis-copatu vix 1. annis scdit, cum D. Benbrick Eboracensis Archiepiscopus & Cardinalis Romanus Regis ad Papam Legatus Romæ ex veneno interiit. Quo cognito Wolceus ad Eboracensem Ecclesiam a Lincolniensi translatus est, Regeq; actiter intercedente Cardinalitiū titulū, atq; legatinā potestatē accepit a Papa. Nihil hominiis elatione atq; gloria insano præter Papatū defuit, cuius (ut postea dicemus) fuit cupidissimus. Et cum omnia tam Ecclesiastica quam ciuilia negocia in eius solius potestate fuissent, Romanæ Ecclesiæ potentia atq; dominatione tanto studio & seueritate tuebatur, vt incredibile videri posset eam sub hoc Imperatore atque duce in Aoglia cadere potuisse. Nam Regem ipsum iuuenem blandis suasionibus quocunque voluit impulit, vt quod de iuris altutis dicit quidam.
units.tr: He was soon also elected Bishop of Lincoln by the same King. He sat in that bishopric scarcely one year, when Bainbridge, Archbishop of York and Cardinal, the King's legate to the Pope at Rome, died of poison. When this was known, Wolsey was transferred from Lincoln to the Church of York, and at the King's urgent intercession he received from the Pope the title of Cardinal and the authority of legate. Nothing that the frenzy of pride and glory could desire was lacking to this man, except the Papacy, for which (as we shall say later) he was most eager. And since all affairs, both ecclesiastical and civil, were in his power alone, he defended the power and dominion of the Roman Church with such zeal and severity that it might seem incredible that under this commander and leader it could have fallen in England. For he drove the young King himself, by smooth persuasions, wherever he wished, so that one may say of him what some say of the law of the kings: the clever man, they say, commands the master.

units.la: Calidus ferunt Dominus imperat.
units.tr: They say the clever man commands the master.

units.la: De hoc Wolceo qui Regem subditus rexit, dictum exiitimari possit. Qui tanto factu & pinione suiinflatus fuit vt cum de maximis Regni causis ad Papa, aut externos Reges iC rti beret, ita plerumq; literas exorsus est.
units.tr: Of this Wolsey, who ruled the King when he was supposed to be ruling, it may be thought that the saying applies. He was so puffed up with such great success and self-importance that, whenever he wrote to the Pope or to foreign kings about the greatest affairs of the realm, he usually began his letters in this way:

units.la: Ego & Rex meus.
units.tr: I and my King.

units.la: Et in hunc modum dominante, Clerus etiam tanquam super bum suum sacerdotium imperitabat populo, in quem omni luxu & libidine exemplo huius Ducis tam maxime lascientem nemo vel sibilare aut hiscere auderet. Sed cum huius authoritate ac potentia Romana vis in Anglia maxime stabilitur & corroborari visa sit, adfuit ei ist ius dolis in se conuersis summa, eaque diuinitus illata calamitas.
units.tr: With this man dominating in such a manner, the clergy also ruled the people as though their priesthood were lord over them, and no one dared even to hiss or gape against those who, following the example of this Duke, indulged in every luxury and lust. But when the Roman power in England seemed to be most firmly established and strengthened by his authority and might, there came upon him, with the turning of his own deceits against himself, a great calamity, and one sent by God.

units.la: Nam hoc ipso anno quo Wolceus ad tuendam Papalem in Anglia Celsitudinem illum Cardinalitij honoris apicem obtinuisset, Martinus Luthe rus Augustinensis Monachus Frederici Saxonix Ducis Capellanus contra Leonem decimum Papam indulgentiarum praetexu pecuniasin Germania colligentem praedicauit. Cui quo magis silentium vel vi, vel precario Pontificii imponere studebant, eo magis eloquendo ac scribendo contra omnes Papales fraudes, rapinas, ac ipsum fucatum atq; adulterinum in gentes Christianas dominatum ex sanctis literis inuectus est. Hunc mox in Heluetia Zuinglius, & Oeculampadius Argentorati sequuti sunt, quorum doctrina Germaniae ac Heluetia paulatim repleta a Pontificiis defecere. Quas res gestas copiosissime e Sleidano & Germanis explicatas, quoniam in huius Archiepiscopi (de quo tractamus) tempora inciderunt, & cum proposito cohaerent, nobis attigisse sufficiat. Eodem autem tempore quo expilatores Papae, contra quos Lutherus praedicabat, grassabantur in Germania venit ab eodem Leone Papa Campeius quidam Romanus Cardinalis ad Henricum Regem cum amplissima omnia de unciendi & absoluendi potestate, suppetias Papae pro Hungariae tuitione cum Turcis (vt simulabat) dimicaturo postulatur. Cuius adueniu tanto motu concitauit ambitiosos Wolcei spiritus, qui metuebat ac superiorem ferre cogeretur, qui parem axuo animo tolerare non poterat, vt eicum 30 vbernimis promissis legatos obuios daret si se collegam saltem suam in hac noua potestate faceret. Ad id Campeius praemiorum pollicitatione allectus, facile adductus est, & remissis illico Romam nuncijs id a Papa impetrarunt. Campeius interea dum haec nuua potestas a Papa mandaretur, Caleti mansit, nec Angliam ingressus est. Reuersis autem cum ea potestate nuncijs Wolceus cum inani ac ostentatoria pompa Douerum proficiscitur, eo Campeius Caleto discedens trahicit. Obiii iam Cardinales inutuis se primum osculis & amplexibus, deinde colloquuis tractaot. Quid multa. Omitto enim id consulto quo nihil est inanius, in eundo atq; redeundo pompae fucum. Ex his duobus Cardinalibus difficile dictus est, vter alterum fraudibus antecessit, sed luxus ac superbiae Wolceus palmam tulit.
units.tr: For in this very year in which Wolsey had obtained that summit of cardinal's honour for the defence of papal majesty in England, Martin Luther, an Augustinian monk and chaplain to Frederick, Duke of Saxony, preached against Pope Leo X, who was collecting money in Germany under the pretext of indulgences. The more the Papists tried to impose silence on him, by force or by persuasion, the more he, speaking and writing against all the papal frauds, robberies, and that counterfeit and adulterous dominion over Christian peoples, drew his arguments from holy letters. Soon after him Zwingli in Helvetia, and Oecolampadius at Strasbourg, followed; and their teaching, filling Germany and Helvetia little by little, drew many away from the Papists. It is enough for us to have touched on these events, which are explained most fully in Sleidan and the German writers, since they fell in the time of this Archbishop of whom we are treating, and they belong to our purpose. But at the same time as the plunderers of the Pope, against whom Luther preached, were raging in Germany, there came from the same Pope Leo to King Henry a certain Roman cardinal, Campeggio, with the most ample powers of binding and loosing, and with a request for help for the Pope, who (so he pretended) was about to fight the Turks for the defence of Hungary. His arrival stirred up the ambitious spirit of Wolsey so greatly, for he feared being forced to bear a superior and could not endure an equal with a calm mind, that he offered the legates, meeting them with the most extravagant promises, if only they would make him at least a colleague in this new power. Campeggio, enticed by the promise of rewards, was easily persuaded, and messengers were at once sent back to Rome, and they obtained this from the Pope. Meanwhile, while this new power was being mandated by the Pope, Campeggio remained at Calais and did not enter England. When the messengers returned with that power, Wolsey set out for Dover with empty and showy pomp, and Campeggio crossed from Calais to meet him. Then the two cardinals, first with mutual kisses and embraces, and then with conversation, began to deal with each other. Why say more? For I deliberately pass over the empty show of pomp in going and coming, which is nothing but vanity. It is hard to say which of these two cardinals outdid the other in deceits, but Wolsey carried off the palm for luxury and pride.

units.la: Hoc enim tempore eius non exemplo solum sed suasu holosericae vestes ab Anglicano Clero suscepta sunt. A quo tanquam splendida & fulgenti carerua stipati Cardinales Regem adeunt, legationis causam exponunt. Rex noo hoc modo, sed quaecunque alia cuiusmomenti negocia Wolceo committit. Is artificiosa & callida oratione Campeio plurimis & Regis & suis muneribus affecto suadet, ne moram in Anglia ducat, sed recurrat illico Romam, se enim ad Romanae Ecclesiae commodum hoc nuper acceptum legatinum negocium curaturum. Campeius discessit, ac Wolceus rem serio aggrestus curiam erexit quam legatinam appellauit. Ea planè praedatoria fuit. Omnium Episcoporum, & caeterorum Ecclesiasticorum iudicium atque praelatorum iura, & exemptorum etiam locorum priuilegia deuorauit, scelerum quorumcunq; veniam & impunitatem 50 quibus libuit, indulsit, ipsam Canuarien fem praerogatiuam heluo inuasit, omnes humani ac diuini iuris habenas & relaxationes vsurpauit. Atque haec effrenata Cardinalis potentia, eo magis insuperabilis visa est, quod Regali simul & Papali authoritate suffulta non modo Pastules Clerum coercuit, sed proceres populumq; prostrauit. Nam in altero Caecellarix munere vt multitudinis beneuolentia collecta iustus iudex videretur, ostendit se popularem, suscepitq; inferioris plebis querelas contra procerum atq; potentiorum, a quibus opprimebatur iniurias, quas sane non minori feuceritate quam caufidicorum, leguleiorum, & formulariorum falsitates, periuria, litigatoriaque cautelas vir dicauit. Repleuit itaq; brcui vtraq; suattibunalia, tam hoc Regio quã illud Papæ nomine exercitatum, tanta multitudine causarum, vt cæteris tam Regiis quã Ecclesiasticis foris exhaustis & exinanitis, é suis foliis delegationes infinitas educeret. His de causis occultum ergafeodium præsulum, procerum & iuris regni peritorum animis ingeocrauit. Sed Regi, Papæ, atque aulæ, multitudinique ita gratus fuit, vt nullius esset iustissima querela coottra hanc gratiam & potentiam potuit præualere. Creuitq; adhuc indies huius Cardinalis monstrosa potentia. Maximiliano enim Imperatore mortuo, Carolus eius oominis quintus Dux Austriæ, & Castiliæ Rex à Germaniæ principibus Cæsar designatus est. Is ex Hispaoiis soluit traiecturus in Belgium, sed in Angliam in itioere venit D. Cathari10 nam Angliæ Reginam, suam amitam visurus. Qui cum Douerüappulisset ab Warhamo Archie. & Cardinali Wolceo, maxima procerum, præsulum, nobilium atq; prælatorum turba stipatus Caotuariam ductus est. Clerus Cantuariensis aliquot miliaribus in splendidissimos capis ex vtraq; viæ parte, odorum suffimentax incenso thure emittens stetit. Rex & ReginaCæsari eiusque matri Castiliæ Reginæ fiunt obuiam. Cantuariæ ab Warhamo Archiepiscopo in Archiepiscopali palatio magnis somptibus, & exquisitissimis epulis excepti sunt. In aula coœoatum est. Cuius supremam partem Cæsar,inferiorem Rex tenuit. Epulis sublatis Cæsar cum Regina, Angliæ Rex cum Cæsaris matre saltant. Omitto reliquam magnificentiam, qua tanti hospitis aduentus celebratus est. Verum Angliæ An.1528 Rex ne Christiani principes(Turcam tum inuadentes)mutuis inter se bellis conflictare20 tur, egit de firmanda in orbe Christiano cum Carolo pace. Quam magni momenti rem perfacilem futuram, si Cæsar, Angliæ, & Galliæ Reges vno foedere iungerentur. Cæsar annuit, staturum se his pactis quæ ioter Angliæ & Galliæ Reges inirentur, & in Belgium mox discessit. Ardebatq; postea Reges inter se de hac salutifera ae perpetua pacè communicare. Itaq; Ardis conuenerunt. At cum de pacis legibus tractandum sit, Rex amplissimam totius rei procurationem sigillo magno Angliæ confirmatâ Cardinali concessit, vt quæcunq; vellet rata & cassa haberet. At Regis Galliæ ,pcuratores qui tanta potestate præditi non erant, huius procurationis amplitudine deterriti, eû ipsi exiguis mâdatorum sui Regis finibus tenebartur, negocio supersedebant, & ad Regem suum referunt aut ipsi intercesseudü tractationi, aut suam aliis authoritatë sine vllaiuris exceptio30 ne plenissimè committendam. Rex Gallia admiratus Angliæ Regem,tâtam in vno homine eodemq; Clericalis ordinis atq; generis obscuri totius fui Regni fiduciam collocaßè,cum ipse nec suorü subditorum quempiâ tanta fide, nec se eû homine parui à nobilibus pêso coniungere dignatus,tum veritus ne si recusata Regis Angliæ cõditione, (screiectoo & repudiato foedus inter eum & Carolum Cæsarem in firmarctur, in omnē euentu ipse confirius seu Cardinali, seu Regis æquitati, eandem sub sui Regni sigillo pröbratoriq; potestatis plenitudinem Wolceo Cardinali concessit, quam Henricus Rex Angliæ cô- cessisset. Ita quod vix vnquam legimas alicui Papæ contigisse, vt Cæsari ac duobus tam excelsis & ioclytis regibus fœderum atq; pacis cõditiones daret, hoc Wolceo Cardinali euenit. Qua principum gratia paulò post vt potentior, sic infolētior factus est. Namq; in40 ter Cæsarem atq; Gallum exortis mox inimicitiis,belloq; vtrinq; parato, hic Cardina- An.1528 listanquam huius septentionalis orbis Papa spectę quadam & obtentu legationis ab Angliæ Rege, adiit vtroq;:sed Regecseu eooniuncte,seu ignaro legatione è sibi finxit & emētitus est ac magnū Regni sigillum q; læsæ maiestatis crimen est,secum eduxit. Quo factū est vt intereatum is aberat, & iudiciorum comitia, & litium expeditiones, & iudicium ac Vicecomitû Comitatibus præfectiones, dū is sua manu ac potestate omniatenetur, incredibili Reip.malo ac detrimento cessarent. In ea prætereaelegatione regali ac splendido luxu quadringentis sexaginta equitibus stipatus ineffit, vasa Regni preciosissima ac ingentem thesaurum exportauit, in epulari lautitie ac delitiis ministrabatur ei à nobilibus & prælatis genibus ad terram curuatis. Quam intolerabilem in Præsbytero superbiâ atq; 50 pompâ Galli, Hispani, & Belgæ, admirantes libellis diffcripferunt. Ex hac Cæsaris & Galli dissensione, dum vtrique inter se contenderent vter alterum in Curia Romana maiori gratia superarct, duæ Romæ factiones quæ adhuc durant, inter Papas atque Cardinales natæ sunt. Ex eo.n.tempore aut Cæsariani, aut Gallicani dicti sunt. Wolceus indole ac naturâ non potuit non esse factiosus & ex alterutra parte, contra antiquum inter Anglos & Burgundos fœdus adhæsit Gallo, præmiis muneribusq; à fide Regi Regnoq; debita deprauatus. Id eò fuit euidentius quod Spurium suum quem cognomento Winterum appellauit,hoc ipso tépore cõmisit tanq; pignus Gallo vt in aula sua instituertur, & Gallorum linguamatq; mores edisceret. Deinde cum à Gallo ad Cæsarë venisset, quanquã Gallus ab icto fœdere prius recesisset, & belli suscipiendi causas dedisset, impudenter tamen conatus est Cæsare ad iniquas Galli pacis conditiones cogere, quibus nisi pareret ineonsulto Angliæ Regeque denunciauit ei bellum. At Carolus Rex eo magis hominis huius Imperium contempsit, quod de Henrici Regis auunculi sui in se amore atq; sensu, tum de veteri Burgundico fœdere, & pristinis capitalibus in Anglos atque Gallos bellis ac inimicitiis, quæ nullo penè æuo reconciliari possint, certum & exploratum habetet. Ita Wolceus, quanquam sibi vilus sit huiusmodi minis metum intulisse Cæsari, tamen inanis atque pretus reuersus est. Eo vero reuerso aurei Gallici Londini passim scatebant. In hac legatione quæ malorum sibi atque Romæ fuit initium, tres insignes ex suo famulatu viros qui claris ingeniis pollebant habuit, Steph. Gardinerum legum Doctorem, Thomam Morum & Crumwellum, ex quibus Morus Gardinero doctior, eoque Gardinerus iuris peritior fuit. At Cromwellus vtroque prudentior atque sanctior. Hoc anno Henricus Angliæ Rex cum accepisset Lutheriana dogmata à Germanis recepta, & approbata etiam fui Regni viscera progressa latius serpisse, ab Wolceo Cardinali Romani pontificis fortissimo satellite instigatus librum de Papæ authoritate & indulgentiis contra Lutherum edidit. Id ita Papæ placuit, vt cum Wolcei Cardinalis suasu blandiri Regi voluit, verum illi & à Domino Deo datum Fidei, defensoris titulum inscripsit. Non aliter ac Hebræorum sacerdotum princeps Annas de mundi Saluatore D. Iesu Christo ac ipse sententiam tulerat, verè tamen olim vaticinatus est, cum necesse esse duxit vt vnus pro populo moreretur. Sic Papa dum Romanam fidem ab Henrico Rege defensam iri putaret, qui eam Euangelica suscepta postea funditus euertit, in veritatem quidem titulo & vaticinio deceptus est. Hunc inscriptum à Papa in bulla Regi titulum Cardinalis Wolceus facundissima oratione, in qua Regem coram præsulibus ac magnatibus & exterorum Regum legatis à pulchritudine, magnanimitate, prudentia omnibusque animi corporisque dotibus in cœlum exsulit, legit, Regiq; tradidit. Qui postea à fæcialibus tubas clangentibus editus atque proclamatus est. Eodem etiam anno Londinensis Episcopatus mortuo Fitzhames (de quo ante diximus) Cuthberto Tonstallo legum Doctori viro eruditissimo ptudentissimoq;, tum publicorum Regni scriniorum custodi delatus est. Hic autè Vicarius Wrhami Archiepiscopi generalis fuit, vitamq; tandem Dunelmensis Episcopus longævus ac tempore satur in Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis familia, à qua primùm ad Aulam prodiit (vt in Matthæi Parker Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi vita inferius dicemus) finiuit. 18. Nouembris Anno 1559. cum annos 85. transegisset. Sepultus est in choro Lamethanæ Ecclesiæ sub marmore, cui hoc Epitaphium eius inscribitur per G. Haddonum.
units.tr: At this time, following his example and at his urging, the English clergy also took up silk garments. Surrounded by a splendid and dazzling retinue, the Cardinals approached the King and explained the purpose of their legation. The King entrusted to Wolsey not only this business but any other matters of importance. Wolsey, with a skilful and crafty speech, persuaded Campeius, who had been loaded with many gifts from both the King and Wolsey himself, not to delay in England but to return to Rome at once, since Wolsey would himself look after the legatine business, lately received, for the benefit of the Roman Church. Campeius departed, and Wolsey, taking the matter seriously, set up the court he called the legatine court. It was truly a court of plunder. It swallowed up the jurisdiction of all the bishops and other churchmen and prelates, and even the privileges of exempt places; it granted pardon and impunity for whatever crimes it pleased; it invaded the Canterbury prerogative itself like a glutton, and seized for itself all the reins and exemptions of human and divine law. This unbridled power of the Cardinal seemed the more invincible because, supported by both royal and papal authority, it not only restrained the lower clergy but also trampled on the nobles and the people. For in his other office, as Chancellor, in order that he might appear a just judge with the goodwill of the multitude, he showed himself a champion of the people and took up the complaints of the common folk against the injuries they suffered from the nobles and the more powerful. These he dealt with, indeed, with no less severity than he showed toward the lawyers, pettifoggers and clerks for their falsehoods, perjuries and litigious tricks. Thus he soon filled both his tribunals, the one exercised in the King's name and the other in the Pope's, with such a multitude of cases that, with the other courts, royal and ecclesiastical alike, exhausted and emptied, he drew out endless commissions from his own pages. For these reasons he secretly bred hatred against himself in the minds of the bishops, nobles and men learned in the law of the realm. Yet he was so pleasing to the King, the Pope, the court and the multitude that no most just complaint against him could prevail against this favour and power. The monstrous power of this Cardinal grew still greater day by day. For when the Emperor Maximilian died, Charles the Fifth of that name, Duke of Austria and King of Castile, was designated Emperor by the princes of Germany. Setting out from Spain, he sailed to cross over into Flanders, but on the journey he came to England to visit his aunt, Queen Catherine of England. When he had landed at Dover, he was escorted to Canterbury by Warham the Archbishop and Cardinal Wolsey, surrounded by a great throng of nobles, bishops and prelates. The clergy of Canterbury stood a few miles out, on both sides of the road, in most splendid copes, sending up the fragrance of burning incense. The King and Queen went to meet Caesar and his mother, the Queen of Castile. At Canterbury they were received by Archbishop Warham in the archiepiscopal palace with great expense and the most exquisite feasts. They dined in the hall. Caesar occupied the upper end, the King the lower. When the feast was over, Caesar danced with the Queen, and the King of England with Caesar's mother. I pass over the rest of the magnificence with which the arrival of so great a guest was celebrated. But in the year 1528 the King of England, so that Christian princes (who were then attacking the Turk) should not be at war with one another, undertook to establish peace in the Christian world with Charles. He said this would be a matter of great moment and very easily achieved if the Kings of Caesar, England and France were joined in one treaty. Caesar assented, saying he would abide by such terms as were agreed between the Kings of England and France, and soon departed for Flanders. Afterwards the Kings were eager to share this healthful and lasting peace between themselves, and so they met at Ardres. But since the terms of the peace were to be discussed, the King granted the Cardinal the fullest powers over the whole business, confirmed under the Great Seal of England, so that whatever he wished he might hold valid and binding. But the procurators of the King of France, who were not endowed with such power, were daunted by the breadth of this commission, and since they were themselves confined within the narrow limits of their own King's instructions, they held back from the negotiation and either reported to their King that they should themselves take part in the discussions, or that their authority should be fully entrusted to others without any legal reservation. The King of France, marvelling that the King of England had placed such great confidence in one man, and a clergyman of obscure birth and family, the whole trust of his realm, while he himself had not deigned to join any of his own subjects with such faith, nor himself with that man in the company of the nobles, and fearing lest, if the King of England's terms were refused and rejected, the treaty between himself and Charles Caesar should be confirmed, in any event he at last granted Wolsey, whether out of regard for the Cardinal or for the King of England's fairness, under the seal of his own realm the same fullness of power, as the King of England had granted him. So it came about that Wolsey, a Cardinal, had the rare distinction, which we can scarcely read of any Pope having enjoyed, of laying down the terms of treaties and peace for Caesar and for two such illustrious and renowned kings. By this favour of princes he soon grew more powerful and also more insolent. For when enmities soon broke out between Caesar and the Frenchman, and war was prepared on both sides, this Cardinal, as if he were the Pope of this northern world, under the pretext of a legation from the King of England, went to both; but the King, either in league with him or unaware of the legation, he had himself invented and falsely claimed, and he carried off the Great Seal, which is a crime of treason against majesty. The result was that, while he was absent, the courts of justice, the dispatch of lawsuits, the appointments of sheriffs and of the vicecounts of counties ceased, while he held all these in his own hand and power, to the incredible harm and detriment of the commonwealth. Moreover, on this legation he rode with royal and splendid luxury, attended by four hundred and sixty horsemen; he carried off the most precious vessels of the realm and an enormous treasure; he was served at table with delicacies and luxuries by the nobles and prelates, who bent their knees to the ground. The French, Spanish and Flemish, marvelling at the intolerable pride and pomp of this priest, described it in pamphlets. From this dissension between Caesar and the French, while each contended with the other as to which should have greater favour in the Roman Curia, two factions arose at Rome between the Popes and the Cardinals, which still endure. From that time they were called either Caesarians or Gallicans. Wolsey, by his nature and disposition, could not but be factious, and he attached himself to one side or the other, contrary to the ancient alliance between the English and the Burgundians, being corrupted by rewards and gifts from the faith owed to his King and realm. This was all the more evident because at this very time he sent his bastard, whom he named Winter, as a pledge to the Frenchman, so that he might be educated in his court and learn the French language and manners. Then, when the son had come from the Frenchman to Caesar, although the Frenchman had earlier withdrawn from that treaty and given the causes for taking up war, Wolsey shamelessly tried to force upon Caesar the unjust terms of the French peace, and he declared war on him without the knowledge of the King of England, unless Caesar obeyed. But King Charles despised this man's authority all the more, because he was certain and assured of the love and feeling of Henry, the King his uncle, toward himself, and of the old Burgundian alliance, and of the ancient capital wars and enmities against the English and the French, which can scarcely be reconciled in any age. Thus Wolsey, although he thought he had put fear into Caesar with threats of this kind, returned empty-handed and despised. Indeed, when he returned, the French crowns were everywhere in London. In this legation, which was the beginning of evils for himself and for Rome, he had three distinguished men from his household who were famous for their talents: Stephen Gardiner, a Doctor of Laws, Thomas More, and Cromwell. Of these, More was more learned than Gardiner, and Gardiner more skilled in law; but Cromwell was more prudent and more upright than both. In this same year, King Henry of England, having learned that the Lutheran doctrines, received and approved by the Germans, had also crept more widely into the very bowels of his own kingdom, was urged by Wolsey, the Roman pontiff's most valiant satellite, and published a book against Luther concerning the authority of the Pope and indulgences. This so pleased the Pope that, at Wolsey's urging, he wished to flatter the King, and he inscribed upon him the title of Defender of the Faith, which he thought was given to him also by the Lord God. Just as the chief priest of the Hebrews, Annas, had pronounced sentence concerning the Saviour of the world, the Lord Jesus Christ, and yet had truly prophesied it long before when he judged that one man must die for the people, so the Pope, thinking that the Roman faith would be defended by King Henry, who afterwards utterly overthrew it when he had embraced the Gospel, was indeed deceived in the title and in the prophecy. Cardinal Wolsey, in a most eloquent speech, in which he extolled the King to the heavens for his beauty, magnanimity, prudence and all the endowments of mind and body, read out this title inscribed by the Pope in the bull, in the presence of the bishops, the magnates and the envoys of foreign kings, and handed it to the King. Afterwards it was published and proclaimed by heralds sounding trumpets. In the same year, when Fitzjames, the Bishop of London (of whom we spoke earlier), died, the see was conferred on Cuthbert Tunstall, a Doctor of Laws, a most learned and prudent man, who was also keeper of the public records of the realm. He had been the general Vicar of Archbishop Warham; he finally ended his life as Bishop of Durham, a long-lived man, full of years, having left the household of the Archbishop of Canterbury, from which he first came to the Court (as we shall say below in the life of Matthew Parker, Archbishop of Canterbury). He died on 18 November 1559, having lived eighty-five years. He was buried in the choir of the church at Lambeth under a marble slab, on which this epitaph by G. Haddon is inscribed.

units.la: Exepfe diplo mate.
units.tr: Extract from the royal diploma.

units.la: In eo autem bello quod nuper (vt diximus) inter Cæsarem & Gallum commotum est, Wolceus ausus non est suadere Regi vt à confœderatione & amicitia Cæsaris ad supiendas Galli partes discederet. In eo enim nihilo se profecturum cernebat, quod & plebs Angliæ mercatoribus à Gallis contra fœdera spoliatis & iniuste tractatis in Gallos incensa fuerat, & Rex Cæsaris legatis accepisset illud (vt diximus) à Wolceo Caleti cœpositum triparitum fœdus à Gallo primò fuisse violatum, Rexq; affinitate & necessitudine Cæsaris, & Galli iniuriis Cæsari adhæsit. Itaque cum in Hispaniis proficisceretur Cæsar, ad firmandam & retinendam cum Angliæ Rege veterem coniunctionem transiit per Angliam. Qui cum pari similiq; ornatu & magnificentia qua (vt ante diximus) exceptus esset, navigauit in Hispanias. Rex verò cum bellum in Gallos per fœciales denunciasset, exercitusq; duos ex optimo militum delectu instruxisset, ad eos elendos Cardinali dedit negocium peeuniæ conficiendæ. Is qui sé vitro omnibus negociis immiscuisset, & in rebus gerendis nihil mite atq; moderatum sapuisset, tam atrox in hoc negocio fuit, vt plebem, cuius benevolentiam curiosa quadam specie non ex animo & ingenuè affectauit, à se penitus abalienauit.
units.tr: In that war which recently broke out between the Emperor and the Frenchman (as we said), Wolsey did not dare to advise the King to abandon his alliance and friendship with the Emperor and go over to the French side. He saw he would gain nothing by it, since the common people of England had been inflamed against the French, who had robbed and unjustly treated English merchants in violation of treaties, and since the King had received from the Emperor's envoys the news (as we said) that the tripartite treaty, begun at Calais by Wolsey, had first been violated by the French. The King therefore clung to the Emperor, both through marriage and kinship and because of the French injuries. So when the Emperor set out for Spain, he passed through England to confirm and keep the old union with the King of England. Having been received with the same equal splendour and magnificence as before (as we said), he sailed for Spain. The King, having declared war on the French through heralds and raised two armies from the best selection of soldiers, gave the Cardinal the task of raising money for them. Wolsey, who had thrust himself into every business and had shown nothing mild or moderate in conducting affairs, was so savage in this matter that he completely alienated the common people, whose goodwill he had sought with a certain showy display rather than sincerely and openly.

units.la: Nam & quintam bonorum partem à singulis exegit, iussitq; vt vnusquisque non à proximis solito more censeretur, sed veram bonorum æstimationem exhibere iureiurando cogeretur. Quod plebi iugum tam intolerabile visum est, vt cunctis iam Reip. ordinibus execrabili fuerit odio. Tü censores designabat qui de Clericorum statu, opibusq; inquirerent. At Clerus cum exprobrabat,quod præter legem aut exemplum à se quicquam sine Synodo, Regis nomine poposcisset. Itaq; Parlamentum Weftmonafterii celebratum est,mandatoq; Regis Warhamus Archiepiscopus Cleri Synodum Londinum conuocauit. In qua Wolceus intolerabili motus elatione, eoq; fastu tumens quo omniū iura violauit,inauditi exempli flagitium commisit. Cum enim ei non fuit in Cantuarienfis prouinciæ Synodo locus,vt omnia ad suam legatioam potestatem raperet,Concilium in templo Paulino Warhamo Archiepiscopo atq; præsidente inceptum Papæ authoritate dissoluit, & idem postridie coram fe legato Papæ Weftmonasterii adesse mandauit. Quod paucis postea diebus simulatoq; subsidium bello gerendo compètens à Clero Regi concessum esset,iterum dimissum fuit. Paulò post Thomas Hannibal Legum Doctor Regis Angliæ Legatus in Romana curia ; Rosam auream insigni artificio fabricatam à Papa Clemente Regi dono missam in Angliam portauit,& Regi in procerum Prefulumq; præsentia eum copiosa testificatione Papalis erga Regem beneuolentiæ Weft- monasterii tradidit. De quo Clemente Papa Romæ mortuo hæc carmina conscriptâ sunt.
units.tr: For he exacted a fifth part of everyone's goods and ordered that each man should not be assessed by his neighbours in the usual way, but be compelled by oath to declare the true value of his goods. This seemed to the people so intolerable a yoke that it became a loathed and execrable hatred among all orders of the realm. He appointed assessors to inquire into the condition and wealth of the clergy. The clergy complained that he had demanded something from them beyond law or precedent, without a Synod, in the King's name. So Parliament was held at Westminster, and at the King's command Archbishop Warham summoned a Synod of the clergy to London. There Wolsey, moved by intolerable arrogance and swollen with the pride by which he violated everyone's rights, committed an outrage unheard of before. Since he had no place in the Synod of the province of Canterbury, and wanted to seize everything for his legatine power, he dissolved by papal authority the council that had been begun in St Paul's with Archbishop Warham presiding, and he ordered the same men to appear before him, the Pope's legate, at Westminster the next day. A few days later, when a pretended subsidy for conducting the war was granted to the King by the clergy, the council was dismissed again. Shortly afterwards Thomas Hannibal, Doctor of Laws and the King's envoy at the Roman court, brought into England a golden rose, skilfully made, which Pope Clement had sent to the King as a gift. In the presence of the nobles and prelates at Westminster he handed it to the King, with ample testimony of the Pope's goodwill towards him. On Pope Clement, who died at Rome, these verses were written:

units.la: Clementem eripuis nobis Clementia fati, Hic est qui fuerat iam dedecus urbis & orbis.
units.tr: Clement, the mercy of fate has snatched Clement from us; he was the disgrace of the city and of the world.

units.la: Wolceus Cardinalis qui(vt diximus)omnium iuraatque priuilegia legatina suâ potestate violauit, Dunelmensem Episcopatum vacantem ingressus est, & Eboraeensi adiunxit. Idemq; alienarum rerum cupidus & insatiabilis, cum omnia experabat,vt in luxum& ostentationem profunderet,cum Richardus Foxus Wintoniēfis Episcopus, cuius(vt diximus)Capellanus fuerat,eiusq; beneficio & commendatione in Regis gratia positus ad tantarum dignitatum culmen, fastigium q; ascenderat. hic seeleratus iogratuiq; ergatam benignum patronum libertus ad eum nunciùm quendam misit, vt quia Foxus cæcus & senio confectus esset,nec commodè potuisset Wintoniensem Episcopatum administrare, valetudini iam studeret, & stipendio contentus Episcopatui cederet.
units.tr: Wolsey the Cardinal, who (as we said) had violated everyone's rights and privileges by his legatine power, entered the vacant see of Durham and joined it to York. Greedy and insatiable for other people's property, and wanting to squander everything on luxury and display, he also dealt with Richard Fox, Bishop of Winchester, whose chaplain he had been (as we said), and who had by his favour and recommendation been placed in the King's good graces and raised to the summit of such great dignities. This wicked man, ungrateful to his kind patron, sent a messenger to him, saying that since Fox was blind and worn out with age and could not conveniently administer the see of Winchester, he should now look to his health and, content with a pension, resign the bishopric.

units.la: Quæ quidem impia ambitiosissimi & auarissimi hominis ingratitudo ita Foxum commouit,vt nuncium hæc responsa refertre iusserit. Etsi ipse in senectute oculis ortbatus candida & atra discernere non potuit, vera tamen a falsis,& iusta ab iniquis potuit. Qua quidem in re meliorem sensum & intuitum quàm oculorum iam habere,cum ceus ingrati hominis maliciam, quam oculis ante non perspexisset,iam animo cernerer. Cauendum autem esse magis Cardinali quam sibi,nec cum pene lippus & tantæ ambitionis atq; cupiditatis tenebris inuolutus sit,in grauiorem cæcitatem ineidat,nec exitum suum prospiciat. Proinde de Wintoniensi Episcopatu gerendo,quem senex atq; cæcus non corporis sed mentis oculis rexerit, solieitus non sit; sed oculorum suorum aciem auertat, ac his quæ sub Rege administrauit negociis intendat De hac Cardinalis impudenti ingratitudine Foxus apud multos conquestus est, vt ea querela sæpius repetita, multorum sermonibus tandem ad Regem qui Foxum diligebat,tránsiit.
units.tr: This impious ingratitude of a most ambitious and greedy man so moved Fox that he ordered the messenger to carry back this reply: though in old age, with his eyes failing, he could not distinguish white from black, he could still distinguish true from false and just from unjust. In this matter he had a better sense and insight than with his eyes, since he now perceived in his mind the malice of the ungrateful man, which he had not seen with his eyes before. The Cardinal, he said, should be more wary of him than he of himself, lest, though nearly blind and wrapped in the darkness of such great ambition and greed, he fall into a graver blindness and not foresee his own end. Therefore he should not be anxious about governing the see of Winchester, which the old and blind man had ruled with the eyes of the mind rather than of the body; rather let him turn away the keenness of his eyes and attend to the business he had carried on under the King. Fox complained of this shameless ingratitude of the Cardinal to many people, and this complaint, often repeated, at length passed through many mouths to the King, who loved Fox.

units.la: Erat tum Foxi Episcòpi Registrarius Iohannes togniometto Cooeus, homo scurrilis sed iocosus,imposturis,rapinis, profusione, omniq; genere nequitiæ ctsi inferioris esset ordinis atq; loci,cum ipso tameo Cardinale conferendus. Hic cum sæpe ad Regem literas & nuncia à Domino suo Foxo perstulisset, cepit audaćter enarrare quam immemor acceptiBeneficii,ingratusq; esset Cardinalis,tum quia eundem si inuisus fuit, de interioribus suis rebus sedulo inquisinit, intellexitq; à chirurgis quibusdam qui Cardinalem curabant,eum ex venerea lue,siue mórbo Gallico quod cum generosioribus: me- tetricibus sæpe rem ac coitsuetudinem haberet,altero oculo captum esse.Disihnum certè supplicium vt qui munificentissimo suo Domino exprobraret cæcitatem; is ex sœdissimo vitio luscus & monoculus fieret. Existimauit autem Coocus nihil potuisse hoc nuncio optatius Domino suo euenire.
units.tr: At that time the registrar of Bishop Fox was John Cooke, a buffoonish but jovial man, given to trickery, robbery, extravagance and every kind of wickedness; although of lower rank and station, he could be compared with the Cardinal himself. Since he had often carried letters and messages from his lord Fox to the King, he began to speak boldly about how forgetful of benefits and ungrateful the Cardinal was. Because he was hated by the Cardinal, he diligently inquired into his private affairs, and learned from certain surgeons who treated him that he had lost the sight of one eye through venereal disease, or the French pox, which he had often caught from intercourse with courtesans of higher rank. It was a fitting punishment indeed: he who had reproached his most generous lord with blindness should himself become one-eyed from a most foul vice. Cooke thought nothing more welcome could have happened to his lord than this news.

units.la: Itaq; arrepto calamo litteras ad Foxum sine mora scripsit, sed loquacitate sua essectum est vt Cardinalis eas literas intercipi & ad se perferri euraret. Er protinus dü in cauponula liberius perpotaret,& inter rabulas festiuus Coocus esset,a lictoribus captus;& in vincula ductus est. Ibi diu à quorumcunq; necessariorum colloquio secreto seruatus est: Sedres à seruulis enunciabatur amicis suis atq; consanguineis, qui de Cooco(cuius anteacta vita tot sceleribus inquinata fuit)penitus actum putabant. Cardinalis illico in his locis in quibus moram aut habitationem Coocus habere consueuit,designauit exploratotes qui ad se de Coociagestis,criminibusq; referrent. Quorum tanta copia relata est, vt cū atrocissima deligerent,rapinis,adulteriis, ac eiusmodi iniuriis ac turpitudinibus prætèrmissis, de furtis atq; proditionibus quibus probatis Coocus vltimam supplicium pateretur, accusationes varias instituebant. Cuius falsus cum propter suam nequitiam, in Cardinalis potentiam à cunctis suis desperaretur, is tamen non conscientia sed D. fui Wintoniensis Episcopi fiducia, nequicquam pertimuit, nec spiritus, audaciamq; remisit. Maioris certe nequitiae atq; pertinaciae neminem reperire Cardinalis potuit, cum quo de capite atque vita, ad suam ipsius magis contumeliā quam cum Cooco contenderet. Qui carceribus eductus per varia actus tribunalia, per varia exagitatus iudicia, cum hominis impudenti nec os defuit, neq; frons, occulta Wintonensis Episcopi gratia non modo cū Regie, sed cum Regius iudicibus atq; causidicis, tum cū tota inquisitorum multitudine quibus Cardinalis inuisus fuit, accusationes omnes deleuit, & vitauit pericula. Omniū iam sermonibus peretebuit atq; ferebatur haec acris contra Coocum concertatio, qua non aliaras vlla maiorem Cardinalis infamiam in vulgus propagauit. Is itaq; incensus nova indices in Coocū finxit crimina, ac veritus Coocus ne, si Dominus suus Wintoniensis Episcopus, qui per aetatem diu viuere iā non posset, moreretur, Cardinalis potentiae nonresisteret, impetrauit ab eo ad Regem literas, quibus datis cum postea Regem in Aula cum Cardinali colloquentem vidisset, flexis genubus, sublatisq; manibus eiulans petiit cum supiritis misericordiam atq; ab omnibus anteactis criminibus absolutionem. Nam etsi a variis accusationibus variis iudiciis absolutus esset, intentare tamen in Cardinalē nō cōfertim vt solebat, sed seorsū accusationes, vt simulatque vna elisa sit, altera atque indies noua Coocus defatigetur. Rex ilico iussit vt praetenta quaecunque illi remittantur. Cum vidisset Cardinalis cuafisse Coocum è suis manibus, eum accepisset, multaq; cum eo colloquutus, hominem, sibi ipsi moribus atq; indole non dissimilem, humanius familiariusq; tractauit. Promisitq; si sibi more gereret, eum in suum famulatum recepturū. Coocusque metu, siue ex animo fidem dedit Cardinali, & sub Regio diplomate à cunctis criminibus absolutus, postquā aliquot annos in causis capitalibus miserè volutaus esset, domū recessit. Obiit deinde Richardus Fox Wintoniensis Episcopus doctrina prudentiaq; venerandus pater, qui Collegium Corporis Christi extruxit Oxonii, viuusq; ei plurima donauit atque tradidit.
units.tr: So, taking up his pen, he wrote a letter to Fox without delay, but through his own talkativeness it came about that the Cardinal took care to have the letter intercepted and brought to him. Straightaway, while Cooke was drinking rather freely in a little tavern and was being witty among the rowdies, he was seized by the lictors and led off to prison. There he was kept a long time, away from any secret conversation with his relatives; but his servants reported to his friends and kinsmen, who thought Cooke (whose past life was stained with so many crimes) utterly lost. At once the Cardinal appointed informers in the places where Cooke was accustomed to stay or live, to report to him Cooke's deeds and crimes.
