So great a quantity was reported that, passing over robberies, adulteries and such injuries and disgraceful acts, they chose the most atrocious, and brought various accusations about thefts and treasons, for which, if proved, Cooke would suffer the final penalty. Though all his friends had given him up for lost, because of his wickedness, in the face of the Cardinal's power, he feared nothing in vain; he relied not on a clear conscience but on the secret favour of the Bishop of Winchester, and he neither lost heart nor boldness. Certainly the Cardinal could find no one of greater wickedness and obstinacy with whom to contend over life and death, and it brought him more shame than Cooke. Led out of prison and dragged through various courts, harassed by various trials, the impudent fellow lacked neither mouth nor brazenness, and through the hidden favour of the Bishop of Winchester he wiped out all the accusations and escaped the dangers, not only with the King's judges and lawyers but also with the whole crowd of inquisitors to whom the Cardinal was hateful. This bitter struggle against Cooke was now on everyone's lips and spread abroad among the common people, and nothing else spread the Cardinal's infamy more widely. Inflamed by this, he invented new charges against Cooke. Cooke, fearing that if his lord the Bishop of Winchester, who by age could not live much longer, should die, he would be unable to resist the Cardinal's power, obtained a letter to the King from him. Having been given it, when he afterwards saw the King in court talking with the Cardinal, he fell on his knees, raised his hands and, wailing, begged with tears for mercy and absolution from all his past crimes. For although he had been acquitted of various accusations in various trials, the Cardinal was still attacking him, not all together as was his habit, but one at a time, so that as soon as one charge was disposed of another new one would wear Cooke down day after day. The King at once ordered that all the pending charges against him be remitted. When the Cardinal saw that Cooke had slipped from his hands, he received him, and after a long conversation treated the man, not unlike himself in character and disposition, more kindly and familiarly. He promised that if Cooke behaved as he should, he would take him into his service. Cooke, either from fear or in good faith, gave the Cardinal his word, and, absolved of all crimes by the royal warrant after being miserably tossed about for some years in capital cases, went home. Then Richard Fox, Bishop of Winchester, a father venerable for his learning and prudence, died; he had built the College of Corpus Christi at Oxford, and while living he gave and handed over very many gifts to it.

units.la: Sed cum in Testamento moriens multa Ecclesiae atq; sedi Wintoniensi aliisq; piè legasset, Cardinalis Episcopatum Wintoniensem vnā cum Eboracensi atq; Dunelmensi fuicepit, bona Richardi Fox defunctū Legatina potestate sequestrauit, Testamentiq; iui tabulas quas (vt multi suspicabatur) à Cooco accepit, aperiri & actis publicis insinuari nō est passus. Legata nulla praestita, sed ab hoc heluone absorpta sunt, inter quę cum copiosissima magnaq; aestimationis cuiusquā generis suppellex, qua quinq; Episcopales aedes instrueretur, relinqueretur, eademq; aestimata singulis ordine succesoribus tradenda essent, ab hoc qui tamen Episcopatū occupauit, quam hereditatem inuasit, expilata est. Huius expilatae hereditatis dedit ipse viuus eodem genere supplicii postea poenas. His totaelerit scelerius & incredibili omnium odio flagrauit. Soli Regi adhuc cordi fuit, qui e: si superbia & cupiditate eius inexplebilem non probasset, propter ea tamen quae procurabat atq; expediebat negocia eum è re sua fuisse credidit. Sed simulatq; comperisset quata fraude atq; simulatione in maxima fide ac momenti rebus vsus sit, repente vna cū Romana authoritate corruit. Ac fraus eius quanquā occultissima atque vaferrima fuit, his tamen quasi scintillis primò emicuit. Diximus ante, etsi Rex à Caesare diffungi noller, Cardinale tamen Gallicarū partium clam fuisse. Itaq; quamcunq; sine suspicione pGallo operam dare sibi licuit, eam sedulo praestitit. Nam simulatq; Caesar repetito & renouato pristino cum Rege(vt diximus) sordere in Hispanias soluisset, omnesGalli Regno exacti sunt. Capitis n poena in eos Gallos qui remanerent sancita est. Deinde Rex atq; Caesar Gallum coniunctis copiis aggrediuntur. At Gallus Mediolanū q; in Caesaris tum ditione atque fide fuit expugnat, caltraque deinde ad Pauiā ponit. Rex Angliae magnā pecuniam Caesarianis militibus, qui tum in Italia sub Borbonii Duce qui à Gallo defecerat, mœrebant, mntuo dedit. Ea pecunia à Veneris D. Pacey Ecclesiae Paulinae Decano Regioque adVenetos oratore fideiubente accepta est. Qui nisi interpellatus ilico pecuniā praestitisset, milites conducti defecissent. At pecunia reprasentata exhilerati, cum Gallus expugnato Mediolano ferociorem in castris nimium securus ac supinus fuisset, in ipsa castra auddaeter inuolant, hostes aut interimunt aut profligant, ipsum Gallum & nonnullos procerates captiuos in Hispanias ad Caesarem mittunt. Hoc pessimè habuit Wolcenm Cardinalem qui omnes artes rationesque iniuit vt pactis inconsulto Caesare inter Regē atque Gallū inducūs, violarentur foedera Burgundica, & inter Caesarem atque Regem nascerentur inde inimicitiae. Eodem enim fere tempore quo haec Mediolani & Pauiae gesta sunt, Iohannes quidam Iokinus vir obscurus, qui in exercenda mercatura bona sua deoxerat, versutus tamen & in dolis Gallicis verlatus obtinuit a Cardinali commeatum, vt a praesidibus Galliae in Angliam tutus atq; clam venire posset. Is cum veniisset delituit in aedibus cuiusdam D. Lark Praebendarii S. Stephani, necad quemquam praeterquam ad Cardinalem idq; nocte ac secreto prodiit. Cum eo agit de induciis. Cardinalis Regi qui de illius decoctì nebulonis aduentu nihil cognouerat, suadet de legati aliquius Gallici, quide induciis aequissimis atq; commodissimis sibi rationibus actur es esset, adventu. Rex conditiones audire non recusauit.
units.tr: But although, in dying, he had bequeathed many things in his will to the Church and to the see of Winchester and to others, in piety, the Cardinal took up the bishopric of Winchester together with those of York and Durham. By his legatine authority he sequestered the goods of the late Richard Fox. He did not allow the tablets of Fox's will, which (as many suspected) he had received from Cooke, to be opened and entered in the public records. None of the legacies was paid. Instead they were swallowed up by this glutton. Among them was left a very large and valuable stock of furnishings of every kind, with which five episcopal residences were to be equipped, and these, once valued, were to be handed down in order to successive bishops. But this man, who nonetheless seized the bishopric, plundered that inheritance which he had invaded. Later he himself paid the penalty for plundering this inheritance, in the same kind of punishment he had inflicted on others. By these and so many other crimes he blazed with an incredible hatred of everyone. Only the King still held him dear. Although the King had not approved of his inexhaustible pride and greed, he nevertheless believed that the business which the Cardinal was managing and handling was to his advantage. But as soon as he discovered what deceit and pretence he had employed in matters of the greatest trust and importance, he suddenly fell, together with his Roman authority. His treachery, though most hidden and most cunning, first flashed out in these sparks. We said before that, although the King did not wish to be separated from Caesar, the Cardinal had nonetheless secretly been on the side of the French. Therefore, whenever he could lend help to the French without arousing suspicion, he zealously provided it. For as soon as Caesar, renewing and reviving his earlier alliance with the King (as we said), set out for Spain, all the French were expelled from the kingdom. For a penalty of death was decreed against any Frenchmen who remained. Then the King and Caesar, with their forces joined, attacked the French. But the French took Milan, which at that time was under Caesar's rule and allegiance, and afterwards pitched camp near Pavia. The King of England lent a large sum of money to Caesar's soldiers, who were then serving in Italy under the Duke of Bourbon, who had defected from the French. This money was received from Venice through Pace, Dean of St Paul's and the King's agent at Venice, who stood surety. Unless he had paid the money at once when called upon, the hired soldiers would have deserted. But when the money was paid out, the soldiers, cheered, boldly flew into the French camp after the French, having taken Milan, had become too arrogant and had grown careless and lax in their camp. They either killed or routed the enemy, and sent the French king himself and several nobles as prisoners to Caesar in Spain. This grieved Cardinal Wolsey badly, and he devised every art and plan to arrange, without Caesar's knowledge, a truce between the King and the French, so that the Burgundian treaties would be broken and enmity would arise between Caesar and the King. For at almost the same time as these events took place at Milan and Pavia, a certain John Joninus, an obscure man who had squandered his goods in trade but was nonetheless crafty and practised in French tricks, obtained from the Cardinal a safe-conduct so that he could come secretly and safely into England from the governors of France. When he arrived he lay hidden in the house of a certain Mr Lark, a prebendary of St Stephen's. He came out to no one except the Cardinal, and that only at night and in secret. With him he negotiated about a truce. The Cardinal, who knew nothing of the coming of that ruined scoundrel to the King, persuaded him that the arrival of some French envoy, who would treat about a most fair and suitable truce, was to be expected. The King did not refuse to hear the terms.

units.la: Venit ꝓ prorinus Brinionus Rhotomagi praeses Galliae Legatus, eodemq; hospitio quo Iohannes Iokinus vsus est. Sed Belgae & Antuerpiani Caesaris subditi, inter quos olim Iokinus mercator bona sua dissipauerat, de eo in Angliam venientè prius cogouerunt, & Caesaris ad Regem oratores certiores fecerunt. Illi Iokinum nocte ad Cardinalem euntem atq; redeuntem saepe observabant, tum explorabant quibus & quantis pollicitationibus Cardinalem, aliosq; nonnullos qui cum Rege tum valebant, solicitaverat de induciis.
units.tr: Immediately Brion, the French governor and envoy at Rouen, came, and he used the same lodging that John Joninus had used. But the Flemings and the men of Antwerp, subjects of Caesar, among whom Joninus, a merchant, had once squandered his goods, learned of him first when he was coming into England, and informed Caesar's ambassadors to the King. They often watched Joninus as he went to and came from the Cardinal at night, and then they tried to find out with what and how great promises he had tempted the Cardinal, and some others who then had influence with the King, about a truce.

units.la: De his omnibus Praetus tum Caesaris Legatus scripsit in Hispanias literas, quas intercipi ac sibi tradi Cardinalis cu rauit ea sq; relcratas legit. Postridie Legatum Prattū conuenit: mirari se aut cur huiusmodi fabulas in literis daret ad Caesarem. At Prattus fui esse officii dixit de rebus tantis Dominum suum admonere, necrecte fecisse Cardinale qui signatas atq; destinatas ad Caesarem literas referrassent. Rumores iam subitò non modo de induciis sed de pace sparsi sunt. Itaq; Legatus Papae Romam scripsit Regem foedos cum Gallo mox iicturum, proinde satius esse Papae cum eodem etiam ocyus quam serius coniungi.
units.tr: Of all this Praet, then Caesar's envoy, wrote a letter to Spain. The Cardinal saw to it that the letter was intercepted and handed to him, and he read it after it had been opened. The next day he met the envoy Praet and asked him why he gave such fables in his letters to Caesar. But Praet said it was his duty to warn his master about such important matters, and that the Cardinal had not acted rightly in opening letters that had been sealed and sent to Caesar. Already rumours of a truce, and not only of a truce but of peace, were suddenly spread abroad. So the Pope's legate wrote to Rome that the King would soon make a treaty with the French, and that it was therefore better for the Pope to join himself to the same side as quickly as possible rather than later.

units.la: Quibus literis motus Papa Gallicam factionem sequutus est, at suo magno (vt dicemus) sequenti anno malo. Sed haec omnium rerum perturbario quam Cardinalis meditabatur, & Gallorum Legatio allato illo de Caesaris victoria, & Galli captiuitate nuncio impedita est. Nam Rex repudiatis Gallis Cuthbertum Tunstallum Londinensem Episcopum, & Richardum Wingfeld militem de belli Gallici progressu legauit ad Caesarē, acinterea de pecuniis quibus bellici sumptus sustentarentur, conficiendis consilium cepit. At Wolceus Cardinalis odio iam aperto secuit in D. Paceum Regium (vt diximus) ad Venetos oratorem, quia se in consulto Duci Burboniae & Caesarianis militibus pecunias ministrabat, sine quibus Caesaris exercitus dissipatus discessisset, Gallusq; Marte superior extitisset.
units.tr: Moved by these letters, the Pope followed the French faction, but in the following year it was to be his great misfortune, as we shall say. But this confusion of affairs that the Cardinal was planning, and the French embassy, were both hindered by the news of Caesar's victory and of the capture of the French king. For the King, having rejected the French, sent Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of London, and Sir Richard Wingfield to Caesar to report on the progress of the French war. Meanwhile he took counsel about raising the money by which the costs of war were to be met. But Cardinal Wolsey, now with open hatred, pursued Pace, the King's agent at Venice (as we said), because he had supplied money to the Duke of Bourbon and to Caesar's soldiers. Without that money Caesar's army would have been scattered and departed, and the French would have prevailed in war.

units.la: Itaenim sine vlla mora atq; difficultate Cardinalis existimauit Regem suo suasu desecturum a Caesare, atq; pactur um cum Gallo. Itaq; dum Paceus apud Venetos ageret, Cardinalis Regem (vt mox dicemus) ita in eum optime de Rege meritum abalienauit, vt nec pecuniapro qua fideuisset restituretur, nec sibi vt legato quicquam etsi crebris literis instati mitteretur. Id quod grauissimū eruditissimū mumq; virū, beneq; sibi conscium in aegritudine incurabile, indeq; In delirium coegit. Nam capto Gallo quod Papae atq; Cardinalem Wolceum intus pupugit, Caesar in Italiam ad tuedas suas ditiones quas superiori aduentu atq; motu Galli turbaras esse cognouerat, proficiscendum sibi statuit. Qui Caesaris aduentus formidabilis Papae fuit, ꝗ paulo ante ex oratoris sui in Angliam literis (vt diximus) cum Gallo foedus iniisset, & cum Caesar Regnum Neapolitanum, Siciliam Insulam, & Mediolanum teneret, ne aduentu & potentia sua totam Italiam occuparet, itaq; Venetos, Florentinos, Vrbinates & caeteras liberas Italiae ditiones atq; ciuitates quodemetu solicitauit, vt coniunctis viribus auerterent & proliberent ab Italia Caesare. Itali itaq; de impediendo Caesare foedus ineunt. Interea nouis conditionibus, & obsidibus datis, Caesar Gallum captiuum relaxauit, & pax etiam inter Regem atq; Gallū stabilita est, quo nihil Papae atq; Italis optatius potuit contingere. Legatos, n. ilico ad Gallum mittunt de eoins liberatione gratulatum, eiq; ostendunt foedus quod de coercendo Caesare inter se pepigisset. Gallus a Papa iuramento Caesari dato solutus & fidefragus eidem se inscripsit Frederi, & copiose ac diserte satis scriptam Apologiā in Caesarē edidit cura fide recessserit. Idem legari postquā cum Gallo transegisset, veniunt ad Regem in Angliā. Is in eiusmodi foedere cum Papa atq; Gallo cohaerere noluit, sed pristinae necessitudinis memor Caesarem vt cauerēt, quod q̃dem gratissimi fuit officii, certiorē facit. Bellum iam attrox violatis inter Caesarē atq; Gallū Papali absolutione foederibus incensum est. Caesar copias belli cas vndique conqisiuit vt In Italiā nauigaret, cumq; cognouisset Cardinalem omnes conatus intendisse, vt Regē ab antiquo foedere Burgundico abduceret, Hugonē Mendosanum virū illustrē atque nobilem oratorem ad cū misit, qui & Galli perfidia Regi declararet, & Regem in veteri necessitudine atq; fide retineret. Gallus itidem suos misit oratores vt Regem ad se alliceret. Verùm tam Gallus quam Cæsar vter sibi Regem magis deuincerret, laborauit. In quo Wolceus boni scilicet Cardinalis officium, ac vt se dignum fuerat, Cæsaris odio fecit. Produxit nunc primum id consilii quod diuino pectore latuisset, vt Cæsare deserto Rex perpetua necessitudine & affinitate iungeretur Gallo. Simulauit inter Gallum & D. Mariam Regis ex D. Catharina filiam nuptias, de quibus cum à Regis Galliæ consiliariis ageretur, Præses Parisiensis, qui in eo consilio fuit, dicebat non fore honorificas illas tanto Regi nuptias, quia D. Maria ex illicito coitu nempe fratris Henrici Regis vera coniuge procreata esset (puria, ideoq; nec iure in hæreditate Regnoq; patris posse succedere. Hoc responsum Cardinalis dolo fabricatum est, & tamen ne is videretur in re tanta obrepere subito Regi, D. Longlandum Lincolniënsem Episcopum Henrici Regis confessorem virum in Theologia Scholastica doctum ad se vocauit.
units.tr: For so the Cardinal thought, without any delay or difficulty, that the King would by his advice withdraw from Caesar and make a treaty with the French. So while Pace was at Venice, the Cardinal (as we shall soon say) estranged the King from him, though he had deserved very well of the King, so that neither the money for which he had stood surety was repaid, nor was anything sent to him as envoy, although he was urgently pressed with frequent letters. This so drove that most learned and most serious man, who was well aware of his own good conduct, into an incurable sickness, and from that into delirium. For when the French king was taken, which pricked the Pope and Cardinal Wolsey within, Caesar decided he must set out for Italy to defend his dominions, which he had learned were disturbed by the French king's earlier coming and movement. This coming of Caesar was a terror to the Pope, who a little before, by letters from his envoy in England (as we said), had made a treaty with the French. And since Caesar held the kingdom of Naples, the island of Sicily and Milan, the Pope feared that by his coming and power he would occupy all Italy. Therefore he stirred up the Venetians, the Florentines, the people of Urbino and the other free states and cities of Italy, out of fear, so that by joining their forces they might turn Caesar away and keep him out of Italy. So the Italians made a league to hinder Caesar. Meanwhile, with new terms and hostages given, Caesar released the captive French king, and peace was also established between the King and the French, than which nothing more welcome could have happened to the Pope and the Italians. For they at once sent envoys to the French king, to congratulate him on his release, and showed him the treaty which they had made with each other for curbing Caesar. The French king, released from his oath to Caesar by the Pope and having broken faith, published at length and in fairly eloquent terms an Apology against Caesar, explaining his withdrawal. After the same envoys had concluded their business with the French, they came to the King in England. He refused to join such an alliance with the Pope and the French, but, mindful of their old friendship, he informed Caesar so that he might take precautions. This was indeed a most welcome service. Now a fierce war broke out between Caesar and the French, the treaties having been violated by the papal absolution. Caesar gathered troops from everywhere for the war, so that he might sail into Italy. And when he learned that the Cardinal had strained every effort to draw the King away from the ancient Burgundian alliance, he sent to him Hugo de Mendoza, an illustrious and noble envoy, who was to make known to the King the French treachery and to keep the King in his old friendship and loyalty. The French likewise sent their envoys to win the King over to themselves. Yet both the French and Caesar laboured to see which of them could bind the King more closely to himself. In this matter Wolsey, as was fitting for a good Cardinal, showed the office of a good man and, as he deserved, incurred Caesar's hatred. Then for the first time he brought forward a plan which had lain hidden in his divine breast: that with Caesar abandoned, the King should be joined to the French by a perpetual alliance and kinship. He arranged a marriage between the French king and the Lady Mary, daughter of the King by Lady Catherine. When this was being discussed by the French king's counsellors, the President of Paris, who was on that council, said that those marriages would not be honourable for so great a king, because Lady Mary had been born of an unlawful union, namely of King Henry with his brother's true wife, and was therefore illegitimate, and so could not by right succeed to the inheritance and kingdom of her father. The Cardinal's answer to this was a contrivance, and yet, so that he might not seem to slip into so great a matter suddenly before the King, he summoned to himself Dr Longland, Bishop of Lincoln, the King's confessor, a man learned in scholastic theology.

units.la: Quæritab eo an iure diuino fratri liceat fratris sui defuncti viduam vxorem ducere. Is de hac quæstione perplexus, vnum aut alterum deliberandi diem petit, ac reuersus nepharias esse & incestas nuptias affirmauit. Tū narrauit ei Cardinalis quid à Regis Galliæ consiliariis responsum fuit, cum inter D. Mariam & Regem Gallię nuptiæ conciliandæ essent. Proinde sui esse officii dixit, cum esset confessor Regius, Regem quam primo tempore admonere, vt repudiata adulterina coniuge, iustas sibi nuptias, é quibus iusta ei & hæreditaria nascatur soboles procuret, ne se mortuo liberis ex hac D. Catharina generatis eiectis, oriatur grauis inter proceres de regno adipiscendo contentio. Hoc consilio, in quo sibi tantum Cardinalis placuit, non potuit inuenirialiut excogitari quicquam regno salutarius, aut sibi, Papæ, atq; curiæ Romanæ perniciousius. Vrait Hcsiodus.
units.tr: He was asked by him whether it was lawful by divine law for a man to take his deceased brother's widow as his wife. Perplexed by this question, he asked for a day or so to consider it, and on returning he declared that such a marriage was unlawful and incestuous. The Cardinal then told him what answer had been given by the counsellors of the King of France when a marriage between the Lady Mary and the King of France was being arranged. He said that, since he was the King's confessor, it was his duty to admonish the King at the earliest opportunity to put away his adulterous wife and procure a lawful marriage, from which a lawful and heritable offspring might be born, so that after his death there would be no serious contention among the nobles over the succession, should the children begotten of this Lady Catharine be cast out. In this counsel, which pleased the Cardinal greatly, nothing more wholesome for the kingdom could have been devised, or more destructive to himself, to the Pope and to the Roman court. As Hesiod says, [...]

units.la: Dum hæc geruntur, Dux Borbonię qui cum Cæsarianis militibus in Italia fuit, Papæ facinus vlturus Romam expugnauit, eaq; capta Papa atq; Cardinales in Arcem quæ Angelica dicitur profugiunt, ædibus suis desertis ac Cæsarianis militibus deteliĉtus prædæ, Illi diuturna obsidione Papam & Cardinales quorum calamitatem ne Romani quidem deplorabant tenuerunt, processiones & cæteras ceremonias Ponuficias cum ornamentis & solennitatibus requisitis indies peregerūt. Hacre in Anglia nunciata Wolceus Cardinalis omne quod restabat virus in Cæsarem euomuit. Ad Regé flebili oratione venit, casum Papæ cū lacbrymis exponit, in Cæsarē acerrime inuehitur, satius esse Regi iudicat ab eius necessitudine & affinitate discedere, quā cū fidei defensor a sanctissimo Papa nominatus fit, hanc inferri Papæ & Ecclesiæ Romanæ contumeliā ppeu. Rex cōmotus decreuit specialibus suis denunciare Cæsari bellū, nisi dimidiū militaris prædæ Pauiæ captū, & Aurelianū ducē sibi redderet, ac Papā liberaret. Cæsar benigne responditse obsidionis Papalis ignarum, de cæteris Regi satisfacturū. At Cardinalis etsi nō subesset belli causa, tamen inconsulto Regead Clarentium scripsit vt bellū denunciaret. Is mandātū peregit. Tū Regē solicitauit vt sororē Regis Galliæ Catharinarepudiata vxorē duceret. Necesse causam eur ea affinitate conciliata timeret 40 Cæsaris potentiā, eoq; magis si Papā mllitib. aut pecuniā iuuaret. Rex pecunias concessit, sed milites noluit. Cardinalis itaq; cū ingenti Thesauro ad Gallū, pficiscitur, Gallus in Italiā exercitū copiosum Regis sumptib. mittit. De nuptiis nouis, & repudiandā D. Catharina agitur, rumores inde varii inter Anglos atq; Gallos exagitātur. Id quod Regi valde displicuit bellū Cæsari denūciatū, & de nouo matrimonio cōciliādo a Cardinali ante quā is prius cognouisset, & D. Catharinaā se legitimē separata esset tractari. Verū eo audaciæ progressus fuit Cardinalis, vt cū omnia sibi licere liberaq; esse putaret. nullis potuit finib' metisq; cōtineri. Ab hac itaq; legatione reuersus Cardinalis cū vidisset alieniori à se animo fuisse Regē q; Cæsari indiceretur bellū, crimē omne impudēter in Clarentinū tràstulit, eiq; simul ac redierit pœnā capitis minatus est. Quod cū a suis familiariḃ. acces50 pisset Claresius, vias sterea & portus à Cardinali obseruari vt præceps antequā Regē cōueniret, ad vltimū supplicū ducereturpoꝛtūRhiā clam ingressus, & adRegē duētus tres Cardinalis literas ostēdit, q bus nisi ciuus bellū indiceret, simile si bi ,pposuit supplicium. Cōmotus bac falsitate & impudēria Rex dixit se nōdū Regiā potestatē gessisse,sed commisisse alteri, cuius se valde pœnituit. Sed ille Cardinalis dolo iniectus matrimonii scrupulus cum Regis animo insedisset altius, nec vllo modo euelli potuisset, nec Rex tā facile vtCardinalis existimauit ad alteras nuptias, nisi priorib.infeĉtis tràsire voluisset, dū Cardinali multō q ante incettius visū est, vtrū Gallicæ nuptiæ, quas istā arrogāter sine Regis cōsensu parauerat, Regi cordi futuræ essent, cepit iā ad hoc quod suasit diuortium lentis atque plumbeis pedibus progredi. Rex vero ad illo Gallicano respondo, atque Cardinalis audacia exanimatus pene & perplexus, seorsim indiescum Praesulibus, doctisq; viris egit de suo matrimonio, qui vna conspiratione & consensu in lege diuinâ vetitû ac prohibitum fuisse affirmabant. Itaq; Rex tardantem Cardinalem incitauit, vt Romam aliquos acceleraret, quia Papa maturè in Angliam mitti procurarent de re tanta legationes. Romana curia (vt colligi & existimari aliter ex antegressis & sequentibus non potest) hanc causam Wolceo Cardinali delegauit, id est, veteranoilli Campeio atque Wolceo, quod perinde fuit.
units.tr: While these things were going on, the Duke of Bourbon, who had been in Italy with Caesar's soldiers, marched on Rome to avenge the Pope's wrongdoing and took the city. The Pope and the Cardinals fled into the fortress called Sant'Angelo, and when their houses were abandoned and Caesar's soldiers were let loose on the plunder, they kept the Pope and the Cardinals under a long siege, whose calamity not even the Romans lamented. Day after day they carried out the processions and the other papal ceremonies with the requisite ornaments and solemnities. When this news reached England, Cardinal Wolsey poured out all the poison that remained in him against the Emperor. He came to the King with a tearful speech, lamented the Pope's plight with tears, and inveighed most bitterly against Caesar. He judged it better for the King to break off his alliance and kinship with him, since he had been named Defender of the Faith by the most holy Pope, than to allow this insult to be inflicted on the Pope and the Roman Church. The King, moved, resolved to declare war on Caesar by his own heralds, unless Caesar returned to him half of the military spoils taken at Pavia, and the Duke of Orleans, and freed the Pope. Caesar replied courteously that he was ignorant of the papal siege and would make satisfaction to the King on the other points. But the Cardinal, although there was no cause for war, nevertheless wrote without the King's knowledge to Clarentius, ordering him to declare war. He carried out the order. Then the Cardinal urged the King to take Catharine, sister of the King of France, as his wife in place of the repudiated one, on the ground that, once such an alliance was made, he need not fear Caesar's power, all the more if the French aided the Pope with soldiers or money. The King granted money but refused soldiers. The Cardinal therefore set off to France with a great treasure, and the French sent a large army into Italy at the King's expense. Talk of new marriages and of repudiating the Lady Catharine went on, and various rumours about it were bandied about among the English and the French. This displeased the King greatly: war had been declared on Caesar, and a new marriage was being arranged by the Cardinal, and the matter of Catharine was being discussed as though she had already been legitimately separated from him, before the Cardinal had first learned of it. Indeed the Cardinal grew so bold that, thinking everything was permitted him and that he was free, he could be restrained by no limits or bounds. Returning from this embassy, the Cardinal, seeing that the King's mind was more alienated from himself, and that war had been declared on Caesar, shamelessly shifted all the blame onto Clarentius and threatened him with capital punishment as soon as he returned. When Clarentius heard this from his friends, he learned that the roads and ports were being watched by the Cardinal's men so that he could be seized before he met the King. He entered the Rhine secretly and, brought before the King, showed him three letters of the Cardinal, by which the Cardinal had set before him a similar punishment unless he declared war on the Emperor. Moved by this falsehood and shamelessness, the King said that he had not yet exercised royal power but had entrusted it to another, and he greatly regretted it. But since the scruple about the marriage, instilled by the Cardinal's trickery, had sunk deeper into the King's mind and could in no way be uprooted, the King did not pass to a second marriage as easily as the Cardinal supposed, unless he wished first to be rid of the earlier one. Meanwhile it seemed far more uncertain to the Cardinal whether the French marriage, which he had arrogantly arranged without the King's consent, would be dear to the King. He began now to move slowly and with leaden feet towards the divorce he had proposed. But the King answered the Cardinal's boldness, and the Cardinal was almost stunned and perplexed; apart from the bishops and learned men, he discussed his own marriage with the King, and they affirmed with one accord and agreement that it had been forbidden and prohibited by divine law. Therefore the King urged the dawdling Cardinal to hasten some men to Rome, so that they might promptly procure legations to England from the Pope on so great a matter. The Roman curia (for it cannot be gathered or judged otherwise from what went before and what follows) entrusted this cause to Cardinal Wolsey, that is, to the old men Campeius and Wolsey, which amounted to the same thing.

units.la: Nam Campeius decennio antecesserat Cardinali in alia (vt diximus) legatione. Nunc autem longis ac molestis itineribus, pedibusq; æger venit in Angliam, vt ex Wolcei sententia de hoc Regali negocio iudicaret. Quod etli prospectum & olfactum antea fuit, tamen quid a Papa & his Cardinalibus meditatum sit res ipsa ac euentus negocii tandem indicauit. Antequam huius causæ cognitionem suscepisset quia vulgus variis de tanta re sermonibus fluctuabatur, Rex Idibus Nouemb. ad Praesules, proceres, consiliariosq; suos huiusmodi orationem habuit.
units.tr: For Campeius had gone before the Cardinal ten years earlier on another embassy, as we have said. Now, however, sick and on foot, after long and tiresome journeys, he came to England, to judge this royal affair in accordance with Wolsey's opinion. Although the scent and suspicion of it had been present earlier, the matter itself and the outcome of the business at last revealed what the Pope and these Cardinals had been planning. Before he undertook the examination of this cause, since the common people were tossed about by various talk on so great a matter, the King on the Ides of November addressed the bishops, nobles and his counsellors with a speech of this kind.

units.la: HENRICI REGIS OCTAVI DE REPVDIANDA D. CATHARINA ORATIO.
units.tr: THE ORATION OF KING HENRY THE EIGHTH CONCERNING THE REPUDIATION OF QUEEN CATHARINE

units.la: ENERANDA & chara nobis Praesulum, procerum, atq; consiliariorum cohors, quos communis Reip. atq; Regni nostri administratio cura coniunxit, haud vos latet diuina Nos, puidentia vigintiiá fermeannis hanc nostram patriam tanta felicitate rexisse, vt & illa ab hostilibus incursionibus tuta semper interea fuerit, & nos in his bellis quæ suscepimus victores semper euasimus. Et quanquam in eo gloriari iure possimus, maiorem tranquillitatem, opes, ac honoris prioribus huc vsque ductis seculis nunquam subditis à maionbus parentibusque nostris Angliæ Regibus quàm à nobis prouenisse, ramen quando cum hac gloria in mente vnà venit ac concurrit mortis cogitatio, veremur ne nobis sine prole legitima decedentibus maiorem ex morte nostra patiamini calamitatem, quàm ex vita fructum ac emolumentum percepistis. Recens enim in quorundam vestrorum animis adhuc est illius cruenti temporis memoria, quod à Richardo 3. cum Aui nostri materni Edwardi 4. statum in controuersiam vocasset, eiusq; hæredes regno atq; vita priuasset, id tum ex historiis notæ sunt illæ diræ strages quæ à clarissimis Angliæ gentibus Eboracensi atq; Lancastrensi, dum inter se de Regno ac Imperio multis suis contenderent, populo eucnerunt.
units.tr: Dear and cherished company of prelates, nobles and counsellors, whom the common administration of our commonwealth and kingdom has joined together, it is not hidden from you that by divine providence we have ruled this our country for almost twenty years with such good fortune that it has always been safe from hostile incursions, and that we have always emerged victorious in the wars we have undertaken. Although we may rightly boast of this, that greater tranquillity, wealth and honour have come to our subjects from us than from our forefathers and parents, the kings of England, in all the centuries past, nevertheless, when the thought of death comes to mind and meets this glory, we fear that if we die without legitimate offspring you will suffer a greater calamity from our death than you have enjoyed benefit from our life. For the memory of that bloody time is still fresh in the minds of some of you, when Richard the Third, having challenged the position of our maternal grandfather Edward the Fourth, deprived his heirs of the kingdom and of their lives. From the histories it is well known what dreadful slaughters came upon the people when the most famous English houses of York and Lancaster contended with each other for the kingdom and the rule.

units.la: Ac illæ exiustis nuptiis inter Henricum septimum, & D. Elizabetham clarissimos nostros parentes contractis, in nobis inde legitima nata sobole sopitæ tandem desierunt: si vero (quod absit) Regalis ex nostris nuptiis stirps, quæ iure deinceps regnare possit non nascatur, hoc regnû aut ciuilibus atq; intestinis se vastabit tumultibus, aurin exterorum Dominationem atq; potestatê veniet. Nam quanquâ forma atq; venustate singulari, quæ magno nobis solatio fuit, filiam D. Mariam ex nobilissima fœmina D. Catharina procreauerimus, tamen à piis atq; eruditis Theologis nuper accepimus, quia eâ quæ Arturi fratris nostri coniunx ante fuerat vxorem duximus, nostras nuptias iure diuino esse vetitas, partumq; inde editum non posse censeri legitimum. Id quod eò vehementius nos angit & excruciat, quod cum superiori anno legatos ad conciliandas inter Aureliarû Ducem, & filiam nostram Mariam nupriasad Franciscum Gallorum Regem misissemus, à quodam eius consiliario responsum est.
units.tr: Those dissensions were at last quieted and ended when our most illustrious parents, Henry the Seventh and Lady Elizabeth, were lawfully united, and legitimate offspring was born to us. But if (God forbid) no royal stock should be born of our marriage that could rightfully reign after us, this kingdom will lay itself waste with civil and internal tumults, and will come under the dominion and power of foreigners. For although we have begotten, by Lady Catharine, a most noble woman, our daughter Lady Mary, who is a great comfort to us in her singular form and grace, we have lately learned from pious and learned theologians that, because we took as wife her who had formerly been the wife of our brother Arthur, our marriage is forbidden by divine law, and the child born of it cannot be regarded as legitimate. This troubles and torments us all the more because, when last year we sent envoys to arrange a marriage between the Duke of Orleans and our daughter Mary, with the King of the French, a certain counsellor of his replied: before any such marriage is discussed, it must first be inquired whether Mary is our legitimate daughter. For (he said) it is established that she was born of Catharine, the widow of his brother, a marriage which is forbidden by divine law.

units.la: Antequam de huiusmodi nuptiis agatur inquirendum esse prius, an Maria fuerit filia nostra legitima. Constat enim (inquit) quod ex D. Catharina fratris sui vidua, cuiusmodi nuptiæ iure diuino interdictæ sunt, suscepta est.
units.tr: Before any such marriage is discussed... (this is the same reply, which the counsellor gave, as reported above).

units.la: Quæ oratio quanto metu ac horrore animum nostrum turbauerit, quia res ipsa æternæ tam animi quàm corporis salutis periculum in se continet, & quam perplexis cogitationibus confectentiam occupat, vos quibus & capitis ant fortunæ, ac multo magis animarum iacturæ imminerent, remedium adhibere velitis, ignorare non posse arbitror. Hæc vna res (quod Deo teste & in Regis oraculo affirmamus) nos impulit, vt per legatos doctissimorum per totum orbem Christianû Theologorû sententias exquireremus, & Romani Pontificis Legatum verû atq; æquum indicium de tanta causa laturum, vt tranquilla deinceps & integra conscientia in coniugio licito viuere possimus, accerseremus. In quo fi ex sacris literis hoc quo viginti iam fere annis gauisi fumus, matrimonium iure diuino permissum esse manifeste liquidoque constabit, non modo ob conscientiæ tranquillitatem, verumetiam ob amabiles mores, virtutesque quibus Regina prædita & ornata est, nihil optatius, nihilque iucundius accidere nobis elt. Nam præterquam quod Regali atque nobili genere progoata est, tanta præterea comitate & obsequio coniugali, tum cæteris animi moribus, ornamentis quæ nobilitatem illustrant, omnes fœminas his viginti annis sic mihi anteire visa est, vt li a cooiugio liber esset ac solutus, si iure diuino liceret, hanc sibi prae cæteris fœminis stabili mihi iure ac fœdere matrimoniali coniungerem. Si vero in hoc iudicio matrimonium nostrum iure diuino prohibitum, ideoque ab initio nullum fritum que fuisse pronuociatur, infœlix hic meus casus multis lachrymis lugendus ac deplorandus erit, non modo quod a tam illustris & amabilis mulieris consuetudine ac cósortio diuertendum sit, sed multo magis quod specie ac similitudine veri coniugii decepti in amplexibus plusquam fornicarum tam multos annos triuimus, nulla legitima prognata nobis sobole, quæ nobis mortuis huius inclyti regni hæreditatem capeleat. Hæc nostræ curæ istæque solicitudines sunt, quæ mentem atque conscientiam nostram dies noctesque torquent & excruciant, quibus auferendis & profligandis remedium ex hac legatione & iudicio opportunum quærimus. Ideoque vos quoru virtuti atque fidei multum attribuimus, rogamus vt certum atque genuinum nostrum hac de re sensum quem ex nostro iam sermone percepistis, populo declaretis, eumque excitetis vt nobiscum vna oraret, vt ad côscientiæ nostræ pacem atque tranquillitatem in hoc iudicio veritas multis iam annis tenebris inuoluta tandem patefiat.
units.tr: How greatly this speech has disturbed our mind with fear and horror, since the matter itself contains a danger to the eternal salvation of both soul and body, and how perplexing the thoughts are that occupy our conscience, I think you cannot be ignorant, you to whom the loss of life and fortune, and much more of souls, is threatened, if you wish to apply a remedy. This one matter (as we affirm before God and on the word of the King) has driven us to seek, through envoys, the opinions of the most learned theologians throughout the Christian world, and to summon the legate of the Roman Pontiff, who will give a true and just judgement in so great a cause, so that we may live thereafter in a licit marriage with a calm and untroubled conscience. If in this, it is clearly and plainly established from the holy Scriptures that the marriage, which we have enjoyed for almost twenty years, was permitted by divine law, nothing could happen to us that is more desirable or more pleasant, not only for the tranquillity of our conscience, but also for the lovable character and virtues with which the Queen is endowed and adorned. For besides that she is born of royal and noble stock, she has in addition, through such courtesy and wifely obedience, and through her other moral qualities and the graces that adorn nobility, seemed in these twenty years to surpass all women, so that, were I free and released from marriage, if divine law allowed it, I would join her to myself before all other women in a firm marital right and covenant. But if in this judgement our marriage is declared forbidden by divine law, and therefore null and void from the beginning, my unhappy case will have to be mourned and lamented with many tears, not only because I must turn away from the company and society of so illustrious and lovable a woman, but much more because, deceived by the appearance and likeness of a true marriage, we have spent so many years in embraces worse than those of fornicators, with no legitimate offspring born to us who could take up the inheritance of this famous kingdom after our death. These are the cares and anxieties that torment and rack our mind and conscience day and night, and for removing and dispelling them we seek a fitting remedy through this embassy and judgement. Therefore, we ask you, to whose virtue and faith we attribute much, to declare to the people the sure and genuine opinion we hold on this matter, which you have already perceived from our speech, and to stir them up to pray with us, so that in this judgement the truth, long wrapped in darkness, may at last be brought to light for the peace and tranquillity of our conscience.

units.la: Hæc cum Rex dixisset magnum ob rei magnitudinem silentium omnes diu tenuit.
units.tr: When the King had said these things, a great silence held all for a long time, because of the greatness of the matter.

units.la: At Legati Regnam adeunt, eiique legationis suæ causam exponunt, quæ tam aduerso & improuiso nuncio attonita atque mœsta, valdeque se mirari ait cur de huiusmodi nuptiis, quæ viginti pene annis omni cōtrouersia carerent, iam subito ambigeretur: incredibile enim esse, vt Inclytissimi Reges Henricus septimus, & Ferdinandus, tum Pontifex Romanus cum prudentissimorum consiliatorum multitudine in re tam clara tantopere hallucinarentur. Ferdinandum autem suum patrem magnis sumptibus à curia Romana dispensationem obtinuisse, vt quanquam Principi Arturo Henrici Regis fratriantea nupta, ab eo, cognita fuerit, liceret tamen cum Henrico Rege matrimonium copulare. Totum autem huius motæ controuersiæ crimen in Wolceum Cardinalem conferebat, quod is in Cæsarem hostiliter affectus, & à Regina propter intolerabilem arrogantiam, luxumque ac libidines in quibus turpiter volutabat, reprehensus esset, has in fœminam tragedias excitaret. Wolceus autem sese leuiter excusauit. & in Gallum omnem facti inuidiam transtulit, se tantum iudicem à Pontifice Romano cum Cardinali Campeio datum asseruit, quod susceptum munus summa æquitate præstiturum promisit. Paulo post cum Legati iudicium atque causæ cognitionem ingrederentur, Warhamus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus cum iamititutam de re tanta litem cerneret, ex Cantebrigiensi, & Oxoniensi Academiis celebriores Theologos & iuris Pontificii atque Cæsarii peritiores accersiuit, qui in eidibus suis Lamethanis indies de hac causa tractabant & differebant. Rex cum animaduerteret quàm grauiter & molestè Regina huius iudicii exercitationem ferebat, permisit ei ne iniuria sibi fieri putaret, vt doctissimos probatissimosque viros eligeret quorum consilio in causa ventilatione veretur. Illa Warhamum Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum, Nicolaum West Elienlem Episcopum Iurisperitos, tum Iohannem Fisher Roffensem, ac Henricum Standishe Asslauensem Episcopos Theologiæ professores elegit. Qui taotum causæ patrocinium præstiterunt, quatorum iure ac scientia potuissent. His deinde legatis atq; Cardinalibus pro tribunali sedeutibus, & iudicio inchoato, Rex & Regina præconis voce ad tribunal vocati sunt. Ille per procuratores comparuit: hæc illis quatuor Episcopis quos supra diximus, aliisq; cōsiliariis, rum illustrium fœminarum multitudine stipata curiam ingressa est, & appellatione ad Papam interpositaCardinalium illorum iudicium recusauit, atque recessit. Legati nihilominus in causa progressi sunt. Sed cum variis dilationibus Rex iudicium procrastinari cerneret, venit ipse cum Regina, & instabat Legatis, vt huius tanti negocii ambiguitatem quæ sola tanta anxietate atq; solicitudine cōscientiā mentemq; suā turbat, vt nihil præterea de publicis ac priuatis reb. statuere aut cogitare penè posset, iudicii definitione dissoluit, Iudicii exitus cuiusuis ac euentu, siue ab hoc cōiugio discedēdū sit(q; minimè vellet) siue in eo manēdū (q; si saluo iure diuino liceat maxime cupiat).
units.tr: Then the legates went to the Queen and explained to her the reason for their embassy. She, astonished and saddened by so adverse and unexpected a message, said she was greatly surprised why such a marriage, which for almost twenty years had been free of all controversy, should now suddenly be called into doubt. For it was incredible that the most illustrious kings Henry the Seventh and Ferdinand, and the Roman Pontiff, with a multitude of the most prudent counsellors, should have been so greatly mistaken in a matter so clear. She said that her father Ferdinand had obtained from the Roman court a dispensation with great expense, so that, although she had been married earlier to Prince Arthur, brother of King Henry, it was nevertheless lawful to join herself in marriage with King Henry. She laid the whole blame for this stirred-up controversy on Cardinal Wolsey, who, being hostile to the Emperor and having been rebuked by the Queen for his intolerable arrogance, his luxury and the lusts in which he shamefully wallowed, was stirring up these tragedies against a woman. Wolsey, however, excused himself lightly, and shifted all the odium of the affair onto the Frenchman. He asserted that he had been given as judge, together with Cardinal Campeggio, only by the Roman Pontiff, and promised that he would discharge the office he had undertaken with the greatest fairness. Shortly afterwards, when the legates entered upon the judgement and the examination of the case, Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury, seeing that so great a dispute had already been started, summoned from the universities of Cambridge and Oxford the more famous theologians and those more skilled in pontifical and imperial law, who day after day discussed and debated this case in his house at Lambeth. The King, perceiving how gravely and grievously the Queen bore the conduct of this judgement, allowed her, so that she might not think herself wronged, to choose the most learned and most approved men, whose counsel she wished to use in the discussion of the case. She chose Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury, Nicholas West, Bishop of Ely, learned in law, and then John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, and Henry Standish, Bishop of St Asaph, professors of theology. These men gave their support to the cause only as far as their right and learning could have done. Then, with the legates and cardinals sitting on the tribunal, and the judgement begun, the King and the Queen were summoned to the tribunal by the voice of a herald. The King appeared through procurators; the Queen entered the court attended by the four bishops we have mentioned and by other counsellors, and with a crowd of illustrious women, and, having lodged an appeal to the Pope, she rejected the judgement of those cardinals and withdrew. Nevertheless the legates proceeded with the case. But when the King saw the judgement being put off by various delays, he himself came with the Queen and pressed the legates to resolve, by a definitive judgement, this uncertainty of so great a matter, which alone troubles his conscience and mind with such anxiety and concern that he could hardly decide or think about anything else, public or private. Whatever the outcome of the judgement, whether he must depart from this marriage (which he would by no means wish) or remain in it (which he most desires, if it is lawful by divine law),

units.la: An. 1529. piat) quòmodo cùmque ires reciderit, baud fore sibi graue, si matura sententia, pnuciata animus tu ancipiti cura liberetur. Eos quib. est cōstrictū & impeditus mœrorib. animo de sua causa facilius colligere & existimare posse, proinde a legatis se petere, ut amputatis confusetis iudiciorum cunctationibus atque tarditatibus, cum tantam acceperint a Papa potestatem, ut exquisitis atque perpensis tam Theologorum quàm Iurisperitorum sententiis ocyus de causa pronuncient. Ac huiusmodi habito sermone Rex discessit, Regina nec verbum quidem Legatis faciens Regem sequuta est. Sed à Legatis reuocata cum ab ea quæreretur, utrum appellationem deferre, & causam Legatorum iudicio permittere vellet, per Procuratorem respondit se staturam appellationi. His gestis discepiationes indies coram Legatis inter Theologos & Iurisperitos de hac quæstione habitæ sunt. ducere uxorem cognitam a fratre decedente sine prole sit prohibitio seu diuinum indispensabilis à Papa. Nam quòd ab Arturo Principe cognita fuerit, etsi id iam Regina negaret, tamen Regis procuratores, & aduocati tribus rationibus euicerunt. 1. Quòd nuptiis inter eam & Principem in Ecclesia Paulina (sicut diximus) celebratis, sequenti nocte concubuerit, & princeps summo mane potum petiit, eoque profundius exhausto, cum ab eo quidam scicitaretur, cur iā solito vehementius sitiisset, respondit quia ea nocte ex Anglia in calidam & feruentem Hispaniarum regionem quæ sitim suam multū auxit profectus esset. Quo indicauit se D. Catharinam Hispanā carnali congressu cognouisse. Deinde Arturo paucis postea mensibus vita functo, Henricus tu Dux Ebor acensis Principaru Wallię, quæ fratre sine liberis decedente ad eum peruenit, vno mense abstinuit, quod D. Catharina secum ex principe grauidam suspicabatur, quæ suspicio nisi ex congressu nasci non potuisset. Postremò quod cum ante nuptias quas cum Henrico Rege contraxisset, pater eius Ferdinadus à Papa Iulio dispensationē impetrasset ut liceret ei ducere fratris sui viduam, tamen quia in ea dispensatione de Carnali copulatione mentio nulla facta fuisset, Regina alteram ab eodem Papa procurauit, in qua haec verba inserta fuerunt. Vxorem à fratre suo prius habitam, vel forsan cognitam. Ex quo suo proptio ad Papam suggestu liquet, eam congressum confiteri, nec ad rem pertinet quod vocem concessionis tam clare vim minuentem Forsan inseruit, cum ipsa quæ hoc suggessit incerta aut dubia eius rei esse non potuit. His probationibus huius facti controuersia, cognita scilicet a priori nec ne fuerit, sublata est. Cum vero ad iuris explicationem ventum esset, utriusque tam Regis quam Reginæ Theologi aduocati illicitas esse nuptias dixerunt, nec posse authoritate aut dispensatione Papali contra ius diuinum conciliari. His iuris facti&q; definitionibus cum expedita causa & ad sententiæ calculum parata atque perdūcta esset, Rexque litis finem ac iudicium sine mora expectarer, Legati confusi ac incerti hærebant tanquam in dilemmate. Prospiciebant enim si pronunciarent Romanam curiam contra ius diuinum (quo minimè facere posset) dispensasse, omnem eius authoritatem eneruarent, sin vero Romanam curiam id remittere ac relaxare posse dicerent, quod ius diuinum posuit atque sanxit, iam Theologos quorum sententiis damnata & explosa fuit ea opinio, timebant. Itaque in hac anciptiti deliberatione dum vtrinq; imminere Romanæ curiæ decus & existimationis iactuam cernerent perplexi & multò quàm antea, vt Terentiani aduocati, incertiores multis cautelis & argutiis litem differebant. Wolceo etiam alia huius dilationis causa fuit, quòd cum is potentia sua anteactis fretus existimauit se Regem ad quascunq; vellet nuptias flectere & allicere posse, videbat his nuptiis dissolutis Regem leĉtissimam foeminam D. Annam Bulley esse ducturum, quæ in Euangelii, & à Romana superstitione, & fastu atq; elatione Cleri, animo toto abhorrebat. Tum multis indiciis indies colligebat, continua procerum interpellatione quibus inuisa & intolerabilis fuit eius libido ac potentia Regis à se animum esse alienioretn. Interea dum haec in Anglia gererentur, Romæ ad papam Regis Legati fuerunt Stephanus Gardiner Legum Doctor, & Franciscus Brian miles. Et Cæsar paulò ante in Italiam venerat, ac Clemens mentem Papam à captiuitate liberauerat, perlatiq; sunt in Anglia rumores Papam aut iam obiisse, aut huiusmodi morbo periclitari, vt euadere mortem non posset, occupauitq; mox Wolceum Papatus ambiendi cupiditas. Itaque Regi sūasit non alia ratione commodius hoc de quo tractabat diuortium procurari posse, quam si is eligeretur Papa, quod promissis se id illico diremptum. Facilem autem esse rem sua & Gallorum Regis gratia Paparu potiri, quòd Cæsar iam ob direptam nuper Romam odio Cardinalibus esset; atq; Romanæ curiæ. Rex cum ad suam etiam magnificentiam Illustrandam hoc multum valiturum existimauit, annuit Wolceo vt suis etiam sumptibus Legatis Romæ amplissimā Dd 4 daretur hoc negocium procurandi potestas. Ad quos etiam tam à Rege quàm à Cardinale literæ dantur, vt omnes Cardinales siue Cæsarianæ siue Gallicæ factionis fuerint, donis, pollicitationibus, blanditiis, minis, omniq; versutiæ genere ad Wolceū Papā eligendum solicitarent. Summa suasionis fuit, vt nisi Regi in Wolceo eligendo morē gerérent, verè dum esse ne cum Romana curia auersum iam & hostem sensisset Cæsarem, si is vna hac de causa desistat, ruituram funditus Romam. Quæ tanta ex miserrima ambitione prouenit Wolceo cæcitas, vt Regem iam de euertenda Romana potentia doceret. Nec interea de sua ruina quæ mox adfuit, prudentius prospicere potuit. Idem tanta tum essertebatur licentia, vt & Cœnobia atque Monasteria, quæ sanctissima illis cæcis temporibus loca putabantur, quæ quoniam aliquo modo violari vulgus summum nepbas existimauit, cie&is Monachis diruit atque profanauit, eoruinq; possessiones atq; prædia ad extruendum magnificentissimum Oxonii Collegium conuertit. Horum tum Cœnobiorum demolitiones vito solertissimo D. Cromwell qui in legatina Cardinalis curia, causisq; ab ea ad Papam per appellatianem translatis multorum negocia procurauit, Romamque frequenter ire ac redire consueuit, ac in itinere dum Germaniam transiret accepit ea quæ a Lutheranis prædicata fuerunt, cömissesunt. Vix enim eo tepore fuit quisquam qui summam esse religionem non putauit, Cœnobiorum bona attingere. At Cardinalis audacia etiam professæ religionis ripas fregit, ac ad tadius Papalis agri calamitatem & inundationem erupit. Cromwellus autem cum de Fratrum atque Monachorum illiciti sociatatibus collegisque, tum de turpi ac desidiosa vita à Germanis accepisset, ipseque Romæ illam opprimendi potestate pro Cardinali tum suo hero atq; Domino procurauerat, subiit id muneris libens nullo conscientiæ stimulo impeditus, ac demum eiecta (vt dicemus) pontificia potestate de cæteris omnibus demoliendis author ac suasor fuit.
units.tr: An. 1529. However the matter turned out, he said, it would not be a burden to him if a decision were pronounced soon and his mind were freed from this uncertain anxiety. Those who are constrained and hindered by sorrow in their own cause can judge it more easily from the outside. Accordingly he asked the legates to cut away the confused delays and tardiness of the courts, since they had received such great power from the Pope, and to pronounce the sentence more quickly after carefully weighing the opinions of theologians and jurists alike. With this speech the King departed. The Queen, saying not a word to the legates, followed the King. But when she was recalled by the legates and asked whether she wished to appeal and to leave the cause to the judgment of the legates, she replied through her proctor that she would stand by her appeal. After these things, disputations on this question were held daily before the legates among theologians and jurists: whether marrying a wife who had been known by a brother who died without offspring is a prohibition of divine law, or something the Pope can dispense with. That she had been known by Prince Arthur, although the Queen now denied it, was nevertheless proved by the King's proctors and advocates on three grounds. (1) After the marriage between her and the Prince had been celebrated in St Paul's (as we have said), she lay with him the same night, and the Prince asked for a drink early in the morning; when he had drained it deeply, and someone asked him why he had been thirstier than usual, he answered that he had set out that night from England into the hot and fiery region of Spain, which had greatly increased his thirst. By this he indicated that he had known Lady Catherine of Spain carnally. (2) Then, a few months after Arthur died, Henry, Duke of York, who came to the title of Prince of Wales when his brother died without children, abstained for a month, because he suspected that Lady Catherine had been made pregnant by the Prince; and this suspicion could not have arisen except from intercourse. (3) Finally, before the marriage she contracted with King Henry, her father Ferdinand had obtained a dispensation from Pope Julius allowing her to marry her late brother's widow. But since that dispensation made no mention of carnal union, the Queen procured another from the same Pope, in which these words were inserted: having first had as wife, or perhaps known, her brother's wife. From this, her own petition to the Pope makes it plain that she admits intercourse. Nor does it matter that the word perhaps was inserted, which so clearly weakens the concession, since she who proposed this could not be uncertain or doubtful about the fact. By these proofs the controversy over the fact, namely whether she had been known beforehand or not, was settled. But when it came to the explanation of the law, the theologians and advocates of both the King and the Queen said that the marriage was unlawful, and that it could not be reconciled with divine law by papal authority or dispensation. When the cause had been thus cleared of its questions of law and fact, and brought ready and prepared to the reckoning of the sentence, and the King was awaiting the end of the suit and the judgment without delay, the legates hung back, confused and uncertain, as if on the horns of a dilemma. For they foresaw that if they pronounced that the Roman court had granted a dispensation against divine law (which it could not do), they would destroy all its authority; but if they said that the Roman court could remit and relax what divine law had established and ratified, they feared the theologians, by whose opinions that view had been condemned and rejected. Therefore, in this two-sided deliberation, while they saw the dignity and reputation of the Roman court threatened on either side, they were perplexed, and, more uncertain than before, like the advocates in Terence, they put off the suit with many cautions and quibbles. There was also another reason for this delay on Wolsey's part. Relying on his past power, he thought he could bend and entice the King to whatever marriage he wished. He saw that once this marriage was dissolved, the King would take as wife the most charming lady, Anne Boleyn, who with her whole heart abhorred the Roman superstition and the pride and haughtiness of the clergy and was devoted to the Gospel. Moreover, from many signs he gathered day by day that the King was becoming estranged from him, through the constant complaints of the nobles, by whom his lust and power had become hateful and intolerable. Meanwhile, while these things were being done in England, the King's legates, Stephen Gardiner, Doctor of Laws, and Sir Francis Bryan, were at Rome with the Pope. Caesar had come into Italy a little earlier, and Clement had freed the Pope from captivity, but rumours spread in England that the Pope had either already died or was in such danger from this illness that he could not escape death. Soon the desire to seek the papacy seized Wolsey. Therefore he persuaded the King that this divorce he was dealing with could be arranged more conveniently in no other way than by his being elected Pope, since with his promises he could bring it to an immediate end. He said it would be an easy matter for him to gain the papacy with the favour of Caesar and the King of France, since Caesar was now hated by the cardinals because of the recent sack of Rome, and so was the Roman court. The King, thinking this would greatly contribute to his own magnificence too, agreed that Wolsey should be given full power to arrange this business at Rome, at his own expense, as well as the legates. Letters were given to them both by the King and by the Cardinal, so that all the cardinals, whether of Caesar's or of the French party, might be urged by gifts, promises, flatteries, threats and every kind of trickery to elect Wolsey Pope. The sum of their persuasion was that unless they complied with the King's wish to elect Wolsey, Rome would surely be utterly ruined, since Caesar, whom they had already perceived as turned away from and hostile to the Roman court, would desert it for this one reason alone. Such was the blindness that the most wretched ambition brought upon Wolsey, that he was already teaching the King how to overthrow Roman power. Nor in the meantime could he foresee more wisely his own ruin, which soon came upon him. At that time he was so given over to license that he destroyed and profaned the convents and monasteries, which in those blind times were thought most holy places, and expelled the monks, thinking it the greatest wickedness for the common people to be harmed in any way; and he turned their possessions and estates to the building of the most magnificent college at Oxford. The demolition of these convents was carried out under the cunning guidance of Master Cromwell, who had served in the Cardinal's legatine court, had transacted much business for many people in causes transferred from it to the Pope by appeal, and was accustomed to go to and fro between Rome and England frequently. On the journey, while passing through Germany, he heard what the Lutherans preached and taught. For at that time there was hardly anyone who did not think it a great offence to touch the goods of convents. But the Cardinal's audacity broke through even the banks of the religion he professed, and burst out to the ruin and flooding of the whole Papal field. Cromwell, indeed, having heard from the Germans of the unlawful associations and gatherings of friars and monks, and of their foul and idle life, and having himself procured, at Rome, the power to suppress them on behalf of the Cardinal, his then lord and master, undertook this office gladly, unhindered by any sting of conscience; and at last, when papal power had been cast out (as we shall relate), he became the author and promoter of the demolition of all the rest.

units.la: Atque hæc de Cardinali ad suprémum mapicem culmenq; elato, nunc de eodem turpiter ac ingeniose deiecto. Romaque cum eo simul collapsa dicendum est. Conatus eius de adipiscendo papatu planè sultus ac inanis fuit. Nam & Clemens adhuc vixit, & Cæsaris in Italia splentia omnes Cardinales recenti calamitate affliotos tenuit, ac Wolcei inimici sui ambitionem fecit irritam. Itaque cum Wolceus Cardinalis sensisset interea, dum frustra tantis gerendis honoribus studuisset, quantas de his nuptiis, inter Cæsarem atque Regem turbas concitauerat, tum veritus ne secutura cum D. Anna Bulleyn nuptiæ ub Euangelium ab illa receptum, sibi atq; Romæ perniciosissimæ forent, omnè dedit operam de reuocandis his quæ etsi iure niterentur, istamen non religione sed ampitione gessisset.
units.tr: So much for the Cardinal raised to the highest peak and summit of honour; now must be told how he was shamefully and cleverly cast down, and how Rome collapsed together with him. His attempt to obtain the papacy turned out wholly foolish and vain. For Clement still lived, and Caesar's presence in Italy kept all the cardinals, who were afflicted by the recent calamity, under his power, and so he made the ambition of his enemy Wolsey futile. And so the Cardinal, having perceived, while he had vainly striven to win such honours, how great the disturbances he had stirred up between Caesar and the King over this marriage, and fearing that the marriage with Anne Boleyn, and the Gospel received by her, would follow and prove most destructive both to himself and to Rome, he took pains to recall those measures which, though supported by law, he had undertaken not from religion but from ambition.

units.la: Quidam ferunt cum dum honoribus inhiaret, ariolos de repellendis his qui suæ ambitioni atque cupiditati obstarent consuluisse, atque accepisse ibi a feemina quæ e-cū apud Regem ratio superaret esse cauendū. Iscam D. Catharinam fore ratus, turbatis nuptiis eam a Rege amore studuit, & iam inter mulieres angu stias constitutus, dum vtrisque pariter inuisus esset, quò se verteret, aut discrimen, in quod suam Romanamque potentiam coniecerat, effugeret, ignoraut. Nam Rex tantam moram & procrastinationem in causa iam explorata atque cogita a Legatis sien haud facile toleraut. Itaque cum accepisset Cæsarem atq; Papam Bononiæ in Italia vnà fuisse, D.Thomam Bulleyn Wiltoniæ Comitē, D.Stokesley & D. Lee Legū Doctores ad eos legauit, a Papa petituros vt suos in Anglia Legatos ad ferendam de illo matrimonio ex iure diuino sententiam sine mora incitaret, a Cæsare verò vt is de hac causa iuxta Theologorum sententias diiudicari pateretur. Cæsar id se æquissime laturum respondit. At Papa permiuit ne separato coniugio cõmuoeretur Cæsaris animus, & Romanæ curiæ in tribuendis dispensationibus facultas, si ratione iuris diuini extenuaretur, sorderet. Itaque cum prolixiores ad impediendum Regis conatum dilationes in animo haberet, respondit, se simulatq; Romam venisset, causam suscepturum, & ex vtraque parte auditis Iurisperitorum & Theologorum sententiis secundùm æquum atque rectum pronunciaturum. Reuersus cum hoc responso Legatis animaduertit Rex, quibus tecbnis Papa suiq; Cardinales eum ludificarent.
units.tr: Some report that while Wolsey was hungry for honours, he consulted fortune-tellers about removing those who stood in the way of his ambition and desire, and that they told him he must beware of a woman who would hold more sway with the King than he did. Thinking this woman was Queen Catherine, he tried to turn the King's affection away from her by stirring up the marriage. Caught between the two women, hated by both, he did not know which way to turn or how to escape the danger into which he had thrown his own and Rome's power. For the King could not easily bear such delay and procrastination in a cause that had already been examined and considered by the legates. So when he learned that Caesar and the Pope were together at Bologna in Italy, he sent Sir Thomas Boleyn, Earl of Wiltshire, and Dr Stokesley and Dr Lee, doctors of law, to them. They were to ask the Pope to urge his legates in England without delay to pronounce sentence on that marriage by divine law, and to ask Caesar to allow the matter to be decided according to the opinions of the theologians. Caesar replied that he would take this most fairly. But the Pope held back, lest the Emperor's mind be stirred by the separation of the marriage, and lest the Roman court's power to grant dispensations be belittled if it were weakened by an argument from divine law. So, intending to frustrate the King's attempt with lengthy delays, he replied that as soon as he came to Rome he would take up the case, hear the opinions of lawyers and theologians from both sides, and pronounce judgment according to what was fair and right. When the legates returned with this answer, the King saw by what tricks the Pope and his cardinals were making a fool of him.

units.la: Quorum contumelias & ludibria cum iam amplius ferre noluit, duobus clarissimis Regni sui proceribus, Norfolciæ, arq; Sufforciæ Ducibus conquestus est, dixitq; quideos facere vellet. Illi Legatos adeunt, de his dilationibus expostulant, iudicium instantet requirunt, Regi perinde fore in vtram partem pronunciet, ita enim eximi & auferri ex animo conscientiæ stimulos quibus affligitur. His latina & facunda oratione respondit Campeius Cardinalis. Nihil sibi fuisse prius quàm Regeni his quibus de coniugio perplexus esset curis liberare, sed hoc mense Iulio transacto neque iure Canonico, nec Ro-manæ
units.tr: When he would no longer put up with their insults and mockeries, he complained to two most distinguished nobles of his kingdom, the Dukes of Norfolk and Suffolk, and said what he wished them to do. They went to the legates, complained about these delays, and demanded that judgment be given without delay, since it would make no difference to the King which way it was pronounced; for thus the goads of conscience by which he was tormented would be removed from his mind. Cardinal Campeggio answered them in Latin, and eloquently. He said that nothing had been more important to him than to free the King from the anxieties by which he was troubled about his marriage; but, the month of July being over, neither canon law nor the custom of the Roman court allowed them to judge controverted causes in the two months that followed, the season of harvest and vintage, before the Ides of October; and if they did otherwise, the whole judgment would have to be considered void and null in law.

units.la: An.1530 manæ curiæ consuetudine licere duobus proximis mensibus instanti messisatque vindemiarum tempore, ante idus Octobris de causis controuersis iudicare, quòd si aliter facerêt, iudicium totum irritum ac iuris viribus cassum esse censendum. At vero duces hoc commento Legatos effugere passi non sunt, Restabat enim adhuc duo dies Iulii ante Calendas Augusti, in quibus quoniam satis deliberatum fuit, petierunt ut causam sententia definirent, ac Legati nō amplius se actu-ros ante Idus Octobris afferebat. Id quod Duces atq; proceres, qui Regem tam indignis modis a Cardinalibus tractari aegre ferebant, ad obscura murmura coegit. Inter quos Carolus Suffolcię Dux manu mensam fortiter discedens percussit, & iureiurando exclamauit, verum esse quod antiquitus dici cōsue10 uit. Nunquam boni quicquam a Romanis Cardinalibus in Anglos esse profectum. Hæc Ducum atq; proceres non obscura indignatio & discessio Cardinales ilupore affecit, qui prorogato ad Idus Octobr. iudicio curiam dimiserunt. Rex etsi ob hanc iniuriam motus & concitatus fuit, tamen placauit vltro ac prudenter spiritus, Idusq; Octob. quos Campeius ad definiendū in causa staturit, expectare decreuit, ne vllius excusationis praetextus Legatis superesset. Conclusi itaque his difficultatibus & angustiis legati omnem ingenii fraudem atq; ius in exploranda cuasione ponebant. Wolceus a quibusdam fidedignis phibetur, cū hanc causam ia tanto discrimine verari intellexerat, secretas de desile adClementem Papam literas, vt quantū posit istis separandis nuptiis impedimento esset, omnee alteris nuptiis futuru Romæ exitiale quantū posit auerteret. In quibus etiā sua 20 temeritatem fassus est, quòd cum contra Cæsaris vim ac potentia de Roma tuenda prospicere atque cauere vellet, eam his turbandis nuptiis ingrauiora periculæ coniecit. Hæ autem vt ferunt literæ a generoso quodam Anglo iuuene, qui non tam libidine quàm consilio scortum quoddam elegans Papæ consuetudine sua tenuit, exploratæ & ad Regem misse sunt.
units.tr: 1530. But the Dukes did not allow the legates to escape by this device. There were still two days of July left, before the Kalends of August; and since these had been fully deliberated, they asked that the cause be settled by sentence, while the legates affirmed that they would act no further before the Ides of October. This so provoked the Dukes and nobles, who were angry that the King was being treated in such unworthy ways by the cardinals, that they broke into low murmurs. Among them, Charles Brandon, Duke of Suffolk, struck the table hard with his fist as he stood up to leave, and swore an oath that the old saying was true: nothing good had ever come from Roman cardinals to the English. The open indignation and departure of the Dukes and nobles struck the cardinals dumb, and they dismissed the court, the judgment having been put off until the Ides of October. The King, though moved and stirred by this insult, nevertheless calmed his spirit of his own accord and wisely, and decided to wait for the Ides of October, which Campeggio had fixed for giving judgment in the case, so that the legates should have no pretext for any excuse. Hemmed in by these difficulties and straits, the legates then put all their cleverness and legal chicanery into searching out a way through the case. Wolsey, when he learned from some trustworthy men that the cause was in such great danger, sent secret letters to Pope Clement, so that, as far as he could, he might hinder the separation of the marriage and turn away as far as possible whatever the other marriage would bring that was ruinous to Rome. In these letters he even confessed his own rashness: he had wanted to look ahead and guard Rome against the power and might of Caesar, yet by disturbing this marriage he had brought greater dangers upon it. These letters, as they report, were intercepted and sent to the King by a certain noble young Englishman, who had kept in close acquaintance with a certain elegant courtesan of the Pope's, not so much from lust as from policy.

units.la: Quibus acceptis & cognita iam Wolcei Cardinalis, dum suis tantum commodis & ambitione omnia metiretur, in vtramq; partem perfidia, Rex Cardinali insci-o legatos suos discedere Roma & in Angliam reuerti iussit. Verum vtcunq; res fit, certum est, cum Rex pro certo haberet Campeium Cardinalem vtq; ad huius matrimonialis cō- trouersiæ finem & exitum in Anglia manuturum, eum paulò post quam iudicium (vt di30 ximus) in Idus Octob. reiudicum ac dilarum fuerit, Clementis Papæ literis Romam subitò fuisse reuocatum.
units.tr: When these letters had been received, and Cardinal Wolsey's treachery was now known, since he measured everything only by his own advantage and ambition, the King, without the cardinal's knowledge, ordered his legates to leave Rome and return to England. However that may be, it is certain that the King was firmly persuaded that Cardinal Campeggio would be the one to bring the controversy over this marriage to an end in England; but shortly after the judgment had been put off and deferred until the Ides of October, as we have said, Campeggio was suddenly recalled to Rome by a letter from Pope Clement.

units.la: Quod cum Regi manifestum dedisset indicium atque signum totius impietatis & impostuæ Papalis, quæ omnia iura diuina & humana libidine sua labefactat, miranda diuini fati potentia excitatus ad tantam improbitatem vlciscendam, superbiamque proftrandam se accinxit.
units.tr: When this gave the King clear evidence and a sign of all the impiety and deceit of the Papacy, which overturns all divine and human laws by its own lust, he was roused by the wonderful power of divine fate and girded himself to avenge such wickedness and to cast down its pride.

units.la: Ac primùm simulatque Campeius Cardinalis discessisset, Rex Wolceum Cardinalem quem ad tantos honores extulerat, post quam nihil in co recte atq; integræ fidei ne erga se quidem esse perspexerat, nec hominem criminosem sed laruam ex dolis, impo-sturis, rapinis, libidine & ambitione contextam ac fabricatam cognouerat, toto animo respuit, & Aula 40 conspectuq; suo prohibuit. Tum cæterorum criminationes, postquam Regis gratia huiusmodi merito caruit, eum totannis tantaq; authoritate in omni fraudé & iniuriarū genere versatū ita opprimebant, vt summū sibi adesse exitium existimauit. Atq; sanè initū est cum qui tot annis tantam tibi firmassèt potentiam, tam paruo momento ranquam oculi ictu concidisse. Verū ei qui ambitione Papam, superbia Cæsarē, dissimulatione Re- gem, fastu proceres, raptinis tenues, iniuriis potentiores, bonosq; omnes impleta a se alienasset, haud facile fuit tamdin consistere. Sed huius quidem repudii rumores no modo Angliam sed Christianum pene orbem totum ita compleuerunt, vt Regiam necc sefuit, quitot annis Cardinalis fraudè & perfidia in varia eaque incerta discrimina venerat, Remp. ipsum capescere, nec alteri amplius vt Cardinali fecit gubernandam comit50 tere. Ac quoniā maximè se conflictari grauariq; conscientia de hoc aricipiti matrimonio sen serat, de eo celeriter curandum existimauit. Campeio Cardinali tum Romam prosectō mense Augusto, quo Legati Papales metiti sunt non licere de causis matrimonialibus agere, Rex vtanimū ab his curis aliquādiu relaxaret, cōsiliumq; interea cum his quos ādos habuit secreto caperet, cum Norfolciæ, Suffolcię, Ducibus, aliisq; suis necessariis Walthamiā oppidū Londini 12. milliaribus distantū venarū aduenit. In quo itinere altam mentis aegritudinē, & in Wolceum Cardinalē indignationem Stephano Gardinero Secretario suo, qui (vt paulò ante diximus) Romæ fuit Regis Legatus, & D. Foxo eleemosinario indicauit, eosq; rogauit vt sedulò ac diligenter inuestigarent quid ad expediendā hanc litem ère maximè sit. Quorum suasu Rex tum nouus ad Papam destinare Legatos commissionem q; ita conceptam, vt ne quid deinceps retardare causam posset procurare pene decreuit. Sed forte (vt aiunt) fortuna, cum hi Doctores in aedibus cuiusdam generosi viri M. Cresley diuertissent, tunc aderat doctrina & pietate insignis quidam Theologus Collegii Iesu Cantabrigiae socius Tho. Cranmerus, qui duos M. Cresley liberos literis instituit, & peste eum Cantebrigiae feruente vna cum dictis adolescentulis eam aestatem Walthamiae triuerat. Quem etsi humili iam tennique vitae conditione contentum, tamen doctrina & veteri Cantabrigiae familiaritate notum cum Gardinerus atque Foxus consepexissent, renouata, vt solet, familiaritate suis expulsis adhibebant, eumq; de Regis causa consulebant.
