Sed praeter doctrinam singularem erat in Cranmero mirifica quaedam grauitas & modestia, vt de rebus magnis non facile nisi meditata sententia proferret, & quo magis cum grauitate diceret, ac fucum iactantiamque vitaret, eo probabiliorem orationem suam effecit. Itaq; grauate ille primo, sed cum a Regis consiliariis vrgeretur quibus sibi parendum putauit, Ego, inquit, de retanta sine metitudine atq; studio haud ita multo adducere vobis possum, sed mea sententia quid a Rex ita mente & conscientia turbetur, nihil neq; causae diuturniorem moram adferre, nec turbatio afflictio atq; conscientiae grauiores dolorum aestus innrere possit, quam Romanarum litium dilationes & anfractus, quibus qui tenentur laqueis vix vnquam se expedire. Proinde satius esse duco, vt omissis forensibus ventilationibus atq; moris, in quibus tanta animi aegritudine Rex iam nimiu diu iactatus sit, tam in nostris quam in externis Academiis exquirantur de hac causa, quae diuino non humano iure definiri potest, Theologorum sententiae. Et si Theologi vel veritas vel licitas esse has nuptias iure diuino pronunciente ac consentiant, Rex non amplius Romanam curiam petat, sed in sua Regione ac prouincia sententiam ferri ac pronunciari iuxta Theologos faciat. Itaque mente hilaris, ac conscientia securus Regiam atq; hac Rep. dignam vitam in legitimo matrimonio quod nobis subditis optandum est, transfigere poterit.
units.tr: As soon as Cardinal Campeggio had left, the King utterly rejected Cardinal Wolsey, whom he had raised to such great honours, once he had seen that there was nothing upright or of true faith in him, not even towards himself; and he had come to know that he was not a criminal man but a mask woven and fashioned from deceits, lies, plunder, lust and ambition. He forbade him the court and his presence. Then the accusations of the others, since he had lost the King's favour, as he deserved, pressed upon him, a man who for so many years had been busy in every kind of fraud and wrong, so that he thought his ruin was at hand. And indeed it is a beginning when one who had for so many years built up such great power falls in as brief a moment as a blink of the eye. But it was not easy for one who had alienated the Pope by ambition, Caesar by pride, the King by dissimulation, the nobles by arrogance, the humble by plunder, the powerful by injuries, and all good men, to hold his ground for long. The rumours of this rejection filled not only England but almost the whole Christian world, so that it was necessary for the King himself to take up the government of the realm, and not to entrust it any longer to another, as he had to the cardinal, who for so many years had through fraud and treachery come into such varied and uncertain dangers. And since he had felt himself most troubled and burdened by conscience about this doubtful marriage, he thought he must deal with it quickly. Then, in August, when Campeggio had set out for Rome, since the papal legates had decided that causes of marriage could not be heard, the King, to relax his mind from these cares for a while, and meanwhile to take counsel in secret with those whom he regarded as his friends, came for hunting to Waltham, a town twelve miles from London, with the Dukes of Norfolk and Suffolk and his other intimates. On this journey he disclosed his deep distress of mind and his indignation against Cardinal Wolsey to Stephen Gardiner, his secretary, who (as we said a little earlier) had been the King's envoy at Rome, and to Dr Foxe, his almoner; and he asked them to inquire carefully and diligently what would be most helpful for settling this dispute. On their advice the King then resolved to send new legates to the Pope, and almost decided to draw up a commission worded so that nothing could afterwards hold up the cause. But by chance (as they say), when these doctors were lodging in the house of a certain gentleman, Master Cressy, there was at that time a certain theologian distinguished for learning and piety, Thomas Cranmer, a fellow of Jesus College, Cambridge, who taught Master Cressy's two sons their letters; and since plague was raging at Cambridge, he had spent that summer at Waltham with these young lads. When Gardiner and Foxe saw him, although he was content with a humble and slender way of life, they knew him for his learning and for their old friendship with him at Cambridge. They renewed their friendship, as is customary, after dismissing their attendants, and consulted him about the King's cause. Besides his outstanding learning, Cranmer had a wonderful gravity and modesty, so that he did not readily put forward his opinion on great matters unless he had thought it over; and the more gravely he spoke, and the more he avoided show and boasting, the more persuasive his speech became. So at first he was reluctant, but when he was pressed by the King's counsellors, whom he thought he must obey, he said: "I cannot give you much in so great a matter without thought and study; but my opinion is this. Since the King is so troubled in mind and conscience, nothing can bring a longer delay to the cause, nor can the disturbance and affliction of his conscience, or the heavier surges of his pain, be relieved, than the postponements and windings of Roman lawsuits, in which those who are caught in their snares can hardly ever free themselves. Therefore I think it better that, setting aside forensic wrangling and delays, in which the King has been tossed about for far too long in such great distress of mind, the opinions of theologians be sought on this matter, which can be settled by divine law rather than human, both in our own universities and in foreign ones. And if the theologians pronounce and agree that this marriage is either true or lawful by divine law, the King need no longer seek the Roman court, but should have sentence passed and pronounced in his own realm and province according to the theologians. So, cheerful in mind and secure in conscience, he will be able to live a royal life worthy of this commonwealth, in a lawful marriage, which we subjects ought to wish for him."

units.la: Haec cum summa grauitate prudentiaq; paucis dixisset, Gardinerus atque Foxus hoc saluberrimum consilium quasi diuinitus datum amplexi, optabant vt ea via Regi ita Romam erranti ante a monstrata fuisset. Itaque postridie cum Cardinerus atque Foxus Regem adluissent, quaesiuit ab his Rex, quid iam de causa sua ageretur. Cui Foxus illum Cranmeri congressum superiori nocte habitum exposuit. Gardinerus vero gloriae cupiditate non dissimilis Wolceo, sub quo aulicus & ambitiosus mores primo imbiberat, dum alienam in se laudem inepte transferre volnit, hoc quod Cranmeri proprium fuit, sibi cepit vendicare. At Rex eius sermone neglecto quaesiuit a Foxo, an is Cranmerus adhuc Walthamiae maneret. Is eum ibi relictum affirmat. Proinde Rex accersiri ad se Cranmerum iussit, cuius (inquit) consilium quod ego rectum esse censeo, si biennio ante cognouissem, infinitis in Romana curia profusis sumptibus pepercisset, & meniae laetiori, magisq; tuta placidaq; conscientia iam vixissem. Venit paulo post ad Regem Cranmerus, cum quo Rex de superiori colloquio, suaque de ea re sententia egit. Cranmerus non minus grauiter atque docte quam ingenue ac modeste quid senserat ac cognouerat eloquutus est. Rex ingenuitatem, facundiam, & doctrinam viri singularem admiratus rogauit vt sententiam quam dixerat in scripta referret, mandauitq; Wiltonio Comiti, vt Cranmerum de causa scripturum sua domo exciperet, ac benigne tractarer. Itaque ex sacris Scripturis, Conciliis, & Patrum Orthodoxorum sententiis Cranmerus libellum conscripsit. In quo Regis cum D. Catharina nuptias lege diuina interdictas, nec Papae nec vlla humana remissione conciliandas esse docuit. Rex perlecto libello rogauit, an ea quae ibi affuerassent, in Romana pontificis curia vel praesentia audetet defendere. Cranmerus constanter & intrepide audere se respondit. Rex confisus hominis ingenio ac doctrina, novam legationem ad Papam profectutam paraui. In ea Wiltoniensis Comes, Tho. Cranmer, D. Stockesley, D. Carnus, D. Benedictus multis doctis ac generosis viris comitantibus profecti sunt. Papa tum fuit Bononiae celeberrima Italiae ciuitate, in qua etiam celebris omnium bonorum artium & scientiarum Academia instituta est. Locus sane huic suscepte legationi si Papa voluisset, ad inquirendum illius quaestionis veritatem percommodus. Quo cum pernenissent Legati, ad Papam perducti oscularI amplius eius ex more pedes noluerunt, sed cum Papa pedem ofeuland nam extendisset, pusillus catulus qui Comitis Wilton fuit, ingressus locum, cum pedem vidisset gemmis auroq; quelucentem, rem tam raram, lasciuus dentibus apprehendit, atque mordit. Id Papa indigne tulit, & inducto ad se illo splendido pede, altero canem abegit. Hoc omne eum Angli in risus & cachinnos profusiores essent, Papa contractis supercilis causam legationis quaesiuit.
units.tr: When he had said this, with great gravity and prudence and in few words, Gardiner and Fox embraced this most wholesome counsel, as though it had been given by God, and wished that this way had been shown earlier to the king, who was wandering so far from the truth in Rome. So the next day, when Gardiner and Fox had visited the king, the king asked them what was now being done about his cause. Fox set out for him the meeting with Cranmer held the previous night. Gardiner, however, not unlike Wolsey, under whom he had first absorbed courtly and ambitious ways, and out of a desire for glory, foolishly tried to transfer to himself another man's praise and claimed for himself what had been Cranmer's own achievement. But the king paid no attention to his speech and asked Fox whether Cranmer was still staying at Waltham. Fox affirmed that he had been left there. Accordingly the king ordered Cranmer to be summoned to him, saying: "If I had learned two years earlier the counsel which I judge to be right, he would have spared the infinite expenses lavished at the Roman curia, and I would have lived now with a happier mind and a more secure and calm conscience." A little later Cranmer came to the king, and the king discussed with him the earlier conference and his own opinion on the matter. Cranmer set out what he thought and had come to understand, no less gravely and learnedly than frankly and modestly. The king, admiring the candour, eloquence and singular learning of the man, asked him to put in writing the opinion he had stated, and commanded the Earl of Wiltshire to receive Cranmer into his house while he wrote about the case, and to treat him kindly. Accordingly, from Holy Scripture, the councils and the opinions of the orthodox Fathers, Cranmer composed a little book, in which he taught that the king's marriage with Lady Catherine was forbidden by divine law and could not be reconciled by any remission from the Pope or any human authority. When the king had read the book through, he asked whether Cranmer would dare to defend, in the Roman curia and in the presence of the pontiff, the things that were set out there. Cranmer replied that he would dare to do so, firmly and fearlessly. The king, confident in the man's talent and learning, prepared a new embassy to be sent to the Pope. In it the Earl of Wiltshire, Thomas Cranmer, Dr Stokesley, Dr Carne and Dr Benet set out, accompanied by many learned and noble men. The Pope was then at Bologna, a most famous city of Italy, where a celebrated academy of all the liberal arts and sciences had also been founded. Indeed the place would have been very well suited to inquiring into the truth of that question, if the Pope had wished it. When the legates arrived there, they were brought to the Pope, but they did not want to kiss his feet in the customary way. When the Pope stretched out his foot for kissing, a little puppy belonging to the Earl of Wiltshire ran into the place, and when it saw the foot shining with gems and gold, so rare a thing, it playfully seized it in its teeth and bit it. The Pope took this badly, and drew the splendid foot back to himself and drove the dog away with the other foot. While the English broke into even more abundant laughter and guffaws at all this, the Pope, knitting his brows, asked the cause of the embassy.

units.la: Eaa
units.tr: These things

units.la: Eā à D. Wiltoniensi Comite exposita est, quicum perorauisset, tradidit Papæ libellum à Cranmero compositum, simulq; adesse iam narrat ex Anglia doctos viros qui quę in illo libro continerentur, ex sacris Scripturis, Conciliis, ac Orthodoxorum Patrū sententiis contra singulos contradicturos essent defensuri. Papa sæpe promisit legatis disputandi & contradicendi diem, verūm cum eadem incertitudine ac perplexitate hæreret, qua sui (vt diximus) in Anglia Legati, Campeius & Wolceus Cardinales antea infixi & confusi sunt, Legatis perhonorificè atque blandè tractatis, tum Cranmero quem illius datiad se deRegis cū Catharina coniunctione opusculi authorē siue cõiecerat, siue mouerat, Pœnitentiario suo in Anglia, Hibernia, & Wallia cõstituto (q; animis omnē soluēdi ro atque ligandi tũ à Papa potestatem continebat) affecto, eum pusillanimis & Cæsarem & Gallum, & Regem maximè pertimeret, nihil ausus est de re tanta statuere, aut litem moris producere, sed Concilium reinfecta, ac ne mota quidem dimisit. His nuncijs Legati reuersi sunt, præter Cranmerum. Qui Regio tacito præcepto Cæsarem & Germaniæ Principis cum reuerteretur, in itinere adiit. Eo tempore Cæsar erat in expeditione contra Turcam Viennam Austriæ ciuitatem expugnaturum. Ibi cum Cranmerus cum Regis nomine conuenisset, atq; quęsiuisset qui ex suis domesticis atq; notis essent contradicturi, datus est ei non vulgaris, sed ob nonnullos libros editos notus vir, in arcana Philosophia, quàm in Theologia peritior Cornelius Agrippa. Is cum facilè Cranmēro in ea causa assensus esset, eadem facilitate suasit cæteris in Cæsaris familia doctis viris ne cum 20 Cranmero à quo veritatem profestam esse dicebat, conienderent. Ita nemine contradicente à Cæsare discessit Cranmerus, & peragrata tota Germania doctissimorum virorum in Academiis & Aulis principum secum conspirantium opiniones & sententias ad Regem in Angliam secum tulit. Interea alii à Rege missi Legati Gallicanas & Italicas Academias petlustrabant, earumq; decisiones cum Germanicis & Cranmero conspirantes, ac sigillis publicis authēticisq; confirmatas in Angliam duxerunt. Quibus peraктis cum Rex quantum in Romāna curia vanitatis & impietatis inesse perspexisset, ac in Wolceo Cardinali veram imaginem & tranquam idæam illius profanæ atque sordidæ Ecclesiæ animaduertisser, tum animi excelsi & inuidi magnitudine cæteris Regibus ac principibus præstitisset, tam im30 purę Ecclesiæ tanquam prostitutæ meretricis dominationem ac libidinem, quæ ipsum in tam diuturnum stuprum adumbrata contra eius diuinum dispensationem induxerat, amplius perferre ac tolerare noluit. Sed cum longè difficilē ac periculosum esse cerneret tam ingentem molem prosterne, secretò prius explorabat quo iure anteactis seculis tanta Papalis potestas primùm in hoc regnum irrepsit. Ac in sacris Scripturis & iure diuino Rexeo periculo quod in matrimoniali sua causa de Cranmero fecerat, neminem libentius quàm eum consuluit. Is non modò in greges & alias Ecclesias, sed in Reges, & Imperia dominationem acquisiuit. Eamq; iam dominationem ac potentiam non le40 ge diuina (vt pontificii volunt) institutam, sed humano potius more, qui valere contra æternitatem non potest, temporis longinquitate præscriptam ac vsucapiam tenere. Ac Wolceus quidem Cardinalis qui de his nuptiis tanquam incestuosis primus conquæstus est, nonnulla Regi in Papam insusurrauit, quotiescunq; suæ ambitioni expedire videbantur. Quæ tamen vera fuerunt, tamen eò minorem authoritatem habuerunt, quò magis à glorioso & inani ingenio profecta sunt. At hic Cranmerus veritatis Theologus, cuiuerba non ex fuco & fallaciis, sed ex doctrina & simplicitate Euangelica prosluebant, Regis optimi clarissimiq; conscientiam eodem penè tempore tam incestus, quàm Papalis dominationis iugo liberauit. Restabat iam in his duobus negotiis nihil quàm vt Rex ab 50 his duobus vinculis, vnum Thori, alterum Papalis religionis se eximeret, aperteque discederet. Quo quidem tempore duo (de quibus antea diximus) insignes ingenio viri à Cardinale abducti & inter Regios cõsiliarios alcripti sunt. Th. Morus, & Th. Crumwell: Ille in iure Angliæ municipali, literisq; Græcis ac Latinis perdoctus fuit, & quanquam Cardinalis superbiam ac tyrannidem exosam haberet, ponificia tamen (quod valde dolendum fuit) (superstitione & caligine ita cæcabatur, vt eidem ad extremam suam perniciem adhærerent. At Crumwell etsi non ita doctrina præstabat, tamen ex vsu rerum in Legatina Cardinalis curia, & appellationibus Romam delatis perceptarum, crebrisq; per Germaniam, Galliam, ac Italiā itineribus ea collegit, quæ vir excellenti ingenio, & summo Euangeli propagandi studio contra Pontificios dolos ac impostturas ad Romanam authoritatem ex Anglia profligandam Regi patefecit atq; produxit. Inter hunc & Cranmerum summam necessitudinem Euangelium conciliauit, vt dum ille experientia, hic doctrina cum stationibus conuentus, tum vtrique Regi intimi atque chari essent, ex harum consilio, & impiis atque odiosis Papæ & Wolcei Cardinalis actis summum supplicium & exitium Romanæ curiæ diuinitus paratum est. Rex enim Parlamentum conuocauit, mandauitque Warhamo Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo vt congregaret in Synodo Clerum. Ac primum Rex Wolcei Cardinalis potentiam minuendam & reprimendam putauit. Itaque Cancellarii munus detraxit, idq; Thomæ Mooro tradidit, deinde quia multorum capitalium criminum reus fuit, præsertim in eo quod Legatinam authoritatem inconsulto Rege, ac sine eius permissu à Papa accepisset, omnia bona sua cepit, ac in fiscum detulit, tum donec de causis eius in Parlamento ageretur, eum in Asheriam qui locus tum Wintoniensis Episcoporatus fuit, relegauit. Archiepiscoporum Eboracensem, & Episcopatum Wintoniensem sibi reliquos fecit. Dunelmensem Episcopatum, Cnthberto Tunstallo, ac Abbatiam S. Albani Norwicensi Priori eontulit. Cardinalis Wolceus cum Londino discederet, vnam ante se gestari errecem, Archiepiscopus videlicet Eboracensis insigne iustitiæ, sustulit, optauitq; vt eam crucem nunquam eorum se gestari permisisset, sed Archiepiscopali sola contentus fuisset, Interea in Parlamento hæc crimina contra Cardinalem obiecta sunt.
units.tr: These were explained by the Earl of Wiltshire, and when he had finished speaking, he handed the Pope the little book composed by Cranmer. At the same time he told him that learned men from England were now present, who would defend and contradict each point contained in that book, from Holy Scripture, the councils and the opinions of the orthodox Fathers. The Pope often promised the legates a day for disputing and contradicting, but since he remained in the same uncertainty and perplexity in which, as we said, the king's legates Campeggio and Cardinal Wolsey had earlier been fixed and confused in England, he treated the legates with great honour and flattery. Then, since he either suspected or was moved to suspect Cranmer as the author of that little work on the king's union with Catherine, he assigned him as his penitentiary in England, Ireland and Wales, a post which carried the power, granted by the Pope, of loosing and binding all souls. Being timid and fearing Caesar and the French, and above all the king, he dared to decide nothing in so great a matter, nor to drag out the lawsuit, but dismissed the council with nothing done and not even stirred. With these reports the legates returned, except Cranmer. On his way back, by the king's silent instruction, he visited Caesar and a German prince. At that time Caesar was on campaign against the Turk, about to storm Vienna, a city of Austria. There Cranmer met him in the king's name and asked which of his household and acquaintances would contradict him. He was given a man who was not ordinary but well known for some books he had published, Cornelius Agrippa, more skilled in occult philosophy than in theology. Agrippa readily agreed with Cranmer in the matter, and with the same readiness he persuaded the other learned men in Caesar's household not to contend with Cranmer, from whom, he said, the truth had come forth. So Cranmer left Caesar with no one contradicting him, and having travelled through all of Germany, he carried back to the king in England the opinions and judgements of the most learned men in the academies and princely courts, who agreed with him. Meanwhile other legates sent by the king visited the academies of France and Italy and brought back to England their decisions, which agreed with the German ones and with Cranmer's, and were confirmed with public seals and authentic signatures. When these things were done, the king had perceived how much vanity and impiety there was in the Roman curia, and had seen in Cardinal Wolsey the true image and, as it were, the idea of that profane and filthy Church. Since he surpassed other kings and princes in the greatness of a lofty and unenvious spirit, he no longer wished to endure or tolerate the domination and lust of so impure a Church, which, like a prostitute, had led him into so long a fornication, contrary to God's divine dispensation. But since he saw that it would be far more difficult and dangerous to overthrow so huge a mass, he first secretly explored by what right, in past ages, so great a papal power had first crept into this kingdom. In the matter of his marriage he had taken a risk with Cranmer, and on the divine law and Holy Scripture he consulted no one more willingly than him. The Papal See had gained dominion not only over flocks and other churches, but over kings and empires. And this domination and power, which was instituted not by divine law (as the Papists want), but rather by human custom, which cannot prevail against eternity, they hold as prescribed and acquired by usucaption through the length of time. Cardinal Wolsey, who was the first to complain of these marriages as incestuous, whispered some things against the Pope into the king's ear whenever they seemed to serve his ambition. Although these things were true, they carried less authority the more they proceeded from a vainglorious and empty mind. But this Cranmer, a theologian of truth, whose words flowed not from deceit and trickery but from the doctrine and simplicity of the gospel, at almost the same time freed the conscience of that best and most illustrious king from the yoke of incest as well as from the yoke of papal domination. Nothing now remained in these two matters except that the king should free himself from these two bonds, one of the marriage bed and the other of papal religion, and openly withdraw. At that time two men of outstanding talent, of whom we spoke earlier, were drawn away from the cardinal and enrolled among the king's counsellors: Thomas More and Thomas Cromwell. The former was learned in the municipal law of England and in Greek and Latin letters. Although he hated the cardinal's pride and tyranny, he was nevertheless, which was very much to be lamented, so blinded by superstition and darkness in papal matters that he clung to them to his final ruin. Cromwell, though he did not excel so much in learning, nevertheless gathered, from his experience of affairs in the cardinal's legatine court, from appeals carried to Rome, and from frequent journeys through Germany, France and Italy, what a man of excellent talent and supreme zeal for spreading the gospel revealed and laid before the king against the tricks and impostures of the Papists, so that Roman authority might be driven out of England. The gospel created the closest bond between him and Cranmer, so that while the one was united with the other, the one by experience and the other by doctrine, and both were intimate and dear to the king, by their counsel and by the impious and odious acts of the Pope and Cardinal Wolsey, the highest punishment and ruin was divinely prepared for the Roman curia. For the king summoned Parliament and ordered Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury, to gather the clergy in synod. First the king thought that Cardinal Wolsey's power should be diminished and curbed. So he took away from him the office of chancellor and handed it to Thomas More. Then, because he was guilty of many capital crimes, especially in having accepted legatine authority from the Pope without the king's knowledge and permission, he seized all his goods and transferred them to the treasury. Then, until his cause was dealt with in Parliament, he banished him to Esher, which at that time was a residence of the bishopric of Winchester. He kept the archbishopric of York and the bishopric of Winchester for himself. He gave the bishopric of Durham to Cuthbert Tunstall, and the abbey of St Albans to the prior of Norwich. When Cardinal Wolsey was leaving London, he had a cross carried before him, the emblem of the archbishop of York, the sign of his jurisdiction. He wished that he had never allowed that cross to be carried before him, but had been content with the archiepiscopal cross alone. Meanwhile in Parliament these charges were brought against the cardinal.

units.la: Quod sine Regis venia a licentia, Legatinam à Papa authoritatem accepisset, eamq; in Anglia contra Regni iura exercuisset.
units.tr: Because he had received legatine authority from the Pope without the King's leave or permission, and had exercised it in England against the rights of the realm.

units.la: Quòd in omnibus literis quas ad Papam, & exteros Principes dedisset, se Regi his verbis præposuisset, Ego & Rex meus.
units.tr: Because in all the letters he wrote to the Pope and to foreign princes, he placed himself before the King with these words: "I and my King."

units.la: Quod magnum Regni sigillum Regno in Belgium, cum ad Cæsarem Legationem obiisset, exportasset.
units.tr: Because, when he went as legate to Caesar in Belgium, he took the great seal of the realm out of the kingdom with him.

units.la: Quod Rege inconsulto bellum Cæsari denunciari à fæciali iussisset.
units.tr: Because, without the King's knowledge, he ordered a herald to declare war on Caesar.

units.la: Quod Gregorium de Casfado militem ad pacificendum nouum inter Regem & Ducem Ferrariæ fœdus, Rege similiter infeio in Italiam misisset.
units.tr: Because, likewise without the King's knowledge, he sent Gregory de Casale, a knight, into Italy to make a new alliance between the King and the Duke of Ferrara.

units.la: Quod morbo Gallico pene putridus, fœtidum ac tristem anhelitum in os Regi inflare ausus esset.
units.tr: Because, almost rotten with the French pox, he dared to breathe foul and sickly breath into the King's face.

units.la: Quòd dum Papatum & Romanos honores impudentissime ambiret, immensum Thesaurum Regno in Italiam emisisset.
units.tr: Because, while he most shamelessly courted the papacy and Roman honours, he sent an immense treasure out of the realm into Italy.

units.la: Hæc & alia nonnulla huius generis crimina confessus, actione de Præmunire in Regio banco conuentus, & earum legum quæ contra prouisores latæ sunt, reus pronunciatus, condemnatus & proscriptus est. Ita qui viginti fere annis non modo Angliam, sed Europam penè rexit, non aliena magis inuidia, quam propria superbia concidit, suoque (vt mox dicemus) præcipitio totum Clerum Anglicanum, ipsiamq; Romam in similē ruinam & occasum traxit.
units.tr: Having confessed these and several other crimes of this kind, he was sued in the King's Bench under the action of praemunire, and was found guilty under the laws passed against providors. He was condemned and outlawed. Thus he who for nearly twenty years ruled not only England but almost all of Europe fell not so much by the envy of others as by his own pride. By his fall (as we shall say presently) he dragged the whole English clergy, and Rome itself, into a similar ruin and downfall.

units.la: Sed Rex vt natura magnanimus, ita mitis atque moderatus fuit. Nam Eboracensem & Wintoniensem Ecclesias, ex quibus copiosum & nimium lautum illi vectigal singulis annis manabat, reseruauit. Id quod hominis ambitione & cupiditate cæcato exitio paulo post fuit. Nam Wolceus his merito priuatus honoribus spiritus, arrogantiamq; nō remisit.
units.tr: But the King, as magnanimous by nature as he was, was also mild and moderate. For he kept back the churches of York and Winchester, from which a plentiful and excessively rich revenue flowed to Wolsey every year. This proved to be the ruin of that man, blinded by ambition and greed, shortly afterwards. For Wolsey, rightly stripped of these honours, did not lay aside his spirit or his arrogance.

units.la: Sed vindictam meditabatur, & solennem ac pomposam in Ecclesia sua Cathedrali Eboracensi intronizationem qua populum deliniret instituit, multisq; sensim de iniuriis quas à Rege pertulisset, cōquestus est, vt mobile vulgus ad seditiones cōcitaret, tū in literis ad Papam, aliosq; datis, in Regē acerbius inuectus est. Ita vt legati & oratores Regii multa connitia & opprobria in Regem à Cardinali fieri audiuerunt. Quæ cum æquis auribus ferre non poterant, ea Regi denuntiabant. His cognitis cum intronizationis tempus aderat, Wolceus omnes proceres, Præsules, milites, & generosos suæ prouinciæ Cawoodi, qui locus adhuc est eius Archiepiscopatus, cōuenire, vt eis stipatus triumpho magis quàm Regio ad Eboracum duceretur, mandauit. Rex qui occultis suppositis exploratoribus de hoc apparatu accepisset, cum animaduerteret eum vindictæ, seditioni & omnibus rebus perturbandis studere, Northumbriæ Comiti qui Regni finibus ad Scotiam positis præsidebat, in mandatis dedit, vt Cardinalem sisteret, & Salopiensi Comiti vt Londinum duceretur, tradetet.
units.tr: But he was planning revenge. He arranged a solemn and showy enthronement in his cathedral church at York, by which he hoped to win over the people. Little by little he complained at length of the injuries he had suffered from the King, so as to stir the fickle crowd to sedition. In letters to the Pope and others he inveighed more bitterly against the King, so that the royal legates and envoys heard many insults and reproaches against the King made by the Cardinal. Since they could not bear these with equanimity, they reported them to the King. When these things were known and the day of the enthronement drew near, Wolsey ordered all the nobles, prelates, soldiers and gentlemen of his province to assemble at Cawood, which is still the seat of his archbishopric, so that he might be led to York surrounded by them, more like a triumph than a royal progress. The King, who had learned of this preparation through secret spies, saw that Wolsey was bent on vengeance, sedition and the disturbance of everything. He gave orders to the Earl of Northumberland, who governed the region on the borders of the realm toward Scotland, to arrest the Cardinal, and to the Earl of Shrewsbury to hand him over to be taken to London.

units.la: Venit itaque Comes Cawoodum, & Cardinalem itineri ad Eboracum iam accinctū, Regio nomine sistit. Id mirum & præter expectationem accexemplum Cardinali visum est, utpote qui fe Cardinalem, Romanæ curiæ membrum, Papæq; legatum iactitauit, cuiusque manus adferre violentas summum esse nefas iudicarit, tandem verò Comitis potentiam veritus necessitate magis quàm sponte parnit. Itaq; famulatu suo à Comite abdicato, bonisq; ad fisçum Regium sequestratis, ipse ad Sheffeldiæ castrum ductus & Salopiensi Comiti traditus est. Eo sic capto omnis illa nobilis & splendida caterua, quæ iter suum Eboracum, & intronizationem illustraret subito dissipata est, in qua vix quisquam fuit qui tam infla- ti & impuri hominis casum deplorabat. Rex cum accepisset eum in custodia Salopiensis Comitis iam fuisse, misit Wilhelmum Kingstonum militem Regis stipatoribus præfe10 ctum, vt eum armata copia in Turrim Londinensem deduceret. Cuius aduentus tanto panore conscium Cardinalis animum perculit, vt in febrem inciderit, sed nihilominus in itinere lenté pergunt, & paulatim Leceftriam peruenerunt. Ibi in Cœnobio diuertunt.
units.tr: The Earl therefore came to Cawood and, in the King's name, placed the Cardinal under arrest. Wolsey was already preparing for the journey to York. This seemed to the Cardinal a strange and unexpected thing: he boasted that he was a Cardinal, a member of the Roman curia and the Pope's legate, and he had judged it the greatest wickedness to lay violent hands on him. Yet at last, fearing the Earl's power, he submitted more from necessity than willingly. So, with his retinue dismissed by the Earl and his goods sequestered to the royal treasury, he was led to Sheffield Castle and handed over to the Earl of Shrewsbury. Once he was taken, that whole noble and splendid crowd which was to adorn his journey and enthronement was suddenly scattered, and among them there was scarcely anyone who lamented the fall of so puffed-up and impure a man. When the King learned that Wolsey was already in the custody of the Earl of Shrewsbury, he sent Sir William Kingston, a knight set over the King's guards, to lead him with an armed force to the Tower of London. The arrival of this man, who was so clearly a cause of fear, struck the Cardinal's mind so that he fell into a fever. Nevertheless they proceeded slowly on the journey and gradually reached Leicester, where they lodged in the abbey.

units.la: Wolceus æger magis quàm ægrotus tam violenta sibi medicamenta adhibuit, vt ex vomitibus & alui profluuio non sine suspicione veneni, dum altera nocte ibi pernoctarent, animam subito effluuit, postridie q; in eodem Cœnobio sine vlla pompa sepultus est. Ac viuus quidem extruxerat sibi morituro egregii sumptus atq; artificii tumulû, cuius pulchritudine delectatus cum inspiciendum semel venisset, à quodam suo Morione, quem ob fatuitatem Patchæ appellabat, admonitus est vt sin eo cumulo cŏdi veller, viuus eum ingrederetur, nam mortuo humilé ac sine specie sepulturam prædicebat. Hic igitur tri-
units.tr: Wolsey, sick rather than ill, applied such violent medicines to himself that, from vomiting and a flux of the bowels, and not without suspicion of poison, he suddenly breathed out his life during the one night they stayed there. The next day he was buried in the same abbey without any pomp. While still alive he had built for himself, as one about to die, a tomb of remarkable expense and workmanship. Delighted by its beauty, he came once to inspect it, and a certain jester of his, whom he called Patch because of his foolishness, warned him that if he wished to be shut into that tomb he should enter it while alive, for he predicted that after death he would have a humble and unsightly burial.

units.la: 20 ftis est & infœlix eius hominis exitus, in quo perfectam & omnibus numeris absolutam totius Romanæ impietatis imaginem intueri liceat, quæ nullus in honoribus modis, nulla in rebus diuinis religio coercuit, quem gloria & aula popularis inflauit, rapinæ locupletarunt, libidines exhauserunt, fraudes & dissimulationes ad tantam calamitatem perduxerunt.
units.tr: Thus the sad and unhappy end of this man may be seen as a perfect image of the whole of Roman impiety, complete in every respect. No religion restrained him in his offices, nor in the sacred duties; popular glory and the court puffed him up, plunder enriched him, lusts wore him out, and frauds and dissimulations brought him to such calamity.

units.la: Ar hoc suum supplicium non sibi proprium atq; peculiare fuit, sed attigit totum Clerum quod suis criminibus communicabat. Nam q; illa rigida prouisionum iuranô modô eos punit, qui Romanas legationes sine Regis licentia suscipiunt, sed qui huiusmodi authoritati parent: minus enim Maiestas Regia ab vtriq; pariter existimatur. Itaq; Clerus Anglicanus qui Cardinali vt Romani Pontificis Legato obtemperabant, ob admif-
units.tr: But this punishment was not his alone and peculiar to him; it touched the whole clergy, which shared in his crimes. For although that strict statute of Provisors punishes in this way those who accept Roman legations without the King's licence, it likewise punishes those who obey such authority, since the royal majesty is thought to be violated equally by both. Hence the English clergy, who obeyed Wolsey as the legate of the Roman Pontiff, were thought to be liable under the action of praemunire, because they had admitted and received papal power. By its force they ought to have been outlawed and adjudged to the King with their goods and persons, unless the King had taken pity on them.

units.la: 30 sam receptamq; Papæ potestatem actione de Præmunire reneri putabatur. Cuius vi pscribi, & cum bonis atq; membris adiudicari Regi debuit, nisi Rex misertus fuisset. Itaq; in superiori synodo, quam ab Warhamo Archiepiscopo conuocatam esse diximus, consilium iniit Clerus de tam dira pœna redimenda. Rex etiâ eò durius multâri voluit Clerum, quod Papali iurisdictione, cuius vsurpationem Regiæ authoritati adueršam plane perspexerat, eum à suo Regioiure eximiri atq; vindicari cernaret.
units.tr: Therefore, in the earlier synod which we said was convened by Archbishop Warham, the clergy took counsel on how to redeem themselves from so dire a penalty. The King wished to punish the clergy all the more harshly because he saw clearly that they were being exempted from his royal law and defended by papal jurisdiction, whose usurpation he perceived to be plainly adverse to royal authority.

units.la: Itaq; etsi in ea synodo multa de statu ecclesiarum atq; Regularium, & Clericali ordine ac vectitia reformando, de vnitis & impropriatis Ecclesiis, de congruis Vicariorum portionibus, deh;rereticis quos appellabant coercendis, multa acta & proposita fuissent; tamen ea deliberatio quæ de auertendo tam atroci supplicio habita est, quia difficilima 40 fuit, cæterà negocia impediebat. Deliberatione diu habita Cantuariensis Prouinciæ Clerus. C M.lib.Eboracensis xviii. M.ea lege concessere, vt suprad his pœnis & sanctionibus soluerentur. At Rex qui solus regnare, nec diuisum & dispertitum de Cleroac populo sio gubernando cum Papa officium amplius gerere voluit, non alia conditione hac oblata pecunia redimere Clerum voluit, quam si ie solum suum totiusq; populi proxime ac secundum Christum protectorem supremumq; caput in ea synodo agnosceret. Huius consilii Cranmerus, & Cromwellus clam authores fuisse existimabant. Clerus animo, toto iam obstinatus, nondum enim quid sibi bic nouus vellet titulus aut quorsum tendere, tprofpexit. Sed nasuti quidam olfecerunt rei exitum, inter quos fuisse Warhamum Archiepiscopum ex his quæ mox dicemus, verisimile est. Magnæ res, deliberatum diu, prò50 erastinationes & prorogationes crebræ, disputatum sæpius grauissimis pœnis & censuris Ecclesiasticis interminatum est omnibus ab Archiepiscopo ne synodi colloquiû emun- ciaretur. Rex per Dide Rochesford, Cromwellum Rotulorum custodem, & Iustiriarios sæpe Clerû de hoc titulo solicitabat, denunciabatq; sine eo, nô remissurû se vlla redeptione violatarû à Clero legû pœnas. Tandé Archiepiscopus cû exq; fuisset Præsulû de eare sententias, ac pleriq; siluissent: quia tacet (in quir) côsentire videtur, respon sumq; ilico fuit. Ergo tacemus omnes. Verû postea cum neq; tutum, neq; e graviate synodi forte cernere- Ee Arch. seq; illudere Regi, frequentes ierunt in sententiâ his verbis conceptam. Ecclesiæ & Cleri Anglicani singularem protectorem, supremum, Dominum & quantum per Christi Legeslicet etiâsupremum caput Regiam Maiestatem recognoscimus.
units.tr: Therefore, although in that synod many matters were enacted and proposed concerning the reform of the state of the churches and of the regulars, and of the clerical order and its discipline; concerning united and appropriated churches; concerning fitting portions for vicars; and concerning the restraint of those they called heretics, nevertheless the deliberation held on averting so atrocious a penalty, because it was most difficult, impeded the other business. After long deliberation the clergy of the Province of Canterbury agreed on this condition: that they be released from the aforesaid penalties and sanctions. But the King, who wished to reign alone and not to have the clergy and people divided and governed in such a way that he shared his office with the Pope, would not redeem the clergy with money offered on any other condition than that in that synod they acknowledge him as the supreme protector and, as far as Christ's law allows, the supreme head of the Church and clergy of England. The authors of this plan were thought to be Cranmer and Cromwell, in secret. The clergy, though wholly obstinate in mind, did not yet see what this new title meant for them or where it was leading. But some shrewd men smelled the outcome, and it is likely that Archbishop Warham was among them, as we shall say presently. The matter was long debated, there were frequent delays and postponements, and the Archbishop repeatedly threatened all with the gravest penalties and ecclesiastical censures, so that the synod's discussion should not be divulged. The King, through Dr. Rochford, Cromwell the Keeper of the Rolls, and the justices, often pressed the clergy on this point, and declared that without it he would not remit the penalties for violating the laws by any payment. At last the Archbishop asked the bishops for their opinions on the matter, and most of them kept silent. Since silence in such a case seems to signify consent, he was answered at once: "So we are all silent." But afterwards, when it seemed neither safe nor in keeping with the dignity of the synod to mock the King, they went in large numbers to the sentence framed in these words: "We acknowledge the King's Majesty as the singular protector, the supreme lord, and, as far as Christ's law allows, also the supreme head of the Church and clergy of England."

units.la: Ee
units.tr: Ee

units.la: Sed Regi difpliceuit hanc anciplitem dubiamq; miugationem & moderatione vetborum a Cleri fui synodo, quæ de Christi lege aut certa fuit, aut certa esse debuit, tam frigidè proferri. Itaq; Cromwello ad synodum iterum nuncio eam aut tolli voluit, aut Clerum irritari suas sanctionum poenas pati. Omnium igitur mox sontentiis Rex sine ambiguitate vfla Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ supremum caput declaratus est. Illeq; titulum in publico Cleri instrumento quo pecunia prædicta concessa fuit, inclusus Regiquè exhibitus est. Rex & pecuniam & titulum accepit ut Clerus deinceps dicatur, sibi a Romano Pontifice eiusq; authoritate cauere. Pontificii iam omnes de duce suo Papa in summam discrimen adducto desperabant. Cumq; Cleri status una cum Papæ & Wolmei Cardinalis vacillare cœpit, populus à iuris Regni periris ineiratus molta in totum Clerum descripta crimina Regi deferebat, Regemq; etsi sæpe contradixerit tandem importunitati suæ, ea quæ in annis 1512.13. Regni sui lata iura sunt, cõcedere adigebat. Nonduum. n. Papæ authoritas profligata fuit, sed præter supremi capitis titulum totus in eadem synodo Clerus in verbo sacerdotii fidem Regi dedit, ne vllas deiceps in synodo ferrent Ecclesiasticas leges, nisi & synodus authoritate Regia congregata, & constitutiones in synodis publicatæ eadem authoritate ratæ essent. In eadem synodo multa in eos quos tum Lutherianos appellabant, quorum indies augebatur numerus, decreta sunt. Libri qui in pontificiam authoritatem & doctrinam diuolgabantur, ipsumq; nouum Testamentum quod à quibusdam piis viris in Anglicanum sermonem versum fuit, quia defectionem à papatu præsunciabant, hæretica iudicata & condemnata fuerunt. Hugo Latimerus pius atque doctus Theologus, nisi propositia tibi ab hac synodo pontificia multa dogmata chirographo suo agnouisset, in cineres flamma versus fuisset. Wilhelmus Tracy defunctus quod in Testamento à pontificia fide recessisset, abrogato testamento sententia synodi exhumatus & combustus est. Hæc synodus in multis de abolendo paparu deliberationibus pendens, sæpius prorogata est. Iamq; nouam dilationem à 6. Kal. Maii, ad quintum Octobris accepit. Interea Warhamus Cantuariam profectus est, ibi Wilhelmi Warhami Cantuariensis Archidiaconi ad fanum S. Stephani prope Cantuariam situs hospitio (in quo adficiando atque reparando multos sumptus effundisset) lethali morbo correptus est, ac in summa fenetute, cum viginti octo annis sedisset, obiit. Postea cadauer eius Cantuariam ductum, in exigoo, quod viuus extruxerat delubro, ad eum locum ubi Thomas Becket quondam interfectus fuit posito, ibidem humatum est. In reliquam tunc pompa sepeliri voluit, vestes lugubres solis pauperibus legauit, executores Ducem Norfolciæ, & D. Winser Baronem instituit. Horum commitat omnia, vrerim in restitutionibus suis amicitia tacita fidei commissa præstarent. Liberari se dilapidationum actionea succesore penit, quia 30. M. librarum in aedificandis & reparandis pluribus Archiepiscopatus sui aedificiis ab eo tempore quo sedere cepit, ad eum usque diem quo obiit effudisset. Consanguineos suos viuus multis ad haereditatem acquisitus prædiis locupletauit. Mortuo (vt diximus) Wolsco Cardinali Stephanus Gardinerus in Wintoniensi Episcopatu, huic Warhamo Thomas Cranmerus successit. Quibus prælulibus proxima historia abioluenda est.
units.tr: But the King was displeased that the clergy's synod had put forward so ambiguous and doubtful a softening, and a moderation of wording, concerning a matter of Christ's law that was, or ought to have been, certain. So he sent Cromwell to the synod again, to demand that the clause be either withdrawn or that the clergy suffer the penalties of the statutes. Consequently, by the votes of all, the King was at once declared, without any qualification, the supreme head of the Church of England. That title was included in the public instrument of the clergy by which the aforesaid sum of money was granted, and it was presented to the King. The King received both the money and the title, so that the clergy should henceforth be said to guard themselves against the Roman Pontiff and his authority. All the Papists now despaired of their leader, the Pope, who had been brought into the greatest danger. When the position of the clergy began to totter along with the Pope's and Cardinal Wolsey's, the people, instructed by men learned in the laws of the realm, laid many crimes against the whole clergy before the King. Although he had often resisted, at last, under their importunity, he was compelled to concede those rights which had been enacted in the years 1512 and 1513 of his reign. For the authority of the Pope had not yet been wholly overthrown; but beyond the title of supreme head, the whole clergy in that same synod pledged their faith to the King, on their word as priests, that they would henceforth enact no ecclesiastical laws in synod unless the synod had been convened by royal authority and the constitutions published in synods were ratified by the same authority. In the same synod many decrees were made against those whom they then called Lutherans, whose number was daily increasing. Books that were spreading papal authority and doctrine, and the New Testament itself, which some pious men had translated into English, were judged heretical and condemned, because they presumed it to be a step away from the papacy. Hugh Latimer, a pious and learned theologian, would have been turned to ashes in the flames, had he not acknowledged with his own signature the many papal doctrines this synod put before him. William Tracy, who was dead, was dug up and burned by sentence of the synod, because in his will he had departed from the papal faith, and the will was annulled. This synod, pending many deliberations on abolishing the papacy, was often prorogued, and now it received a new postponement, from 26 April to 5 October. Meanwhile Warham went to Canterbury, and there, at the hospice of William Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury, at St Stephen's near Canterbury, on which he had spent large sums in furnishing and repairing it, he was seized by a deadly illness and died in extreme old age, after he had sat for twenty-eight years. Afterwards his body was taken to Canterbury and buried there, in the small chapel he had built during his lifetime, placed at the spot where Thomas Becket was once killed. He wished to be buried without further pomp, bequeathed mourning garments to the poor alone, and appointed as executors the Duke of Norfolk and Lord Windsor. He entrusted everything to these men, so that in their restitutions they would fulfil, by tacit friendship, the trust committed to them. He wished to be wholly freed from action for dilapidations by his successor, since he had spent 30,000 pounds, from the time he began to sit until the day he died, in building and repairing many buildings of his archbishopric. While alive he enriched his kinsmen, acquiring for them many estates as inheritances. As we have said, after Cardinal Wolsey's death Stephen Gardiner succeeded to the bishopric of Winchester, and Thomas Cranmer succeeded this Warham. With these prelates the history that follows must now be brought to a close.

units.la: LXVIII. Thomas Cranmerus.
units.tr: LXVIII. Thomas Cranmer.

units.la: Enrico octauo Regi nihil iam prius aut antiquius fuit, quàm quod de pontificia potestate Anglia penitus exterminanda negocium prius inchoauerat, ad finem exitumq; perducere. Cum (vt diximus) aggrediendo Wolsei Cardinalis impostur causam & adiutum patefecerunt. Magnum deinde adiumentum ex eius ruina, & Warhami Archiepiscopi morte accessit. Ac primum quibus solutionum generibus Anglicana Ecclesia à Papis expilata sit inquisitum est, compertumq; fuit centum sexaginta librarum milliaqnadraginta proximis annis pro solis Episcoporum inuestituris Romanæ curiæ fuisse persoluta. Præterea indulgentiarum, dispensationum, similiumq; fraudum immo scopia, insinitis pecuniis Anglos emunxerunt. Rex etiam de eo iuramento quod Episcopis à Papa consecrationem accipientibus præstitum Papæ fuit, certior factus, idem suæ Regiæ authoritati nitinum præiudicare, præiudicatoq; Papali magis quàm Regia potestate & iurisdictione teneri animadiuerit. Itaq; in Parlamento noua iuramenti formula, qua præiatorum fides firmius apertiusq; Regi deinceps astringeretur, concepta atque de-
units.tr: For King Henry VIII nothing was now more important or pressing than to bring to completion and conclusion the business he had begun earlier, namely the total expulsion of papal power from England. As we have said, when the Cardinal Wolsey was attacked, his imposture and his supporters were exposed. A great further help came from Wolsey's fall and from the death of Archbishop Warham. First, an inquiry was made into the various ways in which the English Church had been plundered by the Popes, and it was discovered that in the preceding years one hundred and sixty thousand pounds had been paid to the Roman court for the investitures of bishops alone. Besides this, they had drained the English of infinite sums through indulgences, dispensations and similar frauds. The King was also informed about the oath that bishops who received consecration from the Pope had sworn to the Pope. He saw that this oath was prejudicial to his own royal authority, and that by its prejudice the bishops were bound more to papal than to royal power and jurisdiction. Therefore a new form of oath was drawn up and enacted in Parliament, by which the loyalty of the prelates would henceforth be bound to the King more firmly and openly.

units.la: De hac iura-mento Vide supra in vita H. Dones. descripta fuit. Synodus autem (de qua supra diximus) Warhamo Archiepiscopo mortuo ex præcepto Regio authoritate Priors & Conventus Cantuariensis prorogata est. Præsidebat huic synodo sede Archiepiscopali vacante Londinensis Episcopus Strokesleyus authoritate sibi data à Conventu Cantuariensi. In eaque relatum est Hugonem Latimerum contra Pontificia dogmata, quibus à synodo (ut diximus) assentiri antea compulsus est nuper prædicasse, in quem multis conviciis exagitarum primus omnium Stephanus Gardinerus Wintoniensis Episcopus acerrimam dixit sententiam. Cuius tamen cæteris assensum fit, tamen quia de Regis difficultio tradendum fuit, posthabita & dilata est atrociitas decreti.
units.tr: On this oath, see above in the life of H. Dones, where it was described. The synod (of which we spoke above), after Archbishop Warham's death, was prorogued by royal command and by the authority of the Prior and Chapter of Canterbury. While the archiepiscopal see was vacant, the Bishop of London, Stokesley, presided over this synod by authority given to him by the Chapter of Canterbury. In it, it was reported that Hugh Latimer had lately preached against papal doctrines, to which he had earlier been compelled by the synod (as we have said) to assent. Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, first of all railed against him with many insults and gave the sharpest opinion. Yet, although the rest assented to this, because the matter had to be referred to the King's pleasure, the severity of the decree was set aside and deferred.

units.la: In eo autem matrimoniali negocio, Stephanus Wintrodiensis Episcopus sententias transmarinarum vniuersitatum in membranis authentice scriptas, & sigillis publicis confirmatas produxit, quas oratione breui habita laudauit, &c a Præjactis diligenter euoluit sufficit. Sed dubitatum fuit an de hac lite quæ coram Romano Pontifice penderet, synodo tractare liceret. Bara vero dubitationem à Pontificio aliquo inculcaram supplicavit Strokesleyus Londinensis Episcopus, idemq; Præses synodo, prolata Papali licentia, qua singulis permissum est sententias de re suas liberè proferre, rogauitq; omnes ut de tantæ materiæ deliberatione, ac quid senserint in synodo declararent. Sed quia res magna fuit, multæ dilationes atq; morę consultationis impetratæ & tributæ sunt. Interea Rex dum Papæ mediatabatur excidium, singulorum de Papali authoritate sensus indicijs haud obscuris colegit. Inter quos Thomas Mooτus, quia Regis conatus Pontificis valde suspectus fuit, Cancellarii munere, venia Regis ægrè impetrata, sese abdicabat. Id munus facundissimo viro Tho. Audeley militi delatum est. Præcato quoq; haud fidos Rex habebat, quos aut Pontificiis renebris cæcutire, aut adulatione conciliare sibi honores ac potentiam vellet, ut neret, quod vitium eo maiori habebat odio, quod in Wolceo vafferrimo & intolerabilis nequitiæ viro latissime patuit. Ex omnibus itaque solum Cranmerum tanta prudentia & communicatione dignum iudicauit, cui doctrinam, fidem, ac integritatem singularem ex multis rerum argumentis inesse certò cognouit. Data itaque Cantuariensi conuentui à Rege eligendi facultatem, Thomas Cranmerus Archiepiscopus electus est. At Clemens sepiimus Papa cui Regis animus iam dubius in Romanam sedem fuit, quid ageret incertus fuit, reiicere ne Cranmerum electum an admittere debuit. Vius tandem metu ne Rex cum regno à Romana sede fiamplius irritaretur deficeret, ad Regem primo scripsit solito blandius, obsecrauitq; ut Cantuariensem Ecclesiam Thomamq; Cranmeum ad eandem electum Regio patrocinio tueretur, summum esse Regi duxit & æternæ gratiæ, & humani præconii meritum, si Ecclesias præsertim Metropolitanas defenderet. At imprudè Papa inanem in hac petitione laborem suscepit. Hoc enim Regi iam in animo fuit, Cantuariensem Ecclesiam, aholita Romana, nobilitare, & Anglicanis prouinciis iuta per Papam ablata restituere. Itaq; Clemens Papa nō minus de Crameri erga Romam, quam de Regis fide solicitus indulsit ei quidem facile; ut à duob. vel tribus Catholicis Episcopis quibus vellet sacraretur, sed vetus illud iuramentum concessionis infestuit, quod niss in sacratione præstaret tam Episcopis sacratoribus quam ipso sacrato omni Episcopali administratione interdixit.
units.tr: In the matter of the marriage, Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, produced verdicts of universities overseas, written authentically on parchment and confirmed with public seals. After a brief speech in their praise, he sufficiently went through them carefully. But it was disputed whether the synod could treat of this suit, which was pending before the Roman Pontiff. Stokesley, Bishop of London, however, addressed this doubt, which some papist had pressed, and, as president of the synod, produced a papal licence by which each man was allowed to state his opinion on the matter freely. He asked everyone to declare in the synod what they thought after deliberating on so great a matter. But because the matter was important, many delays and pauses for consultation were obtained and granted. Meanwhile the King, while plotting the ruin of the Pope, gathered from fairly clear signs what each man thought about papal authority. Among them, Thomas More, who was highly suspected of opposing the King's plans, gave up the office of Chancellor, having obtained the King's pardon with difficulty. That office was offered to the most eloquent man Sir Thomas Audley. The King also had few faithful men about him; some he wanted either to blind with papist darkness or to win over by flattery, so that they might gain honours and power for him. He held this fault in greater hatred because it had appeared most widely in Wolsey, a most crafty man of intolerable wickedness. Of all of them, therefore, he judged Cranmer alone worthy of such trust and confidence, since he had clearly recognised in him, from many proofs, his learning, his faith and his outstanding integrity. Therefore, the King gave the Chapter of Canterbury the power to elect, and Thomas Cranmer was elected Archbishop. But Pope Clement VII, whose mind was already doubtful towards the Roman See, was uncertain what to do, whether he should reject Cranmer, once elected, or admit him. At last, fearing that the King, together with the kingdom, would completely fall away from the Roman See if he were further provoked, he first wrote to the King more flatteringly than usual, and entreated him to protect the Church of Canterbury and Thomas Cranmer, elected to it, with royal patronage. He said it would be the greatest merit before eternal grace and human praise for the King to defend the churches, especially the metropolitan ones. But the Pope unwisely undertook a vain labour in this petition. For it was already in the King's mind to ennoble the Church of Canterbury, now that Rome was abolished, and to restore to the English provinces the jurisdiction that had been taken away by the Pope. Therefore Pope Clement, no less anxious about Cranmer's loyalty to Rome than about the King's faith, granted him readily that he might be consecrated by two or three Catholic bishops of his choice. But he insisted on that old oath of obedience, and forbade, unless it were taken at the consecration, both the consecrating bishops and the consecrated man from all episcopal administration.

units.la: Verum in sacratione coram testibus fide dignis, notarijs publicis Crămerus protestatus est, id iuramentum consuetudinis tantum Romanæ, non Christianæ necessitatis fuisse, nec se velle à fide subdito Regi debita eius iuramenti viabducì aut deficere, eoq; iuramento perfunctorie lecto, à Lincolniensi, Exoniensi, & Asiaueni Episcopis sacrationem atq; pallium suscepit, tum Regi ingenuè ac liberaliter iuramento de veraq; plena obedientia dato, temporalibus Archiepiscopatus donatus est. Papæ pro obsoletis illis putidisq; iam bullis 900. aureos ducatos soluit. Iamq; præter opinionem atq; sensum permultorum in Archiepiscopatu Cantuariensi positus, ingressus est authoritate sua in synodum quam (ut diximus) sub Conuentu Cantuariensi Suffraganei tenuerunt.
units.tr: Yet at the consecration, in the presence of trustworthy witnesses and public notaries, Cranmer protested that this oath was only a custom of Rome, not a necessity of Christianity, and that he did not wish to deviate from or fall away from the faith and loyalty owed to his prince by that oath. Having read the oath perfunctorily, he received consecration and the pallium from the Bishops of Lincoln, Exeter and Ely. Then, freely and generously, he gave the King an oath of true and full obedience, and was granted the temporalities of the archbishopric. For those old and now stinking bulls he paid the Pope nine hundred gold ducats. Thus he was placed in the archbishopric of Canterbury beyond the expectation and feeling of very many, and he entered, by his own authority, the synod which (as we have said) the suffragans had held under the Chapter of Canterbury.

units.la: Cuius aduentu quæsitum est iterum de Regis cum D. Catharina coniugio, acrenouata illa tamdiu cori Papæ Legatis (ut in Warhamo diximus) agitata quæstio. Andcere vxorem cognitam à fratre decedente sine prole sit prohibitio iuris diuini indispensabilis à Papa?
units.tr: On his arrival the question was raised again concerning the King's marriage with the Lady Catherine, the question that had been so long debated before the Pope's legates (as we said in the life of Warham) and was now renewed. Is it a prohibition of divine law, indispensable by the Pope, for a man to marry a wife who had been known by his brother, who died without issue?

units.la: Ea res primo ad inferiorem synodi Conuentum relata est. In eo affirmarunt dictam conclusionem quatuordecim, negarunt septem, dubitauit vnus, alteri; iuris esse diuini dixit sed moralis atq; dispensabilis à Papa. In superiori autem patrum Conuentu, in quo Bononiensis, Patauinensis, Parisiensis, aliarumq; vniuersitatum de ea quæstione iudicia recitata sunt, controuersia inter Strokesleyum Londinensem, & Fisherum Roffensem Episcoposaliquandiu tnota,ab omnibus patribus qui duceret sex decim personaliter vel per procuratores,intet fuerunt,praeterquam a 19. Vniuersitatum praedictarum sententus af- sensum est. Sed vt hoc negocium omni tum iuris tum facti controuertia careret, aliud quaesitum est. An carnalis copula inter serenissimum Principem Arturum, & serenissimam Dominam Catharinam ex propositis exhibitis, deductis, & allegatis sit sufficienter probatum. Diximus autem in Warhamo ante quid coram Papae Legatis ad concubitum, & congressum probandum tum propositum fuit. Sed illa prior iuris quaestio Theologorum propria fuit, haec posterior inquisitio facti, ad legum atque Canonum peritos relata est.
units.tr: This question was first referred to the lower house of the synod. There fourteen affirmed the proposed conclusion, seven denied it, one doubted, and another said that it was of divine law but moral and dispensable by the Pope. In the upper house of the Fathers, in which the judgements of the universities of Bologna, Padua, Paris and others on this question were read out, there was for some time a dispute between Stokesley, Bishop of London, and Fisher, Bishop of Rochester. All the Fathers who were present, either in person or by proxy, were sixteen in number, and they assented to the opinions of the said universities, except nineteen. But so that this business might be free from all controversy, both of law and of fact, another question was asked: whether carnal copulation between the most serene Prince Arthur and the most serene Lady Catherine had been sufficiently proved from the exhibited and alleged proofs and arguments. We said in the life of Warham what had earlier been put forward before the papal legates to prove intercourse and cohabitation. But the former question of law belonged to the theologians, while this latter inquiry into fact was referred to experts in laws and canons.

units.la: Qui quinq; aut sex dumtaxat exceptis omnes carnalem copulam luculenter probatam affirmarunt. Quorum etiam sententia ab omnibus patribus praeterquam a Bathonien- si & Wellensi Episcopo approbata est. Hi se gestis tam Parlamenti quam synodus cociliam mandato Regio protogationibus paulatim intermissa sunt. Rex ad D. Catharinam nuncios misit, vt quoniam nepharias & incestas fuisse suas nuptias ex Theologorum ac iurisperitorum tam in Anglia quam in transmarinis Vniuersitatibus constabat, dote ab Arturo Regis fratre malo e, sua; marito contenta diuertere ac discedere sponte vellet. Illa vero in proposito pertinax, respondit se ab eo vinculo dissolui nolle quod patre suo Ferdinando procurante a Papa fuit colligatum. Hoc nuncium Regem, qui Caesarem atque Papam iam coniunctos esse cognouit, vt hanc separationem impedirent, ad abrogandam Papae potestatem citius vehementius impulit. Quod vt tutius petageret, nouo cum Gallo foedus firmauit, eoq; magis quod accepisset proxima aestate Gallum atq; Papa Marsiliis in prouincia conuenturos. Itaq; vt certum Galli animum atq; sensum exploraret, per vtriusq; legatos actum est, vt Reges ad colloquium in finibus vtriusq; inter Calet- um & Bononiam maritimam interpositis conuenirent, fore enim vt mutuis postulatis & desideriis expositis artiori amicitia iungeretur. Ac obuiis iam & congressis Regib. Henricus Angliae Rex quam indignis modis in causa matrimoniali a Papa tractatus ii commemorat: dilationes, moras, cautelas, versutias omnes, & impositas narrat Theologorum ac iurisperitorum non modo in Anglia, sed in Gallia, Germania, ipsaq; Italia sententias profert, & Gillo ostendit. Nunc esse amplius eam Papalem in spiritualib. Dominationem ferendam docet, vt Christianis prouinciis synodicq; imperirarct, & in sanctissimo atque sanctis- simoq; coniugali foedere, non modo populis sed Regibus contra Christi mentem & Scrip- turas illuderet. Quid enim ei in humanis rebus sanctum esse potest, quia a Deo datas co- iugii leges quae tuolis disspensationibus audet violare, aut quod eo a recto depravatiu sexistimari debet, qui quod improbe permissum est, haud finit corrigia peritissimis sanctissimisq; Theologis didicisse se, Romano Pontificii in prinprio tantum territorio atq; prouincia non in alienis esse iudicandi potestatem: eam autem quam iam vendicat non a Christo aut Petro (prout iactitat) sed Principum ignauia & Episcoporum desidia exigui temporis (si ad aeternitatem referatur) praescriptione accepisse: prorinde iturusse se spiritualem eius non iurisdictionem vt appellat sed libidinem, & sacrorum profanatione atq; tyrannidem exterminare Anglia, & se suoq; subditos in sui regni prouinciis synodiq; de cautiss Ecclesiasticis velle iudicari. Petit ad extremum a Gallo vt idem in Gallijs suis efficiat, aut si temporum ratione impeditus id minus adhuc commode facere possit, initum tamen renouatumq; foedus seruet, cum Papae atque Caesare aduersus se non iungatur. Gallus de foedere seruando certo promittit Regi cupere etiam valde se vt Papae eiiciatur tota Gallia, daturumq; operam omnem, vt id tempore quamprimo fiat: nec timendam esse Caesaris atque Papae coniunctam potentiam, se praesertim in fide inuicem data perseuerantibus. Papam autem (facete dixit, ineratenim Francisco Gallorum Regi iucundus orationis lepos) Anglia, Gallia, Germaniaque eiectum, necessario detrudemus vt Caesari Capellanus seruiat. Hoc habito colloquio ad Bononiam itum, atque coniuatum est, co Gallus Regem Caletum reduxit, vbi cum Gallus fiuq; proceres lautius coenassent atque pernoctassent, postridie mutuis datis dextris & amplexibus foedus iterato confirmatum, Gallusque Parisios, Rexin Angliam reuersus est. In hoc reditu quod diu Re me imminebar, exitum habuit. Dilata enim (vt antea diximus) Parlamenti, synodusque, Concilia iterum a Rege indicta sunt. In Parlamento de illis iure diuino prohibitis nuptiis ex prioris synodi & Vniuersitatum praedictarum sententiis decretum est, debuissetque licite potuisse Regem ab illis vetitis nuptiis discedere, & cum integerrima lectissimaq; foemina D. Anna Bullena nuptias licitas, iuriq; diuino ac humano non consentaneas contrahere. Itaq; Cranmerus Archiepiscopus, Londinensi, Wintoniensi, Bathoniensi, ac Lincolniensi Episcopis, aliisq; permultis Praelatis Comitatus Dunnestabliam in Bedfordiensi Comitatu oppidum venit: eoq; D. Catharinam repudii sui sententiam audituram citauit. Eā vero ad iudicium vocatam & non accedentem pronunciauit contumacem, ac à Regis thoro consuetudinem; nuptiali amouit.
units.tr: Only five or six excepted, all of them affirmed that the carnal union had been clearly proved, and their opinion was approved by all the fathers except the bishops of Bath and Wells. Meanwhile, by royal command, the proceedings both of Parliament and of the synod were gradually suspended by successive prorogations. The King sent messengers to Lady Catherine. Since it was established by the judgement of theologians and jurists, both in England and in the universities overseas, that her marriage had been unlawful and incestuous, he asked whether she would of her own accord withdraw and depart, content with the dower given her by Arthur, the King's brother and her husband. She, however, was obstinate in her purpose and replied that she was unwilling to be released from the bond which her father Ferdinand had procured from the Pope. When the King learned that the Emperor and the Pope were now allied to prevent this separation, the news drove him all the more quickly and vehemently to seek the abrogation of the Pope's power. To pursue this more safely, he confirmed a new alliance with the French King, all the more because he had heard that the French King and the Pope would meet at Marseilles in the province the following summer. So, to learn for certain the French King's disposition and feeling, it was arranged through envoys on each side that the two kings should meet for a conference in the borderlands between Calais and maritime Boulogne, since by setting out their mutual demands and desires they would be joined in closer friendship. When the kings had met face to face, Henry, King of England, recounted the shameful ways in which the matrimonial cause had been handled by the Pope: the delays, postponements, cautions and all sorts of trickery. He brought forward the opinions of theologians and jurists not only in England but also in France, Germany and Italy itself, and showed them to Francis. He argued that the papal dominion in spiritual matters should no longer be endured, since it lorded it over Christian provinces and synods and, in the most holy covenant of marriage, mocked not only peoples but kings, against the mind of Christ and the Scriptures. For what in human affairs can be holy to a man who dares to violate, by his dispensations, the laws of marriage given by God? Or what can be thought more depraved, more removed from what is right, than one who does not allow what has been wickedly permitted to be corrected? He said he had learned from the most skilled and holy theologians that the Roman Pontiff has power to judge only in his own territory and province, not in the lands of others. The power he now claims, he said, he received not from Christ or Peter, as he boasts, but through the prescription of a short time (if compared with eternity), by the sloth of princes and the negligence of bishops. Therefore he would drive out of England what the Pope calls his spiritual jurisdiction, but which is in truth lust, the profanation of sacred things and tyranny; and he wished himself and his subjects to be judged in ecclesiastical causes within the provinces and synods of his own kingdom. Lastly, he asked the French King to do the same in his own French lands, or, if the circumstances of the times prevented him from doing so conveniently as yet, at least to keep the alliance made and renewed, and not to join with the Pope and the Emperor against him. The French King firmly promised to keep the alliance, and said that he too greatly wished the Pope to be expelled from all of France, and would do everything in his power to bring this about as soon as possible; nor was the combined power of the Emperor and the Pope to be feared, especially while the kings remained steadfast in the faith they had pledged to one another. "The Pope," he said wittily, for a pleasant turn of phrase came naturally to Francis, King of the French, "once expelled from England, France and Germany, we shall necessarily thrust down so that he serves the Emperor as his chaplain." After this conference they went on to Boulogne and feasted together there; then the French King escorted the King of England back to Calais. There, after the French King and his nobles had dined more lavishly and spent the night, on the following day the alliance was confirmed again with right hands given and embraces exchanged; the French King went back to Paris and the King to England. On this return, that which had long been hanging over the King came to its outcome. For the adjourned Parliament and synod (as we said before) were summoned again by the King. In Parliament it was decreed, on the judgement of the earlier synod and of the universities mentioned, that those marriages were forbidden by divine law; and the King could and should lawfully depart from those forbidden marriages and contract a lawful marriage with the most upright and choice lady, Anne Boleyn, a marriage not at odds with divine and human law. Therefore Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop, with the bishops of London, Winchester, Bath and Lincoln and very many other prelates, came to the town of Dunstable in Bedfordshire, and there summoned Lady Catherine to hear the sentence of her divorce. When she, summoned to judgement, did not appear, he pronounced her contumacious and removed her from the King's bed and from the conjugal relationship.

units.la: Deinde à Rege edictum est nec ea deinceps Regina, sed Arturi Principis fratris sui maioris propter nuptias donatūria vocaretur. Papa contrariam Romæ sententiam tulit, easq; quæ à plerisq; Academiis illicitæ decretæ nuptiæ fuerunt, sua sententia rataς esse voluit. At Rex nihilominus D. Annam Bullenam Thoma Cranmero sacra ministrante vxorem duxit, eamq; in festo Pentecostes proximo ab eadem Thoma Cranmero sacrari Westmonasterii mandauit. Ex his piis nuptiis edita est ad diuturnum Anglicani Regni Imperium atq; patrocinium, æternumque Papalis Dominationis excidium Deo sacrata virgo D. Elizabetha septimo Idus Septemb. quieo anno Dominicus dies fuit, inter horas tertiam atque quartam maturinas. Quam tertio postea die in porticu Ecclesiæ Conuenualis fratrum Minorum de Grinwich ab Episcopo Londinensi baptisatam, Reuerendissimus in Christo pater D. Thomas Cranmerus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus, ac Illustrissimæ viduæ D. Agnes Thomæ quondam Noi folciæ Ducis, &D. Margareta Thomæ quondam Marchionis Dorset relictæ in frequenti nobilium virorum ac mulierum multitudine in sacro Baptismate suscepserunt, diuinis sanè & sacris ministerius huic Angliæ Regno auspiciis. Eodem enim anno tam Parlamenti quam synodus decretis Papalis tota vis sublata & profligata fuit. In Synodo autem superiori hæc disquisitio propositæ est:
units.tr: Then the King issued an edict that she should no longer be called queen, but the dowager Princess, widow of his elder brother Prince Arthur. The Pope pronounced the contrary sentence at Rome and wished that the marriage, which most of the universities had decreed unlawful, should be held valid by his own judgement. But the King nevertheless married Anne Boleyn, with Thomas Cranmer performing the sacred rites, and ordered her to be consecrated at Westminster by the same Thomas Cranmer at the next feast of Pentecost. From this pious marriage was born, for the lasting empire and protection of the English realm and the eternal overthrow of papal domination, the virgin Elizabeth, consecrated to God. She was born on the seventh Ides of September, on the Lord's day, between the third and fourth hours of the morning, in that year. Three days later she was baptised by the Bishop of London in the porch of the conventual church of the Friars Minor at Greenwich. In the sacred baptism she was received, in the presence of a large crowd of noblemen and noblewomen, by the most reverend father in Christ, Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, and by the most illustrious widows Lady Agnes, widow of Thomas, former Duke of Norfolk, and Lady Margaret, widow of Thomas, former Marquis of Dorset. These were divine and holy rites, auspices for this kingdom of England. In that same year, by decrees of Parliament and of the synod, the whole force of papal power was abolished and overthrown. In the earlier synod this question was put forward:

units.la: An Romanus Pontifex habeat maiorem iurisdictionem collatam sibi à Deo in sacra Scriptura in hoc Regno Angliæ quàm alius quiuis extraneus Episcopus?
units.tr: Does the Roman Pontiff have, in this kingdom of England, a greater jurisdiction conferred on him by God in Holy Scripture than any other foreign bishop?

units.la: Ac à patribus quidem omnibus in superiori synodo affirmatum est, nullam iurisdictionis potestatem ex verbo Dei Papæ in Anglia competere: in inferiori autem omnes patribus assensi fuit, præter vnum qui dubitauit, & quatuor qui eam vniuersalem Ecclesiæ administrationis potestatem Papæ tribuebant.
units.tr: Indeed, all the fathers in the upper synod affirmed that the Pope had no power of jurisdiction in England by the Word of God. In the lower synod all the fathers agreed, except one who hesitated and four who attributed to the Pope that universal power of administering the Church.

units.la: Tum ab eadem synodo decretum est, vt Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus non amplius Apostolicæ sedis legatus, sed eius inanis titulí vice Primas & Metropolitanus totius Angliæ in posterum diceretur.
units.tr: Then the same synod decreed that the Archbishop of Canterbury should no longer be called legate of the Apostolic See but, in place of that empty title, should henceforth be called Primate and Metropolitan of all England.

units.la: De his actis publico à Notariis descripto instrumento Archiepiscopus Regem 50 facit certiorem. Itaque in Parlamento de appellationibus iata lex est, ne quis deinceps Romam prouocaret. Reiectaq; iam rursus in sequentem annum sunt Parlamenti synodusque Comitia.
units.tr: The Archbishop informed the King of these proceedings by a public instrument drawn up by notaries. Accordingly, a law concerning appeals was passed in Parliament, that no one should henceforth appeal to Rome. The sessions of Parliament and of the synod were again postponed to the following year.

units.la: Ac quia Pontificia potestate, authoritate synodus ex verbo Dei abdicata, multi liberi impressi & per vulgus dispersi sunt, de his primò censuit synodus, decreuitq; Regiam Maiestatem a tota synodo interpellādam, vt sacra Biblia in Anglicanum sermonem verti atq; transferri mādaret. Ita n. diffecrnia ab omnib. facilius posse, quid iuri diuino congruū atq; consentaneum fuerit. Huic rei Stephanus Gardinerus Wintoniensis Episcopus q Regiab intimis fuit consiliis, occulte quantum in se fuit, restitit. Sed clarissimæ integerrimæque D. Reginæ gratia & intercessione à Rege tandē impetratum est, vt Biblia sacra Anglicana imprimerentur, & p singula ē pla in loco, quo populo legēdi potestas fiat locarentur. Quæ tamē Regis concessio nondū effectū sortita est, qa hæc clarissima Regina capite pau-40 lo post mulctata est. Certam aūt eius rei causam ne hi quidē designant, quūRegia historia descripserunt, sed capiē cōsiterq; morte passa Regē diu fore regnō gerēdo fupsitie, ac ne quæ de sua morte perperā iudicaret pcata est. Synodus verò supiot ne litesç altercationes ex disceptationib. de reb. diuinis oriri ur, decreuit ne ex indocta plebe q qq. de Catholica fide disputaret, similesq; leges in Parlamento latæ sunt. De Rege supremo Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ capite declarando. De Clero Anglicano Regi subiiciendo. Nec quid deinceps amplius Papæ aut Romanæ curiæ quocunq; prextu ex Anglia pēdatur. De Episcopis consecrādis aliisq; q Romæ ante agerebatur, intra regnū pficiendis. De Ecclesiasticorū beneficiorum primitiis atq; decimis Principi in perpetuū soluēdis. His legib. potētia Papalis q nongetis amplius annis in Anglia durauit, quæq; superba adeo & insuperabilis vi a est, inuictissimi Regis impio, integerrimiq; pfulis cōsilio detecta facile cōcidit.
