Neq. n. in humanis reb. quicquā tā stabile atq; firmū est, q. si diuini iuris neruis ac præsidio careat, quo immensum magis ingenio fuctit, ipsa sua magnitudine atq; mole nō ruat, ppcepsad interitū. Quo magis horribilis Romanæ potētiæ casus existimari debuit, q diuina iura fœdauit, gētes Christianas supstitione infatuauit, Templūdei tenuit, ac se supra Deū extulit. Sed Papa ciecto atq; decurbato, residua adhuc in Ecclesia Anglicana fuit Romana collusiones, cuius cōtagione tā multis cā antea fœculis cōtaminauerat. Hæc annis (vt dicemus) sequentib. paulatim expurgata & abstersa est. Ad q alterū Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ fidus à cœlo delapsum est.
units.tr: And because, with papal power and authority renounced by the synod on the basis of God's Word, many books had been printed and scattered among the common people, the synod first considered these matters and decreed that His Royal Majesty should be petitioned by the whole synod to order the holy Bible to be turned and translated into English. For in this way everyone could more easily discern what agreed with and was consonant with divine law. Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, who was among the King's intimate counsellors, resisted this matter secretly as far as he could. But at last, through the favour and intercession of the most illustrious and upright Lady Queen, it was obtained from the King that the English Holy Bible should be printed and placed in each church, in every place, so that the people might have the power to read it. Yet this concession of the King did not yet take effect, because this most illustrious Queen was soon afterwards punished by beheading. Nor do even those who wrote the royal history name a definite cause for this. She suffered death by beheading, and the King was thought to be long in governing the kingdom; and lest anyone judge wrongly about her death, it was ... The earlier synod, so that no quarrels or disputes should arise from debates about divine matters, decreed that no one from the unlearned common people should dispute about the Catholic faith, and similar laws were passed in Parliament. Concerning the declaration of the King as supreme head of the English Church; concerning the subjection of the English clergy to the King; that nothing more should henceforth be paid from England to the Pope or the Roman court under any pretext; concerning the consecration of bishops and the other things formerly done at Rome, to be carried out within the kingdom; and concerning the first fruits and tithes of ecclesiastical benefices, to be paid to the Prince in perpetuity. By these laws the papal power, which had lasted in England for more than five hundred years and which seemed so proud and invincible, was easily overthrown, exposed by the counsel of the most invincible King and of the most pious and upright prelate. For nothing in human affairs is so stable and firm that, if it lacks the sinews and protection of divine right, it will not, however greatly it is tossed about by men's minds, fall by its own greatness and bulk and rush headlong to ruin. All the more dreadful should the fall of Roman power be considered, which defiled divine laws, bewitched Christian nations with superstition, held the temple of God, and exalted itself above God. But with the Pope cast out and overthrown, some remnants of Roman collusion still remained in the English Church, by whose contagion it had been polluted for so many centuries before. These, as we shall say, were gradually purged and wiped away in the following years. To this end another star of the English Church fell, as it were, from heaven.

units.la: Ee Natus n. est Hamptoniæ matre Dorothea Ocob. ex clarissima fœmina D. Iana Seimera Regina, Regitandé filius inclytus Edwardus Princeps, qui patris acta sequutus cū ad regnū, (vt postea dicemus) euectus fuisset, reliquias Pontificias abolevit. Huc Cramerus Archiep. Dux Norfolciæ, & D. Maria Regis filia in sacro baptismate suscepertū. Interim vero insignis q dā & expressa inter Christi & Antichristi membra cōcertatio atq; lucta eminebit. Nam q pfligato Papa, & suscepta Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ defensione, cura, & tutela Rex excelsū ingenii, & multarū rerū viū peritū virū Thomā Cromwellū Vicarii sui in spiritualib. generalē designauit. Hic cū Thoma Cramero Archiep. tanquā in puppi sedit, clauduq; Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ tenuit, prorā q; a Papali littore auertit, & in Christianū portū reduxit. Nam Præletorū fides eo magis dubia & incerta Regi visæ est, q; longa mora & difficultate tāquā tædio abducti sunt a Papa, sibiq; supremi capitis titulū detulissent. Qua suspicione veritus Rex ne opportunitate data ad Papā facilius redirēt, quā recessissent, eorū opera haud ita multū visus est. Etsi in his q; tuā tū iarditate purgare volebat, fuere Steph. Wintoniē sis Episcopus, qui libellū tum edidit de vera Obedientia, in quo à Papa alienissimus fuit, & summā Ecclesiæ gerendæ potestatē, primè ac secūdū Deū attribuit Principi, item Cuthbertus Tunstallus Dunelmēus, Stokeslcyus Lōdin. & Lōglandus Lincoln. Episcopi, q publicis coră Rege concionib. eandē sententiā docte fortiterq; tuebantur. Edmundus etiam Bonerus, postea (vt dicemus) Londinēsis Episcopus tū Archidiaconus Leycestriæ, qui psationem Gardineri libello pfixit, Regisq; Legatus vt Papali potestati renunciaret Romam missus est, eaq; causa Regi atq; Crumwelo charus fuit, donec Episcopalē dignitatē adeptus, reliquis adhuc Pontificiis ritib. solito, ppenfior & amicior visus fit. Permulti alii tum Regis causa in Papā tā profligatū se multa velle iactabant, quorū oratio quia à simulato magis quā vero officio profecta videbatur, authoritate atq; fide caruit. Summa aūt Ecclesiasticarū rerū his duobus, Thomæ Cranmero Archiepiscopo, & D. Cromwello Regis Vicario eōmissæ est. Itaq; altera synodo Nonis Iunii conuocata, D. Cromwellus locū sibi vtpote Regis in spiritualib. Vicario dari petiit, cui Archiepiscopus locū sibi proximū assignauit. In quaetiā synodo libellus à Clero eōpositus est, caulas nōnullas de dignas quare Regia Maiestas se intercesserit generalib. Cleri Concilijs non deberet. Hunc libellū ab omnib; subscriptū D. Cromwellus ex Régis etiam sententia approbauit. Et quia abdicata Papali potestate, retinionis totius reformatio pedetentim sequuta est, operaq; precium erit hoc in loco quomodo Cranmerus, antequam Ecclesiā, & Rempub ingressus lit, instítutus fuerat cōmemorare. Thomas Cranmerus Articleōnēz oppido Nottinghamensis Comitatus Eboracensis prouinciæ generosa iāne familia ortus est. Fuit n in Lincolniensi Comitatu elus nominis vetustus adhuc pagus dictus Granmer, Ystiligi, olim suæ getis atq; stirpis fuerat, indicanto, genii insignia eā ex Normannis, ac vna cum Guihelmo Victore exterisq; illustrib. Normannorum ducibus in Anglia ductam fuisse, quod Henrico Octauo Regeregnante nobilisquidā Gallus nomine Cramerus huc in legatione cum aliis legatis missus eadem insignia tulit: quæ Thomas Cranmerus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus ut generositatis & insignium suorum originē explorarct, ad lauas epulas inuitauit, & inquisitione à fœcialibus habita comperuit ab eadē nobilitatis origine vtroq; stirpe duxisse, nec fuisse quicq̄ ad insignibus dilcriminis aut differentiæ. Patris summa cura fuit, vt in literis puer accurate instituereteur. Ideoq; ad pedagogū ductus est, qui aspernante nimia flexibile atq; facilem, iuuenile suum animū ita pertertur, vt tota reliqua vita memoriam & alacritatē ingenii mulceri in se labefactati tenseri. Verum paterne studia tædio penitus abiu, ecerētq; delereret, pmisit ei aucupium, venationem, equitatum, arcum, aliaq; honesta ludendi exercitia interponere literis. Quibus quidem, cum iam Archiepiscopus relaxarēanimū, & abducēro se à rebus grauioribus vellet, ita vteretur, vt in famulatu suo non fuerit quisquam qui generosum equum salire ac tractare elegantius, aut aues ferasque aucupio aut venatione insequi commodius, intelligentiusque potuisset, serpe et iam etsi oculis infirmis esset, arcum tendens sagitta percussit feram. Ab informatione ista puerili Cantebrigiam venit ad Collegium Iesu nuncupatum, ibi liberalibus perceptis artibus atque Philosophia Artium Magister creatus est lamq; quia Cranmerus vxor e domi xisset, nec Collegiorum sociis esse ex locorum statutis permissa coniugia, collegio cederet coadtus est. Sed cum ne coniugatus quidem literarum studia deseruerit, sed Scholares publicas, disputationes & lectiones frequentaret, in altero Cantebrigiensis Academiæ Collegio quod Buckinghamēnse appellatur, quia doctrina celebratae & vitæ integritate notus fuisset decretum ei est præleotoris salarium. Iuse mereede pubblica docuit, & suus coniugisque inopiam subleuauit. Verum quia non suppetebant abunde facultates, coactus est coniugi & mensam & cœnaculum in eo diuersorio Cantebrigiæ parare quem Delphinatē nuncupant. Eius enim domus materfamilias affinuis illi fuit, quoetiā is vxoris gratia conuenit sæpe. Atque hæc causa fuit cur à pontificiis qui dignitatiā atque famæ integerrimi doctissimique viri posteā detrahebant, indoctas & in campoña non in schoolis educatus diceretur. De quo quidem maleuolorum hominum conuicio plura deinceps dicenda sunt. Verūm alterò a uupiis anno vxor Crameri grauida in puerperio decessit. Postquam obitū ab eodem Iesu Collegio à quo procrearus primò Cantebrigiæ fuit, iterum in pristinum locum repetitus est. Ac tanta quidem doctrinæ laude perereb uit, vt cum Wolceus Cardinalis augustissimum quidem Collegium Oxonii (vt in Warhamo antea diximus) condere inciperet, illuduque doctissimis viris ex toto Regno conquisitis replete statuisset, Cranmerum ad Collegii sui societatem expeteret. Sed Cranmerus cum iam esset in itinere à quibusdam suis necessarijs obuijs admonitus est, vt quoniam se à cæteris artibus ad Theologiæ studium transtulisset, in eaque humilitate magis quàm magnificentiam sectari debuisset, à Collegio Iesu tanquam aptioti commodioi atque suo institutio loco non discederet. Itaque reuersus paulò post Theologiam prælector docuit, ac eiusdem Doctor seu professor à Cantebrigiensibus Theologis ascriptus est. Eaque in Theologiæ gradu existimatione Cantebrigiæ vixit, vt cum hi qui gradum aliquē petuit, attribus maximæ authoritatis & doctrinæ viris antequam gradu donentur examinari debeant, quotiesin Theologia aliquis promouendus esset, D. Cranmerus Academiæ iudicio è tribus censoribus semper vnus fuit. Itaq; à promouendis diligenter explorabat, virum omissis Scoti, Lombardi, ac huiusmodi Theologomachorum argutiis recta & genuinum Christianæ doctrinæ sensum ex sacris Scripturis libasset, aliquum repellebat. Quā de causa Monachis, Fratribus ac toti Scholasticæ tixiæ Theologorum turbæ, qui hoc censore semper in gradus petitione repulsam passi sunt; inuisus fuit. Ac vt Theologiā à barbarie vendicaret, adiecit literas Græcas & Hebraicas, quarum fa nè post suscepit Doctoratus gradum constat eum perstudiosum fuisse. Quibus perceptis antiquissimos tam Græcos quā Latinos Patres euoluit, Cōcilia omnia & antiquitatem ad ipsa Apostolorum tempora inuestigauit, Theologiam totam detracta illa quam sophistæ obduxerant vitiata cute ad viuum refecauit. Quam tamen non doctrina magis quam moribus atque vita expressit. Mita enim temperantia, mira animi lenitate atque placabilitate fuit, vt nulla iniuria aut contumelia ad iram aut vindictam prouocari posset, inimicissimosq; quorum vim ac potentiam etsi depexit ac leuiter tulit, ab offensione tamen ad inimicitias deponendas atq; gratiam ineundam summa sæpe humanitate duxit. Eam præterea constantiam, grauitatem, ac moderationem præ se tulit vt idonus vanietate, rebusq; siue secundis, siue aduersis vunquam turbari animum ex fronte vultuq; collegeres. His naturæ doctrinaq; dotibus ornatus ad Regem Henricum Octauum a occasione quæ illicitis nuptiis de quibus tam iu hoc tractatur quàm in superiore diximus, interuenit, tanquàm faro atque coelitus ductus est. Eiusque ad Papam Clementem & Carolum Cæsarem Legatus à Papa generalis Angliæ pronunciatiatus, à Rege Archidiaconus Tauntonensis creabatur Sed eum sibi (vt diximus) à Rege magnum de antedictis nuptiis negocium mandaretur, quamdiu Cæsarin expeditione contra Turcā Viennam obsidentem detinebatur, morām Norinbergæ fecit, hospitiōque Andreæ Osiandri vsus est, cum quo secunda coniugę ducta contraxit affinitatem. Sed Cæsarem in Hispanias post bellum Viennense in quo Turcæ profligari fuerūt, sequutus, eam in Germania cum consanguineis dimisit, donec in Angliam rediret. Postquam ea (vt dixi mus) redditum Wathamo mortuo ad Archiepiscopale culmen euectus est. Atqi ab his quidem piis & secundis initiis Cranmerus ad Archiepiscoporum gerendum progressus est. Thomæ verò Cromwellius educationem & variosfortunæ eius quos pertulerit, antequā ad Regem ducereturg, siccō pede prætereundos diximus, quoniam ea omnia satis fuse ab aliis traētara fuerunt.
units.tr: Prince Edward, the famous son of King Henry, was born at Hampton in October to the most illustrious lady Jane Seymour, the queen. When he came to the throne, as we shall say later, he followed his father's deeds and abolished the remnants of Popery. Archbishop Cranmer, the Duke of Norfolk, and Lady Mary, the King's daughter, stood as sponsors at his sacred baptism. Meanwhile a remarkable and clearly marked struggle between the members of Christ and of Antichrist came to the fore. When the Pope had been overthrown and the defence, care and protection of the English Church had been taken up, the King appointed Thomas Cromwell, a man of great ability and wide experience in many affairs, as his Vicar-General in spiritual matters. Cromwell, together with Archbishop Thomas Cranmer, sat as if at the stern. They held the rudder of the English Church, turned its prow away from the Papal shore, and brought it back into the Christian harbour. For the bishops' loyalty seemed too doubtful and uncertain to the King, since they had been drawn away from the Pope after long delay and difficulty, as if by weariness, and had granted him the title of supreme head. Fearing that, given the opportunity, they might return to the Pope as easily as they had left him, the King did not think much of their help. Yet among those who wished to clear themselves of this charge of insincerity were Stephen, Bishop of Winchester, who then published a little book on true obedience, in which he was most hostile to the Pope and attributed the highest power of governing the Church, first and second only to God, to the Prince; likewise Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, Stokesley, Bishop of London, and Longland, Bishop of Lincoln, who in public sermons before the King learnedly and courageously defended the same opinion. Edmund Bonner also, later (as we shall say) Bishop of London, who was then Archdeacon of Leicester, prefixed a preface to Gardiner's book and was sent to Rome as the King's envoy to renounce the papal power; for this reason he was dear to the King and to Cromwell, until, having obtained the episcopal dignity, he seemed more inclined and friendly, as usual, to the remaining Popish rites. Many others at that time, for the King's sake, boasted that they wished to do much against a Pope so thoroughly overthrown; but since their speech seemed to come from pretence rather than from genuine duty, it lacked authority and credit. The sum of ecclesiastical affairs was entrusted to these two, Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop, and Lord Cromwell, the King's Vicar. Accordingly, when another synod was convened on the Nones of June, Lord Cromwell asked that the place of honour be given to him, as the King's Vicar in spiritual matters, and the Archbishop assigned him the place next to himself. In this same synod a little book was composed by the clergy, setting out certain reasons why the royal majesty ought not to interpose itself in the general councils of the clergy. Lord Cromwell, subscribed to by all, approved this little book, also with the King's agreement. And since, the papal power having been renounced, the reformation of the whole realm followed gradually, it will be worth the trouble at this point to recall how Cranmer had been brought up before he entered the Church and the commonwealth. Thomas Cranmer was born of a noble family in the town of Aslockton, in Nottinghamshire, in the province of York. For in Lincolnshire there is still an old village of that name, called Cranmer, which was once the seat and stock of his kin, as the family arms indicate: that they were brought into England from the Normans, together with William the Conqueror and other illustrious leaders of the Normans. In the reign of Henry VIII, a noble Frenchman named Cranmer came here on an embassy with other envoys and bore the same arms. Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, wishing to learn the origin of his nobility and of his arms, invited him to a splendid banquet, and by inquiry among the heralds found that both lines derived from the same noble origin, and that there was no difference or distinction in their arms. His father took the greatest care that the boy be carefully instructed in letters. For this reason he was led to a tutor who, by excessive indulgence and easy handling, so spoiled his youthful mind that for the rest of his life his memory and liveliness of wit were, as it were, weakened and impaired. But when he had wholly lost interest in his father's studies, and his father was unwilling to let him waste away, he allowed him to mix in fowling, hunting, riding, archery and other honourable pastimes with his letters. Indeed, when the Archbishop wished to relax his spirit and withdraw from weightier matters, he so enjoyed these that among his household there was no one who could ride and manage a spirited horse more gracefully, or pursue birds and wild beasts by fowling or hunting more skilfully and knowledgeably. Once, though his eyes were weak, he drew his bow and struck a deer with an arrow. From this boyish training he came to Cambridge, to the college called Jesus, where, having taken the liberal arts, he was created Master of Arts in Philosophy. Then, because Cranmer had married and his wife had died, and according to the statutes of the colleges marriage was not permitted to fellows, he was compelled to give up his fellowship in the college. But although he was now married, he did not abandon his literary studies; he frequented public lectures, disputations and readings. Then, in another Cambridge college called Buckingham, he was granted the salary of a reader, because he was known for celebrated learning and integrity of life. He taught by public pay and relieved his own and his wife's poverty. But since his resources were not sufficient, he was forced to prepare a table and lodging for his wife in the inn at Cambridge called the Dolphin. For the mistress of that house was a relative of his, and he often met his wife there. This was the reason why the Papists, who later detracted from the dignity and reputation of this most upright and learned man, said that he was uneducated and brought up in the tavern rather than in the schools. We shall have more to say about this slander of ill-disposed men. But in the second year after that, Cranmer's wife, pregnant, died in childbirth. After her death he was again restored to his former place in the same Jesus College where he had first been educated at Cambridge. And he so excelled in the praise of learning that when Cardinal Wolsey began to found the most splendid college at Oxford (as we said earlier in Warham's time), and wished to fill it with the most learned men sought out from the whole kingdom, he sought Cranmer for the fellowship of his college. But when Cranmer was already on the journey, he was warned by some of his close friends on the way that, since he had turned from the other arts to the study of theology, he ought to seek humility rather than magnificence in it, and should not leave the College of Jesus, as the more suitable and fitting place of his training. And so, returning shortly afterwards, he lectured on theology and was enrolled by the Cambridge theologians as a Doctor or professor of that subject. And he lived in such esteem in the rank of theology at Cambridge that whenever anyone sought that degree, he had to be examined before three censors of the greatest authority and learning before the degree was conferred; and whenever someone was to be promoted in theology, Dr Cranmer was always one of the three censors chosen by the judgement of the University. Accordingly, he carefully examined those to be promoted, and whoever had drawn the true and genuine sense of Christian doctrine from the Holy Scriptures, setting aside the subtleties of Scotus, Lombard and such theological wranglers, he admitted; whoever did not, he rejected. For this reason he was hated by the monks, friars and the whole crowd of scholastic theologians, who, whenever this censor was present, were repulsed in their petition for degrees. And to rescue theology from barbarism, he added Greek and Hebrew letters, in which it is certain that he was most diligent even after taking the doctorate. Having acquired these, he read through the most ancient Fathers, both Greek and Latin, investigated all the councils and antiquity back to the very times of the Apostles, and restored the whole of theology to life, stripping away that corrupted skin which the sophists had drawn over it. Yet he expressed it not so much by teaching as by his morals and way of life. For he had remarkable self-control and wonderful gentleness and placability of spirit, so that no injury or insult could provoke him to anger or revenge; and although he despised and lightly bore his most bitter enemies, whose power and influence he did not fear, he often showed great kindness in laying aside their hostility and making peace with them after offence. Moreover, he displayed such constancy, gravity and moderation that no one could see in his face or countenance any vanity, nor any disturbance of mind whether in prosperity or adversity. Adorned with these gifts of nature and learning, he was brought, as if by chance and as if sent from heaven, to King Henry VIII, through the occasion of those unlawful marriages which are discussed here at length and which we mentioned above. He was declared the Pope's general legate for England to Pope Clement and to Charles Caesar, and was appointed by the King Archdeacon of Taunton. But when the King had given him (as we said) a great matter concerning the aforesaid marriages to handle, while Caesar was detained in the campaign against the Turks besieging Vienna, he stayed at Nuremberg and lodged with Andreas Osiander, with whose family he formed a relationship by marrying a second wife. But after the war of Vienna, in which the Turks were routed, he followed Caesar into Spain, and left his wife in Germany with her relatives until he should return to England. After that (as I have said), on the death of Warham, he was raised to the archiepiscopal summit. And from these pious and fortunate beginnings Cranmer advanced to the conduct of the archbishopric. As for Thomas Cromwell, we said that his education and the various fortunes he endured before he was brought to the King had to be passed over lightly, since all these things have been treated at sufficient length by others.

units.la: Sed cum vices regias in spiritualium administratione gereret, Cranmero Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo scripsit, vt Episcopos conuocaret, in quorum catam ac conuentum Cromwellius ingressus declarauit Regis esse voluntatem ritus ac ceremonias Ecclesiasticas ad scripturarum normam redigere, omniaque ex Ecclesiis delere quae authoritate diuini verbi non niteretur.
units.tr: But while he was exercising the king's authority in ecclesiastical affairs, Cromwell wrote to Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, to summon the bishops. When Cromwell entered their assembly, he declared that it was the king's will to bring the ecclesiastical rites and ceremonies back to the norm of Scripture, and to remove from the churches everything that did not rest on the authority of the divine word.

units.la: Absurdum enim me esse cum in eo saluris æternæ lex continearur, è glossographis, Interpretationibus, aut pontificijs decretis pendere Christianos. Actum q primò est tanquam exepli eausa denoui testamenti fuisse ribus seu sacramentis, de quibus Cromwellius fog auit Alexandrū quendam Alesiū Scotum virum in Theologia perductum, quem secu in consilium adduxerat vt sententiam suā diceret. Is verbo diuino instituta tantum duo, Cœnā, & Baptismum probauit.Contra quem Stokesleyus Londinensis Episcopus,ex Gratiana Decretorum Rhapsodia acriter contendit de illis tum vulgatis & nonis septe sacramentis.Stockesleyum sequuti sunt Eboracensis Archiepisc. Lincolniensis, Bathonienfis, Ciceftrensis,atq; Norwicensis. Tum Cranmerus cum ex hoc cautissime a Cromwellio iniecto scrupulo pontificiam sectam perspexisset, grauissima & doctissima oratione de anthoritate verbi Dei,de vi vsuq; sacramentorum, de humanis traditionibus,de Monachorum & Clericorum votisatq; coelibatu. multisq; aliis, verbi authoritate carent quae differuit.Non esse Episcopalis ordinis & integritatis dixit praeter sanctas Scripturas aliquid, in Cocilio praesertim, affirmate aut statuere, verborum aucupationes, & eiusmodi nugas arcendas a Cocilijs, & reiiciendas ad sophistas in scholis. Quae cum dixisset, Foxus Herefordensis Episcopus,qui ex Germanica legatione in quam a Rege missus esset paulo ante redierat,subiunxit. Non esse iam amplius in tam clara & perspicua propagati Euangelii luce hallucinandi tempus praelatis, ipsi iam plebi apertos oculos radiis atque claritate Euangelii.In Germania passim ad veritatem & amussim Hebraici Graeciq; idiomatis sic in maternam linguam versa sacra Biblia, vt commentariis, glossisq; populus nō egeret, esseq; indoctos in sacris Scripturis periliores quàm pleriosq; praelatos. Itaque tempus ipsum sanos omnes admonere, ne intempreses nimium tanquam ruuulos secentur, sed ad vberrimum Scripturarum fontem recurrerent. Multa vtrinque dicta & responsa, retorta, ac prolata sunt. Cranmero Archiepiscopo, Saributiensis, Elicensis, Herefordensis, Wigorniensis Episcopi, aliique nonnulli praelati adhaeserant. Atq; haec consilii communicatione olfecerunt Cranmerus & Cromwellus qui in pontificia sententia adhuc fortebant, quiqué ad nitorem & puritatem verbi aspirabant. Rex verò ex horum consiliis tum ea quae adumbrata & fucata specie Christianam religionem prae se ferebant, extitit parare apud se decreuisset, primò Idololatriam ex his locis ad quae peregrinantes superstitiosè confluebant, & mortuorum imagines adorabant, sustulit,ipsaque delubra funditus euertit. Deinde manum fratrum,nec non Monialium impuris Coenobiis admouit. Quorum omnium flagitia, ficta quèmitacula ad captandum a populo quaestum diuulgauit. Ac quia data ei a synodo atque Parlamento authoritas fuit, in Anglicana Ecclesia visitandi atque corrigendi, inquisitores per totam Angliam constituti sunt, qui Monasteriorum statum, morésque ac conuersationes Monachorum explorarent. Hi autoritate fusceptapro anno de inquilitis certiorem faciunt. Interea Papa Cöcilium generale indixit Mantuae. Ac Rex promulgauit, non esse penes Papam, sed Caesarem atq; Reges Concilium conuocandorum potestatem. Deinde locum ipsum non esseturum his qui Papae obijcerc vellent ea crimina quorum poenis reus enetetur. Ad extremum Regi ipsi maximè insidiosum, Caesare praesertim atque Gallo mutuo se Marte infestantibus, in quorum alterum incidere sibi necesse sit ex Papae insidijs, quia ex Anglia eiectus Regem excommunicauit, & vindicta atque odio alios in eum Reges excitauit.
units.tr: For it was absurd, he said, that Christians should depend on glossators, interpretations or papal decrees, when the law of eternal salvation is contained in the New Testament. First, by way of example, the rites and sacraments were discussed. On these Cromwell consulted a certain Alexander Alesius, a Scot learned in theology, whom he had brought with him into the council so that he might state his opinion. Alesius approved only two institutions as having been instituted by the divine word, the Supper and Baptism. Against him Stokesley, Bishop of London, argued sharply from the Decretum of Gratian, defending those seven sacraments commonly held. Stokesley was followed by the Archbishop of York and the bishops of Lincoln, Bath, Chichester and Norwich. Then Cranmer, who had perceived from the scruple so cautiously raised by Cromwell that the papist faction was at work, delivered a very weighty and learned speech on the authority of God's word, on the power and use of the sacraments, on human traditions, on the vows of monks and clergy and on celibacy, and on many other matters that lack the warrant of the word. He said that it did not befit the episcopal order and integrity to affirm or establish anything beyond holy Scripture, especially in a council, and that verbal quibbles and such trifles should be kept out of councils and left to the sophists in the schools. When he had said this, Foxe, Bishop of Hereford, who had lately returned from the German embassy to which the king had sent him, added that there was no longer any time for prelates to be deceived in the so clear and plain light of the spreading Gospel, since the common people now had their eyes opened by the rays and brightness of the Gospel. In Germany, he said, the holy Bible had been turned into the mother tongue everywhere, with such fidelity to the Hebrew and Greek idiom, that the people needed no commentaries or glosses, and the unlearned were more skilled in the Scriptures than most prelates. Therefore the very times warned all sensible men not to follow the untaught too closely, as though they were little streams, but to return to the most abundant fountain of Scripture. Many things were said and answered on both sides, turned back and put forward. The bishops of Salisbury, Ely, Hereford and Worcester, and some other prelates, adhered to Cranmer. In this exchange of counsel, Cromwell and Cranmer perceived that those who still clung to papal opinion were striving for the purity and clarity of the Word. The king, however, resolved, on the basis of their counsels, to root out of his realm those things which, under a shadowy and feigned appearance, presented themselves as the Christian religion. First he removed idolatry from those places to which pilgrims flocked superstitiously and adored the images of the dead, and he razed the shrines to the ground. Then he laid hands on the friars and also on the nuns in the impure cloisters. He published abroad the crimes and fictitious miracles of them all, so as to win gain from the people. Since the Synod and Parliament had given him authority to visit and correct the English Church, inquisitors were appointed throughout England to examine the state of the monasteries and the morals and conduct of the monks. Having taken up their authority, these men report to the king each year about those they have examined. Meanwhile the Pope called a general council at Mantua, and the king proclaimed that the power of convening councils belonged not to the Pope but to the Emperor and the kings. He further declared that the place would not be safe for those who wished to bring against the Pope the charges for which he himself deserved punishment. Finally, the danger was especially great for the king himself, since the Emperor and the French king were attacking each other in mutual war, and it was necessary for him to fall into one of their hands because of the Pope's snares, the Pope having been expelled from England and having excommunicated the king and stirred other kings to vengeance and hatred against him.

units.la: Anno sequenti Reginaldus Polus, qui paulò ante in Cardinalium numerum a Paulo Tertio ascriptus erat, quia cum Papa in Regem cōspirasset, Papaeq; nuncius & Legatus Caesarem, Gallum, aliosq; principes in Regem tam sua suasione, quàm pa palibus mandatis prouocassset, Regiam maiestatem laesisse iudicatus, & proscriptus est. Quae hoc in loco tantum attingimus, quia de eo narrando proximus locus futurus est. At proximo huic anno totius poni ficiae improbitatis quasi radix excisa est, totus enim Monachorum cassus atq; Grex, qui à Dunstano (vt diximus) institutus servitium, ab Henr. 8. Regeinquisitionem, Cranmero Archiprasule sanctissimo, Cromwello consiliario sagacissimo ad nihilum tedactus est.
units.tr: In the following year Reginald Pole, who shortly before had been enrolled among the cardinals by Paul III, was judged to have injured the royal majesty and was outlawed. He had conspired with the Pope against the king, and as papal nuncio and legate he had incited the Emperor, the French king and other princes against the king, both by his persuasion and by papal mandates. We touch on this only here, because the next place will be the account of him. But in that very next year the root, as it were, of all papal wickedness was cut out. The whole crew and flock of monks, which had been instituted by Dunstan (as we said), was reduced to nothing by Henry VIII, through the inquiry of Cranmer, the most holy archbishop, and Cromwell, the most shrewd counsellor.

units.la: An.1539 Gardineti Wiotoniensis Episcopi, qui tecens à duabus magoitum momenti legationibus, Cæsare nimirum atq; Gallo, redierat, gratia, versutia & potentia, Rex pootificiorum importunitati, eam legum sœuitiam concedere inuito pene animo coactus est.
units.tr: In 1539, through the favour, cunning and power of Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, who had lately returned from two embassies of great importance, namely to the Emperor and to the French king, the king, forced almost against his inclination by the importunity of the Papists, conceded that savage law.

units.la: Id ex eo perspici potest quòd lata tam cruenta lege, cum sacerdotum io ea, conIugia capite sancita fuissent, Cranmerum non minus ob legis cui interesset ratio, cum ad tempus antecessit, cuius in ea mater. ...
units.tr: This can be seen from the fact that when so cruel a law was enacted, with marriages of priests also sanctioned by capital punishment, Cranmer, no less because of the reasoning of the law in which he was involved, when he went ahead for a time, whose mother in it... ...

units.la: Horū procerum à Rege aduentū expectauit, epulis laute instructis excepit. Illi ex Regis sententia vt eum metu ac solicitudine liberarent, Regis in eum beneuolentiam exponebant, facundiam, grauitatem, modestiam, doctrinam, quæ in eo summa fuerit omnia præterea eius io Parlamento acta atque dicta laudabant, non esse causam vllam quare exposita sua de tantis rebus piè, diserte, atque docte sententia (etsi ea non prætualuit) de disfentiebus (quos in ipsa dissensione ac opinionis diserepantia sibi valde eociliabat) quicquam formidaret ac pertimesceret, Wolecum Cardinalem suos necessarios ac coniunctos nimia opinione sui, ac elatione animi abalienasse, Cramerum etiam in re diuina adueros sibi pietate, elementia, atque facilitate adiungere.
units.tr: The king's nobles, who had been expected to arrive, received him with lavish banquets. In accordance with the king's wishes, in order to free him from fear and anxiety, they set out the king's goodwill toward him and praised his eloquence, gravity, modesty and learning, all of which were in him in the highest degree; they also praised his acts and words in Parliament. There was, they said, no reason why he should fear or dread that his pious, eloquent and learned opinion on such great matters (although it had not prevailed) would alienate those who dissented, whom he had in fact greatly conciliated to himself by that very disagreement. Cardinal Wolsey, they said, had estranged his necessary and close associates by excessive self-regard and haughtiness of spirit, whereas Cranmer would win over to himself, in matters of religion, those who were hostile, by his piety, clemency and affability.

units.la: Sed hic sermo qui Cranmero consolando adhibitus fuit, ad Cromwellii eonuiitum conuersus est.
units.tr: But this speech, which had been used to console Cranmer, was turned against Cromwell.

units.la: Hac tanquam contumelia tactus Cromwellus respondit se Wolcæi mores haud probasse, etsi in famulatu eius aliquandiu fuisset.
units.tr: Stung by this insult, Cromwell replied that he had not approved of Wolsey's manners, although he had been in his service for some time.

units.la: Ex illis duobus Ducibus diuxit vnus, neminem eognouisse magis inter Ctanmeri & Wolcæi consuetudinem atque mores, interfuisset quam Cromwellum, cum & vtrūq; nouerit, & Wolcæi seruus fuisset.
units.tr: Of those two leaders, one remarked that no one knew better the intimacy and manners of Cranmer and Wolsey than Cromwell, since he had known both and had been Wolsey's servant.

units.la: Id ex eo perspici potest quòd tam cruenta lege. Gardinerus Wintoniensis Episcopus Regem vehementius in Euangelicos incitabant, totiusq; crudelitatis in Anglia pootificiæ authores fuerunt. Boneruseum & legatam, & Gardineri gratia, & Norfolciæ Ducis potentia, & Regis inclinatione vacillate causam Euangelii senserat, tuòtes (vtipse purauit) partes sequutus, à Cranmero & Cromwello defecit, adhæsitq; pontificiis.
units.tr: This can be seen from the fact that by so cruel a law, Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, urged the king more vehemently against the evangelicals, and they were the authors of all the papist cruelty in England. Bonner, the legate, and through the favour of Gardiner, the power of the Duke of Norfolk, and the king's inclination, sensing that the cause of the Gospel was wavering, followed (as he himself claimed) the safer side, defected from Cranmer and Cromwell, and adhered to the papists.

units.la: {y} Ioan. 3.
units.tr: {y} John 3.

units.la: Tomimq; huius turbulentissimæ tempestatis sictum in Cromwellum atque Cranmerum pontificii vibrabant. Quibus sublatis ipsi Monachi qui stipendiis iam alebantur ad clavstra se reuersuros speran-bant. Cromwellus breui postea ponrificiorum odiis capitis accusatus, sine fui defensione primus praeter exemplum condemnatus est. Quo non fuit aut religione ergadeum, aut fidelitate in Regem, aut prudentia in Remp. aut in benemeritos gratitudine, aut in omnes pietate, charitate ac benevolentia maiore tunc in Anglia quisquam. Cuius virtus singularis eo est admirabilior, quòd etsi in illa senstina pontificia sub Wolceo Cardinali multis annis versatus omnes Romanas tecbinas & inposturas calluisset, tamen à naturæ bonitate, nunquam corruptus degeneraurit, sed per-cepto Euangelio ab illis animo toto studioq; abhorruit. Verùm ab eius laudibus, quas, ut conuenit, non attigimus, periequi certe non possumus, ad Cranmerum redeamus. Cranmerus iam in ludu & squafore ob Cromwelli necem positus, à pontificiis postulatus, omnium vocibus iactatus, etsi ne minimum temporis momentum sibi a pernicie securum existimauit, tamen nec animo succubuit, nec frontis hilaritatem mutauit, quia constantia, grauitate, ac modestia singulari ipsum Regem à pontificiis pene abductum in Euangelii defensione continuit. Ac Rex pontificiorum iam consuetudine implicatus, etsi undique contraeum quaerelæ variæ deferebantur, quarum tædio concedere hominis insontis sibi; charissimi vnà pontificiis pene cogeretur, diuino tamen instinctu ita conciliatus atque intimo affectu ei deuinctus fuit, vt cum integerrimi patris salus maximè oppugnaretur à pontificiis, atque defpareretur à piis, Rex tamen eum incolumē sal20 uum; vehit. Primum autem Gardinetus Wintoniensis Episcopus pontificiorum iam Coryphæus, saltuosus legista, cuius tum authoritas atq; gratia cum Rege maxima putabatur, multis cum disputationibus in Theologia coram Rege prouocauit. In quibus prudenter animaduertit Rex Cranmerum nunquam ab insita innataq; gravitate modestiaq; recessisse, Gardinerumq; gloriolam magis quàm veritatem affectasse. Itaqi cum Garduerus vt factarum Scripturarum authoritatem imminueret, eos qui vulgariter Apostolorum canones perhibentur eiusdem cum sacris literis potestatis esse, his quibus poterat paralogisinis contenderet, Cranmerus pacato atque moderato sermone ita viomnein eorum quæ dixisset, Rege audiente, labefactauit, vt Rex Gardinero multis præsentibus diceret. Cranmerum in Theologia veteranum esse, neque lacessendum à Ty- 30 ronibus. Verùm Gardinerus fastutumens quofcunq; poterat in Cranmerum incitauit, eo enim sublato nihil obstare putauit ponrificiorum consiliis ac propositis potuisse. Cáruariæ ac in Cantio toto multi Gardinero, pcurante suppositi sunt, qui Cranmerū hæresis clandestinis delatis querelis & accusationibus impetrent. Eodemq; tempore in Parlamento Goltwikus quidam Comitatus Bedfordiensis miles palam affirmauit totius in Angliam hæreticæ sectionis seminarii a Cranmero Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo eiusque familia profluxisse. Proceres nonnulli Regisq; consiliarii cum Rege egerunt, vt quia tanta hæreticæ factionis infamia Cranmerus laboraret, concilio aliquantisper exclusus, in Turri Londinensi carceribus abderetur, donec de fide atq; veritate eorum quæ percrebuissent, inquisitio fieret. 40 Eo enim in consilio sedente, singulos ea quæ scirent ac proferre & indicare vellent, metu celaturos. Rumores per vulgus disseminat Cranmerum tacito Regis iudicio iam esse condemnatum, pœnamq; capitis (prout paulo ante Cromwellus) palam subiturum. Ipse etsi vultu simulassef spem aliquam aperte, tamen intimis amicis lachrymas copiose fudit, tempotumq; magis quàm suam propriam conditionem deploravit. Ab omnibus tam inimicis quam necessariis designatus ad necem vltimumq; supplicium putabatur. Rex has pontificiorum insidias explorabat, & quorsum tenderet, diligenter obseruabat. A cœna semel cum animi relaxandi gratia cimba huc illuc transfuehi vellet, nautam qui proram, tenuit iussit Lametham appellere, & à quibusdam Archiepiscopi seruulis in ponte Lamethano forte stantibus animaduertsum & Regiam cimbam eo appropinquare, res est citò renunciata Archiepiscopo, is celeriter sua domo ad pontem excessit, Regem præternauigantem salutaturus, aut in ripam & in suam domum excepturus. Rex eum cimbam ingredi, ac propter se assidere iussit, secreto eum longoq; sermone detinuit, nautæ interim huc illuc cimbam deducunt. 50 Inter cætera conquestus est sermone satis simulato Rex Angliam à Cromwelli morte hæreticis factionibus atque partibus esse valde perturbatam, timendumq; valde ne si diu huiusmodi litigia atq; altercationes religionis prætextu fouerentur, intestina nascerētur grauiora mala, atque bella ciuilia, proinde protinus pacandas esse de rebus diuinis dissen-
units.tr: Amid this most turbulent storm, the Papists also hurled their darts at Cromwell and Cranmer. With these two removed, the monks, who were already being supported by pensions, hoped to return to their cloisters. Cromwell was soon afterwards accused of a capital crime through the hatred of the Papists, and he was condemned without any defence, the first man ever condemned in such a way. No one in England at that time surpassed him in piety toward God, loyalty to the King, prudence in the commonwealth, gratitude to those who had deserved well, or in kindness, charity and goodwill toward all. His singular virtue is all the more admirable because, although he had spent many years in that papal workshop under Cardinal Wolsey and had mastered all the Roman arts and impostures, he was never corrupted or degenerated from his natural goodness. Once he had grasped the Gospel, he shrank from those things with his whole mind and zeal. But we cannot possibly pursue his praises, which, as is fitting, we have not touched upon; let us return to Cranmer. Cranmer, now placed in prison and squalor because of Cromwell's death, was called to account by the Papists and assailed by everyone's voices. Although he thought he was not safe from ruin even for the smallest moment, he neither gave way in spirit nor changed the cheerfulness of his face, because by his singular constancy, gravity and modesty he kept the King, who had been almost drawn away from the Papists, steadfast in the defence of the Gospel. The King, entangled in the habits of the Papists, was pressed on all sides by various complaints against Cranmer. Wearied by these, he was almost compelled to give up that innocent man, his dearest friend, together with the Papists. Yet, by a divine impulse, he was so won over and so bound to him by inward affection that, although the safety of this most upright father was fiercely attacked by the Papists and despaired of by the godly, the King nevertheless wished him to be safe and sound. First, Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, already the leader of the Papists, a tricky lawyer whose authority and favour with the King were then thought very great, challenged Cranmer in many disputations in theology before the King. In these the King shrewdly noticed that Cranmer never departed from his innate gravity and modesty, and that Gardiner aimed at vainglory rather than truth. Thus, when Gardiner, to diminish the authority of the Scriptures, contended with fallacies that the so-called Canons of the Apostles have the same authority as the sacred writings, Cranmer, with a calm and moderate speech, overturned the whole of what he had said, the King listening, so that the King said to Gardiner, in front of many, that Cranmer was a veteran in theology and was not to be provoked by novices. But Gardiner, swollen with pride, stirred up whomever he could against Cranmer, for he thought that with Cranmer removed nothing could stand in the way of the Papists' plans and purposes. At Canterbury and throughout all Kent, many men were set up at Gardiner's instigation to assail Cranmer with secret informations, complaints and accusations of heresy. At the same time, in Parliament, one Goltwick, a knight of Bedfordshire, openly declared that the seed-bed of the whole heretical sect in England had flowed from Cranmer, the Archbishop of Canterbury, and his household. Some nobles and the King's counsellors urged the King that, since Cranmer labored under so great an infamy of heretical faction, he should be shut out from the council for a while and confined in the prisons of the Tower of London, until an inquiry was made into the truth of the rumours that had spread. For while the council was sitting, they thought that individuals would through fear conceal what they knew and what they wished to bring forward and reveal. Rumours spread among the people that Cranmer had already been condemned by the King's tacit judgement and would openly undergo the capital penalty, as Cromwell had shortly before. Himself, although he had openly feigned some hope in his face, shed copious tears among his intimate friends, and lamented the times more than his own condition. Marked out by all, enemies and friends alike, he was thought destined for death and the ultimate punishment. The King was probing these snares of the Papists and carefully watching where they were tending. Once, after dinner, wishing to be ferried hither and thither in a boat for the sake of relaxing his mind, he ordered the boatman who held the prow to put in at Lambeth. When some of the Archbishop's servants, standing by chance on Lambeth bridge, noticed the royal barge approaching there, the news was quickly reported to the Archbishop. He hastened from his house to the bridge, to greet the King as he sailed past, or to receive him on the bank and at his house. The King ordered him to board the barge and sit beside him; he kept him in secret and long conversation, while the boatmen steered the barge hither and thither. Among other things, the King complained, in a speech that was quite feigned, that England since Cromwell's death had been greatly disturbed by heretical factions and parties, and that it was very much to be feared that if such quarrels and disputes were long fostered under the pretext of religion, graver evils, even civil wars, would arise from within; therefore the disputes over divine matters must be settled at once.

units.la: dissensiones. Id vt fieret consilium habere se ex præsulum, proceru mq; nonnullorum sententiis,explorare quis esset huius tanti mali author atque hæresiarcha,& ad totam reliquam turbam comprescendam,atque sedandam,de eo atroces pœnas sumere, crudeliterque exurere flammis. Ad extremum rogauit a Cranmeto quid de hoc consilio atque hæresiarcha iudicaret. Cranmerus,etsi sibi valde meruit,ingenuo tamen ac placido satis vultu respondit consilium placere,ac esse salubre,nec non ultimo hæresiarchæ supplicio coercendum reliquum hæreticorum gregem,sed paterna quadam in Regem obseruantia,atque modestia monuit ne eos hæreticos esse eenseret, qui contra leges humanas diuino verbo niterentur. Et rectè(inquit Rex)nam & tu denunciatus a multis nobis
units.tr: Dissensions. To bring this about, he said, he had taken counsel from the opinions of bishops and some nobles, and was seeking to find out who was the author and arch-heretic of so great an evil; and that, to restrain and quiet the rest of the mob, he would take savage punishment against him and burn him cruelly in the flames. At last he asked Cranmer what he thought of this plan and of the arch-heretic. Cranmer, although he greatly feared for himself, answered with a frank and fairly calm countenance that the plan pleased him and was wholesome, and that the remaining flock of heretics should indeed be restrained by the ultimate punishment of the arch-heretic. But with a certain fatherly deference and modesty toward the King, he warned him not to think those to be heretics who relied on the divine Word against human laws.

units.la: es,totius nostri Regni hæresiarcha,obstareqi in Cantio ae in tota prouincia tua quo minus illorum 6. Articulorum in Parlamentorum faneitorum fidesa plebe recipiatur, proinde dehis & quid senseris & quid egeris apertenobis indica. Cranmerus in eadem sic adhuc esse sententia, quasi palam in ea lege condenda in Parlamento tum fuisse professus est,nec tamen contra legem iam latam aliquid perpetrasse respondit. Tum Rex remissa paulatim huius sermonis secueritate,lepide ab eo quæsiuit,an interior suus pri-uatusque thalamus ab illis Articulis esset immunis. Cranmerus etsi capitale iam esset ex illis Articulis saeerdotibus coniugari,& Rex eum coniugatum certo sciuisset, respondit sese nupriasante initum ae suscepeum Archiepiscopatum, cum suus ad Cæsarem & ad Papam esset Legatus in Germania contraxisse, verum nein legem tam atroceм committeret,ex quo ea lata fuit coniugem suam non attigisse,sed ad consanguineos necessariofquefuos ex Anglia in Germaniam transtulisse. His apertis ac sine sueo responsis Cranmerus tantam suæ fidei,integritatis & doctrinæ opinionem ingenerauit Regi,vt depofita superioris tristitia & dissimulatione sermonis, Rex eum exhilararet,eorumq; articulorum pœnas non sua causa sanciras diceret,ae institutæ in eum accusationis capita authorcēq; indicaret. Quæ cum Cranmerus falsa & ex Pontificiorum inuidia fabricata confictaque eognouerat,petiit vt dato inquisitore atque iudice de illis ageretur,nam se iudicii diiterimen non pertimescere,Rex ingenuitatitam sancti viri confisus, propriam ei causam inquirendam & explorandam permisit.Sed Cranmerus id iniquum aduersariis visum iridixit,si proprio actorum censor aut explorator statueretur, proinde ali- um iudicem postulauit. At Rex non se alium staturum inquisitorem propriæ vitæ affirmauit, quia tantam in cius vnius fide sincerita tatoque ipsem possiset, vt de propriis, sive bene,siue perperam gestis certo ac sine vllo mendacio veritatem plene referret.Hoc ha bito sermone Rex Cranmerum satis a diuturna mœstitia reuocatum domum remisit, Cranmerus D.Coxum Vicarium suum in spiritualibus generalem,& Antonium Husleyum Notarium, scribam ac Tabellarium suum præcipuū ad inuestigandas has Cantuariæ a pontificiis meditatas machinas cum amplissimis mandatis misit. Quiquod vniut aut alterius mensis moras relevier inchoata, tardeq; progressa traxissent, existimabantur pontificiis occulte fauere.Interim pontificii flagitabant vt Cranmerus hæresis causas,de quibus postulabatur,e publicis carceribus atque custodiis ageret, rati parata
units.tr: "And rightly so," said the King, "for you too have been denounced to us by many as the arch-heretic of our whole realm, and as standing in the way, in Kent and throughout your province, of the people accepting the faith of the Six Articles enacted in Parliament. Therefore tell us openly what you have thought and what you have done in these matters." Cranmer answered that he was still of the same opinion, as he had openly declared in Parliament when that law was being framed; yet he had done nothing against a law already passed. Then the King, gradually relaxing the severity of his speech, asked him playfully whether his inner and private bedchamber was exempt from those Articles. Although it was already a capital offence under those Articles for priests to marry, and the King knew for certain that Cranmer was married, Cranmer replied that he had contracted marriage before taking up and accepting the archbishopric, when he was envoy to the Emperor and the Pope in Germany. But, lest he commit so atrocious a breach, since the law was passed he had not touched his wife; instead, he had transferred her from England to Germany, to her kin and his own near relations. By these frank and unpretentious answers Cranmer so impressed the King with his faith, integrity and learning that, laying aside his earlier gloom and his feigned speech, the King cheered him, said that the penalties of those articles were not enacted on his account, and pointed out the heads of the accusation brought against him and its authors. When Cranmer learned that these charges were false, fabricated and invented out of Papist malice, he asked that they be examined by an appointed inquirer and judge, for he did not fear the peril of judgement. The King, trusting in the candour of so holy a man, allowed him to investigate and examine his own case. But Cranmer saw that this would seem unfair to his opponents if he himself were made the censor or examiner of his own acts; therefore he asked for another judge. But the King affirmed that he would appoint no other examiner of his own life, because he had such confidence in the sincerity of this one man, and was so able, that he could fully and without any lie report the truth about his own deeds, whether well or badly done. With this speech the King, having recalled Cranmer well enough from his long sadness, sent him home. Cranmer sent Dr Cox, his vicar-general in spiritual affairs, and Antony Husley, his notary, scribe and chief messenger, with very ample instructions to investigate these machinations devised at Canterbury by the Papists. But because they dragged out the inquiry, begun and proceeding slowly, through a delay of a month or two, they were thought to be secretly favouring the Papists. Meanwhile the Papists demanded that Cranmer be made to answer the charges of heresy for which he was accused from the public prisons and custody, thinking that they had ready a supply of fabricated proofs to which the accused could not reply.

units.la: (vt de Cromwello ante ad eximus) fictarum probationum quibus reus non respondere t copia,insontem à Regis conspectu abduetum obruere, subitoque supplicio interimere. Rex assiduis pontificiorum importunitatibus oneratus concessit,vt si de aliquo eius in Ecclesiam aut Remp. delicto liquido constaret,ad carceres duceretur. Carolus Suffolciæ Dux paulo ante obierat, Cromwellus(vt diximus) capitis pœna interiit, reliqui consiliarii Gardineri asseclæ ab eoque in Cranmerum incitati conspirabant, vt donec de actis Cranmeri per totam Cantuariensem prouinciam cognoscatur,in Turri Londinensi teneretur.Proximum diem eius incarcerationi statuerunt, sustinuit hoc negocium Rex vt pontificii virus omne suum in Cranmerum euomerent, & tamen eum sartum tectumque habuit.
units.tr: (as we said earlier about Cromwell) of fabricated proofs, to which the accused could not reply, so that an innocent man would be taken from the King's sight, crushed, and quickly destroyed by execution. The King, burdened by the constant importunities of the Papists, agreed that if any offence of his against the Church or the commonwealth were clearly established, he should be led away to prison. Charles, Duke of Suffolk, had died shortly before, and Cromwell had suffered capital punishment, as we have said. The remaining councillors, the followers of Gardiner, were conspiring, and had been incited by him against Cranmer, that until the acts of Cranmer throughout the whole province of Canterbury had been examined, he should be held in the Tower of London. They fixed the next day for his imprisonment. The King allowed this business to go forward so that the Papists might vent all their poison against Cranmer, and yet he kept him safe and sound.

units.la: Namque Antonium Deneum vnum ex intimis suis Cameraris, virum itidem pontificiis aduersum,& Cranmeri amicissimum media fere nocte ab Aula Lamethamı mi- sit aecerfitum Cranmerum. Venit mox ad Regem è somnis experrectus Cranmerus. Narrat his verbis Rex qui eum vellet.
units.tr: For they sent Antony Denny, one of his closest chamberlains, a man likewise hostile to the Papists and a very dear friend of Cranmer, from Lambeth Palace at about midnight to summon Cranmer. Cranmer, roused from sleep, came to the King soon afterwards. The King tells in these words what he wanted with him.

units.la: Instare penè omnes consiliarios, vt quoniam Cant.prouincia, totaque fere Anglia hæreticis sectis inquinata esset,quarum origo ab ea certisque viris peregrinis sed doctis, quos in sua familia teneret, ducta esse credebatur, inquisitione pendente subeat publicam custodiam, nam nisi illud fiat ad fontem & originem penetrari testibus,& probationibus haud posse. Id quod illorum (inquit) desideriis concessimus, ita recte ne an secus tuum esto iudicium, craftuus enim huic rei statutus est dies.
units.tr: Almost all the councillors were urging that, since the province of Canterbury and almost all of England had been polluted by heretical sects, whose origin was believed to be traced to that province and to certain foreign but learned men whom he kept in his household, he should submit to public custody while the inquiry was pending. For (he said) unless this were done, one could not get down to the source and origin by witnesses and proofs. "This we have granted to their wishes," he said; "whether it is right or otherwise, let the judgement be yours, for a day has been set for it tomorrow."

units.la: Cranmerus summas Regi agit gratias quod eum illius decreti etsi nimium seueri ante admoneret uon se recusare dixit careceres, aut subterfugere iudicia, consentiens tamen, tantum petiit ut quoniam doctrina fidesque sua in rebus diuinis in quaestione deerentur daretur satis aequi atqui periti in Theologia iudices. At Rex hae iutegerrimi patris aperiam simplicitatem, fatuitatem appellauit, quod subeundis tam facili animo carceribus se immicissimorum iniuriis permitteret: si enim (inquit) non modo a dignitate tua, sed a luce coelique hominum in carcerum tenebras abducaris, exorientur falsi multi atque periuri testes, qui in praesentiam tuam prodire, aut verbum illum criminatorium in te effertre audeant. Proinde eum neque dignitati neque saluti tuae prospicis, ego tibi consulam ne obuiaris ab infestissimis tibi hostibus. Craste accerseut, haeresis criminationes obiicient, carceribusque mandabunt. Petas ut eum ex consiliariorum meorum numero sis, eodem tecum iure agant, quo ipsi in simile discrimen incident, secum agi optarent, id est, ut accusatores tuos in aperium iudicium proferrent, quos si arguere atqui conuincere non possis, ea quo animo patiaris carceres. Quod si huius aequissimi postulati rationem non habeant, se eo reiecto exequendum decretum pergant, ad meam praesentiam & audientiam prouocees, & ut decreto superseudeant, hoc signo tradito efficies.
units.tr: Cranmer gave the King the greatest thanks, and said that, although he had first warned him that this decree was too severe, he did not refuse the prison or shun the trial, and consented; he asked only that, since his teaching and faith in divine matters were being called in question, fair and skilled judges in theology should be given him. But the King called this simplicity of that most upright father foolishness, because he so readily submitted to imprisonment and allowed himself to be exposed to the injuries of his most bitter enemies. "For if," he said, "you are taken away not only from your dignity but from the light and the company of men into the darkness of a prison, many false and perjured witnesses will arise who will dare to come forward in your presence, or to bring out that accusing word against you. Therefore, since you look neither to your dignity nor to your safety, I will look after you, so that you are not caught by your most hostile enemies. Tomorrow they will summon you, bring charges of heresy, and commit you to prison. Ask that you be treated as one of my councillors, that they deal with you by the same law by which they would wish to be dealt with if they fell into a like peril, that is, that they bring your accusers forward into open judgement; if you cannot then refute and convict them, you may endure the prison as you wish. But if they do not heed this most just request, and refuse it and press on with executing the decree, appeal to my presence and hearing, and you will bring about a stay of the decree by showing this sign."

units.la: His dictis Rex annulum insigne atque notum digito suo detraxit, & Cranmero tradidit, euinq; dimisit. Postridie mane nuncii a Cardinero eiusque aliseclis consiliariis missi Archiepiscopales ianuas Lamethz pulsabant, Cranmerum petunt. Consiliarii in Synodrio Concilii sedebant, quo eum Cranmerus venisset, intromissus non est. Id quod plerisque nobilibus atq; aulicis qui illue erebro transferunt, mirum visum est, Cranmerum Regni Primatem Regis fidissimum atque intimum consiliarium Synedrio exclusum, inter pueros seruulosque dominis tuis famulantes sedere. Nunciabatur ea res D. Butleo Clarissimo Regis Medico, viro Euangelico atque pio, qui indignitate rei permotus venit ad Cranmerum saltem ut abigeret inspectantes rabulas, ae tam Reuerendi patris praesentiam cohonestaret. Sed accersitus mox ad Regem Medicus, se nuper rem insolitam & inauditam vidisse narrat. Quaerit Rex, quaenam ea sit. Cranmerus (inquit) ex Metropolitano & Primate Regni deuenit alienius seruulos, fteritque iam uuius pene horae spacio cum reliquis vnaseruulis pro Synedrii foribus alieu Domino famulans. Adeone (inquit Rex) contumeliose Primatem tractant Consiliarii? Cuius Rei indignitate eorum motus Rex, nuncium mittit ut D. Cranmerus in Synedrium intromittatur. Cui iugresso declaratum est Regem & Consiliarios aceepisse totam Angliam contagione haeresis, quae ab eo eiusque familia manarit, a catholica doctrina penitus esse aueriam & depraueta, proinde eo in Turri Londinensi incluso habendumesse sine mora huius famae quae perere buit celerem Inquisitionem. Craumerus accusatores, testes, tabulas eaque iudicia probarionumque genera, quibus hęc quae obiiciebantin se collegissent, ut palam ostendantur, sibique iu praesentia respondere, sequè defendere liceat poposcit, iniquum esse Primatem Regni atque consiliarium euius fides nunquam dubia fuit, aut in controuersiam veniret, solis suspicionibus ignominiose & cum totius acceusationis causeque praeiudicio detrudi in carceres.
units.tr: When he had said this, the King drew off his signet ring, known to all, from his finger, handed it to Cranmer, and dismissed him. The next morning messengers sent by Gardiner and his fellow councillors knocked at the archiepiscopal gates at Lambeth and sought Cranmer. The councillors were sitting in the council chamber; when Cranmer came there, he was not admitted. This seemed strange to many nobles and courtiers who often went there, that Cranmer, primate of the realm, the King's most faithful and intimate councillor, should be shut out of the council chamber and sit among the boys and servants who waited on your lords. The matter was reported to Dr Butts, the very distinguished royal physician, a man evangelical and pious, who, moved by the indignity of the affair, came to Cranmer, if only to drive away the gawking rabble and to lend dignity to the presence of so reverend a father. But when the physician was summoned to the King, he said that he had just seen an unusual and unheard-of thing. The King asks what it is. "Cranmer," he said, "the Metropolitan and Primate of the realm, has come down to the servants of others, and has been standing for almost an hour now with the other servants at the doors of the council chamber, serving another's lords." "Do the councillors treat the Primate so contemptuously?" said the King. Moved by the indignity of this, the King sends a messenger that Dr Cranmer be admitted to the council chamber. When he had entered, it was declared to him that the King and the councillors had received the report that the whole of England had been infected by the contagion of heresy, which had flowed from him and his household, and had been wholly turned away and corrupted from Catholic teaching; therefore he was to be shut up in the Tower of London, and a swift inquiry into this scandal, which had spread so widely, was to be held without delay. Cranmer asked that the accusers, witnesses, documents, and the kinds of judicial proof by which the things laid against him had been gathered be produced, so that they might be openly shown, and that he might be allowed to answer and defend himself in their presence; it was unjust that the Primate of the realm and a councillor whose faith had never been doubted or called into question should be thrust into prison, disgracefully, on suspicions alone, and to the prejudgement of the whole accusation and cause.

units.la: Multaque alia e commemorat quare secum mitius elementiusque agere oporterent. Sed eum neq; rationibus flecti, nec precibus exorari poterant, Cranmerus dolere se valde dixit quod ab his quibus eum tam diu in communicatione coucilii vixerit, quorumque aequitatem in omni discrimine sperabat, ad Regem prouocare necesse haberet. Itaque annulo Regio tradito se eoram Rege sistere, suoque decreto superseodere iussit. Iiico. D.Ruffell qui postea Comes Bedfordiensis creatus est. Arthon praedixi vobis (inquit) Regem nunquam permissurum, ut Cranmerus careceres parereutur, nisi summae proditionis aut suae Maiestatis grauissime laesae teus fuerit? Ad Regem cum Cranmero mox penitentem est. Isacrio biurgatione consiliarios exagitauit, prudeutiam atque grauitatem remmaiore deiderauit, cur Cranmerus concilii loco excluderetur, eur in seruulorum grege pro ostio staret, & an eorum quisquam tam indignam pati vellet infamiam rogauit. Certoac cum iuramento percussoque dextera pectore affirmauit, se tautis nominibus Craumero deuinctum & obligatum teneri quantis praeteres nemini, eiusque fidem ita cognitam & exploratam habere, vt nunquam maior euiusquam Praelati in suum Regem esse poterit. Proiude omnes qui se diligant, Cranmerum in summo precio & existimatione habeant. His a Rege prolatis cum cæteri metu taciturniores essent, Dux Norfolcię respondit. Nostri sane non fuit institutum, obesse quicquam Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo, sed ut eo inquisitione pendente in custodia publica seruato, innocentiaq; eius ac obiectorum falsitate coguita cum maiori existimatione atq; fama prodiret. At Rex: Nolo (inquit) Cranmerum, aut eos qui mihi chari sunt, hoc exiſtimationis genere, periculoſq; trâctari, sed odia quæ dâ inter vos occulta atq; inuetera tas tragœdias concitare animaduerto, quæ nisi mature sopiantur, ego meas partes interponâ, eaq; compescam. Hic dictis Rex commotus discessit. Consiliarii cum Cranmero singuli dextras iungunt, cum eoq; in gratiam redire studeant.
units.tr: He mentioned many other things as well, showing why they ought to deal with him more gently and mercifully. But since they could be moved neither by his arguments nor won over by his prayers, Cranmer said that he was greatly grieved that he had to appeal to the King against those with whom he had lived so long in the fellowship of the council, and whose fairness he had hoped for in every danger. So, handing over the royal ring, he ordered them to stand before the King, and to desist from their decree. Then Mr Russell, who was later created Earl of Bedford, said: "Did I not tell you, my lords, that the King would never permit Cranmer to be thrown into prison, unless he had committed the greatest treason or gravely injured his Majesty?" Cranmer soon came before the King, who was angry. The King in his rebuke harshly berated the councillors, demanded greater prudence and seriousness from them, asked why Cranmer had been shut out of the council chamber and why he stood at the door among the crowd of servants, and whether any of them would wish to suffer so unworthy a disgrace. Striking his breast with his right hand, he affirmed with certainty and on oath that he was bound and obligated to Cranmer by ties greater than to anyone else, and that he held his loyalty so well known and so tested that no Prelate could ever be more loyal to his King. Therefore all who loved him should hold Cranmer in the highest esteem and regard. When the King had spoken these things, the others, being more silent through fear, the Duke of Norfolk replied: "Certainly it was not our intention to harm the Archbishop of Canterbury in any way, but that, while he was kept in public custody during the inquiry, his innocence and the falsity of the charges might be recognised and he might come forth with greater esteem and reputation." But the King said: "I do not want Cranmer, or those who are dear to me, to be treated in this way, with disgrace and danger; but I notice that secret hatreds and long-standing quarrels are stirring up tragedies among you, and unless these are quickly calmed, I will step in myself and check them." With these words the King, moved, withdrew. The councillors each clasped Cranmer's right hand, and strove to return to his favour.

units.la: Ille mitissimus parer, omnium q; iniuriarum immemor, quæcunq; offensiones facile remisit, & ex animo penitus delerat, ex eo quidem ab inimicorum insidiis securus atque tutus in summa Regis gratia vixit.
units.tr: He, the gentlest of men, forgetful of all wrongs, readily forgave whatever offences had been committed against him and wholly blotted them from his mind; from then on he lived safe from his enemies' snares, and secure in the highest favour of the King.

units.la: Sed cum (vt ante diximus) D. Coxus Cranmeri in spiritualibus Vicarius, cum Antonio Huffæo suo Registrario in illa inquisitione morose, nec sine suspicione, reç; infecta hæreret Cantuariæ, Rex occulte misit D. Leum in legibus Doctorem, vt quid pro Cranmero, vel aduersus eum ageretur exploraret. Is Cantuariam celeriter profectus exquisiuit a quibusdam pijs & reformatis viris, quos Coxus & Huffæus sibi non adhibebant, à quo fonte tanta in Cranmerum infamia inde nasceretur.
units.tr: But since (as we said before) Dr Cox, Cranmer's Vicar-General in spiritual matters, remained at Canterbury with Antony Husley, his registrar, lingering over that inquiry in a slow and not unsuspicious manner, and the business was left undone, the King secretly sent Dr Legh, Doctor of Laws, to find out what was being done for Cranmer or against him. He went quickly to Canterbury and inquired of certain pious and reformed men, whom Cox and Husley did not admit to their counsels, from what source such great infamy against Cranmer had arisen.

units.la: Illi authores Pontificios quosdam præsbyteros designabant, quorum exploratis media tunc nocte edibus, reperiuntur literæ ad concitandos in Cranmerum Pontificios à quodam Gardinero conscriptæ, qui Stephani Gardineti Wintoniensis Episcopi secretarius tum fuit, & paulo post obprodītionem ad patibulum iudicatus & suspensus est.
units.tr: Those authors pointed to certain Papist priests. When their houses were searched at midnight, letters were found, written by one Gardiner to stir up the Papists against Cranmer. He had then been secretary to Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, and shortly after the betrayal he was condemned and hanged on the gallows.

units.la: In his literis tota Pontificiæ in Cranmerum coniurationis machina descripta fuit, quam cum Rex vidisset, cepit suam cum Pontificiis necessitudinem sensim dissuere, indicauitq; Cranmero singula vt cautissime caueret à Pontificiis, voluitq; vt illæ Gardineri literæ ad Pontificiorum infamiam in Parlamento recitarentur. Sed Cranmerus nePontificiorum odium in apertum erumperet, Regi suasit vt celarentur.
units.tr: These letters described the whole machinery of the Papist conspiracy against Cranmer. When the King saw them, he began gradually to loosen his ties with the Papists, and he showed Cranmer each detail so that he might guard most cautiously against them. He wanted Gardiner's letters read out in Parliament to the infamy of the Papists. But Cranmer advised that they be kept secret, lest the Papists' hatred break out into the open.

units.la: Euenit eodem quoque tempore, vt cum integerrimi patriŝgratia contra aduersarios iniurias & calumnias valeret, nobilis quidam Cantius eum adiit, rogauitque vt in quadam petitione ad Regem pro se intercederet.
units.tr: At the same time it happened that, since the upright man's favour with the King counted for much against the injuries and slanders of his adversaries, a certain noble of Kent approached him and asked him to intercede with the King on his behalf in a petition.

units.la: Cranmerus eadem facilitate ductus qua de singulis bene mereri consueuerat, desiderium eius Regi exposuit, Regiq; beneficentiam penè exorauit.
units.tr: Cranmer, moved by the same readiness with which he was accustomed to serve each person well, laid the man's request before the King and almost won the King's kindness.

units.la: Sed Rex cum animo pauliusper voluisset eum ipsum pro quo Cranmerus intercesserat, ministrũatq; socium incepta illius accusationis fuisse, interrogauitan Cranmerus eum pro quo postulasset, inter amicos suos haberet. Crāmerus id quod credidit fassus est pro amico eum se habere.
units.tr: But the King, having for a short while considered the very man on whose behalf Cranmer had interceded, and whether he had been an accomplice in the beginning of that accusation, asked whether Cranmer counted among his friends the man for whom he had petitioned. Cranmer admitted what he believed, that he did count him a friend.

units.la: Rex subiratus, deliras (inquit) hic enim nebulo has omnes tragœdias contra effecit in Cantio, proinde simulat que eum conuenias, nebulonem appellet. Cranmerus id se facere minimè decere respondit. Iussit itaque Rex vt id suo mandato nomine facieret.
units.tr: The King, angered, said: "You are mad! For this scoundrel has brought about all these tragedies in Kent. So go and greet him, and call him a scoundrel." Cranmer replied that it was by no means fitting for him to do that. The King therefore ordered him to do it in his name, by command.

units.la: Sed Cranmerus silentio rem transiit atq; omisit. His gestis emergere iam ceperunt ex inundatione Pontificia, cuius fluctibus diu obruebantur Euangelici.
units.tr: But Cranmer let the matter pass in silence and dropped it. After these events the Evangelicals began to emerge from the Papist flood, under whose waves they had long been overwhelmed.

units.la: Nam in Parlamento nuper conuocato Cranmerus docte, bonisque lateribus suffit, tollendam esse illam diram atque cruentam de prioribus 6. Articulis sanctis pœnam, ant æquiori interpretatione moderandam, ne integerrimi cuiusquam subditi, optimeque de Rege ac Repub. merito salus iniquis ac fraudulentis laqueis irretita in discrimine relinquatur.
units.tr: For in the Parliament recently convened, Cranmer spoke learnedly and with good arguments, saying that the harsh and bloody penalty under the earlier Six Articles should be abolished, or at least moderated by a more equitable interpretation, lest any upright subject, one who deserved well of the King and the commonwealth, be left in danger, his safety caught in unjust and fraudulent snares.

units.la: In quo quidem negocio etsi à Wigorniensi, Ciceftrensi, ac Roffensi Episcopis, quibus cum ante communicabat, quiq; enum consensum atque operam in Parlamento promittebant, in summa periclitatione Gardinero plenis buccis faucibusq; vociferante & reclamante desertus fuerat, solusq; aciem contra Pontificios tenuerat, tamen à Regeipso proceribusque, qui tantam in diuina veritate constantiam vehementiamq; laudabant, adiutus, etsi non tolli penitus legem, tamen æquabili magis atque temperata ratione moderari impetrauit. Verum nondum obfuit Cranmeri sinceritati hæc clandestina & insidiosa Pontificiorum coniunctio. Nam Rex Cranmerum arctiori secum quam vnquam antea necessitudine tenuit, intimaque ei indies communicauit. Pontificios quorum consuetudinem repente præcidere & amputare non poterat, ilieniores tamen habuit, & ad tam intima non admisit. Suasit iam Cranmerus quod saepe antea, vt sacra Biblia in Anglicanum sermonem verterentur, & per singulas Ecclesias distribuerentur singula, cui Gardinerum atq; Pontificios restituisse tam diu antea diximus.
units.tr: In this business, although he had been deserted by the Bishops of Worcester, Chichester and Rochester, with whom he had previously conferred, and who had promised their agreement and help in Parliament, while Gardiner shouted and protested with mouth and throat full, Cranmer alone held the line against the Papists, in great peril. Nevertheless, he was supported by the King himself and by the nobles, who praised such constancy and vehemence in the divine truth. Although the law was not entirely abolished, he obtained that it be moderated by a more even and temperate plan. Yet this secret and treacherous alliance with the Papists did not yet harm Cranmer's sincerity. For the King held Cranmer in a closer bond than ever before and shared his most intimate matters with him daily. The Papists, whose company he could not suddenly cut off and amputate, he nevertheless treated more gently, and did not admit to such intimacy. Cranmer now urged, as he had often urged before, that the holy Bibles be translated into English and distributed to each church, a project which, as we said above, Gardiner and the Papists had delayed for so long.

units.la: Accum Rex tem omnem Ecclesiasticam Cranmeri moderarioni permisisset, in Synodo illaque(vt diximus) cum Parlamento incepta est, Cranmerus de verendis factis Bibliis, de oratione Dominica, Apostolorum Symbolo, & Catalogo vulgari lingua perdiscendis, de Portiferiis vsus Romani abolendis, de matrimonio Vicarius Episcoporum permittendo, de Ecclesiasticis ad statum Ecclesiae Anglicanae legibus componendis, &c de Regis necessitatibus Ecclesiastico subsidio sublenandis egit. Pontifici qui iam eognita Regis voluntate resistere apene non audebant, renitebantur quantum occulte10 poterant. Namque aliquandiu quibus Biblia transferenda committerentur, ambigebant.
units.tr: When the King had then committed the whole ecclesiastical business to Cranmer's management, and in the Synod begun (as we said) alongside Parliament, Cranmer dealt with the translating of the Bibles, the learning by heart in English of the Lord's Prayer, the Apostles' Creed and the Catechism, the abolition of the Roman breviary, the permission of marriage for the bishops' vicars, the framing of ecclesiastical laws for the state of the English Church, and the relieving of the King's needs by ecclesiastical subsidy. The Papists, who now knew the King's will, hardly dared to resist openly, but resisted as far as they secretly could. For for some time they hesitated over to whom the translation of the Bibles should be entrusted.
