units.la: Quidam id negocii Cantebrigiensi & Oxoniensi Academiis delegari volebant, alii certos ex Synodo doctos viros deligabant. Tum de quorundam verborum transferendorum significatione atq; vidi disputatum est, veluti, an Dominus ex sacris literis Anglice the Lord, vel our Lord vertentur, & an Ecclesia transferenda sit the congregation vel p Church, item virum charitas dicenda sit Charitie vel Love.
units.tr: Some wanted this task delegated to the Universities of Cambridge and Oxford; others chose learned men from the Synod. Then there was dispute over the meaning of certain words to be translated: for example, whether the Latin "Dominus" in Holy Scripture should be rendered "the Lord" or "our Lord"; whether "Ecclesia" should be rendered "the congregation" or "the Church"; and likewise whether "charitas" should be rendered "Charitie" or "Love."

units.la: Ad haec in secundo ipsius Decalogi praecepto. Non facies tibi sculptile &c. Gardinerus atq; Pontifi: ii, quia de eiiciendo ex Ecclesiis simulachrorum cultu formidabant, ad finem praecepti addi voluerunt. Eo proposito ne hic diuinum cultum praefies. Atque huiusmodi nugis Regis & Cranmeri in propagandis per Anglicanas Ecclesias sacris literis studium Pontificii impediebant & protrahinabant. Etiamsi illis quantumuis repugnantib. res haec tandem fælicem effectum sortita est.
units.tr: Again, in the second precept of the Decalogue, "Thou shalt not make to thyself any graven image," and so on, Gardiner and the Papists, fearing that the worship of images would be cast out of the churches, wished to add something at the end of the precept, with this aim: that it should not set divine worship before them. By such trifles the Papists hindered and delayed the King's and Cranmer's zeal for spreading Holy Scripture through the English churches. Yet, though they resisted with all their might, the matter at last came to a happy outcome.

units.la: Nam & Anglicana Biblia in singulis Ecclesiis collocata sunt, eaq; legendi faclitas populo facta est cum Ecclesiasticarum legum ad vsum Anglicanae Ecclesiae ferendarum potestas 2. Parlamenti consultis à Rege delegandis concedebatur, vnaq; decretum vt Ecclesiastica iurisdictio a coniugatus qui iuris Ciuilis peritiam habeant, in eoque ab aliqua Vniuersitate doctores cieentur exerceri possit. His paulatim modis ille superstitionis & impietatis tam firmitet a Pontificiis colligatus nodus explicari ac dissolui facile cepit. Ac Rege diuinitus ad tuendam Euangelii fuscepitam causam singulari Cranmeri virtute adducto, conciliatae sunt ei cum pia & Euangelica matrona (quae D. Latimeri defunctae vidua, Marchionisque Northamptonensis soror fuit) Zetati iam fuit contentance nupt iz.
units.tr: For English Bibles were placed in the individual churches, and the people were given easy access to reading them. Parliament granted that the King might delegate the power to enact ecclesiastical laws for the use of the English Church, and also decreed that ecclesiastical jurisdiction might be exercised by married men who had skill in civil law, and by doctors summoned for this purpose from some University. By these gradual steps, that knot of superstition and impiety, so firmly tied by the Papists, began to be easily loosened and dissolved. Since the King, divinely moved, had with Cranmer's singular virtue taken up the cause of the Gospel, a marriage was arranged for Cranmer with a pious and Evangelical matron, the widow of the late Master Latimer and sister of the Marquess of Northampton, and by now he was of an age suited to marriage.

units.la: Quibus valde corroborari Euangelicorum partes existimabantur. Sed bellis iam in hac Pontificiorum rituum profligatione tam in Gallos quam in Scotos vtrinque Anglos infestantes subito exortis, nouae turbae concitatae, iterumq; in Euangel cos magna crudelitate saeuitum est. Namq; Gallo fidem atq; pacta vt solet frangente, Rex Carolus folicitaut, vt mutuis eum coniunctis adiumentis adoriretur. Quorum quidem bellorum exitus et Regi regnoq; secundi fuerint (nam & 15. Scotorum milia in praelio ad Askam fluuium commisso fuisset, & Bolonia maritima Galliae ciuitas oppugnata atq; capta est) tamen authoritate Caesaris Gardinetus atq; Pontificii in Regis gratiam irrepscerunt, quibus praxalentibus flammis iterum & incendio aliquandiu crudeliter in Euangelicos actum est. In quo si modum Pontificii tenere potuissent, causam fortasse suam apud Regem effecissent meliorem.
units.tr: These things were thought greatly to strengthen the side of the Evangelicals. But new wars suddenly broke out, while the Papist rites were being overthrown, with the French and the Scots both attacking the English. New troubles were stirred up, and once again great cruelty raged against the Evangelicals. For when the French, as usual, broke faith and treaties, King Charles urged that they be attacked together with joint forces. Whatever the outcome of these wars was for the King and kingdom (for 15,000 Scots were lost in battle at the river Ask, and Boulogne, a maritime city of France, was assaulted and taken), nevertheless, by the authority of the Emperor, Gardiner and the Papists crept back into the King's favour. With their urging, fires and burning again raged cruelly for a time against the Evangelicals. If the Papists had been able to keep within measure in this, they would perhaps have made their cause better with the King.

units.la: Verum immoderatus eorum furor eo progressus est, vt neque thalamus Regis, neque nuptiae abilla de 6. Articulis inquisitione Pontificiarum falsa esse poterant. Postulabat enim Gardinerus elatus iam ferocia, nö modo Regis cubicularios, sed egregiam illam sincerimamq; matronam D. Catharinam Reginam haereticae factionis. Quae quidem audaciaq; impudentia Regem à Pontificiis in perpetuum alienauit, vt Gardineri consspectum deinceps nunquam ferre potuerit, Norfolciae Ducem, eiusq; hxrilem filiu Surrensem Comitem prodinonis suspectos Turri Londinensi inclusertit. Quorum hic capite damnatus interuitille carceribus septennio detentus, regnante postea Regina Maria liberatus est.
units.tr: But their unrestrained fury went so far that neither the King's bedchamber nor his marriage could be safe from the Papists' false accusations arising from the inquiry into the Six Articles. For Gardiner, now puffed up with fierceness, demanded that not only the King's bedchamber servants but also that outstanding and most sincere matron, Queen Catherine, be branded as members of a heretical faction. This audacity and shameless impudence alienated the King from the Papists for ever, so that he could never afterwards bear the sight of Gardiner. He shut up in the Tower of London the Duke of Norfolk, and his heir, the Earl of Surrey, both suspected of treason. Of these, the son, condemned to death, perished; the Duke, detained in prison for seven years, was freed when Queen Mary reigned afterwards.

units.la: Henricus octauus victoriosissimus Rex profligato iam Papa, eiectaq; illa Monacho atq; fratrum impura turba, lueq; Pontificia, tum promulgato per regnum Euangelio, cum toto regni tempore omnes domi militiaq; sui conatus secundos semper ac foelices exitus habuerunt, tertio Kal. Feb. moritur, ac Regali pompa Windsoriae sepultus est. In Testamento Edwardo Principi minori 9. annis nato haeredi suo sexdecim tutores, ex Episcopis solos Thomam Cranmerum Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum, & Cuthbertum Tonstallum Dunelmensem Episcopum dedit. Gardinerus sibi viuo omni gratia penitus excidetat, & mortui Testamento consilio exclusus est.
units.tr: Henry VIII, the most victorious King, died on the third day before the Kalends of February, the Pope now overthrown, the monk and the impure crowd of friars and the Papist plague cast out, and the Gospel promulgated throughout the kingdom. Throughout his reign all his undertakings, at home and in war, had always had happy and successful outcomes. He was buried at Windsor with royal pomp. In his Will he gave his heir, Prince Edward, then nine years old, sixteen guardians, of whom only two were bishops: Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham. Gardiner, while the King lived, had fallen completely out of all favour, and by the dead King's Will he was excluded from the council.

units.la: Quod Euangelio dilatando, & Romanis paulatim abolendis ritibus, quos Gardinerus mordicus adhuc retinebat maxime profuisse putabatur. Eoque animo ac proposito Regem quidam retulerunt exterminasse eum a primato Concilio, ne is mortuo ad Papismum omnia rursus revocaret, atque Rempub. Pontificiis factionibus perturbaret.
units.tr: Because the spread of the Gospel and the gradual abolition of Roman rites, which Gardiner still stubbornly kept, were thought to be greatly advanced by this, some reported that the king had removed him from the primacy and the council, so that after his death he could not call everything back to Papism and throw the commonwealth into confusion with Papist factions.

units.la: Ac Edwardus eius nominis 6. Rex, annis quidem puerilibus quarto Kal. Martias Regiis ex huius inclyti Angliæ regni more sacris a Reuerendissimo ac integerrimo Patre Cranmero Westmonasterii initiatus est: sed a piis atque eruditis praeceptoribus D. Coxo, & Iohanne Checo Graecis, Latinisque literis institutus, cum sana religione ad praescriptam diuini verbi normam imbutus, aetatem longe suam doctrina virtuteque superauit. Qui Anglicanam Ecclesiam rudem adhuc & informem tam acurate sincera religione perpoliuit, omnesque foeces Pontificias expurgauit, vt a piis omnibus alter Iosias meritò dictus sit.
units.tr: Edward VI, in his boyhood years, was consecrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of March with the royal rites customary in this famous kingdom, by the most reverend and upright father Cranmer at Westminster. Instructed by pious and learned tutors, Dr Cox and John Cheke, in Greek and Latin letters, and imbued with sound religion according to the prescribed rule of the divine Word, he far surpassed his age in learning and virtue. He polished the still crude and unformed English Church so thoroughly with pure religion, and purged out all the Papist dregs, that by all pious people he was rightly called another Josiah.

units.la: Verùm pluribus(ut diximus) ei minori a patre constitutis curatoribus, ne numero suo atque multitudine ad dissensiones facilès essent & proeliues, vnus electus est qui ex cōsiliis reliquorum impuberis Regis tutelam solus administraret. Is fuit Edwardus Seimerus Comes Hertfordensis, totius Regni Camerarius, Regisq; auunculus. Qui suscepta tutela Regis, totius regni atque dominiorum suorum Protector, & Somersetu Dux nuncupatus atque creatus est. Is etiam (quod diuinitus Angliæ datum est) reformandæ ad verbi institutum religioni non minus quam Reip. studuit. Itaque Parlamentum a Rege, Synodo, dusq; a Clero vnà celebrantur. In Synodo Cranmerus Archiepiscopus orationem habita de religione ex verbo Christi instituta populo tradenda, ac reliquis Pontificiis tanquam adulterinis plantis eradicandis consulendum duxit. Sed legum adhuc de 6. Articiilis Hērico Rege regnante latarum (ueritas plerōq; tertuit, quo minus suas de religione reformanda sententias liberè dicerent. Itaq; impetrauit a Rege Cranmerus, vt interim dum illæ leges Parlamento abrogentur, Praelatis de religione in Synodo differentibus atroces illæ rigidæq; pœnæ laxarētur. Quod & concessum est. Ad aliam etiam postulationem progressi sunt Praelati. Animaduerterunt enim omnem vim authoritatemq; Synodi nō modo diminuram, sed penitus fractam & euersam esse, postquam (vt in Warhamo antea diximus) Clerus in verbo sacerdotii Henrico Regi promisissent sine authoritate Regia in Synodo se nihil deleteros. Qua Ecclesiasticarum legum potestate abdicata, populus in Parlamento cepit de rebus diuinis inconsulto Clero sancire, tum absentis Cleri priuilegia & immunitates sensim detrahere, iuraque duriora quibus Clerus inuitus teneretur constituere.
units.tr: But, as we have said, several guardians had been appointed for the boy by his father, lest by their number and multitude they should easily fall into disputes and quarrels; one was chosen who alone would administer the guardianship of the underage king, with the advice of the others. This was Edward Seymour, Earl of Hertford, Lord Chamberlain of the whole kingdom and the king's uncle. Having taken up the guardianship, he was named and created Protector of the king and of all his dominions, and Duke of Somerset. He also (as was given to England by God) worked no less for the reform of religion according to the institution of the Word than for the commonwealth. Thus Parliament, Synod and the clergy were convened together by the king. In the Synod, Archbishop Cranmer gave a speech on the religion instituted from the word of Christ, to be delivered to the people, and advised that the remaining Papist things be uprooted like adulterine plants. But the laws concerning the Six Articles, passed under King Henry, still prevented many from freely stating their views on reforming religion. So Cranmer obtained from the king that, meanwhile, until those laws were repealed by Parliament, those atrocious and harsh penalties should be relaxed while the prelates debated religion in Synod. This was granted. The prelates also advanced another request. For they saw that the whole power and authority of the Synod would not only be diminished but utterly broken and overthrown, since (as we said earlier at Warham) the clergy had promised King Henry, on their priestly word, that they would decide nothing in Synod without royal authority. With this power of ecclesiastical law abdicated, the people in Parliament began to enact decrees on divine matters without consulting the clergy, then gradually to strip away the privileges and immunities of the absent clergy, and to set harsher laws by which the clergy were bound against their will.

units.la: Haec discrimina pati, cum populus de Rep. non de Ecclesia in Parlamentis antiquitus tractare consueuerit, Clericis multo iam acrius atque vigilantius in diuina veritate quam vnquam antea laborantibus, iniquum atque graue visum est. Proinde petierunt, vt quemadmodum Praesules in superiori Parlamento consilio cum procerib[us] coniunguntur, ita in eōdem inferiori Praelati Cleriq; procuratores cum populo permisti de Rep. pariter & de Ecclesia vna consulant. Cuius æquissimi postulati deliberatio quia de religione mature consulendum fuit, in aliud tempus reiecta est. Ac paulo post omnes Papales ceremoniae, missationes, exequiae, sanctorum invocationes, shortuorum expiationes, precationumq; formulae quibus Pontificii blateroenes ignota lingua Deum ac infinitam mortuorum turbam quos inter sanctos relatos esse putabant colebant, caeterasq; nugae e templis & Christianorum coetu sublatae atq; deletae sunt. Purusq; Dei cultus in precibus materna lingua publicè deseripsit, & Sacramentis ad diuini verbi Regulam exptessis & institutis per totam Angliam edirus est. Ad hanc rem a Rege visitatio totius regni generalis decernitur, datiq; cum amplissimis mandatis certi inquisitores, qui singulas dioceses lustrarent, Papismum e templis tollerent, Clerum ad diuini verbi praedicationem excitarent, populumq; ad suscipiendum Euangelium repudiato Papifmo prouocarent. Omniq; Papismus sic abiectus & abstersus est, vt neq; reliquii, neque suspicionis suae quicquam reliquerit. Sed in hac Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ specie quæ tot antea seculis Romanis deliris inquinabatur, iamq; in hoc feliei Edwardi regno, & Cranmeri Praesulatu Euangelica claritate tandem enituit, Pontificii plures pertinacia proteruiaq; incredibili quantuti poterant restituerunt. Nam & Gardinerus Wintoniensis, & Bonerus Londinensis, Ton-stallus Dunelmensis, atque Hethus Rossensis Episcopi, omnes rursus Pontificios sine discrimine proffligari, ve nulla restitutionis superesset spes, indignè ferebant. E quibus Gardinerus indignatione repulsæ quam ab Henrico Rege (vt diximus) ceperat, magis quàm pietatis aut religionis studio Pontifici Romano tam firmiter adhærere putabatur, non id quidem aperte, nam leguum poenas formidabat, sed Pontificias religiones hoc prætextu retineri voluit, quod Rege adhuc minore nihil in religionis aut Reip. statu innouandum esse suadit. Horum auxit contumaciam D. Maria Regis soror, Henrici ex Catharina Hispana filia. Quæ matris ab Henrico Rege repudium indignè tulit, Romanamq; vsurpaticnem eo magis probauit, quod matris suæ nuptias iure diuino prohibitas dispensatione 'ı beatas fecisset. Itaq; Missas, Idolorum cultum, sacrasq; Pontificia publicis legibus sublata, domi suæ celebrauit. Huius exemplum, quia paterno Testamento S. Edwardus Rex sine prole decederet, hæres regni institutus est, permultos in fide Pontificia tenuit atq; deprauauit. Verum Gardineri, Boneri, Tonstallii, necnon Hethi indies crescentes contumaciæ Episcoporuum ami ssione, carceribusq; multatæ sunt.
units.tr: To suffer these dangers seemed unjust and grievous, since the people had traditionally dealt with the commonwealth, not the Church, in Parliaments, and since the clergy were now labouring in divine truth far more keenly and vigilantly than ever before. Therefore they asked that, just as the prelates in the earlier Parliament were joined with the nobles in council, so in the lower house the prelates and proctors of the clergy, mixed with the people, should jointly deliberate on both the commonwealth and the Church. But because the deliberation on this most equitable request had to be taken maturely with regard to religion, it was put off to another time. And a little later, all Papal ceremonies were removed and abolished from the churches and the assembly of Christians: masses, funerals, invocations of saints, expiations for the dead, the formulas of prayer by which the Papist babblers worshipped God in an unknown tongue and the countless crowd of the dead whom they believed to be numbered among the saints, and other trifles. Pure worship of God was publicly set forth in prayers in the mother tongue, and the sacraments, expressed and instituted according to the rule of the divine word, were published throughout all England. For this purpose the king decreed a general visitation of the whole kingdom, and certain inquisitors were appointed with very ample commissions to survey the individual dioceses, to remove Papism from the churches, to rouse the clergy to preach the divine word, and to urge the people to receive the Gospel and reject Papism. Papism was so cast out and wiped away that it left no remnant and no trace of suspicion. But in this form of the English Church, which for so many centuries had been polluted by Roman follies, and which now at last, in the happy reign of Edward and under Cranmer's primacy, shone with evangelical clarity, many Papists, with incredible obstinacy and insolence, restored as much as they could. For Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, Bonner of London, Tunstall of Durham and Heath of Rochester were all indignant that the Papists were everywhere struck down without distinction, so that no hope of restoration remained. Of these, Gardiner, from the resentment of the rejection he had received from King Henry (as we said), was thought to cling more firmly to the Roman pontiff out of anger than from zeal for piety or religion. Not openly, indeed, for he feared the penalties of the laws, but he wished the Papist religion to be kept under this pretext: that, while the king was still a minor, nothing should be changed in the state of religion or the commonwealth. Their obstinacy was increased by Lady Mary, the king's sister, daughter of Henry by Catherine of Spain. She took badly her mother's repudiation by King Henry, and approved the Roman usurpation all the more because she had made her mother's marriage, forbidden by divine law, lawful by dispensation. So she celebrated masses, the worship of idols and the other Papist sacred rites in her own household, though they had been abolished by public laws. Her example held and corrupted very many in the Papist faith, since King Edward was to die without offspring by his father's will and she had been appointed heir to the kingdom. But the bishops Gardiner, Bonner, Tunstall and Heath, whose obstinacy grew daily, were punished by the loss of their bishoprics and by imprisonment.

units.la: Pro D. Maria quæ Cæsaris consanguinea fuit, intercessit per legatos ipsæ Cæsar vt consuetis Pontificiis sacris impune uteretur. Quod Edwardus Rex cum tam perniciosum esse atq; prætiudiciale id exemplicerneret non permisit, vt cum Cranmerus atq; Ridleius vir etiam doctus atq; pius, qui Bonero deprivato in Londinensi Episcopatu successit, instarent & deprecarentur, exoratus nullo pacto voluit, quin lachrymis pro sororis duritie 3 ō atq; exeitate abundè fusis, eam si in pertinacia perseueraret legibus coercendam edixit. Quacum summa pietate coniuncta in Rege adeo iuuenc constantia perspecta Cranmerum atq; Ridleium suæ in eiusmodi causa pro D. Mariæ intercessionis valde puduit.
units.tr: On behalf of Mary, who was a cousin of the emperor, the emperor himself interceded through envoys, asking that she be allowed to use the customary Papist rites with impunity. King Edward, perceiving that such an example would be so pernicious and prejudicial, did not permit it. When Cranmer and Ridley, a man both learned and pious who had succeeded the deprived Bonner in the see of London, pressed and entreated him, he would by no means be persuaded. Rather, with tears shed abundantly over his sister's hardness and obstinacy, he decreed that if she persisted in her stubbornness she should be restrained by laws. Since this great piety in the king was joined with such constancy, so remarkable in one so young, Cranmer and Ridley were deeply ashamed of their intercession for Mary in such a cause.

units.la: Cranmerus Iohannem Checum Regium præceptorem adiens perbeatos fuisse fucia in tam inelyto instituendo Rege labores pronunciauit, qui virtute atq; religione ipsos Præsules & concionatores aduersarentur. Postea Cranmerus Archiepiscopus, vt Euangelicam doctrinam in Cantebrigiensi atq; Oxoniensi Academiis, e quibus ad totius regni institutionem doctores infinitos prodeunt, firmaret, celeberrimos Theologos ab exteris nationibus in Angliam accersuit, Petrum Martyrem Vermilium Florentinum, & Martinum Bucerum Germanum ex Argentorato profectum. Ille Oxonii docuit, hic Cantebrigiæ. Cumhoc etiā Paulus Fagius Hebraicas literas Cantebrigiæ professus est. Ac præter hos Imm. Tremellium, Bernardinum Ochinum, P. Alexandrū, D. Valerandum quos omnes cum liberis atq; eoiugibus abunde alebat: Pb. etiam Melanchthon, atq; Muculus accersiti sunt, sed a patriis recenti se per literas excusabant.
units.tr: Cranmer, approaching John Cheke, the king's tutor, declared that his labours in instructing so famous a king were most blessed, since they were opposed by bishops and preachers who were hostile to virtue and religion. Afterwards Archbishop Cranmer, in order to strengthen evangelical doctrine in the universities of Cambridge and Oxford, from which countless teachers go forth to instruct the whole kingdom, summoned the most celebrated theologians from foreign nations into England: Peter Martyr Vermigli of Florence and Martin Bucer, a German who had come from Strasbourg. The former taught at Oxford, the latter at Cambridge. With Bucer, Paul Fagius also taught Hebrew at Cambridge. Besides these, Immanuel Tremellius, Bernardino Ochino, P. Alexander and D. Valerand were summoned, all of whom he supported abundantly, together with their children and wives. Philip Melanchthon and Musculus were also invited, but they excused themselves by letter, on account of their native lands, having only recently left them.

units.la: In hos aliosq; doctos Theologos tanta beneficentia Cranmerus vsus est, vt collectis quotannis suarum expensarum rationibus nihil sibi ex redditibus reliquisse, superesse potera. Hi tres Cranmeri sumptibus abunde alebantur. Verum Fagius cito mortuus est. Reliqui duo assiduis lectionibus, prædicanonibus atq; disputationibus Papisimum refellebant, & dilatabant Euangelium. Ac Bucerus tertio quo in Anglia venerat anno obiit, cuius funus omnium ordinum Cantebrigiæ concursu, atq; singulorum plancu, carmi- 40 nibus, atq; concionibus declarato cohonestabatur. Petrus Martyr adhuc vixit, continuoq; laboresin Euangelica veritate contra Pontificios tuenda exantlauit. Cranmerus domi ocium omne suum sacris literis impartiuit, scripitq; contra Pontificiorum sententiam illam crassam atq; carnalem in sanctæ Cœnæ Sacramento Christi præsentiam affirmantium, tanta doctrina & argumentorum copia refertum librum, vt ea controuersia a nemine vnquam contra Pontificios accuratius tractata esse videatur. Contra hunc librum Stephanus Gardinerus Wintoniensis Episcopus Turri Londinēsi inclusus furtim & prolixè in eo libro inuectus est, quem Marcum Constantium nominauit. Atq; hunc rursus Cranmero postea mortuo Petrus Martyr doctè refellit & refutauit.
units.tr: Cranmer treated these and the other learned theologians with such generosity that, when he drew up the accounts of his expenses each year, he could have left nothing for himself out of his revenues. These three were abundantly maintained at Cranmer's expense. But Fagius soon died. The other two, by constant lectures, sermons and disputations, refuted Papism and spread the Gospel. Bucer died in the third year after he had come to England, and his funeral was honoured at Cambridge by the gathering of every order and by the lamentations, poems and sermons of individuals. Peter Martyr lived on and continually toiled in defending evangelical truth against the Papists. Cranmer devoted all his leisure at home to Holy Scripture, and wrote a book against the Papist opinion, gross and carnal, of those who affirm Christ's presence in the sacrament of the Holy Supper. It was so full of learning and abundance of arguments that this controversy seems never to have been treated more accurately against the Papists by anyone. Against this book Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, shut up in the Tower of London, secretly attacked it at length in a work which he called by the name of Marcus Constantius. After Cranmer's death, Peter Martyr learnedly refuted and overthrew this book in turn.

units.la: Sed huius Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ status, qui pilis omnibus pergratus Pontificiis, in- 50 uisus fuit, vt ura perbrevis iam ad calamitatem atq; luctum ex lætitia recidit. Namq; Edwardus Rex adolescens ante quā plena pubertate attigisset ex phthisi subito interiit. Cuius vita omnium opiniones incredibili virtute doctrinaq; superauit, mors præter expectationem annis iuuenilibus accidit, in quibus sine vi pauci interierunt. Eo vero mortuo eū regnū D. Mariæ Henrici Regis primogenitæ obuenirret, Pontificii custodia pœnisq; liberati, ac ad pristinas dignitates restituti, in Euangelicos eiectos atque deturbatos omne genus vindictæ supplicioq; parauerunt. Quorum pleriq; fuga & exilio, Pontificiorum vi & immanitate vitata, sed meliora Reginæ Elizabethæ tempora referuntur. Cranmerus cum simile consilium à suis accepisset vt fugeret, Ego vero (inquit si furti, prodiproditionis, parricidii aut cuiusuis sceleris postularer induci ad fugam multo facilius quam in hac causa potuissem. Nunc com de mea non in hominesfed in Deum fide,&facrarumfcrip.urarum veritate contra Pontificios errores agendum esse video, conftatia potius vita cedam,quàm fugitiua euasione regno.
units.tr: But the state of this English Church, most pleasing to all the godly and hateful to the Papists, was turned in a very short time from joy to calamity and mourning. King Edward, a young man, died suddenly of consumption before he reached full manhood. His life surpassed everyone's expectations in incredible virtue and learning, and his death, beyond all expectation, came in his youthful years, when few die except by violence. When the kingdom then passed to Lady Mary, the firstborn daughter of King Henry, the Papists were freed from prison and punishment and restored to their former dignities. They then prepared every kind of vengeance and punishment against the Evangelicals, whom they cast out and overthrew. Many of these fled into exile to escape the force and savagery of the Papists, but better times are recorded under Queen Elizabeth. When Cranmer received similar advice from his friends to flee, he said: "If I were being urged to flee for theft, treason, parricide or any other crime, I could have done so much more easily than in this cause. But now, since I see that my case concerns not my faith in men but my faith in God, and the truth of the holy Scriptures, against the errors of the Papists, I would rather yield up my life by constancy than escape by a fugitive flight from the kingdom."

units.la: Hoc enim in Cranmero admirabile visum est, quod etsi mitissimus ac facillimus in omnibus rebus agendis iudicaretur, tamen fi diuinam veritatem labefactari aut oppugnari à quocunq; tentiret, nemo vnquam in bellis Imperator maiorem animi magnitudinem conftantiamq; declararet. Vt quondam virum quendam magnanimum ac ferocem,&in hac Rep. Principem in causa religionis regnante Rege Edwardo ad duellum lacesseret,quod Ecclesiasticos ritus abolitis Pontificiis ex Cranmeri consilio reformatos improbaret. Verum Cranmero iam in mentem venirillius vaticinii quo Heoricus Octauus Rex Martyrium in hac causa suum praenunciaret. Insignia enim ex genre fuaCrâmerus tribus gruibus quadripartita tulit,quæ Rex Hebricus postea,cum integerrimi patris in veritate diuina constantiam,fi Pontificii praeualerent,in morte ac incendio deliturum profperexerat,ita mntati voluit vt gruibus deletis tres Pellicani mortis Martyriique praeouocii in suis deinceps insignibus ederentur. Nam Pellicani in pullos suos famelicos pietate ducti,eos lethali propriis rostris pectoribus inflicto vulnere, emiffoq;ad animæ defectu cruore satiant. Id quod in Cranmero fore praedixit Rex,vt pro veritate Christianaad pascendum & stabiliendum Christi gregem sanguine quondam Martyr effunderet.
units.tr: For this was admired in Cranmer: although he was judged the gentlest and easiest of men in all his dealings, yet if anyone tried to shake or assail divine truth, no commander in war ever showed greater greatness of spirit and steadfastness. Once, in the reign of King Edward, a certain magnanimous and fierce man, a prince in this commonwealth, challenged him to a duel in a matter of religion, because he disapproved of the ecclesiastical rites reformed by Cranmer's counsel and the Papist practices abolished. But now Cranmer called to mind that prophecy by which King Henry VIII had foretold his martyrdom in this cause. Cranmer bore in his family arms a shield divided into four parts with three cranes. The king, who had foretold that this most upright man would, if the Papists prevailed, perish in death and fire for his constancy in divine truth, wished the arms changed. The cranes were removed and three pelicans displayed in their place in his later insignia, as a sign of death and martyrdom. For pelicans, moved by piety towards their starving chicks, wound them mortally in the breast with their own beaks, and satisfy them with blood poured out until life fails. The king foretold that this would happen to Cranmer: that for the truth of the Christian faith, to feed and establish Christ's flock, he would one day pour out his blood as a martyr.

units.la: Cuius praedictionis euentum iam instare animaduertit, eumq; mente tolerante & intrepida perferendum sibi statuit. Iamq; Regina Maria miffationibus sacrifq; Pontificiis Weftmonafterii pridie Kal. Octob. a Gardinero Wintonienfi Episcopo sine expresso iure aut exemplo,quoniam ea res ad Metropolitanum spectabat, vnda,regnoque initiata est. Omnium autem tam ciuiliumquam Ecclesiasticarum rerum potestas Pontificiis Praesulibus, & Stephano praesertim Gardinero Wintoniensi Episcopo à Regina Maria tradita est. Cranmerus cum Ridleio Londinensi(vt diximus)Episcopo,&Hugone Latimero Oxoniim in carceres missi sunt. Congregataq; Londini Synodus praetextu quidem authoritatis Cantuarienfis Archiepiscopi,&ex Reginæ ad eum mandato,verùm praesidebant ei fine mandato Bonerus,cui Hugone Weftono sacrae Theologiæ professore inferioris Synodi moderatore,quem Proloquutorem vocant,designato,missarum,omniomq; Pontificiorum rituum constitutionem introduxit. Accontra diu atque docte disputabant Walterus Phillips Decanus Roffenfis,Iacobus Haddonus Decanus Exoniensis, Richardus Cheiney Archidiaconus Herefordenfis, Iohannes Philpotus Archidiaconus Wintonienfis, &Iohannes Elmerus Archidiaconus Stohenfis , qui à ceteris multitudine non argumentis vincebantur. Ita enumeratis potius quàm perpeofis singulorum in hac Synodo sententiis Papifmus iterum pene restitutus est.
units.tr: Cranmer saw that the fulfilment of this prediction was now at hand, and he resolved to endure it with a steadfast and fearless mind. Now Queen Mary, on the day before the Kalends of October, at Westminster, had the Mass and the Papist rites introduced throughout the kingdom by Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, without express right or precedent, since the matter belonged to the Metropolitan. The power over all matters, civil as well as ecclesiastical, was handed over by Queen Mary to the Papist prelates, and especially to Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester. Cranmer, together with Ridley, Bishop of London (as we said), and Hugh Latimer, was sent to prison at Oxford. A synod was gathered at London, under the pretext of the authority of the Archbishop of Canterbury and by the Queen's command, but Bonner presided over it without his command, together with Hugh Weston, professor of sacred theology, appointed moderator of the lower house, whom they call the Prolocutor. Bonner introduced the restoration of the Mass and of all the Papist rites. Against them long and learnedly disputed Walter Phillips, Dean of Rochester, James Haddon, Dean of Exeter, Richard Cheyney, Archdeacon of Hereford, John Philpot, Archdeacon of Winchester, and John Elmer, Archdeacon of Stow; but they were overcome by the others' numbers rather than by arguments. Thus the opinions of individuals in this synod were counted rather than weighed, and Popery was almost wholly restored.

units.la: In Parlamento quoque quod eodem tempore celebrabatur, omnes propemodum leges atq; sanctiones,quæ ab Henrico 8. & Edwardo 6. Regibus in Pontificios ferebantur, rescisse & abrogatæ fuerunt. Reginaldus Polus Cardinalis Romanus (de quo proximo loco diéturi fumus) à Regina Maria vt Angliam Pontificiæ potestati iterum subiiceret,accersitus est. Thomas Cranmerus vrmaiori populi odiolaboraret,laesæ Maiestatis ab iniquis & Pontificiis Iudicibus in iudicii forma fine veritate cuinicitur. Qua quidem in re iniquum Cranmerus tulit fui in Mariam iam Reginam olim benemeriti praemiu. Nam cum pater eius Henricus Octauus eam Pontificia factione praefrafam atque contumacem carceribus coercere statuisset, solus Cranmerus intercessit, Regemq; incensum mitigauit. Deindecum eadem à fratre Edwardo Rege Testamento exhæredirata fuisset,longa oratione ne id fieret,etsi frustra,diu contédit. Verum materini repudii memoria aróq; malevolentia ex inuetiorato ac reposito odioqua cunque Cranmeri beneficia exclusit. Itaq; capite iam damnatus Oxonium cum Nicolao Ridleio Lôdioefi(vt diximus)Episcopo ac Hugone Latimero in carceres missus est. Eo Petrus Martyr defunca prius & repulsa sua coniuge in Germaniam obtento comeatu sese conulit. Acqui aliud rursus Parlamentum,aliaq; Synodus inchoantur.
units.tr: In Parliament, which was held at the same time, almost all the laws and sanctions passed by Kings Henry VIII and Edward VI against the Papists were repealed and abrogated. Reginald Pole, the Roman Cardinal (of whom we shall speak in the next place), was summoned by Queen Mary to bring England back under the power of the Pope. Thomas Cranmer, so that he might be more hated by the people, was condemned for treason by unjust and Papist judges, in a legal form but without truth. In this matter Cranmer received an unjust reward for his services to Mary, who was now Queen and to whom he had formerly done good service. When her father Henry had resolved to coerce her with imprisonment, she being stubborn and obstinate in the Papist faction, Cranmer alone interceded and softened the king when he was inflamed. Later, when she had been disinherited by her brother King Edward in his will, he long contended, in a lengthy speech, that this should not be done, though in vain. But the memory of her mother's divorce and her long-stored malice, from a hatred that had been long hidden and kept, shut out from her mind whatever benefits Cranmer had bestowed. And so, already condemned to death, he was sent to prison at Oxford with Nicholas Ridley, Bishop of London (as we said), and Hugh Latimer. Peter Martyr, his wife having died earlier and his position having been rejected, obtained leave and withdrew into Germany. And another Parliament and another Synod were begun.

units.la: In Parlamento Papa suum vsucaptam potentiam (quod nunquam ante euenit) legis vigore recepit.Et vt Pontificia faétio firmaretur,infausta nuptiæ inter PhilippumCæfaris filium & Reginam Mariam conciliatæ sunt,quæ Wintoniæ septimo Kal. Augu.St̃ephano Gardinero miffificante celebrabantur. Tum Polus Cardinalis cum Legatina potestate à Iulio. 3. Papa venit in Angliam aduentuq; suo excommunicationis & interdictisententiasà Papis viginti fere annis in regnum latas in Parlamento relaxauit. Interea Oxonium venerunt à Synodo missi Westonus Proloquutor cum permultis aliis Theologiæ professoribus, vt cum Cranmero, Ridleio, atq; Latimero de sacramentis, & carnalii in eadem Christi præsentia publice disputarent. Qui sanctiparres conuictis atq; contumeliis exploiti potius quam scripturæ, atq; patrum, Conciliorumque auctoritatibus victi, hæretici primò ab Oxoniensi Vniuersitate, deinde à Synodo Londini iudicati sunt.
units.tr: In Parliament the Pope recovered, by force of law, his power, which he had usurped (something that had never happened before). To strengthen the Papist faction, an ill-omened marriage was arranged between Philip, son of the Emperor, and Queen Mary. It was celebrated at Winchester on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, with Stephen Gardiner officiating. Then Cardinal Pole came to England with legatine power from Pope Julius III, and on his arrival in Parliament he relaxed the sentences of excommunication and interdict which the Popes had pronounced against the kingdom for nearly twenty years. Meanwhile Weston the Prolocutor came to Oxford, sent by the Synod, with very many other professors of theology, to dispute publicly with Cranmer, Ridley and Latimer about the sacraments and the bodily presence of Christ in them. Those men, worsted by insults and abuse rather than by Scripture and the authority of the Fathers and councils, were judged heretics, first by the University of Oxford and then by the Synod at London.

units.la: Quarum omnium rerum prolixas narrationes ab aliis explicatas nos in perstrictò compendio consulto omittimus. Tum editas a Bonero Christianorum stragis, Martyrumq; incendia, Gardineri versurias, Poli simulationem & hypocrisim, ruinam denique clademq; regni a Pontificiis paucis annis inuectam commemorare opus esset & imminentium, & ab aliis suscepetum fœlicitatq; atq; copiose expeditum, nobis inane & superuacaneum. Illis itaq; præteremissis ad Cranmeri mactationem, quæ iam instat, propius accedamus. Cardinalis Polus Papæ Legatus honore & cum Regina gratia cunctos anteibat, & quamuis Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum concupiuit, eiusq; fructus authoritate qua fungebatur legatina Cranmero adempt, & sequestrationis præsentia quod suos vsus coluerit, ac Lamethæ habitauit, se tamen pro Archiepiscopo gerere Cranmero adhuc vigente noluit. Verum Stephanus Gardinerus falsa arrogantiaq; tumens, qui ambitione ex Wolcei Cardinalis, cui(vt diximus) primò seruiuit, aulæ familiaq; hausit, nec superiorem ferre potuit, occulteq; quantum potuit restituit, honoremq; Cardinalium, & Legatiunam authoritatem exemplo Magistri sui Wolcei nunciis ad Papam clanculum inietpositis affectauit. In quo defidetio ipsem certam concepetar, quia Papa Julio 3. mortuo, Iohannes Petrus Carafa, qui Cardinalis Theatinus dicebatur ad Papatum euectus est. Iterq; hunc qui iam Paulus 4. Papa vocabatur atq; Polum Cardinalem inuetera&e capnales inimicitiæ, quæ nulla reconciliatione deponi poterant, intercessere. Itaq; gratissimum ei fuit Gardineri de postulando Cardinalatu nuncium, qui Polum omni authoritate exuere, Romam ex Anglia reuocare, ibiq; tam diuturni odii vindictam de eo sumere cogitauit. Hoc callido consilio cum Gardinerus occulte puraretur Cranmerum ab incendio reseruasse, ne Polus Archiepiscopatum ingrederetur, tanta morbi articularis vehementia non modo in eruris sed in ipso coxendice cortepius est, vt a suis Medicis ei mors nunciata sit. Itaq; in lecto decumbentis cadauer ita putridum fœtidumq; ante mortem fuit, vt 3 præsentibus qui cum curabant nihil molestius ipso odore esse potuit. In ipso mortis momento hæc verba eiaculatus est. Errauí cum Petro, non fleni cum Petro. Eo veio moriuo Polus Legatus D. Brookum Briftolienfem Episcopum Papæ Delegatum ad sententiam in Cranmerum ferendam designauit. Cum eo Oxonium vna profectiu sunt Johannes Storeus, & Thomas Martinus legum doctores, qui authoritate fulciti Regia adiumento atq; subsidio forent delegato. Ac longo sermone habito, vt Cranmerum ab his quæ de Religione Christiana tenuisset dogmatibus ad Romanam concordiam reuocaret, illeq; constanter perseueraret, nec abduci a sententia veller, monitus est a Brooke Papali delegato vt intra 8. dies continuos se Romæ eorum Papa sisteret. Id se libenter facturum Cranmerus respondit, si ei a Regina fieret potestas. Verum Papa Cranmeri aduentu nō expectato ante vicesimum diem literis ad Regem Philippū & Reginam Mariam scriptis condemnati & bracchio seculari permitti iussit. Interea Ridleius atq; Latimerus vna cōbulii sum. Quod funestum lugubreq; spectaculum ex summo carceris sui loco conspiciens Cranmerus idem breui expectans, hulus vitæ exitum, genubus flexis, palmisq; ad sidera tentis focilis suis spei fideiq; constantiam in tam horrendo mortis tormento precatus est. Solebant enim viui, postquam delegarorum sententia condemnatiesset, literis indies se ad perseuerantiam mutuo cohortari. Ac paulo post noua potestas Thomæ Thirleby Elienfi, & Bonero Londinensi Episcopis à Papa data est, vt Cranmerum tam Clericali quam Archiepiscopali ordine depriuarent, & flammis eremādum seculari potestati traderet. Id 14. Febr. peractu est. Verū illa literarū consolatoriarū cōsuetudine eū iā Cranmerus catuisset, irrepsit ei subdoli cuiusda fratris Hispani quì Iohannes dictus est, ex Pontificiorum blanditiis rentatio Diabolica, vt proposita vitæ spe, mortisq; terrore, eaquæ antea de religione senserat, docuisset, scriptis & chirographo retractaret. Sed neque Pontificiorū immanitas, nec ficta & adumbrata Poli sanctitas quæ integerrimi cuiusquā sanguine expetiuit, hac retractatione contenta esse poterat. Nam cum in vitæ spem pene eertam venisset Cranmerus, præsto el adfuit ex Poli Cardinalis decreto exitium, venitq; Oxonium Iohannes Colus vir non modo Pontificia prauitate sed in omni vitæ actione peruersus ac difficilis. Is Scholariū & oppidanorum Oxoniensium concione in D. Mariæ templo habita diuinum numen ob Thomæ Moori, & D. Fisheri Roffensis Episcopi exdeq cædes qui Henrico Octaoo regnante capite ob Papismum plectebantur infensum, non alia ratione quam Cranmeri mactatione atq; victima placari posse asseruit. Eò inter duos fratres eductus est è carceribus toga squalida, pannisque obsita Craomerus, quem cū in sua concione Colus hortaretur vt retractationem quam scripto ratam fecisset, iam cunctis audientibus viua voce ederet. Is fide sua in Deum eiusque scriptuntas explicata, omniumq; suorū delictorum veni exorata, ex omnibus quæ vnquam perpetrauit peccatis id gratissimum sibi videri asseruit, quo priori fidei scripto maouq; contra mentem & conscientiam renunciasset. Tum Papam vt Antichristum omnesque pontificios rītus qui Ecclesiam Christi contaminabant exosus, de dextra sua manu quæ subscripsit, simulatque in flammas venisset, primum combureda prædixit. In huiusmodi autem sermone cum progredi vltra veller, pontificiorum clamoribus & conuiciis impeditus, & à loco in quo constiterat violēter tractus est. Indeq; inter duos rut sus Estres ad Martyrium ductus, posti cathena alligatus, aridisque fasciculis circumdatus, simulatque flamma ligoum acceederat, læua in cœlos erecta dexteram primò admouit igni, quam ne bracchio quidem reducto totam combussit, sequeq; iodignam ac Christo ioimicam appellauit, erectusq; corpore nuoquam moto aut declinato sublatis in cœlum oculis cum flamma iam undique ixuiret, ex clamauit. Domine suscipe spiritum meum, atque exspirauit. Hoc fuit tam sancti doctrinque patris gloriosum Martyrium, cuius tota vita diuinis vigiliis lucubrationibus q; transfacta ipsius flamis ad cœlestē immortalitatē translata est. Postquā flāma cadauer eius atq; ligna ad cineres redegisset, repertū est cor eius in cinctibus integrū ac illæsum. Id si pontificii in suæ factionis aliquo cōbusto cōperissent, instar insiguis alicuius miraculi habuissent, cōbustūq; ioter sanctos io papali calēdario retulissent. Sed Cranmerus fide integra nō pontificiacen iura io libro vitæ scriptus cœlestē hæreditatē cū Christo cōsecutus est, vt ù in hominibus gloriari fas esset, nō ab Augustino, Dūstano, Elphego, Anselmo, Thom. Becket, Edmundo, & reliqua pontificia turbassed ab hoc vno qui solus in Christi causa contra Antichristum flammarum incredibili dolore ad cœlos sublatus est, Cantuariensis sedes nobilitata esse videatur. De Martyrioeius hæc carmina conscripta sunt à Rodulpho Skinnero.
units.tr: We deliberately leave out long accounts of all these matters, which others have already set out in full. It would be needless and superfluous for us to recall, in this brief summary, the published accounts by Bonner of the slaughter of Christians and the burning of martyrs, Gardiner's shifts, Pole's pretence and hypocrisy, and finally the ruin and disaster that the Papists brought upon the kingdom within a few years. Others have taken those matters up and treated them fully and successfully. Passing over them, let us come closer to the coming slaughter of Cranmer. Cardinal Pole, the Pope's legate, went before everyone in honour and in the Queen's favour. Although he coveted the archbishopric of Canterbury, he took its revenues from Cranmer by the authority of legate that he exercised, and, by the sequestration, he managed its affairs for his own use and lived at Lambeth. Yet while Cranmer was still alive he refused to act as archbishop. Stephen Gardiner, however, swollen with false arrogance, who had served Cardinal Wolsey first and had absorbed ambition from his household, could not bear a superior. Secretly he restored as much as he could, and, following the example of his master Wolsey, he aspired to the honour of the cardinalate and the authority of legate, sending messages secretly to the Pope. In this hope he was confident, for when Pope Julius III died, John Peter Carafa, who was called the Cardinal of Theate, was raised to the papacy and became Pope Paul IV. Between him and Cardinal Pole there were old and deep enmities that no reconciliation could lay to rest. So the news of Gardiner's request for the cardinalate was most welcome to Paul, who thought it would strip Pole of all authority, recall him from England to Rome, and there take vengeance on him for so long-standing a hatred. With this crafty plan being secretly prepared by Gardiner, Cranmer was spared from the fire, lest Pole should enter the archbishopric. Then such a violence of gout attacked him, not only in the shin but in the hip itself, that his doctors announced death to him. As he lay in bed, his body became so putrid and foul before death that nothing was more troublesome to those who attended him than the smell. At the very moment of death he cried out these words: "I erred with Peter; I did not weep with Peter." When he had died, Pole, the legate, appointed Dr Brooks, Bishop of Bristol, as papal delegate to pronounce sentence on Cranmer. Along with him, John Story and Thomas Martin, doctors of law, set out together for Oxford, so that, supported by royal authority and assistance, they might act as delegates. After a long speech, they tried to bring Cranmer back from the doctrines he held on the Christian religion to agreement with Rome. He persevered constantly and would not be drawn from his opinion. Brooks, the papal delegate, warned him that within eight continuous days he must present himself before the Pope at Rome. Cranmer replied that he would gladly do so if the Queen granted him permission. But the Pope, without waiting for Cranmer's arrival, ordered by letter to King Philip and Queen Mary, written before the twentieth day, that he be condemned and handed over to the secular arm. Meanwhile Ridley and Latimer were burned together. Cranmer, looking down from the highest place of his prison on this mournful and deadly spectacle, expecting that his own end would soon come, knelt, raised his hands to the heavens, and prayed for constancy of hope and faith in so horrible a torment of death. For the living, after the sentence of the delegates had been pronounced, had been accustomed to urge one another daily by letters to perseverance. A little later, the Pope gave new power to Thomas Thirlby, Bishop of Ely, and to Bonner, Bishop of London, to deprive Cranmer of both his clerical and archiepiscopal orders and to hand him over to the secular power to be burned. This was done on 14 February. But Cranmer, wearied by the custom of consoling letters, was approached by a deceitful Spanish friar called John. Through the flattery of the Papists, a diabolical temptation crept upon him: setting before him the hope of life and the terror of death, this man was to persuade him to retract, in writing and by signature, the things he had thought about religion. But neither the savagery of the Papists nor the feigned and pretended holiness of Pole, which sought the blood of the most upright man, could be content with this retraction. For when Cranmer had come almost to a sure hope of life, the death decreed by Cardinal Pole was at hand. John Cole, a man perverse and difficult not only in Papist wickedness but in every action of his life, came to Oxford. At a sermon given to the scholars and townspeople of Oxford in the church of St Mary, he declared that the divine power, angered by the killings of Thomas More and of John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, who had been put to death for Papism under Henry VIII, could be appeased by no other means than the slaughter and sacrifice of Cranmer. Then Cranmer, in a filthy gown and covered with rags, was led out of his prison between two friars. Cole, in his sermon, urged him to deliver aloud, in the hearing of all, the retraction which he had confirmed in writing. Cranmer explained his faith in God and in his Scriptures, and, having begged pardon for all his sins, he said that of all the sins he had ever committed, the one that seemed most grievous to him was that he had, against his mind and conscience, renounced his earlier faith in writing. Then, hating the Pope as Antichrist and all the Papist rites which polluted the Church of Christ, he foretold that his right hand, which had signed, would be the first part burned, as soon as it reached the flames. But when in this speech he wished to go further, he was hindered by the shouts and insults of the Papists and violently dragged from the place where he stood. From there, again between two friars, he was led to the stake. Bound with a chain and surrounded with dry bundles of sticks, as soon as the flame had reached him he raised his left hand to heaven and first put his right hand to the fire. He burned it entirely without drawing back his arm, calling it unworthy and hostile to Christ. Upright in body, never moving or bending, with his eyes lifted to heaven, and with the flame already raging on every side, he cried out: "Lord, receive my spirit," and breathed his last. This was the glorious martyrdom of so holy a teacher and father, whose whole life had been spent in divine watchings and studies, and whose spirit was carried by the flame to heavenly immortality. After the fire had reduced his body and the wood to ashes, his heart was found in the ashes whole and unharmed. If the Papists had found this in the burning of someone from their own faction, they would have held it as some remarkable miracle, and they would have put that burning among the saints in the papal calendar. But Cranmer, with his faith intact, was written in the book of life and not in the papal registers, and he gained the heavenly inheritance with Christ. So it is right to boast in men not of Augustine, Dunstan, Elphege, Anselm, Thomas Becket, Edmund, and the rest of that papal crowd, but of this one man alone, who alone, in Christ's cause against Antichrist, was lifted up to heaven through the incredible pain of the flames. By him alone the See of Canterbury seems ennobled. These verses on his martyrdom were written by Rudolph Skinner.

units.la: S Vccubuit Sanctus præsul Cranmerus iniquæ Pontificum rabie, fraude, dologue periit.
units.tr: The holy prelate Cranmer succumbed to the furious rage, the fraud and the wiles of the Pontiffs, and perished.

units.la: Quid verbis inutile deiecerat esse Papatum, Quod docuit pura quaerere mente Deum.
units.tr: Because he had cast down the Papacy, useless for words, he taught that God is sought with a pure mind.

units.la: Quodque Antichristi subuerterat impia regna, Regnapius Anglis bem tolerata din.
units.tr: And because he had overthrown the impious kingdom of Antichrist, a kingdom not long endured by the English.

units.la: Hinc pius & clemens crudelis addicitur igni, Et dant innocui membra cremanda viri.
units.tr: Hence the pious and gentle man is cruelly given over to the fire, and they give the limbs of the innocent man to be burned.

units.la: Hæc vbi iam ventum est, dextram proiecit in ignem, Proiectamq; tenens talia dicta dedit:
units.tr: When it had come to this, he thrust his right hand into the fire, and, holding it out, he gave these words:

units.la: Primum peccauit, primum & sentire dolorem Debet, ah Christo dextra inimica mea.
units.tr: First it sinned, so first it must feel the pain: my right hand, an enemy to Christ.

units.la: Immotamq; tenet dum deflagrauerat omnis, Ineuerres totam dum cecidisse videt.
units.tr: It held itself unmoved while everything else burned, and it saw the whole of it fall away.

units.la: Catera cum pereant flamma (mirabile dictu) Cor manet illæsum post vbi flamma perit.
units.tr: Though everything else perished in the flame (wonderful to tell), the heart remained unharmed after the flame had died.

units.la: Ecce inuicta fidei cor inuiolabile seruat, Nec medijs flammis corda perire finit.
units.tr: Behold, the invincible heart of faith keeps itself inviolate, and the flames do not let the hearts perish in the midst of them.

units.la: In effigiem Thō. Cranmeri Archiepisc. Cantuariensis Qualtetī Haddoni Carmina.
units.tr: On the Likeness of Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury: Verses by Haddon

units.la: E Tpius, & clemens, Thoma Cranmere fuisti Tempora læta dedit, tempora dura Deus. Totestus Christi crudelis addiceris igni, Nunc daris reddunt tempora læta vicem.
units.tr: You were gentle and merciful, Thomas Cranmer. God gave you happy times and hard times. Cruelly you were doomed to the fire, but now the happy times repay you in turn.

units.la: Eo verò mortuo, sedequē iam vacante capitulum Cantuariense ex mandato Regis & Reginæ Syoodum conuocauit, suasque vices Boneroo Londinensi Episcopo delegauit, vt is consilio præsideret. In hac Synodo decretum est vt dies ille quo pontifici Romano vsurpata illa authoritas restituta fuerit, quotaonis festus dies celebraretur, atque Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ reconciliatio diceretur. Tum quia Regina Maria primitias aliq; decimas Henrico Octauo Regi (vt antea diximus) in perpetuum concessas Clero remisisset, decretum ei est amplissimum ex Cleri beneficiis subsidiū. Multa alia in ea Synodo a Clero postulata, sed nondum impetrata fuerunt. Verum Regina Maria eo animo in Cletum affecta fuit, vt cum decimas & primitias reddidisset, & de restituendis Cœnobiorum ab Henrico Rege deiectorum ablatis prædiis cogitaret, quæ salua conscientia sibi retinenda haud putauit, ideoque Domino Marchiuni Wintoniensi Regni Thesaurano, aliisque suis consiliariis accersitis narrauit, quantum animo dies noctesque de retentis illis Cœnobiorum prædiis turbetur, quorum restitutio est damnosa Regali dignitati futura sit, t o censumque suum atq; sicum maxime extenuabit, tamen nolle se dixit non modo alienaa, sed ne regna plutima, conscientia læsa atq; turbata possidere, proinde voluit vt Cardinalem Polum Papæ legatum, cuius arbitrio atque moderationi hoc negocium tam à se quam à Papa commissum sit, consulant, vt sua conscientia adeo perplexa atque dubia hac cura & solicitudine mature liberetur. At Henricus Rex cū Cœnobia dissoluisset, terrarum permutatione aliisque contractibus ita Cœnobiorum prædia diuisit, vt sibi nō adeo magna pars reliqua fuerit, quin à proceribus, nobilibus, atque plebeiis pleraq; tenerentur. Vt cum Papa, Regina atque Cardinali occulte procurantibus excommunicationis sententia in eunctos huiusmodi prædiorum possessores fulminasset, eaq; bulla(vt aiunt) in Anglia promulganda & denunciada foret, tantus omnium ordinum, ipsorumetiam pontificiorum stupusin eam bullam subito exortus est, vt nisi ea bullare missa Romam sententiaque renocata esset, Papæ omnis potestas totius populi consensu atq; vi iterum cuncidisset. Ipsi enim pontificiorum rituum superstitionissimi cultores denunciabant se eius authoritatem non latiuros, si libera eorum attingeret tenementa. Hoc modo de restitutione Cœnobiorum desperatum est.
units.tr: After his death, while the see of Canterbury stood vacant, the chapter of Canterbury, by the command of the King and Queen, summoned a synod and delegated its functions to Bonner, Bishop of London, so that he might preside over the council. In this synod it was decreed that the day on which that papal authority had been restored should be celebrated every year as a festival, and called the reconciliation of the English Church. Then, since Queen Mary had remitted to the clergy the first-fruits and tenths which King Henry VIII had (as we said before) granted in perpetuity, a very generous subsidy was voted to her from the benefices of the clergy. Many other requests were made by the clergy in that synod, but they had not yet been obtained. Indeed, Queen Mary was so disposed toward the clergy that, having given back the tithes and first-fruits, she considered restoring the estates taken from the monasteries that King Henry had dissolved. She did not think she could keep these with a clear conscience. So she summoned the Lord Marquis of Winchester, the Lord Treasurer of the realm, and her other counsellors, and told them how much, day and night, she was troubled in mind about those monastic estates still held. Their restitution would be harmful to the royal dignity and would greatly diminish her revenue and her wealth. Nevertheless, she said, she was unwilling to possess not only other people's property but not even many kingdoms with her conscience wounded and troubled. Therefore she wished them to consult Cardinal Pole, the Pope's legate, on whose judgment and moderation this matter had been entrusted both by herself and by the Pope, so that her conscience, so perplexed and uncertain, might be freed in good time from this care and anxiety. But King Henry, when he had dissolved the monasteries, had divided the monastic lands by exchanges of territory and other transactions in such a way that not so large a part remained to him that most of it was not held by nobles, gentry and commoners. So when the Pope, with the Queen and the Cardinal secretly promoting it, had hurled the sentence of excommunication against all possessors of such lands, and that bull was (as they say) to be published and proclaimed in England, such a great outcry of all orders, even of the Papists themselves, arose at once against that bull that, unless the bull had been sent back to Rome and the sentence recalled, the whole power of the Pope would have fallen again by the consent and force of the whole people. For the most zealous devotees of the Popish rites themselves declared that they would not tolerate his authority if it touched their freeholds. In this way the restitution of the monasteries was abandoned.

units.la: LXIX. Reginaldvs polvs Cardinalis.
units.tr: LXIX. Reginald Pole, Cardinal.

units.la: Vtvs viri vita tantis laudibus à diserrissimis Italis, & Academiæ Venetæ declamatoribus expresta est, vt nulluis in eo ornando atq; illustrādo orationis elegantia desiderari amplius posset. Verum vsu sæpe venit, vt qui toto orationis apparatu concinnè atque copiosè constructo, coaceruandis texendisq; laudibus tantum studeant, dum consulto præterire quiequam nollent eorum, quæ ad eum de quo scribunt amplificandum faciant, omittant tamen non nonnunquam veritatem, tum nimiæ laudis studio proue ctis falsis criminationibus lacescant eos quos aduersos scripserint. Id quod in Polo celebrando Italis oratoribus commune semper fuit, vt pontificiis partibus obsecuti, neq; in eius encomiis explicandis seruare modum, neque Illustrissimi Regis atque Regni famæ dignitatiq; parcete potuissent. Cuius generis scriptures aut horitatem omnem, fidemq; prudentiam à suis scriptis auertunt, efficiuntq; vt ea iuuenilēs otiosorum hominum declamationes atque Rhetorum progymnasmata potius quàm virtutibus recteq; factis dignæ atque tribuitæ laudes esse videantur.
units.tr: The life of this man has been praised with such great eulogies by the most eloquent Italians, and by the orators of the Venetian Academy, that nothing more elegant in the ornament and illustration of style could be desired. But it often happens that those who, with the whole apparatus of their oratory skilfully and copiously arranged, strive only to heap up and weave praises, while they do not wish to omit deliberately anything that adds to the magnifying of the man they write about, nevertheless sometimes omit the truth; and, carried away by an excessive zeal for praise, they assail with false accusations those whom they have written against. This has always been common among Italian orators in celebrating Pole: being subservient to the Papal party, they could neither keep due measure in unfolding his eulogies nor spare the good name and dignity of the most illustrious King and of the realm. Writings of this kind strip away from their works all authority, all trustworthiness and prudence, and make these youthful declamations of idle men, and rhetorical exercises, seem to be praises rather than the praises which are due to and fitting for virtue and right deeds.

units.la: Neque sanè hæc à nobis ideo dicta sunt, quòd viri, si pontificius saltem fucus ab fuisset, laudes præclaras satis bene meriti, cœlebrationi aut præconum suorum industriæ facultatiq́ue inuideamus. Quid enim nobis gloriosius esse potest quam hominem nostratem, ab Italis præsertim, qui omnem ingenii doctrinæq; landem iure quodam hæreditario atq; peculiariter sibi vindicat, tanta orationis vbertate facundiaq; celebrari? Sed quia ea quæ iam Atchiep. Cantuariensis gessit potißimum nobis explicanda sunt, eiusq; vitæ cursus breuiter perstringendus, ignosci nobis iure poscimus, si multū dissentiamus, permissoq; illis laudatorio in quo exultent Campo, nostram orationem angustis historiæ veritatisq; cancellis concludamus.
units.tr: Certainly we do not say these things because we grudge the man, if at least the papal tinsel had been absent, his well-deserved and splendid praises, nor the industry and abilities of his heralds in celebrating him. For what can be more glorious to us than that a man of our own nation should be celebrated with such richness and fluency of speech, especially by the Italians, who claim for themselves by a kind of hereditary right all the glory of talent and learning? But since we must chiefly explain what the Archbishop of Canterbury did, and briefly set out the course of his life, we rightly ask to be pardoned if we differ greatly, and, leaving to them the field of panegyric in which they may exult, we confine our discourse within the narrow bounds of history and truth.

units.la: Reginaldus Polus patre quidem Richardo equestris ordinis viro, Henrici septimi Regis fratre consobrino, Matre vero Margaretha Edwardi quarti Anglorum quondam Regis neptæ, Georgii Clarentini Ducis filia, atque Comitissa Sarisburiæ nata est. Quorum cuna, indole docili, ac moribus benignis eommodisque prædītus, literis à pueritia domi institutus, cumq; adoleuisset Oxonium ad Magdalenense Collegium missus est. Hunc Henr. Octauus Rex maxime adolescentem amauit, non modo quia paterni materno sanguinis cognatione atque necessitudine coniunctus ei fuit, verum etiam quod literis & doctrina Regiam quondam illustrare stirpem, & in Regni administratione summo sibi adiumento esse posse perspebat. Itaque eum & Exoniensi Decanatu, & amplissimis stipendiis auxit, ut in transmarinis Academiis, & multa scientiarum genera complecti, & exterarum gentium mores atque linguas callere simul posset. Quo Regis beneficio adiutus Polus venit Patauium, quae civitas Venetae ditionis est, habetque doctissimis in omni disciplinarum genere viris florentem atque refertam Academiam. Huc Polus concessit, deditque eloquentiae atque Philosophiae diu pariter operam, adeoque in utraque tandem profecit, ut non magis domestica nobilitate, qua in doctrina & ea famaarque ecclesiasticis tum honorem consecutus. Itaque cum nobilicas generis cum doctrina coniuncta magnum ei amorem & admirationem in Italia peperisset, in patriciorum nobiliumque Venetorum familiaritatem & consuetudinem allectus, a charitate patriae & beneficentissimi Regis obsequin ingratus recessit. Nam cum Henricus Octauus Rex (ut diximus) vsurpatam Papae potestatem Regno exterminare decreuisset, Polum in his quibus animum dedit artibus iam adultum & maturum domum amanter revocavit, ut patriae sibi optime de eo merito Regi in illis pontificiis angustiis atque difficultatibus mutuam gratamque operam rependeret, illumque cunctantem reditumque crebris dilationibus & excusationibus procrastinantem per alios grauissimos doctissimosque viros interpellari, & ne contagione pontificia dnm longius haereret in Italia, inficeretur admoneri curauit. Inter eos tum erat Stokesleius Londinensis, & Cuthbertus Tonstallus Dunelmensis Episcopi, quorum adhuc extant ad eum contra pontificiae potestatis copiosissimae, doctissimaeque scriptae literae. Verum Polus neque amore patriae, neque gratitudine officiorum in Regem motus, sed pontificiis tenebris exaecatus defecit, & Italorum consuetudine ab innata bonitate degeneravit. Ac coniunxit se quidem cum viris tum nobilitate, tum eloquentia, doctrinaque claris. Inter nobiles fuerunt Aloysius Priolus, Gaspar Contarenus, Petrus Bembus patricii Veneti, nec non Pertus Caraffa tum Archiepiscopus Theatinus, patria Neapolitanus, inde vero metu Caesaris ad Venetos profugus in Monasterio literisque delituit. Hiis etiam adiuncti sunt studiorum morumque similitudine Iacobus Sadoletus Episcopus Carpentoractensis in Gallia provincia, & Cnismus Gherius Fanensium Episcopus, tum ex plebeiis in Bononiensi & Patauina Academiis, Tryphon Gabrielius, M. Antonius Passerus cognomento Genua, Lampridius Cremonensis, Lazarus Bonamicus Bassianus, atque eius generis complures qui omnes eloquentiae faciunt, & Philosophiae scientia, literisque Graecis ac Latinis exteros non Italia modo, sed in quacunque alia regione longe antea sibi videbantur. Qui tamen omnes in Latinae nrationis facundia atque copia primas Polo nostro eo cedebant, ut ex literis inuicem ad se crebro datis, ac nupererime Paulo Manutio eloquentissimi viri testimonio enimprobatur. Quorum laudes etsi abfuissent; tamen Polus ipse hac in re locupletissimus suitestis esse poterat, qui ab ipso Sadoleto qui librum desertum & perdoctum de laudibus philosophiae tum conscriptum edidit lacessitus, vt iudicium de eo suum proferret. Polus longis literis ita respondit probari sibi quae de Philosophia scripsisset magnopere omnia, sed mirari se valde quod Romanae Ecclesiae Cardinalis omnium studiorum apicem atque fastigium, hominisque propositum finem in philosophia statuisset. Quae quanquam olim studiorum artium omnium principatum teneret, nunc tamen aduentu verbi deiectam esse scribit, & verbibus Virgilianis Tragedo comparat. Insula dives opum, Priami dum regna manebant, Et in conspectu Tenedos notissima fama, Nunc tantum sinus & statio male fida carinis. Sie Ethnica superstitione delata Theologiam nnn Philosphiam Christiano hmmo ni portum, ad quae totis velis conscendere debet, proponendo esse ait. Eam Poli Epistolae cum Sadoleti respondit qui diligenter contulerit, reperiet Poli, & in argumento, & ornatu facultateq; orationis omniq; tractatione fuisse superiorem. Sed iuuenis ingenii facundiatate cum rerum verborum frequens copia ei sine dicenti, sine scribenti succederet, Asiatic eam redundantiam sequi visus est. Quam vtex libris cum iam cernimus sine studio, sine flaecescente nratione sic tandem decoxit, vt senex in dicendo scribendoque redundantiam omnem & afluentiam a stilo relecauit, saepe etiam sine vbertate peneque succo ieiunis exiit imetur. Verum vtab huius doctrinae ac eloquentiae laude ad ea quae Polus gessit redeamus. Cum Henricus Rex dominatum papalem eiecisset, nec in Angliam rediit Polus vellet, primum stipendio Regina atque Exoniensi Decanatu mulctatus est.
units.tr: Reginald Pole was born, indeed, of a father, Richard, a man of the equestrian order, cousin of King Henry VII, and of a mother, Margaret, granddaughter of Edward IV, former King of the English, and daughter of George, Duke of Clarence, and Countess of Salisbury. Endowed with a docile disposition and kindly and agreeable manners, he was educated at home in letters from boyhood, and when he had grown up he was sent to Oxford, to Magdalen College. King Henry VIII loved him very much while he was still a youth, not only because he was connected with him by the kinship and tie of paternal and maternal blood, but also because he saw that he could by his learning and erudition adorn the royal stock, which had once been illustrious, and could be of the greatest help to himself in the government of the realm. Therefore the King increased his income with the deanery of Exeter and with very ample stipends, so that he could visit the overseas universities, master many kinds of learning, and at the same time become skilled in the customs and languages of foreign peoples. Aided by this kindness of the King, Pole came to Padua, a city in the dominion of Venice, which has a flourishing and well-stocked university of the most learned men in every branch of learning. Pole withdrew there and devoted himself for a long time equally to eloquence and philosophy, and he so profited in both that he gained honour not so much from his domestic nobility as from his learning and the reputation that went with it, and then from his ecclesiastical office. Thus, since his noble birth, joined with learning, had won him great affection and admiration in Italy, and he had been drawn into the friendship and company of the Venetian patricians and nobles, he forgot his love of country and the duty owed to his most kindly King. For when King Henry VIII (as we said) had decided to drive out of the realm the usurped power of the Pope, he lovingly recalled Pole, who was now grown and mature in those arts to which he had devoted himself, so that he might repay his country, which had deserved so well of him, and the King, with mutual and welcome service in those papal difficulties and straits. He also took care that, since Pole hesitated and kept putting off his return with frequent delays and excuses, he should be pressed by other most serious and learned men, and be warned that he should not stay longer in Italy and be infected by papal contagion. Among these at that time were Stokesley, Bishop of London, and Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, whose very copious and learned letters against the papal power written to him still survive. But Pole, moved neither by love of country nor by gratitude for the favours of the King, but blinded by papal darkness, fell away, and by the Italian habit degenerated from his natural goodness. And he joined himself indeed with men distinguished by their nobility, eloquence and learning. Among the nobles were Luigi Priuli, Gasparo Contarini, Pietro Bembo, Venetian patricians, and also Pietro Carafa, then Archbishop of Theate, a Neapolitan by birth, who afterwards, from fear of the Emperor, fled to the Venetians and hid himself in a monastery and among his books. To these were also joined, through similarity of studies and character, Jacopo Sadoleto, Bishop of Carpentras in the French province, and Gian Matteo Giberti, Bishop of Verona, and, from the commoners, in the Bolognese and Paduan academies, Trifone Gabriele, M. Antonio Passero, surnamed Genua, Lampridio of Cremona, and Lazzaro Bonamico of Bassano, and many others of that kind, all of whom were thought by themselves to surpass foreigners, not only in Italy but in any other region, in eloquence, philosophy, and knowledge of Greek and Latin letters. Yet all these yielded the first place in the fluency and abundance of Latin speech to our Pole, as is proved by the letters often sent among them, and most recently by the testimony of the most eloquent man Paolo Manuzio. Even if their praises were absent, Pole himself could be a most abundant witness in this matter, since Sadoleto, who had published a fine and very learned book on the praises of philosophy, challenged him to give his judgment on it. Pole answered in a long letter that everything he had written about philosophy pleased him greatly, but he wondered very much that a Cardinal of the Roman Church had placed the summit and pinnacle of all studies, and the chosen end of a man, in philosophy. Although philosophy once held the leadership of all the arts, he writes, it has now been cast down by the coming of the Word, and he compares it to Troy in Virgil's verses: "The island rich in wealth, while the realms of Priam remained, and Tenedos, famous in the sight of all, now only a bay and an unsafe anchorage for ships." So, he says, philosophy, carried away by Gentile superstition, ought to be set before the Christian man as a harbour, into which he must sail with full sails. Whoever carefully compares Pole's letter with Sadoleto's reply will find Pole superior in the subject matter, the ornament, the ability of his expression and the whole treatment. But since, as a young man, a fluent ease of expression and an abundance of matter came readily to him both in speaking and writing, he seemed to follow an Asiatic exuberance. We see this from his books, which, without care and without a sober style, he at last so boiled down that, as an old man, in speaking and writing he removed all exuberance and profusion from his style, and often seemed to go forth thin and almost dry, lacking juice. But let us return from the praise of this learning and eloquence to what Pole did. When King Henry had cast out the papal dominion, and Pole did not wish to return to England, he was first deprived of his stipend from the Queen and of the deanery of Exeter.

units.la: Quam multõ à pontificiis multò vberius quàm antea subleuatus sprenit atq; contempsit, vixitque eò maiori amplitudine, & cum Italis atque pontificiis arctiori necessitudine, quò magis ab Angliæ Rege, atque sua patria propter ingratitudinem atque pertinaciam (quæ in eam liberali ingenio, tantaque liberarum copia exculto summa vitia cõsentur) desertus atque repudiatus fuit. Papa vero tum Paulus 3. Clementi 7. successisset, cuius Secretarius fuit Petrus Bembus Poli familiarissimus. Is Polus in magna posuit pontificis gratia. Exitimarunt enim pontificii, cum Angli Imperium, iugumq; suum depulisset, partibus suis commodiorem & aptiorem quàm Polum habere se ad suas technas & insidias posse alium neminem. Quem nobilitate doctrinaque celebrem, & quocunque ab his impellerentur flexibilem ac procliuem, & Anglorum proceres, & aliarum gentiū principes ad bellum pro pontifice Romano contra Henricum Regem suscipiendum solicitare & commouere facile posse sperabant. His de causis deferendū eis à pontifice Cardinalitium honorem titulumq; suadebant, vt altiori gradu & authoritate præditus, res in Anglia nouas felicioribus auspiciis moliretur. Hoc consilium à pontifice approbatum est, qui vt virtutis doctrinaque rationem in creandis Cardinalibus potissimum sequi voluerit, non modo ipsum Polum, cuius & vita exterior cultu sincera atque integra, & mores amabiles atque commodi, & summa literarum scientia in omnium oculis versabantur, sed eius etiam familiares & Bembum, Contarenum, Sadoletum, & Petrum Caraffam Archiepiscopum Theatinum, in Cardinalium suorum numerum cooptauit. Qui Cardinalium delectus omnium quæ multis antea seculis contigerunt optimus & celeberrimus habebatur. Ex his Theatinus odio Cæsaris Gallicarum partium fuit, Polus verò Cæsarianus. Quæ res indelebiles inter eos (vt deinceps dicemus) procreauit inimicitias. Hæc Cardinalium delectatio ti. Kal. Jan. an. 1536. facta est. Polus verò Diaconus Cardinalis S. Mariæ in Cosmedin renunciatus est. Verum cum de suffulciendis iam labentibus rebus pontificiis & coercendis in Germania Lutheranis, atq; deturbando ex Anglia Euangelio secretius Romæ ageretur, designati sunt Theatinus, Polus, Cortesius D. Georgii Abbas, Matthæus Gibertus Veronensis Episcopus, qui communicato consilio ea literis mandarent, quæ ad rem communem adferre possint, quorum adhuc extat in Italia scriptum, editumq; de ea re Concilium. Quo expolito solus Polus ad interiorem Papæ familiaritatem, ipsumq; palatium, quia Angloru insidias sed dixit peremiscere, recepit us est. Ibi tutus cum aliquot mensibus in ipsius Papæ sinu gremioq; consedisset, protinus infatuatus & tanq; Circæo exhausto poculo ex Anglo in Italo, ex Christiano in pontificium convertis. Omitto hic quid ab ipsis Italis de nostratibus ad eos mutatis dici solet, quantum & quam monstrosam Metamorphosim, & non modo contra humanā speciē ac naturam sed contra diuinam eam esse fingunt. Et quamuis Poli culpa omnem tam flagitet non modo acerbitate, sed atrocitatem sermonis, tamen ne gravius aliquid in eum dicamus quàm id quòd ab ipsis pontificiis Italiæq; obiectum ei sepe fuit, latini sub suq; simplicitatis specie illud à sapiente alienissimum sane vitium quod à morû facilitate Græci recte appellant. Nam qui Italis pontificisq; adulationibus, conciliis atq; technis in Regis atque patriæ discrimine sic se abduci passus est, vt non modo defertor esset, sed etiam proditor, cuius in eo fœderis, virtutis, amorisque constantiam fuisse iudicaremus? Atilla (credo) simplicitas primò vt in Anglo recta ingenuaq; fuit, sed cum diuturna Romanæ gentis consuetudine versutias eas calluisset, naturalis probitatis externam atque adumbratam retinuit speciem, dissimulationis verò atque fraudis vitium consuetudine contractum in pectore fotum occultauit. Iamque ad omnes artes pontificias Polus cõpositus suscepit ad Gallorum Regem, & ad Belgas duas à Papa laboris & discriminis plenas legationes. Cuius etsi aliæ prætexebantur causæ, tamen habere à Papa in mandatis vnâ voluit vt vtrosque tã, Cæsarem quàm Gallum ad bellum Henrico Regi, Angliæque inferendum, Papæ, Romanæque curiæ nomine solicitaret.
