Sed has (vt in Warhamo & & Cranmero antea diximus) insidias pontificias Henr. Rex non minus prudenter quàm diuinitus anteuertit. Neque enim aut Cæsar aut Gallus cum de finibus ac imperiis tã hostiliter dimicarent Regem audebant irritare, ne ad alteram tum partem inclinato, aduersam partem pessundaret. Ita cum huius tam diu flagrāris belli victoria, cœlitus in Regis potestate posita videretur, vt eam quocunq; vellet transferret, nec pontificiorum cõspirationes atq; doli, nec Polus ingratus & abortius patriæ partus, nec ipsa infernalis potentia quicquam in Regem Euangelii ruentem præualere potuerunt. Polus cum ad has legationes obeundas se se ppararet, consanguineos, affines, atq necessarios in Anglia suos
units.tr: Polus was raised far more generously by the Papists than before, and he scorned and despised the England he had left behind. He lived all the more splendidly, and in closer alliance with the Italians and the Papists, the more he had been deserted and rejected by the King of England and by his own country, because of his ingratitude and obstinacy. (Those are considered the greatest vices in a man of a generous nature, cultivated by such an abundance of liberal learning.) Then Paul III succeeded Clement VII, and Pietro Bembo, Polus's very close friend, was his secretary. Polus gained great favour with the Pope. For the Papists judged that, now that the English had thrown off their empire and yoke, they could find no one more suited or better fitted than Polus for their schemes and plots. They hoped that, because of his noble birth and learning, and because he could be easily swayed and inclined in whatever direction they pushed him, he could readily rouse and stir up both the English nobles and the princes of other nations to take up war against King Henry on behalf of the Roman pontiff. For these reasons they urged that the cardinal's dignity and title be conferred on him, so that, endowed with a higher rank and authority, he might undertake new projects in England under more favourable auspices. The Pope approved this plan. In creating cardinals he wished above all to follow the standard of virtue and learning, and so he admitted into the number of his cardinals not only Polus himself, whose outward life was known to all as sincere and blameless, whose manners were pleasant and agreeable, and whose learning was outstanding, but also his close friends Bembo, Contarini, Sadoleto, and Pietro Carafa, Archbishop of Theate. This choice of cardinals was regarded as the best and most celebrated of all those made in many previous centuries. Of these, the Theatine was hostile to the party of the Emperor Charles and favoured the French, whereas Polus was on the Emperor's side. This difference produced lasting enmities between them, as we shall say later. This appointment of cardinals was made on 17 December 1536. Polus was then named deacon cardinal of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. But when, at Rome, it was discussed more secretly how to prop up the tottering affairs of the Papacy, how to restrain the Lutherans in Germany, and how to overthrow the Gospel in England, the Theatine, Polus, Cortese, abbot of San Giorgio, and Matteo Giberti, Bishop of Verona, were appointed to pool their counsel and commit to writing whatever might contribute to the common cause. A council on that subject, written and published, still survives in Italy. When this business was finished, Polus alone was admitted to the Pope's more intimate favour and to the palace itself, since he said he was avoiding the English plots. There, safe, he settled for some months in the very bosom and lap of the Pope. Then, as if he had drunk from Circe's cup, he was at once bewitched and transformed: from an Englishman into an Italian, from a Christian into a Papist. I pass over here what the Italians themselves are wont to say about our countrymen who have changed over to them, and how great and how monstrous a metamorphosis they claim it is, contrary not merely to human nature but to divine nature. And although Polus's fault would call for language not only harsh but savage, still, so that we may not say anything more severe about him than what the Papists and the Italians themselves often objected to him, we may say that he suffered from that vice, most alien to a wise man, which the Greeks rightly call easiness of disposition, though Latin writers cover it under the appearance of simplicity. For what sort of man was it who allowed himself to be drawn away by Italian flattery, by the councils and plots of the Pope, in a crisis for the King and his country, so that he was not merely a deserter but a traitor too, whose constancy in loyalty, virtue, and love we would judge to have been present in him? Attila's simplicity (I think) was at first upright and frank, as it was in England; but after long acquaintance with Roman customs had made him skilled in those tricks, he kept the outward and shadowy appearance of natural honesty, while the vice of dissimulation and deceit, acquired by habit, he concealed and nursed in his breast. And now, equipped for all the Papal arts, Polus undertook, at the Pope's command, two embassies full of toil and danger: one to the King of France and one to the two Low Countries. Although other reasons were put forward for these, he was willing to have one thing in his instructions from the Pope: that he should urge both the Emperor and the French King, in the name of the Pope and the Roman Curia, to make war on King Henry and invade England. But King Henry, as we said earlier in the cases of Warham and Cranmer, anticipated these Papal plots no less wisely than providentially. For neither the Emperor nor the French King, while they were fighting so bitterly over borders and dominions, dared to provoke the King, lest, if he leaned to one side, he would crush the other. Thus, since the victory in this long-burning war seemed to lie from heaven in the King's power, so that he could transfer it wherever he wished, neither the conspiracies and tricks of the Papists, nor Polus, ungrateful and an abortive offspring of his country, nor infernal power itself, could prevail against the King, who was advancing the Gospel.

units.la: Anglius Ita- lianatus, Ortaboles incet matus. suos nuncijs literisq; confirmauit, vt in pontificia fide conflatrent, & suarum legationum exitum expectarent. Rex hanc coniurationem atque legationum nefarias causas occultis tam Romæ, quàm in Italia, Gallia, atque Germania disponitis exploratoribus ôrquisiuit. Et cum de Poli in Gallias aduentu cognouisset, egit eum Hallo per Legatos vt Polum perduellionis iafæq; maiestatis reum, ad subeundas tanti criminis poenas in Angliam mitteret. Gallus id esse contra religionem iuraq; facialium legatum alicoitus ac præfertim Papæ supplicio concedere existimauit. Sed ne Regem offenderet, Poli legationem non admisit, sed regno eum quàm celeriter discedere iussit. Perplexus Potus festinanter in Belgium contendit, vbi nec à Cæsare quidem receptus est, quia Rex paulò an-te in cum eiusq; matrem Sarisburiæ Comitissam, aliosq; in Anglia Poli condemnatos proscriptionis sententiam in Parlamento tulisset. Iraque Leodium ab Erardo à Marchia Cardinali eius ciuitatis Episcopo inuitatus se recepit. Atquehie non adeo diutur-nam moram fecit, cum Rex ab exploratoribus de eo Leodii commemorante certior factus; à Belgis per legatos, perq; veterea illa Burgundiæ foedera postulauit, ne eum qnem iure sui Regni quondam subditum, nunc aut num hostem & perduellionem iudicaret, in Belgio grassari diutius paterentur, sed suis legatis tradetent. Hoc Regis postulato in publico Belgarum consilio cui tum Erardus Cardinalis Leodiensis Episcopus interfuit declarato, Polo nuneiatum est, ut per Germaniam confestim atq; clam festinarot Romam. Ita Poli discessio eum fugæ similis videretur, ad Papam legationibus inutiliter, aut sitta liceat dicere nulliter perfunctus, turpiter reuersus est. At pontificii cum Polum iam proscriptū, & perduellionem à patria iudicatum ab imaduerterent, cognouerunt eò sua confœderatione recedere saluum atque tutum esse non posse, nec animis infœlici superio: is legationis euentu iam exacerbatis reincepta & imperfecta voluerunt desistere. Itaque nouam obtruduntei legationis eamq; periculosissimam prouinciam. Cæsar rebusin Belgio atque Germania compositis in Hispanias profectus est, eo Papæ iussu Polo proficisc-endum fuit, deinde ad Gallum vt ageret cum vtroque vt fœdus atque amicitiam cum Rege repente præciderint, impetumq; vnâ in eum facerent. Ipse verò aliquo loco siue in Belgio, siue in Gallia finibus subsisteret, vbi totius rei exitum cômodius expectaret, atq; interim de singulis rebus pontificem, certiorem redderet. Cum his mandatis Polus mutato veltitu paucis quibusdam comitibus per equos dispositos profectionem maturauit, magnaque celeritate recta in Hispanias ad Cæsarem qui tum Toleti erat, venit. Cæsar qui retinere Regem in pristino fœdere voluit, sic Polum audiuit, vt alienum esse id tempus exequendis suis postulatis respondoret, & vt eum à se ablegaret, voluit vt Gallum consulat. Quo responso intellexit Polus q; callidè atq; artificiose illusisset ei Cæsar, quòd nulla proposita spe aut vilitate suaissset, vt cum cauta propter quam missus esset derrimento ac ruina sen Galli potestatem, certissimisq; capitis periculis permittetet. Iraque venia reuertendi facile atque cirò impetrata venit Auinionem, indeq; ad familiarem suum Iacobum Sadoletum, Carpentoracti Episcopum ac etiam Cardinalem, vbi tutò paulisper conquiescit, donec de Papæ voluntate cognosceret, quoniam ille duæ ciuitates papalis ditionis fuerunt. Ac paulò post à Pontifice reuocarus erat legationes suæ inanes vtilitatis fuissent, & in nihilum fuissent, tamen quia periculosiorum profectionum laboribus suscepti, pro amplitudine pontificia tuenda se opposuisset Regi atque patriæ, Wirerbiensem Legationem tanquam laborum inutilium præmium & mercedem acceptat Papa. Est autem Witerbiû Episcopalis, & Romanæ ditionis, ciuitas quæ Roma 60 mille passibus distat. Hue tot laboribus exantlatis, iamPapæ lateralis legatus se contulit Polus; ac militari custodia(quia Anglum atque vt dixit insidiantem, suum scilicet vmbram timebat) secinxit ac muniuit, rerumq; haud prosperè gestarum infœlicijuentu stupefactus, eû se frustra Romanæ amplitudinis contra patriam dilatandæ tam diu studuisse senserat; reliquis ceteris actibus & disciplinis totus Theologus esse voluit. Verûm id quod effecit tardius, vt inam suscepisset ocyus. Iam enim à pontifice iis necessitudinibus & honoribus depravatus liquidò ac sincere de sanctis Scripturis existimare ae sentire voluit, sed rei sæpe maiestate & veritate perculsus, animo incertus fluctuabat, & hucillue nunc ad pontificios, nisi ad Euangelicos impulsus est. Id indicabat frequens ad eum Euangelicorum concursus, & Antonii Flaminij dicertissimi oratoris ac Poetæ qui Psalmos Datuidicos in Lyrica vertit carmina confuerudo, tum Immanuelis Tremellii doctissimi viri qui à Iudaica pertinacia ad Christum in Poli familia conuersus, & contra pontificia-am doctrinam edoctus fuit, ac Euangelica dogmata ibidem hausit, nec non à Polo & Flamminio in Baptismo intra domesticos Poli parietes suscepcrus est. Adhæc domus ejus ipsorum Monachorum atq; fratrum Coenobia & Claustra impura deferentium, reliquorumque à pontificia sece deficientium, & ex Italia in Germaniam migrantium portus & occultum perfugium fuit. Praeterea in eos qui Lutheriana haeresis atque sectae in Wintherbiensi provincia postulabantur, neque inquisitione neq; poena seueriori quam animadvertit, sed aliquot ibi annis tanquam in studiis sepultus, & a mundanis rebus tortus abductus atque separatus visus est. Verum nescio quomodo Poli castitas in qua vna virtute omnes Romae Cardinales facile superabat, dum Witerbu contemplaretur, dixit: Nam Papae castello vbi Polus habitabat, adiunctum est Monasterium Coenobium Sanctae Clarae dedicatum. His Monialibus suis vicinis vt in castitate retinerentur, scilicet dicitur proiecisse Polus, earumq; Abbatissam quae nobilis Perusina fuit ad 10 ie eiuocasse sepius. Ex quorum frequenti congressu Pasquillus Romanus qui nullius fama aut dignitatis parcit, sapiusque vera quam falsa narrat, Latinis Italicisq; carminibus Romae diuulgauit, eam e Polo peperisse bis, primò masculinam deinde foeminam prolem, sed de his omnibus quae Witerbii gestit, audiuit (ut postea dicemus) maxime tū, cum ad Papatum electus est. Interea cum inter Caesarem atque Gallum bellum exardesceret, Euangelium in Anglia sit marcetur, ac in Germania fidelium numerus augeretur, Paulus. 5 Papa quo non fuit verumor aut callidior alter, Euangelicam doctrinam alia via profligare aggreditur. Nam Concilium generale indixit Tridenti, cui Polum, Parrisium, & Mortuum Cardinales Legatos suos praefecit, quod interuentu & astu belli inter Caesarem atque Gallum gestus ob militum in Helvetia, Germania, Gallia, ac Hispania, ipsaque 20 saepe Italia delectus atque apparatus mox interruptum cessauit. Intermissio autem aliquatenus eo bello Tridentinum Concilium reuocatum, & Polo aliisque legatis videlicet de Monte & S. Crucis Cardinalibus a Papa gubernandum commissum est. De quo Concilio satis ex Pontificiorum sententia, & concinne scripsit Polus, eumq; libellum ad collegas suos dedicatum emisit in lucem. Sed ne hoc quidem Concilii ad eum quem Pontificii iperabant, exitium quicquam perduxit. Nam & auctus Euangelicorum in Germania numerus ipsum Caesarem ne Concilium ratum haberet adegit. Et polus in variis cogitationes distractus inter Euangelicam & Ponificiam fidem anceps dubiusque pendebat, ac fide sola sine operibus iustificari coram Deo hominiis in Concilio decernendum suadebat, Morellum quendam Hispanum qui eo aduenerat vt contra Euangelicos disputaret, hospitio exceptum suo in eandem sententiam trahebat. Itaq; Euangelicis permultis bonam sui opinionem commouit, & Papam ita Concilio diffidere fecit, vt & is a vocatus, & Cocilium a Tridento Bononiam traductum fuerit. Hoc Caesar indigne tulit vt Concilium in Italiam transferretur, de quo per Piegum Huttadum Oratorem suum edito libello omnibus publice conquestus & contestatus est. Germaniaq; religionis formulam descriptam in eo libro quem Interim appellauit. Quorū vtrumq; Polus iam in Papae conspectu positus edius reiponsis coarguit. Haec Poli varietas & inconstantia vt aliud Romae, aliud alibi de religione sentiret, effecit vt neque sibi, nec alteri cuipiam constare videretur, vcnireque ipsis Italis in eius vitii suspicionem, quod illi Dapocagiae vocant, quo nomine designant eum qui proprii consilii inops, totus pendet ab aliis, cuiusmodi virum imperio aut magistratui gerendo prorsus inutilem & ineptum statuunt. Itaq; cum vita decederet Paulus 3. Papa, conuenerunt in coelauì ex more omnes Cardinales vt communibus votis & suffragiis nouû Papam designarent. In qua electione omnibus ingenii, pollicitationum, numerumque neruis inter duas Cardinalium factiones, Caesarianos scilicet atq; Gallicanos decertatum est Polus ipse Caesarianus ad se traxit & Caesarianos, & eos qui neutrius partis essent. Ex his tum erat Alexander Farnesius Pauli Papae defuncti nepos, cuius praeter caeteros tum magnopere valebat authoritas, adduxitque maximam Cardinalium partem ad Polum eligendum. At qui Gallorum Regis causa aliquid volebant, obiiciebant esse cauendum, ne Polus ad pro pontificatu Caesari nimis addictus, qui conuiuando haud ita pride Romã diripuit, & aduentu protinus suo totam Italiam perturbauit, omnia in eius potestatem permitteret. Itaque habendam esse Gallicorum Cardinalium qui nondum adessent, rationem, eosq; expectandos atque audiendos, quid tam è Galli, quae Caesaris re in eligendo Papa futurum sit, ne factiosus aliquis & in alteram partem nimis propensus ad omnia tumultuose innouandae emergat Papa. Sed nihilominus cum postridie recensferentur iterum in scrutinio suffragia, repertus est maior eorum qui Polo adhaesserunt numerus, quam ut à Gallicanis poterat obsisti. Hie Polus simiditarem, ignaviam seu hypocrisim ostendit aperte suam, rei enim perfecta fecĭæ & ad exitum perductæ nouam dilationem & deliberationem sine causa interpo-suit. Quo animaduerso exortus Cardinalis Theatinus, qui vnà cum Polo aliisque (vt dixi-mus) Cardinalis à Paulo 3. renunciarus est, hic Paparus ipse atq; cupiditate si Polus repul-sam paterentur ductus, ambitionem, hæresis & incõinentiæ suspicionē obiecit Polo. Ambitionem quod præmaturè Pontificatum ambiret: hæresim quod in Germania atq; Tridentina legatione nimis familiariter Lutheranorum consuetudine vsus esset, ac Antonium Flamminium Lutheranismi suspectum domi secum diu habuisset, eumq; præben-dis & Ecclesiasticis dignitatibus locupletasset, tum in Viterbiensi legatione fontibus ple-rumq; pepercisset & paucos modico supplicio, nullos autem morte affecisset: Incontineotiam, quod filiam suam apud Moniales Romæ educandam collocasset. Quos etiam conuiniosos sermones in populum disseminabat, vt Polus in iofamiam ductus Pontificatum non perciperet. Quibus ita vt poterat respondit satis grauiter atq; scite Polus (eam enim vultus grauitatem semper tulit, nullius iniuria aut contumelia, aut casu siue aduerso siue secundo quocunq; vnquam mutaretur) onus Pontificatus existimari a se tanto pondere, vt suscipienti terrorem magis quàm desiderium adferrat.
units.tr: Pole, having arranged for his relatives, connections and close friends in England to be encouraged by messages and letters, so that they would stand firm in the papal faith and wait for the outcome of his missions, was himself meanwhile, along with the Italians, sending out spies to Rome, Italy, France and Germany. The King tracked down this conspiracy and the wicked purposes of these embassies. When he learned of Pole's arrival in France, he persuaded Hallo, through envoys, to demand that Pole, as a traitor and guilty of treason, be sent to England to pay the penalty for so great a crime. The Frenchman judged that it was contrary to religion and to the law of nations to hand over an ambassador to punishment, and especially a man sent by the Pope. Yet, not wishing to offend the King, he refused to receive Pole's embassy and ordered him to leave the kingdom as quickly as possible. Perplexed, Pole hurried into Belgium, where he was not received even by the Emperor, because shortly before the King had pronounced sentence of outlawry in Parliament against him, against his mother the Countess of Salisbury, and against others in England who had been condemned on Pole's account. Therefore he withdrew to Liège, at the invitation of Erard de la Marck, Cardinal and bishop of that city. Nor did he stay there very long, for the King, informed by his spies that Pole was staying at Liège, demanded through envoys from the Belgians, and by those old treaties of Burgundy, that they should not permit a man whom he judged to be a former subject of his realm, and now either an enemy or a traitor, to roam about in Belgium any longer, but should hand him over to his envoys. When this demand of the King was declared in the public council of the Belgians, at which Erard, Cardinal and bishop of Liège, was then present, it was announced to Pole that he should hurry to Rome at once and in secret, by way of Germany. Thus Pole's departure looked like a flight; having carried out his embassy to the Pope fruitlessly, or, if one may say so, without effect, he returned in disgrace. But when the Papists saw that Pole had now been proscribed and judged a traitor to his country, they realised that he could not be safe or secure in their company, and, since their minds were already exasperated by the outcome of the embassy, they wished to abandon the enterprise, which had been begun but not completed. So they thrust upon him a new embassy, a most dangerous task: when the Emperor had settled affairs in Belgium and Germany and set out for Spain, Pole was ordered by the Pope to go to the French King, and to act with both of them so that they might suddenly break off their alliance and friendship with the King and make a joint attack upon him. He himself was to stay somewhere, either in Belgium or on the borders of France, where he could more conveniently await the outcome of the whole affair, and meanwhile keep the Pope informed of each development. With these instructions, Pole, changing his dress and with a few companions, hastened his journey by means of relays of horses, and with great speed came straight into Spain to the Emperor, who was then at Toledo. The Emperor, who wished to keep the King to the former alliance, heard Pole in such a way that he answered that this was not the time to carry out his demands, and, wishing to send him away from himself, told him to consult the French King. By this reply Pole understood that Caesar had cleverly and artfully deceived him, since, without holding out any hope or advantage, he had sent him on a mission that would expose him, to the ruin and loss of the French power, and to the gravest dangers to his life. Therefore, with leave to return easily and quickly obtained, he came to Avignon, and from there to his close friend Jacopo Sadoleto, bishop and also cardinal of Carpentras, where he rested safely for a little while until he learned the Pope's will, since those two cities belonged to the papal dominion. A little later he was recalled by the Pope, and although his embassies had been of no use and had come to nothing, yet, because he had undertaken them with the labours of more dangerous journeys, and had set himself against the King and his country in defence of the papal greatness, the Pope accepted the legation of Viterbo as the reward and wage of his useless labours. Viterbo is an episcopal city in the Roman dominion, sixty miles from Rome. Having endured so many labours, Pole withdrew there, now a legate of the Pope; he fortified and guarded himself with a military guard, since he feared the Englishman, who (as he said) was plotting against him, that is, his own shadow. Stunned by the unhappy outcome of affairs that had not gone well, he realised that he had in vain for so long striven to extend Roman greatness against his country. He wished to be wholly a theologian, setting aside all other activities and studies. Yet he did this more slowly than he should have begun it. For, now corrupted by the Pope with those connections and honours, he wished to judge and think soundly and sincerely about the holy Scriptures, but, often struck by the majesty and truth of the matter, he wavered in an uncertain mind, and was driven hither and thither, now towards the Papists, now towards the evangelicals. This was shown by the frequent gathering of evangelicals to him, and by the familiar company of Antonio Flaminio, a most eloquent orator and poet who had turned the Davidic Psalms into lyric verse; also by Immanuel Tremellius, a most learned man who, converted from Jewish obstinacy to Christ in Pole's household and instructed against papal teaching, drank in evangelical doctrines there, and was baptised by Pole and Flaminio within the walls of Pole's own house. Besides, his house was a harbour and secret refuge for those very monks and brothers who were deserting their cloisters and impure convents, and for the rest who were falling away from the papacy and migrating from Italy into Germany. Moreover, against those who were accused of the Lutheran heresy and sect in the province of Viterbo, he did not proceed by inquisition or by more severe punishment, but seemed to be buried for some years there as among his studies, and drawn away and separated from worldly affairs. But I know not how it was that Pole's chastity, in which alone he easily surpassed all the cardinals at Rome, was called into question while he was being observed at Viterbo. For there was attached to the Pope's castle where Pole lived a convent of nuns dedicated to Saint Clare. It is said that Pole used to visit these nuns, who were his neighbours, in order that they might be kept in chastity, and often summoned their abbess, who was a noble woman of Perugia. From their frequent meetings the Roman Pasquil, who spares no one's reputation and tells more often what is false than what is true, spread abroad in Latin and Italian verses at Rome that she had borne two children to Pole, first a boy and then a girl. But all these things that were done at Viterbo he heard (as we shall say later), chiefly when he was elected to the papacy. Meanwhile, as war was blazing up between the Emperor and the French King, the Gospel was being hindered in England, and the number of the faithful was increasing in Germany, Pope Paul III, than whom there was no more cunning or crafty other man, set about overthrowing evangelical doctrine by another way. For he called a general council at Trent, over which he placed Pole, Parisio and Mortuus, his cardinals and legates. But this council, because of the war between the Emperor and the French King and the levies and preparations of soldiers in Switzerland, Germany, France and Spain, and indeed often in Italy itself, was soon interrupted and ceased. The Council of Trent was recalled after the war had been somewhat interrupted, and was entrusted by the Pope to Pole and the other legates, namely the cardinals of Monte and Santa Croce. Pole wrote about this council, quite fittingly and sufficiently by the opinion of the Papists, and issued a little book dedicated to his colleagues. But not even this council brought about in any way the destruction that the Papists desired. For the growing number of evangelicals in Germany compelled the Emperor himself not to ratify the council. Pole, distracted by various thoughts and wavering between the evangelical and the papal faith, hung in doubt and uncertainty, and he urged that it should be decided in the council that men are justified before God by faith alone without works. He drew into the same opinion a certain Spaniard named Morello, who had come there to dispute against the evangelicals, received him as his guest, and by this won for himself a good reputation among many evangelicals. And he so caused the Pope to distrust the council that both he was recalled and the council was transferred from Trent to Bologna. The Emperor took this badly, that the council should be moved into Italy, and he publicly complained and protested about it to everyone, through his ambassador Pflug, by a published pamphlet; and he set out in that book the form of religion called the Interim for Germany. Pole, now placed before the Pope's eyes, refuted both of these by his replies. This variability and inconstancy of Pole, so that at Rome he judged one thing about religion and elsewhere another, made it seem that he was consistent neither with himself nor with anyone else; and even the Italians came to suspect him of that fault which they call dapocagia, by which name they designate a man who, lacking his own counsel, depends wholly on others; such a man they judge utterly useless and unfit for exercising command or holding office. So when Pope Paul III died, all the cardinals gathered in the conclave, as is customary, to name a new Pope by common votes and suffrages. In this election, with all the powers of wit, promises and numbers, there was a contest between the two factions of cardinals, namely the partisans of the Emperor and the partisans of the French. Pole himself, being on the Emperor's side, drew to himself both the Emperor's supporters and those who belonged to neither party. Among these at that time was Alexander Farnese, nephew of the late Pope Paul, whose authority then carried especially great weight, and he brought the greater part of the cardinals to elect Pole. But those who wanted something for the French King objected that care must be taken lest Pole, too closely devoted to the Emperor, who not long before had plundered Rome during his sojourn there and by his arrival had at once thrown all Italy into confusion, should give everything into his power. Therefore, they said, account must be taken of the French cardinals who were not yet present, and they must be awaited and heard, to see what would happen in the election of a Pope on the part of the French and of the Emperor, lest some factious man, too inclined to one side, should rise up to stir up everything tumultuously as Pope. Nevertheless, when on the following day the votes were counted again in the scrutiny, a greater number of those who had adhered to Pole was found than could be resisted by the Frenchmen. Here Pole openly showed his own rashness, cowardice or hypocrisy: for when the matter was already completed and brought to its end, he interposed a new delay and deliberation without cause. Noticing this, the Theatine cardinal arose, who, together with Pole and the others (as I have said) had been made a cardinal by Paul III. This man, driven by the rage of his own ambition, and by the desire that Pole should be repulsed, charged Pole with ambition, heresy and suspicion of incontinence. Ambition, because he was aspiring prematurely to the papacy; heresy, because in Germany and in the Tridentine legation he had too familiarly used the company of the Lutherans, and had kept Antonio Flaminio, suspected of Lutheranism, long at home with him, and had enriched him with benefices and ecclesiastical dignities; further, that in the Viterbo legation he had spared the heretics too much, and had punished a few with moderate penalties but put none to death. Incontinence, because he had placed his daughter to be brought up among the nuns at Rome. He also spread these slanderous words among the people, so that Pole, brought into infamy, might not obtain the papacy. To these charges Pole replied as well as he could, quite gravely and skilfully (for he always bore that gravity of countenance, which was never changed by any injury or insult, or by any chance, whether adverse or favourable): the burden of the papacy, he said, seemed to him so heavy that it brought fear rather than desire to the one who undertook it. Then, that every suspicion of heresy ought to be far from him, since he had incurred the hatred and offence of the King and his country for the sake of the papal religion. Lastly, the little girl whom he had handed over to the nuns at Rome to be brought up was the daughter of a certain English woman, who had died at Rome, and Pole had presented the girl to the nuns...

units.la: Deindeomnem hæresis suspicionem a se procul abesse debere, qui Pontificiæ religionis causa in Regis atq; patriæ odium offensionemq; incurrisset. Poltremo paruulam quam Monialibus Romæ enutriendam tradiderat, fuisse Anglicanæ cuiusdam multieris, quæ Romæ obierat filiam, eam vero exhibuisse Polum, & Monialibus in disciplinam dedisse, ne puella atq; otiosa se malis artibus daret, dotem ei præterea in publico Romæ loco, quem Fidei-motem appellant, centum aureorum depositisse, ne egesta: egr andæuaad incertos casus extrudatur. Cuius generis munificentias cum in alios perpultos cooferre Polus consueuerat, charitatis atq; pietatis potius officia, quam incontinentiæ signa à bo-nis viris exstimari debent. Has criminationes cum ita diluissetPolus, iterum noctē Papa electus est. Itaq; Farnesius Cardinalis, cæteriq; qui in eam sententiam ibant ad Polū eupidè accurrunt, orantq; vt se de more adorari, & Papæ sanctissimiq; patris nomine saluta-ri parerentur. At is noctumum tempus causabatur, odisse Deum tenebras, lucem recte factis atq; diem designari dicebat, quare procrastinari voluit rem. Quam Poli morani faruitatem appellabantCardinales. Itaq; postridie omnia mutata, & Cardinalium studia inclausi exiret, à Cardinali Theatino de Poli Pontificatu percunctantibus, eiusq; tardeatē quærentibus quibusdam contumeliosissimē responsum est, nihil contingere potuisse in-commodius quam si ille Pontifex renunciaretur, propterea quod omnibus iam se stipirem esse ostendisset, qui neq; oblatum Papatum suscipere t, necaptè recusarer, sed in suspenso rem hærere sinerer. In hus cūctanoribus atq; moris venit Guifianus è Guifiana Cardinalis, cuius maxima fuit ex altera parte potestas, cum quo Farnesius iam Polum tanquam pusillanimum parui faciens, vt cum Gallo saltem iniret gratiam se coniunxit Et cum hi duo reliquorum suffragiis arbitratu suo vterentur, Montius quidam Cardinalis, qui in Concilio Tridentino Poli (vt diximus) collega fuit, Papa declaratus, ac Iulius 3. dictus est. Polus etsi pusillanimitatis aut vecordiæ à plerisq; accusaretur, tamen animi tranquillitarem & oris constantiam non deposuit, quo & librum à se in illa electione mora in Conclavi de Papæ præficiendo compositum, & disertissimam Epistolam qua Pacensi Hispano cuidam Episcopo de non suscepto Pontificatu respondit, edidit. Ac Iulius nouus Papa Polum eò humanius tractauit, quod eius mora quàquam inepta atq; odiosi, Papatum adeptus sit. Itaque Theatinum Cardinalem impostorem ambitiosissimum, qui Poli famam conuitiis (vt diximus) laesit, in Cœclaui præsentem ea quæ contra Polum emisisset reuocare, cinisq; veniam exorare coegit. Cuius rei conceptum odium idem Theatinus postea (vt dicemus) creatus Papa acerbissime in Polum cuomuit.
units.tr: Next, he ought to be far from any suspicion of heresy, since he had incurred the hatred and displeasure of the King and the country for the sake of the Papist religion. Lastly, the little girl whom he had handed over to the nuns at Rome to be brought up was the daughter of an English woman who had died at Rome. Pole had taken the girl in, placed her in the nuns' care for training, so that she, being idle and unoccupied, would not give herself to bad arts. Moreover, he had deposited a dowry of a hundred gold pieces for her in a public place at Rome which they call the Monte della Fede, so that she would not be cast out in need into uncertain chances. Good men ought to regard such generosity, which Pole was accustomed to bestow on other destitute people, as acts of charity and piety rather than signs of wantonness. When Pole had answered these accusations in this way, he was again elected Pope by night. So Cardinal Farnese and the others who were of that opinion eagerly hurried to Pole, and begged that they might be allowed, as is customary, to adore him and to greet him with the name of Pope and Most Holy Father. But he pleaded that it was night, saying that God hates darkness, that light and day are the symbols of good deeds, and so he wished to postpone the matter. The Cardinals called this delay of Pole's a dull sluggishness. So the next day everything had changed, and when the Cardinals' zeal had gone out of the conclave, some asked Cardinal Theatino about Pole's papacy and inquired about his delay, and he answered most abusively that nothing could have happened more inconveniently than for that man to be declared Pope, since he had already shown himself to all as a fool who neither accepted the papacy when offered nor openly refused it, but let the matter hang in suspense. Among these hesitators came Cardinal Guise of the House of Guise, who held the greatest power on the one side. Farnese, now making light of Pole as faint-hearted, joined himself to Guise, so that at least he might win the favour of the Frenchman. When these two made use of the votes of the rest according to their own judgment, a certain Cardinal Monte, who had been Pole's colleague at the Council of Trent (as we have said), was declared Pope and was named Julius III. Although Pole was accused by many of timidity or folly, he did not give up his calm of mind and steadiness of countenance. He published both the book he had written during that election, in the conclave, on the choice of a Pope, and a most eloquent letter in which he replied to a certain Spanish bishop of Pace about the papacy he had not accepted. The new Pope Julius treated Pole all the more kindly because, though Pole's delay had been most unwise and hateful, he had attained the papacy. So he compelled the Theatine Cardinal, an impostor and most ambitious man who had injured Pole's reputation with insults (as we have said), to recall in the conclave, in his presence, what he had said against Pole, and to beg pardon of him. The Theatine, later made Pope (as we shall relate), bitterly vented the hatred he had conceived from this matter against Pole.

units.la: Verum Polus qui Papatum non alieno sed suo tantum vitio carere putabatur, o-mnem iam authoritatem gratiamque apud Italos amisit, qui eos maxime admirantur ac suspiciunt quos in petendis gerendisque honoribus non labefactari aut concidere, sed erigi animo ac attollisenserint. Itaque ex omnium conspectu impetrata à Pontifice potestate in agrum Veronensem ad Cœnobium Mooachorum ordinis Benedictini secessit. Huius Monachorum ordinis ille patronus Romæ fuerat, inrer hos itaque se abdere, & reliquam vitam transigere cum statuisset, toia Italia percrebuit de Edwardi Regis in An-glia morte, &D. Mariæ Reginæ successione nunciū. Id q. Polū qui spiritus animumque dimisserat, magnopere exhilarauit, eumque à seculo pene exclusum, in lucem & humanam societatem, ipsamque Romam prouinciarum Ecclesiasticarum forum atque mercaturam claustro iterum eduxir atque reuocauit. Sperabat enim iam perhonorifi-
units.tr: But Pole, who was thought to lack the papacy not through anyone else's fault but only through his own, now lost all his authority and favour among the Italians. They most admire and esteem those whom they perceive, in seeking and holding office, not to be shaken or cast down, but to be lifted up and raised in spirit. So, out of everyone's sight, having obtained the Pope's permission, he withdrew to the Benedictine monastery in the Veronese territory. He had been the patron of this order at Rome, and having decided to hide among these monks and spend the rest of his life there, news of the death of King Edward in England and the succession of Queen Mary spread throughout all Italy. This greatly cheered Pole, whose spirit and courage had been dismayed. It led him, almost shut out from the world, out of the cloister again into light and human society, and back to Rome itself, the forum and marketplace of the ecclesiastical provinces. For he now hoped for a most honourable

units.la: Gg cum in partiam reditum, quod cerro copnoucrat Reginam Matiam exploso & ciecto E-uangelioad Pontificiam regulam ac doctrinam omnia reduct urum.
units.tr: return to his homeland, since he had clearly learned that Queen Mary had cast out and driven away the Gospel, and that he would bring everything back to the Papist rule and doctrine.

units.la: Exquo duplicem sibi ipem proposuit. Namq; Regina Matia olim fe puro sub matre eius D. Margareta Sarisburiæ Comitissa educanda a matre sua D. Katharina Hispana tradita est, id quod eam ea mente fecisse multi referunt, vt quoniam D. Margareta Georgii quondam Clarentiæ Ducis filia ac superstes hæres fuisset, optauit sæpe D. Katharina, vt Maria sua filia alicui ex eius liberis matrimonio iungeretur, quo magis ei ius Angliæ Regni firmaretur, fi Henricus Octauus Rex sine mascula prole moriretur. Ita cum tantum Diaconatus ordinem suscepisset (quo Papæ licentia abrogati facile potuisset) venitin ipem coniugii Reginalis atq; Regni, aut fi id non possit obtineri, summum hnnorem Ecclefiafticum atq; Legatinam potestatem expectauit a Papa. Ita vtrinq; Regalis aut sacerdotalis Celsitudinis etectus spe, & ab ipsa Regina expectitus ac inuitatus, acceptat a Pontifice Legatina potestate fe accinxit in Angliam. Sed his Polt cogitatifq; apud fe Concilijs, obstabat maxime Cæsar, dum & quid Polus meditaretur olfecit, & eas nuptias Philippo hæredi suo ad tuendas suas contra Gallum partes commodissimas esse ratus est. Itaq; Cæsar de Polo aduentu impediendo cum Dandino Cardinali Pontificis ad fe de pace cum Gallo transigenda Legato communicauit, eumq; rogauit vt Polum salem aliquandiu in Italia retardaret. Is Francifcum quendam Commendinum cum litteris ad Pulum quam celerrime ptoficifci iussit, quibus ne in viam sese daret, monebat. Cæsari enim eam legationem displicere quæ fe inconsulto suscepta fuit, tum Anglos plerofq; ac Lodinenfes maxime ipsum nomen Romani Pontificis, fuafq; legationes executari dicebat, proinde non esse eos adhuc legatina potestate adcundos donec fuationibus ad eum æ-quo animo perferendum adduceretur. Polus cum has Dandini literas accepit, in eo quem diximus Maguzano Cœnobio fuit, nec vltra sibi progrediendum existimauit, æ-quam de Pontificis voluntate cognouisset. Pontifex quoniam Cæsaris potentiam augeri contra Gallum illis Marianis nuptiis noluit, Dandinum quia Polo impedimento, & Cæsari auxilio fuit, à legatione Romam reuocabat, ac vtramq; tam in Angliam, quam ad Cæsarem atq; Gallum de ineunda firmanda q; pace legationem Polo deferebat.
units.tr: From this he proposed a twofold hope to himself. For Queen Mary, when she was a girl, had been handed over by her mother, Lady Catherine of Spain, to be brought up under the care of Lady Margaret, Countess of Salisbury, and many report that she did this with this intention: since Lady Margaret, the daughter and surviving heir of George, once Duke of Clarence, was the one who had survived, Lady Catherine often wished that her daughter Mary might be joined in marriage to one of Margaret's children, so that Mary's right to the kingdom of England might be made firmer, should King Henry VIII die without a male heir. Thus, since Pole had received only the order of deacon (from which he could easily have been released with the Pope's permission), he came to hope for marriage with the Queen and the kingdom. Or, if that could not be obtained, he looked to the Pope for the highest ecclesiastical honour and legatine power. So, buoyed by the hope of attaining royal or priestly eminence on either count, and encouraged and invited by the Queen herself, he accepted legatine power from the Pope and set out for England. But against these plans and designs that Pole had in mind, the Emperor especially stood in the way: he got wind of what Pole was planning, and judged that a marriage between Mary and Pole would be most inconvenient for his son Philip's interests in defending their side against the French. So the Emperor communicated with Cardinal Dandino, the Pope's legate for negotiating peace with the French, and asked him to delay Pole in Italy for some time. Dandino sent a certain Francesco Commendino with letters to Pole, as quickly as possible, warning him not to set out on the journey. He said that the Emperor disliked that legation, which had been undertaken without his consent. Moreover, most of the English and the people of Lodi, he said, were executing the very name of the Roman Pontiff and his legations, and therefore they should not yet be approached with legatine power until they had been brought to bear the matter calmly by persuasion. When Pole received these letters of Dandino's, he remained in the monastery of Maguzzano mentioned above, and did not think he should advance any further until he had learned the Pope's will. The Pope, since he did not want the Emperor's power to grow against the French through that Marian marriage, and since Dandino had been an obstacle to Pole and a help to the Emperor, recalled Dandino from the legation to Rome. He also gave Pole the legation both to England and to the Emperor and the French, to bring about and confirm a peace.

units.la: Ita duplici legationis munere suscepto Polus in itinere pergit. Cumque Tridentum aduentaffet, suos tam ad Cæsarem quam ad Gallum nuncios præmisit, vt de iftalégatione fuoq; ex Italia disceret, ad eofq; aduentu cognoscerent.
units.tr: Thus, with the double charge of the legation undertaken, Pole continued on his journey. When he arrived at Trent, he sent messengers ahead both to the Emperor and to the French king, so that they might learn of his legation and of his departure from Italy, and know of his coming.

units.la: Quæ legatio Cæsaris inceptis tam infausta fuit, vt virum Illustrem Iohannem Mendozam Polo panuluum progresso maxima celeritate obuium eum lueris miserit, in quiblis Cæsar declarauit pergratum illi fore fi fe sistat nec vltra progrediatur, donec quædā magni momenti negocia quibus ea legatio obesse poterit, confecifiet, cum maturum suerit ab ipso Cæsare vltro eum expectandum, quod fi progredi veller, licere ei ex Cæsaris voluntate Leodio vfq; proficisci, sed illic ei necessario commorandum, donec euocetur à Cæfate. His acceptis literis Polus Dilingam quod oppidum haud procul Tildento abest, reuertitur.
units.tr: This legation proved so unfortunate for his undertaking that the Emperor sent the illustrious John Mendoza, with the greatest speed, to meet Pole, who had advanced a little. Mendoza declared in the Emperor's name that it would be most welcome to him if Pole would stop and go no further, until certain matters of great importance, with which that legation might interfere, had been concluded. When the time was ripe, he would be summoned by the Emperor himself. If he wished to proceed, he might go as far as Liège by the Emperor's will, but there he would necessarily have to stay until he was called by the Emperor. Having received these letters, Pole returned to Dillingen, a town not far from Trent.

units.la: Ibi Pontificem dete tota certiorem facit, & ad Cæsarem expostulatorias literas dat quam indignum facinus fit ostendit, Pontificis legatum pacis & religionis causa missum, media Germania in ipsorum hæreticorum oculis & præfentia cum fumino dedecore & contemptu Pontificis, Cæsaris præsertim iussu detineri.
units.tr: There he informed the Pope of everything in full, and wrote a letter of complaint to the Emperor, showing how shameful a deed it was that a legate of the Pope, sent for the sake of peace and religion, should be detained in the middle of Germany, before the eyes and in the very presence of the heretics themselves, to the great dishonour and contempt of the Pope, and especially by the Emperor's order.

units.la: Vetum nullis expostulationibus aut precibus vt in Belgium propius accederet ut pertrare poterat, antequam inter Philippum & Reginam Mariam nuptiæ (quas in Cranmero commemorauit) contractæ, & Parlamenti auctoritate ratæ effent. Sciebat enim Cæfar quanti Polum Mariæ semper ab incunte virtutis ætate feciflet, cauendumq; sibi putauit ne eius aduentus pertutbaret nuptias. Acqa Philippus (cuius aduentus à Reginaia auidè expectabatur) ex Hispaniis nondum in Anglia appulfiset, nec nuptiæ celebratæ. atq; cō-fummatæ effent, vix tandem atq; ægre impetrauit Polus saltem vt Bruxellas ad Cæsarem peruenirct, vbi manendi conditio ei scripta ei fuit tantisper, dum Philippus in Anglia veniffet atq; celebraffet nuptias. Interea de pace cum Cæsare atq; Gallo ex præscripta legatione authoritate à Papa Polus egit, sed frustra. Odia. n. ram diu inueterata, animiq; infesti & exulcerati (edari pacariq; non nisi longa intercessione, dieq; aut ipsa victoria poterat.
units.tr: But by no complaints or prayers could he obtain permission to approach nearer to Belgium, as he could have done, before the marriage between Philip and Queen Mary (which I mentioned under Cranmer) was contracted and ratified by the authority of Parliament. For the Emperor knew how greatly Mary had valued Pole from the earliest years of her youth, and he thought he must take care that Pole's coming would not disturb the marriage. Since Philip, whose arrival was eagerly awaited by the Queen, had not yet landed in England from Spain, and the marriage had not been celebrated and completed, Pole with difficulty at last obtained only that he might reach Brussels to the Emperor, where a condition was written to him that he should remain there for a while, until Philip had come to England and the marriage had been celebrated. Meanwhile Pole, by the authority the Pope had given him in his prescribed legation, negotiated for peace with the Emperor and the King of France, but in vain. For hatreds long rooted, and minds hostile and inflamed, could not be calmed and reconciled except by long intervention, and by time, or by victory itself.

units.la: Itaq; Philippi & Mariæ congressu omnibus ceremoniis peractis & absolutis nuptiis, cum Polus iam nihil impedire suam in Angliam profectiones amplius posse existimaret, cum que spe Regni frustratus, tamen in sacerdotalis culminis possessione sibi esse videretur, occultis inuidiis apud Reginam & Philippum, necnon Cæsarem atque Papam pene supplantatus & a legatione reuocatus est. Quibus omnibus Polis aduersis ipcommodis solum Reginæ iam visendi desiderium atque studium restitit. Illa enim abfuisse tam diu Polum ægre tulit, cumq; cundationis suæ causas cognouisset, legatos ad Cæsarē vt eum bona venia dimitteret, & ad Polum vt veniret misit.
units.tr: So when the marriage of Philip and Mary had been concluded with all the ceremonies completed, Pole, who now thought nothing could prevent his journey to England, was frustrated of his hope of the kingdom. Yet he still seemed to himself to hold the summit of the priestly office. Through hidden jealousies at court with the Queen and Philip, and also with the Emperor and the Pope, he was all but supplanted and recalled from his legation. Against all these adverse circumstances for Pole, only his longing and eagerness to see the Queen stood in the way. She took it hard that Pole had been absent so long, and when she learned the reasons for his delay, she sent envoys to the Emperor to dismiss him with good grace, and to Pole to bid him come.

units.la: Quibus legatis Comitibus, Reginæ instantia Cæsaris venia impetrata, redit io patriam Polus, ex qua non vlla vi sed sua perfidia tamdiu abfuisset, teditq; natura peregrina atq; fera indutus, & Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ carnifex, ac flagellum, cuius iam Patronus atq; tutor esse debuit atq; potuit. Multi enim pii & Euangelici viri, quibuscum (vt antea diximus) sæpe Ecclesiasticis de rebus sermones conferebat, cum aduentus & legationis suæ causas scitent, eum in itinere & Belgio admonuetūt, vt Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ quæ suæ iam esset potestati tradita, prouideret.
units.tr: With these envoys as companions, and with the Emperor's permission obtained at the Queen's urgent request, Pole returned to his homeland, from which he had been absent so long not through any compulsion but through his own treachery. He put on a foreign and savage nature, and became the executioner and scourge of the English Church, whose patron and guardian he ought and could have been. For many pious and evangelical men, with whom (as I said earlier) he had often conferred on ecclesiastical matters, when they learned the reasons for his coming and his legation, warned him on his journey and in Flanders to provide for the English Church, which was now handed over to his power.

units.la: Quibus despectis aut paruipensis respondit se omnium potius in Anglicana Ecclesia laturum incommoda quam schismata & Romanæ vnitatis defectionem. Ipse Immanuel Tremellius Hebræus qui ab eo nomen in Baptismo (vt diximus) accepit, cum Bruxillis beneficentiam modicam qua inopiam suam subleuaret obnixe atq; adeo Christianitatis per eom suscepta nomine peteret, sine ope vlla cum probto atq; minis tepuisse est. His moribus immutatus Polus venit, Iltpatus & Comitatus Italis ac Romanæ curiæ tabellioribus atq; scribis, Angles vero ad se perpaucos admisit, oec nisi eos quos maxima crudelitate in Euangelicos sæuire cerneret, sibi fidos esse duxit iamq; accepta priuā Rege & Regina legationem suam gerendi potestatē tetum erecta Legatina Crux, Potificiæ potestatis indicium coram Polo gesta cum bonorum omnium gemitu & mœrore visa est. Celebratur autem eo tempore quo Polus Legatus Regnum ingressus est, Parlamentum Westmonasterii, quo perhonorificē ductus postquam Steph. Gardinerus Winchonensis Episcopus Regni (vt diximus) Cancellarius, de cuius grato aduocatu quædam ad ptoceres & vniuersum populum præmisisset, Polus patria lingua suis longam orationem habuit, in qua Regi ac Reginæ, procenbus atq; populo gratias summas agebat, quod eorum tanto beneficio omnibus exilii & proscriptionis legibus abrogatis in patriam restitutus esset, fui proinde officii atque gratitudinis fuisse dicebat, hoc meritum ita compentate, vt eom illa a sede Apostolica superiori schismate defecissent, eoque modo ab Vnitate Ecclesiæ atque Regno Dei exulassent, eos authoritate sibi a Papa, Christi stifcilicet Vicario, data ad sedem Romanam, tanquam hæreditatem cœlestem reducere.
units.tr: Scorning or making little of these warnings, he replied that he would sooner bear all the troubles in the English Church than schisms and a falling away from Roman unity. Immanuel Tremellius, the Hebrew, who had received his name at baptism from Pole (as I said), had earnestly begged at Brussels for a modest kindness to relieve his poverty, and sought it in the name of the Christianity he had embraced through Pole. He was, it is said, rejected without any help, with reproach and threats. Pole came changed in these ways. He admitted to himself only a very few Englishmen, but Italians, and the notaries and secretaries of the Roman court. He thought only those men trustworthy who he saw were raging with the greatest cruelty against the evangelicals. Once he had received from the King and Queen, in private, the authority to carry out his legation, a legatine cross was raised throughout the whole kingdom, a sign of papal power, and carried before Pole, to the groans and grief of all good men. At that time, when Pole the legate entered the kingdom, Parliament was sitting at Westminster. He was led there with great honour. Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester and, as I said, Lord Chancellor of the realm, first made some remarks to the nobles and the whole people about his weighty advocacy. Then Pole addressed them at length in his native tongue, giving the highest thanks to the King and Queen, to the nobles and to the people, because by their great kindness, with all the laws of exile and proscription repealed, he had been restored to his homeland. It was, he said, a duty and a matter of gratitude for him to repay this favour in such a way that those who had fallen away from the Apostolic See in the recent schism, and so had been exiled from the unity of the Church and the kingdom of God, might be brought back to the Roman See, by the authority given him by the Pope, namely Christ's Vicar, as to a heavenly inheritance.

units.la: Suæ Legatioois eam maximam fuisse causam vt ad pristinam nobilitatem atque gloriam hæ Insulam restituret, de qua Romana sedes præ omnibus cæteris prouinciis cuam atq; ratione poslimum habendam duxit, quoniā hæc eius fuit peculiaris atq; propria laus, quod ex omnibus orbis terrarum prouinciis hæc vna eaq; tota Christianam fidem primum amplexa est.
units.tr: He held that the greatest reason for his legation was to restore this island to its former nobility and glory. Of this island the Roman See, above all other provinces, had decided that care and account must be taken, because this was its peculiar and proper praise: that of all the provinces of the world, this one, and this one alone, embraced the Christian faith first, and entirely.

units.la: Britannos primùm etsi exterarum & Romanorum Cæsarum Imperio subessent, tamē receptam publicē Christi fidem per totam Insulam promulgasse.
units.tr: He said that the Britons, although they were subject to the rule of foreigners and of the Roman emperors, nevertheless published the Christian faith, once received, publicly throughout the whole island.

units.la: Noo vt cæterē gentes quæ sensim & dioturni temporis accedente paulatim incremeto, & pet paucos eam hauserunt, sed vno eodemq; pene momento ab omnibus simul approbatam diuulgarunt.
units.tr: Not like the other nations, which took it in gradually, with slow increase over a long period, and only a few at a time, but they spread it, approved by all together at almost one and the same moment.

units.la: Britannis exactis etsi Saxones Christi fidē cum incolis exterminassent, tamen Deum ita locum ipsum & Insulam dilexisse, vt eorum Ethnica superstitione excæcatas mentes Euangelii luce tandem illustraverit.
units.tr: Although, after the Britons were driven out, the Saxons drove out the Christian faith along with its inhabitants, nevertheless God so loved this place and island that at last he illumined their minds, blinded by heathen superstition, with the light of the Gospel.

units.la: Hanc Insulæ oobilitatem atque gloriam Dei prouidentiæ atque beneficentiæ foli acceptam fateo dam, sed tamen viam ipsam atque rationem, qua hæc nobilitas atque gloria parta est, a fede Romana nobis primo semperque monstratam & patefactam fuisse.
units.tr: I acknowledge that this nobility and glory of the island is due to the providence and kindness of God alone. Yet the very way and method by which this nobility and glory was won was first and always shown and revealed to us by the Roman See.

units.la: In Romanæ exinde fidei Vnitate nos sempet persenerasse, fuisseq; nostram antiquissimam Romanæ Ecclesiæ subiectionem, eamq; maxima religione & obseruantia ab huius Regni incolis cultam & celebratam, ex Offa & Adolphi Regum exemplis constate, qui maximis sumptibus Romam suis loogiquis itionibus inuisendam putarunt, à qua diuinæ veritatis initia acceperunt.
units.tr: From that time we have always persevered in unity with the Roman faith, and our most ancient subjection to the Roman Church has existed, and it was cultivated and observed by the inhabitants of this kingdom with the greatest reverence and devotion. This is clear from the examples of Kings Offa and Adolf, who thought it right to visit Rome at great expense on their long journeys, since it was from Rome that they had received the beginnings of divine truth.

units.la: Carolum Magnum cum Parisiensem Academiam instituisset, Alcuinum Theologum Magnum & copiosum ex Anglia acciuisse, qui omnis doctrinæ & pietatis fundamenta Lutetiæ poneret.
units.tr: When Charlemagne founded the Academy of Paris, he summoned from England Alcuin, a great and abundant theologian, who would lay the foundations of all learning and piety at Paris.

units.la: Adrianum. 4. Papam fuisse Anglum qui Noruegiam primus Christiana fide imbuit; amorem, patriæ ductus Imperium Hybérniæ, quæ Pontificiæ ditionis fuerat Hęretico. a Anglorum Regi concessit.
units.tr: Adrian IV was an Englishman, who was the first to imbue Norway with the Christian faith. Moved by love of his homeland, he granted the Lordship of Ireland, which had been under Papal jurisdiction, to Henry, King of the English.

units.la: Infinitam benefitiorum multitudinem quibus ab Ecclesia Romana Angli femper ptæ cæteris gentibus affecti fuerunt præterm itt endam, nec non calamitates & ignominias quas ab eo tempore quo à Romana fide defexit, incurrit, prætereundas, tantum Aliam, Græciam, ac nuperrime Germaniam, quæ tot seclis atque factionibus diuulsa & in varias religiones dissipata est, earumque omnium prouinciarum afflictiones & ruinas, postquam a fide Romana defecissent nobis ob oculos proponendis.
units.tr: I pass over the infinite multitude of benefits with which the English have always been favoured above other nations by the Roman Church, and likewise the calamities and disgraces they have incurred since the time they fell away from the Roman faith. Let us set before our eyes only Asia, Greece, and most recently Germany, which has been torn apart by so many centuries and factions and scattered into diverse religions, and the afflictions and ruins of all those provinces since they fell away from the Roman faith.

units.la: Defectionis causam fuisse in illis, radicem omnium malorum auaritiam, in Anglia, uiaius hominis libidinem atq; luxum, & quatiquam multarum diuitiarum ex ea mutatione spes proposita fuerit, omnia tamen non modo ad inopiam, sed ad grandes calamitates perducta sunt.
units.tr: The cause of the defection was, in those places, avarice, the root of all evils; in England it was the lust and luxury of man. And although the hope of much wealth from that change was held out, yet all things have been brought not only to poverty but to great calamities.

units.la: Romanam Ecclesiam cum summa vi agere, & cæterorum Principum ope ac potentia Angliam subiugare potuissët, malùisse tamen ipsam diem opemque diuinam expectare, quæ vastatis Ecclesiis, altaribus euersis, sactis omnibus prophanatis, rebusque desperatis subito adfuit, nam lamisse in Regina pectore religionem, velut in igne extinctum aut cineribus obducto scintillam, quæ paecfacta flammam accendit & illuminauit.
units.tr: The Roman Church could have acted with great force, and with the help and power of the other princes could have subdued England. Yet it preferred to await the day and the divine help, which, when the churches were laid waste, the altars overthrown, all sacred things profaned, and affairs seemed hopeless, came suddenly. For religion had lain hidden in the Queen's breast, like a spark extinguished in fire or covered with ashes, which, when struck, kindled a flame and gave light.

units.la: Ei exhæredatæ, eiectæ, inermi, ac à potentissimis hostibus oppugnatæ de Regni sui iure virgini prætet expectationem humanam datam cœlitus fuisse victoriam, atque imperandi potestatem, vt Vnitati Romanæ adiungeretur iterum Anglia.
units.tr: To her, disinherited, cast out, unarmed, and attacked by most powerful enemies, a virgin, concerning the right of her own kingdom, there was given from heaven, beyond human expectation, victory and the power of rule, so that England might once again be joined to Roman unity.

units.la: Ad eam remex nuptiis cum Philippo Caroli Cæsaris filio Catholico Principe contractis, robur atque vires acceßisse, cuius pater ex omnibus Christianis Principibus maximam nauauit coniungendæ dissipare Ecclesiæ operam, in qua etsi bellorum interuentu exitium nondum secundum habeat, sperandum tamen esse vt quod ille in Vnitate Ecclesiæ inchoauerat a Philippo eius filio pacifico Principe perficiatur, Dauidis atq; Solomonis in extruenda Dei domo Hierosolymis exemplo. Ad hanc vnitatem coniungendam & stabilitendam duas à Deo potestates esse datas, quæ gladiorum instar sunt: Ciuilis ciuiliscet siue temporalis, & Ecclesiastica. Illa in tebelles atq; contumaces morte, proscriptione, exilio, cæterisq; ciuilibus pœnis animaduertit, & penes Reges est. Hæc cœlestium clauium & ligandi atq; absoluendi ab æternis cruciatibus authoritatem continet, eaq; solius est Papæ ac Romanæ curiæ tanquam Christi in terris Vicarii.
units.tr: For this purpose strength and power had come from her marriage with Philip, the Catholic prince, son of the Emperor Charles, whose father, of all Christian princes, had expended the greatest effort in joining together the scattered Church. Although, through the intervention of wars, that effort does not yet have a successful outcome, it is nevertheless to be hoped that what he had begun for the unity of the Church will be completed by his son Philip, a peaceful prince, after the example of David and Solomon in building the house of God at Jerusalem. To join and establish this unity, God has given two powers, which are like swords: the civil, or temporal, power, and the ecclesiastical. The former punishes rebels and the obstinate with death, proscription, exile, and other civil penalties, and it rests with kings. The latter contains the authority of the heavenly keys, of binding and absolving from eternal torments, and this belongs only to the Pope and the Roman court, as Christ's Vicar on earth.

units.la: Ad extremum hanc sibi à Papa commissam pro Anglia ad Romanam fidem reducenda potestatem: Cuius beneficium his qui id tecipere possint impartiri est Quominus autem eius participes esse possint impedimento esse eas leges quæ prævalente ichimate contra Romanam cutiam sancitæ fuerunt. Eas igitur si abrogare & tollere velint, adesse Romanæ Ecclesiæ tanquam charæ matris benedictionem, quæ redeuntibus gremium nunquam claudit.
units.tr: Lastly, he said that the power committed to him by the Pope for bringing England back to the Roman faith is this: its benefit can be granted to those who are able to receive it. But what could prevent them from sharing in it are those laws which were enacted against the Roman court while the schism prevailed. If they wish to repeal and remove these laws, then the blessing of the Roman Church, as of a dear mother, will be present, for she never closes her bosom to those who return.

units.la: Eiusmodi satis diserte cum elegantि ordinis speciæ exposuisset, eorum qui Pontificiis ritibus dediti essent animos ad fe cum admiratione rapuit, vt aperte dicetent se illo de renatos fuisse. Esti non deerant ex plebeiuum in illo Parlamenti conuentu qui Pontificiæ suæque Legatinæ authoritati recipiendæ palam reclamarent.
units.tr: Having set out these matters quite clearly and in an elegant order, he so captured with admiration the minds of those devoted to Popish rites that they openly said they had been reborn through him. Yet there were not lacking some commoners in that Parliament who openly protested against receiving the Pope's and his legate's authority.

units.la: Sed Regis ac Reginæ authoritatem, ac multitudine suffragiorum Papa iam quod nunquam antea contigit legis lacæ ispecie irrepsit in Angliam. Qua constripta & Polu delata Legatinam authoritatem gesit, cuiusq; vigore Regem, Reginam Præsules, procetes; cunctumq; populum & Clerum Anglicanum à schilmatis (vt dixit) seu à Papa defectionis crimine absoluit. Hanc absolutionem Gardinetus Winton. Episcopus, Regni Cæcellarius proximo die Dominico concione pro cruce Paulina denunciauit Dehoe Angliæ ad Papifmum reditu magna Romæ gratulatio facta est, & amplissimus annus Iubileus à Iulio 3. Papa promulgatus. Ad quem missi ex Anglia qui subiectionem ei deferrent Thomas Thutbeius Elienfis Episcopus, Antonius Brown miles Dominus Montague, & Edwardus Carnen miles, cum iam essent in itinere de obitu Iulii Papæ certiores facti. Ei Marcellus successit, qui post succepium Paparum vigesimo die mortem obiit. Itaq; Lega-ti moram in itinere aliquantisper traxerunt, donec nouì Papæ nomine Legatio renoca-ta esset: is fuit Petrus Theatinus Cardinalis (de quo ante dictum est) nunc Paulus. 4. nūcupatus, Polo atq; Cæsari ipsi in sensissimus, Gallicæq; factionis aden studiosus, vt cū inducias quinquennales inter Cæsarem atq; Gallum pactæ essent, eas adiutote Caroln Lotharingio baringio Cardioali frági atq; violari procuraucrit. Huic itaq; oratores Angliæ obedientiam Regni nomine detulerunt, sed Polus huius Papæ in se animum cum ex veteri simultate odioque cognouisset, sibi imminere calamitatem animaduertit. Itaq; reuersis legatis afliduam cum Rege ac Regina operam dedit, vt de Cranmero hæresis supplicio sumpto Cantuariensem Archiepiscopatum obtineret, oe si Legatione abdicatus Romam reuocaretur, malè tractaretur à Papa, qui nonnullos iam Cæsarianos Cardinales quod sibi aduerší sæpe essent, vinculis duríq; pœnis multauit. Diximus in Cranmero antea Stephanum Gardinerum Wintoniensem Episcopum, cui haud igoota fuit hæc inter Papam atque Polum tam diu gesta simultas, occasione opportunitateq; data Cardioalitium honorem & Legatinam potestatem occultis artibus ambiuisse, operamq; dedisse, ne se viuo Polus Cranmerum perimeret. Non quod Cranmero bene, sed quod Polo maleuolebat, illuoíq; oon modo Archiepiscopatu, sed è regno Romam repellere, vt is solus omnia in regno gereret. Sed in hac ambitione & affectatione legationis (vt diximus) mortuus est, ac Crammerus paolo post combustus. Tum Regè ac Regina instantibus impetratum est vt Polus Caoturiensis Archiepiscopus à Papa designaretur. Communis enim cautera ratio Angliæ ad fidem tam nuper aduentante Polo ad Papifmum reuersa, vtionisatq; vindictæ Papalis vim paulisper repressit & eohibuit. Itaq; Papa in Cardinalium suorum cxtu referente Morono Cardinali, qui tum Angliæ protector in Romana curia dicebatur, Polum noo modo Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem nominauit, sed cumulatissimis laudibus simulans celebrauit. Et quia Polus præsbyteratus ordinem nondum suscepit, sed Diaconus tantum esset, accepit à Paulo Papa prouisionis illius vsurpatæ prætextu, titulo generalis admioistratoris Archiepiscopatus, & prouiocia Cantuariensis, dooec præsbyteratu initiaretur, quo suscepto admirabili sua & absoluta potentia decreuit Papa vt administratoris titulus euanesceret, & in Archiepiscopi traosiret. Interea verò dedit in eadem prouisionis bulla facultatem vt ad Archiepiscopatus, Cardinalis, Legatique amplitudinem sustinendam quæcunq; beneficia, dignitates, pensionesq; quocunq; modo ex Ecclesiasticis prouentibus acquisitas, illæsio iure Pontificio cum Archiepiscopatus retineret.
units.tr: But by the authority of the King and Queen and the weight of the votes, the Pope, as had never happened before, crept into England under the appearance of law. Once this was drawn up and carried to Pole, he exercised legatine authority, and by its power absolved the King, the Queen, the prelates, the nobles, and the whole English people and clergy from the crime of schism (as he called it), that is, of defection from the Pope. Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester and Lord Chancellor of the realm, announced this absolution the following Sunday in a sermon at St Paul's Cross. At Rome, when England returned to Popery, there was great rejoicing, and Pope Julius III proclaimed a most ample jubilee. Sent from England to offer submission to him were Thomas Thirlby, Bishop of Ely, Sir Anthony Browne, Lord Montague, and Sir Edward Carne. They were already on their journey when they learned of the death of Pope Julius. Marcellus succeeded him but died twenty days after taking up the papacy. The legates therefore delayed for a while on the road, until the legation was recalled in the name of the new Pope. This was Peter, Cardinal of Theate (of whom we spoke before), now named Paul IV, a man very hostile to Pole and to Caesar himself and very zealous for the French faction. When a five-year truce had been agreed between Caesar and the Frenchman, he saw to it that it was broken and violated through the agency of Cardinal Charles of Lorraine. To this Pope the English envoys therefore offered obedience in the name of the realm. But Pole, having recognised from the old enmity and hatred the Pope's disposition towards himself, saw that disaster threatened him. So, once the legates had returned, he devoted constant effort, with the King and Queen, to obtaining the Archbishopric of Canterbury through the execution of Cranmer for heresy. If he were stripped of the legation and recalled to Rome, he feared he would be badly treated by the Pope, who had already punished with chains and harsh penalties several Caesarian cardinals because they had often opposed him. We said earlier, in the life of Cranmer, that Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, was not unaware of this rivalry between the Pope and Pole, which had lasted so long. When an opportunity and occasion were given, he sought by secret arts the honour of the cardinalate and legatine power, and took care that Pole should not put Cranmer to death while Gardiner lived. This was not because he wished Cranmer well, but because he ill-wished Pole, and wanted to drive him away from the archbishopric and from the realm to Rome, so that he alone might manage everything in the kingdom. But in this ambition and pursuit of the legation (as we said), Gardiner died, and Cranmer was burned shortly afterwards. Then, at the insistence of the King and Queen, it was obtained that Pole be designated Archbishop of Canterbury by the Pope. For the common caution of England, since Pole had so recently returned to Popery, had for a time restrained and checked the force of Papal vengeance and retribution. Accordingly the Pope, on the report of Cardinal Morone, who was then called the protector of England in the Roman curia, named Pole in consistory of his cardinals not only Archbishop of Canterbury but also praised him with the most lavish commendations, though feigning. And because Pole had not yet received the order of the priesthood but was only a deacon, he received from Pope Paul, under the pretext of that provision, the title of general administrator of the Archbishopric and province of Canterbury, until he should be initiated into the presbyterate. Once he had received this, the Pope, by his wonderful and absolute power, decreed that the title of administrator should lapse and pass into that of archbishop. Meanwhile, in the same bull of provision, he granted the faculty that, to sustain the dignity of archbishop, cardinal and legate, Pole might keep along with the archbishopric whatever benefices, dignities and pensions had been acquired in any way from ecclesiastical revenues, without prejudice to Papal law.

units.la: Posthæc sacerdotii ordine suscepto in Ecclesia Conuentuali fratrum Franciscanorum Grenwici vicesimo secundo die mensis Martii, authoritate Papæ à Nicolao Heathoo Eboracensi Archiepiscopo, Londinensi, Elienši, Wigorniensi, Lincolniensi, Roffensi, atq; Alauensi Episcopis præsentibus consecratus est. In hac consecratione Polus iuramentum illud, quod in Denei vita supra descripsimus, dum misla in choro Pontificio ritu cantuq; celebraretur, Regina eum multis proceribus atq; consiliariis inspectantibus, Papæ præstitit. Triduo post qui dies Anouinciationi beatæ Mariæ dedicatus est, Comitibus cum Edmundo Bonero Londinensi Episcopo, & Willielmo Comite Pembrochiæ, ac Edwardo Hastings ordinis Garterii milite, ad Ecclesiæ parochialem de Arcubus Lodini, vbi primo Pontificia sacra fecit, cum Cardinalitus & Legationis suæ insignis, præcedentibus Aduocatis & Procuratoribus generalibus, nec non cæteris ministris Arcuatæ curiæ pethonotificè ductus est. Ibi in solio deaurato, puluinaribus vestimentisq; aureis circumseptoCardinalitio amictu vestitus splendidè consedit. Missa inuitata pené pompa à Wigorniensi Episcopo celebrabatur. Aderat etiam Eliensis Episcopus, quibus à Dauide Polo Derbiensi Archidiacono scriptum quoddam Papale cum pallio datum est, quo accepto illi Mitris redemiti, & Pontificalibus ornamentis ioduti Poli humeris Pallium ea cærimonia verborum; formula (quam in Deneo supra descripsimus) impositum est. Eo indurus Polus suggestum ascendit, & de significatione, vsu, origine materia, artificioque Palli tam exilem & iciunam orationem habuit, vt non modo de Theologia nihil sapuisse, sed in ipsa, cui diu studuerat oratoris facultate atq; copia exaruisse visus est. Acomnibus ritibus Pontificiis absolutis Archiepiscopatus possessionem quâ installationem vocant, hoc solito apparatu & magnificentia interposito procuratore Roberto Collins suo Cantuariæ Commissario quinto Kal. April. ingressus est. His gestis vt datâ fidâ à Papa sese locupletandi potestate exerceret, Episcopatus Wintoniensis iam vacantis in suam arcam inferri iussit redditus. Quem cum ambitiosissimus Antistes Whitus Lincolniensis Episcopus eo cupidius appeteret, quod in dioecesi natus, & Collegio Wickamiensi Wintoniæ præfectus quondam fuisset, petopportunè in istius Legati tanta ad sapiendi authoritate à Papa prædití manus potestatemq; deuenit. Cū quo de mille libris annuis Anglicanis non modo reliquo vitæ suæ tempore sed vno post mortem eius anno soluendis simul atq; pactus esset, Wintoniensem Episcopatū obtinuit. Quæ conuēta quia simoniam redolebant, verùq; à Papa non sine remuneratioe absoluendi fuerunt.
units.tr: Afterwards, having received the order of the priesthood in the conventual church of the Franciscan friars at Greenwich on 22 March, by authority of the Pope, he was consecrated in the presence of Nicholas Heath, Archbishop of York, and the Bishops of London, Ely, Worcester, Lincoln, Rochester and Alauensis. In this consecration Pole took, before the Pope, that oath which we described above in the life of Dene, while Mass was celebrated in the choir in the Papal rite and chant; the Queen was watching, with many nobles and councillors looking on. Three days later, on the day dedicated to the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, he was led in solemn procession, with the earls, Edmund Bonner, Bishop of London, William, Earl of Pembroke, and Edward Hastings, knight of the Order of the Garter, to the parish church of St Mary-le-Bow in London. There, where he first performed Popish rites, he was conducted with the insignia of cardinal and legate, preceded by the advocates and general procurators and the other ministers of the Court of Arches. There, on a gilded throne surrounded by gilded cushions and golden vestments, clothed in his cardinal's garb, he sat down in splendour. A Mass celebrated with almost unbelievable pomp was conducted by the Bishop of Worcester. The Bishop of Ely was also present. To him David Pole, Archdeacon of Derby, handed a certain Papal writing and the pallium. When this was received, the pallium was placed on Pole's shoulders with the words of that ceremony (which we described above in the life of Dene), while he was wearing the mitre and adorned with pontifical ornaments. Thereupon Pole ascended the pulpit and delivered such a thin and meagre oration on the meaning, use, origin, material and making of the pallium that he seemed not only to have no grasp of theology but to have run dry in that very faculty of oratory and copiousness which he had long studied. When all the Popish rites were complete, he took possession of the archbishopric, which they call installation, with this customary pomp and magnificence. His proctor, Robert Collins, his commissary at Canterbury, acted for him on 28 March. When these things had been done, in order that he might exercise the power of enriching himself, granted him by the Pope, he ordered the revenues of the now vacant Bishopric of Winchester to be carried into his own chest. The most ambitious prelate, Whyte, Bishop of Lincoln, desired that see the more eagerly because he had been born in the diocese and had once been warden of Winchester College. Through a fortunate opportunity he came into the hand and power of this legate, who was endowed by the Pope with such authority. With him he agreed to pay a thousand pounds a year in English money, not only for the rest of his own life but also for one year after his death, and so obtained the Bishopric of Winchester. Since these agreements smelled of simony, they were absolved by the Pope, though not without payment.

units.la: Ac Regina Maria cum (vt in Cranmero notea diximus) Ecclesiasticorum beneficiorum ac proucturuum primitias atq; decimas, quæ patri suo, Henrico Octauo Regi, eiusque hæredibus regnique sanccessoribus concessæ fuerunt, Clero remisisset, remque omnem Polo permisit. Cui cum Clerici relaxatione Regia se liberatos primidiarum atq; decimarum onere putassent, nihilominus eas totas integrafq; soluerunt. Cuius rei prætexebatur causa, quod cum Henricus Octauus fratrum Conuentus & Cœnobia Monachorum dediciffet, eorumq; prædia legelata cepisset, clausitq; multitudini annua stipendia quoad viuerent, diplomate publico concedebat. Quibus Polus ex illis decimis ac primitiis satisfaciendum esse suasit, ne cum extenuaris Regiis facultatib. ærarium publicum tantas largitiones ferre non posset, Regina liberalitate sua detrimentum sanciat.
units.tr: Queen Mary, as we noted in Cranmer's life, had remitted to the clergy the first-fruits and tithes of ecclesiastical benefices and parishes, which had been granted to her father, King Henry VIII, and to his heirs and successors in the realm, and she left the whole matter to Pole. Although the clergy thought that by the royal relaxation they had been freed from the burden of first-fruits and tithes, they nevertheless paid them all, in full and entire. The reason pretended for this was that Henry VIII had dissolved the convents of friars and the monasteries of monks and had seized their lands, and, by public charter, had assigned annual stipends to the multitude for as long as they lived.
