Pole persuaded that these should be satisfied out of those tithes and first-fruits, so that the public treasury, with the royal estates diminished, would not be able to bear such largesse, and the Queen's generosity would not suffer loss.

units.la: Ita hæc Reginæ concessio Clero multo magis obfuit, quam profuit. Multi enim ac plerique illius remissionis spe de solucndis primitiis fideliusfores non dederunt, id quod priori coacessionis lege ab Henrico lata fieri sub grani sanctione oportuit. Illi in ins de stipulatione ac fideiussione de primitiis danda vocati, dum in iure contenderent fisci procuratoribus ac ministris, cum consuetæ sportulæ essent pendendæ, miserè plectebantur, soluendiq; tum dilationibus factis earum residua, quæ arrægia dicuntur, mortuis paulo post tam Regina Maria quam Polo Cardinali, maximo Ministerili detrimento Regina Elizabetha regnante iterum repetita sunt, postquam Pontificius Clerus amotus & abdicatus fuisset. Ex quibus quidem primitias atq; decimis cum longe maximus vberrimusque prouentus quotannis Polo inuectus esset, detrahi sane illis modicis Monachorum fratrumq; stipendiis haud ita multum posset, quin ingens inde ei Thesaurus superesset.
units.tr: Thus this grant of the Queen harmed the clergy much more than it helped them. For many, and indeed most, trusting in that remission, did not give sureties for the payment of the first-fruits, which under the earlier law made by Henry had to be given under the sanction of a penalty. Those summoned to court to give a bond and surety for the first-fruits, while contending at law with the procurators and officers of the fisc, were miserably punished when the customary fees had to be paid. When payments were deferred, their residues, which are called arrears, were demanded again in the reign of Queen Elizabeth, after both Queen Mary and Cardinal Pole had died shortly afterwards, and after the Popish clergy had been removed and deposed; this was to the great loss of the ministers. Since from these first-fruits and tithes an by far the greatest and most abundant income was brought in to Pole each year, it could certainly not be much diminished by those modest stipends of the monks and friars, so that an immense treasure remained over for him.

units.la: Hinc ei a patrio more, confuetudineq; degeneratio & abhorrenti, frequentiores cum Italis atq; peregrinis mercatoribus qui cum Anglis contractus intercesserunt, quibus corrasas patriæ pecunias sub vsuris rurpiq; fœnore credidisse fertur.
units.tr: Hence, departing from his country's custom and from his own habits, he began to have more frequent dealings with Italian and foreign merchants who made contracts with the English. He is said to have lent them the money he had scraped together from his homeland at usury and shameful interest.

units.la: Cuirei argumento est, quod Roma venit in Angliam inops, scripsit; Papæ se egere ad tantam dignitatem sustinendam facultatibus, moriensq; antem (vt dixi, mus) on illis in Anglia neglectu suis necessariis, Italos mirum in modo locupletauit. Eodem autem anno, Polus de Ecclesia saltem Cantuariensi bene meritus nouemdeum Ecclesiasticarum beneficia in Cantio sua diœcesi sita, a Regina suæ sedis patronatus iuri concedi impetrauit.
units.tr: Evidence for this is that he wrote that he came to England from Rome poor, and that the Pope needed means to sustain so great a dignity. Dying (as I have said), he had neglected his needs in England and enriched the Italians wonderfully. In the same year Pole, who at least deserved well of the Church of Canterbury, obtained from the Queen that nineteen ecclesiastical benefices lying in his diocese of Kent be granted to the right of patronage of his see.

units.la: Neq; in alia re quacunq; fedi suæ profuit, præterquam in illa longa ad orientem extensa ad Lamethanas ædes adiuncta, & ad ortum posita stratione cum inferioribus & connexis cœnaculis extruenda. Nam quos sumptus in reficiendo Cantuariensi Palatio facere vitus destinasset morte sublatus nunquam præstitit. Celebrauit etiam Londini in Ecclesia Paulina Cleri Synodum in qua ea quæ ad Angliam in perpetuum Romanæ curiæ subiugandam pertinere videbantur in eo libro edidir, quem de Reformatione Angliæ inscripsit, qui liber duodecim capitulis ex decretis constat. In quibus & illud memorabile fauxit. Quia exeplu, inquit, vitæ magna authoritate verbo affert, estq; velut quoddam prædicandi genus, ob id curandu est iis qui alios præsunt, vt cæteris cum morum pulcritudine, vitæq; sanctitate, tu ea propria domu rectè gubernandi laude, qua in Episcopis Apostolus requirit, antecellant. Nullo igitur Præsulis fastu, nulla pompa vtantur, nō vestib. sericis, non preciosa suppellectile, sed eorum mensa frugalis & parca, non plus quam tria, aut ad summum quatuor (quod etiam magis pro huius temporis ratione, indulgedo quia probado concedimus) ciborum genera præter fructus & bellaria, qualefcunq; hospites aut conuiuas habeant, apponantur. Reliqua mensæ condimenta sint charitas, sanctorum librorum lectio, & sermones pii. Domesticorū & equorū numerosa & superflua multitudine abstineat, ac tot ministris contenti sint, quot ad curæ sibi committe administrationem, ac domus regimen, & quotidianos vitæ vsus erut necessarii. Hæc ille. Sed de hac coiuiali parsimonia Cranm. An. Do. 1541 aliquato largi decreuit. Nā piscis aut carnium fercula sibi Archiepiscopo sex, Episcopis quinq, Decanis & Archidiaconis quatuor, inferioribus vero plalatis tria pmisit, bellatiorū aut sibi quatuor, Episcopis tria, cæteris duo concessit. Et si Principi Legatos, aut Regni proceres, Regis cōsiliarios, vel eiusmodi illustriores cōuiuæ accederet, pmissum est vt secundū pfonarū dignitate exciperetur. Sed neq; Cramerus neq; Polus suis sanctionib. Anglicanā conuiuādi luxuriem, penèq; luxu cohibere poterāt, q n paucis mensib. interiectis ad veterē copiā, libertatem q; nulla legevel pscripto coercitam rediit. Proinde optandū est vt cū ex antiq simo gētis more, rerumq; omniū abundātia atque copia vix cerni epnis Anglicanis cæcelli statui possint, vt qa apertis clamoribus hospitalitatem a Clero populus flagitat, in precio victualium, quia census redditusq; Cleri annuus tàtopere diminutus est, in victualium precio talis modus adhibeatur, qualé Edwardum Regem secundum pro Episcoporum & Baronum hospitiis copiosé ac liberaliter tuendis statuit: quas ob rem præcepit ut in Anno 1515. Videlicet ut Bos s in stabulo pinguefiat 24 s. s in pascua 16 s. Item Vaccæ in stabulo pinguefacta 16 s. Ouis cum vellere 10 d. detonsa 14 d. Porcus biennalis 3 s. 4 d. Anser pinguis 1 d. ob. in urbe 3 d. Capo turi 2 d. in urbe 2 d. ob. Galina ruri 1 d. ein urbe 1 d. ob. Duo pulli ruri 1 d. in urbe 1 d. ob. Quatuor Columbæ ruri in urbe 1 d. Oua ruri 2 ‹ in urbe 2 o. 1 d. tantum neq; pluris vænirent. Et hoc tam æquo modo moderato victualium precio statuto, annonæ tamen sequenti eanuiuis epulifi modum idem Rex præscripsit. Vetuitq; primo ne inserioribus ordinis subditi præsulum, atque procerum in epulando sumptum & magnificentiam imitarentur. Deinde vt ipsi præsules atque proceres duabus ferculorum mensæ fuzappositionibus, & in vnaquaque appositione duobus tantum carninm vel piscium plenis ferculis contenti sint, præcepit, tantum eminentioribus præsulibus ac proceribus indulsit, vt inter ferculorum appositiones interponant si velint quintum ferculum. Tertio Aulæ dum & conuiuarum nisi inuitarentur, concursum interdixit. Quì si seruarentur modus in tanta rerum caritate, melioris ad omnes necessitates frugi, & in pauperes indigentesque beneficentiæ iam essemus. Sed ad historiam reuertamur. Æterna iam & immutabilis pontificiis rebus securitas parta existimabatur, namque & pii omnes siin sententia fidequé sterent, aut in exilium, aut in latebras, aut in carceres flammasue actu sunt. Hoc ipso enim anno octoginta quatuor ob eam quā Deum colebant fidem cremati perierunt, quorum maximam partem Boneri Carnificina Londini cōsumpsit, & Clerusin omnem tyrannidem luxumque profusus excurrit. Polus cum ad eum nulla iam Regni obcinendi spes peruenire possit, omnem cum pontificiis dedisse operam putabatur, vt Philippus iure suo potireur Regno, ne si Maria Regina sine sobole moreretur, D. Elizabetha quæ à pontificiis non modò in dogmatibus religionisque instituris dissensit, sed quia vitæ suæ diu insidiabantur, eamque carceribus ac durissima custodia continebant, crudelitate immanitatequè ipsa abhorruit, Regnum iure capescerer. Consilia quedam sceleratissima hac de re quam occultissimé inita, siue à futili quodam consiliarioe nunciata, siue haud obscuris indiciis atq; signis in populi suspicionem adduèta putabantur huiusmodi. Vt Maria non modò inre municipali Regina, sed iure belli victrix Regni promulgaretur, vt eo pretextu omnia publica priuataque iura mutare, Regnumq; quocunq; vellet transferre possit. Sed hoc consilium etsi arridebat primò, tamen quiatam anceps & periculosum fuit, haud diu probabatur. Eoque reiecto visum est ad stabiliendam rem pontificiam maximé facere, si D. Elizabeth aut è medio tolleretur, quod pontificii quantum poterant suadebant, aut Nobili alicui pontificiæ sc s Hispano nuptum daretur.
units.tr: He did nothing else that benefited his see, except that he added to Lambeth House the long gallery stretching to the east and planned a building on the east side, to be built with lower and connected rooms. For death prevented him from ever paying the costs he had intended to spend on restoring the palace of Canterbury. He also held a synod of the clergy in St Paul's in London, in which he published, in that book which he entitled On the Reformation of England, the measures that seemed to subject England to the Roman court forever. That book consists of twelve chapters taken from the decrees, and in them he also sanctioned this memorable point: "Because example, he says, carries great authority in word of life, and is a kind of preaching, it must be taken care of that those who preside over others surpass the rest not only in the beauty of their morals and sanctity of life, but also in that praise of well-ordering their own household, which the Apostle requires in bishops. Therefore let them use no episcopal pride and no pomp, neither silken garments nor costly furnishings; but let their table be frugal and sparing, and let no more than three, or at most four, kinds of food be served, besides fruit and dessert, whatever guests or dinner companions they have (which we also grant, rather as an indulgence, in view of the present state of things, though it is not to be commended). Let charity, the reading of the holy books, and godly sermons be the seasonings of their table. Let them refrain from a large and superfluous number of servants and horses, and be content with as many attendants as are necessary for the administration of the care committed to them, the running of the household, and the daily uses of life." So he wrote. But in regard to this table moderation, Cranmer in the year of our Lord 1541 decided somewhat more liberally. For he allowed fish or meat dishes: six to himself as archbishop, five to bishops, four to deans and archdeacons, and three to lesser prelates. For dessert courses he allowed four for himself, three for bishops, and two for the rest. And if ambassadors of the Prince, or nobles of the realm, or counsellors of the King, or guests of that rank, came to the table, it was permitted that they be received according to the dignity of each person. But neither Cranmer nor Pole could by their decrees restrain English feasting and near-luxury, for within a few months it returned to its old abundance and freedom, which was not restrained by any law or prescribed rule. Therefore it is to be wished that, since by the most ancient custom of the nation, and with the abundance and plenty of all things, English feasts can scarcely be restrained, and since the people openly demand hospitality from the clergy, while the clergy's annual income and rents have been so greatly reduced, a method be adopted for fixing the price of victuals like that which King Edward the Second set for the generous and liberal maintenance of the hospitality of bishops and barons. For this reason he ordered, in the year 1515, namely: that an ox fattened in the stall be priced at 24 shillings, and one on pasture at 16 shillings; likewise a cow fattened in the stall at 16 shillings; a sheep with its fleece at 10 pence, and shorn at 14 pence; a two-year-old pig at 3 shillings 4 pence; a fat goose at 1½ pence in the country and 3 pence in town; a capon at 2 pence in the country and 2½ pence in town; a hen at 1 penny in the country and 1½ pence in town; two chickens at 1 penny in the country and 1½ pence in town; four pigeons in the country at 1 penny, and in town likewise; eggs in the country at 2 pence, and in town at 2½ pence, and no more than this should they be sold for. And although the price of victuals was fixed in so fair and moderate a way, the same King also prescribed a limit for feasts for the following year. He first forbade inferior subjects to imitate the expense and magnificence of prelates and nobles at table. Then he ordered that the prelates and nobles themselves be content, at the two courses of the table, with only two full dishes of meat or fish at each serving; he granted only to the more eminent prelates and nobles that they might place a fifth dish between the courses if they wished. Thirdly, he forbade crowds to gather at the court and in the dining halls unless they were invited. If this moderation were kept in such a dearth of goods, we would be in a better position for all needs, and for beneficence to the poor and the needy. But let us return to our history. An eternal and unchangeable security was now thought to be secured for the papistical cause, for all the godly, whether they stood by the same opinion and faith, were driven either into exile, or into hiding, or into prisons, or to the flames. For in this very year eighty-four persons perished by burning for the faith in which they worshipped God, the greater part of whom the butchery of Bonner consumed in London, and the clergy ran forth poured out into every tyranny and luxury. Since no hope of obtaining the kingdom could now reach Pole, it was thought he had devoted all his effort, together with the papists, to ensure that Philip should take possession of the kingdom by his right, lest, if Queen Mary died without issue, Lady Elizabeth should seize the kingdom by right. She differed from the papists not only in doctrine and the institutions of religion, but, because they had long plotted against her life and kept her in prison and under the harshest custody, she herself abhorred their cruelty and savagery. Certain most wicked plans concerning this matter, undertaken as secretly as possible, whether announced by some foolish counsellor, or brought into the suspicion of the people by not obscure indications and signs, were thought to be of this kind: that Mary should be proclaimed not only Queen by municipal law, but victorious queen of the kingdom by right of war, so that under that pretext she might change all public and private laws and transfer the kingdom wherever she wished. But although this plan at first pleased, because it was so dangerous and hazardous it was soon not approved. And with that rejected, it was thought most effective for establishing the papistical cause that Lady Elizabeth should either be removed from the midst, which the papists urged as much as they could, or be given in marriage to some Spanish noble of papist persuasion.

units.la: Sed Deus opt. maxim. qui huius clarissimæ integerrimæq; principis, ac Regni liberatio salutique simul prospexit, ita pontificiorum consilia irrita inanisque effecit. Hispanos enim pontificios mitiores, minusque cruentos quàm nostrates reddidit, deditque D. Elizabethæ maiorem coram Philippo Rege, quam coram sorore Maria gratiam, vt is misericordia diuinitus doctus eā & mortis metu & seuera pontificiorū custodia leberet. Nuptiæ autem tam sibi quàm sorori suspectæ non placebant. Vtvna eademque opera diuina tam à summo discriminé quam ab externis nuptiis tam ad Regnum ab externa dominatione, quam Ecclesiam à pontificiorum cæcitate tyrannidéq; liberandum vindicaretur. Atque his inuentis ope diuina ad nihilum profligatis, ipsorum pontificiorum res infirmiori itatu ac lubricæ esse ceperunt. Nam Paulus. 4. Papa vt Regnum Neapolitanum, ex quo ad Venetos fuga quondam elapsus Cæsaris vim euasit, ab eius potentia suæ pristinæ libertati restitueret, aut ex eius manu Gallo proderet, cum iam Cæsar in Hispanias secessisset, & Belgium Philippo tradidisset, quinquennales passo ductus induciasadiutore (vt diximus) Lotharingio Cardinali à Gallorumpi, bellumq; denunciari curauit. In quo quamuis Angliæ nulla belli Gallis inferendi causa data fuerit, tamen Regina Maria insano Philippi amore solicitata bellum indixit, ac faluratem sibiregnoq; pacem primo violauit. Cuius rei magno Regni detrimento ac infamia suaquè pernicie iustas pœnas postea (vt dicemus) persoluit.
units.tr: But God, the best and greatest, who looked out at the same time for the liberation and safety of this most illustrious and upright princess and of the kingdom, thus made the counsels of the papists vain and empty. For he made the papist Spaniards milder and less bloody than our own countrymen, and gave Lady Elizabeth greater favour before King Philip than before her sister Mary, so that he, taught by divine mercy, might free her both from fear of death and from the severe custody of the papists. But the marriage, suspect to her as well as to her sister, did not please. So that by one and the same divine work the kingdom might be delivered both from the greatest danger and from foreign marriages, and from foreign domination, and the Church from the blindness and tyranny of the papists. And when these plans had been discovered and, by divine help, overthrown to nothing, the affairs of the papists themselves began to be in a weaker and more slippery state. For Pope Paul IV, wishing to restore the Kingdom of Naples, from which he had once fled to the Venetians and escaped the power of the Emperor, to its former liberty away from his power, or to hand it over to the French from his hand, when the Emperor had already retired into Spain and handed the Low Countries over to Philip, had a five-year truce made, and with the help (as we have said) of the Cardinal of Lorraine, from the French side, he saw to it that war was declared. In this war, although no cause for making war on the French had been given by England, nevertheless Queen Mary, urged on by an insane love of Philip, declared war, and first violated her own safety and the peace of the kingdom. For this, to the great detriment and disgrace of the kingdom and to her own ruin, she afterwards paid the just penalties (as we shall say).

units.la: Hoc à Regina susceptum pro Philippo bellum, Paulum Quartum Papam, qui se cū Gallo cōsœderauit, tanto furore accendit, vt in declarationem diuturni sui in Polū odii aperte crumperer, eoq; magit quòd Polus, qui ab ipso Papa concitatum hoc bellum cognouerat, de eo sedando per literas & legatos, etsi cum magna reuerentia, acriter tamen & vehementer ageret, Id quod pontifice in Polū vehementius irritauit, quòd suis contra Cæsarem & Hispanos pro Regno Neapolitano vindicaret, cupiditate inceptis obstaret, seq; officii muneribus, sui in ea causa quam redarguia quosq; nollet, admoneret. Itaq; Papa abrogata Poli legatione eum Romam revocavit, eiusque loco Petrum Peto Franciscani ordinis virum Cardinalem atque Legatum creavit. At vt in Polum citatum ante quàm Romam adueniret crimimum probationumque copiam exquireret, Moronum Cardinalem Angliæ vt (diximus) in Romana curia protectorem Poli familiarissimum in vincula conjecit. Hæc omnia Mariæ Reginæ priusquam Polo nuncia banturque cum ea ad Papam nuncia... [Transcription of the full page continues as printed; text partially illegible in the scan.]
units.tr: This war undertaken by the Queen on Philip's behalf so inflamed Pope Paul IV, who had allied himself with the French, that he openly burst out in a declaration of his long-standing hatred of Pole. This was all the more so because Pole, who had learned that the Pope himself had stirred up this war, tried to calm it by letters and legates, though with great deference yet sharply and vehemently. This irritated the Pontiff against Pole even more, because Pole defended the interests of his own side against the Emperor and the Spaniards on behalf of the Kingdom of Naples, opposed the Pope's ambitions in his undertakings, and by the duties of his office admonished him about the cause that he was pleading and did not wish to be refuted. So the Pope revoked Pole's legation and recalled him to Rome, and in his place created Peter Peto, a man of the Franciscan order, Cardinal and Legate. And so that he might seek out a supply of charges and proofs against Pole before he arrived in Rome, he threw into chains Cardinal Morone, England's protector in the Roman curia (as we said) and Pole's most intimate friend. All these things were done before the news reached Mary and Pole, and messages were sent with her to the Pope ...

units.la: An.1557 ab Opilione custodiri sine auxilio militari posset. Eo vero amisso cum id populus ægre ferret, suadebant palam in concionibus pontificii Caletum hæreticorum tantummodo portum ac refugium fuisse, nec de eius amissione cuiquam catholico viro dulendum. Sed Regina repentino horrore perculsa, cum externas illas nuptias & Papalem rursus indudam, à se potentiam tantas calamitates & infamiam sibi peperisse cerneret, in summam ægritudinem incidit, quæ viro suo Philippo absente cum nullo in his solatio leniri posset, eam luctuosam & sqnallidam intercus incurabilis occupabat. De quo morbo etsi paucissimis in viris eam laborasse compertum est, tamen Romæ Venetiisque ac in nonnullis Italiæ locis atque civitatibus peterebant tantam fuisse morbi sui vitam, ut quamuis æstatem, tamen hyemem tolerare non posset, ideoque altero anno eam superstitem non fore. Quæ quomodo exteris nota fuerunt, incertum est.
units.tr: In the year 1557 the town could be guarded by Opilio without military aid. When it was lost, the people bore it with great difficulty, and the Papists openly argued in their sermons that Calais had been only a refuge for heretics, and that no Catholic man should grieve at its loss. But the Queen, struck by sudden horror when she saw that those foreign marriages and the renewed Papal power had brought her so many calamities and infamy, fell into deep sorrow, which could not be eased by any comfort while her husband Philip was absent. Meanwhile a sad and squalid disease, incurable, took hold of her. Although it is known that very few men were afflicted by this disease, it was reported in Rome, Venice and some other places in Italy and cities that the life of her illness was such that, although she could endure the summer, she could not endure the winter, and that therefore she would not survive the next year. How these reports came to be known abroad is uncertain.

units.la: At in Anglia Parlamentum atque Synodus celebrabatur. In ea Synodo Polus Clero indicavit quā graviter Regina amissum Caletū ferebat, ideoque ad eam consolandā suasit ut de suis facultatibus ad diuturni belli contra Gallos administrationem l. bentius iam largiusq; promitterent. Ad id Clerus ea conditione adduētus est, ut ab armatorū, virorū & equorum præstatione, cæterisque bellicis sumptibus quibuscunq; immunis esse posset. Quod cum Polo intercedente impetratum est, inierunt tamen priuatum inter le consilium Prælati de comparandis ad fui defensionem, ut in ea Synodo dicebant, cōtra vim dolorum armis. Quo dicto exi stimare conuenit summam suo imperio seu tyrannidi di em iam adesse cognouisse pontificios. Nam Regina ex illa semestri amplius intercute febricula, dum in Parlamento atque Synodo deliberatum est, correpta, die quodam Iouis qui eo anno 17. Novembris fuit, in Regia S. Iacobo dicata inter horas 5. & 6. matutinas obiit.
units.tr: Meanwhile Parliament and a Synod were being held in England. In that Synod Pole told the clergy how grievously the Queen bore the loss of Calais, and therefore urged them to console her by promising more generously and freely from their resources for the continuing war against the French. The clergy were persuaded to this on condition that they be immune from providing armed men, horses and all other military costs. When this was obtained through Pole's intercession, the prelates nevertheless made a private council to prepare arms for their own defence, as they said in that Synod, against the violence of their troubles. From this statement it is fitting to judge that the Papists had perceived that the end of their rule, or tyranny, was now at hand. For the Queen, seized for more than half a year by a low intercurrent fever while matters were being deliberated in Parliament and the Synod, died on a certain Thursday, which that year fell on 17 November, in the royal palace dedicated to St James, between five and six in the morning.

units.la: Quod Henrico patri, Edwardo fratri, sibique fatale videri posset, ut dies Iouis ribus regibus ordine succedentibus mortalis funestusq; fuerit. Eodem anno febris quartana multorum in Anglia, præsertim vero Prælatorum valetudines affixit, neciq; dedit. Quæ cum aliquot pontificios Episcopos extinxisset, Polo geminata vicissitudine accessit, eo quē die ac currime infestant quo Maria obiit. De quo cum accepisset quasi in eodem die vna exspiraut ad terriam horam nuētis cum 38. annos & sex menses vixisset, in Archiepiscopatu vero duos annos, septem menses, tres septimanas, quinq; dies sedisset, legatinamq; potestatem quatuor annos, & sex dies exercuisset. Curpus eius plumbo inclusum curru Cantuariam vectum, ac iustis triduo peractis, laudatione q; latine atq; Anglice habita in sacello Thomæ Becket dicato inhumatum est. Sciatura fuit mediocri, corpore exili, colore candido rubore permisto, vultu latiori, oculis lætis animi placabilem indicantibus. Neque sane aliter existimare conuenit, quin si pontificiis moribus depravatus ad ambitionem, cupiditatem, & sæuitiam non deflexisset, naturæ suæ acingenuitatis prop ter præclaris dotibus doctrinæque virtutisque singularis ornamentis omnibus præstitisset. Sed illa factione à patriæ fuorumq; necessariorum charitate abductus, in testamento pene omnia legauit peregrinis, & Aloysium Priolum patricū Venetū omnium rerum suarum hæredem instituit, cuiusque fidei commisit, ut legata præstaret ac distribueret his, qui eum ex Italia & longinquis partibus in Angliam secuti sunt. Hoc gratitudinis officio fecisse Polum Itali affirmant, qui exul quondam & proscriptus eorum beneficentia subleuatus est. Ipsumque Priolum tanta in alienis bonis temperantia fuisse aiunt, ut fidei commissa abunde præstaret cæteris, nec ex bonis Poliquicquam præter precationum libros Breuiarium scilicet & Diurnale caperet. Illud autē ad æternam immanitatis pontificiæ memoriam infamiam q; contra Polum valebit, quòd eo Legato & acceptante integerrimus doctissimus Archiep. Cranmerus igne cremarus est, quòd Archiepiscopo præterea (quod legimus) accidit nemini, pluresque in illo suæ legationis quadriennio, ferro, flammaq; crudeliter mactati sunt, quam in cuiusquam Regis eorum qui post Lucinm huic Insulæ imperabant longissimo Regno. Ita Cranmerum Martyrē Polum tyrannum eadem Cantuaria celebrat, hic plumbo depressus, illæ cinerbus ascue flamma ad cœlos elatus est. Atqui in hoc breui etiā tæuo, temporis curriculo videmus potentiam & misericordiam Domini, qui quanquam Angliæ meritò castigauit & afflixit; tamen non ita diu deseruit, qui in turbatis pontificiis Reginam Elizabetham aduersia multa sub eis passam eorū potestate & insidiis, ereptam in folio Regni collocauerit viros pios atq; doctos ab exilio atque latebris eduxerit, Reginæq; authoritate, ac eorum ministerio Euangelium multò uberius quàm vnquam antea propagauerit.
units.tr: This could seem fatal to her father Henry, to her brother Edward, and to herself, so that Thursday proved deadly and fatal to the kings succeeding in order. In the same year a quartan fever afflicted and killed many in England, especially prelates. When it had carried off several Papist bishops, it returned to Pole with redoubled regularity, on the very day and hour at which Mary died. When he had heard that they died almost on the same day, at about the third hour of the night, after living thirty-eight years and six months, sitting in the archbishopric two years, seven months, three weeks and five days, and exercising legatine power for four years and six days, his body, enclosed in lead, was carried to Canterbury by cart. After the funeral rites were performed for three days, and eulogies were given in Latin and English, he was buried without honour in the chapel dedicated to Thomas Becket. He was of medium stature, slender of body, with a complexion of white mixed with red, a broad face and cheerful eyes that showed a placid mind. Indeed one ought not to judge otherwise than that, had he not been corrupted by papal ways into ambition, greed and cruelty, he would have excelled in all the fine gifts of his nature and noble birth, and in the outstanding ornaments of learning and singular virtue. But drawn away by that faction from love of his country and his kin, he bequeathed almost everything in his will to foreigners, and appointed Aloysius Priolus, a Venetian patrician, heir of all his goods, entrusting to him the duty of paying and distributing the legacies to those who had followed him into England from Italy and distant parts. The Italians affirm that Pole did this as a duty of gratitude, since he, once an exile and outlaw, had been relieved by their kindness. They also say that Priolus himself was so temperate with others' goods that he paid the entrusted bequests fully to the others, and took from Pole's goods nothing except prayer books, namely the Breviary and the Diurnal. But this will be an eternal memorial to the savagery and infamy of the Papacy against Pole: under his legation, and with his consent, the most upright and most learned Archbishop Cranmer was burned. Moreover (as we read) this happened to no other archbishop; and in those four years of his legation many were cruelly slaughtered by sword and flame, more than in the very long reign of any of the kings who ruled this island since Lucius. Thus Canterbury celebrates Cranmer as a martyr and Pole as a tyrant: the one was pressed down with lead, the other raised to heaven by ashes and flame. But in this short span of time we see the power and mercy of the Lord, who, although he justly chastised and afflicted England, did not abandon her for long. When the papal affairs were in turmoil, he snatched Queen Elizabeth, who under their power and snares had suffered many adversities, and placed her on the throne of the kingdom; he drew pious and learned men out of exile and hiding; and through the Queen's authority and their ministry he has propagated the Gospel far more abundantly than ever before.

units.la: Itaq; quod ab omnibus anterioribus semper Regibus optatum atq; desideratum est; ut Episcopos atque Clerum contra pontificias & externas factiones sibi morigeros atque obsequentes retinerent, hoc illustrissima nostra Regina diuino atque solo Euangelii tuendi beneficio consecuta est. Nec aliud sane magis in hac tam bene constituta Ecclesia Anglicana timendum atque cauendum est, quàm ne Clerus nunc cum maxime in verbo ac veritate laboret, summaque obseruantia Principi pareat, profusorum atque decoctorum praedae ac direptioni proponantur, & imperitorum conuiciis atque contumeliis proscin-datur, populoque fiat ludibrio ac contemptui. Quod si contingat, grauius Dei flagellum, multaque arociora tempora expectanda sunt, quàm illa Mariana fuerunt. Sin verò longaeuam Deus vitam D. Reginae produxerit, vt eos praesidio suo tueatur ac in honore habeat, illis in fide, ac in vigilantia gregis perseuerauerint, Ecclesiam Anglicanam sub Augustissima Principe omnibus diuinis donis florentem, & non modò a pontificiarum, sed aliarum, quae nuper insinuante se Diabolo furtim irrepserunt, factionum iniuriis liberam saluamque retinebimus. Quod faxit ille qui quaecunque velit, facit. Amen.
units.tr: Therefore what all earlier kings always wished and desired, namely to keep bishops and clergy compliant and obedient to them against papal and foreign factions, our most illustrious Queen has obtained by the sole divine benefit of defending the Gospel. Nor indeed is anything more to be feared and guarded against in this well-established English Church than that the clergy, who now labour most in the Word and truth and obey the prince with the greatest respect, should be offered up as prey and plunder to the prodigal and ruined, be torn apart by the insults and abuse of the unskilled, and be made a laughing-stock and object of contempt to the people. If this happens, a heavier scourge of God and far harsher times must be expected than those of Mary. But if God grants our Queen a long life, so that she may protect and honour the clergy with her defence, and they persevere in faith and in vigilance over the flock, we shall keep the English Church, flourishing with all divine gifts under this most august Prince, free and safe not only from the injuries of the papal faction but also from those of the other factions which have lately crept in stealthily, with the Devil insinuating himself. May He who does whatever He wills bring this about. Amen.

units.tr: Henry III, secretly absolved of his oath to the Pope, 175.22. Complains to the Pope of his avarice, 175.56. The Prince of North Wales rebels against him, 176.5. The Pope denies him entry into England, 177.20. At the Council of Lyons he orders the King to be killed, 177.22. The magnates against the Pope, 177.30. Sends legates to the council, 177.54; 178.30. Refuses the Pope's demanded tax, 178.31. Forbids the Pope's legates entry, 179.12. Summons Parliament at London, 179.18. Denounces the Pope, 180.44. Brings forward one asking in the Pope's name, 181.13. Appeals from the Pope to Jesus Christ present, 182.33. Holds Parliament at London, 182.36. Writes a letter to the Pope, 182.37. Gently wins over the King, 182.41. The Pope pledges the kingdom as security for money raised by tax, 185.53. That is his comfort, 185.55. Wages civil war with the barons, 187.2. The Pope calms this through legates, 187.22. Settles all controversies of the Church, 187.38. Builds Westminster Abbey, 189.8. Dies, 189.13.

He acknowledges himself a creature of the Pope (192.28). He unjustly pays four thousand marks to his Creator (192.58). He unjustly seeks five thousand marks from the goods of Robert Kilwardby (193.26). He holds the council at Lambeth (193.36). He complains of the pride of the Archbishop of York concerning the carrying of the cross (193.43). He visits the province and deals in usury (193.57). He answers the Pope's letters about the tenth collected by the King (199.13). He practises usury against the Jews (196.40). He rejects the churches of Winchester and Lichfield (196.47). units.tr: Wilfrid's teaching, 5 4.12. Driven from his see, 5 4.25. Flees to Mercian King, 56.30. Made Bishop of Lichfield, 56.32. Summoned to the Synod, 56.36. Torn apart in the assembly, 56.38. Complains to the Pope, 57.1. Prevails in the cause, 51.25. His will, 57.44.

Statuta Curia de arcubus descri-psit. 202.2. instrumentum 202.3. consensus cum Rege de decima 202.52. papam spiritua-lem Regem temporalem Dominum summo voca-t 202.58. ob contumaciam spoliatur a Rege 203.17. in gratiam recipitur 203.35. prodi-tionis crimen fassus veniam a Rege petiit. 203.40. Roma idcirco datur 207.38. mexi-lium agitur 207.55. ob exilio redit 208.44. Iudicibus veniam praestandi iuramenta reis dat 209.38. prouincie concilium celebrat. 210.13. Templarios damnat 210.15. units.tr: Winchelsey: education, 200.37. The University of Paris, 200.47. Chancellor of Oxford, 200.50. Archbishop of Canterbury there, 201.9. Consecrated at Rome, 201.15. Convenes a synod at London, 201.31. Drew up the statutes of the Court of Arches, 202.2. The instrument, 202.3. Agreement with the King about tithes, 202.52. Calls the Pope spiritual, the King temporal, and the Lord the Highest, 202.58. Deprived by the King for obstinacy, 203.17. Received back into favour, 203.35. Confessed the crime of treason and sought pardon from the King, 203.40. Given to Rome for this reason, 207.38. Led into exile, 207.55. Returns from exile, 208.44. Grants judges permission to administer oaths to the accused, 209.38. Holds a provincial council, 210.13. Condemns the Templars, 210.15. Imposed bread (penance) on a knight accused of manslaughter, 210.40. Procured that the authority of the Church be set out in articles, 211.2. Chastised offending magnates, 211.5. Generosity to the poor, 211.20.

units.la: Walefei educatio 252.54. sit Cantuar. Arch. 253.5. sine pompa unobrem. 253.13. synodum celebrat. 253.17. Trienales decimas Regi concedit 253.17. In synodo subsidium Regi negatur 254.4. Arundel Ebenie sacras. 254.2 4. moritur. 254.27.
units.tr: Walefei: education, 252.54. Becomes Archbishop of Canterbury, 253.5. Without pomp, unobtrusively, 253.13. Celebrates a synod, 253.17. Grants the King the triennial tithes, 253.17. At the synod, aid to the King is refused, 254.4. Arundel consecrates at Ely, 254.24. Dies, 254.27.

units.tr: Wolsey, 309.25. Renounced at Oxford, 309.30. Becomes the King's almoner, 309.35. How he insinuated himself into the King's favour, 310.44. Becomes the King's chancellor, 309.51. Bishop of Lincoln, 309.52. Archbishop of York and Cardinal, 309.53. Writes in the usual literary manner, 310.8. Becomes colleague in legation with Campeggio, 310.32. Legation(s)

units.tr: Courts the court, 310.5. Becomes popular, 310.5. To secure peace, through that procuration, the Kings are entirely consumed, 311.25. Takes the King's little son with him on embassy to Caesar, 310.43. Incredible deceit, 311.47. Hands over his own son to be educated at the French court, 312.47. Caesar declares war on the hostile King, 312.1. Which servants he recommended to the King, 312.9. By a tithe, alienates the people from himself, 312.57. After the synod is dissolved, convenes at Westminster, 313.38. Shamelessly demands that his lord Fox resign the bishopric, 313.25. A child is reported to have been (insulted) by a certain Cone, 313.49. Whom he threw into chains, 313.52. Attacks Bishop Daniel, 313.18. Afterwards treats him humanely, 314.23. Seizes the bishopric of Winchester with Fox's goods, 314.31. Adheres to Galba, 314.42. Warns the Frenchman about affairs, 315.2. Carries letters to Caesar's envoys, 315.22. His pretence in reporting to the King about the Frenchman, 316. Stirs up the King against Caesar, 315.28. Sets out to the French King with a huge army, 315.48. Declares war on Caesar without the King's consent, 316.43. Urges the King to repudiate his wife, 316.37. He arbitrarily decides on the repudiation, 318.48. Seeks the papacy, 319.35. Monasteries, 320.10. Consults soothsayers, 320.35. Writes to the Pope about hindering the marriage, 322.16. Avila is approved, 321.37. Is stripped of the office of chancellor, 324.9. What charges were brought against him, 324.20. Is produced, 324.38. Is admitted into the judgment at York, 324.50. In the King's name, that is, 324.59. Die from violent medicines, 325.13. Buried without pomp, 325.15. 325.16.
